specificity.statement: Well, annual CPI inflation in Australia is currently 3.7 percent; in the UK, it is 3.2 percent; and the OECD average is 3.4 percent... New Zealand is starting from a somewhat stronger position than many other countries.
specificity.explanation: Three named country/bloc figures answering the comparison directly.

specificity.statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, I'd just say to the member that this is a Government that is doing everything it can to turn this economy around, to lift incomes, to create new jobs. If the member wants to get on board, support the Indian free-trade agreement.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspirations ('turn the economy around', 'lift incomes') with no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: No, we're very focused on the fuel crisis, and that's what this Government is doing an exceptionally good job of managing... We're working through commercial options; when we have that resolved, we'll come and talk about it.
specificity.explanation: No timeframe, volume, or mechanism — only 'commercial options' and self-praise.

specificity.statement: Well, this Government doesn't just talk words; we put action and investment to climate change. That's why this country, in the last quarter, has had less emissions produced than in any time since 2010. That's why we're investing in resilience in our roading network; that's why we're investing another $200 million into our flood protection.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete $200 million figure but leaves 'roading resilience' investment unquantified.

specificity.statement: I can. I'm very proud to say we'll have a national flood plan by the end of this year. We are the first Government to do so, and we are taking action and putting investment into climate change, not just words and bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific deliverable and timeframe, though the 'bumper stickers and Post-it notes' tail is rhetorical.

specificity.statement: We are determined to make sure we deliver on our climate change commitments—that means net zero 2050; that means doing everything we can to deliver on our Paris agreements... We have reversed the oil and gas ban so we don't create an energy dry-year risk and high power bills for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete targets (net zero 2050, Paris) and a specific action (oil-and-gas ban reversal).

specificity.statement: We have a renewables boom under way in this country... We have taken a strategic coal reserve behind Huntly; we are looking at extra strategic diesel reserves in Whangārei because we are determined that we are going to lower the cost of energy for New Zealanders so it's affordable and abundant.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions (Huntly coal reserve, Whangārei diesel reserve) though without figures or dates.

specificity.statement: One of them was based on an extreme set of assumptions, including escalating conflict... and, critically, oil prices averaging US$180 a barrel being sustained through quarter two and quarter three. I note that if all of these assumptions did come to pass, inflation could reach over 7 percent. However... oil prices in quarter two are currently US$95 a barrel, which is around half what was assumed in the stylised scenario.
specificity.explanation: Detailed assumptions, oil-price figures, quarters, and the 7% threshold.

specificity.statement: Well, first and foremost, my plan is to ensure that we are responding effectively to the global fuel crisis. The worst thing that could happen for New Zealand would be that we'd run short of fuel.
specificity.explanation: Names fuel-supply actions but offers nothing concrete on the wage question that was asked.

specificity.statement: Because the economy has been going through a challenging recovery following a period of excessively high inflation that was sustained outside of the target band for 33 months in a row, leading to a massive spike in interest rates and a very difficult economic recovery.
specificity.explanation: Concrete '33 months in a row' detail, but otherwise general about the recovery.

specificity.statement: Westpower estimates the scheme will generate enough electricity for 12,000 homes and prevent—Chlöe Swarbrick—129,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. I'm told this is equivalent to taking 69,000 cars off the road annually.
specificity.explanation: Precise quantities: 12,000 homes, 129,000 tonnes CO2, 69,000-car equivalent.

specificity.statement: There are 48 referral applications that have been lodged and found compliant, and 47 substantive applications have been lodged and found complete. If they're all approved, these would authorise the construction of nearly 24,000 new houses, thousands of new retirement village units, and thousands of additional megawatts of new electricity generation.
specificity.explanation: Hard application counts (48, 47) and a concrete projected output (nearly 24,000 houses), though some items are 'thousands of'.

specificity.statement: Well, listen up: the average number of working days for a substantive decision is 126... Auckland Port estimates their application to extend the wharf would have taken more than three years; it took five months and nine days... Green Steel... took seven months and 18 days. They say it would have taken six years under the RMA.
specificity.explanation: Dense with exact figures: 126 working days average, '5 months 9 days', '7 months 18 days', plus named projects.

specificity.statement: Well, the process we're going through is to make sure that we reduce power bills for New Zealanders, that we make sure we protect regional jobs, and we keep the lights on, unlike the previous Government's approach—
specificity.explanation: Lists generic objectives with no price, ratio, or threshold despite that being exactly what was asked.

specificity.statement: Well, unfortunately, after the previous Government made the decision to ban oil and gas exploration, we have seen a significant reduction in gas availability in New Zealand. It is reducing faster than was expected and that is damaging jobs, it is damaging industries across our country... I can tell the member: hope is not a strategy.
specificity.explanation: References a concrete policy (the ban) and effects but quantifies none of the 'significant reduction' or job damage.

specificity.statement: As I said, we are working through a process. Once that process is complete, decisions will be made and they'll be announced.
specificity.explanation: Contentless 'a process… decisions will be made' formulation.

specificity.statement: This Government's recently announced Go Rural programme offers student teachers $4,000 to cover the cost of undertaking a placement in a rural and isolated school... yesterday I announced a further 87 places per year... We're also increasing the number of places available in the Government's Teacher Bonding Scheme by 50 places to 235 per year, supporting teachers with an additional $40,000 over five years.
specificity.explanation: Dense, precise detail: $4,000 placements, 87 extra places, +50 to 235 bonding places, $40,000 over five years, $2.35m/year.

specificity.statement: I directed the Ministry of Education to pick up the phone or personally visit every single school in New Zealand so that we can understand exactly what they're dealing with on the ground.
specificity.explanation: Concrete action (directing the ministry to contact every school) with named outputs (relief-teacher access, conveyance allowance).

specificity.statement: The provision of civil defence payments is a Ministry of Social Development operational decision that is informed by assessments by civil defence, by MSD, and by local communities... Existing MSD services and support have, so far, been able to meet the needs of those impacted.
specificity.explanation: Names the bodies involved in assessment but no thresholds, amounts, or a yes/no on availability.

specificity.statement: Annual figures show that overseas visitor arrivals reached 3.58 million in the year to February 2026, which is an increase of 229,000 people on the previous year. This puts us at 92 percent of the pre-COVID levels.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 3.58 million arrivals, +229,000, 92% of pre-COVID, with timeframe and source (Stats NZ).

specificity.statement: In December, we announced that 13,000 Chinese and Pacific travellers had already visited, with 24,000 total requests approved; that number is now at almost 67,000 visits. With an average visitor spend of $5,300 for Chinese visitors, that's an estimated economic injection of almost $350 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures: 13,000 then 67,000 visits, 24,000 approvals, $5,300 average spend, ~$350m injection.

specificity.statement: I note that the Stats New Zealand Research and Development Survey shows that employment in the sector increased from 28,200 roles in 2022 to 30,600 roles in 2024, with most of that growth in the private sector... Budget 2025 committed more than $1.8 billion to science and innovation.
specificity.explanation: Concrete role counts and a $1.8 billion budget figure with dates.

specificity.statement: We are very focused on ensuring that the critical work that is done in weather forecasting and climate research continues. We're bringing NIWA and MetService together in Earth Sciences so that we can get efficiencies and ensure that we reinvest in improvements to our climate science and our weather forecasting capabilities.
specificity.explanation: Names the NIWA/MetService merger as the mechanism but no detail on staffing or service levels.

specificity.statement: We as a Government sought to try and bring a bit of order to the 28 or so pieces of legislation that refer the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi and a host of arrangements—sometimes "give effect to", sometimes "have regard to", sometimes "honour", sometimes "take account"... We set a group up to bring some coherency to that, and that's what we're doing.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the scope (~28 pieces of legislation) and lists the varied statutory wordings being reviewed.

specificity.statement: By convention, a six-week call for submission corresponds to a six-month report back, or four weeks for a four-month report back. The clerk of the committee originally understood it to be a six-month report back and so issued a submission for the six-week period. However, shortly after the Easter break, it came to his attention that the report back was, in fact, only a four-month report back, and... I instructed him to call for submissions proportional to the report-back date, which, in effect, is the four weeks.
specificity.explanation: Concrete procedural detail: the six-week/six-month and four-week/four-month conventions, dates, and the sequence of events.

specificity.statement: Why did his Government decide to cut flood protection funding at a time when extreme weather is becoming more frequent and severe, by approximately half compared to the former Government?
specificity.explanation: Puts a concrete magnitude (≈half, ~41%) on the alleged flood-protection funding cut against a named comparator.

specificity.statement: If she truly is on the side of construction workers, then why are there 39,570 working-age jobseeker support clients as at the end of January 2026, who have declared construction, mining labourer, or trades worker as their previous occupation?
specificity.explanation: Very precise: 39,570 jobseeker clients, dated end of January 2026, with named occupational categories.

forthrightness.statement: We know, from a previous data release, that petrol prices rose 18.6 percent in the month of March alone, following the start of the conflict... Stats NZ identified that they were the largest contributor to the quarterly inflation rate, adding one percentage point to the total.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages Ryan Hamilton's question on the role of Middle East conflict with concrete data rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: Well, annual CPI inflation in Australia is currently 3.7 percent; in the UK, it is 3.2 percent; and the OECD average is 3.4 percent... New Zealand is starting from a somewhat stronger position than many other countries.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the comparison question with the requested cross-country numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, I'd just say to the member that this is a Government that is doing everything it can to turn this economy around, to lift incomes, to create new jobs. If the member wants to get on board, support the Indian free-trade agreement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why job-losers should have confidence in him, he pivots to general talking points and a deflection to the India FTA without addressing the question.

forthrightness.statement: No, we're very focused on the fuel crisis, and that's what this Government is doing an exceptionally good job of managing... We're working through commercial options; when we have that resolved, we'll come and talk about it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when the promised additional fuel will be secured (a deadline he reportedly missed), he gives no date and defers to 'when resolved'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, this Government doesn't just talk words; we put action and investment to climate change. That's why this country, in the last quarter, has had less emissions produced than in any time since 2010. That's why we're investing in resilience in our roading network; that's why we're investing another $200 million into our flood protection.
forthrightness.explanation: Twice asked specifically why flood-protection funding was cut ~41–50%, he never addresses the cut and instead lists other investments.

forthrightness.statement: We are determined to make sure we deliver on our climate change commitments—that means net zero 2050; that means doing everything we can to deliver on our Paris agreements... We have reversed the oil and gas ban so we don't create an energy dry-year risk and high power bills for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Cabinet deferred climate-adaptation cost-sharing decisions until after the election, he does not address the delay.

forthrightness.statement: We have a renewables boom under way in this country... We have taken a strategic coal reserve behind Huntly; we are looking at extra strategic diesel reserves in Whangārei because we are determined that we are going to lower the cost of energy for New Zealanders so it's affordable and abundant.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Government has any plan beyond 'hope' on adaptation, he pivots to energy supply measures rather than adaptation.

forthrightness.statement: One of them was based on an extreme set of assumptions, including escalating conflict... and, critically, oil prices averaging US$180 a barrel being sustained through quarter two and quarter three. I note that if all of these assumptions did come to pass, inflation could reach over 7 percent. However... oil prices in quarter two are currently US$95 a barrel, which is around half what was assumed in the stylised scenario.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the 7% scenario the question asked about and explains its assumptions rather than evading.

forthrightness.statement: I'd have to go back and look at the Hansard, but as I recall them, the member's questions weren't very precise, and what I'd stressed in answer to those questions was that I hadn't been presented with a forecast, which was the case.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly explains why she didn't volunteer the 7% scenario earlier, but leans on 'the questions weren't precise' to justify the omission rather than fully owning it.

forthrightness.statement: Well, first and foremost, my plan is to ensure that we are responding effectively to the global fuel crisis. The worst thing that could happen for New Zealand would be that we'd run short of fuel.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about a plan for the 70% of workers without an above-inflation pay rise, she redirects to the fuel crisis rather than wages.

forthrightness.statement: That is why the Government moved swiftly to introduce targeted, temporary support to working families who face high costs in supporting their children. We delivered that support, but did it in a way that adhered to the advice that economists the world over are giving, which is: "Do not respond to this crisis in a way that adds to inflation and further weakens your fiscal sustainability."
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the constituent example by acknowledging the hardship is real and describing the support delivered in response.

forthrightness.statement: Because when people ask me whether they should have confidence in me, they need to compare themselves with the alternative, which is that member, and what she is promoting is more taxes, more spending, more borrowing, and more debt—back to the bad old COVID days.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify confidence given more unemployment, a smaller economy and rising inflation, she does not address those metrics and pivots to attacking the alternative.

forthrightness.statement: Well, because if you talk to those in the construction sector, they say one of the most important things for ensuring that there's high levels of construction activity is that interest rates are lower. And on the watch of this Government, there have been successive interest rate reductions, whereas on the watch of the previous Government, they increased at such a rapid rate that it's meant that many construction projects fell over.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages the construction-jobs question by linking activity to interest rates, but does not concede or explain the 20,000-job loss figure.

forthrightness.statement: Because the economy has been going through a challenging recovery following a period of excessively high inflation that was sustained outside of the target band for 33 months in a row, leading to a massive spike in interest rates and a very difficult economic recovery.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 39,570 specific construction/trades jobseekers, she gives a macro narrative and never engages the number.

forthrightness.statement: Well, my thoughts absolutely go out to Jamie and others like him in the economy who are doing everything right... it sounds as if he's someone who's had the gumption to start his own business, to put his own money and time on the line, and to take risks.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the hardship and lists infrastructure support but does not directly say how her 'optimism' helps this specific builder.

forthrightness.statement: I utterly reject the assertion made in the latter part of that question, and it's an assertion that the Labour Party dishonourably continue to make on social media. We have a plan, we have a fuel response plan, we have published that plan, we are taking all of the measures necessary.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the 'no plan' charge by asserting a published fuel response plan exists, though without detailing it here.

forthrightness.statement: There are 48 referral applications that have been lodged and found compliant, and 47 substantive applications have been lodged and found complete. If they're all approved, these would authorise the construction of nearly 24,000 new houses, thousands of new retirement village units, and thousands of additional megawatts of new electricity generation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the 'how many projects' question with specific numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the process we're going through is to make sure that we reduce power bills for New Zealanders, that we make sure we protect regional jobs, and we keep the lights on, unlike the previous Government's approach—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the specific price/cost-benefit thresholds used to judge the LNG terminal, he gives slogans about goals and a swipe at the previous government, not any threshold.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we're working through a procurement process, but on this side of the House we are focused on affordable electricity prices, keeping the lights on, and protecting jobs, and the reality is, you can't run an electricity system on hope that it will rain. That's the Opposition's strategy—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what alternative measures he has sought advice on if LNG does not proceed, he names none and pivots to attacking the Opposition.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, we are working through a process. Once that process is complete, decisions will be made and they'll be announced.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Simon Watts that without LNG there is no plan B for a dry year, he gives a pure process non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: I directed the Ministry of Education to pick up the phone or personally visit every single school in New Zealand so that we can understand exactly what they're dealing with on the ground.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how schools shaped the response — by describing the consultation she ordered and the two issues that surfaced.

forthrightness.statement: The provision of civil defence payments is a Ministry of Social Development operational decision that is informed by assessments by civil defence, by MSD, and by local communities... Existing MSD services and support have, so far, been able to meet the needs of those impacted.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the process and asserts needs are being met, but does not directly answer whether the civil defence payment is available and, if not, why not.

forthrightness.statement: The first step is that there is an assessment by civil defence, by local communities, and by MSD as to whether or not the civil defence payments are required. That is the first step.
forthrightness.explanation: Genter's point of order is upheld in substance — asked about the value of the payment being frozen since 2013, Upston only repeats the assessment 'first step' and never addresses the value.

forthrightness.statement: Annual figures show that overseas visitor arrivals reached 3.58 million in the year to February 2026, which is an increase of 229,000 people on the previous year. This puts us at 92 percent of the pre-COVID levels.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the patsy question on tourism reports with the relevant data.

forthrightness.statement: I note that the Stats New Zealand Research and Development Survey shows that employment in the sector increased from 28,200 roles in 2022 to 30,600 roles in 2024, with most of that growth in the private sector... Budget 2025 committed more than $1.8 billion to science and innovation.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms her statement and supplies data but sidesteps the specific job-loss figure the question put to her.

forthrightness.statement: Of course, it isn't a cut; it is a reallocation of funding to the Advanced Technology Institute.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly contests the 'cut' premise but uses a quoted endorsement to bolster the reframing rather than addressing the lost roles.

forthrightness.statement: We are very focused on ensuring that the critical work that is done in weather forecasting and climate research continues. We're bringing NIWA and MetService together in Earth Sciences so that we can get efficiencies and ensure that we reinvest in improvements to our climate science and our weather forecasting capabilities.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether cutting hazard-monitoring roles risks degrading services, she reassures generally and cites a merger for 'efficiencies' without addressing the degradation risk.

forthrightness.statement: I agree that the Treaty of Waitangi, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, in its two languages was the document signed at the founding of our contemporary nation.
forthrightness.explanation: Carefully reframes Ferris's question (whether Te Tiriti is 'the founding document') into a narrower factual agreement about what was signed, neither fully agreeing nor refusing.

forthrightness.statement: We as a Government sought to try and bring a bit of order to the 28 or so pieces of legislation that refer the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi and a host of arrangements—sometimes "give effect to", sometimes "have regard to", sometimes "honour", sometimes "take account"... We set a group up to bring some coherency to that, and that's what we're doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the rationale for the review but does not directly say what steps protect Treaty-based justice rights from being adversely affected, as asked.

forthrightness.statement: By convention, a six-week call for submission corresponds to a six-month report back, or four weeks for a four-month report back. The clerk of the committee originally understood it to be a six-month report back and so issued a submission for the six-week period. However, shortly after the Easter break, it came to his attention that the report back was, in fact, only a four-month report back, and... I instructed him to call for submissions proportional to the report-back date, which, in effect, is the four weeks.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully explains why the submission period changed from six to four weeks, including the clerk's error and the proportionality convention.

forthrightness.statement: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the claim that he breached ruling 117/1, asserting the proportionality exception applies.

authenticity.statement: What we can control is our own spending, and this Government is determined to take a responsible course in which we do not add fuel to the inflation fire, as was not the case in recent history under previous Governments.
authenticity.explanation: States a fiscal-restraint value consistent with the Government's stated stance, but no delivered action is verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: We are determined to make sure we deliver on our climate change commitments—that means net zero 2050; that means doing everything we can to deliver on our Paris agreements... We have reversed the oil and gas ban so we don't create an energy dry-year risk and high power bills for New Zealanders.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts commitment to net zero 2050 and Paris in the same breath as boasting of reversing the oil-and-gas exploration ban — a visible tension between the climate goal and the action taken.

rigor.statement: Well, because I'd put my economic management record up against his any day of the week. This is a former Prime Minister who drove up spending 84 percent, who actually drove inflation to 32-year highs, 12 or 13 interest rate rises, slowed an economy up, and created unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Cites figures but asserts sole causation between Hipkins and inflation/rate rises without supporting the causal chain.

rigor.statement: That is why the Government moved swiftly to introduce targeted, temporary support to working families who face high costs in supporting their children. We delivered that support, but did it in a way that adhered to the advice that economists the world over are giving, which is: "Do not respond to this crisis in a way that adds to inflation and further weakens your fiscal sustainability."
rigor.explanation: Appeals to 'economists the world over' as authority to justify restraint without citing specifics — a mild appeal-to-authority.

rigor.statement: Because when people ask me whether they should have confidence in me, they need to compare themselves with the alternative, which is that member, and what she is promoting is more taxes, more spending, more borrowing, and more debt—back to the bad old COVID days.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a false-dichotomy framing ('compare with the alternative') instead of defending her own record on the figures cited.

rigor.statement: Well, because if you talk to those in the construction sector, they say one of the most important things for ensuring that there's high levels of construction activity is that interest rates are lower. And on the watch of this Government, there have been successive interest rate reductions, whereas on the watch of the previous Government, they increased at such a rapid rate that it's meant that many construction projects fell over.
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible mechanism (rates → construction) but supports it with 'if you talk to the sector' anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: Well, listen up: the average number of working days for a substantive decision is 126... Auckland Port estimates their application to extend the wharf would have taken more than three years; it took five months and nine days... Green Steel... took seven months and 18 days. They say it would have taken six years under the RMA.
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based before/after case, though the RMA counterfactual durations are proponents' own estimates rather than independent.

rigor.statement: Well, we're working through a procurement process, but on this side of the House we are focused on affordable electricity prices, keeping the lights on, and protecting jobs, and the reality is, you can't run an electricity system on hope that it will rain. That's the Opposition's strategy—
rigor.explanation: Substitutes a dismissive strawman ('run the system on hope') for an actual account of the alternatives.

rigor.statement: Well, unfortunately, after the previous Government made the decision to ban oil and gas exploration, we have seen a significant reduction in gas availability in New Zealand. It is reducing faster than was expected and that is damaging jobs, it is damaging industries across our country... I can tell the member: hope is not a strategy.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a direct causal chain from the ban to job damage without supporting evidence, leaning on the rhetorical 'hope is not a strategy'.

rigor.statement: By convention, a six-week call for submission corresponds to a six-month report back, or four weeks for a four-month report back. The clerk of the committee originally understood it to be a six-month report back and so issued a submission for the six-week period. However, shortly after the Easter break, it came to his attention that the report back was, in fact, only a four-month report back, and... I instructed him to call for submissions proportional to the report-back date, which, in effect, is the four weeks.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a logical chain (report-back length → proportional submission window) to justify the decision.

rigor.statement: I have to dispute what the Hon Dr Duncan Webb's just stated, because under the Speaker's rulings the committee chair can call for a submission period proportional to the report back. I know that the committee clerk actually spoke to the Speaker about this issue, and I'm fully, as the chair of the committee, entitled to do this under the power of the committee and under the Speaker's ruling.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the rebuttal in the Speaker's rulings and the clerk's consultation with the Speaker, though without quoting the specific provision.

rigor.statement: Why should the tens of thousands of New Zealanders who have lost jobs under his leadership have confidence in him when the job that he seems most committed to fighting for is his own?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes job losses with the leadership-vote story rhetorically rather than establishing any causal link.

rigor.statement: If she truly is on the side of construction workers, then why are there 39,570 working-age jobseeker support clients as at the end of January 2026, who have declared construction, mining labourer, or trades worker as their previous occupation?
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete statistic to test the Minister's claimed support for construction workers, a relevant evidential challenge.

rigor.statement: What about the smoke-free generation rules that your Government revoked and repealed? What was the economic impact on the health system as a result of the repealing of that particular piece of legislation, given the Minister's last comments?
rigor.explanation: Tries to connect the smokefree repeal to downstream health-system costs — a relevant line of reasoning, though asserted rather than evidenced here.

strength.statement: I can. I'm very proud to say we'll have a national flood plan by the end of this year. We are the first Government to do so, and we are taking action and putting investment into climate change, not just words and bumper stickers and Post-it notes.
strength.explanation: Concrete commitment with a deadline (national flood plan by year-end), but it is a forward promise not yet delivered — credit pending follow-through.

strength.statement: That is why the Government moved swiftly to introduce targeted, temporary support to working families who face high costs in supporting their children. We delivered that support, but did it in a way that adhered to the advice that economists the world over are giving, which is: "Do not respond to this crisis in a way that adds to inflation and further weakens your fiscal sustainability."
strength.explanation: Claims a specific delivered measure ('we delivered that support') consistent with the later in-work tax credit detail, though the package's adequacy is contested.

strength.statement: I utterly reject the assertion made in the latter part of that question, and it's an assertion that the Labour Party dishonourably continue to make on social media. We have a plan, we have a fuel response plan, we have published that plan, we are taking all of the measures necessary.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete deliverable (a published fuel response plan) but its substance and effectiveness are asserted, not demonstrated.

strength.statement: Well, listen up: the average number of working days for a substantive decision is 126... Auckland Port estimates their application to extend the wharf would have taken more than three years; it took five months and nine days... Green Steel... took seven months and 18 days. They say it would have taken six years under the RMA.
strength.explanation: Demonstrates delivered approvals (projects consented in months) as evidence the fast-track policy is producing results, not just announced.

strength.statement: This Government's recently announced Go Rural programme offers student teachers $4,000 to cover the cost of undertaking a placement in a rural and isolated school... yesterday I announced a further 87 places per year... We're also increasing the number of places available in the Government's Teacher Bonding Scheme by 50 places to 235 per year, supporting teachers with an additional $40,000 over five years.
strength.explanation: Concrete, costed measures, but largely just announced ('yesterday I announced'), so delivery/uptake is still prospective.

divination.statement: Westpower estimates the scheme will generate enough electricity for 12,000 homes and prevent—Chlöe Swarbrick—129,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually. I'm told this is equivalent to taking 69,000 cars off the road annually.
divination.explanation: Forecast of future annual generation/emissions savings from a scheme not yet built; plausible but contingent on completion and output.

specificity.statement: a major announcement was publicised this morning in turning Southland's lignite reserve, I believe it's something like 9 billion tonnes, into urea, and also electricity generation from the hydrogen.
specificity.explanation: Names the resource (Southland lignite), a figure (9 billion tonnes) and the outputs (urea, hydrogen electricity), though hedged with 'something like'.

specificity.statement: Within eight weeks, New Zealand—eight weeks—I've achieved, on behalf of the Government, what the last regime could not do for 1,000 weeks; simply dedicated a small amount of money, relatively speaking, to upgrade 100 million litres' worth of storage; recommissioned a crude tank, to the best of my knowledge, for the purposes of holding additional diesel.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and mechanisms: eight weeks, 100 million litres, a recommissioned crude tank for diesel.

specificity.statement: had the 700 million – odd litres of storage capacity not been terminated in 2021-22, we may very well have had tanks fit for use.
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure (700 million litres) and a year (2021-22).

specificity.statement: No single fuel company has said that they are close or perilously heading towards violating their legal obligations, because punitive damages up to $700 million could be visited upon them.
specificity.explanation: Names the enforcement mechanism and a figure ($700 million punitive damages).

specificity.statement: the solar plant would only operate less than 20 percent of the time, in effect because it's not sunny all the time, it certainly doesn't operate at night, by the time you set what level of energy it generated, the geothermal plant was actually the cheapest by the amount of energy that it generated, and, of course, it's operating close to 100 percent of the time.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies capacity factors (under 20% solar, near 100% geothermal) to support the comparison.

specificity.statement: the evaluation only looks at exits, and not exits into work. How does she know that it's not the case management system or job coaching that is actually achieving work exits and that it is nothing to do with the sanctions? Why did the review not include that?
specificity.explanation: Points to a precise gap in the evaluation (exits vs exits-into-work) but does not cite figures.

specificity.statement: There were 60,000 people in case management, and there are now 70,000. Case management is the most effective programme that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) funds and delivers, and it is the significant increase in the number of people in case management that is a strong correlation to what we are seeing in terms of work exits.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (60,000 to 70,000) tied to a named programme.

specificity.statement: Where there is someone who moves from green into orange, 84.7 percent are resolved after they contact MSD.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure (84.7%) tied to the traffic-light mechanism.

specificity.statement: In terms of the relationship rules, they are longstanding rules, and they are in place because an underpinning principle of the welfare system is that it's based on a household rather than an individual. I know that there are some people who disagree with it and believe that support should be based on each individual. There is no view to changing a longstanding principle of the Social Security Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the principle (household-based, Social Security Act) but gives no figures or mechanism detail.

specificity.statement: One was the Smithfield Alliance in Timaru, with about 700 affected workers, and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) worked very closely on the ground with those workers. The example that the member gave in Tokoroa, project phoenix, was stood up as a combination of work across Government agencies, council, and Toi Ohomai to work really closely with affected workers, and I'm really proud of what MSD have done on the ground.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete cases (Smithfield Alliance, ~700 workers; project phoenix; Toi Ohomai).

specificity.statement: every single person that our Government supports to exit the benefit into work is a victory. It's a win for that individual, their whānau, and the community, and that's what I'll continue to focus on.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no figures, mechanism, or plan.

specificity.statement: During the year in review, there were 69 non-financial sanctions that were applied, and it was not throughout the entire year of the financial review.
specificity.explanation: Cites an exact count (69) with a caveat on the period.

specificity.statement: In terms of the question around job coaching, 45 percent of those participating in phase 1 have so far achieved employment outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure (45%) for a defined cohort (phase 1).

specificity.statement: why are Māori more likely to be investigated for things like welfare fraud than their counterparts when that is not the case for early intervention and facilitation processes which do not show that Māori are disproportionately targeted by these less burdensome and consequential interventions
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes investigation from early-intervention/facilitation and notes the ethnic breakdown driving the concern.

specificity.statement: what does she make of the fact that out of the total sanctions that have been applied, non-financial sanctions, to my understanding, make less than 0.5 percent of total sanctions? A significant amount of money has been spent in updating the Ministry of Social Development's system so that these sanctions could actually be used, but it seems like they're not being used altogether, basically. Does she accept that this could lead to, or be seen as, a failure or a policy failure?
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure (under 0.5% of sanctions) and the system-upgrade spend.

specificity.statement: We know that there are 32,000 fewer jobs under this Government... Kinleith Mill lost 150 jobs, Kinleith plywood 119, and Winstone Pulp's Ruapehu mills—230 there... Toi Ohomai in Tokoroa had 60 job losses in and around the same time that we've seen three closures of wood manufacturing.
specificity.explanation: Itemised job-loss figures by named employer and location, plus an aggregate figure.

specificity.statement: Did the ministry receive any direction in 2024-25 to shift away from equity-focused or Tiriti-based approaches? If so, who made that decision, and how was it justified?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question naming a period and concrete follow-ups (who decided, how justified).

specificity.statement: Yes, we are disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment, but for very good reason... This merger is simply about reducing bloated bureaucracy. We saw, under the previous Government, something like 16,000 extra bureaucrats were appointed.
specificity.explanation: Names the new ministry rationale and a figure (≈16,000 extra staff).

specificity.statement: the ministry has actually produced a record amount of output—a full 4,822 items, which included 896 briefings, probably most to Chris Bishop; 62 Cabinet papers, probably most to Chris Bishop; 452 Official Information Act requests, that's probably a lot for you, Andrew Hoggard!; and many, many more parliamentary questions and pieces of ministerial correspondence.
specificity.explanation: Itemised output counts (4,822 items; 896 briefings; 62 Cabinet papers; 452 OIAs).

specificity.statement: we are not getting rid of the Ministry for the Environment's functions. Its role has always been advisory. We're simply moving these functions to the newly appointed Secretary for the Environment, who I understand—not yet met—is an exceptional operator. I encourage that side of the committee to have some faith in the officials and their expertise.
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism (functions moved to the Secretary) but without statutory detail.

specificity.statement: the isolation of the environment into a separate ministry is that there is a tendency to ignore the advice from the Ministry for the Environment... how do you do proper transport planning in a spatial sense in a region and how do you do land-use planning in a city or a district, without thinking about the environment?
specificity.explanation: Illustrates with concrete planning functions, though without quantification.

specificity.statement: Wellington Water discovered that they installed a pipe from the top of Aro Valley down to Wellington harbour in the early 2000s that has never been connected to any network and, until they started actually going through their records as part of local water restructuring, they didn't even know existed. It had been put in at vast expense in the early 2000s and had just sat there unconnected. All the records are based on paper.
specificity.explanation: Concrete anecdote with location, era, and detail (paper records) to illustrate the case for restructuring.

specificity.statement: there's been decades of under-investment largely because local body politicians have prioritised building convention centres and half-billion - dollar town hall upgrades on the ground of heritage and not focused on the basics.
specificity.explanation: Names categories of spend (convention centres, half-billion-dollar town hall upgrades) but no specific councils or totals.

specificity.statement: we have an under-secretary for the resource management reform say that this Government's Resource Management Act reforms are about ending this integrated management of the Resource Management Act, and we see that in the form of two different bills, being the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill. I'm interested in whether the Minister for resource management reform might want to comment on how that is enabling an integrated approach—having those two different functions.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific bills (Planning Bill, Natural Environment Bill) and the under-secretary's stated position.

veracity.statement: a major announcement was publicised this morning in turning Southland's lignite reserve, I believe it's something like 9 billion tonnes, into urea, and also electricity generation from the hydrogen.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about an announcement and reserve size; plausible and specific but flagged as belief ('I believe'), unverified.

veracity.statement: Within eight weeks, New Zealand—eight weeks—I've achieved, on behalf of the Government, what the last regime could not do for 1,000 weeks; simply dedicated a small amount of money, relatively speaking, to upgrade 100 million litres' worth of storage; recommissioned a crude tank, to the best of my knowledge, for the purposes of holding additional diesel.
veracity.explanation: Storage upgrade is a checkable claim, but '1,000 weeks' framing is rhetorical exaggeration that overstates the contrast.

veracity.statement: had the 700 million – odd litres of storage capacity not been terminated in 2021-22, we may very well have had tanks fit for use.
veracity.explanation: Counterfactual blaming the 2021-22 refinery/storage closure; the underlying fact of lost capacity is real but the 'fit for use' conclusion is speculative.

veracity.statement: No single fuel company has said that they are close or perilously heading towards violating their legal obligations, because punitive damages up to $700 million could be visited upon them.
veracity.explanation: Assertion about what companies have said and the penalty regime; plausible but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: There were 60,000 people in case management, and there are now 70,000. Case management is the most effective programme that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) funds and delivers, and it is the significant increase in the number of people in case management that is a strong correlation to what we are seeing in terms of work exits.
veracity.explanation: Specific operational figures, plausible, but 'most effective programme' is an unquantified assertion.

veracity.statement: Where there is someone who moves from green into orange, 84.7 percent are resolved after they contact MSD.
veracity.explanation: A precise statistic, but 'resolved' is undefined and the figure is used to imply impact it may not show.

veracity.statement: In terms of the question around job coaching, 45 percent of those participating in phase 1 have so far achieved employment outcomes.
veracity.explanation: A precise programme statistic; plausible but not independently checkable here.

veracity.explanation: Precise figures attributed to the select committee report; plausible and sourced, not independently verified here.

veracity.explanation: A specific claim presented as fact ('I am told'); plausible but second-hand and uncorroborated.

veracity.statement: local councils have been the ones responsible for the funding and delivery of, essentially, what's a network utility infrastructure service, which is drinking water and waste water. Unsurprisingly, they have done a poor job of that
veracity.explanation: A sweeping evaluative claim about council performance; the funding-responsibility part is accurate, but 'done a poor job' is a generalisation stated as fact.

strength.statement: One was the Smithfield Alliance in Timaru, with about 700 affected workers, and the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) worked very closely on the ground with those workers. The example that the member gave in Tokoroa, project phoenix, was stood up as a combination of work across Government agencies, council, and Toi Ohomai to work really closely with affected workers, and I'm really proud of what MSD have done on the ground.

forthrightness.statement: No single fuel company has said that they are close or perilously heading towards violating their legal obligations, because punitive damages up to $700 million could be visited upon them.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the question about confidence in fuel-supply obligations with a direct claim about company status and enforcement.

forthrightness.statement: Where there is someone who moves from green into orange, 84.7 percent are resolved after they contact MSD.
forthrightness.explanation: Prime asked why the review measures exits not exits-into-work; the Minister pivots to a different sanctions statistic and notes the evaluation is outside the review period rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the relationship rules, they are longstanding rules, and they are in place because an underpinning principle of the welfare system is that it's based on a household rather than an individual. I know that there are some people who disagree with it and believe that support should be based on each individual. There is no view to changing a longstanding principle of the Social Security Act.
forthrightness.explanation: Menéndez March asked whether she supports the relationship-status policy; she answers clearly — defends the principle and states there is no view to change it.

forthrightness.statement: I don't have that detail in front of me in terms of the disproportionate number that he is suggesting are being investigated. What we do know is, unfortunately, Māori have a disproportionate number of people receiving benefit and then, further down the track, in interventions or, in this case, in investigations. It does then lead to that there's a higher proportion that are also being investigated.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was why disparity emerges specifically at the investigation stage but not in early intervention; she does not address that, citing lack of detail and base rates instead.

forthrightness.statement: The issues related to housing, social housing, homelessness were covered in the annual review debate last night with Minister Potaka, so I won't be covering that.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. In the round, the new ministry, I believe, will lead to improvements of our natural environment over time.

rigor.statement: the solar plant would only operate less than 20 percent of the time, in effect because it's not sunny all the time, it certainly doesn't operate at night, by the time you set what level of energy it generated, the geothermal plant was actually the cheapest by the amount of energy that it generated, and, of course, it's operating close to 100 percent of the time.
rigor.explanation: Sound levelised-cost reasoning: distinguishes nameplate cost from cost-per-energy by accounting for capacity factor; conclusion follows from the premises.

specificity.statement: this bill will seek to allow for a registered offender to present ID in an electronic form. So if an electronic driver’s licence is held by anyone in this country—and this will create the mechanism for that to happen; it’s not saying that will, necessarily, all come in overnight, but it will create the mechanism for that to happen.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete change (registered offenders presenting electronic ID) and the legal mechanism, but the repeated 'create the mechanism' hedging and lack of timing/figures keeps it mid-range.

specificity.statement: For the prostitution reform, the current legislation requires an individual specified in that Act to present a photocopy of their driver’s licence, which would prove rather difficult if you had an electronic copy
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete existing requirement and the practical problem it creates, though without exact section references.

specificity.statement: If there were some safety concerns around State highways as part of the networks, there was not an automatic right for Waka Kotahi to go and, effectively, close down periods or patches of State highway networks. This does provide them the opportunity to do that, but only in circumstances where safety is an issue. It’s not a broad-brush form of authority where they can just go in and shutdown a highway; it needs to be purely related or only related to safety considerations.
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete new power and its explicit limitation to safety circumstances, though without clause numbers or thresholds.

specificity.statement: this bill, in the maritime space, will ensure that the reforms that Maritime New Zealand are undertaking as a result, and in sort of tandem with this bill and this legislation, will bring us into alignment with the Maritime Labour Convention.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete outcome (alignment with the Maritime Labour Convention) and the responsible agency, though without timeframe or detail of the specific standards.

specificity.statement: It’s a failure of this Government of public transport.
specificity.explanation: A bare verdict with no mechanism, figures, or examples to substantiate it.

specificity.statement: new section 61AA says, “(1) The Agency may—(a) stop, divert, or otherwise control traffic on a State highway; or (b) close a State highway (or any part of it) to traffic.” It also goes on to say, “(2) The Agency may only exercise the power under subsection (1) if the Agency considers it appropriate to do so for the protection and safety of the public.”
specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact clause and subsections of the new section 61AA, giving precise legislative detail.

authenticity.statement: at its core, New Zealand First supports this bill because it is firmly rooted in our foundational belief that we need to protect community and country.

specificity.statement: at its core, New Zealand First supports this bill because it is firmly rooted in our foundational belief that we need to protect community and country.

specificity.statement: Health New Zealand's proposing that participating pharmacists be able to provide funded medicines for children and their families for pain and fever management, oral rehydration, and common conditions such as scabies, headlice, and conjunctivitis. The proposal also covers treatment for uncomplicated urinary tract infections and emergency contraception.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates specific conditions and treatments covered, with a June start.

specificity.statement: To support delivery, Health New Zealand has established a $5 million per year extended pharmacy services fund to help ensure these services are available nationwide.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete annual funding figure and its purpose.

specificity.statement: By enabling pharmacists to manage common conditions, we free up GPs to focus on more complex cases, reducing pressure across the system … It is a practical, common-sense step to improve access, affordability, and efficiency in our health system.
specificity.explanation: General claims of system benefit without measures or targets.

specificity.statement: Last week, Retail NZ released a report … It said that an illicit tobacco market already existed and is only going to grow. … It also reduces revenue collection used to fund Government services, and … it allows organised crime groups to line their pockets and expand their reach in our communities.
specificity.explanation: Cites a recent named report but gives no figures.

specificity.statement: Today, I welcomed … a new investment from French fashion house Chanel in New Zealand's fine wool production. … Chanel has invested in a joint-venture company to own a part of and continue to support Lammermoor Station in the Central Otago high country, which produces some of the world's best fine wool for Chanel's garments.
specificity.explanation: Names the investor, the station, and the location.

specificity.statement: Chanel plans to build on Lammermoor's organic status and achieve regenerative organic certification. That would make Lammermoor the world's first fine-wool producing farm with those credentials.
specificity.explanation: Concrete goal (regenerative organic certification) and a distinct claimed milestone.

specificity.statement: New statistics from Land Information New Zealand show average end-to-end assessment time frames for business and productive forestry. Assessments have decreased significantly under this Government, going from an average of 67 working days to 31 working days in the last 12 months.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures and timeframe.

specificity.statement: The changes being made by Amendment Paper 570 are very minor and technical in nature. They mainly relate to the change in approach from 10 Hauraki bills progressing together to third reading and to individual groups being able to progress when they are ready to do so. These changes will affect references to the Pare Hauraki collective redress deed and the timing of transfer of jointly vested properties.
specificity.explanation: Detailed, precise account of the amendments and what they affect.

specificity.statement: Just to be clear, for those who made submissions, this bill does not set up digital drivers' licences; it just provides the framework … I want to acknowledge the submitters who raised concerns about whether or not digital drivers' licences would become compulsory. That is not the Government's intention. … this is a voluntary step that people can take up if they wish to do so.
specificity.explanation: Clarifies precisely what the bill does and does not do.

specificity.statement: In Ōtautahi, we have over 54 percent of our emissions coming from land transport. No, it wasn't going to fix that.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure and locale.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced five changes to how we improve assurance of infrastructure projects. We are simplifying assurance by having one tool that is focused on what Ministers need to make investment decisions. We're transferring responsibility over assurance from the Treasury to the independent, expert Infrastructure Commission. Ministers will now get a two- or three-page fitness assessment for business cases seeking Cabinet endorsement.
strength.explanation: An announcement of changes; describes a decision taken but not yet implemented or shown to deliver.

strength.statement: This Government is finally investing in a bilingual education system more equitably than any other Government that I can remember. That is about raising achievement for Māori students.
strength.explanation: Claims investment but offers no figures or delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I launched Anzac Stories with Archives New Zealand and the National Library. … The stories are of real people, places, animals, and items and are designed with the help of students from Belmont School in Lower Hutt and Adventure School in Porirua.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete initiative actually launched, not merely promised.

strength.explanation: A proposal/announcement; expanded services are proposed, not yet delivered.

authenticity.explanation: Proactively corrects her own earlier statement on the record — words aligned with accuracy.

authenticity.statement: Sadly, life is not static. I can confirm, however, that there a host of areas in New Zealand where it would be very inappropriate to mine. Whether or not those places will be permanently off limits, obviously, waits for a future regime.
authenticity.explanation: Responding to his own 2010 anti-mining quote, he concedes a shift ('life is not static') — an acknowledged change of position.

authenticity.statement: I can provide no better answer than to go to the Good Book: "When I was a child, I thought as a child."
authenticity.explanation: Dismisses his earlier anti-mining views as childish — an open repudiation of a prior position, i.e. a flip.

rigor.statement: It seems, to me, that we should be treating everybody equally, and that's what the coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National says.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the equal-treatment claim in the text of the coalition agreement — an appeal to the agreement as authority rather than to evidence about outcomes, but a coherent premise.

rigor.statement: The question, Minister, is why it is that, at the moment, it appears, you are not supporting this amendment, because it would be consistent with the coalition agreement to support the amendment.
rigor.explanation: Argues the amendment follows from a stated coalition principle; reasoning is clear but rests on the agreement rather than transport evidence.

rigor.statement: Will a consistent set of standing orders override this provision, or will this provision stand and, effectively, trump any form of consistent set of standing orders that the bill that I mentioned would actually present?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine legislative-interaction problem between two bills with clear logical structure.

rigor.statement: Again, is he comfortable that whilst undertaking the same amount of work, there, effectively, would be a potential differential in remuneration levels that would exist there?
rigor.explanation: Highlights an inconsistency — equal work but different remuneration regimes for mayoral vs ministerial appointees.

rigor.statement: All I can say is that, if a subsequent piece of legislation says there is to be a consistent set of standing orders that overrides other standing orders, it will override them. If the subsequent bill does not provide that, it will not override them.
rigor.explanation: Logically sound conditional, though somewhat tautological.

rigor.statement: have some faith in our elected representatives to do the right thing because, ultimately, that's what we elect them for, and if we weren't all here to do the right thing, then we should probably walk out the door and go get another job.
rigor.explanation: Responds to a politicisation-of-appointments concern with an appeal to good faith rather than any safeguard or evidence.

rigor.statement: it would surprise me if anyone could interpret "safe and rapid movement of people and goods" as anything other than addressing issues around congestion.

rigor.statement: the intention of Parliament is the words that are written in the statute, supported by the context and the interpretation and purpose of the text and all that kind of stuff, not the ramblings of Ministers and members in the Chamber.
rigor.explanation: Sound statutory-interpretation reasoning about why his comments should not be read as legislative intent.

rigor.statement: when I actually look at the voting members, it has potential for a tie with no tiebreaker in that there are three appointed by the Minister, three appointed by the mayor—and we understand that already that power of the mayor is quite different from other councils around the country—and then they've got to agree on the chairperson.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete structural deadlock risk by reasoning through the committee's composition.

rigor.statement: they're not thrown out just because it was the other side that started them.
rigor.explanation: Sensible point about wasted spend, linked to the Infrastructure Commission report, though stated generally.

rigor.statement: Why is it necessary, then, for the Government to have such a level of central planning as to impose on Aucklanders the three objectives there?
rigor.explanation: Pointed question reasoning from the new body's stated localist purpose to question central objective-setting.

rigor.statement: Would he not consider then, if those objectives are going to be imposed on Aucklanders, the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read "reducing congestion" as one of the objectives of that plan, given that most Aucklanders tell pollsters and local politicians alike that congestion is their number one problem in Auckland's transport system
rigor.explanation: Backs the proposal with public-opinion evidence, but partly an appeal to popularity.

rigor.statement: Does this allow for the ARTC, for instance, to canvass its intention to sell off some transport assets and to use the proceeds of those to buy other transport assets?
rigor.explanation: Probes a specific, non-obvious implication of the 'likely sources of funding' provision.

rigor.statement: you need to at least, Minister, tell us what Māori means in this piece of legislation? Is it iwi?
rigor.explanation: Argues for definitional clarity, citing the select committee's own commentary that 'consultation with Māori' should be defined.

rigor.statement: how do we know it's delivering on these objectives, and what's the definition or measure that we're using to measure productivity?
rigor.explanation: Demands measurable definitions and a means of verification for the stated objectives — disciplined questioning.

rigor.statement: if there is no specific requirement to think about disabled access then it will often get missed and it will be more expensive to remedy later.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned cause-and-effect drawn from experience with prior regional committee requirements.

rigor.statement: When you look overseas at cities that have really good outcomes, most of the power and the funding is devolved to the city to make the decision about transport priorities. It's not done at a national level.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to overseas examples to support devolution but names no specific cities or data.

rigor.statement: let's face it: most people are just voting on vibes, whether it's for the mayor or the Government of the day.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping unsupported assertion about voter behaviour used to bolster the argument.

specificity.explanation: References a specific named principle in a specific agreement, though the proposed course of action stays general.

specificity.explanation: General aspiration about wanting good transport, no mechanism or measure.

specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the exact definitional gap across clause 12 and new section 48, though the substance is that no definition exists.

specificity.statement: The biggest issue I get is not actually any feeling that is particularly anti the park developing, but it's about this—it's about the transport issues around the park.
specificity.explanation: Concrete about the locus of constituent concern (transport, not development).

specificity.explanation: Names the responsible body, the framework, and the consultation under way, though without timing detail.

specificity.explanation: Anchors the question to a population figure and the specific consultation paragraphs (42D(2)(c)/(d)).

specificity.explanation: Concrete, detailed example with named locations to illustrate accessibility for seniors.

charisma.statement: They want no congestion. They want to be able to use a good public transport system. Those things affect all of us. They affect all people, regardless of whether they are Māori or whether they are non-Māori.
charisma.explanation: Universalising, common-ground framing that emphasises shared interests across groups.

civility.statement: The question, Minister, is why it is that, at the moment, it appears, you are not supporting this amendment, because it would be consistent with the coalition agreement to support the amendment.
civility.explanation: Presses the Minister on policy consistency without any personal attack.

civility.statement: have some faith in our elected representatives to do the right thing because, ultimately, that's what we elect them for, and if we weren't all here to do the right thing, then we should probably walk out the door and go get another job.

civility.statement: I'd encourage the member, if she would like this committee to see some action before November, that we should hurry along and get this bill passed into law as quickly as possible.

civility.statement: the intention of Parliament is the words that are written in the statute, supported by the context and the interpretation and purpose of the text and all that kind of stuff, not the ramblings of Ministers and members in the Chamber.
civility.explanation: Self-deprecating ('ramblings'), no disrespect to others.

civility.statement: While I was on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee and I generally support the direction, I just wanted to tease out some of what I would say were apparent inconsistencies.
civility.explanation: Respectful framing focused on substance.

civility.statement: Why is it necessary, then, for the Government to have such a level of central planning as to impose on Aucklanders the three objectives there?

civility.statement: I have absolutely no idea what the Eden Park precinct is, and I just can't tell my constituents what's in and what's out.
civility.explanation: Wholly constructive — 'It's not a trick question' — focused on getting clarity.

forthrightness.statement: All I can say is that, if a subsequent piece of legislation says there is to be a consistent set of standing orders that overrides other standing orders, it will override them. If the subsequent bill does not provide that, it will not override them.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Utikere's question as fully as logically possible and is candid that a definitive answer is impossible while the other bill's final form is unknown.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of Mr Luxton's questions around the use of the word "Māori", look, I can't answer that directly
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer the core question of what 'Māori' means in the bill, deflecting to the select-committee process and the bill-as-introduced.

forthrightness.statement: it would surprise me if anyone could interpret "safe and rapid movement of people and goods" as anything other than addressing issues around congestion.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages Williams's point about whether congestion is captured in the objectives, arguing it is already covered.

forthrightness.statement: Auckland Council will define the Eden Park precinct area when it develops the Auckland roading classification framework. I'm advised that this work is currently under way and that the local boards are being consulted with on the framework.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers White's question about who defines the precinct and how, including the ministerial-agreement safeguard.

forthrightness.statement: there absolutely is the expectation that it is a joint process shared between the mayor and the Minister, and "joint" is what it says on the tin.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear yes to Utikere's question about whether chairperson appointment is an equal partnership.

forthrightness.statement: the purpose here is very much one that is aligned with expectations, which is restoring democratic accountability for transport and Auckland transport matters back with Auckland Council.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers that he is comfortable with the select committee recommendation and gives a reason, though briefly.

veracity.statement: Would he not consider then, if those objectives are going to be imposed on Aucklanders, the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read "reducing congestion" as one of the objectives of that plan, given that most Aucklanders tell pollsters and local politicians alike that congestion is their number one problem in Auckland's transport system
veracity.explanation: Claim that congestion is Aucklanders' number-one transport problem is commonly cited and plausible but unsourced here.

veracity.statement: there's roughly, say, off his numbers, about 300,000 people who whakapapa Māori in Tāmaki-makau-rau, in Auckland.

veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that many high-performing cities have devolved transport powers, though stated as a sweeping generalisation.

veracity.explanation: Specific factual recollection, appropriately hedged ('I believe'); plausible but not independently confirmed here.

civility.statement: saying there was no use of “agree to disagree” when the bill was introduced and so it must be fine is not really, in a parliamentary process, a suitable answer when members from parties across this House are raising legitimate questions for Aucklanders engaged in the process of a 30-year transport plan that has been through a select committee, had issues identified, and had them flagged in the select committee report
civility.explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the Minister's procedural answer, not the Minister personally; engages the substance of the process.

civility.statement: I’m very concerned, based on the answers that we’ve received in this committee stage, that that is left undefined. Therefore—I shudder to even mention this—but is this creating a separation in legislation between people if we’re going to allow such a term to remain undefined in this important part of the committee stage?
civility.explanation: Raises a charged 'separation' implication but frames it as a question and flags reluctance ('I shudder'); not a personal attack, though leaning toward insinuation.

civility.statement: It was ACT and New Zealand First who said, “Actually, we are concerned about that, because we don’t like the wording there and we think it is impractical.”
civility.explanation: Corrects a misattribution about the proceedings without attacking the Minister personally, framing it as an inaccuracy to fix.

civility.statement: because it said it in 2002, we should just keep on following that up essentially forever and a day until the LTMA one day maybe gets replaced or repealed. I would suggest to you that that is a fairly lazy way of doing things.
civility.explanation: Calls the drafting approach 'lazy' — a jab at the method rather than the person, but verging on a cheap characterisation of the Minister's reasoning.

civility.statement: ensuring that at the end of the process of transition the staff are protected and there’s confidence from the Government that the entities involved will be able to manage that transition smoothly and in a way that is appropriate is, I think, important for some assurance to be given.
civility.explanation: Constructive, focused on staff protection and orderly transition; no personal attack.

rigor.statement: saying there was no use of “agree to disagree” when the bill was introduced and so it must be fine is not really, in a parliamentary process, a suitable answer when members from parties across this House are raising legitimate questions for Aucklanders engaged in the process of a 30-year transport plan that has been through a select committee, had issues identified, and had them flagged in the select committee report
rigor.explanation: Points out that a procedural defence (no 'agree to disagree' at introduction) doesn't address the substantive concerns raised, a reasonable logical objection.

rigor.statement: If tradies, transport users, and ports are not involved in the pre-design of a plan, what is that definition of “Māori” in this part?

rigor.explanation: Grounds the drafting choice in legislative precedent, a relevant evidential basis for the conclusion of consistency.

rigor.explanation: Argues the provision is not novel because it mirrors existing practice; supported by the cited section comparisons, though it sidesteps the definitional point itself.

rigor.explanation: Identifies a logical inconsistency in the bill's definition of the CCO's scope and asks the Minister to resolve it.

rigor.statement: If we mean iwi, we should be saying iwi; if we mean Māori, it’s a very, very large number of people. As I said, roughly one in five New Zealanders, we are told, have some element of Māori whakapapa

charisma.explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement (Green MP crediting a National MP) that builds goodwill across the House.

charisma.statement: the invitation to join us in this bill is still there.
charisma.explanation: Open, inclusive invitation for others to come on board rather than an adversarial framing.

authenticity.statement: We don't believe in extra Government; we believe in limited Government. It is one of our values.
authenticity.explanation: States a party value consistent with the bill's deregulatory aim; no contradiction visible in the text, but unverified against the wider record.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we are very interested in developing more mining in this country because we need critical minerals to make the clean, green transition. That's what we've got in this country. We're going to continue to explore them and develop all our natural resources.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically how he justifies granting a prospecting permit in a UNESCO World Heritage Site, he gives a general pro-mining statement and never addresses the World Heritage point.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I know New Zealanders are not OK about is not having high-paying jobs in regional New Zealand and actually banning oil and gas and mining projects that ends up having Kiwis leave New Zealand to go to Australia to access those jobs in those sectors.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether New Zealanders are OK with trading off a World Heritage area for profit, he pivots entirely to jobs and the oil-and-gas ban rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Again, we will find the balance, but we are prioritising economic growth in this country. We are going to get things done, we're going to get this economy moving, and we're going to offer high-paying jobs to people in regional New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether his Government departed from the 2012 no-mining-in-World-Heritage commitment, he says 'find the balance' but never answers yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: Just remember, 30 percent of this country is in the Department of Conservation estate. We have very important national parks of very high environmental quality, and we'll continue to protect those, obviously.
