charisma.statement: I actually would like to thank the Minister for the generosity of the answers and the engagement that she provided through that committee of the whole House process. It was a very good backwards and forwards exchange.
charisma.explanation: Builds goodwill by crediting an opponent's conduct.

strength.statement: while my party, Te Pāti Māori, supports this bill, we will not let these issues fade. We will monitor implementation closely. We will push for stronger Māori representation. We will advocate for Te Tiriti - consistent planning, for the protection of Māori land and cultural sites, and for transparent reporting of Māori outcomes.
strength.explanation: Clear stated commitments to monitor and advocate, but these are future intentions with no delivery yet shown.

strength.statement: these changes that we're making today are real action after a long period of time of non-delivery. Aucklanders, at long last, are going to get back the power that they rightfully deserve in regards to planning and dealing with transport in their city.
strength.explanation: Claims real delivery via the bill's passage, which is concrete, but the 'power returned' benefit is yet to be realised in practice.

strength.statement: But look, at the end of the day, delivery is happening on this side.
strength.explanation: Asserts delivery in general terms without naming what was delivered.

strength.statement: After 16 long years, it restores democracy by ensuring that elected people are accountable for transport decisions. It ensures accountability by making sure that council is in charge of transport and that the council-controlled organisation is in charge of delivering public transport. It ensures local responsiveness by empowering local boards to make better and greater decisions on transport-related matters
strength.explanation: Describes what the bill does on enactment; concrete structural change but outcomes not yet delivered.

authenticity.statement: these changes that we're making today are real action after a long period of time of non-delivery. Aucklanders, at long last, are going to get back the power that they rightfully deserve in regards to planning and dealing with transport in their city.
authenticity.explanation: Frames passing the bill as fulfilling a promise; consistent with the Government's stated agenda, though delivery of outcomes is unproven.

authenticity.statement: Essentially, what this bill does is it strengthens the laws around anti - money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism. It does this by simplifying the system, by reducing red tape and unnecessary burdens on businesses—which is very important to us in the National Party—and still making sure that authorities are given better and practical tools to recognise risks and tackle crime.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the bill as expressing National's stated value of cutting business compliance costs, consistent with the party's positioning.

authenticity.statement: with this anti -money-laundering third reading that it exactly exemplifies what this Government is all about: reducing business compliance costs, improving regulatory effectiveness and efficiency, continuing regulatory compliance with related international obligations, and providing sufficient funding for the regulatory system, and, of course, one single supervisor.
authenticity.explanation: Ties the bill to the Government's consistent deregulatory agenda.

specificity.statement: Now what we see, in this amendment, is that the purpose is to enable use and development of that land. That is a huge change, and it is one that we are very much opposed to.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete change to the bill's purpose (enabling use and development) but no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: Giving effect to requires active protection, but what we see in the new section 4A is a bit of consultation, a bit of consideration, one or two reports, and that is it. That is not active protection.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific clause (section 4A) and characterises its mechanism, though without quoting wording.

specificity.statement: We had a very short select committee turn-around period and we did not have a regulatory impact statement.
specificity.explanation: Concrete procedural complaints (short turn-around, no RIS), though without dates here.

specificity.statement: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (businesses/charging tourists fund facilities) but no figures or detail on safeguards.

specificity.statement: Last weekend, on Sunday, on the way back from the dairy awards evening in Rotorua, I dropped into the Maungatautari sanctuary and had a look round. It’s just an amazing, amazing thing that’s happened there; the locals have done a lot of great work.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a named place and event but a general impression rather than detailed claims.

specificity.statement: It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill.
specificity.explanation: Vague characterisation with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
specificity.explanation: Names an alleged power but vaguely ('a heck of a lot of powers') without citing the clause.

specificity.statement: This bill is actually quite a small bill—it’s only eight pages long—it has the intention of facilitating the Government’s plan to combine the functions of a number of entities, with those entities being the Ministry for the Environment, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, the Ministry of Transport, and also the local government functions within the Department of Internal Affairs.
specificity.explanation: Names the page count and the precise entities being merged.

specificity.statement: One of the amendments that came from that was to strengthen the feedback from the Secretary for the Environment, who will hand the ultimate responsibility for this new ministry back to Parliament. We have inserted a new clause, and it’s requiring the secretary to report annually to ensure that he’s reporting on the performance of their function, as is required under the Environment Act.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete amendment—an annual reporting requirement on the Secretary.

specificity.statement: Here we have 588 submissions. Again, they are almost unanimous in saying we don’t want this.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact submission count and the direction of submitter sentiment.

specificity.statement: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
specificity.explanation: Names the domains (air, water, ocean, biodiversity) but not specific indicators or figures.

specificity.statement: Bronwyn Hayward from University of Canterbury has pointed out that the assurances in the Cabinet paper that say that stakeholders may fear environmental priorities will be diluted and these concerns are unfounded because other countries successfully integrate similar functions—she could find “no evidence of other countries that have successfully integrated such diverse oversight as Environment” with development and economic objectives. The only ones she could find were the Maldives and Kosovo, which have really unfortunate and concerning conflict of interest issues.
specificity.explanation: Names the expert, the comparison, and the only countervailing examples (Maldives, Kosovo).

specificity.statement: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
specificity.explanation: Exact durations for committee consideration and public hearings.

specificity.statement: The Secretary for the Environment will now be required to report annually on the performance of their Environment Act functions, and that report will sit inside a new ministry, which will be created and will report to this House.
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete annual-reporting mechanism and reporting line to the House.

specificity.statement: We believe that you can protect the environment while also making space for the beautiful humans of New Zealand that live within the environment. We need space for everybody.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational with no mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: But one of the New Zealand First’s election promises was to set up a ministry for infrastructure, absorbing the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and other infrastructure aspects. This is about integrated and spatial planning.
specificity.explanation: Names the promise and the entities to be absorbed, though without timeframe or detail.

specificity.statement: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
specificity.explanation: Names the duration, the courts, and the legal basis.

specificity.statement: They have even started subsidising the fossil fuel industry again: $200 million for the fossil fuel industry.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete dollar figure ($200 million).

specificity.statement: We will indeed be opposing this, and when we get back into Government, we’ll fix this righteous mess they have made.
specificity.explanation: No concrete plan—just a promise to fix the 'mess'.

specificity.statement: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
specificity.explanation: General claim with no mechanism for how development and protection coexist.

specificity.statement: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
specificity.explanation: Names the new ministry and a list of domains, but the 'will support' claims have no mechanism or evidence.

specificity.statement: I will point to the submission by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (PCE), Simon Upton... there is a “real risk with this ‘mega-ministry’ that the trade-offs will [now] be resolved within the organisation” by officials, whereas they should have been and should be elevated to ministerial decision-making where the accountability for those trade-offs will sit.
specificity.explanation: Names the PCE and the specific concern about internal vs ministerial resolution of trade-offs.

specificity.statement: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
specificity.explanation: Exact introduction/reading/submission dates, submission window, hearing time and submission count.

specificity.statement: With regard to clause 9, which replaces section 29 of the Act... It collapses the Ministry for the Environment into a single statutory office, with the Secretary for the Environment personally responsible to the Minister for all environmental functions... A ministry can push back. A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews and then their future roles, and so what we’re seeing here is a deliberate reduction in democratic oversight and accountability for our environment.
specificity.explanation: Cites clause 9/section 29 and the precise structural change.

specificity.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner of the Environment—a former National Party MP, and a man who was appointed to the role by Labour and reappointed by National—said, “For these reasons, the Ministry for the Environment should, in my view, be left out of this merger.”
specificity.explanation: Identifies the official, his background, and quotes his recommendation.

specificity.statement: It has reversed the ban on offshore oil and gas. It has excluded agriculture from the emissions trading scheme (ETS). It has ended the Clean Car Discount. It has gotten rid of the Climate Emergency Response Fund. It has weakened climate reporting... It has cancelled Auckland light rail. It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, itemised list of named policy decisions.

specificity.statement: It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles, such that a light electric vehicle pays exactly the same road-user charge as a 3.5 tonne ute.
specificity.explanation: Concrete comparison with a specific weight figure, even if the underlying claim is questionable.

specificity.statement: This bill is really quite simple. It’s about taking the environment ministry and putting it into another ministry. Nothing’s disappearing. There’s no drama. Cheer up; the sun is shining. I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: Characterises the bill only in the broadest terms, no detail.

specificity.statement: Report the news; don’t be the news. And, for the avoidance of doubt, the news should be the truth—the facts, not someone’s reckons. Everyone has an opinion; don’t mistake it for news.
specificity.explanation: A clear principle but a general exhortation rather than a concrete proposal.

civility.statement: Now what we see, in this amendment, is that the purpose is to enable use and development of that land. That is a huge change, and it is one that we are very much opposed to.
civility.explanation: Pointed disagreement focused on the policy content, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I am asking the members opposite: are they intending to go to Mitre Peak to attend a wine bar? Is this what this bill is about?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical, sensationalised framing that caricatures the bill rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: Giving effect to requires active protection, but what we see in the new section 4A is a bit of consultation, a bit of consideration, one or two reports, and that is it. That is not active protection.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the legal change without disparagement.

civility.statement: Shame on anybody across the aisle there who says that they are “blue-greens”, because this is diminishing every piece of the conservation estate and those settlements.
civility.explanation: 'Shame on' directed at members combined with the sweeping 'every piece' is accusatory and hyperbolic.

civility.statement: I don’t disagree that urban environments have environmental problems that need to be dealt with. Of course that’s an issue—of course it is—and so are our rural environments, as well. You can do both things.
civility.explanation: Respectful, concedes a fair point, no attack.

civility.statement: Disestablishing a Government department that is part of our environmental institutional infrastructure is not a simple thing, and I would remind those members to think about the people who are involved in these workplaces, as well.
civility.explanation: Rebuts the 'simple bill' framing while showing regard for affected officials; substance-focused.

civility.statement: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
civility.explanation: Argues the case without attacking opponents.

civility.statement: Last weekend, on Sunday, on the way back from the dairy awards evening in Rotorua, I dropped into the Maungatautari sanctuary and had a look round. It’s just an amazing, amazing thing that’s happened there; the locals have done a lot of great work.
civility.explanation: Warm, generous acknowledgement of community conservation work; no conflict.

civility.statement: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
civility.explanation: Largely substance-focused, though the 'wine bars in pristine areas' framing edges toward caricature.

civility.statement: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
civility.explanation: Critical but focused on process facts rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: This is an absolute travesty for New Zealand, and this Government should be absolutely ashamed of themselves.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic condemnation ('absolute travesty', 'should be ashamed') aimed at the Government collectively.

civility.statement: A logo on a door in Wellington does not clean a river, and a stand-alone ministry does not make a wetland.
civility.explanation: Pointed rhetoric but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Look, we know there were many submitters who were fearful and worried about the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, and fair enough—it is what we know. This is a bold change, and so we hear them.
civility.explanation: Respectful recognition of opposing concerns.

civility.statement: It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
civility.explanation: Critical but engages the framing of the issue, not persons.

civility.statement: It opens up the door for corporate exploiters. It makes sure there are no winners here. The only winners are those investors who this Government is well reputed for protecting. The loser here is the taiao. We do not support what the Government is intending to do with this bill. Shame on you.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive ('protecting investors', 'corporate exploiters') and ends with 'Shame on you'—accusatory.

civility.statement: This Government, in their one term, will go down in history as the most environmentally destructive Government of New Zealand. I doubt that any Government will be as bad and as anti-environment as this one.
civility.explanation: Sweeping condemnatory characterisation of the Government.

civility.statement: At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense.
civility.explanation: Sharp but argues against the policy and the chair's process, not her character.

civility.statement: This Government has no commitment to the environment.
civility.explanation: Sweeping opening attack on the Government's motives rather than a specific policy critique.

civility.statement: This bill is really quite simple. It’s about taking the environment ministry and putting it into another ministry. Nothing’s disappearing. There’s no drama. Cheer up; the sun is shining. I commend the bill to the House.
civility.explanation: Light and dismissive of the opposition's tone but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Report the news; don’t be the news. And, for the avoidance of doubt, the news should be the truth—the facts, not someone’s reckons. Everyone has an opinion; don’t mistake it for news.
civility.explanation: Pointed advice to media framed generally and good-naturedly ('love you as I do'), not a personal attack.

civility.statement: we members of Parliament need to be resilient. It’s a tough gig. It’s a lot tougher since social media, and the way in which some mainstream media have chosen to adopt social media standards.
civility.explanation: Reflective and measured; mild criticism of media standards without targeting individuals.

rigor.statement: I am asking the members opposite: are they intending to go to Mitre Peak to attend a wine bar? Is this what this bill is about?
rigor.explanation: Strawman/reductio—poses an extreme caricature (a wine bar at Mitre Peak) rather than reasoning from the bill's text.

rigor.statement: Giving effect to requires active protection, but what we see in the new section 4A is a bit of consultation, a bit of consideration, one or two reports, and that is it. That is not active protection.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned legal argument contrasting the 'give effect to' standard with the procedural steps in the new section.

rigor.statement: Shame on anybody across the aisle there who says that they are “blue-greens”, because this is diminishing every piece of the conservation estate and those settlements.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping generalisation ('every piece') asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Disestablishing a Government department that is part of our environmental institutional infrastructure is not a simple thing, and I would remind those members to think about the people who are involved in these workplaces, as well.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable counter to the minimisation argument, though more assertion than evidence.

rigor.statement: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
rigor.explanation: Has a clear means-ends logic (revenue funds facilities) but leans on a vivid anecdotal contrast rather than data.

rigor.statement: It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill.
rigor.explanation: Minimising interjection; asserts simplicity as a reason to dismiss concerns without supporting it.

rigor.statement: The bill will enable the department to use and develop “to the greatest extent”—what does that mean? It is very ambiguous.
rigor.explanation: Legitimately flags vague statutory wording, though stops at raising the question rather than analysing it.

rigor.statement: In fact, it’s mentioned that 50 percent of all international visitors will visit the conservation estate, and what’s wrong with charging them a reasonable amount to they can contribute to the conservation that we wish to deploy on to that land.
rigor.explanation: Uses a relevant statistic to support a user-pays argument; conclusion follows reasonably.

rigor.statement: One of the most often-made comments I get from international visitors who come and visit me is that they can’t believe how much free stuff there is in New Zealand, and this is one of them here.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote—personal impressions from visitors offered as support for the charging policy.

rigor.statement: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
rigor.explanation: The causal 'because they would not be in Government' is an unfalsifiable counterfactual presented as fact.

rigor.statement: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a named evidence source (MfE's own reporting) and the conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: Bronwyn Hayward from University of Canterbury has pointed out that the assurances in the Cabinet paper that say that stakeholders may fear environmental priorities will be diluted and these concerns are unfounded because other countries successfully integrate similar functions—she could find “no evidence of other countries that have successfully integrated such diverse oversight as Environment” with development and economic objectives. The only ones she could find were the Maldives and Kosovo, which have really unfortunate and concerning conflict of interest issues.
rigor.explanation: Cites a named academic and a specific evidentiary finding to rebut the Cabinet paper's claim.

rigor.statement: A logo on a door in Wellington does not clean a river, and a stand-alone ministry does not make a wetland.
rigor.explanation: Memorable but a false framing—reduces opponents to defending a 'logo on a door' rather than the ministry's actual functions.

rigor.statement: I just point you back to how successful the spatial planning in Auckland has been and how integrated that has been, and we need to respond to all of the regions of New Zealand in an integrated way.
rigor.explanation: Argues by analogy from Auckland amalgamation, asserting its success without evidence; the premise is contestable.

rigor.statement: It opens up the door for corporate exploiters. It makes sure there are no winners here. The only winners are those investors who this Government is well reputed for protecting. The loser here is the taiao. We do not support what the Government is intending to do with this bill. Shame on you.
rigor.explanation: Attributes motive and predicts outcomes without supporting evidence in the passage.

rigor.statement: They have allowed the expansion of dairying, Grant McCallum, in the Canterbury Plains, the primary cause of nitrate contamination, the primary cause of climate change.
rigor.explanation: Has an evidentiary basis on nitrates but the climate-change attribution is a loose, unsupported leap.

rigor.statement: I will point to the submission by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (PCE), Simon Upton... there is a “real risk with this ‘mega-ministry’ that the trade-offs will [now] be resolved within the organisation” by officials, whereas they should have been and should be elevated to ministerial decision-making where the accountability for those trade-offs will sit.
rigor.explanation: Builds on a named, authoritative submission and a clear mechanism (where trade-offs and accountability are resolved).

rigor.statement: I will speak to my experience when Labour was in Government and established the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, elevating it from an office that sat within the Department of Internal Affairs... so that independent policy advice pertaining to those matters would actually see the light of day and would not be subsumed in a mega-ministry. This bill is taking us in the opposite direction.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned analogy with a relevant precedent, though the parallel is asserted rather than fully demonstrated.

rigor.statement: With regard to clause 9, which replaces section 29 of the Act... It collapses the Ministry for the Environment into a single statutory office, with the Secretary for the Environment personally responsible to the Minister for all environmental functions... A ministry can push back. A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews and then their future roles, and so what we’re seeing here is a deliberate reduction in democratic oversight and accountability for our environment.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a specific clause to an institutional-independence consequence with a coherent chain (appointment/performance control over a secretary).

rigor.statement: This Government has no commitment to the environment.
rigor.explanation: Absolute generalisation asserted up front without qualification.

rigor.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner of the Environment—a former National Party MP, and a man who was appointed to the role by Labour and reappointed by National—said, “For these reasons, the Ministry for the Environment should, in my view, be left out of this merger.”
rigor.explanation: Marshals a cross-party authority (appointed by both major parties) to lend weight to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: It has reversed the ban on offshore oil and gas. It has excluded agriculture from the emissions trading scheme (ETS). It has ended the Clean Car Discount. It has gotten rid of the Climate Emergency Response Fund. It has weakened climate reporting... It has cancelled Auckland light rail. It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'walk-back on climate' thesis with a series of verifiable examples.

rigor.statement: This Government needs to remember that business is a subset of the environment, not the other way around. Business is a subset of the economy. It is a subset of the environment—the economy is a subset of the environment. We cannot work in business unless we have a livable world.
rigor.explanation: A coherent nested-dependency argument (economy depends on environment), though presented as axiom rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: This bill is really quite simple. It’s about taking the environment ministry and putting it into another ministry. Nothing’s disappearing. There’s no drama. Cheer up; the sun is shining. I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Minimises the change ('nothing's disappearing') by assertion, dismissing the substantive concerns raised without engaging them.

charisma.statement: I don’t disagree that urban environments have environmental problems that need to be dealt with. Of course that’s an issue—of course it is—and so are our rural environments, as well. You can do both things.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the validity of opponents' point about urban environments before making her own, a consensus-seeking move.

charisma.statement: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
charisma.explanation: Concedes common ground with the other side (charging tourists) before drawing a conditional line.

charisma.statement: We believe that you can protect the environment while also making space for the beautiful humans of New Zealand that live within the environment. We need space for everybody.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, warm framing ('space for everybody') seeking to reconcile development and protection.

charisma.statement: Look, we know there were many submitters who were fearful and worried about the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, and fair enough—it is what we know. This is a bold change, and so we hear them.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and validates opponents'/submitters' concerns rather than dismissing them—bridge-building tone.

charisma.statement: It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
charisma.explanation: Reframes the debate inclusively ('and, and' rather than 'either/or'), inviting a both-ways approach.

charisma.statement: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
charisma.explanation: Offers a both-things framing but mostly asserts her side's position rather than reaching across.

veracity.statement: We had a very short select committee turn-around period and we did not have a regulatory impact statement.
veracity.explanation: Factual process claim corroborated by other members; absence of a RIS is confirmed elsewhere in the debate.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister promised all New Zealanders that he would fix the cost of living, but nothing is getting better.
veracity.explanation: 'Nothing is getting better' is an absolute, unsupported characterisation; cost-of-living indicators are mixed, not uniformly static.

veracity.statement: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the bill as letting the Minister sell land 'as he sees fit', an overstatement of the discretionary powers as described.

veracity.statement: In fact, it’s mentioned that 50 percent of all international visitors will visit the conservation estate, and what’s wrong with charging them a reasonable amount to they can contribute to the conservation that we wish to deploy on to that land.
veracity.explanation: Roughly half of international visitors engaging with the conservation estate is broadly consistent with tourism/DOC figures.

veracity.statement: This bill is actually quite a small bill—it’s only eight pages long—it has the intention of facilitating the Government’s plan to combine the functions of a number of entities, with those entities being the Ministry for the Environment, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, the Ministry of Transport, and also the local government functions within the Department of Internal Affairs.
veracity.explanation: Factual description of the bill's length and scope, consistent with the rest of the debate.

veracity.statement: One of the amendments that came from that was to strengthen the feedback from the Secretary for the Environment, who will hand the ultimate responsibility for this new ministry back to Parliament. We have inserted a new clause, and it’s requiring the secretary to report annually to ensure that he’s reporting on the performance of their function, as is required under the Environment Act.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the annual-reporting amendment also referenced by Cameron Luxton.

veracity.statement: Here we have 588 submissions. Again, they are almost unanimous in saying we don’t want this.
veracity.explanation: The 588 figure is corroborated by Priyanca Radhakrishnan; the near-unanimity claim is supported by repeated accounts of submissions opposing the bill.

veracity.statement: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
veracity.explanation: The factual core—no party campaigned on disestablishing the ministry—is plausible and unrebutted, though hard to verify exhaustively.

veracity.statement: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
veracity.explanation: MfE environmental reporting does document declines across several domains, broadly supporting the claim.

veracity.statement: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
veracity.explanation: Precise process figures consistent with Radhakrishnan's 'less than three hours of hearings' account.

veracity.statement: The Secretary for the Environment will now be required to report annually on the performance of their Environment Act functions, and that report will sit inside a new ministry, which will be created and will report to this House.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reporting amendment described by National members.

veracity.statement: I just point you back to how successful the spatial planning in Auckland has been and how integrated that has been, and we need to respond to all of the regions of New Zealand in an integrated way.
veracity.explanation: The success of Auckland's spatial planning is a debated characterisation, not a settled fact.

veracity.statement: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
veracity.explanation: The seabed-mining litigation (Trans-Tasman Resources) did turn substantially on tikanga and Treaty considerations through to the Supreme Court.

veracity.statement: They have allowed the expansion of dairying, Grant McCallum, in the Canterbury Plains, the primary cause of nitrate contamination, the primary cause of climate change.
veracity.explanation: Dairy intensification is indeed a leading driver of nitrate contamination in Canterbury; calling it 'the primary cause of climate change' overstates and conflates issues.

veracity.statement: They have even started subsidising the fossil fuel industry again: $200 million for the fossil fuel industry.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a specific figure for fossil-fuel support; whether it constitutes a 'subsidy' is contested framing, so partly accurate at best.

veracity.statement: At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense.
veracity.explanation: NZ has one of the highest proportions of threatened species, but 'highest level in the world' is an overstatement of a contested ranking.

veracity.statement: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
veracity.explanation: Precise dates and figures consistent with other members' accounts of the truncated process.

veracity.statement: With regard to clause 9, which replaces section 29 of the Act... It collapses the Ministry for the Environment into a single statutory office, with the Secretary for the Environment personally responsible to the Minister for all environmental functions... A ministry can push back. A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews and then their future roles, and so what we’re seeing here is a deliberate reduction in democratic oversight and accountability for our environment.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the accountability difference between a ministry and a statutory office answering to the Minister, though 'deliberate' imputes intent.

veracity.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner of the Environment—a former National Party MP, and a man who was appointed to the role by Labour and reappointed by National—said, “For these reasons, the Ministry for the Environment should, in my view, be left out of this merger.”
veracity.explanation: Simon Upton is a former National MP appointed/reappointed across governments; the cited recommendation matches the PCE's stance referenced elsewhere.

veracity.statement: It has reversed the ban on offshore oil and gas. It has excluded agriculture from the emissions trading scheme (ETS). It has ended the Clean Car Discount. It has gotten rid of the Climate Emergency Response Fund. It has weakened climate reporting... It has cancelled Auckland light rail. It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Most items (offshore oil/gas reversal, ending Clean Car Discount, agriculture out of ETS, cancelling Auckland light rail, RUCs on EVs) match the public record; framing of a few is contestable.

veracity.statement: It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles, such that a light electric vehicle pays exactly the same road-user charge as a 3.5 tonne ute.
veracity.explanation: RUC rates are weight-banded, so a light EV and a 3.5-tonne ute would not generally pay 'exactly the same'—the comparison is misleading.

authenticity.statement: But one of the New Zealand First’s election promises was to set up a ministry for infrastructure, absorbing the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development and other infrastructure aspects. This is about integrated and spatial planning.
authenticity.explanation: Ties the current support to a stated NZ First election promise on integrated planning—words consistent with prior commitment.

authenticity.statement: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a long, consistent 15-year personal record of opposing seabed mining—words backed by a documented track record.

authenticity.statement: I will speak to my experience when Labour was in Government and established the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, elevating it from an office that sat within the Department of Internal Affairs... so that independent policy advice pertaining to those matters would actually see the light of day and would not be subsumed in a mega-ministry. This bill is taking us in the opposite direction.
authenticity.explanation: Draws on her own party's consistent prior action (elevating Ethnic Communities to a ministry) to ground today's opposition.

divination.statement: This Government, in their one term, will go down in history as the most environmentally destructive Government of New Zealand. I doubt that any Government will be as bad and as anti-environment as this one.
divination.explanation: A prediction about future historical judgment; superlative ('most destructive ever') is speculative and hard to substantiate against past governments.

strength.statement: We will indeed be opposing this, and when we get back into Government, we’ll fix this righteous mess they have made.
strength.explanation: Vague future commitment to 'fix' contingent on returning to government, with no mechanism or detail.

strength.statement: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
strength.explanation: Broad promise that one structural change will deliver across many areas, asserted rather than demonstrated.

charisma.statement: I'm proud of the impact this project is having on the infrastructure system—and those members know they're not allowed to say that—showing that you don't need to talk for years and years to get a good decision, when one is possible in just a matter of months.

charisma.statement: Some applicants have said to me that fast track is driving competition in the consenting system... in some cases, this is leading to more reasonable behaviour by councils, acting in a more proportionate way. Isn't competition a wonderful thing?

charisma.statement: Absolutely, and particularly the actions of that great Government Minister Judith Collins. I want to acknowledge her and her 24 years of service to this great country and this Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of a colleague's long service; warm but inward-facing.

charisma.statement: For too long, Government sent the wrong message to farmers that if you do the right thing and invest in preserving or creating wetlands and native bush, you'll be punished with more controls on what you can do on your own land. charisma.statement: I respect the significant responsibility that Ngāi Tahu has in its takiwā and the ongoing relationships and partnerships that it has with the Department of Conservation... charisma.statement: In my past life, I was an environmental lawyer, and I did act for a number of clients on trying to get concessions from the Department of Conservation, and it was very difficult... charisma.statement: Minister Potaka, of all people in this House, knows what is at stake here; knows what it takes to lead our people through settlement; knows what it means to persistently pester the Crown to do what it says it will do.

civility.statement: I'm proud of the impact this project is having on the infrastructure system—and those members know they're not allowed to say that—showing that you don't need to talk for years and years to get a good decision, when one is possible in just a matter of months.

civility.statement: Sorry, I didn't hear the question. I'm actually deaf in the left ear today, and I just would like to hear it again. It's such a good one.

civility.statement: I'm ignoring the OECD! OK. civility.statement: I want to ensure young New Zealanders are ready to take up those opportunities, unlike the other side who are happy to leave them there to rot.

civility.statement: Come on, Greta. Have your turn now. Greta, your turn.

civility.statement: I respect the significant responsibility that Ngāi Tahu has in its takiwā and the ongoing relationships and partnerships that it has with the Department of Conservation... civility.statement: I'm not aware that the member has insights into my diary, but what I am aware of is that I visited many villages right throughout this country, and there are many residents that are very, very comfortable and expressed to me that they are comfortable with the arrangements that they contracted after independent legal advice.
civility.explanation: Mild retort to the loaded 'has his ear' question, then pivots to substance.

civility.statement: In my past life, I was an environmental lawyer, and I did act for a number of clients on trying to get concessions from the Department of Conservation, and it was very difficult... There have been Ministers since back in the day of Eugenie Sage... who have been making that point—that there does need to be a change to this legislation; it needs some work.
civility.explanation: Substantive, acknowledges the other side's case before disagreeing.

civility.statement: But what this bill does is an entire paradigm shift. It's not what we're expecting when we hear speeches from the other side saying, 'Oh, this is just about efficiency and modernisation.' No—this is a paradigm shift.
civility.explanation: Engages the Government's characterisation of the bill rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: I stand today to raise the alarm on this coalition Government's ram raid of conservation in Aotearoa, on the inheritance of our mokopuna.
civility.explanation: 'Ram raid' is a sensational metaphor for the policy; vivid but inflammatory.

civility.statement: Minister Potaka, of all people in this House, knows what is at stake here; knows what it takes to lead our people through settlement; knows what it means to persistently pester the Crown to do what it says it will do.
civility.explanation: Pointed appeal to the Minister's record rather than a personal insult, though it implies inconsistency.

civility.statement: —in the disposals and swap process, and they are not unilateral, Priyanca Radhakrishnan... there is a process which is set out there and it's quite an extensive process... Labour is not interested in the submissions—it's already made its mind up—but I'm looking forward to the submissions and seeing what New Zealanders have to say.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance (the disposal process) but takes a jab imputing Labour has 'already made its mind up'.

forthrightness.statement: The projects are expected to create tens of thousands of jobs and inject billions into the economy. So far, over 8,000 new homes have been approved, about the size of Greymouth.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Cheung's question on expected economic impact with figures.

forthrightness.statement: The Ashbourne project was approved on 21 April: hundreds of news homes and two solar farms in the Waikato. On 1 May, the Pound Road Industrial Development was approved in Canterbury... Over $450 million is expected to be contributed to the economy. Then, on 7 May, also in Canterbury, the Ryans Road Industrial Development was also approved, enabling the development and subdivision of 126 industrial lots.
forthrightness.explanation: Concrete, on-topic update on further approvals.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely, and particularly the actions of that great Government Minister Judith Collins. I want to acknowledge her and her 24 years of service to this great country and this Parliament.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms he stands by the Government's statements and actions as asked.

forthrightness.statement: The Minister explained his comments well, and, actually, I'm quite confident that he did not at any time direct RNZ or TVNZ.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the broadcaster-direction point but sidesteps whether Seymour's conduct met his expectations of Ministers.

forthrightness.statement: The statements that we have made publicly are statements that I support, otherwise they wouldn't have been made.
forthrightness.explanation: Falls back on a generic talking point; never engages with why he expressed support a Minister called 'imprudent'.

forthrightness.statement: Sorry, I didn't hear the question. I'm actually deaf in the left ear today, and I just would like to hear it again. It's such a good one.
forthrightness.explanation: Pure deflection that avoids answering the question about Winston Peters.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first leg of the question: yes, I act in the national interest of New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers only the first clause and ignores why he won't act on Winston Peters as Willis reportedly urged.

forthrightness.statement: All we're doing is giving business confidence and clarity to continue to invest in New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address Swarbrick's question about urgency interfering with an active Supreme Court case; reframes to business confidence.

forthrightness.statement: We have a challenge within this country in making sure we've got abundant supply of electricity, and that's why this Government is doing everything it can to get renewables built and also make sure we've got gas, coal, and other things that we need as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not answer whether Government-owned gentailers should lower prices; pivots to supply.

forthrightness.statement: We expect the gentailers to be giving consumers a fair deal. That's why we are strengthening the Electricity Authority with new powers to make sure that they can increase fines and make sure companies play by the rules.
forthrightness.explanation: After a point of order, partially engages by stating an expectation and a measure, but still avoids the 'excessive profits' framing.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and the way trust is built is by delivering improved outcomes for Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms he stands by his trust-building words and offers his measure of trust.

forthrightness.statement: We think there's a problem with generic Treaty principle clauses. We want to create certainty and make sure that everyone is very clear about their specific roles and obligations to each other.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a rationale but does not engage with whether the changes are consistent with building trust with Māori as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Because we think there's a problem with generic Treaty principle clauses, because when they're open-ended, they create uncertainty and legal risk for everybody.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not say whether he read the cited officials' advice or why Cabinet proceeded against it; repeats a talking point.

forthrightness.statement: Again, we've talked about this before. In terms of the Treaty of Waitangi, article 1 deals with that issue very well.
forthrightness.explanation: Avoids a direct yes/no on whether iwi Māori ceded sovereignty by gesturing at article 1.

forthrightness.statement: Yesterday, I announced the Government's plan to support growth in New Zealand's voluntary nature markets by providing a light-touch assurance framework for private sector programmes. Voluntary nature markets enable private capital to fund projects that protect and restore nature—work such as wetland restoration, native planting, and habitat protection.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what he announced and explains it.

forthrightness.statement: I'll start with what the Government isn't doing in relation to voluntary nature markets: we won't be running a market, and we won't be forcing people into it through heavy-handed regulation. What we will do is offer Government recognition through two pathways: high-quality programmes accredited by reputable international bodies will be recognised by the Government; and domestic providers will be able to have their programmes assessed against market principles.
forthrightness.explanation: Clearly sets out the Government's role as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. We acknowledge that many Kiwis are finding things tough at the moment. That's why our Government's welfare reset is shifting the dial, driving policies to support job growth, to help more people into work.

forthrightness.statement: despite it being challenging, in the last year, we saw 84,000 New Zealanders leave welfare into work. That's why I'm confident that what we are doing is working.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, what we're really proud of is the welfare reset that is enabling—despite there being challenging times and more young people being affected through the jobseeker numbers—84,000 New Zealanders leaving welfare into work.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address the Apprenticeship Boost cut asked about; repeats the 84,000 line.

forthrightness.statement: Ongoing litigation in the High Court where civil claims have been made is creating uncertainty in business confidence in investment... forthrightness.statement: A tort is a claim brought in private law in situations where the conduct of one person causes harm or invades the interest of another person. forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear, direct explanation of the term as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Obviously, Ministers, members of Parliament, and officials engage with those companies on a regular basis. But, as has widely been counted, there is widespread concern across the business community around this decision, and that's where we were looking at it.
forthrightness.explanation: Avoids the specific question of whether he or officials engaged with the named companies being sued; gives a general answer.

forthrightness.statement: This decision does not change New Zealand's climate targets, nor the approach the Government has set for meeting them. Businesses will continue to be required to meet their obligations under the emissions trading scheme.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether existing obligations change—no.

forthrightness.statement: There are more people in work.
forthrightness.explanation: A direct, unqualified answer to a direct question.

forthrightness.statement: The member will hopefully have seen the Stats NZ result last week which showed unemployment falling, which is very positive news... forthrightness.explanation: Does not address the real-wage-growth question; restates the plan.

forthrightness.statement: In fact, what our Government did was rescue the Apprenticeship Boost scheme which the last Government left unfunded with a massive fiscal cliff. We rescued that programme, and I am certain that many Māori and Pasifika will have benefitted.
