rigor.statement: The 2024 ERO or Education Review Office report statistics speak for themselves: 70 percent of employers did not consider NCEA level 1 to be credible; 60 percent of teachers didn’t think it was a reliable measure of what students know and can do; half of parents and 40 percent of students don’t understand how the system works.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy rationale in cited survey evidence, though 'speak for themselves' leans on the data without further analysis.

rigor.statement: It was a standards-based qualification system that was designed to be flexible but, in actual fact, has led to the ability for students to game the system by pulling together random credits that don’t always form a cohesive package of learning or pathway into future study.
rigor.explanation: A plausible mechanism-based critique of credit-accumulation, but the 'gaming' claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: One retired teacher wrote to me to say, “I applaud your strategies and desire to elevate learning outcomes for students. I’m ashamed of the New Zealand Post Primary Teachers’ Association for wanting to choke your timely initiatives.”
rigor.explanation: Supports the policy via selected anecdote and appeal to authority (a principal, a teacher) rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: It’s 1 percent of the total population. It was around 1 percent; it blew out under the last Government to around 1.2 percent, and we’re now going down to about 1 percent. It is larger, in headcount terms, than where it was in 2017, but we’re accounting for population growth in that time. It’s a rough number, and it will take some time to get there
rigor.explanation: Offers a defined methodology (share of population) and acknowledges its roughness and population adjustment.

rigor.statement: there are three facile and fallacious statements and assertions in that member’s statement. Dealing with the last point, as has been extensively litigated, there are no tax breaks for tobacco companies advanced by the Budget... I note that members opposite were arguing on the weekend that bringing back the interest deductibility rules was not a tax increase, which is a little bit inconsistent with their argument today that that is a tax break for landlords.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine apparent inconsistency in the opposition's position on interest deductibility (cannot be both not-a-tax-increase to reverse and a tax break).

rigor.statement: The idea that increasing the size of the Public Service year on year is the answer to New Zealand’s economic problems is precisely the kind of mentality that got us into this mess in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a strawman (that the opposition believes ever-larger Public Service solves all problems) rather than the actual argument.

rigor.statement: We live in a market economy... In the private sector, people lose their jobs and go for new jobs every day of the week... That’s what living in a market economy means, and so, yes, there will be job changes in the Wellington Public Service
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasonable point about labour-market churn but uses it to sidestep the specific count requested.

rigor.statement: these liquidations are a direct result of an overcooked economy where we saw inflation up to 7.3 percent, food inflation up to over 12 percent, where we saw interest rates up—12 consecutive official cash rate increases.
rigor.explanation: Attributes liquidations directly to past conditions via correlation; cites figures but asserts the causation.

rigor.statement: So is the Government working on an energy strategy, as he said to me last week in this House, or was the energy strategy work programme cancelled by his Government, as our Official Information Act request shows, in March this year?
rigor.explanation: Builds a tight contradiction backed by documentary evidence (an OIA) against his prior statement.

rigor.statement: Why is it socialism to invest in renewable energy but not socialism to actively invest hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer funds into fossil-fuel production?
rigor.explanation: Exposes an inconsistency in applying the 'socialism' label selectively to public investment.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct affirmative answer to whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions, though the question is formulaic.

forthrightness.statement: when you increase Government spending by 84 percent, you drive up inflation to 32-year highs, interest rates go up 13 times, the economy slows down, and people lose their jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why 40,000 more are out of work under him; pivots to blaming the previous government's spending rather than addressing his own record.

forthrightness.statement: unemployment has dropped to 5.3 percent, as the member will be aware. That means there are more Kiwis in work, and total hours’ work has increased three quarters in a row.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the unemployment topic but reframes rather than addressing the '14-year high' premise directly.

forthrightness.statement: we have the City Rail Link project, we have major events funding coming, we have an Indian free-trade agreement coming on track. So we’ve got a lot of good things happening that will drive future growth and employment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Auckland unemployment doubled; lists future positives instead of addressing the doubling.

forthrightness.statement: It was utterly unacceptable to come into Government to find that 55 percent of our kids do not go to school regularly. Half our kids hitting high school are not at the standard they need to be at in reading and 80 percent are not at the standard they need to be in mathematics. I’d just ask the question: who was the previous Minister of Education?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 100,000 young NEET; pivots to school attendance/achievement stats and a jab rather than the NEET figure.

forthrightness.statement: Every dollar we have spent has been typically driving $3.20 back into the tourism and hospitality experience. Think about the State of Origin. Think about the changes we’ve made to Eden Park stadium. Think about the events that we’ve attracted to New Zealand, including the Raglan surf that’s going on this week. I hear it’s really good.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a 49% rise in hospitality liquidations; never addresses liquidations, lists events instead and trails into an aside.

forthrightness.statement: No. The New Zealand people voted to put the adults in charge and to turf the teenagers out.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'No' to the question, but the elaboration is a partisan jab rather than reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: We’re very interested in exploring all sorts of energy options for New Zealand. It’s an “and, and, and” strategy. We have a massive renewables boom under way. We need to make sure that we open up opportunities for oil and gas, and, of course, we are supporting fusion, which we think has got some long-term potential as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether he supports nuclear fission energy; answers about fusion and a general 'all options' line, avoiding the actual question (which prompts a point of order).

forthrightness.statement: The work that we have exploratorily supported is that work around fusion, and that, of course, is a new technology which we have some interest in here in Wellington.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked where radioactive waste would be stored and whether iwi were consulted; entirely avoids both by discussing fusion.

forthrightness.statement: I think we should be looking at all hydrogen options, whether it’s clean or orange, or whatever colour.
forthrightness.explanation: Broadly engages Peters' hydrogen question but gives no clear position on the ban point asked.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first leg of the question, no.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, unambiguous 'no' to whether he intends to introduce legislation to repeal the Nuclear Free Zone Act.

forthrightness.statement: what we’re not interested in doing is running up the Public Service from 47,000 to 65,000, with, I think, a 46 percent increase in support and admin roles, and only an 18 percent increase in front-line roles.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly engages the 'what is a front-line service' question by contrasting admin vs front-line growth, but does not actually define a front-line service as asked.

forthrightness.statement: excluded from the baseline savings exercises are the New Zealand Defence Force, the Police, the Ministry for Children Oranga Tamariki, Corrections, the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Education, the Government Communications Security Bureau, the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service, the Education Review Office, the Crown Law Office, the Ministry of Defence, the Serious Fraud Office, and parliamentary agencies.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly lists the excluded agencies, a concrete answer even if it sidesteps the specific service Davidson named.

forthrightness.statement: I look forward to that party’s support of the new National Party policy which is to abolish good character tests for all sexual offending.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he says to victims of violence after a prevention agency's closure; completely pivots to a separate policy and a partisan dig.

forthrightness.statement: We are continuing the previous Government’s work on the sexual violence plan. We want continuity there, but we also want to make sure that we get better return out of the money that we are spending.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages the question on the cost of sexual violence but reframes around value-for-money rather than the closure's impact.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, the Budget will be announced next week and the member will have to wait for that.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer about future front-line cuts; deferral to the Budget is legitimate but still leaves the question unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: we don’t do just strategies and bumper stickers and Post-it notes. That’s what ended the oil and gas ban. We get on, crack on, put the money in, make the investments, and get into action rather than just talk and waffle and more Post-it notes and more bumper stickers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the energy strategy work programme was cancelled (per an OIA); dodges with rhetoric about action vs strategies.

forthrightness.statement: We have an energy strategy. I’ve explained it to the member before, actually. We’re experiencing a massive renewables boom... Equally, we need to make sure we’ve got a strategic coal reserve, a strategy diesel reserve, and we’ve actually got options to explore with investors to discover more gas, as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asserts a strategy exists but does not address Swarbrick's evidence (OIA) that the work programme was cancelled.

forthrightness.statement: What we’re seeing in Auckland is the inevitable effect of years of high inflation and high interest rates under the last Government. The good news for Aucklanders is that inflation and interest rates are now under control under this Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Auckland is succeeding given doubled unemployment; deflects to blaming the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: As I’ve outlined, the key deliverable—which, on this side of House, is what we’re focused on: deliverables and outcomes, not slogans. The last side of the House had six years to deliver for Auckland, which it didn’t
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a 15,000 rise in young Aucklanders not in work/training; does not address the figure, pivots to a slogan-vs-delivery line.

forthrightness.statement: what I can guarantee, and as I’ve outlined already, is that on this side of the House we are focused on delivering economic growth for this country and for Auckland... the Auckland city deal included four areas of growth focus, including Drury, the city centre, Eden Park
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee real Budget relief; declines to guarantee and lists focus areas instead.

forthrightness.statement: It’s 1 percent of the total population. It was around 1 percent; it blew out under the last Government to around 1.2 percent, and we’re now going down to about 1 percent. It is larger, in headcount terms, than where it was in 2017, but we’re accounting for population growth in that time. It’s a rough number, and it will take some time to get there
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the 8,700 figure was derived without knowing which jobs go; gives a population-ratio rationale, a partial but honest answer that concedes it is 'a rough number'.

forthrightness.statement: the Government is focused on growing front-line roles in the Public Service to deliver better services for New Zealand taxpayers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the no-front-line-cuts promise applies to the 8,700 reduction; restates the front-line commitment without confirming whether it holds against the cut.

forthrightness.statement: We live in a market economy... In the private sector, people lose their jobs and go for new jobs every day of the week... That’s what living in a market economy means, and so, yes, there will be job changes in the Wellington Public Service
forthrightness.explanation: Eventually concedes there will be job changes/losses in Wellington, but reframes the zero-sum premise rather than answering 'how many'.

forthrightness.statement: I ask the member to put that question to the young and dynamic Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, because that is the Minister who gets the monthly update from the Companies Office
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many of 188 liquidations were small businesses; redirects to another Minister rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: That is why businesses and manufacturers are going to back this Government for its re-election, and it’s exactly why they will not return the last lot
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what immediate support is being provided to struggling businesses; pivots to campaign messaging without specifics.

charisma.statement: If the member actually cared about working New Zealanders, he’d support Resource Management Act reforms, support job-rich fast-track projects, support the repeal of the oil and gas ban, support council rate caps, support the income-tax thresholds, and I could go on and on and on.
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them appeal to his own side; no attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: No. The New Zealand people voted to put the adults in charge and to turf the teenagers out.
charisma.explanation: Divisive applause line aimed at his own side.

charisma.statement: we don’t do just strategies and bumper stickers and Post-it notes. That’s what ended the oil and gas ban. We get on, crack on, put the money in, make the investments, and get into action rather than just talk and waffle and more Post-it notes and more bumper stickers.
charisma.explanation: Energetic but purely combative, appealing to his own side.

charisma.statement: One retired teacher wrote to me to say, “I applaud your strategies and desire to elevate learning outcomes for students. I’m ashamed of the New Zealand Post Primary Teachers’ Association for wanting to choke your timely initiatives.”
charisma.explanation: Marshals supportive voices but in a one-sided way that does not engage critics' substance.

charisma.statement: The idea that Wellington is a Public Service town and only that is wrong and offensive.
charisma.explanation: Mounts a positive, somewhat inclusive defence of Wellington (Wētā, Xero, Sharesies) though framed combatively.

authenticity.statement: what we’re not interested in doing is running up the Public Service from 47,000 to 65,000, with, I think, a 46 percent increase in support and admin roles, and only an 18 percent increase in front-line roles.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to prioritise front-line delivery while the same exercise cuts services Davidson identifies as front-line; tension between stated value and the cuts.

authenticity.statement: the Government is focused on growing front-line roles in the Public Service to deliver better services for New Zealand taxpayers.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to be growing front-line roles while simultaneously announcing a large headcount reduction; tension between the two is unresolved in the answer.

civility.statement: Te Pāti Māori offers our congratulations to you, Mr Speaker-Elect, on your new role.
civility.explanation: A gracious, respectful congratulation to the incoming Speaker; pure courtesy with no attack.

civility.statement: I apologise for my colleague and co-leader of Te Pāti Māori; I didn’t know she was going to do that. It’s not very good for relations at the start of the year.
civility.explanation: Takes responsibility and apologises on behalf of a colleague to smooth relations — conciliatory rather than combative.

civility.statement: But just to say you and I have had a good relationship over the last three years, and I hope to maintain that, because my first experience of a Speaker here had me kicked out several times. The last Speaker had me suspended.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges a constructive past relationship and expresses hope to maintain it; the references to being ejected are stated matter-of-factly, not as an attack.

civility.statement: I’m looking forward to seeing what you and I can achieve together heading into the next three years.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cooperative tone toward an institutional counterpart.

civility.statement: But I agree, you’ve got a big job ahead of you.
civility.explanation: An agreeable, respectful acknowledgement of the Speaker's role; routine but courteous.

charisma.statement: Te Pāti Māori offers our congratulations to you, Mr Speaker-Elect, on your new role.
charisma.explanation: Warm, goodwill-building opener that extends an olive branch across the House.

charisma.statement: I apologise for my colleague and co-leader of Te Pāti Māori; I didn’t know she was going to do that. It’s not very good for relations at the start of the year.
charisma.explanation: An attempt to repair goodwill and preserve a working relationship, though it appeals mainly to maintaining decorum.

charisma.statement: But just to say you and I have had a good relationship over the last three years, and I hope to maintain that, because my first experience of a Speaker here had me kicked out several times. The last Speaker had me suspended.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building: contrasts past friction with a shared good relationship to set a cooperative tone.

charisma.statement: I’m looking forward to seeing what you and I can achieve together heading into the next three years.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, forward-looking framing of working together across the Chair — consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: We will continue to do that, and we hope that with your support you will allow tangata whenua to freely express themselves in our cultural identity here in Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal inviting the Speaker's support and framing cultural expression as something to be enabled together.

veracity.statement: But just to say you and I have had a good relationship over the last three years, and I hope to maintain that, because my first experience of a Speaker here had me kicked out several times. The last Speaker had me suspended.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that he was repeatedly ejected and previously suspended by a Speaker; consistent with the record of Waititi's clashes in the House (e.g. the 2021 tie/haka suspension).

veracity.statement: We have been really proud of the fact that we’ve been able to hear more te reo Māori in the House. We’ve been proud to be able to hear more waiata in the House and to hear a wairua Māori in this House.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that more te reo Māori and waiata are now heard in the House; broadly accurate as use of te reo in Parliament has increased, though 'more' is unquantified.

specificity.statement: We have been really proud of the fact that we’ve been able to hear more te reo Māori in the House. We’ve been proud to be able to hear more waiata in the House and to hear a wairua Māori in this House.
specificity.explanation: Conveys a real trend but with no figures, mechanism, or timeframe — a general statement of pride.

specificity.statement: We will continue to do that, and we hope that with your support you will allow tangata whenua to freely express themselves in our cultural identity here in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: An aspirational hope to 'freely express' cultural identity with no concrete mechanism or commitment.

strength.statement: We will continue to do that, and we hope that with your support you will allow tangata whenua to freely express themselves in our cultural identity here in Aotearoa.
strength.explanation: States intent to 'continue' but is a soft commitment dependent on the Speaker's goodwill, with no concrete action specified.

charisma.statement: I see the role very much as protection of members’ rights to speak freely in this House, and to go about their business across the country unimpeded.
charisma.explanation: Frames the Speaker's role as protecting all members' rights regardless of party — inclusive, even-handed language.

charisma.statement: I think that that is, unfortunately, the lot of a Speaker, but I’ll do my best to be fair and even across the House.
charisma.explanation: Commits to impartiality across all parties — unifying, reassuring to both sides.

charisma.statement: One of the most important roles of the Speaker is to protect the rights of the minority, and we find ourselves now in the minority in this House.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, acknowledges the Speaker's duty to both Government and Opposition without rancour.

charisma.statement: the Green Party wants to reiterate our commitment to work alongside you to ensure that this Parliament is a family-inclusive Parliament, that we protect our staff and treasure the work that they do, that this Parliament remains accessible, and that we honour our duty of care that we have to each other and in the discourse.
charisma.explanation: Collaborative, inclusive framing — offers to work alongside the Speaker and emphasises care for staff and accessibility.

charisma.statement: the ability of any member to be able to appeal to you to uphold the rules is sometimes the only protection that this Parliament and, ultimately, our democracy has. I would urge you to take the upholding of those Standing Orders as perhaps the most important thing you ultimately do.
charisma.explanation: Respectful direct disagreement with the Speaker-Elect's 'not absolute' view — persuasive and engaging the substance rather than attacking.

charisma.statement: there will be those who come here not to participate in the institution but attempt to make a theatrical point by undermining it. That may be the greatest challenge that you face.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that casts certain (implicitly identified) members as bad-faith, alienating rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: in a democracy where we’re one of only nine for last 100 and so years from 1854, which makes us a special, special country
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared national pride and the cross-House value of preserving democracy — unifying in tone.

specificity.statement: I see the role very much as protection of members’ rights to speak freely in this House, and to go about their business across the country unimpeded.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete functions (free speech, unimpeded movement) but no mechanisms or detail on how.

specificity.statement: I think that that is, unfortunately, the lot of a Speaker, but I’ll do my best to be fair and even across the House.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration ('do my best to be fair') with no concrete standard or mechanism.

specificity.statement: the Green Party wants to reiterate our commitment to work alongside you to ensure that this Parliament is a family-inclusive Parliament, that we protect our staff and treasure the work that they do, that this Parliament remains accessible, and that we honour our duty of care that we have to each other and in the discourse.
specificity.explanation: Lists several aims (inclusivity, staff protection, accessibility) but gives no concrete measures or mechanisms.

rigor.statement: Firstly, can I say that our Standing Orders really are just a guide for how this House works. They’re important and they give us a framework, but they’re not absolute.
rigor.explanation: A defensible interpretive position on the rules, but asserted rather than argued from evidence or precedent.

rigor.statement: One of the most important roles of the Speaker is to protect the rights of the minority, and we find ourselves now in the minority in this House.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point linking the Speaker's protective role to his party's situation, but stated as a premise rather than argued.

rigor.statement: the ability of any member to be able to appeal to you to uphold the rules is sometimes the only protection that this Parliament and, ultimately, our democracy has. I would urge you to take the upholding of those Standing Orders as perhaps the most important thing you ultimately do.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument from his own experience as a sole-MP party that rule enforcement protects minority members; conclusion follows, though largely anecdotal.

rigor.statement: an institution that has worked better to allow people to flourish in self-chosen ways up and down our country than perhaps any other institution imaginable
rigor.explanation: Grand claim resting on rhetorical superlative with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: when people know things are fair, they will behave themselves.
rigor.explanation: A plausible generalisation asserted without evidence — an appeal to common sense rather than a supported claim.

veracity.statement: This is, in fact, your 10th consecutive Parliament, resulting in 27 years of unbroken service, and that is quite simply a remarkable political career.
veracity.explanation: Brownlee was first elected in 1996; 1996–2023 is 27 years of continuous service — the figures are accurate.

veracity.statement: It’s the sixth time that I’ve been sworn in as a member of Parliament, but I can honestly say that every time still feels like a special occasion.
veracity.explanation: Hipkins entered Parliament in 2008; by the 2023 swearing-in this is consistent with six terms — a plausible, accurate self-claim.

veracity.statement: One of the most important roles of the Speaker is to protect the rights of the minority, and we find ourselves now in the minority in this House.
veracity.explanation: After the 2023 election Labour was in opposition; the claim of being in the minority is factually accurate.

veracity.statement: an institution that has worked better to allow people to flourish in self-chosen ways up and down our country than perhaps any other institution imaginable
veracity.explanation: Sweeping superlative ('any other institution imaginable') — hyperbolic and not verifiable.

veracity.statement: in a democracy where we’re one of only nine for last 100 and so years from 1854, which makes us a special, special country
veracity.explanation: A frequently cited claim that NZ is among a small number of continuously democratic states, but the exact count and 1854 baseline are imprecise and contestable.

civility.statement: there will be those who come here not to participate in the institution but attempt to make a theatrical point by undermining it. That may be the greatest challenge that you face.
civility.explanation: Impugns the motives of unnamed members as insincere 'theatrical' actors rather than engaging their conduct on substance.

veracity.statement: They have inherited a set of Government books that are on track to getting back into surplus.
veracity.explanation: At the time, forecast surpluses were repeatedly being pushed out and deficits persisted; the 'on track to surplus' framing was contested and arguably optimistic.

veracity.statement: it was never in recession, despite the fact that the new Prime Minister went up and down the country preaching doom and gloom.
veracity.explanation: Stats NZ data at the time indicated a technical recession (two negative quarters) around late 2022; 'never in recession' overstates the case.

veracity.statement: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
veracity.explanation: Employment rate near record highs and large net job growth over 2017–2023 are broadly consistent with official HLFS data.

veracity.statement: we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders
veracity.explanation: The abolition occurred; the 3 million figure is plausible though uptake counts are hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: 13,000 new public homes under our Government since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Net public housing additions of this order are broadly supported; 'new' figures depend on gross vs net counting.

veracity.statement: 1,800 extra police on the beat under our Government
veracity.explanation: Net police growth of around this scale is broadly consistent with the record, though 'on the beat' framing is generous.

veracity.statement: When we became the Government in 2017, just 2 percent of the cars coming into the market were electric or hybrid vehicles. As we leave office, that is 37 percent—a huge improvement.
veracity.explanation: Direction is correct — EV/hybrid market share rose sharply, partly driven by the clean car rebate; exact end figure is plausible.

veracity.statement: emissions in New Zealand falling for three years in a row
veracity.explanation: Gross emissions did decline over recent years, but attribution to specific policies and the 'three years' precision is harder to verify.

veracity.statement: over the past six years violent crime went up 33 percent; serious assaults went up—I think it doubled; gang membership went up over 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Gang membership and violent-crime increases are directionally supported by Police data; 'I think it doubled' is hedged and the figures are selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Why me? Why did I survive when I was the Minister of Finance who delivered food price inflation of 28 percent—28 percent, faster than at any time since the 1980s
veracity.explanation: Annual food-price inflation peaked around 12%; a '28 percent' figure (likely cumulative over the term) presented as if a single rate is misleading.

veracity.statement: You tripled mortgage interest rates, you crippled family budgets
veracity.explanation: Mortgage rates roughly tripled from pandemic lows to ~7%, but attributing this solely to the government ignores global rates and RBNZ independence.

veracity.statement: Around 40 percent of our kids are not attending school regularly. That is startling and shameful—absolutely shameful.
veracity.explanation: Regular-attendance rates had fallen to around half, so the order of magnitude is broadly defensible depending on definition and term.

veracity.statement: in reading, maths, and science New Zealand has slid even further, and in all three of those subject areas, our results are the worst that they've ever been.
veracity.explanation: NZ's PISA scores did decline to record lows in that cycle, so directionally accurate, though long-run comparability has caveats.

veracity.statement: Simeon Brown has already instructed officials to stop work on the ridiculous $16 billion Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme.
veracity.explanation: The new government did move to stop the scheme; the '$16 billion' figure reflects upper-end cost estimates.

veracity.statement: retail crime has been impacted by an incredible 92 percent. It's cost us actually $2.6 billion extra, and we're all now paying for that crime with higher, higher prices and more inflation.
veracity.explanation: The '92 percent' and '$2.6 billion' figures are vaguely sourced and the causal chain to inflation is asserted rather than demonstrated.

veracity.statement: It is the single-greatest honour of my life to be standing here as part of the largest Green Party caucus ever.
veracity.explanation: The 2023 Green caucus was indeed the party's largest — an accurate, checkable claim.

veracity.statement: the Greens have now not once but twice grown our support after being in a Government arrangement—unheard of. This is an achievement that is unheard of anywhere in the world
veracity.explanation: The NZ Greens did grow support in 2020 and 2023, but 'unheard of anywhere in the world' is sweeping hyperbole that is not established.

specificity.statement: They have inherited a set of Government books that are on track to getting back into surplus.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at fiscal position but gives no figures, dates, or surplus magnitude.

specificity.statement: When Māori thrive, all New Zealanders will thrive.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism, measure, or policy detail.

specificity.statement: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise rate (69.8%) and a job figure (281,000).

specificity.statement: we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a quantified result (3 million prescriptions).

specificity.statement: 13,000 new public homes under our Government since 2017.
specificity.explanation: Specific count and timeframe.

specificity.statement: 1,800 extra police on the beat under our Government
specificity.explanation: Specific headcount figure.

specificity.statement: When we became the Government in 2017, just 2 percent of the cars coming into the market were electric or hybrid vehicles. As we leave office, that is 37 percent—a huge improvement.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages and a clear before/after comparison.

specificity.statement: emissions in New Zealand falling for three years in a row
specificity.explanation: Gives a direction and timeframe but no magnitude or sectoral detail.

specificity.statement: over the past six years violent crime went up 33 percent; serious assaults went up—I think it doubled; gang membership went up over 70 percent.
specificity.explanation: Several concrete percentages, though one is qualified with uncertainty.

specificity.statement: Why me? Why did I survive when I was the Minister of Finance who delivered food price inflation of 28 percent—28 percent, faster than at any time since the 1980s

specificity.statement: the Greens have now not once but twice grown our support after being in a Government arrangement—unheard of. This is an achievement that is unheard of anywhere in the world

civility.explanation: Strong condemnation ('disgraceful') but directed at a policy idea, not a person.

civility.statement: Across the House, I genuinely want to congratulate every new MP on your election to Parliament and I urge you to use your time here well.
civility.explanation: Gracious, cross-party acknowledgement of opponents and colleagues alike.

civility.statement: he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn't just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he's caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn't actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people
civility.explanation: Extended personal attack comparing the opponent to a criminal arsonist — pure character attack, not policy.

civility.statement: we heard from a bitter and a twisted and a negative Chris Hipkins, the one we saw during the campaign over there.
civility.explanation: Direct personal insult ('bitter', 'twisted', 'negative') aimed at character rather than argument.

civility.statement: Why me? Why did I survive when I was the Minister of Finance who delivered food price inflation of 28 percent—28 percent, faster than at any time since the 1980s
civility.explanation: Sarcastic, mocking framing ('Why me?') putting words in an opponent's mouth.

civility.statement: To be strong, a democracy relies on fair and honest debate. ... We owe it to everyone to create a safe space for public debate.
civility.explanation: An appeal to constructive, respectful debate and shared democratic standards.

civility.statement: The leaders of our two biggest parties spent more time telling you who not to vote for, trying to scare people with how things will be under the other lot than they spent time talking about how we build the beautiful future our mokopuna deserve.
civility.explanation: Criticises opponents' campaign conduct but on the substance of their messaging rather than via personal insult.

divination.statement: by this time next year, inflation will be back to the 1 to 3 percent target range.
divination.explanation: A one-year forecast consistent with RBNZ projections at the time; inflation did in fact return to the 1–3% band by late 2024, so a well-founded prediction.

divination.statement: absolutely resolved that for the first time in New Zealand's history, this will be a one-term National Government.
divination.explanation: A multi-year electoral prediction that is highly uncertain and self-interested; no evidential basis beyond aspiration at the time.

charisma.statement: When Māori thrive, all New Zealanders will thrive.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unity-seeking framing that invites a shared interest rather than dividing along ethnic lines.

charisma.statement: as an Opposition and as a future Government, we will seek to bring New Zealanders together, not drive a wedge between Kiwis.
charisma.explanation: Explicit unity message, though framed in contrast to opponents rather than reaching across to them.

charisma.statement: Across the House, I genuinely want to congratulate every new MP on your election to Parliament and I urge you to use your time here well.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, magnanimous tone that reaches across the House.

charisma.statement: the pledge of the coalition Government is that whether you voted for us or not, we will govern for you.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to all voters, signalling intent to govern beyond the base.

charisma.statement: he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn't just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he's caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn't actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing demolition of an opponent; divisive rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Just like there are laws of nature and there are laws of physics, there are laws of politics. Because if you want lower tax, you vote for us.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically punchy but appeals only to supporters.

charisma.statement: To be strong, a democracy relies on fair and honest debate. ... We owe it to everyone to create a safe space for public debate.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying framing that invites the whole House to a common standard.

charisma.statement: The leaders of our two biggest parties spent more time telling you who not to vote for, trying to scare people with how things will be under the other lot than they spent time talking about how we build the beautiful future our mokopuna deserve.
charisma.explanation: Contrasts a hopeful vision against rivals, but the framing still draws an us-vs-them line between the Greens and the big parties.

authenticity.statement: as an Opposition and as a future Government, we will seek to bring New Zealanders together, not drive a wedge between Kiwis.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between the stated unity pledge and the highly combative, attack-heavy speech in which it is delivered.

rigor.statement: the adoption of COVID-19 conspiracy theories as apparent Government policy.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts a policy position as endorsement of conspiracy theories without establishing that link.

rigor.statement: he is actually like an arsonist who, having thrown an accelerant all over the joint and lit the place up, he doesn't just slink off, actually leaving the scene, realising he's caused a huge amount of damage, he doesn't actually fess up, put his hand up, apologise to the New Zealand people
rigor.explanation: Argument by emotive analogy/ad hominem rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Just like there are laws of nature and there are laws of physics, there are laws of politics. Because if you want lower tax, you vote for us.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: dressing partisan claims as inviolable 'laws' like physics, with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: retail crime has been impacted by an incredible 92 percent. It's cost us actually $2.6 billion extra, and we're all now paying for that crime with higher, higher prices and more inflation.
rigor.explanation: Links retail crime to general inflation without establishing the mechanism — a weak causal leap.

strength.statement: We have the highest rate of Kiwis in jobs, with a 69.8 percent employment rate, having created 281,000 new jobs during our time in Government.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivered labour-market outcomes, though jobs growth is only partly attributable to government action.

strength.statement: we abolished prescription charges, which resulted in 3 million free prescriptions for New Zealanders
strength.explanation: A concrete, enacted policy (the $5 charge was removed) with delivered uptake — clear follow-through.

strength.statement: 13,000 new public homes under our Government since 2017.
strength.explanation: Substantial delivered public-housing build, a concrete result over the term.

strength.statement: 1,800 extra police on the beat under our Government
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a recruitment commitment; figure roughly matches the term's net police increase.

strength.statement: Simeon Brown has already instructed officials to stop work on the ridiculous $16 billion Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete early action taken (work halted), a delivered decision rather than mere intent.

strength.statement: we're committed to training no fewer than 500 new front-line police officers in our first two years.
strength.explanation: A firm commitment but stated at the outset with no delivery yet to assess.

strength.statement: We're going to get going on infrastructure, including 13 new roads of national significance and public transport projects that actually get progressed, not just talked and talked and talked about by consultants.
strength.explanation: An announced programme with no delivery yet; follow-through unproven at this stage.

charisma.statement: Mate ururoa mō Niu Tireni, mō Aotearoa New Zealand, mō ngā tāngata katoa.
charisma.explanation: A call to strive 'like a thresher shark' for New Zealand and all its people — inclusive, nation-wide framing that invites everyone in rather than rallying one side against another.

charisma.statement: This is a special place, one which bestows upon us the power to make the laws of our land and exert great control over the people. Please use that power lightly and infrequently.
charisma.explanation: Addressed to the whole House regardless of party; a unifying, restraint-focused appeal that invites shared norms rather than dividing.

charisma.statement: Members opposite do not own Māori. Members opposite do not own the poor. Members opposite do not own the workers. No party and no ideology has a right to claim ownership over anything or anyone.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective and broadens claim to all parties, but the repeated 'members opposite' framing is a partisan rebuttal that appeals chiefly to his own side.

charisma.statement: This is why we are all here: to debate freely; to have an open, robust contest of ideas; to challenge one another in an environment where disputes are resolved by the showing of hands and not by the throwing of fists.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive ('we are all here'), celebrates contest of ideas across the House, and frames Parliament as common ground — bridge-building.

charisma.statement: We can only judge someone on who they are today compared to who they were yesterday.
charisma.explanation: A generous, inclusive principle about forgiveness and growth that invites a shared standard rather than division.

charisma.statement: I started the way I wished to continue, being positive, approachable, connected, and always taking the high road.
charisma.explanation: Emphasis on being positive and approachable signals an inclusive, consensus-oriented style.

charisma.statement: I am here today as the representative of the Napier electorate. For Napier City and Matawai, for rural and urban, for employer and employee, for landlord and tenant—for every person, no matter how they cast their vote.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately inclusive — pairs opposing groups and commits to represent all constituents regardless of vote; strongly consensus-building.

charisma.statement: While I have spent the last 15 minutes talking, I will spend the rest of my career listening, advocating, and delivering, because the Nimon family motto states “I show, not boast”.
charisma.explanation: Humble, listening-oriented framing that lands well across the House.

charisma.statement: I don’t think I have ever seen anything quite as pathetic as the incoming Prime Minister literally sprinting out the door of Parliament to fly back to Auckland because he had been summoned by Winston Peters
charisma.explanation: A combative applause line for his own side; mocks an opponent rather than persuading the undecided.

charisma.statement: On a serious note, though, I respect the fact that New Zealanders at this last election voted for change.
charisma.explanation: Bridging tone that accepts the result and reaches beyond his base, even while disputing the detail.

charisma.statement: I do want to welcome one change, and I want to congratulate New Zealand First for the change, and that is the reversal of National’s policy to allow foreign homebuyers back into the New Zealand housing market.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit a coalition party for a policy reversal — genuine cross-party acknowledgement of a point on which they agree.

specificity.statement: What we’re proposing to do is reinstate every item of business from the last Parliament so that Ministers—and members, actually, for that matter—can have a good opportunity to look at what they may wish to proceed with and items that they may wish to discharge. I think that’s the appropriate constitutional thing to do.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (reinstating all prior business, then prioritising/discharging) but no detail on which items or timeframe.

specificity.statement: she’s now been here for nine years, entering her fourth term as the member of Parliament for Taranaki-King Country.
specificity.explanation: Concrete tenure, term count, and named electorate.

specificity.statement: If we invest thousands in supporting the first thousand days of a child’s life, we can save millions in long-term costs that stem from poor health and poor education.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target (first thousand days) and direction of spend/save, but no figures or mechanisms for delivery.

specificity.statement: If we are sensible with the rules and the regulations that we put in place about who can work in our education and health systems, for example, by allowing those who train in CANZUK countries—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to work here as a right, we will save millions in costs associated with burnout and the constant under-resourcing of those sectors.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (automatic work rights for CANZUK-trained staff) and the sectors affected, though no dollar figures or timeline.

specificity.statement: I am the representative of Napier City, yes, but also the Wairoa District and parts of the Hastings and Gisborne districts. Every township and settlement is equally important to me and I commit to staying connected to all 9,482.6 square kilometres of it.
specificity.explanation: Names the constituent districts and a precise area figure to the decimal; concrete, though the 'staying connected' commitment lacks mechanism.

specificity.statement: You can’t spend your way out of every problem, nor can you regulate your way out of it. All you get is debt and dependency.

specificity.statement: and expects, over the next three years, to see action on the cost of living pressure Kiwi families are facing, with inflation falling faster than Treasury’s pre-election projections, interest rates falling, real incomes continuing to grow, near record-low unemployment being sustained, the Government’s books being returned to surplus at least as quickly as previously forecast, the number of affordable homes built increased, all those on State house waiting lists being accommodated, significant reductions in crime, climate emissions continuing to decline, school attendance materially improving, rates of literacy and numeracy amongst 15-year-olds improving, and material improvements in the overall living standards of all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Sets out an explicit, itemised list of measurable benchmarks (inflation vs Treasury forecast, surplus timing, waiting lists, literacy/numeracy etc.) against which to judge the Government.

specificity.statement: Mega landlords, around 300 of whom stand to get over a million dollars in tax cuts each under this incoming Government, actually get their tax cuts brought forward

specificity.statement: $250 a fortnight is what National promised the average working family—$250 a fortnight—and not “up to”. ... But then we discovered late in the campaign that actually there were only about 3,000 families that were going to benefit from that
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact dollar figure and the number of families benefiting.

rigor.statement: What we’re proposing to do is reinstate every item of business from the last Parliament so that Ministers—and members, actually, for that matter—can have a good opportunity to look at what they may wish to proceed with and items that they may wish to discharge. I think that’s the appropriate constitutional thing to do.

rigor.statement: If we invest thousands in supporting the first thousand days of a child’s life, we can save millions in long-term costs that stem from poor health and poor education.

rigor.statement: If we are sensible with the rules and the regulations that we put in place about who can work in our education and health systems, for example, by allowing those who train in CANZUK countries—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to work here as a right, we will save millions in costs associated with burnout and the constant under-resourcing of those sectors.
rigor.explanation: Coherent supply-side argument linking recognition of overseas training to staffing relief, but the cost-saving conclusion outruns the evidence offered.

rigor.statement: It’s not the State that saved my family; it was my mum. She took responsibility for our situation.

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, the more involved a Government becomes in people’s business, and businesses, for that matter, the worse things seem to get.

rigor.statement: You can’t spend your way out of every problem, nor can you regulate your way out of it. All you get is debt and dependency.

rigor.statement: There is a reason that the Government are now so desperately thrashing around trying to blame the outgoing Government for everything they possibly can—because their numbers didn’t add up before the election and they certainly don’t add up after the coalition negotiations.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the numbers 'don't add up' as a conclusion without presenting the costing detail in this passage; relies on characterisation.

veracity.statement: she’s now been here for nine years, entering her fourth term as the member of Parliament for Taranaki-King Country.
veracity.explanation: Kuriger entered Parliament in 2014, making 2023 her fourth term (2014, 2017, 2020, 2023) and roughly nine years — accurate.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, the more involved a Government becomes in people’s business, and businesses, for that matter, the worse things seem to get.
veracity.explanation: Broad, unfalsifiable-as-stated generalisation ('the worse things seem to get') that overstates a contested correlation as a rule.

veracity.statement: It is unjust to prioritise the niceties of urban Wellington and Auckland when the locals of Tiniroto and Ruakituri are still taking a two-hour detour because the roads have been closed for nearly 10 months.
veracity.explanation: The Cyclone Gabrielle road closures (from mid-February 2023) leaving rural detours by December is broadly accurate; specific locality detail supports it, though 'nearly 10 months' and exact detour length are not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: Mega landlords, around 300 of whom stand to get over a million dollars in tax cuts each under this incoming Government, actually get their tax cuts brought forward
veracity.explanation: Draws on Labour's contested costing of restoring interest deductibility; the 'around 300 getting over a million each' figure is a disputed political estimate presented as established fact.

veracity.statement: $250 a fortnight is what National promised the average working family—$250 a fortnight—and not “up to”. ... But then we discovered late in the campaign that actually there were only about 3,000 families that were going to benefit from that
veracity.explanation: Substantially accurate: National's headline $250-a-fortnight figure applied only to a small subset of families (the much-publicised ~3,000), though framing it as a flat promise rather than a maximum slightly overstates the deception.

civility.explanation: Explicitly elevates reasoned disagreement over conflict; respectful of opponents and institution.

civility.statement: It is unjust to prioritise the niceties of urban Wellington and Auckland when the locals of Tiniroto and Ruakituri are still taking a two-hour detour because the roads have been closed for nearly 10 months.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of governmental priorities framed as injustice, but aimed at policy/allocation rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: what we heard was a plan to take New Zealand backwards—repeated use of words like “stop”, “repeal”, “replace”, “reverse”, and “disestablish”—a plan to go backwards, not a plan to take New Zealand forward.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's programme but engages with the content of the speech rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: a Government that has chosen to prioritise the tobacco lobby over the health and wellbeing of young New Zealanders; a Government that has chosen to prioritise oil and gas companies over our environment; a Government that has chosen to prioritise millionaires instead of salary and wage workers; a Government that has chosen to accept conspiracy theories instead of policy-based facts, evidence, and science.
civility.explanation: A string of 'prioritise X over you' framings that impute bad motives; uses loaded characterisation ('conspiracy theories') that borders on strawman rather than engaging the policies' stated rationale.

civility.statement: I don’t think I have ever seen anything quite as pathetic as the incoming Prime Minister literally sprinting out the door of Parliament to fly back to Auckland because he had been summoned by Winston Peters
civility.explanation: Direct personal ridicule ('pathetic') of the Prime Minister's character/conduct rather than criticism of a policy.

civility.statement: On a serious note, though, I respect the fact that New Zealanders at this last election voted for change.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the electoral verdict against his own party; concedes legitimacy of opponents' mandate.

civility.statement: I do want to welcome one change, and I want to congratulate New Zealand First for the change, and that is the reversal of National’s policy to allow foreign homebuyers back into the New Zealand housing market.
civility.explanation: Gracious, substance-focused, congratulates an opponent rather than attacking.

civility.statement: But what I think New Zealanders will be shocked by is what they have replaced it with: the idea that more young New Zealanders should take up smoking in order to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible.
civility.explanation: Casts the policy as deliberately wanting youth to smoke — a heightened, motive-imputing characterisation that strawmans the Government's stated fiscal rationale.

civility.statement: There is a reason that the Government are now so desperately thrashing around trying to blame the outgoing Government for everything they possibly can—because their numbers didn’t add up before the election and they certainly don’t add up after the coalition negotiations.
civility.explanation: Mocking imagery ('desperately thrashing around') but the substantive charge concerns the costings/fiscal credibility rather than personal character.

divination.statement: If we invest thousands in supporting the first thousand days of a child’s life, we can save millions in long-term costs that stem from poor health and poor education.
divination.explanation: Conditional long-run prediction of fiscal savings; directionally supported by early-childhood evidence but magnitude and timeframe uncertain.

divination.statement: If we are sensible with the rules and the regulations that we put in place about who can work in our education and health systems, for example, by allowing those who train in CANZUK countries—Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to work here as a right, we will save millions in costs associated with burnout and the constant under-resourcing of those sectors.
divination.explanation: Predicts savings and reduced burnout; plausible but the 'save millions' outcome is asserted and depends on uptake and recognition standards.

divination.statement: Tax cuts that aren’t properly funded and the catalogue of spending commitments that we’ve seen in the coalition agreement are more likely to stoke inflation than see inflation coming backwards.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the fiscal package will be inflationary; directionally arguable but contested — the inflation effect of the mix of cuts and spending is genuinely uncertain.

authenticity.statement: It’s not the State that saved my family; it was my mum. She took responsibility for our situation.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the limited-government, individual-responsibility worldview he advances throughout; the personal account aligns with the stated value.

authenticity.statement: I started the way I wished to continue, being positive, approachable, connected, and always taking the high road.
authenticity.explanation: Self-description of a consistent approach; plausible and matches her conciliatory 'bridge' framing, but a self-claim with no external record yet to verify.

strength.statement: Much faith has been placed in me by many people. I intend to work hard to repay that faith—flaws and all.

strength.statement: While I have spent the last 15 minutes talking, I will spend the rest of my career listening, advocating, and delivering, because the Nimon family motto states “I show, not boast”.
strength.explanation: Commitment to 'delivering' but entirely forward-looking and aspirational, with no record yet — announcement of intent, not demonstrated follow-through.

civility.statement: We're not going to have a French Polynesian name that's an insult to everybody in the South Island.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the name Aotearoa as an 'insult' in a sneering, inflammatory way rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: If we'd not got back, these three parties, we were heading off to be Venezuela or Myanmar.

civility.statement: Who settled the central North Island Tribes' 14-iwi settlement? Who settled that? The Māori Wardens—who gave them their start? civility.explanation: Legitimate record contrast undercut by the dismissive 'all talk and no action' jab at opponents.

civility.statement: you can put the tā moko on and dance around and carry on in a way that we find very strange because where I come from, that's conferred upon you; you don't just paint yourself like some tattoo shop.
civility.explanation: Personal, mocking attack on another MP's cultural practice and authenticity rather than any policy substance.

civility.statement: may I remind Winston: you only won five seats; we won six.
