It’s certainly true that there was not a statutory requirement for the Government of the day to respond to Productivity Commission reports, and I agree with him: had there been, perhaps the reports might have got a little bit more coverage and attention.
rigor.explanation: Concedes a genuine structural point (no statutory requirement to respond) and reasons from it.

rigor.statement: On the other hand, James Shaw was a Minister in a Government for six years—in fact, many of the people who have spoken tonight had six years to do exactly that thing. I thank them for making the contribution now, but it’s about six years too late.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque-flavoured point, but grounded in the factual observation that critics held office for six years without making the fix they now demand.

rigor.statement: let me be clear: one of the things I intend to do in this Government as the Minister for Regulation is make sure that regulatory impact analysis is focused on regulation that actually puts restrictions on the use and exchange of private property. There is no need to do regulatory impact analysis on the Government deciding it’s no longer going to operate and spend money on a department
rigor.explanation: Provides a principled rationale for why no RIS is needed to close a department, directly answering Verrall's challenge.

charisma.statement: But if that’s what Mr Seymour thinks, there’s a really simple way of dealing with that: change the commissioners, and then carry on with the Productivity Commission.
charisma.explanation: Constructive suggestion but framed to expose the opponent rather than build common ground.

charisma.statement: surely, improving productivity to drive prosperity for all New Zealanders would be something everyone could agree on.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to shared goals across the House, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I have been listening very carefully, and I’ve got to say that if a competent Opposition is essential to democracy, then our country is in big, big trouble.
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them put-down that rallies his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I have to thank James Shaw for a much more constructive contribution. It’s certainly true that any policy can be improved over time. It’s certainly true that there was not a statutory requirement for the Government of the day to respond to Productivity Commission reports, and I agree with him: had there been, perhaps the reports might have got a little bit more coverage and attention.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges an opponent's valid points and finds common ground; bridge-building across the aisle.

strength.statement: let me be clear: one of the things I intend to do in this Government as the Minister for Regulation is make sure that regulatory impact analysis is focused on regulation that actually puts restrictions on the use and exchange of private property. There is no need to do regulatory impact analysis on the Government deciding it’s no longer going to operate and spend money on a department
strength.explanation: A stated intention as incoming Minister for Regulation rather than a delivered outcome; commitment without follow-through yet shown.

veracity.statement: over the last six years, non - COVID-related spending and borrowing increased at unprecedented rates. This has flowed on to higher inflation and higher interest rates, both hurting New Zealanders daily.
veracity.explanation: Core government spending did rise materially, but 'unprecedented' is hyperbolic and attributing inflation/interest rates chiefly to domestic non-COVID spending ignores global post-pandemic inflation drivers — partly true but misleading.

veracity.statement: Nearly half of the Mt Roskill electorate is from the Asian ethnic group, which is one of the highest percentages of any general electorate and over three times the national average. Over half of the population were born overseas, the fourth-highest share in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Census-consistent demographic claims; Mt Roskill is indeed among the most Asian and migrant-heavy general electorates, figures broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: It is somewhat unsettling to note that the last major project of national significance—and not one that benefitted commuters in either Wellington or Auckland—was the Clyde Dam. The dam was completed 30 years ago
veracity.explanation: Clyde Dam was completed around 1992-93, so roughly 30 years prior is fair; but 'last major project of national significance' is a subjective overstatement ignoring later major infrastructure.

veracity.statement: Farmers are leaving the industry due to unworkable regulations. These are costing enormous amounts of money, eroding property rights, and are ridiculously time-consuming.
veracity.explanation: Directionally reflects real rural concern but is a contested, single-cause attribution offered without figures or evidence.

veracity.statement: Have a look at clause 11 of the bill. What does it do? All employment contracts are terminated.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the bill's effect of ending employees' contracts, citing the clause directly.

veracity.statement: It also did a very substantial piece of work under Steven Joyce called “towards a net-zero economy for New Zealand”, which actually provided a lot of the basis for what became the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, and amongst its many recommendations suggested a feebate scheme for electric vehicles, which became the Clean Car Discount.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the Commission's low-emissions work and its influence on later climate policy and the Clean Car Discount.

rigor.statement: over the last six years, non - COVID-related spending and borrowing increased at unprecedented rates. This has flowed on to higher inflation and higher interest rates, both hurting New Zealanders daily.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain (spending → inflation → interest rates) asserted without evidence and omitting global factors; conclusion does not securely follow from the premise.

rigor.statement: The previous Government focused on metadata and ideas of diversity, equity, and inclusion but never on the root cause of the problems or the real patient outcomes that mattered.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping 'never on the root cause' assertion offered without evidence; absolute claim weakens the reasoning.

rigor.statement: Farmers are leaving the industry due to unworkable regulations. These are costing enormous amounts of money, eroding property rights, and are ridiculously time-consuming.
rigor.explanation: Asserts regulation as the cause of farmer exits without evidence and leans on emotive intensifiers ('ridiculously', 'enormous').

rigor.statement: Why is it that supposed liberals are so illiberal when it comes to hearing opposing views?
rigor.explanation: Loaded rhetorical question with a sweeping generalisation about a group; no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Have a look at clause 11 of the bill. What does it do? All employment contracts are terminated.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a specific, checkable provision of the bill rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: this is a party who’s out to look after themselves and their mates, and they’re trying to get rid of the Productivity Commission.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem motive attribution with no evidence linking the repeal to personal gain.

rigor.statement: It also did a very substantial piece of work under Steven Joyce called “towards a net-zero economy for New Zealand”, which actually provided a lot of the basis for what became the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, and amongst its many recommendations suggested a feebate scheme for electric vehicles, which became the Clean Car Discount.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based, traceable chain from report recommendation to enacted policy supporting his case.

rigor.statement: One of the big disadvantages of the way that the Productivity Commission was designed, of course, was that there’s no requirement upon the Government to respond to its reports... a lot of the time that good work just fell on deaf ears.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete structural design flaw (no obligation to respond) that explains the body's limited impact.

rigor.statement: I have huge respect for the original commissioner Murray Sherwin, and I think they did fantastic work. Unfortunately, the work that they did didn’t transfer into actions, and actions actually matter.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable implementation-gap point, but the claim that the work 'didn’t transfer into actions' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We have simply become a country that is incredibly good at writing reports and setting up working groups, but it has become impossible to get anything done.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping generalisation with hyperbole ('impossible to get anything done') and no supporting evidence.

charisma.statement: I commend the Cabinet's decision to cancel the Interislander replacement contract. It sent a clear message to all those who consider the Government to be a bottomless ATM that this coalition Government will deliver value for taxpayers' money.
charisma.explanation: Confident applause line for his own side; 'bottomless ATM' framing rallies supporters rather than persuading or building consensus.

charisma.statement: I also want to take this opportunity to acknowledge my opponent Michael Wood. He ran a clean and respectful campaign, and I am proud to succeed him in serving the people of Mt Roskill as an electorate MP in Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, bridge-building gesture across party lines that invites goodwill.

charisma.statement: Solutions to these problems must be prioritised right here in Parliament by all of us fellow MPs. None of us can do it alone. We must come together, work together, and make change.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly inclusive, cross-party call to collaborate on crime, inviting all members in.

charisma.statement: Damien O'Connor and Jo Luxton, both of whom I believe share National Party values but have been held hostage by the Labour Party for so long that they suffer from Stockholm syndrome!
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing quip aimed at his own side rather than persuading across the aisle, though delivered good-naturedly.

charisma.statement: We should all be able to agree to disagree in a mature and tolerant manner, and that includes in this House.
charisma.explanation: An inclusive appeal to tolerance and mutual respect across the House.

charisma.statement: this is not, in any way, an indictment on the quality of the work of the Productivity Commission. The Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work over the past decade or so, and that work will remain available as an asset or a taonga for New Zealanders to be a guide for policy formation.
charisma.explanation: Disarming, magnanimous framing that softens a contentious move, though still advancing his own agenda.

charisma.statement: I suspect that this side of the House will have more faith in New Zealanders’ judgment than the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Us-versus-them framing that flatters his own side and disparages opponents rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: the Green Party will be supporting the continued existence of the Productivity Commission—despite the fact that we opposed its establishment in the first place
charisma.explanation: Self-aware framing that disarms the obvious contradiction and reasons through it for the House.

charisma.statement: we would suggest that there would be improvements to the legislation governing the Productivity Commission, such as a requirement on the Government to have to respond to its recommendations and to require Government agencies to respond to its recommendations.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, problem-solving proposal that engages with how to improve rather than merely oppose.

charisma.statement: I’d actually like to commend the Minister, the Hon David Seymour, for actually walking the talk. I think he’s been someone that’s been quite outspoken about the need to cut red tape, and this is really hard, detailed stuff.
charisma.explanation: Warm praise, but directed at a coalition partner and his own side rather than persuading opponents.

specificity.statement: I commend the Cabinet's decision to cancel the Interislander replacement contract. It sent a clear message to all those who consider the Government to be a bottomless ATM that this coalition Government will deliver value for taxpayers' money.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete decision (cancelling the Interislander replacement contract), though the 'value for money' claim is general.

specificity.statement: Firstly, returning our polytechnic to local control through the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (disestablishing Te Pūkenga) and goal (local control), though without timing or detail of the local model.

specificity.statement: For South Taranaki, this could mean the development of offshore wind farms, and I look forward to having input into the creation of a regulatory framework that will enable this.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete project type (offshore wind for South Taranaki) and an enabling action, but hedged ('could') with no scale or timeframe.

specificity.statement: My promise is to work hard for them and to work hard for every constituent in the Whanganui electorate.
specificity.explanation: A vague commitment to 'work hard' with no measurable action, mechanism, or deliverable.

specificity.statement: Nearly half of the Mt Roskill electorate is from the Asian ethnic group, which is one of the highest percentages of any general electorate and over three times the national average. Over half of the population were born overseas, the fourth-highest share in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Precise proportions and rankings rather than vague description of diversity.

specificity.statement: We need to be tougher on crime, especially violent crime. People who commit crimes must face real consequences, and, yes, when released back into the community, they also need to be capable of being productive and law-abiding.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (tougher consequences plus rehabilitation) but no mechanism, measure, or named policy.

specificity.statement: This is why our policy of one hour of reading, writing, and mathematics each day is so important; it sets a good foundation for our Kiwi kids.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy with a quantified requirement (one hour per day of core subjects).

specificity.statement: We need to teach people how to fish rather than giving them a fish.
specificity.explanation: A proverb/slogan that commits to no concrete welfare or training mechanism.

specificity.statement: I'm proud that our Government is willing to invest in our health system by operating a third medical school. We will increase the numbers of healthcare professionals and improve outcomes.
specificity.explanation: The third medical school is a concrete named initiative, but 'increase numbers' and 'improve outcomes' are unquantified.

specificity.statement: the new “Ministry of Regulation” that will, in part, be funded by the funding that would have gone on to the Productivity Commission—approximately $6 million each year
specificity.explanation: Names the funding mechanism and a concrete annual figure (~$6 million) redirected to the new ministry.

specificity.statement: It also did a very substantial piece of work under Steven Joyce called “towards a net-zero economy for New Zealand”, which actually provided a lot of the basis for what became the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, and amongst its many recommendations suggested a feebate scheme for electric vehicles, which became the Clean Car Discount.
specificity.explanation: Names the report, the resulting Act and bodies, and the concrete feebate-to-Clean-Car-Discount link.

specificity.statement: we would suggest that there would be improvements to the legislation governing the Productivity Commission, such as a requirement on the Government to have to respond to its recommendations and to require Government agencies to respond to its recommendations.
specificity.explanation: Offers a concrete legislative fix (mandatory government/agency responses), though without drafting detail or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We have simply become a country that is incredibly good at writing reports and setting up working groups, but it has become impossible to get anything done.
specificity.explanation: A broad lament with no figures, examples, or named instances.

strength.statement: My promise is to work hard for them and to work hard for every constituent in the Whanganui electorate.
strength.explanation: Pure aspiration of effort with no concrete commitment or deliverable to follow through on.

strength.statement: I'm proud that our Government is willing to invest in our health system by operating a third medical school. We will increase the numbers of healthcare professionals and improve outcomes.
strength.explanation: Announced/in-progress policy rather than a delivered outcome; follow-through not yet demonstrated.

civility.statement: I also want to take this opportunity to acknowledge my opponent Michael Wood. He ran a clean and respectful campaign, and I am proud to succeed him in serving the people of Mt Roskill as an electorate MP in Parliament.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of a defeated opponent with no personal attack.

civility.statement: Solutions to these problems must be prioritised right here in Parliament by all of us fellow MPs. None of us can do it alone. We must come together, work together, and make change.
civility.explanation: Respectful, collaborative framing addressed to all MPs without attack.

civility.statement: The previous Government focused on metadata and ideas of diversity, equity, and inclusion but never on the root cause of the problems or the real patient outcomes that mattered.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the previous government's policy focus rather than a personal attack, but the 'never' framing borders on a strawman caricature.

civility.statement: Damien O'Connor and Jo Luxton, both of whom I believe share National Party values but have been held hostage by the Labour Party for so long that they suffer from Stockholm syndrome!
civility.explanation: A jokey jab, but it characterises named opponents as captive/lacking agency rather than engaging their actual positions.

civility.statement: We should all be able to agree to disagree in a mature and tolerant manner, and that includes in this House.
civility.explanation: Explicitly advocates respectful, tolerant disagreement.

civility.statement: Why is it that supposed liberals are so illiberal when it comes to hearing opposing views?
civility.explanation: A rhetorical jab that paints 'liberals' as a bloc, leaning on caricature rather than engaging specific arguments.

civility.statement: this is not, in any way, an indictment on the quality of the work of the Productivity Commission. The Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work over the past decade or so, and that work will remain available as an asset or a taonga for New Zealanders to be a guide for policy formation.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of the very body he is abolishing, focusing on its merits.

civility.statement: I suspect that this side of the House will have more faith in New Zealanders’ judgment than the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: A pointed partisan contrast aimed at the opposition's character (faith in citizens) rather than a specific policy argument.

civility.statement: as Fred Dagg once said—it might as well have been Grant Robertson—“We could always borrow a few billion more.”
civility.explanation: A mocking caricature of a named opponent's fiscal stance rather than engagement with his actual record.

civility.statement: this is a party who’s out to look after themselves and their mates, and they’re trying to get rid of the Productivity Commission.
civility.explanation: Imputes self-interested, cronyist motive to opponents rather than addressing the policy argument.

civility.statement: It’s going to be his show, it’s going to be the little David Seymour show, and he’s going to be able to pontificate about how effective rules and regulations are.
civility.explanation: Personal mockery ('the little David Seymour show', 'pontificate') aimed at the individual rather than the policy.

civility.statement: One of the big disadvantages of the way that the Productivity Commission was designed, of course, was that there’s no requirement upon the Government to respond to its reports... a lot of the time that good work just fell on deaf ears.
civility.explanation: Substantive, even-handed critique of institutional design rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: I have huge respect for the original commissioner Murray Sherwin, and I think they did fantastic work. Unfortunately, the work that they did didn’t transfer into actions, and actions actually matter.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the Commission and its chair while disagreeing on outcomes.

civility.statement: I’d actually like to commend the Minister, the Hon David Seymour, for actually walking the talk. I think he’s been someone that’s been quite outspoken about the need to cut red tape, and this is really hard, detailed stuff.
civility.explanation: Respectful, complimentary engagement crediting a colleague's consistency and effort.

authenticity.statement: We’ve been very clear, as the Government, in our communications with the department that we want to ensure that those people who were working for the Productivity Commission are given every opportunity to find new employment within the Government, that those people do not find themselves unfairly treated throughout this process.
authenticity.explanation: Words of care for staff sit in tension with the bill itself: as Webb notes, clause 11 terminates all employment contracts, so the stated concern is at odds with the mechanism being legislated.

authenticity.statement: the Green Party will be supporting the continued existence of the Productivity Commission—despite the fact that we opposed its establishment in the first place
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges and explains a reversal of his party's earlier opposition; a candid, defensible shift rather than concealed hypocrisy.

divination.statement: Just like his Treaty principles bill, it’s going to be a dead letter. It will be of no effect.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the new ministry will prove ineffective; plausible as partisan rhetoric but unfalsifiable in the near term and highly uncertain.

civility.statement: I’d like to thank the Minister for sharing his CV with us today and also reminding us who the Prime Minister currently is, because if anyone had been sitting in this House this week, they may have been under the mistaken impression that it was David Seymour.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic personal jab at Simeon Brown and a swipe implying Seymour is running the show; mocking rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: It is disingenuous for this finance Minister, this new one, to claim that it is their work that’s doing it.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of a claim, but 'disingenuous' edges toward impugning honesty rather than the policy.

civility.statement: why don’t we just call them the “Hijacked Party”, because they are 8 percent of the vote and they are hijacking 80 percent of the Government’s airtime.
civility.explanation: Derisive nickname for ACT — ridicule rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: it is his responsibility, it’s his Government, it’s his circus, and they are his clowns.
civility.explanation: Calls government ministers 'clowns' — a direct personal/character insult (quoting Grant Robertson but endorsing it).

civility.statement: What we’re seeing is a 21st century version of the old saying, “Where Britain goes, we go.” Except, under this Government, it’s now, “When Washington calls and says, ‘Will you jump?’, we say, ‘How high?’ ”
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature of the government's foreign policy as servile — borders on strawman though aimed at policy not person.

civility.statement: The rural community has likely spent more on the environment than those that criticise them, those that flush the dunny without a thought about where it goes, in their plastic clothes, standing on their plastic carpet, that ignore their own impacts on the environment, and would rather point the finger.
civility.explanation: Mocking, contemptuous caricature of urban critics rather than engaging their arguments.

charisma.statement: I’d like to thank the Minister for sharing his CV with us today and also reminding us who the Prime Minister currently is, because if anyone had been sitting in this House this week, they may have been under the mistaken impression that it was David Seymour.
charisma.explanation: An applause line for her own side that belittles opponents; no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

charisma.statement: why don’t we just call them the “Hijacked Party”, because they are 8 percent of the vote and they are hijacking 80 percent of the Government’s airtime.
charisma.explanation: Purely divisive us-vs-them line aimed at her own side.

charisma.statement: it is his responsibility, it’s his Government, it’s his circus, and they are his clowns.
charisma.explanation: Combative crowd-pleasing attack, no bridge-building.

charisma.statement: We should work to demilitarise the Pacific. We should strengthen the Pacific Islands Forum and urge our friends from outside the region to respect it and take its lead. We should do more for regional economic development in the Pacific—help Pacific nations to protect their exclusive economic zones and ramp up our efforts and commitments on climate mitigation and adaptation, including by giving resettlement opportunities for people whose islands are made uninhabitable by climate change.
charisma.explanation: Offers a positive, constructive alternative agenda rather than only attacking — invites a different vision.

charisma.statement: I will also represent those values for all in my electorate, regardless of whether you voted for me or not.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive commitment to represent everyone, reaching beyond his own supporters.

charisma.statement: I support a multicultural New Zealand. Our country is enriched by migration. With growing Hawke’s Bay industries, immigration is so important, and I’ve been a relentless supporter of the Recognised Seasonal Employment (RSE) scheme, which sees thousands of RSE workers from the Pacific Islands coming to our Hawke’s Bay orchards every year—labour shortages are filled, our economy grows, more jobs are created, and our Pacific neighbours are enriched as they return with money for their families and communities.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, welcoming framing of migration and Pacific workers as mutual benefit.

charisma.statement: Ki a koutou ngā hapū me ngā marae o Te Matau-a-Māui, kia ora, kia kaha, tātou. ... I look forward to working together and standing together to ensure our region, Te Matau-a-Māui, grows together.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across to local iwi with te reo and an explicit invitation to work together — consensus-building and inclusive.

charisma.statement: But we can’t grow our economy at the expense of the environment. After working for an organic grower and exporter, I know we can run profitable businesses while also enhancing our environment for future generations.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground between economic and environmental concerns rather than pitting them against each other.

veracity.statement: Then we heard an announcement in recent days that inflation has dropped from 7.2 percent to 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ annual CPI peaked at 7.3% in mid-2022 and fell to 4.7% in the December 2023 quarter.

veracity.statement: It is disingenuous for this finance Minister, this new one, to claim that it is their work that’s doing it.
veracity.explanation: The inflation fall largely reflects a pre-existing trajectory, but attributing it solely to the prior government is itself contestable; mixed.

veracity.statement: She sold it as annual reductions in back-office expenditure of 6.5 percent, and there were only going to be 24 agencies, 24 specific agencies listed on a Treasury website. What do we have now? Suddenly all departments, including arm’s-length departments, dozens and dozens of agencies. And the 6.5 percent—oops! It’s suddenly grown to 7.5 percent for some of them.
veracity.explanation: Broadly captures a real widening of the savings exercise, but the precise '24 agencies' and '7.5 percent' framing is a partisan characterisation and unverified here.

veracity.statement: Currently, my constituents pay about $4,500 to go up to Christchurch, plus accommodation, plus transport, to be able to access the same services that people in Christchurch get for free.
veracity.explanation: Plausible cost claim about PET scan access, but the figure is asserted without sourcing and cannot be confirmed from the text.

veracity.statement: What I should have said is that the court was not required to determine whether Israel had actually breached its obligations under the genocide convention. However, the court found that there is a plausible case that Israel’s conduct in Gaza may breach its obligations under the genocide convention.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the ICJ provisional-measures ruling of January 2024 — plausible case, no finding of actual genocide.

veracity.statement: We saw this in the hasty decision to send six New Zealand military personnel to take part in the bombing of Yemen to punish Houthi rebels there for their attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.
veracity.explanation: NZ did contribute a small (~6) defence-force team to support strikes on Houthi targets; 'take part in the bombing' overstates a support role.

veracity.statement: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have been bombing the Houthis for much of the past decade with no apparent effect.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — the Saudi/UAE coalition campaigned in Yemen from 2015 without decisively defeating the Houthis; 'no apparent effect' is somewhat sweeping.

veracity.statement: This is the same China that is our largest trading partner.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — China is New Zealand's largest two-way trading partner.

veracity.statement: Is there any evidence that China poses a military threat to New Zealand, that they have some kind of plan to invade us? There isn’t a skerrick of evidence to suggest that.
veracity.explanation: True that no evidence points to an invasion plan, though it sidesteps wider concerns about Chinese assertiveness he himself notes.

veracity.statement: Why don’t we talk about the 25,000 kilometres of waterways fenced off, the over 36,000 culverts or bridges over waterway crossings by the dairy industry alone, the hundreds of thousands of dollars spent on effluent systems per family farm, this country’s 5,000th Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust covenant that was registered in the Wairarapa in 2022, the community catchment groups, the millions of trees planted, or the 2.8 million hectares of woody vegetation that’s already on our farmland?
veracity.explanation: Figures echo dairy-sector and QEII Trust reporting and are plausible, but presented selectively as advocacy without sourcing.

veracity.statement: you should be proud to be a part of the food and fibre sectors that earn 82 percent of this country’s export income—export income that pays the wages of our teachers, our nurses, and our policemen.
veracity.explanation: Primary/food-and-fibre exports are roughly 80%+ of NZ goods exports, but as a share of total export income (incl. services) the 82% figure is overstated.

veracity.statement: How could we have spent 80 percent more to achieve worse outcomes?
veracity.explanation: A loosely-defined '80 percent more for worse outcomes' is a rhetorical figure not tied to a specified baseline or metric.

veracity.statement: I’m proud to stand here as the first female National Party MP for Tukituki, and, wow, did we turn Tukituki blue—a record majority of over 10,000; the biggest majority the seat has ever had.
veracity.explanation: The 'first female National MP for Tukituki' and large 2023 majority are plausible and likely accurate, though 'biggest ever' is asserted without verification here.

veracity.statement: Grandma never got a seat in this House, but she was a woman before her time, when it wasn’t common for women to be MPs, with just eight female MPs being elected that year. I know she would be so proud to see her granddaughter standing here now among 57 other female MPs in this 54th Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Both figures — a handful of women MPs in 1981 and around 58 women in the 54th Parliament — are in line with the historical record.

divination.explanation: Hedged 20-year forecast of US-China conflict, attributed to analysts; plausible but highly uncertain over that timeframe.

strength.statement: We believe in a strong military that can be deployed in the service of New Zealand’s values and to protect our interests. The last Labour Government’s investments in updating military hardware speaks for itself, as does the strong support that we gave the people of Ukraine in their defence of their homeland against the Russian invasion.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivered defence-hardware investment and Ukraine assistance; partly verifiable follow-through.

strength.statement: The four-lane expressway between Hastings and Napier has to happen, a new Hawke’s Bay hospital must be a priority, and water storage in Hawke’s Bay is an absolute must.
strength.explanation: Stated commitments to 'fight for' projects with no delivery mechanism, funding, or timeframe — aspiration at this stage.

This suggests that criminals are using firearms that are either illegally imported, manufactured, or intentionally stripped of serial numbers, making them untraceable. The firearms registry would be unable to capture these illegally held or manufactured firearms.
veracity.explanation: Specific seizure statistics presented as fact; plausible and consistent with police data, though not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Ninety-four percent of people who were present at or subject to a search by police in which firearms were seized last year did not possess a firearms licence. The gangs and criminals are carrying and using firearms illegally, and they're circumventing the firearms registry. Licensed firearms owners are not the problem. That's why the Government is committed to targeting firearms illegally held by the gangs.
veracity.explanation: Statistic presented as fact; plausible but the inference that licence-holders are 'not the problem' is a partial framing.

veracity.statement: As of mid - last year, we were down to 284,000 daily smokers from 573,000 ten years ago.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the long-run decline in NZ daily smoking numbers.

veracity.statement: I was pleased to see police's proactive enforcement response to a gang convoy through Whakatāne last year, which included a response by the Eagle helicopter, to ensure that the rights of law-abiding citizens to move about their towns freely are protected over and above the rights of gang members who choose to block roads, intimidate people, and break the law. veracity.explanation: Specific operational details and arrest figures presented as fact; plausible and concrete.

veracity.explanation: Attendance figure is broadly in line with reported regular-attendance rates, though the precise framing is debatable.

veracity.statement: I think we're incredibly proud of the lowering of smoking rates. It's gone from 16.7 percent down to 8.6 percent and to 6.8 percent in the space of the last decade.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister not find it extraordinary that the Opposition that's raising in the House today this issue nevertheless supported the very same party writing sound policy in 2018-19 which led to the biggest drop in the whole world of cigarette smoking? The unemployment rate is also expected to rise to around 5 percent before beginning to fall again.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays HYEFU forecasts, including the candid per-capita GDP decline.

divination.explanation: GDP/export boost is a forecast of future benefit; plausible per modelling but 'up to' figures are optimistic upper bounds.

veracity.statement: From the year 2000, our population has surged by 72 percent, far surpassing the nationwide average of 38 percent. In the same period, our GDP saw a remarkable increase of 142 percent, compared to the national average of 82 percent.
veracity.explanation: Specific growth statistics for the Western Bay of Plenty; figures are plausible and consistent with the region's known rapid growth, though exact percentages can't be fully verified from the text.

veracity.statement: On top of this, we have the least affordable rental market in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Tauranga/Bay of Plenty has frequently ranked among NZ's least affordable rental markets; broadly defensible but 'the least' is a strong superlative whose accuracy depends on the measure used.

veracity.statement: In New Zealand, we have around 1,700 career firefighters and nearly 12,000 volunteers. Volunteer firefighters represent 86 percent of the front-line workforce and they respond to 70 percent of all vehicle accidents, 71 percent of medical call outs and 85 percent of vegetation fires.
veracity.explanation: These figures align closely with publicly cited Fire and Emergency NZ statistics on volunteer numbers and response shares.

veracity.statement: I am one of three new MPs from Generation Z—the first time this generation has ever had representation in Parliament—and I am proud to be the youngest MP in the National Party.
veracity.explanation: Rutherford (born 1997) entering Parliament with other Gen Z MPs in 2023 is accurate, and being the youngest National MP is consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: New Zealand, as our Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon, aptly put it, is the best country on planet Earth.
veracity.explanation: An unfalsifiable superlative/hyperbole presented as endorsement; not a verifiable factual claim and overstated.

veracity.statement: From the Otago gold rush days to when Chinese miners ventured into New Zealand in pursuit of opportunities; to early Chinese migrants contributing to various sectors of our economy, such as vegetable growers and dairy product exporters
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of Chinese New Zealand history — Otago gold-rush era migration and later roles as market gardeners and merchants.

veracity.statement: After realising I was unsuccessful to become a MP on election night in 2020, I held my 10-month-old baby girl, Amber, in my arms—I felt I had let her down.
veracity.explanation: Her unsuccessful 2020 candidacy is an accurate factual claim.

veracity.statement: my first ancestor came to New Zealand in 1841, to Nelson, on the Whitby, one of the three first ships to settle in the South Island.
veracity.explanation: The Whitby was one of the early New Zealand Company ships to Nelson; the personal/historical detail is specific and broadly consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: The original four Māori seats were established to keep us in our place.
veracity.explanation: The four Māori seats (1867) are historical fact, but the stated motive ('to keep us in our place') is one contested interpretation of their purpose rather than an established fact.

veracity.statement: It was Governor FitzRoy's arrogant refusal to converse with Hōne Heke about Heke's concerns about Te Tiriti that led to conflict in 1845.
veracity.explanation: The Northern War did break out in 1845 amid Heke's grievances; the date and broad cause are accurate, though 'arrogant refusal' is a characterisation and the causes were more complex.

veracity.statement: Matariki has been a huge success.

veracity.explanation: The programme exists and was popular; 'oversubscribed' is plausible but not quantified.

veracity.statement: Prime Ministers Ardern and Hipkins set the bar high, and could never be accused of being fly in, fly out Prime Ministers at Waitangi.

veracity.statement: Māori had unprecedented access to the Government at all levels for the first time ever.
veracity.explanation: Increased iwi-Crown engagement under the sixth Labour Government is real, but 'unprecedented... for the first time ever' is a superlative that overstates a more gradual history.

That's what they care about.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he will say at Waitangi about a bill removing tino rangatiratanga rights; pivots to education and socio-economic outcomes instead of the bill.

forthrightness.statement: I reject the question. We're not changing the Treaty of Waitangi, nor Treaty settlements. What we have is a coalition agreement which we are actioning.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly denies the premise (distancing/leveraging) and gives a reason, but does not engage the substance of why responsibility was delegated to an ACT Minister.

forthrightness.statement: From memory, without checking my information, as of 30 September 2023—again, from memory—the number in Lower Hutt City of people on the wait-list was 623, and I would note that that is a fivefold increase compared to October 2017.
forthrightness.explanation: Andersen asked why he could not provide the Lower Hutt wait-list number; he answers with a specific figure on the spot.

forthrightness.statement: New Zealanders should take the time to learn about Te Tiriti o Waitangi—the Treaty of Waitangi—and come to their own views.
forthrightness.explanation: Jackson asked who New Zealanders should believe (Seymour vs the PM on partnership) and whether he'd reiterate it at Waitangi; the reply deflects to 'come to their own views' without addressing either.

civility.statement: No, the member should not take it as being that. What he should take it as is being that the New Zealand Defence Force has been left in a very difficult position after six—well, actually, the last three years of neglect, and that, clearly, promises that were made by a previous Minister, himself, to Defence around capital funding have not been complied with. So it is outrageous that this debate is being used to attack Defence on funding when, in fact, he's left Defence in the position that they are.
civility.explanation: Turns on Henare personally — 'three years of neglect', broken promises 'by a previous Minister, himself' — rather than engaging the substance neutrally.

civility.statement: Sorry, but the member clearly wasn't listening to the statement I just read out. I didn't actually make that statement. I'm happy to remind him that 15 percent of world trade goes through there, and if anyone really wants to know what happens when our shipping lanes and our supply chains are interrupted, just think back to what happened to New Zealanders and to their lack of buying power when we had the COVID-19 situation.
civility.explanation: Opens with a dismissive jab ('clearly wasn't listening') before addressing the point.

civility.statement: the member may wish to, as she has today—express support for the Houthis. I do not, and nor does this Government. We do not support piracy; we do support New Zealanders' freedom of navigation, being good citizens of the world, and we're very proud of the people who are doing that.
civility.explanation: Mischaracterises Davidson as expressing 'support for the Houthis', which she did not — a strawman and personal imputation.

civility.statement: Look, I don't think any of that has anything to do with the statement that I've made today. But I would say to that member that we all love world peace; we'd just like to see a bit more of it.
civility.explanation: Glib and dismissive but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: This Government's denial—which will lead to some of our questions that I have—that this conflict in Yemen is connected to the war in Gaza is naive and dangerous—at best, wilfully ignorant
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government's position as 'naive', 'dangerous', and 'wilfully ignorant' rather than engaging it on the merits alone.

civility.statement: the experiment of the last five years of having a dual mandate failed spectacularly.
civility.explanation: Strong criticism of a policy choice, not a person.

civility.statement: Minister, how did the Government manage to spend so much more money and yet get so much worse results, and is that an example of the previous finance Minister's fiscal incontinence?
civility.explanation: 'Fiscal incontinence' aimed at the previous finance Minister is a personal jibe rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: How can she reconcile the inclusion of Corrections in the departments to be cut with the commitment in the coalition agreement with ACT to increase its funding, or is this going to be another example of David Seymour's political impotence?
civility.explanation: The substantive part (reconciling cuts with the ACT funding commitment) is legitimate, but it ends in a personal jab ('David Seymour's political impotence').

civility.statement: If the member is specific about exactly what she is asking, she will get that information. And the other point I would note is that the information is publicly available every quarter. The member just needs to learn a little website: www.google.com.
civility.explanation: The 'learn a little website: www.google.com' line is a condescending cheap shot at the questioner rather than engagement with the point.

civility.statement: Does the Minister agree with the very respectable and well-supported National Party members Dame Jenny Shipley, Jim Bolger, Doug Graham, and Chris Finlayson, who all support the partnership principle and are adamant that we should get rid of the Treaty principles bill, and is he planning on discussing that at Waitangi?
civility.explanation: Pointed and partisan but engages the substance via named, credible figures rather than insulting the Minister personally.

rigor.statement: Sorry, but the member clearly wasn't listening to the statement I just read out. I didn't actually make that statement. I'm happy to remind him that 15 percent of world trade goes through there, and if anyone really wants to know what happens when our shipping lanes and our supply chains are interrupted, just think back to what happened to New Zealanders and to their lack of buying power when we had the COVID-19 situation.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the COVID supply-chain analogy as the main support rather than direct evidence on current price effects.

rigor.statement: the member may wish to, as she has today—express support for the Houthis. I do not, and nor does this Government. We do not support piracy; we do support New Zealanders' freedom of navigation, being good citizens of the world, and we're very proud of the people who are doing that.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a position the opponent did not take (strawman) rather than her actual de-escalation argument.

rigor.statement: The Labour Party has made their position clear: that we should not be involved in this conflict. There's no UN resolution in favour of such actions, and there are countries in Europe and Scandinavia that are against joining this conflict.
rigor.explanation: Supports the position with stated reasons (no UN resolution, other nations declining), though the comparators are asserted rather than detailed.

rigor.statement: This Government's denial—which will lead to some of our questions that I have—that this conflict in Yemen is connected to the war in Gaza is naive and dangerous—at best, wilfully ignorant
rigor.explanation: Asserts a connection forcefully but the support (Houthi statements) is provided separately; the labels do most of the work here.

rigor.statement: there is more than a 50 percent chance that violence and conflict will escalate.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in agreement among international-relations experts (appeal to expert consensus) rather than independent evidence.

rigor.statement: On the other hand, non-tradables inflation has stayed stubbornly high. So domestic factors, rather than global factors, are playing the greatest role in driving inflation right now.
rigor.explanation: Uses the tradables/non-tradables split to support the conclusion that domestic factors dominate; the inference follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: the experiment of the last five years of having a dual mandate failed spectacularly.
rigor.explanation: Asserted with hyperbole ('spectacularly') rather than evidence isolating the mandate's effect.

rigor.statement: you shouldn't simply conflate spending more money with getting results for the people we serve. This Government will not fall for that mistake.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable analytical point that inputs are not outcomes, though asserted rather than evidenced here.

rigor.statement: Minister, how did the Government manage to spend so much more money and yet get so much worse results, and is that an example of the previous finance Minister's fiscal incontinence?
rigor.explanation: A loaded question presuming 'worse results' without evidence, leaning on the insult for effect.

rigor.statement: Does the Minister agree with the very respectable and well-supported National Party members Dame Jenny Shipley, Jim Bolger, Doug Graham, and Chris Finlayson, who all support the partnership principle and are adamant that we should get rid of the Treaty principles bill, and is he planning on discussing that at Waitangi?
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority (named senior National figures) as the main support for the position.

charisma.statement: These attacks are actually forcing ships to take the long route around the Cape of Good Hope, and that's adding 10 to 15 days on to that journey—10 to 15 days of extra fuel and of wages—and it means fewer journeys.
charisma.explanation: Plain, relatable framing ('hitting all of us in the pocket—all Kiwis') aimed at persuading, though it rallies its own position rather than seeking cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: Aotearoa has a proud and long custom and history of being a voice for peace and humanitarian concentration and efforts across world conflicts.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared national values of peace, but frames her side's position rather than reaching across to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: We, as a country, cannot wish the evils of the world away. We must stand as a partner in a global society and play our important part in it. This deployment signals our commitment to our shared values of protecting all things democracy, global security, and the importance of global trade.
charisma.explanation: Aspirational, value-based appeal, but addressed to those who already support the deployment rather than persuading sceptics.

charisma.statement: you shouldn't simply conflate spending more money with getting results for the people we serve. This Government will not fall for that mistake.
charisma.explanation: Frames an in-group lesson ('members opposite') rather than building cross-party agreement.

charisma.statement: the legislation about which the Leader of the Opposition is talking was not constructed by him but by New Zealand First, which led to the dramatic fall in tobacco smoking in the first place? And that's a fact.
charisma.explanation: Partisan credit-claiming aimed at his own party's record rather than building consensus.

authenticity.statement: The Labour Party has made their position clear: that we should not be involved in this conflict. There's no UN resolution in favour of such actions, and there are countries in Europe and Scandinavia that are against joining this conflict.
authenticity.explanation: States a clear party position consistent with Labour's stance, with no visible contradiction.

authenticity.statement: In my time as the former defence Minister, my colleagues and I made the decision—and it was the right decision—after the fall of Kabul to evacuate.
authenticity.explanation: Cites his own record to ground his argument about deployment decision-making, consistent with his prior role.

authenticity.statement: Aotearoa has a proud and long custom and history of being a voice for peace and humanitarian concentration and efforts across world conflicts.
authenticity.explanation: States a value (independent, peace-focused foreign policy) consistent with the Greens' long-held positions.

authenticity.statement: I reject the question. We're not changing the Treaty of Waitangi, nor Treaty settlements. What we have is a coalition agreement which we are actioning.
authenticity.explanation: Maintains the line that no Treaty change is intended while advancing a Treaty principles bill to first reading — a tension he resolves by citing the coalition agreement.

authenticity.statement: As has been well canvassed, there is no commitment to support the bill after first reading.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the stated coalition position, though it sits awkwardly with appointing a Minister specifically to progress the bill.

strength.statement: In my time as the former defence Minister, my colleagues and I made the decision—and it was the right decision—after the fall of Kabul to evacuate.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a specific, executed decision (the August 2021 Kabul evacuation) he was responsible for as Defence Minister.

strength.statement: New Zealanders will welcome measures such as cancelling fuel tax increases for the remainder of this term and removing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
strength.explanation: Concrete commitments that the Government did move on, though framed prospectively as part of the plan.

strength.statement: Our savings programme in Budget 2024 is designed to find around $1.5 billion in savings per year, which we'll use to deliver on our policy commitments and fund critical cost pressures.
strength.explanation: A stated programme target at the design stage; delivery not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: I am very proud of our Government's statements and actions around education, particularly banning mobile phones; making sure we have one hour of maths, reading, and writing every day at primary and intermediate schools; and, importantly, reviewing the curriculum.
strength.explanation: Mix of implemented (phone ban) and in-progress measures; partial delivery on stated commitments.

divination.statement: there is more than a 50 percent chance that violence and conflict will escalate.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable prediction of escalation; plausible and consistent with the cited expert view, but probabilistic and uncertain.

veracity.statement: We know that one-in-four New Zealanders’ jobs depends on trade, and the New Zealand - EU free-trade agreement is the result of a longstanding and bipartisan effort by successive New Zealand Governments.
veracity.explanation: The 'one in four jobs depends on trade' figure is a commonly cited NZ statistic, roughly accurate; the bipartisan characterisation is also fair.

veracity.statement: With a GDP of around $27 trillion and a population of 450 million consumers, the EU represents an important and valuable market for New Zealand businesses looking to sell overseas.
veracity.explanation: EU population ~450 million is accurate, but EU nominal GDP is roughly US$18 trillion; $27 trillion overstates it unless on a PPP/other basis.

veracity.statement: As a result of the NZ-EU FTA, New Zealand exporters will benefit from $100 million in additional tariff savings from day one of entry into force.
veracity.explanation: Matches the official MFAT estimate of immediate tariff savings from the agreement.

veracity.statement: From the day of the agreement entering into force, 91 percent of New Zealand’s current trade with the EU will enter duty-free through a combination of tariff elimination and duty-free quotas.
veracity.explanation: The 91 percent duty-free figure aligns with the published terms of the FTA.

veracity.statement: Under the FTA, New Zealand has agreed to protect 1,975 EU geographical indications (GIs) on day one, with the potential for up to 30 additional GIs to be added every three years by mutual agreement.
veracity.explanation: Specific GI numbers consistent with the agreement's terms.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand - EU FTA was commenced in the direction of an agreement under the National Government, concluded under a Labour Government, and now quickly enters into force under a National Government. That’s bipartisan.
veracity.explanation: Accurate timeline of which governments commenced, concluded and implemented the deal.

veracity.statement: There were many who thought that, actually, a trade deal with the EU’s 27 member States would have been virtually impossible to conclude.
veracity.explanation: Fair characterisation of the widely-held scepticism about concluding a 27-state EU deal.

veracity.statement: The National Government brought that model in—and I want to thank you for that—some time ago.
veracity.explanation: Pharmac was established in 1993 under a National government — accurate.

veracity.statement: We’re seeing with other countries that are trying to negotiate with the EU that they’ve hit some hurdles. I know that Australia has decided to park that for some time.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Australia-EU FTA talks were suspended/stalled in 2023 over agricultural access.

veracity.statement: When you look at how investor-State dispute settlement mechanisms have been applied through history, the vast majority of them were on environmental grounds and the vast majority of them found in favour of the litigant and overturned environmental provisions.
veracity.explanation: ISDS has frequently been used against environmental regulation, but the strong 'vast majority' framing overstates a contested empirical record.

veracity.statement: New Zealand had access to around 13 percent of world consumption at tariff rates less than 10 percent. Effectively, what that 13 percent represents is the freely traded world market, which pretty much sets the world price.
veracity.explanation: Directionally plausible that only a small share of global dairy is freely traded and sets the marginal price, but the precise 13 percent figure is hard to verify.

veracity.statement: The EU is New Zealand’s fourth-largest trading partner and one of our most important markets. Under this bill, New Zealand’s conditions of access will be significantly improved, hence this piece of legislation is incredibly valuable to our market.
veracity.explanation: The EU as NZ's fourth-largest trading partner is accurate.

veracity.statement: It was Māori who signed Aotearoa’s first ever trade agreement in 1835, He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence, so that Māori could continue to trade and export our goods overseas without being treated like pirates and having our ships detained.
veracity.explanation: He Whakaputanga (1835) is real and trade/shipping recognition was a motivation, but characterising it as a 'free-trade agreement' is a generous framing of a declaration of independence.

veracity.statement: Whilst this is the first free-trade agreement with the EU to include a specific chapter on Māori trade, the Treaty of Waitangi exception clause allowing more favourable treatment to Māori remains unchanged from previous free-trade agreements dating back to 2001.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Treaty of Waitangi exception originated in the 2001 NZ-Singapore agreement and has been carried in essentially the same form since.

veracity.statement: This just seems ridiculous at a time when Māori are more than 50 percent of forest and fish, 20 percent of sheep and beef, and 12 percent of dairy.
veracity.explanation: These Māori-economy asset shares are broadly in line with commonly cited estimates, though the precise figures vary by source.

veracity.statement: Our fourth-largest, covering about $20-odd billion worth of two-way goods, and one-in-four jobs in New Zealand directly related to that trade importance in our economy.
veracity.explanation: EU as fourth-largest partner, ~$20bn two-way trade and the one-in-four jobs figure are all broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: With respect, the comments by the Māori Party are incorrect; the Treaty provisions in this agreement are as good as they have been in any other agreement. There is no other country in the world that manages to secure the level of protection that we do for a founding document like the Treaty of Waitangi than New Zealand does.
veracity.explanation: It is true NZ's Treaty exception is a notable, internationally unusual protection; the absolute 'no other country in the world' claim is rhetorically strong but defensible given the uniqueness of the clause.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that Europe agreed to no ISDS clauses in this agreement. It’s something that if the new Government and their future trade aspirations bring back ISDS clauses, there will be difficulty in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the NZ-EU FTA does not include investor-State dispute settlement.

veracity.statement: Where the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership went wrong was that the class of investments that could be screened for was closed by that agreement and therefore, after that agreement came into effect, New Zealand could not introduce any new areas of investment to be screened under our screening regime.
veracity.explanation: An accurate, if technical, account of the CPTPP investment-screening constraints that drove NZ's foreign-buyer and forestry rule changes.

veracity.statement: And, for the record, Tim Groser, in retrospect, agrees that under his watch investment protocols were taken too far in some of those trade agreements.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific retrospective view to a National-era trade minister; plausible but presented without citation, so hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: In particular, I want to acknowledge the contribution this makes to our horticultural industry... the farmers in Horowhenua, a $714 million industry, and for them that’s a $46 million saving immediately when this comes into force.
veracity.explanation: Specific local figures that are plausible and consistent with the sector-level tariff-saving estimates cited elsewhere in the debate.

veracity.statement: The fact that there will be, as the Minister said in his opening remarks, $100 million in tariff savings from day one—that’s worth something. That’s worth something to our fantastic onion-growing industry.
veracity.explanation: Reiterates the official $100 million day-one tariff-saving figure accurately.

veracity.statement: Twenty years after I was organising those demonstrations, I found myself as Minister for Trade and Export Growth in our Government here in 2020, welcoming a multi-party delegation of European members of Parliament who said that this EU - New Zealand trade agreement is gold standard.
veracity.explanation: The 'gold standard' praise from EU MPs is reported second-hand; plausible but unverifiable as quoted.

veracity.statement: This agreement has labour standards—it allows the EU and New Zealand to hold each other to account on our climate commitments, on animal welfare, on gender commitments through the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the agreement's inclusion of sustainability, labour and trade-and-gender provisions.

veracity.statement: Under the free-trade agreement, New Zealand’s conditions of access will be significantly improved, with 91 percent of New Zealand’s current goods trade to the EU able to enter duty-free from day one... This will rise to 97 percent after seven years, with estimated tariff savings exceeding $100 million from day one—the highest immediate tariff savings of any New Zealand FTA—growing to $110 million after seven years.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the published FTA terms and official tariff-saving estimates.

veracity.statement: Zespri, another one of our organisations in horticulture that has a massive contribution, said that the agreement would benefit its sector by up to $46 million, which it paid out in 2022 in tariffs on $1 billion of exports.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to Zespri's own submission and consistent with the $46m kiwifruit tariff figure cited elsewhere in the debate.

charisma.statement: We know that one-in-four New Zealanders’ jobs depends on trade, and the New Zealand - EU free-trade agreement is the result of a longstanding and bipartisan effort by successive New Zealand Governments.
charisma.explanation: Frames the deal as cross-party and built by successive governments — inclusive, consensus-building language.

charisma.statement: The New Zealand - EU FTA was commenced in the direction of an agreement under the National Government, concluded under a Labour Government, and now quickly enters into force under a National Government. That’s bipartisan.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits both major parties across time — bridge-building, consensus framing.

charisma.statement: I want to recognise the significant efforts of officials within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade and our skilled trade negotiators, as well as former trade Minister Damien O’Connor for his work on this agreement.
charisma.explanation: Crosses party lines to thank an opponent (O'Connor) and officials — generous, unifying.

charisma.statement: I hope the vote will be unanimous and that the protestations against trade agreements that we’ve seen previously are a thing of the past.
charisma.explanation: Calls for unanimity (unifying), but dismisses past dissent as something to be left behind, which slightly undercuts the inclusiveness.

charisma.statement: It is indeed an advantage to all exporters—and importers of the European products, as well—to get this legislation through. I have to acknowledge the speed with which the EU and its Parliament passed it through, so I want to thank them.
charisma.explanation: Praises the incoming government and EU partners — generous, cross-party and cross-border goodwill.

charisma.statement: The National Government brought that model in—and I want to thank you for that—some time ago.
charisma.explanation: Credits the opposing party for creating Pharmac — generous, bridge-building across the aisle.

charisma.statement: We’re particularly concerned about Māori rights and interests. I want to respect the fact that there were hundreds of Māori advisers and negotiators involved in this. So I respect that they arrived at a point that they were satisfactory, but we do want to pay attention to that.
charisma.explanation: Balances a critical concern with respect for others' input, inviting scrutiny rather than condemnation.

charisma.statement: Volatility is the enemy of farmers all around the world—not each other—and New Zealand should strive, through high-quality trade deals, to show the way forward.
charisma.explanation: Reframes farmers as allies rather than competitors — unifying, common-ground framing across nations.

charisma.statement: I would encourage members speaking to this to get their facts correct before they stand up in this House and make accusations that are actually quite inaccurate and not particularly helpful to the debate.
charisma.explanation: Admonishing rather than persuasive — likely to alienate the members it addresses rather than bring them along.

charisma.statement: Can I pay my accolades to the New Zealand trade team: one of the best trade teams in the world led by one of the best public servants in New Zealand: Vangelis Vitalis... tough as old boots, but as principled as anything and really does a fantastic job for New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Warm, unifying recognition of officials that the whole House can rally behind.

charisma.statement: When we succeed we often do so standing on the shoulders of those who have gone before us. There are two generations of Kiwis that bled in Europe, that stood side by side with them in their darkest hours.
charisma.explanation: Evocative, unifying invocation of shared NZ-Europe history likely to resonate across the House.

charisma.statement: The fact that there will be, as the Minister said in his opening remarks, $100 million in tariff savings from day one—that’s worth something. That’s worth something to our fantastic onion-growing industry.
charisma.explanation: Accepts and amplifies a figure raised by the Minister opposite — cooperative, cross-bench tone.

charisma.statement: You can also believe and understand that this country is a trading nation—we would not exist, we couldn’t survive in the modern world, without open access to international markets. We cannot do otherwise. So that contradiction is one of the great challenges of our foreign policy.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the validity of both pro- and anti-trade concerns, inviting a shared reckoning rather than picking a tribe.

specificity.statement: With a GDP of around $27 trillion and a population of 450 million consumers, the EU represents an important and valuable market for New Zealand businesses looking to sell overseas.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (GDP, population) to size the market.

specificity.statement: As a result of the NZ-EU FTA, New Zealand exporters will benefit from $100 million in additional tariff savings from day one of entry into force.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure and timing (day one).

specificity.statement: Once fully implemented, this FTA has the potential to boost our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year and our GDP by up to $1.4 billion per year.
specificity.explanation: Quantified projections with figures and an annual timeframe, though 'up to' caps rather than commits.

specificity.statement: From the day of the agreement entering into force, 91 percent of New Zealand’s current trade with the EU will enter duty-free through a combination of tariff elimination and duty-free quotas.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage, timing and mechanism (tariff elimination plus quotas).

specificity.statement: Under the FTA, New Zealand has agreed to protect 1,975 EU geographical indications (GIs) on day one, with the potential for up to 30 additional GIs to be added every three years by mutual agreement.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts, cadence and mechanism for adding GIs.

specificity.statement: One was Pharmac... and so we’ve protected the right, against what was an EU demand at the start, to continue to negotiate affordable pharmaceuticals for our country.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific issue (Pharmac, pharmaceutical pricing) protected, though without detailed mechanism.

specificity.statement: We put up the reality that Māori play a bigger part in our economy, and said that we want to ensure that they had opportunities under a trade-for-all policy. So we included that chapter, which, again, is leading the way for international trade agreements.
specificity.explanation: Names the chapter and policy framing but light on substantive detail of what it secures.

specificity.statement: I recall during the dairy downturn of 2014-17, work that was done internationally showed that interfering in the market might well delay the impact, but that impact still came and the recovery took longer than it needed to. This work showed that most countries’ domestic price will follow the world price.
specificity.explanation: Concrete period (2014-17), price-lag figures and a mechanism.

specificity.statement: New Zealand had access to around 13 percent of world consumption at tariff rates less than 10 percent. Effectively, what that 13 percent represents is the freely traded world market, which pretty much sets the world price.
specificity.explanation: Quantified shares and tariff thresholds underpin the argument.

specificity.statement: The EU is New Zealand’s fourth-largest trading partner and one of our most important markets. Under this bill, New Zealand’s conditions of access will be significantly improved, hence this piece of legislation is incredibly valuable to our market.
specificity.explanation: States the ranking but 'significantly improved' and 'incredibly valuable' are unquantified.

specificity.statement: It was Māori who signed Aotearoa’s first ever trade agreement in 1835, He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence, so that Māori could continue to trade and export our goods overseas without being treated like pirates and having our ships detained.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, year and concrete motivation.

specificity.statement: Any trade agreement that is not born off Te Tiriti o Waitangi is not legitimate in the eyes of Te Pāti Māori.
specificity.explanation: A firm standard but without spelling out what Tiriti-based negotiation would concretely require.

specificity.statement: Whilst this is the first free-trade agreement with the EU to include a specific chapter on Māori trade, the Treaty of Waitangi exception clause allowing more favourable treatment to Māori remains unchanged from previous free-trade agreements dating back to 2001.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the clause, its origin year and what has and hasn't changed.

specificity.statement: This just seems ridiculous at a time when Māori are more than 50 percent of forest and fish, 20 percent of sheep and beef, and 12 percent of dairy.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete sector-by-sector percentages.

specificity.statement: Our fourth-largest, covering about $20-odd billion worth of two-way goods, and one-in-four jobs in New Zealand directly related to that trade importance in our economy.
specificity.explanation: Cites trade value, ranking and the jobs ratio.

specificity.statement: Where the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership went wrong was that the class of investments that could be screened for was closed by that agreement and therefore, after that agreement came into effect, New Zealand could not introduce any new areas of investment to be screened under our screening regime.
specificity.explanation: Precise on the legal mechanism (closed investment class, MFN clauses applying to investment not tariffs).

specificity.statement: In particular, I want to acknowledge the contribution this makes to our horticultural industry... the farmers in Horowhenua, a $714 million industry, and for them that’s a $46 million saving immediately when this comes into force.
specificity.explanation: Concrete industry value and immediate saving figures tied to his electorate.

specificity.statement: This agreement has labour standards—it allows the EU and New Zealand to hold each other to account on our climate commitments, on animal welfare, on gender commitments through the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete enforceable areas (labour, climate, animal welfare, CEDAW gender commitments).

specificity.statement: Under the free-trade agreement, New Zealand’s conditions of access will be significantly improved, with 91 percent of New Zealand’s current goods trade to the EU able to enter duty-free from day one... This will rise to 97 percent after seven years, with estimated tariff savings exceeding $100 million from day one—the highest immediate tariff savings of any New Zealand FTA—growing to $110 million after seven years.
specificity.explanation: Dense with precise figures, percentages and timeframes (91%/97%, $100m/$110m, seven years).

specificity.statement: Zespri, another one of our organisations in horticulture that has a massive contribution, said that the agreement would benefit its sector by up to $46 million, which it paid out in 2022 in tariffs on $1 billion of exports.
specificity.explanation: Names the company, the benefit figure, the year and the export value.

divination.statement: Once fully implemented, this FTA has the potential to boost our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year and our GDP by up to $1.4 billion per year.
divination.explanation: A forecast of future export/GDP gains; consistent with MFAT modelling but hedged with 'up to' and dependent on full implementation.

divination.statement: It’s interesting that Europe agreed to no ISDS clauses in this agreement. It’s something that if the new Government and their future trade aspirations bring back ISDS clauses, there will be difficulty in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts political difficulty if a future government reintroduces ISDS — plausible given the historical controversy, but contingent and unfalsifiable in timeframe.

divination.statement: Whilst it will be an incredible boost for many sectors, it’ll also provide an improvement to the returns of dairy and beef and lamb.
divination.explanation: Predicts improved dairy/beef/lamb returns, but other speakers stressed access for those very sectors was disappointing and below expectations, making a meaningful uplift uncertain.

civility.statement: While the deal has not met everybody’s expectations, particularly for dairy and meat, where farmers’ expectations have not been met, when considered as a whole, this FTA nevertheless represents a valuable opportunity for New Zealanders in other sectors.
civility.explanation: Candidly concedes the deal's shortcomings for dairy/meat rather than overselling — honest, substance-focused.

civility.statement: I want to recognise the significant efforts of officials within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade and our skilled trade negotiators, as well as former trade Minister Damien O’Connor for his work on this agreement.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of a political opponent's contribution.

civility.statement: It is indeed an advantage to all exporters—and importers of the European products, as well—to get this legislation through. I have to acknowledge the speed with which the EU and its Parliament passed it through, so I want to thank them.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious acknowledgements throughout.

civility.statement: We’re particularly concerned about Māori rights and interests. I want to respect the fact that there were hundreds of Māori advisers and negotiators involved in this. So I respect that they arrived at a point that they were satisfactory, but we do want to pay attention to that.
civility.explanation: Raises a concern while respectfully acknowledging the Māori advisers involved — substance-focused, no personal attack.

civility.statement: It is disappointing, however, that we could not get access for meat and dairy exports at such a level.
civility.explanation: Candid, measured criticism of the deal's limits without personalising blame.
