civility.statement: We’d like to acknowledge the tangata whenua groups, such as the Federation of Māori Authorities and Te Taumata, who have endorsed and supported this FTA as they continue to strive to do the best for their people.
civility.explanation: Respectfully acknowledges Māori groups who hold the opposite position to his, without disparaging them.

civility.statement: Beneath the surface, however, this is just another form of soft colonisation in 2024, and Te Pāti Māori will not be supporting the bill.
civility.explanation: Charged 'soft colonisation' framing is provocative, but it is aimed at the policy/process rather than a personal attack on an individual.

civility.statement: I would encourage members speaking to this to get their facts correct before they stand up in this House and make accusations that are actually quite inaccurate and not particularly helpful to the debate.
civility.explanation: A pointed rebuke implying other members (Te Pāti Māori) are factually careless; targets their credibility rather than engaging the specific claims, though stops short of a personal insult.

civility.statement: With respect, the comments by the Māori Party are incorrect; the Treaty provisions in this agreement are as good as they have been in any other agreement. There is no other country in the world that manages to secure the level of protection that we do for a founding document like the Treaty of Waitangi than New Zealand does.
civility.explanation: Directly rebuts Te Pāti Māori on the substance ('with respect', focused on the Treaty provisions) rather than attacking them personally.

civility.statement: Can I pay my accolades to the New Zealand trade team: one of the best trade teams in the world led by one of the best public servants in New Zealand: Vangelis Vitalis... tough as old boots, but as principled as anything and really does a fantastic job for New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Generous and respectful tone.

civility.statement: Can I just thank our ambassador to the EU, His Excellency Carl Reaich... and the many European citizens that we employ to work in our embassy but they work to serve New Zealand; they work tirelessly for New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Gracious, detailed recognition of officials by name — respectful and constructive.

authenticity.statement: While the deal has not met everybody’s expectations, particularly for dairy and meat, where farmers’ expectations have not been met, when considered as a whole, this FTA nevertheless represents a valuable opportunity for New Zealanders in other sectors.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges limitations openly rather than claiming an unalloyed win, consistent with the mixed outcome.

authenticity.statement: In the past, the Green Party has often been the lone voice in Parliament when it comes to some of the concerns around free-trade agreements, and I just want to reflect on what some of our concerns have been over the course of the last several decades.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the party's longstanding consistent scepticism on FTAs, setting up a transparent account of where the party has stood.

authenticity.statement: The EU FTA doesn’t contain most of the things that we’ve historically previously been worried about and it does contain some of the things that we wanted to see in those trade agreements, such as enforceable provisions around climate and the environment. So it would be inconsistent of us not to support the EU FTA, given that the very things that we had previously been concerned about have actually been reversed in this agreement.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly reasons that supporting this deal is consistent with the party's prior positions because the agreement reverses their specific past objections — principled application of a stated standard.

authenticity.statement: It is disappointing, however, that we could not get access for meat and dairy exports at such a level.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with ACT/farming constituency concerns; honest about a shortfall while still supporting the bill.

authenticity.statement: Any trade agreement that is not born off Te Tiriti o Waitangi is not legitimate in the eyes of Te Pāti Māori.
authenticity.explanation: States a clear principle consistent with the party's stance and the basis for voting against — a principled, predictable position.

authenticity.statement: We’d like to acknowledge the tangata whenua groups, such as the Federation of Māori Authorities and Te Taumata, who have endorsed and supported this FTA as they continue to strive to do the best for their people.
authenticity.explanation: Concedes that respected Māori bodies back the deal even while he opposes it — candid rather than one-sided.

authenticity.statement: Twenty years after I was organising those demonstrations, I found myself as Minister for Trade and Export Growth in our Government here in 2020, welcoming a multi-party delegation of European members of Parliament who said that this EU - New Zealand trade agreement is gold standard.
authenticity.explanation: Openly reconciles his past anti-trade-agreement activism with later support for this deal — a defensible, transparently explained evolution rather than a hidden flip-flop.

authenticity.statement: Whilst it will be an incredible boost for many sectors, it’ll also provide an improvement to the returns of dairy and beef and lamb.
authenticity.explanation: Sits in mild tension with the repeated cross-party acknowledgement that dairy and meat access fell short — a more optimistic gloss than the deal's terms support.

strength.statement: One was Pharmac... and so we’ve protected the right, against what was an EU demand at the start, to continue to negotiate affordable pharmaceuticals for our country.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete negotiated protection (Pharmac) that was in fact preserved in the final agreement — delivered defensive outcome.

strength.statement: We put up the reality that Māori play a bigger part in our economy, and said that we want to ensure that they had opportunities under a trade-for-all policy. So we included that chapter, which, again, is leading the way for international trade agreements.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete deliverable (the Māori trade chapter) that was actually included in the agreement.

rigor.statement: When you look at how investor-State dispute settlement mechanisms have been applied through history, the vast majority of them were on environmental grounds and the vast majority of them found in favour of the litigant and overturned environmental provisions.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based reasoning citing the historical pattern of ISDS cases to justify the concern, though the specific 'vast majority' claims are stated without source.

rigor.statement: The EU FTA doesn’t contain most of the things that we’ve historically previously been worried about and it does contain some of the things that we wanted to see in those trade agreements, such as enforceable provisions around climate and the environment. So it would be inconsistent of us not to support the EU FTA, given that the very things that we had previously been concerned about have actually been reversed in this agreement.
rigor.explanation: Clear logical entailment: prior concerns were X, this deal removes X and adds the wanted provisions, therefore support follows.

rigor.statement: I recall during the dairy downturn of 2014-17, work that was done internationally showed that interfering in the market might well delay the impact, but that impact still came and the recovery took longer than it needed to. This work showed that most countries’ domestic price will follow the world price.
rigor.explanation: Argues from cited international evidence and a worked example to support the open-markets conclusion; reasoning is coherent though the studies are unnamed.

rigor.statement: When our rural sectors are able to get better returns for our products, the benefit flows through to all our local communities... By earning less for our export products, it limits what we as a nation can buy offshore, such as medicines.
rigor.explanation: A plausible flow-through argument linking export returns to community spending and import capacity, but asserted causally without supporting data.

rigor.statement: Whilst this is the first free-trade agreement with the EU to include a specific chapter on Māori trade, the Treaty of Waitangi exception clause allowing more favourable treatment to Māori remains unchanged from previous free-trade agreements dating back to 2001.
rigor.explanation: Uses the unchanged-since-2001 clause as evidence that protections have not advanced despite the growing Māori economy — a coherent evidentiary point.

rigor.statement: Beneath the surface, however, this is just another form of soft colonisation in 2024, and Te Pāti Māori will not be supporting the bill.
rigor.explanation: Strong sweeping characterisation asserted rather than demonstrated from the specific provisions.

rigor.statement: If there’s a level of dissatisfaction on both sides of the trade agreement, then you’ve probably got the balance about right.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical heuristic ('both sides unhappy means it's balanced') presented as reasoning; intuitive but not logically sound evidence of a good deal.

rigor.statement: With respect, the comments by the Māori Party are incorrect; the Treaty provisions in this agreement are as good as they have been in any other agreement. There is no other country in the world that manages to secure the level of protection that we do for a founding document like the Treaty of Waitangi than New Zealand does.
rigor.explanation: Explains why the clause cannot be re-opened or improved deal-by-deal without endangering it — a coherent structural argument.

rigor.statement: Where the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership went wrong was that the class of investments that could be screened for was closed by that agreement and therefore, after that agreement came into effect, New Zealand could not introduce any new areas of investment to be screened under our screening regime.
rigor.explanation: Detailed, mechanistic explanation of how CPTPP's ratchet/most-favoured-nation provisions constrained investment screening — premises lead clearly to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: When we succeed we often do so standing on the shoulders of those who have gone before us. There are two generations of Kiwis that bled in Europe, that stood side by side with them in their darkest hours.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to history and emotion (wartime sacrifice) to frame the trade relationship rather than an evidentiary argument about the deal's merits.

rigor.statement: You can also believe and understand that this country is a trading nation—we would not exist, we couldn’t survive in the modern world, without open access to international markets. We cannot do otherwise. So that contradiction is one of the great challenges of our foreign policy.
rigor.explanation: Sets out the genuine tension between FTA scepticism and NZ's dependence on trade and reasons honestly about navigating it rather than resolving it glibly.

charisma.statement: To the new and returning members on the other side of the House, congratulations. It is important for our democracy that people are still prepared to stand for Parliament and to take on this unique role. I look forward to working with all MPs over this term.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, bipartisan tone — congratulates opponents and expresses willingness to work across the House.

charisma.statement: while I'll bring a classical liberal lens, I'm always willing to speak with others who share a desire for a better Government—for a better New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Signals openness to working across ideological lines and finding common ground while stating his own position.

charisma.statement: Finally, to everyone in this House: I'm here to debate the issues, to put my views and solutions forward. I look forward to playing the ball, not the man or the woman.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, good-humoured framing directed at the whole House rather than rallying one side.

charisma.statement: giving the benefit of the doubt to your neighbour or saying gidday to the person you pass on the street: little things which maintain trust and openness.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive evocation of shared everyday civic values that invites everyone in rather than dividing.

civility.statement: To the new and returning members on the other side of the House, congratulations. It is important for our democracy that people are still prepared to stand for Parliament and to take on this unique role. I look forward to working with all MPs over this term.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of opponents and of democratic participation; no attack.

civility.statement: Finally, to everyone in this House: I'm here to debate the issues, to put my views and solutions forward. I look forward to playing the ball, not the man or the woman.
civility.explanation: Explicit commitment to issue-focused debate over personal attacks ('play the ball, not the man').

civility.statement: The day kura hourua was stopped by the "kind" previous Government, I decided that, in whatever way I could, I would help the political party who gave—if even for a moment—that chance to Kiwi kids.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic scare-quotes on 'kind' aimed at the previous Government — a pointed jab, though tied to a policy grievance rather than a personal insult.

authenticity.statement: I'm proud only to have ever voted ACT, supporting the party even in the bleakest of times when the liberal flame was almost extinguished.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent long-standing allegiance backed by his stated record of campaigning at four elections and serving on the ACT board — words match a verifiable pattern of action.

authenticity.statement: I was able to get up and speak about what we had done, all without subsidies
authenticity.explanation: Words matched deeds — contrasts his record of completed action against others' stated intentions.

strength.statement: I'm committed to working with David Seymour to deliver a modern, efficient, and effective medicines access process so Kiwis can get the world's best treatments.
strength.explanation: Stated intent in a maiden speech with no delivery yet; commitment to act, not demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: I was able to get up and speak about what we had done, all without subsidies
strength.explanation: Claims delivered (done, not merely intended) environmental action on-farm, distinguishing himself from other farmers who 'intended to do'; some follow-through demonstrated.

strength.statement: With initiatives like partnership schools, we empower parents, students, edu-preneurs, and iwi to forge a new educational path.
strength.explanation: Aspirational framing of a policy direction with no delivery shown.

specificity.statement: I'm committed to working with David Seymour to deliver a modern, efficient, and effective medicines access process so Kiwis can get the world's best treatments.
specificity.explanation: Names a goal (medicines access reform) and a collaborator, but gives no mechanism, figures, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We have seen the growth of catchment groups, and I see dairy farmers talking with pride at how much fencing of waterways they have done.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete developments (catchment groups, waterway fencing) but with no figures or scale.

specificity.statement: The fact is: rules and regulations are crippling innovation and growth.
specificity.explanation: Sweeping slogan with no named regulation, sector, figure, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: With initiatives like partnership schools, we empower parents, students, edu-preneurs, and iwi to forge a new educational path.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (partnership schools) and intended beneficiaries, but no detail on number, funding, or timing.

specificity.statement: Small businesses, the lifeblood of our economy, will excel in this House if we allow them. By unwinding stifling regulation, we can foster a dynamic market that positions New Zealand globally as it's open to business.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration ('unwinding stifling regulation') with no named rules or measures.

specificity.statement: As our leaders get further away from the site of production, further from how buildings are built, food is grown, fish are caught, resources harvested, and services provided, it is no wonder that we have a productivity crisis.
specificity.explanation: Evocative but vague; no measure of productivity or named cause beyond the metaphor.

rigor.statement: It's a great example of where the private sector is doing something no Government could or should do. No Government could manage the complexity, let alone accept the considerable cost and risks involved.
rigor.explanation: An assertion about state vs private capacity drawn from his industry experience, but sweeping ('no Government could') and offered without evidence.

rigor.statement: Farmers are not afraid or reluctant to change; we are constantly looking for better ways to do things.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping generalisation about all farmers supported only by personal anecdote (his own farm changing 'night and day').

rigor.statement: The fact is: rules and regulations are crippling innovation and growth.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic blanket assertion ('crippling') presented as 'the fact' with no evidence.

rigor.statement: Contrary to expectations, statistics reveal a concerning uptick in serious workplace incidents and fatalities. This begs the critical question: how can this worrying trend persist, despite excessive safety protocols?
rigor.explanation: Implies safety protocols cause (or fail to prevent) more harm by juxtaposing them — a correlation-as-causation move with no controlled evidence.

rigor.statement: Big business—who can easily afford to implement complex protocols—enjoy the fact that smaller would-be competitors face barriers to open and grow.
rigor.explanation: A coherent regulatory-capture / fixed-compliance-cost argument, plausible in mechanism but asserted without supporting data.

rigor.statement: As our leaders get further away from the site of production, further from how buildings are built, food is grown, fish are caught, resources harvested, and services provided, it is no wonder that we have a productivity crisis.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that leaders' distance from production causes the productivity crisis — a single-cause claim ('no wonder') with no evidence.

rigor.statement: The only thing that has ever innovated and produced more in this world is private citizens working for themselves, their families, communities, and each other.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping absolute ('the only thing that has ever') presented as self-evident; ignores public-sector and collective innovation, no evidence.

rigor.statement: how does a Government think they can change the direction of a housing supply crisis without changing the real factors which affect our ability to provide houses and actually build more?
rigor.explanation: A reasonable challenge — outcomes won't change unless underlying constraints do — grounded in his trade experience, though the 'real factors' are left unspecified.

veracity.statement: I was able to get up and speak about what we had done, all without subsidies
veracity.explanation: NZ agriculture has operated without significant production subsidies since the mid-1980s reforms — the claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: 20 percent interest rates make life hard
veracity.explanation: Interest rates in 1980s New Zealand did reach around 20%; broadly accurate for the period he describes.

veracity.statement: We have seen the growth of catchment groups, and I see dairy farmers talking with pride at how much fencing of waterways they have done.
veracity.explanation: Catchment groups and waterway fencing did expand materially over the period; broadly accurate though impressionistic.

veracity.statement: The fact is: rules and regulations are crippling innovation and growth.
veracity.explanation: An exaggerated, unqualified claim treating all regulation as harmful; misleading through overstatement.

veracity.statement: Contrary to expectations, statistics reveal a concerning uptick in serious workplace incidents and fatalities. This begs the critical question: how can this worrying trend persist, despite excessive safety protocols?
veracity.explanation: Appeals to unspecified 'statistics'; NZ serious-harm and fatality trends are mixed, so the unqualified 'uptick' claim is partly contestable.

veracity.statement: as the only licensed building practitioner ever elected to this House
veracity.explanation: A specific, plausible biographical claim about his unique trade qualification in Parliament; likely true but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: The only thing that has ever innovated and produced more in this world is private citizens working for themselves, their families, communities, and each other.
veracity.explanation: An overstated universal claim that is straightforwardly contestable; misleading through absolutism.

divination.statement: If the feeling amongst farmers becomes "Why do I bother to do all this, because there is nothing I am doing that is being recognised?", they will give up. They lose hope; they stop doing.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction about farmer behaviour if effort goes unrecognised — plausible and directionally reasonable but unfalsifiable in magnitude and timeframe.

divination.statement: Small businesses, the lifeblood of our economy, will excel in this House if we allow them. By unwinding stifling regulation, we can foster a dynamic market that positions New Zealand globally as it's open to business.
divination.explanation: Prediction that deregulation will produce a dynamic, globally competitive market — directional and optimistic, with no mechanism or magnitude to assess.

divination.statement: I believe strongly that if this doesn't get sorted, then the negative effects on every aspect of Kiwis' lives will lead to a broken future for our country which will be hard to repair.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction that an unresolved housing crisis leads to a 'broken future' — directionally plausible but vague and unfalsifiable in its sweep.

civility.statement: the Government put this bill into urgency and then spent most of Wednesday evening filibustering it in order to make it go slower.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's handling of the process, not a personal attack; 'filibustering' is loaded but aimed at conduct.

civility.statement: this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it. In other words, it is one of the worst examples of poor parliamentary process and governance and oversight that you can get in this Parliament
civility.explanation: Harsh but legitimate criticism of process and governance, not of any person.

civility.statement: if you take that to its logical extreme, you would also disestablish the Treasury... every Government in history has continuously ignored the advice of the Treasury, and yet you don't shut the Treasury down because you ignore its advice.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the opposing argument rather than the person.

civility.statement: I was just wondering if we could invite the member to refer to the bill that is up for debate rather than to debate something that isn't in the bill.
civility.explanation: Polite, procedural point of order with no personal edge.

civility.statement: it's amazing how our perspectives change when we only move a few metres across the House. All of a sudden, the member is understanding the frustrations with the urgency process and the use of it which we spent a lot of time railing against only a few months ago.
civility.explanation: Wry jab about a shift in position; targets the inconsistency, not the person.

civility.statement: Where the Productivity Commission wrote reports—and some of them were worthy; there's no doubt about that—it really contributed little to our economy.
civility.explanation: Concedes the reports' worth before disagreeing; courteous in tone.

civility.statement: Time and again, they have pulled out the shredder and said that they don't like the direction that the country is headed in and decided to rip up that direction, that plan, that blueprint.
civility.explanation: Metaphorical criticism of a pattern of governing; harsh but directed at conduct, not persons.

civility.statement: this is Government by slogan.
civility.explanation: A barbed but impersonal characterisation of the Government's approach.

civility.statement: this is yet another example of our far-right, race-baiting Government's commitment to New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Inflammatory labelling ('race-baiting', 'far-right') — a personal/character attack on the Government.

civility.statement: cancelling the Productivity Commission so that David Seymour can fund his new ministry of regulation razor gang vanity project.
civility.explanation: Derogatory framing ('razor gang vanity project') aimed at a named minister.

civility.statement: Even their leader has applauded the work of the Productivity Commission... he said that the Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work... In the next breath, he cuts their throat. He amputates them at the neck. With friends like David Seymour, who needs enemies?
civility.explanation: Violent imagery and a cutting jab at a named opponent.

civility.statement: he wants to—him and his ACT friends—take from the rich and give them tax cuts instead.
civility.explanation: Imputes self-serving motives to opponents.

civility.statement: the exact policy platform that is being articulated by the Atlas Network is being articulated by not just the ACT Party but by the Taxpayers' Union and the New Zealand Initiative. The question is: who is pulling David Seymour's strings?
civility.explanation: Implies a named minister is a puppet of foreign interests.

civility.statement: This particular bill is a bipartisan bill. It's good that we can, on these types of kaupapa, come together, because it is a really important bill.
civility.explanation: Warm, collaborative tone toward all parties.

civility.statement: We are already very clear that the New Zealand Productivity Commission is no longer serving its intended purposes. We need to seriously get to work and improve the quality of regulation and reduce Government spending. So stop wasting time.
civility.explanation: 'Stop wasting time' is dismissive of the debate but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: this Government does not care for public consultation or engagement in relation to important bills that come before the House.
civility.explanation: Sweeping criticism of the Government's conduct; targets behaviour but generalises.

civility.statement: I think what it is is because it’s a personality issue—a personality issue... If that’s the case—you just don’t like the chair—change it. That’s your discretion as the Minister. Don’t, basically, remove the public debate
civility.explanation: Mildly barbed attribution of motive, but engages the policy choice.

civility.statement: an ideologically driven, one-person-knows-best solution from the Minister David Seymour.
civility.explanation: Characterises a named minister as ideological and arrogant — edges into personal criticism.

civility.statement: I just want to acknowledge the Hon Willie Jackson there. I’m quite new to the House and I learnt some good material there. “Razor gang vanity project”, “social-good vandalism”, and “overseas far-right thinktanks”. There’s some awesome material there that I can use. Thank you for that
civility.explanation: Good-humoured ribbing rather than a sharp attack; lightens the tone.

civility.statement: Has National finally run out of things to disestablish? Maybe they have. Is it now that they’re actually passing Labour legislation because they’ve run out of their own bills to put?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic jab at the Government; rhetorical rather than substantive.

civility.statement: is the point of registering social workers so that they can keep tabs on how many they’re going to fire when they bring in social investment and get rid of the Public Service.
civility.explanation: Imputes a sinister motive to the Government for supporting the bill.

civility.statement: I would oppose that consideration for the simple fact that many of our community members that can go through and become qualified actually are quite busy—very busy looking after their families, going through the cost of living crisis, and other duties.
civility.explanation: Respectful plea to the Minister, focused on the substance.

civility.statement: “Kumbaya” had broken out until Ginny Andersen got to her feet and launched an unprovoked attack on this Government when we were just trying to be the nation’s great unifiers.
civility.explanation: A light but pointed jab at a named opponent, framed humorously.

civility.statement: Can I congratulate the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon on leading the National Party into Government and becoming New Zealand’s 42nd Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Gracious, courteous acknowledgement.

civility.statement: To the Rt Hon Winston Peters, congratulations on leading New Zealand First back into Parliament and Government. People can say many things about the current Deputy Prime Minister and foreign Minister, but you can’t question his commitment to public service.
civility.explanation: Respectful and complimentary.

veracity.statement: the Government put this bill into urgency and then spent most of Wednesday evening filibustering it in order to make it go slower.
veracity.explanation: Plausible characterisation of the urgency debate, but 'filibustering' is an interpretive framing of opponents' speeches rather than an established fact.

veracity.statement: this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it. In other words, it is one of the worst examples of poor parliamentary process and governance and oversight that you can get in this Parliament
veracity.explanation: The factual core (no submissions, no select committee, urgency, no RIS) is accurate for a bill passed under urgency.

veracity.statement: It was referred to as the Clean Car Discount, which was implemented in the last term, and it led to a more than 1,200 percent increase in the uptake of electric vehicles.
veracity.explanation: The Clean Car Discount did sharply lift EV uptake, but a '1,200 percent' figure depends on a low baseline and chosen window, so it likely overstates the typical effect.

veracity.statement: Where the Productivity Commission wrote reports—and some of them were worthy; there's no doubt about that—it really contributed little to our economy.
veracity.explanation: Unsupported and hard-to-verify causal claim about economic contribution.

veracity.statement: we here are working under urgency with this legislation through a process in which there has been no public consultation nor submissions.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the urgency process used for this bill.

veracity.statement: the Productivity Commission was originally an innovation of the ACT Party.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — the Commission (established 2010) was championed by ACT under the confidence-and-supply arrangement; 'innovation of ACT' is a fair shorthand.

veracity.statement: prior to quoting, just advice against the establishment of the accommodation supplement which we now see paid out to the tune of $2 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Accommodation supplement spending in the order of ~$2 billion a year is broadly accurate; the historical-advice claim is harder to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: cancelling the Productivity Commission so that David Seymour can fund his new ministry of regulation razor gang vanity project.
veracity.explanation: Contains a factual kernel (Commission funds redirected to a regulation ministry) wrapped in loaded characterisation.

veracity.statement: he wants to—him and his ACT friends—take from the rich and give them tax cuts instead.
veracity.explanation: Speculative attribution of motive presented as fact; not established in the text.

veracity.statement: the exact policy platform that is being articulated by the Atlas Network is being articulated by not just the ACT Party but by the Taxpayers' Union and the New Zealand Initiative. The question is: who is pulling David Seymour's strings?
veracity.explanation: The claim of an 'exact' shared platform controlled by an overseas network is asserted, not substantiated.

veracity.statement: this Government does not care for public consultation or engagement in relation to important bills that come before the House.
veracity.explanation: Has a factual basis for this bill's process, but 'does not care' is an overgeneralisation.

veracity.statement: It was Bill English who said it was about encouraging high-level debate.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific rationale to a named figure at the Commission's founding; consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: David Seymour was reported in a press conference on 5 September 2023 saying it had been “frankly hijacked” and that he wouldn’t have appointed the chair that it currently has.
veracity.explanation: A datable, attributable quote presented with specifics; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: We have one of the lowest productivities in the world in terms of who we are.
veracity.explanation: NZ does have low labour productivity relative to the OECD, but 'one of the lowest in the world' overstates it across all countries.

veracity.statement: There was a report done by a woman called Gail Pacheco... she looked specifically at pay gaps... Gail Pacheco looked at the wellbeing of people, and she looked at what was going on in terms of breaking the cycle of persistent disadvantage.
veracity.explanation: Describes the Commission's wellbeing/disadvantage work plausibly and checkably.

veracity.statement: In terms of construction costs, we are in the bottom 10 percent of the OECD—the Infrastructure Commission’s told us that.
veracity.explanation: A sourced, plausible claim about NZ's relative construction costs.

veracity.statement: the Social Workers Registration Act initially brought in the rules around this, back in 2003. It established occupation regulations to ensure that social workers are fit to practise and accountable.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 2003 Act and its purpose.

veracity.statement: the reality is that we have come through to 2024 and we are some 700 vacancies short and we just simply don’t have the people that we need.
veracity.explanation: The ~700 social worker vacancy figure is consistent with what is cited elsewhere in the debate.

veracity.statement: is the point of registering social workers so that they can keep tabs on how many they’re going to fire when they bring in social investment and get rid of the Public Service.
veracity.explanation: Speculative motive presented insinuatingly, not evidenced.

veracity.statement: a programme of 6.5 percent cuts to all social services will directly impact people like social workers in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Refers to the Government's baseline savings target; '6.5 percent to all social services' is roughly drawn from announced cut targets.

veracity.statement: around about 700 vacancies for social workers across this country.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the vacancy figure cited by other speakers and the Registration Board.

veracity.statement: section 13 of the Social Workers Registration Act of 2003 provides this alternative experience pathway to registration for people who have had extensive practical experience but who do not have the prescribed qualification.
veracity.explanation: Accurate statement of what section 13 provides.

veracity.statement: the Social Workers Registration Board estimate that there are 700 unfulfilled social worker vacancies currently.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the 700-vacancy figure to the Board; consistent and sourced.

veracity.statement: Can I congratulate the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon on leading the National Party into Government and becoming New Zealand’s 42nd Prime Minister.
veracity.explanation: Luxon becoming the 42nd Prime Minister of New Zealand is accurate.

specificity.statement: this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it. In other words, it is one of the worst examples of poor parliamentary process and governance and oversight that you can get in this Parliament
specificity.explanation: Names concrete procedural defects (submissions, select committee, RIS).

specificity.statement: It was referred to as the Clean Car Discount, which was implemented in the last term, and it led to a more than 1,200 percent increase in the uptake of electric vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and gives a precise quantified outcome.

specificity.statement: It's very easy to make that problem go away: you set up an independent appointments panel. It's at arm's length from the Minister, and appointments are done on the basis of merit, the people who are appointed to the appointments panel are human resources experts and recruitment experts and not Ministers
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative mechanism (independent merit-based appointments panel) though without detail on how it would be constituted.

specificity.statement: we know red tape is a problem, and we will be able to put this money to a better place and to a better spend.
specificity.explanation: Vague — no figures, mechanism, or named destination for the money.

specificity.statement: we here are working under urgency with this legislation through a process in which there has been no public consultation nor submissions.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific procedural omissions (consultation, submissions).

specificity.statement: this is Government by slogan.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-like put-down with no concrete content of its own.

specificity.statement: prior to quoting, just advice against the establishment of the accommodation supplement which we now see paid out to the tune of $2 billion a year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete dollar figure tied to a named policy.

specificity.statement: we've got to drive those sectors that produce, and that's agriculture, that's supporting our exporters, that's supporting our businesses... and that is reducing red tape, reducing regulation, and reducing compliance.
specificity.explanation: Names sectors but offers no mechanism, target, or measure for how regulation would be reduced.

specificity.statement: some of our best Māori social workers had community and life experience... we had actually engaged former gang members... Who better to address some of the domestic violence that was going on in some of the homes that we were working with than ex-gang members who'd turned their lives around?
specificity.explanation: Concrete example (ex-gang members addressing domestic violence) illustrating the point.

specificity.statement: We are already very clear that the New Zealand Productivity Commission is no longer serving its intended purposes. We need to seriously get to work and improve the quality of regulation and reduce Government spending. So stop wasting time.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a conclusion with no detail on how regulation or spending would change.

specificity.statement: It was Bill English who said it was about encouraging high-level debate.
specificity.explanation: Names the person and the stated purpose.

specificity.statement: David Seymour was reported in a press conference on 5 September 2023 saying it had been “frankly hijacked” and that he wouldn’t have appointed the chair that it currently has.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact date, source, and quoted words.

specificity.statement: I think what it is is because it’s a personality issue—a personality issue... If that’s the case—you just don’t like the chair—change it. That’s your discretion as the Minister. Don’t, basically, remove the public debate
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete alternative (replace the chair) within the Minister's power.

specificity.statement: This bill is about evolution. It’s evolution of how we as a country can improve the productivity that we so dearly need.
specificity.explanation: Abstract framing ('evolution') with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: It’s an outcome that will improve people’s lives, it will improve people’s lifestyles, and it will improve people’s livelihoods.
specificity.explanation: Triple platitude with no measure, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: I, for one, during these debates, have learnt that perhaps what we needed to do was actually further depoliticise. We probably needed to move to a model where the person appointed was not appointed by the Minister and we probably needed to move to a model where those reports came to Parliament and we looked at them and we had to respond to them
specificity.explanation: Names concrete reforms (non-ministerial appointment, reports tabled and responded to in Parliament).

specificity.statement: There was a report done by a woman called Gail Pacheco... she looked specifically at pay gaps... Gail Pacheco looked at the wellbeing of people, and she looked at what was going on in terms of breaking the cycle of persistent disadvantage.
specificity.explanation: Names the researcher and the concrete subject matter (pay gaps, persistent disadvantage).

specificity.statement: In terms of construction costs, we are in the bottom 10 percent of the OECD—the Infrastructure Commission’s told us that.
specificity.explanation: Quantified ranking attributed to a named source.

specificity.statement: We don’t need the Productivity Commission anymore; it’s the end of a season.
specificity.explanation: Metaphorical conclusion with no supporting detail.

specificity.statement: the Social Workers Registration Act initially brought in the rules around this, back in 2003. It established occupation regulations to ensure that social workers are fit to practise and accountable.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, year, and its function.

specificity.statement: the reality is that we have come through to 2024 and we are some 700 vacancies short and we just simply don’t have the people that we need.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete shortfall figure to justify the bill.

specificity.statement: a programme of 6.5 percent cuts to all social services will directly impact people like social workers in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Quantified claim tied to a named policy effect.

specificity.statement: this bill allows those that don’t have the necessary qualifications but have the experience—it gives them the opportunity to continue to serve their communities.
specificity.explanation: Clearly states what the bill does (retains the experience pathway).

specificity.statement: around about 700 vacancies for social workers across this country.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete workforce-shortage number.

specificity.statement: I would oppose that consideration for the simple fact that many of our community members that can go through and become qualified actually are quite busy—very busy looking after their families, going through the cost of living crisis, and other duties.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete constraints (family duties, cost of living) but no figures.

specificity.statement: section 13 of the Social Workers Registration Act of 2003 provides this alternative experience pathway to registration for people who have had extensive practical experience but who do not have the prescribed qualification.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact section, statute, and what it does.

specificity.statement: the Social Workers Registration Board estimate that there are 700 unfulfilled social worker vacancies currently.
specificity.explanation: Quantified figure with named source.

rigor.statement: this bill has had no submissions and no select committee hearing, it was put through under urgency, and it has no regulatory impact statement attached to it. In other words, it is one of the worst examples of poor parliamentary process and governance and oversight that you can get in this Parliament
rigor.explanation: Premises (process failures) support the conclusion, though 'one of the worst' is a strong inference from listed facts.

rigor.statement: if you take that to its logical extreme, you would also disestablish the Treasury... every Government in history has continuously ignored the advice of the Treasury, and yet you don't shut the Treasury down because you ignore its advice.
rigor.explanation: A reductio ad absurdum that exposes a flaw in the 'governments ignore it, so abolish it' argument; relies on analogy but the logic holds.

rigor.statement: It's very easy to make that problem go away: you set up an independent appointments panel. It's at arm's length from the Minister, and appointments are done on the basis of merit, the people who are appointed to the appointments panel are human resources experts and recruitment experts and not Ministers
rigor.explanation: Offers a reasoned remedy to the politicisation concern rather than dismissing it.

rigor.statement: it's amazing how our perspectives change when we only move a few metres across the House. All of a sudden, the member is understanding the frustrations with the urgency process and the use of it which we spent a lot of time railing against only a few months ago.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque point — notes Shaw's earlier opposition to urgency, but uses it to deflect rather than defend the current use on its merits.

rigor.statement: Where the Productivity Commission wrote reports—and some of them were worthy; there's no doubt about that—it really contributed little to our economy.
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion that it 'contributed little' with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: Time and again, they have pulled out the shredder and said that they don't like the direction that the country is headed in and decided to rip up that direction, that plan, that blueprint.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a pattern by vivid metaphor rather than cited examples at this point.

rigor.statement: we've got to drive those sectors that produce, and that's agriculture, that's supporting our exporters, that's supporting our businesses... and that is reducing red tape, reducing regulation, and reducing compliance.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that cutting red tape drives productivity without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: this is yet another example of our far-right, race-baiting Government's commitment to New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem labelling substituted for argument; no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Even their leader has applauded the work of the Productivity Commission... he said that the Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work... In the next breath, he cuts their throat. He amputates them at the neck. With friends like David Seymour, who needs enemies?
rigor.explanation: Does land a genuine inconsistency (praising the work while abolishing it), but couched in rhetoric rather than argument.

rigor.statement: he wants to—him and his ACT friends—take from the rich and give them tax cuts instead.
rigor.explanation: Asserts hidden motive with no evidence.

rigor.statement: the exact policy platform that is being articulated by the Atlas Network is being articulated by not just the ACT Party but by the Taxpayers' Union and the New Zealand Initiative. The question is: who is pulling David Seymour's strings?
rigor.explanation: Guilt-by-association / insinuation of hidden control rather than demonstrated linkage.

rigor.statement: some of our best Māori social workers had community and life experience... we had actually engaged former gang members... Who better to address some of the domestic violence that was going on in some of the homes that we were working with than ex-gang members who'd turned their lives around?
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in first-hand experience rather than data — persuasive anecdote supporting the experience pathway.

rigor.statement: I think what it is is because it’s a personality issue—a personality issue... If that’s the case—you just don’t like the chair—change it. That’s your discretion as the Minister. Don’t, basically, remove the public debate
rigor.explanation: Builds a proportionality argument (a lesser remedy exists), though the 'personality issue' premise is speculative.

rigor.statement: I, for one, during these debates, have learnt that perhaps what we needed to do was actually further depoliticise. We probably needed to move to a model where the person appointed was not appointed by the Minister and we probably needed to move to a model where those reports came to Parliament and we looked at them and we had to respond to them
rigor.explanation: Reasoned proposal for de-politicising appointments and mandating parliamentary responses.

rigor.statement: In terms of construction costs, we are in the bottom 10 percent of the OECD—the Infrastructure Commission’s told us that.
rigor.explanation: Cites evidence from a named body to support the point.

rigor.statement: is the point of registering social workers so that they can keep tabs on how many they’re going to fire when they bring in social investment and get rid of the Public Service.
rigor.explanation: Insinuation rather than argument.

rigor.statement: I would oppose that consideration for the simple fact that many of our community members that can go through and become qualified actually are quite busy—very busy looking after their families, going through the cost of living crisis, and other duties.
rigor.explanation: Gives a reasoned ground (time pressure on multi-generational carers) for keeping the four-year window.

charisma.statement: It's very easy to make that problem go away: you set up an independent appointments panel. It's at arm's length from the Minister, and appointments are done on the basis of merit, the people who are appointed to the appointments panel are human resources experts and recruitment experts and not Ministers
charisma.explanation: Constructive, problem-solving tone that engages the opponents' stated concern.

charisma.statement: This particular bill is a bipartisan bill. It's good that we can, on these types of kaupapa, come together, because it is a really important bill.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly welcomes cross-party cooperation and common ground on the social workers bill.

charisma.statement: some of our best Māori social workers had community and life experience... we had actually engaged former gang members... Who better to address some of the domestic violence that was going on in some of the homes that we were working with than ex-gang members who'd turned their lives around?
charisma.explanation: Builds a relatable, inclusive case for valuing non-academic experience.

charisma.statement: I, for one, during these debates, have learnt that perhaps what we needed to do was actually further depoliticise. We probably needed to move to a model where the person appointed was not appointed by the Minister and we probably needed to move to a model where those reports came to Parliament and we looked at them and we had to respond to them
charisma.explanation: Concedes her own side's model was imperfect and offers constructive reform — bridge-building, not point-scoring.

charisma.statement: I just want to acknowledge the Hon Willie Jackson there. I’m quite new to the House and I learnt some good material there. “Razor gang vanity project”, “social-good vandalism”, and “overseas far-right thinktanks”. There’s some awesome material there that I can use. Thank you for that
charisma.explanation: Disarming, self-deprecating opener that engages an opponent warmly.

charisma.statement: “Kumbaya” had broken out until Ginny Andersen got to her feet and launched an unprovoked attack on this Government when we were just trying to be the nation’s great unifiers.
charisma.explanation: Casts his own side as unifiers, but does so by needling an opponent.

charisma.statement: Can I congratulate the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon on leading the National Party into Government and becoming New Zealand’s 42nd Prime Minister.
charisma.explanation: Warm, congratulatory tone toward a coalition partner's leader.

charisma.statement: To the Rt Hon Winston Peters, congratulations on leading New Zealand First back into Parliament and Government. People can say many things about the current Deputy Prime Minister and foreign Minister, but you can’t question his commitment to public service.
charisma.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of an ally, granting credit for commitment to public service.

strength.statement: we know red tape is a problem, and we will be able to put this money to a better place and to a better spend.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to redirect funds with no concrete plan or delivery shown.

strength.statement: It’s an outcome that will improve people’s lives, it will improve people’s lifestyles, and it will improve people’s livelihoods.
strength.explanation: Sweeping aspiration with no concrete action or delivery attached.

authenticity.statement: I, for one, during these debates, have learnt that perhaps what we needed to do was actually further depoliticise. We probably needed to move to a model where the person appointed was not appointed by the Minister and we probably needed to move to a model where those reports came to Parliament and we looked at them and we had to respond to them
authenticity.explanation: Self-critical of the arrangement her own side operated, which lends consistency to her support for an independent body.

divination.statement: a programme of 6.5 percent cuts to all social services will directly impact people like social workers in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts cuts will hit social workers; directionally plausible given announced reductions, magnitude uncertain.

specificity.statement: Today, the House will adjourn until Tuesday, 13 February. In that week, the Government will move urgency to progress multiple stages of the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact date, the legislative process (urgency), and the specific bill.

specificity.statement: I've seen a report showing that the median wage in 2010 was $40,000, and that now it has risen to $65,000.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and a defined timeframe.

specificity.statement: This means that someone earning the median wage back in 2010 was firmly in the 17.5 percent personal income tax bracket, and now they are firmly in the 30 percent tax bracket. Through neglect, the personal income tax scale has failed to keep up with growth in incomes.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific tax brackets and the mechanism (fiscal drag).

specificity.statement: A person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage in 2010 was earning $27,000. After the increase in the minimum wage, a person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage will now be earning more than $48,000, and therefore—like median income earners—will be in the 30 percent tax bracket.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures, hours, and the relevant tax bracket.

specificity.statement: you have to go all the way back to 1 October 2010, when the National Government reduced personal income taxes after Budget 2010. That is 14 years ago. To be fair, personal income tax reductions were legislated for in 2017. However, the incoming Labour Government cancelled them, and then introduced a new top tax rate of 39 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact dates, governments, and the new rate.

specificity.statement: Can the Minister of Finance confirm that wage growth comes from investments and entrepreneurship and productivity growth allowing employers to pay their workers more, and that legislating up the wage from Wellington is not the only or the best way for Kiwis to get ahead—in fact, for the 97.1 percent of workers who are not on the minimum wage, that's the only way for them to get ahead?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (97.1% of workers not on minimum wage) and named mechanisms.

specificity.statement: Colonisation brought to New Zealand things like Westminster democracy, the rule of law, economic development. ... On the other hand, colonisation brought immense suffering for many people. It brought the loss of land for tangata whenua, it brought disease, and it brought illness.
specificity.explanation: Gives named outcomes (Westminster democracy, rule of law, land loss, disease) but no further detail.

specificity.statement: we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers (200 staff, 32 EDs) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: Just last week, guards that were provided through our ED security boost helped to swiftly remedy a fight in Christchurch Hospital's emergency department between gang members.
specificity.explanation: Names the hospital, timing, and a concrete incident.

specificity.statement: Repealing section 7AA is something that I have campaigned on for the last three years.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific provision (section 7AA) and the duration of her position.

specificity.statement: I take this role very seriously, and every report of harm of a child is disappointing. My focus is to make sure that every child—Māori or non-Māori—is safe, loved, and cared for.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational platitude with no mechanism, measure, or commitment.

specificity.statement: The documentation is a range of historical policy positions and notes that were held in New Zealand First policy positions. Some of it relates to things that were passed in the legislation when New Zealand First was in Government. This is a range of points and positions and it's about five pages long.
specificity.explanation: Gives some detail (five pages, NZ First positions) but not the figures, authorship, or dates that would resolve the question.

specificity.statement: I've recently announced $26.8 million of funding for flood resilience projects across the country, of which $12.3 million has been for flood risk mitigation across 13 projects, and $14.5 million for Future of Severely Affected Land Category 2 support across four projects.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise dollar figures and project counts broken down by category.

specificity.statement: Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (500 net) and timeframe (two years).

specificity.statement: Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn't—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (1,800, 1,500, 500) and a clear standards commitment.

specificity.statement: The changes proposed for electric vehicles will ensure that they pay the same amount as a road-user charge as those other light vehicles which pay a road-user charge. There are variances throughout the system, and that is why the coalition agreement with ACT commits this Government to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system based on how much people travel the roads and the weight of their vehicle.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (RUC parity, weight/distance basis) and the coalition commitment, though without figures.

specificity.statement: This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric.
specificity.explanation: Names the date (1 April), the 2% fleet threshold, and the exemption's origin.

specificity.statement: we are going to stop giving around $6 million a year to the Productivity Commission to produce more reports. We are going to take that money and we're going to establish a ministry of regulation, whose job it will be to uphold and enforce the quality of lawmaking in New Zealand and to review the red tape and regulation that stifles so much productive activity up and down this country.
specificity.explanation: Names the saving (~$6m/year), the replacement body, and its functions, though without staffing or timeline detail.

specificity.statement: the bill that is drafted under his care has no provision whatsoever for respecting the employment relationship. It says, quite shortly, quite bluntly that the employment contracts are terminated. Ironically, leases aren't terminated. Ironically, all of the other contracts held by the Productivity Commission are moved to the Treasury, but employment contracts are terminated—end of story.
specificity.explanation: Points to concrete contents of the bill (termination clause vs transferred leases/contracts).

specificity.statement: This is not a Government that builds up; it's a Government that tears down.
specificity.explanation: A broad rhetorical slogan with no concrete detail.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced at the Financial Services Council meeting my intention to simplify regulations, cut red tape, and reduce costs to financial institutions. There were three elements: first of all, the proposal to move from three to two regulators; secondly, to reduce from a maximum of six licences to a single licence; and thirdly, to reform the Conduct of Financial Institutions requirements to make it easier for smaller financial institutions to meet their obligations.
specificity.explanation: Itemised three concrete elements with specific numbers (3→2 regulators, 6→1 licence).

specificity.statement: I announced yesterday that we are looking into the credit contracts Act because our intent is to improve the regulation, which the previous Government has made an absolute hash of—hash of. What we're intending to do is to make sure that vulnerable borrowers are still protected, but, just as importantly, making sure that credit is available to those who need it but have been excluded under the current regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the dual goal (protect vulnerable borrowers / widen credit access) but no mechanism or detail on how Webb's 'what's different' question is answered.

forthrightness.statement: Yes.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Webb's question (whether he'll progress anything other than repeal/disestablish) with a direct affirmative, but supplies no substance or examples.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It's fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can't imagine the psychology of someone who doesn't want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.
forthrightness.explanation: Reaffirms the earlier answer but recasts the question rather than engaging Sepuloni's underlying concern.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I've had assurances from all coalition partners in this Government that they have had no funding from the tobacco industry, and I am confident that there has been no undue influence on the policies of this Government by the tobacco industry.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was who developed/wrote the documents Costello passed to officials; he answers a different question about funding and influence (a point Robertson flagged in a point of order).

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I am confident that there has been no undue influence on the policy formation of this Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeats the non-answer about influence when the repeated question was specifically about authorship of the documents.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. And that question was about as effective as a Marama Davidson etymology lesson.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'Yes' to whether conflicts of interest were declared, then pivots to a jibe.

forthrightness.statement: the member has been in Cabinet, so she'll be aware that the Prime Minister is responsible for all Ministers. In respect of Casey Costello, I have full confidence in her, and I'm sure that, in time, that member will too.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'when will he dismiss Costello' question by effectively declining (full confidence), but does so somewhat obliquely.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I can't answer in respect to that conversation, at this time.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to say whether the PM asked Costello about the document's authorship; non-answer to a direct question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd point out to the member that there are a number of projections for what inflation will be in the year ahead—and that in the last quarter, at 0.5 percent and an annualised rate of 2 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Belich asked her to justify raising the minimum wage below inflation; she offers inflation projections without addressing the justification (Webb's point of order noted this).

forthrightness.statement: I can confirm to the member that that is indeed the wording in the coalition agreement, and the Government is delivering on that commitment.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the coalition-agreement wording asked about, plus a delivery claim.

forthrightness.statement: Of course, the Consumers Price Index is viewed as the standard measure of inflation, but the period which you look at to determine the inflation rate is something that there can be a number of perspectives on.
forthrightness.explanation: Names CPI as the standard measure but hedges on which period was used in the actual advice.

forthrightness.statement: Colonisation brought to New Zealand things like Westminster democracy, the rule of law, economic development. ... On the other hand, colonisation brought immense suffering for many people. It brought the loss of land for tangata whenua, it brought disease, and it brought illness.
forthrightness.explanation: Davidson asked specifically what 'good' outcomes he meant; he names concrete examples and balances them with the harms.

forthrightness.statement: Well, all Government agencies are being asked to make savings. The member will be aware of the coalition Government commitment around looking at the scope, purpose, and the nature of the inquiries of the Waitangi Tribunal. That work has yet to begin, but it will begin in due course.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially addresses the Tribunal budget question with general savings context, but doesn't engage the specific 'fixing bad outcomes of colonisation' tension Davidson raised.

forthrightness.statement: No commitments have been made on what's going to happen in staffing levels. Those decisions are still ongoing and those discussions are still ongoing.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'how can she justify cutting 600 staff' question by disputing the premise (no commitments made) rather than addressing the substance.

forthrightness.statement: I take this role very seriously, and every report of harm of a child is disappointing. My focus is to make sure that every child—Māori or non-Māori—is safe, loved, and cared for.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she will accept responsibility for any further increases in abuse, she pivots to a general statement of focus without answering.

forthrightness.statement: It is unfortunate the actions have been distorted by a media article. The fact is I was asked a question about whether I had sought specific advice. I had not sought specific advice, which is the question I answered, and I referred to a range of advice I had sought from officials.
forthrightness.explanation: Reframes Verrall's question about the RNZ contradiction by drawing a 'specific advice' distinction rather than addressing the apparent inconsistency.

forthrightness.statement: The documentation is a range of historical policy positions and notes that were held in New Zealand First policy positions. Some of it relates to things that were passed in the legislation when New Zealand First was in Government. This is a range of points and positions and it's about five pages long.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly who wrote/collated the notes, she describes the document's provenance generically without naming an author (Webb's point of order noted the authorship question went unanswered).

forthrightness.statement: The pages of notes that were provided to the officials were a compilation of information that was extracted; the authors, I'm not sure of. They were historical policy positions.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked who wrote the note, she says she is unsure of the authors — a non-answer to a repeatedly pressed question, made odd by Verrall's point that a 'historical' document contained a December 2023 proposal.

forthrightness.statement: Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms the coalition commitment asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I became aware as the incoming Minister that Police faced major challenges around recruiting due to the fact that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, they were finding it difficult to fill recruit wings, and we've got many police officers that are fast approaching retirement age.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers when he became aware (as incoming Minister) and gives the reasons, though slightly less precise on the exact 'when'.

forthrightness.statement: I was recently at the Gisborne Police Station and there was a young constable there that had been put in charge of mentoring and identifying young people in the community that may be interested in a career in Police. He has been very successful. In the latest recruit wing, I think there were four that had been recruited through that process and were proudly graduating.
forthrightness.explanation: Andersen asked whether he would rule out lowering recruitment standards; he answers with an anecdote about Gisborne and never addresses standards (her point of order noted this).

forthrightness.statement: Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn't—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
forthrightness.explanation: Now explicitly answers the standards question ('no we will not be dropping standards').

forthrightness.statement: There are variances throughout the system, as I acknowledged. That is why the coalition Government has agreed to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system. This was an issue that was not addressed under the last Government, and this is the first step towards ensuring that all vehicles who use the road pay towards contributing towards maintaining it.
forthrightness.explanation: Genter asked how it is fair that an EV would pay more than double a comparable petrol car for a Wellington–Auckland trip; he retreats to 'variances' and future reform without addressing the specific fairness charge.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I'd be very happy to have a read.
forthrightness.explanation: A complete dodge — mocks the questioner and ignores her substantive question about per-kilometre contribution logic (her point of order asked him to address it).

forthrightness.statement: This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the timing question but reframes around 'all users should pay' rather than the disincentive point asked.

forthrightness.statement: I've appointed Professor Elizabeth Rata because she is a well-recognised and renowned educational expert. Any views that she has expressed in terms of her political views are not relevant to her appointment, which is based on her educational expertise.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question about Rata's appointment with a clear rationale, while declining to endorse or disown her quoted political views.

rigor.statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It's fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can't imagine the psychology of someone who doesn't want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — recasts the opposition as objecting to a Minister wanting to reduce smoking, which was not the criticism.

rigor.statement: In the 15 years that I have been in the House, Prime Ministers are asked about the actions—every action—of a Minister. It is, of course, perfectly possible for the Prime Minister to say that they don't know, because, I agree with Leader of the House, they may well not know all of the details of documents. But that is not the same as simply not answering or avoiding the question.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned procedural argument that draws a clear distinction between not knowing and not answering; concedes the opposing point before rebutting it.

rigor.statement: Ministers are clearly responsible for things they give to their officials—no one's disputing that. The issue is: are they responsible for the generation of that material? I would argue they cannot be, in the same way that if, for example, a Labour Party Minister gave a document to the education ministry—that was the New Zealand Educational Institute or the Post Primary Teachers' Association or the Council of Trade Unions (CTU), for example—they cannot be questioned about the CTU in Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Structured argument distinguishing handling from generation, supported by a relevant parallel example; rests partly on analogy.

rigor.statement: That is what the question is about: was the tobacco industry involved in developing a document that the Minister then gave to officials, at which point it became official material? That's just a matter of transparency; it's not a matter of undue influence; it's not a funding question or anything like that.
rigor.explanation: Cleanly isolates the actual question (transparency over document origin) from the answer given (influence/funding), with clear reasoning.

rigor.statement: This means that someone earning the median wage back in 2010 was firmly in the 17.5 percent personal income tax bracket, and now they are firmly in the 30 percent tax bracket. Through neglect, the personal income tax scale has failed to keep up with growth in incomes.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based on bracket creep, though the loaded 'neglect' conclusion leans on a partisan inference.

rigor.statement: This came from Australia, where the Labor Government has just announced the third in a series of personal income tax reductions. I thought this was highly relevant for New Zealand as it shows that such reductions are commonplace and can be adopted by Governments of all political stripes.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to analogy/precedent (Australia) to support adopting cuts here.

rigor.statement: Of course, the Consumers Price Index is viewed as the standard measure of inflation, but the period which you look at to determine the inflation rate is something that there can be a number of perspectives on.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that the chosen period affects the inflation figure, though it avoids committing to specifics.

rigor.statement: Can the Minister of Finance confirm that wage growth comes from investments and entrepreneurship and productivity growth allowing employers to pay their workers more, and that legislating up the wage from Wellington is not the only or the best way for Kiwis to get ahead—in fact, for the 97.1 percent of workers who are not on the minimum wage, that's the only way for them to get ahead?
rigor.explanation: Economically grounded argument linking productivity to wages, but the 'only way' framing for the 97.1% overstates and is presented as a leading question.

rigor.statement: Colonisation brought to New Zealand things like Westminster democracy, the rule of law, economic development. ... On the other hand, colonisation brought immense suffering for many people. It brought the loss of land for tangata whenua, it brought disease, and it brought illness.
rigor.explanation: Presents a balanced both-sides case rather than asserting one side; reasoning is coherent.

rigor.statement: I am told that there has been a noticeable reduction in the number of people who have been abusive towards staff. This has improved due to the increased presence of security in our EDs and has ensured people feel safer when they access care in their times of need.
rigor.explanation: Relies on anecdote/hearsay ('I am told', firsthand accounts) and asserts causation without data.

rigor.statement: I was recently at the Gisborne Police Station and there was a young constable there that had been put in charge of mentoring and identifying young people in the community that may be interested in a career in Police. He has been very successful. In the latest recruit wing, I think there were four that had been recruited through that process and were proudly graduating.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a single anecdote ('four... recruited') to suggest the target is achievable, without engaging the structural question.

rigor.statement: that member's graph that she continues to raise doesn't take into account the full running costs of those vehicles. As everyone knows, electric vehicles are far cheaper to use and drive, as many members of this House know, but that graph that she uses misinforms the House.
rigor.explanation: Makes a fair point on total running costs but supports it with 'as everyone knows' (appeal to common knowledge) rather than data.
