civility.statement: Can I say to that rather confusing question, there is no statement from this Government or any member of it of getting rid of the Treaty of Waitangi. Anybody else that says otherwise is spreading malice of forethought and we're not going to tolerate it.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the question as 'confusing' and labels contrary claims as 'malice of forethought', though the underlying denial is on-point.

civility.statement: But what we won't do is have this unmandated, unelected judicial woke concoction that that member seeks to subscribe to, which wasn't supported by the greatest scholar ever to come to this House on this matter, Sir Āpirana Ngata—he's our authority. What's yours?
civility.explanation: 'Judicial woke concoction' is dismissive sloganeering aimed at delegitimising opponents rather than debating substance.

civility.statement: They're based on the elite Māori in this country who would never consult with their own people. And out there in New Zealand, the mass majority of Māori have proven that by not even being on the Māori roll subscribed to by that member.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents as 'elite Māori' who don't consult their people, an othering characterisation.

civility.statement: The reality is Kōhanga Reo was started by the National Party. Does that member not know it?
civility.explanation: 'Does that member not know it?' is a mild barb but within robust debate.

civility.statement: No record of having done anything in her whole career, and she wants to know—will somebody tell her?—and she's on the front bench!
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on an opposing member's career and competence with no policy content.

civility.statement: It's preposterous that the Government that was in charge of the original inquiry went to set out their own terms of reference for an inquiry into their own decisions. In short, setting up an inquiry to cover one's derrière is not in the public interest, and we're going to fix it up.
civility.explanation: 'Cover one's derrière' is a colourful jab but the criticism targets the process, not personal character.

civility.statement: Well, members might be interested to know that the cultural report provider Hard 2 Reach, headed by lifetime Mongrel Mob member Harry Tam, boasts on its website that offenders "have received sentence discounts of up to 35 percent because of factors raised in our reports".
civility.explanation: Foregrounds a provider's gang affiliation, edging toward guilt-by-association rather than addressing the reports' merits.

civility.statement: Six years of loose spending, of hopeless, naive law and order policies, of waffle, and of almost comically poor delivery came to an end last year.
civility.explanation: A string of disparagements ('hopeless', 'waffle', 'comically poor') aimed at the previous Government rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: A naive approach to justice exemplified by Labour's only clearly articulated justice sector target to reduce the prison population by 30 percent irrespective of what's happening in our community, on our streets, and in our houses has been followed by a rise in violent crime, an explosion in retail crime, ram raids, gang membership, and paying for the victims of crime.
civility.explanation: 'Naive approach' and the litany framing disparage the opponent's policy, though crime trends are a legitimate subject.

civility.statement: Point of order. Sorry, Mr Speaker, to belabour the point, but that wasn't the question. The question wasn't "Is there one policy?"; it was "What does this particular policy contribute?" Those are actually materially two different questions, and the question that the member asked has not been answered.
civility.explanation: Engages procedurally and on the substance of the question without personal attack.

veracity.statement: It is simple: there is a requisite under the electoral law of this country for declarations to be made. Those declarations have been made. The Electoral Commission has not challenged it, nor has anybody else.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that electoral law requires donation declarations and that they had not been challenged by the Electoral Commission.

veracity.statement: It told me that core Crown expenses have increased markedly since 2017, peaking at 35 percent of GDP in the 2021-22 fiscal year, which is the highest rate in New Zealand in decades.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with Treasury data showing core Crown expenses around 35% of GDP in 2021-22, elevated by COVID spending.

veracity.statement: In fact, Treasury's BIM tells me that after stripping out large one-off expenditures like COVID and after adjusting for the economic cycle, the Government is currently running a structural deficit of around 2 percent of GDP, largely because of growth in Government spending. That is the mess Labour has left us in.
veracity.explanation: Aligns with Treasury's structural deficit estimate; attribution solely to spending growth is a contestable simplification.

veracity.statement: Currently, 60 percent of the children in material hardship are in benefit-dependant homes. There is no dignity in them having poor or worse outcomes because of the family circumstances they were born in.
veracity.explanation: The benefit-dependant share of children in material hardship is a real statistic in that range, though such figures vary by measure and year.

veracity.statement: Recipients of the jobseeker work-ready benefit are now expected to spend, on average, 13 years of the future on a benefit—an increase of almost four years compared to 2017.
veracity.explanation: Drawn from MSD social-outcomes modelling; presented as established fact though Verrall's point of order notes it is projection, not actual experience.

veracity.statement: The modelling estimated that 626,000 New Zealanders who received a benefit in the last year would collectively require another 6.43 million years of income support.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to MSD modelling; the aggregate 'years of support' figure is a projection presented as a concrete fact.

veracity.statement: By 2022, teenagers who go on to welfare were expected to spend, on average, 24 years relying on a benefit—a staggering nine extra years of their lives on welfare.
veracity.explanation: Modelling figure presented as fact; 'a staggering nine extra years' adds rhetorical colour to a projected estimate.

veracity.statement: The empirical evidence that says the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000 when there's been a 50 percent reduction in the number of sanctions applied in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: The underlying numbers are roughly in range, but framing them as evidence sanctions work is misleading.

veracity.statement: In fact, the member may have seen opinion polling by Curia which found that 60 percent of New Zealanders support the principles in the bill and 18 percent oppose it, and maybe it's time for the member to get on board.
veracity.explanation: Cites a real Curia poll, but Curia is a party-aligned pollster and the 60/18 framing of 'support the principles' is contested and selectively favourable.

veracity.statement: Can I say to that rather confusing question, there is no statement from this Government or any member of it of getting rid of the Treaty of Waitangi. Anybody else that says otherwise is spreading malice of forethought and we're not going to tolerate it.

veracity.statement: They're based on the elite Māori in this country who would never consult with their own people. And out there in New Zealand, the mass majority of Māori have proven that by not even being on the Māori roll subscribed to by that member.

veracity.explanation: Kōhanga Reo began in 1982 under a National government via the Department of Māori Affairs, but it was a Māori community-led initiative; 'started by the National Party' overstates the credit.

veracity.explanation: The '55 percent of Māori not even at school' figure is an exaggerated/misleading rendering of attendance statistics (regular attendance rates differ from being chronically absent).

veracity.explanation: The '$500,000 speed bumps' claim he immediately had to correct to ~$490,000 plus traffic management, indicating the original figure was loosely stated.

veracity.explanation: Corrects the figure and cites a source, though the combined framing of the cost remains a debating point.

veracity.explanation: Light-rail consultancy spend in the tens-to-hundreds of millions is broadly documented, but claiming the previous Government 'caused the congestion' is misleading hyperbole.

veracity.statement: I'm advised by officials that since 2017, $26.3 million of taxpayer funding was spent on crafting section 27 reports designed to encourage lighter sentences.
veracity.explanation: Cites an official-sourced cumulative figure; the characterisation 'designed to encourage lighter sentences' editorialises the reports' purpose.

veracity.statement: Well, members might be interested to know that the cultural report provider Hard 2 Reach, headed by lifetime Mongrel Mob member Harry Tam, boasts on its website that offenders "have received sentence discounts of up to 35 percent because of factors raised in our reports".
veracity.explanation: Quotes a verifiable website claim, though singling out one provider implies it is representative of all section 27 reports.

veracity.explanation: Partly true that fiscal stimulus contributed to inflation, but framing it as the dominant cause is misleading given global supply and energy shocks.

veracity.explanation: The growth figures are consistent with his earlier cited data; 'cottage industry is gone' is rhetorical overstatement of a funding change.

authenticity.statement: Just to put on record, the previous Government was not on track to meet the targets. We supported the legislation when it was introduced, we're not making changes to the legislation, and our Government will work incredibly hard to lift children out of poverty.
authenticity.explanation: Claims continued commitment to targets the party supported, but pairs it with an attack on the prior Government's track record rather than her own forward commitment.

authenticity.statement: And given the GDP—given the ratio against the GDP—which is way better than most developed nations, yes, we are going to keep it at 65. On that, you've had our long, 40-year promise.
authenticity.explanation: Keeping the superannuation age at 65 is a long-standing, consistently held NZ First position, so the stated commitment matches the party's record.

authenticity.statement: I may have misspoken; it was a $490,000 speed bump, which had $172,000 of traffic management to construct. I'm happy to table the New Zealand Herald article.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges misspeaking and corrects his own figure, offering a source.

charisma.statement: This Government is introducing a Treaty principles bill to democratise that process of defining the Treaty principles because, for the first time through this representative House of Parliament, all New Zealanders will have a say about what our founding document and our constitutional future means.
charisma.explanation: Uses inclusive 'all New Zealanders' framing, though the framing appeals primarily to supporters of the bill.

charisma.statement: The fact that it has been interpreted through a lens of principles upon which most New Zealanders have had not a chance to have any influence or say, I believe, has diminished its mana and made it a source of division when it should be a source of unity.
charisma.explanation: Frames the bill in terms of unity and enhancing mana, an attempt at bridging language, though contested in effect.

charisma.statement: At bottom it is to try to honour the Treaty and Treaty settlements while at the same time not losing sight of or undermining those core human rights that all people in modern democratic societies expect—equal voting rights, equality before the law, and an equal say in the big decisions affecting their lives. We have to appreciate that there is tension between those two things—
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges genuine tension between competing principles in a measured way, an attempt to frame the debate constructively rather than combatively.

strength.statement: We are committed to training an extra 500 front-line police in the next two years.
strength.explanation: A concrete commitment stated at the outset of the term with delivery still pending — intent, not yet demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: The Government has committed to wider changes to sentencing laws to restore real consequences for crime. That includes capping sentence discounts at 40 percent, and my colleague Minister McKee is leading work to reinstate three strikes legislation.
strength.explanation: States committed policy changes early in the term; delivery is intended but not yet demonstrated.

veracity.statement: This member's bill came about because the addition of mental health – specific features of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Bill were not included at the time that it was passed.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about the legislative history of the Pae Ora Act; broadly consistent with the record that mental-health-specific strategic provisions were not in the original Act, though framed favourably.

veracity.statement: Now, a National Government has gone a long way towards that by having a mental health Minister. We've already committed lots of funding toward mental health, both I Am Hope and, again, I point out the work towards the Cyclone Gabrielle recovery and also the funding for those affected by Cyclone Gabrielle and Cyclone Hale and helping them get the mental health support that they need one year on from that cyclone.
veracity.explanation: The mental health Minister appointment is accurate; the funding claims are vague ('lots of funding') and hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: Recently surveyed, 92 percent of surveyed New Zealanders—in just six years, there's been a 92 percent—sorry—increase in Kiwis reporting that they have unmet mental health needs.
veracity.explanation: Garbled delivery conflating '92 percent of New Zealanders' with 'a 92 percent increase over six years'; the underlying figure is uncited and the confusion makes the claim potentially misleading.

veracity.statement: We had support from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission, we had support from the Mental Health Foundation of New Zealand, we had support from Emerge Aotearoa, and we had support from Mental Health Advocacy and Peer Support Trust.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about named bodies' support; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: there are many people in New Zealand who have experienced mental distress or illness in their life. In fact, half of New Zealanders will do so.
veracity.explanation: 'Half of New Zealanders will experience mental distress/illness in their lifetime' aligns with commonly cited lifetime-prevalence estimates; broadly supported though rounded.

veracity.statement: there is nothing on mental health committed by this Government in its hundred-day plan. There's been a big talk around this, and we on this side are really keen to know what the Minister is going to deliver.
veracity.explanation: Checkable claim that the 100-day plan contained no mental health commitment; plausible given the published plan but stated as absolute.

veracity.statement: this inclusion is being built on the previous Government's investment into mental health. It was the biggest ever investment, to lay a whole new foundation for the mental health system
veracity.explanation: Refers to the 2019 Wellbeing Budget's $1.9bn mental health package, frequently described as the largest such investment; directionally accurate though self-favouring.

veracity.statement: I query how that's going to happen in an environment where the Government is requiring Public Service cuts of between 6.5 and 7.5 percent. I also wonder how Māori will be able to deliver on this, given that there will be the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: The 6.5–7.5% public service savings target and the planned disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority were both real Government policies at the time.

veracity.statement: it was a four-year promise of $63 million for methamphetamine addiction treatment out of a total commitment—or promise—of $179 million. So it's a significant portion of the money, and yet the word "addiction" is not in the nomenclature of the new section 46A mental health and wellbeing strategy provision.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures cited as National's commitments; plausible and checkable but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: successive Governments have commissioned advice on addiction... Both of those recommended that in order to actually meaningfully deal with the issues of substance abuse and addiction, we needed to take them outside of the criminal justice sector and place them squarely within health. And that's something which we've seen no Government, successively, be willing to have a backbone on actually meaningfully implementing.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the recommendations of named inquiries to move addiction from justice into health; well supported.

veracity.statement: Despite the significant investment announced in Budget 2019, almost nobody is satisfied with the state of mental health and addiction services in our country.
veracity.explanation: Budget 2019's mental health investment is real; 'almost nobody is satisfied' is an unquantified hyperbolic generalisation that overstates.

veracity.statement: Our youth suicide rate is a heartbreaking statistic, and it's an area where New Zealand, a country accustomed with leading the world in many areas, unfortunately has the worst record.
veracity.explanation: NZ has among the highest youth suicide rates in the OECD, but 'the worst record' is a strong absolute that has been contested/varies by dataset and year — partly true but overstated.

veracity.statement: Sadly, what we have seen is a prevalence of mental distress amongst Māori, and we are 50 percent higher affected than non. Māori are 30 percent more likely to go undiagnosed than anyone else in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported — Māori do experience higher mental distress and under-diagnosis — but the precise percentages are stated without a source and hard to verify.

specificity.statement: This member's bill came about because the addition of mental health – specific features of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Bill were not included at the time that it was passed.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act and the gap, but does not detail the actual provisions.

specificity.statement: Now, a National Government has gone a long way towards that by having a mental health Minister. We've already committed lots of funding toward mental health, both I Am Hope and, again, I point out the work towards the Cyclone Gabrielle recovery and also the funding for those affected by Cyclone Gabrielle and Cyclone Hale and helping them get the mental health support that they need one year on from that cyclone.
specificity.explanation: Names I Am Hope and the cyclones, but 'lots of funding' gives no amounts, timeframes, or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: Recently surveyed, 92 percent of surveyed New Zealanders—in just six years, there's been a 92 percent—sorry—increase in Kiwis reporting that they have unmet mental health needs.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (92 percent) and timeframe (six years), though muddled and without a named source.

specificity.statement: We have an incredible number of NGOs stepping in to do what the Government should be doing.
specificity.explanation: Vague — no named NGOs, numbers, or specific services.

specificity.statement: We had support from the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission, we had support from the Mental Health Foundation of New Zealand, we had support from Emerge Aotearoa, and we had support from Mental Health Advocacy and Peer Support Trust.
specificity.explanation: Names four specific organisations that supported the amendments.

specificity.statement: there are many people in New Zealand who have experienced mental distress or illness in their life. In fact, half of New Zealanders will do so.
specificity.explanation: Gives a proportion (half) but no source or timeframe definition.

specificity.statement: this inclusion is being built on the previous Government's investment into mental health. It was the biggest ever investment, to lay a whole new foundation for the mental health system
specificity.explanation: Asserts 'biggest ever investment' but gives no dollar figure or year here.

specificity.statement: I query how that's going to happen in an environment where the Government is requiring Public Service cuts of between 6.5 and 7.5 percent. I also wonder how Māori will be able to deliver on this, given that there will be the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (6.5–7.5%) and a named policy (Māori Health Authority disestablishment).

specificity.statement: it was a four-year promise of $63 million for methamphetamine addiction treatment out of a total commitment—or promise—of $179 million. So it's a significant portion of the money, and yet the word "addiction" is not in the nomenclature of the new section 46A mental health and wellbeing strategy provision.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures ($63m of $179m over four years) tied to a specific clause (section 46A) and a textual omission.

specificity.statement: they have shown a strong research database showing the relationship between debt resilience and mental health. That doesn't seem to be included in this. There is no reference to social determinants.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete example (debt resilience, former prisoners and bank accounts) of what is missing from the bill.

specificity.statement: I also wanted to acknowledge and appreciate my colleague the Hon Matt Doocey for the mahi that we've done over the last six years in establishing the Cross-Party Mental Health and Addictions Wellbeing Group.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific cross-party group and a six-year timeframe, though without further detail.

specificity.statement: we need to be willing to invest meaningfully in youth one-stop shops. This is a model which we looked into in our second report out of that cross-party group, which, we found, has phenomenal results for our young people, with a no-wrong-door approach. I find it mind-blowing that we don't have a youth one-stop-shop in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland—in our largest city.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete model (youth one-stop shops, no-wrong-door), cites a specific report, and a concrete gap (none in Auckland).

specificity.statement: Despite the significant investment announced in Budget 2019, almost nobody is satisfied with the state of mental health and addiction services in our country.
specificity.explanation: References a specific budget but the satisfaction claim is vague and unmeasured.

specificity.statement: A one-size-fits-all approach to mental health care can be more harmful than helpful. Individuals need to be able to access care and services that best suit their needs. While we support the devolution of funding to communities and their organisations, we must also ensure that there are strict criteria for funding services and that services are monitored to ensure New Zealanders receive high-quality care.
specificity.explanation: Offers a direction (devolved funding with strict criteria and monitoring) but no mechanisms, amounts, or thresholds.

specificity.statement: We need a coordinated approach that brings together Government agencies, NGOs, and communities to make mental health a priority for everybody.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational platitude with no concrete mechanism for coordination.

specificity.statement: I would like to assure the member in the House that it's not a tick-box situation here. It really is something that I know New Zealand First is very committed to, and I know as a coalition we are very committed to, and we've already said that we will support the Mike King I Am Hope Foundation.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (supporting Mike King's I Am Hope Foundation), but no funding figure or detail.

specificity.statement: One of the things that I have noticed, actually, about some of the wording in the bill is to not only say that we are going to put something in place and speak about it but having outcomes and to have deliverable outcomes. So, yes, it is about measuring, it is about being on top of everything as well, and not just speaking to it but being specific on what these outcomes are going to be.
specificity.explanation: Advocates measurable, deliverable outcomes but does not itself specify any concrete outcome or metric.

specificity.statement: Sadly, what we have seen is a prevalence of mental distress amongst Māori, and we are 50 percent higher affected than non. Māori are 30 percent more likely to go undiagnosed than anyone else in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (50 percent higher affected; 30 percent more likely undiagnosed).

rigor.statement: the reason that's so important is that today, in 2024, mental health is not on an equal footing with physical health. If we don't lead from the top, as a Government, nobody else will.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable framing premise, but 'if we don't lead nobody else will' is an unevidenced sweeping assertion (appeal leaning) rather than a demonstrated causal claim.

rigor.statement: now that we are putting this amendment bill forward, there should be absolutely no opposition to it, because it is such a simple, simple amendment that will have such a massive impact... All of this stuff is absolutely vital, but it's common sense. It's pragmatic. Like I said, absolutely no party should oppose this.
rigor.explanation: Leans on 'it's common sense' and assertion of 'massive impact' rather than evidence that the mandate will change outcomes — appeal to common sense.

rigor.statement: without a strategic plan you cannot look for funding, you cannot make a plan long term, you cannot plan for infrastructure, you cannot plan for long-term funding.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument linking strategy to funding/infrastructure, but stated as absolutes ('you cannot') without evidence; reasonable but overstated logic.

rigor.statement: I query how that's going to happen in an environment where the Government is requiring Public Service cuts of between 6.5 and 7.5 percent. I also wonder how Māori will be able to deliver on this, given that there will be the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based challenge linking funding/staffing cuts to ability to deliver the strategy; conclusion follows from cited policies.

rigor.statement: it was a four-year promise of $63 million for methamphetamine addiction treatment out of a total commitment—or promise—of $179 million. So it's a significant portion of the money, and yet the word "addiction" is not in the nomenclature of the new section 46A mental health and wellbeing strategy provision.
rigor.explanation: Detailed, evidence-anchored argument pointing to a concrete gap between funding priorities and the bill's wording.

rigor.statement: I support it, but it does feel a little bit like sloganeering... great on slogans; how are they going to deliver?
rigor.explanation: Reasonable scepticism, but the 'sloganeering' charge is asserted more than evidenced at this point.

rigor.statement: they have shown a strong research database showing the relationship between debt resilience and mental health. That doesn't seem to be included in this. There is no reference to social determinants.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her critique in research (FinCap's database) and identifies a specific conceptual gap (social determinants); evidence-led reasoning.

rigor.statement: successive Governments have commissioned advice on addiction... Both of those recommended that in order to actually meaningfully deal with the issues of substance abuse and addiction, we needed to take them outside of the criminal justice sector and place them squarely within health. And that's something which we've seen no Government, successively, be willing to have a backbone on actually meaningfully implementing.
rigor.explanation: Cites specific reviews (He Ara Oranga; Turuki! Turuki!) and their consistent recommendation to draw an evidence-based conclusion about a policy gap.

rigor.statement: we need to be willing to invest meaningfully in youth one-stop shops. This is a model which we looked into in our second report out of that cross-party group, which, we found, has phenomenal results for our young people, with a no-wrong-door approach. I find it mind-blowing that we don't have a youth one-stop-shop in Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland—in our largest city.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-referenced ('our second report', 'phenomenal results'), though 'phenomenal' is an unquantified characterisation.

rigor.statement: we have continued to see successive Governments ignore the evidence and advice that they have commissioned, which has not been convenient in fitting with political narrative and not doing that hard stuff.
rigor.explanation: Consistent with her cited examples of commissioned-but-unimplemented advice, though the 'political narrative' motive is asserted.

rigor.statement: A one-size-fits-all approach to mental health care can be more harmful than helpful. Individuals need to be able to access care and services that best suit their needs. While we support the devolution of funding to communities and their organisations, we must also ensure that there are strict criteria for funding services and that services are monitored to ensure New Zealanders receive high-quality care.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument balancing devolution against oversight, though resting on assertion rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: That is not asking for a separatist system; it's actually asking for a targeted approach to stop the horror that we see going on.
rigor.explanation: Pre-empts a strawman ('separatist') and reframes the argument as a targeted, needs-based approach grounded in disparity data.

charisma.statement: the reason that's so important is that today, in 2024, mental health is not on an equal footing with physical health. If we don't lead from the top, as a Government, nobody else will.
charisma.explanation: Confident leadership framing aimed at the whole House, but rallying its own governing-from-the-top theme rather than actively reaching across.

charisma.statement: now that we are putting this amendment bill forward, there should be absolutely no opposition to it, because it is such a simple, simple amendment that will have such a massive impact... All of this stuff is absolutely vital, but it's common sense. It's pragmatic. Like I said, absolutely no party should oppose this.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites all parties to back the bill and frames it as uncontroversial common ground, a consensus-building pitch.

charisma.statement: I'm letting members opposite know that we will support this amendment bill.
charisma.explanation: Opposition openly backing a Government member's bill — a cross-party, consensus-building gesture.

charisma.statement: The Greens will be supporting this bill through the House tonight and through select committee, and encourage members of the public to have their say at that select committee stage.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party support plus an inclusive invitation to the public to participate.

charisma.statement: I also wanted to acknowledge and appreciate my colleague the Hon Matt Doocey for the mahi that we've done over the last six years in establishing the Cross-Party Mental Health and Addictions Wellbeing Group.
charisma.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of a political opponent and emphasis on cross-party collaboration — strongly bridge-building.

charisma.statement: We need a coordinated approach that brings together Government agencies, NGOs, and communities to make mental health a priority for everybody.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive call for a coordinated, whole-of-society approach.

charisma.statement: I would like to assure the member in the House that it's not a tick-box situation here. It really is something that I know New Zealand First is very committed to, and I know as a coalition we are very committed to, and we've already said that we will support the Mike King I Am Hope Foundation.
charisma.explanation: Reassures the opposition member directly and frames commitment as shared across the coalition, a mildly bridging tone.

charisma.statement: I really want to assure the members on the other side that you can rely on us to deliver on this.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across to opposition members in a cooperative, reassuring register.

charisma.statement: First of all, I'd like to confirm that Te Pāti Māori will be supporting this bill. We'll be supporting this bill because it is simple and practical.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party backing of a Government bill, stated cooperatively.

charisma.statement: I think one of the things that Matt has done is he's absolutely shared vulnerability and made it OK, and I think it's really important that we help to destigmatise and use our sphere of influence in the right way. Another thing he did was he reached across cross-parties for engagement, even though one of those cross-parties only had two MPs at times.
charisma.explanation: Warm, specific praise of a political opponent (Doocey) and explicit valuing of cross-party engagement — strongly bridge-building.

charisma.statement: That is not asking for a separatist system; it's actually asking for a targeted approach to stop the horror that we see going on.
charisma.explanation: Seeks to defuse a divisive framing and bring sceptics along to the idea of targeted services.

charisma.statement: with some of the language, the Tiriti principles bill, the smoke-free environment, and the belief that there is an anti-Māori agenda going on out of this House, we fear that we're creating harm. And so we will continue to support movements that appeal for unity.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly commits to supporting unity and de-escalation, an appeal to common ground despite raising grievances.

charisma.statement: to hear the Greens and ACT speaking together on the same topic, New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori, I think is really encouraging.
charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party agreement across the political spectrum — explicitly unifying and consensus-affirming.

charisma.statement: so often the snapshots that get put on TV shows are the heated moments; they show the tension... but it doesn't capture some of the real meaningful work that takes place. I want to commend not just Matt but all of those across the House who have contributed to this.
charisma.explanation: Praises cross-House cooperation and downplays adversarial theatre — inclusive and bridge-building.

strength.statement: Now, a National Government has gone a long way towards that by having a mental health Minister. We've already committed lots of funding toward mental health, both I Am Hope and, again, I point out the work towards the Cyclone Gabrielle recovery and also the funding for those affected by Cyclone Gabrielle and Cyclone Hale and helping them get the mental health support that they need one year on from that cyclone.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for action (a dedicated Minister, I Am Hope funding, cyclone recovery support); appointing a Minister is real, but the funding claims are general and largely early-stage rather than demonstrably delivered.

strength.statement: I would like to assure the member in the House that it's not a tick-box situation here. It really is something that I know New Zealand First is very committed to, and I know as a coalition we are very committed to, and we've already said that we will support the Mike King I Am Hope Foundation.
strength.explanation: Largely assurance and stated intent ('very committed', 'will support'); a named commitment but as-yet undelivered.

strength.statement: I really want to assure the members on the other side that you can rely on us to deliver on this.
strength.explanation: Pure assurance of future delivery with no concrete action or mechanism behind it.

civility.statement: We have an incredible number of NGOs stepping in to do what the Government should be doing.
civility.explanation: Mild self-critical/systemic point about government gaps; not a personal attack but a generalised judgement.

civility.statement: I'm letting members opposite know that we will support this amendment bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, constructive opening toward political opponents.

civility.statement: there is nothing on mental health committed by this Government in its hundred-day plan. There's been a big talk around this, and we on this side are really keen to know what the Minister is going to deliver.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism but directed at the Government's plan/delivery, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I support it, but it does feel a little bit like sloganeering... great on slogans; how are they going to deliver?
civility.explanation: 'Sloganeering' and 'great on slogans' are jabs at the Government's seriousness, but tied to a delivery critique rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: The Greens will be supporting this bill through the House tonight and through select committee, and encourage members of the public to have their say at that select committee stage.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful, process-focused.

civility.statement: successive Governments have commissioned advice on addiction... Both of those recommended that in order to actually meaningfully deal with the issues of substance abuse and addiction, we needed to take them outside of the criminal justice sector and place them squarely within health. And that's something which we've seen no Government, successively, be willing to have a backbone on actually meaningfully implementing.
civility.explanation: 'No Government willing to have a backbone' is a pointed dig, but aimed at successive governments' policy inaction rather than an individual.

civility.statement: we have continued to see successive Governments ignore the evidence and advice that they have commissioned, which has not been convenient in fitting with political narrative and not doing that hard stuff.
civility.explanation: Criticises governments for ignoring evidence for political convenience; harsh but a systemic critique, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: First of all, I'd like to confirm that Te Pāti Māori will be supporting this bill. We'll be supporting this bill because it is simple and practical.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful support.

civility.statement: I think one of the things that Matt has done is he's absolutely shared vulnerability and made it OK, and I think it's really important that we help to destigmatise and use our sphere of influence in the right way. Another thing he did was he reached across cross-parties for engagement, even though one of those cross-parties only had two MPs at times.
civility.explanation: Generous and respectful toward an opponent across the aisle.

civility.statement: with some of the language, the Tiriti principles bill, the smoke-free environment, and the belief that there is an anti-Māori agenda going on out of this House, we fear that we're creating harm. And so we will continue to support movements that appeal for unity.
civility.explanation: Raises a sharp accusation ('anti-Māori agenda') but frames it as a fear about harm and pivots to a call for unity rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: to hear the Greens and ACT speaking together on the same topic, New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori, I think is really encouraging.
civility.explanation: Respectful, positive acknowledgement of opponents working together.

civility.statement: so often the snapshots that get put on TV shows are the heated moments; they show the tension... but it doesn't capture some of the real meaningful work that takes place. I want to commend not just Matt but all of those across the House who have contributed to this.
civility.explanation: Commends colleagues across all parties; constructive and respectful.

authenticity.statement: this inclusion is being built on the previous Government's investment into mental health. It was the biggest ever investment, to lay a whole new foundation for the mental health system
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's record of having made that investment; a defensible claim about her own party's prior action.

forthrightness.statement: In part because the Government sought a mandate at the election to do those things quickly, and in case it has escaped the notice of the member, that mandate was delivered.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the bills warrant bypassing select committee/public participation, he gives a rationale (electoral mandate) but does not engage the loss of public participation itself.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is at No. 19 on the Order Paper, and when the Government is ready to make moves around it, that member will be one of the first to know.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives the order-paper position but evades the substance of how/why the bill is progressing or languishing.

forthrightness.statement: I haven't read the decision of the panel in relation to that particular project, but what I would say in a more general sense is that it is possible to have environmental conditions proposed on projects that mitigate and remedy the environmental effects of a variety of projects, including, for example, renewable energy projects that will help decarbonise the economy and grow the economy at the same time, and I would have thought the member would be in favour of such projects.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about the Hananui salmon farm, he admits he hasn't read the decision and pivots to a general point.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in the sense that Ministers will be able to refer projects. There will be two pathways. One will be there will be a range of projects listed in the legislation, and then the second pathway will be, upon application to the Government, Ministers will be able to refer projects to an expert consenting panel. This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms Shane Jones' characterisation that permits will be granted by politicians and explains the mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member is asking hypothetical questions. I just haven't ruled out the premise of his original question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he would take responsibility for a species extinction, he dismisses the question as hypothetical rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Well, matters for the Cabinet Manual, as the member well knows, are matters for the Prime Minister, but I think I would be right in saying that the Prime Minister expects all Ministers to uphold the principles and the text of the Cabinet Manual.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects responsibility to the PM and gives a general assurance rather than committing to the specific conflict-of-interest steps asked about.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, as I said in answer to the primary question, the modelling that the member refers to is in the absence of any other Government policies and interventions. Our Government fully intends to take other policies and interventions, such that we can have confidence that we will be doing more to help children in poverty than that Minister ever managed to achieve.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about disabled children affected by the indexation change, she pivots to caveats about the modelling and a comparison with the previous minister.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that money will actually go into the consolidated account, where it will help pay for schools, where it will help pay for nurses, where it will help ensure we have police on our streets, where it will help ensure we lock up the offenders that they wanted running free.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the $670m saving funds tax cuts and whether that is fair to the poorest, she reframes the money as funding services and never addresses fairness.

forthrightness.statement: No, I disagree because, actually, the single biggest thing we can do is reduce the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent households. And then the second biggest thing we can do is provide those children a decent education by ensuring they're turning up to school and we're teaching them how to read, write, and do maths. These are tasks that the previous Government ignored. They were prepared to see children trapped in cycles of poverty, and this Government is not.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers (disagrees with the Children's Commissioner) and gives her alternative reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I am simply not aware of the detail of the advice to which the member refers.
forthrightness.explanation: An honest non-answer: she declines on the basis of not knowing the specific advice Kahurangi Carter asked about.

forthrightness.statement: To the first part of the question, I can confirm to the member that that is indeed the wording in the coalition agreement, and that the Government intends to keep its coalition commitments. To the second part, Cabinet has yet to consider the details of this policy and its implementation, so the member will have to wait until it is announced.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the first part (confirms the coalition wording) but defers the cost question to a future announcement.

forthrightness.statement: I can confirm that I have had advice on this issue, and I can confirm that discussions have not yet been had by Cabinet, and I will not be getting ahead of those discussions.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether advice put the retrospectivity cost near $1 billion, she confirms advice exists but declines to disclose its content.

forthrightness.statement: I can see that the member is getting excited because taxpayers might be getting something back from the Government! He should really wait and see when the policy is announced.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether retrospectivity increases Crown costs, she dodges entirely with a rhetorical deflection.

forthrightness.statement: I'm excited about the precedent of tax reduction, for the first time in 14 years. The member opposite had six opportunities to do it, and he couldn't bring himself to let New Zealanders keep more of their own money—and this Government will.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was about the precedent of retrospective tax cuts; she answers a different question about tax reduction generally.

forthrightness.statement: I find it interesting that the member opposite wishes to demonise landlords. If there were no landlords in New Zealand, there would be no tenants. No one would be able to rent a home.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why tax cuts for landlords are a priority while cutting the poorest's incomes, she does not engage the priority/tradeoff question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the mayor and myself have sat down with each other and discussed what the priority projects should be from the remaining funds. The Eastern Busway, City Rail Link trains and stabling, and local roading improvements—that's what we're going to make sure those remaining funds are spent on.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly names the prioritised projects asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I always agree with the Prime Minister, and we will be making sure that the remaining funds go on the priority projects which Auckland Council and the mayor have identified around what are the priority projects for the remaining funds, which is the Eastern Busway, City Rail Link, and local roading projects.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile the PM's 'localism not centralisation' stance with dictating to Auckland Council, he affirms agreement and reasserts the projects without addressing the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: I will never apologise for adding more tools and skills to our young people so that they can cope when they come out of these facilities and have a better chance at life.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the Auditor-General's six recommendations and the lack of evidence for boot camps, she gives a values declaration without addressing either.

forthrightness.statement: establishing the role of New Zealand's first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
forthrightness.explanation: Names concrete actions taken when asked what actions he has taken, though the role's establishment is structural rather than service delivery.

forthrightness.statement: I've enjoyed working with mental health professional bodies to grow the pipeline of mental health professionals, and I look forward to making announcements about this in due course.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether his only real action in 80 days was supporting a former member's bill, he deflects to a future announcement.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I won't be lectured by that member when, today, we published a report in the House from the Auditor-General that says more young people are waiting longer for specialist services when they came into Government—shame on them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he has set a wait-time target and can assure South Islanders, he pivots to attacking the previous government's record.

forthrightness.statement: I've been working with other Government departments to develop a cross-Government approach to mental health, and I look forward to making announcements about that cross-Government approach in due course.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what projects he has advocated for in the first 100 days, he repeats a generic 'in due course' deflection.

forthrightness.statement: I am hearing reports about Australian states picking up this policy, like many other countries are around the world, and I look forward to speaking more positively about it in the future as more data and evidence comes to light as to the success of the policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Peters' question and candidly acknowledges that supporting data is not yet in.

forthrightness.statement: Speaking to the question and, also, as it relates to the primary, the cellphone ban for Wainuiomata will have similar impacts to every other school that I'm hearing from, in that students are interacting more with each other, focusing on their learning, not getting distracted, and, very soon, we are going to have evidence and data to show that this policy is working.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the cancelled Wainuiomata rebuild and classroom shortage, she redirects to the cellphone policy's benefits.

forthrightness.statement: Āna, I do stand by my statement, and our Government deeply cares about inequalities of opportunity that many communities in New Zealand are facing, particularly Māori communities, around housing, health, and education. That's why our view is that the devolution of resources is generally better, to achieve equalities of opportunity such as the recent funding announcement by the superlative Minita Matua tākuta Shane Reti to help with child immunisation rates.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms he stands by his statement and gives a rationale (devolution), with one concrete example.

forthrightness.statement: Ministers including myself are in regular communications with one another about the efforts made to try and help those people who have gone through difficult weather events over the last year or so. As a result, I continue to work with and engage with those Ministers responsible for the kaupapa Māori pathway to support Māori land that has been—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether he was advised before the $63m boost and whether he raised concern about the lack of Māori support, he gives a general statement about communications without answering either.

civility.statement: In part because the Government sought a mandate at the election to do those things quickly, and in case it has escaped the notice of the member, that mandate was delivered.
civility.explanation: 'in case it has escaped the notice of the member' is a condescending dig rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: On behalf of the Minister, as I said in answer to the primary question, the modelling that the member refers to is in the absence of any other Government policies and interventions. Our Government fully intends to take other policies and interventions, such that we can have confidence that we will be doing more to help children in poverty than that Minister ever managed to achieve.
civility.explanation: Comparative jab ('than that Minister ever managed to achieve') but aimed at record, not the person.

civility.statement: Well, that money will actually go into the consolidated account, where it will help pay for schools, where it will help pay for nurses, where it will help ensure we have police on our streets, where it will help ensure we lock up the offenders that they wanted running free.
civility.explanation: 'offenders that they wanted running free' is a misrepresentation/cheap shot against the opposition.

civility.statement: No, I disagree because, actually, the single biggest thing we can do is reduce the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent households. And then the second biggest thing we can do is provide those children a decent education by ensuring they're turning up to school and we're teaching them how to read, write, and do maths. These are tasks that the previous Government ignored. They were prepared to see children trapped in cycles of poverty, and this Government is not.
civility.explanation: 'They were prepared to see children trapped in cycles of poverty' imputes bad faith to opponents.

civility.statement: We think it is shameful that under a time of declining employment, 69,000 more people went on to the jobseeker benefit under Labour, with 50,000 more children living in benefit-dependent households. That is no way out of poverty.
civility.explanation: Pointed ('shameful') but directed at the policy record rather than a person.

civility.statement: I can see that the member is getting excited because taxpayers might be getting something back from the Government! He should really wait and see when the policy is announced.
civility.explanation: Mocking but mild ('getting excited'), not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I'm excited about the precedent of tax reduction, for the first time in 14 years. The member opposite had six opportunities to do it, and he couldn't bring himself to let New Zealanders keep more of their own money—and this Government will.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the opponent's record, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I find it interesting that the member opposite wishes to demonise landlords. If there were no landlords in New Zealand, there would be no tenants. No one would be able to rent a home.
civility.explanation: Mischaracterises the questioner's position ('wishes to demonise landlords').

civility.statement: Under that Government, I would note, rents went up considerably. Well, we want to be a Government that delivers more housing, that actually achieves more affordable housing, unlike that Government, which colossally failed. Remember the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses?
civility.explanation: Sharp attack on the record ('colossally failed') but legitimately policy-focused.

civility.statement: Yesterday, the coalition Government delivered on its promise to repeal the divisive three waters programme that would've taken local decisions away from communities. The vast majority of councils were opposed to Labour's three waters. This Government is delivering on our commitment to restore local council ownership and control of water assets.
civility.explanation: 'divisive three waters programme' is loaded but aimed at the policy.

civility.statement: Yes. Particularly when I said that this Government will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund more cycle lanes, red light cameras, speed bumps, and lowering speed limits across the city.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the projects ('speed bumps') but policy-directed.

civility.statement: As I said, if the Labour Party wants to ask Aucklanders for more money to build speed bumps, get on your bike and enjoy yourselves.
civility.explanation: A dismissive cheap shot ('get on your bike') rather than engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: Well, I won't be lectured by that member when, today, we published a report in the House from the Auditor-General that says more young people are waiting longer for specialist services when they came into Government—shame on them.
civility.explanation: 'shame on them' is a rhetorical jab, though tied to a report finding.

civility.statement: The report findings are clear: things have got worse, there's no workforce plan, and, basically, they failed in mental health.
civility.explanation: Blunt attack on the predecessor's record, anchored to a report but rhetorically charged.

civility.statement: Has the Minister received any reports of requests by the previous Government of their officials as to the unheralded impact of 128,000, a record number, coming to New Zealand in just one year... Were there any reports requested back then by these people now today showing faux concern in the House?
civility.explanation: 'faux concern' imputes bad faith to the opposition members rather than engaging their argument.

civility.statement: if we find ourselves in a situation where members are trying to ask specific questions that are quite narrow in nature in order to elicit a response, and all we get is a general answer that talks about the topic that the question happens to be related to, it somewhat obviates the need for question time at all.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of accountability and question-time function without personal attack.

rigor.statement: In part because the Government sought a mandate at the election to do those things quickly, and in case it has escaped the notice of the member, that mandate was delivered.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the election mandate to justify urgency, but does not address the merits of removing the select committee stage.

rigor.statement: Yes, in the sense that Ministers will be able to refer projects. There will be two pathways. One will be there will be a range of projects listed in the legislation, and then the second pathway will be, upon application to the Government, Ministers will be able to refer projects to an expert consenting panel. This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel.
rigor.explanation: Uses the precedent of the COVID fast-track legislation to argue this is not novel — a reasonable analogy, though leaning on appeal to precedent rather than addressing the concentration-of-power concern.

rigor.statement: No, I disagree because, actually, the single biggest thing we can do is reduce the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent households. And then the second biggest thing we can do is provide those children a decent education by ensuring they're turning up to school and we're teaching them how to read, write, and do maths. These are tasks that the previous Government ignored. They were prepared to see children trapped in cycles of poverty, and this Government is not.
rigor.explanation: Asserts priorities without evidence and leans on an attack rather than substantiating the 'single biggest' claim.

rigor.statement: I find it interesting that the member opposite wishes to demonise landlords. If there were no landlords in New Zealand, there would be no tenants. No one would be able to rent a home.
rigor.explanation: Strawmans the question as 'demonising landlords' and offers a truism rather than addressing the tradeoff.

rigor.statement: Under that Government, I would note, rents went up considerably. Well, we want to be a Government that delivers more housing, that actually achieves more affordable housing, unlike that Government, which colossally failed. Remember the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses?
rigor.explanation: Points to the KiwiBuild shortfall as evidence of failure, but the housing-delivery claim is asserted, not substantiated.

rigor.statement: I will never apologise for adding more tools and skills to our young people so that they can cope when they come out of these facilities and have a better chance at life.
rigor.explanation: Sidesteps the evidence challenge rather than engaging with the Auditor-General's findings.

rigor.statement: The feedback I have received about my vision and priorities for Oranga Tamariki has been overwhelmingly positive.
rigor.explanation: Asserts broad positive reception without evidence; selection toward favourable anecdotes.

rigor.statement: Just last week, I visited a youth justice residence. I had received feedback about a young person there who had heard about our plans to establish military academies. He was very excited about this and said he would be very excited to take part in something like this.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote about one young person as evidence the policy is welcomed.

rigor.statement: A Wellington year 9 dean said she has seen no cellphones in class at all or walking around during school on duty. She noticed students engaging in game playing, like cards, and said that the librarians have been thrilled with the number of books students are taking out and have noticed students are reading in the library much more than last year.
rigor.explanation: Builds the case for the policy on selected anecdotal reports rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: the social workers association themselves have written not only to me this week but also to the Minister for social development to make it clear to her that, actually, their intention is not for it to be reduced to two years.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her opposition to the amendment in documented correspondence from the professional body, with the chain of how a withdrawn submission caused confusion.

rigor.statement: the two population groups, in terms of the social workers, that would be most affected by reducing that time from four years to two years would actually be Māori and Pacific who have been working within their community and iwi organisations, haven't yet finished their qualifications or their registration, and are going to be denied the four years to actually get up to speed and get that registration that we need them to get.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument linking the timeframe change to a workforce-shortage and equity consequence.

rigor.statement: if we find ourselves in a situation where members are trying to ask specific questions that are quite narrow in nature in order to elicit a response, and all we get is a general answer that talks about the topic that the question happens to be related to, it somewhat obviates the need for question time at all.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned procedural argument citing prior practice (Speaker Carter) that narrow questions warrant narrow answers.

specificity.statement: Well, the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is at No. 19 on the Order Paper, and when the Government is ready to make moves around it, that member will be one of the first to know.
specificity.explanation: Cites the No. 19 position but offers no timeframe or concrete plan.

specificity.statement: Yes, in the sense that Ministers will be able to refer projects. There will be two pathways. specificity.explanation: Describes two concrete pathways (listed projects; ministerial referral to an expert panel).

specificity.statement: the proportion of children reporting some level of food insecurity rose sharply in 2023, including 40 percent of Pacific households with children, and the number of children in benefit-dependent households increased during 2023, meaning more children are at risk of poverty.

specificity.statement: the accounts show an increase in core Crown expenses of around 10 percent since the same statement a year ago.

specificity.statement: GDP growth was weaker than expected in the September quarter of last year, contracting 0.3 percent, and growth in the preceding two quarters was revised down.
specificity.explanation: Names the quarter and the precise contraction figure (0.3%).

specificity.explanation: Names the $100m figure and the 2026-27 year.

specificity.statement: The BPS will be released on 27 March.
specificity.explanation: A precise date for a defined deliverable.

The next bill will be passed by the middle of 2024, setting out provisions relating to council service delivery plans and transitional economic regulations. A next bill to provide for the long-term replacement scheme will be introduced in December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names two bills with concrete timeframes (mid-2024; December 2024) and their content.

specificity.statement: Yes. Particularly when I said that this Government will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund more cycle lanes, red light cameras, speed bumps, and lowering speed limits across the city.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (11.5c/litre) and names the projects he opposes funding.

specificity.statement: Well, the mayor and myself have sat down with each other and discussed what the priority projects should be from the remaining funds. The Eastern Busway, City Rail Link trains and stabling, and local roading improvements—that's what we're going to make sure those remaining funds are spent on.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete named projects for the remaining funds.

specificity.statement: My goal is to ensure that Oranga Tamariki is truly a child-centric care and protection agency, where the safety and wellbeing and the best interests of children are at the forefront of social work practice and decision making. One way I intend to do this is by repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (repealing section 7AA) within a broader values statement.

specificity.statement: The latest inflation data from Stats New Zealand shows that the price of building a new house has increased by 41 percent as compared with 2019 prices.

specificity.statement: In Australia, for example, the cost of building a stand-alone house is some 50—five-zero—percent higher in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete comparative figure (50%) but no source detail.

specificity.statement: our coalition agreement with our New Zealand First friends sets out that this Government will amend the Building Act to make it easier to build granny flats—smaller structures, up to 60 square metres—and, in addition, our coalition agreement with the ACT Party also states that the Government will explore allowing builders to opt out of needing a building consent, provided they have long-term insurance for the building work.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (granny flats up to 60m², consent opt-out with insurance) and their source agreements.

specificity.statement: establishing the role of New Zealand's first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
specificity.explanation: Cites the ~$2.5b ring-fenced funding figure.

specificity.statement: the social workers association themselves have written not only to me this week but also to the Minister for social development to make it clear to her that, actually, their intention is not for it to be reduced to two years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail: who wrote, when, and the specific four-vs-two-year point at issue.

specificity.statement: the two population groups, in terms of the social workers, that would be most affected by reducing that time from four years to two years would actually be Māori and Pacific who have been working within their community and iwi organisations, haven't yet finished their qualifications or their registration, and are going to be denied the four years to actually get up to speed and get that registration that we need them to get.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific groups affected and the concrete mechanism (loss of the longer experience pathway).

specificity.statement: Could I ask the Minister whether she is concerned... at how it was the fact that 128,000 immigrants came to New Zealand in the year ended October last year, exacerbating all the conditions that this Government now has to deal with?
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete number and timeframe (128,000; year ended October).

specificity.statement: Āna, I do stand by my statement, and our Government deeply cares about inequalities of opportunity that many communities in New Zealand are facing, particularly Māori communities, around housing, health, and education. That's why our view is that the devolution of resources is generally better, to achieve equalities of opportunity such as the recent funding announcement by the superlative Minita Matua tākuta Shane Reti to help with child immunisation rates.
specificity.explanation: Mostly thematic, though it points to a specific immunisation funding announcement.

specificity.statement: with the social worker sector facing a significant workforce shortage, with an estimated 700 unfilled vacancies and growing demand for social work services due to the impact of COVID-19 and Cyclone Gabrielle, and also the number of students enrolled in social worker qualifications declining, it has been reviewed and looked at to shorten the period.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (700 vacancies) and the specific causes and policy response.

charisma.statement: I haven't read the decision of the panel in relation to that particular project, but what I would say in a more general sense is that it is possible to have environmental conditions proposed on projects that mitigate and remedy the environmental effects of a variety of projects, including, for example, renewable energy projects that will help decarbonise the economy and grow the economy at the same time, and I would have thought the member would be in favour of such projects.
charisma.explanation: Attempts a mild bridge to the Green questioner via shared interest in decarbonisation, but framed as a gotcha rather than genuine common ground.

charisma.statement: Can I make it very clear that we are supporting the bill overall; in fact, it started whilst we were still in Government and it is a good piece of legislation and it is the right thing to do.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party endorsement of the Government's bill, seeking common ground rather than scoring points.

veracity.statement: the proportion of children reporting some level of food insecurity rose sharply in 2023, including 40 percent of Pacific households with children, and the number of children in benefit-dependent households increased during 2023, meaning more children are at risk of poverty.
veracity.explanation: Cites Salvation Army report figures on 2023 food insecurity and benefit dependency; broadly consistent with that report.

veracity.statement: what instead we saw under the last Government's immigration settings was a significant spike in lowly skilled workers at the expense of highly skilled workers.
veracity.explanation: A contestable characterisation of immigration composition presented as fact; directionally arguable but the 'at the expense of' framing overstates a tradeoff.

veracity.statement: the accounts show an increase in core Crown expenses of around 10 percent since the same statement a year ago.
veracity.explanation: A specific fiscal figure drawn from the released six-month financial statements; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: GDP growth was weaker than expected in the September quarter of last year, contracting 0.3 percent, and growth in the preceding two quarters was revised down.
veracity.explanation: Specific GDP figure and revision claim consistent with Stats NZ data of the period.

The vast majority of councils were opposed to Labour's three waters. This Government is delivering on our commitment to restore local council ownership and control of water assets.
veracity.explanation: 'vast majority of councils were opposed' is contestable; council positions on Three Waters were more mixed than stated.

veracity.statement: The feedback I have received about my vision and priorities for Oranga Tamariki has been overwhelmingly positive.

veracity.statement: The latest inflation data from Stats New Zealand shows that the price of building a new house has increased by 41 percent as compared with 2019 prices.
veracity.explanation: A specific, sourced statistic (Stats NZ) on construction cost inflation since 2019; plausible and checkable.

veracity.explanation: The ~128,000 figure is in the range of net/gross migration estimates for the period; 'exacerbating all the conditions' is an asserted causal gloss.

veracity.explanation: Cites a concrete vacancy estimate and demand drivers; broadly consistent with known sector workforce pressures.

divination.statement: Inflation, however, is expected to continue falling, reducing cost of living pressures for New Zealand households.
divination.explanation: Forecast of continued disinflation, consistent with Treasury/RBNZ expectations at the time; plausible but uncertain on magnitude.

divination.statement: high migration means GDP per capita is expected to continue to decline.
divination.explanation: Directionally consistent with high net migration and weak growth at the time; plausible near-term forecast.

divination.statement: Put it this way: I think it is highly unlikely that the full set of forecasts in May will deliver any upside surprises.
divination.explanation: Prediction about the May Budget update; reasoned from weaker growth and lower inflation data, but a directional claim about a future official forecast.

divination.explanation: Forecasts a legislative timetable; plausible given Government control of the order paper but contingent.

divination.explanation: Predicts forthcoming evidence will show the policy works — an optimistic forecast ahead of the data.

authenticity.statement: To the first part of the question, I can confirm to the member that that is indeed the wording in the coalition agreement, and that the Government intends to keep its coalition commitments. To the second part, Cabinet has yet to consider the details of this policy and its implementation, so the member will have to wait until it is announced.
authenticity.explanation: Commits to honouring the stated coalition agreement, consistent with the published commitment.

authenticity.explanation: Action (the repeal) matches the prior stated commitment to restore council control.

strength.explanation: Points to an actually-enacted repeal (passed the previous day), a concrete delivery rather than a mere announcement.

strength.explanation: Backed by the regional fuel tax repeal being progressed in the same plan, though framed by what he won't do.
