strength.explanation: Plans drawn from coalition agreements; stated intent ('will explore') rather than delivered policy.

strength.statement: establishing the role of New Zealand's first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
strength.explanation: Points to creation of a portfolio rather than delivered mental-health outcomes.

strength.statement: I've enjoyed working with mental health professional bodies to grow the pipeline of mental health professionals, and I look forward to making announcements about this in due course.
strength.explanation: No concrete delivery; 'in due course' signals nothing yet achieved.

strength.statement: I've been working with other Government departments to develop a cross-Government approach to mental health, and I look forward to making announcements about that cross-Government approach in due course.
strength.explanation: No concrete advocacy outcome described.

charisma.statement: Apart from the amendment, the legislation itself, as it stands, I think, is supported across the House. It is the right and fair thing to do. It is good for social workers in general, but actually crucial for Aotearoa, because we need to give time for people to take up this experience pathway. We do have a shortage of social workers.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly notes cross-House support and frames the bill as common ground, separating shared agreement from the contested amendment — consensus-building tone.

charisma.statement: any Government, any Minister, has to be nimble and has to be ready to change position when they are presented with quality evidence that suggests that their way forward is not the right way forward. So it’s disappointing to see that this Minister and this Government, when presented with solid evidence and information just this week, are not willing to change their position on this.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective appeal to a shared norm of good governance, but ultimately directed at the opposing side as criticism.

charisma.statement: We acknowledge that the experience pathway is currently an important entry point for Māori practitioners and Pacific communities. The Social Workers Registration Board have recently made changes to the experience pathway application process to make this more accessible for Māori and Pacific practitioners, I believe.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opposition's central concern (Māori/Pacific access) before defending the Government line — finds common ground.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge the Minister has referred to the 2017 sort of heads-up. I acknowledge that. I want to understand then, though, what is the benefit—what is the benefit?
charisma.explanation: Explicitly concedes the Minister's prior point before pressing her own question — disarming, bridge-building approach.

charisma.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
charisma.explanation: Finds common ground with Davidson on the value of lived experience before stating the disagreement.

charisma.statement: I thank the member for his persistence, and I can give him every confidence that we will absolutely, as a Government, be looking at those pieces to ensure that it is—we want to encourage more people into work, and there will be barriers currently, but today is not for debating that; that is for another occasion.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, acknowledges the member's persistence and frames a shared aim of encouraging work.

charisma.statement: On this side of the House, we certainly want to encourage those families to get ahead through work and through less time spent on a benefit.
charisma.explanation: Frames the aim as 'this side of the House', appealing to his own side rather than reaching across the aisle.

civility.statement: Apart from the amendment, the legislation itself, as it stands, I think, is supported across the House. It is the right and fair thing to do. It is good for social workers in general, but actually crucial for Aotearoa, because we need to give time for people to take up this experience pathway. We do have a shortage of social workers.
civility.explanation: Constructive, policy-focused, no personal attack; affirms agreement before raising disagreement.

civility.statement: All of the evidence that the Government is using to actually justify the reduction in time for the extended pathway is now null and void because the most important professional body has come forward and written to the Minister and said to her that there was a mistake in that submission.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's process and use of evidence, but engages the substance rather than attacking character.

civility.statement: any Government, any Minister, has to be nimble and has to be ready to change position when they are presented with quality evidence that suggests that their way forward is not the right way forward. So it’s disappointing to see that this Minister and this Government, when presented with solid evidence and information just this week, are not willing to change their position on this.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's conduct ('disappointing') but framed around responsiveness to evidence, not personal insult.

civility.statement: I feel for the Minister in the chair, the Hon Melissa Lee, because she is not the Minister who is leading the actual bill, but the Minister who is leading the actual bill should be reading her correspondence and should be nimble enough to change her position.
civility.explanation: Shows empathy toward the stand-in Minister, but implies the lead Minister neglected her correspondence — a mild criticism of conduct rather than the person.

civility.statement: To shorten time just to fill a shortage of workforce, this idea is an unsafe way to go—it’s unsafe. I’m talking as a clinician, and I’m talking as an experienced clinician.
civility.explanation: Emphatic and emotive but aimed at the policy ('this idea'), not at a person.

civility.statement: What I heard in your discussion was that you are content with your decision, which sounded to me like the Minister will go on record as rejecting the written record by the national body—two of them, in fact, the tangata whenua body—that the Minister will go on record as being satisfied that that’s the position that’ll be taken, and, in fact, rejecting tangata whenua outwardly, and therefore Māori.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Minister's decision as 'rejecting tangata whenua... and therefore Māori', escalating a policy choice into a charged framing of the Minister's stance.

civility.statement: We acknowledge that the experience pathway is currently an important entry point for Māori practitioners and Pacific communities. The Social Workers Registration Board have recently made changes to the experience pathway application process to make this more accessible for Māori and Pacific practitioners, I believe.
civility.explanation: Respectful and substance-focused.

civility.statement: I seek the committee’s indulgence a little bit, because obviously I’m not an expert in this field—I’m sitting in the chair and I’m trying my very best to actually answer the members.
civility.explanation: Humble, respectful, conciliatory toward members.

civility.statement: did the Minister’s office receive the correspondence that we have been discussing this afternoon and that has been tabled in the committee? Did she receive it on the date that it was sent? Did she read it? Did she consider it and, therefore, did she ignore it and decide to proceed with this tabled amendment, which is reducing it from four years to two years? Did all of that happen before we came into the House today?
civility.explanation: Insistent and pointed but procedurally legitimate; targets the decision process, not the person.

civility.statement: I’m just concerned that if the Minister isn’t in a position to respond to the questions and the comments that have been made by both of the speakers previously, and you take a closure motion on this particular section, then it will go through and we haven’t actually had the question addressed.
civility.explanation: Raises a genuine procedural concern respectfully, focused on getting questions answered.

civility.statement: what advice has she sought on the impacts in the intake of Māori and Pasifika social workers, any advice that she’s sought around the intake of social workers from low socio-economic backgrounds, and what conversations has she had, in between coming into the role and tabling the amendment, with those professional bodies? And other than professional bodies, I’m also interested in what conversations has she had with tertiary education institutions around their ability to adequately train the necessary amount of social workers to meet demand.
civility.explanation: Substantive, policy-focused questioning without personal attack.

civility.statement: because of the current abatement thresholds, it actually eats up what they could be getting from the minimum family tax credit at a much faster rate than would have done, say, in 2006... effectively undermining the goals that she has talked about time and time again of relentlessly supporting people into employment.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Minister of self-contradiction but on policy grounds, engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I acknowledge the Minister has referred to the 2017 sort of heads-up. I acknowledge that. I want to understand then, though, what is the benefit—what is the benefit?
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the opponent's argument while seeking clarification.

civility.statement: unsafe practice can cause deep, irreparable harm. So I do want to make that very clear... At the same time, we have seen that the most enduring and transformational outcomes sometimes only come from those who have shared those very experiences but with the necessary supports around them to be able to safely practise and work with whānau.
civility.explanation: Even-handed, acknowledges the legitimate concern on both sides.

civility.statement: I have said I’m not going to talk about things that are not in this bill, and the abatement rate and abatement thresholds are not in the bill. So, no, I’m not going to answer questions on that.
civility.explanation: Curt but not insulting; a procedural refusal rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful, acknowledges the member's point.

civility.statement: will this in fact have a projected fiscal saving to the Government? Because benefits are going to increase at a slower rate, I’m assuming that will also mean that the family tax credits will increase at a slower rate as well. And has there been work done to understand that because this increases at a slower rate because it tracks main benefits; whether there’s fiscal savings to the Government in the forecast?
civility.explanation: Substantive, neutral, policy-focused question.

civility.statement: I do have a question around the tax implications of such a move and whether the Minister has in fact investigated any of the tax implications and the fiscal implications for such a change, because, of course, greater tax credit to families will, of course, impact the fiscal envelope and the fiscal financials for the Government.
civility.explanation: Courteous, on-topic question to a Minister of his own side.

civility.statement: what engagement or consultation you have specifically had with parents or the community who will be affected by this legislation change... there are many families in our community where the cost of living is really important and they are suffering... the figure is an $18 loss in their income per week.
civility.explanation: Respectful, focused on affected families and the consultation process.

veracity.statement: Apart from the amendment, the legislation itself, as it stands, I think, is supported across the House. It is the right and fair thing to do. It is good for social workers in general, but actually crucial for Aotearoa, because we need to give time for people to take up this experience pathway. We do have a shortage of social workers.
veracity.explanation: NZ did face a documented social worker shortage in this period; claim is accurate and uncontroversial.

veracity.statement: At the last committee stage, we did have it clarified that net wage growth was going to be 5.3 percent versus the Consumers Price Index, which is 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Recounts figures clarified earlier in committee; presented accurately as established in the debate, though the underlying numbers are not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: We acknowledge that the experience pathway is currently an important entry point for Māori practitioners and Pacific communities. The Social Workers Registration Board have recently made changes to the experience pathway application process to make this more accessible for Māori and Pacific practitioners, I believe.
veracity.explanation: Hedged claim ('I believe') about SWRB changes to the application process; plausible but presented tentatively rather than verified.

veracity.statement: The ANZASW provided a submission to the Social Services and Community Committee recommending shortening the time frame to two years. However, we understand that, as the member says, the ANZASW have softened their view on the need for a shorter time frame.
veracity.explanation: Describing the correspondence as the body having 'softened their view' is misleading given the letter stated the submission was a mistake they tried to retract and formally apologised for — understates the reversal.

veracity.statement: yes, a letter was received yesterday, I think it was, in relation to this piece of legislation, and it has been considered—a bit challenging, given the content of the letter suggesting that a submission that had been submitted on behalf of their organisation wasn’t valid, but the select committee process has finished... I’ve made the decision, for a range of other reasons, that the two-year time frame is what the Government will stand with.
veracity.explanation: Says the letter was received 'yesterday', which Sepuloni disputes (stating it went to the office on 13 February) — the timing claim is contested.

veracity.statement: I’m comfortable with my decision. It is really important that part of the consideration was to ensure that we kept the emphasis on transitioning to a mandatory qualification regime, which has been signalled in legislation since 2017... I don’t accept that it is not going to be possible within the two years. I do expect that that will apply some pressure.
veracity.explanation: The mandatory-qualification direction was indeed signalled in the 2017 social worker registration legislation — accurate.

veracity.statement: there’s been no change in the way it is calculated, it has been calculated the same way for quite some time. The only change in this legislation is the threshold... The calculation considers a range of factors: the rate of income taxes, main benefits, and the minimum wage... ensures that sole parents are better off working and receiving the minimum family tax credit than they would be receiving a benefit on an annual basis. In terms of timing, it comes into effect at the start of the tax year.
veracity.explanation: Description of the minimum family tax credit formula and its 'better off in work' design is accurate.

veracity.statement: In terms of the minimum family tax credit work-hours test, “full time” is actually defined as 20 hours or more per week for a sole parent and 30 hours or more combined for a two-parent family.
veracity.explanation: Matches the established Working for Families minimum family tax credit work-hours thresholds.

veracity.statement: what engagement or consultation you have specifically had with parents or the community who will be affected by this legislation change... there are many families in our community where the cost of living is really important and they are suffering... the figure is an $18 loss in their income per week.
veracity.explanation: The '$18 loss per week' figure is asserted without sourcing and contrasted against a '$2' figure mentioned earlier — the magnitude is contested in the debate.

rigor.statement: Apart from the amendment, the legislation itself, as it stands, I think, is supported across the House. It is the right and fair thing to do. It is good for social workers in general, but actually crucial for Aotearoa, because we need to give time for people to take up this experience pathway. We do have a shortage of social workers.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning links the time frame to workforce supply, but the 'crucial' conclusion leans on assertion rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: All of the evidence that the Government is using to actually justify the reduction in time for the extended pathway is now null and void because the most important professional body has come forward and written to the Minister and said to her that there was a mistake in that submission.
rigor.explanation: Sound core argument that the evidentiary basis was retracted, but 'null and void' overstates — the submission still formally exists in the select committee record.

rigor.statement: any Government, any Minister, has to be nimble and has to be ready to change position when they are presented with quality evidence that suggests that their way forward is not the right way forward. So it’s disappointing to see that this Minister and this Government, when presented with solid evidence and information just this week, are not willing to change their position on this.
rigor.explanation: Coherent principle (update positions on new evidence) applied to the case; reasonable though normative.

rigor.statement: pathways take time. Pathways of learning take time, particularly so when systemically it prejudices particularly Māori in the process of registration. And why I know this is because I was one of those that attempted the registration process some while ago.
rigor.explanation: Compelling but rests on personal anecdote and assertion of systemic bias rather than cited data — an appeal to personal experience.

rigor.statement: To shorten time just to fill a shortage of workforce, this idea is an unsafe way to go—it’s unsafe. I’m talking as a clinician, and I’m talking as an experienced clinician.
rigor.explanation: Leans on appeal to her own authority/experience ('as an experienced clinician') rather than presenting evidence for the harm claim.

rigor.statement: it took me more than four years—and I said earlier before that I wouldn’t say what the number was, but it did take me time, and many like me. Why? It’s because we’re working while we’re getting credentials—we’re working while we get on the way; we are on the job.
rigor.explanation: Anecdotal evidence generalised ('many like me'); persuasive but not systematically evidenced.

rigor.statement: What I heard in your discussion was that you are content with your decision, which sounded to me like the Minister will go on record as rejecting the written record by the national body—two of them, in fact, the tangata whenua body—that the Minister will go on record as being satisfied that that’s the position that’ll be taken, and, in fact, rejecting tangata whenua outwardly, and therefore Māori.
rigor.explanation: Slides from 'declined the bodies' advice' to 'rejecting Māori', a leap that overstates the entailment.

rigor.statement: A shorter time frame could also encourage more of an uptake in social worker qualifications. A two-year delay will also provide an opportunity to consider an alternative entry pathway into social worker registration that is more accessible, including for Māori and Pasifika and other communities.
rigor.explanation: Asserts benefits of the shorter timeframe without evidence; reasoning is plausible but unsupported.

rigor.statement: I’m just concerned that if the Minister isn’t in a position to respond to the questions and the comments that have been made by both of the speakers previously, and you take a closure motion on this particular section, then it will go through and we haven’t actually had the question addressed.
rigor.explanation: Logical worry about closure pre-empting answers; sound but modest reasoning.

rigor.statement: what advice has she sought on the impacts in the intake of Māori and Pasifika social workers, any advice that she’s sought around the intake of social workers from low socio-economic backgrounds, and what conversations has she had, in between coming into the role and tabling the amendment, with those professional bodies? And other than professional bodies, I’m also interested in what conversations has she had with tertiary education institutions around their ability to adequately train the necessary amount of social workers to meet demand.
rigor.explanation: Systematically probes the evidence base for the amendment across distinct stakeholder groups before accepting the conclusion.

rigor.statement: being a field educator for social workers, I’ve done guest lectures for social work classes, and it’s really clear that a lot of the people who are able to get registered through the experience pathways are some of the people who are really struggling to enter the professional sector through the traditional pathways. I’ve seen students who are having to work multiple jobs to make ends meet while expected to complete their unpaid labour that they do as part of the degree.
rigor.explanation: First-hand observation used as evidence; persuasive but anecdotal generalisation.

rigor.statement: because of the current abatement thresholds, it actually eats up what they could be getting from the minimum family tax credit at a much faster rate than would have done, say, in 2006... effectively undermining the goals that she has talked about time and time again of relentlessly supporting people into employment.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a clear chain: un-indexed thresholds since 2006 → faster abatement → reduced work incentive → contradicts the stated employment goal.

rigor.statement: unsafe practice can cause deep, irreparable harm. So I do want to make that very clear... At the same time, we have seen that the most enduring and transformational outcomes sometimes only come from those who have shared those very experiences but with the necessary supports around them to be able to safely practise and work with whānau.
rigor.explanation: Balances two competing considerations (risk of unsafe practice vs value of lived experience) and conditions the benefit on adequate supports — nuanced reasoning.

rigor.statement: will this in fact have a projected fiscal saving to the Government? Because benefits are going to increase at a slower rate, I’m assuming that will also mean that the family tax credits will increase at a slower rate as well. And has there been work done to understand that because this increases at a slower rate because it tracks main benefits; whether there’s fiscal savings to the Government in the forecast?
rigor.explanation: Builds a clear causal inference (benefits track inflation → slower increase → tax credits track benefits → likely fiscal saving) and asks for it to be tested.

rigor.statement: I do have a question around the tax implications of such a move and whether the Minister has in fact investigated any of the tax implications and the fiscal implications for such a change, because, of course, greater tax credit to families will, of course, impact the fiscal envelope and the fiscal financials for the Government.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that increased tax credits affect the fiscal envelope; logical but not deeply evidenced.

forthrightness.statement: I have said I’m not going to talk about things that are not in this bill, and the abatement rate and abatement thresholds are not in the bill. So, no, I’m not going to answer questions on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicit refusal to engage Menéndez March's repeated, central question; declines on scope grounds rather than addressing the substance.

forthrightness.statement: there’s been no change in the way it is calculated, it has been calculated the same way for quite some time. The only change in this legislation is the threshold... The calculation considers a range of factors: the rate of income taxes, main benefits, and the minimum wage... ensures that sole parents are better off working and receiving the minimum family tax credit than they would be receiving a benefit on an annual basis. In terms of timing, it comes into effect at the start of the tax year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about how the minimum family tax credit is calculated and when it takes effect.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the minimum family tax credit work-hours test, “full time” is actually defined as 20 hours or more per week for a sole parent and 30 hours or more combined for a two-parent family.
forthrightness.explanation: Returns to and directly answers Menéndez March's earlier part-time-work question with concrete detail.

forthrightness.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not actually answer Davidson's specific question — what the benefit of two years over four is — instead reaffirming the decision.

forthrightness.statement: I thank the member for his persistence, and I can give him every confidence that we will absolutely, as a Government, be looking at those pieces to ensure that it is—we want to encourage more people into work, and there will be barriers currently, but today is not for debating that; that is for another occasion.
forthrightness.explanation: Offers a general assurance but defers the substantive question on abatement thresholds to 'another occasion' without committing to anything concrete.

strength.statement: I do have an amendment here in relationship to that that would actually update the abatement thresholds in line with inflation.
strength.explanation: Backs his critique with a concrete tabled amendment rather than rhetoric alone, but as an opposition member with no governing majority its delivery is uncertain.

veracity.statement: by 2015, the Commerce Commission noted that the numbers of orders per month increased approximately 400 percent after that change—from approximately 200, to over a thousand.
veracity.explanation: Specific attributed statistic (Commerce Commission, ~400% rise from ~200 to over 1,000/month); plausible and consistent with reporting on the 2014 reforms, though not independently confirmable from the text.

veracity.statement: in 2018, over 24,000 attachment orders for civil debt were granted against people on the benefit—beneficiaries. Only around 5,000 of civil attachments were made against people on wages—people who were working.
veracity.explanation: Concrete figures cited from public reporting; the ~24,000 vs ~5,000 split is plausible and aligns with the wider point about beneficiaries being disproportionately targeted.

veracity.statement: In 2020, the Salvation Army also noted that only 14 percent of attachments in 2020 were placed on people who were working and receiving wages, leaving a massive 86 percent of attachment orders against beneficiaries.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to the Salvation Army with a specific 14%/86% split; consistent with the earlier figures and uncontested by other speakers (Arbuckle repeats the 86%).

veracity.statement: Also, the District Court already has the power to limit an attachment order on beneficiaries. Currently, that limit is at 40 percent of their income.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the existing protected earnings mechanism (no more than 40% deductible); Brewer and Nakhle independently confirm this figure.

veracity.statement: recently, last year, we had a coalition of groups including FinCap, Child Poverty Action Group, the Dunedin Budget Advisory Service... the Salvation Army as well as the Nelson Budget Service penning a letter to the former Ministers at the time, calling for attachment orders to be stopped for people on the benefit.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable claim about a named coalition's letter; plausible and uncontested.

veracity.statement: we’re looking at 86 percent of attachments are to beneficiaries—that in itself speaks loudly.
veracity.explanation: Repeats the 86% beneficiary figure cited earlier from the Salvation Army; accurate to the source.

veracity.statement: all of a sudden, if we passed this legislation, we are actually saying, “If you’re on a benefit, you go ahead and you commit a crime, and it doesn’t really matter because the highest amount you’ll get is 5 percent.”
veracity.explanation: Misleading implication that the bill is mainly about offenders escaping reparations, when reparations are a minority of attachment orders and administered separately via the Ministry of Justice.

veracity.statement: In a supplementary answer to question 10 from Te Pāti Māori, I answered that the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000. It is actually 69,100.
veracity.explanation: Replaces an inaccurate figure (76,000) with the precise correct one (69,100).

veracity.statement: in August 2023 a man who received $452.74 a week in benefits payments had $96 a week to cover off his own debt repayments... Then he had $30 a week taken for a private debt collector’s attachment order, $40 went to the Ministry of Justice, $11.00 to the Ministry of Social Development, and $15 in child support. He was left with $356 a week; $270 had to go on rent, giving him $86 a week to live on.
veracity.explanation: Internally consistent itemised example; presented as a real August 2023 case, plausible though unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Other jurisdictions in other countries prohibit entirely the attachment orders in respect of benefit payments. So for New Zealand this is an incredibly modest move.
veracity.explanation: Broadly true that some jurisdictions exempt benefits from attachment (Menéndez March cites Australia); stated generally without naming which, so partially supported.

veracity.statement: the bill only affects attachments issued under the District Court Act, even though attachments and deductions exist in other legislation.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's limited statutory reach.

veracity.statement: there already is a mechanism in the civil court system where 40 percent of a debtor’s net income can be deducted... either party can apply to vary this and to suspend or cancel the attachment order.
veracity.explanation: Correctly states the existing 40% ceiling and the ability to apply to vary/suspend/cancel orders.

veracity.statement: if you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate and the PER is set at 60 percent, meaning that no more than 40 percent of a person’s net earnings can be deducted.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the protected earnings rate (60% protected / 40% maximum deductible).

veracity.statement: deductions can include a range of Government or court orders, including child support, tax administration, student loan repayments, Working for Families overpayments, benefit overpayments, recoverable assistance, and fines or reparation payments. These deductions have priority over civil debt.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate list of deduction types and their priority ordering.

veracity.statement: the fifth Labour Government introduced the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, or the CCCFA legislation, in 2003 during the Clark years, and then it was heavily amended in the Jacinda Ardern years
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the CCCFA was enacted in 2003 under the Clark Government and significantly amended (responsible-lending changes) under the later Labour Government.

veracity.statement: it’s unworkable for a lot of people having to present their Netflix accounts to their bank manager at the ANZ.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic caricature of the CCCFA affordability checks; presents a memto-style exaggeration as fact.

veracity.statement: these people that are going to loan sharks, which are heavily monitored and regulated these days, know exactly what they are agreeing to.
veracity.explanation: Overstated — high-cost lending harm persisted despite regulation, so the blanket claim is misleading.

veracity.statement: a 25-year-old on a single person’s jobseeker benefit is given $337 a week net... What I just heard members from the other side of the House say is that it’s OK to take 40 percent of that in attachment orders. That would leave them with $202 to live off
veracity.explanation: The arithmetic is correct (60% of $337 ≈ $202) and the jobseeker rate is in the right range; the gloss that opponents say it's 'OK' is rhetorical characterisation.

veracity.statement: Mr Arbuckle probably had the most thoughtful comment... Well, in fact, they’re administered through the Ministry of Justice, but that’s a decent question.
veracity.explanation: Correctly notes that criminal reparations are administered through the Ministry of Justice, distinguishing them from the civil-debt attachments the bill targets.

veracity.statement: We heard today that that Government’s actions will see 7,000 more children in poverty
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure attributed to the day's debate; a contestable projection (likely from benefit-indexation modelling) presented without source detail.

veracity.statement: We funded Omāroro Reservoir—35 million litres of drinking water on the city side of the Wellington fault.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about a real Wellington reservoir project; plausible and consistent with her tenure.

veracity.statement: Clean air regulations have now vastly improved people’s health, so regulation is essential.
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported: post-war clean-air regulation (e.g. UK after the 1950s smogs she references) is well documented to have improved respiratory health.

veracity.statement: We’re seeing more and more people choosing to bike, one of the best ways to reduce congestion.
veracity.explanation: Cycling growth and its congestion benefits are broadly supported, but stated generally without figures, so only partially substantiated.

specificity.statement: by 2015, the Commerce Commission noted that the numbers of orders per month increased approximately 400 percent after that change—from approximately 200, to over a thousand.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the timeframe, the percentage, and concrete before/after figures.

specificity.statement: in 2018, over 24,000 attachment orders for civil debt were granted against people on the benefit—beneficiaries. Only around 5,000 of civil attachments were made against people on wages—people who were working.
specificity.explanation: Year, exact counts, and a clear comparison between beneficiaries and wage earners.

specificity.statement: In 2020, the Salvation Army also noted that only 14 percent of attachments in 2020 were placed on people who were working and receiving wages, leaving a massive 86 percent of attachment orders against beneficiaries.
specificity.explanation: Source, year and precise percentages given.

specificity.statement: Also, the District Court already has the power to limit an attachment order on beneficiaries. Currently, that limit is at 40 percent of their income.
specificity.explanation: Names the existing power and the precise 40% threshold.

specificity.statement: The idea of limiting to 5 percent attachment judgments will not incentivise individuals from pushing themselves to taking on that personal responsibility of being mindful of the debts that they incur.
specificity.explanation: References the concrete 5% cap but the predicted effect on behaviour is left general.

specificity.statement: recently, last year, we had a coalition of groups including FinCap, Child Poverty Action Group, the Dunedin Budget Advisory Service... the Salvation Army as well as the Nelson Budget Service penning a letter to the former Ministers at the time, calling for attachment orders to be stopped for people on the benefit.
specificity.explanation: Names numerous specific advocacy organisations and the concrete action (a letter to Ministers calling for a stop), though no date precision.

specificity.statement: if somebody has incurred a huge amount of civil debt while being on benefit, they will know that if they take up employment, they will have to pay that money back sooner or in bigger instalments than it would be because of this legislation. So overall, it’s not going to actually do good for these people
specificity.explanation: Lays out a concrete mechanism but no figures or evidence.

specificity.statement: what happens is a person can get an attachment order and take it along to WINZ and it gets processed through the WINZ computer systems automatically... there are companies that specialise in doing it. So they buy the debt and they get attachment orders on it, and they take these debts along to WINZ—the attachment orders—in bulk lots and get them bulk processed
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete process — debt-buyers, bulk lots, automated WINZ processing — though without figures.

specificity.statement: in August 2023 a man who received $452.74 a week in benefits payments had $96 a week to cover off his own debt repayments... Then he had $30 a week taken for a private debt collector’s attachment order, $40 went to the Ministry of Justice, $11.00 to the Ministry of Social Development, and $15 in child support. He was left with $356 a week; $270 had to go on rent, giving him $86 a week to live on.
specificity.explanation: Highly concrete worked case: exact weekly income, each deduction line-itemised, rent, and residual.

specificity.statement: there already is a mechanism in the civil court system where 40 percent of a debtor’s net income can be deducted... either party can apply to vary this and to suspend or cancel the attachment order.
specificity.explanation: Names the existing 40% mechanism and the variation route, though Webb contests its adequacy.

specificity.statement: this bill harms no one, it’s a step forward to making a positive contribution towards the livelihoods and the lives of people who often are the ones that are most vulnerable in our society
specificity.explanation: General framing of the bill's benefit without mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: if you look at the District Court Act, it already provides for a protected earnings rate and the PER is set at 60 percent, meaning that no more than 40 percent of a person’s net earnings can be deducted.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the PER, and the precise percentages.

specificity.statement: deductions can include a range of Government or court orders, including child support, tax administration, student loan repayments, Working for Families overpayments, benefit overpayments, recoverable assistance, and fines or reparation payments. These deductions have priority over civil debt.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the categories of competing deductions and their priority over civil debt.

specificity.statement: a 25-year-old on a single person’s jobseeker benefit is given $337 a week net... What I just heard members from the other side of the House say is that it’s OK to take 40 percent of that in attachment orders. That would leave them with $202 to live off
specificity.explanation: Exact benefit figure, the 40% rate, and the resulting residual amount.

specificity.statement: We made Wellington this country’s first living wage council.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete, first-of-its-kind policy outcome, though without dates or figures.

specificity.statement: We funded Omāroro Reservoir—35 million litres of drinking water on the city side of the Wellington fault.
specificity.explanation: Names the project and its 35-million-litre capacity and strategic siting.

specificity.statement: I led this city through the 2013 earthquakes, taking decisive action in increasing earthquake resilience funding and partnerships
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a real event and a stated action, but 'increasing funding and partnerships' lacks amounts.

specificity.statement: We’re seeing more and more people choosing to bike, one of the best ways to reduce congestion.
specificity.explanation: Vague trend claim ('more and more') with no quantification.

rigor.statement: The idea of limiting to 5 percent attachment judgments will not incentivise individuals from pushing themselves to taking on that personal responsibility of being mindful of the debts that they incur.
rigor.explanation: An asserted behavioural claim resting on an incentives intuition with no evidence; ignores the counter-argument (later made by Menéndez March) that those with no surplus income cannot 'budget' their way out.

rigor.statement: Yes, circumstances may change, but then the responsibility of taking more debt is a personal one and something that each individual truly needs to get a handle on in life.
rigor.explanation: A values-based appeal to personal responsibility; reasonable as a principle but unsupported and does not engage the evidence about beneficiaries' capacity to repay.

rigor.statement: you can’t actually make life choices when you don’t have the choice. Like, if you get stripped of so much of your money when you literally have no money left to make decisions on how you spend it, it doesn’t matter how good you’re at budgeting; you’re put in that impossible situation where you then have to take more debt to survive.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal argument directly rebutting the 'personal responsibility' framing: removing disposable income forecloses the budgeting choices that argument presumes.

rigor.statement: if somebody has incurred a huge amount of civil debt while being on benefit, they will know that if they take up employment, they will have to pay that money back sooner or in bigger instalments than it would be because of this legislation. So overall, it’s not going to actually do good for these people
rigor.explanation: A logically structured incentive argument (the cap creates a cliff-edge on entering work), but asserted without evidence of magnitude and assuming debtors reason this way.

rigor.statement: lenders will not be lending money to people if they are on benefit because of this legislation, if it goes through.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned from lender incentives but presented as certainty without evidence.

rigor.statement: courts make a judgment based on individual circumstances. So... putting this percentage on whatever amount they are getting through Work and Income actually considers that everybody’s circumstances are exactly the same, which is wrong.
rigor.explanation: A fair point that a flat 5% cap removes individualised judicial discretion; somewhat overstated since a cap sets a ceiling rather than mandating identical treatment.

rigor.statement: all of a sudden, if we passed this legislation, we are actually saying, “If you’re on a benefit, you go ahead and you commit a crime, and it doesn’t really matter because the highest amount you’ll get is 5 percent.”
rigor.explanation: Overgeneralises: most attachment orders are civil debt, not criminal reparations (as Russell and Webb note), so the crime framing misrepresents the bill's reach.

rigor.statement: If you do a crime, you pay—it’s as simple as that. Putting a minimum of 5 percent I just do not think is appropriate... but don’t do the crime in the first place.
rigor.explanation: An oversimplified slogan ('it's as simple as that') that collapses the civil-debt question into crime-and-punishment without addressing the bill's actual scope.

rigor.statement: what happens is a person can get an attachment order and take it along to WINZ and it gets processed through the WINZ computer systems automatically... there are companies that specialise in doing it. So they buy the debt and they get attachment orders on it, and they take these debts along to WINZ—the attachment orders—in bulk lots and get them bulk processed
rigor.explanation: Builds a clear mechanism-based explanation (automated bulk processing) for why beneficiaries are disproportionately hit, directly answering Arbuckle's 'why this bill?' question.

rigor.statement: I agree that reparations to victims of crime should be perhaps further up the list, but that is exactly the sort of issue that could have been discussed through a select committee process. I urge the member that if he wants to make that priority, this is an ideal bill to do it on
rigor.explanation: Concedes the point and offers a constructive procedural resolution (debt prioritisation at select committee).

rigor.statement: in August 2023 a man who received $452.74 a week in benefits payments had $96 a week to cover off his own debt repayments... Then he had $30 a week taken for a private debt collector’s attachment order, $40 went to the Ministry of Justice, $11.00 to the Ministry of Social Development, and $15 in child support. He was left with $356 a week; $270 had to go on rent, giving him $86 a week to live on.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete case to evidence the harm claim, though a single example is anecdotal.

rigor.statement: Other jurisdictions in other countries prohibit entirely the attachment orders in respect of benefit payments. So for New Zealand this is an incredibly modest move.
rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative-jurisdiction benchmark to argue the bill is modest — a reasonable, if undetailed, appeal to precedent.

rigor.statement: the bill only affects attachments issued under the District Court Act, even though attachments and deductions exist in other legislation.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine scope limitation (only District Court attachments), a substantive policy critique echoing Garcia.

rigor.statement: limiting the amount the creditor can receive through attachment orders may also incentivise them to pursue other methods of enforcement. And we’re talking about methods such as seizing property.
rigor.explanation: A plausible unintended-consequences argument (creditors switching to harsher enforcement); reasoned but speculative and unevidenced.

rigor.statement: the quickest and easiest thing is always to blame the person at the bottom of the pile. What about their responsibility to make sure that people don’t get into that debt?
rigor.explanation: Reframes the responsibility argument toward lenders — a fair rhetorical counter, though it asserts rather than evidences the responsible-lending failure.

rigor.statement: this bill harms no one, it’s a step forward to making a positive contribution towards the livelihoods and the lives of people who often are the ones that are most vulnerable in our society
rigor.explanation: 'Harms no one' overstates — it does not engage the opposition's stated harms (lender withdrawal, reparation priority).

rigor.statement: it’s unworkable for a lot of people having to present their Netflix accounts to their bank manager at the ANZ.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a vivid exaggeration rather than evidence to argue the rules are unworkable.

rigor.statement: these people that are going to loan sharks, which are heavily monitored and regulated these days, know exactly what they are agreeing to.
rigor.explanation: Asserts borrowers 'know exactly what they are agreeing to', dismissing the irresponsible-lending evidence Russell raised; unsupported and contestable.

rigor.statement: a 25-year-old on a single person’s jobseeker benefit is given $337 a week net... What I just heard members from the other side of the House say is that it’s OK to take 40 percent of that in attachment orders. That would leave them with $202 to live off
rigor.explanation: Grounds the hardship argument in a concrete calculation, though it frames the opposition's position uncharitably.

rigor.statement: maybe Mr Garcia hasn’t had the misfortune to lose a job by redundancy, or fall sick, or have a car break down when you’re on a low income and have to borrow money to get the kids to school on time. Things go wrong, bad things happen, and people get into debt and can’t pay it back.
rigor.explanation: Makes the substantive point that debt often arises from non-culpable shocks, rebutting the personal-responsibility frame — though it leans on illustrative anecdote and a jab at Garcia.

rigor.statement: I am horrified by this Government’s reckless blanket cancellation of so many walking and cycling projects, robbing today’s children of their independence and health.
rigor.explanation: Asserts harm to children's health and independence as a consequence of cancellations without supporting evidence; leans on an appeal to emotion.

rigor.statement: We won’t become a smart, green country by 2040 with three-year flip-flops cancelling out each other’s policies and Budgets.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument that policy whiplash undermines long-term goals, though offered as assertion rather than with evidence.

rigor.statement: Clean air regulations have now vastly improved people’s health, so regulation is essential.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real historical example to support a regulatory principle, though the leap from one case to 'regulation is essential' is a generalisation.

rigor.statement: Debtors deserve to get their money back.
rigor.explanation: An interjection asserting creditors' right to repayment; a fair principle but stated as a one-line slogan that ignores the bill's capacity-to-pay point (Russell immediately concedes the principle but distinguishes it).

charisma.statement: you can’t actually make life choices when you don’t have the choice. Like, if you get stripped of so much of your money when you literally have no money left to make decisions on how you spend it, it doesn’t matter how good you’re at budgeting; you’re put in that impossible situation where you then have to take more debt to survive.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective but framed against the Government side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: it seems that the Government side is content with the status quo of trapping people in poverty.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that closes down rather than builds cross-party agreement.

charisma.statement: I just want to address the issue that was raised by the member from New Zealand First, worrying about the victims of crime. Actually, he’s got a point. He’s got a good point on that one. I think there is some regard that needs to be given to the priority of debt
charisma.explanation: Explicitly concedes a valid point from an opposing party and turns it into a reason to advance the bill — genuine bridge-building across the House.

charisma.statement: I agree that reparations to victims of crime should be perhaps further up the list, but that is exactly the sort of issue that could have been discussed through a select committee process. I urge the member that if he wants to make that priority, this is an ideal bill to do it on
charisma.explanation: Invites an opponent to bring his own concern into the process, seeking common ground rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: If those members opposite think it’s OK to live on $86 a week, I’d like to see them try and do it themselves.
charisma.explanation: Rallying line aimed at the opposing benches, not consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: the theme that I’ve noticed through the Opposition’s contributions today has been searching for excuses. None of it was particularly logical; none of it really stood out.
charisma.explanation: Reinforces the partisan divide rather than seeking to persuade the other side.

charisma.statement: Mr Arbuckle probably had the most thoughtful comment, which was, essentially, “OK, how does this affect reparation payments for victims of crime?” ... it’s a good question to put to select committee to make sure we strike the right balance there, so well done, Mr Arbuckle.
charisma.explanation: Singles out and praises an opposing MP's point as worthwhile, building a bridge across the House even while disagreeing.

charisma.statement: What we have on the other side of the House is an uncaring Government who really doesn’t understand poverty and who thinks it’s attacking the drivers of crime when it’s increasing the drivers of crime.
charisma.explanation: Strongly divisive us-vs-them framing.

civility.statement: it seems that the Government side is content with the status quo of trapping people in poverty.
civility.explanation: Imputes a callous motive ('content with trapping people in poverty') to opponents rather than engaging their stated reasons.

civility.statement: it was interesting to hear from Paulo Garcia, from the Government side, where he identified the problem right at the beginning. He almost got it right.
civility.explanation: Engages the opponent's actual argument and credits part of it, though with a faintly dismissive 'almost got it right'.

civility.statement: I can clearly see that the intention behind this bill is a good one, but that intention won’t be delivered through this bill
civility.explanation: Acknowledges the bill sponsor's good intent and frames opposition around delivery rather than character.

civility.statement: If you do a crime, you pay—it’s as simple as that. Putting a minimum of 5 percent I just do not think is appropriate... but don’t do the crime in the first place.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the policy/offending question rather than at an individual member.

civility.statement: I just want to address the issue that was raised by the member from New Zealand First, worrying about the victims of crime. Actually, he’s got a point. He’s got a good point on that one. I think there is some regard that needs to be given to the priority of debt
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with an opponent's argument on its merits.

civility.statement: on a day where the Government is eroding the financial ability of beneficiaries in the future, that they’re also voting against this bill... So it’s a double whammy today for anybody who is on a benefit, thanks to the members opposite who proclaim to be fighting the cost of living crisis.
civility.explanation: Harsh and rhetorical ('double whammy') but tied to votes and policy rather than personal abuse.

civility.statement: If those members opposite think it’s OK to live on $86 a week, I’d like to see them try and do it themselves.
civility.explanation: A challenge that imputes a callous attitude to opponents; rhetorical rather than engaging their stated reasons.

civility.statement: the quickest and easiest thing is always to blame the person at the bottom of the pile. What about their responsibility to make sure that people don’t get into that debt?
civility.explanation: Critiques the opposing argument's logic ('blame the person at the bottom') without naming or attacking an individual.

civility.statement: the theme that I’ve noticed through the Opposition’s contributions today has been searching for excuses. None of it was particularly logical; none of it really stood out.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' arguments wholesale as 'excuses' rather than rebutting specific points.

civility.statement: That, frankly, was an embarrassment—an underprepared member coming along, reading the bill, and talking from a list of points about things which are utterly irrelevant. If you’re going to come to this House, treat it with the dignity it deserves.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on Brewer's competence and preparation ('an embarrassment', 'underprepared') rather than his arguments.

civility.statement: Mr Arbuckle probably had the most thoughtful comment, which was, essentially, “OK, how does this affect reparation payments for victims of crime?” ... it’s a good question to put to select committee to make sure we strike the right balance there, so well done, Mr Arbuckle.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused engagement with an opponent's contribution.

civility.statement: What we have on the other side of the House is an uncaring Government who really doesn’t understand poverty and who thinks it’s attacking the drivers of crime when it’s increasing the drivers of crime.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as 'uncaring' and ignorant of poverty — an attack on motive and character rather than their arguments.

civility.statement: maybe Mr Garcia hasn’t had the misfortune to lose a job by redundancy, or fall sick, or have a car break down when you’re on a low income and have to borrow money to get the kids to school on time. Things go wrong, bad things happen, and people get into debt and can’t pay it back.
civility.explanation: Engages the responsibility argument but does so via a pointed personal supposition about Garcia's life experience.

civility.statement: I am horrified by this Government’s reckless blanket cancellation of so many walking and cycling projects, robbing today’s children of their independence and health.
civility.explanation: Charged language ('reckless', 'robbing children') directed at a Government policy; harsh and emotive but aimed at the policy, not an individual.

divination.statement: lenders will not be lending money to people if they are on benefit because of this legislation, if it goes through.
divination.explanation: A prediction that the cap would dry up lending to beneficiaries; directionally plausible but overstated as a categorical outcome ('will not'), and cuts against Russell's counter that this is the point of responsible-lending checks.

divination.statement: We heard today that that Government’s actions will see 7,000 more children in poverty
divination.explanation: Forecasts 7,000 more children in poverty from the indexation change; directionally plausible but the precise magnitude is uncertain.

divination.statement: We won’t become a smart, green country by 2040 with three-year flip-flops cancelling out each other’s policies and Budgets.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction that the 2040 goal fails under short-term policy reversals; plausible and reasoned, but the conditional framing and long horizon make it only loosely falsifiable.

forthrightness.statement: I haven’t had any consultation on this, so I’ve just read today and heard from Mr Webb what the bill’s intention is.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits he has only just seen the bill and lacks consultation, rather than feigning command of it.

forthrightness.statement: In a supplementary answer to question 10 from Te Pāti Māori, I answered that the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000. It is actually 69,100.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, unprompted correction of a specific figure.

authenticity.statement: I haven’t had any consultation on this, so I’ve just read today and heard from Mr Webb what the bill’s intention is.

specificity.statement: it increases the prescribed amount from $34,216 to $35,204.

specificity.statement: We know, looking back over the last 20 years or so, that in most years—around nine out of 10 years—wage increases have been higher than inflation. That is why we made this change

divination.explanation: Predicts rising food-bank and hardship-grant demand; plausible given reduced benefit growth, but unquantified.

civility.statement: What it is is bullying. It is bullying from that side of the House and deliberate distraction tactics—move people's attention away from what they should be focused on, put their attention on the poorest New Zealanders, as if they are to blame, they are the villain
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as 'bullying' and using 'distraction tactics'—an attack on motive rather than engagement with the policy substance.

civility.explanation: Dismissive ('Baloney') but aimed at the Government's claim about itself rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Our communities are served better than a Minister who doesn't actually understand the welfare system she's been put in charge of running
civility.explanation: Personal attack on the Minister's competence rather than her arguments.

civility.statement: So let's cut the BS from the Minister and actually accept that this is a bill that will punish disabled people the hardest.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'BS' framing and emotive 'punish' language directed at the Minister.

civility.statement: Yes, we acknowledge that arguments can be made both ways.
civility.explanation: Respectful framing that legitimises the other side's reasoning.

civility.statement: Why do we want to imagine that somebody will be sitting on benefit for four to five years? That is not the kind of ambition we bring to New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Frames disagreement around 'ambition' without personal insult, though it implies the opponent lacks aspiration for beneficiaries.

civility.explanation: Respectful, reframes the dispute as differing methods rather than differing values.

civility.explanation: Personal jab at the colleague ('stopped reading her notes') rather than her argument.

civility.statement: we are opposing this legislation and the hateful rhetoric that comes with it.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents' rhetoric 'hateful'—a characterisation of motive rather than engagement with their reasoning.

civility.statement: They are anti-Māori, anti-workers' rights, anti-disability, and anti-beneficiaries.
civility.explanation: Sweeping condemnatory labelling of the Government rather than critique of specific policy.

civility.statement: Many of them have expressed values coming from the Christian faith they profess. I would like to see that faith expressed in action, not just words.
civility.explanation: Pointed challenge to opponents' professed faith versus their vote—engages values but edges toward a personal-consistency jab rather than policy substance.

civility.statement: taking from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible.
civility.explanation: Strong moral condemnation of the policy (not a personal insult), but the 'morally reprehensible' framing is heated and assigns bad character to the choice.

civility.statement: The first is that it's not beneficiaries' tax money; it's actually hard-working New Zealanders' tax money and it is being given to beneficiaries.
civility.explanation: Pointed correction of a colleague but framed as a substantive point, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: We've traversed this topic a lot in the last year, in the election campaign, which that side of the House lost overwhelmingly. They lost their seats to large majorities from this side of the House.
civility.explanation: Triumphalist jab about election losses rather than engagement with the policy merits.

civility.statement: some of whom have been smirking and laughing and interrupting my colleagues talking about when their parents passed away from cancer
civility.explanation: Accuses named opponents of mocking colleagues' grief—an attack on conduct/character rather than policy.

civility.statement: Evidence—the evidence; you're rejecting the evidence.
civility.explanation: An interjection challenging the speaker, but pointed at the substance (use of evidence) rather than the person.

rigor.statement: What it is is bullying. It is bullying from that side of the House and deliberate distraction tactics—move people's attention away from what they should be focused on, put their attention on the poorest New Zealanders, as if they are to blame, they are the villain
rigor.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad-faith motive without evidence; rhetorical assertion rather than reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: Our communities are served better than a Minister who doesn't actually understand the welfare system she's been put in charge of running
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem; competence assertion stands in for engagement with the policy.

rigor.statement: the irresponsible spending of the previous Labour Government fuelled inflation.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause attribution that understates the well-documented global drivers of the inflation spike.

rigor.statement: Why do we want to imagine that somebody will be sitting on benefit for four to five years? That is not the kind of ambition we bring to New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Sidesteps the cumulative-loss argument by disputing the premise that people remain on benefits long term, rather than rebutting the modelled losses.

rigor.statement: many of us have experienced poverty, have lived it, and we know what it tastes, smells, and feels like.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal lived experience rather than evidence about the bill's effects.

rigor.statement: It is about also addressing the culture of welfare dependency that we've got in this country, and it is something that seems to be increasing as the years go on
rigor.explanation: Relies on the loaded 'dependency' framing without data to support the claimed increase.

rigor.statement: People like the 311 families who together mass $85 billion collectively without being fairly taxed.
rigor.explanation: Pivots to wealth taxation as a counter to the 'dependency' framing—rhetorically effective but only loosely connected to the bill at hand.

rigor.statement: They are anti-Māori, anti-workers' rights, anti-disability, and anti-beneficiaries.
rigor.explanation: A string of 'anti-' labels asserted without supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: if the main benefit is indexed on cost of living, then the cost of living would have also gone down.
rigor.explanation: Weak reasoning: implies that any future nominal drop in benefits would only follow a fall in the cost of living, which sidesteps the opponents' point about benefits lagging wages over time.

rigor.statement: there's some really clear economic research that shows that lower-income people are more affected by inflation... Lower-income households will be experiencing a higher rate of inflation because of the basket of goods and services that they actually purchase.

rigor.statement: Central to his thinking was the thinking that in terms of the way we set up our society, we would set it up in such a way that we would ensure that our decisions benefited the least well off. rigor.explanation: Builds a structured normative argument from Rawls's framework to a standard for evaluating welfare policy; reasoned, though the link to the specific bill is developed only later.

rigor.statement: past left-wing Governments have done exactly the same thing over the last 31 years. So if they are to say this is a reflection on the coalition Government, it's a reflection on their own practice of the last 31 years.
rigor.explanation: Has a factual basis (CPI indexation was long-standing) but leans on a tu quoque to deflect rather than addressing whether the change reduces benefits relative to wages.

rigor.statement: taking from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible.
rigor.explanation: A value assertion resting on the contested 'to pay for tax cuts' linkage rather than a demonstrated causal claim.

rigor.statement: I have been brought up in a benefit-dependent household. It wasn't my father's fault that my mother got cancer at the age of 35 and that he was a widower at the age of 40 with four children under the age of 11.
rigor.explanation: Personal anecdote and appeal to emotion; powerful but offered as illustration rather than evidence about the bill's aggregate effects.

rigor.statement: The first is that it's not beneficiaries' tax money; it's actually hard-working New Zealanders' tax money and it is being given to beneficiaries.

rigor.statement: those in work have better mental health—have more productive capacity, and have better wellbeing

rigor.statement: she said to me that it was like leaving a violent relationship with her husband and entering a violent relationship with the State.
rigor.explanation: Vivid second-hand anecdote and appeal to emotion used to illustrate benefit sanctions, rather than systematic evidence.

authenticity.statement: The previous Government had a chance to accept my recommendations and amendments to index benefits to wages, or inflation, whichever was higher, to ensure that we guarantee the best and highest possible benefit increases
authenticity.explanation: Criticises both his own former allies (the previous Government) and National, showing a consistently held position rather than partisan convenience.

authenticity.statement: We know, looking back over the last 20 years or so, that in most years—around nine out of 10 years—wage increases have been higher than inflation. That is why we made this change

authenticity.statement: those of us who are parliamentarians, will get a tax cut. Why the heck do I need a tax cut? I find it immoral... I will be donating it to the NGOs that are closing in Nelson
authenticity.explanation: Aligns stated value (rejecting a personal tax cut as immoral) with a committed action (donating it), demonstrating words-match-deeds within the statement.

charisma.statement: Yes, we acknowledge that arguments can be made both ways.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges merit on the opposing side, a bridge-building concession rare in this debate.

charisma.statement: Many of us on this side, we all want the same outcome as the members on the opposite side; however, we just have different paths to getting there.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground by affirming shared goals across the House, distinguishing means from ends.

charisma.statement: those of us who are parliamentarians, will get a tax cut. Why the heck do I need a tax cut? I find it immoral... I will be donating it to the NGOs that are closing in Nelson
charisma.explanation: Emotionally resonant and principled, but rallies her own side rather than persuading opponents.

forthrightness.statement: On review of my response, I acknowledge that there is confusion arising from my understanding of the differentiation between seeking specific advice and accepting advice being offered. I had no intention of misleading the House, and I apologise for any confusion.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

forthrightness.statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) cannot provide this exact measure, as the member was told by the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes the data does not exist before pivoting to a defence of the policy.

forthrightness.statement: around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years... The extension could potentially save 65 lives per year; however, on our current settings, that relates to 22 lives saved.

specificity.statement: we will not sit and let those young people rot on welfare for 24 years.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical commitment with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: The bill amends the Social Security Act 2018 to ensure that income support responds to the increases in the cost of living by indexing main benefits to changes in the Consumers Price Index (CPI). This is the method that has been used for 31 of the last 35 years
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the mechanism (CPI indexing) and a precise historical frequency (31 of 35 years).

specificity.statement: the number of people on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 70,000 during the past six years, while sanctions applied for breaches of work obligations decreased by 35,259.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures (70,000; 35,259) with a defined time window.

specificity.statement: work-ready job seekers were forecast to spend, on average, 13 years on a benefit, and teenagers could become trapped on welfare for 24 years of their working lives.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific forecast durations (13 years average, 24 years).

specificity.statement: for our first hundred days, we had the Families Package introduced, we saw the winter energy payment and the Best Start payment introduced for the first time, we extended paid parental leave, we had the Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill setting minimum standards for rentals... we lifted the minimum wage for our lowest-income workers.
specificity.explanation: Names multiple specific policies, though without figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Last week, the Government took its first steps towards delivering on our promise to extend free breast cancer screening to women aged 70 to 74... that’s why the Government prioritised this crucial initiative in our 100-day plan.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific cohort (70–74) and the 100-day plan, though without dates for full rollout.

specificity.statement: around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years... The extension could potentially save 65 lives per year; however, on our current settings, that relates to 22 lives saved.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 120,000 women, two-yearly cycle, 65 vs 22 lives.

specificity.statement: I can confirm that there were 17 listed projects in the COVID fast-track bill passed by the last Parliament: Te Ara Tupua, the Ngauranga to Petone shared path; the Wellington metro upgrade; Papakura to Pukekohe rail electrification... specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise count (17) and names individual listed projects.

specificity.statement: the time it’s taken to consent major infrastructure has doubled in the last five years, and we now spend... $1.3 billion a year in this country consenting infrastructure—by most measures, some of the most expensive consenting processes in the developed world.
specificity.explanation: Quantified claims: doubling of consenting time, $1.3b annual cost.

specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: $29.2b projected cost, $228m spent, zero metres of track.

veracity.statement: loose fiscal policy has contributed to them being higher than they might otherwise have been
veracity.explanation: Reflects Treasury's stated assessment that fiscal policy contributed to higher interest rates; a defensible but contestable causal claim.

veracity.statement: We’ve been calling for a cessation of hostilities since October last year.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Government's public statements calling for a cessation of hostilities from late 2023.

veracity.statement: They’re not losing anything. We’re adjusting benefits and indexing benefits to inflation so that the purchasing power of those beneficiaries is not eroded.
veracity.explanation: 'Not losing anything' is misleading relative to wage-indexing — recipients lose income they would have received, which is the source of the savings.

veracity.statement: They’re not losing anything, because we’re adjusting benefits by the amount of inflation.
veracity.explanation: Cannot both claim large savings and no loss to recipients relative to the prior indexation; misleading.

veracity.statement: we’re not going to do what that Government did, which was to increase the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 70,000 people—increased it by 58 percent, took the number of sanctions and obligations down by 57 percent. veracity.explanation: Jobseeker-number rise is broadly in the right range; the percentage figures are harder to verify and may be selectively framed.

veracity.statement: since pseudoephedrine cough and cold medicine has been denied from New Zealanders through an effective ban, the price of P has actually gone down, the availability has gone up, and the volume consumed has gone up. The law simply has not worked
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with the meth market trend, though precise causal attribution to the pseudoephedrine ban is contestable.

veracity.statement: The publicly available report states that preliminary modelling shows indexing benefits to inflation in isolation as a policy, in the absence of any other Government policy interventions before 2028, may increase the number of children captured by the before-housing-cost moving line measure and after-housing-cost fixed line measures of child poverty by 7,000.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the official report's modelled figure and its caveats.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) cannot provide this exact measure, as the member was told by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with the framing that MSD does not collate this outcome centrally.

veracity.statement: the number of people on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 70,000 during the past six years, while sanctions applied for breaches of work obligations decreased by 35,259.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker rise is broadly supported; the exact sanctions figure is plausible but selectively framed and unsourced here.

veracity.explanation: Draws on MSD lifetime-liability projections, but the headline figures are worst-case framings that risk overstating typical experience.

veracity.explanation: The $670m savings figure is real, but 'taking from the poorest to pay for tax cuts' is a contestable framing of the fiscal linkage.

veracity.statement: around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years... The extension could potentially save 65 lives per year; however, on our current settings, that relates to 22 lives saved.
veracity.explanation: Presents both modelled estimates with appropriate qualification, consistent with advice received.

veracity.explanation: Factual recall of the COVID fast-track project list; verifiable from the legislation.

veracity.explanation: Cites the Infrastructure Commission / Sense Partners report; figures are sourced though the 'most expensive in the developed world' comparison is looser.

veracity.explanation: The non-delivery and spend figures are broadly accurate; the '$29.2 billion' is a top-end projection presented as the cost.

rigor.explanation: Quantified claim with an apt comparison illustrating opportunity cost; conclusion follows from the figures.
