To offer advice that I need or offer advice that I may not want to hear is the privilege and the purpose of HMAC—to be in that position, to be trusted advisers to the Minister and to us so that we can do a better job. So, yes, to answer that question, I do envisage the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee to proactively offer advice.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct 'yes' to a clear question on whether HMAC can proactively advise, including advice he may not want to hear.

forthrightness.statement: Those appointments—yes, they're ministerial appointments, like, as I say, it's been for the past two years, but of course I will seek advice and consultation from out in the sector and, of course, from IMPBs, as but one group whose voice I need to take into account.
forthrightness.explanation: Arena Williams asked him to name the eight intended appointees and the criteria; he defends the process and confirms consultation but does not name them or the criteria.

forthrightness.statement: I would point you to one of the Māori members on the Health New Zealand board already: Dr Curtis Walker, who clearly is skills-based and brings representation. So it is my intention to have that as an "and and" on the Health New Zealand board.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Henare's question on Māori representation on the Health NZ board with a concrete example and a stated intention.

forthrightness.statement: At the present time, metrics are currently reported quarterly, and this is a feature of the ability of Health Quality and Safety Commission and others to provide robust data. So I would anticipate at this point that quarterly reporting will continue
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a concrete answer to the question of what 'from time to time' reporting means (quarterly).

forthrightness.statement: I've already indicated in the legislation that through Schedule 1, I think it is, locality plans will be paused and localities will be paused while I reconsider their position going forward.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly states that the locality questions are moot because locality plans are paused under the bill.

divination.statement: Is it a reasonable step if that iwi-Māori partnership board turns around and says to Health New Zealand, "This isn't working."—and guess what! That's what they're going to say, because that's been the case for decades
divination.explanation: Predicts IMPBs will tell Health NZ the arrangement isn't working, reasoning from a long historical pattern; directionally plausible but unfalsifiable in specifics.

forthrightness.statement: The Therapeutic Products Act was not fit for purpose. Appropriate regulation of medicines and medical devices is vital to ensure that these products do what they claim, are high quality, and that product approval pathways do not make them inaccessible or unaffordable. We also know that the current fragmented and outdated approach to the regulation of natural health products means that New Zealand is missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity to grow jobs and the economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she wants to repeal the Act, she gives substantive reasons (fitness, accessibility, natural health products), though somewhat general.

forthrightness.statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry. I have received advice that implementing the changes required to meet the commencement date would’ve been extremely challenging. This poses the real possibility of poor outcomes for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers whether repeal will harm safety by arguing implementation, not repeal, posed risk; addresses the question directly enough.

forthrightness.statement: We are confident we will have effective legislation that will deliver good outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether 'big pharma' will be put back in its place, she pivots to a generic confidence statement, answering nothing.

forthrightness.statement: I received a range of advice from officials, and we’re continuing to develop good legislation and programmes to achieve the Smokefree 2025 targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked yes/no whether she was advised repeal would push the smoke-free goal to 2061, she neither confirms nor denies.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, I’ve received a range of advice. Some of that advice was based on statistical data that was not current. In the last three years, we have seen 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with vaping playing a key role. Importantly, 79,000 of those who stopped smoking—36 percent of those who quit—were Māori. We are now receiving statistics where we have a smoking rate of 6.8 percent of New Zealanders daily smoking, which is down from the 8.6 percent, which was one of the statistics that that data was based upon.
forthrightness.explanation: Re-asked the 2061 yes/no question, she again dodges by disputing the data rather than confirming the advice.

forthrightness.statement: We were absolutely committed to achieving the smoke-free targets, and we are going to implement systems that target addicted smokers, and not generalist, virtue-signalling approaches that are unproven.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how she justifies repeal given advice it would close the Māori life-expectancy gap, she restates commitment without addressing the advice.

forthrightness.statement: I have been interviewed on numerous occasions on this issue, and I am looking forward to having media interviews on the effective legislation and regulations that we will introduce to ensure that people who are addicted to nicotine smoking will have the tools to quit, and that youth vaping will decline.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she refuses interviews, she rebuts the premise (says she has been interviewed) and addresses it reasonably directly.

forthrightness.statement: If the member would like to ask a specific question, I’m sure I can give him a proper answer for that. But what I would say to you is: 350 schools were misled by the previous Government: “We’re going to rescope your school; we’re going to redesign it.” Twenty before Christmas; 250, now 350; billions of dollars, lots of promises, no delivery, underfunded—a pattern of behaviour we’ve seen many, many times.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about Botany capex rising from $3.7m (2017) to $11.9m (2022) and which projects were low value, he declines the figures and pivots to a general attack.

forthrightness.statement: What I have seen is the results from the last year, which has seen daily smokers go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent just in the last 12 months, with the legislation that we’re going to readopt.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd seen Treasury advice on $500m extra revenue from repeal, he ignores it and cites smoking-rate stats.

forthrightness.statement: Our Associate Health Minister is very committed to lowering smoking rates. The smoking legislation that we’ve seen over the last decade has actually halved daily smoking in this country. We are very confident that this will continue to lower smoking rates across this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Cabinet was advised of a $5b health cost and 12 deaths/day, he answers neither, restating talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Unlike the previous Government, we don’t discuss stuff that happens in Cabinet—unlike Stuart Nash.
forthrightness.explanation: Refuses the question outright by invoking Cabinet confidentiality.

forthrightness.statement: Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why his Associate Minister rejected raising the tobacco purchase age to 25 despite Ministry advice, he gives a content-free non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we’re going to be a Government that’s going to deliver on our emissions commitments and also grow our economy. We’re not going to turn off growth opportunities in sectors across this country when we’ve had three of the last four quarters left to us in decline by the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out new fossil fuel projects, he restates a both/ways position without answering.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we have been on the record to say that we actually want to overturn the oil and gas ban, because we need gas as a transitory energy source as we make the transition to clean, green energy going forward.
forthrightness.explanation: Still doesn't rule out specific projects, but openly states the pro-gas position underlying the question.

forthrightness.statement: Again, we have not had fast-track consenting legislation come before the Cabinet and it has not yet been discussed. What we have is a very good process to make sure we’re managing potential conflicts of interest, real or perceived. We have clear processes around that that make sure that we’re compliant with the Cabinet Manual.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the conflict-of-interest question by pointing to existing processes, though without specifics.

forthrightness.statement: Because we opposed it from its very conception, we spoke about it extensively in Opposition and opposed it in Opposition, we campaigned on it in the election campaign, and we put it into our 100-day plan as part of forming a new Government. It’s been very well signalled that we do not believe that bureaucracy is the way in which we drive better health outcomes for Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why he introduced the bill before the Tribunal hearing, he justifies the mandate rather than the timing.

forthrightness.statement: No, the tribunal will again have the jurisdiction to consider a claim after the legislation comes into effect. But we have been very, very clear in our opposition to the Māori Health Authority. We do not believe it’s the way in which we deliver better health outcomes for Māori—period.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'No' and a reason (Tribunal retains jurisdiction afterward) to the bypassing-judicial-process question.

forthrightness.statement: We have seen tremendous halving of smoking rates amongst Māori—from memory, something like 37 percent down to 16 percent in the space of a decade—under the legislation that we’re supporting putting back into law. So we’re going to continue to drive smoking rates down for Māori and for non-Māori, and we’re going to continue to get better health outcomes for Māori by using local iwi providers—localism and devolution, not centralisation and control.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the Māori-health framing but reframes rather than directly engaging the contradiction the question posed.

forthrightness.statement: I received Treasury’s briefing to the incoming Minister in November, which has been released, as has the accompanying slide pack. That slide pack contained a paragraph which stated: “Current budget allowances are expected to be sufficient to fund critical cost pressures only, with limited room for new spending in the absence of reprioritisation and savings”.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about advice on the operating allowance, she quotes the relevant released advice directly.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the definition of “cost pressure” depends a little on who’s doing the defining. Say, Mr Robertson would probably define the urgent need for more back-office bureaucrats as a cost pressure. I wouldn’t see it the same way, so I’d be reluctant to endorse the figure that the member has used.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm the 79% figure, she declines to engage with it and reframes the definition.

forthrightness.statement: I am both confident and happy about the fact that we have elected a coalition Government that is doing the hard and essential work of reprioritising low-value spending across Government. Members opposite may have been happy that on their watch the amount spent on consultants and contractors boomed, the number of people hired in back-office roles boomed, and there were low-value programmes, but our Government makes no apologies for being on a drive to ensure that dollars spent go to front-line services.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she regrets calling cost-pressure money a 'buffer', she avoids the question and gives a values statement.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, because our Government is committed to front-line services, and not backroom bureaucracy.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'Yes' to whether she's committed to meeting cost pressures for core services, with a brief reason.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member is going to have to keep up with the changing position of her leader, because this morning, as he detailed, he acknowledged that if he had been faced with the property situation inherited by our Minister of Education, then he too would have said, “Actually, that’s not affordable. We’re going to have to reassess it.”
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she prioritises tax cuts over classrooms/teachers/benefits, she deflects to the Opposition leader's position.

forthrightness.statement: I don’t believe that the people were refusing or misleading in any way. They made it very clear that they had misunderstood the question at select committee... We know that the job seminars do assist people in getting into employment... at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up and 64 received interviews from that.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the credibility question and offers an example, but the example is about interviews, not the stable employment asked about.

forthrightness.statement: As I explained, those outcomes are reported and are recorded on an individual basis; they are just not collated right across the country. So, on an individual basis, someone turning up to a work seminar, it will be recorded whether it was successful in supporting them into employment or not.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if she'll commit to reporting outcomes, she explains current recording but doesn't commit to national reporting.

forthrightness.statement: Starting in Southland, the Bluecliffs land site is situated on a former gravel pit located within Te Waewae Bay... That council has been granted $1.35 million for its remediation. The St Andrews Beach landfill project... have been granted $135,000... Nelson City Council... granted $134,000... And, finally, Gisborne District Council is receiving $4.98 million to develop a remediation plan and carry out remediation works at the former Tokomaru Bay landfill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers which specific projects were funded.

forthrightness.statement: The remedial contamination fund will be used in the way that it’s going to be best used to help the environmental and community outcomes of this country. The 6.5 to 7.5 is being concentrated, as we have been asked to, on the backroom functions, not on the funding that we get out to the grassroots where the work is being done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the fund will be spared the cuts, she answers indirectly that cuts target backroom functions, not grants.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the purpose of the non-consorting legislation is to stop serious gang offenders meeting with particular other serious gang offenders to create crimes. That is a piece of legislation that we’ve learnt from some of the Australian states, and it’s making a real impact on disrupting the gang activity.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the purpose question and cites the Australian precedent.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it will have an impact on gangs’ freedom to intimidate and create fear. Gang members want all the rights of being a New Zealander but none of the responsibility that comes with it. Expressing fear and intimidation is not a form of expression that this Government supports.
forthrightness.explanation: Reframes the freedom-of-expression question to gangs' intimidation rather than directly addressing the civil-liberties concern.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the purpose of this legislative change is to also remove the need for a connection between being a gang member and that specific crime that has been caused... The other point of it is this very simple idea that a political party would campaign in Opposition to do something and, when elected, they do it. That’s what we’re doing in this legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers what the change adds beyond the existing aggravating factor (removes the crime-connection requirement).

forthrightness.statement: We’ll always remain open to any dialogue from any parties and from any citizens, from Māori, from anyone who wants to help us advance the cause of Māori health outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government brought forward disestablishment, bypassing the Tribunal, he gives an open-dialogue platitude that ignores the question.

forthrightness.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal will still be able to critique the legislation after enablement, so we’re very comfortable with the position that we’ve taken. What we’ve also wanted to do is give some surety to staff with the Māori Health Authority so that they can see a vision and a pathway forward.
forthrightness.explanation: Offers two reasons (post-enactment review, staff certainty) for not waiting, partially addressing the timing question.

forthrightness.statement: What I accept is that we will involve Māori in the monitoring and the delivery of health services to improve Māori health outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he accepts the breach will trigger further claims/litigation, he sidesteps to a different commitment.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think it’s brave of that member to ask a question, given that this morning on air she said that all of the properties in her portfolio, when she was the Minister, were funded and factored into the Budget. Just mere hours later, her leader had to correct her and say that he would not guarantee absolutely every single one of them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the inquiry will examine National's earlier property cuts, she ignores it and attacks the questioner.

specificity.statement: The Therapeutic Products Act was not fit for purpose. Appropriate regulation of medicines and medical devices is vital to ensure that these products do what they claim, are high quality, and that product approval pathways do not make them inaccessible or unaffordable. We also know that the current fragmented and outdated approach to the regulation of natural health products means that New Zealand is missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity to grow jobs and the economy.
specificity.explanation: Names concerns (quality, affordability, natural health products) but no figures, mechanisms, or timeframes for the replacement.

specificity.statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry. I have received advice that implementing the changes required to meet the commencement date would’ve been extremely challenging. This poses the real possibility of poor outcomes for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete date (1 September 2026) but the asserted risk is unquantified.

specificity.statement: We are confident we will have effective legislation that will deliver good outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Pure platitude — no mechanism, content, or measure.

specificity.statement: Yes, in particular my statements that I’m absolutely committed to the Smokefree 2025 targets, and to providing practical, targeted help so that smokers who are addicted to nicotine can stop.
specificity.explanation: States a value and 'practical, targeted help' but no concrete programme detail.

specificity.statement: As I said, I’ve received a range of advice. Some of that advice was based on statistical data that was not current. In the last three years, we have seen 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with vaping playing a key role. Importantly, 79,000 of those who stopped smoking—36 percent of those who quit—were Māori. We are now receiving statistics where we have a smoking rate of 6.8 percent of New Zealanders daily smoking, which is down from the 8.6 percent, which was one of the statistics that that data was based upon.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures: 219,000 quitters, 79,000 Māori (36%), 6.8% down from 8.6%.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do. In particular, I stand by the Government’s action to conduct a ministerial inquiry into problems within the school property system—problems driven by a culture of mismanagement under the previous Government’s Ministers of Education, which have resulted in hundreds of projects facing huge escalations in both cost and scope.
specificity.explanation: References 'hundreds of projects' and cost/scope escalation but no precise figures here.

specificity.statement: Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics.
specificity.explanation: Generic boilerplate with no information.

specificity.statement: Again, we have not had fast-track consenting legislation come before the Cabinet and it has not yet been discussed. What we have is a very good process to make sure we’re managing potential conflicts of interest, real or perceived. We have clear processes around that that make sure that we’re compliant with the Cabinet Manual.
specificity.explanation: Refers to 'clear processes' and the Cabinet Manual but describes no actual mechanism.

specificity.statement: Kiwis are continuing to be hit by high inflation and high interest rates. According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data.
specificity.explanation: Names the comparator countries and the source.

specificity.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government. So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, periods, and index named.

specificity.statement: In good news for Kiwis at the checkout, food price data released earlier this month showed food prices are increasing at their slowest annual rate since 2021, at 4 percent. Compared to this time last year, there have been big drops in the price of tomatoes, Mr Hipkins, down 52 percent; and cheese, down 27 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentages and named items (tomatoes 52%, cheese 27%, food 4%).

specificity.statement: Well, just this week, the Government is legislating to end the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering Aucklanders relief at the pump from the start of July after years of being fleeced to pay for projects they don’t want, like cycleways and speed bumps.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a timeframe (relief from start of July).

specificity.statement: I received Treasury’s briefing to the incoming Minister in November, which has been released, as has the accompanying slide pack. That slide pack contained a paragraph which stated: “Current budget allowances are expected to be sufficient to fund critical cost pressures only, with limited room for new spending in the absence of reprioritisation and savings”.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific document and quotes the operative paragraph.

specificity.statement: However, what I would share with her is that what we know is that even before this Government formed, the previous Government had pre-committed 68 percent of this year’s operating allowance, and we know that the sum of the fiscal cliffs they’d left behind, at $7.2 billion, would more than have evaporated the entire operating allowance before we funded another single cost pressure.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages and dollar figures.

specificity.statement: Could I ask the Minister of Finance as to whether or not the Public Interest Journalism Fund, started in December 2020 and still going now—costing a colossal $55 million—is a cost pressure that could have been far more worthily spent on schools and hospitals, and not some woke programme supported by the other side?
specificity.explanation: Names the fund, its start date, and a $55m figure.

specificity.statement: There are 190,000 people on jobseeker benefits. That’s a 70,000 increase under Labour. So, clearly, nothing was working previously and it behoves us to ensure that we try a variety of means to assist people into employment, including work seminars, including job expos.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete numbers (190,000; +70,000) and named interventions.

specificity.statement: I don’t believe that the people were refusing or misleading in any way. They made it very clear that they had misunderstood the question at select committee... We know that the job seminars do assist people in getting into employment... at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up and 64 received interviews from that.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete anecdote with figures (82 attendees, 64 interviews).

specificity.statement: On Saturday, I had the pleasure of announcing that the Government is granting $6.6 million to clean up four historic New Zealand landfill and dump sites which are vulnerable to extreme weather events and coastal erosion.
specificity.explanation: Concrete amount ($6.6m), number of sites (four), and purpose.

specificity.statement: Starting in Southland, the Bluecliffs land site is situated on a former gravel pit located within Te Waewae Bay... That council has been granted $1.35 million for its remediation. The St Andrews Beach landfill project... have been granted $135,000... Nelson City Council... granted $134,000... And, finally, Gisborne District Council is receiving $4.98 million to develop a remediation plan and carry out remediation works at the former Tokomaru Bay landfill.
specificity.explanation: Itemised sites with exact grant figures for each.

specificity.statement: On Sunday, the Government announced a raft of measures aimed at addressing harm caused by gangs. Gangs’ insignia will be banned from public display, gang gatherings will be disrupted by police-issued dispersal notices, gang associates separated by court-issued non-consorting orders, and, finally, we’re giving greater weight to gang membership as an aggravating factor at sentencing.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete, named measures (insignia ban, dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, sentencing factor).

specificity.statement: In the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 new members and there has been significant escalation in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and shootings. Violent crime has increased by 33 percent; gangs play a significant part in this.
specificity.explanation: Quantified claims (3,000 members, 33% rise).

specificity.statement: Well, the purpose of the non-consorting legislation is to stop serious gang offenders meeting with particular other serious gang offenders to create crimes. That is a piece of legislation that we’ve learnt from some of the Australian states, and it’s making a real impact on disrupting the gang activity.
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism and origin but no figures.

specificity.statement: Oh, well, thank you—this Government is making excellent progress. We’ve abolished the prison target reduction, we’re stopping taxpayer funding for section 27 reports, we’ll soon introduce legislation to implement our package to tackle gangs, and my colleague Minister McKee will have further announcements to make on restoring law and order very soon.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions and items.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced a ministerial inquiry into the Ministry of Education’s school property function. This review will address the challenges the Ministry of Education face in not being able to deliver the current pipeline of school infrastructure projects—in particular, the failure to sufficiently implement a value-for-money approach, schools having expectations beyond what could be delivered on, and significant cost escalations.
specificity.explanation: Names the inquiry and the specific issues it will examine.

specificity.statement: In September 2023, the Ministry of Education began a review of property projects. In January, I was informed that up to 350 projects needed to be reviewed for cost-effectiveness. By their own admission, the ministry have advised me that these challenges are due to building-cost increases but also due to scope creep and over-reliance on bespoke designs and over-engineering add-ons, like extensive landscaping and infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Dates, the 350-project figure, and named cause categories.

specificity.statement: I have been talking with principals about their property concerns since the day I became the Minister. Since this announcement, I have already received reports that principals are welcoming this inquiry. On RNZ this morning, Vaughan Couillault of the Secondary Principals Association of New Zealand—SPANZ—said that principals are really pleased that the Minister has listened to the sector.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, organisation, and source.

specificity.statement: by my count, the Government has put 16 bills through urgency and one item of Government business not through urgency. So, recognising your point about the accumulation, there has to be a point at which we’re able to debate whether it’s appropriate for a ratio of 16 urgent items to one to go through the House, because the Government has the majority and is, essentially, railroading the House.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the claim (16 to 1).

specificity.statement: We also campaigned on repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax. The National Party—and I think I’m right in saying that the ACT Party said the same thing—at two successive election campaigns sought a mandate from the New Zealand people to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax, going all the way back to early 2018 when it was introduced.
specificity.explanation: References two campaigns and the 2018 introduction date.

rigor.statement: The Therapeutic Products Act was not fit for purpose. Appropriate regulation of medicines and medical devices is vital to ensure that these products do what they claim, are high quality, and that product approval pathways do not make them inaccessible or unaffordable. We also know that the current fragmented and outdated approach to the regulation of natural health products means that New Zealand is missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity to grow jobs and the economy.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable case but largely assertion; 'missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity' is unquantified.

rigor.statement: Well, we’re going to be a Government that’s going to deliver on our emissions commitments and also grow our economy. We’re not going to turn off growth opportunities in sectors across this country when we’ve had three of the last four quarters left to us in decline by the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: Asserts emissions delivery plus growth without reconciling the tension the question raised.

rigor.statement: Kiwis are continuing to be hit by high inflation and high interest rates. According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data.
rigor.explanation: Cites a data source and draws an inference, though the comparison alone doesn't fully refute the international-driver argument.

rigor.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government. So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Attributes child poverty to 'economic mismanagement' as a slogan ('the price of Labour') beyond what the cost-index data shows.

rigor.statement: There are 190,000 people on jobseeker benefits. That’s a 70,000 increase under Labour. So, clearly, nothing was working previously and it behoves us to ensure that we try a variety of means to assist people into employment, including work seminars, including job expos.
rigor.explanation: 'clearly, nothing was working' is a sweeping inference from a single aggregate, ignoring other drivers.

rigor.statement: I don’t believe that the people were refusing or misleading in any way. They made it very clear that they had misunderstood the question at select committee... We know that the job seminars do assist people in getting into employment... at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up and 64 received interviews from that.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a single anecdote and conflates interviews with employment outcomes.

rigor.statement: In the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 new members and there has been significant escalation in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and shootings. Violent crime has increased by 33 percent; gangs play a significant part in this.
rigor.explanation: Asserts gangs 'play a significant part' in the crime rise without establishing the causal share.

rigor.statement: Well, it will have an impact on gangs’ freedom to intimidate and create fear. Gang members want all the rights of being a New Zealander but none of the responsibility that comes with it. Expressing fear and intimidation is not a form of expression that this Government supports.
rigor.explanation: Argues by characterising gang insignia solely as intimidation, sidestepping the expression trade-off.

rigor.statement: by my count, the Government has put 16 bills through urgency and one item of Government business not through urgency. So, recognising your point about the accumulation, there has to be a point at which we’re able to debate whether it’s appropriate for a ratio of 16 urgent items to one to go through the House, because the Government has the majority and is, essentially, railroading the House.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument from a specific count to a procedural conclusion; 'railroading' is a characterisation.

rigor.statement: The point is, of the 16 bills that have come through this House, a large proportion are affecting communities who are made up of tangata whenua, who are denied the right to come in and be part of an open, transparent select committee, an open, transparent consultation. This is affecting Māori more than anyone else in Aotearoa, which is why we have put this request for an urgent debate.
rigor.explanation: Links urgency use to denial of select-committee scrutiny and disproportionate Māori impact; 'a large proportion' is unquantified.

rigor.statement: the reason why the Government is seeking this urgency motion is to progress the necessary stages of our 100-day plan. The coalition parties collectively campaigned on repealing the Māori Health Authority not because we have an objection to improving Māori health outcomes—in fact, quite the converse—but we campaigned on it because we don’t think a giant new bureaucracy is the right way to go about doing that.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the 'bureaucracy' rationale without evidence that abolition improves outcomes.

rigor.statement: The next point I was going to make is that all three of these bills are repeal bills—in other words, they wipe from the statute book bills that the Parliament passed. Many of them have been through select committees previously. The Government considers urgency is more than justified in this case.
rigor.explanation: Argues urgency is justified because the bills are repeals previously scrutinised — a coherent if contestable point.

rigor.statement: These section 27 reports have cost taxpayers millions of dollars, and have done nothing for victims of crime; in fact they’ve led to further sentencing discounts.
rigor.explanation: Absolute claim ('done nothing') asserted without evidence.

divination.statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry. I have received advice that implementing the changes required to meet the commencement date would’ve been extremely challenging. This poses the real possibility of poor outcomes for New Zealanders.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'real possibility of poor outcomes' from meeting the 2026 commencement date — vague magnitude, cites unseen advice.

divination.statement: There has already been a substantial black market for cigarettes and crime attached to tobacco retailing, and Customs are seeing a high volume of seizures of tobacco, both large and small, and through multiple channels, and an increase in large seizures.
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast that the previous regime would worsen the black market; directionally arguable, evidence mixed.

divination.statement: I have been interviewed on numerous occasions on this issue, and I am looking forward to having media interviews on the effective legislation and regulations that we will introduce to ensure that people who are addicted to nicotine smoking will have the tools to quit, and that youth vaping will decline.
divination.explanation: Predicts youth vaping 'will decline' under the planned regime — plausible but unquantified and uncertain.

divination.statement: Our Associate Health Minister is very committed to lowering smoking rates. The smoking legislation that we’ve seen over the last decade has actually halved daily smoking in this country. We are very confident that this will continue to lower smoking rates across this country.
divination.explanation: Predicts smoking rates will keep falling — plausible given trend, but credits the rolled-back framework.

divination.statement: We have seen tremendous halving of smoking rates amongst Māori—from memory, something like 37 percent down to 16 percent in the space of a decade—under the legislation that we’re supporting putting back into law. So we’re going to continue to drive smoking rates down for Māori and for non-Māori, and we’re going to continue to get better health outcomes for Māori by using local iwi providers—localism and devolution, not centralisation and control.
divination.explanation: Predicts continued falls and better Māori outcomes via iwi providers — plausible aspiration, unproven.

authenticity.statement: Yes, in particular my statements that I’m absolutely committed to the Smokefree 2025 targets, and to providing practical, targeted help so that smokers who are addicted to nicotine can stop.
authenticity.explanation: Professes commitment to Smokefree 2025 while leading the repeal of the 2022 smoke-free measures designed to reach it — a words-vs-actions tension.

authenticity.statement: We were absolutely committed to achieving the smoke-free targets, and we are going to implement systems that target addicted smokers, and not generalist, virtue-signalling approaches that are unproven.
authenticity.explanation: Claims commitment to smoke-free targets while repealing the measures aimed at them.

authenticity.statement: Well, we have been on the record to say that we actually want to overturn the oil and gas ban, because we need gas as a transitory energy source as we make the transition to clean, green energy going forward.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's campaign position on the oil and gas ban.

authenticity.statement: Because we opposed it from its very conception, we spoke about it extensively in Opposition and opposed it in Opposition, we campaigned on it in the election campaign, and we put it into our 100-day plan as part of forming a new Government. It’s been very well signalled that we do not believe that bureaucracy is the way in which we drive better health outcomes for Māori.
authenticity.explanation: Documents a consistent position on the Māori Health Authority from opposition through campaign to government.

authenticity.statement: No, the tribunal will again have the jurisdiction to consider a claim after the legislation comes into effect. But we have been very, very clear in our opposition to the Māori Health Authority. We do not believe it’s the way in which we deliver better health outcomes for Māori—period.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a consistent stated position.

authenticity.statement: In Opposition, we opposed the Māori Health Authority from its very conception—we have opposed it in Opposition. We went to the election campaign and said we would dismantle it. We formed a Government; within a matter of days, we had a hundred-day plan to dismantle it—49 actions in 100 days. That’s what we’re doing.
authenticity.explanation: Words match deeds — a consistent stated position now being acted on.

authenticity.statement: Well, the purpose of this legislative change is to also remove the need for a connection between being a gang member and that specific crime that has been caused... The other point of it is this very simple idea that a political party would campaign in Opposition to do something and, when elected, they do it. That’s what we’re doing in this legislation.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the action as delivering a campaign commitment.

authenticity.statement: We’ll always remain open to any dialogue from any parties and from any citizens, from Māori, from anyone who wants to help us advance the cause of Māori health outcomes.
authenticity.explanation: Professes openness to all dialogue while the action under question is bringing the bill forward ahead of the inquiry.

authenticity.statement: the reason why the Government is seeking this urgency motion is to progress the necessary stages of our 100-day plan. The coalition parties collectively campaigned on repealing the Māori Health Authority not because we have an objection to improving Māori health outcomes—in fact, quite the converse—but we campaigned on it because we don’t think a giant new bureaucracy is the right way to go about doing that.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the motion as delivering a consistent campaign position.

authenticity.statement: We also campaigned on repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax. The National Party—and I think I’m right in saying that the ACT Party said the same thing—at two successive election campaigns sought a mandate from the New Zealand people to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax, going all the way back to early 2018 when it was introduced.
authenticity.explanation: Documents a long-standing, consistent campaign position on the fuel tax.

veracity.statement: As I said, I’ve received a range of advice. Some of that advice was based on statistical data that was not current. In the last three years, we have seen 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with vaping playing a key role. Importantly, 79,000 of those who stopped smoking—36 percent of those who quit—were Māori. We are now receiving statistics where we have a smoking rate of 6.8 percent of New Zealanders daily smoking, which is down from the 8.6 percent, which was one of the statistics that that data was based upon.
veracity.explanation: Cites smoking-rate figures consistent with the period; characterising the 2061 advice as based on 'not current' data is a contestable framing.

veracity.statement: There has already been a substantial black market for cigarettes and crime attached to tobacco retailing, and Customs are seeing a high volume of seizures of tobacco, both large and small, and through multiple channels, and an increase in large seizures.
veracity.explanation: Tobacco black market and rising Customs seizures are broadly supported, though 'substantial' and 'high volume' are unquantified.

veracity.statement: If the member would like to ask a specific question, I’m sure I can give him a proper answer for that. But what I would say to you is: 350 schools were misled by the previous Government: “We’re going to rescope your school; we’re going to redesign it.” Twenty before Christmas; 250, now 350; billions of dollars, lots of promises, no delivery, underfunded—a pattern of behaviour we’ve seen many, many times.
veracity.explanation: The 350-schools figure recurs in his government's messaging but the escalating '20/250/350' and 'billions' are loosely sourced here.

veracity.statement: What I have seen is the results from the last year, which has seen daily smokers go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent just in the last 12 months, with the legislation that we’re going to readopt.
veracity.explanation: The 8.6%→6.8% drop is broadly accurate, but attributing it to legislation 'we're going to readopt' overstates causation.

veracity.statement: Our Associate Health Minister is very committed to lowering smoking rates. The smoking legislation that we’ve seen over the last decade has actually halved daily smoking in this country. We are very confident that this will continue to lower smoking rates across this country.
veracity.explanation: Daily smoking roughly halving over a decade is broadly supported.

veracity.statement: Well, we’re going to be a Government that’s going to deliver on our emissions commitments and also grow our economy. We’re not going to turn off growth opportunities in sectors across this country when we’ve had three of the last four quarters left to us in decline by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: 'three of the last four quarters in decline' is a specific economic claim of contested accuracy as framed.

veracity.statement: We have seen tremendous halving of smoking rates amongst Māori—from memory, something like 37 percent down to 16 percent in the space of a decade—under the legislation that we’re supporting putting back into law. So we’re going to continue to drive smoking rates down for Māori and for non-Māori, and we’re going to continue to get better health outcomes for Māori by using local iwi providers—localism and devolution, not centralisation and control.
veracity.explanation: Māori smoking roughly halving over a decade is directionally supported; the precise 37%→16% is hedged ('from memory') and approximate.

veracity.statement: Kiwis are continuing to be hit by high inflation and high interest rates. According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data.
veracity.explanation: NZ inflation exceeding several peers in the period is broadly defensible, though selective comparison can mislead on the 'international' claim.

veracity.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government. So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
veracity.explanation: The 20%-over-three-years vs 18%-over-nine-years contrast is cited to a source but compares unlike periods, which can mislead.

veracity.statement: In good news for Kiwis at the checkout, food price data released earlier this month showed food prices are increasing at their slowest annual rate since 2021, at 4 percent. Compared to this time last year, there have been big drops in the price of tomatoes, Mr Hipkins, down 52 percent; and cheese, down 27 percent.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific Stats NZ food-price figures that are checkable and broadly plausible for the period.

veracity.statement: I received Treasury’s briefing to the incoming Minister in November, which has been released, as has the accompanying slide pack. That slide pack contained a paragraph which stated: “Current budget allowances are expected to be sufficient to fund critical cost pressures only, with limited room for new spending in the absence of reprioritisation and savings”.
veracity.explanation: Quotes a released document verbatim, readily verifiable.

veracity.statement: However, what I would share with her is that what we know is that even before this Government formed, the previous Government had pre-committed 68 percent of this year’s operating allowance, and we know that the sum of the fiscal cliffs they’d left behind, at $7.2 billion, would more than have evaporated the entire operating allowance before we funded another single cost pressure.
veracity.explanation: Specific claims (68% pre-committed, $7.2b fiscal cliffs) presented as fact; figures are contestable framings of fiscal data.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the legislation that’s seen the most dramatic change in the decrease in smoking levels in this country—that law was written by New Zealand First, and not these people over here that are screaming about it right here, right now—
veracity.explanation: Claims NZ First authored the most effective smoking legislation — an overstated credit claim that is contestable.

veracity.statement: Could I ask the Minister of Finance as to whether or not the Public Interest Journalism Fund, started in December 2020 and still going now—costing a colossal $55 million—is a cost pressure that could have been far more worthily spent on schools and hospitals, and not some woke programme supported by the other side?
veracity.explanation: The $55m Public Interest Journalism Fund figure is broadly in the right range for the programme.

veracity.statement: Has the Prime Minister and his Government considered the fact that there is a preference in using New Zealand coal rather than to be importing inferior Indonesian coal, which was the practice of the former Government?
veracity.explanation: Importing Indonesian coal did occur, but 'inferior' and the framing are contestable assertions presented as fact.

veracity.statement: There are 190,000 people on jobseeker benefits. That’s a 70,000 increase under Labour. So, clearly, nothing was working previously and it behoves us to ensure that we try a variety of means to assist people into employment, including work seminars, including job expos.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker numbers and the rise are broadly in range, though period framing matters.

veracity.statement: In the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 new members and there has been significant escalation in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and shootings. Violent crime has increased by 33 percent; gangs play a significant part in this.
veracity.explanation: Gang membership growth (~3,000+) is broadly cited; the '33 percent' violent crime rise depends on the measure and period and can be selective.

veracity.statement: In September 2023, the Ministry of Education began a review of property projects. In January, I was informed that up to 350 projects needed to be reviewed for cost-effectiveness. By their own admission, the ministry have advised me that these challenges are due to building-cost increases but also due to scope creep and over-reliance on bespoke designs and over-engineering add-ons, like extensive landscaping and infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Attributes causes to ministry advice; the 350 figure recurs across the government's account.

veracity.statement: I have been talking with principals about their property concerns since the day I became the Minister. Since this announcement, I have already received reports that principals are welcoming this inquiry. On RNZ this morning, Vaughan Couillault of the Secondary Principals Association of New Zealand—SPANZ—said that principals are really pleased that the Minister has listened to the sector.
veracity.explanation: Cites a named, checkable on-air endorsement from a sector body.

veracity.statement: by my count, the Government has put 16 bills through urgency and one item of Government business not through urgency. So, recognising your point about the accumulation, there has to be a point at which we’re able to debate whether it’s appropriate for a ratio of 16 urgent items to one to go through the House, because the Government has the majority and is, essentially, railroading the House.
veracity.explanation: Offers a specific, checkable count ('by my count') of urgency use.

veracity.statement: We also campaigned on repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax. The National Party—and I think I’m right in saying that the ACT Party said the same thing—at two successive election campaigns sought a mandate from the New Zealand people to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax, going all the way back to early 2018 when it was introduced.
veracity.explanation: National's repeated opposition to the regional fuel tax since ~2018 is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: These section 27 reports have cost taxpayers millions of dollars, and have done nothing for victims of crime; in fact they’ve led to further sentencing discounts.
veracity.explanation: 'done nothing for victims' is a sweeping claim; s27 reports informing sentencing discounts is partly accurate but 'nothing' overstates.

civility.statement: We were absolutely committed to achieving the smoke-free targets, and we are going to implement systems that target addicted smokers, and not generalist, virtue-signalling approaches that are unproven.
civility.explanation: 'virtue-signalling' dismisses opponents' policy as posturing rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: There has already been a substantial black market for cigarettes and crime attached to tobacco retailing, and Customs are seeing a high volume of seizures of tobacco, both large and small, and through multiple channels, and an increase in large seizures.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents' policy as 'unworkable, woke, virtue-signalling' and an 'experimental prohibition regime'.

civility.statement: Yes, I do. In particular, I stand by the Government’s action to conduct a ministerial inquiry into problems within the school property system—problems driven by a culture of mismanagement under the previous Government’s Ministers of Education, which have resulted in hundreds of projects facing huge escalations in both cost and scope.
civility.explanation: 'culture of mismanagement' attacks the previous government's conduct, but is aimed at policy/administration rather than personal traits.

civility.statement: If the member would like to ask a specific question, I’m sure I can give him a proper answer for that. But what I would say to you is: 350 schools were misled by the previous Government: “We’re going to rescope your school; we’re going to redesign it.” Twenty before Christmas; 250, now 350; billions of dollars, lots of promises, no delivery, underfunded—a pattern of behaviour we’ve seen many, many times.
civility.explanation: 'lots of promises, no delivery' and 'a pattern of behaviour' are accusatory characterisations of opponents.

civility.statement: Unlike the previous Government, we don’t discuss stuff that happens in Cabinet—unlike Stuart Nash.
civility.explanation: A pointed personal jab at Stuart Nash rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government. So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
civility.explanation: 'disastrous economic mismanagement' and 'the price of Labour' are partisan attacks.

civility.statement: Well, just this week, the Government is legislating to end the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering Aucklanders relief at the pump from the start of July after years of being fleeced to pay for projects they don’t want, like cycleways and speed bumps.
civility.explanation: 'being fleeced' and dismissing 'cycleways and speed bumps' are loaded characterisations.

civility.statement: Well, the definition of “cost pressure” depends a little on who’s doing the defining. Say, Mr Robertson would probably define the urgent need for more back-office bureaucrats as a cost pressure. I wouldn’t see it the same way, so I’d be reluctant to endorse the figure that the member has used.
civility.explanation: A swipe at 'back-office bureaucrats' and Robertson, but mild and policy-adjacent.

civility.statement: I am both confident and happy about the fact that we have elected a coalition Government that is doing the hard and essential work of reprioritising low-value spending across Government. Members opposite may have been happy that on their watch the amount spent on consultants and contractors boomed, the number of people hired in back-office roles boomed, and there were low-value programmes, but our Government makes no apologies for being on a drive to ensure that dollars spent go to front-line services.
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of presiding over a 'boom' in waste, partisan but policy-focused.

civility.statement: Well, the member is going to have to keep up with the changing position of her leader, because this morning, as he detailed, he acknowledged that if he had been faced with the property situation inherited by our Minister of Education, then he too would have said, “Actually, that’s not affordable. We’re going to have to reassess it.”
civility.explanation: 'keep up with the changing position of her leader' is a mild dig but engages a real argument.

civility.statement: Could I ask the Minister of Finance as to whether or not the Public Interest Journalism Fund, started in December 2020 and still going now—costing a colossal $55 million—is a cost pressure that could have been far more worthily spent on schools and hospitals, and not some woke programme supported by the other side?
civility.explanation: Dismisses the fund as 'woke stupidity'/'woke programme', deriding rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: We’ve got people who don’t understand Speakers’ rulings here, or Standing Orders, and they’re getting up and showing their ignorance every day—
civility.explanation: A personal disparagement of other members' competence rather than a substantive point.

civility.statement: Well, it will have an impact on gangs’ freedom to intimidate and create fear. Gang members want all the rights of being a New Zealander but none of the responsibility that comes with it. Expressing fear and intimidation is not a form of expression that this Government supports.
civility.explanation: Pointed about gangs but directed at conduct, not personal opponents.

civility.statement: Well, I think it’s brave of that member to ask a question, given that this morning on air she said that all of the properties in her portfolio, when she was the Minister, were funded and factored into the Budget. Just mere hours later, her leader had to correct her and say that he would not guarantee absolutely every single one of them.
civility.explanation: 'it’s brave of that member' is a sarcastic personal jab rather than substance.

civility.statement: The point is, of the 16 bills that have come through this House, a large proportion are affecting communities who are made up of tangata whenua, who are denied the right to come in and be part of an open, transparent select committee, an open, transparent consultation. This is affecting Māori more than anyone else in Aotearoa, which is why we have put this request for an urgent debate.
civility.explanation: Makes a procedural-fairness argument without personal attack.

civility.statement: Members opposite cry crocodile tears about urgency, because I’ve sat where they sit for six years and I realise it’s grim times, and I know exactly what they are going through.
civility.explanation: 'crocodile tears' belittles opponents' objections, though comparatively mild.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, with respect, I think I have a right to raise a point of order without you interrupting. I think it’s probably not just me but it’s certainly me who is a little bit tired of repetitive trifling points of order from someone who hasn’t taken the time to understand the rules, and I’d like you to take a tougher line on him because we’re all getting a little tired of it.
civility.explanation: Disparages another member as not understanding the rules and raising 'trifling' points — a personal swipe.

civility.statement: These section 27 reports have cost taxpayers millions of dollars, and have done nothing for victims of crime; in fact they’ve led to further sentencing discounts.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy rather than a person, though framed sensationally.

strength.statement: In Opposition, we opposed the Māori Health Authority from its very conception—we have opposed it in Opposition. We went to the election campaign and said we would dismantle it. We formed a Government; within a matter of days, we had a hundred-day plan to dismantle it—49 actions in 100 days. That’s what we’re doing.
strength.explanation: Describes a campaigned commitment being implemented via the 100-day plan, though delivery is in progress.

strength.statement: Well, just this week, the Government is legislating to end the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering Aucklanders relief at the pump from the start of July after years of being fleeced to pay for projects they don’t want, like cycleways and speed bumps.
strength.explanation: A campaigned commitment being enacted via legislation with a stated start date — concrete follow-through in progress.

strength.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the legislation that’s seen the most dramatic change in the decrease in smoking levels in this country—that law was written by New Zealand First, and not these people over here that are screaming about it right here, right now—
strength.explanation: Credit-claiming for past tobacco legislation; partly grounded but inflated.

strength.statement: On Saturday, I had the pleasure of announcing that the Government is granting $6.6 million to clean up four historic New Zealand landfill and dump sites which are vulnerable to extreme weather events and coastal erosion.
strength.explanation: A funding announcement with concrete allocation, though delivery (remediation) is yet to occur.

strength.statement: On Sunday, the Government announced a raft of measures aimed at addressing harm caused by gangs. Gangs’ insignia will be banned from public display, gang gatherings will be disrupted by police-issued dispersal notices, gang associates separated by court-issued non-consorting orders, and, finally, we’re giving greater weight to gang membership as an aggravating factor at sentencing.
strength.explanation: Announced measures, not yet legislated/delivered — commitment with delivery pending.

strength.statement: Oh, well, thank you—this Government is making excellent progress. We’ve abolished the prison target reduction, we’re stopping taxpayer funding for section 27 reports, we’ll soon introduce legislation to implement our package to tackle gangs, and my colleague Minister McKee will have further announcements to make on restoring law and order very soon.
strength.explanation: Mixes delivered actions (abolished prison target, stopping s27 funding) with still-to-come legislation.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced a ministerial inquiry into the Ministry of Education’s school property function. This review will address the challenges the Ministry of Education face in not being able to deliver the current pipeline of school infrastructure projects—in particular, the failure to sufficiently implement a value-for-money approach, schools having expectations beyond what could be delivered on, and significant cost escalations.
strength.explanation: A concrete action (inquiry announced) underway, though outcomes pending.

charisma.statement: We’ll always remain open to any dialogue from any parties and from any citizens, from Māori, from anyone who wants to help us advance the cause of Māori health outcomes.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'any parties... anyone' framing, though unanchored to action.

specificity.statement: Legislation to be considered will include the first readings of the Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill, the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, the fast-track consenting bill, and the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill; and the remaining stages of the Legal Services Amendment Bill and the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill.
specificity.explanation: Names each specific bill and its stage — concrete and precise legislative agenda.

specificity.statement: Some of the legislation I’ve just read out is exactly that; the fast-track consenting bill will go to a committee, the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill will go to a committee, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee, and the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee. This is a very hard-working Government—we’ve got a lot on.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bills going to committee, though without detail on the process conditions asked about.

specificity.statement: The bank’s monetary policy committee, which makes its decisions about interest rates independent of the Government, left the official cash rate unchanged at 5.5 percent... Inflation has declined from a peak of 7.3 percent in mid-2022 to 4.7 percent in the December quarter, and the bank’s forecasts show it falling towards the 2 percent mid-point of the target band.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, dates, and the target band.

specificity.statement: New Zealand is dedicated to a clean energy transition and meeting our emissions targets. This Government is committed to deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and removing consenting barriers.
specificity.explanation: Names net-zero-by-2050 and doubling renewables, but no figures or mechanism for 'how'.

specificity.statement: It is targeted to go to 0.23. This is shocking. And in 2017, we were facing it going to 0.21... We left it at 0.34 when we left.
specificity.explanation: Quotes concrete percentage figures and years.

specificity.statement: We have also stopped all work on the separatist agenda called He Puapua, kept secret by the last Government; repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act; abolished the failing Māori Health Authority to ensure we focus on delivering better healthcare for all of those who need it most... based on need, not some woke concept.
specificity.explanation: Names specific Acts and bodies, though framed with loaded labels.

specificity.statement: Recently, as reported, I was present as six gold-plated Harley-Davidson motorcycles, formerly the prized possessions of the Comancheros, were shredded into scrap metal.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail: number, type, owner, action.

specificity.statement: On Sunday, Minister Goldsmith, Minister McKee, and I announced part of the coalition Government’s proposed crackdown on gangs, including banning gang patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, and making gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
specificity.explanation: Lists the concrete proposed measures.

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced that the Government will repeal the Business Payment Practices Act 2023. This piece of legislation was an ineffective, costly solution to the problem of large market players paying invoices late, and evidence from abroad supports the repeal of the Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the rationale, though 'evidence from abroad' is asserted before being detailed.

specificity.statement: Back in 2020, Australia implemented a very similar scheme named the Payment Times Reporting Act. A recent independent review of the scheme’s effectiveness found that despite imposing significant IT compliance costs on businesses, overall payment times had not reduced.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme, year, and review finding.

specificity.statement: I’m working with the Minister of Finance to ensure Government departments—and, in time, some Crown entities—meet the 10-day payment time target... reducing Government entity payment times to an expected target of five working days... We will also proactively publish payment times on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment website.
specificity.explanation: Concrete targets (10-day, five-working-day) and a named mechanism (publishing on MBIE site).

specificity.statement: On Friday, I announced a $5 million boost to the upper North Island community’s fight against the invasive seaweed Caulerpa. This exotic pest arrived in 2021 and has now been found in five locations across Northland and Greater Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, arrival year, and number of locations.

specificity.statement: I read recently in media that Macleans College in Auckland had funded and built five new classrooms in nine months after being advised by the Ministry of Education that it would take three years to deliver the same learning spaces. They did it for $2.5 million.
specificity.explanation: Names the school, timeframes (nine months vs three years), and cost.

specificity.statement: we have seen the number of bureaucrats employed at the Ministry of Education increase in the past six years from 2,500 to 4,400, and yet fewer kids are going to school
specificity.explanation: Concrete headcount numbers and timeframe.

specificity.statement: In the year since January 2023 alone, there’s been a 3 percent increase in the District Court criminal backlog, rising to a total backlog of 37 percent of active cases.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages and timeframe.

specificity.statement: I’m so happy to let that member on that side know that this Government is going to be releasing—as part of our 100-day plan—early next week, our initiatives to address the mess that was left behind for us to fix.
specificity.explanation: Promises an announcement 'early next week' without naming any initiative.

specificity.statement: Plurality is really important to me—that people actually have choices. Despite the Warner Bros. Discovery announcement, I’m confident that New Zealand news media continues to have a diverse range of voices and perspectives available on multiple platforms.
specificity.explanation: General reassurance about 'diverse voices' without concrete measures or evidence.

specificity.statement: However, this Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sector sustainability while still preserving the independence of the fourth estate. There is a range of work under way that aims to ensure the media can continue to function in the current changing landscape.
specificity.explanation: Vague commitment to 'a range of work' with no named policy, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: I want to remind the House about the 49 points of action that we will have completed by this time next week or next Friday. It’s actually 8 March which is the day that we will celebrate the first hundred days of this administration.
specificity.explanation: Names a count (49) and a date (8 March).

forthrightness.statement: Some of the legislation I’ve just read out is exactly that; the fast-track consenting bill will go to a committee, the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill will go to a committee, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee, and the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee. This is a very hard-working Government—we’ve got a lot on.
forthrightness.explanation: Q asked when a bill would go through full process with no urgency, no instruction and a published RIS; he lists bills going to committee but never addresses the 'no instruction' / RIS part, and tacks on a talking point.

forthrightness.statement: That will be over to the House at the time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether bills would go to committee for a full time without instruction; deflects with a non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: I think the member who’s yelling out, who’s a former Minister of Housing, will recall that the funding for social housing places ceases after June 2025, so that is indeed a fiscal cliff. The reality is the last Government didn’t fund places beyond 2025, into 2026 or 2027, because they wanted to create the illusion of a surplus later on.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to funding levels beyond 2025; defers to the Budget and pivots to attacking the predecessors.

forthrightness.statement: I’m happy for the member to meet with Kāinga Ora, as I am indeed happy for all members of Parliament to meet with Kāinga Ora to get a briefing on what they’re up to in their particular local areas, or indeed the Opposition spokesperson.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly grants the request to permit a Kāinga Ora briefing.

forthrightness.statement: Speaking to the point of order, if that member wanted that answer, then an Official Information Act (OIA) request would’ve satisfied them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically which people/organisations/lobbyists were consulted; refuses to name any and redirects to the OIA.

forthrightness.statement: With respect, I am not going to answer a question which was in the purview of the previous administration and Minister. It has got nothing to do with this Government whatsoever.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the cost of the Tamarind clean-up; explicitly declines to answer.

forthrightness.statement: New Zealand is dedicated to a clean energy transition and meeting our emissions targets. This Government is committed to deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and removing consenting barriers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether bonds would breach commitments to abolish fossil-fuel subsidies; pivots to a general clean-energy statement.

forthrightness.statement: As that member will well know, all conversations with all colleagues—including the Prime Minister and, most importantly, the Minister of Finance—are confidential. However, we are pressing on to ensure that on Budget day that member will know, and so that then the only uncertainty at that point in time will be whether or not he is rightfully the leader of the Labour Party.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agreed to 6.5% MFAT savings; declines on confidentiality grounds and defers to the Budget.

forthrightness.statement: I think it was probably legislation that Stuart Nash brought in, because, actually, he was a very good police Minister, unlike the three that followed him.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked precisely which legislation was used; answers only 'probably' and pivots to praising one minister.

forthrightness.statement: I can justify it because, unlike the Labour Party who are gang apologists, we have a deeply capable New Zealand police force that is motivated and wants to go out there and protect the communities that they serve and clamp down on gangs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he justifies the ban given 12 officers calling it unworkable; does not engage the specific concern.

forthrightness.statement: No, but I hope that the example she gave, with Western Australia, shows that the gang patch ban was working because they wanted to leave. And I hope that our gang patch ban forces them over the border as well!
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'no' to the displacement concern but does not address the under-resourced-areas point.

forthrightness.statement: I’m working with the Minister of Finance to ensure Government departments—and, in time, some Crown entities—meet the 10-day payment time target... reducing Government entity payment times to an expected target of five working days... We will also proactively publish payment times on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment website.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how he will ensure timely payment, with specific measures.

forthrightness.statement: Thank you for the question. No, it’s not fair. But we will be working with an industry code... with Business New Zealand to make sure that large businesses do meet their requirements.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'no, it's not fair' to the constituent example, then outlines the response.

forthrightness.statement: Technical advice so far has been that fully eradicating it from New Zealand will be extremely challenging and unlikely with current technology. But this investment will still make a difference for the environment and for the people affected.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes eradication is unlikely rather than overselling the policy.

forthrightness.statement: the answer, I can unequivocally say, is absolutely not. The reason that’s possible is that there has been so much waste in the past six years that you can reduce expenditure by 6.5 percent very easily—hell, some of our coalition partners in this Government would go a lot further.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'absolutely not' to whether cuts will affect learning, though the supporting reasoning is assertion rather than evidence.

forthrightness.statement: I’m so happy to let that member on that side know that this Government is going to be releasing—as part of our 100-day plan—early next week, our initiatives to address the mess that was left behind for us to fix.
forthrightness.explanation: Pressed repeatedly on what specific initiatives she has introduced; repeatedly defers to a future announcement.
