forthrightness.statement: No. But what I am concerned about is resolving the growing court backlog that was allowed to persist under his party’s watch since 2017.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'no' to the concern, but immediately pivots to blaming the Opposition rather than addressing the funding-pressure premise.

forthrightness.statement: Plurality is really important to me—that people actually have choices. Despite the Warner Bros. Discovery announcement, I’m confident that New Zealand news media continues to have a diverse range of voices and perspectives available on multiple platforms.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses media plurality broadly but does not engage the specific question about who produces Sky News' NZ content.

veracity.statement: I think the member who’s yelling out, who’s a former Minister of Housing, will recall that the funding for social housing places ceases after June 2025, so that is indeed a fiscal cliff. The reality is the last Government didn’t fund places beyond 2025, into 2026 or 2027, because they wanted to create the illusion of a surplus later on.
veracity.explanation: The funding end-date / 'fiscal cliff' is a checkable fiscal-baseline claim and broadly defensible; the imputed motive ('illusion of a surplus') is unverifiable editorialising.

veracity.statement: The bank’s monetary policy committee, which makes its decisions about interest rates independent of the Government, left the official cash rate unchanged at 5.5 percent... Inflation has declined from a peak of 7.3 percent in mid-2022 to 4.7 percent in the December quarter, and the bank’s forecasts show it falling towards the 2 percent mid-point of the target band.
veracity.explanation: OCR held at 5.5%, inflation peak 7.3% and 4.7% Dec quarter match the official RBNZ/Stats NZ figures for the period.

veracity.statement: The Reserve Bank was trying to fight inflation with higher interest rates while the Government was busy fuelling it with its high spending and ever-growing debt. By way of metaphor, there’s no point in the Reserve Bank being asked to put its hand on the brake if the Government’s hitting the accelerator at the same time.
veracity.explanation: Partly defensible (fiscal stimulus during tightening) but a contested, one-sided characterisation of the inflation cause.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that under a former administration, gas supply could run out within the next five years. It’s not because of a shortage of gas but a shortage of investment and political wisdom.
veracity.explanation: Underlying gas-decline concern is real, but 'run out in five years' is an overstatement of forecasts.

veracity.statement: Marsden Point, which right now has been allowed to close down in supply when, in a critical phrase of non-supply to this country by tankers, we could’ve supplied 50 percent of the country’s critical needs.
veracity.explanation: Marsden Point was a refinery converted to an import terminal; the '50 percent of critical needs' figure is an unsupported and likely misleading claim.

veracity.statement: It is targeted to go to 0.23. This is shocking. And in 2017, we were facing it going to 0.21... We left it at 0.34 when we left.
veracity.explanation: Specific ODA/GNI percentages cited from memory across multiple periods; partly checkable but mixes years and is selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Recently, as reported, I was present as six gold-plated Harley-Davidson motorcycles, formerly the prized possessions of the Comancheros, were shredded into scrap metal.
veracity.explanation: Describes a reported, verifiable event (confiscated Comanchero motorcycles destroyed).

veracity.statement: Back in 2020, Australia implemented a very similar scheme named the Payment Times Reporting Act. A recent independent review of the scheme’s effectiveness found that despite imposing significant IT compliance costs on businesses, overall payment times had not reduced.
veracity.explanation: Accurately references the Australian scheme and a review finding limited effect; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: On Friday, I announced a $5 million boost to the upper North Island community’s fight against the invasive seaweed Caulerpa. This exotic pest arrived in 2021 and has now been found in five locations across Northland and Greater Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claims about funding and Caulerpa's spread consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: I read recently in media that Macleans College in Auckland had funded and built five new classrooms in nine months after being advised by the Ministry of Education that it would take three years to deliver the same learning spaces. They did it for $2.5 million.
veracity.explanation: Specific, plausible and media-sourced, but presented second-hand ('I read recently in media') without independent verification.

veracity.statement: I’m in possession of correspondence from well-respected Auckland property engineering firms who say that you could easily get rid of 75 percent of the Auckland Ministry of Education staff and be better off.
veracity.explanation: A sweeping, unsubstantiated assertion attributed to anonymous correspondence.

veracity.statement: we have seen the number of bureaucrats employed at the Ministry of Education increase in the past six years from 2,500 to 4,400, and yet fewer kids are going to school
veracity.explanation: Staffing-growth figures are broadly in line with reported Ministry headcount increases; 'fewer kids going to school' conflates attendance with enrolment.

veracity.statement: In the year since January 2023 alone, there’s been a 3 percent increase in the District Court criminal backlog, rising to a total backlog of 37 percent of active cases.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific, checkable court-backlog statistics; plausible and consistent with reported trends.

veracity.statement: Considering the fact that when the Warner Bros. Discovery came for help to the previous Government’s Minister of broadcasting and they said no, I can say that that is a very rich question coming from the member.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the prior government declined to help WBD; plausible but unsubstantiated in the text.

veracity.statement: you cannot move around the Beehive without stumbling over lobbyists. We’ve got the tobacco lobby, the oil and gas lobby, the fishing lobby, the forestry lobby, the mining lobby, the gun lobby. They’re all in the building, and they are the ones setting the agenda of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Exaggerated framing presented as fact; the claim that lobbyists 'set the agenda' is unsubstantiated.

veracity.statement: We have seen, this week, the repeal of a policy that was going to do real and meaningful work around saving the lives of New Zealanders—the work around the smoke-free legislation that was world leading. And what did we see? We saw a Government that repealed it under urgency at a point where lives will be lost.
veracity.explanation: The legislation was widely described as world-leading and was repealed under urgency; 'lives will be lost' is a contested projection stated as fact.

veracity.statement: We’re seeing Air Marshal Short saying that the 6.5 percent cuts from Defence would mean they had to divest themselves of capability.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific claim to a named official; plausible and checkable, though presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: Then, of course, this Government has already stopped that mind-bogglingly wasteful experience called the Auckland light rail.
veracity.explanation: Factually accurate that the Government cancelled Auckland light rail; 'mind-bogglingly wasteful' is loaded editorialising.

civility.statement: I think the member who’s yelling out, who’s a former Minister of Housing, will recall that the funding for social housing places ceases after June 2025, so that is indeed a fiscal cliff. The reality is the last Government didn’t fund places beyond 2025, into 2026 or 2027, because they wanted to create the illusion of a surplus later on.
civility.explanation: Engages the funding substance but imputes a deliberate bad motive to the previous government.

civility.statement: I’m happy for the member to meet with Kāinga Ora, as I am indeed happy for all members of Parliament to meet with Kāinga Ora to get a briefing on what they’re up to in their particular local areas, or indeed the Opposition spokesperson.
civility.explanation: Cooperative, respectful response to an opponent's request.

civility.explanation: Legitimate policy criticism of the prior government, but framed combatively.

civility.statement: In taking this course of action... has he considered an alternative approach in which the Government simply appropriates money from the magic money tree at the end of the garden?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'magic money tree' framing that caricatures the Opposition's fiscal stance.

civility.statement: This sovereign risk is a result of the economic vandalism threatened by some, and their woke fellow travellers, who have no comprehension at all of international business and investment.
civility.explanation: 'Economic vandalism', 'woke fellow travellers', 'no comprehension' — personal disparagement, not policy critique.

civility.statement: As that member will well know, all conversations with all colleagues—including the Prime Minister and, most importantly, the Minister of Finance—are confidential. civility.statement: We have also stopped all work on the separatist agenda called He Puapua, kept secret by the last Government; repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act; abolished the failing Māori Health Authority to ensure we focus on delivering better healthcare for all of those who need it most... based on need, not some woke concept.
civility.explanation: 'separatist agenda', 'woke concept' are pejorative framings rather than neutral description.

civility.statement: Did you hear what she said? “That’s two Rs.”. See what the problem is? She doesn’t even get the great theme; all around Western society where they spoke English, it was three Rs, but genius over here knows better.
civility.explanation: Mocking a colleague ('genius over here') for sport, even if light-hearted.

civility.statement: And for those who are protesting over there, how on earth did they think they’d ever get a proper inquiry if they didn’t have proper terms of reference? An inquiry designed to cover your derrière is not an inquiry.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'cover your derrière' framing of opponents' prior process.

civility.statement: I think it was probably legislation that Stuart Nash brought in, because, actually, he was a very good police Minister, unlike the three that followed him.

civility.explanation: 'Gang apologists' is a personal/partisan smear rather than engagement with the resourcing concern raised.

civility.statement: Thank you for the question. No, it’s not fair. But we will be working with an industry code... with Business New Zealand to make sure that large businesses do meet their requirements.
civility.explanation: Engages respectfully with the substance of an opposition member's constituent case.

civility.statement: I think the Opposition is going to have a real problem here in that they have confused spending money with delivering results, because if spending $100 billion of borrowed money on every problem actually worked, this country wouldn’t have any problems after the last Government.
civility.explanation: Caricatures the Opposition's approach for rhetorical effect.

civility.statement: No. But what I am concerned about is resolving the growing court backlog that was allowed to persist under his party’s watch since 2017.
civility.explanation: Frames the issue as the opponent's fault ('under his party's watch').

civility.statement: Considering the fact that when the Warner Bros. Discovery came for help to the previous Government’s Minister of broadcasting and they said no, I can say that that is a very rich question coming from the member.
civility.explanation: Deflects with a 'very rich question' jab at the questioner's own side.

civility.statement: And when we look back, what has our new Government achieved over the last 100 days? A whole lot of going backwards... with no sense that if you’re going to repeal, you’re meant to replace as well.
civility.explanation: Pointed but largely policy-directed critique of the Government's record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: you cannot move around the Beehive without stumbling over lobbyists. We’ve got the tobacco lobby, the oil and gas lobby, the fishing lobby, the forestry lobby, the mining lobby, the gun lobby. They’re all in the building, and they are the ones setting the agenda of this Government.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Government's integrity rhetorically rather than engaging specific decisions.

civility.statement: I did note in question time today, though, that David Seymour must have got so excited when he heard about 7.5 percent cost cuts, he read that as 75 percent at the Ministry of Education.
civility.explanation: Personal mockery of a named member, though riffing on his own '75 percent' remark.

civility.statement: We have seen, this week, the repeal of a policy that was going to do real and meaningful work around saving the lives of New Zealanders—the work around the smoke-free legislation that was world leading. And what did we see? We saw a Government that repealed it under urgency at a point where lives will be lost.
civility.explanation: Strong but substantively-grounded criticism of a policy decision.

civility.statement: That’s what this coalition Government has had to do during its first hundred days: stop the bleeding, the wasteful profligate spending, the arrogant assumption that they know best on every issue.
civility.explanation: Partisan framing ('arrogant assumption') but directed at the previous government's approach.

civility.statement: Then, of course, this Government has already stopped that mind-bogglingly wasteful experience called the Auckland light rail.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the prior policy.

rigor.explanation: Coherent fiscal/monetary argument but leans on the brake/accelerator analogy and asserts a contested causal claim without evidence.

rigor.statement: In taking this course of action... has he considered an alternative approach in which the Government simply appropriates money from the magic money tree at the end of the garden?
rigor.explanation: A loaded, strawman framing rather than reasoned argument.

rigor.explanation: Reframes the displacement objection (gangs moving elsewhere) as success, dodging whether the problem is solved or just relocated.

rigor.explanation: Cites a comparable jurisdiction and an independent review to support the conclusion; clear evidence-to-claim link.

rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic strawman ('every problem', 'wouldn't have any problems') rather than a sound argument.

rigor.statement: I’m in possession of correspondence from well-respected Auckland property engineering firms who say that you could easily get rid of 75 percent of the Auckland Ministry of Education staff and be better off.

rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two figures to imply causation without establishing the link.

rigor.statement: You see, there’s a thing called the sunk cost fallacy, and just because money has been spent on something in the past does not mean that continuing to waste money is a good idea.

rigor.explanation: Claims savings can be found 'very easily' from 'waste' without specifying where.

rigor.explanation: Hyperbole and a sweeping causal claim ('setting the agenda') offered without evidence.

rigor.statement: I’m a committed electric vehicle (EV) driver and a fan. I don’t understand why people wouldn’t be driving an EV. But I do understand the negative impacts of putting in place a policy that would punish those who aren’t able to, for a variety of reasons, use EVs.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned distinction between liking EVs and opposing a policy that penalises non-users, though the 'punish' framing is assertion.

divination.statement: I’m advised that under a former administration, gas supply could run out within the next five years. It’s not because of a shortage of gas but a shortage of investment and political wisdom.
divination.explanation: Five-year forecast of gas supply running out; directionally consistent with declining NZ field output but magnitude/timeframe uncertain.

divination.statement: Technical advice so far has been that fully eradicating it from New Zealand will be extremely challenging and unlikely with current technology. But this investment will still make a difference for the environment and for the people affected.
divination.explanation: Realistic, evidence-grounded prediction that full eradication is improbable with current technology.

And what did we see? We saw a Government that repealed it under urgency at a point where lives will be lost.
divination.explanation: Predicts lives will be lost from the smoke-free repeal; directionally supported by public-health modelling, magnitude/timeframe uncertain.

strength.statement: New Zealand is dedicated to a clean energy transition and meeting our emissions targets. This Government is committed to deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and removing consenting barriers.
strength.explanation: Restates a standing aspiration/commitment rather than demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: We have also stopped all work on the separatist agenda called He Puapua, kept secret by the last Government; repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act; abolished the failing Māori Health Authority to ensure we focus on delivering better healthcare for all of those who need it most... based on need, not some woke concept.
strength.explanation: Lists repeals/abolitions that were actually enacted in the term — demonstrated follow-through on coalition commitments.

strength.statement: On Sunday, Minister Goldsmith, Minister McKee, and I announced part of the coalition Government’s proposed crackdown on gangs, including banning gang patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, and making gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
strength.explanation: An announcement of proposed measures rather than enacted delivery.

strength.statement: Last week, I announced that the Government will repeal the Business Payment Practices Act 2023. This piece of legislation was an ineffective, costly solution to the problem of large market players paying invoices late, and evidence from abroad supports the repeal of the Act.
strength.explanation: Announced repeal in progress, consistent with the Government's stated programme.

strength.statement: However, this Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sector sustainability while still preserving the independence of the fourth estate. strength.explanation: Stated intent to support the sector with no concrete action described.

strength.statement: Then, of course, this Government has already stopped that mind-bogglingly wasteful experience called the Auckland light rail.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a commitment actually delivered (cancellation), though delivery here is stopping rather than building.

authenticity.statement: We have also stopped all work on the separatist agenda called He Puapua, kept secret by the last Government; repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act; abolished the failing Māori Health Authority to ensure we focus on delivering better healthcare for all of those who need it most... based on need, not some woke concept.
authenticity.explanation: Actions cited align with the publicly stated coalition agreement positions.

authenticity.statement: I’m a committed electric vehicle (EV) driver and a fan. I don’t understand why people wouldn’t be driving an EV. But I do understand the negative impacts of putting in place a policy that would punish those who aren’t able to, for a variety of reasons, use EVs.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges his own pro-EV stance yet supports repealing the EV-favouring policy, giving a consistent, non-self-serving rationale.

civility.statement: Look, first of all, I want to congratulate Todd Stephenson on bringing this here today, and I acknowledge, of course, that he was a lawyer in the great city of Dunedin and went to the fabulous University of Otago Law School about the same time as the current speaker.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of an MP from another party; no attack.

civility.statement: I think there was a very important caveat from Dr Duncan Webb about the importance that these programmes are well funded, and my colleague Ginny Andersen also expressed concern around that 6.5 percent cut that is happening to Corrections.
civility.explanation: Engages with substantive funding concerns and credits colleagues by name; policy-focused.

civility.statement: I would like to spend the last few seconds of my call to say that my heart goes out to the wife and daughters of Efeso and that they be courageous at this time.
civility.explanation: Respectful, compassionate tribute to a deceased colleague's family.

civility.statement: I join the House, I think, in thinking very much that this was a man who loved his family and who doesn’t get to see his children grow up and they don’t get to have him there any more, and that’s the bit that means the most to me in the situation.
civility.explanation: Heartfelt tribute to Efeso Collins; entirely respectful and humane.

civility.statement: Now, this is a piece of legislation that is, at heart—and Toni has a good heart—about rehabilitation and not abandoning people, and supporting people when they are willing to make a move.
