civility.explanation: Generous to an ACT colleague and focused on constructive collaboration.

civility.statement: This week has been a really hard one for the Labour Party in this House. We found the smoke-free legislation really difficult. It has been one of those things which really hurt a lot of people.
civility.explanation: Reflective and non-combative even while referencing a politically charged issue.

civility.statement: And congratulations to Todd—a first-term MP having his bill drawn from the biscuit tin. Luck was in his favour that day.
civility.explanation: Good-natured congratulation of a member from another party.

civility.statement: To the Government members who spoke in relation to the bill: Cameron, Jamie, Paulo, and Tom—I want to thank you for your comments and your support. Yes, you have nailed the intent of what we are trying to do here.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of opponents' contributions.

civility.statement: I also totally accept what was said about Corrections. Again, it is, like many Government departments, one that is having trouble recruiting and retaining staff. So I do want to acknowledge those issues, and I think they correctly identified some of the things that we can discuss at the select committee.
civility.explanation: Credits opponents for correctly identifying problems; constructive and substantive.

civility.statement: Let me finish this off because I’ve only got a minute and I’m sure we want to get out of here. So, look, I think we can address some of these concerns in the select committee. I think that we can have a robust and productive discussion, and let’s actually do something to, hopefully, enhance our criminal justice system, with all those caveats and concerns in place.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges critics' caveats and frames the path ahead as shared work.

charisma.statement: Look, first of all, I want to congratulate Todd Stephenson on bringing this here today, and I acknowledge, of course, that he was a lawyer in the great city of Dunedin and went to the fabulous University of Otago Law School about the same time as the current speaker.
charisma.explanation: Friendly cross-party congratulation that builds goodwill on a bipartisan bill.

charisma.statement: During the election campaign, I was standing for the seat of Dunedin. I went to visit some of the people in this programme, as did members from across this House—both sides of the House—and had some of the most interesting conversations I had during the campaign.
charisma.explanation: Notes the visits were cross-party, reinforcing a unifying, bipartisan frame.

charisma.statement: I join the House, I think, in thinking very much that this was a man who loved his family and who doesn’t get to see his children grow up and they don’t get to have him there any more, and that’s the bit that means the most to me in the situation.
charisma.explanation: Speaks for the whole House in shared grief, an inclusive unifying note.

charisma.statement: Now, this is a piece of legislation that is, at heart—and Toni has a good heart—about rehabilitation and not abandoning people, and supporting people when they are willing to make a move. I think that we all agree with that purpose. We might have some gnarly bits to work through in the select committee, but I think we’re all prepared to do that.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks common ground, affirms shared purpose across parties, and frames disagreements as workable together.

charisma.statement: And congratulations to Todd—a first-term MP having his bill drawn from the biscuit tin. Luck was in his favour that day.
charisma.explanation: Light, generous cross-party tone that reinforces the collaborative mood.

charisma.statement: We want to be tough and crack down on the causes of crime, but, at the same time, we also want to have strong and thorough rehabilitative programmes in place for prisoners to prepare them for release.
charisma.explanation: Balances a law-and-order message with rehabilitation, reaching toward common ground, though framed for its own side.

charisma.statement: To the Government members who spoke in relation to the bill: Cameron, Jamie, Paulo, and Tom—I want to thank you for your comments and your support. Yes, you have nailed the intent of what we are trying to do here.
charisma.explanation: Names and thanks members across parties, actively cultivating cross-bench goodwill.

charisma.statement: I also totally accept what was said about Corrections. Again, it is, like many Government departments, one that is having trouble recruiting and retaining staff. So I do want to acknowledge those issues, and I think they correctly identified some of the things that we can discuss at the select committee.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory acknowledgement builds consensus toward joint select-committee work.

charisma.statement: Let me finish this off because I’ve only got a minute and I’m sure we want to get out of here. So, look, I think we can address some of these concerns in the select committee. I think that we can have a robust and productive discussion, and let’s actually do something to, hopefully, enhance our criminal justice system, with all those caveats and concerns in place.
charisma.explanation: Closes on a collaborative, forward-looking note that invites all sides into a productive process.

authenticity.statement: My father, when I was growing up, was a regular visitor to the prisons and was also involved over 30 years ago in establishing Moana House, which is mainly known for being a residential programme to rehabilitate men, mainly Māori and Pasifika men, who mainly have drug issues and have been in the justice system.
authenticity.explanation: Her stated commitment to rehabilitation is grounded in a concrete family record, lending consistency between values and lived experience.

authenticity.statement: During the election campaign, I was standing for the seat of Dunedin. I went to visit some of the people in this programme, as did members from across this House—both sides of the House—and had some of the most interesting conversations I had during the campaign.
authenticity.explanation: Backs her professed support for rehabilitation with a concrete personal action (visiting the programme during the campaign).

authenticity.statement: This week has been a really hard one for the Labour Party in this House. We found the smoke-free legislation really difficult. It has been one of those things which really hurt a lot of people.
authenticity.explanation: Candid, self-revealing admission of her party's difficulty rather than spin; consistent honest tone.

authenticity.statement: I also totally accept what was said about Corrections. Again, it is, like many Government departments, one that is having trouble recruiting and retaining staff. So I do want to acknowledge those issues, and I think they correctly identified some of the things that we can discuss at the select committee.
authenticity.explanation: Openly concedes weaknesses in his own bill's implementation context rather than defending it uncritically.

specificity.statement: My father, when I was growing up, was a regular visitor to the prisons and was also involved over 30 years ago in establishing Moana House, which is mainly known for being a residential programme to rehabilitate men, mainly Māori and Pasifika men, who mainly have drug issues and have been in the justice system.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme (Moana House), its purpose, target population and rough timeframe.

specificity.statement: “Rehabilitative programmes” is defined in the Corrections Act 2004, so we don’t see it on the bill in front of us, but that means a programme designed to reduce reoffending by facilitating the rehabilitation of prisoners sentenced to imprisonment and their reintegration into society.
specificity.explanation: Cites the named statute and the precise legal definition rather than speaking vaguely.

specificity.statement: In the Justice Committee, we have gone through an overview of the Ministry of Justice and the Department of Corrections, and the fact that the number of prisoners—whether in youth facilities or in Corrections facilities—are so many, and that the time that they spend there is considerable: over one year, sometimes close to two years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough quantitative range (one to nearly two years) but no precise statistics.

specificity.statement: So the bill seeks to bring in, through clause 4, a definition of what a “rehabilitative programme” is. Through clause 5, it requires that offenders who have not done a rehabilitative programme be considered as ineligible for parole; but, conversely, for the Parole Board to then say to them that if they’re able to do a programme within the next 12 months, then that would be the best thing. Clause 6 also establishes a very strong incentive for offenders in that space, in that once they complete a rehabilitative programme, they would then become eligible for parole.
specificity.explanation: Walks through the bill clause by clause with concrete mechanisms and a 12-month timeframe.

specificity.statement: I’d love to see—and I’m not sure if it’s in scope—us look at the capacity to bring rehabilitation in as an offering to people on remand, because they sit on remand, at the present time, for far too long, lost and without those opportunities.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete extension (rehabilitation for remand prisoners) but without a mechanism or detail on delivery.

specificity.statement: We want to be tough and crack down on the causes of crime, but, at the same time, we also want to have strong and thorough rehabilitative programmes in place for prisoners to prepare them for release.
specificity.explanation: States twin aims but no concrete measures, figures, or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: Now, the National Party is supporting this to the select committee stage because we’re interested to hear the feedback that we receive from the industry groups and firsthand from the general public.
specificity.explanation: Clear about the procedural stage and rationale, though general about what feedback is sought.

specificity.statement: I was actually lucky enough, earlier in the week, to talk to another great man who hails from Dunedin—he’s no longer there—Sir Ron Young, who’s actually the chair of the New Zealand Parole Board. He reached out to me and generously gave me some of his time to give me some of his thoughts. He talked about the fact that the Parole Board is doing some of this victim-offender rehabilitation work.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific source and the substance of his input, though the 'work' itself is described loosely.

veracity.statement: “Rehabilitative programmes” is defined in the Corrections Act 2004, so we don’t see it on the bill in front of us, but that means a programme designed to reduce reoffending by facilitating the rehabilitation of prisoners sentenced to imprisonment and their reintegration into society.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes the definition to the Corrections Act 2004 and paraphrases its substance correctly.

veracity.statement: I think there was a very important caveat from Dr Duncan Webb about the importance that these programmes are well funded, and my colleague Ginny Andersen also expressed concern around that 6.5 percent cut that is happening to Corrections.
veracity.explanation: Reports a specific 6.5 percent Corrections cut; directionally consistent with budget reporting at the time but the precise figure/scope is hard to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: In the Justice Committee, we have gone through an overview of the Ministry of Justice and the Department of Corrections, and the fact that the number of prisoners—whether in youth facilities or in Corrections facilities—are so many, and that the time that they spend there is considerable: over one year, sometimes close to two years.
veracity.explanation: Claim about lengthy remand/incarceration times is broadly consistent with known NZ remand data, though the figures are imprecise.

veracity.statement: We know our prison population suffer a lot from illiteracy. They’re illiterate, often, and they’re also suffering from things like ADHD. They’ve often had trauma. They’ve often had violence in their past.
veracity.explanation: Claims of high rates of illiteracy, neurodiversity and trauma among prisoners are broadly supported by NZ corrections research, though stated loosely.

veracity.statement: Prisoners, as we know, face many barriers to gaining employment post their release from prison, such as poor literacy, numeracy, and educational underachievement. This results in many offenders unfortunately falling back into criminal activity.
veracity.explanation: Claims about literacy/numeracy barriers driving reoffending align with established corrections research.

veracity.statement: The paramount consideration of the Parole Board when considering someone for release is the safety of the community.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the statutory paramount consideration of the NZ Parole Board (community safety).

veracity.statement: I was actually lucky enough, earlier in the week, to talk to another great man who hails from Dunedin—he’s no longer there—Sir Ron Young, who’s actually the chair of the New Zealand Parole Board. He reached out to me and generously gave me some of his time to give me some of his thoughts. He talked about the fact that the Parole Board is doing some of this victim-offender rehabilitation work.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim that he consulted the Parole Board chair Sir Ron Young; consistent and plausible.

rigor.statement: So the bill seeks to bring in, through clause 4, a definition of what a “rehabilitative programme” is. Through clause 5, it requires that offenders who have not done a rehabilitative programme be considered as ineligible for parole; but, conversely, for the Parole Board to then say to them that if they’re able to do a programme within the next 12 months, then that would be the best thing. Clause 6 also establishes a very strong incentive for offenders in that space, in that once they complete a rehabilitative programme, they would then become eligible for parole.
rigor.explanation: Lays out the bill's logical structure clearly, connecting each clause to the incentive it creates.

rigor.statement: The impacts are great. We will reduce the prison population in the process, we will give people opportunities to improve themselves, and ensure that victimisation is itself reduced.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable cause-and-effect chain (rehabilitation reduces reoffending) but asserted as certainty without evidence.

rigor.statement: We know our prison population suffer a lot from illiteracy. They’re illiterate, often, and they’re also suffering from things like ADHD. They’ve often had trauma. They’ve often had violence in their past.
rigor.explanation: Uses the documented profile of the prison population to argue for rehabilitation; reasonable but leans on generalisation without citing figures.

rigor.statement: Prisoners, as we know, face many barriers to gaining employment post their release from prison, such as poor literacy, numeracy, and educational underachievement. This results in many offenders unfortunately falling back into criminal activity.
rigor.explanation: Coherent causal argument from employment barriers to reoffending; reasonable but evidence is asserted rather than cited.

divination.statement: The impacts are great. We will reduce the prison population in the process, we will give people opportunities to improve themselves, and ensure that victimisation is itself reduced.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will reduce the prison population and victimisation; plausible in direction but unsubstantiated and contingent on funding/implementation.

forthrightness.statement: I’d love to see—and I’m not sure if it’s in scope—us look at the capacity to bring rehabilitation in as an offering to people on remand, because they sit on remand, at the present time, for far too long, lost and without those opportunities.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly flags her own uncertainty about whether the idea is in scope rather than overclaiming.

forthrightness.statement: Now, the National Party is supporting this to the select committee stage because we’re interested to hear the feedback that we receive from the industry groups and firsthand from the general public.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly states his party's position and the reason for it.

civility.statement: I'm surprised at that member, Jamie Arbuckle, actually, because, as I understand it, he's double-dipping with the Marlborough District Council.
civility.explanation: Hedged personal insinuation ('double-dipping') aimed at a named member rather than engaging the substance of his argument.

civility.statement: So the other side of the House are doing what they always do. They say, "Well, let's have the same rules for everyone, because everyone should be a bit like me."
civility.explanation: Caricatures opponents' position rather than quoting it; mild strawman.

civility.statement: So I'm disappointed that the parties on the other side of the House have chosen to once again take a narrow view of democracy—an exclusive view of democracy—and not try to use the very tools we've got at our disposal to have a more inclusive, more effective, and more robust democratic framework.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the opponents' approach to democracy that stays on the policy rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: this is just bizarre that the Government, which is holding itself out to be wanting to get New Zealand moving, to look after rural communities, is suddenly saying, "Oh, except when it comes to local democracy."
civility.explanation: Critical and a touch sensational ('bizarre') but aimed at the Government's stance rather than a person.

civility.statement: all we've seen in this House over the last hundred days is legislation getting ran through with no due process, under urgency, no select committee hearings.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused criticism of the Government's legislative process, tipping into hyperbole.

civility.statement: Oh, put the handbrake on; let's go back 50 years, because that's what this Government likes to do. They are so backward
civility.explanation: Derogatory characterisation ('so backward', 'go back 50 years') rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: if Ingrid Leary's worried about bizarre comments, she should take hers, wrap them in cellophane, and put them on a plinth; I haven't heard anything so bizarre in a long time.
civility.explanation: Personal mockery of a named member rather than engagement with her argument.

civility.statement: Geez, we had it during the last one; you were getting told how long you're allowed to stay in the shower. I don't like the thought of Grant Robertson inspecting me in the shower, quite frankly!
civility.explanation: Sensationalised mockery naming an individual; misrepresents past policy for comedic effect.

civility.statement: this simply shows a Wellington-knows-best approach to how local government and how local communities should be operating ... Legislation like this is just another example of Labour's Wellington-knows-best approach to local government, which imposes rules on councils
civility.explanation: Criticises the legislative approach rather than individuals, though relies on a recurring caricature.

civility.statement: I do just want to take a moment to acknowledge that today was the funeral of our parliamentary colleague Efeso Collins ... my thoughts, and those of ACT, are with his family, friends, and especially his wife and daughter today.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous tribute to a colleague across party lines.

civility.statement: I am looking for all parties to support this bill to the first reading. It may not be the perfect solution, but I hope that we can have a constructive debate about it and have the select committee look at it.
civility.explanation: Frames the debate as constructive and collaborative rather than adversarial.

civility.statement: I'm very proud that the National Party sent a significant delegation led by the Prime Minister ... Efeso was someone who had that unique ability, both as a person and as a politician, to walk so well in so many worlds.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful tribute to a deceased colleague from another party.

civility.statement: if I look at what was launched at the weekend by Minister Mitchell: "Masher Mitchell" as they call him now—not "Crusher Collins", but "Masher Mitchell"—and Goldie, colloquially known as the Hon Paul Goldsmith, introduced legislation to ban gang patches. And hasn't that gone down so well
civility.explanation: Jokey nicknames for colleagues are light-hearted rather than hostile, but the digression and 'gone down so well' boosterism stray from substantive debate.

civility.statement: Corrections funds rehabilitation and prison-educated programmes, as the member will know. And with 6.5 percent cuts looming over the service, I don't think it's unreasonable for us to say that we certainly have some concerns as to how these pathways will continue to be funded sufficiently
civility.explanation: Raises a substantive funding concern respectfully while still supporting the bill.

civility.statement: This is a really nice bill for ACT. I'm quite impressed. So good on you. ... I'm being nice; this is a great bill. We like it. It's a good bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous tone toward a political opponent's work.

rigor.statement: I'm surprised at that member, Jamie Arbuckle, actually, because, as I understand it, he's double-dipping with the Marlborough District Council.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks Arbuckle's situation ('as I understand it') instead of his reasoning.

rigor.statement: So the other side of the House are doing what they always do. They say, "Well, let's have the same rules for everyone, because everyone should be a bit like me."
rigor.explanation: Strawman — invents a self-centred motive ('everyone should be a bit like me') the other side did not state.

rigor.statement: What about people who suffer from a disability? What about people who have to organise transport, a wheelchair, and whatever other equipment their disability might require?
rigor.explanation: A legitimate access argument, but leans on appeal to emotion via accumulated rhetorical questions rather than evidence on participation rates.

rigor.statement: This is just a common-sense bill. It makes no sense to say, "You can participate, you just can't vote." The reason we get elected to democratic positions is to vote.
rigor.explanation: Coherent point that voting is the core function of an elected representative, but rests partly on an appeal to 'common sense'.

rigor.statement: We know that when we have more participation, we get better decisions.
rigor.explanation: Plausible general claim asserted as known fact without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: if we go to clause 4 inserting new clause 25A(6) in Schedule 7 of the principal Act—it's just a short bill, but subclause 6 says that when a local authority is including things in its standing orders, it can also add any other requirements that it considers are "appropriate to maintain public confidence in the transparency and integrity of decision-making processes and the conduct of members".
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the bill's actual text, showing safeguards exist; evidence-based rebuttal.

rigor.statement: Once again, this Government—interested in Auckland, interested in building roads up north, interested in everything that happens in the North Island—is not thinking about the consequences for the people of the South Island.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the Government ignores the South Island without evidence; leans on geographic generalisation.

rigor.statement: I point you to Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023. It's already given them the ability to do this. All they have to do is change their standing orders.
rigor.explanation: Cites the existing statute as evidence the bill is redundant; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: we don't believe in this age-old, from-the-left, "Wellington knows best. We'll tell you how to do it. We've got all the answers." We heard it from them not just with this; we heard it from three waters
rigor.explanation: Uses analogies (three waters, Te Pūkenga, health) to support the centralisation critique, but characterises opponents' position via a strawman slogan.

rigor.statement: Geez, we had it during the last one; you were getting told how long you're allowed to stay in the shower. I don't like the thought of Grant Robertson inspecting me in the shower, quite frankly!
rigor.explanation: Strawman / ridicule with no evidentiary basis for the 'inspecting me in the shower' claim.

rigor.statement: Before I came to this House, I was an elected member on a community board ... They were running businesses from homes, they were juggling commitments with full-time jobs, some were parents with young kids, and some had mobility or accessibility issues and that made it difficult for them to attend every meeting.
rigor.explanation: Uses first-hand observation of busy board members as evidence for the access problem, though anecdotal.

rigor.statement: there's a real risk here in not doing this, and that is that representation becomes a luxury for those who can afford it. People won't seek office. People won't be able to represent their communities, because they can't take the time off work, off family, off study
rigor.explanation: Logical chain from access barriers to who can serve, though the conclusion is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Standing order 13.11, "Conditions for attending by audio or audio-visual link": "[The] Chairperson may give approval for a member to attend meetings by electronic link, either generally or for a specific meeting." ... So the Bay of Plenty Regional Council has this provision already in their standing orders.
rigor.explanation: Brings documentary evidence ('receipts') to support the 'solution in search of a problem' claim; conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: this time last year less than 20 percent of sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run facilities were attending rehabilitation programmes ... closer to 10 percent of the onsite prison population are actually enrolled in any rehabilitation programme.
rigor.explanation: Marshals data to argue the problem is real and the incentive is needed; reasoning is evidence-led.

rigor.statement: I accept there are likely to be some capacity and operational issues in what I'm putting forward, but I believe that the select committee is well placed to look at these issues
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges the limitations and capacity risks of his own proposal rather than overstating it — intellectually honest reasoning.

rigor.statement: rather than branding prisons as the "University of Crime" and focusing on reducing the prison population, regardless of how much crime is happening, this Government, this coalition Government, is confronting the real reasons behind crime and looking at rehabilitation as a key part of our success
rigor.explanation: Strawman of the opposing approach ('regardless of how much crime is happening') and asserts the Government addresses 'real reasons' without evidence.

rigor.statement: Corrections funds rehabilitation and prison-educated programmes, as the member will know. And with 6.5 percent cuts looming over the service, I don't think it's unreasonable for us to say that we certainly have some concerns as to how these pathways will continue to be funded sufficiently
rigor.explanation: Links a specific funding constraint to a concrete operational risk for the bill — evidence-based, measured reasoning.

rigor.statement: we have some concerns that parole could be denied due to Corrections resources rather than just the merits of the parole application.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a clear logical flaw in the bill — that a resourcing gap, not the prisoner's conduct, could block parole; conclusion follows from the staffing premises.

rigor.statement: From New Zealand First's point of view, we're a party of common sense. It makes common sense that if you're in that situation, you would take the opportunity to try to improve your life.
rigor.explanation: Repeated appeal to 'common sense' substitutes for evidence; assertion rather than argument.

rigor.statement: I always look at it from the victim's point of view. ... if the victim could actually look and see that someone's making an effort to try to change their life, that actually makes you feel better.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion via the victim's feelings; a reasonable framing but not evidence for the policy's effectiveness.

rigor.statement: One of my portfolios for New Zealand First is horticulture. It was quite interesting hearing that that is a programme that has great uptake. Carpentry—something that this country has a deficit of, at the moment, in our building industry. So why don't we teach it?
rigor.explanation: Connects programme uptake to a skills shortage sensibly, but the building-industry deficit claim is asserted without data.

rigor.statement: we would not want to see a failure of resourcing stopping someone from receiving their treatment if they accept it, and we would not want anyone to be prevented from having a fair right of being reviewed by the Parole Board.
rigor.explanation: Articulates the same resourcing-vs-fairness risk with clear conditional logic; principled and coherent.

rigor.statement: resources are so constrained in Corrections that 12 out of the 18 prisons are not giving the legal entitlement of a visit a week.
rigor.explanation: Uses the visit-entitlement data as concrete evidence of system-wide resource constraints relevant to the bill.

rigor.statement: what I would not want to see is someone who is ready to be put back into the community but hasn't done a rehabilitative programme—not because they don't want to but because the resources aren't there.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clean distinction between a prisoner's refusal (which should count) and a system failure (which should not), making the logical flaw in the bill explicit.

rigor.statement: when this comes to select committee, we've got to (a) be confident that this isn't just flag waving, that it really can make a concrete change operationally.
rigor.explanation: Sets an evidentiary test (operational, concrete change vs symbolic 'flag waving') for evaluating the bill.

veracity.statement: Kenepuru Road, which, as you can imagine, goes up to Kenepuru Sound and out to the outer Sounds, is still impassable.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about ongoing storm damage to Kenepuru Road; consistent with the protracted Marlborough Sounds road repairs after the 2021-22 weather events, though 'impassable' may be slightly overstated.

veracity.statement: I can tell you that out of the 78 councils, four of the 10 biggest regional councils by land are based in the South Island, and for territorial authorities nine out of 10 of them.
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claim about council size and location; directionally plausible given the large South Island land areas but the precise 'nine out of 10' figure is hard to verify and likely imprecise.

veracity.statement: all we've seen in this House over the last hundred days is legislation getting ran through with no due process, under urgency, no select committee hearings.
veracity.explanation: True that the coalition used urgency heavily in its first 100 days, but 'all we've seen... no due process' is a sweeping overstatement that ignores bills that did follow normal process.

veracity.statement: I point you to Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023. It's already given them the ability to do this. All they have to do is change their standing orders.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 made permanent the ability for councils to allow remote attendance via their standing orders.

veracity.statement: Environment Canterbury is our largest regional council. It's over 44,000 kilometres squared. That's bigger than Denmark. It's four times the size of Jamaica. It's 20,000 times the size of Monaco
veracity.explanation: Environment Canterbury covers roughly 45,000 km², comparable to Denmark (~43,000 km²); the comparisons are broadly accurate, if rhetorically selected.

veracity.statement: Standing order 13.11, "Conditions for attending by audio or audio-visual link": "[The] Chairperson may give approval for a member to attend meetings by electronic link, either generally or for a specific meeting." ... So the Bay of Plenty Regional Council has this provision already in their standing orders.
veracity.explanation: Quotes a specific standing order to substantiate that councils already permit remote attendance; verifiable and consistent with the existing legal framework.

veracity.statement: The Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 made permanent the ability for elected members to meet remotely if the council's standing orders allow this.
veracity.explanation: Accurate statement of what the 2023 Act did regarding remote participation.

veracity.statement: As of 2023, around 56.5 percent of people with serious convictions are reconvicted within two years following release, and again another 35.8 percent are reimprisoned after two years following prison.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific recidivism figures consistent with the order of magnitude of NZ Corrections reconviction/reimprisonment data, though exact figures are hard to verify.

veracity.statement: Our own Corrections department estimates that around 60 percent of prisoners have literacy and numeracy skills below that of NCEA level 1 ... One in four prisoners are two steps below the adult learning progressions
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Corrections estimates of very low prisoner literacy/numeracy; broadly accurate figure attributed to the department.

veracity.statement: this time last year less than 20 percent of sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run facilities were attending rehabilitation programmes ... closer to 10 percent of the onsite prison population are actually enrolled in any rehabilitation programme.
veracity.explanation: Specific enrolment figures presented with caveats about remand prisoners; plausible and consistent with known low programme uptake, though precise figures are uncertain.

veracity.statement: one such programme is the special treatment unit for violent offenders—reported a 54 percent completion rate for the year 2022-23. Having a bit of compulsion will try to get that rate up.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific completion-rate statistic for a named programme and year; plausible Corrections figure though not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Police Commissioner Coster told the Justice Committee that the Western Australia example was working a treat and they are going to do their best to emulate it.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a strong endorsement ('working a treat') to the Police Commissioner about WA gang-patch laws; the effectiveness of that model is contested and the paraphrase likely overstates a more qualified evidence picture.

veracity.statement: We are not interested in reducing the prison population by 30 percent; that's another action point that's been delivered. We're getting rid of that ridiculous goal.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the coalition moved to scrap the previous prison-population reduction target; 'ridiculous' is editorial.

veracity.statement: Corrections funds rehabilitation and prison-educated programmes, as the member will know. And with 6.5 percent cuts looming over the service, I don't think it's unreasonable for us to say that we certainly have some concerns as to how these pathways will continue to be funded sufficiently
veracity.explanation: Refers to a 6.5 percent savings demand on Corrections; broadly consistent with the across-government savings targets of the period, though the precise figure as applied to Corrections is contestable.

veracity.statement: In the briefing to the incoming Minister in 2023, Corrections stated that they have faced some pressures retaining and recruiting staff ... These pressures have impacts on the provision of those services in prisons, including access to rehabilitation and education programmes
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes staffing-pressure concerns to the Corrections briefing to the incoming Minister, a documented source.

veracity.statement: In 2016, Corrections estimated that around 65 percent of the prison population had literacy levels that were below NCEA level 1. ... Corrections also found that 48 percent of Pākehā are below NCEA level 1 competency and 62 of Māori and Pasifika are below that level.
veracity.explanation: Cites Corrections' 2016 literacy estimates with ethnic breakdowns; consistent with published figures, attributed to source.

veracity.statement: resources are so constrained in Corrections that 12 out of the 18 prisons are not giving the legal entitlement of a visit a week.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim based on his own written parliamentary questions about statutory weekly prison visits; presented as sourced and plausible, though not independently verified here.

specificity.statement: Kenepuru Road, which, as you can imagine, goes up to Kenepuru Sound and out to the outer Sounds, is still impassable.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific road and its location to ground the argument.

specificity.statement: This is just a common-sense bill. It makes no sense to say, "You can participate, you just can't vote." The reason we get elected to democratic positions is to vote.
specificity.explanation: States a principle about the purpose of office without concrete mechanisms or figures.

specificity.statement: We know that when we have more participation, we get better decisions.
specificity.explanation: Broad assertion with no measure of how much participation improves which decisions.

specificity.statement: I can tell you that out of the 78 councils, four of the 10 biggest regional councils by land are based in the South Island, and for territorial authorities nine out of 10 of them.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete counts (78 councils, four of 10, nine of 10) to support the South Island point.

specificity.statement: if we go to clause 4 inserting new clause 25A(6) in Schedule 7 of the principal Act—it's just a short bill, but subclause 6 says that when a local authority is including things in its standing orders, it can also add any other requirements that it considers are "appropriate to maintain public confidence in the transparency and integrity of decision-making processes and the conduct of members".
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause, schedule and quoted statutory wording to rebut the 'anti-democratic' charge.

specificity.statement: I point you to Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023. It's already given them the ability to do this. All they have to do is change their standing orders.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise Act and the concrete mechanism (amending standing orders).

specificity.statement: I love supporting our local councils. Horowhenua Council, Kāpiti Coast Council—we've got great people in our community; I trust them to make the decisions that are best for them
specificity.explanation: Names specific councils but the 'trust them to decide' point remains general.

specificity.statement: Environment Canterbury is our largest regional council. It's over 44,000 kilometres squared. That's bigger than Denmark. It's four times the size of Jamaica. It's 20,000 times the size of Monaco
specificity.explanation: Concrete area figure and multiple scale comparisons to convey the council's size.

specificity.statement: Standing order 13.11, "Conditions for attending by audio or audio-visual link": "[The] Chairperson may give approval for a member to attend meetings by electronic link, either generally or for a specific meeting." ... So the Bay of Plenty Regional Council has this provision already in their standing orders.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact standing order number, council, and quoted text.

specificity.statement: The Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 made permanent the ability for elected members to meet remotely if the council's standing orders allow this.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and precisely describes the change it made.

specificity.statement: As of 2023, around 56.5 percent of people with serious convictions are reconvicted within two years following release, and again another 35.8 percent are reimprisoned after two years following prison.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages and a defined timeframe.

specificity.statement: Our own Corrections department estimates that around 60 percent of prisoners have literacy and numeracy skills below that of NCEA level 1 ... One in four prisoners are two steps below the adult learning progressions
specificity.explanation: Concrete proportions tied to a recognised benchmark (NCEA level 1, adult learning progressions).

specificity.statement: this time last year less than 20 percent of sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run facilities were attending rehabilitation programmes ... closer to 10 percent of the onsite prison population are actually enrolled in any rehabilitation programme.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies enrolment for both sentenced and total on-site populations.

specificity.statement: one such programme is the special treatment unit for violent offenders—reported a 54 percent completion rate for the year 2022-23. Having a bit of compulsion will try to get that rate up.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, the completion rate, and the year.

specificity.statement: Police Commissioner Coster told the Justice Committee that the Western Australia example was working a treat and they are going to do their best to emulate it.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Coster), the forum (Justice Committee), and the jurisdiction.

specificity.statement: the clanger, I suppose, is clause 5, which inserts new section 24A in the principal Act, to require that an offender who has not completed a programme, indicated in their management plan under section 51 of the Corrections Act 2004, must not be considered for parole.
specificity.explanation: Precisely identifies the clause, the new section, and the cross-referenced Corrections Act provision and its effect.

specificity.statement: In the briefing to the incoming Minister in 2023, Corrections stated that they have faced some pressures retaining and recruiting staff ... These pressures have impacts on the provision of those services in prisons, including access to rehabilitation and education programmes
specificity.explanation: Names the source document and the specific pressures (staffing, ratios, service provision).

specificity.statement: From New Zealand First's point of view, we're a party of common sense. It makes common sense that if you're in that situation, you would take the opportunity to try to improve your life.
specificity.explanation: Vague positioning statement with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: One of my portfolios for New Zealand First is horticulture. It was quite interesting hearing that that is a programme that has great uptake. Carpentry—something that this country has a deficit of, at the moment, in our building industry. So why don't we teach it?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete programmes (horticulture, carpentry) and links them to a labour-market gap, though without figures.

specificity.statement: in this, it has, at subsection 3, that if people actually do these courses and upskill themselves, there's an incentive—parole can actually be brought forward.
specificity.explanation: Points to the specific subsection and describes its concrete incentive mechanism (bringing parole forward).

specificity.statement: In 2016, Corrections estimated that around 65 percent of the prison population had literacy levels that were below NCEA level 1. ... Corrections also found that 48 percent of Pākehā are below NCEA level 1 competency and 62 of Māori and Pasifika are below that level.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages, year, source, and population breakdowns.

specificity.statement: resources are so constrained in Corrections that 12 out of the 18 prisons are not giving the legal entitlement of a visit a week.
specificity.explanation: Exact ratio (12 of 18) tied to a defined legal entitlement.

specificity.statement: when this comes to select committee, we've got to (a) be confident that this isn't just flag waving, that it really can make a concrete change operationally.
specificity.explanation: States a criterion for committee scrutiny but in general terms.

charisma.statement: So the other side of the House are doing what they always do. They say, "Well, let's have the same rules for everyone, because everyone should be a bit like me."
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing ('what they always do') that rallies his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: So I'm disappointed that the parties on the other side of the House have chosen to once again take a narrow view of democracy—an exclusive view of democracy—and not try to use the very tools we've got at our disposal to have a more inclusive, more effective, and more robust democratic framework.
charisma.explanation: Frames his side as inclusive and the other as 'exclusive' — rhetorically effective but appeals mostly to his own side.

charisma.statement: Oh, put the handbrake on; let's go back 50 years, because that's what this Government likes to do. They are so backward
charisma.explanation: Alienating, dismissive framing that shuts down rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: Once again, this Government—interested in Auckland, interested in building roads up north, interested in everything that happens in the North Island—is not thinking about the consequences for the people of the South Island.
charisma.explanation: Regional us-vs-them framing (North Island vs South Island) that divides rather than builds cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: if Ingrid Leary's worried about bizarre comments, she should take hers, wrap them in cellophane, and put them on a plinth; I haven't heard anything so bizarre in a long time.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing put-down that rallies his own side and alienates the other.

charisma.statement: we don't believe in this age-old, from-the-left, "Wellington knows best. We'll tell you how to do it. We've got all the answers." We heard it from them not just with this; we heard it from three waters
charisma.explanation: Partisan 'from-the-left' framing that appeals to his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I love supporting our local councils. Horowhenua Council, Kāpiti Coast Council—we've got great people in our community; I trust them to make the decisions that are best for them
charisma.explanation: Warm, locally-grounded appeal, but framed around his own communities and the localism position rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: this simply shows a Wellington-knows-best approach to how local government and how local communities should be operating ... Legislation like this is just another example of Labour's Wellington-knows-best approach to local government, which imposes rules on councils
charisma.explanation: Repeated partisan slogan ('Wellington-knows-best') that frames Labour negatively rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I do just want to take a moment to acknowledge that today was the funeral of our parliamentary colleague Efeso Collins ... my thoughts, and those of ACT, are with his family, friends, and especially his wife and daughter today.
charisma.explanation: Builds a shared, unifying moment in the House transcending party division.

charisma.statement: I am looking for all parties to support this bill to the first reading. It may not be the perfect solution, but I hope that we can have a constructive debate about it and have the select committee look at it.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites all parties in and concedes imperfection — consensus-seeking and humble.

charisma.statement: I accept there are likely to be some capacity and operational issues in what I'm putting forward, but I believe that the select committee is well placed to look at these issues
charisma.explanation: Openness to scrutiny and improvement invites cross-party engagement.

charisma.statement: I'm very proud that the National Party sent a significant delegation led by the Prime Minister ... Efeso was someone who had that unique ability, both as a person and as a politician, to walk so well in so many worlds.
charisma.explanation: Generous, bridge-building remembrance that honours a political opponent.

charisma.statement: if I look at what was launched at the weekend by Minister Mitchell: "Masher Mitchell" as they call him now—not "Crusher Collins", but "Masher Mitchell"—and Goldie, colloquially known as the Hon Paul Goldsmith, introduced legislation to ban gang patches. And hasn't that gone down so well
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing for his own benches; celebrates the Government's record rather than persuading the other side.

charisma.statement: rather than branding prisons as the "University of Crime" and focusing on reducing the prison population, regardless of how much crime is happening, this Government, this coalition Government, is confronting the real reasons behind crime and looking at rehabilitation as a key part of our success
charisma.explanation: Partisan contrast that appeals to his own side rather than building consensus on a bill that has cross-party support.

charisma.statement: Labour will be supporting this bill to the select committee. ... we're going to support this bill because it actually is congruent with Labour's work to support people into work and to support people into work through gaining those skills
charisma.explanation: Crosses party lines to back an ACT bill and frames it as common ground.

charisma.statement: I always look at it from the victim's point of view. ... if the victim could actually look and see that someone's making an effort to try to change their life, that actually makes you feel better.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic framing that could appeal broadly, though it rallies around sentiment rather than persuasion of opponents.

charisma.statement: This is a really nice bill for ACT. I'm quite impressed. So good on you. ... I'm being nice; this is a great bill. We like it. It's a good bill.
charisma.explanation: Genuine cross-party praise for an ACT bill; warm and consensus-building.

charisma.statement: we would not want to see a failure of resourcing stopping someone from receiving their treatment if they accept it, and we would not want anyone to be prevented from having a fair right of being reviewed by the Parole Board.
charisma.explanation: Frames concerns as collaborative ('happy to collaborate') rather than oppositional.

charisma.statement: what I would not want to see is someone who is ready to be put back into the community but hasn't done a rehabilitative programme—not because they don't want to but because the resources aren't there.
charisma.explanation: Constructive framing — supports sending the bill to committee while flagging a fixable problem, inviting cross-party refinement.

authenticity.statement: this is just bizarre that the Government, which is holding itself out to be wanting to get New Zealand moving, to look after rural communities, is suddenly saying, "Oh, except when it comes to local democracy."
authenticity.explanation: Targets a claimed inconsistency in the Government (pro-rural vs opposing rural access) — a low-authenticity signal about opponents, not about Leary herself.

authenticity.statement: Before I came to this House, I was an elected member on a community board ... They were running businesses from homes, they were juggling commitments with full-time jobs, some were parents with young kids, and some had mobility or accessibility issues and that made it difficult for them to attend every meeting.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds his support for the bill in his own prior service on a community board, aligning stated position with lived experience.

authenticity.statement: It has been longstanding ACT policy that we'd actually like to do something in the prisoner rehabilitation space. Now, I know that might seem counterintuitive to some people or their perception of ACT, but we do believe in actually giving people a fair go
authenticity.explanation: Presents the bill as consistent with longstanding ACT policy and acknowledges it cuts against ACT's tough-on-crime image — a candid alignment of position and action.

authenticity.statement: We're proud that when we were in Government, we made mental health treatment, family violence counselling services, and alcohol and drug treatment all much more readily available right across prisons in New Zealand.
authenticity.explanation: Her support for the rehabilitation bill is consistent with the record she claims of expanding prison treatment services.

divination.statement: there's a real risk here in not doing this, and that is that representation becomes a luxury for those who can afford it. People won't seek office. People won't be able to represent their communities, because they can't take the time off work, off family, off study
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced candidacy and narrower representation if the bill fails; directionally plausible but the magnitude and causation are uncertain and unquantified.

strength.statement: We are not interested in reducing the prison population by 30 percent; that's another action point that's been delivered. We're getting rid of that ridiculous goal.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivering an 'action point' (abandoning the target); a deliverable framed as done, though it is a reversal rather than a build.

strength.statement: We're proud that when we were in Government, we made mental health treatment, family violence counselling services, and alcohol and drug treatment all much more readily available right across prisons in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of expanded prison treatment services under the previous Government; plausible direction of travel but 'much more readily available right across' is a self-assessment without verification of scale.

forthrightness.statement: Labour will be supporting this bill to the select committee. ... we're going to support this bill because it actually is congruent with Labour's work to support people into work and to support people into work through gaining those skills
forthrightness.explanation: Directly states Labour's position (supporting the bill) and the reason, leaving no ambiguity.

civility.statement: It has, effectively, waited for the clock to run down at the expense of members of the public and the community to be able to have an adequate say on the provisions contained within this bill, and so that is rather unfortunate in terms of the use of urgency.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's process and use of urgency, but focused on the action rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I’ll put the Minister out of his misery and say that we are prepared, on this side of the House, to support this through to select committee—albeit a very, very short process indeed.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured and respectful toward the Minister while stating a position.

civility.statement: But I really do start to question the motives of the Government when they, effectively, remove the Clean Car Discount, when they effectively remove other rebates, when they are not seeming to incentivise the uptake.
civility.explanation: Questions the Government's motives, edging toward imputing bad faith rather than engaging only the policy.

civility.statement: I heard the Minister say in his speech that the previous Government had done no work on this, and I have to say that is patently untrue because, obviously, they’d all gone out and done some consultation on it, firstly.
civility.explanation: Calls the claim 'patently untrue' — harsh but directed at the statement, not the person.

civility.statement: I look forward to hearing more submissions at the select committee about this and finding ways that people in the public think we can improve the income stream to pay for our roads, because there is no free lunch, and particularly when it comes to roading, which has been underfunded by no small amount in the last six years—but I am glad to hear that Labour is supporting this bill.
civility.explanation: Mild partisan criticism of past underfunding, but constructive in tone.

civility.statement: this Government has campaigned to build 15 new roads and are pledging $500 million to fix potholes. The one pothole they cannot fix, however, is the $24 billion pothole in their budget.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical 'pothole' jab mocking the Government's fiscal position rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: By disincentivising electric vehicles while at the same time cutting public transport, this Government is fuelling climate change.
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing of the Government as 'fuelling climate change', though aimed at policy effect.

civility.statement: We heard the Minister who introduced this bill making wild claims that no work has been done on this in the previous Government and then in the next breath talking about the work the previous Government had been doing around road-user charges (RUCs) come 1 March 2024.
civility.explanation: 'Wild claims' is pointed, but the critique targets the contradiction rather than the person.

civility.statement: It is Labour’s position that that is not enough time to delve into some of the issues which need to immediately be addressed within this bill.
civility.explanation: States a procedural objection respectfully and substantively, even praising the committee chair elsewhere.

civility.statement: Show that we can achieve both those objectives: the objective of good quality legislative scrutiny, not scrutiny by exhaustion, and also looking after our members so that they can return to their important legislative tasks and their important constituency tasks with the appropriate degree of energy and attention.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful appeal focused on process and wellbeing rather than attack.

specificity.statement: It has, effectively, waited for the clock to run down at the expense of members of the public and the community to be able to have an adequate say on the provisions contained within this bill, and so that is rather unfortunate in terms of the use of urgency.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete concern (truncated public say due to urgency) but no figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Because I have one of my constituents who said not actually just—look, he has no problem, actually, with moving to a RUC approach for his vehicle, but he has some concerns about the weight variance and perhaps there should be a different rate when it comes to those that weigh less than one tonne. The threshold in this bill is setting it at 3½ tonnes.
specificity.explanation: Names specific weight thresholds (1 tonne, 3½ tonnes) and a concrete policy concern.

specificity.statement: if you were driving a pure electric vehicle on a return trip between Wellington and Auckland, how much would they pay in road-user charges under this proposal? It’s $98.80. How much would a plug-in hybrid Prius pay? ... That vehicle on the same exact trip would pay $94.78. ... a conventional fossil fuel Prius would pay, in fuel excise duty, $42.92 for the exact same trip.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures for a defined trip across three vehicle types.

specificity.statement: this was signalled by the previous Minister of Transport Simon Bridges, when he was in that role, that at 2 percent of the fleet this exemption would be removed, and that time has come.
specificity.explanation: Names the 2% trigger and the originating Minister.

specificity.statement: I took the opportunity to have a look at what the weight of EVs is, and even relatively small vehicles like a Fiat 500 electric vehicle are 1,400-plus kilograms. So that kind of vehicle would still be caught. You’ve got to have a very, very small vehicle not to be caught by the 1,000 kilograms.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete model and weight figures (1,400kg vs the 1,000kg threshold).

specificity.statement: Our policy would see the use of both accessible and efficient free public transport: free for tamariki, free for students, free for community service cardholders, and made free for everyone within five years.
specificity.explanation: Names specific beneficiary groups and a five-year timeframe.

specificity.statement: As I’ve been driving around the roads of Northland, observing the state of those roads and observing the number of electric vehicles and hybrids, along with all the other users on the road, it’s become apparent to me that all people using the road should pay their fair share.
specificity.explanation: General appeal to fairness with no figures, rates, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: We know that 44 percent of our energy-related emissions in New Zealand comes from the transport sector and 20 percent of all of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from transport, and the bulk of vehicle fleet, light-duty passenger vehicles are the vast majority. Heavy vehicles only make up 4 percent, and this piece of legislation is only looking at heavy vehicles and light vehicles. But we know that 4 percent of heavy vehicles make up 25 percent of transport’s total emissions.
specificity.explanation: Dense with precise statistics on emissions shares by sector and vehicle class.

specificity.statement: in 2009, the previous National Government exempted electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles from paying road-user charges to encourage their uptake. This exemption was always planned to end when EVs hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet, and, right now, New Zealand has reached that target.
specificity.explanation: Provides a date, the originating government, and the 2% threshold.

specificity.statement: It is Labour’s position that that is not enough time to delve into some of the issues which need to immediately be addressed within this bill.
specificity.explanation: Asserts insufficient time but defers the concrete reasons to later in the speech.

specificity.statement: The Labour Party is proposing that the Minister reconsider the motion and put a six-month report-back date in it. Then we will be happy to vote for it through to select committee and to participate in a completely bipartisan way.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete ask (six-month report-back date) as the condition.

specificity.statement: it’s absolutely appropriate that they do take calls of submissions from the public about the rate at which those particular vehicles pay—whether it be the $53 for the hybrids or the $73 per thousand kilometres for the electric vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Cites the concrete proposed rates ($53 for hybrids, $73 per 1,000km for EVs).

specificity.statement: This is not a simple one-line, one-clause bill. It actually has amendments to a primary Act—which is the Road User Charges Act 2012—and then it looks to change secondary legislation, and then my reading of this piece of legislation is that it inserts brand new schedules which would require scrutiny.
specificity.explanation: Names the primary Act and the specific structural changes (secondary legislation, new schedules).

specificity.statement: I move, That the motion be amended by adding the words “but not on Saturdays, despite any Standing Order to the contrary.”
specificity.explanation: A precise, concrete amendment with exact wording.

charisma.statement: I’ll put the Minister out of his misery and say that we are prepared, on this side of the House, to support this through to select committee—albeit a very, very short process indeed.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle to offer support, though paired with a caveat about process.

charisma.statement: I look forward to hearing more submissions at the select committee about this and finding ways that people in the public think we can improve the income stream to pay for our roads, because there is no free lunch, and particularly when it comes to roading, which has been underfunded by no small amount in the last six years—but I am glad to hear that Labour is supporting this bill.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes public submissions and acknowledges Labour's support, though includes a jab at the previous Government's record.

charisma.statement: we’ve heard from the Labour Party member Tangi Utikere as well that in fact they were working on exactly this thing.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges common ground with the Opposition on the policy direction.

charisma.statement: The Labour Party is proposing that the Minister reconsider the motion and put a six-month report-back date in it. Then we will be happy to vote for it through to select committee and to participate in a completely bipartisan way.
charisma.explanation: Offers a concrete path to cross-party cooperation and 'bipartisan' participation conditional on a fair process.

charisma.statement: It is fundamentally important to the design of our democracy to have a meaningful select committee process and that is even more important because of the fact that we do have a single House; we don’t have an Upper House which is taking the opportunity to scrutinise the legislation once it’s passed and that gives, in my view, more constitutional significance and importance to the select committee process.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared democratic values likely to resonate across the House rather than a partisan attack.

charisma.statement: Show that we can achieve both those objectives: the objective of good quality legislative scrutiny, not scrutiny by exhaustion, and also looking after our members so that they can return to their important legislative tasks and their important constituency tasks with the appropriate degree of energy and attention.
charisma.explanation: Frames the ask around shared goals (quality scrutiny and members' wellbeing) likely to appeal across parties.

rigor.statement: Because I have one of my constituents who said not actually just—look, he has no problem, actually, with moving to a RUC approach for his vehicle, but he has some concerns about the weight variance and perhaps there should be a different rate when it comes to those that weigh less than one tonne. The threshold in this bill is setting it at 3½ tonnes.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point grounded in a constituent example, but leans on a single anecdote.

rigor.statement: But I really do start to question the motives of the Government when they, effectively, remove the Clean Car Discount, when they effectively remove other rebates, when they are not seeming to incentivise the uptake.
rigor.explanation: Cites concrete policy removals to support the point, but jumps to motive rather than evidenced effect.

rigor.statement: Treasury had given advice that if you are to provide a financial incentive to increase the number of electric and low-emissions vehicles coming into the country that it would make more sense for that incentive to be at the point of purchase or registration of the vehicle. Which is why, later on, we developed the policy—alongside best practice international evidence about what works—of the Clean Car Discount and Clean Car Standard.
rigor.explanation: Cites Treasury advice and international evidence to justify a point-of-purchase incentive; conclusion follows from premises.

rigor.statement: if you were driving a pure electric vehicle on a return trip between Wellington and Auckland, how much would they pay in road-user charges under this proposal? It’s $98.80. How much would a plug-in hybrid Prius pay? ... That vehicle on the same exact trip would pay $94.78. ... a conventional fossil fuel Prius would pay, in fuel excise duty, $42.92 for the exact same trip.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based comparison sourced from the Minister's own written answers; conclusion (EVs charged more than double) follows.

rigor.statement: So the combination of this Government’s policies and actions—to get rid of the Clean Car Discount, to probably water down the Clean Car Standard, they’ve indicated they will do that, and to now overcharge electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid vehicles—will be that we will get fewer low-emissions and zero-emissions vehicles into the country—
rigor.explanation: Links a chain of named policy changes to a predicted outcome consistent with incentive theory.

rigor.statement: I took the opportunity to have a look at what the weight of EVs is, and even relatively small vehicles like a Fiat 500 electric vehicle are 1,400-plus kilograms. So that kind of vehicle would still be caught. You’ve got to have a very, very small vehicle not to be caught by the 1,000 kilograms.
rigor.explanation: Backs the point with specific researched data (vehicle weights) and reasons clearly to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: Julie Anne Genter asked why we are doing it at pace. Well, it’s always been around 31 March. That’s the time the exemption expires. It’s got to be done by then.
rigor.explanation: Gives a clear, factual reason (statutory expiry date) for the timing.

rigor.statement: this Government has campaigned to build 15 new roads and are pledging $500 million to fix potholes. The one pothole they cannot fix, however, is the $24 billion pothole in their budget.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a metaphor and rhetorical contrast rather than evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: By disincentivising electric vehicles while at the same time cutting public transport, this Government is fuelling climate change.
rigor.explanation: States a causal chain but sweeping and asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: As I’ve been driving around the roads of Northland, observing the state of those roads and observing the number of electric vehicles and hybrids, along with all the other users on the road, it’s become apparent to me that all people using the road should pay their fair share.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning rests on personal anecdotal observation ('driving around Northland') rather than data.

rigor.statement: We know that 44 percent of our energy-related emissions in New Zealand comes from the transport sector and 20 percent of all of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from transport, and the bulk of vehicle fleet, light-duty passenger vehicles are the vast majority. Heavy vehicles only make up 4 percent, and this piece of legislation is only looking at heavy vehicles and light vehicles. But we know that 4 percent of heavy vehicles make up 25 percent of transport’s total emissions.
rigor.explanation: Uses data to argue heavy vehicles are a disproportionate emissions source that the bill overlooks.

rigor.statement: it will have an ongoing effect on the emissions of our vehicle fleet as a whole when people hang on to their older vehicles that do not use EV technology.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal argument linking removed incentives to slower secondary-market fleet turnover.

rigor.statement: They meant that New Zealand had one of the highest rates of increase of uptake in electric vehicles in our fleet in the world, and when we take away those options for people, it means that we will see an ongoing effect over several decades in terms of what is available not only in the primary vehicle purchasing market but also for the secondary vehicle purchases, which is most New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Connects policy removal to long-run secondary-market effects with a coherent but unquantified chain.

rigor.statement: It is fundamentally important to the design of our democracy to have a meaningful select committee process and that is even more important because of the fact that we do have a single House; we don’t have an Upper House which is taking the opportunity to scrutinise the legislation once it’s passed and that gives, in my view, more constitutional significance and importance to the select committee process.
