specificity.explanation: Exact figure, timeframe, and a concrete historical benchmark.

specificity.statement: The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures and timeframe.

specificity.statement: I particularly stand by my commitment to give tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the upcoming Budget in May.
specificity.explanation: Names the deliverable (tax relief) and timeframe (May Budget), though without amounts.

specificity.statement: Look, the member can list a bunch of assertions that are completely incorrect but it doesn't reflect well on her. Because we are committed to funding the school lunch programme, we are committed to funding disability services, we are committed to sustaining good front-line services—our Budget will reflect that.
specificity.explanation: Names programmes and an efficiency mechanism (cutting consultants/back office) but no figures.

specificity.statement: We are wanting to grow this economy so we can drive more prosperity in this economy and lift wages and incomes for everybody.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: The deal's very simple in New Zealand: you have rights to a State house when you need it, but you also have responsibilities to look after it like it's your own house. That's the deal.
specificity.explanation: Articulates a clear principle but no operational detail.

specificity.statement: Completely appropriate, but what I'd say to you: the purpose of fast-track consenting is it's taking too long to get anything done in this country. We have built an obstruction economy. We are here to get things done. That's why we're taking fast track, introduced by David Parker, beefed it up, put it on steroids, and are actually going to get some outcomes for some people.
specificity.explanation: Some concrete framing ('introduced by David Parker', fast-track) but mostly slogans ('obstruction economy', 'on steroids').

specificity.statement: KO records hundreds of serious incidents every month, including alleged illegal activity, harassment, intimidation, threatening behaviour, and verbal abuse. Despite this, only three people were evicted last year for bad behaviour.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts and a named contrast to justify the change.

specificity.statement: To give you the exact numbers, in 2017, tenants' rent debt was $1 million; six years later, it has ballooned to $21 million. At the moment, there are more than 450 Kāinga Ora tenants who each owe more than $10,000.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, dates, and thresholds.

specificity.statement: We've made it clear that we expect Kāinga Ora to move families into vacant homes much more quickly than they are currently doing. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of homes vacant at any given time, and when the wait-list is over 25,000 people, that is not OK.
specificity.explanation: Concrete expectation and wait-list figure, though 'hundreds, if not thousands' is loose.

specificity.statement: Well, we've been very clear that the coalition agreement says that we will deliver 500 additional police officers in two years, and the Prime Minister is absolutely right in restating that.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure and timeframe from the coalition agreement.

specificity.statement: Police destroyed over 35,000 cannabis plants and prevented $128 million going into the pockets of gangs through Operation Emerald. Based on the drug harm index, the estimated social harm prevented by Operation Emerald last year was $127 million.
specificity.explanation: Precise operational figures and a named methodology (drug harm index).

specificity.statement: We are introducing five key targets that clearly spell out faster cancer treatment, improved immunisation for children, shorter stays in emergency departments, and shorter wait times for both first specialist assessments and planned care.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five named target areas, though the numeric thresholds aren't given here.

specificity.statement: In 2015, when targets were still at the forefront of Government policy, the immunisation rates for children stood at just over 93 percent. Today, that number is worrisome, at 83 percent. This is well behind countries like the UK, Australia, and Canada.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures, years, and international comparators.

specificity.statement: I am aware of the potential for gaming targets and will keep a close eye on this. There will be mechanisms to ensure that our health targets will remain robust. These include quality assurance processes to validate data, clinical engagement with discussions on emerging concerns, and the use of independent agencies such as the Health Quality and Safety Commission to support reviews, as needed.
specificity.explanation: Names mechanisms and an institution, if not their detailed operation.

specificity.statement: The fund for the equipment and modification of services has been increased by 10 percent. So the misleading statements from the Opposition about funding cuts is completely incorrect. The issue is the policy settings that were put in place by the previous Government that has seen a blowout in the funds available.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (10% increase to one fund), though not for the broader funding picture queried.

specificity.statement: Pharmac is changing its processes so that it can assess a funding application at the same time Medsafe is assessing an application for regulatory approval of the same product. This means that medicines will be able to be considered sooner for funding in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (parallel Pharmac/Medsafe assessment) and its intended effect.

specificity.statement: I'm very proud of the way that the three parties in this coalition Government are working to actually get things done for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Vague, content-free affirmation.

strength.statement: Our Government believes in rights and responsibilities, so if you contribute to a culture of intimidation and abuse, it's time to change your behaviour, and if you don't, you may not keep your taxpayer-funded State house.
strength.explanation: Backed by a same-day directive to Kāinga Ora, but follow-through and actual evictions remain to be delivered.

strength.statement: We've made it clear that we expect Kāinga Ora to move families into vacant homes much more quickly than they are currently doing. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of homes vacant at any given time, and when the wait-list is over 25,000 people, that is not OK.
strength.explanation: States a delivered directive (letter of expectation) but the move-in outcomes are yet to be demonstrated.

strength.statement: Well, we've been very clear that the coalition agreement says that we will deliver 500 additional police officers in two years, and the Prime Minister is absolutely right in restating that.
strength.explanation: Reaffirms a target not yet delivered; the question itself flags doubt about achievability.

strength.statement: We are introducing five key targets that clearly spell out faster cancer treatment, improved immunisation for children, shorter stays in emergency departments, and shorter wait times for both first specialist assessments and planned care.
strength.explanation: Announces a policy framework; delivery against the targets is still to come.

strength.statement: Pharmac is changing its processes so that it can assess a funding application at the same time Medsafe is assessing an application for regulatory approval of the same product. This means that medicines will be able to be considered sooner for funding in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: A specific delivered process change, though its impact on actual access is yet to materialise.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can tell you I'm not going to take any lectures from that member about economic management. That was a Government that was characterised by spending more, taxing more, borrowing more, and we heard from the new finance spokesperson they want to continue to do more of it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a yes/no about a $5.6bn shortfall and 'huge gap' in costings; answers neither, pivots to attacking the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we've inherited a struggling economy from the previous Government's economic mismanagement, and we've got some big fiscal challenges ahead of us, but we're the Government that's going to fix it. We'll do it; that's what we always do, and we're going to clean up after your last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Still does not confirm or deny the specific $5.6bn shortfall question; deflects to general blame and aspiration.

forthrightness.statement: What I can reassure the member about is that this is a Government that's going to give tax relief to working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers who actually deserve a tax break after 14 years of not getting one, particularly from that previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which of two costings (IRD's $155m vs the Government's $716m gambling figure) is correct; answers a different question about tax relief.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can tell the member the numbers that we're not going to be doing. We're not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We're not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We're not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether benefit-indexation savings would fall $1.3bn short; refuses the figure and recites attack lines instead.

forthrightness.statement: I think what's great is we care about renters, a group that the Labour Party used to care about a lot. Actually, we're increasing the supply of rental properties, we're lowering costs that have just been passed through to renters—because under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether landlord tax-cut costings blew out by $800m; does not address the figure and pivots to renters.

forthrightness.statement: What we will be doing is increasing the supply of rental property and putting downward pressure on rent, as he has received in formal advice before in Government. That's why his policies didn't work.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the simple question whether tenants will get $800m of rent reductions; never answers, asserts general 'downward pressure'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, look, I can tell you it is ironic that you are trying to lecture me on economics after six years of being in Government, of actually causing huge damage to our books, having had economic mismanagement and vandalism on a scale we've never seen before, an 84 percent increase in Government spending. You drove up domestic inflation, you drove up interest rates, the last three quarters of the last year's economic growth went down, and you've got rising unemployment.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address whether his own 'rock solid numbers' claim holds given the cited blowouts; turns to attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: I agree that that definition of "prudent" is met. What I question is whether New Zealanders can see $123 billion worth of value generated by that Government for the $123 billion worth of debt that they have saddled this and future generations with.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes the Treasury 'prudent' point asked about, then reframes — a substantive if partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: I'll give the member a little instruction on coalition Government, because the Government's tax and fiscal plans reflect coalition negotiations which resulted in a number of amendments to the proposals that National and other parties campaigned on.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile breaking the 'no new taxes' line (app tax, petrol, vehicle fees); deflects to a general 'coalition negotiations' explanation rather than addressing each.

forthrightness.statement: Look, the member can list a bunch of assertions that are completely incorrect but it doesn't reflect well on her. Because we are committed to funding the school lunch programme, we are committed to funding disability services, we are committed to sustaining good front-line services—our Budget will reflect that.
forthrightness.explanation: Rebuts the premise and lists commitments, but defers proof to the future Budget rather than answering the specific cuts alleged.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely, including those State tenants who have been abused and victimised by their neighbours. Take Cheyne Smith, who's been a Kāinga Ora (KO) tenant since 2015 and described the actions of some of his neighbouring KO tenants. He said, "I've been beaten, the house has been robbed, egged, bottled. Visitors were assaulted, vehicles got stolen. It was a nightmare."
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms he stands by the 'safety net' statement quoted, then reframes via an anecdote — answers but redirects emphasis.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we don't want to actually see KO tenants being evicted from KO housing, but, actually, the parents are adults and they have a choice to make about whether they want to meet their obligations and their responsibilities. That is the first port of call.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee no children made homeless; does not give a guarantee, shifts responsibility to parents.

forthrightness.statement: We are wanting to grow this economy so we can drive more prosperity in this economy and lift wages and incomes for everybody.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he cares about evidence of rising homelessness/poverty or is governing 'on vibes'; replies with an unrelated economic-growth platitude.

forthrightness.statement: Completely appropriate, but what I'd say to you: the purpose of fast-track consenting is it's taking too long to get anything done in this country. We have built an obstruction economy. We are here to get things done. That's why we're taking fast track, introduced by David Parker, beefed it up, put it on steroids, and are actually going to get some outcomes for some people.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about constitutional advice on adding projects after select committee; asserts 'completely appropriate' without citing any advice, then pivots to general justification.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely rubbish. I mean, the bottom line here is that we have an obstruction economy. We've actually taken an awful long time to consent something, and it's costing a huge amount of money. We want to actually deliver on our climate goals, something that I think the Green Party would want to identify and align with us around, but you can't take eight years to consent a wind farm and two years to build it.
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the 'pork barrelling' quote outright, then makes a substantive efficiency argument — partial engagement.

forthrightness.statement: I respect the role of the president of the Police Association and he respects our role. The police and the Police Association are engaged in good-faith negotiations, and they carry on.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to Cahill's 'slap in the face' criticism; declines to engage the substance, citing live negotiations.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we've been very clear that the coalition agreement says that we will deliver 500 additional police officers in two years, and the Prime Minister is absolutely right in restating that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly reconciles the two cited statements, affirming the 500-in-two-years commitment.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the offer made by the previous Government was rejected by the police—[Interruption]—that's right, and they failed to really act on that quickly. Whereas the incoming Government—we take it seriously, we've acted quickly, and we negotiate in good faith.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Peters' steer about last year's pay, but uses it largely to contrast with the previous Government rather than detail the timeline.

forthrightness.statement: Comments like that show a lack of respect or understanding for the outstanding job our police officers do, in often difficult situations and circumstances, keeping our community safe and slowing down and disrupting the flow of harmful drugs into our communities.
forthrightness.explanation: Patsy question, but he does reject the characterisation while not engaging the substance of 'ineffective'.

forthrightness.statement: I am aware of the potential for gaming targets and will keep a close eye on this. There will be mechanisms to ensure that our health targets will remain robust. These include quality assurance processes to validate data, clinical engagement with discussions on emerging concerns, and the use of independent agencies such as the Health Quality and Safety Commission to support reviews, as needed.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly acknowledges the risk asked about (gaming) and lists concrete safeguards.

forthrightness.statement: The biodiversity collaborative stakeholder group did not actually reach a consensus in the end. There was a minority statement, by a number of groups, so there was no consensus on an outcome. The decision was not taking into account what the biodiversity stakeholder group—actually, they didn't land on a decision.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the premise (what the group got wrong) by contesting that they reached an agreed position at all.

forthrightness.statement: I do not have those numbers on hand at the moment. I can come back to it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the proportion of native species threatened/at risk; doesn't answer but honestly concedes he lacks the figure and offers to follow up.

forthrightness.statement: No consultation has been undertaken in this. There will be consultation going into what will be the future use of SNAs. Basically, this was signalled in our coalition agreement in the 100-day plan.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and plainly answers whether Māori landowners were consulted: 'No consultation has been undertaken.'

forthrightness.statement: How we will encourage this is by encouraging the behaviour that has already been happening. As I have said to this House a number of times, in my time in farming, I have seen a complete mind shift from farmers, who are doing more and more every day on protecting biodiversity on their farm, encouraging more of it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how biodiversity on private land will be protected once council requirements are removed; answers with 'encouraging existing behaviour' rather than a protective mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, the increase in the use of these services has caused a funding blowout, and it is somewhat disingenuous for the member of that party, who put the policies in place that set up the situation that Whaikaha is now facing in terms of flexibility of purchasing and ring-fencing the funding, taking it out of a demand-funding situation.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why there was no consultation on the changes; doesn't address consultation, redirects blame to the previous Government's settings.

forthrightness.statement: The fund for the equipment and modification of services has been increased by 10 percent. So the misleading statements from the Opposition about funding cuts is completely incorrect. The issue is the policy settings that were put in place by the previous Government that has seen a blowout in the funds available.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers by citing a 10% increase, but sidesteps the commitment-to-increase-support question by reframing as a settings problem.

forthrightness.statement: So the priority has been that the funding must be spent on the person with the disability, when, in the past, the previous Government allowed such flexibility for carers to be able to spend on such things for themselves as pedicures, as massages, as overseas travel.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a carer's specific concern with a general principle rather than the individual's situation.

forthrightness.statement: I'm very proud of the way that the three parties in this coalition Government are working to actually get things done for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Seymour's question asks him to confirm whose costing estimate the deductibility impact is closer to; answers with a generic pride-in-coalition line, not the figure.

rigor.statement: Well, I can tell you I'm not going to take any lectures from that member about economic management. That was a Government that was characterised by spending more, taxing more, borrowing more, and we heard from the new finance spokesperson they want to continue to do more of it.
rigor.explanation: Slogan-style characterisation ('spending more, taxing more') offered without evidence and not responsive to the claim.

rigor.statement: Well, I can tell the member the numbers that we're not going to be doing. We're not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We're not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We're not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it.
rigor.explanation: Lists 'what we're not doing' as a rhetorical deflection rather than engaging the costing premise.

rigor.statement: Is the IRD correct that his Government's proposed tax on offshore online casino operators will raise $155 million over four years, or are the "rock-solid" costings that he and Nicola Willis produced correct, suggesting the change will bring $716 million of revenue over the same period—a difference of over $500 million?
rigor.explanation: Sets up a clear evidence-based contradiction between official advice and the Government's costings.

rigor.statement: The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.
rigor.explanation: Cites Treasury on a ~2% structural deficit, but folds COVID-driven debt into a blame narrative without fully isolating causes.

rigor.statement: so Governments should always be thinking about the next shock that's around the corner, not just maxing out the credit card today.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable prudence argument (build fiscal headroom before shocks), but leans on the 'credit card' analogy rather than data.

rigor.statement: I agree that that definition of "prudent" is met. What I question is whether New Zealanders can see $123 billion worth of value generated by that Government for the $123 billion worth of debt that they have saddled this and future generations with.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical value-for-money framing; asserts no value without itemised evidence.

rigor.statement: Absolutely, including those State tenants who have been abused and victimised by their neighbours. Take Cheyne Smith, who's been a Kāinga Ora (KO) tenant since 2015 and described the actions of some of his neighbouring KO tenants. He said, "I've been beaten, the house has been robbed, egged, bottled. Visitors were assaulted, vehicles got stolen. It was a nightmare."
rigor.explanation: Leads with a single vivid anecdote to justify policy rather than systemic evidence.

rigor.statement: Absolutely rubbish. I mean, the bottom line here is that we have an obstruction economy. We've actually taken an awful long time to consent something, and it's costing a huge amount of money. We want to actually deliver on our climate goals, something that I think the Green Party would want to identify and align with us around, but you can't take eight years to consent a wind farm and two years to build it.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete consenting-timeline example, though the 'eight years to consent a wind farm' figure is illustrative rather than sourced.

rigor.statement: KO records hundreds of serious incidents every month, including alleged illegal activity, harassment, intimidation, threatening behaviour, and verbal abuse. Despite this, only three people were evicted last year for bad behaviour.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable incentive argument (no consequences → no behaviour change) grounded in the eviction data.

rigor.statement: To name just one example, we saw the elderly Whangārei couple subject to death threats from the patched Black Power Kāinga Ora tenants next door. They allegedly threatened to slit the 82-year-old man's throat and watch him bleed out.
rigor.explanation: Vivid individual anecdotes used to carry the policy argument; emotionally charged rather than systemic evidence.

rigor.statement: Comments like that show a lack of respect or understanding for the outstanding job our police officers do, in often difficult situations and circumstances, keeping our community safe and slowing down and disrupting the flow of harmful drugs into our communities.
rigor.explanation: Responds to the 'ineffective' characterisation with an appeal to respect for police rather than addressing the effectiveness critique on its merits.

rigor.statement: I am aware of the potential for gaming targets and will keep a close eye on this. There will be mechanisms to ensure that our health targets will remain robust. These include quality assurance processes to validate data, clinical engagement with discussions on emerging concerns, and the use of independent agencies such as the Health Quality and Safety Commission to support reviews, as needed.
rigor.explanation: Anticipates a known failure mode and names specific mitigations and an independent body.

rigor.statement: The biodiversity collaborative stakeholder group did not actually reach a consensus in the end. There was a minority statement, by a number of groups, so there was no consensus on an outcome. The decision was not taking into account what the biodiversity stakeholder group—actually, they didn't land on a decision.
rigor.explanation: Makes a factual point about lack of consensus, though somewhat muddled in delivery.

rigor.statement: Because the current use of SNAs are an unjustified intrusion on private property rights, and they are a barrier to the great work that landowners have already been doing on their farms.
rigor.explanation: Asserts SNAs are 'unjustified' and a 'barrier' as conclusions without supporting evidence; value-laden premise.

rigor.statement: I think rural New Zealand are sick and tired of being portrayed as people who don't care about their land. Our land is so important to us—it is vital. Up and down this country, I see more and more farmers engaging in planting activities on their farms, creating wetlands, planting off streams, riparian planting—this is all happening.
rigor.explanation: Offers observational/anecdotal evidence ('I see more and more farmers') of voluntary conservation rather than data.

rigor.statement: How we will encourage this is by encouraging the behaviour that has already been happening. As I have said to this House a number of times, in my time in farming, I have seen a complete mind shift from farmers, who are doing more and more every day on protecting biodiversity on their farm, encouraging more of it.
rigor.explanation: Relies on personal anecdote of a 'mind shift' rather than evidence that voluntary action will substitute for regulation.

rigor.statement: So the priority has been that the funding must be spent on the person with the disability, when, in the past, the previous Government allowed such flexibility for carers to be able to spend on such things for themselves as pedicures, as massages, as overseas travel.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the restriction with a few emotive 'pedicures, massages, overseas travel' examples that characterise the prior flexibility unflatteringly rather than showing scale.

veracity.statement: What I can reassure the member about is that this is a Government that's going to give tax relief to working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers who actually deserve a tax break after 14 years of not getting one, particularly from that previous Government.
veracity.explanation: '14 years of not getting one' is misleading — there were tax threshold/relief changes within that period.

veracity.statement: Well, I can tell the member the numbers that we're not going to be doing. We're not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We're not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We're not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it.
veracity.explanation: '84 percent' spending and the '$5 billion to $100 billion' debt framing are cherry-picked/loose nominal figures presented as damning; partly grounded but misleading.

veracity.statement: I think what's great is we care about renters, a group that the Labour Party used to care about a lot. Actually, we're increasing the supply of rental properties, we're lowering costs that have just been passed through to renters—because under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week.
veracity.explanation: 'Average rents went up $170 a week' is a cumulative figure over the full previous term presented as if a single jump — directionally true but selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Well, look, I can tell you it is ironic that you are trying to lecture me on economics after six years of being in Government, of actually causing huge damage to our books, having had economic mismanagement and vandalism on a scale we've never seen before, an 84 percent increase in Government spending. You drove up domestic inflation, you drove up interest rates, the last three quarters of the last year's economic growth went down, and you've got rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Mix of supportable claims (negative growth quarters, rising unemployment) and loose/inflated ones ('84 percent', 'drove up interest rates').

veracity.statement: Net core Crown debt, according to the latest forecasts, is now 44 percent of GDP—44 percent—a considerable increase in only five years. To put it in perspective, members, 44 percent of GDP is the highest that net debt has been as a proportion of the overall economy in 30 years, comparable only with the period from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s.
veracity.explanation: Net core Crown debt around 43–44% of GDP and the 30-year historical comparison are broadly accurate per forecasts.

veracity.statement: The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.
veracity.explanation: Figures are in line with official debt trajectory; accurate though attribution of cause is partisan.

veracity.statement: KO records hundreds of serious incidents every month, including alleged illegal activity, harassment, intimidation, threatening behaviour, and verbal abuse. Despite this, only three people were evicted last year for bad behaviour.
veracity.explanation: The 'only three evictions' figure was widely cited from KO data; broadly accurate as the basis for the policy.

veracity.statement: To give you the exact numbers, in 2017, tenants' rent debt was $1 million; six years later, it has ballooned to $21 million. At the moment, there are more than 450 Kāinga Ora tenants who each owe more than $10,000.
veracity.explanation: Cited as official KO arrears data; presented accurately though framed for effect.

veracity.statement: Police destroyed over 35,000 cannabis plants and prevented $128 million going into the pockets of gangs through Operation Emerald. Based on the drug harm index, the estimated social harm prevented by Operation Emerald last year was $127 million.
veracity.explanation: Plant counts are concrete, but the dollar 'harm prevented' figures rest on modelled assumptions presented as fact.

veracity.statement: In 2015, when targets were still at the forefront of Government policy, the immunisation rates for children stood at just over 93 percent. Today, that number is worrisome, at 83 percent. This is well behind countries like the UK, Australia, and Canada.
veracity.explanation: Childhood immunisation rates did fall to around the low-80s%; the 93%→83% decline is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: No consultation has been undertaken in this. There will be consultation going into what will be the future use of SNAs. Basically, this was signalled in our coalition agreement in the 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Candid factual statement consistent with the policy process described.

veracity.statement: The fund for the equipment and modification of services has been increased by 10 percent. So the misleading statements from the Opposition about funding cuts is completely incorrect. The issue is the policy settings that were put in place by the previous Government that has seen a blowout in the funds available.
veracity.explanation: The 10% EMS increase may be accurate, but using it to call all 'funding cuts' claims 'completely incorrect' overstates, given the restrictions on flexible funding.

authenticity.statement: I think what's great is we care about renters, a group that the Labour Party used to care about a lot. Actually, we're increasing the supply of rental properties, we're lowering costs that have just been passed through to renters—because under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to be 'on the side of renters' while the question is about cuts benefiting landlords; consistency contestable from the text.

authenticity.statement: I particularly stand by my commitment to give tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the upcoming Budget in May.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a campaign commitment she is positioned to deliver; consistency pending the Budget.

authenticity.statement: I'll give the member a little instruction on coalition Government, because the Government's tax and fiscal plans reflect coalition negotiations which resulted in a number of amendments to the proposals that National and other parties campaigned on.
authenticity.explanation: Effectively acknowledges campaign positions were changed, attributing reversals to coalition deals rather than owning the broken promise.

divination.statement: What we will be doing is increasing the supply of rental property and putting downward pressure on rent, as he has received in formal advice before in Government. That's why his policies didn't work.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased supply and 'downward pressure on rent' as a result of the policy; plausible direction but unquantified and contested.

specificity.statement: Doing both the regulatory assessment to see if it’s safe at Medsafe and the funding assessment to see if it is a good use of taxpayer funds at Pharmac at the same time is common sense. It’s a change that costs nothing but it will help Kiwis in need by shaving up to nine months off the approval process.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (parallel Medsafe/Pharmac assessment) and a quantified benefit (up to nine months), though no firm dates.

specificity.statement: Yes. In fact, I have been looking at Budget documents that show that Pharmac’s funding over the next three years was left by the previous Government as reducing by several hundred million dollars each year for the next four years. In total, to maintain the level of pharmaceutical funding that New Zealanders are used to, the Government would have to find nearly $2 billion of extra funding over four years, and that is something that this Government is now working very hard to do in challenging economic conditions.
specificity.explanation: Cites figures (several hundred million per year, nearly $2 billion over four years) and a source (Budget documents).

specificity.statement: The coalition Government is based in part on an ACT-National coalition agreement which contains a commitment to updating the rules for Medsafe to speed up the processing of new medicines for regulatory approval to within 30 days if two recognised overseas regulators have already approved it.
specificity.explanation: Precise: a 30-day target conditional on two recognised overseas regulators' prior approval.

specificity.statement: On 1 January 2025, the income inclusion rule and under-taxed profits rule will be enacted, and on 1 January 2026, the domestic income inclusion rule will be enacted.
specificity.explanation: Names specific rules and exact commencement dates.

specificity.statement: Inland Revenue estimates that there are at least 400,000 trusts. In 2022, approximately 76,000 trusts paid taxes at the trustee tax rate. To help mitigate the risk of over-taxation, we are proposing a $10,000 trustee income de minimis. This will mean that a further 27,000 trusts will not be affected by the 39c tax rate. Based on this, only 12 percent of all trusts would be affected by the 39c tax rate.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures: 400,000 trusts, 76,000, $10,000 de minimis, 27,000 exempted, 12 percent affected.

specificity.statement: So a person could be better off by $600 if they kept the income below $10,000, or if you set up a number of trusts, you could maybe spread all the income across a number of trusts to try to get around that top tax rate... But the compliance costs of running a trust, of getting it set up, and of doing all the processing for it is probably more than the $600 is worth.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers and a worked example (10 trusts of $10,000 vs one of $100,000).

specificity.statement: So what we’ve said is that in actual fact, what should happen is that for that sum of money, the appropriate tax rate should be determined by looking at the average tax rate over the previous four years and applying that rate.
specificity.explanation: States the precise mechanism (four-year average tax rate) for backdated lump sums.

specificity.statement: we have a tax system in this country that sees the top 311 families pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise group (top 311 families) and a quantified comparison.

specificity.statement: It is not the version of the bill which will come into effect after the Government uses its three-headed taniwha majority to push through the changes for repealing back to the two-year brightline test and those interest deductibility changes, as well as removing depreciation deductions.
specificity.explanation: Specifically names the three amendments (two-year brightline, interest deductibility, depreciation deductions).

specificity.statement: While the average person in Aotearoa is paying 20.2 percent in tax, the wealthy are only paying 9.4 percent, and they are the ones that usually benefit from these trusts.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise comparative percentages.

specificity.statement: Again, what it does is it gives support to the 2 percent who control 50 percent of this country’s wealth and continue to get the tax breaks that this Government is so openly supportive of
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete (if inaccurate) figures rather than vague language.

specificity.statement: the proposed changes in the lodged Amendment Paper—which we’re not discussing right now—will reinstate interest deductibility, reduce the brightline test from 10 years to two years, and remove depreciation deductions for commercial and industrial buildings.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise changes and the bracket shift (10 years to two).

specificity.statement: A fair taxing tax system is— ... fairness is a core principle of our society; that is agreed to by members of the public.
specificity.explanation: Vague value statement with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: rather than a person getting a lump-sum payment and they’re getting fully taxed on the year that they received that backdated lump-sum payment, this bill changes it to look over the four previous tax years. We believe that this was bringing greater fairness into the system, because a lot of these ACC clients and MSD clients, through no fault of their own, were absolutely eligible for these backdated payments
specificity.explanation: States the concrete change (four-year look-back) for ACC/MSD backdated lump sums.

specificity.statement: the Finance and Expenditure Committee has accepted the Government’s advice that a $10,000 trustee income de... minimis be introduced. So that has been done, and this is excellent as it will stop people trying to set up multiple trusts and avoid taxation.
specificity.explanation: Names the $10,000 de minimis and its anti-avoidance purpose.

specificity.statement: there were 67 interested groups of written submissions and individuals that we received and considered. As the select committee, we also heard oral evidence from 25 submitters.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts of written submissions (67) and oral submitters (25).

specificity.statement: I am honoured to be part of a team that was able to see across all the differences and rise above, stand back, and finally, agree on something, so that we can highlight New Zealand’s dedication to forming tax policies that are modern, that are efficient, and that are effective.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational language ('modern, efficient, effective') with little concrete detail.

divination.statement: Doing both the regulatory assessment to see if it’s safe at Medsafe and the funding assessment to see if it is a good use of taxpayer funds at Pharmac at the same time is common sense. It’s a change that costs nothing but it will help Kiwis in need by shaving up to nine months off the approval process.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the process will be shortened by 'up to nine months' — plausible and bounded, but unverified outcome.

divination.statement: we recently had Treasury officials in, who I questioned about the productivity implications of our tax system, and they made it abundantly clear that were we to introduce the capital gains tax, we would not only generate the revenue necessary to invest in the infrastructure that all New Zealanders deserve but also that we would have a fundamentally more productive economy.
divination.explanation: Predicts a CGT would yield a more productive economy; directionally arguable but the magnitude and certainty are uncertain.

divination.statement: we will not be letting this Government get away with increasing inequality, which, they know full well and their advice bears out, will occur as a result of them progressing this policy agenda.
divination.explanation: Predicts the policy agenda will increase inequality; directionally supported by distributional arguments but unquantified.

divination.statement: the Finance and Expenditure Committee has accepted the Government’s advice that a $10,000 trustee income de... minimis be introduced. So that has been done, and this is excellent as it will stop people trying to set up multiple trusts and avoid taxation.
divination.explanation: Predicts the de minimis 'will stop people' setting up multiple trusts; plausible but the threshold reduces rather than fully stops the incentive.

rigor.statement: Doing both the regulatory assessment to see if it’s safe at Medsafe and the funding assessment to see if it is a good use of taxpayer funds at Pharmac at the same time is common sense. It’s a change that costs nothing but it will help Kiwis in need by shaving up to nine months off the approval process.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable cost/benefit argument, but leans partly on the 'common sense' appeal rather than presented evidence.

rigor.statement: Inland Revenue estimates that there are at least 400,000 trusts. In 2022, approximately 76,000 trusts paid taxes at the trustee tax rate. To help mitigate the risk of over-taxation, we are proposing a $10,000 trustee income de minimis. This will mean that a further 27,000 trusts will not be affected by the 39c tax rate. Based on this, only 12 percent of all trusts would be affected by the 39c tax rate.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion (12 percent affected) follows logically from the cited counts and the de minimis threshold.

rigor.statement: As I’ve said many times before, we do not have a broad based - low rate tax system. There is a significant gap in our tax system where capital income is not treated as income for income tax purposes.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific structural feature (untaxed capital income) to support the claim; argument is logically connected.

rigor.statement: So a person could be better off by $600 if they kept the income below $10,000, or if you set up a number of trusts, you could maybe spread all the income across a number of trusts to try to get around that top tax rate... But the compliance costs of running a trust, of getting it set up, and of doing all the processing for it is probably more than the $600 is worth.
rigor.explanation: Quantifies the avoidance incentive ($600) and weighs it against compliance costs to justify the threshold; conclusion follows from premises.

rigor.statement: So what we’ve said is that in actual fact, what should happen is that for that sum of money, the appropriate tax rate should be determined by looking at the average tax rate over the previous four years and applying that rate.
rigor.explanation: Explains the fairness logic of averaging over four years to avoid lump-sum bracket distortion; reasoned and balanced.

rigor.statement: we have a tax system in this country that sees the top 311 families pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in cited IRD reporting rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The tax system has only been there to service the wealthy and actually put a pinch on the working class and the poorer whānau.
rigor.explanation: Emotive generalisation with no evidence supplied for the absolute claim.

rigor.statement: Our tax system allows the wealthy to illegally avoid tax through housing, investment funds, property, and through trusts
rigor.explanation: Rests on the avoidance/evasion conflation, undermining the logical basis of the claim.

rigor.statement: this change is, essentially, retrospective, as investors who may have previously been willing to wait five years or 10 years to sell their property will now be able to sell much sooner and pay no additional tax
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument about the effect of shortening the brightline window, though 'retrospective' is a loose characterisation of a prospective rule change.

rigor.statement: A fair taxing tax system is— ... fairness is a core principle of our society; that is agreed to by members of the public.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to popularity ('agreed to by members of the public') rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: this omnibus bill with the Government amendments will certainly restore a lot of fairness to those mum and dad landlords that dominate our landscape. In fact, about 80 percent of landlords in New Zealand own one property—they are mum and dad landlords.
rigor.explanation: Uses a relevant statistic, but 'restore a lot of fairness' is an evaluative leap presented as following from it.

rigor.statement: rather than a person getting a lump-sum payment and they’re getting fully taxed on the year that they received that backdated lump-sum payment, this bill changes it to look over the four previous tax years. We believe that this was bringing greater fairness into the system, because a lot of these ACC clients and MSD clients, through no fault of their own, were absolutely eligible for these backdated payments
rigor.explanation: Explains the mechanism and the fairness rationale, with the conclusion following from the over-taxation problem described.

rigor.statement: the Finance and Expenditure Committee has accepted the Government’s advice that a $10,000 trustee income de... minimis be introduced. So that has been done, and this is excellent as it will stop people trying to set up multiple trusts and avoid taxation.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable link between threshold and avoidance behaviour, but 'will stop' overstates a partial deterrent.

rigor.statement: From the many, many doors that I have knocked on and phone calls that I have made, the fact is that most of the households here are mums and dads who really just wanted the two years back, because they need the flexibility
rigor.explanation: Generalises a policy conclusion from personal canvassing — an appeal to anecdote rather than representative evidence.

veracity.statement: It will also bring us into line with countries such as Australia and Canada, which do it and have been doing it exactly the way that we now will.
veracity.explanation: Comparative factual claim about Australia and Canada running concurrent assessment; broadly accurate, though 'exactly the way' overstates the precision of the parallel.

veracity.statement: Yes. In fact, I have been looking at Budget documents that show that Pharmac’s funding over the next three years was left by the previous Government as reducing by several hundred million dollars each year for the next four years. In total, to maintain the level of pharmaceutical funding that New Zealanders are used to, the Government would have to find nearly $2 billion of extra funding over four years, and that is something that this Government is now working very hard to do in challenging economic conditions.
veracity.explanation: Framing of funding being 'left' reducing by the previous Government is a contested political characterisation of baseline/forecast figures rather than a clean factual cut.

veracity.statement: On 1 January 2025, the income inclusion rule and under-taxed profits rule will be enacted, and on 1 January 2026, the domestic income inclusion rule will be enacted.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's enacted commencement dates for the GloBE rules.

veracity.statement: Inland Revenue estimates that there are at least 400,000 trusts. In 2022, approximately 76,000 trusts paid taxes at the trustee tax rate. To help mitigate the risk of over-taxation, we are proposing a $10,000 trustee income de minimis. This will mean that a further 27,000 trusts will not be affected by the 39c tax rate. Based on this, only 12 percent of all trusts would be affected by the 39c tax rate.
veracity.explanation: Cites IRD estimates; figures are consistent with the committee's reported analysis.

veracity.statement: As I’ve said many times before, we do not have a broad based - low rate tax system. There is a significant gap in our tax system where capital income is not treated as income for income tax purposes.
veracity.explanation: Defensible expert claim that NZ lacks a comprehensive capital income tax, though 'broad based' is partly a matter of definition.

veracity.statement: we have a tax system in this country that sees the top 311 families pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with IRD's high-wealth individuals research showing the wealthiest pay roughly half the median effective rate; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: prior to Christmas, under urgency, this Government introduced legislation which repealed requirements for the IRD to report against a set of tax principles, basically to showcase to New Zealanders whether the tax system is working efficiently and fairly... Spooky stuff—spooky stuff—as far as the tax debate here in Aotearoa New Zealand is concerned!
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the Tax Principles reporting requirement was repealed under urgency in late 2023; characterisation of purpose is fair.

veracity.statement: we recently had Treasury officials in, who I questioned about the productivity implications of our tax system, and they made it abundantly clear that were we to introduce the capital gains tax, we would not only generate the revenue necessary to invest in the infrastructure that all New Zealanders deserve but also that we would have a fundamentally more productive economy.
veracity.explanation: 'Made it abundantly clear' likely overstates the strength of Treasury's testimony on productivity effects of a CGT.

veracity.statement: The tax system has only been there to service the wealthy and actually put a pinch on the working class and the poorer whānau.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping hyperbole; 'only been there to service the wealthy' is an overstatement not supported as an absolute.

veracity.statement: While the average person in Aotearoa is paying 20.2 percent in tax, the wealthy are only paying 9.4 percent, and they are the ones that usually benefit from these trusts.
veracity.explanation: The 20.2 percent vs 9.4 percent figures align with IRD's high-wealth effective-tax-rate findings; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Our tax system allows the wealthy to illegally avoid tax through housing, investment funds, property, and through trusts
veracity.explanation: Misleading: using trusts/property to reduce tax is lawful avoidance, not 'illegal' evasion; the statement conflates the two.

veracity.statement: Again, what it does is it gives support to the 2 percent who control 50 percent of this country’s wealth and continue to get the tax breaks that this Government is so openly supportive of
veracity.explanation: Wealth-concentration figure is overstated; NZ data more closely supports the top ~10 percent holding around half, not the top 2 percent.

veracity.statement: the proposed changes in the lodged Amendment Paper—which we’re not discussing right now—will reinstate interest deductibility, reduce the brightline test from 10 years to two years, and remove depreciation deductions for commercial and industrial buildings.
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of the three amendments the Government had foreshadowed.

veracity.statement: this omnibus bill with the Government amendments will certainly restore a lot of fairness to those mum and dad landlords that dominate our landscape. In fact, about 80 percent of landlords in New Zealand own one property—they are mum and dad landlords.
veracity.explanation: The claim that the large majority of landlords own a single property is broadly supported by IRD data, though '80 percent' is an approximation.

veracity.statement: there were 67 interested groups of written submissions and individuals that we received and considered. As the select committee, we also heard oral evidence from 25 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable procedural figures presented as fact with no evident misleading framing.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. In fact, I have been looking at Budget documents that show that Pharmac’s funding over the next three years was left by the previous Government as reducing by several hundred million dollars each year for the next four years. In total, to maintain the level of pharmaceutical funding that New Zealanders are used to, the Government would have to find nearly $2 billion of extra funding over four years, and that is something that this Government is now working very hard to do in challenging economic conditions.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he had seen reports of risks to medicine access, he answers 'Yes' directly and substantiates it.

forthrightness.statement: The coalition Government is based in part on an ACT-National coalition agreement which contains a commitment to updating the rules for Medsafe to speed up the processing of new medicines for regulatory approval to within 30 days if two recognised overseas regulators have already approved it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what steps he is taking, he responds with concrete named commitments rather than generalities.

charisma.statement: There have been significant changes and modifications as a result of the Finance and Expenditure Committee working across party lines in order to listen to feedback from a large number of people making consultation and inputs into this bill... and, again, I acknowledge those members of that committee for their contribution.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party, consensus-oriented framing that credits the whole committee rather than rallying one side.

charisma.statement: It is not the version of the bill which will come into effect after the Government uses its three-headed taniwha majority to push through the changes for repealing back to the two-year brightline test and those interest deductibility changes, as well as removing depreciation deductions.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically vivid but combative, rallying her own side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: there will be parts of this bill that this side of the House will absolutely agree with and we will provide our support for this second reading; however, the last bit that is on the Table, by the new Minister of Revenue, the new father, we will have a lot to say on during the committee of the whole House stage
charisma.explanation: Measured, good-humoured framing that signals genuine agreement where it exists before flagging disagreement.

charisma.statement: I’d like to acknowledge, actually, the Government members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee. They’ve come on to the bill at quite a sort of a difficult stage, but the work that we did within the select committee, particularly on the revision-tracked version of the bill, was very cordial.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit Government members and characterise the work as cordial — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This was, I think, a process where we actually did improve the bill at the select committee... we actually did listen to submitters and some of the... problems that were raised and the issues they saw as problematic, and we actually did address them.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises collaborative, responsive process; constructive though appealing mainly to a shared sense of good faith.

charisma.statement: I am honoured to be part of a team that was able to see across all the differences and rise above, stand back, and finally, agree on something, so that we can highlight New Zealand’s dedication to forming tax policies that are modern, that are efficient, and that are effective.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, consensus-celebrating tone that credits cross-party agreement; aimed at common ground.

civility.statement: There have been significant changes and modifications as a result of the Finance and Expenditure Committee working across party lines in order to listen to feedback from a large number of people making consultation and inputs into this bill... and, again, I acknowledge those members of that committee for their contribution.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of members across the House; entirely policy and process focused.

civility.statement: As I’ve said many times before, we do not have a broad based - low rate tax system. There is a significant gap in our tax system where capital income is not treated as income for income tax purposes.
civility.explanation: Directly takes issue with the Minister's characterisation on substance, with no personal attack.

civility.statement: prior to Christmas, under urgency, this Government introduced legislation which repealed requirements for the IRD to report against a set of tax principles, basically to showcase to New Zealanders whether the tax system is working efficiently and fairly... Spooky stuff—spooky stuff—as far as the tax debate here in Aotearoa New Zealand is concerned!
civility.explanation: Engages a real legislative action, but 'spooky stuff' is rhetorical sensationalism rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: It is not the version of the bill which will come into effect after the Government uses its three-headed taniwha majority to push through the changes for repealing back to the two-year brightline test and those interest deductibility changes, as well as removing depreciation deductions.
civility.explanation: 'Three-headed taniwha majority' and 'push through' are colourful us-vs-them framing, though directed at the coalition rather than an individual.

civility.statement: we will not be letting this Government get away with increasing inequality, which, they know full well and their advice bears out, will occur as a result of them progressing this policy agenda.
civility.explanation: 'Get away with' and imputing that they 'know full well' attributes bad intent rather than debating the policy alone.

civility.statement: there will be parts of this bill that this side of the House will absolutely agree with and we will provide our support for this second reading; however, the last bit that is on the Table, by the new Minister of Revenue, the new father, we will have a lot to say on during the committee of the whole House stage
civility.explanation: Distinguishes agreement from disagreement on substance and process, with no personal attack.

civility.statement: I’d like to acknowledge, actually, the Government members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee. They’ve come on to the bill at quite a sort of a difficult stage, but the work that we did within the select committee, particularly on the revision-tracked version of the bill, was very cordial.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of opponents' contribution.

civility.statement: This was, I think, a process where we actually did improve the bill at the select committee... we actually did listen to submitters and some of the... problems that were raised and the issues they saw as problematic, and we actually did address them.
civility.explanation: Process- and submission-focused, no attacks; credits the cross-party committee work.

authenticity.statement: As I’ve said many times before, we do not have a broad based - low rate tax system. There is a significant gap in our tax system where capital income is not treated as income for income tax purposes.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly consistent with her prior stated position ('as I've said many times before'), signalling a held position rather than a shift.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that depends on the decisions that the House makes at the time. There's plenty of business to get on with.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether there will finally be a sitting week without urgency, he gives a non-committal 'it depends' and pivots to 'plenty of business' — avoids a yes/no.

forthrightness.statement: My highest priority is delivering on the Government's 100-day plan to begin stopping the implementation of new significant natural areas, known as SNAs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about his most immediate portfolio priority and names the specific commitment.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, the Government's new approach is part of a wider response to end large-scale use of emergency housing and to get New Zealanders, tamariki, and whānau into homes faster.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the approach will result in more New Zealanders on the streets, he says 'Yes' but then reframes to the Government's aspiration rather than addressing the homelessness risk asked about.

forthrightness.statement: We receive advice on housing matters on a regular basis, and the advice that we've received is that we will continue to focus on ending the large-scale use of emergency housing and getting whānau and tamariki into homes faster.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether he has advice/evidence that those losing grants will find housing and not end up on the streets, he gives a non-answer about receiving advice 'on a regular basis' and repeats the slogan.

forthrightness.statement: We need bold and radical solutions to end the housing crisis that has been exacerbated under the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Used in response to a pointed question about reducing access to grants; deflects to aspiration and blame.

forthrightness.statement: I can guarantee that this Government is committed to getting New Zealanders—tamariki and whānau—out of emergency housing and into homes faster.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he can guarantee his policies won't leave more people homeless, he offers a guarantee about a different thing (commitment to the goal), sidestepping the actual question.

forthrightness.statement: Certain expenditure is always warranted, but none of it will amount to the $1.2 billion that vanished on three waters.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically how much would be set aside for failed fast-track projects, he gives no figure and pivots to attacking Three Waters.

forthrightness.statement: There are two ways projects can be fast tracked: they can either be referred by the joint decision of the Ministers of infrastructure, regional development, and transport upon an application, or by being listed in Schedule 2A of the bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers 'how will projects be fast tracked' by laying out the two mechanisms.

forthrightness.statement: Therefore, more social housing is not created directly as a result of this policy change.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many additional social houses result from the Priority One category, he candidly admits none are created directly by it.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. That's a key design choice of the regime. We're proud of it.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms that the ultimate approve/decline decision sits with Ministers rather than independent experts — an unflattering admission given the question.

forthrightness.statement: The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: we're prohibiting the display of gang insignia in all public places; we're giving the police the ability to require gang members to disperse from gatherings that disrupt the public; we're creating new non-consorting orders to stop specified gang members from associating; and, finally, we're amending the Sentencing Act to make gang membership, on its own, an aggravating factor at sentencing.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers what the legislation will do, enumerating each measure.

forthrightness.statement: Why? Because we don't agree with that analysis. Actually, we've seen a 50 percent increase in gang membership under the previous Government, and we want to stop that, because we believe that law-abiding citizens should be going about their business without being intimidated by gangs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly responds that he disagrees, but doesn't engage the specific Chief Science Adviser finding cited.

forthrightness.statement: Well, of course, we'd be happy if the gangs relocated somewhere else and cleared out of this country and left our people alone.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about Ministry of Justice advice that NZ's unitary structure leaves no jurisdiction for gangs to relocate to, he gives a quip rather than addressing the substantive point.

forthrightness.statement: Well, yes, I do, from time to time. We don't necessarily agree with every piece of advice that we get from officials here in Wellington, and we treat all advice with respect, but, fundamentally, when a Government is elected to deliver on a policy to keep our country safe, we will deliver on that policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes' to whether it is acceptable to disagree with officials' advice, then explains his reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: The bill has been introduced, albeit, yes, under urgency, to meet the 100-day commitment to get it into the House, and the reason why it's under urgency is to send it to a committee as soon as possible so the public can have their say on this extremely important piece of legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the urgency point candidly and gives a direct rationale, though it doesn't fully address the withheld schedules raised.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sustainability. As I have previously stated, the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is currently before select committee, and I'm awaiting the committee's report.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what actions she has taken given the Newshub/TVNZ job losses, she points to a bill in progress but offers no new action — a partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: The Hon David Seymour has his own views and he is responsible for his comments. As a shareholding Minister, it would be irresponsible for me to interfere in TVNZ's editorial independence.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Seymour's comment, she declines to say yes or no, deflecting to editorial-independence grounds rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: That member does not even know that that photo was taken at the New Zealand Open, and I was there as the Minister responsible for funding the Major Events Fund. However, … at the time when the announcement was made this morning, I was in my office doing work …
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the 'luxury resort' insinuation by explaining the photo's context and her whereabouts.

veracity.statement: These show that consumer confidence continues to rise, albeit off a very low base, and business confidence is on a strong upward trend, despite levelling out in February.
veracity.explanation: ANZ surveys did show rising consumer and business confidence off low bases in early 2024; the 'levelling out in February' caveat is candid. Broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: In 2022 and 2023, consumer confidence fell to the lowest level ever reported in this survey—lower than the global financial crisis and lower than during the COVID lockdowns
veracity.explanation: ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer confidence did hit record lows in 2022-23; the GFC/COVID comparison is broadly defensible though selective in framing.

veracity.statement: Landowners are already voluntarily protecting areas of native biodiversity—over 180,000 hectares are already protected through QEII National Trust. Put together, that would be our fifth-largest national park, all voluntarily.
veracity.explanation: QEII National Trust covenants cover roughly 180,000+ hectares — consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: Can I please reiterate that we will support those with genuine need to have emergency housing, but our aspiration is to end the large-scale use of emergency housing, particularly in places like Hamilton and Waikato, where there are over 500 kids living in emergency housing right now.
veracity.explanation: The figure of 500+ children in emergency housing in the Hamilton/Waikato area is consistent with reported figures of the time.

veracity.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to whether or not he's received any reports that say his task now to solve this problem has been massively exacerbated by bringing in 148,000 immigrants as at December last year?
veracity.explanation: Net migration to December 2023 was in the order of 126,000-133,000; the 148,000 figure appears to use a larger/selective measure (e.g. arrivals), so directionally true but overstated.

veracity.statement: Certain expenditure is always warranted, but none of it will amount to the $1.2 billion that vanished on three waters.
veracity.explanation: The '$1.2 billion that vanished' is a contested, rhetorically loaded characterisation of Three Waters spending rather than an established fact of money lost.

veracity.statement: So between 18 months ago and two years, up until June 2025, there are 6,000 new social housing places, delivered both by Kāinga Ora and by the community housing sector.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with Budget 2022/2023 social housing build commitments, though these were largely funded under the previous Government — context the opponent disputes.

veracity.statement: Under the funding track we inherited, in writing Kāinga Ora was planning to sell 10,000 State houses.
veracity.explanation: 'Planning to sell 10,000 state houses' is a contested characterisation of Kāinga Ora's asset management/funding pressures rather than an established sales plan; misleading framing.

veracity.statement: Well, very good news: last night, the Government passed legislation to axe the 11.5c per litre fuel tax for Aucklanders. … This tax is gone on 1 July.
veracity.explanation: The Auckland regional fuel tax was indeed repealed effective 30 June/1 July 2024 — accurate.

veracity.statement: Well, 57.8 percent of Aucklanders voted for the coalition Government at the last election
veracity.explanation: Aggregating three parties' Auckland votes into 'voted for the coalition Government' is a misleading construction; voters chose individual parties, not a coalition that formed afterwards.

veracity.statement: On Tuesday, we introduced and have now passed legislation to stop taxpayer funding of section 27 cultural reports that proliferated under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget.
veracity.explanation: Section 27 report legal-aid spending of around $7m is broadly in line with reported figures, though 'proliferated' is a characterisation.

veracity.statement: Because the gangs have been recruiting faster than the police over the past six years, from 6,000-odd in 2018, to 9,000 at present—a 50 percent increase.
veracity.explanation: The National Gang List did grow from roughly 6,000 toward 9,000 over this period; the ~50% figure is broadly accurate, though 'recruiting faster than the police' is a rhetorical comparison.

veracity.statement: Retail crime has indeed exploded in the previous six years, with reported victims of retail crime up by 110 percent.
veracity.explanation: A large rise in retail-crime victimisation is supported by survey data, but 'exploded' and the precise 110% figure depend on the measure and base period chosen.

veracity.statement: That member does not even know that that photo was taken at the New Zealand Open, and I was there as the Minister responsible for funding the Major Events Fund. However, … at the time when the announcement was made this morning, I was in my office doing work …
veracity.explanation: Offers a specific factual correction (New Zealand Open, Major Events Fund role) which is plausible but unverifiable from the text.

specificity.statement: These show that consumer confidence continues to rise, albeit off a very low base, and business confidence is on a strong upward trend, despite levelling out in February.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (ANZ) and direction with some nuance, but cites no figures.

specificity.statement: In 2022 and 2023, consumer confidence fell to the lowest level ever reported in this survey—lower than the global financial crisis and lower than during the COVID lockdowns
specificity.explanation: Specific time period and comparative benchmarks (GFC, COVID), though no index numbers.

specificity.statement: My highest priority is delivering on the Government's 100-day plan to begin stopping the implementation of new significant natural areas, known as SNAs.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy action (stopping new SNAs) tied to the 100-day plan, but no mechanism detail yet.

specificity.statement: Landowners are already voluntarily protecting areas of native biodiversity—over 180,000 hectares are already protected through QEII National Trust. Put together, that would be our fifth-largest national park, all voluntarily.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete hectare figure and a vivid comparative scale.

specificity.statement: The way to protect biodiversity on private land is to work collaboratively with landowners, including farmers, foresters, and iwi, to incentivise the sustainable use of land, and to show them that their work to protect the biodiversity is valued and then they will want to do more.
specificity.explanation: States an approach (collaboration, incentives) but no concrete mechanism or funding.

specificity.statement: We need bold and radical solutions to end the housing crisis that has been exacerbated under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: 'Bold and radical solutions' is a slogan with no concrete mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Can I please reiterate that we will support those with genuine need to have emergency housing, but our aspiration is to end the large-scale use of emergency housing, particularly in places like Hamilton and Waikato, where there are over 500 kids living in emergency housing right now.
specificity.explanation: Names a location and a concrete number of children affected.

specificity.statement: We are determined to cut through the thicket of red and green tape holding New Zealand back by fast tracking consents for projects of regional and national significance whilst protecting Treaty settlements and the environment.

specificity.statement: So it is a very good change in the bill that people will be able to have that lump-sum payment assessed across a four-year period.

specificity.statement: In fact, they only reach the threshold of being attached to these rules once they’ve reached €750 million, which provides them the position of having the effective rate of 15 percent.

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (deferral of tax liability on insurance proceeds) and the affected group.

specificity.explanation: Exact rate ($76/1,000km), date (1 April), and affected vehicle class.
