civility.statement: I want to finish off by saying Melissa Lee to the media industry is what disability Minister Penny Simmonds is to the disability sector: utterly hopeless.
civility.explanation: Direct personal insult ('utterly hopeless') aimed at two named ministers.

civility.statement: they won’t support it because they’re in the pocket of the lobbyists. They’re in the pocket—we all know this. They’re in the pockets of the property developers
civility.explanation: Imputes corruption to opponents; he was made to withdraw and apologise.

civility.statement: I do want to acknowledge Nancy Lu, the previous speaker from the Government. It is a really hard decision to put your children into early childhood education (ECE), and I support the decision making that she had to make for her children
civility.explanation: Warmly acknowledges an opponent's personal contribution before disagreeing on policy.

civility.statement: last year, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance continually stood by their statements that their numbers were solid as a rock, or rock-solid... They said that tax cuts were going to arrive from 1 April 2024.
civility.explanation: Critique of the Government's fiscal promises framed with a light musical motif rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: They don’t understand what it’s like to live in regional New Zealand; they just live in little electorates in town.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of opponents as out-of-touch townies rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: while National goes around claiming that they care about freedom and choice and economic productivity, every action they are taking will achieve the exact opposite of what they claim to care about, and anyone who knows anything at all about urban transportation or transportation economics knows this.
civility.explanation: Challenges the consistency of opponents' stated values; pointed but aimed at their policy claims, with a touch of condescension.

civility.statement: the Government didn’t do it at all; it was the Opposition that brought it in, slipped it through the select committee, and now the Government’s trying to claim credit for the changes.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of claiming undue credit; a pointed but process-focused charge rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: is the Government committed to a transition through to a low-carbon transport fleet? I think it is important that the Minister stand up and commit to that.
civility.explanation: A direct, respectful challenge focused on policy commitment rather than the Minister personally.

civility.statement: I’d like to ask the question that I think most of my constituents would want to know the answer to: does it still make sense economically for people to buy an electric vehicle if they are in that setting, given the law that we’re going to pass?
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused question to the Minister.

civility.statement: I’d like to acknowledge that there was really good work done by the select committee over the issue of plug-in hybrids
civility.explanation: Credits cross-party committee work before pressing her question.

charisma.statement: I want to start this discourse by thanking our hard-working health professionals, both clinical and non-clinical, for their continued support and commitment to serving New Zealanders and maintaining our health system.
charisma.explanation: Warm and inclusive toward the sector but does not reach across the political aisle.

charisma.statement: And I do, of course, have to acknowledge the other side for their work, but I will congratulate Mr McClay for his work and making sure that we got it into force quickly and efficiently.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the Opposition's contribution to the FTA, a cross-party courtesy, though the bulk of credit stays partisan.

charisma.statement: We aren’t going to get wealthy growing mega Government bureaucracies and shuffling paper back and forth.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but appeals only to his own side's worldview, drawing an us-vs-them contrast.

charisma.statement: We’re seeing a Minister completely out of her depth.
charisma.explanation: Combative, alienating, no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

charisma.statement: I do want to acknowledge Nancy Lu, the previous speaker from the Government. It is a really hard decision to put your children into early childhood education (ECE), and I support the decision making that she had to make for her children
charisma.explanation: Gracious, cross-aisle goodwill that finds common ground on a shared parental experience.

charisma.statement: They don’t understand what it’s like to live in regional New Zealand; they just live in little electorates in town.
charisma.explanation: Rallies a regional in-group by belittling urban MPs; divisive rather than bridging.

charisma.statement: while National goes around claiming that they care about freedom and choice and economic productivity, every action they are taking will achieve the exact opposite of what they claim to care about, and anyone who knows anything at all about urban transportation or transportation economics knows this.
charisma.explanation: Confident and earlier consensus-minded, but this line draws a hard contrast that appeals to her own side.

charisma.statement: if it is this Government’s intention that that fast-track bill is used to decrease emissions, then can I suggest a consideration that that bill... be restricted to projects that will decrease carbon emissions.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive suggestion to the Minister rather than just attacking, inviting engagement.

charisma.statement: I’d like to ask the question that I think most of my constituents would want to know the answer to: does it still make sense economically for people to buy an electric vehicle if they are in that setting, given the law that we’re going to pass?
charisma.explanation: Frames the question around ordinary constituents' concerns in plain terms, seeking a useful answer rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: I’d like to acknowledge that there was really good work done by the select committee over the issue of plug-in hybrids
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges shared good work, a small consensus-building gesture.

rigor.statement: Gloriavale is not some quaint, outdated community. It’s an oppressive, backward, harmful, and evil institution, run by a small group of controlling men.
rigor.explanation: A heated characterisation, though one he goes on to support with a list of convictions; this sentence alone is assertion-heavy.

rigor.statement: In 1995, the very founder was convicted of three charges of indecent assault against a 19-year-old. The overseeing shepherd, Howard Temple, is currently facing 27 charges of sexual offending. In 2023, Jonathon Benjamin was convicted of 26 charges of sexual offending.
rigor.explanation: Marshals concrete evidence (convictions and charges) to support the claim of systemic harm.

rigor.statement: It’s a sign of an incompetent Government—a Government that doesn’t care, and a Government that’s too obsessed with its own chaos to look after people.
rigor.explanation: Asserts incompetence and indifference without logical linkage to evidence beyond the single funding decision.

rigor.statement: Basic human rights are not a priority for this Government. Children are not a priority for this Government.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from one agency-defunding decision to a sweeping claim about priorities; overreaches the evidence.

rigor.statement: We aren’t going to get wealthy growing mega Government bureaucracies and shuffling paper back and forth.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a contrast between trade and 'shuffling paper' without supporting argument.

rigor.statement: his own ministry reports that over just a six-year period, our country’s area of indigenous vegetation cover decreased by over 12,000 hectares, and we currently have the highest proportion of threatened species per capita in the world.
rigor.explanation: Uses the opponent's own ministry's evidence to rebut his claim — a strong, sourced argument.

rigor.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment points out that only 2 percent of Government expenditure goes toward nature.
rigor.explanation: Backs the 'no balance' argument with a cited authority and a concrete figure.

rigor.statement: this Government has been breathtakingly reckless in prioritising short-term profits over the long-term health and wellbeing of our environment and communities.
rigor.explanation: A strong conclusion that she partly supports elsewhere, but this sentence is assertion-led.

rigor.statement: I want to finish off by saying Melissa Lee to the media industry is what disability Minister Penny Simmonds is to the disability sector: utterly hopeless.
rigor.explanation: Pure derogation by analogy with no supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: they won’t support it because they’re in the pocket of the lobbyists. They’re in the pocket—we all know this. They’re in the pockets of the property developers
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem 'in the pocket' allegation asserted with 'we all know this' rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Most OECD countries pay about 14 percent—14—of average income. However, the highest costs are observed in New Zealand where net childcare costs for working families can reach as high as 38 percent of average earnings.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative data to justify the policy, a reasonable evidence-based argument.

rigor.statement: For the first time in my public service history, there is no clear indication of what the operating allowance is for the Budget. They said that it’s going to be less than $3.5 billion.
rigor.explanation: Infers ongoing coalition negotiations from the missing allowance — a reasonable but speculative inference ('that only points to one thing').

rigor.statement: A recent NZIER report indicated that the economic benefits of just building the Dome Valley extension to Te Hana was approximately $500 million per year.
rigor.explanation: Supports the case for the road with a cited economic study rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: They don’t understand what it’s like to live in regional New Zealand; they just live in little electorates in town.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem about opponents' residences rather than a substantive rebuttal.

rigor.statement: If the previous Government had continued to build this road as planned, it would be close to finished and we would be about to reap the huge gains that follow.
rigor.explanation: Plausible counterfactual but asserted, leaning on the prior NZIER figure rather than fully argued.

rigor.statement: In Queenstown, for example, they dropped the bus fares to $2 for a flat fare, made the transfer free, made the buses run every 15 minutes, and what happened? They raised more revenue than when the bus fares were higher.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete worked example to support the claim that lower fares can raise ridership and revenue.

rigor.statement: we now have the highest car ownership rate in the entire world. And our entire dairy exports—$19 billion—do not pay for our annual imports of vehicles and fuel to run them, which is now at $22 billion.
rigor.explanation: Marshals trade-balance figures to argue car dependence is an economic drag.

rigor.statement: the Minister... was forced to admit that putting speed limits up to 50 from 30 kilometres an hour around schools only saves 15 seconds—that’s 1 percent of the average car journey... if a pedestrian or vulnerable road user is struck by a car, they have a 300 percent increased chance of fatality.
rigor.explanation: Weighs a tiny time saving against a large fatality-risk increase — a clear cost-benefit argument grounded in figures.

rigor.statement: while National goes around claiming that they care about freedom and choice and economic productivity, every action they are taking will achieve the exact opposite of what they claim to care about, and anyone who knows anything at all about urban transportation or transportation economics knows this.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sweeping 'exact opposite' claim and leans on an appeal to expert consensus ('anyone who knows anything... knows this') rather than fully demonstrating it here.

rigor.statement: if we don’t have some sort of support or financial incentive to electrify the fleet, it will slow down, and that has very serious consequences for meeting our greenhouse gas reduction targets later in the period.
rigor.explanation: Logical chain from incentive removal to slower electrification to target risk, supported by the cited industry submission.

rigor.statement: a heavy vehicle is 625 times greater impact on the road than a light vehicle—625.
rigor.explanation: Uses the road-damage ratio to argue RUC relativity between heavy and light vehicles is out of line with impact.

rigor.statement: the Government didn’t do it at all; it was the Opposition that brought it in, slipped it through the select committee, and now the Government’s trying to claim credit for the changes.
rigor.explanation: A factual provenance claim about who originated the PHEV change, plausible but asserted.

rigor.statement: On Monday, I heard an interesting article on Radio New Zealand—actually, it was the CEO of the Motor Trade Association... pointing to the reality that with the changes in this piece of legislation, there is no incentive for people to move from combustion engines into e-vehicles, because at an average of 14,000 kilometres, it will be about $1,064 paid in road-user charges (RUC), which would be equivalent to diesel on the same road.
rigor.explanation: Backs the 'no incentive' claim with a sourced calculation (average km × RUC rate compared to diesel).

rigor.statement: in 2012, the National Government increased the weights and then decreased the funding for roading. If we’re trying to catch up, why did the Minister not bring in some adjustment
rigor.explanation: Links a past policy decision to current road dilapidation to justify revisiting RUC relativities.

rigor.statement: if it is this Government’s intention that that fast-track bill is used to decrease emissions, then can I suggest a consideration that that bill... be restricted to projects that will decrease carbon emissions.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a conditional policy argument linking the fast-track bill to emissions outcomes and proposes a concrete refinement.

divination.statement: When it comes into force, it will increase our exports via the EU by $1.8 billion annually—a substantial amount from a Government that is focused on trade and trading with the world.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a $1.8b annual export increase; plausible and based on modelling but an estimate of future trade outcomes.

divination.statement: If the Government bulldozes on with this short-sighted, reckless approach to nature, we will ultimately face dire consequences, and Aotearoa deserves much better.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'dire consequences' but too vague on magnitude and timeframe to be readily falsifiable.

divination.statement: It could bring hundreds of millions of dollars into the industry—hundreds of millions of dollars—but they won’t support it because they’re in the pocket of the lobbyists.
divination.explanation: Predicts the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill would bring 'hundreds of millions' to the industry; an optimistic, unquantified forecast.

divination.statement: If the previous Government had continued to build this road as planned, it would be close to finished and we would be about to reap the huge gains that follow.
divination.explanation: A counterfactual prediction about a road's completion and benefits; not directly falsifiable and rests on contested assumptions.

divination.statement: if we don’t have some sort of support or financial incentive to electrify the fleet, it will slow down, and that has very serious consequences for meeting our greenhouse gas reduction targets later in the period.
divination.explanation: Predicts EV uptake will slow without incentives, jeopardising emissions targets; directionally well-supported but magnitude uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: the Government has agreed that there should be a lower plug-in hybrid rate. That is why we sent it to select committee, to test that issue, and Cabinet agreed that the rate should be $38.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to questions about the PHEV rate, he directly states the agreed figure and the process; answers that part squarely.

forthrightness.statement: Ultimately, lots of other questions have been raised around fuel economy: charging infrastructure, other issues—fuel economy standards. Those aren’t relevant to the bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to substantive questions from O'Connor, Genter and Brooking about incentives and emissions, he declines to engage by ruling them out of scope rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: If the member reads the Order Paper, he will see that the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is no longer on the Order Paper.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he plans to introduce a replacement now the Government scrapped the bill; he only notes the bill is off the Order Paper and never addresses the replacement question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as the member knows from his time in Government, the Government intention to progress bills is announced in due course, and when they make their way on to the Order Paper, they get reflected on the Order Paper.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether there will be a replacement for the Kermadec bill; gives a generic process answer and declines to confirm or deny.

forthrightness.statement: the operating allowance for the most recent Budget in 2023 was announced as being $2.6 billion in Budget 2020, but as the years went by, it was raised to $2.7 billion, then to $4 billion, then to $4.5 billion, and then to $4.8 billion—some $2.2 billion more than indicated three years earlier.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when she will announce future Budget allowances; she answers (Fiscal Strategy Report) and gives a worked historical example, though pivots to a partisan point.

forthrightness.statement: No, that's another one from the Labour Party fantasy file—the same file they get their idea that a new tax will somehow make New Zealand more prosperous.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she broke convention because coalition Budget negotiations broke down; she denies it ('No') but substitutes ridicule for any explanation.

forthrightness.statement: I often agree with Nicola Willis, although I have observed that, from time to time, she does fall short of perfection.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with her own 2023 promise that no cuts would be made to front-line services; deflects with a joke and reframes rather than affirming the promise.

forthrightness.statement: I've been assured that MPI is not proposing any reductions to its front-line services and that statutory staff—such as veterinarians, animal welfare, fishery, food-compliance officers, and biosecurity teams at the border—remain.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what evidence assures her MPI cuts won't harm biosecurity response; gives a concrete assurance about protected roles, though it is an assurance rather than the evidence requested.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm getting a bit of a flavour for what the last regime might have been like—interrogations and evidence—but, actually, that doesn't at all marry up with what we saw in practice, does it, which is that spending got completely out of control, resources were tied up in the back office, the headcount in public agencies exploded, and New Zealanders were left wondering, if spending's increased by 80 percent in just six years, what have we the people got to show for it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she interrogated chief executives' assurances and, if not, why the public should believe no front-line cuts are being made; she pivots to attacking the previous Government instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: I have also been advised by officials that expenditure information from providers indicates that, in a number of instances, individualised funding has been used to purchase Lotto tickets, alcohol, and tobacco. Clearly, the system set up under the previous Government did not have appropriate settings in place.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the reports contained figures or only anecdotal evidence; she describes the range of sources and examples but does not clearly state whether actual figures existed.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can confirm that carers that were accessing the funding for care services such as massages, hairdressers, pedicures, and other appearance or therapeutic services, or for purchasing Lotto tickets, alcohol, or tobacco will be impacted.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm at least 26,000 carers will be impacted; she confirms impact but reframes around the contested spending categories rather than the number.

forthrightness.statement: Whaikaha advised me that they had a comprehensive engagement and communication plan in place. Clearly, that did not happen. I have apologised that that did not happen, as did the chief executive (CE) of Whaikaha.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether she or her office signed out the wording used in Whaikaha's 18 March announcement; she answers a different question about the communication plan, prompting repeated points of order that the specific question was not addressed.

forthrightness.statement: I contacted the Otago Regional Council to release them from the obligation that had been placed on them by the previous Minister for the Environment, to ensure that I extended the date for their statutory deadline for notifying their freshwater planning instrument so that it was in line with all other councils.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she regrets contacting ORC to slow its water plan; she confirms the contact and reframes it as alignment rather than answering the 'regret' framing.

forthrightness.statement: there is a marine reserve around each Kermadec island out to 12 nautical miles, there are regulations prohibiting bottom trawling, there is a minerals reservation—prevents new mining permits, and there are a range of marine wildlife regulations.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she regrets extended Kermadec protection being taken off the table; she does not address regret but does substantively list existing protections.

forthrightness.statement: I reject that assertion.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a loaded, opinion-laden question ('powerless to protect the environment') with a flat rejection rather than substantive engagement, though the question invites little else.

forthrightness.statement: The report said that 51 percent of teachers mention device use reduced the ability to concentrate and may be one of the causes of worsening behaviour. We've already taken action to ban cellphone use in our classrooms, and the feedback has been overwhelmingly positive. Feedback from Hornby High School was that they had no reports of cyber-bullying since the ban was introduced.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what action the Government has already taken on classroom behaviour; she directly names the cellphone ban and supporting evidence.

forthrightness.statement: All of the seven rules of firearm safety are important. However, during the roar, rule No. 4, identify your target beyond reasonable doubt, is mainly the one to be emphasised. Failure to properly identify a target could lead to tragedy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which of the seven rules is most important; she directly names rule No. 4 and explains why, despite a preamble that all matter.

forthrightness.statement: It is important that licensed firearms owners follow the guidelines for the storage and transportation of firearms and ammunition to the letter. These guidelines have changed significantly over the past couple of years, so it's important that licensed firearm owners revise them again and understand what their new requirements are.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice she'd give owners travelling with firearms; gives a direct, on-topic answer about storage/transport guidelines.

forthrightness.statement: I've already delivered two of the commitments from the ACT-National coalition agreement in my portfolio: to repeal the fair pay agreement system and expand the 90-day trials to apply to all businesses. I've also implemented a moderate annual increase in the minimum wage, as required by the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice she's seen on the policies' impact on workers; she lists deliveries and notes each RIS mentioned worker impacts, partially addressing the question.

forthrightness.statement: I have only received very early policy scoping advice on contracting arrangements, so the member will have to wait for further policy decisions to be made, but one thing that's very clear from the coalition agreement's intentions is that this Government intends to clarify the law to make certain for both businesses and workers what are employment or contracting arrangements.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee workers can keep clarifying employment status in the Employment Court; she declines to engage and defers to future advice.

forthrightness.statement: As I have suggested earlier, I have only received very early policy scoping advice on the contracting arrangements. This is very early in my work programme, and I'm very excited to clarify the law about the role of contracting arrangements and employment law arrangements within existing New Zealand law.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to acknowledge minimum-wage workers' vulnerability to contractor exploitation and ensure court access; she repeats 'early scoping advice' and does not address the vulnerability point.

forthrightness.statement: There are many, many people who sign contracting arrangements every day who are very satisfied with the terms of their contracts—90 percent of people who are in contracting arrangements are satisfied or very satisfied with being self-employed and not being employees, and we should uphold their rights to continue to be contractors.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a friendly question about clarifying status before starting work with a direct, on-point answer.

forthrightness.statement: Yesterday, I was pleased to announce the establishment of a Science System Advisory Group. This group will help us explore the well-documented issues facing the science sector and will be chaired by Professor Sir Peter Gluckman... The Science System Advisory Group has been tasked with delivering two reports: the first in June 2024 and the second in October 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what recent announcement she made in the portfolio; she answers directly with the relevant announcement.

forthrightness.statement: I've had a look at that and it's actually about just over $400,000 for the entire system—which is pretty amazing, considering that was pretty much what one Government agency might have spent on gifts for its outgoing CEO.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how much the review will cost; she gives a concrete figure (~$400,000) before adding a jab.

forthrightness.statement: That Te Ara Paerangi was, frankly, a waste of paper. In fact, the forestry people should have taken back the money... that was a waste of space. This is actually about getting things done. And unlike a previous Minister in this role, I actually get stuff done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the new group isn't duplicative of existing documented work; she does address it by claiming the earlier work was empty, but mainly through dismissal.

forthrightness.statement: Because the Hon Casey Costello is my associate, and she is assisting me as part of her delegation in the delivery of the 500, and I think it's a fair recognition of her that the last 1,800 was a great New Zealand First policy and the next 500 is another great New Zealand First policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why his office told the Herald that Costello holds responsibility for the 500; he explains her delegated role but reframes around crediting NZ First rather than the 'primary responsibility' wording.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think the member is getting a bit hung up on the word "primary"... I can assure her that myself and my very competent associate will be working together to deliver the 500 police officers over the next two years.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm on the record that the Herald response naming Costello as having primary responsibility was incorrect; he dodges by minimising the word 'primary' and never confirms or denies.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I agree. Non-sworn staff have a critically important role to play in the Police.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with OIA-released Police advice that retaining non-sworn staff is necessary to deliver 500 officers; he answers directly and affirmatively.

forthrightness.statement: Well, firstly, it's not a 6.5 percent cut. As an incoming Government, it became obvious—although we had very clear ideas—that the previous Government has left a shambles behind. You are economic—or the previous Government are economic vandals.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to not cutting non-sworn roles this and next financial year; he disputes the premise and attacks the previous Government without committing either way.

forthrightness.statement: These changes will mean around 1,900 fewer dams will be impacted by the new regulations, reducing compliance costs by more than $13.3 million. It will also better align dam safety regulations with the requirement for dams over 4 metres to also have a building consent.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what impact the changes will have; answers directly with concrete effects.

forthrightness.statement: I've gone from the champion of the provinces to the leader, the leading politician, who is going to ensure that the fishing industry is not demonised or driven out of existence by stupid Green policies.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he shares fishers' opposition to seabed mining; he ignores the seabed-mining question entirely (confirmed by a sustained point of order) and self-promotes.

forthrightness.statement: The processes that are in play pertaining to applicants seeking to gain access to the half a trillion dollars' worth of wealth on the bed of the sea are entitled to go through that process. That is shared space enjoyed also by quota owners.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he communicated fishers' opposition to seabed mining when meeting Straterra; he discusses applicants' process entitlements instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: The decision that the member refers to is a decision of the Cabinet... nothing in the Kermadecs will change as a consequence of the overdue decision today, whether it's noddies on land or pufferfish at the sea.
forthrightness.explanation: Pressed again on whether he shares the fishing industry's opposition to seabed mining; he deflects to collective Cabinet responsibility and flippant imagery.

forthrightness.statement: We're working with our coalition partners to fund front-line services such as Gumboot Friday and the I Am Hope charity. This Government is also working to establish the mental health innovation fund to increase access to mental health services in this term of Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what evidence-based initiatives the next Suicide Prevention Action Plan is considering and how they address Māori/non-Māori disparities; names some funded services but does not tie them to evidence or the disparity asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I do not have that information to hand. I am sure the Minister will be able to respond in writing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what procurement process was used for I Am Hope to receive $6 million; she does not answer and defers to a written reply.

forthrightness.statement: As I have stated before, the coalition Government is committed to reducing suicide rates in New Zealand and better health outcomes for all New Zealanders. This is why we are focused on committing delivering of services close to home and as close to hapū as possible.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what specific Māori-targeted suicide-prevention initiatives are being funded; she restates a general commitment without naming any.

civility.statement: If the member reads the Order Paper, he will see that the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is no longer on the Order Paper.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive ('if the member reads the Order Paper') but no personal attack.

civility.statement: That is why I take any comments about future allowances with a large grain of salt when those comments come from the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Partisan dig at an opponent party, but aimed at their fiscal record rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: The Public Finance Act does not require anything from the finance Minister with regard to Budget allowances, and, in fact, it makes no mention of Budget allowances whatsoever. What is highly embarrassing is for someone to publicly accuse a Minister of breaching an Act of Parliament while getting basic facts wrong, and I am disappointed in the Opposition spokesperson Barbara Edmonds.
civility.explanation: Names and criticises an opponent's competence ('getting basic facts wrong'), but the criticism is tied to a substantive factual dispute.

civility.statement: No, that's another one from the Labour Party fantasy file—the same file they get their idea that a new tax will somehow make New Zealand more prosperous.
civility.explanation: 'Labour Party fantasy file' belittles opponents rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: The Labour Party's convention was every time they said they'd stick to a spending limit, the next opportunity they had, they broke it. Well, this Government is going to break that convention.
civility.explanation: Critiques the opponent's record on spending limits rather than the person, but in a sweeping accusatory form.

civility.statement: Well, I'm getting a bit of a flavour for what the last regime might have been like—interrogations and evidence—but, actually, that doesn't at all marry up with what we saw in practice, does it, which is that spending got completely out of control, resources were tied up in the back office, the headcount in public agencies exploded, and New Zealanders were left wondering, if spending's increased by 80 percent in just six years, what have we the people got to show for it.
civility.explanation: 'Last regime' and mocking 'interrogations and evidence' frame the exchange combatively.

civility.statement: I've had a look at that and it's actually about just over $400,000 for the entire system—which is pretty amazing, considering that was pretty much what one Government agency might have spent on gifts for its outgoing CEO.
civility.explanation: Tacks a sarcastic dig (CEO gift comparison) onto an otherwise substantive answer.

civility.statement: That Te Ara Paerangi was, frankly, a waste of paper. In fact, the forestry people should have taken back the money... that was a waste of space. This is actually about getting things done. And unlike a previous Minister in this role, I actually get stuff done.
civility.explanation: Disparages prior work as 'a waste of paper/space' and takes a personal swipe at a predecessor's competence.

civility.statement: Well, firstly, it's not a 6.5 percent cut. As an incoming Government, it became obvious—although we had very clear ideas—that the previous Government has left a shambles behind. You are economic—or the previous Government are economic vandals.
civility.explanation: 'Economic vandals' is a personal/partisan slur rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: I've gone from the champion of the provinces to the leader, the leading politician, who is going to ensure that the fishing industry is not demonised or driven out of existence by stupid Green policies.
civility.explanation: 'Stupid Green policies' is a dismissive partisan jab rather than engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: The decision that the member refers to is a decision of the Cabinet... nothing in the Kermadecs will change as a consequence of the overdue decision today, whether it's noddies on land or pufferfish at the sea.
civility.explanation: Flippant ('noddies on land or pufferfish at the sea') but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I can respond that any loss of a young life is an unspeakable tragedy. The suicide rates in New Zealand are unacceptably high and disproportionately affect some groups in New Zealand, including Māori men. That's why this coalition Government is so focused on improving access to mental health.
civility.explanation: Respectful, sober engagement with a sensitive topic.

civility.statement: And, of course, the last Government didn't do much, but I do acknowledge their support of this legislation thus far into the House. I do want to acknowledge that they have supported this legislation thus far.
civility.explanation: Mild jab paired with genuine acknowledgement of cross-party cooperation.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the Minister for his approach to not only the committee stage but being flexible and adaptive in what has been generally a really good working process for working through what is a very detailed piece of legislation. So the reality is that we’re putting it back to its original purpose. That option still exists and will continue to exist.
specificity.explanation: Describes the mechanism (free-funded reports removed, option retained) but no figures.

specificity.statement: Well, we are making sure that we actually have a fair system. That is fair and stands up for the victims of crime; it doesn’t stand up for the offenders.
specificity.explanation: Vague 'fair system' framing with no mechanism.

specificity.statement: No, I don’t find it acceptable, and that’s why we’re working so hard on lowering crime.
specificity.explanation: No concrete solution offered.

specificity.statement: We need both city densification and we need to open up new greenfields and new green spaces, too.
specificity.explanation: States a direction but no policy or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Does he find it acceptable that Māori women make up 64 percent of the female prison population while Māori men make up 50 percent of the male prison population, and, if not, what are his Government’s solutions to reduce that number and ensure it doesn’t increase as a result of this policy?
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages framing a concrete question.

specificity.statement: Just two hours ago, the Government completed another key commitment from our 100-day plan, the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MOU) for a third medical school. This is the first step in a process to help increase the number of New Zealand - trained doctors.
specificity.explanation: Names the action, timing, and purpose.

specificity.statement: With this initiative we aim to retain more New Zealanders in our domestic medical school programmes, given more than 300 New Zealand students each year have been training in Australian medical schools.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (300+ students/year in Australia) as the rationale.

specificity.statement: I am confident that the Local Water Done Well will be implemented cheaper than the previous Government’s three waters reform that cost the taxpayers over $1.2 billion with very little to show for it.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure ($1.2bn) but no costing for his own 'cheaper' alternative.

specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures, named projects, and a ring-fencing commitment.

specificity.statement: Well, of the, I think, $700 million that has been raised to date, around $340 million—almost half of it—remains unspent, so that’s a fail on the former Government. The second point is around over $100 million was spent on safety improvement projects, which was basically speed bumps, and then a whole lot of other bus lanes and cycle lanes received funding as well.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figures given, but not the percentage actually requested.

specificity.statement: Well, that’s a very good question, and this is all about the cost of living for Aucklanders. specificity.explanation: Per-fill savings figures by vehicle type.

specificity.statement: There will be two further bills progressing through Parliament to transition to Local Water Done Well. specificity.explanation: Two named bills with scope and a December timeframe.

specificity.explanation: Concrete historical framing and the policy choice stated.

specificity.statement: The difference this year will be approximately $2, and our Government is absolutely focused on, first of all, reducing the number of people on jobseeker benefit, because we’ve seen a blowout in dependency under the last Government, and also we are focused on reducing the cost of living and the pressures that households—those receiving benefits and on low incomes—are facing.
specificity.explanation: Gives the $2 figure; 'blowout in dependency' is unquantified.

specificity.statement: That’s the way it’s been for many years, and I don’t forecast it’s going to change.
specificity.explanation: Offers no detail or rationale.

specificity.explanation: Dated announcement and named coalition-agreement basis.

specificity.explanation: Names the vacancy, who resigned, and the process to fill it.

specificity.explanation: Council-by-council allocations down to ring-fenced sub-amounts.

specificity.statement: The message to the people affected by Cyclone Gabrielle is that this Government is listening and working as hard as it can to speed up this recovery. We are behind you.
specificity.explanation: Reassurance with no concrete commitment of its own.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we are making sure that we actually have a fair system. That is fair and stands up for the victims of crime; it doesn’t stand up for the offenders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what work ensures Māori/low-income won't be unfairly sentenced; answers with a slogan, not the work.

forthrightness.statement: No, I don’t find it acceptable, and that’s why we’re working so hard on lowering crime.

strength.statement: we made a significant announcement of $63 million to support and accelerate the clean-up of silt and debris in both Tairāwhiti and Hawke’s Bay.

rigor.explanation: Uses supply/price trends to argue the precursor ban failed; conclusion follows reasonably, though 'no difference' is a strong inference from those two indicators.

rigor.statement: This position was supported by advice we received from the Ministry of Health, which consulted with the New Zealand Police, the New Zealand Customs Service, and the National Drug Intelligence Bureau.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the low-meth-risk claim in named official sources and their consultation chain rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: if the pharmacies don't want to wear the risk of storing pseudoephedrine, then, simply, they don't have to store it.
rigor.explanation: A valid point that pharmacy participation is opt-in, but it sidesteps Verrall's safety concern rather than fully engaging the risk to those who do stock it.

strength.statement: So it's time now for Stride Property to put up or sell, because it is just now unacceptable... It's time for Stride to sell.
strength.explanation: An advocacy demand rather than a delivered outcome; describes pressing for action without evidence of follow-through he has secured.

specificity.statement: This Government owes it to Kiwis to focus on delivering on the things that matter most to them, like shorter wait times for emergency care and elective treatments, safer communities with less violent crime, and more kids at school and achieving the skills they need to live a better life.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy areas (ED wait times, elective treatments, violent crime, school attendance) but no figures, mechanisms, or timeframes here.

specificity.statement: We’re not here to manage decline; we’re here to get things done and deliver better outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Slogan with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Well, what we are doing is we’re making sure we rebuild this economy, we restore law and order, and we deliver better health and education for Māori and non-Māori.
specificity.explanation: Lists broad goals with no concrete action.

specificity.statement: We can’t just shut down the world’s best farmers and send agricultural production offshore, making global greenhouse gas emissions worse in the process. We believe “no additional warming” is a fair basis for methane targets in particular.
specificity.explanation: Names 'no additional warming' as the basis but no figures or timeframes for the target.

specificity.statement: It is an absolute travesty that only 47 percent of our kids go to school regularly in this country—a legacy of the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete attendance figure.

specificity.statement: The Suicide Prevention Office is not being considered for closure.
specificity.explanation: A clear, unambiguous factual claim, though no supporting detail.

specificity.statement: Yes, and especially the target that I announced yesterday for 75 percent fewer households in emergency housing. Too many children are being raised in motels, and my Government is focused on reversing the huge growth seen under the previous Government and its homelessness Minister.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete 75% reduction target for emergency-housing households.

specificity.statement: I’d just say to you that the Government supports mining on a responsible basis, and there’s a process under way.
specificity.explanation: Vague reference to 'a process under way' with no detail.

specificity.statement: What our fiscal intentions and objectives are, are to return to surplus; to get debt heading down as a percentage of GDP, rather than going up, as it has been over the past five years; and to reduce Government spending as a proportion of the overall economy.
specificity.explanation: Clear directional objectives (surplus, debt-to-GDP down, spending share down) but no figures or dates in this line.

specificity.statement: Well, the half-year update, in December, forecast that core Crown spending in the current 2023-24 financial year will be 33.4 percent of GDP. Now, to put that in context, core Crown spending in 2018-19—just five years ago—was only 28 percent of GDP. Now, clearly, COVID disruptions were a factor in this increase, but the crucial thing is that unlike in other countries, there was no attempt to bring Government spending back down again after the temporary disruption passed.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, years, and source (half-year update).

specificity.statement: New Zealand currently has a structural deficit, and there are only three broad options to deal with that: borrowing to cover that deficit, which is unsustainable; taxing New Zealanders more, which most of the members opposite think’s a great idea, but which we’re not big fans of; or reining back on spending. We will do the last of these. We intend to control growth in core Crown spending so that it reduces as a percentage of GDP, and, over time, our objective is to bring spending down towards 30 percent of GDP.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target of ~30% of GDP, though without a firm date.

specificity.statement: I particularly stand by my statement that hard-working Kiwis deserve personal income tax relief. Given that they’ve been waiting 14 years for it, the coalition Government will be delighted to deliver it to them in the Budget in May.
specificity.explanation: Commits to tax relief in a named timeframe (Budget in May) but no figures or thresholds.

specificity.statement: There needs to be a greater focus on supporting people off welfare and into work, because the previous Government failed to capitalise on long periods where employers were crying out for staff—and when they left office, there were 70,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit. We now have almost 190,000 people in New Zealand receiving the jobseeker benefit, and that’s approximately the size of Hamilton.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers (70,000 increase, ~190,000 total).

specificity.statement: The Taylor Fry report that was published in December last year showed the forecast of the future years expected that people would spend—the forecast of the future years expected that people would spend on welfare. For a jobseeker benefit, they are estimated to spend, on average, 13 future years on welfare. For those who move on to welfare under the age of 25, they are forecast to spend 19 future years on main benefit.
specificity.explanation: Named report, date, and precise projected-years figures (13 and 19 years).

specificity.statement: In February, we announced the first two actions to reset the welfare system. Firstly, work check-ins will begin for people who’ve been on the jobseeker benefit for more than six months to ensure that they are taking action to find work and getting the support they need. Secondly, we reversed Labour’s light-touch approach to benefit sanctions and made our expectation clear: those who can work should work, and job seekers have responsibilities to become work-ready and find a job.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (six-month work check-ins, reinstated sanctions) with a timeframe (February).

specificity.statement: Our Government is focused on reducing the number of job seekers by 50,000, and we believe that a job is better than no job and that a job is a path to a better job.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 50,000 figure but otherwise relies on the 'a job is a path to a better job' platitude.

specificity.statement: The number of people on the jobseeker benefit is, unfortunately, expected to increase in the coming months due to the challenging economic circumstances: jobseeker benefit recipients are expected to peak at 198,500 in January 2025.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure and date.

specificity.statement: That’s why the Government is amending the Building Act to remove artificial barriers to the use of building products from overseas by recognising overseas building product standards from trusted jurisdictions and requiring building consent authorities to accept products that are equivalent to, or better than, those already in use in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (Building Act amendment, recognition of overseas standards, mandating BCAs accept equivalent products).

specificity.statement: The cost of building a house has increased by 41 percent in the last five years, and it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than Australia.
specificity.explanation: Two precise comparative figures with timeframe.

specificity.statement: First of all, we’re going to see a lot more data. This Government’s view is that we should tell the people and trust the people, rather than try and obscure the facts from them. We’ll be rolling out a communications plan to improve awareness of the importance of attendance from term 2 this year onwards. We’ll also be updating the public health guidance to help schools and parents decide if a student is well enough to attend.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions (communications plan from term 2, updated public health guidance) but limited detail on scale or mechanism.

specificity.statement: from the start of next year, we’ll be mandating daily attendance data to be reported by all schools
specificity.explanation: Concrete measure (mandatory daily attendance reporting) with a timeframe (start of next year).

specificity.statement: actually, the Ministry of Education has been upgrading its IT software so that the student management systems from the school can automatically push the data each day. This is an object lesson for the Labour Party. You see, we’re actually going to able to do more with less money, using innovation and technology.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (automated daily data push from school management systems).

specificity.statement: Resources will play a critical role in our export-led recovery, and as part of my strategy as the climate-smart mining Minister, I have announced that settings will be developed to enable investors and other stakeholders to explore the potential of naturally occurring hydrogen as a contribution to lessening our reliance on overseas hydrocarbon fuels, boosting our resilience, and ensuring that there is a suitable framework enabling people to find this potential sooner rather than later.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete focus (natural hydrogen settings) but 'settings will be developed' leaves the mechanism and timing vague.

specificity.statement: Not only will a critical-minerals list and associated strategies be delivered, not only will studies be completed, but we will ensure, where people want to invest in the minerals sector in New Zealand, there is certainty and no more of this nonsense, such as no more mining on Department of Conservation land.
specificity.explanation: Names deliverables (critical-minerals list, strategies, ending the DOC-land mining ban) but no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: we are telling global investors, we are telling Kiwi investors, our country is moving from “cancel economics” to “can-do economics”. We are open for business. We will have a legislative framework that rewards risk taking, rewards investment, and restores the place of the extractive sector to a place of pride that it enjoyed with the development, originally, of the party sitting on the other side of the House.
specificity.explanation: Sloganistic; promises a 'framework' with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: What we will have are targets that reduce the number of children and whānau in emergency housing. We’ve established that target and announced it yesterday through the Prime Minister, rather than sitting by and talking about how we’re going to help whānau Māori in emergency housing and to see those numbers go up by several hundred.
specificity.explanation: References an established target but gives no figure for it here.

specificity.statement: At the core, these arrangements will recognise the mountains within the national park as a legal personality, to be named Te Kāhui Tupua. The land of Egmont National Park will also be vested in Te Kāhui Tupua. Once the land is owned by Te Kāhui Tupua, the national park will be renamed Te Papa-Kura-o-Taranaki—the highly regarded and treasured lands of Taranaki. The highest mountain will also be granted a name change to a sole te reo name, Taranaki maunga.
specificity.explanation: Detailed, concrete description of the legal arrangements: legal personality, vesting, specific new names.

specificity.statement: Taranaki maunga was first confiscated in 1865 by the Crown as a punishment for the so-called rebellion of Māori during the Land Wars.
specificity.explanation: Names the year, actor, and historical context.

specificity.statement: ACT supports historical Treaty settlements and has traditionally supported the personhood of historical and culturally significant bodies such as Te Awa Tupua—the Whanganui River.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete precedent (Te Awa Tupua / Whanganui River) supporting the position.

specificity.statement: I acknowledge the horrendous injustices when in 1865, the Crown unfairly punished Māori by confiscating 1.2 million acres of Taranaki land, including Taranaki maunga.
specificity.explanation: Names the year and the precise area confiscated.

strength.explanation: Announcement of intent to develop settings; no delivery.

strength.explanation: Forward commitments stated; delivery not yet demonstrated.

charisma.statement: We’re not here to manage decline; we’re here to get things done and deliver better outcomes.
charisma.explanation: Confident rallying line for his own side; no attempt to build cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: Again, what I’d say to you is there is no place for racism in New Zealand—period—and whether you are a new New Zealander or you’ve been here for some time, the same standard holds for everybody.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'same standard for everybody' framing, but sidesteps the substance rather than bringing people along on it.

charisma.statement: we are telling global investors, we are telling Kiwi investors, our country is moving from “cancel economics” to “can-do economics”. We are open for business. We will have a legislative framework that rewards risk taking, rewards investment, and restores the place of the extractive sector to a place of pride that it enjoyed with the development, originally, of the party sitting on the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Punchy 'can-do economics' rallying rhetoric aimed at his own side and investors; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This Parliament will continue a bipartisan effort towards Treaty negotiations. Given the significance of this bill for all New Zealand, it is my honour to begin today’s reading.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly frames Treaty settlements as a shared, bipartisan, all-of-New-Zealand endeavour — unifying and consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge the Hon Chris Finlayson, who signed the terms of negotiation with Ngā Iwi o Taranaki in 2017 and began the process of negotiation. I also acknowledge my immediate predecessor, the Hon Andrew Little, who concluded negotiations last year, after six years of discussion.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits both a National and a Labour predecessor, reaching across party lines.

charisma.statement: actions are important, so we now need to take what is in that agreement and put it into action—a great wero for Tama Potaka.
charisma.explanation: Constructive cross-bench challenge framed positively as a 'wero' (challenge) to the Minister, rather than an attack.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what we are doing is we’re making sure we rebuild this economy, we restore law and order, and we deliver better health and education for Māori and non-Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he is doing to regain the trust of the Iwi Chairs Forum after their withdrawal; he recites generic priorities and never addresses trust or the Forum.

forthrightness.statement: I disagree completely. We may disagree with the previous administration and the way they went about things, but we are here to make sure we improve outcomes for Māori, because you can talk about it, as the previous Government did, but outcomes for Māori went backwards under the last six years across a range of measures. We’re saying enough is enough, and I look forward to that member’s support for many of the programmes that we have.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the impact of specific policies (Fast-track, Treaty principles bill, 7AA, Māori wards, Māori Health Authority) on iwi mistrust; he engages none of them and pivots to attacking the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: Again, what I’d say to you is there is no place for racism in New Zealand—period—and whether you are a new New Zealander or you’ve been here for some time, the same standard holds for everybody.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to choose between the justice Minister's view and the report's documented findings on colonial racism; he restates a general principle without taking a side.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it’s something that we’ve talked about in Opposition for some time, it’s something that we’ve campaigned on, and all we’re saying is we’re making sure we’ve got complementary work going on to make sure we have the latest knowledge around methane science. From there, we can set targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government is commissioning a second review when a legally required independent expert review already exists; he never addresses the duplication.

forthrightness.statement: That’s not what we’re saying. What we’re saying is we’re reviewing the science base on methane to make sure we do that. I’d just say to the member I really look forward to her adjusting the Green Party website to come out in support of our GE policy so that we can actually drive emissions down.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Climate Change Commission that reducing methane targets shifts the burden to households and businesses; he denies the premise and pivots to a jibe about the Greens' GE position.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I said, we have an ambitious Government, and that is fantastic because what we observed over the last six years was a Government that spent more, borrowed more, taxed more, and delivered worse outcomes. Your Government had six years. You did very little; you failed at it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the straightforward question of whether the truancy announcement was approved by Cabinet; gives no answer and attacks the previous Government instead (Hipkins raised a point of order on exactly this).

forthrightness.statement: No. Again, what the Minister announced was that was our proposal, and there’s more work to be done on that, and that will come towards Cabinet in due course.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the traffic light system details were approved by Cabinet; he answers directly ('No') and explains the status.

forthrightness.statement: I mean, I reject the premise of the question. We have a fantastic plan to tackle school attendance in New Zealand—something the previous administration, the previous Minister for 5½ years, didn’t seem to care about.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Simmonds was reprimanded but Seymour was not for announcing un-approved decisions; he rejects the premise and changes subject without addressing the asymmetry.

forthrightness.statement: The Suicide Prevention Office is not being considered for closure.
forthrightness.explanation: After repeated evasions, gives a direct flat denial to the question of whether the Office was being considered for closure.

forthrightness.statement: I’d just say to you that the Government supports mining on a responsible basis, and there’s a process under way.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project will not be listed in the Fast-track Approvals Bill; he gives no guarantee and offers a generic line.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely. That is a Minister that is determined to grow this country, to do the right thing by this country, who thinks deeply about where it’s going, and he has my total backing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in Shane Jones's impartiality across his overlapping resources/regional-development/fisheries portfolios; affirms confidence but does not address the conflict-of-interest concern.

forthrightness.statement: What our fiscal intentions and objectives are, are to return to surplus; to get debt heading down as a percentage of GDP, rather than going up, as it has been over the past five years; and to reduce Government spending as a proportion of the overall economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the patsy question about her fiscal-policy announcements with the three stated objectives.

forthrightness.statement: Well, if the member had actually looked at her own questions, she asked whether all of this would be subject to final Cabinet approval. Well, Cabinet has not given final approval to the Budget yet.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers (Cabinet has not yet approved the Budget) but deflects via the member's question wording rather than addressing whether vote Ministers approve savings plans beforehand.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government is focused on reducing the number of job seekers by 50,000, and we believe that a job is better than no job and that a job is a path to a better job.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to ensuring the 50,000 get jobs paying at least a living wage that match their skills; she restates the target and a slogan, not addressing job quality at all.

forthrightness.statement: The number of people on the jobseeker benefit is, unfortunately, expected to increase in the coming months due to the challenging economic circumstances: jobseeker benefit recipients are expected to peak at 198,500 in January 2025.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes numbers will rise short-term despite her own reduction target, rather than dodging the unfavourable forecast.

forthrightness.statement: As the Minister of Climate Change, I have not received advice from officials saying the science of methane’s impact on climate change is settled. However, I do meet with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, who shares their reports with me on a regular basis. This Government has commissioned a review to ensure that we have the latest science as part of our coalition agreement.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the primary question about advice received and explains the review's basis.

forthrightness.statement: The review that the member is citing was undertaken nearly five years ago. It is an imperative for this coalition Government to use the latest science available, and that’s what our review will undertake.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the timing point but sidesteps the substance of the chief economist's claim that the science is already comprehensively done.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not going to pre-empt a review that hasn’t actually started yet, but what I can be clear about is this review will be comprehensive, it will have integrity, and the results, once received, will be in addition to the work undertaken by the Climate Change Commission, and we’ll go from there.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee any target/Act changes would proceed by cross-party consensus as before; he declines to commit, citing that the review hasn't started.

forthrightness.statement: Once again, the review hasn’t actually been started yet, so I am unable to make comments in regard to what that review will indicate. But what is clear is that all industries within this country need to play their part in order to reduce emissions, to enable us to hit our targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out using the review to justify less ambitious targets than the Paris commitment; he declines to rule it out, deferring to the un-started review.

forthrightness.statement: As you have heard through the last few months, we are ruthlessly focused on delivering on the genuine needs of Māori: education, health, and housing, particularly the over 1,500 Māori whānau who are living in the emergency housing disaster that the malfeasance of the previous Government created.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he will deliver more homes for Māori having disestablished the associate Māori housing role; he restates focus areas without addressing the disestablished role.

forthrightness.statement: What we will have are targets that reduce the number of children and whānau in emergency housing. We’ve established that target and announced it yesterday through the Prime Minister, rather than sitting by and talking about how we’re going to help whānau Māori in emergency housing and to see those numbers go up by several hundred.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will match the previous Government's $750m targeted Māori housing investment; he pivots to the emergency-housing target and never addresses the funding.

forthrightness.statement: We are absolutely committed to delivering on the genuine needs of all New Zealanders, to ensure that there are sufficient houses to accommodate people, unlike the previous Government, which curated a situation where there are now five times as many whānau on the social housing wait-list as there was when they started.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Kāinga Ora that it will keep increasing public housing if funded; he gives a generic commitment and attacks the prior record instead.

forthrightness.statement: As we are all aware, we have inherited a significant fiscal cliff, left behind for us by the previous Government. But we are absolutely committed to actually delivering on the housing needs of Māori and all New Zealanders, unlike the development aspirations of the previous Ministers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Kāinga Ora chair that up to 10,000 houses may need to be sold without funding past 2025; he does not engage with the figure and pivots to a 'fiscal cliff' line.

veracity.statement: I disagree completely. We may disagree with the previous administration and the way they went about things, but we are here to make sure we improve outcomes for Māori, because you can talk about it, as the previous Government did, but outcomes for Māori went backwards under the last six years across a range of measures. We’re saying enough is enough, and I look forward to that member’s support for many of the programmes that we have.
veracity.explanation: "Outcomes for Māori went backwards under the last six years across a range of measures" is selective — some Māori indicators improved, others worsened; the unspecified "range" overstates a mixed record.

veracity.statement: We can’t just shut down the world’s best farmers and send agricultural production offshore, making global greenhouse gas emissions worse in the process. We believe “no additional warming” is a fair basis for methane targets in particular.
veracity.explanation: 'World's best farmers' is hyperbole; the leakage point is partly defensible but presented without quantification.

veracity.statement: It is an absolute travesty that only 47 percent of our kids go to school regularly in this country—a legacy of the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: The ~47% regular-attendance figure is broadly in line with 2022–23 data, but attendance decline is driven heavily by COVID/illness, so pinning it solely on the previous Government is misleading.

veracity.statement: Well, the half-year update, in December, forecast that core Crown spending in the current 2023-24 financial year will be 33.4 percent of GDP. Now, to put that in context, core Crown spending in 2018-19—just five years ago—was only 28 percent of GDP. Now, clearly, COVID disruptions were a factor in this increase, but the crucial thing is that unlike in other countries, there was no attempt to bring Government spending back down again after the temporary disruption passed.
veracity.explanation: The 33.4% and 28% core-Crown-spending figures align with HYEFU/Treasury data; the 'no attempt to bring spending down' framing is contestable but she concedes COVID as a factor.

veracity.statement: I particularly stand by my statement that hard-working Kiwis deserve personal income tax relief. Given that they’ve been waiting 14 years for it, the coalition Government will be delighted to deliver it to them in the Budget in May.
veracity.explanation: 'Waiting 14 years' is rhetorical — tax thresholds had not been indexed, but to say there was no relief at all overstates it.

We now have almost 190,000 people in New Zealand receiving the jobseeker benefit, and that’s approximately the size of Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: The ~190,000 jobseeker figure and the rise under the previous Government are broadly accurate; the Hamilton-size analogy is apt.

For a jobseeker benefit, they are estimated to spend, on average, 13 future years on welfare. For those who move on to welfare under the age of 25, they are forecast to spend 19 future years on main benefit.
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific figures to a named, dated actuarial source (Taylor Fry); consistent with that valuation's methodology.

veracity.statement: The cost of building a house has increased by 41 percent in the last five years, and it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than Australia.
veracity.explanation: Both figures are in line with widely cited construction-cost and trans-Tasman comparison data from the period.

veracity.statement: actually, the Ministry of Education has been upgrading its IT software so that the student management systems from the school can automatically push the data each day. This is an object lesson for the Labour Party. You see, we’re actually going to able to do more with less money, using innovation and technology.
veracity.explanation: Plausible factual claim about IT upgrades, but unverified and paired with the rhetorical 'do more with less' assertion.

However, I do meet with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, who shares their reports with me on a regular basis. This Government has commissioned a review to ensure that we have the latest science as part of our coalition agreement.
veracity.explanation: Claim about not receiving 'settled science' advice is plausible but contestable given the existing expert review the Greens cited.

veracity.statement: The review that the member is citing was undertaken nearly five years ago. It is an imperative for this coalition Government to use the latest science available, and that’s what our review will undertake.
veracity.explanation: The 'nearly five years ago' timing of the cited work is roughly right, but the implication that it is therefore outdated is an inference, not established.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge the horrendous injustices when in 1865, the Crown unfairly punished Māori by confiscating 1.2 million acres of Taranaki land, including Taranaki maunga.

civility.statement: I hope that this is a demonstration of how we can continue to work effectively to review our position on a range of issues and work cooperatively across the House to come up with sensible solutions.

charisma.statement: We had a whole lot of things when the Labour Party was part of the Government which were to incentivise this, and I'd urge the new Government to keep on thinking about new incentives, because some of those incentives have been taken away because of recent changes.
charisma.explanation: Constructively urges the incoming government to continue a policy direction — cross-party appeal rather than attack.

charisma.statement: It's something I can't influence in the same way, but I can encourage all the parties to think very seriously about the value of that garden to the community.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to all parties; seeks common ground rather than confrontation.

charisma.statement: How do we work together across the House?
charisma.explanation: Explicit, inclusive invitation to cross-party cooperation on the issue.

charisma.statement: I hope that this is a demonstration of how we can continue to work effectively to review our position on a range of issues and work cooperatively across the House to come up with sensible solutions.

charisma.statement: I do acknowledge Takutai Tarsh Kemp's speech in terms of the experience and the work that places like Manurewa Marae have, trying to fill those gaps... I want to acknowledge that the member Casey Costello has just also run us through some of the controls.

divination.statement: A Government that has given tax breaks to landlords, that's mislaid their cast-iron promise to fund our hospital, and that's repealed three waters, leading to looming massive rises to rates.

divination.statement: This is just going to allow more things to come—increased crime. It's another avenue for the ram raids to happen... It's going to increase crime, it's going to increase youth offending.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased crime, ram raids and youth offending from the reclassification; contested by evidence that meth supply has shifted away from pseudoephedrine, and timeframe is unstated.

divination.statement: I don't wish for any harm to come to anyone, but if there are ram raids, then that is on his shoulders.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction of ram raids resulting from the storage decision; contested and timeframe-free.

authenticity.statement: So myself and the then Minister Jan Tinetti visited the school and engaged heavily with the Ministry of Education, and we actually got that rebuild back on track.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with a record of advocacy for the school; the claimed action matches the stated commitment, unverified externally.

authenticity.statement: On the daily, in my mahi, when I was the CEO of Manurewa Marae, a lot of these families visited our marae for help. They need kai. They need housing. They need drug awareness programmes.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds her opposition in her own prior frontline record at Manurewa Marae; words consistent with her stated work.

authenticity.statement: What the Greens are supporting in this bill is the consistency with taking a harm reduction approach, and consistency with previous positions that we have held.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly frames the vote as consistent with the party's long-held harm-reduction stance; plausible and aligned with the Greens' record.

specificity.statement: especially our announcement of new targets for at least 80 percent of students regularly attending school and 80 percent of year 8 students at or above the expected curriculum level for their age in reading, writing, and maths
specificity.explanation: Names concrete percentage targets and the specific domains (reading, writing, maths), though no timeframe.

specificity.statement: Finally we have a Government that’s getting New Zealand back on track, getting our kids back to school, and making sure they’re going to do well.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level claim with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Well, what I can say to that member is that we finally have a Government that can walk and chew gum at the same time.
