rigor.statement: every electricity generator in the country will tell you that unless you do planning reform, none of those decarbonisation goals are achievable
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority plus 'every'/'none' absolutes — sweeping claim presented without specific evidence.

rigor.statement: One thing in and of itself won’t fix our productivity disease. One thing by itself won’t, but 50 things cumulatively and collectively will make a difference.
rigor.explanation: Sensible point that productivity has many contributing factors rather than a single fix.

rigor.statement: We know that there’s 3 megatonnes out of emissions budget 2, which is 37 percent of all emissions that need to come from energy and industry sector in emissions budget 2 alone. There’s another 4 megatonnes in emissions budget 3, which is 22 percent
rigor.explanation: Uses quantified gaps to press the case that cancelling GIDI leaves measurable holes.

rigor.statement: we also know that this Government has received advice that simply doubling renewable electricity is insufficient to meet the targets that have been set.
rigor.explanation: Cites received advice to challenge reliance on a single supply-side measure.

rigor.statement: When is she going to address the structural problems that are predicted to go out to 2060—that are sitting in the briefing to the incoming Minister that is now her responsibility?
rigor.explanation: Anchors the challenge in long-run fiscal projections from the official briefing rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: if you could tax your way to prosperity, her side would’ve won the Cold War
rigor.explanation: False analogy/strawman equating a capital gains tax with Cold War-era command economies.

rigor.statement: They had $2 billion they started with, then they came back to the Government for another $1.2 billion, and they used it to go out and bid up the price of building materials, of land, of project managers, of builders.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim about price effects asserted without evidence; selectively framed.

rigor.statement: Sydney, Melbourne—they’ve all had a capital gains tax and they’ve all had housing at 10 times income, because it doesn’t work.
rigor.explanation: Correlation-as-causation — infers CGT 'doesn't work' from high prices in CGT cities, ignoring supply and other drivers.

rigor.statement: housing is about supply and demand. If there are not enough houses for the number of people, you get a shortage and the price rises because demand outstrips supply
rigor.explanation: Sound basic supply-demand reasoning, though it treats a single factor as the whole explanation for housing costs.

rigor.statement: I think the model under the prior Government was to write blank cheques and throw them over the fence.
rigor.explanation: Slogan-like characterisation ('blank cheques over the fence') offered in place of evidence.

charisma.statement: My debate is with your arguments and not with your capability, and I look forward to continuing to have debates about the argument.
charisma.explanation: De-escalating, respectful gesture toward an opponent that lowers the temperature of the exchange.

charisma.statement: There is nothing dirty about working people wanting a bit more money to pay for the swimming lessons, a bit more money so they can afford a pack of chocolate biscuits, a little bit more money so they don’t need to worry about whether they can afford shoes for their kids this winter.
charisma.explanation: Vivid, relatable rhetoric — rhetorically effective, but aimed at rallying its own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I would just remind the Minister of Finance that in the Finance and Expenditure Committee, we worked quite constructively across the aisle and quite collaboratively on a number of issues.
charisma.explanation: Invokes shared cross-party work to build a bridge after taking offence — consensus-seeking rather than combative.

charisma.statement: I just make the point to the member that it is possible to protect the environment and the values that underpin the environment at the same time as expediting the consent of projects that we need.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the environmental concern of opponents and frames a both/and position, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: any change to our domestic targets would require legislative change in terms of what I think is a piece of legislation this House can be proud of in the multipartisan way in which we came to setting those targets
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the cross-party origins of the climate targets, framing them as a shared achievement.

charisma.statement: this Government says to the next generation, “We’re going to solve the problems by building for everyone.”—building more infrastructure, building more renewable energy, building new homes.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'for everyone' framing with a forward-looking vision, though delivered as a contrast against opponents.

veracity.statement: What we saw over the past six years was an alternative approach, which saw Government spending increase 80 percent in just six years and yet didn’t see value delivered for those extra dollars.
veracity.explanation: Core Crown spending did rise substantially over the period, but 80% appears overstated in nominal terms and the 'no value' claim is contestable.

veracity.statement: the $1.2 billion—am I correct, members?—that was invested on the three waters reform programme that went absolutely nowhere; the tens of millions of dollars that were wasted on a failed TVNZ-RNZ merger; the more than $100 million that was spent on an Auckland light rail fantasy that was dead on arrival
veracity.explanation: Figures are in a defensible ballpark, but 'went absolutely nowhere'/'fantasy' are loaded characterisations that overstate.

veracity.statement: we have been advised that we are still on track to achieve the emission reduction for the first emission reduction plan, and we are soon to consult on our plan for the second emission-reduction period.
veracity.explanation: Emissions budget 1 being on track was broadly consistent with advice at the time; unverifiable in detail from the text.

veracity.statement: the largest of which, the one that that member is so proud of, was handing out massive cheques to profitable private, often multinational, companies
veracity.explanation: GIDI did fund decarbonisation by firms, but 'massive cheques to multinationals' selectively frames a co-funding scheme.

veracity.statement: The Treasury”, here on page 9—and I quote—“has identified slow productivity growth as one of New Zealand’s long-term economic performance challenges.
veracity.explanation: Accurately conveys a well-established Treasury position on NZ's productivity challenge.

veracity.statement: That showed us that the top 311 families in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of average New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Closely matches the IRD high-wealth individuals report's headline finding on effective tax rates.

veracity.statement: we’re also an outlier amongst the OECD for not having a capital gains tax, stamp duty, wealth tax, or otherwise
veracity.explanation: NZ is indeed unusual in the OECD for lacking a general CGT; 'outlier' broadly fair though some members also lack certain capital taxes.

veracity.statement: it, basically, settled on the conclusion that the major issue that is driving school non-attendance in this country is inequality and poverty.
veracity.explanation: Reflects a real finding of the inquiry, though 'the major issue' simplifies a multi-factor conclusion.

veracity.statement: Take a wind farm, for example: two years to build it; 7-10 years to consent it.
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with known consenting delays, though the specific years are an illustrative range.

veracity.statement: The amount of time it takes to get a consent doubled in a five-year period from 2014 to 2019.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with commonly cited RMA processing-time data, but the precise doubling is unverified here.

veracity.statement: Port of Tauranga, for example, is right now engaged in a lengthy battle to add another berth to its existing port infrastructure when 60 percent of New Zealand’s exports by value go through the Port of Tauranga.
veracity.explanation: Tauranga is NZ's largest port, but '60 percent of exports by value' appears overstated against its actual trade share.

veracity.statement: One thing in and of itself won’t fix our productivity disease. One thing by itself won’t, but 50 things cumulatively and collectively will make a difference.
veracity.explanation: NZ's long-running productivity lag is well documented, though 'disease' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: We know that there’s 3 megatonnes out of emissions budget 2, which is 37 percent of all emissions that need to come from energy and industry sector in emissions budget 2 alone. There’s another 4 megatonnes in emissions budget 3, which is 22 percent
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the order of magnitude of the relevant emissions budgets, though unverified in detail here.

veracity.statement: we also know that this Government has received advice that simply doubling renewable electricity is insufficient to meet the targets that have been set.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Climate Change Commission advice that the ETS/supply measures alone are insufficient; not independently confirmed in the text.

veracity.statement: we are committed to about $30 billion of expenditure on health every year. That’s what health costs us every year. Education costs us about $20 billion a year. Now, here’s the thing, New Zealand super costs us about $95 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Health (~$30b) is roughly right, but NZ Super costs around $20–22b a year, not $95b — a large factual error.

veracity.statement: the Minister has promised tax cuts, but personal income tax delivers about 52 percent of our tax revenue at the moment
veracity.explanation: Personal income tax is roughly half of core Crown tax revenue, so the figure is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: They had $2 billion they started with, then they came back to the Government for another $1.2 billion, and they used it to go out and bid up the price of building materials, of land, of project managers, of builders.
veracity.explanation: Funding figures are loosely in range, but the claim that the spend pushed up housing/input prices is contestable and one-sided.

veracity.statement: Sydney, Melbourne—they’ve all had a capital gains tax and they’ve all had housing at 10 times income, because it doesn’t work.
veracity.explanation: Those cities do have high price-to-income ratios, but the list mixes jurisdictions (e.g. Hong Kong's CGT regime) and the causal claim is unsupported.

veracity.statement: Emissions budget 1 is pretty much in order and on track. Emissions budget 2 has risks in regards to delivery, and that is something that we are monitoring through.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the prevailing assessment that EB1 was on track while EB2 carried delivery risk.

divination.statement: every electricity generator in the country will tell you that unless you do planning reform, none of those decarbonisation goals are achievable
divination.explanation: Prediction that decarbonisation goals are unachievable without planning reform; directionally plausible but stated as a certainty.

veracity.statement: The context was the brutal invasion of the Waikato, the shameless invasion, where Cameron's troops bypassed the warriors and went to Rangiaowhia and killed children and women and elderly people, and two days after that atrocity, Rewi Maniapoto's house was looted and burnt.
veracity.explanation: Historical claims about the Rangiaowhia attack and the looting/burning of Rewi Maniapoto's house are broadly consistent with the documented record of the Waikato invasion.

veracity.statement: Even Governor Grey himself visited in 1849, and he said, “Never have I seen a more thriving and contented population in any part of the world.” And the invasion of the Waikato was explicitly to take that abundance from Māori.
veracity.explanation: The Grey quote and the economic context of the prosperous Waikato are consistent with the historical record.

veracity.statement: Within 10 days of the attack—on that day of “terrible savagery”, as O’Sullivan calls it—Kihikihi was divided up by the military surveyors into acreages to be given to the soldiers who committed the atrocities.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the documented post-invasion confiscation and military settlement of the Waikato; attributes a characterisation to a named source.

veracity.statement: Three hundred people were present at Ō-Rākau pā, which was encircled by 1,400 British soldiers. The battle lasted for three days, and it has been estimated that more than half of the pā’s occupants were killed. Seventeen British soldiers were also killed in the battle.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with standard historical accounts of Ō-Rākau.

veracity.statement: The battle of Ō-Rākau was a tragedy—a tragedy born out of misunderstanding, mistrust, a clash of conflicting world views.
veracity.explanation: Framing the battle as mutual 'misunderstanding' omits the documented fact that it followed a deliberate Crown invasion and confiscation; true in part but missing context that changes its meaning.

veracity.statement: Three hundred people to defend Ō-Rākau against 1,500 soldiers. This war lasted over three days and it was the confiscation of 12,000 square kilometres of land.
veracity.explanation: Largely accurate, though the '1,500 soldiers' figure is higher than the ~1,400 cited by other speakers; the broader Waikato confiscation figure is roughly right.

veracity.statement: I vividly remember 10 years ago at the 150-year commemoration at Ō-Rākau. I was 11 years old, standing, doing the haka, as Prime Minister at the time, John Key, arrived.
veracity.explanation: A checkable personal/historical recollection with no apparent distortion.

veracity.statement: The battle of Ō-Rākau was, of course, a bloody battle—300 versus 1,400, with about 150 casualties from the pā. It was the final stand for the Waikato Wars.
veracity.explanation: Figures and characterisation as the final Waikato battle match the historical record.

veracity.statement: Rewi Maniapoto, a great leader, a warrior, whose father signed the Treaty—who signed the Treaty because they believed that their rights and their values would be upheld, and they weren’t.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the general historical understanding that Treaty signatories expected protections that were not honoured; the specific paternal-signature detail is plausible but harder to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: this legislation will give effect to certain provisions of the deed of agreements relating to the Ō-Rākau site, dated 31 October 2023, when the Crown and Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato signed this deed... this bill enables the record of title for the Ō-Rākau site to be held in the names of the ancestors who fought at this battle
veracity.explanation: An accurate, checkable description of the bill's content and the underlying deed.

veracity.statement: The Government accounts for 2022-23 showed an increase of revenue to $153 billion, but it also showed an increase in expenditure from $151 billion to $161.8 billion... the operating balance before gains and losses... showed a $9.4 billion deficit, which is $2.5 billion larger than the Budget had projected.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures from the official Government accounts, presented without evident distortion.

veracity.statement: It’s costing people with higher interest rates now than they would have needed to be, had the Reserve Bank not continued to have one foot on the accelerator and the other one on the brake. I think that was pretty poor management on their part
veracity.explanation: A plausible counterfactual claim about rate costs that cannot be definitively verified.

veracity.statement: they oversaw a period of some of the highest inflation we have seen in a generation, which delivered, in substantive terms, a cost of living crisis which saw New Zealanders’ real purchasing power eroded, thereby grossly undermining their wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: Inflation was indeed historically high and eroded purchasing power, though the framing omits the global drivers of that inflation.

veracity.statement: oversaw the magnificent contribution of increasing Government spending by 80 percent. Yet I am still to find a New Zealander who can point, for me, to an area of public life that they thought got 80 percent better.
veracity.explanation: The '80 percent' figure is a contested headline number whose baseline and timeframe are unstated, making it misleading as presented.

specificity.statement: The context was the brutal invasion of the Waikato, the shameless invasion, where Cameron's troops bypassed the warriors and went to Rangiaowhia and killed children and women and elderly people, and two days after that atrocity, Rewi Maniapoto's house was looted and burnt.
specificity.explanation: Names the commander, specific places, and the sequence and timing of events.

specificity.statement: Even Governor Grey himself visited in 1849, and he said, “Never have I seen a more thriving and contented population in any part of the world.” And the invasion of the Waikato was explicitly to take that abundance from Māori.
specificity.explanation: Cites a date and a sourced quotation to support the claim.

specificity.statement: Within 10 days of the attack—on that day of “terrible savagery”, as O’Sullivan calls it—Kihikihi was divided up by the military surveyors into acreages to be given to the soldiers who committed the atrocities.
specificity.explanation: Names a place, a timeframe ('within 10 days'), and the mechanism (military surveyors dividing land for soldiers).

specificity.statement: Three hundred people were present at Ō-Rākau pā, which was encircled by 1,400 British soldiers. The battle lasted for three days, and it has been estimated that more than half of the pā’s occupants were killed. Seventeen British soldiers were also killed in the battle.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete numbers: defenders, attackers, duration, casualties on both sides.

specificity.statement: Let us strive to build a future where the lessons of history serve as a beacon of hope, guiding us towards a more inclusive society. Let us honour the memory of those who fought and fell on both sides of the conflict, recognising that their sacrifices have helped shape this fabric of our nation.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational framing with no concrete mechanism or commitment.

specificity.statement: Three hundred people to defend Ō-Rākau against 1,500 soldiers. This war lasted over three days and it was the confiscation of 12,000 square kilometres of land.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers for defenders, attackers, duration, and land confiscated.

specificity.statement: I vividly remember 10 years ago at the 150-year commemoration at Ō-Rākau. I was 11 years old, standing, doing the haka, as Prime Minister at the time, John Key, arrived.
specificity.explanation: Specific personal detail anchored to a dated event and a named person.

specificity.statement: The battle of Ō-Rākau was, of course, a bloody battle—300 versus 1,400, with about 150 casualties from the pā. It was the final stand for the Waikato Wars.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers for combatants and casualties.

specificity.statement: I would encourage members of the audience to submit on this bill, so that myself and other members from across the House can learn your stories and your tūpuna stories... Of course, we want this bill to go as quickly through the House as possible, but we also want to hear from you.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (submitting to select committee) but timing is loose ('very shortly').

specificity.statement: this legislation will give effect to certain provisions of the deed of agreements relating to the Ō-Rākau site, dated 31 October 2023, when the Crown and Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato signed this deed... this bill enables the record of title for the Ō-Rākau site to be held in the names of the ancestors who fought at this battle
specificity.explanation: Names the deed, its date, the parties, and the precise legal mechanism (title held in ancestors' names).

specificity.statement: History matters profoundly, and that’s why this bill is so important. It ensures through legislation that the history of Ō-Rākau will also be remembered. It will be a living history, and through the innovation of placing the title in the name of your tīpuna, this history will always speak from the source.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concrete mechanism (vesting title in tīpuna names) though the broader claims stay general.

specificity.statement: The Government accounts for 2022-23 showed an increase of revenue to $153 billion, but it also showed an increase in expenditure from $151 billion to $161.8 billion... the operating balance before gains and losses... showed a $9.4 billion deficit, which is $2.5 billion larger than the Budget had projected.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures for revenue, expenditure, deficit, and the variance from Budget projections.

specificity.statement: The official cash rate is raising interest rates to slow the economy down, whereas the funding for lending programme is giving banks cheaper access to money, and, effectively, having the opposite effect of the OCR, and we wondered about the wisdom of that.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific instruments (OCR, funding for lending) and explains their opposing mechanisms.

specificity.statement: given that the Budget Policy Statement’s wellbeing objectives have changed... what is her plan for ensuring that there is robust quantitative evidence; what are the measures she will be using to compare to a previous measure of wellbeing; and what type of statistics will she be looking for to ensure the robustness of that evidence?
specificity.explanation: A focused, multi-part question naming the specific report, objectives, and the kind of evidence sought.

specificity.statement: I am proud to be part of a Government and to be a Minister of Finance who is going to cut that crap and focus on results, and isn’t going to focus on pages and pages of reports about wellbeing, because, frankly, it was just talk. We’re going to walk the walk.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level ('focus on results', 'walk the walk') with no measure, metric, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: oversaw the magnificent contribution of increasing Government spending by 80 percent. Yet I am still to find a New Zealander who can point, for me, to an area of public life that they thought got 80 percent better.
specificity.explanation: Offers a figure but no breakdown or comparator for the claimed spending increase.

specificity.statement: you can stamp your Budget with the word “wellbeing” as nicely as you like, and you can write as many pages of verbiage about wellbeing as you like, but if you don’t deliver low, stable inflation, fair tax, and effective spending, then none of that is worth the paper that it is written on.
specificity.explanation: Names three desired outcomes (low inflation, fair tax, effective spending) but no measures or targets.

civility.statement: The context was the brutal invasion of the Waikato, the shameless invasion, where Cameron's troops bypassed the warriors and went to Rangiaowhia and killed children and women and elderly people, and two days after that atrocity, Rewi Maniapoto's house was looted and burnt.
civility.explanation: Charged language ('shameless invasion', 'atrocity') but directed at documented historical actions of Crown forces, not a present opponent.

civility.statement: There is no dignity for the Crown. There is nothing, no morsel of honour, but only shame for the Crown in this battle—and for Cameron and for Governor Grey and for von Tempsky, that ruthless murderer.
civility.explanation: 'Ruthless murderer' is a personal denunciation; aimed at a historical figure but rhetorically heavy and sweeping.

civility.statement: But I do worry when I hear backwards steps, sometimes, from this coalition Government in terms of their commitment to the history of this country.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's direction but framed as policy concern, not personal attack.

civility.statement: when I hear people talking about balancing history, sometimes that sounds to me like they don’t want to talk about our history
civility.explanation: Imputes a motive to unnamed others but stays on the substance of how history is taught.

civility.statement: Shane Jones runs away from that—he’s too busy doing his fast-track stuff.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at a named colleague ('runs away') rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: He’s in the wrong bloody party, but he’s still our Minister—he’s still our Minister.
civility.explanation: Light, affectionate ribbing of a cross-bench Minister rather than a hostile attack.

civility.statement: Tēnei tangata e tū nei, nāku anō i whāngai te pūtea ki a Rangiriri kia whakakanohitia mai ai te wāhanga e rerekē ana. Horekau koutou i pōhiri i ahau kia haramai ki te kaupapa mō te huakitanga.
civility.explanation: Pairs the claim with a grievance about not being invited to the opening ('be careful, I'm back'), a self-regarding aside.

civility.statement: It’s costing people with higher interest rates now than they would have needed to be, had the Reserve Bank not continued to have one foot on the accelerator and the other one on the brake. I think that was pretty poor management on their part
civility.explanation: Criticises the Reserve Bank's management on substance rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: Given the Minister has failed to address my question about what are the quantitative evidence measures she’s going to use, I will quote from the Treasury economist Dominick Stephens
civility.explanation: Pointedly notes the non-answer but keeps the exchange on substance and cites an authority.

civility.statement: I am proud to be part of a Government and to be a Minister of Finance who is going to cut that crap and focus on results, and isn’t going to focus on pages and pages of reports about wellbeing, because, frankly, it was just talk. We’re going to walk the walk.
civility.explanation: 'Cut that crap' is dismissive and coarse rather than engaging the substance of the question.

civility.statement: they oversaw a period of some of the highest inflation we have seen in a generation, which delivered, in substantive terms, a cost of living crisis which saw New Zealanders’ real purchasing power eroded, thereby grossly undermining their wellbeing.
civility.explanation: Harsh but legitimate criticism of the previous Government's economic record.

civility.statement: oversaw the magnificent contribution of increasing Government spending by 80 percent. Yet I am still to find a New Zealander who can point, for me, to an area of public life that they thought got 80 percent better.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm ('magnificent contribution') used to belittle the opposing record.

rigor.statement: Even Governor Grey himself visited in 1849, and he said, “Never have I seen a more thriving and contented population in any part of the world.” And the invasion of the Waikato was explicitly to take that abundance from Māori.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion (the invasion targeted Māori abundance) is supported by cited evidence rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: when I hear people talking about balancing history, sometimes that sounds to me like they don’t want to talk about our history
rigor.explanation: An inference from others' rhetoric, hedged ('sounds to me'), but not evidenced beyond impression.

rigor.statement: The Government accounts for 2022-23 showed an increase of revenue to $153 billion, but it also showed an increase in expenditure from $151 billion to $161.8 billion... the operating balance before gains and losses... showed a $9.4 billion deficit, which is $2.5 billion larger than the Budget had projected.
rigor.explanation: Builds a concern about structural deficits from the cited numbers rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The official cash rate is raising interest rates to slow the economy down, whereas the funding for lending programme is giving banks cheaper access to money, and, effectively, having the opposite effect of the OCR, and we wondered about the wisdom of that.
rigor.explanation: Clearly identifies a logical tension between two policy levers operating in opposite directions.

rigor.statement: It’s costing people with higher interest rates now than they would have needed to be, had the Reserve Bank not continued to have one foot on the accelerator and the other one on the brake. I think that was pretty poor management on their part
rigor.explanation: Reasoned counterfactual following from his earlier point, though leaning on the accelerator/brake analogy.

rigor.statement: Given the Minister has failed to address my question about what are the quantitative evidence measures she’s going to use, I will quote from the Treasury economist Dominick Stephens
rigor.explanation: Reinforces the point by quoting a named Treasury economist rather than asserting.

rigor.statement: they oversaw a period of some of the highest inflation we have seen in a generation, which delivered, in substantive terms, a cost of living crisis which saw New Zealanders’ real purchasing power eroded, thereby grossly undermining their wellbeing.
rigor.explanation: Links inflation to eroded wellbeing coherently, but attributes it wholly to the previous Government without addressing external causes.

rigor.statement: oversaw the magnificent contribution of increasing Government spending by 80 percent. Yet I am still to find a New Zealander who can point, for me, to an area of public life that they thought got 80 percent better.
rigor.explanation: Rests on a rhetorical anecdote ('I am still to find a New Zealander') and an implied premise that spending should map linearly onto outcomes.

rigor.statement: you can stamp your Budget with the word “wellbeing” as nicely as you like, and you can write as many pages of verbiage about wellbeing as you like, but if you don’t deliver low, stable inflation, fair tax, and effective spending, then none of that is worth the paper that it is written on.
rigor.explanation: Makes a defensible point that outcomes matter more than documents, but caricatures the alternative as mere 'verbiage'.

charisma.statement: There is no dignity for the Crown. There is nothing, no morsel of honour, but only shame for the Crown in this battle—and for Cameron and for Governor Grey and for von Tempsky, that ruthless murderer.
charisma.explanation: Morally forceful but rallies the sympathetic rather than seeking to bring the unconvinced along.

charisma.statement: Let us strive to build a future where the lessons of history serve as a beacon of hope, guiding us towards a more inclusive society. Let us honour the memory of those who fought and fell on both sides of the conflict, recognising that their sacrifices have helped shape this fabric of our nation.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, reconciliation-oriented language reaching across the conflict's two sides.

charisma.statement: We are moving forward. We will be guided on the wise words of pāpā Tom Roa: “Utua te kino ki te pai.” [Respond to evil with goodness.]
charisma.explanation: Reconciliatory, forward-looking framing that invites a constructive response despite grievance.

charisma.statement: I would encourage members of the audience to submit on this bill, so that myself and other members from across the House can learn your stories and your tūpuna stories... Of course, we want this bill to go as quickly through the House as possible, but we also want to hear from you.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive invitation that emphasises cross-House listening and brings the public into the process.

charisma.statement: I know that these debates—well, not so much debates. These types of kōrero that we have with regards to Treaty settlements and whatnot are very bipartisan, and I acknowledge that and I’ve always acknowledged all sides during this type of debate.
charisma.explanation: Bipartisan framing that credits opponents and seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: But I do worry when I hear backwards steps, sometimes, from this coalition Government in terms of their commitment to the history of this country.
charisma.explanation: Mildly oppositional; voices concern about the other side rather than reaching toward them.

charisma.statement: So we want him to carry our dreams, carry our moemoēās, carry our kaupapa, challenge his friends, challenge the ACT Party.
charisma.explanation: Singles out the ACT Party as an adversary to be challenged rather than seeking to persuade them.

charisma.statement: Shane Jones runs away from that—he’s too busy doing his fast-track stuff.
charisma.explanation: A dismissive aside aimed at a colleague; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: He’s in the wrong bloody party, but he’s still our Minister—he’s still our Minister.
charisma.explanation: Warm cross-party embrace of Minister Potāka while gently noting the partisan divide.

charisma.statement: History matters profoundly, and that’s why this bill is so important. It ensures through legislation that the history of Ō-Rākau will also be remembered. It will be a living history, and through the innovation of placing the title in the name of your tīpuna, this history will always speak from the source.
charisma.explanation: Affirming, unifying framing of the bill's purpose.

charisma.statement: you can stamp your Budget with the word “wellbeing” as nicely as you like, and you can write as many pages of verbiage about wellbeing as you like, but if you don’t deliver low, stable inflation, fair tax, and effective spending, then none of that is worth the paper that it is written on.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective but combative and dismissive of the opposing approach rather than consensus-seeking.

authenticity.statement: I know that these debates—well, not so much debates. These types of kōrero that we have with regards to Treaty settlements and whatnot are very bipartisan, and I acknowledge that and I’ve always acknowledged all sides during this type of debate.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent personal record of acknowledging all sides; plausible and self-consistent within the speech but not independently verified.

strength.statement: Tēnei tangata e tū nei, nāku anō i whāngai te pūtea ki a Rangiriri kia whakakanohitia mai ai te wāhanga e rerekē ana. Horekau koutou i pōhiri i ahau kia haramai ki te kaupapa mō te huakitanga.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for actually providing funding to Rangiriri that was delivered (a concrete action), though the claim is self-reported.

strength.statement: I am proud to be part of a Government and to be a Minister of Finance who is going to cut that crap and focus on results, and isn’t going to focus on pages and pages of reports about wellbeing, because, frankly, it was just talk. We’re going to walk the walk.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to focus on results with no delivery yet demonstrated.

forthrightness.statement: I am proud to be part of a Government and to be a Minister of Finance who is going to cut that crap and focus on results, and isn’t going to focus on pages and pages of reports about wellbeing, because, frankly, it was just talk. We’re going to walk the walk.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked twice for the specific wellbeing measures and statistics she would use, she never names any, pivoting entirely to dismissing the previous Government's approach.

strength.statement: In particular, I stand by the Government's “phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents and students and schools
strength.explanation: Refers to a concrete policy (the school phone ban) that this Government actually implemented in its first term, not merely an aspiration.

strength.statement: We've got the Reserve Bank focused on a single target of fighting inflation, we've actually made sure we've introduced our Family Boost policy to give families that are struggling with childcare costs some support and subsidy, and we're making sure that we're going to give tax relief in this Budget for low and middle income working New Zealanders.
strength.explanation: Mix of delivered (RBNZ mandate change) and yet-to-come (Budget tax relief) actions; follow-through partial at this date.

strength.statement: Our RMA reforms have two broad objectives. The first thing is to make it easier to get things done by unlocking capacity for housing and business growth, enabling delivery of quality infrastructure; doubling renewable energy; and enabling primary sector growth and development. Our second objective is to safeguard the environment and human health, adapt to climate change, and improve regulatory quality in the resource management system.
strength.explanation: Describes a multi-phase delivery programme partly underway (a bill introduced) but with the major repeal-and-replace still a future commitment.

strength.statement: These priorities will support the Government to be laser-focused on ensuring that at least 80 percent of our kids are at curriculum by 2030.
strength.explanation: A concrete target announced but, at this stage, only foundational work begun — delivery is aspirational, not demonstrated.

strength.statement: We have committed to an additional 500 police officers. We are bringing new legislation and that will deal with violent gangs. We are bringing legislation in that will actually put tougher consequences around these violent retail, youth, and juvenile offenders.
strength.explanation: Commitments stated and legislation in train, but delivery (the 500 officers, the new laws) is still in progress at this point.

specificity.statement: In particular, I stand by the Government's “phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents and students and schools
specificity.explanation: Names a specific, identifiable policy, but offers no figures or mechanism beyond the policy label.

specificity.statement: I am proud to lead a Government that makes the changes that we need to ensure our kids are well set up for a great future, because we're getting our country back on track.
specificity.explanation: Pure slogan (“back on track”, “well set up for a great future”) with no concrete measure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to putting downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two years; we're making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws right between tenants and landlords.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy mechanisms (brightline 10→two years, interest deductibility) though without figures or timeframes for rent effects.

specificity.statement: We've got the Reserve Bank focused on a single target of fighting inflation, we've actually made sure we've introduced our Family Boost policy to give families that are struggling with childcare costs some support and subsidy, and we're making sure that we're going to give tax relief in this Budget for low and middle income working New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names specific policies (single RBNZ target, Family Boost, Budget tax relief) but without dollar amounts or thresholds.

specificity.statement: Since Labour came into power, we have seen a 33 percent increase in violent crime, resulting in an increased number of victimisations.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage and timeframe, though no absolute numbers or source.

specificity.statement: To restore law and order by getting repeat violent and sexual offenders off the streets. We're sending a message to the criminals: think twice, because if you commit a violent or sexual offence, you're going to be going away for longer.
specificity.explanation: Clear about the intended outcome (longer sentences for second/third strikes) but vague on scale or detail.

specificity.statement: At the half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more over the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Treasury), the count (nine) and a dollar threshold ($100m), and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside for future years.
specificity.explanation: Names the amount, the fiscal year, the purpose, and the exact expiry date.

specificity.statement: We will be putting in more money to improve health services in this Budget. We will be putting in more money to improve education and we will be putting in more money to strengthen law and order.
specificity.explanation: Lists spending areas (health, education, law and order) but with no amounts or measures.

specificity.statement: As we've said a number of times, both publicly and in the House, no projects have been selected for the fast-track process. Cabinet has made a decision to set up a thorough and independent panel process for the selection of projects to be included in the schedule of the bill.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete process (independent panel, select committee submissions) though without names or dates.

specificity.statement: So we're open to sensible changes, but I can tell the House two things: the core of it will remain—it will be a one-stop shop process in which all of the relevant permits are dealt with at the same time—and it will be a genuine fast-track process. The clue's in the name.
specificity.explanation: Clear on the unchangeable core (one-stop-shop, all permits together) but vague on which “sensible changes” are actually on the table.

specificity.statement: Our RMA reforms have two broad objectives. The first thing is to make it easier to get things done by unlocking capacity for housing and business growth, enabling delivery of quality infrastructure; doubling renewable energy; and enabling primary sector growth and development. Our second objective is to safeguard the environment and human health, adapt to climate change, and improve regulatory quality in the resource management system.
specificity.explanation: Lays out structured objectives and concrete aims (doubling renewables, three-phase reform, 20 coalition commitments) though without timeframes for most.

specificity.statement: One thing that I would say is that under the last Government where some of these outcomes went haywire, we saw an increase of 98,000 through to 130,000 Māori on main benefits, and we are committed to supporting Minister Upston and others to get this country back on track.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete before/after numbers (98,000 to 130,000), though no precise dates.

specificity.statement: This week, I announced six education priorities which will drive decision making and build a world-leading education system for New Zealand students. These priorities are establishing a clear year-by-year curriculum that details the knowledge, skills, and competencies that kids need to succeed, implementing evidence-based approaches to teaching literacy and numeracy, introducing more consistent reporting, strengthening teacher training, targeting effective learning support and interventions, and using data and evidence to drive decision making.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates six concrete priority areas, though each is a direction rather than a costed, dated measure.

specificity.statement: The equity gap is stubbornly wide; 20 percent of our tamariki Māori are at curriculum for maths at the end of year 8, and in 2022, almost 10,000 kids left school with no qualifications at all.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise statistics with cohorts and a year (20% of Māori at curriculum in maths, ~10,000 leaving in 2022).

specificity.statement: These priorities will support the Government to be laser-focused on ensuring that at least 80 percent of our kids are at curriculum by 2030.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise target figure (80%) and date (2030).

specificity.statement: The latest advice that I received from police in relation to front-line safety is that there was a 45.5 percent increase in assaults on police since 2018.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact percentage and a baseline year.

specificity.statement: I think that we're in a terrible situation as a country where, under the previous Government, we've seen a massive increase in violent crime: a 33 percent increase. We've seen a 76 percent increase in gang members. Those gang members are carrying firearms; they're willing to use them.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete percentages, though without sources or exact periods.

specificity.statement: Well, what I'd say to that is that this Government is committed to making sure that our police have got all the intelligence, all the tools, all the resources that they need to go out there and keep the public safe.
specificity.explanation: Vague reassurance (“all the intelligence, all the tools”) with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: We have committed to an additional 500 police officers. We are bringing new legislation and that will deal with violent gangs. We are bringing legislation in that will actually put tougher consequences around these violent retail, youth, and juvenile offenders.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (500 extra officers) and legislative streams, though without dates.

specificity.statement: The Government is bringing forward a review of earthquake-prone buildings to provide greater certainty for Kiwis. While this review is under way, all current remediation deadlines will be extended by four years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (review plus a four-year extension of remediation deadlines), though the review's outcomes remain open.

specificity.statement: This Government has an ambitious target to double the value of exports over the next decade, continue to support major events, increase foreign direct investment, and improve the Government procurement system by reducing red tape and bureaucracy.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete headline target (double exports in a decade) but the other items are broad directions without measures.

specificity.statement: Well, I have seen one commentator—who should know better—describe this $1.77 billion commitment to continue funding much-needed medicines as “fiscal jiggery-pokery”. Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-pokery” to describe the practice of funding medicines for one year only and then taking it away again.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the point in the concrete $1.77b medicines commitment versus one-year funding.

charisma.statement: I am proud to lead a Government that makes the changes that we need to ensure our kids are well set up for a great future, because we're getting our country back on track.
charisma.explanation: Confident and positive but appeals only to his own side; no attempt to bring opponents along.

charisma.statement: I suspect there would have been a little less noise had half of the Government benches not been looking at their phones during the Prime Minister's answer.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective barb that plays to his own side rather than building any consensus.

charisma.statement: It's very disappointing to see representatives from Te Pāti Māori not even speaking about the victims of crime but more about cuddling and cotton-wooling those criminals instead.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that demonises opponents rather than persuading or finding common ground.

charisma.statement: If you're going to go away and consider this matter, could I just suggest that one of the marvellous things about a democracy is robust debate. If people aren't prepared to put other sides of the story or hear other people out—they just want to shout in the way that's happening now—then this Parliament will deteriorate very rapidly.
charisma.explanation: Invokes democratic debate and hearing others out, but the broader point is aimed at chiding opponents rather than building bridges.

forthrightness.statement: It depends on their circumstances, but if the member would like to put the question in writing, we'll get him a proper answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the average weekly cost to families of ending half-price public transport for under-25s, he gives no figure and defers to a written question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern about that constituent, but what I'd say is that help is on the way, because we are going to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about someone being $70 a fortnight worse off from the transport change, he pivots entirely to tax-relief talking points without addressing the figure.

forthrightness.statement: I'd just say to that member, again, help is on the way to low and middle income New Zealanders doing it tough in a cost of living crisis created by that member's previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about parents paying more for under-13s' transport and school lunch cuts, he again repeats the “help is on the way” line without addressing either cost.

forthrightness.statement: This Government is committed to putting downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two years; we're making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws right between tenants and landlords.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether $2.9b of landlord tax cuts will lower rents given an 8.3% surge, he lists policies but never directly answers whether rents will fall.

forthrightness.statement: isn't it good that inflation hit 4 percent—the lowest it's been for three years—we're on our way.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which of a long list of rising costs reflects his cost-of-living commitment, he lists Government measures and the inflation figure rather than addressing the listed costs.

forthrightness.statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three-strikes legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws have shown reductions in both minor and serious violent crimes, along with decreased arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what evidence she has that three strikes reduces crime, she cites a specific source (a Ministry evidence brief) and US studies — a direct, on-topic answer.

forthrightness.statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief which cited US studies showing similar three-strike laws have reduced serious violent crimes and reduced arrest rates for offenders who had received a first or second strike.
forthrightness.explanation: Confronted with specific 2022 US research showing no deterrent effect and disproportionate impact on African Americans, she does not engage it and repeats her earlier evidence-brief point.

forthrightness.statement: At the half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more over the forecast period.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what challenges she faced putting together the Budget, she gives a direct, detailed answer.

forthrightness.statement: This is a novel new policy from the Labour Party today. They're going to be subsidising everyone's insurance bill, I see.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether people facing rising insurance premiums and rates will be better off in the Budget, she mocks the question instead of answering it.

forthrightness.statement: I'm surprised by that question. I've actually been giving the Opposition member the benefit of the doubt. That question was well beneath her and I'm not going to honour it with an answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Expressly refuses to answer the question about saving her own job ahead of front-line workers.

forthrightness.statement: There will be no hidden fiscal cliffs established for a future Government to deal with, and there will never be, under this Government's watch, a fiscal cliff left for essential medicines—shame on you.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether all Budget items will be baselined, she answers that there will be very few time-limited items and reviews beforehand — a fairly direct answer.

forthrightness.statement: We will be putting in more money to improve health services in this Budget. We will be putting in more money to improve education and we will be putting in more money to strengthen law and order.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee every New Zealander will be better off, she declines the guarantee and pivots to areas of spending.

forthrightness.statement: All New Zealanders benefit from a strong economy, and we as a Government are embarking on a significant project to rebuild an economy that has been drastically weakened by a period of prolonged, very high inflation that has eroded people's real incomes and purchasing power, that has led to a significant increase in interest rates, that is in turn leading to four of the past five quarters having been in recession and very challenging economic conditions.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how 12,000 newly unemployed will benefit from tax cuts, she gives a general economic narrative rather than addressing those people directly.

forthrightness.statement: As we've said a number of times, both publicly and in the House, no projects have been selected for the fast-track process. Cabinet has made a decision to set up a thorough and independent panel process for the selection of projects to be included in the schedule of the bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether projects have been selected (no) and describes the panel process and the public's ability to submit to select committee.

forthrightness.statement: So writing a letter to someone which is, essentially, a press release letting them know that the fast-track process is open does not raise any concerns like the member is raising.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the conflict-of-interest line of questioning by characterising the letter as a courtesy/press release, but dismisses rather than addresses the specific conflict allegation.

forthrightness.statement: So we're open to sensible changes, but I can tell the House two things: the core of it will remain—it will be a one-stop shop process in which all of the relevant permits are dealt with at the same time—and it will be a genuine fast-track process. The clue's in the name.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he'll commit to reducing concentrated ministerial powers, he says he's open to changes but defers to the select committee without committing.

forthrightness.statement: I am committed to Māori and New Zealand's success, and this coalition Government is committed to good government. There is a consultation process under way at Te Puni Kōkiri, and that's an operational matter that I'll leave to the Tumu Whakarae of Māori Development to progress.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether cutting Te Puni Kōkiri jobs contributes to Māori success, he restates his commitment and deflects to it being an operational matter.

forthrightness.statement: I agree with Minister Seymour, who has observed that having one out of three Māori kids going to school is an absolute failure and we need to get more Māori children back to school.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees TPK analysis adds little value and if that drives the job cuts, he answers on school attendance instead — a different topic.

forthrightness.statement: One thing that I would say is that under the last Government where some of these outcomes went haywire, we saw an increase of 98,000 through to 130,000 Māori on main benefits, and we are committed to supporting Minister Upston and others to get this country back on track.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how removing te reo, Treaty provisions and the Māori Health Authority contributes to Māori success, he pivots to benefit numbers rather than the policies named.

forthrightness.statement: This week, I announced six education priorities which will drive decision making and build a world-leading education system for New Zealand students. These priorities are establishing a clear year-by-year curriculum that details the knowledge, skills, and competencies that kids need to succeed, implementing evidence-based approaches to teaching literacy and numeracy, introducing more consistent reporting, strengthening teacher training, targeting effective learning support and interventions, and using data and evidence to drive decision making.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what announcements she has made on education priorities, she answers directly and completely.

forthrightness.statement: The latest advice that I received from police in relation to front-line safety is that there was a 45.5 percent increase in assaults on police since 2018.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice he's received on frontline officer safety, he gives a specific figure from that advice — a direct answer.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I'd say to that is that this Government is committed to making sure that our police have got all the intelligence, all the tools, all the resources that they need to go out there and keep the public safe.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether moving the Firearms Safety Authority out of police would preserve frontline access to intelligence, he gives a generic commitment instead of addressing the transfer.

forthrightness.statement: We have committed to an additional 500 police officers. We are bringing new legislation and that will deal with violent gangs. We are bringing legislation in that will actually put tougher consequences around these violent retail, youth, and juvenile offenders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he'll resolve police advice that the Arms Act and coalition timings are incompatible, he lists policy commitments rather than addressing the timing conflict.

forthrightness.statement: First of all, I'd like to say I disagree with the member's interpretation of the advice, as asked in the question. If you take the advice as it was stated in full, which said, “Traditional bootcamp models of strict discipline are likely to be detrimental to young people with a history of abuse and family violence.”, yes, I do agree. The advice also noted that programmes which include elements of counselling and have primary focus on rehabilitation are significantly more effective.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question directly, quotes the advice in full, distinguishes her programme from a “traditional bootcamp,” and states where she agrees.

forthrightness.statement: An evaluation of that programme showed positive results, with improvements in attitude and motivation of the young people to address their offending. However, it was also found that the lack of robust support once the young person left the programme meant that the improvements in outcomes were not realised to the extent that they might have been.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether an 86% reoffending rate signals success, she doesn't address that figure but does acknowledge limitations of the earlier programme.

forthrightness.statement: What the evidence does show us is what we are doing now is not working. We can't accept the status quo. We need to make sure that we are giving these young people the tools they need to be the best that they can be.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name a single evidence-based reason for pursuing bootcamps, she pivots to “the status quo isn't working” without naming any supporting evidence.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is bringing forward a review of earthquake-prone buildings to provide greater certainty for Kiwis. While this review is under way, all current remediation deadlines will be extended by four years.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what announcements the Government has made on building and construction, he answers directly with the specific measure.

forthrightness.statement: There are many decisions that this Government makes and one of the things that we are actually trying to do is grow the economy, and some of the decisions that that Government put through were actually a bad idea and we cancelled them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what she says to the forestry and wood-processing sector after axing their plan, she gives a generic justification rather than addressing that sector.

forthrightness.statement: The tech industry is very well supported by this Government, and one of the great Ministers—Judith Collins—is actually very focused on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to NZTech's specific plea to retain the industry-led framework, she gives a generic reassurance and deflects to another Minister.

civility.statement: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern about that constituent, but what I'd say is that help is on the way, because we are going to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten.
civility.explanation: No personal insult, but the “long forgotten” jab is a partisan dig rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I suspect there would have been a little less noise had half of the Government benches not been looking at their phones during the Prime Minister's answer.
civility.explanation: A witty dig at the Government benches over the phone policy; partisan and mildly mocking but not a personal attack on character.

civility.statement: Nicola Willis has a repeated history of giving answers that fly directly in the face of rulings that you have given repeatedly since you took up your tenure as Speaker—but she's also very clever because she puts the dig in right in the last few words.
civility.explanation: Procedural criticism of an opponent's conduct in the House rather than a personal insult, though pointedly accusatory.

civility.statement: It's very disappointing to see representatives from Te Pāti Māori not even speaking about the victims of crime but more about cuddling and cotton-wooling those criminals instead.
civility.explanation: Strawmans opponents as caring only about “cuddling and cotton-wooling” criminals rather than engaging their evidence-based questions.

civility.statement: I remember that meeting vividly because what I saw in the eyes of their officials was what I felt, which was abject horror at the situation the previous Government was prepared to leave Pharmac in.
civility.explanation: Attacks the previous Government's choices dramatically but stays on the policy/fiscal substance rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: This is a novel new policy from the Labour Party today. They're going to be subsidising everyone's insurance bill, I see.
civility.explanation: Strawmans a question about cost pressures as a Labour policy to “subsidise everyone's insurance bill”.

civility.statement: And I would point that member to the colleagues either side of her on that front bench, who actively chose not to adjust tax thresholds, even while inflation ate away at people's incomes, who actively chose to pour fuel on the inflation fire while a cost of living crisis surged, who actively chose to spend money on a TVNZ and RNZ merger when New Zealanders couldn't pay for their groceries.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the previous Government's policy choices rather than personal character.

civility.statement: There will be no hidden fiscal cliffs established for a future Government to deal with, and there will never be, under this Government's watch, a fiscal cliff left for essential medicines—shame on you.
civility.explanation: The substantive commitment is undercut by the closing “shame on you” personal rebuke to the questioner.

civility.statement: Because there was a period when the babysitters were in control, they had the credit card and they were charging everything upon it—the TVNZ-RNZ merger and new jobs tax over here; $1.2 billion on three waters over here.
civility.explanation: The “babysitters” metaphor belittles the previous Government but targets its spending conduct rather than individuals.

civility.statement: Well, I'm proud to say this coalition Government is ending the war on farmers. The last Government loaded on the regulations, putting unnecessary costs on farmers and growers.
civility.explanation: “War on farmers” is loaded, sensational framing of the previous Government's regulations rather than neutral policy critique.

civility.statement: If you're going to go away and consider this matter, could I just suggest that one of the marvellous things about a democracy is robust debate. If people aren't prepared to put other sides of the story or hear other people out—they just want to shout in the way that's happening now—then this Parliament will deteriorate very rapidly.
civility.explanation: Appeals to robust-debate norms but pairs it with the dismissive “sensitive people... need to just harden up” jab.

civility.statement: Can I ask the Minister—not to be speculative in this case—is it a fact that no member or Minister or party in the Government has taken $350,000 illegally from a charity, as is the fact publicly known now?
civility.explanation: Uses a question to level an accusation of illegal conduct at opponents rather than engage the fast-track substance.

civility.statement: Will she be the only New Zealander better off by saving her own job ahead of the jobs of front-line workers?
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister as prioritising her own job over workers' — a personal, character-directed jab rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: Well, I have seen one commentator—who should know better—describe this $1.77 billion commitment to continue funding much-needed medicines as “fiscal jiggery-pokery”. Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-pokery” to describe the practice of funding medicines for one year only and then taking it away again.
civility.explanation: Turns a critic's phrase back on the previous Government's funding practice; pointed but engages the substance of the fiscal argument.

veracity.statement: But what I'd say to that member is we are not going to see a $170 per week increase in rents, as we saw under his administration.
veracity.explanation: Rents did rise substantially under the previous Government; the $170/week figure is directionally defensible but presented without timeframe, so partly contextual.

veracity.statement: isn't it good that inflation hit 4 percent—the lowest it's been for three years—we're on our way.
veracity.explanation: NZ annual CPI was 4.0% in the March 2024 quarter, the lowest since 2021 — accurate; the “we're on our way” credit-claim is the softer part.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three-strikes legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws have shown reductions in both minor and serious violent crimes, along with decreased arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes.
veracity.explanation: Three-strikes deterrent evidence is mixed-to-negative in much of the literature; selectively citing favourable US findings is partly misleading.

veracity.statement: Since Labour came into power, we have seen a 33 percent increase in violent crime, resulting in an increased number of victimisations.
veracity.explanation: The 33% figure is a commonly cited measure of rising victimisations over the period but is contested and sensitive to the baseline chosen.

veracity.statement: At the half-year update in December, Treasury identified nine instances of these fiscal cliffs where, in each case, the costs of continuing funding were $100 million more over the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim attributed to Treasury's HYEFU; consistent with the Government's fiscal-cliffs narrative though framed favourably.

veracity.statement: The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside for future years.
veracity.explanation: The $350m one-year Pharmac top-up and its expiry are real budget facts, presented with the Government's framing of “no funding set aside”.

veracity.statement: And I would point that member to the colleagues either side of her on that front bench, who actively chose not to adjust tax thresholds, even while inflation ate away at people's incomes, who actively chose to pour fuel on the inflation fire while a cost of living crisis surged, who actively chose to spend money on a TVNZ and RNZ merger when New Zealanders couldn't pay for their groceries.
veracity.explanation: The factual cores (unadjusted thresholds, the proposed merger spend) are real; the inflation-causation framing is contestable.

veracity.statement: All New Zealanders benefit from a strong economy, and we as a Government are embarking on a significant project to rebuild an economy that has been drastically weakened by a period of prolonged, very high inflation that has eroded people's real incomes and purchasing power, that has led to a significant increase in interest rates, that is in turn leading to four of the past five quarters having been in recession and very challenging economic conditions.
veracity.explanation: The macro claims (high inflation, rising interest rates, multiple recessionary quarters) broadly match the data for the period.

veracity.statement: One thing that I would say is that under the last Government where some of these outcomes went haywire, we saw an increase of 98,000 through to 130,000 Māori on main benefits, and we are committed to supporting Minister Upston and others to get this country back on track.
