charisma.explanation: Generously acknowledges the Minister's genuine prior commitment, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: There was a robust line of questioning, shared quite well between both the Government and the Opposition.
charisma.explanation: Bipartisan, generous framing of the committee's work across the aisle.

charisma.statement: We’ve just heard from the chair of our select committee, Katie Nimon, and I’d like to say thank you to her for chairing those hearings so well.
charisma.explanation: Gracious cross-bench courtesy that builds goodwill.

charisma.statement: And to be fair to the previous Government and the previous Minister, I think that that was acknowledged as well. So the work that was started, unfortunately not completed or well-completed over that six-year period, but I think we’re on the same track... So I think we’re on a similar page there.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks common ground with the opposition and credits their direction while disagreeing on execution.

charisma.statement: I have to acknowledge the previous Government’s role in bringing in literacy and numeracy co-requisites at high school. It showed us that so many of our kids can’t read, write, and do maths at a basic level.
charisma.explanation: Credits the opposing party's reform as useful, reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: Well, once again, this is why the member’s side lost the Cold War. You see, there used to be a belief that if we had a Government that could tell people where to invest and what to invest in... then we’d all be better off.
charisma.explanation: Plays to his own side by ridiculing the opponent rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: Oh no, we’ve gone from anti-business sentiment to outright xenophobia. There’s now totally unfounded accusations that early childhood education centres are actually funnelling money that they should have paid tax on into foreign corporations.
charisma.explanation: Combative dismissal that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: Can I firstly thank the Minister for acknowledging the funding that has been given to those two schools in Palmerston North. I know those schools pretty well, and the fact that they were funded under the previous Government, I know, is a testament to the success of the focus in that space.
charisma.explanation: Gracious tone, though it also claims credit for his own side's funding.

authenticity.statement: That is why addressing the cost of living, when the coalition Government came in, was and still is the number one priority.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a stated government priority; consistent with the coalition's messaging but no action evidenced in the text.

authenticity.statement: I picked up He Poutama Rangatahi, which was actually a National Party initiative that was put on hold back around 2017.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledging the policy's National origin while championing it signals a consistent, non-partisan stance on the programme.

strength.statement: I picked up He Poutama Rangatahi, which was actually a National Party initiative that was put on hold back around 2017.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete action — reviving a stalled programme — though delivery detail is in the following claims.

strength.statement: And I do want to ask the question about He Poutama Rangatahi that saw over 12,000 young people engaged in the programme, resulting in 77 percent of those young people—77 percent, Minister—engaging in employment, education, or training.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered programme with measured outcomes under his ministership.

strength.statement: Again, in our time as Government, we brought that back and that saw 79 percent of those who participated in that programme gain positive employment outcomes. That’s a very significant percentage; 85 percent retaining employment for at least six months. And we committed over $95 million for the fund which delivered 63 Māori-lead projects and will support over 4,000 Māori across Aotearoa.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for reviving and funding a programme with stated employment outcomes — delivery, not mere announcement.

veracity.statement: the vast majority of the transport budget under the previous Labour Government was spent on highways and local roads; that, in fact, nearly $1 billion was spent on State highway improvements
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about spending under the previous government; ~$1bn on State highway improvements and a majority on roads is broadly consistent with the NLTF allocations of that period, though framed to favour her argument.

veracity.statement: not even 3 percent—not even 3 percent—of the transport budget was spent on walking and cycling improvements
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claim that walking/cycling was under 3% of the transport budget; consistent with the marginal share these modes historically received.

veracity.statement: now we’re in a situation where New Zealand has the highest car ownership in the entire world because people don’t have a choice because of decades of insufficient investment in alternatives
veracity.explanation: NZ is among the highest in car ownership per capita, but 'highest in the entire world' is an overstatement of a contested ranking; the causal claim about underinvestment is plausible but unproven.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister of Transport confirm that the amount in the draft Government policy statement which he has just referred to is only 1 percent of the transport budget on walking and cycling improvements, and a lower percentage than in the previous year
veracity.explanation: Specific quantitative claim about the draft GPS allocation; plausible given the policy direction but presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: The single most inconvenient thing for someone trying to drive somewhere is not someone on a bike, it’s not someone on public transport; it’s the other cars and trucks that are clogging up our roads and damaging the roads, along with extreme weather events which are caused by carbon emissions.
veracity.explanation: Claims about congestion sources and road damage from heavy vehicles are accurate; the emissions-to-extreme-weather link is broadly supported though stated sweepingly.

veracity.statement: for the last six years, we’ve had a Government—ex-Government—which used to say, “We’re going to build Auckland light rail, and we’re going to start it in 2021.” Well, they had six years and nothing happened.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that Auckland light rail was repeatedly promised and not delivered after six years, though 'nothing happened' glosses over planning work that did occur.

veracity.statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
veracity.explanation: CRL main works began under the previous National-led government and the project's cost rose to roughly $5.5bn; figures and attribution are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: The last Government spent an awful lot of time talking about things, talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery—absolutely no delivery.
veracity.explanation: The ~$227m spent on Auckland light rail planning/consultancy with no construction is broadly accurate; 'glossy documents' is rhetorical colour.

specificity.statement: the vast majority of the transport budget under the previous Labour Government was spent on highways and local roads; that, in fact, nearly $1 billion was spent on State highway improvements
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures ($1bn) and a specific category (State highway improvements) drawn from the annual review report.

specificity.statement: not even 3 percent—not even 3 percent—of the transport budget was spent on walking and cycling improvements
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise figure and named spending category, though the repetition is rhetorical.

specificity.statement: Can the Minister of Transport confirm that the amount in the draft Government policy statement which he has just referred to is only 1 percent of the transport budget on walking and cycling improvements, and a lower percentage than in the previous year
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (1%) and a year-on-year comparison tied to the specific GPS document referenced.

specificity.statement: I would point her to page 29 of the draft Government policy statement on transport, which invests in public transport services, public transport infrastructure, and walking and cycling improvements.
specificity.explanation: Points to a specific document and page and named investment categories, but provides no figures.

specificity.statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, a dollar figure, and the expected benefit.

specificity.statement: I am incredibly proud of our track record of delivering in public transport infrastructure, because we actually got stuff started and we will get things done.
specificity.explanation: General self-praise with no figures, projects, or timeframes in this sentence.

specificity.statement: The last Government spent an awful lot of time talking about things, talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery—absolutely no delivery.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure and the specific programme it was spent on.

specificity.statement: what Aucklanders want and what Aucklanders voted for is delivery, and that is what this Government is focused on.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level claim about what voters want with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: People in the regions need roads.
specificity.explanation: A brief general assertion with no detail on which roads, funding, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: I still haven’t heard from the Minister whether or not he accepts that the Clean Car Discount’s initiative did increase the uptake of electric vehicles—that was the question that I asked and he still has neglected to address that.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy (Clean Car Discount) and the precise question said to be unanswered.

rigor.statement: the vast majority of the transport budget under the previous Labour Government was spent on highways and local roads; that, in fact, nearly $1 billion was spent on State highway improvements
rigor.explanation: Argument built on cited budget percentages from the committee report rather than appeals, with the conclusion following from the figures.

rigor.statement: now we’re in a situation where New Zealand has the highest car ownership in the entire world because people don’t have a choice because of decades of insufficient investment in alternatives
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal argument linking underinvestment to car dependence, but leans on a superlative claim and asserts causation without direct evidence.

rigor.statement: The single most inconvenient thing for someone trying to drive somewhere is not someone on a bike, it’s not someone on public transport; it’s the other cars and trucks that are clogging up our roads and damaging the roads, along with extreme weather events which are caused by carbon emissions.
rigor.explanation: Sound underlying logic that congestion comes from cars not active modes, and that heavy vehicles damage roads; the leap to weather events from emissions is a directionally supported but compressed argument.

civility.statement: Although I know the National Party cannot help but believe in their own talking points that have nothing to do with reality
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of opponents as detached from reality rather than engaging their substance.

civility.statement: for the last six years, we’ve had a Government—ex-Government—which used to say, “We’re going to build Auckland light rail, and we’re going to start it in 2021.” Well, they had six years and nothing happened.
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive criticism of a delivery record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: The last Government spent an awful lot of time talking about things, talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery—absolutely no delivery.
civility.explanation: Harsh but largely policy/record-focused criticism, with some sensationalising ('glossy documents').

civility.statement: I still haven’t heard from the Minister whether or not he accepts that the Clean Car Discount’s initiative did increase the uptake of electric vehicles—that was the question that I asked and he still has neglected to address that.
civility.explanation: Legitimate procedural criticism that his specific question went unanswered, focused on conduct in the debate rather than personal attack.

charisma.statement: Although I know the National Party cannot help but believe in their own talking points that have nothing to do with reality
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that mocks the other party rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: what Aucklanders want and what Aucklanders voted for is delivery, and that is what this Government is focused on.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident appeal to the electorate's mandate, but speaks to its own side rather than building cross-party consensus.

forthrightness.statement: I would point her to page 29 of the draft Government policy statement on transport, which invests in public transport services, public transport infrastructure, and walking and cycling improvements.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm specific budget percentages, he deflects to a page reference listing categories without confirming or denying the numbers asked about.

forthrightness.statement: page 29 of the draft Government policy statement—and I’m happy to give her a copy—does include investment in public transport services, does include investment in public transport infrastructure, and does include investment in walking and cycling improvements.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked to confirm the 1% figure and the year-on-year decline, he repeats the page-29 reference without addressing the specific question.

strength.statement: for the last six years, we’ve had a Government—ex-Government—which used to say, “We’re going to build Auckland light rail, and we’re going to start it in 2021.” Well, they had six years and nothing happened.
strength.explanation: Describes the previous government's repeated non-delivery on a flagship promise — a low-strength record for those responsible.

strength.statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a major project that was genuinely started under National and is nearing completion — substantive follow-through, though credited to a prior government.

strength.statement: I am incredibly proud of our track record of delivering in public transport infrastructure, because we actually got stuff started and we will get things done.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivery record but leans on 'got stuff started' and the future 'will get things done' — partial/in-progress rather than completed delivery.

strength.statement: The last Government spent an awful lot of time talking about things, talking about Auckland light rail, spending $227 million on business case reports and consultancy reports and glossy documents and no delivery—absolutely no delivery.
strength.explanation: Characterises the opponent's spend-without-delivery — a low-delivery record for those responsible.

divination.statement: The last National Government started the City Rail Link, and it’s soon going to be completed, and that is $5 billion of investment into our rail network in Auckland, which is going to unlock significant opportunities for Aucklanders wanting to use public transport.
divination.explanation: Prediction that CRL is 'soon going to be completed' and will unlock public transport use; well-founded given the project's near-complete status.

specificity.statement: I think the member will agree that the learning support system is broken.
specificity.explanation: A blunt characterisation ('broken') with no figures or detail; relies on surrounding context.

specificity.statement: The wait times have increased, the numbers have increased, and, as we all know, the worst thing for a child is to be on a wait-list.
specificity.explanation: States a direction of change but gives no figures, baselines, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: we spend an awful amount of money on learning sport; well—well—over a billion dollars and potentially a lot more once we start collecting up all the things we spend money on.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough magnitude but explicitly admits the full figure is not collated.

specificity.statement: it will be my focus, with the backing of the ministry, to make sure that we are evaluating and monitoring all of the things that we do so that we can shift money into things that are working and stop doing things that are not working.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (evaluation, reallocation) but no programmes, amounts, or dates.

specificity.statement: we're prioritising period products—meeting front-end need, shifting some of that back-end resource.
specificity.explanation: Concrete example of the back-to-front-end shift, though no figures.

specificity.statement: you will see from us a clear quarterly action plan of delivery.
specificity.explanation: Names a cadence (quarterly) and a deliverable type, but no actual content or measures.

specificity.statement: schools, for example, have to fill out a million forms through a million different channels to try and access support. We want to streamline things.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete problem (access friction) but 'streamline' is a vague remedy with no detail.

specificity.statement: it's so important that, actually, when you learn to be a teacher, you learn about neurodiversity, you learn about dyslexia, you learn about trauma-informed teaching.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete content areas for initial teacher education, though no mechanism, timing, or requirement detail.

specificity.statement: how would the Minister and the ministry plan to achieve our Learning Support Action Plan 2019-2025 when expert roles directly supporting neurodivergent and disabled students and teachers and schools will be lost in the Ministry of Education cuts?
specificity.explanation: Pointed, concrete question naming a specific plan and a specific tension (expert roles lost to cuts).

specificity.statement: along with Minister Stanford and Cabinet colleagues, we've been working very quickly to get the basic ideas around policy decisions around charter schools made. And we're doing that in order that we can pass legislation and have the first charter schools open in term 1, 2025. That is our goal.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target (legislation and first schools open in term 1, 2025).

specificity.statement: It will happen fast, and it will happen bigger than it has happened previously.
specificity.explanation: Vague comparatives ('fast', 'bigger') with no figures or definition.

specificity.statement: we will be having two types. There will be those that people are more familiar with from the last time New Zealand had charter schools... But there will also be charter schools which used to be State schools that have converted to charter school status... And, critically, they're contracted and accountable for school achievement and school attendance.
specificity.explanation: Describes two concrete models and an accountability mechanism, though without numbers or dates.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has the highest species extinction rate in the world. I'm going to say that again: the highest species extinction rate in the world. Sixty-three percent of our ecosystems are threatened. Those ecosystems are the home of our native species, of which 4,000 are either at risk or threatened with extinction. That includes 90 percent of our seabirds, 82 percent of our native birds, 94 percent of our reptiles, and 72 percent of our native freshwater fish.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete percentages across multiple species groups.

specificity.statement: One of the times when I really burnt a chunk of my political capital was to secure the $1.3 billion for Jobs for Nature in Budget 2020.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure ($1.3 billion), programme, and budget year.

specificity.statement: in that time, it has empowered 10,000 of our most precarious citizens in some of our most fragile, remotest regions in the country, and they have done the most incredible work restoring our rivers, our estuaries, our forests, and our bush.
specificity.explanation: Gives a headcount and concrete restoration domains, though no detailed outcomes.

specificity.statement: New Zealand was the first country in the world to introduce that measure. The United Kingdom was the second. There are now three dozen countries.
specificity.explanation: Concrete ordering and a count of adopting countries.

specificity.statement: I am giving myself a five-year mission to boldly reduce or remove 150 million tonnes of climate pollution from global emissions by 2030.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete figure (150 million tonnes) and date (2030).

specificity.statement: We became the first support party to increase our support after a term in Government. And then, in 2023, we did it again.
specificity.explanation: Concrete electoral claim with the relevant years.

specificity.statement: we actually invest as much as the international benchmark. We're investing enough; what they're saying is we are not getting value out of it. They're saying we're investing about 5 to 6 percent of GDP in infrastructure, but if we were to get what we need to get out of it, with the way we do it currently, we'd need to invest about 10 percent, so about 4 percent of GDP, essentially, being wasted in our processes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages of GDP for current spend, required spend, and waste.

specificity.statement: New Zealand ranks in the bottom 10 percent of high-income countries in terms of the amount of infrastructure we deliver per unit of capital invested.
specificity.explanation: A precise comparative ranking with a defined metric.

specificity.statement: roughly speaking, we should be investing about 60 percent in maintenance, 40 percent in new, but we are investing probably about 30 percent in maintenance. So we're way under
specificity.explanation: Gives target and actual maintenance/new split ratios.

specificity.statement: we need a population strategy and we need an immigration strategy, and we haven't had one of those worthy of the name for all of those 40-odd years.
specificity.explanation: Names two specific strategy gaps but no content or proposed mechanism.

specificity.statement: They talked about two substations that were caught in Cyclone Gabrielle: an older one failed; a newer one didn't. Of course, what that did is it kept the lights on in that area
specificity.explanation: A specific real-world example, though without named locations.

specificity.statement: Transpower told us that its assets are ageing. They said that most of the grid is 60-plus years old and that some of the assets are over 80 years old.
specificity.explanation: Concrete asset-age figures.

specificity.statement: Traffic management is costing us 40 percent of the cost of some of the projects that we're undertaking.”—40 percent. If you could knock that down to a reasonable, say, 10 percent, imagine how much money that is leaving in their pockets
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete percentages for traffic-management cost and a target reduction.

specificity.statement: Our State highways have been peppered with 62,000 potholes in the last year
specificity.explanation: Precise number over a defined period.

specificity.statement: In the last six years, they didn't start and complete one single major infrastructure project, pavement rehabilitation on our State highways declined 27 percent
specificity.explanation: Concrete claims with a percentage and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: they cancelled the roads of national significance programme. They then had to reheat that with the New Zealand Upgrade Programme, which has been faced with delays, cancellations, cost escalations, and, ultimately, an Auditor-General's report which was incredibly damning
specificity.explanation: References specific programmes and an Auditor-General report, though no figures.

specificity.statement: $228 million had been spent on simply doing nothing but writing more and more business cases and glossy documents.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure tied to a named project.

specificity.statement: we've been given very clear evidence that there's a $200 billion hole between the last Government's aspirations and what was actually funded
specificity.explanation: States a concrete figure, though without breakdown.

specificity.statement: We will invest more in road maintenance, but we will also ensure we're getting better value for money out of every single dollar that is being spent.
specificity.explanation: Direction of travel (more maintenance, better value) but no amounts, targets, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: there is, I think, up to $2.3 billion allocated to public transport services as part of that draft Government policy statement... there are a range of concessions which still exist in place which Auckland Transport, Wellington, and Christchurch have all put in place... The Government will continue to support SuperGold, Total Mobility, and Community Connect
specificity.explanation: Names a funding figure and specific concession schemes.

specificity.statement: Over $300 million of taxpayers' money put into the scheme... which could have gone to health, education, law and order, all of those other priorities.
specificity.explanation: Cites a total cost figure, though without precise period.

specificity.statement: on the very day that the Government has cut or scrapped subsidies for those aged under 25... how will this Government continue to support an increased use of public transport in New Zealand in light of the recent decisions that the Government has taken?
specificity.explanation: A precise, well-targeted question tying a specific decision (under-25 subsidy cut) to a specific goal.

specificity.statement: we also heard from the Ministry of Transport that the Clean Car Discount at the time saw an increase in the uptake of electric vehicles (EVs)—actually more than was anticipated and expected.
specificity.explanation: States a directional effect attributed to a source, but no figures.

specificity.statement: we did hear about the “roads of National Party significance” and that it would come at a minimum cost estimate of between $30 and $46 billion, which leaves... a fiscal hole of $8 billion to $22 billion for him.
specificity.explanation: Concrete cost-range and fiscal-gap figures.

civility.statement: I think the member will agree that the learning support system is broken.
civility.explanation: Critical of the inherited system but framed as a shared assessment rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: in the last six years, not a lot of action. Things have not got better; things have got worse. And, frankly, I'm not interested in writing another glossy strategy. I'm not interested in doing another review.
civility.explanation: Legitimate criticism of the previous government's approach, but the dismissive 'glossy strategy' framing edges toward rhetoric.

civility.statement: Learning support—much worse. Academic achievement—much worse. Kids going to school—much worse. A lot of glossy documents; not a lot of doing.
civility.explanation: Attacks the predecessor's record; legitimate critique but delivered as repetitive, sloganistic rhetoric.

civility.statement: First of all, I would like to reject the Associate Minister's claim before. I was asking a valid question—“can he ensure”—and I get called xenophobic. But that's OK; I forgive that member.
civility.explanation: Rebuts a charge against him but does so without retaliation, ending with a gracious 'I forgive that member'.

civility.statement: I would also like to join my colleagues in thanking all the members of the Education and Workforce Committee, and the chair, and, of course, all the Ministers as well.
civility.explanation: Courteous, inclusive thanks extended across the committee and ministers.

civility.statement: in recent years we have got the balance wrong with New Zealand education policy: enormous amounts of micro-management of what shape classroom they have and how they operate under the Common Practice Model, but almost no accountability for whether students actually attend and actually achieve. The charter school policy flips that script
civility.explanation: Critiques policy settings rather than people, in measured terms.

civility.statement: There are some in the new Government who seem to want to put these endangered species on the fast track to oblivion.
civility.explanation: Imputes a destructive motive to opponents with the hyperbolic 'fast track to oblivion'.

civility.statement: I know that the current Minister is more interested in the quid than the quo, but, Christopher, if you let them unwind the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity, I will haunt you!
civility.explanation: A pointed jab at the Minister, but delivered as good-humoured banter rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I understand it's usual procedure for the Opposition to ask more questions than the Government, but, in fact, everybody contributed significantly to asking good questions, and I think we got a lot out of it.
civility.explanation: Even-handed, generous acknowledgement of contributions from across the committee.

civility.statement: the last Government was focused on trying to tell people to get out of their cars and trying to tell them to drive really, really slowly, rather than actually trying to stay focused on the basics.
civility.explanation: Caricatures opponents' transport policy in mocking terms rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: In the last six years, they didn't start and complete one single major infrastructure project, pavement rehabilitation on our State highways declined 27 percent
civility.explanation: Pointed attack on the record; harsh but largely aimed at policy delivery rather than persons.

civility.statement: $228 million had been spent on simply doing nothing but writing more and more business cases and glossy documents.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'glossy documents' framing rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: this was the reverse Robin Hood scheme that the last Government thought was the best thing. Ultimately, though, I think what the last Government did was very good for Elon Musk. Elon Musk did very well out of it. I think it was something like $115 million of subsidies for Elon Musk.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'reverse Robin Hood' and the Elon Musk framing target the policy through ridicule.

civility.statement: we did hear about the “roads of National Party significance” and that it would come at a minimum cost estimate of between $30 and $46 billion, which leaves... a fiscal hole of $8 billion to $22 billion for him.
civility.explanation: The 'roads of National Party significance' pun is a mild partisan jab within otherwise substantive questioning.

veracity.statement: The wait times have increased, the numbers have increased, and, as we all know, the worst thing for a child is to be on a wait-list.
veracity.explanation: Claims rising wait times and numbers — directionally plausible for learning support but unquantified and unverified here.

veracity.statement: we spend an awful amount of money on learning sport; well—well—over a billion dollars and potentially a lot more once we start collecting up all the things we spend money on.
veracity.explanation: Over a billion dollars on learning support is plausible; hedged with 'potentially a lot more', so not overstated.

veracity.statement: in the last six years, not a lot of action. Things have not got better; things have got worse. And, frankly, I'm not interested in writing another glossy strategy. I'm not interested in doing another review.
veracity.explanation: 'Things have got worse' is a sweeping claim with mixed support and no specific evidence cited.

veracity.statement: Learning support—much worse. Academic achievement—much worse. Kids going to school—much worse. A lot of glossy documents; not a lot of doing.
veracity.explanation: Attendance and achievement did decline, but the blanket 'much worse' is hyperbolic and uncited.

veracity.statement: schools, for example, have to fill out a million forms through a million different channels to try and access support. We want to streamline things.
veracity.explanation: 'A million forms through a million different channels' is obvious hyperbole.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has the highest species extinction rate in the world. I'm going to say that again: the highest species extinction rate in the world. Sixty-three percent of our ecosystems are threatened. Those ecosystems are the home of our native species, of which 4,000 are either at risk or threatened with extinction. That includes 90 percent of our seabirds, 82 percent of our native birds, 94 percent of our reptiles, and 72 percent of our native freshwater fish.
veracity.explanation: These figures align closely with widely cited NZ environmental and DOC statistics; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: in that time, it has empowered 10,000 of our most precarious citizens in some of our most fragile, remotest regions in the country, and they have done the most incredible work restoring our rivers, our estuaries, our forests, and our bush.
veracity.explanation: The 10,000-jobs figure for Jobs for Nature is broadly in line with reported scale; 'most incredible' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: New Zealand was the first country in the world to introduce that measure. The United Kingdom was the second. There are now three dozen countries.
veracity.explanation: NZ is widely credited as first to legislate mandatory climate-related financial disclosures; the claim is well supported.

veracity.statement: Last week... we got the news that New Zealand's emissions fell for the third year in a row.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported gross-emissions declines over the period, though the framing omits which inventory measure.

veracity.statement: we also got the news that we were on track to meet our target of net zero long-lived gases before 2050, in fact; before 2050. At least, we were on track as of last July.
veracity.explanation: The 'on track as of last July' claim is plausibly accurate but time-bound and dependent on retained policy.

veracity.statement: the zero carbon Act, the Climate Change Commission, the emissions targets and our five-year emissions budgets, our 2030 target under the Paris Agreement, and our 2050 net zero targets all seem to have largely survived the change of Government when very little else has.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the core climate framework persisted, though hedged with 'seem to' and 'largely'.

veracity.statement: We became the first support party to increase our support after a term in Government. And then, in 2023, we did it again.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the Greens' vote share rose in 2020 and again in 2023, unusual for a governing support party.

veracity.statement: we actually invest as much as the international benchmark. We're investing enough; what they're saying is we are not getting value out of it.
