specificity.explanation: Names the committee and the concrete step (writing to request Fonterra attend), though no timing.

specificity.statement: When I look at the number on one of the pages in this document, it talks about the at-risk land species: 3,283 threatened, at-risk land species.
specificity.explanation: Exact count (3,283) attributed to the source document.

specificity.statement: It’s also estimated that 192 million tonnes of soil are lost to erosion every year, and 44 percent of that comes from our pastures.
specificity.explanation: Precise tonnage and percentage attribution.

specificity.statement: Our isolated island, as we’ve heard, is a biodiversity hotspot and it’s something to be celebrated, but we know that so many species—4,000—are threatened and at risk of extinction.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number of at-risk species.

specificity.statement: The one thing I want to touch on in my last minute is the role of community-led incentives around catchment groups. That is the way forward in this country. We’ve got over 290 catchment groups.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete count of catchment groups, though the 'way forward' framing around it is general.

specificity.statement: We experienced these ourselves first hand, particularly on the East Coast with Cyclone Gabrielle. ... Tens of thousands of people were displaced in the middle of a cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: Names the event and region and a rough magnitude of displacement.

specificity.statement: It projects an increase from 17 percent of the population being over the age of 65 in 2023 to 24 percent of the population by 2053.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages and years.

specificity.statement: It also noted that the sector currently generates around $13 billion each year and employs just under 100,000 people as at the end of March 2022.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, headcount, and a dated reference point.

specificity.statement: The long-term insight briefings are about the Public Service Act 2020 mandating Government departments to develop and publish long-term insight briefings every three years.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and the three-year cadence.

specificity.statement: 86 percent, not that long ago, of those over 65 owned their own home. That’s projected to be lower than 50 very shortly, and that’s a worry.
specificity.explanation: Gives figures but 'very shortly' leaves the timeframe loose.

specificity.statement: So we’re going to have to address Māori and Pacific housing. That is going to require a change in attitude to programmes that are effective, directed, directly targeting ... There were programmes; there aren’t now. Perhaps that could be reconsidered.
specificity.explanation: Points to a category of targeted programmes now discontinued, but names no specific programme, funding, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: This is why we continue to advocate, especially for multigenerational housing—I think that’s something we don’t have in our housing stock, is that diversity.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete housing type (multigenerational/universally designed homes) but no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: So Autism New Zealand, they have indicated that 2 percent of people in New Zealand suffer from autism, which is around 93,000 individuals.
specificity.explanation: Cites a source, a percentage, and a headcount.

specificity.statement: You look at the number of nought to four-year-olds as a proportion of the population, it’s half what it was in 1961—half what it was.
specificity.explanation: Names the age band, the comparison year, and the magnitude.

specificity.statement: Back in 1948, the average age expectancy for men was 66.7; for women it was 68.5. Now, for men, it’s 80 or over 80; and for women it’s about 83 or 84.
specificity.explanation: Gives dated figures for both sexes.

specificity.statement: In 1986 ... 79 percent of Europeans and Asians owned their own home; it’s now 51 percent. For Māori, 54 percent; it’s now 40 percent. For Pasifika, 51 percent; it’s now 31 percent.
specificity.explanation: Breaks down before/after homeownership rates by ethnic group with figures.

civility.statement: The previous speaker, the Hon Julie Anne Genter, might think that increasing taxes is a good thing, but if you’re printing a heck of a lot of money and you believe in modern monetary theory, I guess that is what you would think is a good thing.
civility.explanation: Attributes a caricatured position (loving tax and MMT) to a named opponent rather than engaging her actual argument — mild strawman/misrepresentation.

civility.statement: Well, I have to say, I’ve gone through it and it’s just a word salad.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the report rather than substantive engagement, though aimed at a document not a person.

civility.statement: It was typical of Ministry for the Environment reports: it had lots of very nice warm words, lots of aspirational goals, lots of pretty pictures.
civility.explanation: Sharp but directed at the quality of a report rather than a person; borders on sneering but stays on the work.

civility.statement: I’m not sure if the previous speaker, Scott Simpson, has actually read the document.
civility.explanation: A personal jab implying an opponent didn't read the report, rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: It’s astounding that these decisions look set to favour corporations and lobbyists at the expense of the awesome sustainable future.
civility.explanation: Imputes motive (serving corporations/lobbyists) to the Government rather than engaging the substance of the decisions.

charisma.statement: The previous speaker, the Hon Julie Anne Genter, might think that increasing taxes is a good thing, but if you’re printing a heck of a lot of money and you believe in modern monetary theory, I guess that is what you would think is a good thing.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side against a named opponent rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I do agree with the previous speakers; I think this is a worthwhile exercise.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges cross-party agreement and finds common ground on the value of the debate.

charisma.statement: This is challenging. This is hopeful. This is scary. But I believe that all of us, on all sides of the House, need to make sure we read this, we understand it, but then of course we put this into practice.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive call for all parties to engage and act together — consensus-seeking and bridge-building.

charisma.statement: But, unfortunately, with this Government at the reins, it looks increasingly unlikely that this beautiful 2050 future is possible.
charisma.explanation: Blames the sitting Government rather than seeking cross-party buy-in on shared goals.

charisma.statement: The only way to deal with climate change is with system change. None of this will be achieved to its ultimate extent without indigenous leadership and knowledge.
charisma.explanation: Advances a distinct worldview compellingly but frames the solution as requiring one group's leadership, appealing more to its own base than broadening consensus.

charisma.statement: At least it has to be said that there appears now to be a consensus in Parliament, on both sides, that the solution to this is in increasing supply. Where the disagreement in that debate appears to be is what role the State has to play in that.
charisma.explanation: Identifies genuine cross-party common ground (supply) and frames the disagreement narrowly and fairly — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: So we’re going to have to address Māori and Pacific housing. That is going to require a change in attitude to programmes that are effective, directed, directly targeting ... There were programmes; there aren’t now. Perhaps that could be reconsidered.
charisma.explanation: Offered as a constructive suggestion ('perhaps could be reconsidered') inviting the Government to act rather than attacking.

charisma.statement: It’s great to be able to speak on this long-term insights briefing. I think this is an excellent initiative of the 53rd Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Praises a cross-parliamentary process (originating under the previous Parliament) rather than scoring partisan points — mildly unifying.

rigor.statement: It is not a surprise that the cost of building skyrocketed when we were printing so much money that it had no alternative because, as the great Milton Friedman said, “Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon”.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal monetary explanation but leans heavily on an appeal to authority (Friedman) and treats a contested monetarist claim as settled; some logic but a gap in evidence.

rigor.statement: It’s only with true property rights that you can create wealth in a society, and it is only with wealth in a society that you can secure a healthy, prosperous, and sustainable environment.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping two-step 'only with X can you get Y' chain stated as necessity with no evidence; over-strong entailment.

rigor.statement: It was typical of Ministry for the Environment reports: it had lots of very nice warm words, lots of aspirational goals, lots of pretty pictures.
rigor.explanation: A critique of vagueness that he then supports by quoting the committee's own report, but the opening is assertion by characterisation.

rigor.statement: I quote: “While the Long-term Insights Briefing articulates an integrated worldview, the committee considers the report did not significantly contribute to an increased understanding of the issues ... they need to go beyond stating the obvious and bring new insights.”
rigor.explanation: Supports his criticism with a direct quotation from the previous Labour-majority committee's own conclusion — evidence rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: It’s astounding that these decisions look set to favour corporations and lobbyists at the expense of the awesome sustainable future.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a corporate-capture motive without evidence; appeal to indignation.

rigor.statement: The only way to deal with climate change is with system change. None of this will be achieved to its ultimate extent without indigenous leadership and knowledge.
rigor.explanation: States necessity claims ('only way', 'none... without') as absolutes without evidence for the exclusivity; strong assertion over demonstrated entailment.

rigor.statement: At least it has to be said that there appears now to be a consensus in Parliament, on both sides, that the solution to this is in increasing supply. Where the disagreement in that debate appears to be is what role the State has to play in that.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes the point of agreement from the point of dispute, a disciplined framing of the debate.

rigor.statement: People aren’t having babies. That’s why our ageing population is increasing—because it’s too expensive and too unstable to raise a family under these conditions.
rigor.explanation: A plausible causal link between housing cost and low birth rates, but presented as the single explanation for ageing, which also reflects rising longevity; some evidence, over-simplified.

rigor.statement: There are some people who would like to see the house prices fall. The problem is that we saw that post-COVID ... people did is say, “Well, actually, there is no money in building houses because the house prices are falling, the cost of building is going up.”, and people stopped building houses. So that didn’t solve the problem at all.
rigor.explanation: Uses a recent real-world episode to argue that falling prices deter construction; a coherent evidence-based causal argument, though it treats one episode as decisive.

strength.statement: This Government has got a long-term vision to reduce the cost of housing, by opening up the laws from which we plan, finance, and fund infrastructure, and taking steps like the Hon Chris Penk has done in making it easier to import materials into this country to provide some competition.
strength.explanation: Describes in-progress action on building materials rather than delivered results; follow-through as yet unclear.

strength.statement: I am going to be writing to the Finance and Expenditure Committee and asking Fonterra to attend and explain to this Parliament why they are using these extraordinary powers.
strength.explanation: A concrete stated action within his power, but announced rather than yet delivered; follow-through unverified.

authenticity.statement: I did hear from the other side of the House around Jobs for Nature. That’s something New Zealand First is proud of and was proud of in 2017-2020. Those Jobs for Nature catchment groups are something we’ve got to encourage and keep supporting.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent position: NZ First backed Jobs for Nature in the 2017-2020 coalition and he says they still support it — words align with the party's prior record.

authenticity.statement: This is why we continue to advocate, especially for multigenerational housing—I think that’s something we don’t have in our housing stock, is that diversity.
authenticity.explanation: States an ongoing advocacy position consistent with the Greens' housing platform, though no specific action is cited to confirm follow-through.

veracity.statement: the median house price in my electorate, Tāmaki Makaurau, now being over $1 million, way out of the price range of our whānau
veracity.explanation: Auckland's median house price was around or above $1 million in 2024, so this is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: tonight 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, or in unlivable houses that are making them sick
veracity.explanation: The ~100,000 figure matches Census-derived 'severe housing deprivation' counts, but framing it as people 'sleeping rough tonight' overstates and mischaracterises that category (which includes crowded/temporary housing).

veracity.statement: 30,000 tamariki will be hospitalised this year because of substandard housing
veracity.explanation: Estimates of housing-related child hospitalisations are in this range, but the flat causal attribution ('because of substandard housing') is stronger than the evidence supports.

veracity.statement: There are currently 94,000 unoccupied houses in this country doing nothing but collecting dust.
veracity.explanation: Census counts of unoccupied dwellings are near this figure, but 'doing nothing but collecting dust' is misleading — the count includes holiday homes, homes between tenancies, and dwellings unfit for occupation.

veracity.statement: Māori make up 60 percent of homelessness in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Māori are heavily over-represented in homelessness, but the 60% figure is higher than most published measures (which are closer to a third to half depending on definition).

veracity.statement: just yesterday, this Government confirmed it will be scrapping first-home grants, further locking Māori, Pasifika, and rangatahi out of homeownership
veracity.explanation: The Government did confirm the axing of First Home Grants around this time (Budget 2024); the factual core is accurate, with the 'locking out' consequence being an interpretive claim.

veracity.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they're giving to landlords.
veracity.explanation: The savings and cost figures are roughly in the right range, but calling the restoration of mortgage interest deductibility a '$3 billion handout' to landlords is a contested, loaded characterisation of a tax-rule change.

specificity.statement: the median house price in my electorate, Tāmaki Makaurau, now being over $1 million, way out of the price range of our whānau
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure ($1M) tied to a named location, though the median is approximate.

specificity.statement: tonight 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, or in unlivable houses that are making them sick
specificity.explanation: Concrete number and enumerated circumstances, but the category is loosely defined.

specificity.statement: 30,000 tamariki will be hospitalised this year because of substandard housing
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and timeframe, though source and causal basis are unstated.

specificity.statement: just yesterday, this Government confirmed it will be scrapping first-home grants, further locking Māori, Pasifika, and rangatahi out of homeownership
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy change and timing, though the impact is asserted rather than quantified.

specificity.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they're giving to landlords.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures, a timeframe, and a proportional comparison.

specificity.statement: The free breakfast programme still exists to this very day, and the scarfie shuttles branched off into a very successful local business called Airport Shuttles Dunedin, still run by the taxi driver Divesh, whom we partnered with many years ago.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete programmes, a business, and a partner, giving verifiable detail.

divination.statement: tonight 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, or in unlivable houses that are making them sick
divination.explanation: A claim about a specific near-term outcome ('tonight'); directionally reflects deprivation data but the precise headline figure is uncertain and likely inflated for rough sleeping.

divination.statement: if members opposite shatter the Shawist legacy of working across the aisle to achieve wins for climate, then they'll make climate another front in our culture wars, and—I promise—that's not a war that they'll win, but it's not a war that we will win either
divination.explanation: A conditional prediction that abandoning cross-party consensus turns climate into a no-win culture war; plausible and even-handed but inherently uncertain.

divination.statement: When overseas markets and our trade agreements are demanding that New Zealand live up to our PR brand of being clean and green, backtracking would be dangerous to our nature and our prosperity as a country.
divination.explanation: Predicts economic/environmental harm from weakening climate policy given trade pressures; directionally supported but magnitude uncertain.

rigor.statement: That is enough empty houses to put roofs over the heads of every single person who's experiencing homelessness in Aotearoa right now, yet in Aotearoa, we're happy to allow tamariki to sleep in cars.
rigor.explanation: The premise-to-conclusion step conflates counted 'unoccupied dwellings' with housing that is available, habitable, and in the right locations — an oversimplification that doesn't logically follow.

rigor.statement: When overseas markets and our trade agreements are demanding that New Zealand live up to our PR brand of being clean and green, backtracking would be dangerous to our nature and our prosperity as a country.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a real market/trade rationale, though it asserts the consequence rather than citing specific evidence.

rigor.statement: Too often, central government tells local communities what to do, but it doesn't give them the resources to do it.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable structural point drawn from his own local-government experience, but offered as a generalisation without specific evidence.

civility.statement: This would save the Crown $245 million over four years, which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they're giving to landlords.
civility.explanation: Legitimate fiscal criticism, but the sensationalised 'handout' framing pushes toward rhetoric over neutral description.

civility.statement: Members opposite should be very careful as to whether they want New Zealand's hard-won consensus sacrificed at the altar of political expediency.
civility.explanation: A pointed warning aimed at policy/political conduct rather than a personal attack, though somewhat admonishing in tone.

strength.statement: The free breakfast programme still exists to this very day, and the scarfie shuttles branched off into a very successful local business called Airport Shuttles Dunedin, still run by the taxi driver Divesh, whom we partnered with many years ago.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete initiatives he helped start that had lasting follow-through, though at student-association scale and self-reported.

charisma.statement: Members opposite should be very careful as to whether they want New Zealand's hard-won consensus sacrificed at the altar of political expediency.
charisma.explanation: Frames the appeal around shared consensus but does so as a warning to opponents rather than an inclusive invitation.

charisma.statement: if members opposite shatter the Shawist legacy of working across the aisle to achieve wins for climate, then they'll make climate another front in our culture wars, and—I promise—that's not a war that they'll win, but it's not a war that we will win either
charisma.explanation: Combative in setup but lands on shared loss and the case for cooperation rather than one-sided triumph.

charisma.statement: So, instead of war, let's have peace. Instead of conflict, let's have consensus.
charisma.explanation: Explicit, inclusive call for cooperation and consensus over conflict.

charisma.statement: we must ensure that the hard-won climate consensus that we've all worked for here across the aisle holds and that we forge a new one that goes faster and further in protecting climate and nature
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-aisle common ground and building a shared, more ambitious consensus.

charisma.statement: To my friends, enemies, and frenemies across the aisle, I promise that my door will always be open to you to hear you out, because dialogue is the first step to consensus.
charisma.explanation: Directly invites opponents in and frames dialogue as the route to consensus — strongly bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I implore this House to make sure that when it's considering legislation on any issue to do with Te Tiriti o Waitangi—whether it is removing clauses from legislation, minimising the value of those clauses, minimising the value of Te Tiriti o Waitangi—they think twice about doing that
charisma.explanation: An appeal to the whole House to reflect before acting; persuasive and addressed to all members, but implicitly aimed at the current government's Treaty-clause agenda so only partly cross-party.

charisma.statement: what I am trying to remind my colleagues across the House is when we talk about iwi being generous and patient, my goodness do we acknowledge in this case for Whakatōhea and hapū that this is an incredibly significant day today.
charisma.explanation: Directly addresses colleagues across the House and invites shared acknowledgement; inclusive tone.

charisma.statement: I am proud to be speaking on the third reading for the ACT Party in support of this bill, to give our shoulder to your effort of seeking justice.
charisma.explanation: Signals cross-party unity behind the settlement; frames his party as supporting a shared cause.

charisma.statement: At one level, we are combatants, adversaries, in the context of politics, but we are all here to, in a patriotic sense of duty, grow the wealth, the prosperity, and robustness of us all on this journey.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reaches across partisan lines and frames a common national purpose; strongly consensus-building.

charisma.statement: you will seize the opportunity and work and build on the collaborative nature of the mahi that has been carried out over the last three to five years and create New Zealand's largest and most profitable and most desirable new platform of marine, blue ocean growth
charisma.explanation: Encouraging and forward-looking, casting the iwi as national leaders.

charisma.statement: this is ultimately about creating a future for the people of Whakatōhea and a place where all of us can—and I mean all people in this country—come together and create a future for our children.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately inclusive ('all people in this country'), building a unifying national frame around the settlement.

charisma.statement: I've seen firsthand the impact of Treaty settlements, the ability they bring for iwi to build homes, to start businesses, to fashion schools, to deliver medical services, to directly assist their whānau, and to see language and tikanga flourish anew
charisma.explanation: Positive, inclusive framing of settlements as enabling flourishing; encouraging rather than divisive.

civility.statement: I implore this House to make sure that when it's considering legislation on any issue to do with Te Tiriti o Waitangi—whether it is removing clauses from legislation, minimising the value of those clauses, minimising the value of Te Tiriti o Waitangi—they think twice about doing that
civility.explanation: Pointed on a live political issue but stays policy-focused and respectful, with no personal attack.

civility.statement: what I am trying to remind my colleagues across the House is when we talk about iwi being generous and patient, my goodness do we acknowledge in this case for Whakatōhea and hapū that this is an incredibly significant day today.
civility.explanation: Respectful, engages the House constructively without attacking anyone.

civility.statement: I am proud to be speaking on the third reading for the ACT Party in support of this bill, to give our shoulder to your effort of seeking justice.
civility.explanation: Wholly respectful and supportive, no adversarial content.

civility.statement: At one level, we are combatants, adversaries, in the context of politics, but we are all here to, in a patriotic sense of duty, grow the wealth, the prosperity, and robustness of us all on this journey.
civility.explanation: Generous toward political opponents, emphasising shared duty over conflict.

civility.statement: There can be no legitimacy in our nationhood if it is not set in a principle of justice for Māori. We must know our history honestly and understand its impact to this very day. If we do not, then we will also not recognise the perpetuation of those injustices in the policy actions of today.
civility.explanation: Makes a strong moral claim but focuses on principle and history, not personal attack.

civility.statement: this is ultimately about creating a future for the people of Whakatōhea and a place where all of us can—and I mean all people in this country—come together and create a future for our children.
civility.explanation: Warm and inclusive with no adversarial content.

civility.statement: I saw firsthand how damaging and difficult that policy could be, and that Whakatōhea saw that up close and continues to feel the pain of that policy.
civility.explanation: Criticises a Crown policy, not any individual; harsh but legitimate.

specificity.statement: I implore this House to make sure that when it's considering legislation on any issue to do with Te Tiriti o Waitangi—whether it is removing clauses from legislation, minimising the value of those clauses, minimising the value of Te Tiriti o Waitangi—they think twice about doing that
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete category of action (removing/minimising Treaty clauses) but no specific bill, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: They also need to look at relativity as well—relativity between the settlements—because some are a lot better than others, one would have to say.
specificity.explanation: Raises the concept of relativity but gives no figures or named comparisons.

specificity.statement: the Greens have always been very, very clear that Te Tiriti was never supposed to be a transactional and a settlement approach. It is and has always been in the vision of all of our tūpuna that it is about an enduring relationship
specificity.explanation: A framing principle (relationship vs transaction) with no mechanism or concrete measure.

specificity.statement: if you live on an isolated part of this country, as is the case where I hail from in the very Far North, or are Whakatōhea, we need to be strategic and work collaboratively with the Crown and other private sector investors to make the resources that we have at our doorstep more valuable and turn them into a flow of goods and services.
specificity.explanation: Names a strategy (collaboration with Crown and private investors to add value) but no concrete instruments or figures.

specificity.statement: in May 1840, seven Whakatōhea rangatira signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, and by 1864 had developed a thriving agricultural economy, constructing a shipping fleet and trading extensively with the growing Auckland settlement.
specificity.explanation: Names dates, the number of rangatira, and concrete economic detail (fleet, trade with Auckland).

specificity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, the Whakatōhea iwi is based on the Eastern Bay of Plenty... with a land interest of about 200,000 hectares, and comprises of six hapū.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures — population, hectares, number of hapū — and a location.

specificity.statement: it confers 5,000 hectares of marine space to go to Whakatōhea for aquaculture endeavours; and two, that it allows for the Waitangi Tribunal to continue its Waitangi Tribunal district inquiry Wai 1750 pertaining to Whakatōhea, and to make findings, but not recommendations; two firsts of its kind in a Treaty settlement.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanisms — 5,000ha of marine space, named inquiry Wai 1750, and the findings-not-recommendations carve-out.

specificity.statement: I would like to talk about the redress of kotahi rau miriona tāra [$1 million] and that that sum is there for the future and the sustenance of Whakatōhea and for your young people to take full advantage of. I note there are 33 vesting sites as well as part of the cultural redress.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete redress figures and 33 vesting sites; highly detailed (the te reo 'kotahi rau miriona' literally means one hundred million, though the English gloss reads $1 million).

specificity.statement: There's no good having aquaculture if we don't have a water system that takes our paru water away and keeps our clean water clean. So your future is also reliant upon the decisions that happen in this country to make sure we look after the quality of our water, our beaches, and our kai moana.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the dependency (water quality) but no specific policy, standard, or measure.

specificity.statement: I've seen firsthand the impact of Treaty settlements, the ability they bring for iwi to build homes, to start businesses, to fashion schools, to deliver medical services, to directly assist their whānau, and to see language and tikanga flourish anew
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete categories of outcome (homes, businesses, schools, medical services) but no figures or named cases.

veracity.statement: They also need to look at relativity as well—relativity between the settlements—because some are a lot better than others, one would have to say.
veracity.explanation: Treaty settlement quanta and terms do vary substantially between iwi; a defensible general claim, though unquantified here.

veracity.statement: back in the early 1990s when Whakatōhea initiated and wanted to see some recognition for the many grievances and the Crown breaches of Te Tiriti, particularly in the iwi rohe, there was a go for a comprehensive settlement in the early 1990s. And then iwi members raised concerns that the negotiators had gone beyond their mandate and the settlement package was insufficient.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the documented history of Whakatōhea's failed 1990s settlement attempt and the mandate/adequacy concerns raised.

veracity.statement: It is a paradise, and it was a paradise in 1864 and it was burnt in 1865, 1866, and for 180 years after.
veracity.explanation: The core historical fact (raupatu/burning from 1865) is accurate, but '180 years after' is loose hyperbole — 1865 to 2024 is roughly 159 years.

veracity.statement: It was Parekura Horomia and Michael Cullen who, in 2005-06, took us to Ōpōtiki, where it became evident that one day we would have infrastructure built in Ōpōtiki.
veracity.explanation: A specific, plausible historical recollection consistent with the Ōpōtiki harbour/aquaculture development history involving those Labour ministers.

veracity.statement: a man by the name of Mokomoko was wrongly accused of murdering the missionary Völkner, and he was taken to Mt Eden Prison and he was hanged.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the historical record of Mokomoko's wrongful conviction and execution for Völkner's death, later the subject of a Crown pardon.

veracity.statement: in May 1840, seven Whakatōhea rangatira signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, and by 1864 had developed a thriving agricultural economy, constructing a shipping fleet and trading extensively with the growing Auckland settlement.
veracity.explanation: Matches the agreed historical account in the deed of settlement; the signing and pre-1864 Whakatōhea economy are well documented.

veracity.statement: te reo Māori is part of the Austronesian languages... we have this connection from Madagascar, on one side, to the Easter Islands and Hawaii, on the other, and Philippines, Taiwan to the North.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: te reo Māori is an Austronesian language and the family's geographic spread from Madagascar to Rapa Nui/Hawaii and up to Taiwan is well established linguistically.

veracity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, the Whakatōhea iwi is based on the Eastern Bay of Plenty... with a land interest of about 200,000 hectares, and comprises of six hapū.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the settlement documentation for Whakatōhea; figures are stated as approximate and are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: it confers 5,000 hectares of marine space to go to Whakatōhea for aquaculture endeavours; and two, that it allows for the Waitangi Tribunal to continue its Waitangi Tribunal district inquiry Wai 1750 pertaining to Whakatōhea, and to make findings, but not recommendations; two firsts of its kind in a Treaty settlement.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the bill's distinctive aquaculture and Tribunal provisions.

veracity.statement: They enacted the only cavalry attack in New Zealand's history, and the lives of 45 men and women were tragically stolen as a result at Te Tarata Pā.
veracity.explanation: The Te Tarata deaths reflect the historical account, but the sweeping 'only cavalry attack in New Zealand's history' superlative is harder to verify and may be overstated.

authenticity.statement: I can speak for myself. I know why I did it; I know why my whānau, hapū, and iwi did it. It was for our future generations.
authenticity.explanation: Speaks from his own experience as a settlement negotiator, giving a consistent personal motive; grounded in his own record rather than abstract.

authenticity.statement: the Greens have always been very, very clear that Te Tiriti was never supposed to be a transactional and a settlement approach. It is and has always been in the vision of all of our tūpuna that it is about an enduring relationship
authenticity.explanation: States a long-standing party position consistent with the Greens' consistent public stance on Te Tiriti; plausible and consistent from the text.

authenticity.statement: I saw firsthand how damaging and difficult that policy could be, and that Whakatōhea saw that up close and continues to feel the pain of that policy.
authenticity.explanation: Draws on her own record as a former Office of Treaty Settlements negotiator to critique the 'large natural groups' policy, consistent with a firsthand account.

divination.statement: you will seize the opportunity and work and build on the collaborative nature of the mahi that has been carried out over the last three to five years and create New Zealand's largest and most profitable and most desirable new platform of marine, blue ocean growth
divination.explanation: An optimistic forecast that Whakatōhea aquaculture will become NZ's largest/most profitable marine platform; directionally plausible given the 5,000ha allocation but the superlative outcome is uncertain over an unspecified timeframe.

rigor.statement: if you live on an isolated part of this country, as is the case where I hail from in the very Far North, or are Whakatōhea, we need to be strategic and work collaboratively with the Crown and other private sector investors to make the resources that we have at our doorstep more valuable and turn them into a flow of goods and services.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument: settlements confined to mana whenua boundaries disadvantage isolated iwi, therefore collaborative investment is needed; premise-to-conclusion reasoning holds.

rigor.statement: There can be no legitimacy in our nationhood if it is not set in a principle of justice for Māori. We must know our history honestly and understand its impact to this very day. If we do not, then we will also not recognise the perpetuation of those injustices in the policy actions of today.
rigor.explanation: A structured argument with clear entailment (know history → recognise ongoing injustice), though the opening premise about legitimacy is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: There's no good having aquaculture if we don't have a water system that takes our paru water away and keeps our clean water clean. So your future is also reliant upon the decisions that happen in this country to make sure we look after the quality of our water, our beaches, and our kai moana.
rigor.explanation: Sound conditional reasoning: aquaculture value depends on water quality, therefore water-quality decisions matter to the settlement's payoff; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Over this past summer, I read Dr Ned Fletcher's book titled The English Text of the Treaty of Waitangi... What is, I believe, incredibly clear is that tino rangatiratanga was the very essence of what was agreed to
rigor.explanation: Grounds his claim about tino rangatiratanga in cited scholarship (Fletcher, Carpenter), which is better than assertion, but leans on appeal to authority rather than presenting the evidence itself.

strength.statement: After 14 years, this is a Government that is finally delivering income tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the Budget. The last Government's response to inflation was more spending, more taxes, and more debt.
strength.explanation: Claims imminent delivery of tax relief in the Budget; the tax cuts were in fact delivered days later, so a real commitment with follow-through, though stated pre-delivery.

strength.statement: Well, what I can confirm is that this is a Government that is going to solve the housing crisis, unlike his Government that had six years to do it and didn't deliver. We're here to deliver.
strength.explanation: 'Going to solve the housing crisis' is aspirational assertion with no mechanism attached in this answer.

strength.statement: Ministers have gone line by line through the funding they are responsible for to evaluate whether it represents the best use of precious taxpayer dollars. As I said yesterday, this line-by-line process has uncovered more than 240 individual saving initiatives for inclusion in Budget 2024.
strength.explanation: Describes savings work actually undertaken and heading into the Budget, showing follow-through on a stated fiscal approach.

strength.statement: This includes finding $442 million in savings at Corrections so we can reinvest in our prisons and front-line corrections officers; finding $99 million from within the New Zealand Defence Force to reinvest in defence personnel and equipment; stopping work on the income insurance scheme, another name for a job tax; stopping work on so-called industry transformation plans; stopping work on Lake Onslow; repealing the Clean Car Discount; exiting the Crown's contribution to Let's Get Wellington Moving... and continuing the school lunch programme... in a way that saves taxpayers approximately $107 million a year.
strength.explanation: Announced concrete decisions already taken to stop spending, indicating delivery rather than mere intent.

strength.statement: Last week, I was proud to announce that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million to funding 1,500 new social homes... They do an outstanding job housing people in need, currently providing over 13,000 social houses around New Zealand...
strength.explanation: An announced funding allocation heading into the Budget — a commitment, but delivery is prospective.

strength.statement: On 7 May, I announced a new online data dashboard which makes daily attendance data available to the public and parents in a more timely way. The interactive dashboard will be updated once a week to show a national average and also regional breakdowns of how many students attended school each and every day.
strength.explanation: Describes an already-launched tool, showing delivery of a stated transparency initiative.

strength.statement: Last week, I announced $53 million over the next four years to attract, train, and retain teachers—the greatest asset that we have in our education system... This investment will support an additional 1,500 teachers into the workforce and help to give our kids a world-leading education.
strength.explanation: An announced funding commitment; delivery of the 1,500 teachers is prospective.

strength.statement: I recently announced $67 million of investment into structured literacy approaches... reading-recovery contracts due to expire at the end of this year will not be renewed as this Government commits to consistent use of best practice in our schools. Teaching staff who are employed under the ministry-allocated 271 full-time equivalent reading-recovery roles have already been offered the opportunity to retrain... The ministry advise that, therefore, current reading-recovery teachers may not necessarily lose their jobs.
strength.explanation: A funded, decided policy shift underway, though outcomes for staff are still unfolding.

strength.statement: Budget 2024 will provide $24 million over four years to contract the I Am Hope Foundation to provide young people aged between five to 25 years with free mental health counselling services through the Gumboot Friday initiative. This will enable Gumboot Friday to provide more than 15,000 young New Zealanders access to free mental health counselling services each year.
strength.explanation: A funded Budget commitment; delivery is forthcoming rather than demonstrated.

strength.statement: This settlement provides financial, commercial, and cultural redress funds totalling $100 million. The deed and the bill provide the transfer of 33 cultural redress sites. The deed and bill include acknowledgments of the Crown's breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi and an apology from the Crown to Te Whakatōhea.
strength.explanation: Describes a settlement being enacted at third reading — a concrete commitment delivered through legislation.

civility.statement: After 14 years, this is a Government that is finally delivering income tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the Budget. The last Government's response to inflation was more spending, more taxes, and more debt.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused characterisation of the previous Government's fiscal record; no personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, I think you heard us declare in February—and we partnered with both Australia and Canada at the time—that we did not want to see Israel undertake military operations in Rafah, because it would have catastrophic implications and impact on people. Obviously, we are a country that upholds international law and we expect Israel to be compliant with the ICJ ruling.
civility.explanation: Measured, substance-focused response to a charged question.

civility.statement: In the context that that statement was made, yes, and I can confirm that this Government will be delivering tax relief in this year's Budget, supporting Kiwis with the cost of living, with more detail to come on Thursday. And like him—though I don't agree with Labour's tax policy at the election; he's already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he's going to flip-flop on GST too.
civility.explanation: 'Flip-flopped' is a pointed criticism of an opponent's consistency, bordering on personal but tied to policy positions.

civility.statement: Again, you'll have to wait till Thursday, but what I can say to that member is that this is a Government that believes, after 14 years, that working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers, the same people the Labour Party and the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions used to care about, actually need support.
civility.explanation: Jab that Labour and the CTU 'used to care about' workers is a mild partisan dig.

civility.statement: Well, what I can confirm is that this is a Government that is going to solve the housing crisis, unlike his Government that had six years to do it and didn't deliver. We're here to deliver.
civility.explanation: Contrasts with the previous Government's record; partisan but aimed at performance, not the person.

civility.statement: Absolutely. And I also appreciate the opportunity to help the member understand economics, which is when you increase spending, you increase domestic inflation; that lifts interest rates, that slows the economy down, and that raises unemployment.
civility.explanation: 'Help the member understand economics' is a mild condescending dig in an otherwise substantive answer.

civility.statement: Well, again, the member didn't listen to my earlier answers to earlier questions which was that the Minister for Infrastructure has said that he is open to sensible changes to the legislation that can improve it. But, again, I make no apologies. We are going to get things done because we're not going to spend the time like the last six years of a Labour-Greens Government that just talked a lot, a lot of bumper stickers, and didn't get stuff done.
civility.explanation: 'Talked a lot, a lot of bumper stickers' is a dismissive characterisation of opponents' record.

civility.statement: Look, again, I just say to the member: we have policies, as you well know, through the Cabinet Office for managing conflicts, perceived or real. I would just encourage that member maybe to think and focus on managing her own personnel, not ours.
civility.explanation: 'Manage her own personnel, not ours' is a personal deflection at the questioner rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I want to thank the Minister for his question and just say the irony was not lost on me.
civility.explanation: Light, good-humoured reply endorsing a colleague's point about printed placards relying on mining; no attack.

civility.statement: According to the most recent advice I have received, the Government's baseline savings exercise will remove around 2,250 roles from Government departments, as well as closing around 1,150 vacancies. Further savings initiatives additional to our baseline exercise will remove a little over 500 roles. The number is subject to change... My heart goes out to anyone losing their job but Budget 2024 has required us to carefully reprioritise taxpayers' dollars.
civility.explanation: The 'magic money tree' and 'fleecing' lines about the Opposition are pointed jabs alongside an otherwise substantive answer.

civility.statement: No, in the next two years—you should listen up, mate; I answered that last week... around 500 new homes of the 1,500 will be allocated quickly, using the existing pipeline of community housing provider opportunities, with three objectives in mind: firstly, value for money from Government investment; secondly, contributing towards our target of getting people out of emergency housing motels; and a balanced approach between achievability and building capability in historically underserved regions.
civility.explanation: 'You should listen up, mate' is a mild personal dig at the questioner.

civility.statement: Well, that, unsurprisingly, is Kāinga Ora's perspective. I prefer the findings of the independent review.
civility.explanation: Dismissive but aimed at an organisation's stance, not a person.

civility.statement: Well, there are a number of factual inaccuracies there. Firstly, I didn't ask the reviewers not to involve Kāinga Ora—you should have listened to my last answer. The reviewers did talk to Kāinga Ora... this Government has a different attitude to that, and the public can see for itself the financial disaster that is that organisation.
civility.explanation: 'You should have listened' plus 'financial disaster' — pointed toward the organisation and a slight dig at the questioner.

civility.statement: One of the great tragedies of the last few years is that the social licence for social housing, which plays a very important role in housing vulnerable New Zealanders, has been eroded due to Kāinga Ora. Our Government seeks to rebuild the social licence to house vulnerable people in communities and make sure they have a warm, dry home.
civility.explanation: Critical of an agency's performance while framing a constructive goal; no personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, sadly, the name Kāinga Ora has become synonymous up and down the country with poor housing outcomes and a poorly performing organisation.
civility.explanation: Criticism directed at the organisation's performance, not individuals.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I'm sure that you should have gone to Specsavers.
civility.explanation: A jab (albeit jocular) at the Speaker's eyesight; a cheap quip rather than substance.

civility.statement: So far this term, we've seen that there is a real problem with fewer students attending each Friday. We've also seen a gradual decline in attendance over the last four weeks, which we might attribute to the winter season where more and more people have been calling in sick... in the last week to Friday 24, 90.8 percent of schools reported their data voluntarily... We're now at nearly 91 percent... We will aim for 100 percent when it becomes mandatory next year.
civility.explanation: Ends with a swipe at Jan Tinetti / the previous Government's honesty, a partisan edge.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister have any advice for people who say they are opposed to mining but live a luxuriant lifestyle thanks to the benefit of it every single day of their life?
civility.explanation: Frames opponents as hypocrites ('luxuriant lifestyle'); partisan point-scoring.

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the ability to hold up colour laser-printed images all day, every day, in Parliament is reliant on a vast array of materials, from printer toner to the metal in the printer to the fibre-optic cables that transmitted the signal—you name it, it all comes from mining—and would the words "hypocritical actions" come to the Prime Minister's mind?
civility.explanation: Explicitly labels opponents' conduct 'hypocritical', a character-tinged jab.

civility.statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they're doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.
civility.explanation: Harsh on the programme's philosophy but focused on methods, not the questioner.

civility.statement: At the heart of reading recovery, they believe in teaching children the habits of poor readers. The three-cueing system: look at the picture, guess the word... We know from all of the evidence from structured literacy in-class teaching that the need for remedial reading drops by up to two-thirds... I would also like to quote a very learned person... And that person was Jan Tinetti.
civility.explanation: Turning Tinetti's own past praise of structured literacy against her is a sharp but legitimate debating move.

civility.statement: Well, my message to that woman is firstly, thank you so much for being a teacher. We value you. The ministry has already contacted all of those reading recovery teachers, offered them retraining in evidence-based structured literacy, and many of them are taking that up.
civility.explanation: Respectful and appreciative toward the teacher despite the confrontational framing of the question.

civility.statement: Is it the Prime Minister's view that MMP has delivered far greater representation of Māori in this Parliament than any other left-wing, woke idea or—dare I say it—ethnic preference idea?
civility.explanation: Loaded framing ('woke', 'ethnic preference') that needles opponents rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware, in terms of the setting of future policy, that the latest records show that the Green MPs have the highest aviation expenditure record of every party in Parliament?
civility.explanation: A hypocrisy jab at the Greens dressed as a question; partisan point-scoring.

civility.statement: Could the Minister advise us as to why the Māori people, and, dare I say it, the esteem of the Māori language, have suffered from the ignominy of a disastrous housing policy such as Kāinga Ora, which has seen so many people without a home in a country they thought they could get a home in?
civility.explanation: Emotive attack on a policy/agency; heavy on rhetoric though aimed at policy, not a person.

civility.statement: Did any of your Ministers get $350,000 in taxpayers' charity money, fail to declare it, and when challenged, shouted by way of defence "That's racism."—did any of your Ministers commit that sin?
civility.explanation: A pointed personal attack on an opposition figure framed as a rhetorical question ('commit that sin').

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I wonder, Mr Speaker, whether you could indicate what ministerial responsibility the Prime Minister has for previous election results.
civility.explanation: A procedural point challenging the relevance of Peters' question; dry and rule-based rather than personal.

civility.statement: If he disagrees with the International Energy Agency and the independent Climate Change Commission and the world's top scientists that there is no future in fossil fuels or coalmining, from who is he actually getting his advice?
civility.explanation: Sharp but aimed at the basis of his policy position rather than his character.

civility.statement: Te Tāwharau is made up of hapū and general representatives, people who have supported the settlement and some who did not. I know that all of you will work together in the best interests of the people to make the most out of the settlement and the opportunities that lie ahead.
civility.explanation: Respectful and generous toward all sides, including dissenters.

civility.statement: I ask the House to think of those who have passed and the efforts of many Te Whakatōhea who have worked tirelessly across the generations to reach this day... While many have passed on over the century of struggle towards this day, you and your descendants carry their memories into a more prosperous future.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful tone with no partisan edge in a cross-party settlement moment.

veracity.statement: After 14 years, this is a Government that is finally delivering income tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the Budget. The last Government's response to inflation was more spending, more taxes, and more debt.
veracity.explanation: Characterising Labour's inflation response as 'more spending, more taxes, more debt' is a partisan simplification with some basis but missing context.

veracity.statement: Well, I think you heard us declare in February—and we partnered with both Australia and Canada at the time—that we did not want to see Israel undertake military operations in Rafah, because it would have catastrophic implications and impact on people. Obviously, we are a country that upholds international law and we expect Israel to be compliant with the ICJ ruling.
veracity.explanation: The February joint statement with Australia and Canada opposing a Rafah offensive is on the public record.

veracity.statement: What I can say to him is our Budget is designed to lower Government spending, to lower inflation so we lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and we actually keep people in employment. The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy's in recession, and rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The '84 percent' spending rise and 'all-time high' claims are contestable and lack the context of the COVID period.

veracity.statement: I have told that member a few times over the last few weeks that she will have to await Budget day to find the full set of commitments that we are progressing... we have already announced our commitment to a $1.8 billion boost for Pharmac. The second thing I would say is that across the coalition agreements... there are a number of commitments and not all of them will be delivered in our first Budget.
veracity.explanation: The '$1.8bn boost for Pharmac' claim is verifiable; the 'massive hole/fiscal cliffs' framing is contestable partisan characterisation.

veracity.statement: Well, sadly, the name Kāinga Ora has become synonymous up and down the country with poor housing outcomes and a poorly performing organisation.
veracity.explanation: A sweeping generalisation about nationwide reputation stated as fact; unverifiable and rhetorically inflated.

veracity.statement: At the heart of reading recovery, they believe in teaching children the habits of poor readers. The three-cueing system: look at the picture, guess the word... We know from all of the evidence from structured literacy in-class teaching that the need for remedial reading drops by up to two-thirds... I would also like to quote a very learned person... And that person was Jan Tinetti.
veracity.explanation: The 'habits of poor readers' framing of three-cueing is a contested characterisation; the two-thirds figure is asserted without citation.

veracity.statement: A report by the Auditor-General earlier this year found that despite a $1.9 billion investment into mental health by the previous Government, young people in need of mental health support are waiting longer to access care.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific finding to the Auditor-General with a figure ($1.9bn); broadly consistent with reporting, though 'waiting longer' compresses a nuanced finding.

veracity.statement: A 2023 ImpactLab assessment found that every $1 invested in I Am Hope results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays a real ImpactLab assessment, though such SROI figures rest on modelling assumptions presented without caveat.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware, in terms of the setting of future policy, that the latest records show that the Green MPs have the highest aviation expenditure record of every party in Parliament?
veracity.explanation: The 'highest aviation expenditure' claim is a verifiable per-party statistic, but stated without a cited source.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that that very speech he's referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency's assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises that the IEA critical-minerals demand figure is conditioned on rapid decarbonisation.

veracity.statement: It's 138 years since the Crown confiscated 144,000 acres of Whakatōhea land and moved its people to the Ōpape Native Reserve. Te Whakatōhea took their first petition to Parliament 110 years ago to seek an inquiry into the confiscation of their land... in 1949, the Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board was established by legislation and the iwi received £20,000 in the compensation.
veracity.explanation: A detailed historical account (144,000 acres, 1949 board, £20,000) consistent with the settlement record.

forthrightness.statement: Well, just that—that it's actually the founding document of New Zealand; we'll continue to honour it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he meant by his Waitangi Day statement that Tiriti obligations bind both sides; he affirms honouring it but does not engage the specific meaning asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think that question mischaracterises what we're doing. What we're asking for is, actually, making sure that when there are references to the Treaty in legislation, that it's actually very specific to the application of that legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how removing Treaty references from 40+ statutes meets Tiriti obligations; partially reframes but does not directly answer the obligation question.

forthrightness.statement: We don't believe a Māori Health Authority actually delivers better health outcomes for Māori—period. We think there's other ways to deal with that. We think we can do that through working and partnering with local iwi health organisations, as an example.
forthrightness.explanation: Rejects the framing but does give a clear position on one of the listed policies (Māori Health Authority), while not addressing the others.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think you heard us declare in February—and we partnered with both Australia and Canada at the time—that we did not want to see Israel undertake military operations in Rafah, because it would have catastrophic implications and impact on people. Obviously, we are a country that upholds international law and we expect Israel to be compliant with the ICJ ruling.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what actions the Government will take on ICJ obligations; points to a prior joint statement and an expectation of compliance, but names no new action.

forthrightness.statement: In the context that that statement was made, yes, and I can confirm that this Government will be delivering tax relief in this year's Budget, supporting Kiwis with the cost of living, with more detail to come on Thursday. And like him—though I don't agree with Labour's tax policy at the election; he's already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he's going to flip-flop on GST too.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms the prior statement 'in the context' but deflects into an attack rather than confirming the $250 figure directly.

forthrightness.statement: Again, you'll have to wait till Thursday, but what I can say to that member is that this is a Government that believes, after 14 years, that working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers, the same people the Labour Party and the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions used to care about, actually need support.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many extra dollars a minimum-wage worker will keep; defers to Thursday and pivots to talking points, never giving a number.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, the member will have to wait until Thursday, but what I appreciate is the question about the tax calculator, because I do want to say to the few people that are watching this broadcast today, get on board, go check out the official tax calculator on Thursday, and see how much benefit you're going to get.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm the calculator showed $2/week for minimum-wage workers; entirely avoids confirming or denying and redirects to Thursday.

forthrightness.statement: Again, that'll be dependent upon their individual circumstances, but what's great is that we have restored interest deductibility, we've reduced the brightline test, and we're balancing laws between tenants and landlords so we get a greater supply of rental properties in the housing market.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many dollars a property investor will keep; does not give a figure but does name the relevant policy changes.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I can confirm is that this is a Government that is going to solve the housing crisis, unlike his Government that had six years to do it and didn't deliver. We're here to deliver.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm the $288/week per property figure; refuses to engage the number and pivots to a housing attack line.

forthrightness.statement: What I can say to him is our Budget is designed to lower Government spending, to lower inflation so we lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and we actually keep people in employment. The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy's in recession, and rising unemployment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee the Budget won't trigger Reserve Bank rate hikes; gives no guarantee and instead recites the fiscal narrative.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I'd just say to that member is I would encourage her to read an excellent speech given by the Minister for Resources, Shane Jones, in the last week... Here's the deal: every electric vehicle (EV), every smartphone, every solar panel, every wind farm needs minerals. We can't just make them out of thin air.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether more coal/oil/gas is consistent with a livable planet; sidesteps to minerals for the clean transition rather than addressing fossil fuels.

forthrightness.statement: Again, what I'd say to you is that it's a very thoughtful speech and there's no way we can deliver our transition to a clean economy without minerals.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confronted that the cited speech assumes a fossil-fuel phase-out; does not engage the contradiction and repeats the minerals line.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd just encourage all leaders of political parties here in this House to support the oil and gas ban reversal and also support the fast-track legislation that's going through the House.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a friendly question about anti-mining hypocrisy by pivoting entirely to a call to back Government bills.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I reject the premise of that question, but what I'd just say to that member is, look, here's the deal: we need minerals—we need critical minerals—in order to make the transition to a clean future.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about sacrificing great spotted kiwi habitat for coalmines; rejects the premise and repeats the minerals point without addressing the conservation concern.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, we do. And as I said before, and as you've heard the Minister for Infrastructure say, the process is before select committee... But we make no apologies for adapting something that David Parker brought in the previous Government to actually fast-track and get things done in this country. We're going to build things.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms the processes exist but does not answer the specific question of how many times they were used on the Fast-track Bill.

forthrightness.statement: What I'd just say to the member is that we've got a bill that's through the select committee process right now... But I make no apologies. We are going to stop the talking and we're going to get things done in this country. New Zealanders are expecting us to deliver more infrastructure, more windfarms, more renewable energy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether a conflict process was used for Minister Jones's dinner with coalmining executives; does not answer and pivots to delivery rhetoric.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, the member didn't listen to my earlier answers to earlier questions which was that the Minister for Infrastructure has said that he is open to sensible changes to the legislation that can improve it. But, again, I make no apologies. We are going to get things done because we're not going to spend the time like the last six years of a Labour-Greens Government that just talked a lot, a lot of bumper stickers, and didn't get stuff done.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not commit to the specific change asked about (panel decision-making powers); reverts to a general openness plus an attack.

forthrightness.statement: Look, again, I just say to the member: we have policies, as you well know, through the Cabinet Office for managing conflicts, perceived or real. I would just encourage that member maybe to think and focus on managing her own personnel, not ours.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what would constitute a conflict under the Cabinet Manual; gives no definition and redirects with a personal jab.

forthrightness.statement: This includes finding $442 million in savings at Corrections so we can reinvest in our prisons and front-line corrections officers; finding $99 million from within the New Zealand Defence Force to reinvest in defence personnel and equipment; stopping work on the income insurance scheme, another name for a job tax; stopping work on so-called industry transformation plans; stopping work on Lake Onslow; repealing the Clean Car Discount; exiting the Crown's contribution to Let's Get Wellington Moving... and continuing the school lunch programme... in a way that saves taxpayers approximately $107 million a year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked where savings were made; answers with a detailed list, though caveats the rest to Budget day.

forthrightness.statement: According to the most recent advice I have received, the Government's baseline savings exercise will remove around 2,250 roles from Government departments, as well as closing around 1,150 vacancies. Further savings initiatives additional to our baseline exercise will remove a little over 500 roles. The number is subject to change... My heart goes out to anyone losing their job but Budget 2024 has required us to carefully reprioritise taxpayers' dollars.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question on Public Service job losses with numbers rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: I stand by the full statement I made in question time last Tuesday, which was, "Tax relief in the Budget will be fully funded through savings and revenue initiatives. These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party's tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements. There will also be other savings in the Budget [and] these savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services."
forthrightness.explanation: Directly reconfirms the quoted statement she was asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I have told that member a few times over the last few weeks that she will have to await Budget day to find the full set of commitments that we are progressing... we have already announced our commitment to a $1.8 billion boost for Pharmac. The second thing I would say is that across the coalition agreements... there are a number of commitments and not all of them will be delivered in our first Budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to funding 13 promised cancer treatments; defers to Budget day but candidly signals not all commitments land in the first Budget.

forthrightness.statement: No. There will be an official Government tax calculator. It will be hosted on the Treasury website, it will be available from 2 p.m. on Thursday, and you should go and check it out.
forthrightness.explanation: Denies the premise (that she took the calculator down knowing the $250 wouldn't materialise) and gives concrete detail on the replacement, though avoids the underlying $250 claim.

forthrightness.statement: No, in the next two years—you should listen up, mate; I answered that last week... around 500 new homes of the 1,500 will be allocated quickly, using the existing pipeline of community housing provider opportunities, with three objectives in mind: firstly, value for money from Government investment; secondly, contributing towards our target of getting people out of emergency housing motels; and a balanced approach between achievability and building capability in historically underserved regions.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers when the homes will be prioritised (500 quickly, within two years) with reasons.

forthrightness.statement: The balance of the 1,500 places, which will be about a thousand, will likely be allocated using an active-purchaser approach, which officials will be developing throughout the rest of 2024. This is a concept developed in the independent review of Kāinga Ora...
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses what happens with the remaining places.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that, unsurprisingly, is Kāinga Ora's perspective. I prefer the findings of the independent review.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the review can be thorough given Kāinga Ora's stated limited engagement; sidesteps the engagement point by simply preferring the review.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there are a number of factual inaccuracies there. Firstly, I didn't ask the reviewers not to involve Kāinga Ora—you should have listened to my last answer. The reviewers did talk to Kāinga Ora... this Government has a different attitude to that, and the public can see for itself the financial disaster that is that organisation.
forthrightness.explanation: Rebuts specific factual claims in the question (that he told reviewers to exclude Kāinga Ora), though characterises the concerns as not credible without detail.

forthrightness.statement: I recently announced $67 million of investment into structured literacy approaches... reading-recovery contracts due to expire at the end of this year will not be renewed as this Government commits to consistent use of best practice in our schools. Teaching staff who are employed under the ministry-allocated 271 full-time equivalent reading-recovery roles have already been offered the opportunity to retrain... The ministry advise that, therefore, current reading-recovery teachers may not necessarily lose their jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many teachers will lose jobs; gives context and the 271 FTE figure but lands on the hedged 'may not necessarily lose their jobs' rather than a number.

forthrightness.statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they're doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains why she is cutting the programme despite the favourable report.

forthrightness.statement: Well, my message to that woman is firstly, thank you so much for being a teacher. We value you. The ministry has already contacted all of those reading recovery teachers, offered them retraining in evidence-based structured literacy, and many of them are taking that up.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to a named teacher's concern about losing her job with a direct account of the retraining offer, though it doesn't guarantee her job.

specificity.statement: Well, I think that question mischaracterises what we're doing. What we're asking for is, actually, making sure that when there are references to the Treaty in legislation, that it's actually very specific to the application of that legislation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a general principle (references should be specific to the legislation) without concrete examples or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Again, that'll be dependent upon their individual circumstances, but what's great is that we have restored interest deductibility, we've reduced the brightline test, and we're balancing laws between tenants and landlords so we get a greater supply of rental properties in the housing market.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy levers (interest deductibility, brightline test) but no dollar amounts.

specificity.statement: Ministers have gone line by line through the funding they are responsible for to evaluate whether it represents the best use of precious taxpayer dollars. As I said yesterday, this line-by-line process has uncovered more than 240 individual saving initiatives for inclusion in Budget 2024.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count (240+ initiatives) and a described process, though the individual measures aren't itemised here.

specificity.statement: This includes finding $442 million in savings at Corrections so we can reinvest in our prisons and front-line corrections officers; finding $99 million from within the New Zealand Defence Force to reinvest in defence personnel and equipment; stopping work on the income insurance scheme, another name for a job tax; stopping work on so-called industry transformation plans; stopping work on Lake Onslow; repealing the Clean Car Discount; exiting the Crown's contribution to Let's Get Wellington Moving... and continuing the school lunch programme... in a way that saves taxpayers approximately $107 million a year.
specificity.explanation: Highly specific: named programmes with dollar figures ($442m, $99m, $107m/yr) and concrete cancellations.

specificity.statement: According to the most recent advice I have received, the Government's baseline savings exercise will remove around 2,250 roles from Government departments, as well as closing around 1,150 vacancies. Further savings initiatives additional to our baseline exercise will remove a little over 500 roles. The number is subject to change... My heart goes out to anyone losing their job but Budget 2024 has required us to carefully reprioritise taxpayers' dollars.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for role reductions (2,250 roles, 1,150 vacancies, 500+ further) with appropriate caveats.

specificity.statement: What an excellent question from the Minister, because this is the new normal. We are a Government that every day, every week, every Budget will strive to make the most impact out of every taxpayer dollar. That's what New Zealanders do in their own household budgets, that's what small businesses do in their own businesses, and that's what a good Government should do too.
specificity.explanation: Answer to a soft patsy question stays at the level of slogans ('new normal', 'most impact out of every dollar') with no measures.
