specificity.statement: I have told that member a few times over the last few weeks that she will have to await Budget day to find the full set of commitments that we are progressing... we have already announced our commitment to a $1.8 billion boost for Pharmac. The second thing I would say is that across the coalition agreements... there are a number of commitments and not all of them will be delivered in our first Budget.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete $1.8bn Pharmac figure while leaving the cancer-drug commitment unresolved.

specificity.statement: No. There will be an official Government tax calculator. It will be hosted on the Treasury website, it will be available from 2 p.m. on Thursday, and you should go and check it out.
specificity.explanation: Names the host (Treasury website), the time (2 p.m.) and the day.

specificity.statement: Last week, I was proud to announce that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million to funding 1,500 new social homes... They do an outstanding job housing people in need, currently providing over 13,000 social houses around New Zealand...
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: $140m, 1,500 new homes, 13,000 existing CHP homes.

specificity.statement: No, in the next two years—you should listen up, mate; I answered that last week... around 500 new homes of the 1,500 will be allocated quickly, using the existing pipeline of community housing provider opportunities, with three objectives in mind: firstly, value for money from Government investment; secondly, contributing towards our target of getting people out of emergency housing motels; and a balanced approach between achievability and building capability in historically underserved regions.
specificity.explanation: Gives numbers, timeframe and three stated objectives.

specificity.statement: The balance of the 1,500 places, which will be about a thousand, will likely be allocated using an active-purchaser approach, which officials will be developing throughout the rest of 2024. This is a concept developed in the independent review of Kāinga Ora...
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the balance (~1,000) and names the mechanism (active-purchaser approach) and timeframe, though the approach is still under development.

specificity.statement: On 7 May, I announced a new online data dashboard which makes daily attendance data available to the public and parents in a more timely way. The interactive dashboard will be updated once a week to show a national average and also regional breakdowns of how many students attended school each and every day.
specificity.explanation: Concrete date, mechanism (weekly-updated dashboard) and content (national and regional breakdowns).

specificity.statement: So far this term, we've seen that there is a real problem with fewer students attending each Friday. We've also seen a gradual decline in attendance over the last four weeks, which we might attribute to the winter season where more and more people have been calling in sick... in the last week to Friday 24, 90.8 percent of schools reported their data voluntarily... We're now at nearly 91 percent... We will aim for 100 percent when it becomes mandatory next year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (90.8%, ~85% to 91%) and concrete patterns (Friday dips, four-week decline).

specificity.statement: This Government has set a goal that by 2030, 80 percent of students will be attending school at least 90 percent of the time. That compares with term 4 last year, when only 46 percent reached that target, and term 1 this year, where the figure was closer to 53... When you have 80 percent of students attending 90 percent of the time, you actually require a daily rate of approximately 94 percent. I'll also just correct what I said earlier; I was relaying term 3 and 4 last year, not term 4 last year and term 1 this year in the earlier part of my answer.
specificity.explanation: Named target (80% by 2030), baselines (46%, ~53%) and a derived daily-rate figure (~94%).

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced $53 million over the next four years to attract, train, and retain teachers—the greatest asset that we have in our education system... This investment will support an additional 1,500 teachers into the workforce and help to give our kids a world-leading education.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($53m over four years, 1,500 teachers) tied to a named purpose.

specificity.statement: We're also faced with a projected shortage of up to 680 secondary school teachers in the next three years. The Education Review Office (ERO) found that half of our graduating teachers felt unprepared for the classroom.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific projected shortfall (up to 680 teachers) and a named source (ERO) with a figure.

specificity.statement: This funding includes 1,200 new on-site teacher-training places, a stipend for the trainees, contribution towards their tuition fees, and funding to support host schools... We're also investing in relocation grants for an additional 300 overseas teachers, supports for schools in early childhood education with teacher recruitment costs, and 670 scholarships and awards for teachers.
specificity.explanation: Detailed breakdown with multiple concrete numbers (1,200 places, 300 relocation grants, 670 scholarships) and mechanisms.

specificity.statement: I recently announced $67 million of investment into structured literacy approaches... reading-recovery contracts due to expire at the end of this year will not be renewed as this Government commits to consistent use of best practice in our schools. Teaching staff who are employed under the ministry-allocated 271 full-time equivalent reading-recovery roles have already been offered the opportunity to retrain... The ministry advise that, therefore, current reading-recovery teachers may not necessarily lose their jobs.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($67m, 271 FTE roles) and a definite decision on contract non-renewal.

specificity.statement: I was in the airport at Wellington yesterday... a mother whose young son, she told me, had dyslexia. In year 8, he was reading between a year 1 and year 2 level. With a structured literacy intervention, he gained that entire primary school—six years of reading—so that he was ready to start high school...
specificity.explanation: Detailed and concrete about the individual case (year 8, year 1–2 level, six years' gain), though it's one story.

specificity.statement: Budget 2024 will provide $24 million over four years to contract the I Am Hope Foundation to provide young people aged between five to 25 years with free mental health counselling services through the Gumboot Friday initiative. This will enable Gumboot Friday to provide more than 15,000 young New Zealanders access to free mental health counselling services each year.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: $24m over four years, ages 5–25, 15,000+ young people per year, named provider.

specificity.statement: I'm advised MPs' inboxes and social media accounts have been overwhelmed with positive feedback following this announcement. Comments I've read include Melanie from Thames, who commented, "Great..." Rachel from Wellington said, "This is fantastic news..."
specificity.explanation: Names individuals but the content is vague endorsement, not substantive detail about the policy.

specificity.statement: A report by the Auditor-General earlier this year found that despite a $1.9 billion investment into mental health by the previous Government, young people in need of mental health support are waiting longer to access care.
specificity.explanation: Named source and dollar figure with a concrete claim about outcomes.

specificity.statement: A 2023 ImpactLab assessment found that every $1 invested in I Am Hope results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70.
specificity.explanation: Precise cited figure ($1 → $5.70) and named source and year.

specificity.statement: Does he agree with the then Leader of the Opposition, Christopher Luxon, who stated on 19 September 2023, regarding the National Party's proposed tax cuts, that "for an average household income family with young kids, that would mean $250 a fortnight"?
specificity.explanation: Precise: exact date, exact quoted figure ($250 a fortnight) and attribution.

specificity.statement: Can he confirm that a typical property investor can expect to keep an additional $288 per week per property, or 144 times what a minimum-wage worker can expect to keep?
specificity.explanation: Highly specific figures ($288/week/property; 144x a minimum-wage worker's gain).

specificity.statement: Is he aware that that very speech he's referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency's assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific 'six times more rare minerals' IEA assessment and its stated premise.

specificity.statement: How do policies such as the Fast-track Approvals Bill, the Treaty Principles Bill, the removal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, the ministerial alienation of te reo Māori, and the disestablishment of Māori wards and the Māori Health Authority meet the Crown's obligations to Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates specific named policies and legislative changes rather than a vague grievance.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his statement that "we have well-established processes for managing ministerial conflicts of interest", and, if so, how many times have those "well-established processes" been used during the development of the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
specificity.explanation: Precise: quotes the PM's exact prior statement and asks for a countable figure tied to a specific bill.

specificity.statement: Where in the coalition agreement does it say that she will introduce or consider a tax on utes as outlined in advice received by the Minister of Revenue?
specificity.explanation: Concrete, document-anchored question referencing named advice and a specific measure (a tax on utes).

specificity.statement: This settlement provides financial, commercial, and cultural redress funds totalling $100 million. The deed and the bill provide the transfer of 33 cultural redress sites. The deed and bill include acknowledgments of the Crown's breaches of the Treaty of Waitangi and an apology from the Crown to Te Whakatōhea.
specificity.explanation: Concrete quantum ($100m), 33 cultural redress sites, and named elements (acknowledgments, apology).

specificity.statement: It's 138 years since the Crown confiscated 144,000 acres of Whakatōhea land and moved its people to the Ōpape Native Reserve. Te Whakatōhea took their first petition to Parliament 110 years ago to seek an inquiry into the confiscation of their land... in 1949, the Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board was established by legislation and the iwi received £20,000 in the compensation.
specificity.explanation: Dense with dates, figures and named places/entities.

rigor.statement: We don't believe a Māori Health Authority actually delivers better health outcomes for Māori—period. We think there's other ways to deal with that. We think we can do that through working and partnering with local iwi health organisations, as an example.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the Authority doesn't deliver better outcomes 'period' without evidence; the alternative (iwi partnerships) is offered as assertion.

rigor.statement: What I can say to him is our Budget is designed to lower Government spending, to lower inflation so we lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and we actually keep people in employment. The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy's in recession, and rising unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Coherent chain from spending to inflation to rates, but leans on selectively framed figures ('84 percent', 'all-time high').

rigor.statement: Absolutely. And I also appreciate the opportunity to help the member understand economics, which is when you increase spending, you increase domestic inflation; that lifts interest rates, that slows the economy down, and that raises unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Presents a simplified causal chain as settled economics; directionally defensible but omits the conditions under which it holds.

rigor.statement: Well, what I'd just say to that member is I would encourage her to read an excellent speech given by the Minister for Resources, Shane Jones, in the last week... Here's the deal: every electric vehicle (EV), every smartphone, every solar panel, every wind farm needs minerals. We can't just make them out of thin air.
rigor.explanation: True that clean tech needs minerals, but this is used to deflect a question about fossil-fuel extraction, a partial non-sequitur.

rigor.statement: Yes, we do. And as I said before, and as you've heard the Minister for Infrastructure say, the process is before select committee... But we make no apologies for adapting something that David Parker brought in the previous Government to actually fast-track and get things done in this country. We're going to build things.
rigor.explanation: Notes the fast-track concept originated with Labour's David Parker — a fair tu quoque, but not a full defence of the conflict-of-interest process.

rigor.statement: What an excellent question from the Minister, because this is the new normal. We are a Government that every day, every week, every Budget will strive to make the most impact out of every taxpayer dollar. That's what New Zealanders do in their own household budgets, that's what small businesses do in their own businesses, and that's what a good Government should do too.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the household-budget analogy rather than evidence about government finances.

rigor.statement: One of the great tragedies of the last few years is that the social licence for social housing, which plays a very important role in housing vulnerable New Zealanders, has been eroded due to Kāinga Ora. Our Government seeks to rebuild the social licence to house vulnerable people in communities and make sure they have a warm, dry home.
rigor.explanation: Asserts an erosion of 'social licence' caused by Kāinga Ora as fact; plausible but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: So far this term, we've seen that there is a real problem with fewer students attending each Friday. We've also seen a gradual decline in attendance over the last four weeks, which we might attribute to the winter season where more and more people have been calling in sick... in the last week to Friday 24, 90.8 percent of schools reported their data voluntarily... We're now at nearly 91 percent... We will aim for 100 percent when it becomes mandatory next year.
rigor.explanation: Draws data-based observations and offers a tentative causal hypothesis (winter illness) with appropriate hedging.

rigor.statement: This Government has set a goal that by 2030, 80 percent of students will be attending school at least 90 percent of the time. That compares with term 4 last year, when only 46 percent reached that target, and term 1 this year, where the figure was closer to 53... When you have 80 percent of students attending 90 percent of the time, you actually require a daily rate of approximately 94 percent. I'll also just correct what I said earlier; I was relaying term 3 and 4 last year, not term 4 last year and term 1 this year in the earlier part of my answer.
rigor.explanation: Works through the arithmetic linking the target to a required daily rate; coherent reasoning.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister have any advice for people who say they are opposed to mining but live a luxuriant lifestyle thanks to the benefit of it every single day of their life?
rigor.explanation: A patsy question built on a tu quoque / hypocrisy framing rather than an argument about mining policy itself.

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the ability to hold up colour laser-printed images all day, every day, in Parliament is reliant on a vast array of materials, from printer toner to the metal in the printer to the fibre-optic cables that transmitted the signal—you name it, it all comes from mining—and would the words "hypocritical actions" come to the Prime Minister's mind?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical gotcha invoking hypocrisy; the everything-needs-mining point doesn't engage the actual dispute over fossil-fuel extraction.

rigor.statement: We're also faced with a projected shortage of up to 680 secondary school teachers in the next three years. The Education Review Office (ERO) found that half of our graduating teachers felt unprepared for the classroom.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy rationale in an ERO finding and a workforce projection rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they're doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.
rigor.explanation: Engages the cited research by questioning its comparison baseline — a substantive rebuttal — but 'we know the evidence backs that up' asserts rather than cites.

rigor.statement: At the heart of reading recovery, they believe in teaching children the habits of poor readers. The three-cueing system: look at the picture, guess the word... We know from all of the evidence from structured literacy in-class teaching that the need for remedial reading drops by up to two-thirds... I would also like to quote a very learned person... And that person was Jan Tinetti.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific mechanism (three-cueing) and cites a quantified benefit (remedial need down two-thirds), though the evidence source is unnamed.

rigor.statement: I was in the airport at Wellington yesterday... a mother whose young son, she told me, had dyslexia. In year 8, he was reading between a year 1 and year 2 level. With a structured literacy intervention, he gained that entire primary school—six years of reading—so that he was ready to start high school...
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote to support the policy — an appeal to anecdote rather than aggregate evidence.

rigor.statement: I'm advised MPs' inboxes and social media accounts have been overwhelmed with positive feedback following this announcement. Comments I've read include Melanie from Thames, who commented, "Great..." Rachel from Wellington said, "This is fantastic news..."
rigor.explanation: Uses a curated selection of supportive comments as evidence of merit — an appeal to popularity/anecdote.

rigor.statement: A report by the Auditor-General earlier this year found that despite a $1.9 billion investment into mental health by the previous Government, young people in need of mental health support are waiting longer to access care.
rigor.explanation: Cites an independent report to argue spending alone didn't improve access — a reasonable evidential move.

rigor.statement: A 2023 ImpactLab assessment found that every $1 invested in I Am Hope results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70.
rigor.explanation: Cites an external return-on-investment study, but leans on a single commissioned analysis to justify the contract.

rigor.statement: Is it the Prime Minister's view that MMP has delivered far greater representation of Māori in this Parliament than any other left-wing, woke idea or—dare I say it—ethnic preference idea?
rigor.explanation: A leading question built on charged labels rather than argument.

rigor.statement: Could the Minister advise us as to why the Māori people, and, dare I say it, the esteem of the Māori language, have suffered from the ignominy of a disastrous housing policy such as Kāinga Ora, which has seen so many people without a home in a country they thought they could get a home in?
rigor.explanation: Loaded, conclusion-laden question ('disastrous', 'ignominy') that assumes its own premise about Kāinga Ora.

rigor.statement: Did any of your Ministers get $350,000 in taxpayers' charity money, fail to declare it, and when challenged, shouted by way of defence "That's racism."—did any of your Ministers commit that sin?
rigor.explanation: Guilt-by-association jab rather than engagement with any policy argument.

rigor.statement: Can he confirm that a typical property investor can expect to keep an additional $288 per week per property, or 144 times what a minimum-wage worker can expect to keep?
rigor.explanation: Presents a concrete quantified contrast to argue the policy is regressive; the 144x ratio is a pointed but arithmetic-based framing.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that more coalmining and oil and gas drilling is consistent with a livable planet or meeting our climate goals, as he has said that he is committed to?
rigor.explanation: Frames a genuine tension between stated climate goals and policy, though phrased as a pointed question.

rigor.statement: Is he aware that that very speech he's referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency's assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
rigor.explanation: Turns the Minister's own cited source against the argument, noting the IEA figure presupposes a fossil-fuel phase-out — a precise logical point.

rigor.statement: If he disagrees with the International Energy Agency and the independent Climate Change Commission and the world's top scientists that there is no future in fossil fuels or coalmining, from who is he actually getting his advice?
rigor.explanation: Marshals authoritative bodies to press the point, but the 'from who is he getting his advice' framing leans on appeal to authority and rhetorical challenge.

rigor.statement: Does he agree with Standard & Poor's that "unabated mines face the risk of becoming stranded assets as the global economy works towards decarbonisation" and his idea of "a modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand"?
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific ratings-agency assessment to argue the economic case against the policy — evidence-anchored.

rigor.statement: How do policies such as the Fast-track Approvals Bill, the Treaty Principles Bill, the removal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, the ministerial alienation of te reo Māori, and the disestablishment of Māori wards and the Māori Health Authority meet the Crown's obligations to Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
rigor.explanation: Builds a cumulative case from concrete examples, though framed as a leading question presuming breach.

divination.statement: In the context that that statement was made, yes, and I can confirm that this Government will be delivering tax relief in this year's Budget, supporting Kiwis with the cost of living, with more detail to come on Thursday. And like him—though I don't agree with Labour's tax policy at the election; he's already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he's going to flip-flop on GST too.
divination.explanation: Predicts Hipkins will 'flip-flop on GST too' — a falsifiable political forecast, offered as a partisan bet with little evidence.

divination.statement: This Government has set a goal that by 2030, 80 percent of students will be attending school at least 90 percent of the time. That compares with term 4 last year, when only 46 percent reached that target, and term 1 this year, where the figure was closer to 53... When you have 80 percent of students attending 90 percent of the time, you actually require a daily rate of approximately 94 percent. I'll also just correct what I said earlier; I was relaying term 3 and 4 last year, not term 4 last year and term 1 this year in the earlier part of my answer.
divination.explanation: The 80%-by-2030 target implies a forecastable outcome; ambitious relative to the current ~53% baseline.

divination.statement: We're also faced with a projected shortage of up to 680 secondary school teachers in the next three years. The Education Review Office (ERO) found that half of our graduating teachers felt unprepared for the classroom.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a shortage of up to 680 secondary teachers within three years; plausible workforce projection, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: Does he agree with Standard & Poor's that "unabated mines face the risk of becoming stranded assets as the global economy works towards decarbonisation" and his idea of "a modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand"?
divination.explanation: Invokes the forecast that unabated mines risk becoming stranded assets under decarbonisation; directionally supported but timeframe/magnitude uncertain.

authenticity.statement: I stand by the full statement I made in question time last Tuesday, which was, "Tax relief in the Budget will be fully funded through savings and revenue initiatives. These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party's tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements. There will also be other savings in the Budget [and] these savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services."
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms her earlier statement in full and in context rather than walking it back — a consistency signal.

authenticity.statement: This Government has set a goal that by 2030, 80 percent of students will be attending school at least 90 percent of the time. That compares with term 4 last year, when only 46 percent reached that target, and term 1 this year, where the figure was closer to 53... When you have 80 percent of students attending 90 percent of the time, you actually require a daily rate of approximately 94 percent. I'll also just correct what I said earlier; I was relaying term 3 and 4 last year, not term 4 last year and term 1 this year in the earlier part of my answer.
authenticity.explanation: Volunteers a correction to his own earlier misstatement, a signal of candour and consistency with the record.

authenticity.statement: Does he agree with the then Leader of the Opposition, Christopher Luxon, who stated on 19 September 2023, regarding the National Party's proposed tax cuts, that "for an average household income family with young kids, that would mean $250 a fortnight"?
authenticity.explanation: Tests the PM's consistency against his own prior specific claim — probing words-vs-delivery, though the judgement is about Luxon, not Hipkins.

authenticity.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that more coalmining and oil and gas drilling is consistent with a livable planet or meeting our climate goals, as he has said that he is committed to?
authenticity.explanation: Probes a possible words-vs-actions gap between the PM's stated climate commitment and expanding fossil-fuel extraction; the consistency judgement targets Luxon.

charisma.statement: Te Tāwharau is made up of hapū and general representatives, people who have supported the settlement and some who did not. I know that all of you will work together in the best interests of the people to make the most out of the settlement and the opportunities that lie ahead.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges those who opposed the settlement and calls for unity in the common interest — inclusive, bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I ask the House to think of those who have passed and the efforts of many Te Whakatōhea who have worked tirelessly across the generations to reach this day... While many have passed on over the century of struggle towards this day, you and your descendants carry their memories into a more prosperous future.
charisma.explanation: Warm, unifying acknowledgement that honours the iwi's multi-generational effort and invites shared reflection.

veracity.statement: It was the same Shane Jones who keeps rubbishing the Waitangi Tribunal, and they want us to shut the tribunal down.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about Jones's/NZ First's stated public position on the Waitangi Tribunal, which is broadly consistent with their public statements about scaling back the Tribunal.

veracity.statement: It is now the biggest full-time employer of people in the rohe, with nearly 200 people
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable employment claim about the Whakatōhea mussel operation; plausible and consistent with public reporting on the venture.

veracity.statement: as part of this settlement, the Crown Regional Holdings Limited shares will transfer to the iwi, increasing its shareholding to just under 48 percent
veracity.explanation: Concrete factual claim about the settlement terms, presented as verifiable detail of the bill.

veracity.statement: This is why economies that are poor tend to be the worst environmental vandals. Economies that are wealthy and prosperous tend to look after the environment, and there's a direct correlation.
veracity.explanation: Contains a grain of truth (environmental-Kuznets-type patterns) but overstated and missing context, so partly misleading as a blanket claim.

veracity.statement: We see in the documents supplied with the bill that the officials have said we don't even know if this is a problem. We don't even know if consents are being stopped, because the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy is being considered in those consents.
veracity.explanation: Cites the bill's own supplementary analysis to claim officials found weak evidence of the problem the change addresses; a checkable, evidence-grounded claim.

veracity.statement: There was official advice that said there was no time for consultation, none with iwi Māori, no assessment of the Treaty impacts, including on the Crown's Treaty settlements or commitments.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim attributed to official advice in the supplementary analysis reports; presented as verifiable and consistent with the bill's rushed timeline.

veracity.statement: 50 of Aotearoa's top freshwater experts and leaders were so concerned about it that they actually organised and wrote a letter to the Prime Minister and Ministers, clearly and concisely stating their concerns.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claim about a specific expert letter; consistent with reported freshwater-scientist opposition to the reforms.

veracity.statement: The advice from officials made it clear that it is not possible to quantify how many new coalmines or extensions for existing coalmines would be affected by the proposed changes—that there is a risk of irreparable damage to, and loss of, wetlands if a consent pathway is to be provided.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific, checkable point to the supplementary analysis report about unquantified scope and wetland risk.

civility.statement: It was the same Shane Jones who keeps rubbishing the Waitangi Tribunal, and they want us to shut the tribunal down.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of a named colleague, but directed at his public position and record rather than a personal insult ('rubbishing' is mildly loaded).

civility.statement: Don't listen to Shane Jones—he'll just waffle on with Winston's carry on, you know.
civility.explanation: Dismissive personal jab at a colleague ('waffle on', 'carry on') rather than engagement with his argument.

civility.statement: But I also recognise that when you hear some of the kōrero coming out from some of these MPs on the other side, you can see that they're conflicted—you see?
civility.explanation: Generous toward opponents, recognising their genuine obligations rather than attacking them.

civility.statement: I think the Whakatōhea kaupapa is the best example of how badly the Treaty settlement process went.
civility.explanation: Critical of the process/system rather than a person; harsh assessment but legitimate substantive criticism.

civility.statement: Stand tall; go well. You have brought dignity and grace in the face of extreme adversity. We wish you all the very best.
civility.explanation: Respectful, warm and dignified address; no attacks, focused on honouring the iwi.

civility.statement: I hear the member over the other side going on simplistically and tritely about destroying the environment. This is not about that; this is about simplifying and reducing the red tape that holds our economy back
civility.explanation: Characterises the opponent's contribution as 'simplistic and trite', dismissing rather than engaging, bordering on strawman.

civility.statement: I think it would be worth just everyone just taking a breath and dialling it down a touch, because I don't think the Speaker intended any offence. I think it would be a shame if we left the third reading and moved on to the later items of business in a spirit where there was acrimony across the Parliament, because I actually think there's unanimous agreement for reconciliation.
civility.explanation: Respectful, seeks to lower the temperature and preserve dignity for all sides during a tense point of order.

civility.statement: That moment then was a completely unnecessary interruption and an affront to an otherwise very dignified and positive process, and I support the call for you to make an apology.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Speaker's action pointedly but frames it around dignity and process rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: You didn't use any of your cultural support that you could have to have ensured that the mana of this kaupapa and the mana of our iwi was respected. There was a very wrong done here today, and they must be apologised to before they leave.
civility.explanation: Direct, forceful criticism of the Speaker's handling, but focused on the specific failing (not using cultural support) rather than personal abuse.

civility.statement: I find it extremely insulting that one of our rangatira was cut off—which is part of the protocol of the waiata today. I call for an apology from the Speaker today, to Te Whakatōhea, for rudely interrupting what was—
civility.explanation: A procedural grievance framed strongly ('rudely interrupting', 'extremely insulting'); assertive and heated but tied to a specific tikanga breach, not a personal attack.

charisma.statement: Don't listen to Shane Jones—he'll just waffle on with Winston's carry on, you know.
charisma.explanation: Combative, in-group framing that dismisses rather than persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: But I also recognise that when you hear some of the kōrero coming out from some of these MPs on the other side, you can see that they're conflicted—you see?
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges good faith and internal conflict in opponents, a bridging gesture, though still partly framed for his own side.

charisma.statement: I reject the proposition that you can have the economy or you can have the environment. Actually, modern economies that grow look after the environment and modern economies that are growing quickly—that provide jobs and growth for their people—provide the prosperity and the revenue to do all sorts of things in the environment that we would want to do.
charisma.explanation: Confident reframing that appeals mainly to his own side rather than winning over the opposition it addresses.

charisma.statement: I think it would be worth just everyone just taking a breath and dialling it down a touch, because I don't think the Speaker intended any offence. I think it would be a shame if we left the third reading and moved on to the later items of business in a spirit where there was acrimony across the Parliament, because I actually think there's unanimous agreement for reconciliation.
charisma.explanation: De-escalating, consensus-seeking intervention that appeals to shared ground ('unanimous agreement for reconciliation') across the House.

charisma.statement: We've been misunderstood for the last 180 years. Come on—all it is is an apology.
charisma.explanation: Emotive, in-group appeal to historical grievance; rallies his side more than it builds cross-bench consensus.

rigor.statement: The tribunal should be alive for ever and a day. It does not shut down just because we complete Treaty settlements. If we shut if the tribunal down, are we saying we're going to trust the Crown for ever and a day?
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason (settlements don't equal Crown trustworthiness) linking premise to conclusion, but rests partly on rhetorical assertion rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: I reject the proposition that you can have the economy or you can have the environment. Actually, modern economies that grow look after the environment and modern economies that are growing quickly—that provide jobs and growth for their people—provide the prosperity and the revenue to do all sorts of things in the environment that we would want to do.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies a false-dichotomy framing and gives a mechanism (revenue funds remediation), but the claimed link is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: This is why economies that are poor tend to be the worst environmental vandals. Economies that are wealthy and prosperous tend to look after the environment, and there's a direct correlation.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a 'direct correlation' as a sweeping generalisation without citing data, and treats correlation as if it settles the causal argument.

rigor.statement: As the Hon Shane Jones would no doubt point out if he was here, coal is required for food production, energy security, and industrial production such as steel manufacturing. If it's not mined domestically, all we do is import coal and steel with potential flow-on costs—increasing greenhouse gas emissions.
rigor.explanation: Gives a substitution/leakage argument (domestic vs imported coal) that reasons to its conclusion, though the emissions comparison is asserted, not quantified.

rigor.statement: Of those six, five of them are amendments to regulations. There is no need for primary legislation to make these changes.
rigor.explanation: Substantive procedural argument distinguishing regulatory amendments from primary legislation, with a conclusion that follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: It is, first, the quality of the water body that comes first. Second comes the ability for humans to use that water—so things like drinking water; that's important. Third is the consumptive use—that's the ability to make money from the water. How can there be any discussion of rebalancing that hierarchy unless you intend for profit to come over the environment and to come over people?
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the defined hierarchy to a conclusion, but the closing rhetorical question presses a slightly loaded either/or framing.

rigor.statement: This bill is being sent to totally the wrong select committee. It is going to primary production, and I have nominated the Environment Committee. I think that is where this bill should go to, because, of course, it is about amending the Resource Management Act (RMA), and what committee has always considered things to do with the Resource Management Act?
rigor.explanation: Argues from a clear premise (bill amends the RMA) to the conclusion that the Environment Committee should consider it.

rigor.statement: We see in the documents supplied with the bill that the officials have said we don't even know if this is a problem. We don't even know if consents are being stopped, because the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy is being considered in those consents.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the critique in the official advice rather than assertion, though summarised selectively.

rigor.statement: 50 of Aotearoa's top freshwater experts and leaders were so concerned about it that they actually organised and wrote a letter to the Prime Minister and Ministers, clearly and concisely stating their concerns.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority (expert consensus) to carry the argument, though it is a relevant and named authority.

rigor.statement: The science is crystal clear that if we want to prevent a future filled with climate catastrophe and extreme weather, then fossil fuels need to stay in the ground.
rigor.explanation: Leans on 'the science is crystal clear' (appeal to authority) and hyperbolic framing rather than laying out the specific evidence chain.

rigor.statement: The advice from officials made it clear that it is not possible to quantify how many new coalmines or extensions for existing coalmines would be affected by the proposed changes—that there is a risk of irreparable damage to, and loss of, wetlands if a consent pathway is to be provided.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the environmental concern in the official advice rather than assertion alone.

rigor.statement: You didn't use any of your cultural support that you could have to have ensured that the mana of this kaupapa and the mana of our iwi was respected. There was a very wrong done here today, and they must be apologised to before they leave.
rigor.explanation: Points to a concrete remediable failing to support the demand for an apology, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We've been misunderstood for the last 180 years. Come on—all it is is an apology.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a sweeping historical framing and emotional appeal rather than engaging the Speaker's stated reasoning.

authenticity.statement: I'm probably the only one who keeps booting the other side, you know—I can't help it.
authenticity.explanation: Candid self-acknowledgement that his combative style is consistent and habitual — words openly match his own conduct in the House.

specificity.statement: It is now the biggest full-time employer of people in the rohe, with nearly 200 people
specificity.explanation: Names a figure and a defined region, though 'nearly 200' is approximate.

specificity.statement: By 2034, the next 10 years, it expects to be employing in the order of 320 people, be operating out of the new harbour entrance, have many more vessels in the ocean, and will fair be pumping along.
specificity.explanation: Gives a headcount target and timeframe, though 'many more vessels' and 'pumping along' are vaguer.

specificity.statement: as part of this settlement, the Crown Regional Holdings Limited shares will transfer to the iwi, increasing its shareholding to just under 48 percent
specificity.explanation: Names the specific entity, the mechanism (share transfer), and a precise resulting shareholding figure.

specificity.statement: The share transfer in the settlement arrangement, with them having sole access to 5,000 hectares of seabed for aquaculture, is a game-changer.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise area figure and the resource involved, though 'game-changer' is rhetorical framing.

specificity.statement: For too long, New Zealand's farmers have been tangled up in red and green tape which has prevented them from unlocking productivity on their own farm.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical framing ('red and green tape') with no specific regulation, figure, or mechanism named at this point.

specificity.statement: It repeals the problematic and contentious low-slope map and associated requirements from stock exclusion regulations, reducing costs for farmers.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact regulatory instrument being repealed (low-slope map, stock exclusion regulations) and the intended effect.

specificity.statement: Of those six, five of them are amendments to regulations. There is no need for primary legislation to make these changes.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the claim (five of six) and identifies the precise legislative mechanism at issue.

specificity.statement: It is, first, the quality of the water body that comes first. Second comes the ability for humans to use that water—so things like drinking water; that's important. Third is the consumptive use—that's the ability to make money from the water. How can there be any discussion of rebalancing that hierarchy unless you intend for profit to come over the environment and to come over people?
specificity.explanation: Lays out the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy precisely, tier by tier, before drawing her inference.

specificity.statement: This bill is being sent to totally the wrong select committee. It is going to primary production, and I have nominated the Environment Committee. I think that is where this bill should go to, because, of course, it is about amending the Resource Management Act (RMA), and what committee has always considered things to do with the Resource Management Act?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific committees and the concrete procedural objection.

specificity.statement: There was official advice that said there was no time for consultation, none with iwi Māori, no assessment of the Treaty impacts, including on the Crown's Treaty settlements or commitments.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the concrete gaps (no consultation, no iwi consultation, no Treaty impact assessment).

divination.statement: By 2034, the next 10 years, it expects to be employing in the order of 320 people, be operating out of the new harbour entrance, have many more vessels in the ocean, and will fair be pumping along.
divination.explanation: Ten-year forecast of employment and expansion; plausible given the settlement's asset transfer but contingent on markets and delivery.

divination.statement: As the Hon Shane Jones would no doubt point out if he was here, coal is required for food production, energy security, and industrial production such as steel manufacturing. If it's not mined domestically, all we do is import coal and steel with potential flow-on costs—increasing greenhouse gas emissions.
divination.explanation: Predicts that curtailing domestic mining leads to imports and higher emissions; directionally plausible but magnitude uncertain and contested.

divination.statement: The science is crystal clear that if we want to prevent a future filled with climate catastrophe and extreme weather, then fossil fuels need to stay in the ground.
divination.explanation: Broad prediction linking continued fossil-fuel use to climate catastrophe; directionally supported by climate science but too sweeping to score highly.

specificity.statement: For every $1 invested in I Am Hope, it results in a social return to New Zealand of $5.70.
specificity.explanation: A precise numerical ROI figure ($1 → $5.70).

specificity.statement: This funding will help Gumboot Friday give more than 15,000 young New Zealanders access to free mental health counselling services each year.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete beneficiary count (15,000/year) and the service.

specificity.statement: I Am Hope has over 500 accredited counsellors and, with this funding, 300 more are on the way.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for current (500) and planned (300) counsellors.

specificity.statement: I am advised that between 16 April 2014 and 16 April 2024 only two residence applications for recognised refugee or protected persons were declined based on determinations that an applicant did not meet the acceptable health standards requirements. These applications in both cases were subsequently granted their residence by ministerial intervention.
specificity.explanation: Precise date range, exact count (two), and the outcome of each case.

specificity.statement: I refute the claim that this creates barriers. What it is actually doing is ensuring that those medical needs can be fully assessed and services provided to meet those needs. charisma.explanation: Constructive, consensus-seeking suggestion that identifies where the House could actually agree.

charisma.statement: It is rare as a Parliament that we do get to have conversations and debates where we take the political tension down around what the long-term future and opportunities and challenges for our country are in order to get beyond the petty politics of the day and think about the future—to think about that long-term, intergenerational future.

charisma.statement: we do need to take the heat out of some of these conversations and realise that we do need to find some of the areas where we can find common ground and find what we can do that is in the interests of our of our globe and of our nation.

authenticity.statement: I was the Mayor of Wellington when we actually introduced a Māori ward, and, actually, I was proud to be part of doing that.

authenticity.statement: All three Government parties campaigned on this, leading up to the last election, and were voted in accordingly—in quite a contrast, perhaps, to 2021, where we saw the first changes to representation and Māori wards not campaigned on at all in 2020.

authenticity.statement: This is the fundamental tenet of democracy: that we tell people what we're going to do, they vote for us, and now we're doing it.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts consistency between campaign commitments and legislative action as a principle.

authenticity.statement: Labour will stick up for Māori; it will stick up for those "activist mayors"... and we will stick up for those outcomes that we see when we have more Māori representatives around the council table—more cohesion, more expertise in te taiao, and the representation of Māori people around the council table.

authenticity.statement: Restoring the right to local referendums on Māori wards is a commitment under both the ACT and New Zealand First coalition agreements. strength.statement: I was the Mayor of Wellington when we actually introduced a Māori ward, and, actually, I was proud to be part of doing that.

specificity.statement: I rise to support this New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill because it aligns with this Government's plans to strengthen our economy and provide for our ageing population.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bill but the stated rationale ('strengthen our economy', 'provide for our ageing population') is general, with no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: The fund adds to Crown wealth, improves the ability of future Governments to pay for superannuation, and reduces the tax burden of the cost of superannuation on future generations of New Zealanders.

specificity.statement: We've already heard tonight that the fund sits at over $70 billion and is projected to reach $110 billion by the end of the decade. It really has a healthy return of 11.9 percent—so huge opportunity for investment.

specificity.statement: Coming from Hawke's Bay, it's heartening to see that we've got this Government investing in our roads of national significance and the four-lane expressway in Hawke's Bay, which will get that wine to port faster.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete project (four-lane expressway, roads of national significance) and its intended benefit, but no cost, scope, or timeframe.

veracity.statement: The fund adds to Crown wealth, improves the ability of future Governments to pay for superannuation, and reduces the tax burden of the cost of superannuation on future generations of New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the purpose and effect of the NZ Super Fund, which was established to pre-fund future superannuation costs; broadly correct though framed favourably.

divination.explanation: Forecasts the fund reaching $110bn by ~2030; plausible given growth and contributions but depends on market returns over the remaining years, so uncertain.

veracity.statement: There are 290 catchment groups now in this country. They have proliferated throughout from Southland to Northland.

veracity.statement: A recent report from the University of Canterbury revealed 24 percent of New Zealand's native vegetation—approximately 2.4 million hectares—is on sheep and beef farms.

veracity.statement: The total Māori package at last year's Budget was just over $825 million.

veracity.statement: Our tax relief packages will increase the take-home income of 83 percent of New Zealanders over the age of 15 and 94 percent of households.

rigor.statement: We will be on a pathway to becoming the next Venezuela or like the former apartheid South Africa.

civility.explanation: Heightened, sensational language, though aimed at Government conduct rather than an individual.

civility.explanation: Personal jab at Parker's appearance ('dishevelled') and a strawman that Woods's 'only response' is more tax.

civility.statement: the previous guy—Grant Robertson—concealed a lot of the size of the deficit because they refused to actually fund a whole lot of things past one or two years

civility.statement: The Minister, in answer to written question No. 11262, in 2024, said that the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki is not a front-line role. Anyone who thinks that a Government agency can run without a chief executive needs a 101 on how our Government works.
civility.explanation: Mocking tone ('needs a 101') but directed at the substance of the front-line/back-office classification.

civility.statement: They are prioritising landlords over our most vulnerable children. This is about choices and this Government has got its priorities wrong.
civility.explanation: Pointed values framing of a budgeting choice; harsh but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: The previous Government spent six years undermining the future of farming with a raft of unnecessary, often conflicting, rules and regulations that were bad for farmers and rural communities.
civility.explanation: Sweeping but policy-directed criticism of the prior government's regulatory approach.

civility.statement: In the words of some of our constituents, this is a Government that has unleashed an unholy or ruthless assault on Māori.
civility.explanation: Highly charged 'ruthless assault' language, though attributed to constituents and aimed at Government policy.

civility.statement: We've not heard from the Māori Party; we've heard from a party of radical extremists—so motivated in their commitment that they couldn't even file their own question today. That's how diligent they are.
civility.explanation: 'Radical extremists' plus a sarcastic dig; personal/party attack rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: We will be on a pathway to becoming the next Venezuela or like the former apartheid South Africa.
civility.explanation: Alarmist comparison used to discredit opponents.

civility.statement: The Māori Party pales in comparison to the great past Māori leaders such as Carroll, Ngata, Pomare, and Buck.

civility.statement: when you spend $350,000 of taxpayers' charity money illegally on an election campaign, they should be called out.

civility.statement: Under the previous Government—their soft-on-crime approach—crime is out of control and people in Mt Roskill don't feel safe anymore.

civility.statement: less than 40 percent will have the opportunity to make an oral submission, and that is outrageous and that is wrong. This Government is taking New Zealand backwards.

civility.statement: The trust deed has been carefully reviewed, and I don't think there is any lack of clarity in the proposed deed, in clause 1.1.17... I would suggest to the Chamber that that amendment is not needed, and I won't be supporting it.

civility.statement: I'm just confirming that the charitable purpose has been expanded to assist any women in the Canterbury area who are in need of support, regardless of social status, formal education, or other characteristics?

charisma.statement: Tonight at 11.59, submissions close on Māori wards, and I invite the people of New Zealand to unite with us in upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi and providing the important voice of Māori at the decision-making table in local government.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'unite with us' invitation, but frames unity around one side's cause rather than genuine cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: We've not heard from the Māori Party; we've heard from a party of radical extremists—so motivated in their commitment that they couldn't even file their own question today. That's how diligent they are.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: The Māori Party pales in comparison to the great past Māori leaders such as Carroll, Ngata, Pomare, and Buck.
charisma.explanation: Divisive framing that excludes rather than seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: Our Government intends to fix all of these things for New Zealand, to lift every New Zealander, Māori and non-Māori, together as one. That is the only way our country will succeed.
charisma.explanation: Unifying 'together as one' language, but embedded in an otherwise combative speech and paired with 'the only way' framing.

strength.statement: That Labour Government came in in 2017 and cancelled the former National Government's commitment to the Woodend Bypass, and it's brilliant to be part of a coalition Government that will reinstate that commitment and start construction in its first term.
strength.explanation: A commitment to reinstate and 'start construction', i.e. announced/intended rather than yet delivered.

strength.statement: It was also a privilege to stand with the Prime Minister and the transport Minister, Simeon Brown, to announce $63 million towards Coastguard and Surf Life Saving—$19 million for Coastguard, $44 million for Surf Life Saving.
strength.explanation: A concrete funding announcement he is associated with delivering, though still an announcement.

strength.statement: This Government is ambitious for New Zealand, with a plan to double agricultural exports over the next 10 years.
strength.explanation: A ten-year aspiration with no delivery yet or concrete mechanism described.

strength.statement: In Budget 2023, $200 million was invested through the Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga programme... it approved and contracted well over a thousand homes, enabled 1,700 infrastructure sites to see more green sites to allow building, it also supported 415 repairs to existing homes

forthrightness.statement: The new deed, in modern language, simply says any woman who's in need of financial support can be supported by the trust fund.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First, as a party, we have always campaigned on and we continue to address and meet with groups who are concerned about gender ideology... authenticity.explanation: The stated position is consistent with NZ First's publicly campaigned stance on gender and language, and she ties the amendment to that record.

charisma.statement: I do want to make sure that in the future we don't undermine what is an occasion where the Parliament comes together in the spirit of unanimity to support the Treaty settlements process with something like that happening again. I don't think the mana of the House was upheld, but I don't think the mana of the people in the gallery were being upheld either.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground and unanimity, acknowledges both the House and the gallery — bridge-building rather than partisan.

charisma.statement: So whether you're a farmer or a tradie, an entrepreneur or an innovator, my message is simple: we're a Government for you.

charisma.statement: Compared to recent years, there will be less verbiage, fewer pretty pictures, and a lot more substance.
charisma.explanation: A confident applause line for her own side that takes a swipe at predecessors rather than building consensus.

civility.statement: I do want to make sure that in the future we don't undermine what is an occasion where the Parliament comes together in the spirit of unanimity to support the Treaty settlements process with something like that happening again. civility.statement: Karanga is not only reserved for women—and those who are representative of iwi who use karanga and waerea to be able to do that would attest to that and affirm that that is actually a common practice where karanga and waerea are used in the same vein.

civility.statement: We don't believe in taking six years to do Auckland light rail—to think about it, to talk about it, to do some Post-it note sessions, to have a lovely strategy... We're going to build a 30-year pipeline of proper projects, not just ideas, and we're going to get things done.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'Post-it note sessions / lovely strategy' framing of opponents, though aimed at policy rather than the person.

civility.statement: thank you very much for overspending by 84 percent Government spending, thank you for driving up inflation to record highs, thank you for driving up interest rates to record highs... and thank you for raising unemployment—no wonder construction firms are doing it tough.

civility.explanation: Concedes question time is robust and criticises the conduct/answers rather than attacking the person.

civility.statement: it would be a bit rich for the member to expect that in six months of Government, we would then take responsibility for six years of actions which have contributed to the levels of child poverty today... she was the Minister of homelessness while thousands of children went to bed each night in a motel room, and it all got worse on their watch.
civility.explanation: 'Minister of homelessness' is a personal, mocking label rather than substantive policy critique.

civility.statement: One more sleep to go, heigh-ho-hippy-ho, and we hope to see tax relief for many Māori and all New Zealanders.

civility.statement: This is a piece of wardrobe that creates drive-by shootings and gang conflicts, and markets to and targets young men for gang recruitment, and to earn the right to wear one, you have to show that you have the propensity to commit violent crime. veracity.statement: Vui Mark Gosche was a Cabinet Minister under the Helen Clark Government, and I also have a range of other senior Ministers who've been appointed to public roles: Steve Maharey; Michael Cullen; Ruth Dyson... Annette King; Trevor Mallard; Phil Goff. The list goes on.

veracity.statement: It identified that of the 4 percent of New Zealanders who are highly victimised, Māori are disproportionately represented, comprising 30 percent of that group. This is twice the rate of the rest of the population.
