specificity.statement: under section 58, any beverage which is made by the fermentation of fruit, vegetables, or grain, is, in fact, wine. That’s what section 58 of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act says.
specificity.explanation: Pins the claim to a named section and the exact statutory criterion.

specificity.statement: if you have a wine grown—say, a very fine pinot noir in Bannockburn—and you are selling that in Queenstown or somewhere on the road nearby, does the member imagine that that would count as a winery cellar door?
specificity.explanation: Grounds the abstract definitional question in specific locations and a specific product.

specificity.statement: there are cideries that could be included as well. There are craft breweries that could be included as well. You think of the Nelson area and the specialist hops that are grown there.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete producer types and a real region/product (Nelson hops) to argue for a broader definition.

civility.statement: It is fitting that the member across the House Greg O’Connor, having been in law enforcement himself and having had a lot of experience dealing with situations like this, is the member who brings this amendment bill into the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of a member from another party; focused on substance and experience with no personal attack.

civility.statement: I think it’s very significant that we are doing this in a way that is united across this House.
civility.explanation: Collegial and constructive, framing the debate as shared work rather than contest.

civility.statement: I thank the Greens for coming around on this bill and supporting it.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of another party's support, no point-scoring.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the members of the Green Party—Tamatha Paul and Kahurangi Carter—for their decision to listen to the submissions, to hear the arguments, to review the evidence, and to balance that against the strongly held views of their party and their principles, and to, I guess, come to the conclusion that, on balance, it is a bill worth supporting.
civility.explanation: Respectful and substance-focused acknowledgement of opponents changing position.

charisma.statement: It is fitting that the member across the House Greg O’Connor, having been in law enforcement himself and having had a lot of experience dealing with situations like this, is the member who brings this amendment bill into the House.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the House to credit an opponent's expertise, building goodwill and cross-party consensus on the bill.

charisma.statement: I think it’s very significant that we are doing this in a way that is united across this House.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly celebrates cross-House unity, emphasising common ground over division.

charisma.statement: I would love to see, in the Budget tomorrow, some money go into making our net safer for our children, and stopping a lot of the stuff that comes into New Zealand by putting money into the safety of our net—and let’s see whether it happens; it’s the kind of thing that should be cross-party.
charisma.explanation: Invites cross-party action and frames child safety as common ground beyond one side.

charisma.statement: I thank the Greens for coming around on this bill and supporting it.
charisma.explanation: Warmly recognises an opposing party's shift, reinforcing consensus.

charisma.statement: We don’t just look after our own region. We take the logical position. We’re representatives of all New Zealanders and we need to make sure we’re looking after New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a national, inclusive frame ('representatives of all New Zealanders') to make her case.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge the members of the Green Party—Tamatha Paul and Kahurangi Carter—for their decision to listen to the submissions, to hear the arguments, to review the evidence, and to balance that against the strongly held views of their party and their principles, and to, I guess, come to the conclusion that, on balance, it is a bill worth supporting.
charisma.explanation: Publicly praises opposing-party members for engaging with evidence, modelling and rewarding cross-party consensus-building.

rigor.statement: With the awareness that this law change could impinge on human rights of registered sex offenders in terms of exposing them to more punishment, there have been steps proposed and accepted by the Justice Committee to ensure that all registered offenders are aware that this bill is going to happen.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges the human-rights counter-consideration and links it to a concrete mitigation (delayed commencement, notification), rather than ignoring the trade-off.

rigor.statement: We don’t just look after our own region. We take the logical position. We’re representatives of all New Zealanders and we need to make sure we’re looking after New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a consistency principle (equal treatment) against regional favouritism; reasoned but leans on a general appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: I cannot see why we would distinguish and keep this for those people who are in small business. They’re manufacturing product of this kind in a region like Blenheim, and not do that for the people of Morningside, who actually do have incredible breweries going, and they are there, and they are in exactly the same position. That’s like-for-like.
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument by analogy: like cases (small regional wineries vs urban craft breweries) should be treated alike; identifies a relevant parity.

rigor.statement: at the moment, they cannot provide samples in the part of the premises which sells the bottles of wine—or they can actually provide samples; they cannot charge to recover the cost of those samples.
rigor.explanation: Accurately isolates the operative distinction underpinning the bill's rationale.

rigor.statement: you could have a cellar door in Bluff and a vineyard up in Marlborough, and the retail premises would be strictly, under this definition, on the same piece of land.
rigor.explanation: Reductio ad absurdum showing that a 'same land' amendment fails because the South Island is one land parcel; exposes a genuine drafting flaw.

rigor.statement: So, when you’re talking about alcohol harm minimisation, going from 40 to 35, or 35 to 30, is not making a significant amount of difference.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned scepticism about marginal harm reduction, supported by the shot-glass/teaspoon comparison, though the conclusion leans partly on rhetorical intuition.

rigor.statement: To be a wine, the minimum amount of alcohol you can have to be classed as a wine under the law is 8.5 percent. There are a lot of beers over 8.5 percent, and so why would you have a different tasting amount like that if it’s similar to wine?
rigor.explanation: Uses an alcohol-strength comparison to argue against differential tasting sizes; a coherent point but glosses the categorical legal differences he elsewhere relies on.

rigor.statement: We had evidence from Olivia Doonan from Tūpari Wines, and their vineyard’s in the Awatere Valley and it’s quite remote. They have a cellar door in the railway station at Seddon, which is 13 kilometres away.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 10km amendment with a concrete real-world counterexample (a legitimate cellar door 13km from the vineyard), evidence directly on point.

rigor.statement: Pernod Ricard, which own Church Road, they gave evidence to the select committee about their difficulties. Even though they have a restaurant, they were having difficulty getting staff to staff the restaurant on the weekend, and, therefore, they had to close their cellar door.
rigor.explanation: Supports the bill's purpose with a concrete illustrative case of the problem it solves.

rigor.statement: the questions you asked were quite valid. The issue is that wine is defined in the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act, so it has to be referred to in that way. We can’t expand the definition of it in this bill. So you could bring in a member’s bill for ciders and so on and have them treated similarly, but you wouldn’t be able to do it in the way this is being done in this bill.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the refusal to expand in a concrete procedural constraint (statutory definition, out-of-scope ruling).

rigor.statement: So it could be that the grapes are grown in Waipara, in the Canterbury region—fantastic wine comes from there—but the cellar door could be in Blenheim or Christchurch. It could be a great distance away, because that’s what a “winery cellar door” means.
rigor.explanation: Careful textual reading of the definition, using concrete geography to show it permits distant cellar doors — a logically supported concern.

rigor.statement: My concern that I expressed in committee to the member was that this was, in fact, creating an anti-competitive environment where people didn’t have the same abilities to compete, that grape wine had a competitive advantage by an unequal regulation.
rigor.explanation: Frames the objection as a principled fairness/competition argument (unequal regulation confers advantage), logically connecting premise to conclusion.

rigor.statement: An arbitrary 10-kilometre radius actually may not fit be fit for purpose from one location to the next.
rigor.explanation: Raises a valid one-size-fits-all objection to the fixed radius, though stated as a concern without supporting data (Smith later supplies the example).

rigor.statement: if you have a wine grown—say, a very fine pinot noir in Bannockburn—and you are selling that in Queenstown or somewhere on the road nearby, does the member imagine that that would count as a winery cellar door?
rigor.explanation: Probes the definition with a concrete graduated test case to pin down how the licensing officer's 'opinion' would apply.

rigor.statement: there are cideries that could be included as well. There are craft breweries that could be included as well. You think of the Nelson area and the specialist hops that are grown there.
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument that comparable producers should get comparable treatment, illustrated with real examples.

veracity.statement: To be a wine, the minimum amount of alcohol you can have to be classed as a wine under the law is 8.5 percent. There are a lot of beers over 8.5 percent, and so why would you have a different tasting amount like that if it’s similar to wine?
veracity.explanation: The 8.5% classification claim is contested moments later by Duncan Webb, who notes it is the Wine Act (not the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act) that governs alcohol content — suggesting a misattribution.

veracity.statement: We had evidence from Olivia Doonan from Tūpari Wines, and their vineyard’s in the Awatere Valley and it’s quite remote. They have a cellar door in the railway station at Seddon, which is 13 kilometres away.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable factual claim about submitted evidence and a real distance; plausible and unchallenged.

veracity.statement: Pernod Ricard, which own Church Road, they gave evidence to the select committee about their difficulties. Even though they have a restaurant, they were having difficulty getting staff to staff the restaurant on the weekend, and, therefore, they had to close their cellar door.
veracity.explanation: Specific attributable factual claim about select-committee evidence; plausible and unchallenged in the text.

veracity.statement: under section 58, any beverage which is made by the fermentation of fruit, vegetables, or grain, is, in fact, wine. That’s what section 58 of the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act says.
veracity.explanation: Confident, specific citation of statutory text to support his amendment; plausible and left unrebutted, though asserted rather than shown.

forthrightness.statement: “Snack food” is defined in regulation 10, and it includes items such as potato chips, crisps, biscuits, crackers, processed seeds, and nuts.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Lemauga Lydia Sosene's question about what counts as snack food, citing the exact regulation and examples.

forthrightness.statement: the questions you asked were quite valid. The issue is that wine is defined in the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act, so it has to be referred to in that way. We can’t expand the definition of it in this bill. So you could bring in a member’s bill for ciders and so on and have them treated similarly, but you wouldn’t be able to do it in the way this is being done in this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Celia Wade-Brown's question on why the wine definition is narrow, giving the scope/legal reason and an alternative route.

forthrightness.statement: Personally, if someone brought a member’s bill allowing brewers to have cellar doors in a similar way under the licences that wineries have, I would support that, subject to it meeting all the right criteria, but I haven’t done that work on brewers, nor have I done it on distillers.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes he simply hasn't done the work on beer/distillers rather than manufacturing a substantive objection.

authenticity.statement: Personally, if someone brought a member’s bill allowing brewers to have cellar doors in a similar way under the licences that wineries have, I would support that, subject to it meeting all the right criteria, but I haven’t done that work on brewers, nor have I done it on distillers.
authenticity.explanation: States a consistent principle (open to extending the same treatment to brewers) but it is a hypothetical position with no action yet taken to verify against.

authenticity.statement: My concern that I expressed in committee to the member was that this was, in fact, creating an anti-competitive environment where people didn’t have the same abilities to compete, that grape wine had a competitive advantage by an unequal regulation.
authenticity.explanation: Notes he raised the same concern in committee, indicating a consistently held position across stages.

strength.statement: For the first time in 14 years, hard-working New Zealanders will get to keep more of their own money through our Government's tax relief.
strength.explanation: Concrete tax relief actually enacted in this Budget with the Minister responsible, not just promised.

strength.statement: From 31 July, personal income tax thresholds will rise. They will rise from $14,000 to $15,600; from $48,000 to $53,500; and from $70,000 to $78,100.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislated change being delivered from a set date, not merely aspired to.

strength.statement: In Budget 2024, the Government is investing an additional $8.2 billion in the health system, including $665 million of reprioritisation.
strength.explanation: An announced Budget investment; delivery of outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: It still staggers me that the previous Government funded a bunch of medicines until 30 June this year only... Thankfully, this Government has fixed that appalling problem.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete delivery — $1.77b to Pharmac to close the funding gap.

strength.statement: This Budget delivers on the commitment made in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to add 500 additional front-line police officers.
strength.explanation: Funds recruitment/retention; officers not yet on the beat, so delivery in progress.

veracity.statement: For the first time in 14 years, hard-working New Zealanders will get to keep more of their own money through our Government's tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Income tax thresholds were indeed largely unchanged since 2010 (~14 years); broadly accurate though framed rhetorically.

veracity.statement: The official cash rate went from 0.25 percent to 5.5 percent and has remained there for a year.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the RBNZ OCR path and its plateau at 5.5%.

veracity.statement: In 2017-18, net core Crown debt was under 20 percent of GDP. It is now over 43 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with Treasury debt figures across the period.

veracity.statement: I said in the Budget Policy Statement that the final operating allowance for Budget 2024 would be less than $3.5 billion, which was the allowance set by the previous Government. The final allowance in this year's Budget is in fact $3.2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the published Budget documents.

veracity.statement: By comparison, the final operating allowances for the last two Labour Budgets were $5.9 billion in 2022 and $4.8 billion in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Figures accord with the previous government's Budget allowances.

veracity.statement: the eligibility for the independent earner tax credit will be extended from $48,000 a year to $70,000 a year of income. This will help an estimated 420,000 additional people, most of whom will get the full $20 boost a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Estimate presented as modelled ('estimated'); plausible but not independently confirmable from text.

veracity.statement: This package of tax relief is identical in most respects to that set out in National's election tax plan.
veracity.explanation: Structure matched, but delivered amounts fell short of headline campaign figures (e.g. the '$250' case), so 'identical' is generous.

veracity.statement: The median full-time wage and salary earner now earns $73,000 a year and is in one of the highest tax brackets.
veracity.explanation: Median full-time earnings figure is roughly right; 'one of the highest tax brackets' is framing but defensible under bracket creep.

veracity.statement: Analysis from Treasury shows that an estimated 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight, and 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to Treasury analysis; framed as estimates, plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: Tax relief in this Budget puts $3.7 billion a year back into the pockets of New Zealanders. This tax relief is fully funded. Some of the funding is from revenue measures, but mostly it comes from savings.
veracity.explanation: 'Fully funded... mostly from savings' is contested — the opposition argues net borrowing rises; partly true but disputed.

veracity.statement: we are ending the failed policy that was first-year fees free. That policy failed its goal of lifting participation, and it failed to support students to complete their studies.
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported by official reviews of the fees-free scheme.

veracity.statement: New Zealand remains on track to reach the emission reduction goals of our first emission reduction period.
veracity.explanation: Partly supported for the first budget period, but omits risk to later periods flagged by critics.

veracity.statement: $10 billion worth of tax cuts; $12 billion worth of borrowing. You don't need an abacus to figure out that this is a Government borrowing to pay for tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Figures are roughly in the ballpark, but the causal 'borrowing to pay for tax cuts' framing is contested/misleading.

veracity.statement: $250 per fortnight, the average family with children was promised by this Government, and what are they getting? Sixty dollars per fortnight under the tax cuts that the Government has delivered.
veracity.explanation: National's '$250' was an 'up to' maximum case; comparing it to the $60 average overstates the gap somewhat, though the shortfall is real.

veracity.statement: superannuitants—a couple on superannuation—promised $13 a week by National before the election gets $4.30. That's $2.15 per person. That's less than a packet of chewing gum. I am astounded Winston Peters agreed to that.
veracity.explanation: The comparison figures are plausible; presented pointedly but not obviously false.

veracity.statement: The $2.9 billion in tax breaks for landlords has so far resulted in rents going up more.
veracity.explanation: Causal claim that interest-deductibility restoration drove rents up 'more' is not well supported by evidence.

veracity.statement: when early childhood education providers get an increase of just 2 percent and schools get an increase of only 3 percent—for some schools and not for others—that's not keeping up with inflation.
veracity.explanation: Figures are contestable but the inflation comparison is a defensible reading.

veracity.statement: this year's Budget makes it clear that child poverty in New Zealand is increasing, and it is going to continue to increase and the measures that the Government has implemented in this Budget mean more children are going to be pushed below the poverty line.
veracity.explanation: Supported by projections in Budget documents, though causation to specific measures is asserted.

veracity.statement: A minimum-wage worker will be lucky to get 30c an hour extra in their pay as a result of the tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: The small per-hour gain for minimum-wage earners is broadly plausible.

veracity.statement: A high-income person who has just one investment property will be getting an extra $2,085 a year in tax cuts, and an extra $15,000 a year in the tax breaks that are being dished out for landlords; $330, at least, a week better off compared to a minimum-wage worker, who gets just 30c an hour.
veracity.explanation: Figures are a plausible worked example but present a maximal contrast case as typical.

veracity.statement: Five-thousand jobs cut and counting—that's just in the public sector—with tens of thousands of jobs across the country going under this year's Budget.
veracity.explanation: Public-sector figure is plausible; 'tens of thousands across the country' is speculative extrapolation.

veracity.statement: 27,000 more people going on to the Jobseeker benefit, which is what this Government's Budget is forecasting.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the figure to the Budget's own forecasts, making it checkable and likely accurate.

specificity.statement: For the first time in 14 years, hard-working New Zealanders will get to keep more of their own money through our Government's tax relief.
specificity.explanation: Names a timeframe (14 years) but 'keep more of their own money' lacks amounts here.

specificity.statement: The official cash rate went from 0.25 percent to 5.5 percent and has remained there for a year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures and timeframe.

specificity.statement: In 2017-18, net core Crown debt was under 20 percent of GDP. It is now over 43 percent of GDP.
specificity.explanation: Concrete years and percentages of GDP.

specificity.statement: I said in the Budget Policy Statement that the final operating allowance for Budget 2024 would be less than $3.5 billion, which was the allowance set by the previous Government. The final allowance in this year's Budget is in fact $3.2 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact figure and the prior benchmark.

specificity.statement: By comparison, the final operating allowances for the last two Labour Budgets were $5.9 billion in 2022 and $4.8 billion in 2023.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures for named years.

specificity.statement: the Government intends to get back to surplus in 2027-28.
specificity.explanation: Names a target year, though contingent on forecasts.

specificity.statement: From 31 July, personal income tax thresholds will rise. They will rise from $14,000 to $15,600; from $48,000 to $53,500; and from $70,000 to $78,100.
specificity.explanation: Exact thresholds and start date.

specificity.statement: the eligibility for the independent earner tax credit will be extended from $48,000 a year to $70,000 a year of income. This will help an estimated 420,000 additional people, most of whom will get the full $20 boost a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Named thresholds, headcount and per-fortnight amount.

specificity.statement: The median full-time wage and salary earner now earns $73,000 a year and is in one of the highest tax brackets.

specificity.statement: Analysis from Treasury shows that an estimated 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight, and 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Precise household counts and thresholds attributed to a source.

specificity.statement: Tax relief in this Budget puts $3.7 billion a year back into the pockets of New Zealanders. This tax relief is fully funded. Some of the funding is from revenue measures, but mostly it comes from savings.
specificity.explanation: Names the annual figure and funding mix at a high level.

specificity.statement: In Budget 2024, the Government is investing an additional $8.2 billion in the health system, including $665 million of reprioritisation.
specificity.explanation: Named total and reprioritisation component.

specificity.statement: This Budget delivers on the commitment made in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to add 500 additional front-line police officers.
specificity.explanation: Named target (500) with $226m attached.

specificity.statement: More than $68 billion is forecast to be spent on infrastructure by the Crown, Crown entities, and KiwiRail over the next five years.
specificity.explanation: Named total, entities and timeframe.

specificity.statement: when early childhood education providers get an increase of just 2 percent and schools get an increase of only 3 percent—for some schools and not for others—that's not keeping up with inflation.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete percentage increases by sector.

specificity.statement: schools will be laying off teacher aides as a result of this year's meagre Budget increase.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete consequence (teacher aide layoffs) but no numbers.

specificity.statement: A minimum-wage worker will be lucky to get 30c an hour extra in their pay as a result of the tax cuts.
specificity.explanation: Concrete per-hour figure for a defined group.

specificity.statement: A high-income person who has just one investment property will be getting an extra $2,085 a year in tax cuts, and an extra $15,000 a year in the tax breaks that are being dished out for landlords; $330, at least, a week better off compared to a minimum-wage worker, who gets just 30c an hour.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures for a defined scenario and comparison.

specificity.statement: Five-thousand jobs cut and counting—that's just in the public sector—with tens of thousands of jobs across the country going under this year's Budget.
specificity.explanation: Gives a public-sector number but the wider claim is vague.

specificity.statement: 27,000 more people going on to the Jobseeker benefit, which is what this Government's Budget is forecasting.
specificity.explanation: Concrete number tied to a source.

authenticity.statement: I said in the Budget Policy Statement that the final operating allowance for Budget 2024 would be less than $3.5 billion, which was the allowance set by the previous Government. The final allowance in this year's Budget is in fact $3.2 billion.
authenticity.explanation: Delivered an allowance ($3.2b) consistent with her own prior BPS commitment (less than $3.5b) — words match action.

authenticity.statement: This package of tax relief is identical in most respects to that set out in National's election tax plan.
authenticity.explanation: Signals delivery of the party's campaign commitment; structure of the package broadly matches the election plan.

authenticity.statement: This Budget delivers on the commitment made in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to add 500 additional front-line police officers.
authenticity.explanation: Ties Budget action to a written coalition commitment — words matching agreement.

authenticity.statement: Fortunately, the parties in this coalition Government are the parties of the worker. We want working people to keep more of what they earn.
authenticity.explanation: 'Parties of the worker' sits in tension with the below-inflation minimum wage rise the opposition highlights.

divination.statement: the Government intends to get back to surplus in 2027-28.
divination.explanation: Forecast surplus 2027-28 ($1.5b); plausible but on deteriorating revenue forecasts already pushed out a year, so uncertain.

divination.statement: New Zealand remains on track to reach the emission reduction goals of our first emission reduction period.
divination.explanation: Forecast of meeting the first emissions budget; plausible but contested given cuts to climate initiatives.

divination.statement: More than $68 billion is forecast to be spent on infrastructure by the Crown, Crown entities, and KiwiRail over the next five years.
divination.explanation: Five-year forecast of capital spend; directional but subject to reprioritisation.

divination.statement: What I can say to them is that better times lie ahead. The economy is robust and it will recover.
divination.explanation: Prediction of recovery consistent with Treasury forecasts of growth picking up, but generic and unhedged on timing.

divination.statement: schools will be laying off teacher aides as a result of this year's meagre Budget increase.
divination.explanation: Prediction of layoffs from below-cost funding; directionally plausible but magnitude/certainty unproven.

divination.statement: this year's Budget makes it clear that child poverty in New Zealand is increasing, and it is going to continue to increase and the measures that the Government has implemented in this Budget mean more children are going to be pushed below the poverty line.
divination.explanation: Prediction of rising child poverty is broadly consistent with the Budget's own Child Poverty Report projections.

divination.statement: 27,000 more people going on to the Jobseeker benefit, which is what this Government's Budget is forecasting.
divination.explanation: Cites a forecast rise in Jobseeker numbers; plausible on the deteriorating labour-market outlook.

rigor.statement: Tax relief in this Budget puts $3.7 billion a year back into the pockets of New Zealanders. This tax relief is fully funded. Some of the funding is from revenue measures, but mostly it comes from savings.
rigor.explanation: Asserts funding source without addressing the fungibility/deficit critique.

rigor.statement: we are ending the failed policy that was first-year fees free. That policy failed its goal of lifting participation, and it failed to support students to complete their studies.
rigor.explanation: Claim of policy failure aligns with evaluations that fees-free didn't lift participation, but no evidence cited in text.

rigor.statement: This year's Budget is the clean-up job New Zealand needs. After six years of economic mismanagement, we are welcoming in a new era of careful Government spending, lower taxes for hard-working New Zealanders, and a strong focus on rebuilding the economy.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping characterisation asserted without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: $10 billion worth of tax cuts; $12 billion worth of borrowing. You don't need an abacus to figure out that this is a Government borrowing to pay for tax cuts.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes real figures but treats money as non-fungible, ignoring the savings/reprioritisation funding claim.

rigor.statement: $250 per fortnight, the average family with children was promised by this Government, and what are they getting? Sixty dollars per fortnight under the tax cuts that the Government has delivered.
rigor.explanation: Compares a best-case promise to an average outcome without noting the 'up to' qualifier.

rigor.statement: The $2.9 billion in tax breaks for landlords has so far resulted in rents going up more.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation on a complex market outcome with no supporting mechanism or data.

rigor.statement: when early childhood education providers get an increase of just 2 percent and schools get an increase of only 3 percent—for some schools and not for others—that's not keeping up with inflation.
rigor.explanation: Compares specific funding increases against inflation — a coherent, checkable argument.

rigor.statement: this Government is reverting back to trickle-down economics—the idea that if you give more people at the top more money, everyone else will benefit; despite 40 years of very clear evidence that that simply is not the case.
rigor.explanation: Labels the policy 'trickle-down' (a strawman of a broad-based threshold change) and asserts '40 years of evidence' without citing it.

rigor.statement: A high-income person who has just one investment property will be getting an extra $2,085 a year in tax cuts, and an extra $15,000 a year in the tax breaks that are being dished out for landlords; $330, at least, a week better off compared to a minimum-wage worker, who gets just 30c an hour.
rigor.explanation: Structured comparison, though selects an extreme case to dramatise the gap.

rigor.statement: A Government that wants to fund tax cuts by increasing gambling and increasing the smoking of tobacco has certainly lost its moral compass.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical moral framing rather than evidenced argument about the revenue measures.

civility.statement: It still staggers me that the previous Government funded a bunch of medicines until 30 June this year only... Thankfully, this Government has fixed that appalling problem.
civility.explanation: Harsh ('appalling') but aimed at a funding decision/policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: we are ending the failed policy that was first-year fees free. That policy failed its goal of lifting participation, and it failed to support students to complete their studies.
civility.explanation: Criticises a policy, not a person.

civility.statement: This year's Budget is the clean-up job New Zealand needs. After six years of economic mismanagement, we are welcoming in a new era of careful Government spending, lower taxes for hard-working New Zealanders, and a strong focus on rebuilding the economy.
civility.explanation: 'Six years of economic mismanagement' is a partisan swipe at predecessors, though aimed at record not persons.

civility.statement: this House has no confidence in the Government because it is taking New Zealand backwards, it has no plan to tackle the cost of living crisis, it has failed to deliver on the promises it has made to New Zealanders, and it is prioritising the interests of landlords and property owners over hard-working Kiwis.
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing ('prioritising landlords') rather than engaging the Budget's substance.

civility.statement: $10 billion worth of tax cuts; $12 billion worth of borrowing. You don't need an abacus to figure out that this is a Government borrowing to pay for tax cuts.
civility.explanation: 'You don't need an abacus' is a mild jab but stays on the policy.

civility.statement: superannuitants—a couple on superannuation—promised $13 a week by National before the election gets $4.30. That's $2.15 per person. That's less than a packet of chewing gum. I am astounded Winston Peters agreed to that.
civility.explanation: Directs a personal 'astounded Winston Peters agreed' jab at a named MP, plus a belittling comparison.

civility.statement: this Government is reverting back to trickle-down economics—the idea that if you give more people at the top more money, everyone else will benefit; despite 40 years of very clear evidence that that simply is not the case.
civility.explanation: Attacks the framing of the policy rather than a person, but via caricature.

civility.statement: A Government that wants to fund tax cuts by increasing gambling and increasing the smoking of tobacco has certainly lost its moral compass.
civility.explanation: 'Lost its moral compass' is a character/values attack rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: I note that Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon said that they would resign if they didn't deliver tax cuts. They've clearly chosen to prioritise their jobs over the jobs of the thousands of New Zealanders whose jobs are now at risk as a result of this year's Budget.
civility.explanation: Personal attack imputing self-interested motives to named opponents.

charisma.statement: Fortunately, the parties in this coalition Government are the parties of the worker. We want working people to keep more of what they earn.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but appeals only to its own side's framing.

charisma.statement: What I can say to them is that better times lie ahead. The economy is robust and it will recover.
charisma.explanation: Reassuring tone aimed at struggling households, though not cross-party.

charisma.statement: This year's Budget is the clean-up job New Zealand needs. After six years of economic mismanagement, we are welcoming in a new era of careful Government spending, lower taxes for hard-working New Zealanders, and a strong focus on rebuilding the economy.
charisma.explanation: Rallies own side by disparaging opponents rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge and thank the Associate Ministers of Finance—David Seymour, Shane Jones, and Chris Bishop—who were heavily involved in putting this Budget together. It has benefited considerably from their ideas, advice, and input.
charisma.explanation: Gracious and collaborative in tone but confined to coalition colleagues, not across the aisle.

charisma.statement: this House has no confidence in the Government because it is taking New Zealand backwards, it has no plan to tackle the cost of living crisis, it has failed to deliver on the promises it has made to New Zealanders, and it is prioritising the interests of landlords and property owners over hard-working Kiwis.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them mobilisation of the opposition, not consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: superannuitants—a couple on superannuation—promised $13 a week by National before the election gets $4.30. That's $2.15 per person. That's less than a packet of chewing gum. I am astounded Winston Peters agreed to that.
charisma.explanation: Scores a partisan point rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: When Māori in New Zealand thrive, the whole country will thrive, and non-Māori New Zealanders have nothing to be afraid of from that.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, reassuring framing that seeks to bring different groups along rather than divide.

charisma.statement: I note that Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon said that they would resign if they didn't deliver tax cuts. They've clearly chosen to prioritise their jobs over the jobs of the thousands of New Zealanders whose jobs are now at risk as a result of this year's Budget.
charisma.explanation: Combative point-scoring that demonises opponents rather than persuading.

civility.statement: Look, we are sick and tired of failed university student union politicians. They couldn't run the university school tuck shop.
civility.explanation: Belittling personal attack on opponents' competence rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: Now, back to the Greens. Facing 54 years, my friend, of never ever having made a Cabinet—54 years of never being in Cabinet.
civility.explanation: A jab at an opponent, though tied to a real political fact.

civility.statement: from the Greens you heard the modern version of Das Kapital, this utopian world, when she said this, straight out of the book itself, “To each according to their need”. That's communism.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents opponents' position to label them, a deliberate strawman.

civility.statement: These Green MPs, of course, are the highest aviation taxpayer-paid cost takers of all of Parliament. These Green MPs spend more time on aeroplanes than all the rest of us in terms of cost—about four times my party's cost.
civility.explanation: Harsh but aimed at a record; slides into insinuation about their conduct.

civility.statement: they just go to the nearest bush and find a frog and say, “This is going be under grave endangerment”, and media rush off and put them on night after night. They never ever do anything out there. They have no constituency offices.
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature of opponents' work; sensationalised ridicule.

civility.statement: When was the time Willow ever hit the ground hard and went around the place and put in some spade work for her party?
civility.explanation: Personal attack on an individual MP's work ethic rather than her arguments.

civility.statement: Two-thirds of our new spending goes to health, education, and law and order. That's our decisive reply to the fearmongering and scaremongering led by that crowd over there.
civility.explanation: Legitimate defence but dismisses opponents as 'fearmongering'.

civility.statement: Today the Māori Party organised a protest on Parliament's forecourt and then didn't even turn up in this House to find out what was in the Budget.
civility.explanation: Criticism of conduct rather than person, but framed to belittle.

civility.statement: never been seen in this Parliament since 1854. Since 1854, never been seen.
civility.explanation: Sensationalised exaggeration to mock opponents.

civility.statement: What I've just quoted to you today in both respects, to the president of the Māori Party, what he said then and what they're doing now, is an example of hypocrisy that is palpable, profound, precise, predictable, preferential, punitive, and pathetic.
civility.explanation: An alliterative pile-on labelling opponents 'pathetic'; targets character.

civility.statement: this Government made a clear attack on the rights of our babies and mokopuna through whakapapa in section 7AA. This Government is trying to create another stolen generation, and we won't stand for it.
civility.explanation: Strong charged framing of opponents' intent, though tied to a specific policy.

civility.statement: you have created the colonial trauma, the colonial violence, and what you do is you then reward yourselves by ensuring that you fund yourself on the trauma that you have created amongst our people.
civility.explanation: Sweeping accusation of bad faith against opponents; charged rather than policy-specific.

civility.statement: They watched while the last Government said that they needed every one of those dollars... and then they wasted it on three waters, on TVNZ-RNZ mergers, on more officials in the back office.
civility.explanation: Pointed attack on the previous government's programmes; targets policy though loaded with 'wasted'.

civility.statement: We've heard from the Greens member her proposal for a wealth tax—it's economic illiteracy. You can't tax your country into prosperity.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the proposal as 'economic illiteracy' — a swipe at the proposer's competence.

civility.statement: They're going to spend a lot more time in the wilderness before Kiwis look to them for salvation again.
civility.explanation: A gibe at opponents, mild and non-personal.

civility.statement: the party of workers does not take away cheap public transport for kids. It does not take away healthy school lunches. It does not put costs back on prescription charging.
civility.explanation: Harsh but engages specific policy choices rather than personal character.

charisma.statement: Look, we are sick and tired of failed university student union politicians. They couldn't run the university school tuck shop.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-vs-them mockery that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: some of us here are on a mission. We're out to save our country. We're out to make it one of the greatest countries in the world again, which we once were.
charisma.explanation: Rousing but appeals only to his own side; no bridge-building.

charisma.statement: from the Greens you heard the modern version of Das Kapital, this utopian world, when she said this, straight out of the book itself, “To each according to their need”. That's communism.
charisma.explanation: Demonises the other side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: there's nothing to fear from us. And I am willing to bring you along with us.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, invites opponents in rather than demonising them.

charisma.statement: we are not so much dealing with a cost of living crisis, as this Government campaigned on... we are dealing with a cost of greed crisis
charisma.explanation: A sharp reframing slogan that rallies her own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: we have made a change from the approach of previous Governments, in which the Opposition would find out about what bills were being introduced at the moment they were introduced... by providing copies of the bills to the Opposition at 2 o'clock when the Budget was introduced. So they've had a reasonable amount of time. I accept it's not an ideal amount of time, but at least it's more time than any Opposition in the past has had.
charisma.explanation: Concedes it is 'not ideal' and frames a procedural improvement toward the Opposition — a conciliatory note.

rigor.statement: Look, we are sick and tired of failed university student union politicians. They couldn't run the university school tuck shop.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem; attacks the people, not the substance of their policy.

rigor.statement: from the Greens you heard the modern version of Das Kapital, this utopian world, when she said this, straight out of the book itself, “To each according to their need”. That's communism.
rigor.explanation: Guilt-by-association/strawman equating a phrase with communism; no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: they just go to the nearest bush and find a frog and say, “This is going be under grave endangerment”, and media rush off and put them on night after night. They never ever do anything out there. They have no constituency offices.
rigor.explanation: Strawman and hyperbole with no evidence for the sweeping 'never ever do anything' claim.

rigor.statement: hundreds of thousands over the last three years have left or fled this country under a Labour Government. That's the most blistering commentary of how bad they were.
rigor.explanation: Correlation-as-causation and cherry-picked figure to indict the previous government.

rigor.statement: I am 20 percent of this country. I expect nothing less than 20 percent of the total Budget in this country.
rigor.explanation: Population-share entitlement to total budget is a non-sequitur; the premise doesn't entail the conclusion.

rigor.statement: if I make up 50 percent of the male prison population, then te iwi Māori should receive 50 percent of that budget. If I make up 64 percent of the female prison population, I deserve that proportion of the budget. If Māori tamariki make up 80 percent of Oranga Tamariki, I deserve that proportion of the budget.
rigor.explanation: Accurate statistics used to reach a proportional-budget claim that doesn't strictly follow.

rigor.statement: Matatini was given $38 million by Labour. You have given it $48 million over three years, which is less than the annual receiving of Matatini. It's less; it's $16 million a year over three years.
rigor.explanation: Makes an annualisation argument, though the comparison framing could be selective.

rigor.statement: you have created the colonial trauma, the colonial violence, and what you do is you then reward yourselves by ensuring that you fund yourself on the trauma that you have created amongst our people.
rigor.explanation: Assertion of motive without evidence linking funding decisions to deliberate self-reward.

rigor.statement: If our people are dying seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori, why not allow us to access superannuation before that? Follow the science. Follow the data.
rigor.explanation: A data-grounded premise leading to a coherent policy proposal, though the entailment is a values argument.

rigor.statement: If we are 50 percent of the social housing waiting list, we demand 50 percent of the stock. It makes absolute sense. These statistics are yours. This data is yours.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to official data but the proportional entitlement claim is asserted, not derived.

rigor.statement: even Michael Cullen's Tax Working Group said that if you don't adjust tax brackets for inflation, you destroy the progressivity of the tax system
rigor.explanation: Cites an authoritative source to support the fiscal-drag point; valid appeal, though the source is invoked selectively.

rigor.statement: two adults earning $150,000 each, per annum. Well, those are pretty well-off people in the first place, and they're going to get one of the biggest tax cuts going. They'll end up about $2,000 better off.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Government's own example to argue regressive prioritisation; conclusion follows from the cited figures.

rigor.statement: in the briefing to the incoming Minister... Treasury set out... a huge fiscal risk in out-years... there is a long-term risk where we know that Crown revenue is going to fall significantly under Crown expenditure.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the critique in Treasury projections rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: both the IMF and the OECD, in line with market economic orthodoxy, have argued: for Aotearoa New Zealand to implement a capital gains tax... in order to have a more productive and fairer tax system
rigor.explanation: Appeals to authoritative institutions to counter the Government's selective citation; reasoned.

rigor.statement: We had a report that told us that the top 311 families in this country pay an effective tax rate of less than half of that of the average New Zealander. But, more so than that, they hold more wealth combined then the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific empirical report to support the inequality argument.

rigor.statement: We've heard from the Greens member her proposal for a wealth tax—it's economic illiteracy. You can't tax your country into prosperity.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a slogan-conclusion with no evidence engaging the wealth-tax case.

rigor.statement: the poorest New Zealanders are not getting that relief, that the wealthiest New Zealanders are getting two times the relief of minimum wage workers.
rigor.explanation: A distributional argument grounded in the bill's own numbers.

rigor.statement: the Treasury... says that “the reintroduction of rental property interest deductibility for tax purposes, and changes to the bright-line rules [are] all expected to have [an] … upward impact [on rents]. Rents are forecast to continue rising rapidly over the early years of projection”.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Government's own official forecast to support the critique.

veracity.statement: Tobacco taxes went up in December last year.
veracity.explanation: NZ tobacco excise indexation did take effect in that period; broadly accurate factual correction.

veracity.statement: Now, back to the Greens. Facing 54 years, my friend, of never ever having made a Cabinet—54 years of never being in Cabinet.
veracity.explanation: The Greens/predecessors had not been in Cabinet as of 2024; the framing is broadly accurate though rhetorically rounded.

veracity.statement: These Green MPs, of course, are the highest aviation taxpayer-paid cost takers of all of Parliament. These Green MPs spend more time on aeroplanes than all the rest of us in terms of cost—about four times my party's cost.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim about relative travel costs that is plausible but unverified and selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Two-thirds of our new spending goes to health, education, and law and order. That's our decisive reply to the fearmongering and scaremongering led by that crowd over there.
veracity.explanation: A specific budget-allocation claim, broadly consistent with the Government's framing of Budget 2024, though the 'two-thirds' figure is a headline characterisation.

veracity.statement: Tax relief in Budget 2024 leaves $3.7 billion in taxpayers' pockets.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reported scale of the Budget 2024 tax package.

veracity.statement: Core Crown debt—what we New Zealanders owe—had gone under Labour and the Greens from 20 percent of GDP to 43 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate that net core Crown debt roughly doubled as a share of GDP over the period, though endpoints depend on the measure used.

veracity.statement: Budget 2024 invests $1.2 billion over three years in what was once the Provincial Growth Fund but is now the Regional Infrastructure Fund.
veracity.explanation: Matches the announced Regional Infrastructure Fund figure.

veracity.statement: hundreds of thousands over the last three years have left or fled this country under a Labour Government. That's the most blistering commentary of how bad they were.
veracity.explanation: Uses gross departures while ignoring arrivals; misleading as net migration was positive, and attributing emigration to the government is unsupported.

veracity.statement: Today the Māori Party organised a protest on Parliament's forecourt and then didn't even turn up in this House to find out what was in the Budget.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate account of Te Pāti Māori's protest and initial absence, though 'didn't even turn up' is contested since they later spoke.

veracity.statement: never been seen in this Parliament since 1854. Since 1854, never been seen.
veracity.explanation: Obvious hyperbole/false as literal claim about attendance.

veracity.statement: In the past seven months, I have witnessed nearly every single right be stripped away from us, from our reo, from our health, to our taiao, to our justice system, to Māori wards, housing
veracity.explanation: 'Nearly every single right...stripped away' is hyperbole; policy changes occurred but rights were not literally removed.

veracity.statement: this Government made a clear attack on the rights of our babies and mokopuna through whakapapa in section 7AA. This Government is trying to create another stolen generation, and we won't stand for it.
veracity.explanation: 'Trying to create another stolen generation' is a contested, inflammatory characterisation of the 7AA amendment, not a demonstrable fact.

veracity.statement: How extraordinary is it that kura and kōhanga reo have only been funded less than 1 percent over the last decade by successive Governments.
veracity.explanation: A specific funding claim that is plausible but ambiguous (1 percent of what) and unverified.

veracity.statement: Despite this approach, kura kaupapa continues to be amongst the highest performing educational systems in the country.
veracity.explanation: A favourable performance claim that is partly supported but not clearly established across metrics.

veracity.statement: The word “Māori” is not even mentioned once in this Budget within health, education, and police.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about Budget wording, plausible as rhetoric but likely selective across the full documents.

veracity.statement: In 1856, Dr Featherston said, “We must soften the pillow of the dying Māori race.”
veracity.explanation: A widely cited historical quotation attributed to Featherston; accurate in substance.

veracity.statement: We now make up a million people. One in five people here in Aotearoa are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Māori are roughly 20 percent of NZ's population, about a million people.

veracity.statement: if I make up 50 percent of the male prison population, then te iwi Māori should receive 50 percent of that budget. If I make up 64 percent of the female prison population, I deserve that proportion of the budget. If Māori tamariki make up 80 percent of Oranga Tamariki, I deserve that proportion of the budget.
veracity.explanation: The cited over-representation statistics are close to reported figures for Māori in prisons and Oranga Tamariki.

veracity.statement: Matatini was given $38 million by Labour. You have given it $48 million over three years, which is less than the annual receiving of Matatini. It's less; it's $16 million a year over three years.
veracity.explanation: Specific funding comparison presented as fact; plausible but relies on comparing a lump sum to an annualised figure, which may mislead.

veracity.statement: If our people are dying seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori, why not allow us to access superannuation before that? Follow the science. Follow the data.
veracity.explanation: The Māori/non-Māori life-expectancy gap of roughly 7 years is well documented.

veracity.statement: We've allowed you 150 years to establish yourselves here as a Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate as a broad-brush reference to the age of NZ's Parliament.

veracity.statement: Tonight in this House, we are going to reduce taxes paid by working people for the first time in 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Personal income tax thresholds had not been adjusted for 14 years; broadly accurate, though 'reduce taxes' via threshold shifts is a framing.

veracity.statement: So we are changing that threshold to $15,600... The new threshold for paying the 30 percent rate will be $53,501. That is $5,500 annually, which will be taxed more fairly at the lower rate of 17.5 percent instead of 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: Matches the legislated Budget 2024 threshold changes.

veracity.statement: I'll leave you with these numbers: 727,000 households getting at least $75 more a fortnight; 187,000 households getting at least $100 more a fortnight; on average, households getting $60 a fortnight; and, on average, households with children getting $78 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Official Budget modelling figures, though averages can obscure distribution (as opponents noted).

veracity.statement: even Michael Cullen's Tax Working Group said that if you don't adjust tax brackets for inflation, you destroy the progressivity of the tax system
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Tax Working Group's noted concern about fiscal drag.

veracity.statement: Even a minimum wage earner, if they work a few more hours a week, is paying 30c on the dollar in tax.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the marginal-rate effect of unindexed thresholds; accurate as a marginal (not average) rate claim.

veracity.statement: They watched while the last Government said that they needed every one of those dollars... and then they wasted it on three waters, on TVNZ-RNZ mergers, on more officials in the back office.
veracity.explanation: Names real programmes but characterising all as 'wasted' is a contestable value judgement.

veracity.statement: Someone who earns $50,000 a year will end up with a tax cut of $15 a week. Someone who earns $60,000 a year, because of the interaction with the independent earner tax credit, will end up with $25 a week. Someone who earns $70,000 a year will end up with $15 a week. Someone who earns $80,000 a year will end up with $20 a week.
veracity.explanation: Weekly-equivalent figures broadly consistent with the package, reframing the Government's fortnightly numbers.

veracity.statement: two adults earning $150,000 each, per annum. Well, those are pretty well-off people in the first place, and they're going to get one of the biggest tax cuts going. They'll end up about $2,000 better off.
veracity.explanation: The high-income couple gain is consistent with the threshold changes.

veracity.statement: in the briefing to the incoming Minister... Treasury set out... a huge fiscal risk in out-years... there is a long-term risk where we know that Crown revenue is going to fall significantly under Crown expenditure.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Treasury's long-term fiscal sustainability warnings.

veracity.statement: both the IMF and the OECD, in line with market economic orthodoxy, have argued: for Aotearoa New Zealand to implement a capital gains tax... in order to have a more productive and fairer tax system
veracity.explanation: The IMF and OECD have indeed recommended NZ consider capital gains taxation.

veracity.statement: under the tax settings today as in this legislation, an average four-person family would receive approximately $126 from this Government. But under the Green Party's tax plan, which we went to this election with, they would receive more than double that, at $288.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the Greens' own modelling; a partisan comparison but internally specified.

veracity.statement: We had a report that told us that the top 311 families in this country pay an effective tax rate of less than half of that of the average New Zealander. But, more so than that, they hold more wealth combined then the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Closely matches the 2023 IRD high-wealth individuals report findings.

veracity.statement: it is landlords—who this Government handed a $2.9 billion tax cut to, only to increase the cost of housing, as the Reserve Bank of this country says.
veracity.explanation: The interest-deductibility restoration figure and Reserve Bank commentary on upward rent pressure are broadly supported, though '$2.9 billion tax cut' framing is contested.

veracity.statement: ACT is proud to be part of a coalition Government that's already found $7.5 billion in savings in last year's mini-Budget, and another $1.5 billion in ongoing savings... veracity.explanation: Cites real savings measures, though '$486 million just knocking around' is a rhetorical characterisation.

veracity.statement: the poorest New Zealanders are not getting that relief, that the wealthiest New Zealanders are getting two times the relief of minimum wage workers.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the package's distributional pattern where higher earners gain more in dollar terms.

veracity.statement: This Budget is a Budget of broken promises... people were expecting the $250 a fortnight that National went out and told them they were getting.
veracity.explanation: The '$250' figure was a maximum for a specific household type, so 'told them they were getting' is a contestable characterisation.

Someone who earns $80,000 a year will end up with $20 a week.

specificity.statement: two adults earning $150,000 each, per annum. Well, those are pretty well-off people in the first place, and they're going to get one of the biggest tax cuts going. They'll end up about $2,000 better off.

specificity.explanation: Precise figures on families, effective rates and comparative wealth.

specificity.statement: it is landlords—who this Government handed a $2.9 billion tax cut to, only to increase the cost of housing, as the Reserve Bank of this country says.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, the beneficiary and a cited source.

specificity.statement: we are not so much dealing with a cost of living crisis, as this Government campaigned on... we are dealing with a cost of greed crisis
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical label with no concrete mechanism attached.

specificity.statement: ACT is proud to be part of a coalition Government that's already found $7.5 billion in savings in last year's mini-Budget, and another $1.5 billion in ongoing savings... That includes $107 million found from the Healthy School Lunches programme... We've found $486 million just knocking around in the bottom drawer at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete savings figures tied to named programmes and agencies.

specificity.statement: finally, from 31 July this year, the taxation thresholds will change... the money is going to be in their pockets for them to choose how they would like to spend their money.

specificity.statement: the poorest New Zealanders are not getting that relief, that the wealthiest New Zealanders are getting two times the relief of minimum wage workers.

strength.statement: Tonight in this House, we are going to reduce taxes paid by working people for the first time in 14 years.

strength.statement: the FamilyBoost payment will ensure that working families can get up to 25 percent of a rebate of every dollar of childcare fee that they pay. The effect is up to $150 more for those families every fortnight.

authenticity.statement: This Budget is a Budget of broken promises... people were expecting the $250 a fortnight that National went out and told them they were getting.

divination.statement: They're going to spend a lot more time in the wilderness before Kiwis look to them for salvation again.

forthrightness.statement: Just to get rid of the surprise for the Government members, the Green Party will be opposing this bill today.

forthrightness.statement: finally, from 31 July this year, the taxation thresholds will change... the money is going to be in their pockets for them to choose how they would like to spend their money.
forthrightness.explanation: States clearly that NZ First supports the bill and why.

veracity.statement: for someone on an average income, they're going to end up with $102 more a fortnight

veracity.statement: a single person earning $55,000 will be better off by $51 a fortnight

veracity.statement: every member of Parliament is walking away with 80 bucks a fortnight that we don't need. I don't need 40 bucks a week.

veracity.statement: Our tax relief in this Budget puts $3.7 billion a year back into the pockets of New Zealanders.

veracity.explanation: Contested by Woods citing Treasury that the cuts are debt-funded ($12b borrowed for $10b of cuts); 'fully funded from savings' is at best partial.

veracity.statement: all of those tradies, all of those truck drivers, all of those nurses… who were sick of the $100 billion and absolutely nothing to show for it. They want tax relief that goes back into their pocket. They know how to spend it better than the Government
veracity.explanation: '$100 billion and absolutely nothing to show for it' is hyperbole; much of that spending funded Covid support and services.

veracity.statement: the most that anyone will get… from the shift in the tax thresholds is $25 a week… that's the amount that someone earning about $60,000 a year will get, in conjunction with the independent earner tax credit.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the ~$25/week maximum from thresholds combined with the IETC for that income band.

veracity.statement: we have 30 years of evidence that the neoliberal ideology does not deliver that. It does not work. That's the facts.

veracity.statement: Last time that Government were in charge, Māori unemployment went up to 14.5 percent.

veracity.statement: this Government has actually cut 500 Kāinga Ora homes, and another few hundred are on the block.

veracity.statement: Contrast that with Labour, where successive quarter after quarter unemployment was below 4 percent… It saw Māori unemployment come down to record lows.

veracity.statement: The debt track that we are on sees us borrowing $12 billion to deliver $10 billion worth of tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the argument that the cuts are debt-funded; the precise 12-for-10 framing is a stylised summary of the fiscal figures.

veracity.statement: On page 19 of this document, the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update… you can see that rents are forecast to continue rising rapidly… "the reintroduction of rental property interest deductibility for tax purposes, and changes to the bright-line rules [are] expected to have [an upward] impact."

rigor.statement: We are the party of health. We are the party of education. We are the party of welfare. We are the party of the environment.

rigor.statement: all we are doing is shifting costs from one pocket to another… families who now have, perhaps, some more money in their pocket… have to, at the same time, pay increased public transport fares… pay more in excise tax… having to pay incredibly increased rates… having to pay more to register their car.

rigor.statement: It leads to an incredibly unequal society where people increasingly… end up living in gated communities and having to pay private armed guards because the crime gets worse because you've got people who are starving outside the walls of that gated community.

rigor.statement: the changes that they've made to the clean car legislation are going to mean higher-emissions vehicles, higher emissions from road transport.

rigor.statement: Mr Meager doesn't know what day of the week it is when he's a Māori, even though he's the "great brown hope" according to some of his mates in the media… Tama Potaka should hang his head in shame after this pathetic—

authenticity.statement: We are the party of health. We are the party of education. We are the party of welfare. We are the party of the environment.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent long-term Labour identity; plausible from the historical record but asserted rather than evidenced here.

authenticity.statement: We don't only talk but we also do what we said we were going to do, and we will continue to deliver for everyone in New Zealand so that they can have greater certainty in what is coming and have faith in us that we will deliver.

authenticity.statement: Contrast that with Labour, where successive quarter after quarter unemployment was below 4 percent… It saw Māori unemployment come down to record lows.
