authenticity.statement: National candidates were out there telling the voters of New Zealand they could expect $250 a fortnight in tax cuts… what has been delivered to them today? Well, it certainly is not $250 a fortnight.
authenticity.explanation: The charge is about opponents' words-vs-delivery, which is a signal about them rather than about Woods.

authenticity.statement: I see we did under Sir Bill English and Steven Joyce. We actually did in 2017, but that Government reversed it.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a consistent National record of pursuing threshold cuts, aligning current action with prior positions.

divination.statement: the changes that they've made to the clean car legislation are going to mean higher-emissions vehicles, higher emissions from road transport.
divination.explanation: Forecasts higher transport emissions from axing the Clean Car Discount; directionally consistent with evidence that price signals shifted EV uptake, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: if you needed a lesson in how to kill off any building of rentals, that speech was it. That's how you kill the rental market—put rent controls in.
divination.explanation: Predicts rent controls would suppress rental construction; a common economic view but stated as certainty without evidence.

divination.statement: the FamilyBoost tax credit… creates a continuous incentive for early childhood centres to continue putting prices up.
divination.explanation: Predicts subsidy pass-through into higher ECE fees; a recognised risk of demand-side subsidies but the magnitude is uncertain.

strength.statement: We don't only talk but we also do what we said we were going to do, and we will continue to deliver for everyone in New Zealand so that they can have greater certainty in what is coming and have faith in us that we will deliver.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery in the abstract without identifying a concrete implemented commitment.

civility.statement: that was quite a sad, pathetic, and embarrassing speech from Chris Hipkins
civility.explanation: Name-calling directed at the person ('sad, pathetic, embarrassing') rather than the substance of his argument.

civility.statement: I’m not sure he actually wrote that speech, and I’ll tell you why. It’s because Helen Clark is writing the foreign policy stuff, we’ve got David Parker and the “Piketty Pirates” writing all the tax policy, and we’ve got Michael Wood and Craig Renney doing everything else.
civility.explanation: Belittling insinuation ('Piketty Pirates') that Hipkins is a puppet who can't write his own speech.

civility.statement: Last year, he was campaigning against David Parker and against Grant Robertson on having a capital gains tax; now, he’s miraculously for it.
civility.explanation: Legitimate criticism of a policy reversal, but delivered with a sarcastic 'miraculously'.

civility.statement: They hired 18,000 more public servants, and yet they delivered worse results.
civility.explanation: Harsh but aimed at the record and staffing decisions rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: he is the arsonist that returns to the scene of the fire that he lit, and then he tries to criticise us as a fire brigade putting it out
civility.explanation: Extended personal-attack metaphor casting the opponent as an arsonist.

civility.statement: But Labour and the Greens don’t like roads. I don’t think they even like tunnels—that’s the reality of it. But, more importantly, they don’t like building anything—they don’t like building anything.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents opponents' views rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I want to put a serious challenge to the Labour Party and to the Green Party and just say very simply that if you cared about housing affordability—if you genuinely cared about it—if you genuinely cared about climate change, and if you cared about energy independence... you would back these reforms.
civility.explanation: Questions opponents' motives instead of their arguments.

civility.statement: we just lost half a decade with Chris Hipkins as education Minister where nothing was achieved
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism of the record with dismissive exaggeration.

civility.statement: Do you think they solved three waters with $1.2 billion of taxpayers’ money? No, they didn’t—no, they didn’t.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical attack, but anchored to real expenditure.

civility.statement: Today, the coalition Government showed us their true colours. It’s a mean and nasty Budget. That’s what it is.
civility.explanation: Charged 'mean and nasty' language, but aimed at the Budget/government rather than an individual.

civility.statement: I actually feel aroha for Minister Karen Chhour, who I know is serious about her work to prevent violence.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous framing of a political opponent's intentions.

civility.statement: every time I hear Marama Davidson, I appreciate and miss James Shaw just a little bit more. Someone should call the physics department, because she actually managed to slow down time—the last five minutes of her speech felt like about 15.
civility.explanation: Personal mockery of a colleague's delivery, not her argument.

civility.statement: They actually forgot to vote against the “White people’s Budget”, the “White people’s Budget” that is brought about by a Cabinet of 20 that has eight Māori members.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic point-scoring off Te Pāti Māori's conduct.

civility.statement: I’m looking up through the beautiful glass ceiling of this Chamber trying to find those flying saucers that dropped them off on this planet, because I don’t think they’ve been here with us on Earth in recent times.
civility.explanation: Mocking personal ridicule of opposition MPs (Swarbrick and colleagues).

civility.statement: On the other side of the House, fundamentally, you don’t own yourself, you don’t own your life, and you don’t own your money. You are the prisoner of collectivism
civility.explanation: Misrepresents opponents' beliefs rather than engaging them.

civility.statement: replay that speech—because it was going to put Mogadon totally out of business. After five minutes, he ran out of puff.
civility.explanation: Mocks Hipkins personally (his speech as a sleeping pill) rather than its content.

civility.statement: There were crocodile tears for the elderly, having done nothing to advance the SuperGold card in the time they had it.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'crocodile tears' jab, but tied to a criticism of the record.

civility.statement: Gee, there’s not many people that can eat a banana sideways, but you could.
civility.explanation: A purely personal insult aimed at an interjecting member.

civility.statement: It doesn’t look like a party’s that’s going to be back in three years, does it? Or, for that matter, six years. Because—I’ll tell you why—it hasn’t got a leader.
civility.explanation: Attack on Labour's leadership, harsh but aimed at political capacity rather than personal traits.

charisma.statement: that was quite a sad, pathetic, and embarrassing speech from Chris Hipkins
charisma.explanation: Demeans an opponent to rally his own side; makes no attempt to persuade or bridge.

charisma.statement: he is the arsonist that returns to the scene of the fire that he lit, and then he tries to criticise us as a fire brigade putting it out
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own benches by vilifying the opponent.

charisma.statement: But Labour and the Greens don’t like roads. I don’t think they even like tunnels—that’s the reality of it. But, more importantly, they don’t like building anything—they don’t like building anything.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: I want to put a serious challenge to the Labour Party and to the Green Party and just say very simply that if you cared about housing affordability—if you genuinely cared about it—if you genuinely cared about climate change, and if you cared about energy independence... you would back these reforms.
charisma.explanation: Framed as a challenge but impugns opponents' sincerity rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Today, the coalition Government showed us their true colours. It’s a mean and nasty Budget. That’s what it is.
charisma.explanation: Rallies her own side rather than persuading the undecided.

charisma.statement: I actually feel aroha for Minister Karen Chhour, who I know is serious about her work to prevent violence.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges an opponent's good faith — a bridging move across party lines.

charisma.statement: The single most important thing that this Budget has shown us is that we must make this a one-term Government.
charisma.explanation: Combative call to unseat the government; rallies supporters rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: we see you, we hear you, and we will always fight for you in these halls of power
charisma.explanation: Empathetic, inclusive appeal to struggling constituents, though within a partisan frame.

charisma.statement: every time I hear Marama Davidson, I appreciate and miss James Shaw just a little bit more. Someone should call the physics department, because she actually managed to slow down time—the last five minutes of her speech felt like about 15.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing put-down aimed at his own side.

charisma.statement: It shouldn’t matter if you’re black, white, Cuban, or Asian... As New Zealanders in the 21st century, we are all New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, universalist appeal — though deployed as a rebuttal to Te Pāti Māori rather than to build consensus with them.

charisma.statement: I’m looking up through the beautiful glass ceiling of this Chamber trying to find those flying saucers that dropped them off on this planet, because I don’t think they’ve been here with us on Earth in recent times.
charisma.explanation: Applause-line derision rather than persuasion.

charisma.statement: On the other side of the House, fundamentally, you don’t own yourself, you don’t own your life, and you don’t own your money. You are the prisoner of collectivism
charisma.explanation: Sharply divisive framing that shuts down dialogue.

charisma.statement: replay that speech—because it was going to put Mogadon totally out of business. After five minutes, he ran out of puff.
charisma.explanation: Derisive applause line, not persuasion.

veracity.statement: I’m not sure he actually wrote that speech, and I’ll tell you why. It’s because Helen Clark is writing the foreign policy stuff, we’ve got David Parker and the “Piketty Pirates” writing all the tax policy, and we’ve got Michael Wood and Craig Renney doing everything else.
veracity.explanation: Unsubstantiated claim that others authored Hipkins' speech; rhetorical insinuation, not fact.

veracity.statement: Last year, he was campaigning against David Parker and against Grant Robertson on having a capital gains tax; now, he’s miraculously for it.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that Hipkins ruled out CGT/wealth tax in 2023 before later softening, though 'miraculously for it' overstates the shift.

veracity.statement: Just six months ago, he thought that exploring AUKUS pillar 2 was a good idea, just like our Government did, and now, no, he’s not doing that.
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate that Labour signalled openness to exploring AUKUS Pillar 2 before cooling on it.

veracity.statement: They hired 18,000 more public servants, and yet they delivered worse results.
veracity.explanation: Public service headcount grew substantially under Labour, though 18,000 is at the high end; 'worse results' is an asserted judgement.

veracity.statement: He increased Government spending by 84 percent, and he taxed everyone a lot more in the process. He borrowed more. We went from $5 billion to almost $100 billion worth of debt. We’re now paying $9 billion in interest payments
veracity.explanation: Interest and spending-growth figures are in the ballpark, but the '$5 billion to almost $100 billion' framing cherry-picks a low starting base and is misleading about net debt.

veracity.statement: Inflation hit a 30-year high, interest rates went right through the roof, we’ve had the economy in recession for four of the last five quarters
veracity.explanation: Inflation reaching a 30-year high is accurate and the recession claim is roughly right on a per-capita basis; 'through the roof' is hyperbole.

veracity.statement: From 31 July, 94 percent—94 percent—of all New Zealand households are going to receive some tax relief from this year’s Budget. That’s right—up to $102 for an average-income household, who may well then be eligible for up to another $150 of FamilyBoost support
veracity.explanation: Uses the government's own framing; '94 percent' and 'up to' capture very small amounts, making the headline generous.

veracity.statement: Half the kids show up at high school not ready to go. They don’t know the basics well enough. Over half the kids aren’t attending school 90 percent of the time
veracity.explanation: Regular attendance below 50% is broadly accurate; the 'not ready' claim is looser and less precisely sourced.

veracity.statement: we just lost half a decade with Chris Hipkins as education Minister where nothing was achieved
veracity.explanation: 'Nothing was achieved' is hyperbolic and not literally accurate.

veracity.statement: So $1.8 billion to lock in permanent funding for Pharmac after Labour put those medicines at risk for everyday Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: 'Labour put those medicines at risk' is contestable partisan spin attached to a factual funding figure.

veracity.statement: Do you think they solved three waters with $1.2 billion of taxpayers’ money? No, they didn’t—no, they didn’t.
veracity.explanation: The ~$1.2bn spent on the since-repealed Three Waters reform is a roughly accurate figure; 'solved' is a rhetorical framing.

veracity.statement: Sixty-three thousand—63,000—tamariki woke up in poverty this morning in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Cites a real child-poverty figure broadly consistent with one of the official measures.

veracity.statement: Four thousand—4,000—of our native species are threatened with extinction, and yet there is no new funding to protect them.
veracity.explanation: New Zealand has roughly 4,000 threatened/at-risk species — broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: The Child Poverty Report... is clear that this Budget will see child poverty flat-line.
veracity.explanation: Represents the report's projection; directionally supported.

veracity.statement: This Government has slashed $40 million from the fund that was supposed to support iwi and hapū to build Māori housing.
veracity.explanation: Māori housing funding was reduced; the precise figure is a specific claim.

veracity.statement: They have chosen to cut $178 million from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority—EECA—which funded things like the hugely successful Warmer Kiwi Homes programme.
veracity.explanation: References real EECA funding changes; figure is a specific verifiable claim.

veracity.statement: Greenhouse gas figures released by Stats New Zealand today, showing further decreases in emissions, are proof that the green initiatives of the last two terms were working.
veracity.explanation: Emissions did decrease, but the causal attribution to Green initiatives is overstated.

veracity.statement: the Clean Car Discount made a massive dent in our overall emissions—a massive dent—stuff that was actually starting to work.
veracity.explanation: The Clean Car Discount lifted EV uptake, but 'a massive dent in overall emissions' is hyperbole.

veracity.statement: I couldn’t find a single new initiative for family violence and sexual violence prevention funding. I looked in Justice, Corrections, Ministry of Social Development, Police, Public Service, Health, Education—I couldn’t find anything.
veracity.explanation: A claim of absence that is plausible but hard to fully verify from the text.

veracity.statement: It’s actually free to vote for us, and we’ve already saved you hundreds of millions, if not billions, of dollars. Is that a good deal or what?
veracity.explanation: Loose, unsubstantiated savings claim with no breakdown.

veracity.statement: when Jacinda Ardern came out and said, “I’m going to tilt the market towards first-home buyers.” What happened, when she put more tax on landlords, is that rents went up $200 in three years
veracity.explanation: Rents did rise, but pinning the increase solely on interest-deductibility changes is a contested, unsupported causal claim.

veracity.statement: that average income household is going to pay up to $103 less tax a fortnight
veracity.explanation: Uses the government's 'up to' figure — accurate at the top of the range but generous as a typical case.

veracity.statement: what Brooke van Velden has done by cancelling the fair pay agreements... it also saved, I think, something like $65 million.
veracity.explanation: A hedged savings claim presented tentatively.

veracity.statement: Our Government—our Government is 40 percent Māori, twice as much as the rest.
veracity.explanation: Cabinet composition claim (eight of twenty Māori members) is broadly checkable and roughly accurate.

veracity.statement: on forecast growth charts, the International Monetary Fund last year had us—of the 159 countries they measured in terms of GDP growth, they had us 158.
veracity.explanation: A specific ranking claim that appears cherry-picked from one particular IMF forecast measure.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders are voting with their feet, leaving our shores in a mass, Old Testament exodus of people.
veracity.explanation: Net citizen migration loss was real, but 'mass, Old Testament exodus' is hyperbole.

veracity.statement: There were crocodile tears for the elderly, having done nothing to advance the SuperGold card in the time they had it.
veracity.explanation: The claim Labour 'did nothing' on the SuperGold card is contestable and overstated.

veracity.statement: he mentioned the failed trickle-down theory of economics... but he forgot to say it was Labour who brought it in—after March 1984.
veracity.explanation: Historically accurate that the 1984 free-market reforms were introduced under a Labour government.

rigor.statement: They hired 18,000 more public servants, and yet they delivered worse results.
rigor.explanation: Implies causation between headcount and outcomes without evidence supplied in the text.

rigor.statement: he is the arsonist that returns to the scene of the fire that he lit, and then he tries to criticise us as a fire brigade putting it out
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical metaphor substituting for an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: But Labour and the Greens don’t like roads. I don’t think they even like tunnels—that’s the reality of it. But, more importantly, they don’t like building anything—they don’t like building anything.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping strawman generalisation about opponents' positions.

rigor.statement: I want to put a serious challenge to the Labour Party and to the Green Party and just say very simply that if you cared about housing affordability—if you genuinely cared about it—if you genuinely cared about climate change, and if you cared about energy independence... you would back these reforms.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — equates disagreement with the reforms to not caring about the underlying goals.

rigor.statement: Half the kids show up at high school not ready to go. They don’t know the basics well enough. Over half the kids aren’t attending school 90 percent of the time
rigor.explanation: Marshals attendance/achievement data to support the education argument, though figures are approximate.

rigor.statement: Today, the coalition Government showed us their true colours. It’s a mean and nasty Budget. That’s what it is.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion asserted as conclusion before evidence.

rigor.statement: Greenhouse gas figures released by Stats New Zealand today, showing further decreases in emissions, are proof that the green initiatives of the last two terms were working.
rigor.explanation: Treats a correlation (emissions fell) as 'proof' of causation, ignoring other drivers.

rigor.statement: the Clean Car Discount made a massive dent in our overall emissions—a massive dent—stuff that was actually starting to work.
rigor.explanation: Overstated causal claim with emphatic repetition rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: I couldn’t find a single new initiative for family violence and sexual violence prevention funding. I looked in Justice, Corrections, Ministry of Social Development, Police, Public Service, Health, Education—I couldn’t find anything.
rigor.explanation: Describes a systematic search across multiple votes to substantiate the claim of absence.

rigor.statement: When people have a home, when people have incomes, and when communities are well and strong, we need to understand that is violence prevention.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned link between social conditions and violence prevention, evidence-informed but asserted rather than cited.

rigor.statement: when Jacinda Ardern came out and said, “I’m going to tilt the market towards first-home buyers.” What happened, when she put more tax on landlords, is that rents went up $200 in three years
rigor.explanation: Attributes a multi-causal rent rise to a single policy.

rigor.statement: Income tax is levied on income, and income is a business or an activity’s revenue minus its expenses, and interest is a legitimate expense. So when you’re in business, you can deduct your interest costs from your tax bill.
rigor.explanation: A coherent, principled argument from the definition of income to the case for interest deductibility.

rigor.statement: when we say that we’re cutting taxes, that is not spending—we are taking less of people’s money in the first place
rigor.explanation: A defensible logical distinction between reducing revenue and increasing expenditure.

rigor.statement: They actually forgot to vote against the “White people’s Budget”, the “White people’s Budget” that is brought about by a Cabinet of 20 that has eight Māori members.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'White people's Budget' label with a concrete factual counter (Māori Cabinet numbers).

rigor.statement: A plumber that can do five jobs in a day is more productive than one that does three jobs and spends a whole lot of time sitting in traffic.
rigor.explanation: A relevant illustrative analogy supporting the productivity/infrastructure argument.

rigor.statement: someone at an early childhood centre was actually told by the Ministry of Education that they had to wash nappies at 60 degrees centigrade—not 59, not 61—60 degrees centigrade.
rigor.explanation: Uses a single vivid anecdote to argue a broad point about over-regulation.

rigor.statement: On the other side of the House, fundamentally, you don’t own yourself, you don’t own your life, and you don’t own your money. You are the prisoner of collectivism
rigor.explanation: Strawman caricature of opponents' actual positions.

rigor.statement: Today, our country has just changed gears—from reverse and backwards to forwards and progress.
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion with no supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: New Zealanders are voting with their feet, leaving our shores in a mass, Old Testament exodus of people.
rigor.explanation: Emotive hyperbole rather than a measured claim.

rigor.statement: he mentioned the failed trickle-down theory of economics... but he forgot to say it was Labour who brought it in—after March 1984.
rigor.explanation: Exposes an inconsistency in the opponent's attack using an accurate historical reference.

specificity.explanation: Cites concrete percentages and dollar figures.

specificity.statement: we see you, we hear you, and we will always fight for you in these halls of power

rigor.statement: Of course, National have a habit of doing this. They have a habit of, effectively, switching out the lights and keeping people in the dark

rigor.statement: The debate from the other side of the House is trying to put this perspective forward—that the incident that took place on Friday night would have all been fixed if iReX hadn't been cancelled. Well that is, quite frankly, completely untrue—completely untrue
rigor.explanation: Partly a strawman — Labour argued the grounding highlights the need for replacement, not that new ferries would have prevented this specific incident; the maintenance point that follows is more sound.

rigor.statement: over the last number of years, when the last Government was in charge, there was so much focus on the big shiny new ferries, they lost sight of the focus on actually maintaining what they already had
rigor.explanation: Plausible causal claim but asserted rather than evidenced in this passage.

rigor.statement: I have a letter here which the former finance Minister Hon Grant Robertson sent to KiwiRail on 19 September 2023, saying, "We note that KiwiRail under-scoped the landside infrastructure in 2021, meaning the decision to procure two large rail-enabled ships at the time was premature."
rigor.explanation: Backs the argument with a dated documentary source from the opposing side, letting the evidence carry the point.

rigor.statement: They made the point in the meeting that there are a large number of ships of this age which operate around the world and which operate safely.
rigor.explanation: Cites the TAIC's expert view to rebut the 'ferries too old to be safe' framing — relevant authority, though second-hand.

rigor.statement: I think, just there, members of the New Zealand public have seen a shining example of why it is that we have an approximate $200 billion infrastructure deficit in this country. We constantly see the chopping and changing of legacy parties in charge, binning projects that the other one did not like, with no meaningful plan on the horizon.
rigor.explanation: Cites an infrastructure-deficit figure and a general pattern, but the causal link to this incident is asserted.

rigor.statement: In Budget 2024, the budget for Crown company monitoring—that's all Crown companies; not just State-owned enterprises (SOEs)—was roughly $5 million, whereas the net asset value of SOEs alone was roughly $40 billion. That's a management fee of 0.1 percent. Even the cheapest private equity funds charge around 1 percent plus performance fees.
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based comparison with figures and a computed ratio to support the under-monitoring claim.

rigor.statement: ACT's policy is to add KiwiRail to the mixed-ownership model. By selling 49 percent of the Government's shares, this would ensure KiwiRail has the accountability and flexibility needed to keep the ferry service running properly
rigor.explanation: Asserts the causal benefit of partial privatisation; the supporting argument follows but 'would ensure' overstates certainty.

rigor.statement: The investment statement prepared by Treasury in 2022 helps confirm this. The Government stake in listed companies significantly outperformed their cost of capital, whereas Government stakes in unlisted companies underperformed.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a named Treasury document and a like-for-like performance comparison.

rigor.statement: roughly one-sixth of the package is for the ferries; one-sixth is for the port of Marlborough end; and a whopping four-sixths—two-thirds of it—is for the port of Wellington end. That reflects the complexity of that end.
rigor.explanation: Uses the cost breakdown to support the point that landside infrastructure, not the ferries, drove the blowout.

rigor.statement: The big problem here was that KiwiRail, I think, were exceedingly arrogant... They ordered the ferries before they had anywhere to put them—they ordered the ferries before they had anywhere to put them.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'arrogant' characterisation of the organisation with a concrete procurement-sequencing point, though partly rhetorical.

rigor.statement: They're cancelling a contract which that member Andy Foster just told this House was a good deal: $551 million for ferries, which will enable a resilient crossing of the Cook Strait
rigor.explanation: Points to a genuine tension in the opposing benches — Foster called the ferry deal good while the government cancels it.

rigor.statement: New Zealand, as a sovereign nation, has a very good reputation for not breaking our promises. We've just broken a $550 million promise with a major commercial player in the marine and wider heavy industry sector. The Hyundai Dockyard is not going to rush to build us our new vessels.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned link from contract repudiation to reputational cost, though the reputation premise is asserted.

rigor.statement: So members opposite are wilfully deluding themselves when they pretend that the Government had any other option but to repudiate the contract with Hyundai, because no one had done the hard work about the land-side infrastructure costs required.
rigor.explanation: Presents repudiation as the only option (false-dichotomy tinge), though grounded in the real landside-cost problem.

rigor.statement: We actually had a great deal on those ferries—$551 million for ferries—and members on the Government benches continue to push the false assertion that those ferries wouldn't have been able to traverse the Tory Channel. That is not correct. Those ferries were being custom-built specifically to be able to navigate the perils.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason (custom-built to navigate) to rebut the claim, but asserts 'that is not correct' without evidence.

civility.statement: If the Government can prioritise nearly $3 billion in tax cuts for landlords, they can prioritise a resilient, safe, and reliable ferry service between the North and South Islands.
civility.explanation: A pointed but policy-level jab at spending priorities rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Of course, National have a habit of doing this. They have a habit of, effectively, switching out the lights and keeping people in the dark
civility.explanation: Sweeping characterisation of an opponent party as deliberately deceptive, more rhetoric than substance.

civility.statement: We are being seen as the laughing stock in maritime circles, not just here in New Zealand but all around the world.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist framing, though aimed at the situation rather than a person.

civility.statement: The debate from the other side of the House is trying to put this perspective forward—that the incident that took place on Friday night would have all been fixed if iReX hadn't been cancelled. Well that is, quite frankly, completely untrue—completely untrue
civility.explanation: Robust but directed at the argument rather than the person.

civility.statement: over the last number of years, when the last Government was in charge, there was so much focus on the big shiny new ferries, they lost sight of the focus on actually maintaining what they already had
civility.explanation: Criticism of the previous government's priorities — harsh but a legitimate policy critique.

civility.statement: the question for the Minister and for Government members is to show us the money, to show us the plan and the contribution, because right now we are left with far more questions than we have answers to as to what occurs in 2026.
civility.explanation: Demands substance from the government without personal attack.

civility.statement: But I say to him and to the Opposition: let's stop playing politics with this; let's work together to try and find the solution.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful invitation rather than an attack.

civility.statement: The big problem here was that KiwiRail, I think, were exceedingly arrogant... They ordered the ferries before they had anywhere to put them—they ordered the ferries before they had anywhere to put them.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism directed at a state-owned enterprise's conduct rather than at an individual.

civility.statement: This knee-jerk, political point-scoring, "shoot from the hip" Government has the chutzpah to come down to this House and give the Labour members a lecture on working together.
civility.explanation: String of pejorative characterisations of the government rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: So the questions as I see them are these: has the contract for the new Interislander ferries been terminated, and, if so, what is that penalty? We don't have that information—that hasn't been offered by the Government.
civility.explanation: Frames pointed accountability questions substantively rather than as personal attack.

civility.statement: one of the reasons why this Government is having to deal with an horrendous financial and fiscal situation is that the previous Government was out of control in its spending, and no more simple example of that was the fact that the replacement of ferries blew out from $700 million to over $3 billion.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused criticism of fiscal management.

civility.statement: I do want to say, though, that there's been some pretty feisty debate here, but this is too important to be politicking about.
civility.explanation: Explicitly rejects point-scoring in favour of constructive focus.

civility.statement: So I do say to this Government, let's work hard on this. Let's not just dismiss it because it was expensive and the last Government's idea. Let's look carefully at the real options, and let's not under-invest in our infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful and forward-looking.

civility.statement: That is a curious rewriting of history by the former Minister, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb.
civility.explanation: Accuses an opponent of rewriting history — pointed but framed around the record rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: So members opposite are wilfully deluding themselves when they pretend that the Government had any other option but to repudiate the contract with Hyundai, because no one had done the hard work about the land-side infrastructure costs required.
civility.explanation: 'Wilfully deluding themselves' imputes bad faith to opponents rather than engaging their argument.

civility.statement: We need to stop with the heckling and the blame games and have a proper plan so that we can actually get across the strait safely and resiliently.
civility.explanation: Rejects heckling and blame in favour of constructive problem-solving.

strength.statement: She seems to think that it's all right; it's only a few years. Well, a few years are a few years far too late. We had a plan. We were prepared to deliver a safe, reliable, and sustainable option.
strength.explanation: Claims Labour was 'prepared to deliver', but the iReX plan was cancelled amid major cost blowouts and was never delivered — intent with unclear follow-through.

strength.statement: One of the very simpler alternatives is not to build—not to take on much larger ferries that require different port infrastructure, but, actually, to get ferries that fit in within the current port infrastructure so that we do not have to spend so much money
strength.explanation: Describes a direction under advice rather than a decided, delivered policy.

charisma.statement: I think, just there, members of the New Zealand public have seen a shining example of why it is that we have an approximate $200 billion infrastructure deficit in this country. We constantly see the chopping and changing of legacy parties in charge, binning projects that the other one did not like, with no meaningful plan on the horizon.
charisma.explanation: Criticises both major parties even-handedly and frames a shared systemic problem, though it stops short of inviting collaboration.

charisma.statement: But I say to him and to the Opposition: let's stop playing politics with this; let's work together to try and find the solution.
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-party appeal to collaborate on a shared problem.

charisma.statement: This knee-jerk, political point-scoring, "shoot from the hip" Government has the chutzpah to come down to this House and give the Labour members a lecture on working together.
charisma.explanation: Combative, us-vs-them framing that rejects rather than reciprocates the collaboration offer.

charisma.statement: I do want to say, though, that there's been some pretty feisty debate here, but this is too important to be politicking about.
charisma.explanation: Calls the House above the partisan fray toward shared seriousness.

charisma.statement: So I do say to this Government, let's work hard on this. Let's not just dismiss it because it was expensive and the last Government's idea. Let's look carefully at the real options, and let's not under-invest in our infrastructure.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking appeal to set partisanship aside and examine options together.

charisma.statement: We need to stop with the heckling and the blame games and have a proper plan so that we can actually get across the strait safely and resiliently.
charisma.explanation: Calls for an end to point-scoring and a shared focus on a solution.

divination.statement: we also are going to continue to see price inflation for the purchasing of these new ships
divination.explanation: Near-term prediction of rising ship prices; directionally consistent with inflationary trends and delivery delays, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: we are likely to see more groundings of these ships; we are likely to see more issues eventuate
divination.explanation: Prediction of further incidents; plausible given the fleet's age and history, but 'groundings' specifically is uncertain.

divination.statement: New Zealand, as a sovereign nation, has a very good reputation for not breaking our promises. We've just broken a $550 million promise with a major commercial player in the marine and wider heavy industry sector. The Hyundai Dockyard is not going to rush to build us our new vessels.
divination.explanation: Predicts reputational/commercial fallout affecting future dealings with Hyundai; plausible but not certain, timeframe open-ended.

divination.statement: I've got a pretty good take on the fact that these new ferries—smaller ferries, three of them—are going to be $300 million each. So that's the best part of a billion dollars already. Getting out of the contract's another 200 million.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the replacement cost of a not-yet-decided option; a self-described estimate, magnitude uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: Well, like I say, the proper investigatory agencies are looking into what caused this particular trap and how it's going to be dealt with.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Swarbrick's interjection 'What are you going to do about it?', deflects to the investigating agencies rather than stating what the Government will do.

authenticity.statement: Now, look, I do want to be clear: I was the former Minister for State Owned Enterprises; iReX was very, very difficult. It's accurate to say that the costs blew out—they did.
authenticity.explanation: Concedes a damaging fact against his own former project and role rather than denying it — words matched to record.

authenticity.statement: Now, I'm not a shareholding Minister in relation to this—I'm not an expert on it—but those are the facts as they appear to be.
authenticity.explanation: Openly flags the limits of his own role and knowledge rather than overclaiming authority.

authenticity.statement: This Government is committed to restoring rail to its rightful place in New Zealand. Bigger, better ships, with new technology are yet another step on that journey … These will be the first brand-new purpose built ferries New Zealand has had in over 25 years.
authenticity.explanation: Quoted from Peters' 2020 statement championing the new rail-enabled ferries; his party is now in the government cancelling that same project, indicating a position reversal (as Swarbrick highlights).

veracity.statement: Interest rates are high. The official cash rate is at elevated levels. Inflation is still outside the band, at over 4 percent.
veracity.explanation: Mid-2024 the OCR was at a cyclical high (5.5%) and annual CPI inflation was ~4%, just above the 1-3% target band — accurate.

veracity.statement: every year that Grant Robertson was the Minister of Finance, he exceeded his Budget allowance
veracity.explanation: Operating allowances were revised up/exceeded in several Robertson budgets, but 'every year' is a sweeping absolute that overstates the pattern.

veracity.statement: That's how we ended up with an 80 percent increase in Government spending in six years
veracity.explanation: Core Crown expenses rose very substantially 2017-2023, but ~80% is at the high end and sensitive to measure (nominal vs COVID one-offs), so somewhat overstated.

veracity.statement: Treasury advised there is a structural deficit.
veracity.explanation: Treasury did identify a structural component to the deficit in Budget documents — accurate.

veracity.statement: Isn't it interesting that the Labour Party have not promised to bring back the First Home Grant?
veracity.explanation: At the time Labour had criticised the cut without pledging reinstatement — a fair characterisation, though framed rhetorically.

veracity.statement: On average, households benefit by 60 bucks a fortnight; households with children, $78 a fortnight; 94 percent of households will benefit from the tax package in this Budget.
veracity.explanation: Broadly matches the government's own tax-package modelling averages, though 'average' masks wide variation and understates how many gain little.

veracity.statement: after 14 years of fiscal drag... More and more people are pushed into higher and higher tax brackets, paying more and more of their money to the Government every year
veracity.explanation: Income tax thresholds had been unchanged since 2010, so bracket creep over 14 years is factually accurate.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders were promised much on the campaign trail—not least $250 a fortnight in tax cuts from the National Party on the hustings... they've found that it is way short of that.
veracity.explanation: National advertised up to ~$250/fortnight for a specific household type; most households received considerably less, so 'way short' is directionally accurate though the $250 was always a maximum case.

veracity.statement: They've found they'll have to be paying for prescriptions again in many cases... the free lunches in their child's school will be reduced to nothing more than a snack.
veracity.explanation: The $5 prescription co-payment was reinstated for many and school-lunch funding per child was cut sharply — accurate, though 'nothing more than a snack' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: New Zealand's debt as a percentage of GDP has risen.
veracity.explanation: Forecast net core Crown debt as a share of GDP was rising over the period — accurate.

veracity.statement: Unemployment, according to the Budget, is due to peak this year at 5.3 percent... that represents hundreds and thousands of New Zealanders who will be without work
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites the Budget's own unemployment peak forecast of 5.3%.

veracity.statement: that side of the House, when they were in Government, managed to clock up an extra 70,000 people on the jobseeker benefit
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker numbers rose materially under the previous government, but the exact 70,000 and attribution over what baseline is contestable.

veracity.statement: After signing on for a benefit, somebody could go for up to 12 months with zero contact—zero.
veracity.explanation: Directionally reflects gaps in prior case-management contact, but 'up to 12 months with zero contact' is a worst-case framing presented as typical.

veracity.statement: the previous Government set it up with a big fanfare and they set these wildly high expectations but actually didn't address the fundamental issues of funding the disability support service
veracity.explanation: Whaikaha did face funding pressures, but the claim the previous government 'did nothing' despite a Cabinet paper is a contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: they are going to have $2.4 billion of new operating allowances for each of those next two years. But guess what! What Treasury, what the Government's own officials say, is that you need at least $2.5 billion. That's $100 million more than the Government has already allocated themselves just to keep the lights on
veracity.explanation: Consistent with commentary that allowances were tight relative to cost pressures, though the neat $100m gap simplifies contested numbers.

veracity.statement: We see hints of that in the changes to the school lunches programme, which takes the average cost per child from approximately $8 to $2.
veracity.explanation: Broadly matches the reported sharp reduction in per-child school-lunch funding.

veracity.statement: We heard from that very climate Minister that the market was working properly, when the emissions trading scheme (ETS) auction failed last week... It puts a $700 million hole in their revenue plan
veracity.explanation: An ETS auction did fail to clear in 2024, creating a forecast revenue shortfall; the $700m figure is a reasonable but rounded estimate of the fiscal impact.

veracity.statement: Our offshore liabilities are looking to be somewhere between $3.7 billion and $24 billion for offshore mitigation... even if we were to meet our very own emissions reductions budgets, that we will have to pay others to reduce their emissions.
veracity.explanation: Cites a genuine officials' estimate range for meeting NZ's Paris NDC via offshore mitigation; the wide range honestly reflects the uncertainty.

veracity.statement: alongside shredding the work programme that was already under way at the Climate Change Commission to price agricultural emissions—the only sector in our economy that is currently not priced under the ETS but also represents 5 percent of our GDP and half of our emissions
veracity.explanation: Agriculture is unpriced under the ETS and accounts for roughly half of NZ's gross emissions — accurate on the key facts.

veracity.statement: their own working group to apparently do this work by 2030, which... has no budget allocated to it. They can't tell us the terms of reference, who the members are, or how much this new working group is going to cost.
veracity.explanation: Plausible account of scrutiny-week answers, though a one-sided recounting of what officials could/couldn't confirm.

veracity.statement: there are tons of international bodies, the likes of the International Monetary Fund and the OECD, who have pointed out one of the key things we could do is fix our tax system with a capital gains tax.
veracity.explanation: The IMF and OECD have repeatedly recommended NZ broaden capital taxation — accurate.

veracity.statement: it's been 14 years since New Zealanders have had tax relief... in 2017, the Hon Steven Joyce legislated tax relief, and the very, very, very first thing the Labour Party did when they came into power was to repeal the tax relief
veracity.explanation: Thresholds were unchanged since 2010, and Labour did cancel National's legislated-but-not-yet-effective 2017 threshold changes on taking office — substantially accurate.

veracity.statement: the last National Government made the tough decisions to start the City Rail Link, which would double the capacity of our rail network in Auckland
veracity.explanation: CRL was jointly funded/started under the previous National government and is projected to roughly double rail capacity — broadly accurate, if simplified on origins.

veracity.statement: Public transport subsidies: gone. Free prescriptions: gone. Bare minimum wages for people with intellectual disabilities: gone. Proper school lunches: gone. The second year of the Apprenticeship Boost: gone.
veracity.explanation: This list of reversed/cut programmes broadly corresponds to actual Budget decisions, though 'gone' compresses some partial changes.

veracity.statement: some people, as a result of this Budget, will face a personal income tax rate of 128 percent. For every single extra dollar they earn, they will be taxed $1.28
veracity.explanation: A 128% figure can arise as an effective marginal rate including benefit abatement, but labelling it a 'personal income tax rate' conflates tax with abatement and is misleading.

veracity.statement: 'And we are replacing the Pinzgauer and Unimogs.' That was already well under way under the Labour Government. In fact, we received the first tranche of those replacement vehicles while still in power.
veracity.explanation: The NZDF vehicle replacement programme did begin under the previous government with early deliveries — a checkable and plausible claim.

specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (over 4 percent) but describes rates only as 'high'/'elevated' without numbers.

specificity.statement: That's how we ended up with an 80 percent increase in Government spending in six years

specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy reversals though without figures.
