specificity.statement: Does he accept that the overall health Budget funding has actually reduced by 4.5 percent per capita, and, if so, will he increase funding to sustainable levels so that our health system isn't on its knees?
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific 4.5% per-capita reduction figure.

specificity.statement: How will slashing up to 3,000 jobs from the organisation that employs doctors and nurses help to get more doctors and nurses on the front line to serve our people?
specificity.explanation: Cites the 'up to 3,000 jobs' figure.

specificity.statement: Will he then commit to voting against the proposed Treaty principles bill at second reading?
specificity.explanation: Asks for a specific, concrete commitment (vote against at second reading).

rigor.statement: it happens to be a circumstance of 8 September 2023 when the Chief Ombudsman ordered Mr Hipkins to apologise. No urgent debate happened as a consequence of that, so let's just get on with it.
rigor.explanation: Counters Hipkins' precedent argument with a specific counter-example, though brief.

rigor.statement: the House has routinely, in the past, on several occasions, debated using the urgent debate procedure reports that have been produced by the Auditor-General, who was also an Officer of Parliament... you're actually shutting down what has in the past been quite an important source of material that has generated urgent debates in the House.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned analogy from precedent: Auditor-General is also an Officer of Parliament, so the Speaker's logic proves too much.

rigor.statement: The member opposite is interjecting to say that inflation could have come lower quicker—he's 100 percent correct. If he hadn't done so much more wasteful spending, we wouldn't be here now.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim with no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Did the Ministry of Health advise the Government that heated tobacco products would likely compound existing concerns about youth uptake in addition to nicotine products, and that addiction rates for snus can be higher than for smoked tobacco products, and that snus can increase the risk of certain types of cancer?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in specific official advice.

rigor.statement: Which is a greater priority for the Government in its decision making around tobacco: advice from the Ministry of Health and health experts that the Government's approach would increase addiction—particularly amongst young New Zealanders—and increase the risk of certain types of cancer; or the lobbying of the tobacco industry?
rigor.explanation: Frames the choice as a false dichotomy between health advice and lobbying.

rigor.statement: We have looked at the evidence from previous military-style programmes, both in New Zealand and internationally, to understand what will give these young people taking part the best chance for success... lessons have been learnt from the Military-style Activity Camp programme... The research shows that when family are involved and supportive, the chances of success are much greater.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to evidence and prior-programme lessons, though evidence on bootcamp efficacy is contested.

rigor.statement: What is correct is that an increase in back-office staff from 2018 to the current time, of 2,500, has contributed to the current financial position.
rigor.explanation: Attributes a March deficit to a six-year staffing trend without bridging the timing gap.

rigor.statement: Why did her Budget barely provide enough to keep the lights on in health, insufficient funding to achieve at least four of the Government's five health targets, but prioritised a $2.9 billion tax break for landlords?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes health funding against landlord tax relief with some evidential grounding.

rigor.statement: Will she guarantee that the additional $1.4 billion of savings she wants will not come at the cost of front-line services to patients, given, when adjusted for inflation, total operating health expenditure only increased by 0.4 percent in her Budget?
rigor.explanation: Inflation-adjusted framing gives an evidence-based challenge.

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the Ministry for the Environment and Treasury have estimated that this country is potentially liable for anywhere near $24 billion if we fail to meet our Paris Agreement obligations to 2030—that is 6 years from now—which his Government's decisions are demonstrably making it harder to do?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in official cost estimates.

rigor.statement: Is reducing emissions at least cost a great improvement on past policies where Governments sought to reduce carbon emissions at a cost many times greater than the emissions trading scheme (ETS) price, or, in other words, chose to take less carbon dioxide out of the air than they could have if they took a least-cost approach?
rigor.explanation: Coherent marginal-abatement argument that spending above the ETS price buys less abatement per dollar.

rigor.statement: Is it appropriate for a Minister who clearly has no understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi to be directing Pharmac to ignore the Treaty?
rigor.explanation: Loaded question presupposing both the Minister's ignorance and the 'ignore the Treaty' claim.

rigor.statement: Is repealing Māori wards, which the tribunal ruled breaches the principle of partnership and our right to representation, an example of his Government honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a specific tribunal finding.

rigor.statement: How does the Minister for Māori Crown relations feel being wheeled out by this Government to answer a question that was directed to the Prime Minister, simply because he is Māori, and the Prime Minister wants to distance himself from the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
rigor.explanation: Assumes motive ('simply because he is Māori') without evidence.

rigor.statement: do two of the top three in this Parliament who have got Māori background... or the highest percentage of Māori and Pasifika in a Cabinet, or the highest percentage in the country, in terms of Parliament, represent progress or the kind of retard comment we've just heard?
rigor.explanation: Cites representation statistics but embeds them in a personal attack.

rigor.statement: Why won't she put as much effort into improving the health of New Zealanders as she will into helping Philip Morris?
rigor.explanation: Built on a presupposition rather than argument.

rigor.statement: Well, it's very irresponsible for the member to come into this House and tell the country that Police have said they are withdrawing from family harm incidents. That is not true... having uniformed police officers standing in someone's lounge room trying to settle an argument between a mother and daughter over an iPhone charger is not a good use of police time.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a systemic claim with a single anecdote (iPhone-charger callout).

civility.statement: the House has routinely, in the past, on several occasions, debated using the urgent debate procedure reports that have been produced by the Auditor-General, who was also an Officer of Parliament... you're actually shutting down what has in the past been quite an important source of material that has generated urgent debates in the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful, procedural, engages the substance of the ruling.

civility.statement: being over 7 percent for most of 2022, when I recall the member was the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Pointed dig linking inflation to Hipkins' tenure, but a legitimate political point.

civility.statement: The member opposite is interjecting to say that inflation could have come lower quicker—he's 100 percent correct. If he hadn't done so much more wasteful spending, we wouldn't be here now.
civility.explanation: Partisan attack blaming opponent's 'wasteful spending'.

civility.statement: especially our actions to fix Health New Zealand after a botched merger from the previous Government... a significant investment in front-line services with a record $16.7 billion in this year's Budget... We're taking decisive action to fix those problems by installing commissioners and giving them a mandate to deliver New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
civility.explanation: 'Botched merger' is criticism of the prior government's policy, legitimate but sharp.

civility.statement: Did the Ministry of Health advise the Government that heated tobacco products would likely compound existing concerns about youth uptake in addition to nicotine products, and that addiction rates for snus can be higher than for smoked tobacco products, and that snus can increase the risk of certain types of cancer?
civility.explanation: Substantive, policy- and evidence-focused question.

civility.statement: I didn't ask what the Government was trying to achieve; I asked whether the Ministry of Health had advised the Government that, basically, it could increase the uptake of tobacco, increase addiction to tobacco, and increase cancer. The Prime Minister hasn't addressed that.
civility.explanation: Fair procedural point restating the unanswered question without personal attack.

civility.statement: Which is a greater priority for the Government in its decision making around tobacco: advice from the Ministry of Health and health experts that the Government's approach would increase addiction—particularly amongst young New Zealanders—and increase the risk of certain types of cancer; or the lobbying of the tobacco industry?
civility.explanation: Insinuates the government is swayed by tobacco lobbying, though tied to a policy dispute.

civility.statement: I would say to the young lady that I am sorry for what she has been through. I would also say to the young lady that we have taken learnings from what has happened in the past and we have put processes in place to make sure that those horrendous acts that have happened in the past will not continue. What we cannot continue to do is do nothing. These young people deserve better, and their families deserve better.
civility.explanation: Empathetic and respectful toward an abuse survivor's concern.

civility.statement: What does she say to Cara Mackey, who survived abuse in care, who says, "The policies that are being implemented at the moment, such as the reintroduction of bootcamps, are recreating the context in which abuse in State care was allowed to flourish."?
civility.explanation: Pointed but relays a survivor's substantive concern rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: I'm seriously saying that six years of that Government and two years of a botched reform is seriously affecting where we are now.
civility.explanation: Partisan but aimed at policy/record, not the person.

civility.statement: We have record numbers of nurses employed in our health system right now... If that member wants to get up in this House and defend hiring hundreds and thousands more health bureaucrats while waiting lists got longer, she's welcome to do so.
civility.explanation: Strawmans the opponent as defending 'health bureaucrats'.

civility.statement: It is fair to ask that member to depart from her high horse when she campaigned on exactly the same amount of funding for Health New Zealand as this Government delivered.
civility.explanation: 'High horse' is a mild personal jab, though the funding-parity point is substantive.

civility.statement: Why did her Budget barely provide enough to keep the lights on in health, insufficient funding to achieve at least four of the Government's five health targets, but prioritised a $2.9 billion tax break for landlords?
civility.explanation: Pointed with mild hyperbole ('keep the lights on') but policy-focused.

civility.statement: Will she guarantee that the additional $1.4 billion of savings she wants will not come at the cost of front-line services to patients, given, when adjusted for inflation, total operating health expenditure only increased by 0.4 percent in her Budget?
civility.explanation: Substantive, no personal attack.

civility.statement: inflation is down to 3.3 percent, the lowest in three years; and more good news as personal income tax relief is coming next week for the first time in 14 years, as we campaigned on, letting Kiwis—hard-working Kiwis, the people that the Greens and Labour used to care about—get more of their own money.
civility.explanation: 'People that the Greens and Labour used to care about' is a partisan jab.

civility.statement: I would love it if the Greens came out and actually cared about emissions, and actually support our fast-track legislation so we can double the amount of renewable electricity in this country and lower our emissions in the process. Please, please join us.
civility.explanation: Implies opponents don't genuinely care about emissions.

civility.statement: compared to the previous administration, which failed to fund core Pharmac needs to the tune of $1.8 billion, we found 54 new medicines at $600 million to improve the lot of 175,000 Kiwis.
civility.explanation: Dig at the previous administration but framed around funding.

civility.statement: Is it appropriate for a Minister who clearly has no understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi to be directing Pharmac to ignore the Treaty?
civility.explanation: Contains a personal denigration ('no understanding') of the Minister.

civility.statement: Is repealing Māori wards, which the tribunal ruled breaches the principle of partnership and our right to representation, an example of his Government honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the policy and its ruling.

civility.statement: How does the Minister for Māori Crown relations feel being wheeled out by this Government to answer a question that was directed to the Prime Minister, simply because he is Māori, and the Prime Minister wants to distance himself from the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
civility.explanation: Accusatory, imputes tokenism and evasive motive rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Does the Minister think that attending a close relation's tangi is a case of being wheeled out of this Parliament, as has been put by that last idiotic questioner?
civility.explanation: 'Idiotic questioner' is a direct personal insult of another member.

civility.statement: do two of the top three in this Parliament who have got Māori background... or the highest percentage of Māori and Pasifika in a Cabinet, or the highest percentage in the country, in terms of Parliament, represent progress or the kind of retard comment we've just heard?
civility.explanation: Uses the slur 'retard' to characterise a colleague's comment.

civility.statement: is it a fact that this question is set in 2022, five years after the Labour Party was in Government, which demonstrates that they did sweet Fanny Adams about this issue when they were in power?
civility.explanation: Dismissive partisan jab ('sweet Fanny Adams').

civility.statement: Is it correct that annual returns submitted to the Ministry of Health show $4,044,956.49 worth of heated tobacco products were sold in New Zealand in 2022, and that $3,924,816.06 of those sales were by the tobacco company Philip Morris?
civility.explanation: Factual, document-based question with no personal attack.

civility.statement: Why won't she put as much effort into improving the health of New Zealanders as she will into helping Philip Morris?
civility.explanation: Loaded, accusatory framing presupposing she prioritises a tobacco company.

civility.statement: Can the Minister name a single thing she has done for the health of New Zealanders that is greater than the benefits she has provided for Philip Morris?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical gotcha presuming the Minister has done nothing net-positive for health.

civility.statement: I'm not sure what the member means by "ongoing colonisation". We are a country. That is our history. The focus of this Government is to rectify the problems that have come alongside colonisation and to build on the many successes.
civility.explanation: Measured tone despite a contentious exchange.

civility.statement: Well, it's very irresponsible for the member to come into this House and tell the country that Police have said they are withdrawing from family harm incidents. That is not true... having uniformed police officers standing in someone's lounge room trying to settle an argument between a mother and daughter over an iPhone charger is not a good use of police time.
civility.explanation: 'Very irresponsible' targets the member, though largely a policy defence.

civility.statement: How does he propose to make New Zealanders feel safer when there are 124 fewer police officers in New Zealand than when he took office?
civility.explanation: Substantive, on the record and staffing.

civility.statement: How does he propose to make New Zealanders feel safer when the National Gang Unit he announced would be operational by 1 July was not stood up by that date and now has only five staff members in it?
civility.explanation: Pointed accountability question grounded in specifics.

civility.statement: How does he propose to make New Zealanders feel safer when Police have advised him they will be pulling out of family violence now and this will be done "regardless of the readiness of partner agencies" and Police have warned him in briefings that this could result in "threat to life"?
civility.explanation: Serious accusation but sourced to official advice, not personal abuse.

civility.statement: Does he accept that the overall health Budget funding has actually reduced by 4.5 percent per capita, and, if so, will he increase funding to sustainable levels so that our health system isn't on its knees?
civility.explanation: Pointed but focused on funding, with mild hyperbole ('on its knees').

civility.statement: How will slashing up to 3,000 jobs from the organisation that employs doctors and nurses help to get more doctors and nurses on the front line to serve our people?
civility.explanation: 'Slashing' is loaded but the challenge is substantive.

divination.statement: the market's expectation and the Reserve Bank's expectation is that inflation will fall within the 1 to 3 percent target range this calendar year.
divination.explanation: Prediction consistent with RBNZ forecasts and subsequently borne out (inflation returned to band late 2024).

divination.statement: Current high interest rates are necessary to get rid of inflation but are a handbrake on the economy. Together with tax relief—which is coming next week—lower inflation and lower interest rates will give New Zealanders the real cost of living relief they deserve. When interest rates fall, the economy will start recovering, which means higher incomes and more jobs.
divination.explanation: Predicts economic recovery, higher incomes and jobs when rates fall; plausible but optimistic and uncertain.

divination.statement: Emissions budget 1 has been delivered, emissions budget 2 is being delivered, emissions budget 3 will be delivered, but we have time for that to happen, and the draft for a plan is out there.
divination.explanation: Predicts future emissions budgets will be met; uncertain given criticised plan.

strength.statement: especially our actions to fix Health New Zealand after a botched merger from the previous Government... a significant investment in front-line services with a record $16.7 billion in this year's Budget... We're taking decisive action to fix those problems by installing commissioners and giving them a mandate to deliver New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
strength.explanation: Concrete action (commissioner appointment, budget) underway; delivery of outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: we're very proud to see smoking go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent in the last 12 months, and we're going to continue that march.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a decline largely driven by long-running trends and prior policies.

strength.statement: Last Saturday, alongside Acting Prime Minister David Seymour, I launched the military-style academy pilot at Te Au Rere youth justice residence in Palmerston North. Ten young males will begin a pilot next Monday, 29 July... a three-month residential stage in a youth justice residence, followed by a nine-month stage focused on supporting the young people to transition back into the community.
strength.explanation: Pilot actually launched, showing follow-through on a stated commitment (though results pending).

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced the appointment of a commissioner to Health New Zealand, due to deteriorating performance issues... This includes Health New Zealand currently overspending at the rate of approximately $130 million a month. This is unsustainable, despite our Government's record investment in health of $16.68 billion in this year's Budget.
strength.explanation: Concrete action taken (commissioner appointed).

strength.statement: inflation is down to 3.3 percent, the lowest in three years; and more good news as personal income tax relief is coming next week for the first time in 14 years, as we campaigned on, letting Kiwis—hard-working Kiwis, the people that the Greens and Labour used to care about—get more of their own money.
strength.explanation: Tax relief actually being delivered on schedule.

strength.statement: Emissions budget 1 has been delivered, emissions budget 2 is being delivered, emissions budget 3 will be delivered, but we have time for that to happen, and the draft for a plan is out there.
strength.explanation: EB1 was met, but partly due to prior settings; EB2/EB3 delivery asserted, not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: compared to the previous administration, which failed to fund core Pharmac needs to the tune of $1.8 billion, we found 54 new medicines at $600 million to improve the lot of 175,000 Kiwis.
strength.explanation: Delivered Pharmac funding boost matching the Budget 2024 announcement.

strength.statement: Our Government's pothole repair targets include 95 percent of potholes on high volume national and arterial State highways to be repaired within 24 hours of identification, and 85 percent of potholes on regional, primary collector, and secondary collector State highways repaired within 24 hours of identification.
strength.explanation: Announces targets; delivery against them is not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Already, we have delivered a record $2.07 billion for State highway pothole prevention over the next three years. That's a 91 percent increase in funding compared to the previous three years under Labour.
strength.explanation: Funding allocated, though repair outcomes are future.

strength.statement: Last week, I announced that 4,000 additional job seekers aged 18 to 24 will receive support from a case manager over the phone. Fifteen hundred young people were receiving this new service at the beginning of July, and the roll-out to 4,000 young job seekers will be complete in two months.
strength.explanation: Rollout already partly delivered (1,500 receiving it).

strength.statement: In Ōpōtiki last year, we saw the Mongrel Mob take over the town. Schools were closed, roads were closed, and the town was, effectively, held under siege. This year's anniversary of that event was policed proactively... we've funded 500 additional police officers, and we are on track to deliver those 500 additional police officers.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete policing action; the 500 officers are in progress, not yet delivered.

forthrightness.statement: What I'd just say to the member is we are determined to lower smoking rates across this country... We're going to try it—do a 12-month trial and see how it goes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Ministry of Health advised that heated tobacco could raise youth uptake, addiction and cancer risk; pivots entirely to intentions.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we absolutely did, because we want to encourage people to move away from smoking, take up vaping, try heated tobacco products to lower smoking rates.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the government did increase tobacco excise in December, answering the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: What I'd say to that member, as I've said, is we are determined to deliver on an outcome of less daily smokers in New Zealand... We've got a 12-month trial on it. We'll review it and see how it goes, but we're going to do everything to get an outcome.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which was the greater priority—health advice or tobacco lobbying—he answers neither and returns to talking points.

forthrightness.statement: I would say to the young lady that I am sorry for what she has been through. I would also say to the young lady that we have taken learnings from what has happened in the past and we have put processes in place to make sure that those horrendous acts that have happened in the past will not continue. What we cannot continue to do is do nothing. These young people deserve better, and their families deserve better.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the concern but does not rebut the specific claim that bootcamps recreate the abuse context.

forthrightness.statement: What is correct is that an increase in back-office staff from 2018 to the current time, of 2,500, has contributed to the current financial position.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile two conflicting official explanations, he substitutes his own framing rather than resolving the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: I'm seriously saying that six years of that Government and two years of a botched reform is seriously affecting where we are now.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a six-year staffing change suddenly hit the books in March, he deflects into partisan blame.

forthrightness.statement: What I accept is the biggest contribution to health of roughly $16.67 billion across three Budgets in our last Budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to accept a 4.5% per-capita funding cut, he neither confirms nor denies and pivots to a gross figure.

forthrightness.statement: there were some proposals from front-line agencies, mostly for capital expenditure, that were not progressed in Budget 2024. By definition, Budgets are about prioritising; they are not about funding everything an agency or Minister might propose. That would be fiscally irresponsible in the extreme.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers yes and concedes some funding requests were declined.

forthrightness.statement: We have record numbers of nurses employed in our health system right now... If that member wants to get up in this House and defend hiring hundreds and thousands more health bureaucrats while waiting lists got longer, she's welcome to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a hiring freeze covers front-line nurses, she avoids it and reframes as a bureaucrat-hiring attack.

forthrightness.statement: I would love it if the Greens came out and actually cared about emissions, and actually support our fast-track legislation so we can double the amount of renewable electricity in this country and lower our emissions in the process. Please, please join us.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to define 'least cost', he does not and pivots to renewables and attacks.

forthrightness.statement: All three parties in the coalition Government oppose the creation of Māori wards. We're making this a decision for local communities. And if they wish to create them, they can; if they don't, they won't.
forthrightness.explanation: States the position clearly but sidesteps the Tribunal-breach premise of the question.

forthrightness.statement: We are prioritising the health and wellbeing of the individual child—that is the primary consideration with the change that has been made.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile removing s7AA with the State abuse report, he restates a principle without addressing the tension.

forthrightness.statement: we are committed to achieving Smokefree Aotearoa 2025... we are choosing to do a programme of work that will ensure that there are tools available to achieve the target audience quitting smoking. We will continue to do so. There is no relationship with the tobacco industry.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked precise factual questions about Philip Morris sales and safety-mechanism timing, she restates commitments and denies a relationship instead.

forthrightness.statement: They ignore the fact that the first thing I did as a Minister was raise excise tax, and that we are continuing to meet with quit-smoking groups to ensure they have the best tools.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially rebuts the 'name one thing' challenge but does not engage the Philip Morris specifics.

forthrightness.statement: yes, recognising that there will always be a wide variety of opinions as to what that means in practice and in every particular situation, and also recognising, in doing so, the need never to lose sight of the basic expectations of people living in a modern democratic society of equality before the law and equal say in matters affecting their lives.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'yes' to whether the Government has a responsibility to uphold the Treaty, with qualifications.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not sure what the member means by "ongoing colonisation". We are a country. That is our history. The focus of this Government is to rectify the problems that have come alongside colonisation and to build on the many successes.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly deflects by querying the term rather than engaging the substance.

forthrightness.statement: I've already laid out for the member that this incoming Government (1) funded the Police properly, because the previous Government hadn't; and (2) we've funded 500 additional police officers, and we are on track to deliver those 500 additional police officers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 124 fewer officers than when he took office, he does not address the figure and pivots to funding and future recruits.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it's very irresponsible for the member to come into this House and tell the country that Police have said they are withdrawing from family harm incidents. That is not true... having uniformed police officers standing in someone's lounge room trying to settle an argument between a mother and daughter over an iPhone charger is not a good use of police time.
forthrightness.explanation: Denies wholesale withdrawal but does not engage the specific 'threat to life' briefing warning.

charisma.statement: I would say to the young lady that I am sorry for what she has been through. I would also say to the young lady that we have taken learnings from what has happened in the past and we have put processes in place to make sure that those horrendous acts that have happened in the past will not continue. What we cannot continue to do is do nothing. These young people deserve better, and their families deserve better.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the concern and appeals to shared care for young people.

charisma.statement: I would love it if the Greens came out and actually cared about emissions, and actually support our fast-track legislation so we can double the amount of renewable electricity in this country and lower our emissions in the process. Please, please join us.
charisma.explanation: Invitation to 'join us' undercut by the implication the Greens don't care about emissions.

charisma.statement: yes, recognising that there will always be a wide variety of opinions as to what that means in practice and in every particular situation, and also recognising, in doing so, the need never to lose sight of the basic expectations of people living in a modern democratic society of equality before the law and equal say in matters affecting their lives.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges a range of views and appeals to shared democratic values.

authenticity.statement: inflation is down to 3.3 percent, the lowest in three years; and more good news as personal income tax relief is coming next week for the first time in 14 years, as we campaigned on, letting Kiwis—hard-working Kiwis, the people that the Greens and Labour used to care about—get more of their own money.
authenticity.explanation: 'As we campaigned on' — delivering the tax relief matches the campaign commitment.

authenticity.statement: They ignore the fact that the first thing I did as a Minister was raise excise tax, and that we are continuing to meet with quit-smoking groups to ensure they have the best tools.
authenticity.explanation: Cites her own concrete action (raising excise) to counter the claim she favours tobacco interests.

veracity.statement: Every single family that I've talked to has told me they are struggling so, so bad.
veracity.explanation: Anecdotal universal claim ('every single family') that is unverifiable and rhetorically absolute; cost-of-living pressure was real but the sweeping framing is exaggerated.

veracity.statement: attacks on Māori ward representation; demolishing the Māori Health Authority; removing section 7AA provisions at Oranga Tamariki; rushing through the fast-track approvals bill; a 45 percent cut from Matariki funding; erasing te reo Māori from the Public Service; $40 million cut for supply and capability of Māori housing; ... a $96.7 million cut to Māori Development, including Te Tumu Paeroa; ... a $35.5 million cut, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority; a $9.5 million cut to claimant funding for historical Treaty claimants
veracity.explanation: The itemised cuts track Budget 2024 measures closely (Māori Health Authority disestablishment, s7AA repeal, Matariki funding reduction, etc.); largely accurate though presented in the most adverse framing.

veracity.statement: 50 percent of the male prison population is Māori; 64 percent of the female prison population is Māori; 80 percent of Oranga Tamariki is Māori.
veracity.explanation: Male (~52%) and female (~65%) prison figures are close to official data; the '80 percent of Oranga Tamariki' figure overstates the ~68-70% of tamariki in care who are Māori, so directionally true but the last figure is inflated.

veracity.statement: We're dying seven to 10 years earlier than anybody else.
veracity.explanation: Māori life expectancy is roughly 7 years lower than non-Māori; 'seven to 10 years' is at the higher edge but broadly accurate as a health-inequity statistic.

veracity.statement: Māori are not mentioned once in the priority areas of this Budget. The Māori development section of the Budget summary only talks about savings; it makes no mention of new Government commitments.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about the Budget's framing; plausibly accurate that Māori did not feature in headline priorities and that the Vote emphasised savings, but stated absolutely without citation.

veracity.statement: the Māori economy sits at $70 billion and is projected to reach $100 billion in the next five years
veracity.explanation: The ~$70bn figure aligns with contemporary asset-base estimates of the Māori economy.

veracity.statement: 100,000 people in Aotearoa will be sleeping rough on the streets, in tents, in cars, in garages, and unlivable houses
veracity.explanation: The ~100,000 figure derives from severe housing deprivation counts that mostly capture crowded/temporary housing, not literal rough sleeping; conflating the two overstates street homelessness and is misleading.

veracity.statement: Māori currently make up 50 percent of the social housing wait-list, and by no doubt they will be some of this one over here's whanaunga. Therefore, they should be given 50 percent of the social housing Budget
veracity.explanation: Māori share of the social housing register is around half, so the statistic is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: they've saved $245 million over four years—which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they're giving to—guess who! That's right, the landlords. They've also cut Māori housing by $40 million and action to address rangatahi homelessness by $20 million.
veracity.explanation: The interest-deductibility restoration is close to $2.9bn and the housing cut figures are plausible; calling deductibility a '$3 billion handout to landlords' is a contestable but common characterisation of a tax change.

veracity.statement: kura and kōhanga reo have been funded less than 1 percent over the last decade and yet kura kaupapa continue to be the highest-performing educational systems in this country.
veracity.explanation: The 'highest-performing educational systems' claim is a strong assertion not clearly supported by comparable national data, and 'funded less than 1 percent' is ambiguous (of what); mixed.

veracity.statement: Te Matatini is receiving $1 million less per year—that's a 5 percent cut. Matariki funding has been cut by 45 percent overall.
veracity.explanation: The Matariki 45% reduction matches the figure cited elsewhere in the debate; the Te Matatini figures are specific and plausible.

veracity.statement: This Budget removes half-price transport and $5 prescription fees. They have cut minimum wage, benefit increases, support for disabled communities, while putting $1.9 million into what? Prisons.
veracity.explanation: Removal of half-price public transport and the $5 prescription subsidy is accurate, but 'cut minimum wage' is false — the minimum wage was raised (modestly), not cut; the mixture of true and false claims is misleading.

veracity.statement: On 31 July this year, next week, New Zealanders will experience tax relief for the first time in 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Income-tax thresholds had not been adjusted since around 2010, so 'first time in 14 years' for threshold-based relief is broadly defensible, though minor tax changes occurred in between.

veracity.statement: It gives average-income households up to $102 a fortnight, plus FamilyBoost childcare payments of up to $150 per fortnight for eligible families. A single person earning $55,000 a year will be better off by $51 a fortnight; a working couple both earning $150,000 a year will be better off by around $80 a fortnight; a single adult working 40 hours on the minimum wage will be better off by about $25 per fortnight
veracity.explanation: The headline figures match the Government's published tax-package examples; 'up to' framing quotes maximums, which are accurate for the cited cases.

veracity.statement: Our tax package is funded through savings and new revenue measures, meaning it will not add to Government debt.
veracity.explanation: The package was presented as funded by savings and revenue measures; whether it added to debt depends on fiscal accounting, so broadly the official framing but contestable.

veracity.statement: The first year fees-free policy was an expensive failure and it did not deliver its aim of more students going to tertiary education, nor did it increase participation; in fact, there were fewer fulltime-equivalents in tertiary education in 2023 than there were in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Evaluations did find first-year fees-free had little effect on enrolment, and tertiary EFTS did decline over the period; broadly accurate, though attributing the decline to the policy alone omits other factors.

veracity.statement: We are investing $651 million over four years to deliver an extra 500 police officers and provide them with the tools they need to do their jobs.
veracity.explanation: Moments later he cites '$191 million over four years to recruit 500 extra officers' for the same commitment, so the $651m/$191m figures for '500 officers' are internally inconsistent and one is likely conflating different funding lines.

veracity.statement: an authoritarian and oppressive disciplinary regime in respect of young people leads to trauma and harm. It's been tried and it's failed.
veracity.explanation: Prior NZ boot-camp trials did show high reoffending, so 'been tried and failed' is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: on Q+A recently, the Minister actually was quite clear that he wasn't doing this to deter criminals; he just wanted to put more people inside. He just wanted more people in jail.
veracity.explanation: Rests on a paraphrase of a media interview that cannot be verified here and may compress the Minister's actual argument.

veracity.statement: it cuts anything and everything to do with the environment.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic — several environment lines were cut but 'anything and everything' overstates it; more accurate detail follows.

veracity.statement: The Budget explicitly stops advocacy for the environment, and we see that with the Environmental Legal Assistance Fund—that's cut, gone. We see the Community Environment Fund, funding community hubs and the like—gone.
veracity.explanation: These environmental funds were indeed cut/discontinued in Budget 2024, so the factual core is accurate; 'explicitly stops advocacy' adds interpretive spin.

veracity.statement: the Prime Minister's answers to questions today, which were, frankly, outrageous, when he said that the Greens should support the fast-track bill because it will do more for renewable energy. That is not what that bill says.
veracity.explanation: A contestable rebuttal — the fast-track bill was framed as enabling projects broadly rather than mandating renewable outcomes, so her characterisation is arguable but she offers no bill text to prove it.

veracity.statement: There is no Treaty clause in that piece of legislation; there is nothing for any group of Māori that is not a settled iwi.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track bill as introduced lacked a Treaty clause, so the core claim is broadly accurate; the 'nothing for non-settled iwi' extension is an interpretive gloss.

veracity.statement: the Climate Emergency Response Fund—that's gone from this Budget. There's nothing happening to actually reduce carbon emissions; the focus is only on offsetting with pine trees
veracity.explanation: The CERF's ring-fenced status was substantially unwound, so that element is defensible, but 'nothing happening to reduce emissions' and 'only pine trees' are overstated absolutes given other policy settings.

veracity.statement: One of them is the project known as SouthPAN ... We're providing 25 percent of the cost of that; Australia's stumping up, obviously, the other three-quarters, and we're going to get a 50:50 share in that—a pretty good deal, if you ask me.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the trans-Tasman SouthPAN arrangement in which NZ contributes a minority share for an equal operational benefit; broadly accurate, framing aside.

rigor.statement: Every single family that I've talked to has told me they are struggling so, so bad.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote — generalises from her own conversations to all New Zealanders with no data.

rigor.statement: when you have a blanket policy—like the 20 hours or the 30 hours that the Labour Party campaigned on during the last election—when you have, basically, a blanket policy out there for anyone to just get it for free, you have also provided financial assistance to families who don't necessarily need it, but it is their right to have it. What we are doing with the FamilyBoost is actually targeting the support that we can give to families who really, really do need it.
rigor.explanation: A coherent targeting-vs-universalism argument, but leans on assertion (that FamilyBoost genuinely reaches those most in need) without evidence on take-up or the compliance burden of collecting invoices.

rigor.statement: a Government—a Pākehā Government—that has released a Pākehā Budget for a Pākehā economy; always has been for the last 100 years. It's not a 100-day plan; this is a 100-year plan to continue to entrench a Pākehā economy, lock out any type of Māori economy
rigor.explanation: Framing/hyperbole ('100-year plan') asserted rather than demonstrated, though it precedes a detailed evidential list.

rigor.statement: attacks on Māori ward representation; demolishing the Māori Health Authority; removing section 7AA provisions at Oranga Tamariki; rushing through the fast-track approvals bill; a 45 percent cut from Matariki funding; erasing te reo Māori from the Public Service; $40 million cut for supply and capability of Māori housing; ... a $96.7 million cut to Māori Development, including Te Tumu Paeroa; ... a $35.5 million cut, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority; a $9.5 million cut to claimant funding for historical Treaty claimants
rigor.explanation: Marshals a detailed evidential list to support the 'anti-Māori Budget' conclusion; the inference is well-supported even if the ethnic framing is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: If Māori make up 20 percent of this country's population, a "by Māori, for Māori, to Māori" approach means that Māori should get 20 percent of the total Budget.
rigor.explanation: A clear proportional-share argument, but the premise that population share should equal Budget share is asserted as self-evident rather than argued, and later he himself says need would justify more — a slight internal tension.

rigor.statement: 50 percent of the male prison population is Māori; 64 percent of the female prison population is Māori; 80 percent of Oranga Tamariki is Māori.
rigor.explanation: Uses data to ground the over-incarceration argument, though the Oranga Tamariki figure is not sourced.

rigor.statement: Māori are not mentioned once in the priority areas of this Budget. The Māori development section of the Budget summary only talks about savings; it makes no mention of new Government commitments.
rigor.explanation: Points to the document's own structure as evidence of neglect — reasonable inference, though a single omission is treated as decisive.

rigor.statement: We don't need reform. Reform is just a sugar-coated mechanism to make us better servants to the system. We need constitutional transformation.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorically framed dichotomy (reform vs transformation) asserted rather than argued from evidence.

rigor.statement: Māori currently make up 50 percent of the social housing wait-list, and by no doubt they will be some of this one over here's whanaunga. Therefore, they should be given 50 percent of the social housing Budget
rigor.explanation: Proportional-allocation argument built on a real statistic, but the leap from wait-list share to identical Budget share is asserted, and 'whanaunga' is an aside rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: they've saved $245 million over four years—which is about 8 percent of the $3 billion handout they're giving to—guess who! That's right, the landlords. They've also cut Māori housing by $40 million and action to address rangatahi homelessness by $20 million.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes savings against the deductibility cost to argue misplaced priorities; the '8 percent' comparison is apt, though 'handout' loads the framing.

rigor.statement: kura and kōhanga reo have been funded less than 1 percent over the last decade and yet kura kaupapa continue to be the highest-performing educational systems in this country.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts low funding with high performance to argue value, but the performance premise is stated without evidence.

rigor.statement: This Government and its coalition will be remembered for being the meanest-spirited Government ever.
rigor.explanation: Superlative appeal to emotion ('meanest ever') with no evidential basis.

rigor.statement: the all-out war that you're waging on tangata whenua and, indeed, the poor
rigor.explanation: Hyperbole ('all-out war') substituting for argument.

rigor.statement: Our tax package is funded through savings and new revenue measures, meaning it will not add to Government debt.
rigor.explanation: States the funding mechanism, which supports the no-new-debt conclusion, but offers no figures reconciling costs and offsets.

rigor.statement: The first year fees-free policy was an expensive failure and it did not deliver its aim of more students going to tertiary education, nor did it increase participation; in fact, there were fewer fulltime-equivalents in tertiary education in 2023 than there were in 2017.
rigor.explanation: Backs the 'failure' claim with an enrolment comparison, but the 2017-vs-2023 figure is offered as causal proof when confounders (demographics, labour market) are ignored.

rigor.statement: this Government has TikTok policies for justice, because you only have to go—and I do go online and look at the members and the Ministers in the justice sector and see what they're saying, and they're full of three-line slogans, but no policy and no real evidence.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a lack of evidence behind the policies but supports it mainly with the rhetorical 'TikTok' characterisation rather than examples at this point.

rigor.statement: an authoritarian and oppressive disciplinary regime in respect of young people leads to trauma and harm. It's been tried and it's failed.
rigor.explanation: Draws on the established evidence that punitive boot-camp models produce poor reoffending outcomes; a supportable claim, though the evidence is referenced generally rather than cited.

rigor.statement: We know that broken families cause crime, that families with a person in jail are more likely for a child to grow up and be in jail, and that the educational outcomes, the financial outcomes for those families, they will be adverse and be more likely to result in criminal offending. We should be attacking those causes of crime.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from intergenerational-incarceration and social-determinants evidence to a causes-of-crime conclusion; the logic follows, though correlations are stated as 'cause' without nuance.

rigor.statement: Te Ao Mārama, the initiatives of the court which are working, which are taking young people at the earliest opportunity and shifting them away from the conveyor belt of court, trial, prison, and return again—now, those programmes that the courts have been initiating have been put on hold by this Government cutting the budget for them
rigor.explanation: Asserts the programmes 'are working' as premise for opposing the cut, but offers no outcome data to substantiate their effectiveness.

rigor.statement: it cuts anything and everything to do with the environment.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping absolute ('anything and everything') offered before the supporting detail; overstated as a standalone claim.

rigor.statement: the Climate Emergency Response Fund—that's gone from this Budget. There's nothing happening to actually reduce carbon emissions; the focus is only on offsetting with pine trees
rigor.explanation: Anchors on a real change (CERF) but generalises to 'nothing' and 'only offsetting', which does not follow from the single fact.

rigor.statement: New Zealand needs the foreign direct investment. We need that capital to build infrastructure and other facilities in New Zealand that are, sadly, lacking and have been lacking for far too many years.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable capital-shortfall argument for FDI, but stated as assertion without figures on the investment gap or infrastructure deficit.

specificity.explanation: Vague — no figures, mechanisms or measures, just an impressionistic 'so, so bad'.

specificity.statement: This Government has put forward what we promised and we have given people the choice. But also, we are clear on the consequences of people not meeting their delivery.
specificity.explanation: Abstract — no named promise, figure or mechanism identified.

specificity.statement: Smoke and mirrors; that's all this is.

specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures broken down by household type and income level.

specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, timeframe and a quantified reach target with a defined age band elsewhere.

civility.explanation: Hyperbolic superlative directed at a bill (a policy) rather than a person.

civility.statement: Can someone tell Mr "Know-it-all" Seymour that the Treaty is part of our constitution and he and his stupid party are wrong?
civility.explanation: Personal insult ('Know-it-all') and disparagement of a party as 'stupid' rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: We see you, we feel you, and we want justice for you. That is our duty as people of this House. You deserve justice.
civility.explanation: Respectful, compassionate acknowledgement of survivors with no partisan edge.

civility.statement: I want to first pause and acknowledge what this afternoon will truly be about, what this day will be about and acknowledge your strength, your grace, and your perseverance in being here today.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of survivors, setting aside his own agenda.

civility.statement: He either doesn't know or he simply does not care.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Minister's competence or intent personally rather than his policy.

civility.statement: Instead, we get a Minister fixated on removing road cones and fixing potholes. The biggest pothole we've got in New Brighton is the river between Hawke Street and Pages Road.
civility.explanation: A pointed, belittling jab at the Minister's priorities, though delivered as rhetoric rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: To every person who took part, I say thank you for your exceptional strength, your incredible courage, and your confronting honesty... I cannot take away your pain, but I can tell you this: you are heard, and you are believed.
civility.explanation: Respectful, survivor-centred acknowledgement free of partisanship.

civility.statement: I would also like to acknowledge the previous Labour Government who commenced this important inquiry almost six years ago.
civility.explanation: Gracious recognition of a political opponent's contribution.

civility.statement: whilst a formal apology is still some time away, we are sorry. As a society and as a country, we are sorry.
civility.explanation: Sincere, respectful apology to survivors with no partisan framing.

rigor.statement: Saying changes in back-office staff that happened over six years could cause a budget blowout in March of this year is totally ridiculous.
rigor.explanation: Contains a genuine temporal argument (gradual six-year change can't cause a sudden March blowout) but leans on ridicule rather than data.

rigor.statement: That's what Margie Apa, Chief Executive of Te Whatu Ora Health New Zealand, said yesterday at a press conference. She said, "In relation to better than expected international recruitment and improved retention after COVID.", she said, "We found ourselves actually over-correcting much faster than we had expected."
rigor.explanation: Backs her claim about the overspend cause by citing a named, authoritative source (the CE) with a direct quote.

rigor.statement: They knew that the allocation was going to be insufficient well ahead of Budget day and they did nothing to address it.
rigor.explanation: Asserts intent and inaction as fact without fully establishing the causal chain.

rigor.statement: It does remind me of some of the members on the other side of the House when they did actually try to bring in hate speech laws, which, again, this Government got rid of, which would have actually severely undermined the rights of Kiwis to have a free and open debate.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sweeping consequence ('severely undermined the rights') without evidence or engagement with the actual proposal.

rigor.statement: by opposing measures that would have the effect of making housing more affordable and more available to people, by not being prepared to support any changes that would actually enable that, they remind me of that famous expression that "Everyone wants to go to heaven, but no one wants to die."
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal to analogy and a strawman that the Opposition rejects any affordability measure, without evidence.

rigor.statement: it is a false choice to say we can either have quality versus affordability, or sustainability versus affordability.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies a false-dichotomy framing, though the claim that productivity resolves the trade-off is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: the Treaty principles were developed and passed in 1987 by Justice Robin Cooke, who described the '87 lands case as "perhaps as important for the future of our country as any that has come before a New Zealand Court."
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a concrete legal precedent and authority.

rigor.statement: Not even the secretary of Justice, Andrew Kibblewhite, supports the Treaty principles Bill. To quote him: "it's a novel interpretation of article 2: there's no support for it in legislation, judicial interpretation, [and] expert opinion."
rigor.explanation: Marshals a named official source with a direct quote to support the argument, rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: Hokianga is mighty—40,000 hectares strong, massive blocks of whenua Māori, and yet our land is prone to flooding. Our land is steep and often unusable for kāinga.
rigor.explanation: Explains the apparent paradox (much land, little housing) with concrete physical reasons—flooding and steep terrain.

rigor.statement: He either doesn't know or he simply does not care.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy that excludes other explanations and impugns motive.

rigor.statement: If there's a tsunami coming, we will not have an hour. If there's a tsunami coming, we will not have a traffic management plan and staff directing cars... people won't be able to get out fast enough, and those who don't get out could die.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference from observed evacuation times, though it dramatises a worst case without probabilities.

rigor.statement: the PPP... hasn't always delivered what the New Zealand Government clients need, what the contractors need, or what the users of public infrastructure need. That's why it's time for an update.
rigor.explanation: Concedes weaknesses in the existing model and links them to the case for reform, though without specific examples.

rigor.statement: the shameful history of abuse in State care has led to prisons overflowing with some of the survivors of that abuse. Gangs contain survivors of that abuse.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the causal link in survivor testimony quoted from the report rather than mere assertion.

veracity.statement: That's what Margie Apa, Chief Executive of Te Whatu Ora Health New Zealand, said yesterday at a press conference. She said, "In relation to better than expected international recruitment and improved retention after COVID.", she said, "We found ourselves actually over-correcting much faster than we had expected."
veracity.explanation: Quotes attributed to the CE appear accurate; the nursing-recruitment explanation is a plausible and evidenced account of the overspend.

veracity.statement: They knew that the allocation was going to be insufficient well ahead of Budget day and they did nothing to address it.
veracity.explanation: Partly supported by her committee account but the Government's knowledge and inaction is contested; a one-sided characterisation.

veracity.statement: On 1 March this year, those of us diligently sitting in the Health Committee heard from Te Whatu Ora about their budget troubles.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about a select committee hearing that is plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: They went to the election with a tax plan that didn't add up
veracity.explanation: A contested political characterisation of the coalition's tax plan presented as fact.

veracity.statement: It does remind me of some of the members on the other side of the House when they did actually try to bring in hate speech laws, which, again, this Government got rid of, which would have actually severely undermined the rights of Kiwis to have a free and open debate.
veracity.explanation: Characterisation of the prior hate-speech proposals as gutting free speech is contested and overstated.

veracity.statement: some 20 percent of New Zealand's carbon emissions are directly involved in the construction and in the use of buildings.
veracity.explanation: Broadly in line with estimates for combined embodied and operational building emissions, though figures vary by methodology.

veracity.statement: One in 10 workers is directly employed in the management of the built environment.
veracity.explanation: A plausible order-of-magnitude figure for the construction/built-environment workforce, but unsourced and imprecise.

veracity.statement: the Treaty principles were developed and passed in 1987 by Justice Robin Cooke, who described the '87 lands case as "perhaps as important for the future of our country as any that has come before a New Zealand Court."
veracity.explanation: The 1987 Lands case and Cooke's role are real and the quote is broadly accurate, though 'developed and passed' loosely describes a judicial precedent, not legislation.

veracity.statement: This nation is built upon a Treaty. That is a historical fact, and while New Zealand is certainly a multicultural society, it was founded on a Treaty with the indigenous peoples of this country. That makes us stronger, not weaker.
veracity.explanation: The founding-Treaty framing is historically well grounded; the 'stronger not weaker' clause is a value judgement.

veracity.statement: Fifty percent of Māori are in jails at the moment
veracity.explanation: Demonstrably false as stated; the real figure is that roughly half the prison population is Māori, not that half of all Māori are imprisoned.

veracity.statement: Not even the secretary of Justice, Andrew Kibblewhite, supports the Treaty principles Bill. To quote him: "it's a novel interpretation of article 2: there's no support for it in legislation, judicial interpretation, [and] expert opinion."
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific, checkable position to a named official; presented as an accurate quote.

veracity.statement: he and this Government have arrogantly told Government departments to use their English names more prominently than Māori. They told Corrections to no longer have Treaty provisions in their legislation... directing Pharmac to stop wasting time on the Treaty.
veracity.explanation: The underlying directives are broadly real, but characterised in loaded terms ('arrogantly', 'wasting time') that colour the facts.

veracity.statement: But in Hokianga we have our kaumātua, we have our whānau, and we have our mokopuna in tents, in their vehicles, in shacks—kāinga kore in their own tūpuna whenua. They live without water and heating.
veracity.explanation: Plausible, first-hand account of housing deprivation in Hokianga, consistent with known Northland housing conditions.

veracity.statement: The Pages Road Bridge is our vital lifeline. It carries traffic and utilities, like water, fibre, and power, into New Brighton... Our current bridge was badly damaged in 2011. It's only had a temporary repair since. It's not safe. It's not strong.
veracity.explanation: Checkable claims about earthquake damage and interim repair that are broadly accurate, though 'not safe' is his characterisation.

veracity.statement: This is part of our Government's Budget 2024—a $466 million investment for school property growth.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable Budget 2024 figure presented as fact and plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: That area of Takanini is in fact the second-fastest growing area in the country.
veracity.explanation: A specific ranking claim presented as fact; plausible for Flat Bush/Takanini but unsourced and hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: the PPP... hasn't always delivered what the New Zealand Government clients need, what the contractors need, or what the users of public infrastructure need. That's why it's time for an update.
veracity.explanation: A fair, evidence-consistent acknowledgement that past NZ PPPs have had mixed results.

veracity.statement: the experience of some children and young people at Lake Alice Hospital did amount to torture. Patients at Lake Alice were given electric shocks without anaesthetic, as well as painful and immobilising paraldehyde injections. These so-called treatments were not administered for medical reasons; they were used for punishment and emotional control.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects well-documented findings, including UN Committee against Torture rulings, about Lake Alice.

veracity.statement: The report has taken six years to write, and it is almost 3,000 pages long, comprising 16 volumes.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable facts about the report that match its known scale.

veracity.statement: The State and its institutions not only allowed this abuse to happen; it then denied you your voice and, worse, covered up the extent of the atrocities that took place.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the royal commission's findings of abuse and systemic cover-up.

veracity.statement: the shameful history of abuse in State care has led to prisons overflowing with some of the survivors of that abuse. Gangs contain survivors of that abuse.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported by the report and the cited 'pipeline to prison' testimony, though 'overflowing' generalises.

specificity.explanation: Concrete description of living conditions (tents, vehicles, no water/heating) though without figures.

charisma.statement: we see robust debates, often of ideas that we don't agree with, but they're allowed to be expressed and we try to win each other over.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing that values persuasion and tolerance of opposing views rather than defeating opponents.

charisma.statement: I see Mr Cameron Luxton, MP, nodding. He is the only member of this House who is actually a licensed building practitioner. I asked him his view on these matters, and I asked the view of those who are actually engaged in building in this country
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, credits colleagues and practitioners across the coalition; consensus-building in tone though within his own side.

charisma.statement: This nation is built upon a Treaty. That is a historical fact, and while New Zealand is certainly a multicultural society, it was founded on a Treaty with the indigenous peoples of this country. That makes us stronger, not weaker.
charisma.explanation: Attempts an inclusive national framing ('makes us stronger') though embedded in a combative speech.

charisma.statement: We must work together in this country, not against each other. Labour want to work with Māori; ACT wants to work against them.
charisma.explanation: Opens with a unity appeal but immediately collapses into an us-vs-them contrast that alienates rather than persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: We see you, we feel you, and we want justice for you. That is our duty as people of this House. You deserve justice.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, framing justice as a shared duty of the whole House.

charisma.statement: To every person who took part, I say thank you for your exceptional strength, your incredible courage, and your confronting honesty... I cannot take away your pain, but I can tell you this: you are heard, and you are believed.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive, and validating language intended to bring survivors and the nation together.

charisma.statement: I would also like to acknowledge the previous Labour Government who commenced this important inquiry almost six years ago.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party credit given on a solemn national issue, building consensus rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: whilst a formal apology is still some time away, we are sorry. As a society and as a country, we are sorry.
charisma.explanation: Speaks for the country as a whole, an inclusive collective acknowledgement.

charisma.statement: This must be bigger than politics. We owe it to the survivors and to future generations to finally deliver justice and to finally end the ongoing abuse that happens in State care. This work will extend beyond the life of any one Government, so we should work together to make sure that happens.
charisma.explanation: Explicit call for cross-party cooperation and shared responsibility beyond partisan advantage.

divination.statement: If there's a tsunami coming, we will not have an hour. If there's a tsunami coming, we will not have a traffic management plan and staff directing cars... people won't be able to get out fast enough, and those who don't get out could die.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction of fatal outcomes in a tsunami given the current bridge; plausible but the scenario and timing are uncertain.

divination.statement: Mill Road is on the list of seven roads of national significance, and work will begin in three years.

divination.statement: This Government is committed to replacing the Resource Management Act, though, by July 2026.

veracity.statement: According to the definition outlined by the Solicitor-General, the children who were sent to Lake Alice went through torture.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributed factual claim; the Solicitor-General did conclude the treatment at Lake Alice met the legal definition of torture, and this is well documented.

veracity.statement: Time and time again, the report points out Māori being disproportionately affected, being massively overrepresented in numbers of children and young people taken from their homes and put into State care.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the royal commission's findings and long-standing data on Māori overrepresentation in state care; accurate.

veracity.statement: This report was six years in the making. The response cannot be rushed. It needs to be considered with respect and care.

veracity.explanation: Matches the royal commission's headline estimates (~655,000 through care 1950–2019; ~200,000 abused); accurate.

veracity.statement: Terrified, having to attest in the CCTV against a defence lawyer. And what happened? That caregiver got 13 months of community service.

veracity.statement: At the boot camps on Great Barrier, boys were forced to dig their own graves. They were made to lie face down in those holes while they were being shot at.

charisma.statement: There is no time to digest. We needed time to digest, but they were quick to uplift, quick to move. Quick to ruin us. Quick to displace us.
charisma.explanation: Combative rebuttal that rallies her own side against 'them'; little attempt to bring opponents along.

charisma.statement: We welcome this report. We welcome the opportunity to work through the 138 recommendations in that report.
charisma.explanation: Constructive and welcoming, positioning the response as shared work rather than partisan opposition.

charisma.statement: You have heard acknowledgments from all parties in the House this afternoon. You have heard all parties saying they are committed to this issue and that they want to work on resolving these issues and ensuring it doesn’t happen again.

charisma.statement: There are some who have already tried to bring politics into today. We should not do that.
charisma.explanation: Calls for setting politics aside, but does so with a finger-pointing framing that faults unnamed others rather than fully inviting them in.

charisma.statement: Government and State and Government alone cannot fix this problem; it actually rests on all New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing that shares responsibility across all New Zealanders rather than one side.

rigor.statement: This report was six years in the making. The response cannot be rushed. It needs to be considered with respect and care.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference (large complex report → careful response) but also a convenient justification for delay, with no evidence weighed on the survivors' urgency.

rigor.statement: they’re saying how sorry it is, but it continues to create mega-prisons, removes section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and experiments with our rangatahi and justice in boot camps.
rigor.explanation: Argues Government hypocrisy by pointing to specific contradictory actions as evidence, though the 'experiments' framing is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: The State failed in three ways. It failed to run safe institutions of its own.
rigor.explanation: Opens a clearly structured three-part analysis (unsafe institutions, absent oversight, cover-up) with each claim grounded in the report's findings and following logically.

rigor.statement: people on this side with the Government have not apologised today because we believe it is so important that we make sure that this report and its recommendations are properly considered and the form of apology and anything else that goes with it is not done to those survivors but actually created with them, so that it is genuine.
rigor.explanation: Gives an explicit, coherent justification for withholding the apology (co-creation makes it genuine) that follows from its premise.

rigor.statement: Government and State and Government alone cannot fix this problem; it actually rests on all New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable claim that institutional fixes alone are insufficient, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Everyone who’s ever done PSYC 101 has heard of the Milgram experiment and the Stanford prison experiments. We can hardly claim ignorance as an excuse.
rigor.explanation: Marshals relevant established psychology on how power corrupts to argue the harms were foreseeable, though it leans on the well-worn appeal to those experiments rather than the report's own data.

rigor.statement: As Mahatma Gandhi said, “The true measure of any society can be seen in how it deals with the most vulnerable”.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority (a quotation) as a moral premise rather than argued evidence.

rigor.statement: for years, successive Governments have spent more time, effort, and money trying to hide that reality, to save its own reputation, as opposed to saving the lives of innocent children.
rigor.explanation: The cover-up claim has some support in the report, but the 'more money on hiding than helping' comparison is asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: The best chance we have of protecting our tamariki from State abuse is to keep them out of it in the first place.
