civility.statement: some councils have made a real hash of their water infrastructure assets. We don’t have to walk too far from this building to see that bubbling up in the street ourselves.
civility.explanation: 'made a real hash' is blunt criticism of councils' performance, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: it is a “Henry VIII” clause; let’s be clear: we looked at the guidelines and absolutely it fits within that. However, the clause doesn’t pose a constitutional risk, because Parliament actually had a policy that that will give effect to.
civility.explanation: Engages the Law Society's concern substantively and acknowledges it rather than dismissing it.

civility.statement: You may well have been misled. You may well have been led down the garden path by a Government that went on the campaign hustings, saying one thing, but has come to the House with a piece of legislation that does the exact opposite.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of misleading voters; an integrity attack rather than pure policy critique.

civility.statement: $1.2 billion of wasteful spending on consultants, on your controversial, divisive three waters—$1.2 billion worth of wasteful spending with nothing, absolutely nothing, to show for it.
civility.explanation: Repetitive, hyperbolic attack ('wasteful', 'divisive') rather than measured critique.

civility.statement: What happened in Havelock North was a tragedy. People died because the water that came out of their taps that should have been safe was not. This is a deeply serious problem which we need to solve.
civility.explanation: Respectfully acknowledges an opposing member's point and frames the issue as a shared problem.

civility.statement: What they said was, “We’re OK. We’ve spent the money. We don’t care about our neighbours. We don’t care about the people one town over... We’re OK. To hell with them.” That was the gist of their submission.
civility.explanation: Puts hostile words into a submitter's mouth to caricature the opposing position.

civility.statement: On that side of the House, they are saying to some district councils, to some areas of the country: “To hell with you—to hell with you. We don’t care that you’ve got to put your rates up... To hell with you.”
civility.explanation: Repeatedly attributes callous words ('to hell with you') to opponents they did not say.

civility.statement: What New Zealanders don’t need is the waste of time.
civility.explanation: A mild rhetorical jab rather than a personal attack.

divination.statement: To the people of Northland, they’re cast on their own. To the people of Tairāwhiti, they’re gone. The top of the South Island: they’re on their own. The West Coast of the South Island: they’re on their own.
divination.explanation: Predicts small/rural regions will be left without viable water arrangements under the new model; directionally plausible given scale arguments but overstated and long-term.

divination.statement: When you look at the projected rates increases across the country, not just this year but next year and every year for the next 10 years, they have all jumped up significantly since this Government repealed water reform.
divination.explanation: Forecasts sustained higher rates over 10 years; plausible directionally, magnitude and attribution uncertain.

divination.statement: if we can’t treat our waste water to drinking-water standard and put it into a river, put it into a stream, put it into the harbour, because of some kind of cultural constraint, this country’s never going to succeed.
divination.explanation: Sweeping prediction that the country 'will never succeed' absent this change; implausibly absolute.

charisma.statement: To the people of Northland, they’re cast on their own. To the people of Tairāwhiti, they’re gone. The top of the South Island: they’re on their own. The West Coast of the South Island: they’re on their own.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective roll-call, but appeals to his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: It’s your fault. I say to the members opposite: you’ve all done this.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-vs-them; makes no attempt to bring the other side along.

charisma.statement: We would have liked to see the required time frame be a minimum of 30 years and have really clear expectations on councils that these plans would consider climate change as recommended by numerous submitters.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, solution-oriented framing though pitched from the party's position.

charisma.statement: it gets rid of co-governance, which was that awful, divisive, race-based solution to everything that the previous Labour Government tried to impose
charisma.explanation: Deliberately divisive framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: off you go to the Opposition benches for a very, very, very, very, very, very, very long time.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing jab that entrenches division.

charisma.statement: when we talk about water in local government, sometimes we forget that central government is not particularly good at this at all either. In fact, when we talk about water in local government, sometimes we forget that central government is not very good at managing its assets either. It’s got to get better at it.
charisma.explanation: Concedes fault on his own side of government, a bridge-building acknowledgement rather than pure attack.

charisma.statement: We’ve heard the comment that 10 years is not long enough. Actually, I’d be inclined to agree; a longer term is a good thing, because these assets are going to be assets which, by and large, should be lasting 100 years.
charisma.explanation: Openly agrees with an opposition (Green) point and reasons across the divide, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: You may well have been misled. You may well have been led down the garden path by a Government that went on the campaign hustings, saying one thing, but has come to the House with a piece of legislation that does the exact opposite.
charisma.explanation: Directed at 'viewer land' to rally against the Government rather than persuade across the aisle.

charisma.statement: My young babies were drinking the water and becoming sick. Our whole community literally felt like we were being poisoned by the water.
charisma.explanation: Personal, emotive testimony that connects with listeners, though it appeals to feeling rather than building cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: On that side of the House, they are saying to some district councils, to some areas of the country: “To hell with you—to hell with you. We don’t care that you’ve got to put your rates up... To hell with you.”
charisma.explanation: Highly divisive framing designed to vilify the other side, not persuade it.

charisma.statement: We were going to share the cost across the country, because that’s what we do as New Zealanders: we look after each other.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'we look after each other' appeal, but framed as a partisan contrast with the other side.

authenticity.statement: So what will we do? Well, this Government’s delivering on what ACT campaigned on and what the coalition Government agreed on.
authenticity.explanation: Claims consistency between ACT's campaign and the legislation; plausibly matches their stated position, unverified in detail here.

authenticity.statement: when we talk about water in local government, sometimes we forget that central government is not particularly good at this at all either. In fact, when we talk about water in local government, sometimes we forget that central government is not very good at managing its assets either. It’s got to get better at it.
authenticity.explanation: Willingness to admit central government's own asset-management failings signals consistency over spin.

authenticity.statement: My young babies were drinking the water and becoming sick. Our whole community literally felt like we were being poisoned by the water.
authenticity.explanation: First-hand lived experience lends genuine consistency between her advocacy and her personal stake.

strength.statement: So what will we do? Well, this Government’s delivering on what ACT campaigned on and what the coalition Government agreed on.
strength.explanation: Enacting-legislation claim, but this is a preliminary bill still in progress rather than delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: Look, we’re a Government of delivery and we are delivering good legislation which is going to deliver local democracy and going to deliver good water infrastructure.
strength.explanation: Repeated 'delivery' claim about a preliminary bill still in progress; announcement/aspiration more than demonstrated delivery.

rigor.statement: one of the comments that was made from that side of the House where he suggested that we should all just stand together as one. Sadly, for Māori, this country doesn't have a very good track record of that.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'stand as one' point by appealing to historical record; reasonable but leans on general assertion rather than laid-out evidence at this point.

rigor.statement: our tīpuna went away and fought together as one; we went and we fought for Aotearoa as one. When they came back, they were left landless, didn't have access to the grants for homes, and some were even excluded from the RSA—Returned Services Association
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete historical example to support the claim that 'stand as one' has failed Māori; evidence-based anecdote with a clear point.

rigor.statement: what about the 52 local and regional councils who say, "No, this is not what we want. We've been through the process and we say no, kahore, leave us alone to be local, manage local, and govern locally."
rigor.explanation: Turns the government's 'localism' rhetoric back on it by citing council opposition — a fair argument, though the number is unsourced here.

rigor.statement: the director-general... will have to ensure that they meet those costs themselves... we've got a situation where far too often we see in regional and local government where, under the auspices of the various statutes, risks are overstated and costs are understated. This is an attempt to invert that particular equation.
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent mechanism (cost-borne reviews to force cost-benefit discipline) but asserts 'risks overstated, costs understated' without evidence.

rigor.statement: Those lines were driven by, as I said earlier today, quackery from the Greens, who don't believe in development, who don't believe in jobs, who don't believe in using our natural resources.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/ad hominem: attributes bad-faith absolutes to opponents with no evidence.

rigor.statement: if you live in a people's paradise and you're poor, you're going to wake up tomorrow, believing you might be in paradise, but you'll still be poor.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical flourish attacking a caricatured Green worldview; witty but no evidential content.

rigor.statement: Amenity values should play second fiddle to jobs, economic growth, and industry in coastal New Zealand. We don't want a situation where, if you are blessed with owning a flash house, you decide that you don't want to see King Salmon expand in a particular area of the Sounds
rigor.explanation: Frames opposition as wealthy NIMBYs — a partial strawman — though it does articulate a genuine prioritisation argument.

rigor.statement: we heard eight councils who submitted to this process, many of them from areas that have coastal permits in operation in their particular rohe. Seven of the eight were in opposition to this particular bill.
rigor.explanation: Uses council submission data to argue local-government opposition; evidence-based point.

rigor.statement: The regulatory impact statement for the bill, they quote, confirms "the status quo is working efficiently and effectively and provides for better environmental and Treaty outcomes than the other [proposed] options." To proceed with the extension proposal would be worse than doing nothing.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the government's own regulatory impact statement — a strong evidentiary source directly supporting his conclusion.

rigor.statement: Does it smell like vested interests lobbying to us? It smells like a bucket of fish guts left in the sun for a week.
rigor.explanation: Insinuation of vested interests via metaphor rather than direct evidence, though preceded by a Law Society quote.

rigor.statement: we made a very simple proposal: not that fish farms should be banned, but that fish farms should be subject to the status quo scrutiny of local councils when assessed. They just should not be given this free consent, and they represent a tiny percentage of the total number of farms but with a potentially large impact.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes finfish farms by their outsized environmental impact and proposes a proportionate, narrowly-targeted carve-out — logically structured.

rigor.statement: A lot of the people that were in support of this bill were iwi Māori—they were iwi Māori in the fisheries space... iwi Māori that spoke to tino rangatiratanga, self-determination, to run their business and afford themselves economic activity in their practice.
rigor.explanation: Counters the 'anti-Māori' framing with the point that Māori commercial interests backed the bill — a relevant, if partial, rebuttal.

rigor.statement: There were 1,100 submissions heard and 1,000 were against this bill. We continuously hear that side of the House talk about democracy... but then every day since then, they've ignored democracy.
rigor.explanation: Uses submission numbers to argue democratic disregard — evidence-backed premise, but 'ignored democracy every day' is a broad rhetorical leap.

rigor.statement: this bill undermines tangata whenua rights. It undermines community autonomy. It undermines environmental protections. It shifts the clean-up costs and the pollution costs of anything to the public—to the public.
rigor.explanation: Lists concrete claimed harms (rights, autonomy, environment, cost-shifting); structured but asserted rather than evidenced in this passage.

rigor.statement: Ngāti Toa pointed out that, potentially, this creates new grievances under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—new grievances. Environmental experts highlighted the severe potential impact on marine biodiversity
rigor.explanation: Cites named submitters and expert input to support the Treaty and biodiversity risks she alleges.

rigor.statement: some of them are ancient, before I was even born—they're from back in the 1970s and have not been tested, have not been reviewed. The environmental impact has not been assessed nor any cultural impact assessments completed, so how can we say we just let them carry on doing what they've been doing for so long, to 2050?
rigor.explanation: Argues from the age and un-reviewed status of consents to the risk of extending them unexamined — a coherent, premise-to-conclusion argument.

rigor.statement: may I go to Marlborough District Council who provided their opinion saying that this proposal, in its blunt form, involves risk of "unintended consequences that will be detrimental to Marlborough's coastal environment." ... They've got 324 marine consents due by the end of 2024... they started in 2019 reviewing these resource consents... and they've got 101 left for this year to review.
rigor.explanation: Marshals a council's quoted submission plus concrete review data (324 consents, 101 remaining) to argue the existing process works — well-evidenced.

rigor.statement: May I go to Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki, another iwi of mine. They are in this industry, they're doing the mahi, but, ultimately, they are saying that this legislation is Trump-esque. This bill does not represent all the voices of the aquaculture sector.
rigor.explanation: Notes even an iwi within the industry opposes the bill — a relevant point that industry support is not uniform.

veracity.statement: our tīpuna went away and fought together as one; we went and we fought for Aotearoa as one. When they came back, they were left landless, didn't have access to the grants for homes, and some were even excluded from the RSA—Returned Services Association
veracity.explanation: Māori WWII veterans were widely excluded from rehabilitation land/home grants and some faced RSA exclusion — well documented historically.

veracity.statement: what about the 52 local and regional councils who say, "No, this is not what we want. We've been through the process and we say no, kahore, leave us alone to be local, manage local, and govern locally."
veracity.explanation: Many councils that had established Māori wards opposed being forced to poll; the '52' figure is asserted and hard to verify precisely from the text.

veracity.statement: the bill will amend the legislation around Māori wards in local government to how it was before the previous Government rushed legislation through by stealth in 2021—so that it's back to where the wider community had a fair chance to help decide whether to add Māori wards to their local area.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the 2021 change removed the poll mechanism; 'by stealth' is a loaded editorial characterisation that overstates the process.

veracity.statement: All three parties were clear about the fact that they were intending to do this during the election campaign—and beforehand, actually, back in 2021, when the changes were brought in almost by stealth.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the parties signalled this; 'all three... clear' is somewhat generalised.

veracity.statement: The overwhelming majority of submissions—the overwhelming majority—actually 1,000 of the 1,100, were absolutely opposed to this bill
veracity.explanation: Consistent with other members' figures (~91% opposed); credible submission count for this bill.

veracity.statement: There were only 13 days that submitters had an opportunity to submit.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about the truncated submission window, consistent with the acknowledged short timeframe.

veracity.statement: we heard eight councils who submitted to this process, many of them from areas that have coastal permits in operation in their particular rohe. Seven of the eight were in opposition to this particular bill.
veracity.explanation: Precise, checkable submission tally (7 of 8 councils opposed); a measured factual claim.

veracity.statement: every single regional and local council in this country opposed this legislation—every single one of them, even the Marlborough regional council, which has, incidentally, 80 percent of the commercially grown seafood in New Zealand, in Marlborough; 600 marine farms
veracity.explanation: 'Every single... council in this country' is likely hyperbole — his colleague noted 7 of 8 submitting councils opposed; Marlborough's share/farm figures are roughly right but the universal claim overstates.

veracity.statement: The regulatory impact statement for the bill, they quote, confirms "the status quo is working efficiently and effectively and provides for better environmental and Treaty outcomes than the other [proposed] options." To proceed with the extension proposal would be worse than doing nothing.
veracity.explanation: RIS wording is quoted; such statements did flag the status quo as preferable, though the excerpt may be selectively framed.

veracity.statement: we heard that 91 percent of the submissions were against this legislation, including the Iwi Chairs Forum, including numerous iwi, including ocean users, the New Zealand Angling and Casting Association, New Zealand Sport Fishing Council, the New Zealand Underwater Association
veracity.explanation: The 91% figure aligns with the ~1,000/1,100 opposed cited by others; the named organisations are plausible submitters.

veracity.statement: A lot of the people that were in support of this bill were iwi Māori—they were iwi Māori in the fisheries space... iwi Māori that spoke to tino rangatiratanga, self-determination, to run their business and afford themselves economic activity in their practice.
veracity.explanation: Some iwi fisheries interests did support the certainty the bill offered; a defensible characterisation of part of the 10% in favour, though selective.

veracity.statement: The sector generated, in 2023, $763 million, including $575 million of export revenue; and the sector employs over 3,000 people—3,225 people to be exact.
veracity.explanation: Figures are in line with reported NZ aquaculture revenue/employment for the period; precise and broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Officials actually spoke to us and said that it was costing about $6 million at the moment in terms of these reconsenting processes.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific cost figure to officials; plausible but unverifiable from the text and lower than other cited figures.

veracity.statement: Then we heard from Moana, which is the largest Māori-owned seafood company, a fully integrated oyster farming operation with 28 farms. They spoke about their concerns around the consenting process and then having to go through these processes over and over and over again with the same information
veracity.explanation: Moana is indeed a large Māori-owned seafood company; the characterisation of its submission is plausible.

veracity.statement: There were 1,100 submissions heard and 1,000 were against this bill. We continuously hear that side of the House talk about democracy... but then every day since then, they've ignored democracy.
veracity.explanation: The 1,000/1,100 submission figures match other members' accounts and are credible.

veracity.statement: Ngāti Toa pointed out that, potentially, this creates new grievances under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—new grievances. Environmental experts highlighted the severe potential impact on marine biodiversity
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific concerns to Ngāti Toa and environmental experts; consistent with iwi and expert submissions referenced elsewhere in the debate.

veracity.statement: there's some 1,200 marine farms across the motu and we know 60 percent-odd are oyster farms.
veracity.explanation: Plausible order-of-magnitude figures for NZ marine farms and oyster share; broadly consistent with sector data.

veracity.statement: one month of consultation targeted and focused; one hui on 1 March with iwi... Iwi had one week to reply and get notice that they're going to call the one hui for iwi to be consulted on this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable process claims consistent with the truncated timeframe others described.

veracity.statement: may I go to Marlborough District Council who provided their opinion saying that this proposal, in its blunt form, involves risk of "unintended consequences that will be detrimental to Marlborough's coastal environment." ... They've got 324 marine consents due by the end of 2024... they started in 2019 reviewing these resource consents... and they've got 101 left for this year to review.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures attributed to Marlborough District Council; plausible and internally consistent.

veracity.statement: We heard from Gary Hooper, the chief executive at Aquaculture New Zealand, who reminded us that the aquaculture sector earns $780 million annually in revenue, employs over 3,000 people, and has the potential to grow exponentially.
veracity.explanation: Revenue/employment figures broadly match those Wedd cited and sector reporting; 'grow exponentially' is aspirational.

veracity.statement: The aquaculture sector is estimated to be facing $28 million in expenditure to renew the consents of 300 farms.
veracity.explanation: A specific cost estimate presented without a clear source; sits alongside a different ($6m) figure cited by a colleague, so uncertain.

veracity.statement: Just like we've passed legislation delivering Kiwis tax cuts for the first time in 14 years so they can keep more of what they earn—one more sleep—so too are we delivering for the aquaculture industry
veracity.explanation: Personal income tax thresholds had not shifted for many years, but 'first tax cuts in 14 years' glosses over prior tax changes (e.g. 2010) — partly true but framed to overstate.

civility.statement: The clear message here is: you do what you're told.
civility.explanation: Uncharitable characterisation of the government's intent rather than engagement with the bill's stated rationale.

civility.statement: this bill is clearly an attack on Māori
civility.explanation: Strong characterisation of the bill's purpose; targets the policy but frames intent as hostile.

civility.statement: just bringing it back to basics, without hurling abuse at each other, because we're all human beings
civility.explanation: Explicitly disavows personal abuse and appeals to shared humanity amid a heated debate.

civility.statement: Those lines were driven by, as I said earlier today, quackery from the Greens, who don't believe in development, who don't believe in jobs, who don't believe in using our natural resources.
civility.explanation: 'Quackery' plus a caricature of Green MPs' motives — personal denigration and strawman rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: we are pro-growth politicians. We don't catastrophise all these apparent risks, that it's going to ruin the environment; that's the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' environmental concerns as 'catastrophising' — belittling of the argument but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: we had the same sort of issue from what is clearly an incompetent Minister for Oceans and Fisheries who just cannot even get the basics right.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on the Minister's competence rather than critique of the policy.

civility.statement: Does it smell like vested interests lobbying to us? It smells like a bucket of fish guts left in the sun for a week.
civility.explanation: Colourful insinuation of corrupt lobbying; vivid rhetoric aimed at the bill's backers rather than substance.

civility.statement: You should look up "democracy", Mister Minister.
civility.explanation: Condescending jab at the Minister rather than a substantive point.

civility.statement: I want to sort of touch on a couple of notable remarks from the Opposition members—I think they're very salient, a couple that I absolutely agree with, and that was the collegiality of the committee and how we worked, I would say, to progress the bill forward.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges opponents' valid points and the committee's collegiality — respectful, cross-bench tone.

civility.statement: I do note—being in the role of the committee chair... there were some in iwi Māori that were divergent from me and this side of the House that said it was too prescriptive... Waikato-Tainui noted that they were in opposition to the bill. They maintained that that was problematic.
civility.explanation: Fairly reports iwi opposition against his own position, including naming Waikato-Tainui — candid and even-handed.

civility.statement: the desperation of twilight politicians whose retorts sound like desperate boars, because their snouts have got no other direction but to take, take, take.
civility.explanation: Sustained personal insult likening a Minister/MPs to greedy boars — character attack, not policy critique.

civility.statement: May I go to Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki, another iwi of mine. They are in this industry, they're doing the mahi, but, ultimately, they are saying that this legislation is Trump-esque. This bill does not represent all the voices of the aquaculture sector.
civility.explanation: Reports an iwi's pejorative 'Trump-esque' label; the substance (not representing all sector voices) is policy-focused though the epithet is loaded.

charisma.statement: The clear message here is: you do what you're told.
charisma.explanation: Rallies her own side against the government; adversarial framing, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: just bringing it back to basics, without hurling abuse at each other, because we're all human beings
charisma.explanation: Attempts to lower the temperature and speak across the divide, though still defending her side's bill.

charisma.statement: Those lines were driven by, as I said earlier today, quackery from the Greens, who don't believe in development, who don't believe in jobs, who don't believe in using our natural resources.
charisma.explanation: Purely divisive us-vs-them attack; alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: if you live in a people's paradise and you're poor, you're going to wake up tomorrow, believing you might be in paradise, but you'll still be poor.
charisma.explanation: Effective applause line for his own side, but mocks opponents rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: we are pro-growth politicians. We don't catastrophise all these apparent risks, that it's going to ruin the environment; that's the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Confident but purely tribal: draws a sharp us-vs-them line rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: we had the same sort of issue from what is clearly an incompetent Minister for Oceans and Fisheries who just cannot even get the basics right.
charisma.explanation: Combative opener aimed at the Minister; does not build any bridge.

charisma.statement: in the spirit of trying to get some compromise around this, we offered up a 10-year extension period, albeit reluctantly. Again, that did not find favour with Government members on the committee.
charisma.explanation: Describes concrete attempts at cross-committee compromise (5- and 10-year options), signalling willingness to find middle ground.

charisma.statement: even went to the extent of offering up an opportunity, by way of amendment, to, effectively, cap the cost of review at 50 percent. So 50 percent of the total cost would be the maximum figure that could be recoverable by the council.
charisma.explanation: Frames Labour as offering reasonable middle-ground amendments to make the bill workable.

charisma.statement: we made a very simple proposal: not that fish farms should be banned, but that fish farms should be subject to the status quo scrutiny of local councils when assessed. They just should not be given this free consent, and they represent a tiny percentage of the total number of farms but with a potentially large impact.
charisma.explanation: Presents modest, reasonable amendments and invites the government to reconsider — a persuasive, moderate register.

charisma.statement: I want to sort of touch on a couple of notable remarks from the Opposition members—I think they're very salient, a couple that I absolutely agree with, and that was the collegiality of the committee and how we worked, I would say, to progress the bill forward.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits the other side and seeks common ground on process, building goodwill.

charisma.statement: the desperation of twilight politicians whose retorts sound like desperate boars, because their snouts have got no other direction but to take, take, take.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative denigration; alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: by 2050, when these permits are finished, this Minister is not going to be here. We're not going to be here. This is the legacy of bloated capitalism which doesn't give a heck about this next generation. This is going to be the mess for our mokopuna and the future generations to clean up.
charisma.explanation: Emotive appeal to her own base framed as 'bloated capitalism'; rousing but not consensus-seeking.

specificity.statement: this bill is clearly an attack on Māori
specificity.explanation: A sweeping characterisation with no specific mechanism named in this line.

specificity.statement: the bill will amend the legislation around Māori wards in local government to how it was before the previous Government rushed legislation through by stealth in 2021—so that it's back to where the wider community had a fair chance to help decide whether to add Māori wards to their local area.
specificity.explanation: Clearly states what the amendment does and the reference year 2021.

specificity.statement: if these councils choose to retain their Māori wards until the 2025 local elections, they will be required to hold a poll at next year's local elections.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism and timeframe: retention triggers a binding poll at the 2025 local elections.

specificity.statement: this bill seeks to also address the increasing pressures within the domain of postal delivery of voting papers. So it will amend some of the local election time frames to allow increases for postal delivery and for the voting period.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete provision (extended postal/voting timeframes), though without exact figures.

specificity.statement: their permits will be extended until 2050
specificity.explanation: Concrete outcome and date: existing marine-farm permits extended to 2050.

specificity.statement: the director-general... will have to ensure that they meet those costs themselves... we've got a situation where far too often we see in regional and local government where, under the auspices of the various statutes, risks are overstated and costs are understated. This is an attempt to invert that particular equation.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete cost-recovery mechanism, though the 'egregious cases' threshold is vague.

specificity.statement: Amenity values should play second fiddle to jobs, economic growth, and industry in coastal New Zealand. We don't want a situation where, if you are blessed with owning a flash house, you decide that you don't want to see King Salmon expand in a particular area of the Sounds
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete value trade-off and a real-world example (King Salmon expansion in the Sounds).

specificity.statement: The overwhelming majority of submissions—the overwhelming majority—actually 1,000 of the 1,100, were absolutely opposed to this bill
specificity.explanation: Gives precise numbers: 1,000 of 1,100 opposed.

specificity.statement: There were only 13 days that submitters had an opportunity to submit.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure: a 13-day submission window.

specificity.statement: in the spirit of trying to get some compromise around this, we offered up a 10-year extension period, albeit reluctantly. Again, that did not find favour with Government members on the committee.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact alternative proposed (10-year extension) and its fate at committee.

specificity.statement: even went to the extent of offering up an opportunity, by way of amendment, to, effectively, cap the cost of review at 50 percent. So 50 percent of the total cost would be the maximum figure that could be recoverable by the council.
specificity.explanation: Concrete policy detail: a 50% cap on recoverable review costs.

strength.statement: the only way we're going to get that opportunity again is if you vote for a Labour Government in 2026. That's the aim. And if you vote for us, we'll bring this kaupapa back.

divination.statement: I'm sure many will get across the line and retain their Māori wards.
