veracity.explanation: Presents specific financing figures as fact; broadly consistent with the Local Water Done Well announcement, though verifiability from the text alone is limited.

veracity.statement: Yes. We inherited an economy in recession, a broken health system following a botched merger, and an education system that has been failing too many children for too long.
veracity.explanation: New Zealand was in technical recession in 2023–24 (accurate), but 'broken' health system and 'failing' education are loaded characterisations rather than verifiable facts.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, we're not stopping the construction; we are actually getting on and fixing the fundamentals in this economy. We inherited an economy that was in recession, interest rates that were at record highs, and inflation was well outside the bounds.
veracity.explanation: Recession and above-target inflation are accurate, but 'interest rates that were at record highs' is misleading — the OCR peak of 5.5% was well below historical highs.

veracity.statement: Well, answering both those two questions, the person who first drafted the legislation is the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, namely Simon Upton. This was in 1991. He was told back then it wouldn't work... Of course, he's entitled to his opinion and so are those other councils, except they're dramatically wrong. Why do we have Ngāi Tahu waiting all this time and all this money for a simple resource consent?... why don't we focus on that as being our purpose, rather than this constant big-city, small-minded complaint?
veracity.explanation: Simon Upton was the Minister for the Environment who introduced the RMA in 1991 — broadly accurate, though 'first drafted' overstates a minister's personal authorship.

veracity.statement: In the six years before we took over, the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent.
veracity.explanation: A specific historical statistic presented as fact; broadly in line with the rise in jobseeker numbers over that period, though the exact figure would need verification.

veracity.statement: Yes. Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.
veracity.explanation: The component figures appear precise, but characterising $207m of intercompany debt as part of 'total debt' is contested by the questioner and arguably overstates external indebtedness.

veracity.statement: Did the Minister include in his announcement that out of the only 182 submissions who were able to submit as part of the truncated 10-day deadline, only 19 explicitly supported the bill, 18 percent of councils missed out on even having their voice heard, and of those who did, all of them submitted that "the cost and resource implications are both unclear and significant for councils, making it challenging to plan or fund the reforms"?
veracity.explanation: Presents specific submission statistics as fact; plausible and internally consistent, though not verifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister consider Māori employment rates to be back on track when, under her watch, in just nine months, Māori unemployment has increased from 8.2 percent to 9.1 percent?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific Māori unemployment figures (8.2% to 9.1%) presented as fact; directionally consistent with rising unemployment over the period.

veracity.statement: How does stopping the construction of schools, hospitals, and houses, when 6,000 people in the construction industry have lost their jobs, help the economy?
veracity.explanation: The '6,000 construction jobs lost' figure is presented as fact; plausible given the downturn but the framing that the Government 'stopped' construction is contestable.

veracity.statement: How does giving the tobacco industry a $216 million tax break, leaving less money for health, help the economy?
veracity.explanation: The '$216 million tax break' framing of the tobacco excise change is a specific figure but a contested characterisation of the policy.

veracity.statement: Can he guarantee that the proposed review of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, which has admitted more than 700 Māori and Pasifika students to medical school in the last 10 years, will not lead to its disestablishment?
veracity.explanation: The 700-plus admissions figure is presented as fact and is plausible for MAPAS, though not verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: Well, the member's discussing the bill, which was before the House, which relates to water service delivery plans. The announcement made today is about the financing models which are now available for councils to be able to invest sustainably into their water services and actually make it happen and get things done. So that's what this Government has done with Local Water Done Well. We've got a plan, we've got the financing, and now it's up to councils to take the leadership to ensure that they can deliver for their local communities. What we campaigned on, we're delivering.
authenticity.explanation: 'What we campaigned on, we're delivering' claims consistency between promise and action; plausible given the repeal of three waters, but delivery here is partial.

authenticity.statement: I acknowledge that the extension means that it is theoretically possible that life-safety risk in some buildings won't be addressed as quickly as originally intended. However, I do think it is very important to stress in the same breath that in many cases these buildings are not being remediated anyway.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly concedes a downside of his own policy (delayed life-safety remediation) rather than glossing over it, showing consistency between claim and acknowledged trade-off.

authenticity.statement: I cannot make guarantees about anything. What I can guarantee is that Oranga Tamariki will get back to their core purpose, which is the care and protection of young people in their care and children that come to their attention. If a child is unsafe and needs care and protection, that's what will happen.
authenticity.explanation: Honestly refuses to over-promise ('I cannot make guarantees about anything'), consistent with a candid rather than spin posture.

rigor.statement: Yes. We inherited an economy in recession, a broken health system following a botched merger, and an education system that has been failing too many children for too long.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping inherited-mess framing with little evidence beyond assertion; leans on blame rather than data.

rigor.statement: Again, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, we have inherited a number of challenges as a Government, which we are having to clean up with the mess left behind by the previous Government. They were spending like drunken sailors, they were borrowing, they had interest rates and inflation through the roof, and this Government has been elected to fix this economy.
rigor.explanation: Relies on hyperbolic characterisation ('drunken sailors', 'through the roof') with no evidence linking to the question asked.

rigor.statement: No. This bill responds to longstanding and widespread concerns by the aquaculture sector about the costs and uncertainty and mahi—that means work—associated with re-consenting processes for existing marine farms under the Resource Management Act. This process of re-consenting is inhibiting aquaculture growth. These marine farmers, many of whom are Māori, don't want the unnecessary costs and uncertainty; they want to be allowed to refocus their efforts on investment, on jobs, and on exports.
rigor.explanation: Offers a cause (re-consenting costs inhibit growth) but supports it with sector sentiment rather than data.

rigor.statement: Well, answering both those two questions, the person who first drafted the legislation is the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, namely Simon Upton. This was in 1991. He was told back then it wouldn't work... Of course, he's entitled to his opinion and so are those other councils, except they're dramatically wrong. Why do we have Ngāi Tahu waiting all this time and all this money for a simple resource consent?... why don't we focus on that as being our purpose, rather than this constant big-city, small-minded complaint?
rigor.explanation: Makes a genuine point about consenting delays (Ngāi Tahu example) but leans on ad hominem framing of critics and an appeal to the author's 1991 role.

rigor.statement: As I explained, unfortunately we inherited an economy that saw the previous Government absolutely mismanage the economy, and, unfortunately, New Zealanders are paying the price. For every New Zealander that loses a job right now, it comes back to the broken economy that we inherited and the damage that that side did.
rigor.explanation: Attributes 'every' job loss to the inherited economy with no evidence — a sweeping causal claim.

rigor.statement: The earthquake-prone building system attempts to manage risk by requiring earthquake-prone buildings to be remediated by set time frames. However, many building owners are currently unable to meet deadlines due to high remediation costs and excessive layering of regulations. This is why we have acted with urgency to bring forward the review to provide certainty and ensure we have a good balance between protecting lives and real-world costs.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a coherent problem-to-action chain (deadlines unmet due to cost → review to rebalance), though 'excessive layering of regulations' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: I acknowledge that the extension means that it is theoretically possible that life-safety risk in some buildings won't be addressed as quickly as originally intended. However, I do think it is very important to stress in the same breath that in many cases these buildings are not being remediated anyway.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges the counter-consideration and gives a reasoned rebuttal (many buildings weren't being remediated anyway).

rigor.statement: I refer the member to the $22 million Oranga Tamariki has already recovered from the last financial year where services weren't delivered, with more expected to come. In previous years, some providers have accumulated significant surpluses and this is unacceptable. Every cent of taxpayer funding that providers receive needs to reach the children and young people for its intended purpose, not sit idle in their bank accounts.
rigor.explanation: Backs the claim with a recovery figure (evidence) but also relies on a single lawyer's emailed anecdote to bolster it.

rigor.statement: Debt to the Crown is debt, just as intercompany debt is real debt. Te Pūkenga has over $251 million worth of debt.
rigor.explanation: Defends the total via assertion ('debt is debt') rather than addressing the questioner's point that intercompany borrowings net out internally; a definitional claim treated as self-evident.

rigor.statement: That's the half-year surplus. So when you run a polytechnic or an ITO your income comes early, your income comes in the first half of the year, your expenditure goes throughout the year. It will bounce around a little bit, but that $28 million was their half-year to date surplus.
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible mechanistic explanation (income front-loaded, expenditure spread) for the apparent contradiction.

rigor.statement: Te Pūkenga hasn't posted a surplus yet. However, I can advise the member that in October 2022 a business case was done that was going to require Te Pūkenga to have over $900 million spent on it to make it fully operational. The Minister at the time understandably rejected that. They came back and said, "Oh, well, over five years, it will need over $400 million to be operational."
rigor.explanation: Supports the disestablishment case with concrete cost figures, though the reasoning selectively frames the merger costs.

veracity.statement: These games were historic for New Zealand, not just for matching our record tally of 20 medals in Tokyo but for clinching the most gold medals New Zealand has ever won and finishing 11th on the medal table, ahead of such sporting powerhouses with far bigger populations, such as Canada, Spain, and Sweden.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ won a record 10 golds and 20 total medals in Paris and finished around 11th on the gold-medal table, ahead of larger nations.

veracity.statement: But what makes this all the more special is that 14 of these 20 medals were won by our extraordinary women athletes and women's teams.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Paris results, where the large majority of NZ medals came from women athletes and women's teams.

veracity.statement: In October 2018, the then New Zealand Government launched a strategy to address the inequities women and girls experience in sport and recreation, the women and girls in sport initiative. As we can see, the results of this initiative have been massive, and not only in the Olympics.
veracity.explanation: The 2018 initiative is real; the sweeping attribution of 'massive' results to it is not established.

veracity.statement: Ellesse Andrews became the second New Zealander to win gold in track cycling, after Sarah Ulmer in 2004.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Sarah Ulmer won track cycling gold in Athens 2004; Andrews is the next NZ track cycling gold medallist.

veracity.statement: alcohol and drugs are the number one cause of fatal crashes on New Zealand roads; in fact, around 30 percent of deaths on our roads involve drug-drivers.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with NZ road-toll data on impairment as a leading factor, though the precise 30% figure is contestable.

veracity.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
veracity.explanation: Ngata did write on the Treaty in 1922, but characterising it as settling that Māori 'ceded sovereignty' omits the contested nature of that reading.

veracity.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation. That then leads to high levels of interest rates. When interest rates go up, that leads to recession, which is what we've been experiencing—thank you to the previous Labour Government!—and, in turn, that leads to rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The debt figure ($5b to $100b) and '84 percent increase in spending' are exaggerated/selective, and global factors in NZ inflation are omitted.

veracity.statement: having projects with names doesn't mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn't make it happen; it's just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that's what that is.
veracity.explanation: The reported spend on light rail with no delivery is broadly accurate, though the exact figure is approximate.

veracity.statement: I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank's monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent. What's more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the August 2024 OCR cut to 5.25% and the RBNZ forecast track; framed as the Bank's own forecast.

veracity.statement: The Reserve Bank's latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Correctly attributes a specific forecast figure to the RBNZ; presented as a forecast, not fact.

veracity.statement: We invested every single dollar gained from savings at Oranga Tamariki back into Oranga Tamariki, which, overall, had increased funding in the Budget.
veracity.explanation: The overall-funding-increased claim sits alongside acknowledged provider-level cuts, so it is true at aggregate level but omits context.

veracity.statement: During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent. Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed
veracity.explanation: The figures may be accurate, but the framing implies a causal link the data alone do not establish.

veracity.statement: Under the last Government, OT was allowing providers who were under-delivering on their contracts to keep unused funding, they were funding services that weren't core business, and they were duplicating services in various parts of New Zealand. If the last Government had taken this same approach to contracting now, at least $132 million more could have gone to the children, rather than letting some bank accounts build up.
veracity.explanation: Contains specific claims about under-delivery and a $132m figure that are asserted without external substantiation in the text.

specificity.statement: These games were historic for New Zealand, not just for matching our record tally of 20 medals in Tokyo but for clinching the most gold medals New Zealand has ever won and finishing 11th on the medal table, ahead of such sporting powerhouses with far bigger populations, such as Canada, Spain, and Sweden.
specificity.explanation: Names the medal tally, the record, the table position, and specific comparator countries.

specificity.statement: But what makes this all the more special is that 14 of these 20 medals were won by our extraordinary women athletes and women's teams.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (14 of 20) tied to a defined group.

specificity.statement: Ellesse Andrews became the second New Zealander to win gold in track cycling, after Sarah Ulmer in 2004.
specificity.explanation: Names the athlete, the precedent, and the year.

specificity.statement: alcohol and drugs are the number one cause of fatal crashes on New Zealand roads; in fact, around 30 percent of deaths on our roads involve drug-drivers.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage tied to a defined cause of road deaths.

specificity.statement: our Government is taking action, with more funding for roadside tests as part of a package of $1.3 billion for road policing in the next three years. But we know funding isn't enough, which is why we're setting targets for alcohol and drug tests so we see better results for where the money is spent.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, a timeframe, and a mechanism (targets for tests).

specificity.statement: having projects with names doesn't mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn't make it happen; it's just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that's what that is.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete spend figure and timeframe for Auckland light rail.

specificity.statement: I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank's monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent. What's more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names the basis-point change, the resulting rate, and a forecast figure with a year.

specificity.statement: The Reserve Bank's latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact figure, the quarter, and the source.

specificity.statement: During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent. Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed
specificity.explanation: Provides precise figures for benefit growth and sanction counts.

specificity.statement: Yes, but since then the independent review has found that the disability support system was in a much worse state than we first understood. Access to disability support services is a postcode lottery based on where someone lives, not their level of need, and Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People lacks the capabilities necessary to deliver disability support services effectively, partly due to their rushed establishment under the last Government.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete problems (postcode lottery, capability gaps) though without figures.

specificity.statement: I'm advised that 34 services across 25 providers will have their funding increased, with a total increase of at least $18.7 million. On top of that, Oranga Tamariki (OT) will be procuring at least 50 new services, and this will include additional services for high and complex needs, and the expansion of the Fast Track programme by $7.6 million.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise counts of services and providers, dollar figures, and named programmes.

charisma.statement: I stand in support of the motion and endorse the words of the Prime Minister in congratulating all of our athletes, who did an absolutely stellar job at the Olympics in Paris.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party endorsement of a Government motion; unifying and consensus-building across the aisle.

charisma.statement: Firstly, I'd also like to start by opening up and saying thank you to the host nation, France, and particularly Paris. Thank you for welcoming the world to your backyard and showing us the beauty of your iconic venues and the rich culture and history held above and below the Parisian streets.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, inclusive, outward-looking tone that builds goodwill rather than partisan division.

charisma.statement: But, importantly, this is a Government that wants to get things built, and I really appreciate the member's interest in the area of infrastructure and I'd ask him to come on board and support our fast-track legislation.
charisma.explanation: Invites the opposition to come on board and acknowledges their interest, a mildly consensus-seeking gesture within a partisan exchange.

charisma.statement: We've taken the genius idea from David Parker about fast-track provisions; we're putting it in and expanding it further.
charisma.explanation: Credits an opposition MP's idea ('genius idea from David Parker'), an unusually bridge-building acknowledgement across party lines.

charisma.statement: Well, I'd say to each of those social service providers that the Government values what you do. You play a significant role in helping New Zealanders in need, and our Government wants to work with you to ensure we can make the maximum impact for the people you serve.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive address to affected providers seeking to bring them along.

civility.statement: I stand in support of the motion and endorse the words of the Prime Minister in congratulating all of our athletes, who did an absolutely stellar job at the Olympics in Paris.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious, and constructive toward political opponents.

civility.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation. That then leads to high levels of interest rates. When interest rates go up, that leads to recession, which is what we've been experiencing—thank you to the previous Labour Government!—and, in turn, that leads to rising unemployment.
civility.explanation: Charged language ('vandalism') aimed at a party's record; harsh but directed at policy rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: having projects with names doesn't mean they are actually projects, so spending six years on Auckland light rail and spending $250 million to $300 million doesn't make it happen; it's just a Post-it note slogan bumper sticker—that's what that is.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'Post-it note slogan bumper sticker' framing, but aimed at a project rather than a person.

civility.statement: When the Prime Minister eventually leaves office, does he anticipate spending his first year out combing the world for statistics to show how badly he buggered the economy?
civility.explanation: A mocking, personalised jibe ('buggered the economy') rather than engagement with policy substance.

civility.statement: if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she's delusional.
civility.explanation: Personal insult ('delusional') built on a strawman of the questioner's position.

civility.statement: I would like to thank Labour MP Greg O'Connor for his endorsement and for confirming that common sense hasn't been completely extinguished from the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: A partisan jab implying the Labour Party generally lacks common sense, though relatively light in tone.

civility.statement: Under the last Government, OT was allowing providers who were under-delivering on their contracts to keep unused funding, they were funding services that weren't core business, and they were duplicating services in various parts of New Zealand. If the last Government had taken this same approach to contracting now, at least $132 million more could have gone to the children, rather than letting some bank accounts build up.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the previous government's contracting, but directed at policy and administration rather than personal attack.

rigor.statement: In October 2018, the then New Zealand Government launched a strategy to address the inequities women and girls experience in sport and recreation, the women and girls in sport initiative. As we can see, the results of this initiative have been massive, and not only in the Olympics.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between a 2018 initiative and 2024 Olympic success; plausible but the causal chain is claimed rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Is it a fact that 102 years ago, in a major thesis, Sir Āpirana Ngata set out the very circumstances of the Treaty and he said that Māori ceded sovereignty—far closer to the action as he was, as were other Māori leaders of that time?
rigor.explanation: Leans on appeal to authority and proximity ('far closer to the action'); Ngata's 1922 view is real but the sovereignty question is historically contested.

rigor.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation. That then leads to high levels of interest rates. When interest rates go up, that leads to recession, which is what we've been experiencing—thank you to the previous Labour Government!—and, in turn, that leads to rising unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Presents a causal chain with figures, but attributes inflation to a single cause and ignores global inflation drivers; a monocausal narrative.

rigor.statement: if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she's delusional.
rigor.explanation: Strawman fallacy: recasts the question as demanding no contract ever change, then attacks that caricature.

rigor.statement: During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent. Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed
rigor.explanation: Infers causation from correlation between falling sanctions and rising benefit numbers, ignoring confounders like COVID-era labour market shifts.

rigor.statement: I would like to thank Labour MP Greg O'Connor for his endorsement and for confirming that common sense hasn't been completely extinguished from the Labour Party.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a talkback-radio endorsement as evidence for a policy's merit — appeal to authority/anecdote.

rigor.statement: Under the last Government, OT was allowing providers who were under-delivering on their contracts to keep unused funding, they were funding services that weren't core business, and they were duplicating services in various parts of New Zealand. If the last Government had taken this same approach to contracting now, at least $132 million more could have gone to the children, rather than letting some bank accounts build up.
rigor.explanation: Offers a specific counterfactual figure but the causal claim ('could have gone to the children') is asserted, not evidenced.

strength.statement: our Government is taking action, with more funding for roadside tests as part of a package of $1.3 billion for road policing in the next three years. But we know funding isn't enough, which is why we're setting targets for alcohol and drug tests so we see better results for where the money is spent.
strength.explanation: Announced funding and targets that are in progress; delivery not yet demonstrated at the time of the statement.

forthrightness.statement: Our position is that the Crown is sovereign.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether he believes Māori ceded sovereignty, he pivots to a statement about Crown sovereignty rather than answering yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: But, as I've said to you, the position is very clear: Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown.
forthrightness.explanation: After several evasive answers he finally gives a direct answer to the repeated question of whether Māori ceded sovereignty.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that is a function of bad economic mismanagement and vandalism from the previous administration that created something called inflation, and inflation works because if you have an 84 percent increase in spending—wasteful spending, much of it—you increase debt from $5 billion to $100 billion, and you hire 18,000 more public servants, you get high levels of domestic inflation. That then leads to high levels of interest rates. When interest rates go up, that leads to recession, which is what we've been experiencing—thank you to the previous Labour Government!—and, in turn, that leads to rising unemployment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what responsibility he takes for a 26% drop in consents and 6,000 lost construction jobs, he takes none and redirects entirely to blaming the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: We invested every single dollar gained from savings at Oranga Tamariki back into Oranga Tamariki, which, overall, had increased funding in the Budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the tax-cut accusation and offers a counter-claim, but reframes rather than addressing the specific provider cuts raised.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd say to each of those social service providers that the Government values what you do. You play a significant role in helping New Zealanders in need, and our Government wants to work with you to ensure we can make the maximum impact for the people you serve.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what she says to named providers who lost funding and staff, she offers reassurance without addressing the funding reductions.

forthrightness.statement: That's why we've introduced a traffic light system. We want people to be really clear about where they are, whether they're at green, orange, or red, so they don't lose any entitlement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether it is harder to find work when someone loses half their benefit, she pivots to describing the traffic-light system rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government of course is committed to the vision and principles of Enabling Good Lives, particularly the principle that talks about mainstream first and ensuring that disabled people are supported to access mainstream services before specialist disability services.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly engages the reconciliation asked for by selecting one principle, but does not directly address the pause.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, but since then the independent review has found that the disability support system was in a much worse state than we first understood. Access to disability support services is a postcode lottery based on where someone lives, not their level of need, and Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People lacks the capabilities necessary to deliver disability support services effectively, partly due to their rushed establishment under the last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes she is updating an earlier position and explains why, rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that 34 services across 25 providers will have their funding increased, with a total increase of at least $18.7 million. On top of that, Oranga Tamariki (OT) will be procuring at least 50 new services, and this will include additional services for high and complex needs, and the expansion of the Fast Track programme by $7.6 million.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the 'how many providers and by how much' question with concrete numbers.

forthrightness.statement: It is the same amount of funding—no cuts have been made to funding. What we are doing is reprioritising that funding to where it will make the biggest impact.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm whether the Independent Children's Monitor and Chief Children's Commissioner had written raising concerns, she does not confirm the letters and instead restates her funding message.

authenticity.statement: Our Government of course is committed to the vision and principles of Enabling Good Lives, particularly the principle that talks about mainstream first and ensuring that disabled people are supported to access mainstream services before specialist disability services.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms commitment to Enabling Good Lives while having paused it, creating tension between the stated value and the action taken.

rigor.statement: It means that consultation is being reduced for the setting up of the water services entities. That’s interesting, because that’s a reduction in democratic participation, and we know that a lot of what this Government has talked about has been the need for bottom-up organisation, and it’s been the need for localism—for decisions to be taken at the most local level possible—but this alternative consultation seems to run against that.
rigor.explanation: Draws a reasoned tension between the government's stated commitment to localism and a clause that reduces required consultation; conclusion follows, though the 'reduction' is asserted rather than demonstrated with figures.

rigor.statement: The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation. In fact, a local government entity could overrule what the people in the area that it administers want.
rigor.explanation: Logical inference that a 'once only' floor permits a council to consult minimally; sound but leans on a hypothetical rather than evidence of it happening.

rigor.statement: Look, that’s a “may”—that’s a “may”—and local government entities may well take that path, and they could engage in more consultation. The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation.
rigor.explanation: Correctly distinguishes a discretionary 'may' from a mandatory floor, showing the Minister's rebuttal doesn't address her point; clean logical entailment.

rigor.statement: I would like the Minister—if he could, please—just to reconcile those two explanations that he’s given, because they do actually pull against each other slightly and I think we deserve a little better than that.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine inconsistency between the Minister's 'clarification' rationale and his 'streamlining' rationale; argument turns on a real contradiction.

rigor.statement: Clause 37(3)(i): the word “quality” is puzzling me. It says, “quality performance measures and statistics:” Now, as someone who plays around with ambiguity and words myself, does this mean “measures of performance quality and statistics”, or does it mean “performance measures that are quality performance measures, because they are high quality, and statistics of high quality”?
rigor.explanation: Careful parsing of an adjectival ambiguity with the two possible readings laid out; disciplined close reading.

rigor.statement: I gave the Minister the example of the regulated airports which do not fit within the Commerce Commission’s model easily, and we have now 20 years to look back at how that has been applied by the Commerce Commission, and has been criticised and has been recently very roundly criticised by the two parties which are subject to that regulation.
rigor.explanation: Supports the claim that the Commerce Commission is a poor fit with a concrete precedent (20 years of airport regulation and its criticism); evidence-based, though the criticism is characterised rather than quoted.

rigor.statement: The third most important protection set out in that section 137 of the Local Government Act is that currently councils who enter into these relationships are required to retain the ownership of the infrastructure assets that people in their cities and their regions have built up over generations.
rigor.explanation: Substantive legal argument, but the 'built up over generations' framing leans partly on an emotive/heritage appeal alongside the statutory point.

rigor.statement: I have asked the Minister twice to address questions, to allay the fears of members on this side of the House that his intention here is to make it easier and simpler for councils to privatise their water assets and sell them out of local body ownership without appropriate consultation.
rigor.explanation: The privatisation worry is grounded in the section 137 argument he develops, but the leap from a consultation change to an intent to enable asset sales is inferential.

rigor.statement: The reason I mention that is because non-financial measures specifically may affect or may be of interest to members of the public. To give a few examples: things like water quality, water security—I’m not an expert on this, but, potentially, stormwater drainage speed.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned link from clause 37(3)(f) non-financial measures to a public interest in consultation; candidly flags the limits of his expertise.

rigor.statement: I would assume that that would have been the logical order first—that they would consult and they would go, “On balance, based on subclause (4), it’s not sufficient. Let’s consult again.” As opposed to, “We’ll consult once. We don’t need to do it again, but if we do want to do it, let’s consider have we thought about all of the views?”
rigor.explanation: Works through the intended sequencing of clauses 52(2)–(4) to expose that the section 78(1) balancing may only be triggered after a decision to reconsult; coherent structural reasoning.

rigor.statement: Standard & Poor’s, the credit rating agency—the agency which has assessed this work and assessed alternative proposals for water reform—have said that this is likely going to lead to significant increases in the cost of borrowing, which is of course what we have been saying all along.
rigor.explanation: Cites an external, credible authority (S&P) to support the affordability critique rather than mere assertion; relevant evidence marshalled to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: The Minister knows that councils haven’t accounted for the 30 years of upgrading and maintaining that is required and was the scope of the original assessment and rationale for water reform in the first place because long-term plans only go out 10 years.
rigor.explanation: Concrete methodological critique—that a 10-year long-term-plan basis cannot capture a 30-year investment need—with a clear causal link; a strong analytical point.

rigor.statement: This is, ultimately, a political solution to an issue that they created. They want to wash their hands of it, hand it back to councils, and then when it inevitably turns sour, say, “Well, that’s their fault for not sorting themselves out.”
rigor.explanation: Speculative attribution of political motive presented as fact; not evidenced and leans on rhetorical framing.

rigor.statement: I know from councils that I’ve spoken to that their council actually, obviously, supported the idea of Māori wards, but now they are faced with the reality of voting for a referendum and, therefore, imposing a cost on their ratepayers, and so they’re thinking about scrapping it altogether—a perverse outcome.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Māori wards case as an analogy to illustrate how mandated costs can drive a perverse choice; illustrative but rests on anecdote ('councils I've spoken to').

rigor.statement: in the AP, it changes the wording to specify “may” at clause 49(a)(i), and then “must” at paragraphs (ii) and (iii). So while the wording was less specific, less directive, in the version of the bill we’ve got, it becomes clearer in the Amendment Paper.
rigor.explanation: Careful reading that isolates exactly what changed and asks a targeted question about why; disciplined analysis.

rigor.statement: why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion—which leaves it open to a council to then turn its mind to any further consultation—rather than actually saying, “Well, you need to consult once.”
rigor.explanation: Offers a concrete, well-reasoned drafting fix ('at least once') that would preserve the clarification while removing the incentive to consult minimally; the logic connects cleanly to his concern.

civility.statement: It means that consultation is being reduced for the setting up of the water services entities. That’s interesting, because that’s a reduction in democratic participation, and we know that a lot of what this Government has talked about has been the need for bottom-up organisation, and it’s been the need for localism—for decisions to be taken at the most local level possible—but this alternative consultation seems to run against that.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the policy's effect on democratic participation, engaging the substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation. In fact, a local government entity could overrule what the people in the area that it administers want.
civility.explanation: Focused on the policy consequence, not on any individual; harsh-but-legitimate critique.

civility.statement: Look, I’d just like to thank the Minister for that answer, because that does really clarify why you only have that requirement to only do it once with the substantive reason behind it. That’s very, very helpful, thank you, Minister, and I’m sure that will help in this process.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of a satisfactory answer from a political opponent; respectful and constructive.

civility.statement: I would like the Minister—if he could, please—just to reconcile those two explanations that he’s given, because they do actually pull against each other slightly and I think we deserve a little better than that.
civility.explanation: Mild reproach ('we deserve a little better') but stays on the substance of the two explanations rather than attacking the person.

civility.statement: I have asked the Minister twice to address questions, to allay the fears of members on this side of the House that his intention here is to make it easier and simpler for councils to privatise their water assets and sell them out of local body ownership without appropriate consultation.
civility.explanation: Imputes a privatisation 'intention' to the Minister, edging toward motive-attribution, but framed as a fear to be allayed and tied to a genuine legal concern about section 137.

civility.statement: I find it ironic that the Opposition has become the defender of wanting to maintain ownership, and welcome them to the party, because that is exactly where the Government is at. That is what this Government is delivering is actually restoring council ownership. Welcome back into the tent. We thank you that you have finally rejected the position that you’ve taken for the last six years.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'welcome back into the tent' jab that scores points off Labour's supposed reversal rather than engaging Williams's section 137 concern.

civility.statement: The Hon Deborah Russell has been repeating the question around penalties that’s already been addressed. Penalties represent an upper limit.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive ('has been repeating') but not a personal attack; a brusque procedural point.

civility.statement: The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
civility.explanation: Firm and repetitive but not disrespectful; stays on the substance.

civility.statement: This is, ultimately, a political solution to an issue that they created. They want to wash their hands of it, hand it back to councils, and then when it inevitably turns sour, say, “Well, that’s their fault for not sorting themselves out.”
civility.explanation: Imputes bad-faith motive (deliberately setting councils up to blame later) rather than engaging the policy on its merits.

civility.statement: in the AP, it changes the wording to specify “may” at clause 49(a)(i), and then “must” at paragraphs (ii) and (iii). So while the wording was less specific, less directive, in the version of the bill we’ve got, it becomes clearer in the Amendment Paper.
civility.explanation: Neutral, technical query focused entirely on the drafting; entirely respectful.

civility.statement: why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion—which leaves it open to a council to then turn its mind to any further consultation—rather than actually saying, “Well, you need to consult once.”
civility.explanation: Constructive, solution-oriented question that engages the Minister's stated intent rather than attacking him.

specificity.statement: It means that consultation is being reduced for the setting up of the water services entities. That’s interesting, because that’s a reduction in democratic participation, and we know that a lot of what this Government has talked about has been the need for bottom-up organisation, and it’s been the need for localism—for decisions to be taken at the most local level possible—but this alternative consultation seems to run against that.
specificity.explanation: Ties the general 'localism' claim to the concrete consultation-once mechanism she identifies in the clause, but no figures in this sentence.

specificity.statement: Clause 37(3)(i): the word “quality” is puzzling me. It says, “quality performance measures and statistics:” Now, as someone who plays around with ambiguity and words myself, does this mean “measures of performance quality and statistics”, or does it mean “performance measures that are quality performance measures, because they are high quality, and statistics of high quality”?
specificity.explanation: Precise, clause-level textual analysis identifying a concrete drafting ambiguity in clause 37(3)(i).

specificity.statement: I gave the Minister the example of the regulated airports which do not fit within the Commerce Commission’s model easily, and we have now 20 years to look back at how that has been applied by the Commerce Commission, and has been criticised and has been recently very roundly criticised by the two parties which are subject to that regulation.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific analogous regime (regulated airports) and a 20-year track record rather than speaking in generalities.

specificity.statement: The third most important protection set out in that section 137 of the Local Government Act is that currently councils who enter into these relationships are required to retain the ownership of the infrastructure assets that people in their cities and their regions have built up over generations.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific statutory protection (section 137 ownership retention) and its practical effect on asset ownership.

specificity.statement: The reason I mention that is because non-financial measures specifically may affect or may be of interest to members of the public. To give a few examples: things like water quality, water security—I’m not an expert on this, but, potentially, stormwater drainage speed.
specificity.explanation: Grounds an abstract question about 'interested parties' in concrete examples of non-financial measures (water quality, water security, stormwater drainage).

specificity.statement: I would assume that that would have been the logical order first—that they would consult and they would go, “On balance, based on subclause (4), it’s not sufficient. Let’s consult again.” As opposed to, “We’ll consult once. We don’t need to do it again, but if we do want to do it, let’s consider have we thought about all of the views?”
specificity.explanation: Precise cross-referencing of subclauses (2), (3), (4) and section 78(1) to make the point concrete.

specificity.statement: Greater Wellington Regional Council is the only regional council which is a water supplier and so, therefore, is covered; all other regional councils are not.
specificity.explanation: Names the entity and the precise reason (sole regional-council water supplier) for the carve-out.

specificity.statement: In relation to the member Arena Williams’ question around the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Commission is well practised in using these tools and the Infrastructure Commission does not have the experience in economic regulation.
specificity.explanation: General assertion of experience with no reference to the advice, tools, or comparison Williams asked about.

specificity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.
specificity.explanation: Names section 137 and specifies that the bill's changes are confined to consultation requirements.

specificity.statement: The purpose of this part is to support councils in terms of setting up water service council-controlled organisations and joint local government arrangements as part of our Local Water Done Well approach. By supporting councils to set up joint organisations between councils, there’s a faster consultation, a streamlined consultation process that’s been put in place.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (joint CCOs, streamlined consultation) and the policy label, but no figures, timeframes, or detail on how consultation is streamlined.

specificity.statement: Standard & Poor’s, the credit rating agency—the agency which has assessed this work and assessed alternative proposals for water reform—have said that this is likely going to lead to significant increases in the cost of borrowing, which is of course what we have been saying all along.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and the mechanism (cost of borrowing) but no figures for the predicted increase.

specificity.statement: The Minister knows that councils haven’t accounted for the 30 years of upgrading and maintaining that is required and was the scope of the original assessment and rationale for water reform in the first place because long-term plans only go out 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Precise on the 10-year vs 30-year mismatch and its consequence for the cost figures.

specificity.statement: I know from councils that I’ve spoken to that their council actually, obviously, supported the idea of Māori wards, but now they are faced with the reality of voting for a referendum and, therefore, imposing a cost on their ratepayers, and so they’re thinking about scrapping it altogether—a perverse outcome.
specificity.explanation: A concrete real-world example, but the councils and numbers are unnamed.

specificity.statement: in the AP, it changes the wording to specify “may” at clause 49(a)(i), and then “must” at paragraphs (ii) and (iii). So while the wording was less specific, less directive, in the version of the bill we’ve got, it becomes clearer in the Amendment Paper.
specificity.explanation: Precise textual comparison of the reported bill versus Amendment Paper 65, down to the may/must changes at named subparagraphs.

specificity.statement: why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion—which leaves it open to a council to then turn its mind to any further consultation—rather than actually saying, “Well, you need to consult once.”
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause and proposes precise alternative wording.

charisma.statement: Look, I’d just like to thank the Minister for that answer, because that does really clarify why you only have that requirement to only do it once with the substantive reason behind it. That’s very, very helpful, thank you, Minister, and I’m sure that will help in this process.
charisma.explanation: Warm, bridge-building tone that credits the Minister and lowers the temperature.

charisma.statement: I find it ironic that the Opposition has become the defender of wanting to maintain ownership, and welcome them to the party, because that is exactly where the Government is at. That is what this Government is delivering is actually restoring council ownership. Welcome back into the tent. We thank you that you have finally rejected the position that you’ve taken for the last six years.
charisma.explanation: Partisan us-vs-them point-scoring rather than persuading or finding common ground.

charisma.statement: why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion—which leaves it open to a council to then turn its mind to any further consultation—rather than actually saying, “Well, you need to consult once.”
charisma.explanation: Attempts to find a middle path acceptable to the Minister's streamlining goal while addressing the Opposition's concern; a mildly consensus-seeking move.

veracity.statement: I gave the Minister the example of the regulated airports which do not fit within the Commerce Commission’s model easily, and we have now 20 years to look back at how that has been applied by the Commerce Commission, and has been criticised and has been recently very roundly criticised by the two parties which are subject to that regulation.
veracity.explanation: Claim that airport economic regulation has been criticised by regulated parties is broadly accurate; 'very roundly' is somewhat rhetorical.

veracity.statement: The third most important protection set out in that section 137 of the Local Government Act is that currently councils who enter into these relationships are required to retain the ownership of the infrastructure assets that people in their cities and their regions have built up over generations.
veracity.explanation: Characterisation of section 137 protections is broadly accurate; the claim that they would not carry over is contested by the Minister.

veracity.statement: Greater Wellington Regional Council is the only regional council which is a water supplier and so, therefore, is covered; all other regional councils are not.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Greater Wellington is the regional council that acts as a bulk water supplier (via Wellington Water), unlike other regional councils.

veracity.statement: In relation to the member Arena Williams’ question around the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Commission is well practised in using these tools and the Infrastructure Commission does not have the experience in economic regulation.
veracity.explanation: Broadly plausible that the Commerce Commission has more economic-regulation experience than the Infrastructure Commission, but asserted without evidence.

veracity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.
veracity.explanation: A definite claim that section 137 is unaltered; plausible but flatly contested by Williams's reading of the either/or drafting, so unverifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Standard & Poor’s, the credit rating agency—the agency which has assessed this work and assessed alternative proposals for water reform—have said that this is likely going to lead to significant increases in the cost of borrowing, which is of course what we have been saying all along.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific view to S&P about higher borrowing costs; consistent with reported ratings-agency commentary on the debt-cap changes, though paraphrased.

veracity.statement: The Minister knows that councils haven’t accounted for the 30 years of upgrading and maintaining that is required and was the scope of the original assessment and rationale for water reform in the first place because long-term plans only go out 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that council long-term plans span 10 years while the original water-reform assessment used a 30-year horizon; the inference about undercounting follows.

forthrightness.statement: Greater Wellington Regional Council is the only regional council which is a water supplier and so, therefore, is covered; all other regional councils are not.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Russell's question about why there are separate rules for Greater Wellington Regional Council with a clear reason.

forthrightness.statement: In relation to the member Arena Williams’ question around the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Commission is well practised in using these tools and the Infrastructure Commission does not have the experience in economic regulation.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a reason for choosing the Commerce Commission but does not answer Williams's actual question about what expert advice he received, so only partly responsive.

forthrightness.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Williams's repeated question about whether section 137 protections survive, giving a clear yes.

forthrightness.statement: The Hon Deborah Russell has been repeating the question around penalties that’s already been addressed. Penalties represent an upper limit.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the penalties question ('upper limit') but curtly and by asserting it was already addressed rather than fully engaging.

forthrightness.statement: The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Restates the once/may position but sidesteps Utikere's specific question about why it can't read 'at least once'; asserts clarity instead of engaging the proposed amendment.

divination.statement: Standard & Poor’s, the credit rating agency—the agency which has assessed this work and assessed alternative proposals for water reform—have said that this is likely going to lead to significant increases in the cost of borrowing, which is of course what we have been saying all along.
divination.explanation: Forecast that the financing changes will lead to significant increases in borrowing costs; directionally plausible and backed by a ratings agency, but magnitude and timing uncertain.

civility.statement: I actually refuse to stand here and be lectured by a member of that previous Government, which made absolutely no progress when it came to the safety of the wellbeing of our young people. The state of Oranga Tamariki when I took over was absolutely disgusting, and I’m not going to allow that to continue.
civility.explanation: Refuses to engage the criticism and attacks the previous Government with charged language ('absolutely disgusting'), rather than addressing the substance.

civility.statement: the reality is those of us who are Māori know that before we’re going to have a renaissance with respect to what’s going on with young people, we have to fix our own place up first. I am saying it to every Māori, including myself, and not taking this judgmental view that she is.
civility.explanation: Largely makes a values point and includes himself, but ends with a pointed jab characterising Ngarewa-Packer as 'judgmental'.

civility.statement: I have been given the opportunity, on behalf of the Government, to lead this reform in the firearms space. What is really important is that we as a Government, as a whole, agree with the process as we move through the transparent process of four firearms reform phases. I’m really happy with the opportunity that I have been given to make New Zealand a safer place, because that side failed to do that post-2019.
civility.explanation: Ends with a partisan jab ('that side failed to do that post-2019') rather than addressing the substance.

civility.statement: I’d just caution the member against misrepresenting that particular language, and I would go so far as to say possibly scaremongering. As most members will know, this phrase is a typical safeguard used and found often in the Commerce Act to protect consumers in industries where there is monopoly characteristics. In this scenario, people won’t be able to choose to go to a different water services provider, so this clause will ensure consumers are being charged a fair price.
civility.explanation: Accuses the member of 'scaremongering' but immediately grounds the rebuttal in the substance of the clause rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: The Minister keeps telling us it’s not about that; it’s bottom-up, not top-down. This all seems, to me, to be very top-down.
civility.explanation: Challenges the Minister's characterisation on the substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: Repetition! Very repetitive.
civility.explanation: A dismissive interjection heckling the speaker rather than engaging the substance of the debate.

veracity.statement: I actually refuse to stand here and be lectured by a member of that previous Government, which made absolutely no progress when it came to the safety of the wellbeing of our young people. The state of Oranga Tamariki when I took over was absolutely disgusting, and I’m not going to allow that to continue.
veracity.explanation: 'made absolutely no progress' is a sweeping, unquantified claim about the previous Government — hyperbolic and hard to sustain literally.

veracity.statement: yes. That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee.
veracity.explanation: The 2019 post-Christchurch Arms Act reform was widely criticised as rushed; the characterisation is directionally accurate though the exact figures are her framing.

veracity.statement: Last week, the Prime Minister and I announced that we are overturning the nearly 30-year effective ban on gene technology, for the benefit of New Zealand. We will establish new legislation and a dedicated regulator based on the Australian regime. The science has matured, other countries have embraced gene technology, and it has potential to treat cancers, increase agricultural production, lower emissions, adapt to a changing climate, and, ultimately, grow the economy. Gene tech is already being used safely in 29 other countries, including many of our trading partners such as Australia, China, Japan, the US, Canada, and many European countries.
veracity.explanation: The 'used safely in 29 other countries' framing is broadly consistent with widespread international GM adoption, though 'safely' and the count are her characterisation.

veracity.statement: This policy will allow many more New Zealanders to access highly effective cancer treatments, including CAR T-cell therapy developed at Wellington’s Malaghan Institute, and this treatment has already successfully treated patients with cancer for the handful of those who were able to participate in its trial.
veracity.explanation: The Malaghan Institute's CAR T-cell trial is real and treated a small number of patients; the claim is consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is an agricultural nation, which is why around half of our emissions come from agriculture.
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate — agriculture accounts for about half of New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions.

veracity.statement: If we look at what has happened in the United Kingdom with Thames Water, there’s been the most appalling extraction of profits and the most appalling water pollution. That’s happened in part because of the profit motive.
veracity.explanation: Thames Water's profit extraction and pollution problems are well documented; 'most appalling' is hyperbolic and the causal claim is her interpretation.

veracity.statement: Dr Woods has further asked around protections against privatisation. Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions. This bill only relates to local government water service providers.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Local Government Act 2002 containing safeguards on divestment of water assets; plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: The genesis of New Zealand’s change in the management of water arose from the drinking-water problems that we had at Havelock North, where under-investment by the then council for many years led to thousands of people becoming ill from contaminated water, and some of them dying.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 2016 Havelock North campylobacter outbreak, which sickened thousands and was linked to deaths, and drove water-reform inquiries.

veracity.statement: When I think back in my own area in the Hutt Valley, you know, significant money was spent on a new event centre and redoing the town hall, and even subsidising a local business owner to build a hotel in the centre of Lower Hutt. People could argue that those ratepayers’ funds probably could have been better spent in securing that we didn’t have sewage pouring up in people’s backyards and that we had adequate infrastructure in place to serve the new builds that were going on across the Hutt Valley.
veracity.explanation: The referenced Lower Hutt spending on civic facilities is broadly consistent with public record, though presented selectively.

veracity.statement: In some situations, the Commerce Commission is the regulator of infrastructure providers who have a weighted assets return ratio on their infrastructure, and that’s how they are primarily regulated in their law—say, for example, the three regulated airports which come under the Commerce Commission’s purview.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Commerce Commission does regulate the major airports under an information-disclosure/asset-return regime.

rigor.statement: I actually refuse to stand here and be lectured by a member of that previous Government, which made absolutely no progress when it came to the safety of the wellbeing of our young people. The state of Oranga Tamariki when I took over was absolutely disgusting, and I’m not going to allow that to continue.
rigor.explanation: Assertion and dismissal of the critic with no evidence offered; leans on emotive characterisation ('disgusting').

rigor.statement: the reality is those of us who are Māori know that before we’re going to have a renaissance with respect to what’s going on with young people, we have to fix our own place up first. I am saying it to every Māori, including myself, and not taking this judgmental view that she is.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a general claim about needing to 'fix our own place up first' without evidence; rhetorical rather than reasoned.

rigor.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I do not agree with Mr Cahill, because legislation actually has restrictions around the legal transfer of firearms—part of the reason why we need to have people involved in the consultation that actually understand the legislation.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason (existing transfer restrictions) rather than mere assertion, but does not substantiate that those restrictions address the risk raised.

rigor.statement: If we look at what has happened in the United Kingdom with Thames Water, there’s been the most appalling extraction of profits and the most appalling water pollution. That’s happened in part because of the profit motive.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real overseas analogy (Thames Water) to support a causal concern, but the 'in part because of the profit motive' link is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: This phrase, “ability to extract excessive profits”, is quite a telling phrase, because the implication is that the whole purpose of this scheme, the whole purpose of this legislation, is not just to ensure that New Zealanders have access to good drinking water, that the waste water is appropriately treated, and that stormwater systems are set up so that people aren’t affected by stormwater, but it implies that there is a profit motive.
rigor.explanation: Infers a broad 'profit motive' purpose from a single standard drafting phrase — a stretch that the Minister later characterises as a common consumer-protection safeguard, so the inference over-reaches.

rigor.statement: So I want to know who is going to be making that judgment about what is an excessive profit as opposed to a reasonable profit and what that judgment is going to be based on. Is it going to be based on the number of rateable households? Is it going to be based on the number of people using the water supply? Is it a return on investment?
rigor.explanation: Systematically probes the undefined term by laying out candidate definitions rather than asserting a conclusion.

rigor.statement: we want some certainty from the Minister in the chair around what protections are in place to stop the privatisation of these assets, to ensure that these do stay public assets and that these are things that will continue to be owned by the people that have built them up over many, many, many generations.
rigor.explanation: Links the concern logically to the clauses on innovation and business models she has just queried.

rigor.statement: we have seen in a previous bill around waste management that once we started charging levies for the work of a commission, we are straddling a very dangerous territory between what is considered a levy and what is considered a tax.
rigor.explanation: Draws on a prior legislative precedent to raise a genuine levy-versus-tax distinction, though the 'dangerous territory' framing is asserted.

rigor.statement: The concern I have here is that subclause 42(1)(a) talks about it in the context of the person both knowingly and actively contravening an obligation to disclose information. Now, under criminal law, we see that fulfils a requirement of both mens rea and actus reus... under clause 45 an individual who then decided not to disclose the information would get a lower penalty than someone who may have just aided or abetted someone under clause 42(2), which has a chance of getting a much higher penalty.
rigor.explanation: Careful, structured legal reasoning comparing mens rea/actus reus across clauses and drawing a clear internal-inconsistency conclusion from the penalty amounts.

rigor.statement: I’d just caution the member against misrepresenting that particular language, and I would go so far as to say possibly scaremongering. As most members will know, this phrase is a typical safeguard used and found often in the Commerce Act to protect consumers in industries where there is monopoly characteristics. In this scenario, people won’t be able to choose to go to a different water services provider, so this clause will ensure consumers are being charged a fair price.
rigor.explanation: Gives a coherent monopoly/consumer-protection rationale tied to the Commerce Act for why the phrase exists.

rigor.statement: And $5 million for not providing information seems like a very high amount. I’d like to know why it’s so high and if it does just relate to those information disclosures, and how that compares to other legislation where there are these penalty clauses for not disclosing information.
rigor.explanation: Frames a proportionality question and seeks a comparative benchmark rather than merely objecting.

rigor.statement: The Minister keeps telling us it’s not about that; it’s bottom-up, not top-down. This all seems, to me, to be very top-down.
rigor.explanation: Draws an inference of inconsistency from the levy and centralised requirements, but states the 'top-down' conclusion more than she evidences it here.

rigor.statement: The genesis of New Zealand’s change in the management of water arose from the drinking-water problems that we had at Havelock North, where under-investment by the then council for many years led to thousands of people becoming ill from contaminated water, and some of them dying.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy rationale in a documented case and a plausible causal chain.

rigor.statement: It wouldn’t be necessarily that the full weight of that dollar amount would be brought to bear against a territorial authority, having not met its obligations. We think that that maximum amount is set at the appropriate level because, of course, the penalties go to conduct... rather than the nature of the entity being public or private that is relevant.
rigor.explanation: Offers a conduct-versus-entity-type rationale, but relies on the assertion that consistency with the Commerce Act settles proportionality.

rigor.statement: When I think back in my own area in the Hutt Valley, you know, significant money was spent on a new event centre and redoing the town hall, and even subsidising a local business owner to build a hotel in the centre of Lower Hutt. People could argue that those ratepayers’ funds probably could have been better spent in securing that we didn’t have sewage pouring up in people’s backyards and that we had adequate infrastructure in place to serve the new builds that were going on across the Hutt Valley.
rigor.explanation: Uses illustrative examples to argue a trade-off; the 'could have been better spent' point is framed as opinion ('people could argue').

rigor.statement: In some situations, the Commerce Commission is the regulator of infrastructure providers who have a weighted assets return ratio on their infrastructure, and that’s how they are primarily regulated in their law—say, for example, the three regulated airports which come under the Commerce Commission’s purview.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a reasoned comparison between airport regulation and the new water powers to frame her question.

forthrightness.statement: I have been assured that that young person has been supported to complete their sentence at another youth justice residence. I’ve also been advised that there is one other young person who will be joining the programme, so now there will be 10 young people within that programme, and all of them are doing well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why 10% left the boot camp and for a guarantee the rest won't, she describes support for the departed youth and adds a new participant, but neither explains the departure nor gives the guarantee sought.

forthrightness.statement: That would be a question for Oranga Tamariki in writing, so they could give you a specific answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to explain a record 790 Māori tamariki entering State care in eight months, she declines to answer and redirects the questioner to write to the agency.

forthrightness.statement: Green means a beneficiary is on track and complying with all their work obligations. Orange means a job seeker has failed an obligation and must re-comply within five days. Red means a job seeker has breached their obligations, which will result in sanctions being imposed.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers the question 'How will the traffic light system work?' with the actual mechanics.

forthrightness.statement: Job seekers will be required to reapply for their benefit every six months, and they must also complete a mandatory job seeker profile. This will enable the Ministry of Social Development to match people with job vacancies. There will also be new, non-financial sanctions that will be available next year, and past failures will be counted against a job seeker’s record for two years, instead of one.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'how else does it affect job seekers' with specific additional measures.

forthrightness.statement: yes.
