veracity.statement: It is a $200 billion, $300 billion nuclear submarine deal, and there will be other things that are attached to it as well.
veracity.explanation: AUKUS is a very large defence programme, but the cited figures are loose and the range is wide/imprecise.

veracity.statement: Despite all of the militaries being in the Pacific, there are actually only four sort of island nations that actually have those types of militaries.
veracity.explanation: Broadly reflects that few Pacific island states maintain militaries, but 'sort of' hedging and the exact count of four is imprecise.

veracity.statement: I'm very happy to report to you that only in the first 10 months, we already have a huge increase in vaccination rates, with over 69,000 vaccinations being delivered.
veracity.explanation: Cites a concrete delivery figure; 'huge increase' is a subjective gloss without a baseline.

veracity.statement: We know that breast cancer is one of the most common cancers in women, affecting one in nine Kiwi women.
veracity.explanation: The roughly one-in-nine lifetime breast-cancer statistic for NZ women is accurate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is relatively rare as one of only three nations with similar systems with a three-year term.
veracity.explanation: NZ is among a very small group of democracies with a three-year term; the exact count of three is plausible but imprecise.

veracity.statement: The Australian Federal Parliament has a three-year term but, interestingly, all of the states have over the past few decades shifted to a four-year term, and some will argue that that works well.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Australian federal parliament has a three-year term while the states have moved to four-year terms.

rigor.statement: They decided then to restructure the entire system during a pandemic. During COVID, the worst time to restructure. And, of course, outcomes went down. Emergency department wait times increased, wait times for elective operations increased, everything went back. Immunisations for our children went backwards—appalling—and it became harder to get a GP appointment.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the restructure caused the declines ('of course') without isolating it from pandemic effects — post hoc reasoning.

rigor.statement: They think unions come first when it comes to our health system. They think, actually, it's the unions which matter first, because what were all the supplementaries about? Unions, unions, unions—nothing about the patients.
rigor.explanation: Infers Labour's core beliefs from the topic of a few supplementary questions — hasty generalisation and strawman.

rigor.statement: No. There are other options in terms of what we can do to provide concrete into our community. There are land-based options that exist already.
rigor.explanation: Points to land-based alternatives, a reasonable counter, but offers no supporting detail on feasibility.

rigor.statement: It's only going to impact your taiao. It's only going to impact the pātaka kai. You won't be able to go fishing or have your mokopuna swim in the moana.
rigor.explanation: Predicts specific consequences without citing the environmental evidence for them.

rigor.statement: You can't build houses without sand.
rigor.explanation: One-line false-necessity that treats sea sand mining as the only option.

rigor.statement: Unlike the last Government, that wanted to centralise everything under their failed socialist experiment, we know Wellington doesn't know best.
rigor.explanation: Loaded characterisation with no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Everything ACT touches is bad faith.
rigor.explanation: Universal claim ('everything') with no evidence — hasty generalisation.

rigor.statement: who would you believe with regard to tino rangatiratanga? Richard Prebble or my uncle Moana Jackson, who said that we would never give away our independence? Eighty thousand Māori giving away their tino rangatiratanga to 2,000 settlers—come on!
rigor.explanation: Advances a historical argument about the implausibility of ceding sovereignty, but leans on an appeal to a trusted authority ('my uncle') and a rhetorical binary.

rigor.statement: the first two competencies are entirely related to ethnicity and the Treaty. Before you even get to patient care, how you actually should be looking after your patients is entirely based on ethnicity.
rigor.explanation: Overstates the competencies into a false dichotomy between Treaty content and patient care.

rigor.statement: They don't understand that $16 billion extra is actually a boost; it is not a cut. This is extra money above inflation and above population growth, because we are turning around this healthcare system.
rigor.explanation: Makes the above-inflation/above-population claim without supplying the figures that would establish it.

rigor.statement: we heard that the combined DHBs have a lower output than the individual DHBs. That is surely a sign of a complete failure of a reform when that actually happens.
rigor.explanation: Leaps from a single output metric to 'complete failure of a reform' — overbroad conclusion.

rigor.statement: including a lady called Margaret, who had a pacemaker put in in under 48 hours
rigor.explanation: A single anecdote offered as evidence of system quality — appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: Well, the trumpets blew and the floor parted and in entered the emperor Christopher Luxon. As he paraded through the ball, everyone exclaimed how fine his clothing was, how well tailored it was, except for one little boy with his mouth agape, by the name of Mike Hosking.
rigor.explanation: Persuasion by literary metaphor rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: about 10 percent of those that returned said, "Actually, the lunch programme is working quite well." When I looked into it and said, "Why is it working quite well?", it was because they haven't actually gone into the new lunch programme yet. That 10 percent are still working with providing their own lunches
rigor.explanation: Interrogates a counter-signal in her own survey data and explains the confound rather than ignoring it.

rigor.statement: but instead of taking responsibility, this Government likes to vilify and blame parents, because they are the ones that are living in poverty because of their policies.
rigor.explanation: Attributes poverty directly to 'their policies' without supporting causal evidence.

rigor.statement: it looks like one of the sides of that geopolitical tension has just basically given up and is busy berating the President of the Ukraine in an appalling display of terrible diplomacy.
rigor.explanation: Strong evaluative claim ('appalling', 'terrible') offered without specifics.

rigor.statement: The primary argument against is that the New Zealand Parliament faces relatively few checks and balances, and that argues for more regular opportunities for the electorate to pass judgment on the Government's success or otherwise and, if they're not happy, to throw them out.
rigor.explanation: Fairly and accurately states the strongest counter-argument to his own bill before responding to it.

rigor.statement: A clean question is a good question. If the question is "Four years or three years—yes or no?", that's a question that's very easy to communicate and to discuss, whereas talking about—and it's pretty arcane stuff to ordinary New Zealanders—how many seats on select committee an Opposition party should have, that's not something that's going to be very exciting.
rigor.explanation: Clear reasoning that a simple referendum question aids public understanding, with a plausible objection to bundling the select-committee mechanism.

rigor.statement: Also, we are not excited about the idea of no one being quite sure how long Parliament will be until a decision has been made by the Prime Minister. That's a kind of uncertainty which I'm not sure the electorate would be happy with.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete structural drawback — indeterminacy of the term length — as a reasoned objection.

strength.statement: we're going to be making sure that we can help support general practice to take nurses straight into general practice through incentivising them at $15,000 in urban areas and $20,000 in rural communities
strength.explanation: Announced policy with delivery still in progress — intent stated, follow-through not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: a 24/7 digital service so that wherever you are, any day, anytime you'll be able to access a doctor or a nurse practitioner
strength.explanation: Announcement of a future service; delivery unproven.

strength.statement: 100 doctor training spaces for internationally trained doctors who are living here in New Zealand unable to work in general practice because there are no training spaces. We are fixing that and making sure they've got training spaces.
strength.explanation: Stated action in progress; delivery not yet verifiable.

strength.statement: Not only have we brought back health targets but for the first time in New Zealand, we've brought in mental health targets to hold us to account, as a Government, on delivering better mental health.
strength.explanation: A concrete accountability mechanism introduced, though outcomes remain to be delivered.

strength.statement: increasing psychiatry registrar places by 50 percent; doubling the number of clinical psychology interns by 100 percent
strength.explanation: Concrete workforce actions attributed to the government; partly in-progress.

strength.statement: We've announced a $1 million fund that will train 100 new peer support workers to go out and provide lived experience peer support work.
strength.explanation: Announced fund; training and delivery still ahead.

strength.statement: the Auditor-General was scathing of the last Government for not having a mental health workforce plan. We published that in our first year
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered output (published workforce plan) against a prior gap.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced money for the Wellington City Mission to scale up their Crisis Café with peer support workers.
strength.explanation: Concrete, recently-actioned funding decision.

strength.statement: This is why this Government will invest $15 million, for two years, for Māori health providers to help lift immunisation rates.
strength.explanation: Committed investment; outcomes still to be realised.

strength.statement: I'm very happy to report to you that only in the first 10 months, we already have a huge increase in vaccination rates, with over 69,000 vaccinations being delivered.
strength.explanation: Claims early delivered results on a stated commitment.

strength.statement: This is why this Government invested $30.2 million to extend free breast-screening for women aged 70 to 74; we make sure they can accept treatment as early as possible.
strength.explanation: Concrete funded expansion of a service; implementation underway.

strength.statement: Under this Government, we have already increased placements in our medical schools by 75 each year for our medical school. But it's not enough. We think we can do more, so we added another 25 this year so we can actually increase to 639 annually from 2026.
strength.explanation: Describes staged, partly-delivered increases to medical training places.

forthrightness.statement: No. There are other options in terms of what we can do to provide concrete into our community. There are land-based options that exist already.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts Collins's interjection ('You can't build houses without sand') by naming an alternative.

forthrightness.statement: The ACT Party doesn't need to be reined in, because we're a constructive part of this Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Jackson's charge that ACT needs reining in, giving a clear position.

forthrightness.statement: no decisions have been made on whether the bill will proceed beyond this point, and the intention is that we want to hear what New Zealanders think during the select committee process, and so all New Zealanders will have an opportunity to have their say.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly states the process is undecided rather than overstating certainty.

forthrightness.statement: It may be indeed that this is a rare case of a genuinely open select committee process, because we on this side of the House are taking a similar approach. We think it's a fair question and we look forward to a select committee process
forthrightness.explanation: Clearly states Labour's position of qualified support.

divination.statement: It's only going to impact your taiao. It's only going to impact the pātaka kai. You won't be able to go fishing or have your mokopuna swim in the moana.
divination.explanation: Forecasts loss of fishing and swimming from sand mining over a 35-year horizon — plausible harm but strongly stated and uncertain in magnitude.

authenticity.statement: but I'm not standing up here claiming that we've cleaned up all the mess that was left to us.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly qualifies his own side's progress rather than overclaiming — words tempered to match the actual state of delivery.

authenticity.statement: It is the position of the Greens that we should steer clear of AUKUS, regardless of who is in the White House, but Trump's transactional and hyper-aggressive foreign policy makes the case incredibly clear and stronger than ever that we should walk away from this.
authenticity.explanation: States a consistent, principled party position held 'regardless of who is in the White House' — words aligned with a stable stance.

specificity.statement: The Waikato Expressway is a great example of the impact that modern, reliable infrastructure can make for families and for businesses, and now we’re bringing the same experience to Northland—more jobs, more growth, more connectivity, and more opportunity for every New Zealander living north of Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete comparator (Waikato Expressway) but the benefits are listed as vague slogans ('more jobs, more growth') with no figures, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Why has the number of rough sleepers in Auckland increased by 53 percent over the last four months, and is it a coincidence that that occurred at the same time his Government kicked 690 Auckland households out of emergency housing?
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (53 percent increase, 690 households, four-month window).

specificity.statement: Well, I am incredibly proud of our record on housing, unlike that last Government. We have stable rents; we have 4,000 to 5,000 people off the social housing wait-list, which went up four times under Minister Megan Woods; and, importantly, we’ve taken 2,000 kids out of motel accommodation and got them into proper homes and houses through community housing providers in Kāinga Ora (KO).
specificity.explanation: Provides several concrete figures (4,000–5,000 off wait-list, 2,000 kids out of motels).

specificity.statement: When this Government came into office, there were 3,141 households in motels thanks to the last Government. Today, there are 591. We have put more families out of motels and into proper homes, where kids should be raised. Almost 2,000 kids now live in houses, not in motels.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures (3,141 down to 591 households, almost 2,000 kids).

specificity.statement: Each year, Treasury does two sets of forecasts: one to accompany the Budget, and another at the half-year update. In an election year, as a bonus, there’s also a pre-election update. Looking ahead, the next Treasury forecasts will be those that accompany the Budget, on 22 May.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact date (22 May) and the forecasting cadence.

specificity.statement: I expect the Treasury’s forecast to show a return to growth in the December quarter of last year, then picking up over this calendar year. Consistent with other forecasts, they are also likely to show unemployment peaking in the first half of 2025 and then declining.
specificity.explanation: Gives directional predictions with rough timeframes (December quarter, first half of 2025) but no magnitudes.

specificity.statement: the number of people unemployed predicted at the pre-election update was 165,000. The half-year update confirmed exactly the same number. If the member wishes to say that this is a result of Government policies, I would commend to her that she then explain why the previous Labour Government were predicting exactly the same levels of unemployment.
specificity.explanation: Cites the precise forecast figure (165,000) across two updates.

specificity.statement: Why, then, are there 6,248 fewer filled jobs than this time last year, according to Statistics New Zealand?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (6,248 fewer filled jobs) with a named source and timeframe.

specificity.statement: This is an investment in the upper North Island area—the economic powerhouse of the country, with 53.7 percent of our population and 55 percent of GDP. This is an investment in growth and productivity.
specificity.explanation: Provides precise population and GDP share figures, though the closing sentence is a generic slogan.

specificity.statement: Formal procurement will begin this week on the first section. Registered parties will be invited to submit a formal expression of interest, with a request for proposal in mid-2025 for up to three short-listed bidders. The preferred bidder is expected to be announced early next year, and a public-private partnership contract finalised by the middle of the year, with construction expected to begin soon afterwards on the first section from Warkworth to Te Hana, which is expected to start in late 2026.
specificity.explanation: Detailed procurement timeline with named stages, places (Warkworth to Te Hana), and dates (mid-2025, late 2026).

specificity.statement: We’re training more doctors and nurses, we’re paying them more, and we’re creating more opportunities for them to work in primary care, serving the community. We’re putting more funding into GP clinics so that they can enrol more patients, and we’re introducing a 24/7 digital platform so that Kiwis can see a doctor when they need it.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (GP funding, 24/7 digital platform) but omits amounts, targets, and timeframes.

specificity.statement: I am advised that in February 2025, a total of 720 procedures were completed at Tōtara Haumaru. As the member will be aware, this is different to the 15,500 procedures evenly distributed, as the facility was opened with the intention of delivering 2,000 elective procedures in the first financial year. I am advised that Health New Zealand is on track to deliver against this target.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise figures (720 procedures, 2,000 first-year target, 15,500 full capacity).

specificity.statement: I can observe, as does the census data from 2018 to 2023, that severe housing deprivation actually increased over 10 percent during those five years.
specificity.explanation: Names the data source, period (2018–2023), and a rough magnitude (over 10 percent).

specificity.statement: This includes yesterday’s announcement of a $3 million boost to secure more international business events in New Zealand. This investment will allow Tourism New Zealand to increase their annual conference bid development from 90 to 110 bids, attract high-value incentive programmes, and sell New Zealand as a world-class location for business events.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific amount ($3 million) and a measurable target (from 90 to 110 bids).

specificity.statement: The additional investment in securing business events will deliver more than $30 million in incremental spend to the economy. Business event participants spend, on average, $175 more a day than other visitors and often travel during the off-peak season.
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete figures ($30 million, $175/day per participant).

specificity.statement: our exports to India fell by $550 million. In the very same period of time, Australia increased their exports by $7 billion into that market.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise comparative figures ($550 million fall vs Australia's $7 billion increase).

specificity.statement: Sense Partners, an economic consultancy, estimate that halving approval times for agricultural products could lift productivity in the sector by $272 million. Conversely, losing EU market access for fruit and vegetables due to delayed product approvals ... is estimated to risk a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar loss.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures ($272 million productivity gain, quarter-billion-dollar risk) and a named source.

specificity.statement: we’ve announced recently critical infrastructure streamlined proposals, whereby incentive payments of an additional 15 percent of the value of the land will be made available to landowners for early agreement; an additional 5 percent of the value of the land in addition, as a recognition payment ... and a streamlined objection process, whereby the landowner ... can object directly to the decision maker.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise mechanisms and figures (15 percent incentive, 5 percent recognition payment, direct objection process).

specificity.statement: this bill makes a targeted change to align the legislation with the practices of agencies and the courts for more than 10 years. It does this by amending section 30M of the Bail Act and inserting several new sections to codify the usual practice taken by Corrections to enable the efficient and practical management of the large population of defendants on electronically monitored bail.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision amended (section 30M of the Bail Act) and the concrete purpose of the change.

specificity.statement: Concerns have been raised that the current law may, in fact, require the courts to approve each and every absence for the roughly 2,000 defendants subject to electronic monitoring. This would place an untenable burden on the courts and justice agencies, and it would be less responsive to the circumstances of the defendant, with consequences for public safety.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the affected population (roughly 2,000 defendants) and identifies the concrete operational problem.

charisma.statement: The Waikato Expressway is a great example of the impact that modern, reliable infrastructure can make for families and for businesses, and now we’re bringing the same experience to Northland—more jobs, more growth, more connectivity, and more opportunity for every New Zealander living north of Auckland.
charisma.explanation: Upbeat and confident, appeals to a broad 'every New Zealander' audience, but is essentially a one-sided sales pitch rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I have, however, within my arsenal, a small piece of humility, which is to say that, while our Government should be driving policies on a daily basis that will help the growth outlook, we should always be mindful that there are factors that remain outside of our control, not least of which are global economic conditions and the decisions made by other Governments.
charisma.explanation: The 'small piece of humility' framing is rhetorically deft but still lands as a jab at the questioner rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I mean, this just characterises the Greens’ position, doesn’t it? It’s a de-growth agenda of living in a hermit kingdom.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them mockery that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: The Government’s moving urgency this afternoon not with any pleasure but because it is necessary in order to advance the bail amendment changes that we want Parliament to deal with as quickly as possible, and for legal reasons we want to come into effect as quickly as possible.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to smooth cross-House relations by noting the Opposition was given advance copies, a mildly consensus-oriented gesture.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the incident we saw last week was unacceptable and not something we want to see at all. I think the Minister has fronted really clearly on that, actually suspending those type of lunches.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he'll wait until term 2 given kids are going hungry, he acknowledges the incident but defends the Minister rather than addressing the timing the question raised.

forthrightness.statement: That is what we have been assured: that, despite the liquidation, the school lunches programme is not at risk. Obviously, that’s a commercial matter, but our key thing is to make sure that we are getting what we have contracted for and that that is delivered.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for a guarantee that insolvency won't leave kids hungry, he reports an assurance rather than personally guaranteeing, but does engage the substance.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I can say is that we’re getting more people out of emergency housing, we’re taking more people off the social housing wait-list, and rents are stable.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked whether Auckland homelessness is increasing or decreasing, he pivots to unrelated talking points and never answers the binary question.

forthrightness.statement: They are able to come to the Government and actually ask for and get the assistance that they need, and we will take anyone’s efforts to come and actually get the support that they need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm whether every person sleeping rough can access housing under his settings, he describes a process rather than confirming or denying the specific claim.

forthrightness.statement: Each year, Treasury does two sets of forecasts: one to accompany the Budget, and another at the half-year update. In an election year, as a bonus, there’s also a pre-election update. Looking ahead, the next Treasury forecasts will be those that accompany the Budget, on 22 May.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers when the next forecasts will be released, with a specific date.

forthrightness.statement: given my experience of forecast revisions last year, I am not holding out hope for an overall positive fiscal surprise. That seems unlikely, but it is still early days.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly lowers expectations rather than spinning; a frank, non-evasive answer about the fiscal outlook.

forthrightness.statement: I have to say the Greens are totally deluded on economics. I mean, I don’t know how to say it any other way, but, honestly, that is a question that just makes no sense, and I reject it.
forthrightness.explanation: Refuses to answer the question about privatisation and public ownership, simply rejecting it.

forthrightness.statement: I am advised that in February 2025, a total of 720 procedures were completed at Tōtara Haumaru. As the member will be aware, this is different to the 15,500 procedures evenly distributed, as the facility was opened with the intention of delivering 2,000 elective procedures in the first financial year. I am advised that Health New Zealand is on track to deliver against this target.
forthrightness.explanation: Provides the specific monthly figure asked for and explains the discrepancy with the projected annual capacity.

forthrightness.statement: As the member will be aware, the last Government, which built Tōtara Haumaru, failed to allocate the funding to operate it. It’s a bit like the Yes Minister show, isn’t it, where you’ve got an empty hospital and nothing is actually able to be done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by wanting private-sector delivery while public facilities are underutilised, he pivots to blaming the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: I think the answer to that question is that Kiwis needing elective surgery don’t care who is providing it; they want it done in a timely manner, and under the last Government the number of people waiting more than four months for elective treatment increased by 2,500 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile Luxon's and his own statements on privatisation, he sidesteps the contradiction and reframes around wait times.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve been advised that Health New Zealand will be both insourcing and outsourcing in order to achieve that number by the end of this year so that we can make sure we are increasing the number of elective surgeries being done.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses how the target will be met (insourcing and outsourcing) but doesn't directly confirm the specific milestone figure the question put to him.

forthrightness.statement: In the context in which that statement was made, yes. Emergency housing was intended to be a last resort—not the first resort—and it remains a last resort in most towns and cities in Aotearoa New Zealand for those with a general need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers that he stands by the statement and explains the qualification he attaches to it.

forthrightness.statement: I sense and completely understand the member’s and the Opposition’s frustration at our successful delivery and commitment around over 3,000 children leaving emergency housing in the last 15 months and 2,000 by way of the Priority One decision making.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'll meet front-line providers on camera and tell them they're wrong, he avoids the yes/no and reframes around delivery statistics.

forthrightness.statement: we remain committed to delivering improved access for Kiwi exporters through a trade agreement with India this term.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question by reaffirming the first-term commitment, though he softens 'free-trade agreement' to 'improved access ... through a trade agreement'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it will be called a comprehensive economic partnership agreement, like the one with the UAE in six months and the NZ-Gulf Corporation Council that the previous Government said wasn’t possible—all done within a year. But I won’t be negotiating via this Chamber or the media with any Government around the world.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out signing an agreement that excludes dairy, he declines to answer, citing a refusal to negotiate in the Chamber.

forthrightness.statement: The Government’s moving urgency this afternoon not with any pleasure but because it is necessary in order to advance the bail amendment changes that we want Parliament to deal with as quickly as possible, and for legal reasons we want to come into effect as quickly as possible.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the reason for urgency, though 'for legal reasons' is left somewhat unspecified.

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that yesterday’s on-time delivery for the healthy school lunch programme was 99.74 percent; and is that better than the delivery of the vaccine roll-out, which someone forgot to order?
civility.explanation: Uses a patsy question to land a partisan cheap shot ('the vaccine roll-out, which someone forgot to order') rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Why has the number of rough sleepers in Auckland increased by 53 percent over the last four months, and is it a coincidence that that occurred at the same time his Government kicked 690 Auckland households out of emergency housing?
civility.explanation: 'kicked ... out of emergency housing' is loaded, but the underlying point is a legitimate policy criticism.

civility.statement: I can stand here with great confidence and say that a Labour-led Government, at this juncture in history, would have done more economic vandalism—
civility.explanation: 'economic vandalism' is a sensationalised partisan characterisation rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: I mean, this just characterises the Greens’ position, doesn’t it? It’s a de-growth agenda of living in a hermit kingdom.
civility.explanation: Caricatures an opponent's position ('hermit kingdom') rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: I have to say the Greens are totally deluded on economics. I mean, I don’t know how to say it any other way, but, honestly, that is a question that just makes no sense, and I reject it.
civility.explanation: 'totally deluded' is a dismissive attack on the opposing party rather than an engagement with the question.

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that New Zealanders have been bringing capital from across the seas since Kupe showed up in a sailboat with some kumara, but, sadly, xenophobic attitudes have been here nearly as long?
civility.explanation: Frames opponents of foreign capital as 'xenophobic', an insinuating characterisation rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: As the member will be aware, the last Government, which built Tōtara Haumaru, failed to allocate the funding to operate it. It’s a bit like the Yes Minister show, isn’t it, where you’ve got an empty hospital and nothing is actually able to be done.
civility.explanation: The 'Yes Minister' jibe mocks the prior Government but targets its record rather than a person directly.

civility.statement: Will the Minister promise not to return from India, as a trade Minister once did, promising that he had secured $500 million of potential orders when it was zero?
civility.explanation: A pointed jab at a past Labour minister framed as a question; targets a past record but with a barbed, sensationalised edge.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that yesterday’s on-time delivery for the healthy school lunch programme was 99.74 percent; and is that better than the delivery of the vaccine roll-out, which someone forgot to order?
veracity.explanation: The 99.74% on-time figure is precise and later confirmed by Luxon; the vaccine jibe is a misleading exaggeration of past events.

veracity.statement: Well, I am incredibly proud of our record on housing, unlike that last Government. We have stable rents; we have 4,000 to 5,000 people off the social housing wait-list, which went up four times under Minister Megan Woods; and, importantly, we’ve taken 2,000 kids out of motel accommodation and got them into proper homes and houses through community housing providers in Kāinga Ora (KO).
veracity.explanation: Mixes verifiable claims with selective framing; 'stable rents' and the wait-list movement are contestable and the numbers are stated without the fuller context the Opposition disputes.

veracity.statement: When this Government came into office, there were 3,141 households in motels thanks to the last Government. Today, there are 591. We have put more families out of motels and into proper homes, where kids should be raised. Almost 2,000 kids now live in houses, not in motels.
veracity.explanation: Figures are concrete but the reduction is contested by opponents who argue people moved to the street; 'into proper homes' omits that disputed context.

veracity.statement: Each year, Treasury does two sets of forecasts: one to accompany the Budget, and another at the half-year update. In an election year, as a bonus, there’s also a pre-election update. Looking ahead, the next Treasury forecasts will be those that accompany the Budget, on 22 May.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of Treasury's standard forecasting schedule.

veracity.statement: the number of people unemployed predicted at the pre-election update was 165,000. The half-year update confirmed exactly the same number. If the member wishes to say that this is a result of Government policies, I would commend to her that she then explain why the previous Labour Government were predicting exactly the same levels of unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The forecast-consistency claim is plausible and checkable, though selectively deployed.

veracity.statement: Why, then, are there 6,248 fewer filled jobs than this time last year, according to Statistics New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific, checkable number to Statistics New Zealand; plausible and sourced.

veracity.statement: This is an investment in the upper North Island area—the economic powerhouse of the country, with 53.7 percent of our population and 55 percent of GDP. This is an investment in growth and productivity.
veracity.explanation: The 53.7% population / 55% GDP figures are plausible and checkable; broadly consistent with upper North Island shares.

veracity.statement: I am advised that in February 2025, a total of 720 procedures were completed at Tōtara Haumaru. As the member will be aware, this is different to the 15,500 procedures evenly distributed, as the facility was opened with the intention of delivering 2,000 elective procedures in the first financial year. I am advised that Health New Zealand is on track to deliver against this target.
veracity.explanation: Reports advised operational figures with reasonable context; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: I think the answer to that question is that Kiwis needing elective surgery don’t care who is providing it; they want it done in a timely manner, and under the last Government the number of people waiting more than four months for elective treatment increased by 2,500 percent.
veracity.explanation: The '2,500 percent' increase is a striking figure that reads as hyperbole and likely reflects a very low base, potentially misleading without context.

veracity.statement: I can observe, as does the census data from 2018 to 2023, that severe housing deprivation actually increased over 10 percent during those five years.
veracity.explanation: Cites census data for a specific period and magnitude; plausible and sourced, though deployed to deflect the front-line-provider point.

veracity.statement: The additional investment in securing business events will deliver more than $30 million in incremental spend to the economy. Business event participants spend, on average, $175 more a day than other visitors and often travel during the off-peak season.
veracity.explanation: The per-day spend figure is checkable; the $30 million total is a forward projection presented as fact.

veracity.statement: our exports to India fell by $550 million. In the very same period of time, Australia increased their exports by $7 billion into that market.
veracity.explanation: Specific and checkable figures, though comparing NZ and Australia to India is a selective framing that omits scale differences.

rigor.statement: Why has the number of rough sleepers in Auckland increased by 53 percent over the last four months, and is it a coincidence that that occurred at the same time his Government kicked 690 Auckland households out of emergency housing?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two figures to imply causation via 'is it a coincidence', a suggestive correlation-as-causation framing rather than demonstrated causation.

rigor.statement: the outlook for global bond yields means that finance costs are likely to be greater than they were at the half-year update. That is to say, the costs of servicing New Zealand’s debt will be higher.
rigor.explanation: Links premise (global bond yields) to conclusion (higher finance costs) with clear entailment.

rigor.statement: the number of people unemployed predicted at the pre-election update was 165,000. The half-year update confirmed exactly the same number. If the member wishes to say that this is a result of Government policies, I would commend to her that she then explain why the previous Labour Government were predicting exactly the same levels of unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific figure and a consistency argument (Labour's own pre-election forecast matched) to rebut the causation claim; reasoning largely follows.

rigor.statement: I have, however, within my arsenal, a small piece of humility, which is to say that, while our Government should be driving policies on a daily basis that will help the growth outlook, we should always be mindful that there are factors that remain outside of our control, not least of which are global economic conditions and the decisions made by other Governments.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges exogenous factors and uncertainty rather than overclaiming control, a measured caveat, though it also sidesteps the forecast challenge.

rigor.statement: I can stand here with great confidence and say that a Labour-led Government, at this juncture in history, would have done more economic vandalism—
rigor.explanation: A counterfactual assertion offered with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: I mean, this just characterises the Greens’ position, doesn’t it? It’s a de-growth agenda of living in a hermit kingdom.
rigor.explanation: Strawmans the Greens' position instead of rebutting the actual argument about ECE profits.

rigor.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that New Zealanders have been bringing capital from across the seas since Kupe showed up in a sailboat with some kumara, but, sadly, xenophobic attitudes have been here nearly as long?
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical patsy leaning on a loaded historical analogy rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: our exports to India fell by $550 million. In the very same period of time, Australia increased their exports by $7 billion into that market.
rigor.explanation: Uses the comparison to argue Labour underperformed, but the Australia analogy ignores relevant differences in market size and mix.

rigor.statement: Sense Partners, an economic consultancy, estimate that halving approval times for agricultural products could lift productivity in the sector by $272 million. Conversely, losing EU market access for fruit and vegetables due to delayed product approvals ... is estimated to risk a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar loss.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a named consultancy's estimates with quantified upside and downside.

rigor.statement: this bill makes a targeted change to align the legislation with the practices of agencies and the courts for more than 10 years. It does this by amending section 30M of the Bail Act and inserting several new sections to codify the usual practice taken by Corrections to enable the efficient and practical management of the large population of defendants on electronically monitored bail.
rigor.explanation: Explains the change as aligning law with long-standing practice, a coherent rationale, though asserted rather than evidenced in detail.

rigor.statement: Concerns have been raised that the current law may, in fact, require the courts to approve each and every absence for the roughly 2,000 defendants subject to electronic monitoring. This would place an untenable burden on the courts and justice agencies, and it would be less responsive to the circumstances of the defendant, with consequences for public safety.
rigor.explanation: Lays out the problem (per-absence court approval), the affected population, and the practical consequences in a logically connected way.

strength.statement: Well, I am incredibly proud of our record on housing, unlike that last Government. We have stable rents; we have 4,000 to 5,000 people off the social housing wait-list, which went up four times under Minister Megan Woods; and, importantly, we’ve taken 2,000 kids out of motel accommodation and got them into proper homes and houses through community housing providers in Kāinga Ora (KO).
strength.explanation: Claims delivered outcomes (kids moved from motels, wait-list reductions) rather than mere aspiration, though the figures are self-reported.

strength.statement: When this Government came into office, there were 3,141 households in motels thanks to the last Government. Today, there are 591. We have put more families out of motels and into proper homes, where kids should be raised. Almost 2,000 kids now live in houses, not in motels.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered reduction in motel households, a concrete claimed outcome rather than an announcement.

strength.statement: We’re training more doctors and nurses, we’re paying them more, and we’re creating more opportunities for them to work in primary care, serving the community. We’re putting more funding into GP clinics so that they can enrol more patients, and we’re introducing a 24/7 digital platform so that Kiwis can see a doctor when they need it.
strength.explanation: Describes announced actions and intents rather than demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: I sense and completely understand the member’s and the Opposition’s frustration at our successful delivery and commitment around over 3,000 children leaving emergency housing in the last 15 months and 2,000 by way of the Priority One decision making.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivered outcome (over 3,000 children leaving emergency housing in 15 months) rather than mere intent.

strength.statement: This includes yesterday’s announcement of a $3 million boost to secure more international business events in New Zealand. This investment will allow Tourism New Zealand to increase their annual conference bid development from 90 to 110 bids, attract high-value incentive programmes, and sell New Zealand as a world-class location for business events.
strength.explanation: Describes a fresh announcement and intended effect rather than demonstrated delivery.

authenticity.statement: Well, I am incredibly proud of our record on housing, unlike that last Government. We have stable rents; we have 4,000 to 5,000 people off the social housing wait-list, which went up four times under Minister Megan Woods; and, importantly, we’ve taken 2,000 kids out of motel accommodation and got them into proper homes and houses through community housing providers in Kāinga Ora (KO).
authenticity.explanation: A 'proud of our record' claim invited by a patsy-style comparison; consistency with actual outcomes is contested and not verifiable from the text.

authenticity.statement: In the context in which that statement was made, yes. Emergency housing was intended to be a last resort—not the first resort—and it remains a last resort in most towns and cities in Aotearoa New Zealand for those with a general need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms a prior position and explains the consistency, though the practical consistency is contested by the questioner.

authenticity.statement: we remain committed to delivering improved access for Kiwi exporters through a trade agreement with India this term.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a pre-election commitment; consistency with the eventual outcome cannot be judged from the text.

divination.statement: I expect the Treasury’s forecast to show a return to growth in the December quarter of last year, then picking up over this calendar year. Consistent with other forecasts, they are also likely to show unemployment peaking in the first half of 2025 and then declining.
divination.explanation: Forecasts growth returning and unemployment peaking in H1 2025 then declining; plausible and aligned with other forecasts but uncertain.

divination.statement: the outlook for global bond yields means that finance costs are likely to be greater than they were at the half-year update. That is to say, the costs of servicing New Zealand’s debt will be higher.
divination.explanation: Predicts higher debt-servicing costs; well-reasoned from the stated bond-yield outlook and near-term.

divination.statement: given my experience of forecast revisions last year, I am not holding out hope for an overall positive fiscal surprise. That seems unlikely, but it is still early days.
divination.explanation: Predicts no positive fiscal surprise, hedged and uncertain by her own admission.

divination.statement: Formal procurement will begin this week on the first section. Registered parties will be invited to submit a formal expression of interest, with a request for proposal in mid-2025 for up to three short-listed bidders. The preferred bidder is expected to be announced early next year, and a public-private partnership contract finalised by the middle of the year, with construction expected to begin soon afterwards on the first section from Warkworth to Te Hana, which is expected to start in late 2026.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the procurement and construction schedule; plausible for an announced project but subject to slippage.

divination.statement: The additional investment in securing business events will deliver more than $30 million in incremental spend to the economy. Business event participants spend, on average, $175 more a day than other visitors and often travel during the off-peak season.
divination.explanation: Forecasts $30 million in incremental spend from the investment; plausible but an unverified projection.

divination.statement: Sense Partners, an economic consultancy, estimate that halving approval times for agricultural products could lift productivity in the sector by $272 million. Conversely, losing EU market access for fruit and vegetables due to delayed product approvals ... is estimated to risk a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar loss.
divination.explanation: Predicts productivity gains and market-access risks; plausible modelled estimates but inherently uncertain.

charisma.statement: It’s good to see a relative sense of unity across the House on this piece of legislation, bar our friends in Te Pāti Māori, but I don’t think we’ll see much of that ever happening.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges cross-House unity but undercuts it with a dismissive swipe at Te Pāti Māori, mixing an inclusive note with an exclusionary one.

charisma.statement: I think that’s the main problem we have with this Government: we do not have a plan to break the cycle of crime. We have a Government that’s very interested in locking people up but not so interested in looking to the solutions to stop that cycle occurring again and again.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing attacking the Government's motives rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I know that our Government absolutely has a plan to crack down on crime. That’s why we want to get through this bill very quickly and get back to those other bills, like the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, which I’m very, very excited about passing very soon in this House.
charisma.explanation: Purely rallies the Government side with no attempt to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: The Labour Party’s giving this bill a good going over, because that’s our job as Opposition, but fundamentally we’re cooperating with the Government on fixing this legislation. We’re here to make it better.
charisma.explanation: Frames the Opposition's role as constructive and cooperative, seeking to improve the bill jointly rather than obstruct.

charisma.statement: have you heard of innocent until proven guilty? Have you heard of not depriving people of rights who’ve yet to be convicted of a crime? Well, I wonder sometimes with the attitude of that Government.
charisma.explanation: Combative appeal to principle that casts the Government as the antagonist rather than inviting them along.

charisma.statement: I do actually think that this is something that the Greens will be supporting, but I also think that if this is something that the Minister considers... is not actually within the scope of this bill... I would very much encourage... the Minister that if it’s not being introduced as part of this bill, that it is considered at a later date.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party gesture: backs another party's amendment and constructively offers the Minister an alternative path forward.

civility.statement: It’s good to see a relative sense of unity across the House on this piece of legislation, bar our friends in Te Pāti Māori, but I don’t think we’ll see much of that ever happening.
civility.explanation: A mild partisan jab at another party rather than a personal attack; borderline dig.

civility.statement: There’s been several contributions from the other side of the House that have almost been flippant to the fact that questions have been raised on this side of the House.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents' contributions as 'flippant' — pointed criticism of their conduct in debate rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: There is no need to wander and waffle. This is a required change, and I commend it to the House.
civility.explanation: Implicit dig at prior speakers ('wander and waffle') but light and impersonal.

civility.statement: I think that’s the main problem we have with this Government: we do not have a plan to break the cycle of crime. We have a Government that’s very interested in locking people up but not so interested in looking to the solutions to stop that cycle occurring again and again.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's policy priorities harshly but stays on policy rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: It might be that the Minister is going to table an amendment—I’m sure he will; he usually does: he doesn’t usually get it right the first time around
civility.explanation: A personal dig at the Minister's competence rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: have you heard of innocent until proven guilty? Have you heard of not depriving people of rights who’ve yet to be convicted of a crime? Well, I wonder sometimes with the attitude of that Government.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical questions implying the Government disregards fundamental rights — pointed but aimed at policy attitude.

civility.statement: One of the things that was concerning to me before, when the member who proposed this tabled amendment was speaking on this, was that we were hearing members from the Government parties laughing. I genuinely think that for someone to be granted the fundamental right and their civil and political rights under our international governance is actually no laughing matter.
civility.explanation: Rebukes Government members' conduct (laughing) while framing the point around rights rather than insulting individuals.

specificity.statement: This is a pragmatic change—really good legislation. We’re doing it quickly so we can ensure nothing falls through the cracks, so I commend it to the House.
specificity.explanation: Generic praise ('pragmatic', 'really good') with no mechanism, figure, or detail about what the bill does.

specificity.statement: This bill simply ensures that the practice that’s been happening for a number of years now is compliant with the Bail Act and that the existing authorisations continue to be valid.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (compliance with the Bail Act, validating existing authorisations) but without section-level detail.

specificity.statement: Some other contributions have noted the escalating proportion of people incarcerated through our corrections system—I think it is even up as high as 42 or 45 percent—who are actually on remand
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure but hedges it as a range and attributes it vaguely to 'some other contributions'.

specificity.statement: There is no need to wander and waffle. This is a required change, and I commend it to the House.
specificity.explanation: Bare endorsement with no detail about the change itself.

specificity.statement: It would be, from our perspective, a difficult position to oppose this bill due to some of the very key reasons that people may need to be on electronic bail and not be at their specific address—for example, for the seeking of urgent medical treatment.
specificity.explanation: Gives an illustrative example but no figures or scope detail.

specificity.statement: I rise to support the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill because this is a common-sense approach, it rectifies a process. It’s all about ensuring that we have safe electronic monitoring in our community, and I commend it to the House.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level support ('common-sense', 'safe') with no mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: electronic bail is definitely not the same to home detention, and those two should not be conflated. Electronic bail... is something which offenders are granted before conviction but prior to sentence, whereas home detention is punishment in itself.
specificity.explanation: Precise about the difference and the stage in the process, though without statute references.

specificity.statement: 43 percent of people in prison in New Zealand are not sentenced and are awaiting court processes, which is a lot higher than other countries... the UK, for example, has only 18.3 percent of prisoners in that space.
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures for two jurisdictions to make the comparison.

specificity.statement: I know that our Government absolutely has a plan to crack down on crime. That’s why we want to get through this bill very quickly and get back to those other bills, like the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, which I’m very, very excited about passing very soon in this House.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific companion bill but the 'plan to crack down on crime' is asserted without detail.

specificity.statement: The majority of people in this circumstance—there’s about 2,000 at any given time; in fact, right now it’s 1,859 people—are there for serious violent offences, and that is why they’ve been put on electronic bail.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact current figure (1,859) plus a rough standing number and the reason for their status.

specificity.statement: Firstly, there was an operational review by the Ministry of Justice conducted to simplify the language used in bail notices, and that work gave rise to questions as to whether the standard practice, which was Corrections approving defendants as being absent, was clearly enabled under the Bail Act... Since late 2024, some judicial decisions have also raised questions
specificity.explanation: Identifies the two triggers and a rough timeframe, though stops short of naming cases.

specificity.statement: Ministers were made aware of the issue in late 2024. We were formally briefed on 20 February this year, and agreed to drafting a Cabinet paper, which was completed before introducing this bill. We moved swiftly when the issue was raised.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete dates and steps (late 2024, 20 February briefing, Cabinet paper).

specificity.statement: I only knew this was a problem because I knocked on a door of someone who was electronically monitored on election day and she said, “I’m not allowed to vote.” And I said, “Well, surely Corrections has helped you out.” She said, “No.” So I asked Corrections, “What assistance do you give to people on electronic monitoring?” And they said, “None.”
specificity.explanation: Concrete illustrative account, though no data on how many EM-bail voters are affected.

specificity.statement: I propose that seeing as we’re looking at the very question of when you’re allowed out from your electronic monitoring, we should add to that “to vote in a general election or referendum by attendance at the nearest voting place”.
specificity.explanation: A precise, drafted amendment naming the exact right and mechanism to be added to section 30L(1)(b).

specificity.statement: one of the things that I want to specifically focus on is actually new section 30MB(2)(b)(i)... does the EM assessor actually trump the information provided by the court? How is inconsistency in the detail resolved?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints an exact clause and poses a precise, concrete question about how court/assessor conflicts resolve.

specificity.statement: We’ve had an illegal act for a long time. Has anybody done an audit of it in terms of which situations this discretion has been used and what the context is in terms of who’s been given that bail for how long, for what purposes, and what the possible complication is there?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the concrete dimensions an audit should cover (who, how long, what purposes).

veracity.statement: This bill simply ensures that the practice that’s been happening for a number of years now is compliant with the Bail Act and that the existing authorisations continue to be valid.
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of the bill's retrospective validation purpose, consistent with the Minister's later account.

veracity.statement: Some other contributions have noted the escalating proportion of people incarcerated through our corrections system—I think it is even up as high as 42 or 45 percent—who are actually on remand
veracity.explanation: The remand share (~43%) is roughly correct; the hedged 42–45% range is directionally accurate but imprecise.

veracity.statement: this has been in practice for over a decade, so I’m not 100 percent clear of the exact reason to necessitate the urgency.
veracity.explanation: The decade-plus practice claim matches the Minister's account (since 2013).

veracity.statement: electronic bail is definitely not the same to home detention, and those two should not be conflated. Electronic bail... is something which offenders are granted before conviction but prior to sentence, whereas home detention is punishment in itself.
veracity.explanation: Accurate legal distinction between EM bail (pre-conviction) and home detention (a sentence).

veracity.statement: 43 percent of people in prison in New Zealand are not sentenced and are awaiting court processes, which is a lot higher than other countries... the UK, for example, has only 18.3 percent of prisoners in that space.
veracity.explanation: NZ's high remand share is well documented; the specific UK 18.3% comparison is plausible but presented without a cited source.

veracity.statement: It is concerning that we have a Government, now, who has significantly cut back funding in public services while still wanting to significantly increase our prison population.
veracity.explanation: A contestable characterisation of funding 'cuts' alongside prison expansion; partly supportable but framed as attack without figures.

veracity.statement: The majority of people in this circumstance—there’s about 2,000 at any given time; in fact, right now it’s 1,859 people—are there for serious violent offences, and that is why they’ve been put on electronic bail.
veracity.explanation: Presents a precise operational figure as fact; plausible from ministerial briefing but not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: let’s face it; let’s just get it right—Corrections have done something illegal, right? They’ve breached the law; they’ve been acting outside of the law. There’s a risk, in this piece of legislation, that we simply look at what they’ve been doing and say, “The problem is you’ve been acting illegally. The fix is to permit it retrospectively.” That’s a topsy-turvy kind of way to approach a problem.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the practice as having operated outside the Act — consistent with the Minister's own account of non-compliance.

rigor.statement: Of the people on bail, many have not been convicted of a crime at all, and because of the presumption of innocence, they should be confined—and I think most people would agree—in the least restrictive way which is still consistent with community safety, which is obviously paramount and incredibly important.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument from the presumption of innocence to a least-restrictive-means principle balanced against community safety; leans slightly on an appeal to consensus ('most people would agree').

rigor.statement: This is a retrospective bill, and I’ve thought about the comments to make about that, because usually retrospectivity is something that we shy away from in lawmaking, for a very good reason: it shouldn’t be that people act in a certain way and this House then subsequently changes the law—or the rules of engagement—under which they operate. It’s not a good way to make law
rigor.explanation: Clear principled reasoning about why retrospective lawmaking is generally objectionable, with the rationale spelled out.

rigor.statement: It would be, from our perspective, a difficult position to oppose this bill due to some of the very key reasons that people may need to be on electronic bail and not be at their specific address—for example, for the seeking of urgent medical treatment.
rigor.explanation: Supports the position with a concrete practical justification (urgent medical treatment).

rigor.statement: I rise to support the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill because this is a common-sense approach, it rectifies a process. It’s all about ensuring that we have safe electronic monitoring in our community, and I commend it to the House.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to 'common sense' rather than any evidence or reasoning.

rigor.statement: electronic bail is definitely not the same to home detention, and those two should not be conflated. Electronic bail... is something which offenders are granted before conviction but prior to sentence, whereas home detention is punishment in itself.
rigor.explanation: Draws a precise, correct conceptual distinction to head off a common conflation.

rigor.statement: 43 percent of people in prison in New Zealand are not sentenced and are awaiting court processes, which is a lot higher than other countries... the UK, for example, has only 18.3 percent of prisoners in that space.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete cross-country comparison to support the claim that the system is an outlier.

rigor.statement: There’s been recent sort of indications from the court that it does need to go back to the court, and if that was followed for all these—there’s been, on average, 30,000 a month—then that would seriously clog up the court system, which we’re wanting to avoid and that’s why this legislation is before us.
rigor.explanation: Links the volume (30,000 absences/month) to a concrete consequence (court congestion) to justify the urgency.

rigor.statement: I have given it full and fair consideration, but it is a separate policy issue, because this bill is amending only section 30M—it doesn’t amend section 30L, which is a separate policy issue.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the rejection in a concrete legislative-scope distinction (section 30M vs 30L).

rigor.statement: let’s face it; let’s just get it right—Corrections have done something illegal, right? They’ve breached the law; they’ve been acting outside of the law. There’s a risk, in this piece of legislation, that we simply look at what they’ve been doing and say, “The problem is you’ve been acting illegally. The fix is to permit it retrospectively.” That’s a topsy-turvy kind of way to approach a problem.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the logical inversion in curing illegality by retrospectively legalising the practice rather than designing the correct delegation.

rigor.statement: I only knew this was a problem because I knocked on a door of someone who was electronically monitored on election day and she said, “I’m not allowed to vote.” And I said, “Well, surely Corrections has helped you out.” She said, “No.” So I asked Corrections, “What assistance do you give to people on electronic monitoring?” And they said, “None.”
rigor.explanation: Persuasive single anecdote plus a follow-up inquiry, but rests on one case rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: if that’s the basis for us to do that under urgency, there is a general concern that even when we’re looking at things like the regulatory systems bills, when we are looking at improvements on the current system, it still requires us to go through the entire process, including all of the readings and select committee.
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument: if routine 'it's working' improvements still get full process, using urgency here is inconsistent — a reasoned procedural objection.

rigor.statement: one of the things that I want to specifically focus on is actually new section 30MB(2)(b)(i)... does the EM assessor actually trump the information provided by the court? How is inconsistency in the detail resolved?
rigor.explanation: Constructs a specific hypothetical to expose a potential gap in the drafting.

rigor.statement: We’ve had an illegal act for a long time. Has anybody done an audit of it in terms of which situations this discretion has been used and what the context is in terms of who’s been given that bail for how long, for what purposes, and what the possible complication is there?
rigor.explanation: Presses for empirical grounding (an audit of past use) before enacting a retrospective law — evidence-seeking reasoning.

rigor.statement: I’m also concerned there’s a pattern in our system of, when we’ve got a problem, simply—simply burying the problem and appealing and appealing and appealing when we actually know there’s a problem.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a systemic pattern of burying problems via serial appeals, but offers it as suspicion without evidence for this case.

divination.statement: some of the changes that this Government have brought in—legislative changes—will see our prison population continue to grow, and it will continue to put pressure, not on just the prison infrastructure, but all of those support services that go with that infrastructure
divination.explanation: Forecasts prison-population growth from sentencing/legislative changes — directionally plausible given the reforms, though magnitude and timeframe are unstated.

divination.statement: There’s been recent sort of indications from the court that it does need to go back to the court, and if that was followed for all these—there’s been, on average, 30,000 a month—then that would seriously clog up the court system, which we’re wanting to avoid and that’s why this legislation is before us.
divination.explanation: Predicts serious court clogging if each absence had to return to court — plausible given the cited monthly volume.

forthrightness.statement: Firstly, there was an operational review by the Ministry of Justice conducted to simplify the language used in bail notices, and that work gave rise to questions as to whether the standard practice, which was Corrections approving defendants as being absent, was clearly enabled under the Bail Act... Since late 2024, some judicial decisions have also raised questions
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Webb's question about how the issue arose, naming both the operational review and judicial decisions.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not going to name the specific cases, because a Minister shouldn’t comment on matters before the courts, because there may be appeals.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer the specific request to identify the cases, giving a sub judice reason for the non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: Ministers were made aware of the issue in late 2024. We were formally briefed on 20 February this year, and agreed to drafting a Cabinet paper, which was completed before introducing this bill. We moved swiftly when the issue was raised.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the repeated questions about the timeline with dated specifics.

forthrightness.statement: I have given it full and fair consideration, but it is a separate policy issue, because this bill is amending only section 30M—it doesn’t amend section 30L, which is a separate policy issue.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly responds to Webb's voting-rights amendment, declining it with a stated scope reason.

forthrightness.statement: Just quickly, in relation to the first question about who prevails when there’s inconsistency, the court prevails.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct, unambiguous answer to Xu-Nan's specific question about inconsistency resolution.

civility.statement: That was the most ridiculous contribution from Hamish Campbell I’ve heard.
civility.explanation: A dismissive cheap shot ridiculing a named colleague's contribution rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: that doesn’t mean that I don’t have every faith in the Corrections department and those officers and look at them and think they’ll be acting in good faith, but it’s also the sort of thing I need context to understand.
civility.explanation: Expresses good faith in the officials being criticised while pressing for information; no personal attack.

civility.statement: It’s our job, as the Opposition, to ask you these questions, but it’s also your job, Minister, to answer the questions when they are reasonable.
civility.explanation: Frames the exchange in terms of mutual parliamentary duties rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: I agree wholeheartedly with the previous speaker, Helen White. It’s not a frivolous matter, and nobody would say that it is.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's point, focused on substance.

civility.statement: My new section—which, knowing you and your previous record, you’ll take it away, tidy it up a bit, and call it your own
civility.explanation: A light, semi-jocular dig at the Minister's habit of adopting others' amendments; teasing rather than a serious personal attack.

civility.statement: as noted, this is under urgency, this stage of the process is our only real opportunity to uncover and to pick up potential problems that may not have been spotted before through the Minister’s own process or through the officials’ process. It is incumbent upon us to ask questions, be they big ones or little ones.
civility.explanation: Justifies the questioning on procedural grounds without attacking anyone personally.

civility.statement: It just really feels like scrambled eggs; it feels like that to us. It’s retrospective, which is never a good principle, and the principle of certainty means that all people under the law need to be able to rely on that certainty.
civility.explanation: Colourful criticism ('scrambled eggs') aimed at the legislation and its retrospectivity, not at any person.

civility.statement: this isn’t really creating electronic monitoring, so the title we’ve got is actually a little misleading and you could run through any number of more accurate titles like, “Oops” or something like that. Because that’s what it is, right? It’s fixing up an “oops” that has grown over time
civility.explanation: Mocking of the bill's title and drafting, but directed at the legislation/process rather than a person.

rigor.statement: what those latest sections do is not kind of ameliorate it, they wildly change it, so I think “subject to” is entirely the wrong thing to say, because it doesn’t limit the scope of section 30M—which is what “subject to” means: it means you can do all this except what it says there—the latest sections extend substantially the powers of electronic monitoring (EM) assessors.
rigor.explanation: Close textual reasoning: defines what 'subject to' entails and shows the drafting does the opposite, with the conclusion following from the premise.

rigor.statement: if the assessor is, under (c), specifying all of the details, how can the language be right in (1)(b), which says that the assessor is authorising, “in their discretion, the defendant to be absent from the EM address in line with the authorisation’s— … (ii) details specified under subsection (2).”
rigor.explanation: Traces cross-references between subsections to expose a potential circularity, reasoning carefully from the text.

rigor.statement: why doesn’t this legislation save everyone a lot of time by setting out that list of the standard conditions and then say to the court, “Well, the court can just adopt the standard conditions, or it could vary the standard conditions, but it doesn’t have to restate them all the time.”
rigor.explanation: Offers a reasoned, evidence-based drafting alternative grounded in the observation that most cases use standard conditions.

rigor.statement: legislation should provide a right of appeal if the rights or interests of a particular person are affected by an administrative decision.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee guidelines and applies them to the bill's administrative decisions.

rigor.statement: I want to refer the Minister of Justice to paragraph 6, which states, “If the Act is amended as proposed, it is likely to improve the speed and suitability of authorisations.”—which is fine—but “If Judges are required to set the conditions for absence … they may find it necessary to make a more generous allowance than is required.”
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument from the Bill of Rights consistency report, quoting it to test whether the change restricts freedom of movement.

rigor.statement: as noted, this is under urgency, this stage of the process is our only real opportunity to uncover and to pick up potential problems that may not have been spotted before through the Minister’s own process or through the officials’ process. It is incumbent upon us to ask questions, be they big ones or little ones.
rigor.explanation: Sound reasoning that urgency removes select-committee scrutiny, though offered as a general justification rather than an evidenced claim.

rigor.statement: It just really feels like scrambled eggs; it feels like that to us. It’s retrospective, which is never a good principle, and the principle of certainty means that all people under the law need to be able to rely on that certainty.
rigor.explanation: Invokes the legal principle of certainty coherently, though the 'scrambled eggs' framing leans on rhetoric.

rigor.statement: What I wanted to ask the Minister is perhaps whether he would agree to an amendment to include clarification that that same definition applies to this new bill, because it’s really fundamental to the work that has to be undertaken in this bill
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine definitional gap (no EM assessor definition in the bill) and reasons to a targeted fix.

rigor.statement: Corrections or Police, or there have also been known as private companies or private security groups, are in these assessor roles; we must remember that private security are not Crown and therefore it’s a breach of Te Tiriti.
rigor.explanation: Advances a syllogism (private security are not Crown, therefore a Tiriti breach) but the premise about private companies filling assessor roles is asserted and contested, leaving a logical gap.

rigor.statement: this isn’t really creating electronic monitoring, so the title we’ve got is actually a little misleading and you could run through any number of more accurate titles like, “Oops” or something like that. Because that’s what it is, right? It’s fixing up an “oops” that has grown over time
rigor.explanation: A fair point that the title overstates what the bill does, but delivered as rhetorical mockery rather than a developed argument.

specificity.statement: what those latest sections do is not kind of ameliorate it, they wildly change it, so I think “subject to” is entirely the wrong thing to say, because it doesn’t limit the scope of section 30M—which is what “subject to” means: it means you can do all this except what it says there—the latest sections extend substantially the powers of electronic monitoring (EM) assessors.
specificity.explanation: Names precise provisions (s30M, 'subject to') and the exact drafting effect at issue.
