specificity.explanation: Precise on which provisions are non-retrospective and the exact trigger (offence committed on/after commencement).

specificity.statement: But what I am saying is, perhaps, we should learn from this and start thinking about where else in the justice sector we can use interventions which identify risk and intervene before the event rather than after the event.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel ('risk-based, prevent before the event') but names no specific policy, area, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: I was involved throughout the whole select committee process, and we received 22 submissions and heard from five oral submitters.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts of written (22) and oral (5) submissions.

specificity.statement: While preliminary findings from PhD research commissioned by the Police indicate that the register may reduce the likelihood of reoffending by 40 to 70 percent, the final findings will not be published until 2026. Further longitudinal study on recidivism is not due for interim reporting until 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the quantified effect range, and specific reporting years (2026, 2027).

specificity.statement: That means honouring our cross-party agreement to honour Te Aorerekura, that action plan and that work plan, working with communities for prevention so that we can eliminate family and sexual violence in Aotearoa.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete plan (Te Aorerekura) but the associated commitment ('working with communities', 'eliminate violence') stays high-level.

specificity.statement: At the end of the day, this is a Government that I am proud to work with, that puts the victim first and the perpetrator second.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-style contrast ('victim first, perpetrator second') with no concrete measure or mechanism.

divination.statement: This bill will go a long way to creating more competition so that we can bring down those prices and ensure that we can get families into their first homes.
divination.explanation: Predicts lower prices and more first-home buyers from increased competition; plausible direction but no magnitude or timeframe, and price effects of product-standards liberalisation are uncertain.

divination.statement: But as the member on the other side of the House said, this is also about risk mitigation. This is about doing something smart, and this is why our register has been successful and will continue to be successful, because it does allow for that risk mitigation component and allow the offenders themselves to contribute to controlling their behaviour.
divination.explanation: Predicts the register 'will continue to be successful'; plausible given the tentative evidence but asserted more confidently than the preliminary data supports.

strength.statement: This bill will go a long way to creating more competition so that we can bring down those prices and ensure that we can get families into their first homes.
strength.explanation: Backs a bill at second reading — an announcement/aspiration stage, not delivered outcomes; follow-through on affordability unproven.

rigor.statement: Time to get rid of the red tape which has been holding the construction industry back, let’s be honest.
rigor.explanation: Asserts red tape is 'holding the industry back' as a given without evidence; leans on a familiar political trope rather than a demonstrated causal claim.

rigor.statement: Additionally, initial findings from research commissioned by Police indicates that the New Zealand register is achieving a 40 percent to 70 percent reduction in the likelihood of recidivism.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based and hedged as preliminary rather than asserted as settled fact; supports the conclusion proportionately.

rigor.statement: Evidence from overseas jurisdictions has indicated that sex offender registers have no or very little impact on child sex reoffending rates or public safety unless they are supported by an active risk management framework.
rigor.explanation: Concedes contrary evidence and conditions the claim on a stated mechanism (risk management framework), rather than overclaiming register benefits.

rigor.statement: The seven additional qualifying offences will not apply with retrospective effect. They will only apply if a person commits one or more of the additional qualifying offences on or after the date the bill commences.
rigor.explanation: Directly engages the section 7 Bill of Rights concern and explains how the design limits the retrospective incursion.

rigor.statement: The bill represents a careful balance that recognises the right of the community to be protected from child sex offenders as well as the rights of the offenders themselves.
rigor.explanation: Presents the issue as an explicit rights-balancing exercise rather than an absolute claim.

rigor.statement: It is a more onerous obligation, but it’s an obligation of the same kind. It’s not a massive change. … Again, it is more onerous, but it’s a change in degree rather than a change in kind.
rigor.explanation: Structured legal reasoning distinguishing change 'in degree' from 'in kind' to weigh the retrospectivity concern; premises support the modest-harm conclusion.

rigor.statement: It was reassuring to me to be told that, whilst the data and the studies aren’t absolutely robust at this stage, there was very promising evidence that this kind of intervention had a genuine reduction in offending and, consequently, a reduction in the numbers of victims.
rigor.explanation: Updates position on evidence while explicitly noting the data 'aren’t absolutely robust'; caveats match the strength of the claim.

rigor.statement: While preliminary findings from PhD research commissioned by the Police indicate that the register may reduce the likelihood of reoffending by 40 to 70 percent, the final findings will not be published until 2026. Further longitudinal study on recidivism is not due for interim reporting until 2027.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly weighs the evidence as preliminary and calls for evaluation over time; conclusion is proportionate to the evidence.

rigor.statement: The key question for this House is whether we as legislators think this conflict with the NZBORA is justified. The Attorney-General did not, and it’s important that we consider this advice really carefully.
rigor.explanation: Frames the decision as an explicit justified-limitation test under the Bill of Rights, engaging the actual legal question.

rigor.statement: How can you even contemplate putting the perpetrators’ rights ahead of a young person not being sexually violated?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy/strawman: recasts a nuanced concern about retrospective NZBORA breaches as choosing offenders' rights over children's safety.

rigor.statement: Sometimes we have to put the most common-sense thing at the forefront of our decision making. The biggest common-sense issue here is the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill, with the purpose of keeping children and young people in our community safe.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to 'common sense' substitutes for engaging the rights and evidence questions others raised; asserts rather than argues.

rigor.statement: When you have an offender who tells you in his interview, admitting to the crime, that it was OK, he always gave her a bag of lollies afterwards, you get to know the evilness that exists in that kind of mentality.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single vivid anecdote and an appeal to emotion ('evilness') to motivate the policy rather than evidence about the register's effect.

civility.statement: The bill represents a careful balance that recognises the right of the community to be protected from child sex offenders as well as the rights of the offenders themselves.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges offenders' rights alongside community protection; measured, non-inflammatory framing of a charged topic.

civility.statement: Look, we support this bill, and it’s actually a really good example … of good justice policy because it is looking at risk and taking all reasonable steps to ameliorate it. It’s not waiting for a disaster to happen and waiting for crime to occur.
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused support for an opponent's legislation.

civility.statement: It is a more onerous obligation, but it’s an obligation of the same kind. It’s not a massive change. … Again, it is more onerous, but it’s a change in degree rather than a change in kind.
civility.explanation: Engages the Attorney-General's objection on its merits without disparagement.

civility.statement: I must say, I do respect the Attorney-General’s opinion, and I know that it’s well-thought-out and that her team in justice do a good job of that analysis.
civility.explanation: Explicit respect for those he disagrees with; models disagreement without denigration.

civility.statement: The key question for this House is whether we as legislators think this conflict with the NZBORA is justified. The Attorney-General did not, and it’s important that we consider this advice really carefully.
civility.explanation: Treats the rights objection seriously and respectfully rather than dismissing it.

civility.statement: There was the talk of inconsistencies with the bill, but, my goodness, the inconsistencies within that speech are actually gobsmacking. It’s left me speechless, to be perfectly honest.
civility.explanation: Mocks the opposing speech as 'gobsmacking' rather than engaging its substance; dismissive tone over policy critique.

civility.statement: How can you even contemplate putting the perpetrators’ rights ahead of a young person not being sexually violated?
civility.explanation: Misrepresents the opponent's position and imputes bad priorities rather than addressing the actual argument.

civility.statement: This is an important piece of legislation, and, as the Minister of Police talked about, it is administrative in nature, but it is a very important piece of legislation. I will applaud Minister Chhour on her previous contribution—that this is about putting the children at the heart.
civility.explanation: Courteous, acknowledges colleagues; restates the bill's character without attacking others.

civility.statement: But as the member on the other side of the House said, this is also about risk mitigation. This is about doing something smart, and this is why our register has been successful and will continue to be successful, because it does allow for that risk mitigation component and allow the offenders themselves to contribute to controlling their behaviour.
civility.explanation: Credits an opponent's contribution and engages the substantive risk-mitigation rationale.

charisma.statement: The bill represents a careful balance that recognises the right of the community to be protected from child sex offenders as well as the rights of the offenders themselves.
charisma.explanation: Frames the bill as a reasonable middle ground, inviting broad support rather than rallying one side.

charisma.statement: Look, we support this bill, and it’s actually a really good example … of good justice policy because it is looking at risk and taking all reasonable steps to ameliorate it. It’s not waiting for a disaster to happen and waiting for crime to occur.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party endorsement of a government bill, framed around shared goals (preventing harm) rather than partisan point-scoring.

charisma.statement: I must say, I do respect the Attorney-General’s opinion, and I know that it’s well-thought-out and that her team in justice do a good job of that analysis.
charisma.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of others' work helps build cross-bench goodwill.

charisma.statement: But what I am saying is, perhaps, we should learn from this and start thinking about where else in the justice sector we can use interventions which identify risk and intervene before the event rather than after the event.
charisma.explanation: Invites a forward-looking, cross-sector conversation grounded in a shared preventive principle.

charisma.statement: That means honouring our cross-party agreement to honour Te Aorerekura, that action plan and that work plan, working with communities for prevention so that we can eliminate family and sexual violence in Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a cross-party agreement and shared prevention goal, seeking common ground across the House.

charisma.statement: There was the talk of inconsistencies with the bill, but, my goodness, the inconsistencies within that speech are actually gobsmacking. It’s left me speechless, to be perfectly honest.
charisma.explanation: Confrontational and directed at riling her own side against the Greens, not persuading or bridging.

charisma.statement: How can you even contemplate putting the perpetrators’ rights ahead of a young person not being sexually violated?
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them, alienating framing that shuts down the cross-party dialogue she claims to want.

charisma.statement: At the end of the day, this is a Government that I am proud to work with, that puts the victim first and the perpetrator second.
charisma.explanation: A confident applause line for her own side that implicitly casts opponents as prioritising perpetrators.

charisma.statement: This is an important piece of legislation, and, as the Minister of Police talked about, it is administrative in nature, but it is a very important piece of legislation. I will applaud Minister Chhour on her previous contribution—that this is about putting the children at the heart.
charisma.explanation: Warm and affirming, though the appreciation is directed at coalition partners rather than across the aisle.

charisma.statement: But as the member on the other side of the House said, this is also about risk mitigation. This is about doing something smart, and this is why our register has been successful and will continue to be successful, because it does allow for that risk mitigation component and allow the offenders themselves to contribute to controlling their behaviour.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly builds on an opposition member's point, reaching across the House to frame shared ground on risk mitigation.

authenticity.statement: It was reassuring to me to be told that, whilst the data and the studies aren’t absolutely robust at this stage, there was very promising evidence that this kind of intervention had a genuine reduction in offending and, consequently, a reduction in the numbers of victims.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his stated prior scepticism — he changes his stance because the evidence shifted, and says so, rather than contradicting himself.

rigor.statement: So I think that was a bit of a missed opportunity to put that in the primary legislation, which would have strengthened the bill.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned constitutional/legislative argument: criteria are broadly agreeable and could sit in primary legislation which gets more scrutiny than regulations; conclusion follows from the premise, no fallacy.

rigor.statement: As 90 percent of our building products are imported, we may as well be importing ones of a higher standard from countries that have better building standards.
rigor.explanation: Uses a factual premise (near-total import dependence) to defuse the concern that the bill increases imports; logical and evidence-anchored.

rigor.statement: But it ended up costing about the same amount as a building built out of New Zealand products because of the hurdles of compliance. Every time an inspector turned up, you had to get 12,000 pages out and go through, “Was this allowed?”, “Was this not allowed?”
rigor.explanation: First-hand anecdote used to illustrate compliance cost; persuasive lived-experience evidence but a single case, and '12,000 pages' is likely hyperbolic.

rigor.statement: That's not a great way, though, of getting house prices down for people who want to buy them, because as soon as you start doing that, what happens is that the cost of building starts becoming much more expensive than the cost of buying something that's already there, and people just say, “I'm not going to build new houses.”
rigor.explanation: Coherent economic argument: falling values below replacement cost deters new construction, so price falls don't solve supply; premises entail the conclusion.

rigor.statement: So should the Government, at the very least, be standing alongside the people who are reliant on these products which are approved through this scheme if something goes wrong?
rigor.explanation: Builds a liability argument step by step (product approved overseas, then by the Minister/ministry on the Crown's behalf) to conclude the Crown should share responsibility; logically structured.

rigor.statement: No one wants to be hobbled by too much red tape, but don't take away too much, then you're going to have to apologise for what you took away before. So it is about a watch, analyse, assess, so we're watching this progress all the time, because ultimately, if we fail, we fail our communities, we fail our people.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable balancing argument that deregulation has a floor of safety; sound in direction but general and not evidence-backed.

rigor.statement: That means the Government then needs to own up to its other decisions that are actually leaving people living in mouldy, cold, damp homes. We shouldn't be taking this bill in isolation; we should be seeing it as part of a holistic project.
rigor.explanation: Argues the bill must be judged in the context of other housing policy levers; a reasonable systemic point, though the 'mouldy, cold, damp homes' link is asserted rather than evidenced here.

rigor.statement: But the report identifies that the Regulations Review Committee finally agreed that, actually, given the urgency that sometimes might be needed to address some of the concerns around criteria changing, in a circumstance where criteria may need to be changed at short notice in order to prevent or mitigate risk when it comes to building failure or product use that might be subject to failure, that actually it was appropriate in those circumstances for that provision to sit with the regulations through secondary legislation.
rigor.explanation: Explains, via the committee's stated reasoning, why urgency/risk-mitigation justifies secondary legislation — directly rebutting Genter's concern with a coherent rationale.

rigor.statement: If we think back to the report—I think it was 2022—from the Commerce Commission that talked about the lack of competition in the building sector in some products, actually increasing the number of products available will drive down prices, will stop people being able to just ramp up their prices when there's a limited supply in the market, and that makes it cheaper for the average Kiwi household to build a house.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the argument in the 2022 Commerce Commission study and applies standard competition economics (more supply → downward price pressure); logically sound though the price effect is asserted.

rigor.statement: When that door got slammed shut—back in those awful COVID years—on our supply chain, if people hadn't worked out how big an issue supply chain resilience was, well, they worked it out pretty quickly, because suddenly we made it way too hard for shipping and freight companies to come to New Zealand. Supply lines dried up. If we have more supply coming in, if we have different supply chains, then, if something would happen that would interrupt one shipping lane, maybe another one can carry it and we can bring in different products.
rigor.explanation: Uses the COVID supply-chain disruption as evidence that diversified supply improves resilience; a reasonable, well-structured inference.

rigor.statement: So you put the three together: more products gets us cheaper homes; consenting pathways gets us faster homes; and the third part, around consenting authorities, ensures this will be done.
rigor.explanation: Organised premise-to-effect summary of the mechanism; coherent, though each causal link is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Very low productivity by international standards—in an industry which itself is plagued by low productivity globally. The most terrible health and safety record in the construction industry, in New Zealand. A demonstrative lack of competition and the presence of anti-competitive practices in the market.
rigor.explanation: Lays out the sector's structural problems as premises before endorsing the bill; grounded in known issues, if delivered as a rapid list rather than fully evidenced.

rigor.statement: In fact, plasterboard is a celebrated case study of how incumbent market players used their market position to keep out products that were highly successful internationally but unable to get a toehold in this little market at the bottom of the South Pacific—to the detriment of the final consumers, the homeowners, homebuyers.
rigor.explanation: Uses plasterboard as a concrete case study to substantiate the anti-competition claim, linking market structure to consumer harm; evidence-based reasoning.

rigor.statement: Arena Williams mentioned earlier in the debate with plasterboard the fact that we have this quite unusual practice in New Zealand of using plasterboard as a structural material when it gets tacked up on the framing. It's not used in that way overseas, so we have to be careful about the way that materials are used to make sure that the new materials are appropriate given the way that they might be used here.
rigor.explanation: Raises a specific, technically valid caveat (NZ uses plasterboard structurally as bracing, unlike overseas) to argue overseas approvals must be applied carefully; sound reasoning.

rigor.statement: We often forget, but New Zealand is a really small trading nation in the scheme of the world. We are a small trading nation, so anything we can do to remove barriers to high-quality products entering the New Zealand market, to increase consumer choice, and to increase competition and provide greater resilience to the supply disruptions is a really good thing.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable argument linking small-market status to the value of removing barriers; coherent but the benefits are asserted as a list.

rigor.statement: But Labour is cautious about the product substitutions for plasterboard being approved in groups. They are used in a structurally different way in other countries. It may be that the rules in other countries for plasterboard should not apply here because of the way it is used by New Zealand house builders.
rigor.explanation: Applies the specific technical concern (NZ's structural use of plasterboard) to argue against blanket group approvals; a reasoned, qualified caution.

civility.statement: So I think that was a bit of a missed opportunity to put that in the primary legislation, which would have strengthened the bill.
civility.explanation: Substantive critique of the bill's drafting approach, not a personal attack; engages the policy design directly.

civility.statement: if only building Treaty relationships, or building hapū and iwi relationships had the same interest and effort that this Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards, and Certification Schemes) Amendment Bill had.
civility.explanation: A pointed but good-humoured jab at the Government's Treaty engagement; criticises priorities rather than attacking a person, though it is a rhetorical dig.

civility.statement: That means the Government then needs to own up to its other decisions that are actually leaving people living in mouldy, cold, damp homes. We shouldn't be taking this bill in isolation; we should be seeing it as part of a holistic project.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of Government housing outcomes but aimed at decisions/policy, not personal attack.

veracity.statement: As 90 percent of our building products are imported, we may as well be importing ones of a higher standard from countries that have better building standards.
veracity.explanation: The '90 percent imported' figure is directionally accurate for NZ's high reliance on imported building materials, though the precise share is uncertain; the inference is reasonable.

veracity.statement: It was incredibly cheap material to bring in; a piece of plasterboard was $10 compared to the same purchased plasterboard in New Zealand for $25 a sheet.
veracity.explanation: Plausible anecdotal price comparison consistent with known NZ plasterboard price concerns, but a single unverified personal example.

veracity.statement: In Wellington City, where I have the sad pleasure at the moment of owning a house, the house prices have dropped by about 25 percent, or the house values have dropped by about 25 percent, over the last three years—I think it's 22 percent, to be more exact.
veracity.explanation: Wellington house values did fall roughly 20–25% from their 2021–22 peak; the figure and his self-correction to ~22% are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: One of the things he did say in introducing this legislation a while back is that the cost of building a house in New Zealand is about 50 percent more than the cost of building a house over the Ditch in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Repeats a commonly cited comparison; broadly in line with estimates that NZ build costs substantially exceed Australia's, though '50 percent' is a contested round figure.

veracity.statement: He also said that the productivity has not improved since 1985—1985.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the well-documented long-run stagnation of NZ construction-sector productivity, though 'not improved since 1985' is a stylised claim attributed to the Minister.

veracity.statement: But for those of us—for example, I was in local government for much of that time—that cost this city something like $150 million trying to clean up the mess that was made by substandard products and by substandard processes which were put in place to build those things.
veracity.explanation: Plausible order-of-magnitude figure for Wellington's leaky-homes liability from someone who was in local government at the time; hedged ('something like') and unverified here.

veracity.statement: It's wild to me when I've met peers from much colder countries who come here and they say they experience, for example, the winter here in a much more severe way than they would in their own home countries.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the well-documented poor thermal performance of NZ housing making indoor winters feel colder than in better-insulated colder-climate countries; anecdotal but well-supported.

veracity.statement: There were 44 submissions that were received. Many of them, actually, were quite technical in nature, and then, of course, we had nine submitters that provided oral evidence to the committee.
veracity.explanation: Specific procedural facts about the select committee process (44 submissions, 9 oral), the kind of detail readily verifiable and consistent with other speakers.

veracity.statement: If we think back to the report—I think it was 2022—from the Commerce Commission that talked about the lack of competition in the building sector in some products, actually increasing the number of products available will drive down prices, will stop people being able to just ramp up their prices when there's a limited supply in the market, and that makes it cheaper for the average Kiwi household to build a house.
veracity.explanation: The 2022 Commerce Commission market study did find competition in key building products was not working well; accurately characterised.

veracity.statement: Very low productivity by international standards—in an industry which itself is plagued by low productivity globally. The most terrible health and safety record in the construction industry, in New Zealand. A demonstrative lack of competition and the presence of anti-competitive practices in the market.
veracity.explanation: The NZ construction sector's low productivity, poor safety record and competition problems are well-documented; broadly accurate, though 'most terrible' is rhetorical emphasis.

veracity.statement: In fact, plasterboard is a celebrated case study of how incumbent market players used their market position to keep out products that were highly successful internationally but unable to get a toehold in this little market at the bottom of the South Pacific—to the detriment of the final consumers, the homeowners, homebuyers.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the well-known plasterboard/Gib market-dominance concerns highlighted by the Commerce Commission study.

veracity.statement: It was the market study in 2022 under our Government—as with most of the good things coming through this House these days, the genesis is in the last Labour Government and it's good to see support from across the House for this bill.
veracity.explanation: True that the 2022 Commerce Commission market study originated under the Labour Government; the sweeping 'most of the good things' rider is partisan hyperbole that overstates the point.

veracity.statement: Arena Williams mentioned earlier in the debate with plasterboard the fact that we have this quite unusual practice in New Zealand of using plasterboard as a structural material when it gets tacked up on the framing. It's not used in that way overseas, so we have to be careful about the way that materials are used to make sure that the new materials are appropriate given the way that they might be used here.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ does use plasterboard for bracing in a way that differs from many overseas uses, a genuine standards-transfer risk.

veracity.statement: One of the points that hasn't quite been canvassed yet, though, is around the 2022 market study, done by the Commerce Commission, on residential building supplies, where they said they found that competition for the supply of key building products was not working as well as it could be.
veracity.explanation: Accurately restates the Commerce Commission's 2022 residential building supplies market study finding on weak competition.

veracity.statement: We often forget, but New Zealand is a really small trading nation in the scheme of the world. We are a small trading nation, so anything we can do to remove barriers to high-quality products entering the New Zealand market, to increase consumer choice, and to increase competition and provide greater resilience to the supply disruptions is a really good thing.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of NZ as a small trading nation, used correctly to motivate reducing import barriers.

veracity.statement: Back in December of 2022, the Commerce Commission released the final report of its residential building supplies market study, which found, of course, that competition for the supply and acquisition of key building products is not working as well as it could.
veracity.explanation: Precisely accurate: the Commerce Commission's residential building supplies market study final report was released in December 2022 with that finding.

veracity.statement: Related to this legislation and housing overall, of course, is the 200,000 apprentices and trainees that were funded under the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the scale of Labour's apprenticeship/trades-training support (e.g. Apprenticeship Boost and free trades training), though '200,000' is a large headline figure that bundles several schemes.

charisma.statement: I hope that the Minister will consider having some cross-party consultation on those regulations and ensure that there's very thorough consultation with the sector, but also the different players across the sector, not just the few big ones but the people who are really at the cutting edge of being passionate about and wanting to deliver more environmentally friendly, healthy homes.
charisma.explanation: Opposition MP inviting cross-party consultation and broad inclusion; consensus-seeking and bridge-building rather than combative.

charisma.statement: The Hon Julie Anne Genter just made some comments that it would be lovely to see more things built in New Zealand—100 percent agree. That's why we're New Zealand First.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly agrees with an opposition MP and finds common ground before pivoting to a party line; acknowledges an opponent's valid point.

charisma.statement: No one wants to be hobbled by too much red tape, but don't take away too much, then you're going to have to apologise for what you took away before. So it is about a watch, analyse, assess, so we're watching this progress all the time, because ultimately, if we fail, we fail our communities, we fail our people.
charisma.explanation: Offers qualified support while framing shared stakes ('we fail our people'), a measured, bring-along tone.

charisma.statement: The Green Party is supporting this bill, but we continue to encourage the Government to set a framework so that the decisions that the Minister is able to do in relationship to what this bill prescribes have some good guiding principles to make this bill enduring and so that it can adapt over the years.
charisma.explanation: Opposition support paired with a constructive suggestion; collaborative rather than combative framing.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge our colleague Cameron Luxton, who actually brought quite an insight to the select committee as someone who, prior to coming to this place, was actively involved in this particular sector.
charisma.explanation: A Labour MP crediting a Government-side colleague's expertise; cross-party goodwill and consensus tone.

charisma.statement: It was the market study in 2022 under our Government—as with most of the good things coming through this House these days, the genesis is in the last Labour Government and it's good to see support from across the House for this bill.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes cross-House support for the bill, a consensual note, undercut slightly by the partisan credit-claim.

authenticity.statement: One of the main things that even motivated me to get involved in politics after I moved here was seeing the quality of buildings and infrastructure in New Zealand and thinking, “Wow. Things could actually be a lot better with some changes from central government policy, regulations, and funding.”
authenticity.explanation: Ties her support for building-quality reform to a long-stated personal motivation, consistent with her Green record on housing/energy efficiency, though unverifiable from the text alone.

authenticity.statement: Because I built 16 homes before I came to this job—just before I came, by the way—in a tiny little place, all the way in Te Kao. Sixteen homes. And here's how we built them: we built them with our own product out of our forests. We built them with our own kaimahi.
authenticity.explanation: Her advocacy for locally sourced, self-built healthy homes is backed by her own prior action of doing exactly that in Te Kao.

authenticity.statement: It was the market study in 2022 under our Government—as with most of the good things coming through this House these days, the genesis is in the last Labour Government and it's good to see support from across the House for this bill.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit consistent with Labour's actual record of commissioning the study, though framed to maximise partisan ownership.

authenticity.statement: Related to this legislation and housing overall, of course, is the 200,000 apprentices and trainees that were funded under the last Government.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's actual record of investing in apprenticeships, aligning the party's stated priority with a delivered programme.

specificity.statement: But I'm sure that everyone in New Zealand would like to see and could understand the economic benefit to New Zealand of us processing more of our wood here, for example, for cross-laminated timber, which could then be used in sustainable buildings as framing instead of seal—low-carbon, sustainably forested, locally produced.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (onshore processing of cross-laminated timber for framing) but no figures, timeframe, or funding detail.

specificity.statement: It was incredibly cheap material to bring in; a piece of plasterboard was $10 compared to the same purchased plasterboard in New Zealand for $25 a sheet.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($10 vs $25 a sheet) drawn from a specific first-hand example.

specificity.statement: But it ended up costing about the same amount as a building built out of New Zealand products because of the hurdles of compliance. Every time an inspector turned up, you had to get 12,000 pages out and go through, “Was this allowed?”, “Was this not allowed?”
specificity.explanation: Concrete illustrative detail about compliance burden, though the page figure is illustrative rather than precise.

specificity.statement: We're going to get affordable housing back, tradies are going to be happy, we're going to get that sort of lifestyle in New Zealand that we expect of a property-owning democracy.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe attached to the outcome.

specificity.statement: In Wellington City, where I have the sad pleasure at the moment of owning a house, the house prices have dropped by about 25 percent, or the house values have dropped by about 25 percent, over the last three years—I think it's 22 percent, to be more exact.
specificity.explanation: Concrete location, magnitude (~22–25%) and timeframe (three years).

specificity.statement: But for those of us—for example, I was in local government for much of that time—that cost this city something like $150 million trying to clean up the mess that was made by substandard products and by substandard processes which were put in place to build those things.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (~$150 million) and cause (substandard products/processes).

specificity.statement: What it does is it reduces the expected time to process and to recognise those overseas products. Something like two years to about three to eight months is the expectation.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the expected effect (from ~two years to three–eight months), a concrete mechanism-linked figure.

specificity.statement: Because I built 16 homes before I came to this job—just before I came, by the way—in a tiny little place, all the way in Te Kao. Sixteen homes. And here's how we built them: we built them with our own product out of our forests. We built them with our own kaimahi.
specificity.explanation: Concrete: 16 homes, named location (Te Kao), method (own forest product, own kaimahi, local collaboration).

specificity.statement: So we had an opportunity, for example, in the Kāinga Ora building programme to really sit in place and retain our construction workforce to develop them and support them so that, alongside what this bill is aiming to do, we have a really well-supported, well-paid construction workforce that allows us to build the best possible buildings that we can have in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete lever (Kāinga Ora programme and workforce retention) but no figures or defined mechanism for how it would be delivered.

specificity.statement: There were 44 submissions that were received. Many of them, actually, were quite technical in nature, and then, of course, we had nine submitters that provided oral evidence to the committee.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts of submissions and oral submitters.

specificity.statement: When that door got slammed shut—back in those awful COVID years—on our supply chain, if people hadn't worked out how big an issue supply chain resilience was, well, they worked it out pretty quickly, because suddenly we made it way too hard for shipping and freight companies to come to New Zealand. Supply lines dried up. If we have more supply coming in, if we have different supply chains, then, if something would happen that would interrupt one shipping lane, maybe another one can carry it and we can bring in different products.
specificity.explanation: Explains a concrete mechanism (multiple shipping lanes/supply chains providing redundancy) though without figures.

specificity.statement: So you put the three together: more products gets us cheaper homes; consenting pathways gets us faster homes; and the third part, around consenting authorities, ensures this will be done.
specificity.explanation: Cleanly maps the bill's three components to distinct claimed effects (cheaper, faster, enforced), a structured and concrete account.

specificity.statement: Back in December of 2022, the Commerce Commission released the final report of its residential building supplies market study, which found, of course, that competition for the supply and acquisition of key building products is not working as well as it could.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the report, the date (December 2022) and the finding.

specificity.statement: We discussed the issue of liability extensively, and I'm encouraged with the Minister's direction of travel, which will be to do a review around the liability settings.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete next step (a review of liability settings) but gives no scope, timeframe, or detail.

divination.statement: We're going to get affordable housing back, tradies are going to be happy, we're going to get that sort of lifestyle in New Zealand that we expect of a property-owning democracy.
divination.explanation: Predicts affordable housing returns from this reform; optimistic and unquantified given building products are only one modest cost factor.

divination.statement: If we think back to the report—I think it was 2022—from the Commerce Commission that talked about the lack of competition in the building sector in some products, actually increasing the number of products available will drive down prices, will stop people being able to just ramp up their prices when there's a limited supply in the market, and that makes it cheaper for the average Kiwi household to build a house.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased product supply will drive down building prices; directionally plausible on competition grounds but magnitude uncertain since products are one of many cost drivers.

strength.statement: Because I built 16 homes before I came to this job—just before I came, by the way—in a tiny little place, all the way in Te Kao. Sixteen homes. And here's how we built them: we built them with our own product out of our forests. We built them with our own kaimahi.
strength.explanation: Describes concretely delivered homes (16, built with local timber and workforce) for which she was responsible — words backed by demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: Related to this legislation and housing overall, of course, is the 200,000 apprentices and trainees that were funded under the last Government.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered workforce-funding programme under the last Government; a real, implemented policy, though the headline number aggregates multiple initiatives.

specificity.statement: Offenders will now be required to report that a child will be residing at the same address at least 48 hours before that in fact occurs, rather than 72 hours previously.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism with exact figures (48 hours vs previous 72 hours) and the precise change being made.

specificity.statement: Registered offenders must now go and report their intended travel overseas at least seven days in advance, instead of the 48-hour requirement. They will also be required to report their return to New Zealand within 72 hours electronically, or they're able to do this by telephone as well.
specificity.explanation: Precise timeframes (7 days, 72 hours), the old requirement, and reporting methods named.

specificity.statement: While it's great to see this bill here, it would be great to see other great things provided to our children as well, like a hot, healthy lunch; like a warm, dry home; and making sure that their mums and dads earn enough money to be able to pay for the bills.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at desirable outcomes (lunches, warm homes, higher pay) but names no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Personally, in my view, I don't really care if a few rights are breached if our children are protected. If people have done something to put our children in harm—I'm sorry, but, personally, I don't care if a few rights are breached in our pursuit of keeping children protected.
specificity.explanation: Emotive stance with no detail on which rights, what balancing test, or how protection is achieved.

specificity.statement: Certainly, preliminary results show that there's something as robust as a 40 to 70 percent reduction in likelihood of reoffending when they look at the effectiveness and the efficacy of that register.
