What does that mean for those who are—if the definition is what I suspect it will be with respect to settlements—yet to settle
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused questioning aimed at improving the bill.

authenticity.statement: as a migrant who grew up speaking English as a second language, I could not understand a lot of things. And, yes, I was that child who interpreted for my parents, but how many times do you actually see parents going through pieces of legislation?
authenticity.explanation: Personal lived experience consistent with her stated position on the topic.

authenticity.statement: I worked in Child, Youth and Family Services—which was called CYFs back then—in 1989 and 1990. I registered as one of the first family group conference coordinators and was a care and protection social worker and youth justice social worker
authenticity.explanation: Grounds her advocacy in relevant lived professional experience consistent with her stance.

divination.statement: its repeal will not only breach Te Tiriti but actively put tamariki Māori at risk.
divination.explanation: Open-ended prediction of harm to tamariki Māori; directionally supported by the Tribunal and royal-commission evidence, but magnitude and timeframe are uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: First of all, I’ll just give an answer to the Hon Willow-Jean Prime around the reporting and the obligations of assessing outcomes for Māori children. This bill does not alter those obligations in any way.
forthrightness.explanation: Prime asked specifically about the statutory duty in 7AA(2)(a) to reduce disparities, not reporting; the Minister pivots to reporting obligations, which Prime repeatedly flags as not the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: I do not feel it’s necessary to have separate obligations based on race. We should be treating all our children with the same level of respect and care and making sure that they are all taken care of, in a way.
forthrightness.explanation: Does eventually give a reason for the repeal (opposition to race-based obligations), though still not identifying where the specific CE duty goes.

forthrightness.statement: I'm very proud of the efforts of our Government to help New Zealanders with the cost of living. That's why we're getting control of Government spending, that's why inflation's coming down, that's why interest rates are coming down. I just note that that member didn't support tax relief for the first time in 14 years for low and middle income workers. We're doing everything we can to put money back in Kiwis' pockets.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why the Government is raising power bills by up to $25/month, he never addresses transmission charges and pivots to generic talking points plus an attack on Labour.

forthrightness.statement: What is improving the situation for Kiwis' households is making sure that inflation is coming down, interest rates are coming down, and the economy is starting to grow. It was fantastic to see the economy grow at 0.7 percent in quarter four last year. Importantly, Labour didn't vote for tax relief, Labour didn't vote for Working for Families credits, and Labour didn't vote for FamilyBoost.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether higher car registration, parking-fine taxes and insurance levies increase or decrease cost of living, he answers neither and recites unrelated talking points.

forthrightness.statement: We don't set insurance premiums, but what we can control is the environment—which is an economy that's incredibly well managed—to make sure that we're bringing spending down, to make sure that we're bringing inflation down and interest rates down, and that the economy's growing so people have more money in their pockets and they can access higher-income jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the household insurance levy the Government is itself consulting on raising, he deflects with 'we don't set insurance premiums' and generic economic lines.

forthrightness.statement: It's a Government agency. They have a separate board; they can make their own decision.
forthrightness.explanation: After being corrected that the question was about the levy the Government does set, he offloads responsibility to the agency's board rather than answering the cost-of-living question.

forthrightness.statement: I'm proud of the fact that we are increasing entitlements by roughly the amount of inflation. But what I'm also proud about is the fact that real wage growth has grown for five quarters in a row, after declining for 13 quarters in a row under that Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether below-inflation minimum-wage rises increase the cost-of-living crisis for low earners, he partly concedes the point on entitlements but pivots to a favourable wage-growth comparison.

forthrightness.statement: In answering part of that question—my focus is on making sure we run a great economy so New Zealanders can get ahead. We inherited a situation where the economy was run into the ground. We are making sure that we do everything we can to get growth back into New Zealand so we get money back into Kiwis' pockets so they can get out of the mess that we've inherited thanks to that last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly answers only 'part of' a detailed question listing multiple fee increases, and retreats to blaming the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: On Sunday, I outlined the Government's next steps to drive more competition in the supermarket sector and deliver better grocery prices for Kiwi shoppers. I announced two things: first, a formal request for information (RFI) process to identify what is needed to support a significant, national-scale competitor to enter our grocery market. Second, I announced that I have commissioned specialist external advice on ways in which the existing supermarket duopoly could be restructured to improve competition.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about her recent supermarket announcements, itemising both concrete steps.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the first thing I would note is that our Cabinet is mindful of the fact that the minimum wage is paid by employers—small businesses and medium businesses up and down the country—and we are conscious that in recent years, they have undertaken a very difficult period in which they have faced significant inflation and rising interest rates. We want to ensure that they are now in a context where, given the choice between letting a worker go and hiring a new worker, we minimise the costs that they face and ensure that we do not put New Zealanders' jobs at risk.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a 35c/hour minimum-wage rise below inflation makes a difference to people's lives, she reframes around employer costs and never addresses the worker's living standards.

forthrightness.statement: In our first Budget, what we did was we ensured that we were able to offer tax relief to millions of New Zealanders, fully funded by savings across government, and what we can say is that that has allowed many New Zealanders to have more money in their bank accounts than would otherwise be the case.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether removing free public transport for under-25s and cutting subsidies affects quality of life, she pivots entirely to Budget tax relief.

forthrightness.statement: Well, picking up on the last part of that question, it's important to note that minimum-wage workers are in families with a range of different household circumstances, and what we have been advised is that in many cases, those workers will be eligible for additional Working for Families and accommodation supplement support, such that in some cases, a minimum wage increase will actually be eroded by the abatement in those payments that would occur otherwise.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages one strand of the multi-part question but sidesteps the direct challenge about rising costs versus a 35c raise.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm incredibly proud that in a very short period of time, this Government has ended what I think is one of the blights on New Zealand's social policies—the fact that we have taken 2,000 children out of squalid motel rooms and we have put them into proper, dry homes; the fact that we have taken 5,000 people off the State social housing wait-list who are desperate to get a home—that is fantastic.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he is more proud of between rising homelessness and cutting service funding, he ignores the framing and asserts his own achievements.

forthrightness.statement: There will always be Government support for people in need of housing. That has not changed.
forthrightness.explanation: A flat reassurance that dodges the specific question about denials of support causing rangatahi to sleep rough.

forthrightness.statement: Well, under iReX, both yards were proposed to lift by a metre at huge expense. There's a lot of stone and concrete with new buildings, roads, and a rail on top. It was far beyond the modest alterations we had planned in 2020. They said lifting yards would mean extreme weather events would not disturb the ferry operations. That would have cost hundreds and billions of dollars alone. Here's the point: why build a halo around a car yard when you could increase the culverts to stop the build-up of water in the first place?
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how the marshalling yards differ from iReX with a specific engineering contrast.

forthrightness.statement: Later this year. We will not approach this like Wellington Water, by which we mean revealing our budget while negotiating the price. That turns a buyer's market into a seller's market. When these ship and port agreements, when they are signed, the member will know the total cost and the shares between the Government and the ports.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains why he won't disclose costs and when they will be known, but declines to give the actual figure asked about.

forthrightness.statement: The reality was that Nicola Willis, as Minister of Finance, inherited a nightmare. She was facing a blowout which Treasury forecast to go to $4 billion and beyond when she was going to be— I know it's rubbish. That's your specialty—that's why I'm talking about it. It's total rubbish.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether his plan beats the earlier deal, he defends the earlier Minister and attacks the questioner rather than making a clean comparison.

forthrightness.statement: I won't comment on individual cases, as that member will understand, given investigations that are ongoing, but I just say that I am very, very proud of the police, and I back our police.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to address the specific alleged incidents (with an ongoing-investigation justification) and substitutes a general endorsement of police.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'll take my advice from the Police, and if that is a tool that they wish to have, I back them with any tools that they need to do their job. But I'm very proud that our police are out there on the beat. They've increased the beat police by 30 percent, and the public are feeling safer in their businesses, in their homes, and in their community, and that's a good thing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will support mandatory body cameras, he neither commits nor refuses, deferring to police advice and pivoting to beat numbers.

forthrightness.statement: I don't agree, with statements that I have seen, that there is structural, racial discrimination in the Police at all.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear, direct answer to whether he accepts discrimination in the Police, unlike his surrounding evasions.

forthrightness.statement: Look, well, there's no decisions that have been made, but I just say to that member, we want to make sure we get our tax and regulatory settings as good and as competitive as they can be so that we can unleash growth in this economy. We want growth, growth, growth. We want that above everything else.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government is considering $1.2 billion in corporate tax cuts given 46% of retail firms paid no income tax, he offers no rationale on the figures and retreats to a growth slogan.

forthrightness.statement: I disagree with that member because, as I said, 98.1 percent of those who are on benefit are complying with their work obligations. They're taking the steps they need to. The economic conditions we inherited mean it's a very challenging labour market, but, despite that, there has been an 11 percent increase on last year of people leaving the jobseeker benefit and going to a job.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to the Salvation Army's view that sanctions had little to do with people finding jobs, she cites a compliance statistic that does not address the effectiveness-of-sanctions question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I've said, it would be great for this side of the House if we didn't inherit the unfortunate economic climate that we did. We always knew—and Treasury forecasts from the previous Government as well as from our Government expected unemployment rates to rise. That is indisputable. What is on record, though, is our success in actually getting people off the jobseeker benefit into work. We're still ambitious. We have a target—50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker is a target that's worth working for.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the community can have confidence given 22,000 more jobseekers and the Kinleith closure, she does not address Kinleith and reframes around forecasts and her target.

forthrightness.statement: The New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey Cycle 7, taken from October 2023 to October 2024, showed that, for the first time since the introduction of the Police module to the survey, the proportion of people with high trust and confidence in Police increased from 67 percent to 69 percent. This coincided with the proportion of people with no trust and confidence in Police dropping to its lowest level, at 2 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the friendly question about reports on trust and confidence in Police.

forthrightness.statement: The delegation for school lunches is the responsibility of the Associate Minister, and any decisions around that are decisions for the Prime Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she won't step in to fix the lunch programme given evidence of nutritionally inadequate meals, she deflects entirely to delegation and the PM.

forthrightness.statement: In response to the second part of the question, I understand that yesterday, I think, around 112,000 meals were delivered, and the on-time delivery rate was 99.5 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly supplies the specific delivery figures asked for by Seymour.

forthrightness.statement: We think profit is a good thing. Excessive profit is a bad thing.
forthrightness.explanation: A concise, direct answer to whether he thinks profit is good in the supermarket context, drawing a clear distinction.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member seems to have a challenge or a problem with organisations making a profit. My point is that that is a good thing. They are investing, they're taking risks, they're investing capital in order to drive growth, and we support that.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage the specific claim that profits drove over half of pandemic-era inflation.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I just reject totally the way the member is characterising profits. The reality is that corporates and businesses, people out there, 97 percent of our businesses in New Zealand are small businesses. They are people who take a risk, they invest their capital, they build a business, they employ people, they grow an economy, they create opportunity and choices for families.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly reframes rather than addressing whether corporate profiteering can be harmful.

forthrightness.statement: As I've commented before in this House in response to a similarly searching line of question previously, we want to make it more affordable and also to enable people to build more on time. For that reason, we are working on the building costs, which have increased by 40 percent since 2019, and we're taking decisive action this week with, all going well, the passage of the overseas building products legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the affordability question and names the specific legislative action being progressed.

forthrightness.statement: The answer is, of course, absolutely not, and we have designed the legislation in such a way that will ensure that only equal or higher standards from overseas are to be met in New Zealand in order for the scheme to qualify.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear, direct 'absolutely not' to whether the bill will lower building standards, with the mechanism that guards against it.

civility.statement: I'm very proud of the efforts of our Government to help New Zealanders with the cost of living. That's why we're getting control of Government spending, that's why inflation's coming down, that's why interest rates are coming down. I just note that that member didn't support tax relief for the first time in 14 years for low and middle income workers. We're doing everything we can to put money back in Kiwis' pockets.
civility.explanation: Pointed dig that the member 'didn't support tax relief' but stays on policy/voting record rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: In answering part of that question—my focus is on making sure we run a great economy so New Zealanders can get ahead. We inherited a situation where the economy was run into the ground. We are making sure that we do everything we can to get growth back into New Zealand so we get money back into Kiwis' pockets so they can get out of the mess that we've inherited thanks to that last Government.
civility.explanation: 'Run into the ground' and 'the mess we've inherited' are harsh but aimed at the previous Government's economic record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: The alternative approach is that of the last Government, where they sprayed the money hose around, crossed their fingers, and hoped, and what that delivered was a cost of living crisis that made many New Zealanders worse off.
civility.explanation: 'Sprayed the money hose around, crossed their fingers, and hoped' is a derisive caricature of the previous Government's fiscal approach rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Well, under iReX, both yards were proposed to lift by a metre at huge expense. There's a lot of stone and concrete with new buildings, roads, and a rail on top. It was far beyond the modest alterations we had planned in 2020. They said lifting yards would mean extreme weather events would not disturb the ferry operations. That would have cost hundreds and billions of dollars alone. Here's the point: why build a halo around a car yard when you could increase the culverts to stop the build-up of water in the first place?
civility.explanation: 'Blindingly obvious to some of us, but not to those in charge' is a jab at predecessors but stays largely on the policy substance.

civility.statement: The previous Government's plan included—unbelievably—multi-storey new terminals with concrete so thick there was barely any room for the passengers and fixtures; so flash, even Louis XIV would have been embarrassed. While some may regret the absence of a Taj Mahal in Picton and the Sydney Opera House in Wellington, the people paying their taxes will not.
civility.explanation: Heavy sarcasm and hyperbole ('Taj Mahal', 'Louis XIV would have been embarrassed') mocking the previous plan rather than engaging its rationale.

civility.statement: Because the option was to buy two massive ferries for which there was no infrastructure, and repeat what's happening in Tasmania right now. They've got two new ferries and no infrastructure—they can't even use the ships. What's wrong with that? Well, it's not moron time over here.
civility.explanation: 'It's not moron time over here' is a demeaning jab that abandons substantive engagement.

civility.statement: The reality was that Nicola Willis, as Minister of Finance, inherited a nightmare. She was facing a blowout which Treasury forecast to go to $4 billion and beyond when she was going to be— I know it's rubbish. That's your specialty—that's why I'm talking about it. It's total rubbish.
civility.explanation: 'That's your specialty' aimed at the questioner is a personal cheap shot rather than criticism of policy.

civility.statement: I've seen a recent media query to Police that asked them to comment on a poll run by The Star newspaper in Christchurch, which shows 82 percent of respondents feel safer as a result of beat patrols. The Canterbury metro area commander responded, noting that the poll aligned with the feedback that Police have been receiving and a 5.8 percent reduction of victimisations in his area. On this side of the House, we back our police. That stands in stark contrast to some people who now think that the Green Party has raised some legitimate issues with regards to our police.
civility.explanation: Closing 'stark contrast to some people who now think the Green Party has raised legitimate issues' is a partisan swipe rather than engagement.

civility.statement: But I just reject the member's degrowth mindset from her party. That is not what New Zealand needs right now. If you are a working New Zealander and you want to create a future for your kids or your grandkids, you need growth. For that to happen, we need free enterprise, and we need companies and businesses to be able to make profits.
civility.explanation: 'Degrowth mindset from her party' is a dismissive characterisation but attacks a policy stance rather than the person.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister, or any member of his Cabinet, tend to take the views of someone who started a small business which went bust on them in about five weeks, and then comes to this Parliament and starts preaching to the rest of us?
civility.explanation: A personal attack on Swarbrick's business history framed to discredit her rather than engage her argument on profit.

civility.statement: By the way, Whānau Ora is a perfect expression of all of those things, but—no surprises—this has also been taken away by the Government. Why? Because it works.
civility.explanation: 'No surprises' and the sardonic 'because it works' imputes bad faith to the Government but stops short of personal attack.

civility.statement: I really want to echo the previous speaker on the fact that we are having conversations around child protection, which is incredibly important, on the same day as we, as a Government, are looking to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act. I think, in that sense, we do wonder if child protection is at the heart of the Government's decision making.
civility.explanation: Raises a pointed contrast between the bill and the section 7AA repeal, framed as a question about priorities rather than an insult.

veracity.statement: What is improving the situation for Kiwis' households is making sure that inflation is coming down, interest rates are coming down, and the economy is starting to grow. It was fantastic to see the economy grow at 0.7 percent in quarter four last year. Importantly, Labour didn't vote for tax relief, Labour didn't vote for Working for Families credits, and Labour didn't vote for FamilyBoost.
veracity.explanation: NZ Q4 2024 GDP growth of 0.7% is consistent with the official Stats NZ figure; the Labour voting claims are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: We don't set insurance premiums, but what we can control is the environment—which is an economy that's incredibly well managed—to make sure that we're bringing spending down, to make sure that we're bringing inflation down and interest rates down, and that the economy's growing so people have more money in their pockets and they can access higher-income jobs.
veracity.explanation: The 'we don't set insurance premiums' framing is misleading; as Hipkins points out on a point of order, the question was about the levy portion the Government does set and is consulting on increasing.

veracity.statement: I'm proud of the fact that we are increasing entitlements by roughly the amount of inflation. But what I'm also proud about is the fact that real wage growth has grown for five quarters in a row, after declining for 13 quarters in a row under that Government.
veracity.explanation: The 'five quarters up, 13 quarters down' real-wage claim is a checkable statistic presented without source; directionally plausible but selectively framed.

veracity.statement: The Government is currently consulting on a proposal to increase household insurance costs by $400 to $948 per year per household.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual claim about a live consultation; the figures are precise and plausibly sourced from the proposal, though unverifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Well, of course, the number one driver of this is the fact that all the evidence points to a lack of competition in the New Zealand supermarket sector, and in particular the fact that New Zealanders are paying more for their groceries than counterparts in other countries.
veracity.explanation: That NZ grocery prices are relatively high and competition is limited is broadly supported by Commerce Commission findings, though 'all the evidence' overstates it.

veracity.statement: Well, I'm incredibly proud that in a very short period of time, this Government has ended what I think is one of the blights on New Zealand's social policies—the fact that we have taken 2,000 children out of squalid motel rooms and we have put them into proper, dry homes; the fact that we have taken 5,000 people off the State social housing wait-list who are desperate to get a home—that is fantastic.
veracity.explanation: The 2,000 children and 5,000 off the waitlist figures are specific and roughly consistent with reported reductions, though the 'off the wait-list' framing is contested.

veracity.statement: The member's line of questioning is not acknowledging that we had 3,141 families and households in motel accommodation in New Zealand—completely and utterly unacceptable. This Government—a Government that cares about outcomes, cares about people and making sure they find housing—has reduced that to 591 families. We now have 2,000 kids out of motels and in proper houses.
veracity.explanation: The motel-family reduction figures are specific and plausibly official, though the exchange disputes whether people are being housed or simply denied emergency support.

veracity.statement: Well, I'll take my advice from the Police, and if that is a tool that they wish to have, I back them with any tools that they need to do their job. But I'm very proud that our police are out there on the beat. They've increased the beat police by 30 percent, and the public are feeling safer in their businesses, in their homes, and in their community, and that's a good thing.
veracity.explanation: 'Increased the beat police by 30 percent' is a specific but unsourced claim, and 'the public are feeling safer' is asserted without the survey detail.

veracity.statement: Yes. We have been working hard to create a more proactive welfare system to support more job seekers into work. In the year to February 2025, there were 67,281 exits from the jobseeker benefit into work—an increase of 11 percent from the year before—despite the challenging economic conditions. We also know our policies are working because 98.1 percent are at green under the traffic light system, which means they are meeting their work obligations.
veracity.explanation: Specific administrative statistics presented without source; plausible but the 'proves our policies are working' inference is contestable.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey Cycle 7, taken from October 2023 to October 2024, showed that, for the first time since the introduction of the Police module to the survey, the proportion of people with high trust and confidence in Police increased from 67 percent to 69 percent. This coincided with the proportion of people with no trust and confidence in Police dropping to its lowest level, at 2 percent.
veracity.explanation: Attributes precise figures to a named official survey; plausible and sourced, though selectively highlights favourable movements.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that the school lunch programme has been contracted to deliver meals at the same nutritional level as last year and the years prior, when, none the less, up to 40 percent of meals were found not to meet the contracted standard, and can she confirm or at least tell the House what yesterday's on-time delivery numbers were?
veracity.explanation: Embeds a factual claim that up to 40% of meals under the old model failed the contracted standard; a specific but unsourced statistic used to reframe the criticism.

veracity.statement: Well, I just reject totally the way the member is characterising profits. The reality is that corporates and businesses, people out there, 97 percent of our businesses in New Zealand are small businesses. They are people who take a risk, they invest their capital, they build a business, they employ people, they grow an economy, they create opportunity and choices for families.
veracity.explanation: '97 percent of our businesses in New Zealand are small businesses' is close to the commonly cited figure for small enterprises.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister accept that a fixation on profit at all costs leads to a rising cost of living for New Zealanders, as found in analysis through the COVID period that rising profits contributed to more than half of domestic inflationary pressure?
veracity.explanation: The claim that profits drove over half of domestic inflationary pressure reflects one contested analysis; the magnitude is debated among economists.

veracity.statement: As I've commented before in this House in response to a similarly searching line of question previously, we want to make it more affordable and also to enable people to build more on time. For that reason, we are working on the building costs, which have increased by 40 percent since 2019, and we're taking decisive action this week with, all going well, the passage of the overseas building products legislation.
veracity.explanation: 'Building costs increased by 40 percent since 2019' is a specific, plausible but unsourced figure.

veracity.statement: Seventy percent of children in State care are tamariki Māori, and 80 percent of those who face abuse within the system are Māori. In 2017, it was revealed that 37 percent of victims of sexual violence within Child, Youth and Family care services were Māori.
veracity.explanation: The figures align in direction with reported over-representation of Māori in State care and abuse, though presented without precise sourcing.

specificity.statement: The Government is currently consulting on a proposal to increase household insurance costs by $400 to $948 per year per household.
specificity.explanation: Names an exact dollar range per household and ties it to a specific consultation proposal.

specificity.statement: On Sunday, I outlined the Government's next steps to drive more competition in the supermarket sector and deliver better grocery prices for Kiwi shoppers. I announced two things: first, a formal request for information (RFI) process to identify what is needed to support a significant, national-scale competitor to enter our grocery market. Second, I announced that I have commissioned specialist external advice on ways in which the existing supermarket duopoly could be restructured to improve competition.
specificity.explanation: Names the RFI mechanism and the commissioning of external advice on structural options, though without dollar figures.

specificity.statement: Well, the RFI is proceeding at pace and will close after six weeks. In mid-2025, once I've considered the evidence from the RFI and the Commerce Commission's additional work, I will bring further recommendations to Cabinet. Depending on what I hear, I may seek Cabinet's mandate to progress further design work on structural options to improve competition in the grocery sector. If legislation is needed, I would want to introduce it before the end of the year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeline (six-week close, mid-2025 Cabinet recommendations, legislation before year end) with defined next steps.

specificity.statement: Well, I'm incredibly proud that in a very short period of time, this Government has ended what I think is one of the blights on New Zealand's social policies—the fact that we have taken 2,000 children out of squalid motel rooms and we have put them into proper, dry homes; the fact that we have taken 5,000 people off the State social housing wait-list who are desperate to get a home—that is fantastic.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete numbers for children moved and people removed from the waitlist.

specificity.statement: The member's line of questioning is not acknowledging that we had 3,141 families and households in motel accommodation in New Zealand—completely and utterly unacceptable. This Government—a Government that cares about outcomes, cares about people and making sure they find housing—has reduced that to 591 families. We now have 2,000 kids out of motels and in proper houses.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 3,141 families reduced to 591, and 2,000 children out of motels.

specificity.statement: Look, well, there's no decisions that have been made, but I just say to that member, we want to make sure we get our tax and regulatory settings as good and as competitive as they can be so that we can unleash growth in this economy. We want growth, growth, growth. We want that above everything else.
specificity.explanation: 'Growth, growth, growth' and 'settings as good as they can be' name no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Yes. We have been working hard to create a more proactive welfare system to support more job seekers into work. In the year to February 2025, there were 67,281 exits from the jobseeker benefit into work—an increase of 11 percent from the year before—despite the challenging economic conditions. We also know our policies are working because 98.1 percent are at green under the traffic light system, which means they are meeting their work obligations.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 67,281 exits, an 11% increase, and 98.1% meeting work obligations.

specificity.statement: Well, as I've said, it would be great for this side of the House if we didn't inherit the unfortunate economic climate that we did. We always knew—and Treasury forecasts from the previous Government as well as from our Government expected unemployment rates to rise. That is indisputable. What is on record, though, is our success in actually getting people off the jobseeker benefit into work. We're still ambitious. We have a target—50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker is a target that's worth working for.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target (50,000 fewer on jobseeker) but gives no timeframe or mechanism.

specificity.statement: The New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey Cycle 7, taken from October 2023 to October 2024, showed that, for the first time since the introduction of the Police module to the survey, the proportion of people with high trust and confidence in Police increased from 67 percent to 69 percent. This coincided with the proportion of people with no trust and confidence in Police dropping to its lowest level, at 2 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the survey, the period, and exact percentage movements (67% to 69%, no-confidence at 2%).

specificity.statement: Yes, in the context they were given. In particular, my commitment to delivering a knowledge-rich, year-by-year, world-leading and internationally comparable curriculum. Yesterday, the Ministry of Education released the draft year 7 to 13 English curriculum for consultation. The draft also proposes a new requirement for year 12 and 13 students to consider at least one work by Shakespeare, one 19th century text, and texts by New Zealand authors as part of their studies.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific draft curriculum released and concrete new requirements (Shakespeare, a 19th-century text, NZ authors for years 12–13).

specificity.statement: In response to the second part of the question, I understand that yesterday, I think, around 112,000 meals were delivered, and the on-time delivery rate was 99.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete numbers: ~112,000 meals and a 99.5% on-time rate.

specificity.statement: We think profit is a good thing. Excessive profit is a bad thing.
specificity.explanation: States a principle but defines no threshold for what counts as 'excessive'.

specificity.statement: As I've commented before in this House in response to a similarly searching line of question previously, we want to make it more affordable and also to enable people to build more on time. For that reason, we are working on the building costs, which have increased by 40 percent since 2019, and we're taking decisive action this week with, all going well, the passage of the overseas building products legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names the cost increase, the timeframe, and the specific bill being passed this week.

specificity.statement: Currently, each of the 67 different building consent authorities approves building products, and because the councils currently have joint and several liability, they can be on the hook for as much as 100 percent of the total cost of a failure. And, therefore, they're extremely risk-averse and only approve familiar products. For this reason, there's often little competition and we see the establishment of effective near monopolies.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 67 consent authorities and the liability mechanism driving the problem the bill targets.

specificity.statement: Seventy percent of children in State care are tamariki Māori, and 80 percent of those who face abuse within the system are Māori. In 2017, it was revealed that 37 percent of victims of sexual violence within Child, Youth and Family care services were Māori.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete percentages and a dated finding to characterise the over-representation of Māori children.

specificity.statement: Our understanding—and I'll come to that—around the section 7 report by the Attorney-General is that, domestically and internationally, the evidence on the registry is inconclusive; however, despite that, what we can see internationally is that, when we have registries which are restricted to law enforcement use and are coupled with comprehensive supervision and treatment programmes, including what we're seeing in Aotearoa New Zealand, it does suggest that they may contribute to reducing the recidivism rates.
specificity.explanation: References the section 7 report and specific conditions (law-enforcement-restricted registries plus supervision and treatment) without quantifying effects.

specificity.statement: First of all, it requires offenders to report if a child is going to be living at the same address as them 48 hours prior to it happening, rather than currently it being up to 72 hours after that child moves into the location that they are at or vice versa. Secondly, it requires offenders to report if they are attending education or training courses, and clarifies that voluntary work does require reporting.
specificity.explanation: Itemises the precise reporting-obligation changes with concrete timeframes (48 hours prior vs 72 hours after) and categories.

strength.statement: Well, the RFI is proceeding at pace and will close after six weeks. In mid-2025, once I've considered the evidence from the RFI and the Commerce Commission's additional work, I will bring further recommendations to Cabinet. Depending on what I hear, I may seek Cabinet's mandate to progress further design work on structural options to improve competition in the grocery sector. If legislation is needed, I would want to introduce it before the end of the year.
strength.explanation: A sequenced, in-progress work programme rather than delivered policy; follow-through on legislation is contingent and not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: The member's line of questioning is not acknowledging that we had 3,141 families and households in motel accommodation in New Zealand—completely and utterly unacceptable. This Government—a Government that cares about outcomes, cares about people and making sure they find housing—has reduced that to 591 families. We now have 2,000 kids out of motels and in proper houses.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete, quantified delivery on reducing emergency motel use, though critics argue outcomes shifted to homelessness rather than housing.

strength.statement: Yes. By Christmas 2029, two brand new ferries will have rail on them and it will save the taxpayer billions.
strength.explanation: A firm commitment with a date, but at the announcement stage with no delivery yet demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Well, of course, the number one driver of this is the fact that all the evidence points to a lack of competition in the New Zealand supermarket sector, and in particular the fact that New Zealanders are paying more for their groceries than counterparts in other countries.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy in an evidence claim about competition and cross-country price comparisons rather than an appeal or slogan.

rigor.statement: Well, the first thing I would note is that our Cabinet is mindful of the fact that the minimum wage is paid by employers—small businesses and medium businesses up and down the country—and we are conscious that in recent years, they have undertaken a very difficult period in which they have faced significant inflation and rising interest rates. We want to ensure that they are now in a context where, given the choice between letting a worker go and hiring a new worker, we minimise the costs that they face and ensure that we do not put New Zealanders' jobs at risk.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reasonable employment-cost argument, but leans on a jobs-at-risk framing without evidence quantifying the trade-off.

rigor.statement: The alternative approach is that of the last Government, where they sprayed the money hose around, crossed their fingers, and hoped, and what that delivered was a cost of living crisis that made many New Zealanders worse off.
rigor.explanation: Relies on mockery and a causal assertion that Labour spending 'delivered' the cost-of-living crisis without evidence.

rigor.statement: Well, picking up on the last part of that question, it's important to note that minimum-wage workers are in families with a range of different household circumstances, and what we have been advised is that in many cases, those workers will be eligible for additional Working for Families and accommodation supplement support, such that in some cases, a minimum wage increase will actually be eroded by the abatement in those payments that would occur otherwise.
rigor.explanation: Makes a genuine, technically substantive point about abatement offsetting minimum-wage gains, attributed to official advice.

rigor.statement: Well, under iReX, both yards were proposed to lift by a metre at huge expense. There's a lot of stone and concrete with new buildings, roads, and a rail on top. It was far beyond the modest alterations we had planned in 2020. They said lifting yards would mean extreme weather events would not disturb the ferry operations. That would have cost hundreds and billions of dollars alone. Here's the point: why build a halo around a car yard when you could increase the culverts to stop the build-up of water in the first place?
rigor.explanation: Presents a real cost-versus-alternative argument (culverts vs lifting yards) but leans on ridicule ('halo around a car yard') and unsupported cost figures.

rigor.statement: Later this year. We will not approach this like Wellington Water, by which we mean revealing our budget while negotiating the price. That turns a buyer's market into a seller's market. When these ship and port agreements, when they are signed, the member will know the total cost and the shares between the Government and the ports.
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent negotiating-strategy rationale for withholding the budget figure rather than a mere refusal.

rigor.statement: Because the option was to buy two massive ferries for which there was no infrastructure, and repeat what's happening in Tasmania right now. They've got two new ferries and no infrastructure—they can't even use the ships. What's wrong with that? Well, it's not moron time over here.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real-world analogy (Tasmania's ferries without usable infrastructure) to justify the approach, though it rests on an analogy and no data.

rigor.statement: I don't agree, with statements that I have seen, that there is structural, racial discrimination in the Police at all.
rigor.explanation: Flatly rejects the finding of the Understanding Policing Delivery report without engaging its evidence, an assertion against the cited research.

rigor.statement: Yes. We have been working hard to create a more proactive welfare system to support more job seekers into work. In the year to February 2025, there were 67,281 exits from the jobseeker benefit into work—an increase of 11 percent from the year before—despite the challenging economic conditions. We also know our policies are working because 98.1 percent are at green under the traffic light system, which means they are meeting their work obligations.
rigor.explanation: Cites data, but treating rising exits and high compliance as proof the policy 'works' ignores the broader rise in total jobseeker numbers.

rigor.statement: I disagree with that member because, as I said, 98.1 percent of those who are on benefit are complying with their work obligations. They're taking the steps they need to. The economic conditions we inherited mean it's a very challenging labour market, but, despite that, there has been an 11 percent increase on last year of people leaving the jobseeker benefit and going to a job.
rigor.explanation: The 98.1% compliance figure is a non sequitur to whether sanctions actually help people find work.

rigor.statement: Well, as I've said, it would be great for this side of the House if we didn't inherit the unfortunate economic climate that we did. We always knew—and Treasury forecasts from the previous Government as well as from our Government expected unemployment rates to rise. That is indisputable. What is on record, though, is our success in actually getting people off the jobseeker benefit into work. We're still ambitious. We have a target—50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker is a target that's worth working for.
rigor.explanation: Reasonably invokes bipartisan Treasury forecasts of rising unemployment, but sidesteps the causal link between her sanctions and the rise.

rigor.statement: I've seen a recent media query to Police that asked them to comment on a poll run by The Star newspaper in Christchurch, which shows 82 percent of respondents feel safer as a result of beat patrols. The Canterbury metro area commander responded, noting that the poll aligned with the feedback that Police have been receiving and a 5.8 percent reduction of victimisations in his area. On this side of the House, we back our police. That stands in stark contrast to some people who now think that the Green Party has raised some legitimate issues with regards to our police.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a self-selecting newspaper poll as evidence people feel safer; the 82% figure is not a rigorous measure.

rigor.statement: Well, the member seems to have a challenge or a problem with organisations making a profit. My point is that that is a good thing. They are investing, they're taking risks, they're investing capital in order to drive growth, and we support that.
rigor.explanation: Mischaracterises the question (about profit's link to inflation) as the member having 'a problem with profit' — a strawman that avoids the cited analysis.

rigor.statement: Well, I just reject totally the way the member is characterising profits. The reality is that corporates and businesses, people out there, 97 percent of our businesses in New Zealand are small businesses. They are people who take a risk, they invest their capital, they build a business, they employ people, they grow an economy, they create opportunity and choices for families.
rigor.explanation: Answers a question about excessive corporate profiteering by shifting to sympathetic small-business framing, dodging the distinction being asked about.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister, or any member of his Cabinet, tend to take the views of someone who started a small business which went bust on them in about five weeks, and then comes to this Parliament and starts preaching to the rest of us?
rigor.explanation: Pure ad hominem — attacks the speaker's background instead of the substance of the profiteering claim.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister accept that a fixation on profit at all costs leads to a rising cost of living for New Zealanders, as found in analysis through the COVID period that rising profits contributed to more than half of domestic inflationary pressure?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a specific cited analysis rather than assertion, though 'at all costs' framing loads the question.

rigor.statement: Currently, each of the 67 different building consent authorities approves building products, and because the councils currently have joint and several liability, they can be on the hook for as much as 100 percent of the total cost of a failure. And, therefore, they're extremely risk-averse and only approve familiar products. For this reason, there's often little competition and we see the establishment of effective near monopolies.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a clear causal chain — joint-and-several liability → risk aversion → limited product approval → weak competition — that follows logically.

rigor.statement: By the way, Whānau Ora is a perfect expression of all of those things, but—no surprises—this has also been taken away by the Government. Why? Because it works.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the Government removed Whānau Ora 'because it works' — a rhetorical claim of motive offered without evidence.

rigor.statement: Our understanding—and I'll come to that—around the section 7 report by the Attorney-General is that, domestically and internationally, the evidence on the registry is inconclusive; however, despite that, what we can see internationally is that, when we have registries which are restricted to law enforcement use and are coupled with comprehensive supervision and treatment programmes, including what we're seeing in Aotearoa New Zealand, it does suggest that they may contribute to reducing the recidivism rates.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes inconclusive overall evidence from the conditions under which registries may reduce recidivism, and hedges appropriately.

rigor.statement: We will be putting forward Amendment Papers to consider during the committee stage that will ensure that this bill follows the purpose and the intent around child protection and, at the same time, is done in a way that is most consistent with our New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. And we would request that the Government consider these amendments seriously.
rigor.explanation: Frames the amendments around a specific legal concern (Bill of Rights consistency and the retrospective element flagged by the Law Society).

rigor.statement: I really want to echo the previous speaker on the fact that we are having conversations around child protection, which is incredibly important, on the same day as we, as a Government, are looking to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act. I think, in that sense, we do wonder if child protection is at the heart of the Government's decision making.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two policies on the same day to imply inconsistent motives, a reasonable rhetorical point but not a rigorous demonstration.

authenticity.statement: There will always be Government support for people in need of housing. That has not changed.
authenticity.explanation: The blanket claim that support 'has not changed' sits in tension with community providers in the same exchange reporting they cannot get support for people who urgently need housing.

divination.statement: Yes. By Christmas 2029, two brand new ferries will have rail on them and it will save the taxpayer billions.
divination.explanation: Forecasts delivery of two rail-enabled ferries by Christmas 2029 and multi-billion savings; large infrastructure timelines and savings claims of this kind frequently slip, making the prediction uncertain.

charisma.statement: The previous Government's plan included—unbelievably—multi-storey new terminals with concrete so thick there was barely any room for the passengers and fixtures; so flash, even Louis XIV would have been embarrassed. While some may regret the absence of a Taj Mahal in Picton and the Sydney Opera House in Wellington, the people paying their taxes will not.
charisma.explanation: Colourful and entertaining for his own side but ridicules opponents rather than building any cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: But I just reject the member's degrowth mindset from her party. That is not what New Zealand needs right now. If you are a working New Zealander and you want to create a future for your kids or your grandkids, you need growth. For that to happen, we need free enterprise, and we need companies and businesses to be able to make profits.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side around growth and free enterprise while labelling the opponent's position a 'degrowth mindset', doing nothing to persuade the other side.

charisma.statement: We will be putting forward Amendment Papers to consider during the committee stage that will ensure that this bill follows the purpose and the intent around child protection and, at the same time, is done in a way that is most consistent with our New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. And we would request that the Government consider these amendments seriously.
charisma.explanation: Supports the bill while constructively inviting the Government to weigh amendments seriously — a bridge-building, cross-party posture.

charisma.statement: So, ultimately, this bill is another example of the National-led coalition Government's focus on law and order, and I commend it to the House.
charisma.explanation: A standard partisan framing that credits the coalition rather than reaching across the House, though the topic itself had broad support.

specificity.statement: This bill addresses two longstanding issues with current settings for sexual violence by stopping child victims of sexual violence being questioned about consent in most circumstances and by changing name suppression settings to empower victims.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete mechanisms (questioning about consent; name suppression) but without figures or dates.

specificity.statement: In the case of sexual offending, the court will no longer be able to grant permanent name suppression to a convicted adult offender unless the victim agrees.
specificity.explanation: Precise legal mechanism and condition stated clearly.

specificity.statement: in 2023, permanent name suppression was granted to 76 convicted offenders of one or more sexual offences.
specificity.explanation: Exact figure and year.

specificity.statement: Last week, we passed the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act, which strengthens real consequences for crime and improves the trust that New Zealanders have in the justice system.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act but describes effects in generic terms.

specificity.statement: Our target is to reduce the number of victims of serious crime by 20,000 people.
specificity.explanation: A numeric target, but no timeframe or mechanism attached in this statement.

specificity.statement: Well, there is no doubt about it, we have some real longstanding challenges in our healthcare system. That's why this Government is spending an extra $17 billion, it's why it's actually hiring more workforce, it's put back in place targets, and with respect to Nelson, it's been fantastic to see a rapid response from the Minister to put a clinical team in there
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure and a concrete Nelson intervention amid generic claims.

specificity.statement: we have 2,000 more nurses in the system than we did when we came to power, they are paid well—relative to their New South Wales counterparts—attrition is low
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure and comparators.

specificity.statement: But four months for an elective surgery—waiting more than four months—went up 2,500 percent under the last Government. Waiting more than four months for a first surgery—for a specialist appointment, went up by over 6,500 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures and thresholds cited.

specificity.statement: this is a Government that has taken 5,000 people off the State house wait-list, this is a Government that has taken 2,500 families out of squalid motel rooms, and this is a Government that has taken 2,000 kids out of motel rooms and got them in proper homes.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete figures.

specificity.statement: we have funded literacy and numeracy resources in te reo Māori for the first time across the country, along with professional learning and development. We launched a world-first phonics check in te reo Māori, we've refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa
specificity.explanation: Names concrete initiatives (te reo resources, phonics check, curriculum refresh).

specificity.statement: we have five RT: Māori teachers in Southland, three in Invercargill, where there is only one kura kaupapa. Two of them are in Mosgiel, in English-medium schools with no Māori language funding.
specificity.explanation: Granular counts by location used to make the point.

specificity.statement: Our Going for Growth With Māori framework has three focus areas: increasing infrastructure investment to drive jobs and sustainable growth, accelerating Māori business exports, and further unlocking the potential of Māori land.
specificity.explanation: Names three defined focus areas but without figures, mechanisms, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: the investment alongside the exemplary Parininihi ki Waitotara Incorporation to explore the potential of a large-scale solar farm that can serve 8,500 homes.
specificity.explanation: Named partner and a concrete capacity figure (8,500 homes), though still at 'explore the potential' stage.

specificity.statement: it is really important that the New Zealand public have confidence in the not-for-profit sector and charitable organisations, especially when those organisations are funded by central government using their tax. So it is important that we have a system where it is clear that those who should pay tax are and that those charities are robust and acting with integrity.
specificity.explanation: General principles, no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: This has already led to key initiatives, including Health New Zealand's elective boost, which will deliver an additional 10,579 elective procedures by June to reduce wait times.
specificity.explanation: Exact procedure figure and a month deadline.

specificity.statement: What excuse can he possibly have when his Government froze hiring in public hospitals, causing the number of people seeing a specialist within four months to fall from 66.3 percent to 61.2 percent within a year?
specificity.explanation: Exact figures and timeframe.

specificity.statement: The four key areas that we've announced to rein in cowboy builders include: (1) giving more tools to the statutory boards for builders, plumbers, and electricians, allowing them to initiate investigations; (2) making information public when a builder has been suspended for disciplinary reasons; (3) introducing a waterproofing class for licensed building practitioners so that Kiwis can have confidence in those vulnerable wet areas of their homes; and (4) establishing codes of ethics for key trades so that disciplinary action can be taken in the event that tradespeople engage in deceptive practices.
specificity.explanation: Four enumerated, concrete measures with clear mechanisms.

specificity.statement: So far, I've announced that Cabinet has agreed to: a carve-out for small, low-risk businesses from general health and safety at work requirements; free up land for recreational use by ensuring landowners will not be responsible if someone is injured on their land while doing recreational activities; clarify the distinction between governance and operational management, health and safety responsibilities, to reduce directors' fear and risk of over-compliance; make critical risk the primary purpose of the Health and Safety at Work Act, and clarify the boundaries between the Act and regulatory systems that already manage the same risk; and set up a hotline for reporting excessive road cone use.
specificity.explanation: Enumerated Cabinet decisions, each a concrete change.

specificity.statement: Last week, the Government passed the Customer and Product Data Act. That's an Act that provides a framework for open banking, open electricity, and open other economic sectors as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the sectors it covers.

specificity.statement: In 1867, the first four Māori came into our Parliament: Patterson from Ngāi Tahu; Mete Kingi from the West Coast of the North Island; Nene Russell, the nephew of the great Tāmati Wāka Nene; and Te Moananui from the Tai Rāwhiti.
specificity.explanation: Names individuals, iwi/regions, and the year.

specificity.statement: What has our side of the House done: $60 million worth of geothermal energy will flow from Māori land, in many respects.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure but the outcome ('will flow...in many respects') is vaguely framed.

strength.statement: This bill addresses two longstanding issues with current settings for sexual violence by stopping child victims of sexual violence being questioned about consent in most circumstances and by changing name suppression settings to empower victims.
strength.explanation: Bill is at 'the next stage' — legislating in progress, not yet enacted, so delivery is partial.

strength.statement: Last week, we passed the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act, which strengthens real consequences for crime and improves the trust that New Zealanders have in the justice system.
strength.explanation: Claims a law actually passed last week — delivered legislation rather than mere announcement.

strength.statement: Well, there is no doubt about it, we have some real longstanding challenges in our healthcare system. That's why this Government is spending an extra $17 billion, it's why it's actually hiring more workforce, it's put back in place targets, and with respect to Nelson, it's been fantastic to see a rapid response from the Minister to put a clinical team in there
strength.explanation: Describes spending and hiring in progress; delivery on outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: this is a Government that has taken 5,000 people off the State house wait-list, this is a Government that has taken 2,500 families out of squalid motel rooms, and this is a Government that has taken 2,000 kids out of motel rooms and got them in proper homes.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered movement of families out of motels; broadly consistent with reduced emergency-motel use.

strength.statement: we have funded literacy and numeracy resources in te reo Māori for the first time across the country, along with professional learning and development. We launched a world-first phonics check in te reo Māori, we've refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa
strength.explanation: Claims delivered programmes rather than aspirations.

strength.statement: This has already led to key initiatives, including Health New Zealand's elective boost, which will deliver an additional 10,579 elective procedures by June to reduce wait times.
strength.explanation: Committed target with a mechanism, but delivery is prospective.

strength.statement: The four key areas that we've announced to rein in cowboy builders include: (1) giving more tools to the statutory boards for builders, plumbers, and electricians, allowing them to initiate investigations; (2) making information public when a builder has been suspended for disciplinary reasons; (3) introducing a waterproofing class for licensed building practitioners so that Kiwis can have confidence in those vulnerable wet areas of their homes; and (4) establishing codes of ethics for key trades so that disciplinary action can be taken in the event that tradespeople engage in deceptive practices.
strength.explanation: Announced measures; implementation still to follow, so delivery is prospective.

strength.statement: So far, I've announced that Cabinet has agreed to: a carve-out for small, low-risk businesses from general health and safety at work requirements; free up land for recreational use by ensuring landowners will not be responsible if someone is injured on their land while doing recreational activities; clarify the distinction between governance and operational management, health and safety responsibilities, to reduce directors' fear and risk of over-compliance; make critical risk the primary purpose of the Health and Safety at Work Act, and clarify the boundaries between the Act and regulatory systems that already manage the same risk; and set up a hotline for reporting excessive road cone use.
strength.explanation: Cabinet agreement reached but legislation not yet drafted or passed.

strength.statement: Last week, the Government passed the Customer and Product Data Act. That's an Act that provides a framework for open banking, open electricity, and open other economic sectors as well.
strength.explanation: Names legislation actually passed the prior week — delivered rather than promised.

strength.statement: What has our side of the House done: $60 million worth of geothermal energy will flow from Māori land, in many respects.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for funding, but the benefit is prospective ('will flow').

veracity.statement: in 2023, permanent name suppression was granted to 76 convicted offenders of one or more sexual offences.
veracity.explanation: Precise, checkable statistic presented as fact; plausible and specific, not verifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Well, I think the member will find that the next iteration of the New Zealand Victims of Violent Crime Survey is showing continued great success towards our target, and in contrast to the previous Government—
veracity.explanation: Asserts 'continued great success' against a challenge that the official survey shows no substantial progress; optimistic and unsubstantiated in context.

veracity.statement: we have 2,000 more nurses in the system than we did when we came to power, they are paid well—relative to their New South Wales counterparts—attrition is low
veracity.explanation: Specific comparative headcount claim, plausible but contested and hard to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: But four months for an elective surgery—waiting more than four months—went up 2,500 percent under the last Government. Waiting more than four months for a first surgery—for a specialist appointment, went up by over 6,500 percent.
veracity.explanation: Enormous percentage rises likely computed off a very low base, presented for dramatic effect — technically-derived but potentially misleading.

veracity.statement: this is a Government that has taken 5,000 people off the State house wait-list, this is a Government that has taken 2,500 families out of squalid motel rooms, and this is a Government that has taken 2,000 kids out of motel rooms and got them in proper homes.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures, but 'off the wait-list' framing is contested and omits the reported rise in rough sleeping.

veracity.statement: we don't have strong, centralised data on homelessness.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — New Zealand lacks robust centralised rough-sleeping data.

veracity.statement: we have funded literacy and numeracy resources in te reo Māori for the first time across the country, along with professional learning and development. We launched a world-first phonics check in te reo Māori, we've refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa
veracity.explanation: Several checkable specific claims presented as fact.

veracity.statement: we have five RT: Māori teachers in Southland, three in Invercargill, where there is only one kura kaupapa. Two of them are in Mosgiel, in English-medium schools with no Māori language funding.
veracity.explanation: Precise distributional claim, plausible and internally consistent, unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: There are more clinical staff working at Nelson Hospital today than there was when she was the Minister—there are more there today than when she was the Minister
veracity.explanation: Specific comparative staffing claim, plausible but contested given the questioner's hiring-freeze framing.

veracity.statement: What excuse can he possibly have when his Government froze hiring in public hospitals, causing the number of people seeing a specialist within four months to fall from 66.3 percent to 61.2 percent within a year?
veracity.explanation: Cites precise before/after percentages; specific and checkable, causation attributed to the hiring freeze is arguable.

veracity.statement: The Deputy Prime Minister makes a very good point, because, surely, New Zealand is the only country on the planet that is transitioning from gas to coal.
veracity.explanation: 'Only country on the planet' is a sweeping, dubious claim used rhetorically and not substantiated.

veracity.statement: In 1867, the first four Māori came into our Parliament: Patterson from Ngāi Tahu; Mete Kingi from the West Coast of the North Island; Nene Russell, the nephew of the great Tāmati Wāka Nene; and Te Moananui from the Tai Rāwhiti.
veracity.explanation: Historical claim about the first Māori MPs of 1867, broadly accurate in substance.

divination.statement: Our target is to reduce the number of victims of serious crime by 20,000 people.
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast of a large crime reduction; ambitious and uncertain against current survey trends.

divination.statement: We will only become a small, advanced leading economy if the Māori economy grows, prospers, and sustains.
divination.explanation: Conditional forecast tying national economic success to Māori economic growth; directionally plausible but unfalsifiable in magnitude.

divination.statement: This has already led to key initiatives, including Health New Zealand's elective boost, which will deliver an additional 10,579 elective procedures by June to reduce wait times.
divination.explanation: Forecasts delivery of a precise number by June; plausible but yet to be realised.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think the member will find that the next iteration of the New Zealand Victims of Violent Crime Survey is showing continued great success towards our target, and in contrast to the previous Government—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly about using a tweet's statistics over the official survey; does not address the methodology criticism and pivots to asserting 'great success'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there is no doubt about it, we have some real longstanding challenges in our healthcare system. That's why this Government is spending an extra $17 billion, it's why it's actually hiring more workforce, it's put back in place targets, and with respect to Nelson, it's been fantastic to see a rapid response from the Minister to put a clinical team in there
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the problem and describes the Nelson response, but does not directly address why avoidable emergency surgeries were occurring.

forthrightness.statement: this is a Government that has taken 5,000 people off the State house wait-list, this is a Government that has taken 2,500 families out of squalid motel rooms, and this is a Government that has taken 2,000 kids out of motel rooms and got them in proper homes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why multiple agencies report rising rough sleeping; recites housing achievements rather than engaging the rough-sleeping data.

forthrightness.statement: we don't have strong, centralised data on homelessness.
forthrightness.explanation: Candid concession of a data gap rather than deflecting outright.

forthrightness.statement: As I've said in my previous answers, there will always be support available for people who need it. Nothing has changed in that regard.

specificity.statement: one in six New Zealanders is affected in this way.

rigor.statement: we just want to make sure that something like this has those kind of checks and balances in place so that we don't have to come back in a few years' time to relitigate something like this because we have found that the processes that were put forward have somehow inadvertently traumatised or retraumatised complainants.
