charisma.statement: Why wouldn’t the Government want to consider the prospect of having a right of appeal, not to dispute matters of fact but maybe just matters of law, so that people can have confidence in the process.
charisma.explanation: Frames the ask constructively and invites the Government in ('why wouldn't the Government want to consider'), seeking common ground rather than attacking.

charisma.statement: We recognise that the fee—$468—reflects the costs that are incurred to run the disputes tribunal, but we also must recognise that $468 is actually quite a lot for many working people, especially people on very low incomes, like the minimum wage, or lower if they’re part-time, of course. When you consider that the filing fee for the District Court is $260—almost half—surely there could be some wriggle room there, some flexibility.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opposing rationale (fee reflects cost) before making his case, an even-handed, bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: They could have been bills that started under us and this Government has finished off, or that this Government has introduced, building on work that the previous Government had done. There has been broad support. Here comes another one.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits cross-party continuity, acknowledging the current Government finishing Labour's work and vice versa — consensus-building rather than partisan.

civility.statement: I want to come back to the rather glib comment from my friend in the ACT Party who talked about congratulating the Green Party in terms of joining the user-pays movement. I think that my friend misses the point.
civility.explanation: Rebuts an opponent's point ('glib', 'misses the point') but stays on the substance of user-pays and uses the collegial 'my friend' — pointed but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I mean, you only have to look over there to see that many people make lots of mistakes!
civility.explanation: A cheap shot at MPs opposite ('look over there') rather than engaging their arguments — a jab at people, albeit light-toned.

civility.statement: I’ve had that happen to me when I’ve put an amendment forward to Chris Bishop. He’s said, “Yep, good idea, but nah.”
civility.explanation: Names a specific minister to illustrate amendments being brushed off, but the tone is light and self-deprecating rather than a personal attack.

strength.statement: At second reading, Government shared with the House its intention to submit an Amendment Paper to maintain a six-month implementation period for the new information privacy principle to help agencies prepare to comply. It has since been decided to extend this period to a full year.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete change carried through via an Amendment Paper agreed in committee of the whole House — delivery on the stated intent, though a procedural adjustment.

charisma.statement: while we may have disagreed on different things politically, that you have huge respect across the House, and that, actually, we want to thank you for your service to this House and to this place, and importantly, also, for the intellect and the passion. We want to wish you well for your future—well done.
charisma.explanation: Gracious cross-aisle tribute to a departing opponent (David Parker); acknowledges disagreement while extending genuine respect — bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I can assure the member that our diplomats are in fact engaging with the US administration to make clear our position that that is not our effective tariff rate... we will continue to fight for our exporters—both in terms of their access to the US market but also through increasing their access to other markets—by continuing to pursue trade agreements throughout the world.
charisma.explanation: 'We are humble enough to know there are some global events we can't control' is a measured, reassuring register, though addressed to its own supporters.

charisma.statement: Success has many fathers, but in relation to this case, the Hon Shane Jones has been the driving force behind this excellent policy, because he’s seen the impact of small units in the Far North and what an impact it can have on families.
charisma.explanation: Generously shares credit with a coalition colleague; warm, collegial tone.

civility.statement: while we may have disagreed on different things politically, that you have huge respect across the House, and that, actually, we want to thank you for your service to this House and to this place, and importantly, also, for the intellect and the passion. We want to wish you well for your future—well done.
civility.explanation: Respectful, warm, focused on the person's service and intellect rather than partisan point-scoring.

civility.statement: I think everybody understands that it is in our brutal national interest—that’s why this coalition Government has said that we will meet our commitments, and that’s why we are staying in Paris, because we want our farmers to do well. We are not going to punish our farmers, and we’re not going to send farming out of this country, like the last Labour - Green Government was proposing to do.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused but includes a partisan jab about the previous government 'sending farming out of this country'.

civility.statement: Well, I can name several of them. But I would just say to that member: we want to end the oil and gas ban; we want that member to support fast-track legislation—but they didn’t. Why? Because 22 projects enabled a 30 percent increase in renewable electricity—that’s a good thing. But if the member really cared about these issues, instead of pretending that he does, he would have backed the fast-track legislation.
civility.explanation: 'instead of pretending that he does' impugns the questioner's sincerity — a personal jab.

civility.statement: We have some crocodile tears from the Leader of the Opposition, because I am incredibly proud of our foreign Minister, and he is out there in the world doing the business for New Zealand. He is hugely respected by everybody in the foreign affairs community... I just would compare and contrast his record versus your record in Government.
civility.explanation: 'Crocodile tears' dismisses the questioner's concern as insincere — a personal characterisation rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I’ve heard the “defund defence” narrative on top of the “defund the police” narrative from the degrowth Greens, but actually it is the defence forces that show up and look after our people and the people in the Pacific because of their abilities and their capabilities and the assets that they have.
civility.explanation: 'degrowth Greens' and imputing a 'defund defence' agenda are dismissive characterisations of opponents.

civility.statement: you and your party were part of a Government that had put 23,000 more kids into poverty in the last year of your Government. Our Budget last year identified that it would lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
civility.explanation: 'it’s all rather sanctimonious to talk about values' characterises the opponent rather than the argument.

civility.statement: Does he think it enhances or diminishes New Zealand’s international reputation as a clean, green economy when his Minister of Foreign Affairs indicates that New Zealand was wrong to sign the Paris Agreement, travels to the Pacific—one of the regions of the world most affected by climate change—and questions the global scientific consensus on climate change, and his Government dismantles almost all proactive action to reduce New Zealand’s emissions?
civility.explanation: Pointed and rhetorically loaded but targets the Government's stated positions and record rather than making personal insults.

civility.statement: As a matter of education, if the economy is growing at 0.7 percent or annualised at 2.8, how could you possibly describe that as being a recession?
civility.explanation: 'As a matter of education' is mildly condescending, but the substance is a legitimate data-based point.

civility.statement: Why did his Government choose to cut $2.4 billion on climate mitigation when the New Zealand Defence Force themselves have identified climate change as one of the biggest risks we face to national security?
civility.explanation: Sharp but wholly policy-focused; no personal attack.

civility.statement: As is sometimes the case with that member, I would have to check that paraphrasing of my comment in the context in which it was made to assure that she is actually accurately representing my statements.
civility.explanation: 'As is sometimes the case with that member' is a mild dig at the questioner's accuracy.

civility.statement: Two very pertinent examples of that are, firstly, Pharmac funding, where it became clear after the Budget that without considerable uplift in funding for Pharmac, they would have been left to delist medicines... Another pertinent example is the school lunch programme, which, again, had not been funded into out-years, even though Labour campaigned on continuing that programme.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the previous finance Minister ('extraordinary position') is pointed but tied to the fiscal substance.

civility.statement: Does she regret cancelling and delaying housing, hospital, and school builds, which has caused the collapse of the construction sector and the deepest recession seen in 30 years?
civility.explanation: Loaded and accusatory framing, though aimed at policy decisions rather than the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Success has many fathers, but in relation to this case, the Hon Shane Jones has been the driving force behind this excellent policy, because he’s seen the impact of small units in the Far North and what an impact it can have on families.
civility.explanation: Respectful and good-humoured, crediting others rather than attacking anyone.

civility.statement: Well, if the member had listened to my primary answer, she would have noted that the vacancy rate increased substantially in 2023... We are taking action to ensure we have the front-line staff in place in Tairāwhiti to ensure they can get the care that they need after a significant drop under the previous Government.
civility.explanation: 'if the member had listened to my primary answer' is a mild put-down, but the criticism is about the record, not the person.

civility.statement: No, it’s not this Government’s policy to defund the Police.
civility.explanation: Reaches for a 'defund the Police' jab at the opposition rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Does he agree with Myles Thomas that “Melissa Lee said she could not do anything. Paul Goldsmith is saying he won’t do anything for a little while longer.”, and, if so, how long does he expect it to be before he gets fired for inaction and incompetence, just like she did?
civility.explanation: Predicting the Minister will be 'fired for inaction and incompetence' is a personal attack on competence rather than a policy critique.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what I know is that it’s important and in our national interest to meet that commitment, and that’s what you’ve seen this coalition Government do. The farmers that I’ve talked to up and down this country, they tell me, very clearly, they don’t want multinational companies or competing countries kicking New Zealand products off the shelf.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his Deputy PM's specific statement about the Paris target; pivots to farmers and national interest without addressing the question.

forthrightness.statement: This is a coalition Government that is going hard on economic growth because it is in our national interest to do so. We are always going to put Kiwis first, and that is going to be primary in all of our decision making.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Peters' 'why on earth we’re doing this' remark; answers with generic growth slogans, does not engage.

forthrightness.statement: I think everybody understands that it is in our brutal national interest—that’s why this coalition Government has said that we will meet our commitments, and that’s why we are staying in Paris, because we want our farmers to do well. We are not going to punish our farmers, and we’re not going to send farming out of this country, like the last Labour - Green Government was proposing to do.
forthrightness.explanation: Does give a clear answer to whether NZ is pulling out — confirms staying in Paris — though wrapped in deflection about the DPM's comments.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can name several of them. But I would just say to that member: we want to end the oil and gas ban; we want that member to support fast-track legislation—but they didn’t. Why? Because 22 projects enabled a 30 percent increase in renewable electricity—that’s a good thing. But if the member really cared about these issues, instead of pretending that he does, he would have backed the fast-track legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name one policy that has actually reduced emissions; claims he can name several but pivots to oil-and-gas and fast-track policy rather than naming an emissions-reducing one.

forthrightness.statement: We have some crocodile tears from the Leader of the Opposition, because I am incredibly proud of our foreign Minister, and he is out there in the world doing the business for New Zealand. He is hugely respected by everybody in the foreign affairs community... I just would compare and contrast his record versus your record in Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the DPM's conduct diminishes NZ's reputation; entirely deflects to praising the Minister and attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the major one that we’re facing right now is actually economic growth. That’s why this Government is prioritising economic growth above and beyond everything else, because we want working New Zealanders to be able to work hard, to get money in their back pocket, and to do well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether climate change is one of the biggest threats facing NZ; reframes to economic growth without answering the yes/no.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve heard the “defund defence” narrative on top of the “defund the police” narrative from the degrowth Greens, but actually it is the defence forces that show up and look after our people and the people in the Pacific because of their abilities and their capabilities and the assets that they have.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government cut $2.4b on climate mitigation; never addresses the cut, redirects to defence.

forthrightness.statement: you and your party were part of a Government that had put 23,000 more kids into poverty in the last year of your Government. Our Budget last year identified that it would lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to explain the $3b poverty vs $3b military comparison; sidesteps into a counter-attack on Labour's record.

forthrightness.statement: I know that there are 2,000 kids out of emergency housing and I know that there are 2,500 families out of emergency housing, and, importantly, we know that 80 percent of the people that have left emergency housing now have proper homes to live in. As for the other 20 percent, nothing has changed.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically where the denied applicants end up sleeping; answers with exit statistics and asserts 'nothing has changed' rather than saying where they go.

forthrightness.statement: What I can say is that our Government’s support has not changed, and if there are people who need housing support, they will be able to access it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee emergency housing access for those fleeing family violence; gives a general reassurance rather than the requested guarantee.

forthrightness.statement: To make a few facts clear, the New Zealand Government delivered more classrooms in the past year than were delivered by the previous Government in the year prior to that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she regrets cancelling/delaying builds causing the construction downturn; rebuts with a classroom comparison rather than addressing the cancellations.

forthrightness.statement: As is sometimes the case with that member, I would have to check that paraphrasing of my comment in the context in which it was made to assure that she is actually accurately representing my statements.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she stands by her February assurance that NZ would not be directly affected by tariffs; declines to engage, questioning the paraphrase instead.

forthrightness.statement: I can assure the member that our diplomats are in fact engaging with the US administration to make clear our position that that is not our effective tariff rate... we will continue to fight for our exporters—both in terms of their access to the US market but also through increasing their access to other markets—by continuing to pursue trade agreements throughout the world.
forthrightness.explanation: Substantially addresses the trust/'could have been worse' challenge by describing diplomatic engagement and market-access strategy.

forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages the vacancy-rate premise of the question with counter-data, though reframes the trend to his advantage.

forthrightness.statement: In the pipeline, Health New Zealand has 11.1 fulltime-equivalent senior medical officers who have accepted offers and are preparing to start work in Tairāwhiti. forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about people losing vision for want of an ophthalmologist; responds with general SMO recruitment figures rather than the ophthalmology-specific action.

forthrightness.statement: Well, if the member had listened to my primary answer, she would have noted that the vacancy rate increased substantially in 2023... We are taking action to ensure we have the front-line staff in place in Tairāwhiti to ensure they can get the care that they need after a significant drop under the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the recruitment progress but reframes the 'was the response inadequate' question into an attack on the 2023 decline under the previous Minister.

forthrightness.statement: The unemployment numbers of 5.1 percent are exactly what was forecast by Treasury under the previous Government. Unfortunately, we are dealing with the realities of high Government spending, inflation, high interest rates that lead to a recession; it leads to higher unemployment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the plan hasn't let Kiwis 'share in prosperity'; rebuts the premise and attributes unemployment to inherited conditions rather than answering directly.

forthrightness.statement: I’m proud of the Employment Action Plan, where we have multiple Ministers working across to ensure that we are getting traction and supporting more Kiwis into work. If that member has a question more specifically about an initiative, she needs to direct it to the Minister responsible.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the loss of school-lunch supply jobs squares with a regional-resilience goal; deflects entirely, telling the member to ask another Minister.

forthrightness.statement: No, it’s not this Government’s policy to defund the Police.
forthrightness.explanation: A planted question about Wellington Central feedback; answered with a partisan slogan rather than any actual feedback.

specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures and timeframes (23,000; 17,000; 'last year').

specificity.statement: It has been fantastic to see 2,000 kids come out of motels and actually put into safe, dry homes, and 2,500 families, as well.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures — 2,000 children and 2,500 families out of emergency motels.

As for the other 20 percent, nothing has changed.
specificity.explanation: Gives an 80/20 split, though 'nothing has changed' for the 20% is vague.

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete share (70%) and the transmission mechanism (regional exposure to US tariffs).

specificity.statement: At the half-year update, trading partner growth was already forecast to be modest—at around 2.5 percent in the June 2026 year. specificity.explanation: Precise figures and timeframes for partner growth (2.5%→2%) and inflation (2.5% + up to 0.5%) for the June 2026 year.

specificity.explanation: Names concrete actions (diplomatic engagement on the effective rate, pursuing trade agreements) but no figures or timelines.

specificity.statement: Last year, alongside a 54 percent increase in foot patrols, aggravated robberies in the Wellington district dropped by 33.6 percent. Being visible is a critical part of successful policing.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures — 54% more foot patrols, aggravated robberies down 33.6% in the Wellington district.

specificity.statement: based on news reports I’m aware of, approximately 71 jobs have been lost at New Zealand Media and Entertainment (NZME), 48 at TVNZ, four from The Spinoff, and 27 from Whakaata Māori. All of those people have our sympathy.
specificity.explanation: Itemised job-loss figures by outlet (71 NZME, 48 TVNZ, 4 Spinoff, 27 Whakaata Māori).

specificity.statement: I moved swiftly to introduce the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill to repeal restrictions on Sunday advertising; why the Government made changes to eligibility criteria for the screen production rebate, which saw shows such as Shortland Street benefit as a result; and why the Government’s currently consulting on proposals for a media reform package.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (the Sunday-advertising bill, screen-rebate criteria changes, media-reform consultation) and an example beneficiary (Shortland Street).

specificity.statement: The target that was set for those Government cost savings was achieving $1.5 billion worth of savings and tasking the Government agencies with either 6.5 or 7.5 of their baseline budget... will deliver—given the environment that she inherited—$23 billion worth of savings over a four-year period. Because of this initiative and essential action, the deficit is $1.1 billion smaller than it would have been without those savings.
specificity.explanation: Multiple figures (1.5b target, 6.5/7.5% baseline, 23b over four years, 1.1b smaller deficit).

authenticity.statement: I think everybody understands that it is in our brutal national interest—that’s why this coalition Government has said that we will meet our commitments, and that’s why we are staying in Paris, because we want our farmers to do well. We are not going to punish our farmers, and we’re not going to send farming out of this country, like the last Labour - Green Government was proposing to do.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts a firm coalition position of staying in Paris, but this sits in visible tension with his own Deputy PM's quoted anti-Paris statements he is being pressed on.

veracity.statement: Well, I can name several of them. But I would just say to that member: we want to end the oil and gas ban; we want that member to support fast-track legislation—but they didn’t. Why? Because 22 projects enabled a 30 percent increase in renewable electricity—that’s a good thing. But if the member really cared about these issues, instead of pretending that he does, he would have backed the fast-track legislation.
veracity.explanation: '22 projects enabled a 30 percent increase in renewable electricity' is a specific but loosely-framed claim conflating fast-track approvals with realised emissions reduction.

veracity.statement: we have our Emissions Reduction Plan 2 Budget and plan, which suggests that our Government is actually on track to deliver Net Carbon Zero potentially six years earlier.
veracity.explanation: Claim of being 'on track' to beat the target is contestable and sits awkwardly with the cuts being challenged in the question.

veracity.statement: you and your party were part of a Government that had put 23,000 more kids into poverty in the last year of your Government. Our Budget last year identified that it would lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
veracity.explanation: Both figures are specific but selectively framed; the '23,000' and '17,000' are projections/single-year snapshots presented without their qualifications.

veracity.statement: It has been fantastic to see 2,000 kids come out of motels and actually put into safe, dry homes, and 2,500 families, as well.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and broadly consistent with the reduction in motel use, though these are the Government's own favourable framing.

veracity.statement: I know that there are 2,000 kids out of emergency housing and I know that there are 2,500 families out of emergency housing, and, importantly, we know that 80 percent of the people that have left emergency housing now have proper homes to live in. As for the other 20 percent, nothing has changed.
veracity.explanation: The '80 percent have proper homes' figure is the Government's tracked-outcome claim; the fate of the untracked 20% is glossed.

veracity.statement: As a matter of education, if the economy is growing at 0.7 percent or annualised at 2.8, how could you possibly describe that as being a recession?
veracity.explanation: Cites a 0.7% quarterly / 2.8% annualised figure; directionally consistent with a return to growth, though selectively omits the preceding contraction.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister not think it’s just axiomatic that if China, India, the United States, and Russia were signed up—that’s almost 60 percent of the emissions in this world at the moment—then targets could be met?
veracity.explanation: Those four economies do account for a very large share of global emissions; the aggregate figure is roughly in the right range.

veracity.statement: Though unwelcome, the tariffs that have been imposed on New Zealand are likely to be modest in comparison with the impact for many other countries. The most significant impact for New Zealand of the current uncertainty will be through disruptions to the global economy.
veracity.explanation: Reasonable characterisation of a small, trade-exposed economy's exposure to US tariffs relative to larger exporters.

veracity.statement: The Asian region, including Australia, accounts for 70 percent of New Zealand’s international trade. There is a risk of slower growth in the region because many economies there have significant exposures to the new US tariff regime.
veracity.explanation: Asia-plus-Australia is a dominant share of NZ trade; 70% is in the plausible range though rounded.

veracity.statement: To make a few facts clear, the New Zealand Government delivered more classrooms in the past year than were delivered by the previous Government in the year prior to that.
veracity.explanation: A checkable comparative claim presented favourably; plausible but the framing ('year prior to that') is selective.

veracity.statement: Two very pertinent examples of that are, firstly, Pharmac funding, where it became clear after the Budget that without considerable uplift in funding for Pharmac, they would have been left to delist medicines... Another pertinent example is the school lunch programme, which, again, had not been funded into out-years, even though Labour campaigned on continuing that programme.
veracity.explanation: Both examples are broadly grounded in real Budget-cycle issues, but framed to attribute maximum fault to the predecessor.

veracity.statement: The Deputy Prime Minister makes a good point, which is that on our watch we have seen inflation return to the target band, interest rate reductions occur, and we have seen in the last three months of last year a return to growth above that which was forecast by consensus economists.
veracity.explanation: Inflation returning to band and rate cuts are verifiable; 'growth above consensus forecast' in the final quarter is a specific, checkable claim presented favourably.

veracity.statement: in the case of one recent asthma medication, 16 months for Medsafe to tell the New Zealand people it is safe for them to use a medication that is already widely used and legal in countries such as Australia, the UK, United States, Switzerland, Japan, Canada, and Singapore.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable illustrative claim used to support the reform; plausible though single-example.

veracity.statement: Many—most notably, filling in a significant fiscal cliff in Pharmac funding last year and then boosting Pharmac funding by around $600 million.
veracity.explanation: The ~$600m Pharmac boost is a real, verifiable Budget commitment.

veracity.statement: I’m advised the current senior medical officer (SMO) vacancy rate is 38.55 percent in Tairāwhiti. I’m further advised there has been an increase in fulltime-equivalent senior medical officers from 49.1 in December 2023 to 55 at the end of March this year, in Tairāwhiti, after a steep decline from 57.2 in December 2022 to 49.1 in December 2023.
veracity.explanation: Disputes the questioner's 44% figure with a sourced 38.55%; his framing selects the decline to 2023 as the baseline to show improvement.

veracity.statement: The unemployment numbers of 5.1 percent are exactly what was forecast by Treasury under the previous Government. Unfortunately, we are dealing with the realities of high Government spending, inflation, high interest rates that lead to a recession; it leads to higher unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The 5.1% figure and the claim it matched a prior Treasury forecast are checkable; presented to deflect responsibility, omitting policy contributions to unemployment.

veracity.statement: Last year, alongside a 54 percent increase in foot patrols, aggravated robberies in the Wellington district dropped by 33.6 percent. Being visible is a critical part of successful policing.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable statistics presented favourably; the causal attribution is asserted rather than demonstrated.

veracity.statement: based on news reports I’m aware of, approximately 71 jobs have been lost at New Zealand Media and Entertainment (NZME), 48 at TVNZ, four from The Spinoff, and 27 from Whakaata Māori. All of those people have our sympathy.
veracity.explanation: Sourced to news reports and appropriately hedged ('approximately', 'I’m aware of'); consistent with reported redundancies.

veracity.statement: The target that was set for those Government cost savings was achieving $1.5 billion worth of savings and tasking the Government agencies with either 6.5 or 7.5 of their baseline budget... will deliver—given the environment that she inherited—$23 billion worth of savings over a four-year period. Because of this initiative and essential action, the deficit is $1.1 billion smaller than it would have been without those savings.
veracity.explanation: Figures are presented in a partisan committee speech and are internally jarring (a $1.5b target 'delivering' $23b), suggesting conflation of different savings measures.

rigor.statement: I’ve heard the “defund defence” narrative on top of the “defund the police” narrative from the degrowth Greens, but actually it is the defence forces that show up and look after our people and the people in the Pacific because of their abilities and their capabilities and the assets that they have.
rigor.explanation: Builds a strawman ('defund defence' narrative) and answers a question about climate mitigation with an appeal to defence-force heroism — no logical link.

rigor.statement: Does he think it enhances or diminishes New Zealand’s international reputation as a clean, green economy when his Minister of Foreign Affairs indicates that New Zealand was wrong to sign the Paris Agreement, travels to the Pacific—one of the regions of the world most affected by climate change—and questions the global scientific consensus on climate change, and his Government dismantles almost all proactive action to reduce New Zealand’s emissions?
rigor.explanation: Chains several factual premises toward a reputational conclusion, but 'dismantles almost all proactive action' is an overstatement that weakens the logic.

rigor.statement: As a matter of education, if the economy is growing at 0.7 percent or annualised at 2.8, how could you possibly describe that as being a recession?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in specific growth figures and a definitional point about what constitutes a recession.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister not think it’s just axiomatic that if China, India, the United States, and Russia were signed up—that’s almost 60 percent of the emissions in this world at the moment—then targets could be met?
rigor.explanation: Cites a large emissions share to argue about target attainability, but the logic (their participation makes 'targets met') is loosely stated and the 'almost 60 percent' is approximate.

rigor.statement: Why did his Government choose to cut $2.4 billion on climate mitigation when the New Zealand Defence Force themselves have identified climate change as one of the biggest risks we face to national security?
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific cut figure and appeals to the NZDF's own risk assessment to expose a tension in the Government's position.

rigor.statement: The Asian region, including Australia, accounts for 70 percent of New Zealand’s international trade. There is a risk of slower growth in the region because many economies there have significant exposures to the new US tariff regime.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from trade concentration to a slower-growth risk with a coherent causal chain.

rigor.statement: At the half-year update, trading partner growth was already forecast to be modest—at around 2.5 percent in the June 2026 year. Following the recent tariff announcements, Treasury’s initial assessment is that partner growth will be closer to 2 percent in the 2026 year. Similarly, at the half-year update, global inflation was forecast at 2.5 percent... Treasury’s current assessment is that global inflation could rise by as much as 0.5 percent in that year.
rigor.explanation: Attributes figures to Treasury, distinguishes prior forecast from revised assessment, and links tariffs to the revision.

rigor.statement: there were a number of factors which Treasury now acknowledge they were over-optimistic about, including trends around revenue collection, including the way that they accounted for future labour productivity, and, overall, this had the effect of flattering the outlook at the pre-election update.
rigor.explanation: Identifies concrete mechanisms and their directional effect ('flattering the outlook') rather than a bare assertion.

rigor.statement: Two very pertinent examples of that are, firstly, Pharmac funding, where it became clear after the Budget that without considerable uplift in funding for Pharmac, they would have been left to delist medicines... Another pertinent example is the school lunch programme, which, again, had not been funded into out-years, even though Labour campaigned on continuing that programme.
rigor.explanation: Uses specific cases to support the general claim about short-term-only funding; coherent, though presented one-sidedly.

rigor.statement: Does she regret cancelling and delaying housing, hospital, and school builds, which has caused the collapse of the construction sector and the deepest recession seen in 30 years?
rigor.explanation: Asserts a direct causal chain from build cancellations to sector collapse and 'deepest recession in 30 years' without establishing the link — overstated causation.

rigor.statement: if two other recognised countries have certified a particular medication, the expectation is it will become legal in New Zealand within 30 days.
rigor.explanation: Clear rule with defined criteria; the 'duplicating work' rationale follows logically from the premise.

rigor.statement: in the case of one recent asthma medication, 16 months for Medsafe to tell the New Zealand people it is safe for them to use a medication that is already widely used and legal in countries such as Australia, the UK, United States, Switzerland, Japan, Canada, and Singapore.
rigor.explanation: Uses the example and comparator-country track records to argue duplication, a coherent evidence-based case.

rigor.statement: The unemployment numbers of 5.1 percent are exactly what was forecast by Treasury under the previous Government. Unfortunately, we are dealing with the realities of high Government spending, inflation, high interest rates that lead to a recession; it leads to higher unemployment.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal chain (spending→inflation→rates→recession→unemployment) that is economically plausible but conveniently exculpatory.

rigor.statement: Last year, alongside a 54 percent increase in foot patrols, aggravated robberies in the Wellington district dropped by 33.6 percent. Being visible is a critical part of successful policing.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes patrol increase and robbery decrease to imply causation ('alongside'); suggestive but stops short of establishing the link.

rigor.statement: The target that was set for those Government cost savings was achieving $1.5 billion worth of savings and tasking the Government agencies with either 6.5 or 7.5 of their baseline budget... will deliver—given the environment that she inherited—$23 billion worth of savings over a four-year period. Because of this initiative and essential action, the deficit is $1.1 billion smaller than it would have been without those savings.
rigor.explanation: Ties savings to a smaller deficit with a counterfactual, but the leap between the stated target and headline savings figure is unexplained.

divination.statement: we have our Emissions Reduction Plan 2 Budget and plan, which suggests that our Government is actually on track to deliver Net Carbon Zero potentially six years earlier.
divination.explanation: Prediction of reaching net carbon zero 'six years earlier'; optimistic given the Government has cut mitigation spending, and hedged with 'potentially'.

divination.statement: Though unwelcome, the tariffs that have been imposed on New Zealand are likely to be modest in comparison with the impact for many other countries. The most significant impact for New Zealand of the current uncertainty will be through disruptions to the global economy.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that direct tariff impact will be modest and that the main channel will be global-economy disruption; plausible and consistent with NZ's trade profile.

divination.statement: At the half-year update, trading partner growth was already forecast to be modest—at around 2.5 percent in the June 2026 year. Following the recent tariff announcements, Treasury’s initial assessment is that partner growth will be closer to 2 percent in the 2026 year. Similarly, at the half-year update, global inflation was forecast at 2.5 percent... Treasury’s current assessment is that global inflation could rise by as much as 0.5 percent in that year.
divination.explanation: Forward forecasts of growth and inflation; sourced to Treasury and hedged, but inherently uncertain.

divination.statement: The Defence Capability Plan outlines planned commitments of $12 billion over the next four years, including a $9 billion increase to baseline funding. The plan will raise New Zealand’s defence spending from the current level of approximately 1 percent of GDP to 2 percent of GDP within eight years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts reaching 2% of GDP within eight years — a commitment spanning beyond the current term and dependent on future budgets, so uncertain.

strength.statement: It has been fantastic to see 2,000 kids come out of motels and actually put into safe, dry homes, and 2,500 families, as well.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered reduction in emergency-housing motel use; a real trend, though the 'where did people go' concern is unaddressed.

strength.statement: The Government plans to stick to our fiscal strategy, including remaining with our intention to endeavour to return the books to an operating balance before gains and losses excluding ACC gains and losses surplus in the 2027-28 fiscal year, and to continue our efforts to reduce net debt.
strength.explanation: A restated commitment with a dated target; delivery is prospective and hedged with 'endeavour to', so intent rather than demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: Many—most notably, filling in a significant fiscal cliff in Pharmac funding last year and then boosting Pharmac funding by around $600 million.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered action — filling the Pharmac funding cliff and adding ~$600m — which corresponds to an actual funding decision.

strength.statement: We consulted on 60 square metres without building or resource consent; we’ve decided to increase that to 70 square metres. We’ll be amending the Building Act and resource consenting system to make it easier to build granny flats, or, as they’re known in the legal parlance, minor residential units.
strength.explanation: A concrete decision announced with a clear mechanism, but implementation (the amendment) is still pending — announcement rather than delivered.

strength.statement: The Defence Capability Plan outlines planned commitments of $12 billion over the next four years, including a $9 billion increase to baseline funding. The plan will raise New Zealand’s defence spending from the current level of approximately 1 percent of GDP to 2 percent of GDP within eight years.
strength.explanation: An announced multi-year plan, not yet delivered; describes intended investment rather than demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: I moved swiftly to introduce the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill to repeal restrictions on Sunday advertising; why the Government made changes to eligibility criteria for the screen production rebate, which saw shows such as Shortland Street benefit as a result; and why the Government’s currently consulting on proposals for a media reform package.
strength.explanation: Mix of delivered (bill introduced, rebate criteria changed) and in-progress (consultation) actions; partial follow-through.

specificity.statement: In terms of addressing the structural deficit, is the Minister considering addressing that issue of uneven capital income taxation?
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy issue (uneven capital income taxation) and grounds it in specific reports (Treasury annual review p.9, IMF), though the question itself doesn't specify a mechanism.

specificity.statement: So the rule in the Income Tax Act is quite straightforward. A person may claim a tax deduction to the extent to which they earn income. Of course, a large amount of the income on residential rental properties is capital gains, which are currently untaxed. Therefore, there is no good reason to have the interest deductibility.
specificity.explanation: Names the Income Tax Act rule, the untaxed-capital-gains mechanism, and the new-builds carve-out elsewhere in her turn.

specificity.statement: we know that the costs of meeting our international obligations are going to range from somewhere between $3.3 billion and $23.7 billion.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete dollar figures for the obligation range.

specificity.statement: The alternative course is that which was taken by the last Government, which chose to be incredibly fiscally imprudent, taking debt from less than 20 percent of GDP to more than 40 percent of GDP. For the benefit of members of this House, that is an addition to New Zealand’s debt of $100 billion.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: debt from <20% to >40% of GDP and a $100 billion addition.

specificity.statement: First, setting a higher bar for new initiatives in our Budgets to ensure that they actually deliver on New Zealanders’ most important priorities. That means we won’t be investing hundreds of millions of dollars in consultancy reports, in light rail projects that go nowhere, in policy analysts to develop jobs taxes that are dumped in the rush of an election campaign.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete targets (consultancy spend, light rail, the jobs/income-insurance tax) but frames the 'higher bar' strategy without amounts or thresholds.

specificity.statement: instead of delivering classrooms at a cost of $1.2 million, appoint a prudent Minister of Education who says, “We need to make the dollars go further”, gets the cost down to more like $800,000, and is able to deliver more classrooms than the previous Government did—in a year.
specificity.explanation: Concrete per-classroom cost figures ($1.2m down to ~$800k) and a comparative delivery claim.

specificity.statement: Prudent: in our first Budget, finding $23 billion worth of reprioritisations to ensure that we could fund fiscally neutral tax relief for New Zealanders who had been assaulted by a cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete reprioritisation figure ($23 billion) tied to a named outcome (tax relief).

specificity.statement: Moves like making sure that people don’t have to jump through red tape and hoops to put a granny flat in their backyard are actually a way of enhancing productivity. Getting rid of the productivity-sapping Resource Management Act, which has been weaponised against development, against investment, and against housing, will be good for productivity. We’ve published a document—and the member should read it—called Going for Growth, which summarises a number of actions across five key themes.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete levers (granny-flat rules, RMA repeal, the Going for Growth document and its five themes) but stops short of quantified impacts.

specificity.statement: Here’s what happened: we had a cost of living crisis that was intergenerational in its significance, with inflation blowing out to 7.3 percent, strangling many families... We then had a Reserve Bank that was forced to drive up interest rates... and we then had the crushing effect that those high interest rates had on economic activity, and a significant economic slowdown.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the argument with a concrete inflation figure and a clear causal sequence.

specificity.statement: That will be a matter for Treasury and that will be a matter that we update at the Budget when it’s published on 22 May.
specificity.explanation: Names the Budget publication date (22 May) as the point of update.

specificity.statement: I think the most objective measure of housing need is the social housing wait-list. On the watch of the last Government, that wait-list, which determines those who are in need of social housing support, quadrupled. On our watch, that social housing list is reducing, which reflects the fact that we have been effective in making sure that more New Zealanders are able to access appropriate housing.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete metric (the wait-list) and its direction, though without figures.

specificity.statement: This Government has published an emphatic emission reduction plan for the second emission reduction period, which demonstrates very clearly our ability to meet our domestic emission requirements, and, sensibly, we’ve aligned our international commitments for the future with our domestic efforts.
specificity.explanation: Refers to a named plan (second emissions reduction plan) but asserts 'very clearly' able to meet requirements without detail.

specificity.statement: Our Government has been progressing a significant reform agenda there... highlighted last week, when we said, “Actually, you don’t need to jump through those hoops anymore. If you want to put a 70-square-metre granny flat in your backyard so that your teenage son doesn’t have to have unaffordable housing, so that your kaumātua can continue to live with your family... ‘Cut the red tape; make it happen.’”
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete measure (consent-free 70-square-metre granny flats) though the broader RMA/consenting reforms remain described in general terms.

specificity.statement: We published a summary of initiatives, which included every single savings initiative, demonstrating how we got out $1.5 billion worth of savings from the public agencies... There had been a habit of putting lots of money into the policy work needed to support go-nowhere initiatives such as Lake Onslow, such as Auckland Light Rail, such as the income insurance scheme.
specificity.explanation: Concrete savings figure ($1.5 billion) and named cancelled programmes (Lake Onslow, Auckland Light Rail, income insurance).

specificity.statement: I would actually like a meaningful back and forth on this, because I think it is relevant to the people of this country... what specific assumptions is Treasury presently making when it comes to forecasting productivity and the impact that Government spending or Government spending cuts may have on that model, and does she have any issues with the way that Treasury is currently inputting those assumptions or is she completely fine with it?
specificity.explanation: A precisely scoped question about named modelling assumptions (productivity forecasting and spending impacts) in Treasury's fiscal strategy model.

specificity.statement: I’d bring us back to the promise that was made in the coalition agreement that decisions would be made based on data and evidence. So if the Minister herself is saying that Treasury is simply modelling those projections extrapolated from the past, how then does she seek to get a sense of an understanding of the efficacy of the spending or the cuts that she is making?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the challenge in the named coalition commitment and the specific modelling limitation.

specificity.statement: our Paris Agreement NDC out to 2030 has been foreshadowed, actually under successive Governments, including the last Government, to not be met—they are not capable of being met—by domestic efforts. So we are going to have to engage in purchasing offshore credits.
specificity.explanation: Concrete on the mechanism (offshore credit purchases) and the timeframe (2030 NDC).

specificity.statement: We had Treasury and the Ministry for the Environment in 2023 tell us that the bill that we were potentially looking at paying—the constructive liability—was anywhere between $3 billion to $24 billion, but the floor was $3 billion, and the orders of magnitude would be determined by how much effort we were to make domestically.
specificity.explanation: Cites the source agencies, year, and the $3–24bn range with the driver of the variance.

specificity.statement: I know the Minister initiated a cost-saving initiative of around 6.5 to 7.5 percent. I wonder if she could elucidate on... whether there were some sectors or departments which actually yielded greater savings, what areas they were and, in fact, whether there were any unexpected areas or surprises or insights... or what it revealed going through that process and any indications of potential further savings going forward.
specificity.explanation: Cites the concrete savings-target band (6.5–7.5%) and asks for specific sectoral breakdowns and insights.

specificity.statement: Since she has taken office, the economy has plunged into recession, 22,000 more Kiwis are on jobseeker, 33,000 more are unemployed, the construction sector has lost thousands of jobs, building consents are down 7.2 percent, front-line health services are struggling or even closing across the country, and in Wellington, homelessness has risen by 37 percent. Does the Minister still think her Government’s policies have had nothing to do with this?
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures (22,000 jobseeker, 33,000 unemployed, consents -7.2%, homelessness +37%).

specificity.statement: the interest deductibility—the reinstatement of it—had a price tag of $2.9 billion, and yet the Minister is talking about incentivising productive assets... Why does she believe that a $2.9 billion interest deductibility... would help to incentivise more productive investment into the productive side of the economy when it’s quite clear it’s giving residential housing investment a bigger lift because now they’re able to deduct the interest deductibility from it?
specificity.explanation: Attaches a concrete cost ($2.9 billion) to the named policy and pinpoints the mechanism (deduction favouring residential rental investment).

specificity.statement: The Minister of Finance should know that the Public Finance Act requires Treasury to use its best professional judgments in preparing all of those forecasts... So my question, then, is to the Minister of Finance: what reports should the Opposition and members of the public depend on in order to get forecasts... At the moment, all I hear is that it’s just the Minister of Finance was right and every single body else is wrong.
specificity.explanation: References the statutory basis and named documents (PREFU, CEFA 2023) rather than speaking in generalities.

specificity.statement: We’ve heard excellent results about the growth of the Māori economy recently. What targeted initiatives does the Minister of Finance have to support this growth, and has the Minister done any forecasting about the impact that tariffs will have on the Māori economy?
specificity.explanation: Asks about two concrete things — targeted Māori-economy initiatives and tariff-impact forecasting — though the initiatives are unnamed.

specificity.statement: they are pretty confident that we are actually investing the right amount, roughly speaking, of our GDP in infrastructure; what we’re not doing is we’re not getting good value for money from that. There are three reasons for that: one of them is that we don’t have a clear pipeline at the moment; secondly, our regulatory processes are very, very expensive; and, third, some of our delivery processes are not particularly good.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete drivers (pipeline, regulatory cost, delivery) and the 60% maintenance benchmark elsewhere in his turn.

specificity.statement: in the education sector, we are not supporting the investment that needs to be made in pilot training and that is going to leave us with a significant shortage of pilots. It’s already occurring and it’s going to get worse over the next two or three years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a mechanism (underinvestment in pilot training) and a rough timeframe (next two to three years).

specificity.statement: there’s a $6 billion shortfall in what is needed in the land transport plan—at least $6 billion. How is the Minister going to fund that?
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the land-transport funding gap ($6 billion, 'at least') and puts a direct funding question to the Minister.

specificity.statement: we have “roads of National Party significance” or 17—... 15 of those projects are in the North Island and only two of them are in the South Island... how can he ensure that there is an adequate amount of funding going into road maintenance instead of sucking money from there into the “roads of National Party significance”?
specificity.explanation: Cites the number of projects and their regional split, and the maintenance-vs-new-build trade-off.

rigor.statement: In terms of addressing the structural deficit, is the Minister considering addressing that issue of uneven capital income taxation?
rigor.explanation: Builds the question on cited evidence — Treasury's structural-deficit finding and the IMF's tax-reform report — with a clear line from premise to the revenue question.

rigor.statement: But Minister, I put it to you that it’s also prudent to consider future revenue streams to address the structural deficit that has been identified by the IMF, by Treasury, by a number of agencies. Can the Minister consider what might be prudent on the revenue side?
rigor.explanation: Appeals to converging expert bodies (IMF, Treasury, agencies) to argue revenue must be considered; reasonable though light on specifics.

rigor.statement: So the rule in the Income Tax Act is quite straightforward. A person may claim a tax deduction to the extent to which they earn income. Of course, a large amount of the income on residential rental properties is capital gains, which are currently untaxed. Therefore, there is no good reason to have the interest deductibility.
rigor.explanation: A structured tax argument from a stated principle (deduction tied to taxable income) to a conclusion; contestable but logically laid out.

rigor.statement: but the simple fact is that that debt was accumulated and frittered away.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping conclusion ('frittered away') asserted without the itemised evidence her own preceding sentence says would be needed to judge it.

rigor.statement: I would note that while the member is always happy to impose new taxes on New Zealanders to steal from them today, she is not ever advocating that that be done in order to improve our fiscal position.
rigor.explanation: Emotive framing ('steal from them') substitutes for argument about the revenue proposal on its merits.

rigor.statement: We now have a position from the Labour Party, different from that enunciated by Chris Hipkins yesterday, in which they oppose New Zealand making the contributions required to our defence force to ensure we are ready to contribute to global peace and security, that we are ready to deploy when natural disasters occur in the Pacific... If your argument is that we shouldn’t be investing in defence, then I’d invite you to sit closer to Chlöe Swarbrick.
rigor.explanation: Recasts a question about the opportunity cost of $12b defence spending as outright opposition to defence — a strawman — then an ad hominem 'sit closer to Swarbrick'.

rigor.statement: Well, there are two separate parts to the question. First, in terms of its productivity assumptions, Treasury has looked at historical trends of where labour productivity has been and, long story short, it’s a bad and sad story, which is that labour productivity in New Zealand has been falling for many years and has been below par... they feed forward, test that against other assumptions about the economy, and then provide their best estimate of future labour productivity.
rigor.explanation: Explains the actual methodology (historical trend → forward estimate) rather than sloganeering.

rigor.statement: Well, that’s a very confused argument from the member Chlöe Swarbrick, because it makes two wrongful assumptions. The first is that all Government spending is good spending... The second assumption that the member has made is that the only way that we drive productivity forward is through our spending decisions.
rigor.explanation: Isolates two premises to rebut and offers a real counter-point (regulatory, not just spending, levers), though it partly re-characterises the member's actual question.

rigor.statement: Moves like making sure that people don’t have to jump through red tape and hoops to put a granny flat in their backyard are actually a way of enhancing productivity. Getting rid of the productivity-sapping Resource Management Act, which has been weaponised against development, against investment, and against housing, will be good for productivity. We’ve published a document—and the member should read it—called Going for Growth, which summarises a number of actions across five key themes.
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasonable non-spending productivity argument, but 'weaponised' and the asserted productivity link lean on rhetoric over evidence.

rigor.statement: Here’s what happened: we had a cost of living crisis that was intergenerational in its significance, with inflation blowing out to 7.3 percent, strangling many families... We then had a Reserve Bank that was forced to drive up interest rates... and we then had the crushing effect that those high interest rates had on economic activity, and a significant economic slowdown.
rigor.explanation: Constructs an evidence-referenced causal narrative, but presents a contested single-cause story as settled empirical proof.

rigor.statement: the facile simplification which, sometimes, this debate is reduced to, forgets the fact that in New Zealand, we do have land taxes; we just call them rates. Rates are charged on those who own property and landholdings; they are not charged on those who do not own land and property.
rigor.explanation: A clever framing point, but equating council rates with a land tax elides the design differences the tax debate is actually about.

rigor.statement: as I have laboriously highlighted to her senior colleague Barbara Edmonds, the unemployment forecasts that we currently have are exactly the same as was presented by Minister Robertson at the pre-election fiscal update.
rigor.explanation: Uses the pre-existing forecast to argue against attributing current unemployment to her government — a logically relevant point.

rigor.statement: we are not a Government that is going to send more than $20 billion overseas into a carbon market to wear a hair shirt for New Zealanders... The alternative course is to wear a hair shirt and pretend that somehow, by spending $20 billion overseas, Donald Trump’s going to change his mind on the Paris Agreement. Well, pull me another one!
rigor.explanation: Fixes on the top of a $3–24bn range as if it were the proposal, then mocks a strawman (that offshore credits aim to change Trump's mind), rather than addressing the actual obligation question.

rigor.statement: It is, I think, a significant assumption to then equate that that will require $20 billion worth of purchases of credit by New Zealand. That is the assumption that I have rejected... feeding into that assumption are all sorts of things about (1) the quantum of how far short of our Paris commitment we will be; (2) what the cost of credits would be internationally, and, in fact, whether they could be purchased; (3) whether that is the mechanism by which we would meet our obligation.
rigor.explanation: Enumerates the genuine uncertainties (shortfall size, credit price/availability, mechanism) that make the $20bn top-of-range figure contestable — a substantive, well-structured point.

rigor.statement: Interest deductibility has been a rule in our tax system for many decades, under successive Governments, and the principle has always been that it should be equally applied to different asset classes, lest we create significant distortions in the economy—so all we have done is restore things to a tax principle that had long been the case.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a stated tax-neutrality principle to justify the reinstatement; a coherent argument, though it sidesteps the untaxed-capital-gains asymmetry Edmonds and Russell raise.

rigor.statement: It can also be true that sometimes, just like every other set of forecasters in the world, they get it wrong. That is the nature of forecasts. They are a best estimate of future events. It is also true to characterise that Treasury, along with others, got their forecasts prior to the election wrong.
rigor.explanation: Draws a legitimate distinction between respecting Treasury's methodology and noting forecasts can be wrong; internally coherent.

rigor.statement: What I meant by that was while Treasury... has an independent forecasting function... it is always also the case that the Treasury has the Minister of Finance as its responsible Minister and, therefore, is beholden to that Minister when it comes to decisions, for example, like how big the operating allowance should be.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes independent forecasting from ministerial decision-making coherently, if self-servingly applied.

rigor.statement: I’d bring us back to the promise that was made in the coalition agreement that decisions would be made based on data and evidence. So if the Minister herself is saying that Treasury is simply modelling those projections extrapolated from the past, how then does she seek to get a sense of an understanding of the efficacy of the spending or the cuts that she is making?
rigor.explanation: Builds a logical challenge: if productivity is extrapolated from past trends, the model can't isolate the efficacy of current spending choices — a coherent evidentiary point.

rigor.statement: We had Treasury and the Ministry for the Environment in 2023 tell us that the bill that we were potentially looking at paying—the constructive liability—was anywhere between $3 billion to $24 billion, but the floor was $3 billion, and the orders of magnitude would be determined by how much effort we were to make domestically.
rigor.explanation: Correctly ties the cost range to domestic mitigation effort rather than presenting a single scare figure.

rigor.statement: My reference to the Minister of Climate Change is that he is internationally responsible for and chairing negotiations with other countries to facilitate what it looks like to purchase offshore credits... yet we simultaneously are getting press releases from the Minister of Climate Change about memoranda of understanding that are being signed internationally that will count towards our nationally determined contribution.
rigor.explanation: Points to a concrete contradiction — the Climate Change Minister is negotiating offshore-credit MoUs while the Finance Minister denies an intention to purchase credits — as evidence for her claim.

rigor.statement: Since she has taken office, the economy has plunged into recession, 22,000 more Kiwis are on jobseeker, 33,000 more are unemployed, the construction sector has lost thousands of jobs, building consents are down 7.2 percent, front-line health services are struggling or even closing across the country, and in Wellington, homelessness has risen by 37 percent. Does the Minister still think her Government’s policies have had nothing to do with this?
rigor.explanation: Stacks correlated indicators to imply the government caused them, without isolating policy effects from the pre-existing downturn — a post-hoc framing.

rigor.statement: the interest deductibility—the reinstatement of it—had a price tag of $2.9 billion, and yet the Minister is talking about incentivising productive assets... Why does she believe that a $2.9 billion interest deductibility... would help to incentivise more productive investment into the productive side of the economy when it’s quite clear it’s giving residential housing investment a bigger lift because now they’re able to deduct the interest deductibility from it?
rigor.explanation: Argues a specific inconsistency — a 'productivity' rationale for a measure that channels investment into non-productive residential housing — a coherent evidentiary challenge.

rigor.statement: The Minister of Finance should know that the Public Finance Act requires Treasury to use its best professional judgments in preparing all of those forecasts... So my question, then, is to the Minister of Finance: what reports should the Opposition and members of the public depend on in order to get forecasts... At the moment, all I hear is that it’s just the Minister of Finance was right and every single body else is wrong.
rigor.explanation: Cites the Public Finance Act obligation to argue Treasury's forecasts are professionally grounded, then presses a legitimate question about which sources are reliable; the closing generalisation is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: they are pretty confident that we are actually investing the right amount, roughly speaking, of our GDP in infrastructure; what we’re not doing is we’re not getting good value for money from that. There are three reasons for that: one of them is that we don’t have a clear pipeline at the moment; secondly, our regulatory processes are very, very expensive; and, third, some of our delivery processes are not particularly good.
rigor.explanation: Relays the Infrastructure Commission's evidence-based diagnosis with a clear premise-to-cause structure (right quantum, poor value, three named reasons).

rigor.statement: there’s a $6 billion shortfall in what is needed in the land transport plan—at least $6 billion. How is the Minister going to fund that?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a figure raised at select committee rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: we have “roads of National Party significance” or 17—... 15 of those projects are in the North Island and only two of them are in the South Island... how can he ensure that there is an adequate amount of funding going into road maintenance instead of sucking money from there into the “roads of National Party significance”?
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete geographic breakdown (15 North Island vs 2 South Island of 17) to argue skewed priorities, though the partisan 'roads of National Party significance' label editorialises the point.

civility.statement: In terms of addressing the structural deficit, is the Minister considering addressing that issue of uneven capital income taxation?
civility.explanation: Substantive, policy-focused question with no personal attack.

civility.statement: But Minister, I put it to you that it’s also prudent to consider future revenue streams to address the structural deficit that has been identified by the IMF, by Treasury, by a number of agencies. Can the Minister consider what might be prudent on the revenue side?
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of 'prudence' and presses on policy, without personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, the Minister didn’t answer my question, which is: what’s prudent in terms of revenue?
civility.explanation: Fair, direct observation that the question was dodged; targets the conduct of the answer, not the person.

civility.statement: I just want to help the Minister with her understanding of interest deductibility. I know she had to get people in to explain provisional tax to her recently.
civility.explanation: A condescending personal jab implying the Minister lacks basic tax competence, rather than engaging the argument.

civility.statement: Is the Minister committed to meeting our Paris obligations?
civility.explanation: Direct, legitimate policy question.

civility.statement: The alternative course is that which was taken by the last Government, which chose to be incredibly fiscally imprudent, taking debt from less than 20 percent of GDP to more than 40 percent of GDP. For the benefit of members of this House, that is an addition to New Zealand’s debt of $100 billion.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-directed criticism of the previous government's fiscal record.

civility.statement: but the simple fact is that that debt was accumulated and frittered away.
civility.explanation: Dismissive but aimed at spending decisions rather than a person.

civility.statement: I would note that while the member is always happy to impose new taxes on New Zealanders to steal from them today, she is not ever advocating that that be done in order to improve our fiscal position.
civility.explanation: Frames taxation as 'stealing' and characterises the member's motives — a loaded, uncharitable strawman rather than engagement with her actual argument.

civility.statement: We now have a position from the Labour Party, different from that enunciated by Chris Hipkins yesterday, in which they oppose New Zealand making the contributions required to our defence force to ensure we are ready to contribute to global peace and security, that we are ready to deploy when natural disasters occur in the Pacific... If your argument is that we shouldn’t be investing in defence, then I’d invite you to sit closer to Chlöe Swarbrick.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents the member's position and uses a dismissive jab rather than answering.

civility.statement: Well, that’s a very confused argument from the member Chlöe Swarbrick, because it makes two wrongful assumptions. The first is that all Government spending is good spending... The second assumption that the member has made is that the only way that we drive productivity forward is through our spending decisions.
civility.explanation: 'Very confused argument' is a mild put-down but she does engage the substance.

civility.statement: Well, that was a string of poorly evidenced assertions in lieu of a question. I found many assertions that were wrong in there. First of all, the member has already been corrected in this House on her use of data when it relates to construction jobs, where she uses a selective measure that Stats NZ themselves say is novel, and she ignores the stat which shows there has actually been increases in construction jobs.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the question as 'poorly evidenced assertions' but does engage specific data points.

civility.statement: we are not a Government that is going to send more than $20 billion overseas into a carbon market to wear a hair shirt for New Zealanders... The alternative course is to wear a hair shirt and pretend that somehow, by spending $20 billion overseas, Donald Trump’s going to change his mind on the Paris Agreement. Well, pull me another one!
civility.explanation: Relies on ridicule ('hair shirt', 'pull me another one!', 'another tree you can climb up') instead of engaging the substance.

civility.statement: It’s a delight to get a lecture from the previous tax lecturer, and I look forward to hearing her lectures in the future on why New Zealanders should be taxed more and how that’s somehow going to drive our economy forward... Here’s a spoiler alert: she’s not going to be able to do that.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic personal framing ('previous tax lecturer', 'spoiler alert') rather than engaging Russell's point about new-builds and supply.

civility.statement: Barbara Anderson is apparently a New Zealand fiction writer, so she does have something in common with Barbara Edmonds.
civility.explanation: A personal jab implying Edmonds fabricates fiction — character-directed sarcasm rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: It’s not Treasury’s fault that Grant Robertson chose outlandish, extravagant operating allowances. In fact, it was probably the advice of the Treasury at the time that that was a very bad idea.
civility.explanation: 'Outlandish, extravagant' targets a former minister's decisions rather than his character, but is heated and the Treasury-advice claim is speculative ('probably').

civility.statement: I would actually like a meaningful back and forth on this, because I think it is relevant to the people of this country... what specific assumptions is Treasury presently making when it comes to forecasting productivity and the impact that Government spending or Government spending cuts may have on that model, and does she have any issues with the way that Treasury is currently inputting those assumptions or is she completely fine with it?
civility.explanation: Respectful, substantive, and directly engages the policy detail.

civility.statement: we’re just kind of confronted with this post-truth belligerence.
civility.explanation: A pointed characterisation of the Minister's manner of answering; critical of conduct rather than a personal insult, but combative.

civility.statement: I know the Minister initiated a cost-saving initiative of around 6.5 to 7.5 percent. I wonder if she could elucidate on... whether there were some sectors or departments which actually yielded greater savings, what areas they were and, in fact, whether there were any unexpected areas or surprises or insights... or what it revealed going through that process and any indications of potential further savings going forward.
civility.explanation: A neutral, substantive question inviting elaboration.

civility.statement: the interest deductibility—the reinstatement of it—had a price tag of $2.9 billion, and yet the Minister is talking about incentivising productive assets... Why does she believe that a $2.9 billion interest deductibility... would help to incentivise more productive investment into the productive side of the economy when it’s quite clear it’s giving residential housing investment a bigger lift because now they’re able to deduct the interest deductibility from it?
civility.explanation: Sharp but policy-focused, no personal attack.

civility.statement: The Minister of Finance should know that the Public Finance Act requires Treasury to use its best professional judgments in preparing all of those forecasts... So my question, then, is to the Minister of Finance: what reports should the Opposition and members of the public depend on in order to get forecasts... At the moment, all I hear is that it’s just the Minister of Finance was right and every single body else is wrong.
civility.explanation: Largely substantive; the 'everybody is wrong except the Minister' line is pointed but aimed at her conduct in debate.

civility.statement: We’ve heard excellent results about the growth of the Māori economy recently. What targeted initiatives does the Minister of Finance have to support this growth, and has the Minister done any forecasting about the impact that tariffs will have on the Māori economy?
civility.explanation: A constructive, non-adversarial question.

civility.statement: everybody across the committee, doesn’t matter which party they come from, is asking good questions and trying to get good answers out of the agencies, and that’s what I like to see.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of colleagues across the aisle.

civility.statement: we have “roads of National Party significance” or 17—... 15 of those projects are in the North Island and only two of them are in the South Island... how can he ensure that there is an adequate amount of funding going into road maintenance instead of sucking money from there into the “roads of National Party significance”?
civility.explanation: The nickname is a partisan jab, but it targets the policy programme rather than a person, and the underlying question is substantive.

civility.statement: for someone who rides a motorbike like I do, the journey is the most important—far more important than the destination. And we’re talking about the journeys here. That is how we get from A to B, how New Zealanders move around the country, and how our economy gets goods and services shifted around.
civility.explanation: Genial and collegial, crediting the chair's work before raising disagreements.

veracity.statement: So the rule in the Income Tax Act is quite straightforward. A person may claim a tax deduction to the extent to which they earn income. Of course, a large amount of the income on residential rental properties is capital gains, which are currently untaxed. Therefore, there is no good reason to have the interest deductibility.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate description of the deductibility/income-matching principle and untaxed capital gains, though 'no good reason' is her framing.

veracity.statement: we know that the costs of meeting our international obligations are going to range from somewhere between $3.3 billion and $23.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Cites a real range from the 2023 Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment (echoed by Swarbrick), though presenting it as a settled 'cost' overstates a hypothetical, caveat-laden figure.

veracity.statement: The alternative course is that which was taken by the last Government, which chose to be incredibly fiscally imprudent, taking debt from less than 20 percent of GDP to more than 40 percent of GDP.
