Since then, police have come across and seized more than 8,500 firearms in the line of duty—firearms that criminals never intended to hand in in 2019.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure and firearm counts given.

specificity.statement: as a result of the decisions that this Government has made around prioritising children to go into emergency housing, 1,110 kids have moved from emergency housing into warm, safe, dry homes between April and the end of July.
specificity.explanation: Exact count and date range tied to a named policy (Priority One).

specificity.statement: Eighty percent of our exports of goods and more than 350,000 jobs come from the rural sector.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentage and job figure.

specificity.statement: restore common sense to intensive winter grazing and stock exclusion rules, introduce pragmatic rules on on-farm water storage, and introduce legislation to cease the implementation of new significant natural areas. We've also repealed the burdensome log traders legislation
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete list of regulatory changes, though without dates or magnitudes.

specificity.statement: hydro storage, which is currently among the lowest since 1992; natural gas production, which has dropped 27.8 percent in production in the first three months of this year; and wind generation, which has also been below average since April this year, meaning 250 gigawatts less energy has been produced than was expected.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete metrics and percentages.

specificity.statement: $101 million has been allocated to 42 consented priority flood resilience schemes ... the key point of the fund is that we are willing to contribute up to 60 percent of the cost with relevant authorities, who must ensure they have resource consents
specificity.explanation: Names the funding total, number of schemes, and the co-investment share.

specificity.statement: for every $4 that the gentailers have paid out in dividends, only $1 has actually gone back into the productive capacity—i.e., invested in generative capacity.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete ratio to characterise gentailer behaviour.

specificity.statement: Many who have considered this at length recognise that those words in that founding document uphold tino rangatiratanga, the highest chieftainship, of the hapū of Māori, at which point it is clear that the 500 rangatira who signed our founding agreement understood they were certainly not giving up their sovereignty.
specificity.explanation: References the specific concept and the ~500 signatories rather than speaking in generalities.

civility.statement: We're hearing submissions. We're taking as wide as possible a look at this in the interests of New Zealand's long-term safety, and not trying to make cheap political points out of it on the way through.
civility.explanation: Implies the questioner is scoring 'cheap political points' — a mild swipe rather than a personal attack, but not engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I'd invite the people in the gallery up there to go and read the coalition agreement and stop wasting Parliament's time.
civility.explanation: 'Stop wasting Parliament's time' is a dismissive jab rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: we take the view of the most learned Māori or, dare I say it, lawyer to come to this Parliament, who got a degree in two years flat ... he set out what Māori then believed and which we believe today, unlike these new people who decide in their woke manner, like Willie Jackson—all over the place. He doesn't even stand up for the greatest leader Ngati Porou ever had, and decides he knows better.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on Willie Jackson ('woke', 'all over the place', 'decides he knows better') rather than engaging his position.

civility.statement: there are no principles to the Treaty of Waitangi. In 1987, five judges wrestling over the Lands case—... those five judges couldn't agree, either. So stop coming here with your unlearned humbug.
civility.explanation: 'Unlearned humbug' and (immediately prior) 'she knows nothing about the law' are direct personal disparagement.

civility.statement: If the Leader of the Opposition is going to come to the House and quote members, then he has to have an accurate quote. He can't make things up ... Quite simply, I didn't say that.
civility.explanation: A pointed point of order accusing the questioner of fabrication, but tied to a specific factual complaint about a misquote rather than gratuitous insult.

civility.statement: I simply wish to withdraw and apologise for my earlier interjection.
civility.explanation: Voluntarily withdraws and apologises for an interjection — respectful conduct.

civility.statement: Oh, I presume she's not meaning the same Buller hospital that several months after she opened it in May last year was temporarily closed. I presume it's that same hospital.
civility.explanation: A factual jab at the questioner's history, sarcastic in tone but tied to a real event.

civility.statement: They missed all of the warning signs, they failed to address any of the problems, and they utterly let down a generation of Kiwi kids and they deprioritised maths from the regionally allocated professional learning and development (PLD) fund. If that member wants to know why she's sitting on that side of the House, this is a perfect example.
civility.explanation: Sweeping condemnation capped with a personal 'why she's sitting on that side of the House' jab rather than engaging the question.

civility.statement: In 2019, the previous Government allowed only three days for select committee submissions and changed the Arms Act in just 10 days. This undemocratic process marginalised and disrespected those who deserved a say on the laws that are impacting them.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the previous process ('undemocratic', 'disrespected') aimed at conduct rather than persons.

civility.statement: for the last six years, the last Government demonised gas production in New Zealand and it has left us with a shortage in the energy needed ... the only project they had on the table was a phantom project for 2038. They thought that was the answer. They have left New Zealand with an insecure energy sector, and they should take responsibility.
civility.explanation: 'Demonised', 'phantom project', and 'they should take responsibility' are combative characterisations of the previous government rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Well, we need more wind, we need more gas, we need more hydro—we need more energy in this country. And the last Government's decisions—the reckless policies of the last Government—have meant that this country's energy has been put at risk.
civility.explanation: 'Reckless policies of the last Government' is a repeated inflammatory characterisation (raised as a point of order).

civility.statement: it is heartbreaking to see the hollowing out of regional New Zealand—in particular, the effect of Fred Flintstone economics now being brought home to bear—when former decision makers, former Ministers, did nothing to increase the resilience and the security of energy supply.
civility.explanation: 'Fred Flintstone economics' mocks opponents' policy rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Speakers' ruling 171/5(1) makes it clear—and this is not in dispute—that a "Government has the right to transfer a question,"; however, not in any way that it "obstructs the answer." When the question intended to ask a Minister to stand by a statement that he had made, and then that be transferred, there is no possible way that another Minister can answer that question.
civility.explanation: Procedural, respectful, and focused on the rules rather than personalities.

civility.statement: I'd like to think that in my interactions with you, you'd consider that we do so in a respectful manner.
civility.explanation: Explicit commitment to respectful conduct toward the Chair.

veracity.statement: It would not be respectful or democratic for me to seek to answer on behalf of another party's leader. But I can say, in comparison with a previous coalition I was in in 2017 to 2020, at this present time, what you see over this side of the House is the epitome of harmony.
veracity.explanation: 'The epitome of harmony' is spin/hyperbole about a coalition visibly split over the Treaty principles bill, the very subject of the question.

veracity.statement: there are no principles to the Treaty of Waitangi. In 1987, five judges wrestling over the Lands case—... those five judges couldn't agree, either. So stop coming here with your unlearned humbug.

veracity.statement: particularly continuing Labour's work which began in September 2021 on AUKUS Pillar Two, with the help of the honest Hon Andrew Little's endorsement.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the previous Labour government engaged with AUKUS Pillar Two discussions, though framing it as settled 'work' overstates the position.

veracity.statement: every party in Parliament except the ACT Party voted in favour of it, and his party, the National Party ... indicated before the election it would keep the firearms register
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the record: the 2020 firearms registry legislation passed with wide support and ACT opposed; National's pre-election signalling on keeping the register is fairly characterised.

veracity.statement: the Reserve Bank's monetary policy committee last week cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the August 2024 RBNZ decision to cut the OCR by 25bp to 5.25%.

veracity.statement: a drop from a 7 percent mortgage rate to 6 percent for a family with a 25-year, $500,000 mortgage means their repayments would reduce by $145 a fortnight
veracity.explanation: The order of magnitude is right for such a loan; presented as one illustrative example rather than a universal claim.

veracity.statement: Vote Health will receive nearly $30 billion in funding this year, with Budget 2024 also seeing the largest ever commitment to funding for the sector, with a boost of $16.68 billion across three Budgets.
veracity.explanation: The ~$30bn Vote Health figure and the $16.68bn multi-Budget uplift align with Budget 2024 announcements; 'largest ever' is a defensible but promotional framing.

veracity.statement: given that 22 percent of students met the curriculum benchmark, clearly some of them had been taught it ... the result was that 78 percent of kids weren't where they needed to be to experience success at high school.

veracity.statement: More people were convicted of a firearm-related offence in 2023 than in 2019; it is up 18 percent. From 2019 to 2023, almost 2,000 gang members were charged with unlawful possession of firearms.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific conviction-trend and gang-charge figures; directionally plausible but the causal implication that the 2019/2020 law changes are to blame is not established by these numbers alone.

veracity.statement: of those 70 percent of A category firearms that have been found by New Zealand Police, 65 percent of them don't actually have a serial number on them. veracity.statement: as a result of the decisions that this Government has made around prioritising children to go into emergency housing, 1,110 kids have moved from emergency housing into warm, safe, dry homes between April and the end of July.
veracity.explanation: The 1,110 figure is internally consistent across answers; whether these placements are net-new and durable is not demonstrated.

veracity.statement: Eighty percent of our exports of goods and more than 350,000 jobs come from the rural sector.

veracity.statement: hydro storage, which is currently among the lowest since 1992; natural gas production, which has dropped 27.8 percent in production in the first three months of this year; and wind generation, which has also been below average since April this year, meaning 250 gigawatts less energy has been produced than was expected.
veracity.explanation: Low hydro storage, a sharp gas-production fall, and below-average wind in 2024 are consistent with reporting of the winter 2024 energy squeeze; precise figures unverified here.

veracity.statement: for the last six years, the last Government demonised gas production in New Zealand and it has left us with a shortage in the energy needed ... the only project they had on the table was a phantom project for 2038. They thought that was the answer. They have left New Zealand with an insecure energy sector, and they should take responsibility.
veracity.explanation: The exploration-ban framing is contested; gas decline has multiple causes, so the mono-causal blame is misleading.

veracity.explanation: A specific dividend-to-reinvestment ratio; plausible as a criticism but unsourced and not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Many who have considered this at length recognise that those words in that founding document uphold tino rangatiratanga, the highest chieftainship, of the hapū of Māori, at which point it is clear that the 500 rangatira who signed our founding agreement understood they were certainly not giving up their sovereignty.
veracity.explanation: The te reo text upholding tino rangatiratanga is well-founded; the flat claim that sovereignty was 'certainly not' ceded is a contested historical/legal interpretation.

rigor.statement: we take the view of the most learned Māori or, dare I say it, lawyer to come to this Parliament, who got a degree in two years flat ... he set out what Māori then believed and which we believe today, unlike these new people who decide in their woke manner, like Willie Jackson—all over the place. He doesn't even stand up for the greatest leader Ngati Porou ever had, and decides he knows better.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority (Ngata) to settle a contested constitutional question rather than argument from the text of the Treaty.

rigor.statement: there are no principles to the Treaty of Waitangi. In 1987, five judges wrestling over the Lands case—... those five judges couldn't agree, either. So stop coming here with your unlearned humbug.
rigor.explanation: Uses judicial disagreement as if it proved no principles exist — a non-sequitur — mixed with the ad hominem close.

rigor.statement: They missed all of the warning signs, they failed to address any of the problems, and they utterly let down a generation of Kiwi kids and they deprioritised maths from the regionally allocated professional learning and development (PLD) fund. If that member wants to know why she's sitting on that side of the House, this is a perfect example.
rigor.explanation: Mostly assertion and blame ('missed all', 'failed to address any') with only the PLD point as evidence.

rigor.statement: The previous Government spent more than $150 million on two firearms confiscations, promising to get illegal firearms off the streets once and for all. rigor.explanation: Reasonable point but relies on the assumption that later seizures indict the earlier scheme rather than reflecting ordinary policing.

rigor.explanation: Answers a systemic question about people left sleeping in cars with a single favourable anecdote (appeal to anecdote), which does not address the general risk.

rigor.statement: for the last six years, the last Government demonised gas production in New Zealand and it has left us with a shortage in the energy needed ... the only project they had on the table was a phantom project for 2038. They thought that was the answer. They have left New Zealand with an insecure energy sector, and they should take responsibility.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the current shortage largely to the 2018 exploration ban while downplaying hydro and wind factors he himself cited — a selective causal claim.

rigor.explanation: Colourful ridicule plus a sweeping 'did nothing' claim, with no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Speakers' ruling 171/5(1) makes it clear—and this is not in dispute—that a "Government has the right to transfer a question,"; however, not in any way that it "obstructs the answer." When the question intended to ask a Minister to stand by a statement that he had made, and then that be transferred, there is no possible way that another Minister can answer that question.
rigor.explanation: Builds a disciplined argument from specific Speakers' Rulings, concedes the points against him, and shows why the transfer obstructs the answer — premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: He asked two completely separate—related but separate—issues in the one question. The Government felt it best that I answered that question. Therefore, we've transferred it. I'm very happy to answer the question and account for it.
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent counter-argument that the second limb (housing funding) is his responsibility, engaging McAnulty's structure directly.

rigor.statement: Many who have considered this at length recognise that those words in that founding document uphold tino rangatiratanga, the highest chieftainship, of the hapū of Māori, at which point it is clear that the 500 rangatira who signed our founding agreement understood they were certainly not giving up their sovereignty.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the sovereignty argument in the te reo text (tino rangatiratanga) and the signatories' understanding, though 'many recognise' leans partly on authority.

rigor.statement: every time we lean into Te Tiriti, we actually assert a principle of nationhood that is based on legitimacy. And every time we choose to not lean into that Treaty, we choose a version of nationhood that is based on the spoils of war in a sense.

divination.statement: This shows steady reductions from the current rate of 5.25 percent to a 3 percent OCR by mid-2027. The financial markets are more forward-leaning than this. divination.explanation: Reports RBNZ and market forecasts for the OCR path to 3%; plausible but forecast-dependent over a multi-year horizon.

divination.statement: Our ambitious target of doubling exports by value over 10 years is an opportunity to work with the primary sector and to grow the economy

strength.statement: revitalising the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme and increasing the cap for the coming season to 20,750 workers—increasing by 1,250.
strength.explanation: A concrete, announced administrative change she is responsible for; delivery is stated but only just taking effect.

strength.statement: in the last nine months under this Government, we have rewritten and completed the draft maths curriculum, which was sent out for consultation last week and has had overwhelmingly positive feedback.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete deliverable (completed draft curriculum, out for consultation) she is responsible for; it is a draft in consultation rather than fully implemented.

strength.statement: as a result of the decisions that this Government has made around prioritising children to go into emergency housing, 1,110 kids have moved from emergency housing into warm, safe, dry homes between April and the end of July.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivered outcome under his responsibility; the figure is repeatedly asserted but not independently verified here.

strength.statement: restore common sense to intensive winter grazing and stock exclusion rules, introduce pragmatic rules on on-farm water storage, and introduce legislation to cease the implementation of new significant natural areas. We've also repealed the burdensome log traders legislation
strength.explanation: Mix of delivered actions (repealed log-trader law) and in-progress items ('introduce legislation'), so partial follow-through.

strength.statement: Our ambitious target of doubling exports by value over 10 years is an opportunity to work with the primary sector and to grow the economy
strength.explanation: A stated aspiration/target with no mechanism yet demonstrated to deliver it.

strength.statement: $101 million has been allocated to 42 consented priority flood resilience schemes ... the key point of the fund is that we are willing to contribute up to 60 percent of the cost with relevant authorities, who must ensure they have resource consents
strength.explanation: A concrete allocation with conditions; delivery of the schemes is prospective rather than complete.

charisma.statement: every time we lean into Te Tiriti, we actually assert a principle of nationhood that is based on legitimacy. And every time we choose to not lean into that Treaty, we choose a version of nationhood that is based on the spoils of war in a sense.
charisma.explanation: Eloquent and reflective, inviting Pākehā New Zealanders in, but frames the alternative starkly ('spoils of war'), appealing mainly to those already sympathetic.

civility.statement: a host of the questions to date have been riddled with falsehoods. That has the effect of acting as an echo chamber, undermining fair consideration on the basis of natural justice at a time where a final decision has not been made.
civility.explanation: Blanket accusation that opponents' questions are 'riddled with falsehoods' impugns motives rather than engaging specifics.

civility.statement: Fast track, of course, started life as an inspired piece of thinking from the “Piketty pirate” David Parker, and we have proudly stolen it and made it even better.
civility.explanation: 'Piketty pirate' is a mild personal jibe, but paired with genuine credit to Parker for the idea.

civility.statement: Well, I’d just say to the member that Ministers are responsible for their own policy development processes and how they work with their agencies, and each Minister will operate differently, as we have seen with Erica Stanford, as Minister of Education, operating very differently from that member as Minister of Education.
civility.explanation: Turns a substantive question into a personal comparison unfavourable to the questioner.

civility.statement: There is a separation between the Parliament, between the executive, and the judiciary. It is well respected that not only Ministers but members of Parliament should not be criticising the judiciary.
civility.explanation: Focuses on the constitutional substance of ministerial conduct rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Almost every one of the Prime Minister’s answers is talking about the previous Government, rather than the Government that he’s the Prime Minister of.
civility.explanation: A pointed but legitimate procedural observation about the PM's evasive pattern, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: Is the Prime Minister surprised that the leader of the Labour Party believes “communist” is a critical term?
civility.explanation: A rhetorical jab framing Hipkins as naive rather than engaging the ministerial-conduct issue.

civility.statement: Is the price gained by a particular type of generation, such as gas, partly a feature of it being available to run on cold nights when people want energy and there’s nothing else, and, if so, is this an example of how keeping the lights on requires an understanding not of Instagram bumper stickers but the real, practical world?
civility.explanation: 'Instagram bumper stickers' belittles opponents' position rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Despite all of those cries of wolf, they are the same.
civility.explanation: 'Cries of wolf' is a mild dig but attached to a direct answer.

civility.statement: Why did she give the tobacco industry a $216 million tax break when the Treasury was already warning that there will be difficult funding trade-offs with other areas of the health system and suggested any extra investment “could be prioritised in areas such as primary care or acute mental health”?
civility.explanation: Pointed 'tax break for the tobacco industry' framing but built on substantive policy evidence.

civility.statement: Well, the member’s characterisation is offensive and wrong. We are running a very clean and transparent process when it comes to the projects we listed in Schedule 2.
civility.explanation: 'Offensive and wrong' rebukes the questioner, though the process defence is substantive.

civility.statement: The member opposite might still be thinking it’s 2023 and she’s the Minister—well, she ain’t. We have an energy crisis in New Zealand caused by the policies that she left behind. She should take some responsibility.
civility.explanation: Mocking, personal put-down of the questioner rather than engaging the cost figures she raised.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I would really appreciate your reflection on the Hansard because this is a really basic thing that we are consistently, as the Greens, trying to get straight answers out of our Prime Minister and are completely unable to.
civility.explanation: A measured procedural complaint about non-answers rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Between 2018 and 2023, when the Greens were in Government, New Zealand imported 5.6 million tonnes of coal and nearly a million tonnes a year.
civility.explanation: Partisan blame framing, but centred on a factual coal-import claim rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Well, I would agree with the member that the bumper sticker end-of-oil-and-gas ban didn’t think through the second- and third-order consequences. It was classic, old-school Government, wasn’t it?—made a statement, made a bumper sticker, but didn’t follow through with the plan.
civility.explanation: 'Bumper sticker' mockery of the previous policy, but aimed at the decision rather than a person.

civility.statement: Energy security now trumps all sorts of falsehoods and woke-ism.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opposing views as 'falsehoods and woke-ism' rather than engaging them.

civility.statement: This is why the Government is overturning the dangerous, juvenile, ridiculous oil and gas ban.
civility.explanation: Stacked pejoratives ('dangerous, juvenile, ridiculous') aimed at the previous policy are sensationalist rather than substantive.

civility.statement: Speaking to the point of order. Sir, what is happening with this House that the beauty of language and robust expression suddenly are turning the other side into sobbers?
civility.explanation: Mocks opponents as 'sobbers' rather than addressing the point of order's substance.

civility.statement: Why did she release this single document as a document under the Official Information Act if it is, as she has just claimed, not a document?
civility.explanation: Pointed but focused on the inconsistency of the answer, not the person.

civility.statement: we want to protect ratepayers from excessive rates hikes and prevent councils from wasting money on nice-to-have pet projects like rain gardens on top of bus stops, and $490,000 speed bumps by implementing a rate cap similar to those in some Australian states.
civility.explanation: 'Nice-to-have pet projects' is dismissive but aimed at spending choices, not people.

rigor.statement: a host of the questions to date have been riddled with falsehoods. That has the effect of acting as an echo chamber, undermining fair consideration on the basis of natural justice at a time where a final decision has not been made.
rigor.explanation: Asserts falsehoods and 'echo chamber' effect without identifying any specific false claim; conclusion outruns evidence.

rigor.statement: Again, the comments are descriptive, not critical. That’s exactly what has happened. It’s on the public record. They might not be the words that I’d use, but he’s perfectly free to do so.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an implausible semantic claim that labelling a judge 'communist' is descriptive rather than critical.

rigor.statement: There is a separation between the Parliament, between the executive, and the judiciary. It is well respected that not only Ministers but members of Parliament should not be criticising the judiciary.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a sound constitutional principle (separation of powers) that supports his conclusion.

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister surprised that the leader of the Labour Party believes “communist” is a critical term?
rigor.explanation: Loaded rhetorical question that assumes its own contestable premise.

rigor.statement: Is the price gained by a particular type of generation, such as gas, partly a feature of it being available to run on cold nights when people want energy and there’s nothing else, and, if so, is this an example of how keeping the lights on requires an understanding not of Instagram bumper stickers but the real, practical world?
rigor.explanation: Contains a genuine point about dispatchable generation value but bundled into a dismissive rhetorical framing.

rigor.statement: No, but I do agree with the Labor Party Prime Minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, who said, “Gas in particular has a key role to play as a flexible source of energy, helping to smooth the transition to renewables.”
rigor.explanation: Rebuts one expert by citing another authority rather than engaging the cost/emissions argument on its merits.

rigor.statement: Why has the Minister not sought advice on renewable energy solutions as an alternative, given it costs $200 to $300 per megawatt-hour to generate electricity from LNG and the 2023 Generation Investment Survey put the cost of new generation from renewables at $90 per megawatt-hour?
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based cost comparison to support the challenge, drawing on a cited survey.

rigor.statement: Why would the gentailers currently invest in renewable energy when, under the status quo, since partial privatisation under the former National-led Government, they have paid out nearly $11 billion in dividends by burning fossil fuels, nearly 2½ times more than what they invested in new power generation?
rigor.explanation: Uses a quantified incentive argument, though the causal link between privatisation and under-investment is asserted more than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Well, I would agree with the member that the bumper sticker end-of-oil-and-gas ban didn’t think through the second- and third-order consequences. It was classic, old-school Government, wasn’t it?—made a statement, made a bumper sticker, but didn’t follow through with the plan.
rigor.explanation: Asserts unconsidered 'second- and third-order consequences' as a slogan rather than laying out the causal chain.

rigor.statement: Energy security now trumps all sorts of falsehoods and woke-ism.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical labelling substitutes for argument.

rigor.statement: Why did she release this single document as a document under the Official Information Act if it is, as she has just claimed, not a document?
rigor.explanation: Sharp logical challenge exposing an internal contradiction in the Minister's account.

rigor.statement: Is it correct that Labour’s fast-track law included in its purpose to support the economy, the requirement “while continuing to promote the sustainable management of natural and physical resources.”, whereas the purpose clause in his bill does not refer to sustainable management?
rigor.explanation: Builds a precise textual comparison to test the Minister's 'same law' claim.

rigor.statement: if you think about mining, every electric vehicle (EV)... you need mining to make sure you’ve got an EV, you’ve got a smartphone, you’ve got solar power, and you need to make sure, wind farms need minerals.
rigor.explanation: Valid general point that green tech needs minerals, but used to sidestep the specific question about a polluted river.

rigor.statement: the public response has been overwhelmingly positive. Ratepayers who are facing an average rates hike of over 15 percent this year have welcomed our call for councils to tighten their belts and focus on core services... Christchurch Mayor Phil Mauger supported the move, viewing it as a much-needed war on waste.
rigor.explanation: Supports 'overwhelmingly positive' with an editorial and one mayor's endorsement—an appeal to popularity and cherry-picked reactions.

charisma.statement: Fast track, of course, started life as an inspired piece of thinking from the “Piketty pirate” David Parker, and we have proudly stolen it and made it even better.
charisma.explanation: Credits an opponent's original idea (a cross-party nod) but wraps it in a mocking nickname, so it appeals to his own side more than it builds bridges.

charisma.statement: So, if you care about climate change, care about energy security and a thriving economy, my message to Labour and the Greens is to get on board and vote for the fast-track legislation.
charisma.explanation: Invites the Opposition to support the bill, but the 'if you care' framing implies they may not, weakening the consensus appeal.

charisma.statement: As a Government, we want to ensure that the workforce of social workers is helped and empowered to meet the needs of our communities.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive acknowledgement of the profession that seeks broad support.

forthrightness.statement: We are doing the job in this Government of lowering daily smoking rates. We’ve made tremendous progress, and I know the Minister is working incredibly hard to do that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which of two people was correct and whether nicotine is as harmful as caffeine; pivots entirely to smoking-rate talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’d just say to the member that Ministers are responsible for their own policy development processes and how they work with their agencies, and each Minister will operate differently, as we have seen with Erica Stanford, as Minister of Education, operating very differently from that member as Minister of Education.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agreed with Costello's claim and was comfortable with it; answers neither, deflecting to ministerial autonomy.

forthrightness.statement: You’d have to ask the Minister about that, but what I’d say is that he was being descriptive, not critical.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects responsibility for a Minister's conduct despite the PM being accountable for it, then offers only a semantic reframing.

forthrightness.statement: Again, the comments are descriptive, not critical. That’s exactly what has happened. It’s on the public record. They might not be the words that I’d use, but he’s perfectly free to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially addresses whether calling a judge a communist is acceptable, but leans on a 'descriptive not critical' distinction rather than answering the Cabinet Manual point.

forthrightness.statement: Despite all of those cries of wolf, they are the same.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether the ratings are higher, lower or the same as under the previous Government: the same.

forthrightness.statement: The Government decided to do none of these things. It decided to keep funding intact for these initiatives and increased the combined pharmaceutical budget and charged this against the Budget 2025 operating allowance.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the funding-source question in detail, though reframes away from the 'tobacco tax break' characterisation the questioner used.

forthrightness.statement: tax relief out the door, fiscally neutrally; inflation down; interest rates down; stable ratings from the ratings agencies—the Budget was pretty good.

forthrightness.statement: No, but I do agree with the Labor Party Prime Minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, who said, “Gas in particular has a key role to play as a flexible source of energy, helping to smooth the transition to renewables.”
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'no' to the quoted expert, then substitutes a counter-authority for justification.

forthrightness.statement: The member opposite might still be thinking it’s 2023 and she’s the Minister—well, she ain’t. We have an energy crisis in New Zealand caused by the policies that she left behind. She should take some responsibility.
forthrightness.explanation: Dodges the specific LNG-vs-renewables cost comparison, answering with blame instead.

forthrightness.statement: We want to see an energy system where we double the amount of renewables and we also turn on huge quantities of gas so that we actually have the security that we need in this country to keep the lights on, to keep people in work, and to make sure that working New Zealanders don’t pay high electricity prices.

forthrightness.statement: What I can say is, yeah, reliability of energy supply is very important to determine profitability of our gentailers. We’ll keep an eye on how much money they’re making; we have a bit of a review going on within the energy sector, but they need confidence to invest.
forthrightness.explanation: On re-asking he engages the topic of gentailer profitability but still never says whether fossil or renewable generation is more profitable.

forthrightness.statement: As I first answered to the member on 31 January, a range of information from various sources was provided to officials. This was then scanned into a single document by officials and subsequently released to Radio New Zealand on 9 July 2024 under the Official Information Act (OIA).
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the provenance question but sets up the contested 'compilation, not a document' framing pressed later.

forthrightness.statement: Yet again, as I’ve stated, it was a compilation of information, which was subsequently scanned by the health officials to form a document.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeats a formula rather than reconciling 'no specific document written' with releasing a single document.

forthrightness.statement: We want to get more jobs, we want to have an economy growing, and we want people to have more houses.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether communities, iwi and hapū being locked out of a voice is acceptable; answers with generic goals.

veracity.statement: Last week, Fitch Ratings announced it was maintaining New Zealand’s long-term foreign currency debt rating at AA+ with a stable outlook. AA+ is a very strong rating, being only one notch below the highest possible rating of AAA.

veracity.statement: tax relief out the door, fiscally neutrally; inflation down; interest rates down; stable ratings from the ratings agencies—the Budget was pretty good.

veracity.statement: We’re facing the driest hydrological year since 1992, with less wind generation than forecast and a 25.8 percent downgrade in gas production this year, following a 12 percent downgrade last year.

veracity.statement: We know that around 50 countries around the world already import LNG, including Japan and the UK, with Australia set to open its first terminal this year.

veracity.statement: with spot prices averaging up to $800 a megawatt-hour on the week of 11 August, LNG comes in a lot lower than that cost
veracity.explanation: Compares crisis spot prices to LNG generation cost rather than to firmed-renewable cost the question asked about, which is somewhat misleading.

veracity.statement: Why would the gentailers currently invest in renewable energy when, under the status quo, since partial privatisation under the former National-led Government, they have paid out nearly $11 billion in dividends by burning fossil fuels, nearly 2½ times more than what they invested in new power generation?
veracity.explanation: Figures are plausible and specific but presented without sourcing and unverified here.

forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages Smith's question on savings, restating the fiscal target and why tighter allowances are needed, before confirming more savings work continues.

forthrightness.statement: We then funded individual initiatives, including some that have been very warmly received by New Zealanders, if opposed by the Labour Party, including things like funding Gumboot Friday mental health services for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers Edmonds' health-funding question by pointing to funded initiatives, but pivots to a partisan point rather than the specific cost-pressure figures asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I am proud to be a member of a party that campaigned on funding additional medicines—a campaign that that member has never made—and that actually delivered on that not only for those in need of those cancer treatments but delivered on that for multiple other patients by using the Pharmac model.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Edmonds' question on why cancer-drug costings were done after the Budget by asserting delivery pride rather than addressing the timing/prioritisation actually asked about.

divination.statement: our fiscal strategy is that we wish to get debt back down under 40 percent of GDP. In order to do that, we need to get the books back into surplus. If we had stuck with the operating allowances left to us by the outgoing Government, that date of balanced books wouldn’t come until the 2030-31 fiscal year, obviously far too long to be running in the red.
divination.explanation: A counterfactual projection that surplus would slip to 2030-31 under the previous allowances; plausible but a contestable modelled forecast.

strength.statement: I am proud to be a member of a party that campaigned on funding additional medicines—a campaign that that member has never made—and that actually delivered on that not only for those in need of those cancer treatments but delivered on that for multiple other patients by using the Pharmac model.
strength.explanation: Claims a campaign commitment on medicines was delivered via Pharmac; delivery did occur, though Edmonds notes cancer-drug costings came after the Budget and under public pressure, tempering the follow-through claim.

strength.statement: I have commissioned from the Treasury advice saying, “What’s a way that we can do this, bearing in mind our current fiscal constraints? ... I have not yet received that advice, but this is something that I, in good faith, would like to make happen.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to establish a Parliamentary Budget Office backed only by commissioning advice not yet received; aspiration with minimal delivery so far.

rigor.statement: is it appropriate to allocate $29 million to the serious youth offender and boot camps initiatives, given that the core features of boot camps—strong discipline in a military-style environment—have repeatedly proven to be ineffective to reducing—and, in some cases, increase—reoffending rates?
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in an appeal to a body of evidence on boot-camp effectiveness; conclusion (question the spend) follows, though the evidence base is asserted rather than cited.

rigor.statement: if the model that works, that is being reinvested in, is a kaupapa Māori model—and let’s use, for example, the boot camp model in Palmerston North. If mātauranga Māori and Māori culture has been, indeed, used to make that its point of difference, then why aren’t you saying that that’s the model that’s best utilised instead of letting it get branded as being a military versus a Māori cultural solution for Māori rangatahi?
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point that if the effective element is kaupapa Māori it should be credited as such; rests on an unverified premise about what makes the pilot work.

rigor.statement: comparing that to the military-style academy that we have started the pilot on is not a fair comparison. We have staff that have been trained to deal with the issues with these young people. These young people are assessed before they even start the pilot programme to recognise if there are any disabilities, neurodiversity issues, learning issues—anything that we feel may make the process not OK for them.
rigor.explanation: Draws a distinction (trained staff, prior assessment) to rebut the analogy to the abuse-era boot camp; reasoning is coherent though claims of training/assessment are asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: Yep, but there are plenty of services that provide women’s counselling, and it is a duplication of service that can be provided somewhere else, when that money could be used towards our children.
rigor.explanation: Offers a duplication rationale for the cut, but the claim that equivalent services exist elsewhere is asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: Do you know what was happening with them before the military-style academy? Nothing. They sat in a youth justice facility, like a holding pen on the way to prison. That’s how we treated them—we gave up on them.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical framing that presents a false dichotomy (either boot camp or 'nothing') and leans on emotive language rather than evidence about prior interventions.

rigor.statement: The only person responsible for that hurt or harm is the person who was the perpetrator of that harm. We can do as much as we can in resourcing front line so they have the tools to step in and do what they need... I just want to thank them for all the hard work that they do, because it’s not easy when you are blamed for the hurt and harm that happened before you even arrived.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that perpetrators bear responsibility, but leans on emotional appeal to social workers' distress rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: When the Minister responded to that plea that they will close, on 8 August, she stated to them that she’s been assured that there will be no impact on front-line roles, such as social workers... I would just like to understand why the Minister wrote that to a group that services 486 wāhine and 460 tamariki
rigor.explanation: Builds a case from a specific dated statement and figures to highlight an inconsistency, though it is the Minister's consistency, not Andersen's, being probed.

rigor.statement: why then make the decision to put $27 million into boot camps when all of the evidence shows that that doesn’t work, when for all of the survivors of State care abuse it is triggering because some of them have been in boot camps... Why not put the $27 million into what she could see was already working for young people: wraparound supports, multi-agency approach, supporting not just the young person but their siblings and the entire whānau?
rigor.explanation: Contrasts a claimed evidence base against the boot-camp spend and proposes an alternative; strong structure but 'all of the evidence' is a sweeping assertion.

rigor.statement: I have heard from many organisations, including Kia Puāwai Functional Family Therapy, which in 2023 had a 96 percent improved living situation key performance indicator (KPI) in relation to the support to 252 rangatahi in Te Tai Tokerau. Can the Minister explain to the committee what direction she will provide her ministry regarding the contracting services in the 2024-25 Budget if a 96 percent KPI is not considered value for money?
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete performance figure to challenge the 'value for money' rationale; a strong evidential hook though drawn from a single program.

rigor.statement: I asked the Minister at the scrutiny week how much per participant, per child, the boot camp was. The Minister said... “we can’t go into [too] much detail around that”. The announcement came and went, and the detail around that has never come to the surface. How much is the pilot per child, per participant?
rigor.explanation: Builds a tight accountability argument: a question deferred to a future announcement that then never disclosed the figure.

rigor.statement: I’m quite frankly sick and tired of the politicisation of what looking after children in New Zealand looks like... Aren’t we all just Kiwis here? I am fascinated that in a modern country this becomes a political football. It’s certainly becoming a political football on the left.
rigor.explanation: Relies on emotive framing and a one-sided attribution of blame rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: we know, through peer-reviewed assessment that was derived from councils’ own numbers, that there needs to be up to $185 billion spent over the next 30 years. The Minister claims that it is less than half of that, not by looking at councils’ own numbers and projections over 30 years but by looking at councils’ projections from their long-term plans... because it’s only 10 years out.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific methodological flaw — using 10-year long-term-plan figures to project a 30-year need — a substantive, logically-structured critique.

rigor.statement: why don’t they listen to neither of us and listen to the credit rating agencies instead? Ultimately, it’s the credit rating agencies that determine the cost of borrowing. Borrowing is the reality when it comes to this water infrastructure. We cannot escape that fact.
rigor.explanation: Sound reasoning: defers to an independent arbiter (credit rating agencies) on borrowing cost rather than asking listeners to take his word, though the agencies' verdict is asserted.

rigor.statement: if you look at South Wairarapa as an example, they have had rates increases of 20 percent in the last two years, and they still don’t have the money to upgrade their roads; they still don’t have the money to upgrade their water system... They have stopped developments in Greytown and Martinborough—no more new builds.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete case study to illustrate the affordability problem; a well-chosen anecdote though generalising from one council.

rigor.statement: It was really disappointing hearing the Minister of Local Government talk about the positive nature of getting rid of Te Mana o te Wai considerations when setting waste-water standards... Te Mana o te Wai, as was pointed out really clearly by a number of submitters, was designed as a cohesive whole. It has a number of elements, and to pick out just one... is very short-sighted.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that removing one element from an integrated framework undermines it, referencing submitters, though the harm is asserted rather than quantified.

specificity.statement: is it appropriate to allocate $29 million to the serious youth offender and boot camps initiatives, given that the core features of boot camps—strong discipline in a military-style environment—have repeatedly proven to be ineffective to reducing—and, in some cases, increase—reoffending rates?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure ($29m), the named initiatives, and the specific mechanism (military-style discipline) she is challenging.

specificity.statement: if the model that works, that is being reinvested in, is a kaupapa Māori model—and let’s use, for example, the boot camp model in Palmerston North. If mātauranga Māori and Māori culture has been, indeed, used to make that its point of difference, then why aren’t you saying that that’s the model that’s best utilised instead of letting it get branded as being a military versus a Māori cultural solution for Māori rangatahi?
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete example (Palmerston North model) and a specific mechanism (mātauranga Māori), though the question stays conceptual.

specificity.statement: comparing that to the military-style academy that we have started the pilot on is not a fair comparison. We have staff that have been trained to deal with the issues with these young people. These young people are assessed before they even start the pilot programme to recognise if there are any disabilities, neurodiversity issues, learning issues—anything that we feel may make the process not OK for them.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete features — trained staff, pre-programme assessment for disability/neurodiversity — but without figures or documented protocols.

specificity.statement: the 10 that are currently in the programme have gone through a process. Actually, they are there voluntarily. They have gone through a process with their family, with the courts, with the judge, working through a sentencing plan, through family group conferences, and they are there voluntarily. They can leave this programme, while it’s a pilot, any time that they would like and for any reason
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number (10 participants) and the specific process steps (courts, sentencing plan, family group conferences).

specificity.statement: In regards to North Shore Women’s Centre, North Shore Women’s Centre were contracted for multiple services. I think it’s around six or seven services that they were contracted for. They were contracted for around $596,000—two services have been discontinued, so they are still being funded for those other services.
specificity.explanation: Cites the contract value (~$596,000), number of services (six or seven), and that two were discontinued.

specificity.statement: in regards to the to the military-style academy, these young people have been sentenced to at least two crimes of 10 years or more, proven in court. These are our most serious repeat youth offenders.
specificity.explanation: Attempts a concrete criterion for participant selection but the phrasing is imprecise.

specificity.statement: Epuni was an absolute disgrace. That has now been—refurbished and actually made fit for purpose. Hell yes, repainted. That place was like a youth justice facility. Those kids did not commit a crime. It is a care and protection unit where those young people deserve to be in an environment where they are not treated like criminals
specificity.explanation: Names a specific facility and the action taken (refurbishment) but without cost, timeframe, or scope detail.

specificity.statement: North Shore Women’s Centre wrote to her last month and explained that the cut to their contract for Oranga Tamariki services would mean, for them, the loss of two front-line social worker jobs... they will, effectively, close in April of next year without that funding now being in place.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail: two front-line jobs, a 38-year-old organisation, closure in April, and later 486 wāhine and 460 tamariki served.

specificity.statement: why then make the decision to put $27 million into boot camps when all of the evidence shows that that doesn’t work, when for all of the survivors of State care abuse it is triggering because some of them have been in boot camps... Why not put the $27 million into what she could see was already working for young people: wraparound supports, multi-agency approach, supporting not just the young person but their siblings and the entire whānau?
specificity.explanation: Names the figure ($27m) and a concrete alternative (wraparound, multi-agency, whānau supports).

specificity.statement: I have heard from many organisations, including Kia Puāwai Functional Family Therapy, which in 2023 had a 96 percent improved living situation key performance indicator (KPI) in relation to the support to 252 rangatahi in Te Tai Tokerau. Can the Minister explain to the committee what direction she will provide her ministry regarding the contracting services in the 2024-25 Budget if a 96 percent KPI is not considered value for money?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named provider, a precise KPI (96%), a client count (252 rangatahi), a region, and the Budget year.

specificity.statement: How do you plan on meeting that despite repealing section 7AA, decreasing the funding to contractors, which include iwi and Māori organisations, by $30 million and, further, not investing any more money into work programmes to support iwi-led care organisations?
specificity.explanation: References the section 7AA repeal, a $30 million funding decrease, and the specific success matrix on page 153 of the Vote.

specificity.statement: I asked the Minister at the scrutiny week how much per participant, per child, the boot camp was. The Minister said... “we can’t go into [too] much detail around that”. The announcement came and went, and the detail around that has never come to the surface. How much is the pilot per child, per participant?
specificity.explanation: Presses a precise, answerable question (cost per participant) and documents the history of it being unanswered.

specificity.statement: This model also reduces the projected water bill increases for Aucklanders from 25.8 percent this year down to just 7.2 percent and, crucially, allows for Watercare to continue with their capital programme of investing in capital infrastructure to clean up our harbours through the Central Interceptor project.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (25.8% down to 7.2%), a named entity (Watercare), and a named project (Central Interceptor).

specificity.statement: councils stay in control. They will determine their preferred delivery arrangements, starting with the development of water service delivery plans within 12 months of this bill’s enactment. These plans will show how councils will deliver drinking-water, waste-water, and stormwater services in a financially sustainable way
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete mechanism (water service delivery plans), the 12-month timeframe, and the three service types covered.

specificity.statement: we know, through peer-reviewed assessment that was derived from councils’ own numbers, that there needs to be up to $185 billion spent over the next 30 years. The Minister claims that it is less than half of that, not by looking at councils’ own numbers and projections over 30 years but by looking at councils’ projections from their long-term plans... because it’s only 10 years out.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure ($185 billion), a 30-year horizon, and the precise source of the discrepancy.

specificity.statement: if you look at South Wairarapa as an example, they have had rates increases of 20 percent in the last two years, and they still don’t have the money to upgrade their roads; they still don’t have the money to upgrade their water system... They have stopped developments in Greytown and Martinborough—no more new builds.
specificity.explanation: Named district, precise figure (20% over two years), named towns (Greytown, Martinborough), and concrete consequences.

specificity.statement: This bill does nothing for the likes of the Tararua District. They’ve got around 10,000 ratepaying units and the fourth-largest roading network in the country. They need to find $600 million over the next 30 years
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: ~10,000 rating units, fourth-largest roading network, $600m over 30 years.

specificity.statement: The first opportunity that I want to reflect on was how truncated the actual process was in the consultation—if you can call it a consultation—on this bill. It was hugely limited, to the extent that not all councils even got to submit on this bill and actually have their say.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete deficiency (not all councils got to submit) though without numbers or dates.

veracity.statement: is it appropriate to allocate $29 million to the serious youth offender and boot camps initiatives, given that the core features of boot camps—strong discipline in a military-style environment—have repeatedly proven to be ineffective to reducing—and, in some cases, increase—reoffending rates?
veracity.explanation: The claim that boot camps have repeatedly proven ineffective (and sometimes increase reoffending) aligns with the general research consensus, though stated broadly.

veracity.statement: the 10 that are currently in the programme have gone through a process. Actually, they are there voluntarily. They have gone through a process with their family, with the courts, with the judge, working through a sentencing plan, through family group conferences, and they are there voluntarily. They can leave this programme, while it’s a pilot, any time that they would like and for any reason
veracity.explanation: Factual claims about numbers and voluntariness; plausible but not independently verifiable from the text, and 'voluntary' is contestable for court-directed participants.

veracity.statement: In regards to North Shore Women’s Centre, North Shore Women’s Centre were contracted for multiple services. I think it’s around six or seven services that they were contracted for. They were contracted for around $596,000—two services have been discontinued, so they are still being funded for those other services.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual figures presented; hedged ('around', 'I think') and not verifiable here, and reframes 'cut' as reprioritisation.

veracity.statement: in regards to the to the military-style academy, these young people have been sentenced to at least two crimes of 10 years or more, proven in court. These are our most serious repeat youth offenders.
veracity.explanation: Garbled and likely overstated claim ('two crimes of 10 years or more'); the characterisation of participants as the most serious repeat offenders is asserted without clear support.

veracity.statement: The purpose of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 is all about promoting the wellbeing of children, young persons, their whānau, and communities. This means supporting and protecting children and young people, including preventing them from suffering harm to their development or wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of the statutory purpose of the Oranga Tamariki Act.

veracity.statement: North Shore Women’s Centre wrote to her last month and explained that the cut to their contract for Oranga Tamariki services would mean, for them, the loss of two front-line social worker jobs... they will, effectively, close in April of next year without that funding now being in place.
veracity.explanation: Relays specific claims sourced to the centre's own letter; accurate as a report of their position though the closure is a projection.

veracity.statement: I have heard from many organisations, including Kia Puāwai Functional Family Therapy, which in 2023 had a 96 percent improved living situation key performance indicator (KPI) in relation to the support to 252 rangatahi in Te Tai Tokerau. Can the Minister explain to the committee what direction she will provide her ministry regarding the contracting services in the 2024-25 Budget if a 96 percent KPI is not considered value for money?
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claim sourced to the organisation; plausible but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: This model also reduces the projected water bill increases for Aucklanders from 25.8 percent this year down to just 7.2 percent and, crucially, allows for Watercare to continue with their capital programme of investing in capital infrastructure to clean up our harbours through the Central Interceptor project.
veracity.explanation: A specific projected reduction presented as fact; plausible but a forward projection whose realisation is contested by opposition speakers.

veracity.statement: The previous Government’s approach—an unpopular, mega-bureaucratic, co-governed model—was costly and overwhelmingly rejected by voters at the last election.
veracity.explanation: 'Overwhelmingly rejected by voters' overstates an election outcome driven by many factors; partly true, partly spin.

veracity.statement: This Government has done that in as simple a time as nine months. We didn’t spend hundreds of millions on consultants. We didn’t need an army of consultants to do this. We just needed to have clear direction, look at the innovation that came through the LGFA, make decisions, and get on with it.
veracity.explanation: The 'nine months / no army of consultants' claim is a favourable characterisation that is difficult to verify and partly rhetorical.

veracity.statement: we know, through peer-reviewed assessment that was derived from councils’ own numbers, that there needs to be up to $185 billion spent over the next 30 years. The Minister claims that it is less than half of that, not by looking at councils’ own numbers and projections over 30 years but by looking at councils’ projections from their long-term plans... because it’s only 10 years out.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the $185bn figure to peer-reviewed analysis of councils' data; plausible and specific but contested by the Minister.

veracity.statement: if you look at South Wairarapa as an example, they have had rates increases of 20 percent in the last two years, and they still don’t have the money to upgrade their roads; they still don’t have the money to upgrade their water system... They have stopped developments in Greytown and Martinborough—no more new builds.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claims about rates and halted developments; plausible but unverified in text.

veracity.statement: The first opportunity that I want to reflect on was how truncated the actual process was in the consultation—if you can call it a consultation—on this bill. It was hugely limited, to the extent that not all councils even got to submit on this bill and actually have their say.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that some councils could not submit; specific and plausible though unverified in the text.

civility.statement: I absolutely agree. That was absolutely horrific what happened in that boot camp. They had staff that were not trained to look over those young people.
civility.explanation: Directly and respectfully acknowledges the merit of an opponent's (the Greens') point rather than dismissing it.

civility.statement: Yep, but there are plenty of services that provide women’s counselling, and it is a duplication of service that can be provided somewhere else, when that money could be used towards our children.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the funding decision without personal attack, while acknowledging the service is 'valid'.

civility.statement: When the Minister responded to that plea that they will close, on 8 August, she stated to them that she’s been assured that there will be no impact on front-line roles, such as social workers... I would just like to understand why the Minister wrote that to a group that services 486 wāhine and 460 tamariki
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the substance of a documented contradiction (assurance of no front-line impact vs a centre losing social workers) without personal insult.

civility.statement: why then make the decision to put $27 million into boot camps when all of the evidence shows that that doesn’t work, when for all of the survivors of State care abuse it is triggering because some of them have been in boot camps... Why not put the $27 million into what she could see was already working for young people: wraparound supports, multi-agency approach, supporting not just the young person but their siblings and the entire whānau?
civility.explanation: Challenges the policy and its evidence base directly, including acknowledging the Minister's differing view, without personal attack.

civility.statement: it was very good, actually, when I referred to Kotahi te Whakaaro and Circuit Breaker and Oranga Tamariki’s role in that, that the Minister said... “because it has shown good results, and that across the table, around the table, multi-agency approach really works well”
civility.explanation: Acknowledges where the Minister was right ('it's great that you said that') before pressing the disagreement.

civility.statement: I couldn’t help but notice the previous Labour member, the Hon Carmel Sepuloni, seemed to get a bit more than she bargained for.
civility.explanation: A mild cross-bench dig at a colleague rather than engagement with substance, though not a serious personal attack.

civility.statement: I’m quite frankly sick and tired of the politicisation of what looking after children in New Zealand looks like... Aren’t we all just Kiwis here? I am fascinated that in a modern country this becomes a political football. It’s certainly becoming a political football on the left.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents ('on the left') as politicising children's welfare — an accusatory characterisation rather than engagement with their arguments.

civility.statement: The previous Government’s approach—an unpopular, mega-bureaucratic, co-governed model—was costly and overwhelmingly rejected by voters at the last election.
civility.explanation: Loaded, pejorative characterisation ('mega-bureaucratic') of an opponent's policy; criticism of policy but leaning on sensational framing.

civility.statement: I just don’t believe him—and there are many New Zealanders around who don’t either—because I find the Minister to be about as disingenuous as you can get.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on the Minister's honesty ('disingenuous as you can get') rather than his argument.

civility.statement: He failed short of making that promise, because he knows, in his heart of hearts, that rates will continue to go up, because the advice that he has received is that this approach by this Government will still result in rates increasing.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith ('he knows in his heart of hearts') to the Minister, edging into a character claim rather than pure policy critique.

civility.statement: they have the gall, after doing those two things, to turn around and stand up in front of councils and lecture them in a patronising, cynical, and arrogant way and tell them it’s their fault.
civility.explanation: String of character descriptors ('patronising, cynical, and arrogant') aimed at the Government rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I have to reflect that I’m disappointed that this, ultimately, is a bill of missed opportunities—and I have to agree with my colleague across the House on that. We know, to solve these challenges, that whatever the model for reform is, it needs to be connecting our councils with communities. It needs to be taking a longer-term view. It needs to be incorporating mandatory considerations like climate change
civility.explanation: Measured, policy-focused critique framed as missed opportunities rather than personal attack.

charisma.statement: I absolutely agree. That was absolutely horrific what happened in that boot camp. They had staff that were not trained to look over those young people.
charisma.explanation: Concedes a valid point raised by opponents, building goodwill and common ground across party lines.

charisma.statement: That is the reason why the fast-track programme will continue and that we are investing more money into that service—because it worked and it worked well. We are also extending the age group up to the age of 16 because that is important too. When you have something that is working, you invest in it.
charisma.explanation: Signals cross-party pragmatism ('I don't politicise that'), a bridge-building note amid an otherwise combative session.

charisma.statement: Do you know what was happening with them before the military-style academy? Nothing. They sat in a youth justice facility, like a holding pen on the way to prison. That’s how we treated them—we gave up on them.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically forceful and emotive but rallies via a stark us/them 'we gave up on them' framing rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: Yes, there are iwi-led programmes within the military-style academy programme. There’s also defence-designed programmes within the military-style academy, and whilst there is a higher percentage of Māori within youth justice and a higher percentage of Māori within this programme, it’s not just a programme for Māori children; it’s a programme for all children
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'programme for all children' framing that acknowledges te ao Māori matters to her, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: The only person responsible for that hurt or harm is the person who was the perpetrator of that harm. We can do as much as we can in resourcing front line so they have the tools to step in and do what they need... I just want to thank them for all the hard work that they do, because it’s not easy when you are blamed for the hurt and harm that happened before you even arrived.
charisma.explanation: Warm, defending of front-line social workers, though appeals to its own framing rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: it was very good, actually, when I referred to Kotahi te Whakaaro and Circuit Breaker and Oranga Tamariki’s role in that, that the Minister said... “because it has shown good results, and that across the table, around the table, multi-agency approach really works well”
charisma.explanation: Credits the Minister's own words and a point of agreement, an attempt to build on common ground before the challenge.

charisma.statement: I visited a youth justice facility with you about a month ago. I noticed that the people there seemed to already know you, and then you told me that you’d been back there just two weeks later to hear from the people some more. I’ve heard you mention visiting quite a number of Oranga Tamariki facilities up and down New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Friendly, warm framing but a leading softball question to a coalition ally that appeals only to its own side.

charisma.statement: I’m quite frankly sick and tired of the politicisation of what looking after children in New Zealand looks like... Aren’t we all just Kiwis here? I am fascinated that in a modern country this becomes a political football. It’s certainly becoming a political football on the left.
charisma.explanation: The 'aren't we all just Kiwis' unity appeal is undercut by immediately blaming 'the left', so it rallies one side rather than bridging.

charisma.statement: why don’t they listen to neither of us and listen to the credit rating agencies instead? Ultimately, it’s the credit rating agencies that determine the cost of borrowing. Borrowing is the reality when it comes to this water infrastructure. We cannot escape that fact.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective invitation to distrust both political sides and check a neutral source, but framed within a partisan attack.

charisma.statement: I have to reflect that I’m disappointed that this, ultimately, is a bill of missed opportunities—and I have to agree with my colleague across the House on that. We know, to solve these challenges, that whatever the model for reform is, it needs to be connecting our councils with communities. It needs to be taking a longer-term view. It needs to be incorporating mandatory considerations like climate change
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the House to acknowledge agreement with a Labour colleague and frames constructive principles for reform, seeking common ground.

forthrightness.statement: In regards to North Shore Women’s Centre, North Shore Women’s Centre were contracted for multiple services. I think it’s around six or seven services that they were contracted for. They were contracted for around $596,000—two services have been discontinued, so they are still being funded for those other services.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Andersen's challenge with concrete detail on the contract rather than deflecting, though she does not address the specific claim that the centre will close.

forthrightness.statement: That is the reason why the fast-track programme will continue and that we are investing more money into that service—because it worked and it worked well. We are also extending the age group up to the age of 16 because that is important too. When you have something that is working, you invest in it.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Sepuloni's question about whether the previous Government's programme continues — yes, extended and funded — though sidesteps the request for the latest recidivism results.

strength.statement: Epuni was an absolute disgrace. That has now been—refurbished and actually made fit for purpose. Hell yes, repainted. That place was like a youth justice facility. strength.statement: We have put standard operating practices in place in these youth justice facilities. We have set a standard of, “You are going to get some training”—which they never got before.
