forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm not sure if that member remembers, but the last Government had a programme called the New Zealand Upgrade Programme, which allocated capital to building a range of transport projects. So if that member wants to lecture this Government for investing in the critical infrastructure, maybe he should answer that question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he would divert schools/hospitals funding to roads, he pivots to attacking the previous Government's record rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: That proposal has been put forward by the New Zealand Transport Agency. It's out for consultation. Ultimately, that roading project is a major upgrade and will have a significant benefit, particularly for freight operators, who will have an incredibly efficient and modern reliable piece of infrastructure.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers by attributing the toll to NZTA and noting consultation, but does not engage the claim that the road was 'already paid for' by the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: There are programmes in our prison system, not the least of which is Hōkai Rangi, but if many of the prisoners practised their culture, they wouldn't be there in the first place.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what consultation with Māori occurred before removing Treaty provisions, he ignores the question entirely and offers a cultural aside.

forthrightness.statement: Firstly, there are no obligations in terms of the prison system under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—which is best described as the Treaty of Waitangi, an indivisible document not to be dismembered. In respect of initiatives to deal with the disproportionate number of Māori, it's about time this House thought about the disproportion of Māori victims.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the Treaty-obligation premise but pivots away from how Corrections will be held accountable, redirecting to victims.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I am aware of the disproportionate statistics. Māori are twice as likely to be victims of violent crime. Māori are 60 percent likely to be the victims of a higher nature than ordinary New Zealanders. Stop lecturing about people in jail and start thinking about the victims of their crime, who are substantially Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the overrepresentation happened, he acknowledges the stats but never addresses causation, redirecting to victimisation.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, a sum of $80 million was set aside in the recent Budget. But I want to make the point: Māori are not in jail because of colonisation. Māori are in jail because of self-responsibility and the need for whānau to refresh and remake themselves so that the values that Kiwis take for granted underlying our society are not trashed and are not explained away by some distant colonial event.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to a refreshed Hōkai Rangi strategy, he cites $80m but does not commit, pivoting to a claim about causes of imprisonment.

rigor.statement: Well, I'm not sure if that member remembers, but the last Government had a programme called the New Zealand Upgrade Programme, which allocated capital to building a range of transport projects. So if that member wants to lecture this Government for investing in the critical infrastructure, maybe he should answer that question.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a tu quoque ('you did it too') deflection rather than addressing the funding-tradeoff premise.

rigor.statement: There are programmes in our prison system, not the least of which is Hōkai Rangi, but if many of the prisoners practised their culture, they wouldn't be there in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Unsupported causal claim that practising culture would keep people out of prison; no evidence.

rigor.statement: Firstly, there are no obligations in terms of the prison system under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—which is best described as the Treaty of Waitangi, an indivisible document not to be dismembered. In respect of initiatives to deal with the disproportionate number of Māori, it's about time this House thought about the disproportion of Māori victims.
rigor.explanation: Asserts there are no Te Tiriti obligations and shifts frame to victims rather than engaging the accountability question.

rigor.statement: As I said, a sum of $80 million was set aside in the recent Budget. But I want to make the point: Māori are not in jail because of colonisation. Māori are in jail because of self-responsibility and the need for whānau to refresh and remake themselves so that the values that Kiwis take for granted underlying our society are not trashed and are not explained away by some distant colonial event.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses colonisation and asserts 'self-responsibility' as the cause with no evidence; a sweeping mono-causal claim.

rigor.statement: For the first time in a long time, I actually agree with Chris Hipkins, because it is true that if New Zealand became one of the only countries in the world to put in place a wealth tax, then we would see a horde of New Zealanders who've invested their money and their capital and their energy and time in New Zealand leaving New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Cites his opponent's own concession as support (a reasonable move), but the capital-flight conclusion is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Well, he is a man, and perhaps that is the issue: Winston Peters needed to go to a man. He couldn't go to Nicola Willis herself and so bypassed her to go directly to the Prime Minister.
rigor.explanation: Attributes Peters bypassing Willis to sexism as speculative inference with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: Just for context, currently in section 127 of the Education and Training Act, there are four primary objectives. The consultation means that only one of those will remain, which is around educational achievement, and the part—subsection (1)(d)—on giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi will be moved down and deprioritised.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the specific legislative text to the conclusion; logically connected, though the practical effect is his inference.

rigor.statement: by the way, in any other country, it is compulsory for you to learn the official languages of that country in their schooling system.
rigor.explanation: Overgeneralised appeal used to support the argument; the universal claim is unsupported.

rigor.statement: For someone that uses that to get to and from work on a weekly basis each day, that is going to add a minimum of an extra $21.50 per week for those vehicles that utilise that.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable arithmetic extrapolation from the toll to weekly commuting cost, though it assumes daily two-way use.

rigor.statement: isn't it reasonable that retail margins of major supermarket brands increasing is something that the Government should be concerned about? And isn't it reasonable that Cabinet should be worried about sustained high levels of profitability and market share in our sector which make it uncompetitive and ultimately lead to higher costs for consumers at the checkout?
rigor.explanation: Draws on the Grocery Commissioner's report (rising margins, entrenched market share) to argue for regulation; evidence-linked reasoning, though framed rhetorically.

rigor.statement: For decades, Kiwi consumers have been paying out more than our counterparts overseas—say, in Europe, with a flourishing supermarket sector with five major players who all compete on different things, not only price but range—and we deserve that now.
rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative-market analogy to argue for more competition; reasonable but the European comparison is generalised.

rigor.statement: In fact, the former Labour Prime Minister gave $2.7 million to the Mongrel Mob. What a great idea that was to get on top of meth addiction! rigor.explanation: Post hoc / false-cause fallacy: treats national crime and gang-membership trends as caused by one grant, with no evidence of a causal link.

rigor.statement: She told me that her partner, who's a builder, has just lost a job. It was a renovation job in that town. It was going to be $80,000. That won't be going ahead.
rigor.explanation: Uses a single constituent anecdote to illustrate the mill closure's local impact; illustrative and specific, but an anecdote rather than systemic evidence.

civility.statement: Well, I'm not sure if that member remembers, but the last Government had a programme called the New Zealand Upgrade Programme, which allocated capital to building a range of transport projects. So if that member wants to lecture this Government for investing in the critical infrastructure, maybe he should answer that question.
civility.explanation: Combative ('wants to lecture') but aimed at the argument, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: There are programmes in our prison system, not the least of which is Hōkai Rangi, but if many of the prisoners practised their culture, they wouldn't be there in the first place.
civility.explanation: Dismissive framing implying prisoners' cultural failings; borders on disrespect rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: Yes, I am aware of the disproportionate statistics. Māori are twice as likely to be victims of violent crime. Māori are 60 percent likely to be the victims of a higher nature than ordinary New Zealanders. Stop lecturing about people in jail and start thinking about the victims of their crime, who are substantially Māori.
civility.explanation: 'Stop lecturing' is a dismissive rebuke of the questioner rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: the comfort food of the Labour Party is tax. Particularly the comfort food for the Labour Party is more and new taxes on New Zealanders: capital gains taxes and wealth taxes.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'comfort food' framing directed at a party's policy preference; ridicule but not a personal attack on a named individual.

civility.statement: Under the last Government, spending went up by 70 percent in six years and debt went through the roof. When we came into Government, debt had hit $100 billion, and we find ourselves in a situation where the Government is having to grapple with tough fiscal decisions because of the wanton mismanagement and reckless fiscal profligacy of the last Government.
civility.explanation: 'Wanton mismanagement and reckless fiscal profligacy' is charged, sensationalised language.

civility.statement: Recently, we've seen the self-appointed executive director of the judiciary—that would be the Hon Shane Jones, a Cabinet Minister—calling a judge a communist. The Attorney-General, Judith Collins, told him off; Jones' own party leader, Winston Peters, told him off, but Christopher Luxon is yet to do so. In fact, he implicitly supported Jones' comments when he described them as "merely descriptive".
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'self-appointed executive director' jab, but the substance is a legitimate critique of ministerial conduct.

civility.statement: We now have a Minister tearing up the Cabinet Manual and the only person who is unwilling to chastise him is his groupie, the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: 'Groupie' is a belittling personal label aimed at the Prime Minister rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Well, he is a man, and perhaps that is the issue: Winston Peters needed to go to a man. He couldn't go to Nicola Willis herself and so bypassed her to go directly to the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Insinuates sexist motive; an accusation about character rather than a substantiated policy point.

civility.statement: Why is he prepared to allow funding that would be used to build new schools and hospitals to be used to pay for the items in his roading plan, such as the roads of National Party significance?
civility.explanation: 'Roads of National Party significance' is a partisan snipe embedded in an otherwise legitimate funding-priorities question.

civility.statement: This Government is now suggesting that a toll of $4.30 or $8.60 be placed over a 24-hour period. That is absolutely uncalled for. It is outrageous, it is a disgrace, and I tell you what, it is a kick in the guts for the people of the Tararua district and the Manawatū region.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic 'outrageous / disgrace / kick in the guts' language, though directed at the policy rather than a person.

civility.statement: The gaslighting continues—gaslighting, it's so 2021. We're over it.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'gaslighting' accusation and flippant retort aimed at hecklers rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: In fact, he's not in it—in it is the Minister for Regulation, who today announced himself as the "White Knight" for the supermarket, and he will find himself among friends: "Big Supermarket Seymour" alongside "Big Airlines Luxon" and "Big Tobacco Chris Bishop".
civility.explanation: String of belittling nicknames ('Big Supermarket Seymour', 'Big Tobacco Chris Bishop') targeting individuals rather than their arguments.

civility.statement: In fact, the former Labour Prime Minister gave $2.7 million to the Mongrel Mob. What a great idea that was to get on top of meth addiction! In fact, the results of that investment we have seen a 33 percent increase in violent crime, a 51 percent increase in gang membership—what a crazy idea.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'what a great idea / what a crazy idea' framing, though aimed at a policy decision.

civility.statement: What I think we have to do when we're in Government is stand up for people. We need to see the systems errors and the mismanagement that is there, and we need to try and step in and assist people in systemic ways.
civility.explanation: Respectful, policy-focused framing with no attack; earlier she explicitly respected the Speaker's ruling while stating her disagreement.

civility.statement: Politicians need to stop and actually listen to rural folk.
civility.explanation: A heartfelt, respectful appeal for attention to rural communities, not an attack.

civility.statement: We don't need any more vacuous sermons on what we should be doing in rural New Zealand. We need people that actually listen to us, and this side of the House we're invested in that.
civility.explanation: 'Vacuous sermons' is a mild dig at opponents' rhetoric, embedded in an otherwise earnest and respectful appeal.

charisma.statement: the comfort food of the Labour Party is tax. Particularly the comfort food for the Labour Party is more and new taxes on New Zealanders: capital gains taxes and wealth taxes.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for his own side but purely combative caricature of opponents, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: We will fight the next election on lower taxes versus more and new taxes from the Labour Party.
charisma.explanation: A clear rallying dividing-line, but frames politics as combat between two sides rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: When we are learning a new language, it expands our horizons. Language connects. Language builds understanding. It allows us to be able to relate to each other and understand why we do things in the way that we do.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, warm framing that invites others in via personal experience, though it appeals mainly to those already sympathetic.

charisma.statement: In fact, he's not in it—in it is the Minister for Regulation, who today announced himself as the "White Knight" for the supermarket, and he will find himself among friends: "Big Supermarket Seymour" alongside "Big Airlines Luxon" and "Big Tobacco Chris Bishop".
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing attack line for her own side; does not seek to persuade the undecided or build consensus.

charisma.statement: From a council point of view, that is fixing roads, it's making sure our local assets are well maintained, it's focusing on flood protection, it's focusing on the infrastructure that is going to get us ahead—that is going to get our communities flourishing.
charisma.explanation: 'Back to basics' framing is positive but appeals to her own side's view of what councils should do.

charisma.statement: We don't need any more vacuous sermons on what we should be doing in rural New Zealand. We need people that actually listen to us, and this side of the House we're invested in that.
charisma.explanation: Sincere and moving, but the 'this side of the House' framing claims the virtue of listening for his own side rather than uniting across the House.

authenticity.statement: It is a 11.5 kilometre stretch of road. authenticity.explanation: Claims Labour committed to and funded the road; consistent with the prior Government's stated position, defending its own record.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First is excited about our commitment to an independent inquiry into COVID-19, which will be delivered as phase 2 of Labour's royal commission of inquiry into COVID-19, lessons learnt. Now, this wasn't our first choice; our leader, Mr Peters, detailed as such.

authenticity.statement: We have an independent royal commission with new commissioners, as promised. We have wide-ranging terms of reference, as promised. The inquiry will take a year, as promised. And finally, a report will be delivered in early 2026, and with this report, be it a lesson for future parliamentarians.
authenticity.explanation: Repeatedly matches outcomes to campaign commitments ('as promised'); words and delivered actions align on this policy.

authenticity.statement: This follows legislation introduced in 2023 by Labour to create a new set of powers for the Commerce Commission and the new Grocery Commissioner to monitor and give reporting annually about the state of our grocery sector. This is something National vociferously opposed at the time, but then on the election campaign started talking about because they know it matters to ordinary New Zealanders.
authenticity.explanation: This is a hypocrisy charge against National (opposed then embraced), which is a signal about them, not the speaker; noted per the rubric as a low-authenticity signal about the opponent.

authenticity.statement: This Government and this Minister cancelled the industry transformation plan. No work progressed. Labour put real money into the sector. It knew that it was really important we create new products out of timber. There was a structural timber project that was created: $57 million went into that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated advanced-manufacturing priorities; defends her party's prior record and actions.

civility.statement: I applaud people like Mark for standing up in this House, speaking out, being prepared to have those difficult conversations so that the New Zealand public knows that it’s OK to not be OK and to talk about it out in public.

civility.statement: what I thought was commendable from SkyCity was their understanding in that, after they heard this story presented to the select committee, they publicly apologised for how they treated the gift card holder who lost their credit.

civility.statement: I wish also to commend the Hon Chris Bishop, who worked with Ashley Jones and was also instrumental in getting—maybe not this particular bill—this idea to the House, and, especially, my dear friend and former colleague Angie Warren-Clark, whose bill this was, when it was drawn out from the ballot.
civility.explanation: Generously credits a political opponent (Minister Bishop) and others; respectful and collegial.

civility.statement: We know that, at the termination of dissolution, that abusive relationship can continue, and, therefore, we want to make sure that there is some level of protection. If there’s property, if there’s custody issues of those things, in the speed and haste of terminating the relationship we aren’t further victimising the applicant in this matter.
civility.explanation: Raises a substantive reservation about the bill respectfully, explicitly seeking the member's response and framing it as shared concern.

civility.statement: It’s always great to come together when there is unanimous agreement across the House. It always feels nice. Of course, today, we’re here because we are wanting to reduce the harm that family violence causes, and we all know how long these ramifications can go on for—trauma for a lifetime, in some cases.
civility.explanation: Wholly constructive and respectful, focused on the shared harm-reduction goal.

civility.statement: It was done because the previous Government didn’t feel it necessary to have a statutory strategic plan to better address improving mental health outcomes.
civility.explanation: A pointed but policy-focused contrast with the previous Government, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: To have a strategy is good news, but without a workforce plan, without funding, without transparent procurement, without localised solutions to mental health, the strategy is at risk of sitting on the shelf gathering dust as we continue to experience this really shameful crisis in our country that is the mental health crisis, particularly of our youth.
civility.explanation: Harsh critique of the policy's sufficiency but aimed at substance (implementation gaps), not at any person.

civility.statement: My challenge is to the Government members: thank you for your words, thank you for what sounds good; when are you going to back it up with action? When are we going to see funding? When are we going to see a workforce plan.
civility.explanation: Sharp challenge but courteously framed (thanking members) and directed at the policy delivery, not personal character.

civility.statement: it’s really great to work together on issues like this in a cross-partisan way if we’re able to. I think one of the most special moments that I’ve had in the admittedly brief period of time that I’ve been in this House for was yesterday with the tributes to King Tuheitia and how we all came together as a House.
civility.explanation: Entirely respectful and collegial across party lines.

civility.statement: Well done to you, Katie, on having your bill read in the House, but also to you, Minister Doocey—fantastic work on introducing this piece of work to the House.
civility.explanation: Cordial cross-party congratulations; respectful and collegial.

charisma.statement: I applaud people like Mark for standing up in this House, speaking out, being prepared to have those difficult conversations so that the New Zealand public knows that it’s OK to not be OK and to talk about it out in public.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle to praise an opponent's contribution and invites a shared, unifying conversation about suicide.

charisma.statement: Parmjeet Parmar has listened to 12 excellent contributions across the House from all the other political parties. She’ll be standing up 11 votes in favour for the ACT Party and voting in support of this legislation, because it’s about the consumer, it’s about businesses in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Good-humoured, inviting framing that tries to coax an opposing party onside rather than attack them, though clearly rhetorical.

charisma.statement: I wish also to commend the Hon Chris Bishop, who worked with Ashley Jones and was also instrumental in getting—maybe not this particular bill—this idea to the House, and, especially, my dear friend and former colleague Angie Warren-Clark, whose bill this was, when it was drawn out from the ballot.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party acknowledgment that builds goodwill and frames the bill as a shared achievement.

charisma.statement: we absolutely, New Zealand First, are totally committed to doing anything we can to ensure we reduce the impacts of family violence. But I think we’re being disingenuous if we suggest that the dissolution is “That’s it. You’re free and clear.”
charisma.explanation: Affirms shared commitment to the bill's goal while dissenting on detail, keeping the tone consensus-oriented rather than combative.

charisma.statement: It’s always great to come together when there is unanimous agreement across the House. It always feels nice. Of course, today, we’re here because we are wanting to reduce the harm that family violence causes, and we all know how long these ramifications can go on for—trauma for a lifetime, in some cases.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-House unity and shared purpose, an inclusive consensus-building framing.

charisma.statement: My challenge is to the Government members: thank you for your words, thank you for what sounds good; when are you going to back it up with action? When are we going to see funding? When are we going to see a workforce plan.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective challenge that supports the bill while pressing the Government, but largely appeals to her own side's scepticism.

charisma.statement: it’s really great to work together on issues like this in a cross-partisan way if we’re able to. I think one of the most special moments that I’ve had in the admittedly brief period of time that I’ve been in this House for was yesterday with the tributes to King Tuheitia and how we all came together as a House.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-party collaboration and a shared unifying moment; inclusive and consensus-building.

charisma.statement: we’re an isolated place with not a lot of amenities. It’s very important that we have things like mental health and wellbeing strategies to make sure we can address what is faced by many people in rural communities who feel isolated, not just physically and geographically but also very often from broader society. Making sure that we speak about people in a way that is uplifting and not tearing them down on any kind of characteristic, be it rural or urban alike, is very important.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to lift up rural and urban people alike, seeking common ground rather than division.

charisma.statement: It was a privilege, in the 52nd Parliament, to be part of the initial cross-party mental health and wellbeing group, and it was really there, through that group that we established cross-party, that we were really able to raise the issue of, in particular, suicide.
charisma.explanation: Highlights cross-party collaboration on a difficult issue, reinforcing a consensus-building, inclusive approach.

specificity.statement: That’s what this legislation is about: it’s about simply moving one year to three years for gift cards; it’s about simply saying that the one-year arbitrary time line we see on most gift cards in the country is not fair.

specificity.statement: he cited a case of a person who purchased $1,500 worth of Mobil gift cards. He contacted Mobil as soon as he realised the gift cards had expired, but they refused to do anything to help.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($1,500, 12 months vs two years) and a named company anchor the example precisely.

specificity.statement: these are the definitions of those that were excluded: a card supplied in substitution for returned goods; a pre-paid card or voucher redeemable for phone credit, internet access, or other similar services; a debit card, credit card, pre-paid travel card, or any other similar product; and a card or voucher supplied as part of a customer loyalty programme.
specificity.explanation: Precise, itemised list of the categories excluded from the bill's minimum expiry period.

specificity.statement: Because we believe in personal responsibility.
specificity.explanation: States a guiding principle but no mechanism or detail about how it applies to gift-card expiry.

specificity.statement: what it does is it ensures that, in cases of family violence proven by there being a final protection order against either one or both parties, the person who is being given protection by the order can apply to have a marriage or a civil union dissolved immediately rather than waiting for a two-year separation period to occur.
specificity.explanation: Precisely states the legal trigger (final protection order) and effect (immediate dissolution vs two-year wait).

specificity.statement: Clause 6 in the bill introduces new section 39A into the Family Proceedings Act 1980, and that new section 39A(6)(c) says that the matters in section 45 of the Family Proceedings Act have to be addressed, and those are the matters around the custody of children.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and cross-referenced statutory provisions to rebut a concern about child custody.

specificity.statement: we absolutely, New Zealand First, are totally committed to doing anything we can to ensure we reduce the impacts of family violence. But I think we’re being disingenuous if we suggest that the dissolution is “That’s it. You’re free and clear.”
specificity.explanation: The commitment ('doing anything we can') is a values statement without a concrete mechanism, though tied to a specific amendment elsewhere.

specificity.statement: This bill strengthens the commitment to mental health and wellbeing by requiring the Minister of Health to consult with the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission in the preparation of strategic documents, including health strategies, the New Zealand Health Plan, and the Government policy statement, and to prepare and determine a mental health and wellbeing strategy.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory mechanisms (consultation with the Commission, specific strategic documents, a mandated strategy) the bill introduces.

specificity.statement: I am excited to see a health system in five to 10 years’ time that, because of a good strategy, will have addressed these barriers and will see less Kiwis taking their own lives and more Kiwis living with good mental health and wellbeing.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough timeframe but no concrete targets or measures for the improvement.

specificity.statement: despite assurances from the Government that there is no front-line freeze, there are hiring freezes, certainly in my electorate in Taieri, in Southland, where advertisements for mental health nurses have disappeared, where pregnant women who are in the mental health sector—nurses that I door-knocked on the other day—said they could not, as a fulltime-equivalent, get somebody to take over part of their shift because there is an effective hiring freeze.
specificity.explanation: Grounds the claim in named electorates and concrete examples (nurse advertisements, shift cover), though without numbers.

specificity.statement: We want to see an acknowledgment of the kind of holistic things that make up health, including secure housing, including making sure that we’ve got a well-resourced public health system that can deal with people and pick up people when they’re down. We want to make sure that there are jobs for young people.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete determinants of mental health (housing, public health capacity, jobs) but as broad directions without mechanisms or measures.

We had a great presentation from Minister Doocey on the big screen talking about the importance of people talking about—and mates; talking to mates on construction sites, making sure that you’re actually checking in.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific, recent, named event and initiative (MATES in Construction launch, Auckland) grounding his point about construction-sector mental health.

specificity.statement: Half of all women patients accessing mental health care are victims of current or recent family violence. Childhood exposure to family violence is implicated in one-fifth of youth suicides. One in nine women victims sustains a brain injury related to domestic violence, which then doubles the likelihood of developing mood disorders.
specificity.explanation: Precise quantified claims (half, one-fifth, one in nine) rather than vague assertions.

He contacted Mobil as soon as he realised the gift cards had expired, but they refused to do anything to help.
veracity.explanation: Recounts a specific Consumer NZ submission example with figures; plausible and sourced, though the underlying case is asserted second-hand.

veracity.statement: We are lucky to now have a mental health Minister—the first of its kind.
veracity.explanation: Matt Doocey is New Zealand's first dedicated Minister for Mental Health, so the factual claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: It was done because the previous Government didn’t feel it necessary to have a statutory strategic plan to better address improving mental health outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the previous Government did not legislate a mandated mental-health strategy, but the characterisation of motive ('didn't feel it necessary') is a contestable gloss.

veracity.statement: despite assurances from the Government that there is no front-line freeze, there are hiring freezes, certainly in my electorate in Taieri, in Southland, where advertisements for mental health nurses have disappeared, where pregnant women who are in the mental health sector—nurses that I door-knocked on the other day—said they could not, as a fulltime-equivalent, get somebody to take over part of their shift because there is an effective hiring freeze.
veracity.explanation: Specific but anecdotal, first-hand claims of an effective hiring freeze contradicting Government assurances; plausible yet unverified and locally sourced.

veracity.explanation: Elevated suicidality among trans people is well supported, though the specific 'five or six times' multiplier is uncertain; she appropriately hedges ('depending on which research you read').

veracity.statement: Half of all women patients accessing mental health care are victims of current or recent family violence. authenticity.statement: Because we believe in personal responsibility.

rigor.statement: a lot of strategies just fail at the strategy phase because there’s no implementation plan behind it. So we definitely— ... And we definitely want to see resourcing behind it.

rigor.statement: we’re an isolated place with not a lot of amenities. specificity.statement: GDP results for the June quarter will come out next Thursday. These are also likely to be weak, with many forecasters picking a negative quarter.
specificity.explanation: Gives the release timing and expected direction.

specificity.statement: Business confidence has risen sharply and is now at its highest level in a decade.
specificity.explanation: Concrete comparative claim ('highest in a decade').

specificity.statement: About the worst thing I can think of is imposing a capital gains tax on businesses, because a capital gains tax would increase the tax that businesses pay. It would tax small-business owners when they sell up and retire. It would increase taxes on productive assets, while exempting the family home, thereby encouraging people to put more and more money into their house.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete mechanisms (retirement sales, productive-asset taxation, home exemption).

specificity.statement: Our targets are tightly focused on five things that really matter: faster cancer treatment, increasing childhood immunisation, shorter stays in emergency departments, and shorter wait times for surgery.
specificity.explanation: Lists named target areas, though says 'five' while enumerating four.

specificity.statement: we are planning to establish more community infusion centres so that patients can access their chemotherapy closer to home. We're also looking to expand the number of beds in operating theatres in public hospitals and make greater use of capacity in private hospitals.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms (infusion centres, theatre beds, private capacity) but no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Our Government has already invested more money into health than any Government in New Zealand's history, with the system receiving around $30 billion a year.
specificity.explanation: Provides a headline dollar figure.

specificity.statement: from 1 October, schools and kura with years 0 to 3 students will receive between $500 and $5,000 per year over the next four years to support them to buy structured literacy resources to drive support for students in their reading achievement.
specificity.explanation: Exact start date, dollar range, duration and target cohort.

specificity.statement: trials of the new phonics check in 80 primary schools are about to begin in both English and, for the first time, a purpose-built phonics check tool in te reo Māori, prior to a nationwide roll-out next year.
specificity.explanation: Names the number of schools, both languages, and a rollout timeframe.

specificity.statement: From term 1, 2025, this Government has reprioritised $33 million of funding from Reading Recovery directly into interventions which align with structured literacy, to ensure consistency of approach. This support includes 271 fulltime-equivalent roles, as was the case under Reading Recovery.
specificity.explanation: Precise date, dollar figure, funding source, and FTE count.

specificity.statement: There is a three-year multiple entry visa that is available, and we know that, since 2022, 25,000 people have applied for that three-year multiple entry visa.
specificity.explanation: Names the visa type, timeframe, and applicant count.

specificity.statement: Overall, a record $2.6 billion is available for disability support services this financial year due to this Government's decision to inject an additional $1.1 billion over five years in Budget 2024.
specificity.explanation: Precise headline and incremental figures with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: There is a pause and a maintenance of the existing funding while a rapid review is undertaken to understand why residential care costs have gone up beyond the level of inflation. That rapid review will have answers by the beginning of early 2025.
specificity.explanation: Gives the mechanism (rapid review) and a rough timeframe.

specificity.statement: The Gangs Bill and the Sentencing Amendment Bill will prohibit the display of gang patches in public places and, in the case of repeat offences, prohibit possession, full stop. Police will have the ability to issue dispersal notices to break up gang gatherings that disrupt the public, and to issue non-consorting orders to prevent specific gang members from associating.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete new powers and offences under the named bills.

specificity.statement: over the past six years, gang membership increased by 51 percent and at the same time violent crime in our communities went up by 33 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise percentages and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: as of last week, the wait time for passports has returned to normal and New Zealanders are now advised to allow up to two weeks to receive their passport. After a software upgrade in March caused unexpected delays to passport processing, with expected wait times pushed up to 10 weeks, I've been focused on reducing passport wait times as a top priority.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete wait-time figures and the cause and timing of the delay.

specificity.statement: In 2020, as part of a suite of law changes made in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government introduced a temporary exemption to the Gambling Act, which allowed three large class 3 licence holders—the Heart Foundation, the Coastguard, and Countdown Kids Charitable Trust—the ability to continue selling their lottery tickets via remote means, such as by telephone and the internet.
specificity.explanation: Names the year, the exemption, the licence class, and the specific organisations.

specificity.statement: This bill will ensure that a longstanding fundraising tool remains fit for purpose for the community organisations who depend on it to fund their operations.
specificity.explanation: States the purpose but the concrete mechanism is elaborated elsewhere.

specificity.statement: There are 180,000 people in New Zealand who suffer from heart diseases, and we know that the Heart Foundation depends on this lottery in order to raise the funds to pay for that research, to pay for that education.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete number and links it to the funding rationale.

specificity.statement: two-thirds—66 percent—of their funding comes from donations, lotteries, memberships, sponsorships, and grants. The remaining one-third comes from the Government's assistance.
specificity.explanation: Precise funding breakdown for Coastguard.

specificity.statement: Surf Lifesaving New Zealand and the Royal New Zealand Coastguard will receive a funding boost of $63.6 million over four years, this Government has announced. That's right—$19 million for Coastguard and $44 million for Surf Lifesaving.
specificity.explanation: Total and itemised amounts with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: Why has he failed to condemn Shane Jones for calling a judge a communist when his Deputy Prime Minister, Winston Peters, says, "It should not have been said."?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific incident and quotes the contrasting position to sharpen the question.

civility.statement: Oh, to you she might be, but you know nothing about it, do you?
civility.explanation: Direct personal put-down of another member's knowledge, no engagement with substance.

civility.statement: the banality of ignorance is to be ignorant without knowing it, and that's what you've heard over there.
civility.explanation: Insult framed as aphorism, characterising opponents as ignorant.

civility.statement: So our point is that of course we want discussion and consultation on the widest number of things, and democracy sometimes takes time.
civility.explanation: Measured, focused on process rather than persons.

civility.statement: But I can think of all sorts of court cases which are a gross waste of the public's time and money, where the mahi has been done when that person is not even here, and, of course, the court case is now involving taxpayers paying for the court proceedings as we speak—and that member from the Green Party would know all about that case, wouldn't she?
civility.explanation: Ends with a personal insinuation directed at the questioner.

civility.statement: if you look at the coalition agreement, two parties have agreed to support it to a first reading only. Now, I'll say it one more time, for the media's sake: read the coalition agreement.
civility.explanation: Answer laced with a condescending jab at the media/questioner.

civility.statement: If I'd been away on Celebrity Treasure Island, I'd probably have lost the plot too, but the reality is that we all did that, and here we've got an extraordinary circumstance where the Deputy Prime Minister of that time is now being accused of talking to the Prime Minister. How horrifying is that!
civility.explanation: Mocking personal reference to the questioner and sarcastic dismissal.

civility.statement: if they know so much about economics, why didn't they stop Grant Robertson from blowing the whole purse? Both of you. But the reality is—I respect Mr Renney but, on this occasion, he let himself down academically terribly.
civility.explanation: Personal disparagement of opponents and of the named adviser.

civility.statement: worsened, of course, by the appalling decision made by the then Minister of Energy and Resources to shut down, for example, Marsden Point, covertly as part of a deal, and she's never ever told anybody about that, including colleagues on her side of the House.
civility.explanation: Accuses a named opponent of covert dealing and concealment.

civility.statement: Actually, Ngata did not say that about article 2. He said it was about their positions and possessions. That's the difference. I would ask her to go back and read that old treatise from 1922—102 years old now—and read it with great clarity, and for that member's sake, I'll make sure it has got pictures.
civility.explanation: The 'I'll make sure it has got pictures' jibe is a personal put-down of the questioner.

civility.statement: The section that has been changed was implemented by the Labour Party in the first place in 2019 and 2020. They should have perhaps been a bit more careful with what they put in the law if they were worried about what subsequent Governments may do.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the party's past law-making rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I don't see that there's a political risk in having somebody with a whole lot of firearms safety background, education, and knowledge being in charge of firearms legislative changes. We can certainly do, and will do, a heck of a lot better than what that side of the House did when they've caused more harm in the community and loss of trust and confidence in the New Zealand Police.
civility.explanation: Turns the answer into an attack on the opposition's record.

civility.statement: detailed policy work will take place next year, because this year we had to get on top of the huge number of migrant exploitation cases that the Government left us, thank you very much.
civility.explanation: The sarcastic 'thank you very much' jab lowers civility while staying on policy record.

civility.statement: This side of the House does support this bill. We know there are always some risks around opening up gambling, which is why we do welcome submissions from the public to say, "Are there areas we need to strengthen in this bill?"
civility.explanation: Constructive and respectful, focused on the merits and safeguards.

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister think of anything that is a bigger waste of the public's time than allowing a six-month - long select committee process on a divisive so-called Treaty principles bill when the majority of Government has already committed to opposing that very bill?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded ('so-called', 'waste of the public's time') but aimed at the policy/process, not the person.

civility.statement: Why has he failed to condemn Shane Jones for calling a judge a communist when his Deputy Prime Minister, Winston Peters, says, "It should not have been said."?
civility.explanation: A hard accountability question, but grounded in a documented contrast rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Is it correct that coalition partner New Zealand First blocked her from delivering on this campaign promise earlier than next year, and, if so, why did she allow herself to be bullied out of delivering on an election promise by a minor party?
civility.explanation: The 'allow herself to be bullied' framing is a loaded, belittling characterisation.

charisma.statement: Oh, to you she might be, but you know nothing about it, do you?
charisma.explanation: Belittling and alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: So our point is that of course we want discussion and consultation on the widest number of things, and democracy sometimes takes time.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to democratic process but frames the disagreement as one-sided.

charisma.statement: This bill will ensure that a longstanding fundraising tool remains fit for purpose for the community organisations who depend on it to fund their operations.
charisma.explanation: Frames the measure around shared community benefit, inviting broad support.

charisma.statement: This side of the House does support this bill. We know there are always some risks around opening up gambling, which is why we do welcome submissions from the public to say, "Are there areas we need to strengthen in this bill?"
charisma.explanation: Cross-party support for a Government bill, inviting public input — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: One major way to reduce the harm associated with gambling is to ensure that community groups are not dependent on gambling revenue.
charisma.explanation: Reframes the debate toward a broadly shareable goal of proper community funding.

charisma.statement: The National Party enthusiastically supports the first reading of this Government bill.
charisma.explanation: Signals cross-chamber unanimity on a broadly supported measure.

rigor.statement: the banality of ignorance is to be ignorant without knowing it, and that's what you've heard over there.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem dressed up as a maxim rather than an argument.

How horrifying is that!
rigor.explanation: Strawmans the question through sarcasm rather than addressing the Budget-bid process concern.

rigor.statement: We did see the economics of the former adviser to the Labour Party, Mr Renney. It is grossly wrong and can be proven with the greatest of ease
rigor.explanation: Asserts the analysis is 'grossly wrong' and easily disproven without offering any evidence.

rigor.statement: if they know so much about economics, why didn't they stop Grant Robertson from blowing the whole purse? Both of you. But the reality is—I respect Mr Renney but, on this occasion, he let himself down academically terribly.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem and rhetorical question in place of engaging the figures.

rigor.statement: About the worst thing I can think of is imposing a capital gains tax on businesses, because a capital gains tax would increase the tax that businesses pay. It would tax small-business owners when they sell up and retire. It would increase taxes on productive assets, while exempting the family home, thereby encouraging people to put more and more money into their house.
rigor.explanation: Builds a chain from CGT to reduced investment incentives, but leans on assertion and a favourable framing rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: over the past six years, gang membership increased by 51 percent and at the same time violent crime in our communities went up by 33 percent.
rigor.explanation: Marshals statistics but implies causation between the two trends without establishing it.

rigor.statement: I think it was freedom of expression, and, yes, I do agree with that. We are limiting the freedom of expression of gang members, but we're also conscious of the fact that New Zealanders have the right to be safe in their communities and to go about their lives without being fearful of violent and intimidatory gangs. If that means preventing a segment of society from associating with each other, preventing them from displaying gang patches, we think that is justified.
rigor.explanation: Openly weighs a rights trade-off against public safety rather than denying the tension.

rigor.statement: That is a tough piece of sentencing which will only be involved if somebody repeatedly flouts the law and is convicted three times within five years. So it's very, very easy to avoid—and that is simply not to be convicted three times in five years for flouting the gang legislation.
rigor.explanation: Explains the three-strikes threshold clearly but does not address the railroading critique it was asked about.

rigor.statement: two-thirds—66 percent—of their funding comes from donations, lotteries, memberships, sponsorships, and grants. The remaining one-third comes from the Government's assistance.
rigor.explanation: Uses the figures to support the argument that community groups are over-reliant on gambling revenue.

rigor.statement: One major way to reduce the harm associated with gambling is to ensure that community groups are not dependent on gambling revenue.
rigor.explanation: A coherent policy inference linking dependency to harm, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Surf Lifesaving New Zealand and the Royal New Zealand Coastguard will receive a funding boost of $63.6 million over four years, this Government has announced. That's right—$19 million for Coastguard and $44 million for Surf Lifesaving.
rigor.explanation: Directly counters the prior speaker's claim with concrete data.

rigor.statement: Can the Prime Minister think of anything that is a bigger waste of the public's time than allowing a six-month - long select committee process on a divisive so-called Treaty principles bill when the majority of Government has already committed to opposing that very bill?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical framing that presumes its conclusion rather than arguing it.

rigor.statement: Is it correct that coalition partner New Zealand First blocked her from delivering on this campaign promise earlier than next year, and, if so, why did she allow herself to be bullied out of delivering on an election promise by a minor party?
rigor.explanation: A complex question that assumes an unestablished premise ('blocked', 'bullied').

forthrightness.statement: Sometimes in life, as in politics, chronology matters. If the bill doesn't get into the second reading or the third reading, there will not be a referendum, will there? So, accordingly, some of us are not concerned about that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by his 'divisive' remark and why Cabinet seeks referendum advice; addresses the contingency but dodges the stand-by question.

forthrightness.statement: But I can think of all sorts of court cases which are a gross waste of the public's time and money, where the mahi has been done when that person is not even here, and, of course, the court case is now involving taxpayers paying for the court proceedings as we speak—and that member from the Green Party would know all about that case, wouldn't she?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what is a bigger waste of time than the bill's select committee process; pivots to unrelated court cases.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the reality is that on this side of the House, we've always been open-minded, prepared to hear others' views, and to have a discussion, and that's what we were saying when we looked at this matter and we still look forward to that process.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked who benefits from a six-month select committee process; never names a beneficiary.

forthrightness.statement: if you look at the coalition agreement, two parties have agreed to support it to a first reading only. Now, I'll say it one more time, for the media's sake: read the coalition agreement.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether they might change their minds — support is to first reading only.

forthrightness.statement: As with the process of coalition Governments, we improve the outcome by consultation, and that's what happened here.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the PM failed to condemn Shane Jones; gives a vague process line rather than an answer.

forthrightness.statement: If I'd been away on Celebrity Treasure Island, I'd probably have lost the plot too, but the reality is that we all did that, and here we've got an extraordinary circumstance where the Deputy Prime Minister of that time is now being accused of talking to the Prime Minister. How horrifying is that!
forthrightness.explanation: Partly explains all ministers wrote to the PM, but wraps it in mockery.

forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether $4m for a bill they won't support is wasteful; attacks the source instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that that matter is under review, but if you go back to 1988, that's what I said back then, and I still stand by it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if market structure caused Ruapehu job losses; gestures at consistency and a review rather than answering directly.

forthrightness.statement: worsened, of course, by the appalling decision made by the then Minister of Energy and Resources to shut down, for example, Marsden Point, covertly as part of a deal, and she's never ever told anybody about that, including colleagues on her side of the House.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to separating gentailers; deflects to blame rather than committing.

forthrightness.statement: Because we have an undertaking, which we gave to another party, and we stick by our word.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why he won't kill the bill now — a coalition undertaking.

forthrightness.statement: I've seen the latest ANZ Business Outlook survey, which includes a measure of firms' current activity compared to a year ago. This measure improved slightly compared to the previous survey but is still weak, reflecting where the economy is at the moment.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what recent economic reports she has seen with a concrete example.

forthrightness.statement: GDP results for the June quarter will come out next Thursday. These are also likely to be weak, with many forecasters picking a negative quarter.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers when GDP figures will be released.

forthrightness.statement: I do stand by the $1.4 billion of reprioritisation, which will improve patient outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the $1.4b figure, though the ED-death premise is deflected to the coroner.

forthrightness.statement: I accept the assurances that Health New Zealand have made to me.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he can be trusted given front-line hiring-freeze reports; defers to unverified assurances rather than addressing the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: The section that has been changed was implemented by the Labour Party in the first place in 2019 and 2020. They should have perhaps been a bit more careful with what they put in the law if they were worried about what subsequent Governments may do.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether she issued drafting instructions to amend section 74A; redirects to blaming the prior government rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Matters that have gone through Cabinet will be made public at a time that is meant to be made public, and I guess when that happens, the member will well know at that time.

strength.statement: as of last week, the wait time for passports has returned to normal and New Zealanders are now advised to allow up to two weeks to receive their passport. After a software upgrade in March caused unexpected delays to passport processing, with expected wait times pushed up to 10 weeks, I've been focused on reducing passport wait times as a top priority.

specificity.statement: it bans the manufacture, sale, supply, and distribution of disposable vapes. Disposable vapes are disproportionately used by children and young people.

specificity.statement: That has been a contributing factor to recent rapid reductions in smoking rates, with nearly 230,000 people quitting smoking in the last three years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure and timeframe (~230,000 over three years).

specificity.statement: These tougher penalties will be backed by a far greater enforcement capability, with 16 dedicated smoking and vaping officers to be in place by December.

specificity.statement: new applications will also need the store to be at least 100 metres from an early childhood education centre (ECE). With nearly 4,500 ECEs around New Zealand, this will further restrict the places specialist vape retailers can establish.

specificity.explanation: Repeated slogan-like assertion ("legislation that works") with no added mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: the committee heard evidence that, in the last two years, there has only been one prosecution for a vape retailer that has sold to youth

specificity.statement: what we would like to see is that the Government is going to take a really bold and visionary plan when it comes to achieving a smoke-free Aotearoa, regardless of if it is going to be cigarette tobacco, regardless of if it’s going to be heated tobacco products, regardless of if it’s going to be vapes, and take a more holistic approach and a more long-term approach

specificity.statement: vapes will still be widely available for those people who choose to use them, who are adults, 18 and over, in order to reduce the harm that smoking causes them, but they will not be widely available to children and young people, and that is what this bill aims to achieve.

specificity.statement: noting that part of the appeal of these products to youth is that they’re inexpensive, brightly coloured, and easy to conceal

specificity.statement: Last week, I hosted Mount Roskill’s first youth vaping awareness seminar. More than 60 concerned parents and community members came together to listen to the seminar and raise their concerns.
specificity.explanation: Gives location, timing and an attendance figure.

specificity.statement: It’s banning the manufacture, sale, supply, and distribution of disposable vapes; increasing penalties for unlawful sales of regulated products to minors; imposing retail visibility restrictions for vaping products, including early childhood education centres; and proximity restrictions for specialist vape retailers.
specificity.explanation: Clearly enumerates the four concrete measures in the bill.

specificity.statement: There’ll be people who are in the manufacturing sector who will want to have an opportunity to speak on this. specificity.explanation: Lists affected sectors but is repetitive and adds little concrete detail beyond restating the four named groups.

specificity.statement: I happen to think that there should be no flavours for vapes available, other than those flavours that are allowed for tobacco, because, at the end of the day, vapes are a cessation device.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete policy position (restrict flavours to those allowed for tobacco) with a clear rationale.

specificity.statement: I used to smoke. I no longer smoke, but I do vape. I vape a tobacco-flavoured vape product. I’ve managed to reduce the level of my nicotine in half in the time. I am slowly weening myself off nicotine—exactly what these are intended to do.
specificity.explanation: Concrete personal detail: tobacco flavour, nicotine halved, progressive weaning.

veracity.statement: it bans the manufacture, sale, supply, and distribution of disposable vapes. Disposable vapes are disproportionately used by children and young people.
veracity.explanation: The claim that disposable vapes are disproportionately used by youth is broadly supported by NZ youth vaping data.

veracity.statement: That has been a contributing factor to recent rapid reductions in smoking rates, with nearly 230,000 people quitting smoking in the last three years.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported rapid falls in NZ daily smoking prevalence 2020-2023; specific figure plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: from Ministers who have cut the tax on heated tobacco products by 50 percent, from Ministers who have stretched out the smoke-free goal for our country that was set by the National Government in 2011, from 2025—so close—to now 2061, as a direct result of the actions that they have taken to make sure that they support their big tobacco friends
veracity.explanation: The HTP tax cut is accurate, but the '2061' figure is a disputed modelling projection presented as fact, and the motive claim is unverifiable.

veracity.statement: from Ministers who have failed to tell their Cabinet colleagues about the $46 billion that the smoke-free generation and the Labour Government’s policies would have resulted in had they not come along and wiped them all away
veracity.explanation: The ~$46b refers to contested long-run health-system savings modelling; presented as a settled fact it is misleading.

veracity.statement: We know that 5,000 people per year in New Zealand die from smoking and that there are still 330,000 smokers in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: ~5,000 smoking-related deaths per year is the standard cited NZ figure; ~330,000 smokers is consistent with recent prevalence data.

veracity.statement: the committee heard evidence that, in the last two years, there has only been one prosecution for a vape retailer that has sold to youth
veracity.explanation: Specific evidentiary claim attributed to committee evidence; plausible but not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: what we have seen in some of the latest data is that a lot of people who do take up vaping have never smoked before.
veracity.explanation: Supported by NZ data showing rising vaping uptake among never-smokers, especially youth.

veracity.statement: certain flavouring, when heated, may produce or may create certain effects in our body—some of which may be considered carcinogenic. There’s still a lot more work that needs to be done in this area
veracity.explanation: Cautious claim consistent with emerging but unsettled evidence on heated-flavouring by-products.

veracity.statement: The research shows that nicotine is no more harmful than caffeine, but cigarette tar is very harmful, and that’s why vaping or inhaling water vapour is a much preferable alternative to smoking cigarettes.
veracity.explanation: The nicotine-equals-caffeine equivalence is a contested, misleading talking point, and vape aerosol is not 'water vapour'.

veracity.statement: Last week, I hosted Mount Roskill’s first youth vaping awareness seminar. More than 60 concerned parents and community members came together to listen to the seminar and raise their concerns.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable personal claim about an event he hosted; plausible and concrete.

veracity.statement: simply saying that it’s just water vapour, when the science hasn’t fully shown the true impact of vaping right around the world—and in fact, you only need a quick Google search or to read some of the more in-depth research that’s coming out of Otago at the moment showing the impact of vaping on lungs.
veracity.explanation: Correct that long-term vaping effects remain unsettled and rebuts the misleading 'water vapour' framing; references Otago research.

veracity.statement: within their first 100 days, they went about effectively dismantling that opportunity for the first time in New Zealand’s history to have a smoke-free generation coming through the ranks.
veracity.explanation: Accurately references the government's early-term repeal of the smokefree-generation legislation.

veracity.statement: The BBC reported on 13 August last year that New Zealand’s vaping crisis data showed that under Labour, the number of teenagers in New Zealand who vaped regularly tripled—it tripled—between 2019 and 2021
veracity.explanation: Regular youth vaping did rise sharply over this period and he cites a specific source; the exact 'tripled' magnitude is harder to confirm.

veracity.statement: Also, under the previous Labour Government, the number of vape shops in New Zealand exploded to 7,500.
veracity.explanation: The 7,500 figure conflates all retailers permitted to sell vapes with dedicated 'vape shops', which risks overstating the point.

veracity.statement: Like everything else, Labour created the youth vaping crisis and this Government is here to fix it.
veracity.explanation: Overstated causal claim; the crisis has multiple drivers, not a single party's creation.

veracity.statement: They’ve spent more time considering the tax cuts to tobacco companies than they have actually looking at the legislation that might address youth vaping.
veracity.explanation: Unsupported comparative claim about time spent, presented as fact.

rigor.statement: it bans the manufacture, sale, supply, and distribution of disposable vapes. Disposable vapes are disproportionately used by children and young people.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning links an evidence-based premise (youth over-use disposables) to the policy conclusion (ban them) with clear entailment.

rigor.statement: from Ministers who have cut the tax on heated tobacco products by 50 percent, from Ministers who have stretched out the smoke-free goal for our country that was set by the National Government in 2011, from 2025—so close—to now 2061, as a direct result of the actions that they have taken to make sure that they support their big tobacco friends
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal motive with no evidence; mixes a real fact (HTP tax halved) with a contested projection to draw an ad hominem conclusion.

rigor.statement: the committee heard evidence that, in the last two years, there has only been one prosecution for a vape retailer that has sold to youth
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete data point to support the argument that enforcement is inadequate.

rigor.statement: although this puts a ban on disposable vapes—which is a step in the right direction—it doesn’t ban or limit non-disposable vapes. For one, it doesn’t limit the number of retailers who potentially will be selling vaping products
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific logical gap between the bill's stated aim and its scope (disposables only, no retailer limits).

rigor.statement: what we have seen in some of the latest data is that a lot of people who do take up vaping have never smoked before.
rigor.explanation: Grounds a challenge to the 'cessation tool' framing in cited data trends.

rigor.statement: certain flavouring, when heated, may produce or may create certain effects in our body—some of which may be considered carcinogenic. There’s still a lot more work that needs to be done in this area
rigor.explanation: Appropriately hedged ("may") and explicitly acknowledges evidentiary uncertainty rather than overstating.

rigor.statement: The research shows that nicotine is no more harmful than caffeine, but cigarette tar is very harmful, and that’s why vaping or inhaling water vapour is a much preferable alternative to smoking cigarettes.
rigor.explanation: Vague appeal to 'the research shows' with no citation, resting a conclusion on a disputed premise.

rigor.statement: vapes will still be widely available for those people who choose to use them, who are adults, 18 and over, in order to reduce the harm that smoking causes them, but they will not be widely available to children and young people, and that is what this bill aims to achieve.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable articulation of the bill's intended trade-off, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: noting that part of the appeal of these products to youth is that they’re inexpensive, brightly coloured, and easy to conceal
rigor.explanation: Grounds the bill's product-removal rationale in specific, plausible product characteristics driving youth uptake.

rigor.statement: simply saying that it’s just water vapour, when the science hasn’t fully shown the true impact of vaping right around the world—and in fact, you only need a quick Google search or to read some of the more in-depth research that’s coming out of Otago at the moment showing the impact of vaping on lungs.
rigor.explanation: Cites Otago research but leans on a weak appeal ('a quick Google search') rather than specific evidence.

rigor.statement: the LAPs, or the local alcohol policies, in Auckland have finally recognised that there are far too many alcohol stores in South Auckland—let’s actually change the settings and the plan to make sure that we’re not opening more closer to schools in poorer socio-economic communities... Well, we’re looking to do the same with vaping, so why don’t we go harder?
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to alcohol outlet policy; a reasonable comparison but relies on the analogy holding rather than direct evidence.

rigor.statement: what the hell did they do for six years? What did they do about vaping for six years? With 65 MPs—65 MPs!
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical questions and the '65 MPs' flourish substitute for an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: The BBC reported on 13 August last year that New Zealand’s vaping crisis data showed that under Labour, the number of teenagers in New Zealand who vaped regularly tripled—it tripled—between 2019 and 2021
rigor.explanation: Anchors the claim to a dated, named source, though used to assign blame rather than analyse causes.

rigor.statement: Like everything else, Labour created the youth vaping crisis and this Government is here to fix it.
rigor.explanation: Monocausal 'Labour created the crisis' claim is an oversimplified attribution with no supporting mechanism.

rigor.statement: on a day where the Government have gone black and blue defending this idea that they have to put the Treaty principles bill through a full select committee hearing, even though that’s not in the coalition agreement, we are now debating as a House to put through a piece of legislation... rigor.explanation: Points to a genuine procedural inconsistency (full process for one bill, truncated for this) to support the argument.

rigor.statement: I happen to think that there should be no flavours for vapes available, other than those flavours that are allowed for tobacco, because, at the end of the day, vapes are a cessation device.

authenticity.statement: The Government is committed to achieving smoke-free 2025 and to reducing youth vaping.

charisma.explanation: Frames a shared community-benefit goal, though within an urging-the-government register.

divination.statement: If no action is taken, it is likely that these cheap, disposable vaping products will continue to find their way into the hands of young people.
divination.explanation: A conditional prediction about continued youth access absent intervention; plausible and consistent with current trends, though unquantified.

specificity.statement: I was out in Auckland on Saturday night, seeing the fantastic results from having more cops out on the beat. We know that visible policing can have a real impact, with serious assaults down 22 percent in the last year in the Auckland CBD.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (22% down) and location (Auckland CBD) and timeframe (last year), though the causal mechanism is asserted rather than detailed.

specificity.statement: Does he believe his Government's decision to cut billions of dollars from infrastructure projects like schools, State houses, and hospitals has contributed in any way to the fact that there are over 8,000 fewer people employed in building and construction today compared to when he became Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Grounds the question in a concrete figure (over 8,000 fewer construction jobs) and a defined baseline (since he became PM).

specificity.statement: it has been seen in some areas that the catch of the sea is reducing, like the snapper that has already been mentioned, but each person has their own autonomy. They have their own autonomy; I do too, I have my own autonomy. And so it is up to Te Ohu Kaimoana to come up with the right path for themselves.
specificity.explanation: Deliberately abstract and metaphorical, committing to nothing concrete.

specificity.statement: As a small example, look to our Minister of Finance, who has supported the undertakings of Te Matatini for the next three years.

specificity.statement: Does he accept the findings of the tribunal that this Government has breached the Te Tiriti o Waitangi at every stage of their Treaty principles bill, Māori wards policy, the removal of section 7AA, and now the Takutai Moana bill?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four specific policies said to breach the Treaty, grounding the question concretely.

specificity.statement: This morning, I announced that from today that low to middle income families with young children will be able to register with Inland Revenue for FamilyBoost. As members know, this is a new payment to help parents and caregivers meet the costs of early childhood education.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the agency, the eligible group and effective date, though the headline answer leaves amounts to follow-up questions.

specificity.statement: Parents and caregivers are eligible for a payment towards their early childhood education fees, up to a maximum fortnightly payment of $150. Payments will be made quarterly as a lump sum, so parents and caregivers can get up to $975 a quarter, up to 25 percent of their early childhood fees after the 20 hours ECE and Ministry of Social Development childcare subsidy have been taken into account.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures ($150 fortnightly, $975 quarterly, 25%), mechanism and interaction with existing subsidies fully spelled out.

specificity.statement: These payments will make a real difference to more than 100,000 Kiwi families—that's 140,000 Kiwi kids. I note that members opposite are grumbling about this. They would take that money away.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the reach (100,000 families, 140,000 children), though the impact claim itself is general.

specificity.statement: Are the increasing company liquidations, which are up 19 percent year on year, and insolvencies up 23 percent from the first quarter of the year and 36 percent higher than the same period a year ago contributing to the brain drain?
specificity.explanation: Grounds the question in multiple precise figures (19%, 23%, 36%) with defined comparison periods.

specificity.statement: we are paying for 200 LATs and 150 teacher certificate renewals to make it easier for former teachers to come back into the class, and we'll be prioritising applications from previously certified teachers. specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers (200 LATs, 150 renewals) and named mechanisms (website, navigator, direct contact) rather than aspiration.

specificity.statement: We know that winter illness has increased markedly since 2019. specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete causes and consequences (rostering home, combining classes) with a reference year (2019).

specificity.statement: On Sunday, I announced that this coalition Government has agreed to amend the Employment Relations Act to provide greater certainty and clarity for businesses and workers in contracting relationships. This was an ACT-National coalition commitment and it was also a priority in the Government's quarter three plan.

specificity.statement: There are four criteria for the gateway test. These criteria are that there must be a written agreement with the worker specifying they are an independent contractor, not an employee; the business does not restrict the worker from working for another business, including competitors; the business does not require the worker to be available to work on specific days or times, or the worker can subcontract the work; and the business does not terminate the contract if the worker does not accept an additional task or engagement.
specificity.explanation: Lays out all four precise legal criteria of the test in concrete, checkable terms.

specificity.statement: No, that is not correct... I did meet with Uber—yes, that's true. I did ask a range of things within our meeting. specificity.explanation: Names the operations and lists precise seizure figures (206kg meth, $9.2m assets, etc.).

specificity.statement: from 1 January to 31 July this year, there were 22 percent fewer serious assaults in the Auckland CBD than last year; within that, there were 18 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury... nationwide there have been 6 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury, 15 percent fewer burglaries, 10 percent fewer aggravated robberies, and 10 percent fewer stabbings. specificity.explanation: Dense with precise, sourced figures across multiple crime categories and geographies with a defined date range.

specificity.statement: We're also capping the sentence discounts that judges can apply at 40 percent, preventing repeat discounts for youth and remorse, and implementing a sliding scale for early guilty pleas.
