specificity.statement: We're investing in te reo language. We're developing and resourcing structured literacy in our schools and offering te reo modification there. specificity.statement: Yeah, we've got schools that will be able to access free decodable books and other resources in reo from the ministry where they're directly receiving cash funds to actually supplement this with other materials they might need. specificity.explanation: Gestures at concrete areas (emergency housing, tax relief) but without figures or the specific data requested.

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that in Budget 2024, the Government allocated an additional $12 million of capital expenditure to kōhanga reo, a form of early childhood education school choice that is actually valued by parents who want their children to learn te reo Māori whether they be Māori or non-Māori?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($12m capital) and its Budget 2024 source, though framed as a supportive planted question.

specificity.statement: from 2 September, buy now, pay later services will be regulated under the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act... The key elements are, first, buy now, pay later providers must comply with responsible lending rules... Second, when consumers sign up or request an increase in their credit limit, buy now, pay later providers must undertake credit checks. Third, buy now, pay later providers must disclose their key terms, including their default fees. Fourth, buy now, pay later providers must join an external dispute resolution scheme. And, finally, buy now, pay later providers must also offer relief for those experiencing financial hardship.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five concrete regulatory requirements with an effective date and the governing Act.

specificity.statement: it's interesting that Afterpay report that 95 percent of their customers paid on time in the first quarter of this year. This is broadly in line with Centrix's figure. That data showed that only 8 percent of people missed the payment—i.e., 92 percent hit the payment—and that, of all of Afterpay's people, only 1 percent applied for an application for full financial hardship, and all of them were granted relief.
specificity.explanation: Cites multiple concrete figures (95%, 92%, 8%, 1%) attributed to named sources (Afterpay, Centrix).

specificity.statement: Does he, the Minister, agree with the WAI11 settlement claim that says, "the Māori language is an essential part of Māori culture, and must be regarded as a taonga, a valued possession"; if the Minister is in agreement, what is the reason for the reduction in funding for Māori TV?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question in a specific cited authority (WAI11) and a concrete policy (Māori TV funding reduction).

veracity.statement: I was out in Auckland on Saturday night, seeing the fantastic results from having more cops out on the beat. We know that visible policing can have a real impact, with serious assaults down 22 percent in the last year in the Auckland CBD.
veracity.explanation: The 22% figure is repeated and corroborated by Minister Mitchell later in the session citing official CBD data; plausible and consistent, though selectively framed.

veracity.statement: But what I would just say to that member is that there is no doubt about it, it is a tough time for New Zealanders at the moment and people are losing their jobs. And that member has to ask the question: why is that? It is because the economy is in recession. The economy is in recession because interest rates are sky-high. Interest rates are sky-high because inflation went through the roof. And why did inflation go through the roof? Because of wasteful Government spending.
veracity.explanation: 'The economy is in recession' was broadly accurate at the time, but the monocausal attribution to 'wasteful Government spending' is a simplification that omits global inflation drivers.

veracity.statement: there's actually been more money put into school buildings—that's what we're doing.
veracity.explanation: Directly disputes Hipkins' claim of a $2b cut; the truth is contested and depends on baseline/reprioritisation framing, so the flat assertion is at best partial.

veracity.statement: We did not cut anything from school buildings.
veracity.explanation: A categorical denial contradicting repeated opposition claims of billions cut from school build/maintenance; the reality involved reprioritisation, making the absolute claim misleading.

veracity.statement: How does it start? You have an 84 percent increase in spending, it drives record levels of inflation, that drives high levels of interest rates, that puts the economy into recession, that drives unemployment. That is the history of economics that we've been trying to articulate to that member... We are where we are today because of woeful, uneducated economic management.
veracity.explanation: The '84 percent increase in spending' is a contestable and likely cherry-picked figure; presented without period definition it is misleading.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is focused on rebuilding the economy, fixing the mess that we've inherited so that people can get ahead. You see lower levels of inflation, you've seen interest rate cuts, you've seen the highest level of business confidence we've had in 10 years—then we'll get economic growth, then we'll keep people in employment.
veracity.explanation: 'Highest level of business confidence we've had in 10 years' aligns with confidence surveys of the period; 'interest rate cuts' and falling inflation were broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Does he believe his Government's decision to cut billions of dollars from infrastructure projects like schools, State houses, and hospitals has contributed in any way to the fact that there are over 8,000 fewer people employed in building and construction today compared to when he became Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: The construction employment decline figure is broadly consistent with contemporaneous data, though the embedded causal attribution is contestable.

veracity.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to whether it's a fact that the tribunal came down with a finding after having a hearing on a bill that they hadn't even read—that that is the actual chronological fact here, that they were talking about a bill, the contents of which they had never seen and hadn't read?
veracity.explanation: Frames a contestable characterisation of the Waitangi Tribunal's urgent hearing process as settled 'chronological fact'; the premise is disputed and one-sided.

veracity.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement... The Government inherited a mess after six years of economic mismanagement by Labour and it will take time to turn that around... We are focused on supporting our economy to grow, and we are already seeing inflation coming back under control, interest rates decreasing, and business confidence rising. These are the green shoots of economic recovery.
veracity.explanation: 'Inflation coming back under control, interest rates decreasing, business confidence rising' were broadly accurate trends at the time; 'green shoots' is optimistic framing.

veracity.statement: Are the increasing company liquidations, which are up 19 percent year on year, and insolvencies up 23 percent from the first quarter of the year and 36 percent higher than the same period a year ago contributing to the brain drain?
veracity.explanation: The liquidation/insolvency figures are broadly consistent with contemporaneous reporting; the causal link to 'brain drain' is the contestable part left as a question.

veracity.statement: I'd also like to acknowledge our outstanding police force, who announced today the conclusion of three significant operations targeting the Comancheros: Operations Scuba, Brewer, and Avon. The operations have seen nearly every member of the Comancheros in New Zealand face charges, have seized 206 kilograms of methamphetamine, $9.2 million in assets seized, $1.275 million in cash, five properties, 14 vehicles, and 15 firearms.
veracity.explanation: Detailed operational figures attributed to a same-day police announcement; specific and verifiable, presumed accurate.

veracity.statement: Well, I think the Hon Willie Jackson is right: get your numbers right. I'm not sure if the member has. She doesn't have a good track record of it... but the most immediate focus for us is dealing with the violent retail crime... And the good news is that violent aggravated robberies in this country are down 10 percent.
veracity.explanation: 'Violent aggravated robberies... down 10 percent' is consistent with figures he repeats elsewhere in the session, though it answers a different metric than asked.

veracity.statement: from 1 January to 31 July this year, there were 22 percent fewer serious assaults in the Auckland CBD than last year; within that, there were 18 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury... nationwide there have been 6 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury, 15 percent fewer burglaries, 10 percent fewer aggravated robberies, and 10 percent fewer stabbings. Auckland Council have reported 35 percent less crime in the CBD, and Heart of the City says that retail thefts have dropped by 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Figures are attributed to specific sources (Auckland Council, Heart of the City) and consistent with the PM's earlier claim; a favourable but sourced selection of statistics.

veracity.statement: Is the most recent Crime and Victims Survey correct when it notes that between 2018 and 2023, "there was no significant difference in the overall violent offence prevalence rate", as reported by Stuff?
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites a Crime and Victims Survey finding, though selectively used to counter the government's narrative.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that in Budget 2024, the Government allocated an additional $12 million of capital expenditure to kōhanga reo, a form of early childhood education school choice that is actually valued by parents who want their children to learn te reo Māori whether they be Māori or non-Māori?
veracity.explanation: The $12m kōhanga reo allocation appears to be a real Budget item; presented favourably but factually grounded.

veracity.statement: it's interesting that Afterpay report that 95 percent of their customers paid on time in the first quarter of this year. This is broadly in line with Centrix's figure. That data showed that only 8 percent of people missed the payment—i.e., 92 percent hit the payment—and that, of all of Afterpay's people, only 1 percent applied for an application for full financial hardship, and all of them were granted relief.
veracity.explanation: Figures are sourced but selectively favourable; relying on the provider's own (Afterpay) on-time rate to rebut a consumer-harm claim is somewhat one-sided.

veracity.statement: As I said before, 99 percent of people who use buy now, pay later actually meet all their payments, and the 1 percent who have applied for hardship have all been granted proper full relief for their situation.
veracity.explanation: The '99 percent meet all their payments' figure sits awkwardly against his own earlier '92 percent hit the payment / 8 percent missed', suggesting a rounded-up or conflated statistic.

strength.statement: I was out in Auckland on Saturday night, seeing the fantastic results from having more cops out on the beat. We know that visible policing can have a real impact, with serious assaults down 22 percent in the last year in the Auckland CBD.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered crime reduction, but attributes it to more police 'on the beat' — partial, early-stage delivery rather than a fully demonstrated programme outcome.

strength.statement: As a small example, look to our Minister of Finance, who has supported the undertakings of Te Matatini for the next three years.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered/committed funding action as evidence of the government's Treaty endeavours.

strength.statement: This morning, I announced that from today that low to middle income families with young children will be able to register with Inland Revenue for FamilyBoost. As members know, this is a new payment to help parents and caregivers meet the costs of early childhood education.
strength.explanation: Announces a policy going live 'from today', showing delivery of a stated commitment, though it is an announcement of a just-opened registration.

strength.statement: we are paying for 200 LATs and 150 teacher certificate renewals to make it easier for former teachers to come back into the class, and we'll be prioritising applications from previously certified teachers. We've set up a website, paid for a navigator at the Teaching Council to help people with the process, and the ministry and the Teaching Council will start to contact out-of-service teachers.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete, funded actions already agreed with the Teaching Council, showing delivery, though it is a short-term measure just being kicked off.

strength.statement: On Sunday, I announced that this coalition Government has agreed to amend the Employment Relations Act to provide greater certainty and clarity for businesses and workers in contracting relationships. This was an ACT-National coalition commitment and it was also a priority in the Government's quarter three plan.
strength.explanation: Points to delivery of a specific coalition commitment, though at the announcement stage rather than enacted law.

strength.statement: I'd also like to acknowledge our outstanding police force, who announced today the conclusion of three significant operations targeting the Comancheros: Operations Scuba, Brewer, and Avon. The operations have seen nearly every member of the Comancheros in New Zealand face charges, have seized 206 kilograms of methamphetamine, $9.2 million in assets seized, $1.275 million in cash, five properties, 14 vehicles, and 15 firearms.
strength.explanation: Credits enforcement results, though acknowledges police (not the minister) as the deliverer of the operations.

strength.statement: from 1 January to 31 July this year, there were 22 percent fewer serious assaults in the Auckland CBD than last year; within that, there were 18 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury... nationwide there have been 6 percent fewer serious assaults resulting in injury, 15 percent fewer burglaries, 10 percent fewer aggravated robberies, and 10 percent fewer stabbings. Auckland Council have reported 35 percent less crime in the CBD, and Heart of the City says that retail thefts have dropped by 50 percent.
strength.explanation: Presents delivered crime reductions as early signs of the government's plan, hedged as 'only very early signs of progress.'

strength.statement: Since 1 July, 97 people have been referred by police for support with accommodation, addiction, and family wellbeing. Additionally, there has been a 68 percent drop in the number of households in emergency housing in the Auckland CBD. This has enabled the exit of two emergency housing motels in the CBD.
strength.explanation: Describes tangible cross-agency delivery, though qualified with 'there is still an enormous amount of work to do.'

strength.statement: Yesterday, the Government introduced the sentencing reform package, delivering on a range of coalition commitments and making a number of changes to restore real consequences of crime while also putting victims at the heart of the justice system. It's got three objectives: making sure that the punishment fits the crime; restoring the principle of personal responsibility for offending; and better recognising victims.
strength.explanation: Points to introduction of legislation delivering coalition commitments, but introduction is an early step, not enactment.

civility.statement: So I'd encourage that member, if he's serious about restoring law and order and keeping communities safe, to back our gang laws so we can get on with the job and clean up the mess that he left behind.
civility.explanation: Frames an invitation to support legislation but tacks on 'the mess that he left behind', a pointed jab at the opponent's record rather than the substance.

civility.statement: That is the consequence in the history of economics. I hope that you learn something about economics on the UK trip.
civility.explanation: A personal, condescending jab implying the opponent is ignorant of economics rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: How does it start? You have an 84 percent increase in spending, it drives record levels of inflation, that drives high levels of interest rates, that puts the economy into recession, that drives unemployment. That is the history of economics that we've been trying to articulate to that member... We are where we are today because of woeful, uneducated economic management.
civility.explanation: 'Woeful, uneducated economic management' is harsh and edges toward disparaging the opponent's competence rather than the policy.

civility.statement: I wish the member understood economics. I hope that he can learn about financial discipline in the UK.
civility.explanation: Repeated personal jab impugning the opponent's understanding rather than addressing substance.

civility.statement: Where the Prime Minister decides to start attacking the questioner personally, that is going to provoke a certain sort of response.
civility.explanation: A reasonable point-of-order observation about personal attacks, though partly self-serving in justifying his own side's crowd noise.

civility.statement: Which of these best reflects his so-called laser-like focus on outcomes: fewer homes being built, fewer classrooms being upgraded, fewer jobs in building and construction, or record numbers of Kiwis simply giving up and leaving the country?
civility.explanation: Uses 'so-called' and loaded framing ('giving up') to mock the PM's slogan; harsh and rhetorical though still tied to policy outcomes.

civility.statement: Could I ask the Prime Minister: does he not think he should contact the UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer about a visitor soon to come to his conference and warn him that sliding polls are contagious?
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at Hipkins' polling framed as a question; light parliamentary banter but a cheap shot rather than substance.

civility.statement: has he heard the saying that a stopped watch tells the time right twice a day?
civility.explanation: A mocking dig implying an opponent (Willie Jackson) is only occasionally right; personal jab rather than engagement.

civility.statement: the Waitangi Tribunal has many opinions and documents. And so I acknowledge those types of documents, but some of the bills that the member has spoken about have yet to come before this House of Parliament... it should not be left to other Governments who have contributed little but discourse, but we have also seen the results of our Prime Minister and these, my colleagues, that consistently strengthen the economy, health, and education of the Māori communities all across the country.
civility.explanation: 'Other Governments who have contributed little but discourse' is a dismissive characterisation of opponents rather than engagement with the findings.

civility.statement: It was not us that arranged this financial path, but instead it was the prior Government that arranged for the reduction in funding to be spent on this issue. But the House, this den of lions, should be aware that this issue, the Aotearoa New Zealand public media entity, is an endeavour that wastes money, wastes funding, and wastes initiatives in the darkness.
civility.explanation: Characterising the public media entity as something that 'wastes money... in the darkness' is dismissive rhetoric rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Does he accept the findings of the tribunal that this Government has breached the Te Tiriti o Waitangi at every stage of their Treaty principles bill, Māori wards policy, the removal of section 7AA, and now the Takutai Moana bill?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory but anchored to cited Tribunal findings and specific policies rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: These payments will make a real difference to more than 100,000 Kiwi families—that's 140,000 Kiwi kids. I note that members opposite are grumbling about this. They would take that money away.
civility.explanation: 'Members opposite are grumbling' and 'they would take that money away' is a mild partisan characterisation rather than a substantive engagement.

civility.statement: the comment that the Prime Minister made when he was the Leader of the Opposition is an accurate one, and I think that the member opposite needs to reflect on what she thinks a Government would have changed in 10 months... I'll tell you one thing that wouldn't help this economy right now, and that's more debt and more taxes, which is what that party say they stand for.
civility.explanation: Characterises Labour as standing for 'more debt and more taxes' — a partisan framing rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: What New Zealanders can have confidence in is that they have a Government that is delivering what it said it would, that has delivered tax relief in a fiscally neutral way, that is getting Government spending under control so that debt can come back down... as "Mr 12 Percent" can tell you.
civility.explanation: 'Mr 12 Percent' is a mocking nickname aimed at Hipkins' polling — a personal dig rather than substance.

civility.statement: Well, I think the Hon Willie Jackson is right: get your numbers right. I'm not sure if the member has. She doesn't have a good track record of it... but the most immediate focus for us is dealing with the violent retail crime... And the good news is that violent aggravated robberies in this country are down 10 percent.
civility.explanation: 'She doesn't have a good track record of it' is a personal dig at the questioner's competence rather than engaging the figure.

civility.statement: the member will be well aware from her time as justice and police Minister that the New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey has up to a two-year lag time. What we're seeing is a crime hangover from her time as sole-charge Minister for public safety.
civility.explanation: 'Crime hangover from her time as sole-charge Minister' personalises the blame onto the questioner.

civility.statement: Well, it amazes me that the member is standing and asking a question like that when it is the previous Government that was responsible for a large part of the lag on those figures... if they'd had a bit more focus and they'd actually applied some targets and taken it seriously, like this Government is doing, then maybe they might have actually avoided the fact that, yes, we're going to have to work hard to achieve our targets.
civility.explanation: 'It amazes me that the member is standing and asking a question like that' is a dismissive framing of the questioner.

civility.statement: Why did the Government choose to base its crime reduction target on the Crime and Victims Survey rather than on Police data, as National did when in Opposition?
civility.explanation: A pointed but substantive question about methodological consistency, engaging policy rather than personality.

civility.statement: Is it true that he tried to protect consumers, as he says, by preventing buy now, pay later providers from charging excessive fees if he was only to be overruled by David Seymour?
civility.explanation: Implies internal weakness/being overruled — a pointed political framing, but tied to a substantive policy question about fee protections.

civility.statement: Does he agree that te reo Māori is a taonga to be handed down to future generations? If so, why is he allowing his Government to deprioritise te reo in schools when evidence shows that bilingual children learn faster than monolingual children?
civility.explanation: Challenging but respectful, engaging the policy of prioritisation rather than attacking the person.

civility.statement: Does he, the Minister, agree with the WAI11 settlement claim that says, "the Māori language is an essential part of Māori culture, and must be regarded as a taonga, a valued possession"; if the Minister is in agreement, what is the reason for the reduction in funding for Māori TV?
civility.explanation: A substantive, policy-focused challenge citing a Tribunal claim, respectful in tone.

civility.statement: Is the Minister going to stop blaming the previous Government and show some courage and make a bid for Whakaata Māori next year, or is he going to do nothing?
civility.explanation: 'Show some courage' impugns the minister's character rather than engaging purely on the funding merits, though tied to a real policy ask.

charisma.statement: So I'd encourage that member, if he's serious about restoring law and order and keeping communities safe, to back our gang laws so we can get on with the job and clean up the mess that he left behind.
charisma.explanation: Nominally invites the member to 'back our gang laws' but does so combatively, casting the opponent as the source of the problem rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: That is the consequence in the history of economics. I hope that you learn something about economics on the UK trip.
charisma.explanation: Belittling and alienating; shuts down dialogue rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: I wish the member understood economics. I hope that he can learn about financial discipline in the UK.
charisma.explanation: Dismissive and alienating; no attempt at persuasion or common ground.

charisma.statement: any company that goes into liquidation is of concern because what that represents is someone's effort, their hope, their investment coming to a very sad end, often affecting many New Zealanders and their families.
charisma.explanation: Shows empathy for affected people, an inclusive and humane framing, though it precedes a pivot back to partisan blame.

charisma.statement: This good feedback is due to the fact that we listened, we consulted with principals and teachers, and we acted on their suggestions.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises listening and consultation with the sector, a consensus-building framing, though somewhat self-congratulatory.

charisma.statement: Yes, we do. I think this week, for example, is a great opportunity for people to expand their knowledge of te reo. We encourage that. We value te reo Māori as an official language of New Zealand. I've enjoyed trying to learn. Personally, I've struggled with it, but I encourage all New Zealanders to do the same.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, self-deprecating and encouraging tone that invites all New Zealanders in.

charisma.statement: I'm incredibly proud that this is a Government that's focused on improving outcomes for Māori and non-Māori... when I think about the efforts that we've made moving many Māori young people out of emergency housing into dry, safe, good homes... giving tax relief for Māori families to support them in a cost of living crisis. We are a Government focused on outcomes, and we're improving them for Māori and non-Māori.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises improving outcomes 'for Māori and non-Māori', an inclusive unifying framing.

forthrightness.statement: But what I would just say to that member is that there is no doubt about it, it is a tough time for New Zealanders at the moment and people are losing their jobs. And that member has to ask the question: why is that? It is because the economy is in recession. The economy is in recession because interest rates are sky-high. Interest rates are sky-high because inflation went through the roof. And why did inflation go through the roof? Because of wasteful Government spending.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a specific question (how many building/construction jobs were affected by a $2b school cut), he never gives a number and pivots entirely to a general recession narrative.

forthrightness.statement: there's actually been more money put into school buildings—that's what we're doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Still does not answer the jobs question posed, offering a general rebuttal instead.

forthrightness.statement: This is a Government that is focused on rebuilding the economy, fixing the mess that we've inherited so that people can get ahead. You see lower levels of inflation, you've seen interest rate cuts, you've seen the highest level of business confidence we've had in 10 years—then we'll get economic growth, then we'll keep people in employment.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to pick which failure reflects his 'laser-like focus', he ignores the multiple-choice framing and delivers a general recovery message.

forthrightness.statement: the statement of the tribunal has indeed been heard. Soon we will receive the thoughts and advice of the officials and advisers of the Government, and we will be able to respond.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for his response to the Tribunal's finding that the Crown's actions would be a gross Treaty breach, he acknowledges hearing it but defers any actual answer.

forthrightness.statement: the bill that the member has referred to has yet to be enacted. At the appropriate time, we know that it will be up to Parliament to enact it.
forthrightness.explanation: Dodges whether he stands by the Crown's actions by resorting to the technicality that the bill is not yet enacted.

forthrightness.statement: To the Speaker, absolutely. At the appropriate time, it will be up to our ministerial colleague Minister Goldsmith to bring it before each of the members of this House.
forthrightness.explanation: After the question was re-read, he gives a direct 'absolutely' (yes he stands by the Crown's actions) but then immediately defers substance to another minister.

forthrightness.statement: it has been seen in some areas that the catch of the sea is reducing, like the snapper that has already been mentioned, but each person has their own autonomy. They have their own autonomy; I do too, I have my own autonomy. And so it is up to Te Ohu Kaimoana to come up with the right path for themselves.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Peters' factual question about the Tribunal reading the bill with an oblique metaphor about autonomy, avoiding the substance.

forthrightness.statement: it is not for me to apologise to that question. It is my humility and my honour to support our Prime Minister at this time and the direction of this coalition Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he justifies his place in a government the Tribunal says seeks to erase Crown duties to Māori, he offers a loyalty statement instead of any justification.

forthrightness.statement: the Waitangi Tribunal has many opinions and documents. And so I acknowledge those types of documents, but some of the bills that the member has spoken about have yet to come before this House of Parliament... it should not be left to other Governments who have contributed little but discourse, but we have also seen the results of our Prime Minister and these, my colleagues, that consistently strengthen the economy, health, and education of the Māori communities all across the country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he accepts the Tribunal's findings of Treaty breaches at every stage, he neither accepts nor rejects them and pivots to government achievements.

forthrightness.statement: The rise and fall of the support funding for Māori TV has been observed. With each successive Government it shifts back and forth; this is nothing new. However, I support the board and the executive leadership of Māori TV. It is not for me; it is for them to choose the appropriate path for the administration of the reo Māori channel online-only.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he is comfortable with policies pushing the channel online-only, he acknowledges funding shifts but deflects responsibility for the decision onto the board.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement... The Government inherited a mess after six years of economic mismanagement by Labour and it will take time to turn that around... We are focused on supporting our economy to grow, and we are already seeing inflation coming back under control, interest rates decreasing, and business confidence rising. These are the green shoots of economic recovery.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms she stands by her statement but reframes the question (why 55,800 left) around inheritance and recovery rather than the emigration figure.

forthrightness.statement: the comment that the Prime Minister made when he was the Leader of the Opposition is an accurate one, and I think that the member opposite needs to reflect on what she thinks a Government would have changed in 10 months... I'll tell you one thing that wouldn't help this economy right now, and that's more debt and more taxes, which is what that party say they stand for.
forthrightness.explanation: Agrees with the Luxon quote but sidesteps whether emigration is due to lack of opportunity, pivoting to attack the opposition's fiscal stance.

forthrightness.statement: any company that goes into liquidation is of concern because what that represents is someone's effort, their hope, their investment coming to a very sad end, often affecting many New Zealanders and their families.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges liquidations are concerning but does not address whether they are contributing to the brain drain as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Well, this is a matter I differ to the Prime Minister on. They're his targets, he set them, and they're very good indeed.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why reducing emigration isn't a government target, she deflects to the PM's target-setting without addressing the substance.

forthrightness.statement: What New Zealanders can have confidence in is that they have a Government that is delivering what it said it would, that has delivered tax relief in a fiscally neutral way, that is getting Government spending under control so that debt can come back down... as "Mr 12 Percent" can tell you.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how predicted negative GDP growth gives confidence, she recites achievements without engaging the GDP forecast.

forthrightness.statement: No, that is not correct... I did meet with Uber—yes, that's true. I did ask a range of things within our meeting. I don't always stick to the talking points that my officials provide for me. However, we did provide around 20 people that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) consulted with a draft policy. That was not the policy that we've ended up with. There were seven unions that were consulted by MBIE, and I note that some of the changes that they suggested were actually implemented in our model.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the insinuation that Uber authored the policy, concedes the meeting happened, and supplies specifics (20 consulted, 7 unions) to answer the core of the question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think the Hon Willie Jackson is right: get your numbers right. I'm not sure if the member has. She doesn't have a good track record of it... but the most immediate focus for us is dealing with the violent retail crime... And the good news is that violent aggravated robberies in this country are down 10 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not confirm or deny the specific 17% retail-crime figure asked about, redirecting to violent aggravated robberies being down 10%.

forthrightness.statement: the member will be well aware from her time as justice and police Minister that the New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey has up to a two-year lag time. What we're seeing is a crime hangover from her time as sole-charge Minister for public safety.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly engages by noting the survey's lag but avoids conceding the 'no significant difference' finding, pivoting to blame.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it amazes me that the member is standing and asking a question like that when it is the previous Government that was responsible for a large part of the lag on those figures... if they'd had a bit more focus and they'd actually applied some targets and taken it seriously, like this Government is doing, then maybe they might have actually avoided the fact that, yes, we're going to have to work hard to achieve our targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address whether he needs to reduce victims by 50,000 to meet the target, deflecting to criticism of the prior government.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, we do. I think this week, for example, is a great opportunity for people to expand their knowledge of te reo. We encourage that. We value te reo Māori as an official language of New Zealand. I've enjoyed trying to learn. Personally, I've struggled with it, but I encourage all New Zealanders to do the same.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by his statement encouraging te reo learning, with a candid personal note about struggling.

forthrightness.statement: We're investing in te reo language. We're developing and resourcing structured literacy in our schools and offering te reo modification there. We've got a new phonics check, which is a world first in te reo Māori. We've got a curriculum-aligned mathematics programme, and all those resources will be free to schools and also available in te reo Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'how is his Government protecting te reo' with a list of programmes, addressing the question if not the deprioritisation critique.

forthrightness.statement: Yeah, we've got schools that will be able to access free decodable books and other resources in reo from the ministry where they're directly receiving cash funds to actually supplement this with other materials they might need. As I said, we've got a phonics check, we've got the Māori structured literacy programme, we're accrediting providers to work across New Zealand professional development.
forthrightness.explanation: Reiterates programme lists but sidesteps the specific challenge about deprioritising te reo despite evidence bilingual children learn faster.

forthrightness.statement: I don't have that number with me, but if you'd like to put that in writing, I can get an answer to you.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how cutting Whakaata Māori funding revitalises te reo, he declines to engage and defers to a written answer.

forthrightness.statement: I'm incredibly proud that this is a Government that's focused on improving outcomes for Māori and non-Māori... when I think about the efforts that we've made moving many Māori young people out of emergency housing into dry, safe, good homes... giving tax relief for Māori families to support them in a cost of living crisis. We are a Government focused on outcomes, and we're improving them for Māori and non-Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Peters' pointed maths question ($12m vs $6,000 per kura) with a broad statement of pride in Māori outcomes rather than the figure.

forthrightness.statement: from 2 September, buy now, pay later services will be regulated under the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act... The key elements are, first, buy now, pay later providers must comply with responsible lending rules... Second, when consumers sign up or request an increase in their credit limit, buy now, pay later providers must undertake credit checks. Third, buy now, pay later providers must disclose their key terms, including their default fees. Fourth, buy now, pay later providers must join an external dispute resolution scheme. And, finally, buy now, pay later providers must also offer relief for those experiencing financial hardship.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'no' to whether changes make things worse and substantiates it, though he initially skirts the 'one in five forgo essentials' premise.

forthrightness.statement: The reason why we made the exception for buy now, pay later is that we wanted to protect this as an important source of finance for people, and the model did not work under the CCCFA provisions as they were currently proposed. That's why we accepted them, because we think it's important that people have access to buy now, pay later services.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the rationale for the fee exception but does not confirm or deny the specific claim that he was overruled by David Seymour.

rigor.statement: But what I would just say to that member is that there is no doubt about it, it is a tough time for New Zealanders at the moment and people are losing their jobs. And that member has to ask the question: why is that? It is because the economy is in recession. The economy is in recession because interest rates are sky-high. Interest rates are sky-high because inflation went through the roof. And why did inflation go through the roof? Because of wasteful Government spending.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a causal chain (spending→inflation→interest rates→recession) but presents it as self-evident with no supporting figures, a plausible-but-unevidenced argument.

rigor.statement: How does it start? You have an 84 percent increase in spending, it drives record levels of inflation, that drives high levels of interest rates, that puts the economy into recession, that drives unemployment. That is the history of economics that we've been trying to articulate to that member... We are where we are today because of woeful, uneducated economic management.
rigor.explanation: Presents a causal chain anchored on an '84 percent increase in spending' figure, but treats correlation as settled causation and ignores confounders like the global pandemic and inflation.

rigor.statement: Which of these best reflects his so-called laser-like focus on outcomes: fewer homes being built, fewer classrooms being upgraded, fewer jobs in building and construction, or record numbers of Kiwis simply giving up and leaving the country?
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical multiple-choice framing that assumes causation between the government and each listed outcome rather than establishing it.

rigor.statement: Where a Government Minister is being questioned on a Government bill, I don't think they can give an answer like the one the Minister just gave. It is a Government piece of legislation, and they have to be able to answer for it.
rigor.explanation: A coherent procedural argument that ministers are accountable for government legislation regardless of technical enactment status; logically grounded.

rigor.statement: We know that winter illness has increased markedly since 2019. This has been compounded by additional classroom release time and out of classroom time for professional learning and development. Even with an increase in the number of relief teachers overall, the pressures have meant that schools are rostering home classes and year groups.
rigor.explanation: Sets out a reasoned diagnosis linking specific drivers (winter illness, release time) to the relief-teacher shortage, though the evidentiary basis is asserted rather than cited.

rigor.statement: the member will be well aware from her time as justice and police Minister that the New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey has up to a two-year lag time. What we're seeing is a crime hangover from her time as sole-charge Minister for public safety.
rigor.explanation: The two-year lag point is a legitimate methodological caveat, but 'crime hangover from her time' substitutes attribution for evidence.

rigor.statement: We're also capping the sentence discounts that judges can apply at 40 percent, preventing repeat discounts for youth and remorse, and implementing a sliding scale for early guilty pleas. We've seen too many examples of people convicted of serious violent and sexual crimes having their sentences discounted away and ending up on home detention.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the change with 'too many examples' — an anecdotal appeal rather than quantified evidence, though the policy detail is clear.

rigor.statement: the Government is concerned that in recent years, the courts have imposed fewer prison sentences and, at the same time, the prevalence of violent and serious crime in our communities has increased. Tougher sentencing will restore real consequences for crime. It will put more serious offenders in prison for longer to prevent them creating new victims.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes fewer prison sentences with rising crime to imply causation, and assumes longer sentences prevent victims — both contested by criminological evidence.

rigor.statement: it's interesting that Afterpay report that 95 percent of their customers paid on time in the first quarter of this year. This is broadly in line with Centrix's figure. That data showed that only 8 percent of people missed the payment—i.e., 92 percent hit the payment—and that, of all of Afterpay's people, only 1 percent applied for an application for full financial hardship, and all of them were granted relief.
rigor.explanation: Marshals data to counter the premise, but conflates 'paid on time' with 'no harm', which does not directly address the one-in-five forgoing essentials.

rigor.statement: Does he agree that te reo Māori is a taonga to be handed down to future generations? If so, why is he allowing his Government to deprioritise te reo in schools when evidence shows that bilingual children learn faster than monolingual children?
rigor.explanation: Marshals an evidence claim (bilingual children learn faster) to press a policy point, engaging on substance, though the cited evidence is stated rather than sourced.

rigor.statement: Is the Minister going to stop blaming the previous Government and show some courage and make a bid for Whakaata Māori next year, or is he going to do nothing?
rigor.explanation: Frames the choice as a false dichotomy ('make a bid... or do nothing') and leads with 'stop blaming the previous Government', an assumption baked into the question.

divination.statement: This is a Government that is focused on rebuilding the economy, fixing the mess that we've inherited so that people can get ahead. You see lower levels of inflation, you've seen interest rate cuts, you've seen the highest level of business confidence we've had in 10 years—then we'll get economic growth, then we'll keep people in employment.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'then we'll get economic growth, then we'll keep people in employment' — directionally plausible given easing conditions but uncertain in timing and magnitude.

divination.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement... The Government inherited a mess after six years of economic mismanagement by Labour and it will take time to turn that around... We are focused on supporting our economy to grow, and we are already seeing inflation coming back under control, interest rates decreasing, and business confidence rising. These are the green shoots of economic recovery.
divination.explanation: 'Green shoots of economic recovery... brighter days are ahead' is a directional forecast, plausible but uncertain.

divination.statement: the Government is concerned that in recent years, the courts have imposed fewer prison sentences and, at the same time, the prevalence of violent and serious crime in our communities has increased. Tougher sentencing will restore real consequences for crime. It will put more serious offenders in prison for longer to prevent them creating new victims.
divination.explanation: Predicts tougher sentencing will 'prevent them creating new victims'; the deterrent/incapacitation effect claimed is optimistic relative to the mixed evidence base.

authenticity.statement: It was not us that arranged this financial path, but instead it was the prior Government that arranged for the reduction in funding to be spent on this issue. But the House, this den of lions, should be aware that this issue, the Aotearoa New Zealand public media entity, is an endeavour that wastes money, wastes funding, and wastes initiatives in the darkness.
authenticity.explanation: Disclaims responsibility for the funding reduction by blaming the previous government, while defending the current settings — a tension between disowning the cut and standing by it.

authenticity.statement: This good feedback is due to the fact that we listened, we consulted with principals and teachers, and we acted on their suggestions.
authenticity.explanation: Claims consultation drove the policy; consistent with the quoted supportive feedback in the answer, but unverifiable from the text alone.

authenticity.statement: On Sunday, I announced that this coalition Government has agreed to amend the Employment Relations Act to provide greater certainty and clarity for businesses and workers in contracting relationships. This was an ACT-National coalition commitment and it was also a priority in the Government's quarter three plan.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly links the action to a prior ACT-National coalition commitment, showing words matched to a pre-stated pledge.

authenticity.statement: Yes, we do. I think this week, for example, is a great opportunity for people to expand their knowledge of te reo. We encourage that. We value te reo Māori as an official language of New Zealand. I've enjoyed trying to learn. Personally, I've struggled with it, but I encourage all New Zealanders to do the same.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms his pro-te-reo statement; the personal admission of trying to learn lends some consistency, though contested against funding-cut criticisms raised.

veracity.statement: Engari me mōhio hoki ka tika, ka nui te whakamoumou i te pūtea i tērā Kāwana tawhito. [But it is appropriate to also be aware that that previous Government wasted a lot of funding.]
veracity.explanation: Sweeping, unquantified claim that the previous Government 'wasted a lot' of funding; no figures or examples given to verify.

veracity.statement: In Budget ’24, the Government boosted Vote Education by $2.93 billion over the next four years to improve student outcomes despite very tough fiscal times.
veracity.explanation: Concrete Budget figure that is checkable against Budget documents; presented as fact.

veracity.statement: There is, of course, the $67 million for structured literacy and $53 million for an additional 1,500 teachers.
veracity.explanation: Checkable Budget line items presented as fact.

veracity.statement: we have put in an enormous injection—over $1.3 billion of investment over four years—into school properties so our kids can learn in safe, warm, dry buildings and so that the portfolio can be expanded to accommodate more students.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable investment figure, though 'enormous' is editorial.

veracity.statement: This is the largest increase in maintenance, upgrade, and redevelopment funding that has been delivered in at least three years, and I understand from the ministry that this injection is more than the last six years combined.
veracity.explanation: Strong comparative claim ('more than the last six years combined') hedged with 'I understand from the ministry'; plausible but not independently substantiated here.

veracity.statement: we’re also investing $456 million to expand the property portfolio to manage roll growth by delivering an additional 8,000 student places, which we’re well on the way to doing.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim; the delivery-progress element is asserted.

veracity.statement: There was $478 million of funding for the school lunch programme, which was new money because this had come to an end
veracity.explanation: Figure is checkable; 'new money because this had come to an end' is a framing claim about continuation funding that could be contested.

veracity.statement: There’s an additional 100 full-time teacher equivalents in learning support—so that’s six Curriculum leads, three leadership advisers, 85 learning support roles, including 10 early intervention teachers, 19 speech language therapists, 10 schoolwide practitioners, 20 intern psychologists, 13 educational advisers
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable figures presented as recent fact.

veracity.statement: 45 percent of our 14- and 15-year-olds recently passed a foundational numeracy assessment at high school, which is the NCEA corequisite. That is a terrible result for our kids.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific, checkable pass-rate figure from recent corequisite assessments consistent with reported results.

veracity.statement: around 10,000 kids last year didn’t get NCEA at all, and their trajectory is grim because we know that those kids end up in youth justice, they end up on benefits, and they end up not participating in society to their full potential.
veracity.explanation: The 10,000 figure is a concrete checkable claim; the causal characterisation is broadly directionally supported but generalised.

veracity.statement: I seem to recall somewhere around 25 kids for the $4 million that we were spending. It wasn’t good use of money, and it was a pilot, a small pilot that was actually for tertiary intervention.
veracity.explanation: About Te Kawa Matakura; hedged recollection ('I seem to recall ~25 kids for $4m') that Ferris disputes (he calls it a $22m leadership programme), leaving the factual basis contested.

veracity.statement: every school who’s done this approach has seen enormous results for their tamariki Māori, unsurprisingly, because they both follow the science of learning, explicit teaching, a structured curriculum
veracity.explanation: Universal claim ('every school... enormous results') is a sweeping generalisation unlikely to hold without exception.

veracity.statement: We also put teachers on the green list fast track to residence for our secondary school teachers, which has meant we’ve got 50 percent more of them coming into the country since last year.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable outcome claim attributed to a concrete policy.

veracity.statement: the requirement for teaching in a charter school is that you need to be a registered teacher or have a LAT, which is no different than exactly what we have now in every single school in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about charter school staffing rules; broadly accurate on registration/LAT but charter schools have exemption provisions that make 'no different' an over-simplification.

veracity.statement: the member’s party has a very strange questionnaire out, stirring up some weird fear and untruths, but, actually, there is no removing or reducing of the Treaty obligation in section 127
veracity.explanation: The claim that section 127 changes remove/reduce no Treaty obligations is genuinely contested (Xu-Nan argues reordering to a secondary clause reduces its force); asserted flatly here.

veracity.statement: We heard, during the select committee hearings, that the overall learning support for this Budget had reduced by $5.449 million from the previous year.
veracity.explanation: Specific checkable figure attributed to a hearing; not contested by the Minister on the numbers.

veracity.statement: I got an email from people within the Ministry of Education who had not long left, who said that those teams had been disbanded and many of the people had lost their jobs due to those cuts and had absolutely no belief that that role would be able to carry on and that the fidelity of PB4L School-Wide would be able to continue.
veracity.explanation: First-hand-sourced claim about PB4L teams being disbanded; plausible and specific but rests on unnamed correspondents.

veracity.statement: I met a principal last week of a big school in Auckland who said she’d lost five in the previous week that are going to be leaving at the end of this term... Of those five, four got positions over in Australia—which, again, worries me, too, that we’re competing on an uneven market.
veracity.explanation: A specific reported account; plausible and modest in its claim, but unverifiable second-hand.

veracity.statement: the vast majority of principals and teachers are saying that the change is happening too fast to be effective. Now, none of these people disagree with the reason for the change and none of these people just agree that change has to happen, but they are questioning the capacity around that change
veracity.explanation: Cites survey findings from NZPF and NZEI; broadly consistent with reported sector sentiment though 'vast majority' is a summary characterisation.

veracity.statement: this particular programme was not introduced as a COVID measure, it was not funded as part of the COVID measures; it was introduced in 2019 and it was funded for four solid years when it was announced in 2019, prior to COVID.
veracity.explanation: Factual correction of the Summary of Initiatives; Stanford subsequently partly concedes it began in 2019 (with a later COVID boost), supporting the core of the claim.

veracity.statement: In round four of the evaluation for this... it states that 63,730 students over four years have benefited from this, it funded 211 projects in 223 schools—and the overall evaluation being very good. That also includes lifting attendance.
veracity.explanation: Figures attributed to a named evaluation; specific and checkable, though presented from one side.

veracity.statement: By devaluing one of them, deprioritising one of them, it means that if you deprioritise them to a secondary clause... if they don’t meet the objective, the primary objective, then a school does not need to consider it. That’s how schools will interpret that particular piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Contested reading of section 127's effect on Te Tiriti obligations; directly disputed by the Minister, so verifiability is unresolved from the text.

veracity.statement: Australia offers scholarships and $40k scholarships. We’re seeing bursaries in the UK and Canada; we’re seeing places like Singapore, Denmark, and Finland fully funding their degree so that the students don’t then have to get a student loan
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that these jurisdictions offer teacher-training financial incentives, though details are summarised.

veracity.statement: Māori education, historically and currently, only receive around 1 percent of the education budget, which is not surprising—that’s an equal amount to what Treaty settlements equate to.
veracity.explanation: The '1 percent' and the settlement-equivalence framing are rough, unsourced figures presented as fact; hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: given that we’ve seen a $4 million cut out of education with Te Pae Roa vanishing—Te Pae Roa’s goal was to increase Māori children’s participation in kōhanga reo kura and wharekura by 30 percent by 2040
veracity.explanation: Specific claims about the cut and the programme's goal; broadly checkable though the Minister frames Te Pae Roa's disbandment differently (replaced by a new advisory group).

veracity.statement: kura kaupapa, Māori medium education outperforms—outperforms; and has been doing it for 30 years—mainstream delivery.
veracity.explanation: Claim that Māori-medium consistently outperforms mainstream is directionally supported for some cohorts/measures but stated absolutely without the specific metric.

veracity.statement: Reports that I am hearing are that it is less per capita, that many are having to descale because it has not been prioritised, and that they cannot afford to do the work they are asked to do in the contract on the funding that they are being provided.
veracity.explanation: Relayed reports (hedged 'reports I am hearing') that Māori-medium structured-literacy PLD funding is inadequate; plausible but second-hand and unquantified.

civility.statement: Engari me mōhio hoki ka tika, ka nui te whakamoumou i te pūtea i tērā Kāwana tawhito. [But it is appropriate to also be aware that that previous Government wasted a lot of funding.]
civility.explanation: Broad-brush attack on the previous Government's record rather than a specific policy critique; more assertion than argument.

civility.statement: koinei hoki te wero mō ngā mema Pāremata o tērā taha: kaua e riro mā te Kāwanatanga me ā koutou pahupahu e whakanui te pūtea. [this is indeed the challenge for the members of Parliament on that side—don’t leave increasing the funding up to the Government and your ranting.]
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents' contributions as 'pahupahu' (ranting), a dismissive framing.

civility.statement: e kaikā ana mātou ko ngā tāngata pēnei i a Matua Tararā nei ki te whakatakoto i te reo Māori, ehara i te reo pahupahu. [we and people like Minister Jones here are keen to lay out the Māori language, not mere rants.]
civility.explanation: Contrasts 'us' with the opposition's 'hot air'/'rants' ('kōrero hōhonu, kakī hōhonu'), disparaging opponents' sincerity.

civility.statement: The previous Government had a pilot running and it was extraordinarily successful—150 teachers a year. We’ve doubled those numbers off the back of that
civility.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of an opponent's initiative rather than criticism.

civility.statement: I said I just wanted to thank the previous Minister, the Hon Jan Tinetti, for her question because I know that she’s passionate about learning support, as am I, which is why it’s one of my six priority areas.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of a political opponent's genuine commitment to the issue.

civility.statement: I was astounded at the fact that previous Ministers in the Labour Government never went through that exercise of going, “Hey, ministry, give me a line by line of everything we spend in learning support”
civility.explanation: Pointed dig at the competence/diligence of named predecessors rather than engaging a policy substance directly.

civility.statement: Having some fancy artist come in to help paint a mural at the front of the school is a “nice to have”, but when kids can’t read, write, and do maths, I’m sorry, but I’m going to prioritise that every single day of the week.
civility.explanation: Reduces the Creatives in Schools programme to 'a fancy artist painting a mural', a diminishing caricature of the opponent's point.

civility.statement: the member’s party has a very strange questionnaire out, stirring up some weird fear and untruths, but, actually, there is no removing or reducing of the Treaty obligation in section 127
civility.explanation: Characterises the opponent's party as spreading 'weird fear and untruths' rather than engaging their specific interpretation of section 127.

civility.statement: You had $153 million for charter schools, whereas the research is very questionable around the effects of charter schools for our young people. I want to know how you can reconcile that allocation with the urgent need for funds for students with existing gaps in their learning.
civility.explanation: Pointed but policy-focused; challenges a funding decision, not the Minister personally.

civility.statement: That data is also given at individual education plan meetings—IEPs—where Ministry of Education personnel are at those meetings. That data is freely available from schools... I just don’t think that saying that we don’t have the data washes, Minister.
civility.explanation: Direct, pointed rebuttal ('doesn't wash') but aimed at the substance of the Minister's data claim, not at her character.

civility.statement: the vast majority of principals and teachers are saying that the change is happening too fast to be effective. Now, none of these people disagree with the reason for the change and none of these people just agree that change has to happen, but they are questioning the capacity around that change
civility.explanation: Concedes the goal of the reform is shared before criticising the pace—fair engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: They don’t want it to muck up; they want to get it right.
civility.explanation: Generous, good-faith characterisation of those raising concerns.

civility.statement: It is $12 million over 4 years. It is roughly $3 million a year. This is miniscule compared to the lavishness that the Minister has funded for other projects, such as $153 million for charter schools.
civility.explanation: 'Lavishness' is a loaded characterisation, but the critique stays focused on funding choices rather than the person.

civility.statement: Reports that I am hearing are that it is less per capita, that many are having to descale because it has not been prioritised, and that they cannot afford to do the work they are asked to do in the contract on the funding that they are being provided.
civility.explanation: Neutral, substance-focused question about funding sufficiency with no personal attack.

rigor.statement: Engari me mōhio hoki ka tika, ka nui te whakamoumou i te pūtea i tērā Kāwana tawhito. [But it is appropriate to also be aware that that previous Government wasted a lot of funding.]
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion of waste with no evidence or mechanism supplied.

rigor.statement: Mehemea he whā kē ngā pou kia whakatairangatia ai te reo Māori, kua rite rānei te wā me whakawhāiti i aua poupou e whā kia kaua rawa atu te pūtea e moumoutia... mā te whakahiato i aua poupou e whā? [If there are four pillars of revitalisation... has the time come to amalgamate those four pillars so funding is not wasted...?]
rigor.explanation: Efficiency argument (consolidate entities to reduce duplication) is coherent but framed as a leading question with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: I was astounded at the fact that previous Ministers in the Labour Government never went through that exercise of going, “Hey, ministry, give me a line by line of everything we spend in learning support”
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical astonishment used as argument; asserts a negative (they 'never' did it) without evidence.

rigor.statement: Having some fancy artist come in to help paint a mural at the front of the school is a “nice to have”, but when kids can’t read, write, and do maths, I’m sorry, but I’m going to prioritise that every single day of the week.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus false dichotomy—frames arts as opposed to literacy/numeracy rather than complementary.

rigor.statement: 45 percent of our 14- and 15-year-olds recently passed a foundational numeracy assessment at high school, which is the NCEA corequisite. That is a terrible result for our kids.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete statistic to justify prioritising numeracy; conclusion follows from the evidence cited.

rigor.statement: around 10,000 kids last year didn’t get NCEA at all, and their trajectory is grim because we know that those kids end up in youth justice, they end up on benefits, and they end up not participating in society to their full potential.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-anchored on the numbers but the causal leap to specific outcomes is asserted with 'we know' rather than shown.

rigor.statement: I seem to recall somewhere around 25 kids for the $4 million that we were spending. It wasn’t good use of money, and it was a pilot, a small pilot that was actually for tertiary intervention.
rigor.explanation: Cost-per-participant reasoning is legitimate but rests on uncertain remembered figures.

rigor.statement: You had $153 million for charter schools, whereas the research is very questionable around the effects of charter schools for our young people. I want to know how you can reconcile that allocation with the urgent need for funds for students with existing gaps in their learning.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts a spending choice against the evidence base for its effectiveness and asks for justification—an evidence-oriented challenge, though 'research is very questionable' is asserted not cited.

rigor.statement: I got an email from people within the Ministry of Education who had not long left, who said that those teams had been disbanded and many of the people had lost their jobs due to those cuts and had absolutely no belief that that role would be able to carry on and that the fidelity of PB4L School-Wide would be able to continue.
rigor.explanation: Relies on anecdotal testimony from former officials rather than documented evidence, though it directly rebuts an on-record assurance.

rigor.statement: That data is also given at individual education plan meetings—IEPs—where Ministry of Education personnel are at those meetings. That data is freely available from schools... I just don’t think that saying that we don’t have the data washes, Minister.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete data source (IEP meetings with ministry staff present) to counter the 'no data' claim; a substantive logical challenge.

rigor.statement: I met a principal last week of a big school in Auckland who said she’d lost five in the previous week that are going to be leaving at the end of this term... Of those five, four got positions over in Australia—which, again, worries me, too, that we’re competing on an uneven market.
rigor.explanation: Argument from a single anecdote (one principal, five teachers) generalised to a systemic retention/competition problem.

rigor.statement: the vast majority of principals and teachers are saying that the change is happening too fast to be effective. Now, none of these people disagree with the reason for the change and none of these people just agree that change has to happen, but they are questioning the capacity around that change
rigor.explanation: Grounds the critique in named survey sources and carefully distinguishes agreement-with-goal from concern-about-pace.

rigor.statement: this particular programme was not introduced as a COVID measure, it was not funded as part of the COVID measures; it was introduced in 2019 and it was funded for four solid years when it was announced in 2019, prior to COVID.
rigor.explanation: Corrects a factual premise underpinning the funding decision, citing the programme's actual origin and funding history.

rigor.statement: In round four of the evaluation for this... it states that 63,730 students over four years have benefited from this, it funded 211 projects in 223 schools—and the overall evaluation being very good. That also includes lifting attendance.
rigor.explanation: Uses evaluation data (including attendance) to counter the claim that programmes lack evidence of impact.

rigor.statement: It is $12 million over 4 years. It is roughly $3 million a year. This is miniscule compared to the lavishness that the Minister has funded for other projects, such as $153 million for charter schools.
rigor.explanation: Proportionality argument comparing programme cost to benefit and to other spending; reasonable, though 'lavishness' is editorial.

rigor.statement: As someone who has stood in front of a classroom for a number of years, I can tell you that is not actually what gets ākonga to school. It is having a safe environment, it is knowing that they can wake up in the morning knowing that they love what they are doing... It’s having a balanced curriculum.
rigor.explanation: Counters the Minister's claim but leans on personal teaching experience (appeal to anecdote/authority) rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: By devaluing one of them, deprioritising one of them, it means that if you deprioritise them to a secondary clause... if they don’t meet the objective, the primary objective, then a school does not need to consider it. That’s how schools will interpret that particular piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument about how statutory reordering (primary vs secondary objective) changes the operative obligation; logical though the interpretive conclusion is asserted.

rigor.statement: Australia offers scholarships and $40k scholarships. We’re seeing bursaries in the UK and Canada; we’re seeing places like Singapore, Denmark, and Finland fully funding their degree so that the students don’t then have to get a student loan
rigor.explanation: Uses international comparison to argue NZ should fund teacher training upfront; a reasoned comparative case.

rigor.statement: Māori education, historically and currently, only receive around 1 percent of the education budget, which is not surprising—that’s an equal amount to what Treaty settlements equate to.
rigor.explanation: Sets up an argument from proportion but the underlying figure and the settlement analogy are asserted without support.

rigor.statement: kura kaupapa, Māori medium education outperforms—outperforms; and has been doing it for 30 years—mainstream delivery.
rigor.explanation: Central premise of his funding argument, but the outperformance claim is asserted rather than evidenced in the exchange.

forthrightness.statement: koinei hoki te wero mō ngā mema Pāremata o tērā taha: kaua e riro mā te Kāwanatanga me ā koutou pahupahu e whakanui te pūtea. [this is indeed the challenge for the members of Parliament on that side—don’t leave increasing the funding up to the Government and your ranting.]
forthrightness.explanation: Answering Hūhana Lyndon's question about who is at fault for low Māori TV funding; deflects into challenging the opposition rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Tāria te wā he kaupapa tērā hei wānangatanga mā ngā ohu me ngā hapori maha e kaikā ana ki te whakanui i tō tātou reo. Engari mō tēnei wā, nau mai ki te Wiki o te Reo Māori. [At the appropriate time, that is a subject for the boards and many communities... But for the time being, welcome to Māori Language Week.]
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the future direction for Māori TV if funding is not increased; pivots to 'at the appropriate time' and a Māori Language Week greeting without answering.

forthrightness.statement: every school who’s done this approach has seen enormous results for their tamariki Māori, unsurprisingly, because they both follow the science of learning, explicit teaching, a structured curriculum
forthrightness.explanation: Ferris asked why Māori-medium education is not funded more given its outperformance; she pivots to promoting structured literacy rather than the funding question asked.

forthrightness.statement: 1,200 additional places in the on-site training programme over the next four years... “Here’s a $20,000 package. If you would like to come and teach, we will pay you a stipend, we will pay your fees...” The TeachNZ scholarship, which is worth $10,000—492 places in the last year.
forthrightness.explanation: Xu-Nan asked specifically about bursaries/paid placement and enticing people into teaching; she answers with existing incentive programmes but does not directly commit to the new measures asked about.

charisma.statement: koinei hoki te wero mō ngā mema Pāremata o tērā taha: kaua e riro mā te Kāwanatanga me ā koutou pahupahu e whakanui te pūtea. [this is indeed the challenge for the members of Parliament on that side—don’t leave increasing the funding up to the Government and your ranting.]
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing aimed at 'that side'; combative rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: e kaikā ana mātou ko ngā tāngata pēnei i a Matua Tararā nei ki te whakatakoto i te reo Māori, ehara i te reo pahupahu. [we and people like Minister Jones here are keen to lay out the Māori language, not mere rants.]
charisma.explanation: Divides the House into serious language advocates vs ranters; alienating rather than unifying.

charisma.statement: The previous Government had a pilot running and it was extraordinarily successful—150 teachers a year. We’ve doubled those numbers off the back of that
charisma.explanation: Credits the previous Government's pilot as successful and builds on it—a cross-party, magnanimous acknowledgement.

charisma.statement: I said I just wanted to thank the previous Minister, the Hon Jan Tinetti, for her question because I know that she’s passionate about learning support, as am I, which is why it’s one of my six priority areas.
charisma.explanation: Finds common ground with the opposition on shared values before disagreeing.

charisma.statement: Having some fancy artist come in to help paint a mural at the front of the school is a “nice to have”, but when kids can’t read, write, and do maths, I’m sorry, but I’m going to prioritise that every single day of the week.
charisma.explanation: Dismissive of the opposing view rather than seeking to persuade the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: the member’s party has a very strange questionnaire out, stirring up some weird fear and untruths, but, actually, there is no removing or reducing of the Treaty obligation in section 127
charisma.explanation: Attacks the opposing party's motives, shutting down dialogue rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: the vast majority of principals and teachers are saying that the change is happening too fast to be effective. Now, none of these people disagree with the reason for the change and none of these people just agree that change has to happen, but they are questioning the capacity around that change
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges common ground ('none disagree with the reason for the change') to build a constructive case.

charisma.statement: They don’t want it to muck up; they want to get it right.
charisma.explanation: Frames critics as constructive partners who share the goal, inviting a collaborative response.

specificity.statement: Tāria te wā he kaupapa tērā hei wānangatanga mā ngā ohu me ngā hapori maha e kaikā ana ki te whakanui i tō tātou reo. Engari mō tēnei wā, nau mai ki te Wiki o te Reo Māori. [At the appropriate time, that is a subject for the boards and many communities... But for the time being, welcome to Māori Language Week.]
specificity.explanation: No timeframe, mechanism, or funding commitment; defers everything to unspecified future discussion.

specificity.statement: Mehemea he whā kē ngā pou kia whakatairangatia ai te reo Māori, kua rite rānei te wā me whakawhāiti i aua poupou e whā kia kaua rawa atu te pūtea e moumoutia... mā te whakahiato i aua poupou e whā? [If there are four pillars of revitalisation... has the time come to amalgamate those four pillars so funding is not wasted...?]
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete proposal—amalgamating the four language pillars so funding flows to Māori TV—though without mechanism detail.

specificity.statement: In Budget ’24, the Government boosted Vote Education by $2.93 billion over the next four years to improve student outcomes despite very tough fiscal times.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure ($2.93 billion) and timeframe (four years) tied to a named vote.

specificity.statement: There is, of course, the $67 million for structured literacy and $53 million for an additional 1,500 teachers.
specificity.explanation: Two named dollar figures attached to specific programmes and a headcount (1,500 teachers).

specificity.statement: we have put in an enormous injection—over $1.3 billion of investment over four years—into school properties so our kids can learn in safe, warm, dry buildings and so that the portfolio can be expanded to accommodate more students.
specificity.explanation: Names amount ($1.3b) and timeframe (four years) with a stated purpose.

specificity.statement: This is the largest increase in maintenance, upgrade, and redevelopment funding that has been delivered in at least three years, and I understand from the ministry that this injection is more than the last six years combined.
