rigor.statement: Aotearoa is one of the countries where the majority of the population speak one language. If you go to Europe, there are many who speak two, three, and even four languages. ... The education system needs to be more diligent in supporting that aspect.
rigor.explanation: Comparative reasoning (multilingual Europe vs monolingual NZ) supporting a case for bilingual education; broad-brush but coherent.

divination.statement: Let me tell Te Pāti Māori that out there in the real world, where Māori work sometimes two or three jobs, they won’t be voting for you at the next election—be as certain as that
divination.explanation: Electoral prediction that Māori voters will abandon Te Pāti Māori; partisan, optimistic and uncertain, timeframe = next election.

divination.statement: you wait until this new legislation comes out in November and a clear message is sent to the gangs. Our police control our streets, towns, and rural communities, not the gangs.
divination.explanation: Predicts the impact of not-yet-passed November legislation on gang behaviour; timeframe stated, outcome uncertain.

specificity.statement: out there they want the real things that people want in this country regardless of race: decent houses, a health system that delivers, education escalators, and First World jobs. And that’s what this Government is setting out to do.
specificity.explanation: Lists broad goal areas (houses, health, education, jobs) but no mechanisms, figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: our transition fuel is—what? It’s Indonesian coal, and it should be natural gas.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific fuel source but no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: you wait until this new legislation comes out in November and a clear message is sent to the gangs. Our police control our streets, towns, and rural communities, not the gangs.
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe (November) but not the content of the powers.

specificity.statement: District-level gang disruption units are what we’re going to see, and that is fantastic. ... giving those units enhanced powers: dispersal notices, preventing gang gatherings, enforcing the upcoming ban—and I am excited—on gang patches in public spaces.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms: district gang disruption units, dispersal notices, gathering bans, patch ban.

specificity.statement: the new legislation that’ll cap sentence discounts of 40 percent—the slippery, slippery slope that ends up giving people every discount under the sun, that ends up with them walking back out on to the street to further intimidate and terrorise our communities.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 40 percent cap figure but frames the rest emotively.

specificity.statement: Let’s just take the last 20 seconds to talk about the FamilyBoost: money into the back pockets of everyday Kiwis who are working hard to rebuild our economy. We want to support them, so it’s up to $150 a fortnight. That opened yesterday, and the first payment will come from 1 October; three-monthly invoices is all that they need.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure ($150/fortnight), open date, first payment date (1 October), and process detail.

specificity.statement: We’ve also stopped the paying of the cottage industry that became the section 27 cultural reports that went from $3,000 taxpayer dollars per month to $6 million per annum. That has stopped.
specificity.explanation: Cites figures ($3,000/month rising to $6m/annum) and a concrete action.

specificity.statement: The first thing that we did as part of the ACT coalition agreement was abolish Labour’s prison reduction targets. ... These are all ACT policies, because we listened, we heard, and we have implemented.
specificity.explanation: Names specific policies (prison targets, three-strikes, section 27 reports).

specificity.statement: We have prioritised victims by making sure that the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, which is now an Act, allows victims to be heard either by audio or audiovisual, instead of having to be retraumatised every time they go into the court.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act and its concrete effect (audio/audiovisual participation).

specificity.statement: What is the energy trilemma? That is ensuring that we have energy security that means that we have a reliability of supply with minimal disruption. It’s also talking about the energy equity that is making sure that we have affordable energy ... The last one of the trilemma is energy sustainability. That’s mitigating the potential effects on the environment but also climate change impacts
specificity.explanation: Defines each concept clearly but stops short of figures or specific policy measures.

specificity.statement: it’s nearly 160 years ago that the very first well was successfully found for oil. It was the Alpha well. It was found down by where Port Taranaki sits today, and that was back in 1865 ... it’s thought to be the first well in the Commonwealth
specificity.explanation: Names the well, location and year.

specificity.statement: The recently appointed commissioner, who we understand is only working a couple of days a week, has recently asked Health New Zealand to make $1.4 billion in savings and we are seeing the cuts that are coming from that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the figure and the source of the savings demand.

specificity.statement: we started our new public transport system in Nelson last year, and guess what we’ve seen since that change! The number of young people in Nelson using the bus has gone down.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the group (young people) and direction of change, but no figures.

specificity.statement: This legal assistance fund is $600,000, it’s available when there’s some environmental public interest, and it’s a contestable fund that people contest when they think that something is important and needs clarification from the court.
specificity.explanation: States the fund size and its precise purpose/mechanism.

specificity.statement: the total cut has been $617 million over the next four years. ... I’m talking about the cuts to the Ministry for the Environment, the $65 million decrease there; cuts to the Environmental Protection Authority; Department of Conservation, $48 million decrease
specificity.explanation: Aggregate figure plus itemised per-agency cuts with dollar amounts.

specificity.statement: since 2017, the environmental Vote appropriation tripled over that time, from 2017 until 2023. During that time, there were quite specific programmes ... in terms of their Resource Management Act programme and also some time-limited freshwater programmes and also a number of time-limited Jobs for Nature programmes. The peak funding for the ministry was always going to be in that 2023-2024 period, and, from that, it was always scheduled to reduce.
specificity.explanation: Names the driving programmes and the peak period, though without dollar figures.

specificity.statement: There is not a cut to the EPA. The EPA have been exceeding their budget by over $4 million. They are being asked to meet or have a break-even position.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure and the required outcome (break-even).

specificity.statement: There are cuts to Te Tuatara o Pukekohe—Integrated Catchment Management Plan, the tangata whenua capability building, and the freshwater farm plans. We see a swathe of cuts to investment in water protection, but accompanied by the cuts to collection of data and environmental monitoring of drinking-water and groundwater nitrate monitoring.
specificity.explanation: Itemises named programmes and specific monitoring functions being cut.

specificity.statement: Aotearoa is one of the countries where the majority of the population speak one language. If you go to Europe, there are many who speak two, three, and even four languages. ... The education system needs to be more diligent in supporting that aspect.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a direction (education system supporting multilingualism) but no concrete mechanism or measure.

charisma.statement: out there they want the real things that people want in this country regardless of race: decent houses, a health system that delivers, education escalators, and First World jobs. And that’s what this Government is setting out to do.
charisma.explanation: 'Regardless of race' gestures at inclusiveness but is embedded in a partisan claim for the Government.

charisma.statement: My message today is that I implore everybody in this House, including the Opposition, to take this matter very seriously. ... I ask the Opposition to make sure that you can come to the table and look at what’s right for New Zealand as a whole.
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-party appeal inviting the Opposition to collaborate on the national interest.

charisma.statement: one of my biggest regrets in my life is not being able to become fluent in te reo. It is a language that I’m incredibly proud of. ... I’m so pleased that we have it accommodated as an official language, but also spoken in this Whare that we enjoy today.
charisma.explanation: Warm, respectful personal reflection reaching across cultural lines toward te reo and colleagues who spoke it.

charisma.statement: it is on all of us to uphold te reo Māori, to champion te reo Māori, to do our best to practise te reo Māori, and also, as some of my colleagues have called out, to fund te reo Māori and to champion it.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'all of us' framing inviting shared responsibility, though the funding point leans partisan.

charisma.statement: do not be afraid. You are welcome to the Māori language. Welcome to the language of this land. Welcome to the language that has not harmed any other language, that has not harmed any other person. ... Do not be afraid, those of you in this House. Do not be afraid, those of you outside this House.
charisma.explanation: Warm, repeated welcome extended to those inside and outside the House; explicitly bridge-building and reassuring rather than divisive.

charisma.statement: Why would anyone fear the Māori language? The Māori language has not harmed anyone. The Māori language has not trampled on anyone’s dignity.
charisma.explanation: Seeks to disarm opposition to te reo through reassurance rather than attack.

charisma.statement: So what I say to us all, honour the Māori language, and speak the Māori language. Not only for this day but for ever and ever and ever.
charisma.explanation: Uplifting, inclusive call addressed to 'us all', though mainly rallying those already sympathetic.

charisma.statement: He said, let us not unite to abase the Government, but let us stand united with the Government as sustenance for us all, and for the environment as well. ... Through collaboration, through unity ... Let us unite to be stronger for the future generations.
charisma.explanation: Endorses an explicitly cross-partisan message of standing united with the Government for the common good — consensus-seeking rather than divisive.

strength.statement: the very successful operations that have led to the arrest and the taking down of the entire Comanchero gang in New Zealand
strength.explanation: Claims credit for enforcement results as Police Minister; some real action but framed expansively.

strength.statement: you wait until this new legislation comes out in November and a clear message is sent to the gangs. Our police control our streets, towns, and rural communities, not the gangs.
strength.explanation: Announced/forthcoming legislation, not yet delivered; commitment with follow-through pending.

strength.statement: District-level gang disruption units are what we’re going to see, and that is fantastic. ... giving those units enhanced powers: dispersal notices, preventing gang gatherings, enforcing the upcoming ban—and I am excited—on gang patches in public spaces.
strength.explanation: Measures are 'going to see' / 'upcoming'; announced rather than yet delivered.

strength.statement: Let’s just take the last 20 seconds to talk about the FamilyBoost: money into the back pockets of everyday Kiwis who are working hard to rebuild our economy. We want to support them, so it’s up to $150 a fortnight. That opened yesterday, and the first payment will come from 1 October; three-monthly invoices is all that they need.
strength.explanation: Policy has actually opened for applications with a set payment date — delivery, not mere aspiration.

strength.statement: We’ve also stopped the paying of the cottage industry that became the section 27 cultural reports that went from $3,000 taxpayer dollars per month to $6 million per annum. That has stopped.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered cut to section 27 report funding, consistent with the coalition's actions.

strength.statement: The first thing that we did as part of the ACT coalition agreement was abolish Labour’s prison reduction targets. ... These are all ACT policies, because we listened, we heard, and we have implemented.
strength.explanation: Lists concrete measures presented as delivered, consistent with the coalition record.

strength.statement: We have prioritised victims by making sure that the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, which is now an Act, allows victims to be heard either by audio or audiovisual, instead of having to be retraumatised every time they go into the court.
strength.explanation: Points to a bill that has actually passed into an Act — a delivered legislative change.

strength.statement: We are delivering, and there’s so much more that we’re going to do; 12 months, we’ve got 24 left to go.
strength.explanation: Blends a delivery claim with forward aspiration and no new specifics.

authenticity.statement: The first thing that we did as part of the ACT coalition agreement was abolish Labour’s prison reduction targets. ... These are all ACT policies, because we listened, we heard, and we have implemented.
authenticity.explanation: Ties campaign positions directly to enacted actions ('we listened, we heard, and we have implemented') — words matching deeds.

forthrightness.statement: There is not a cut to the EPA. The EPA have been exceeding their budget by over $4 million. They are being asked to meet or have a break-even position.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Brooking's EPA question with a clear position and a figure, though it reframes rather than fully engaging the future-roles point.

forthrightness.statement: this Government considered prioritisation of funding and they did not meet the priorities that we considered we wanted to fund at this time.
forthrightness.explanation: In answer to why these funds were cut, gives a circular 'they weren't a priority' response without naming the priorities.

rigor.statement: it is not a failure of funding, with the increase of the $1.1 billion; it is a failure of the system—the system that the previous Government set up in a rush and set these very high expectations and then left it to be.
rigor.explanation: Asserts systemic rather than funding failure and blames the prior government's rushed setup; a causal claim leaning partly on assertion without evidence shown in the text.

rigor.statement: It made six findings: “(1) Delivery of DSS is inconsistent, (2) The DSS 2024/25 appropriation will be breached if spending is not controlled, (3) There is inadequate budgetary control and commercial rigor, (4) The two areas of largest cost growth are flexible funding provisions and residential facilities-based care, (5) The new departmental agency is not set up in a manner that enables it to manage effectively the nature and scale of its appropriation, (6) Current policy settings and service design do not allow the Ministry to administer and deliver DSS effectively”.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in an independent review's documented findings rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: To quote my colleague Shane Jones about the nephs on the couch, there were too many nephs on the couch.
rigor.explanation: Anecdote and colloquial slogan offered as diagnosis of the benefit system rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: they have, as I say, longstanding networks. They’ve got a proven track record. I have seen, as I hope you’ve seen too, they’ve got a recent impact report done that shows they’re returning $4.90 for every dollar invested, which is quite impressive, and that work is being undertaken by Sir Bill English’s ImpactLab, which is quite a reputable outfit.
rigor.explanation: Uses an evidenced impact figure but leans partly on appeal to authority ('reputable outfit', Sir Bill English) to bolster it.

rigor.statement: why it is that she continues to say in the House that there is no funding freeze, that disabled people are getting more funding to support them and more access to services, when disabled people and disabled people’s organisations are telling the media and are telling politicians in the House that that is simply not the case, that their access to support has been frozen
rigor.explanation: Frames a contradiction between official statements and reported experience, inviting the Minister to reconcile them.

rigor.statement: how would going ahead with the wage supplement to top up the wages of disabled workers to bring them from $2 an hour, in some cases, to the minimum wage have resulted in job losses?
rigor.explanation: Presses for the causal basis of the Minister's job-loss claim rather than asserting a counter-claim.

rigor.statement: can she then tell us, finally, that the reason why she decided to cut the wage supplement is to pay for tax cuts?
rigor.explanation: Advances an alternative causal explanation (tax cuts) as conjecture without evidence, framed conditionally.

rigor.statement: Where is the evidence that jobs would be lost, as the Minister has said—on record—given that Aotearoa Disability Enterprises can’t actually back that up? All they wanted to see was the detail of the policy that she has now scrapped. Where is the Minister’s evidence?
rigor.explanation: Demands the evidentiary basis of a specific claim and cites that the named enterprise body cannot corroborate it.

rigor.statement: Why did the Minister choose not to strengthen Whaikaha if she’s placing all of this blame on the fact that the previous Government set up Whaikaha quickly?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a logical tension in the Minister's position (blame the quick setup, yet dismantle rather than strengthen).

rigor.statement: It was set up quickly—they get that; this Minister does not seem to get that—but the next steps were to then strengthen the functions and the financial structures of Whaikaha.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reasoned justification (avoid dropped services, then strengthen) for the sequencing decision.

rigor.statement: the only major new road is the Warkworth to Wellsford Road, which actually has a consent, and there are not consents for other roads. If there was fast-track legislation in place, why were there not consents for all of these other roads which, actually, New Zealanders need? That last Government cancelled those roads
rigor.explanation: Argument for fast-track need is reasonable, but the causal blame on the prior government is asserted and internally strained.

rigor.statement: the most recent benefit-cost analysis for the Mount Victoria tunnel was 0.2, which means it was losing money.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete benefit-cost ratio to argue the project's costs outweigh benefits, a logically connected evidence-based point.

rigor.statement: why has he promised and committed to a series of projects for which we don’t know the true cost and we have no idea of the actual economic benefit? Why is it that the Government has proposed to spend tens of billions of dollars on projects for which we do not have any economic evidence?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in the Transport Agency chair's own committee admission that economic evaluation is incomplete.

rigor.statement: The Minister has just claimed that the last Government cancelled roads, yet he’s announced a road that’s going to start construction that was funded by the last Government. It’s completely inconsistent.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete internal contradiction in the Minister's claims (cancelled roads vs a last-Government-funded road now proceeding).

rigor.statement: there is a graph which says, “Revenue and expenditure 2024-25 to 2034.”, and it shows an enormous gap opening up between expenditure intentions and net revenue from about 2027... an additional $1 billion from 2027 that, as of yet, has no planned revenue
rigor.explanation: Points to a specific published document and figure to argue an unfunded gap in transport spending intentions.

rigor.statement: This is not a new road. This is a replacement road. This is nine months from being finished. This is a seven-year project
rigor.explanation: Uses the road's status to argue the toll is inappropriate — a logically relevant point, though the evidence is asserted.

rigor.statement: the Treasury has indicated that they only had one hour to review the limited information that was provided by the Ministry of Transport and, on that basis, they recommended not including the additional capital funding for the GPS in the Budget package as it had not been through the same assessment process
rigor.explanation: Builds a challenge to the funding's credibility on cited official advice rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The Minister’s not answering it, so we’ll take that as a yes.
rigor.explanation: Treats a non-answer as confirmation — a rhetorical inference not logically warranted by silence.

rigor.statement: Now, we know that Labour absolutely hate motorways, because the road from Pūhoi to Warkworth, they labelled the “holiday highway”—the “holiday highway”
rigor.explanation: Infers a sweeping stance ('hate motorways') from a single nickname — overgeneralisation.

rigor.statement: We were told, in the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, by the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA), that, in fact, over quite some period of time, they’ve been investing at about 50 percent of the amount of money that they should have been investing to keep the roads at the right level. An increase of 91 percent basically takes it to pretty much where they should be.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited committee evidence to contextualise the 91% increase as restoring adequate maintenance investment.

civility.statement: it is not a failure of funding, with the increase of the $1.1 billion; it is a failure of the system—the system that the previous Government set up in a rush and set these very high expectations and then left it to be.
civility.explanation: Harsh but legitimate criticism of the previous government's system design rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: that former Minister should have made sure the organisation was set up to be successful, because disabled people have paid the price for that, and I think that’s really unfortunate.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the former Minister's setup decisions; targets performance/record rather than personal insult, but is accusatory.

civility.statement: To quote my colleague Shane Jones about the nephs on the couch, there were too many nephs on the couch.
civility.explanation: Repeats a derogatory characterisation of young unemployed people ('nephs on the couch'); demeaning rather than policy-focused.

civility.statement: why it is that she continues to say in the House that there is no funding freeze, that disabled people are getting more funding to support them and more access to services, when disabled people and disabled people’s organisations are telling the media and are telling politicians in the House that that is simply not the case, that their access to support has been frozen
civility.explanation: Harsh but substantive challenge contrasting the Minister's claims with the sector's lived experience; not a personal attack.

civility.statement: why the Minister made the decision not to include any disabled people on the panel that did the review of Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People, given the motto that has been used already in this House, “Nothing about us without us”
civility.explanation: Pointed but respectful question focused on process legitimacy rather than character.

civility.statement: She’s insulting the intelligence of people in this House by skirting around this answer and not giving straight-up information
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's evasiveness with charged language ('insulting the intelligence'); borders on personalising but is aimed at the non-answer.

civility.statement: can she then tell us, finally, that the reason why she decided to cut the wage supplement is to pay for tax cuts?
civility.explanation: An accusatory hypothesis about motive, though offered as a question tied to the substantive funding trade-off.

civility.statement: Where is the evidence that jobs would be lost, as the Minister has said—on record—given that Aotearoa Disability Enterprises can’t actually back that up? All they wanted to see was the detail of the policy that she has now scrapped. Where is the Minister’s evidence?
civility.explanation: Forceful but substance-focused, challenging evidence rather than character.

civility.statement: Why did the Minister choose not to strengthen Whaikaha if she’s placing all of this blame on the fact that the previous Government set up Whaikaha quickly?
civility.explanation: Harsh yet legitimate; engages the reasoning of the decision.

civility.statement: And 62,000 potholes, thank you, Suze Redmayne—62,000 potholes in their last year in Government. That’s the type of stats they’re very proud of. They’re very proud of the fact that they left our roads absolutely riddled with potholes.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic strawman imputing pride in potholes to opponents; ridicule rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: Auckland light rail didn’t even get a business case delivered... it had got to $29.2 billion.
civility.explanation: Repeated 'Auckland light fail' mockery is a derisive jab rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: the last Government spent something like $70 million on Dome Valley, and the reality is they didn’t consider resilience as part of any of the work—they didn’t consider resilience.
civility.explanation: Critique of the prior government's works decisions; harsh but aimed at policy delivery.

civility.statement: the most recent benefit-cost analysis for the Mount Victoria tunnel was 0.2, which means it was losing money.
civility.explanation: The added 'I’m not sure if members opposite understand what a benefit-cost analysis is' is a mild condescending jab within otherwise substantive argument.

civility.statement: the Minister is taking up lots of time for this debate, not talking about the Estimates and what’s in his plan but shouting about things that previous Governments did or did not do. Could I ask the Minister to try and stay on track
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's debating conduct ('shouting') but is a legitimate procedural complaint about relevance, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: I want to know what the Minister would say if he actually had the guts to turn up to that meeting in Woodville last night.
civility.explanation: Personal jab impugning the Minister's courage ('had the guts') rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: The Government is treating the people of Manawatū, Tararua, Hawke’s Bay, and Wairarapa with disgrace. They are treating them with disrespect.
civility.explanation: Heated, hyperbolic condemnation ('disgrace', 'disrespect') that sensationalises rather than engaging the tolling policy's substance.

civility.statement: is his focus on tolling as an action to simply address the $6 billion financial hole that is in his Government’s transport plans.
civility.explanation: Adversarial framing but directed at the transport plan's finances rather than the person.

civility.statement: Now, we know that Labour absolutely hate motorways, because the road from Pūhoi to Warkworth, they labelled the “holiday highway”—the “holiday highway”
civility.explanation: Strawman attributing to Labour that they 'absolutely hate motorways', an exaggerated characterisation rather than engagement.

civility.statement: If I could just take this opportunity, with your indulgence, to acknowledge that this is Aotearoa New Zealand Social Workers’ Day and acknowledge the hard work they do.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous, and wholly constructive.

civility.statement: it appears that everyone else is coming up with plans for the Waitematā Harbour crossing but you... what is your plan? What’s the time line when the public can expect to hear from you on some sort of a plan?
civility.explanation: Pointed jab ('everyone else... but you') but focused on the policy gap rather than personal attack.

veracity.statement: the increase in costs is over 30 percent—right? Understanding what is driving the increase in costs is pretty fundamental in stabilising the ship, and that is exactly what we are doing.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claim of >30% cost increase in residential care despite fewer people; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: the National Party policy was to maintain the minimum wage exemption.
veracity.explanation: Verifiable claim about National's 2020/2023 policy stance; plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: an increase of 1,500 people exiting the jobseeker benefit into work. That’s 1,500 more than at the same time last year, and yet look at the economic conditions we’re in today. I think that’s a remarkable result, and I’m very proud of that.
veracity.explanation: Specific comparative statistic on jobseeker exits; plausible but unverified and framed favourably against economic conditions.

veracity.statement: Addressing the child poverty one: we don’t forecast the number of children in material hardship.
veracity.explanation: Immediately contradicted in-House ('You actually do'); material hardship is in fact a forecast Child Poverty Reduction Act measure, making the claim misleading.

veracity.statement: young people who go on to the jobseeker benefit under the age of 25, their future years on benefit is 19 years—19 years, and 23 if they’re Māori.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to the Taylor Fry actuarial report; specific figures that are plausible and sourced but unverified here.

veracity.statement: a nine-year programme of work that was broken into three horizons of three years was only funded for two of the first three years, which was a bit strange.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim about the programme's funding horizons; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: they have, as I say, longstanding networks. They’ve got a proven track record. I have seen, as I hope you’ve seen too, they’ve got a recent impact report done that shows they’re returning $4.90 for every dollar invested, which is quite impressive, and that work is being undertaken by Sir Bill English’s ImpactLab, which is quite a reputable outfit.
veracity.explanation: Specific $4.90-per-dollar claim attributed to a named impact report; plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: It outlines a 91 percent increase in funding for road maintenance on our State highways, a 50 percent increase in road maintenance on our local roads, a 40 percent increase in public transport services funding, a significant investment in completing the rail network rebuild of $159 million to complete the rail network rebuild
veracity.explanation: Specific budget figures presented as fact; plausible and sourced to the GPS but unverified here.

veracity.statement: And 62,000 potholes, thank you, Suze Redmayne—62,000 potholes in their last year in Government. That’s the type of stats they’re very proud of. They’re very proud of the fact that they left our roads absolutely riddled with potholes.
veracity.explanation: The 62,000 figure may be accurate, but the 'very proud' framing is a misleading characterisation of opponents' position.

veracity.statement: Auckland light rail didn’t even get a business case delivered... it had got to $29.2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific escalation figures ($1.2b to $29.2b) for Auckland light rail; directionally consistent with reported cost growth, presented pointedly.

veracity.statement: the only major new road is the Warkworth to Wellsford Road, which actually has a consent, and there are not consents for other roads. If there was fast-track legislation in place, why were there not consents for all of these other roads which, actually, New Zealanders need? That last Government cancelled those roads
veracity.explanation: Consent claim is checkable; the 'cancelled those roads' assertion is contested and partly undercut by his own announcement of a last-Government-funded road.

veracity.statement: the last Government spent something like $70 million on Dome Valley, and the reality is they didn’t consider resilience as part of any of the work—they didn’t consider resilience.
veracity.explanation: Hedged spend figure ('something like $70 million') plus a categorical 'didn't consider resilience' claim that is a sweeping characterisation.

veracity.statement: the most recent benefit-cost analysis for the Mount Victoria tunnel was 0.2, which means it was losing money.
veracity.explanation: Specific BCR claim consistent with published low ratios for the project; plausible but unverified in text.

veracity.statement: More than two-thirds of those projects that regional and local councils applied for did not receive funding, so a huge number of projects are not going to be funded.
veracity.explanation: Specific two-thirds figure on unfunded public transport applications; plausible but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: the Treasury has indicated that they only had one hour to review the limited information that was provided by the Ministry of Transport and, on that basis, they recommended not including the additional capital funding for the GPS in the Budget package as it had not been through the same assessment process
veracity.explanation: Detailed claim about Treasury's advice; plausible and specific but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: is his focus on tolling as an action to simply address the $6 billion financial hole that is in his Government’s transport plans.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific '$6 billion financial hole' as fact within a leading question; contested and unsubstantiated in the text.

specificity.statement: the increase in costs is over 30 percent—right? Understanding what is driving the increase in costs is pretty fundamental in stabilising the ship, and that is exactly what we are doing.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure and mechanism (rapid pricing review) but leaves the driver undefined pending review.

specificity.statement: What we are doing at this point in time is stabilising the system before we seek to improve it.

forthrightness.statement: We are not explicitly exempting charter schools from the pan tax; we’re giving them the same exemption that State schools have. Depending on the council, they will face the same challenge that State schools would have. We’re not trying to differentiate them here; we’re just putting them in the same position as State schools.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Tinetti's question about whether charter schools are exempted from the pan tax — clarifies they get the same treatment as State schools.

forthrightness.statement: it might be more practical to recognise that what this legislation really does is it devolves the decision making to a group of people who are accountable, who are putting themselves and their professional reputations… on the line with this, and I think trusting their judgment is better than the House trying to micromanage or specify.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Tinetti's ask to codify community support by explaining why he won't, rather than saying yes/no to amending the bill — partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: I don’t believe it’s ever right to say that all Pacific people think or believe the same, so it’s not necessarily true that a school would be antithetical to Pacific people, because Pacific people actually have a wide range of views.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the theme of Utikere's question but sidesteps the specific 'no other option for a zoned family' scenario until his later answer.

authenticity.statement: This is one of the headline pieces of work that came out of the National Party election manifesto, and I’m pleased to be bringing it to this final stage of the House
authenticity.explanation: Claims to be delivering on a specific National election manifesto commitment; words match the party's campaign position.

authenticity.statement: It has always been New Zealand First’s policy to see it as an aggravating factor to be a gang member while you’re being sentenced, so today seeing that implemented is something that we have campaigned on and is now being implemented into legislation.
authenticity.explanation: Ties the vote to a long-standing, campaigned-on party policy — words consistent with prior position and action.

strength.statement: This is one of the headline pieces of work that came out of the National Party election manifesto, and I’m pleased to be bringing it to this final stage of the House
strength.explanation: A campaigned-on commitment being enacted into law at third reading — demonstrated follow-through, not mere announcement.

strength.statement: It has always been New Zealand First’s policy to see it as an aggravating factor to be a gang member while you’re being sentenced, so today seeing that implemented is something that we have campaigned on and is now being implemented into legislation.
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment being enacted into legislation.

veracity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent over the past five years, alongside violent crime increasing by 33 percent.
veracity.explanation: Gang-list growth of roughly 50% over five years is broadly supported; the 33% violent-crime figure is timeframe-dependent and more contestable.

veracity.statement: Just one in every 400 New Zealanders are identified as gang members, yet they are linked to nearly one in five serious violent crime offences and around one in five homicides, around one in four kidnapping and abductions, and one in four of all crimes caused by illicit drug offences.
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with police attributions of gang links to serious crime, though 'linked to' is a loose causal framing that overstates certainty.

veracity.statement: We know that because 80 to 90 percent of gang members experienced abuse in State care.
veracity.explanation: A widely cited figure attributed to the Royal Commission; the precise 80–90% applied specifically to gang members is a strong reading of the evidence.

veracity.statement: The reason that I say that is because 75 percent of gang members are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reporting that three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.

veracity.statement: Māori by population make up a million people in New Zealand—a million; I’ve just googled the stats
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate — the Māori population is close to but somewhat below a million.

veracity.statement: But why are we not talking about the victims of crime? It’s so often, to the member’s remarks about Māori and Māoridom … the victims are disproportionately Māori.
veracity.explanation: Māori being over-represented among crime victims is broadly supported.

veracity.statement: in 2017, there were just over 5,000 registered gang members; by 2023, we had over 8,600 members, a 50 percent increase—a 50 percent increase
veracity.explanation: Consistent with National Gang List growth figures over that period.

veracity.statement: They poured millions of dollars—taxpayers’ dollars—and gave it to gangs. Their way of fixing gang behaviour was to give them money. No wonder people were joining gangs, because it was a free money tree.
veracity.explanation: Misleading characterisation; funding went to programmes and providers, not to gangs as a 'free money tree'.

veracity.statement: I remember a time in my lifetime when a more enlightened, in this regard at least, leader of the National Party shook hands with members of the gangs, visited them on marae, and on his death, Sir Robert Muldoon had Black Power performing a haka at his funeral.
veracity.explanation: Muldoon's engagement with gangs and Black Power's presence at his funeral are historically documented.

veracity.statement: They chose Tupou only because of the colour of his clothing. [They] shot Tupou three times. Tupou was only 21 years old and worked as a machine operator to support his parents. He was not a gang member or even affiliated with a gang … He was murdered only because he chose to wear blue that day.
veracity.explanation: Quotes a documented news report of a real killing; the underlying facts are accurate.

veracity.statement: The findings of the royal commission on abuse in State care suggest that 80 to 90 percent of gang members were victims of abuse … If we’re serious as a Parliament about removing the social harm caused by gangs, we would be looking to stop our kids being abused in State care in the first place.
veracity.explanation: The 80–90% figure is commonly cited from the inquiry, though a strong specific reading.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon told the country during the Paddy Gower election debate that he would demand 500 heavily armed police to storm a gang funeral just to remove a gang patch.
veracity.explanation: A contentious characterisation of debate remarks; the '500 heavily armed police to storm a funeral' framing likely exaggerates what was said.

veracity.statement: We’ve talked about it in prior readings when we looked at the Whanganui example … asking Michael Laws, who was mayor at the time, “How did that work out?” … the result of the answer was that the gangs just left town. It’s like, “Cool. So where are they going to go when the gang patches are banned over all of New Zealand?” That is not a solution.
veracity.explanation: Characterisation of the Whanganui outcome is broadly consistent with reporting, though summarised.

veracity.statement: We had the Police Association who specifically stated that there was a risk to the trust and confidence in New Zealand Police if we made a law in this House that was then unable to be enforced by a front-line police officer because there would be insufficient numbers or capacity capability to do that work.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with concerns raised in the submissions process.

specificity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent over the past five years, alongside violent crime increasing by 33 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages over a defined period.

specificity.statement: Just one in every 400 New Zealanders are identified as gang members, yet they are linked to nearly one in five serious violent crime offences and around one in five homicides, around one in four kidnapping and abductions, and one in four of all crimes caused by illicit drug offences.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete ratios across crime categories.

specificity.statement: If an offender is convicted three times within five years, a court order will be made against them, banning them from owning any gang insignia for the next five years and preventing them from continuing to reoffend.
specificity.explanation: Names exact thresholds (three convictions, five-year window, five-year ban) and the mechanism.

specificity.statement: A dispersal notice will require the group to leave an area and not associate in public for seven days.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism and duration (seven days).

specificity.statement: I look forward to the commencement of this bill in November so that law-abiding Kiwis can enjoy the summer with less risk of violent crime, drug dealing, and general fear, disruption, and intimidation, which gangs have gotten away with peddling for far too long.
specificity.explanation: Names a commencement month but the promised outcome is broadly framed.

specificity.statement: If you’re pursuing an offence—someone’s got a firearm, they’ve run into a house, then you’re looking for that firearm—but if you’re just wondering whether they’ve got a gang patch that they’re not entitled to, you’re going to shake down the entire house.
specificity.explanation: References dated official briefings (7 March, 7 June 2024) and their specific concerns.

specificity.statement: It has always been New Zealand First’s policy to see it as an aggravating factor to be a gang member while you’re being sentenced, so today seeing that implemented is something that we have campaigned on and is now being implemented into legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific mechanism (gang membership as an aggravating sentencing factor).

specificity.statement: in 2017, there were just over 5,000 registered gang members; by 2023, we had over 8,600 members, a 50 percent increase—a 50 percent increase
specificity.explanation: Exact figures and years.

specificity.statement: We actually have wānanga with them. We actually bring them into a space and say, “What is happening? How can we awhi you to make better choices? What programmes can we develop to help?” That’s what we need to do. That’s a solution.
specificity.explanation: Describes a marae-based engagement approach but without concrete detail on scale or delivery.

specificity.statement: This Government is banning all gang insignia in public places because New Zealanders deserve to feel safe in their communities. We are cracking down on gangs.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete measure (public insignia ban) but wraps it in a general safety slogan.

specificity.statement: The situation with law and order in New Zealand, a majority of reasonable people living throughout New Zealand would agree, is a situation that has slipped down to very difficult, scary, and uncomfortable levels.
specificity.explanation: Vague characterisation with no figures or defined measure.

specificity.statement: We had the Police Association who specifically stated that there was a risk to the trust and confidence in New Zealand Police if we made a law in this House that was then unable to be enforced by a front-line police officer because there would be insufficient numbers or capacity capability to do that work.
specificity.explanation: Names the source and the specific enforcement-capacity concern.

divination.statement: I look forward to the commencement of this bill in November so that law-abiding Kiwis can enjoy the summer with less risk of violent crime, drug dealing, and general fear, disruption, and intimidation, which gangs have gotten away with peddling for far too long.
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced crime/fear over the coming summer; optimistic and contested by evidence on patch bans' effectiveness.

divination.statement: this bill, which will only result in more people being in prison—more wasted human potential—and which will not make our communities any safer
divination.explanation: Predicts more imprisonment and no safety gain; directionally plausible on incarceration, safety outcome uncertain.

charisma.statement: We get the intimidation in public places issue; it’s real. We agree that it needs to be addressed, but no one is intimidated by a gang patch in someone’s top drawer.
charisma.explanation: Concedes the opponent's valid concern about public intimidation before drawing the distinction — a bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: Human rights are called human rights because they’re universal, and we’ve got to be very cautious about saying, “Well, we don’t like that group of people. They’re not the kind of members of society I like, so they shouldn’t enjoy the same rights as everyone else.”
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared principle but is framed to persuade his own side.

charisma.statement: there’s a million Māori people and overwhelmingly they’re not in gangs. They’re bloody good people going about their lives, adding to New Zealand society, the tax take, the overall wellbeing of New Zealand as a whole.
charisma.explanation: Warm acknowledgement of the wider Māori community, though deployed to rebut the opposition.

charisma.statement: I don’t pick winners and losers based on race; I pick people. They either want to be in there or they don’t. They break the law or they don’t.
charisma.explanation: An individual-responsibility appeal that rallies his side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I would rather be with a policeman in a dark alley any day of the week than a gang member, and on that, I commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-them applause line rather than a consensus-building appeal.

charisma.statement: We actually have wānanga with them. We actually bring them into a space and say, “What is happening? How can we awhi you to make better choices? What programmes can we develop to help?” That’s what we need to do. That’s a solution.
charisma.explanation: Offers a compassionate, inclusive alternative approach rather than attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: I remember a time in my lifetime when a more enlightened, in this regard at least, leader of the National Party shook hands with members of the gangs, visited them on marae, and on his death, Sir Robert Muldoon had Black Power performing a haka at his funeral.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle by praising a former National leader's approach as a model.

charisma.statement: perhaps the gang was the only refuge on this earth where they felt they could be safe, and they went to that refuge and they found that they could get a home there. They had a place to exist—the despised of our society—and now, through this legislation, we’re coming for them there too.
charisma.explanation: Seeks to build compassion but frames the other side as lacking it.

charisma.statement: We must eradicate gangs and we must eradicate the causes of gangs. This bill isn’t the whole solution, but it is a step in the right direction.
charisma.explanation: Concedes the importance of addressing causes and frames the bill modestly, softening the partisan divide.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge the kōrero of the previous member James Meager. It is a rightful kōrero and it’s something that many of us have dealt with for many, many years. However, we cannot go along with this type of legislation.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly validates an opponent's speech as 'rightful' before dissenting — a genuine bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: When you have a man who was the mob boss, who did 10 years in prison, whose life now is absolutely committed to turning around people’s lives, has no time for gang members, you should listen … What works is mahi. What works is knitting communities together. What works is giving people a sense of purpose, not just playing tough guy.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, offers named practitioners and a positive vision of what works.

charisma.statement: Willie Jackson says there are better ways. Well, frankly, I don’t want to understand gangs, because we know enough. We know enough about the misery that they peddle in our community.
charisma.explanation: Combative and one-sided rather than persuasive to the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: This Government is banning all gang insignia in public places because New Zealanders deserve to feel safe in their communities. We are cracking down on gangs.
charisma.explanation: Rallies supporters ('great day for New Zealand') without any cross-party appeal.

charisma.statement: We’ve heard here today about the fact that gangs are a problem, and of course they are. Crime is a problem. No one’s sticking up for gangs. The pathway that people end up in gangs is also heartbreaking—no one’s disputing that.
charisma.explanation: Concedes common ground (gangs and crime are real problems) before pressing the disagreement.

rigor.statement: We get the intimidation in public places issue; it’s real. We agree that it needs to be addressed, but no one is intimidated by a gang patch in someone’s top drawer.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent public/private distinction, though the 'top drawer' framing simplifies the search-power argument.

rigor.statement: If you’re pursuing an offence—someone’s got a firearm, they’ve run into a house, then you’re looking for that firearm—but if you’re just wondering whether they’ve got a gang patch that they’re not entitled to, you’re going to shake down the entire house.
rigor.explanation: Grounded in cited Ministry of Justice advice and draws a clear logical contrast between evidence-gathering and open-ended search.

rigor.statement: Human rights are called human rights because they’re universal, and we’ve got to be very cautious about saying, “Well, we don’t like that group of people. They’re not the kind of members of society I like, so they shouldn’t enjoy the same rights as everyone else.”
rigor.explanation: A principled universality argument with clear logical entailment.

rigor.statement: This bill is largely window dressing, and the idea that a flag on a boat is prohibited but a flag on a house is not is incoherent.
rigor.explanation: Points to a genuine internal inconsistency, though asserted rather than fully evidenced.

rigor.statement: What I want people to understand about this bill and about the Government’s attack on gangs is that it is simply a marketing exercise. It is a PR strategy to look tough on crime but does nothing to make our communities tangibly safer.
rigor.explanation: An assertion of motive; the supporting evidence comes later rather than here.

rigor.statement: we cannot arrest our way out of the gang problem.
rigor.explanation: Slogan-like framing, but reflects an evidence-based criminological position she then supports.

rigor.statement: We know that because 80 to 90 percent of gang members experienced abuse in State care.
rigor.explanation: Cites the largest royal commission inquiry as support for the causal claim.

rigor.statement: This bill, in my eyes, is about persecuting Māori, because not all gangs have been treated equally in this bill. We just heard about that at question time: what about white supremacists? What about swastikas?
rigor.explanation: The swastika/white-supremacist omission is a concrete inconsistency, though the 'persecuting Māori' inference is asserted.

rigor.statement: there’s a million Māori people and overwhelmingly they’re not in gangs. They’re bloody good people going about their lives, adding to New Zealand society, the tax take, the overall wellbeing of New Zealand as a whole.
rigor.explanation: Valid statistical point that most Māori aren't in gangs, used to sidestep the disproportionate-impact argument rather than engage it.

rigor.statement: I don’t pick winners and losers based on race; I pick people. They either want to be in there or they don’t. They break the law or they don’t.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — reduces gang involvement to a binary choice, ignoring the structural drivers he had just conceded.

rigor.statement: But why are we not talking about the victims of crime? It’s so often, to the member’s remarks about Māori and Māoridom … the victims are disproportionately Māori.
rigor.explanation: Reframes toward victims with a factually grounded point about disproportionate Māori victimisation.

rigor.statement: They poured millions of dollars—taxpayers’ dollars—and gave it to gangs. Their way of fixing gang behaviour was to give them money. No wonder people were joining gangs, because it was a free money tree.
rigor.explanation: Relies on caricature and a rhetorical 'money tree' rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Why is it that Black Power insignia is named and a swastika isn’t? Why aren’t white supremacist gangs named? Why is it just those of us who are brown?
rigor.explanation: Highlights a genuine inconsistency in which symbols are proscribed, via rhetorical questions.

rigor.statement: perhaps the gang was the only refuge on this earth where they felt they could be safe, and they went to that refuge and they found that they could get a home there. They had a place to exist—the despised of our society—and now, through this legislation, we’re coming for them there too.
rigor.explanation: An empathetic causal narrative linking state-care abuse to gang refuge; leans heavily on emotional appeal.

rigor.statement: They chose Tupou only because of the colour of his clothing. [They] shot Tupou three times. Tupou was only 21 years old and worked as a machine operator to support his parents. He was not a gang member or even affiliated with a gang … He was murdered only because he chose to wear blue that day.
rigor.explanation: A single dramatic anecdote deployed as an emotional counter to the opposition rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: We must eradicate gangs and we must eradicate the causes of gangs. This bill isn’t the whole solution, but it is a step in the right direction.
rigor.explanation: A measured, non-overclaiming characterisation of the bill's role.

rigor.statement: The findings of the royal commission on abuse in State care suggest that 80 to 90 percent of gang members were victims of abuse … If we’re serious as a Parliament about removing the social harm caused by gangs, we would be looking to stop our kids being abused in State care in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Cites royal commission findings and draws a coherent prevention-focused conclusion.

rigor.statement: This heavy-handed approach is doing no good in terms of our community. We’re just pandering to the “Let’s be tough on crime brigade”, rather than finding actual solutions.
rigor.explanation: Asserts ineffectiveness; consistent with his broader evidence but stated as conclusion here.

rigor.statement: When you have a man who was the mob boss, who did 10 years in prison, whose life now is absolutely committed to turning around people’s lives, has no time for gang members, you should listen … What works is mahi. What works is knitting communities together. What works is giving people a sense of purpose, not just playing tough guy.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to lived-experience authority; persuasive but anecdotal rather than data-driven.

rigor.statement: Willie Jackson says there are better ways. Well, frankly, I don’t want to understand gangs, because we know enough. We know enough about the misery that they peddle in our community.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly rejects understanding causes — closes off reasoning rather than advancing it.

rigor.statement: We’ve talked about it in prior readings when we looked at the Whanganui example … asking Michael Laws, who was mayor at the time, “How did that work out?” … the result of the answer was that the gangs just left town. It’s like, “Cool. So where are they going to go when the gang patches are banned over all of New Zealand?” That is not a solution.
rigor.explanation: Uses a prior real-world precedent (Whanganui ban) to argue displacement rather than resolution — evidence-based reasoning.

rigor.statement: The situation with law and order in New Zealand, a majority of reasonable people living throughout New Zealand would agree, is a situation that has slipped down to very difficult, scary, and uncomfortable levels.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity / common sense ('a majority of reasonable people would agree') in place of evidence.

rigor.statement: We had the Police Association who specifically stated that there was a risk to the trust and confidence in New Zealand Police if we made a law in this House that was then unable to be enforced by a front-line police officer because there would be insufficient numbers or capacity capability to do that work.
rigor.explanation: Cites the Police Association's submission to support an enforceability concern — a sourced argument.

civility.statement: To hear the Minister stand up in question time today and say with a straight face that he hadn’t talked to the Attorney-General about this invasion of fundamental rights—he should hang his head.
civility.explanation: Personal disparagement ('hang his head', later 'ashamed of himself') aimed at the Minister rather than the substance.

civility.statement: This bill is largely window dressing, and the idea that a flag on a boat is prohibited but a flag on a house is not is incoherent.
civility.explanation: Dismissive ('window dressing') but the incoherence point engages the bill's substance.

civility.statement: What I want people to understand about this bill and about the Government’s attack on gangs is that it is simply a marketing exercise. It is a PR strategy to look tough on crime but does nothing to make our communities tangibly safer.
civility.explanation: Harsh ('marketing exercise') but aimed at the policy's design rather than a person.

civility.statement: This bill, in my eyes, is about persecuting Māori, because not all gangs have been treated equally in this bill. We just heard about that at question time: what about white supremacists? What about swastikas?
civility.explanation: Imputes a discriminatory motive to the Government, but is anchored to a substantive point about unequal treatment of symbols.

civility.statement: They poured millions of dollars—taxpayers’ dollars—and gave it to gangs. Their way of fixing gang behaviour was to give them money. No wonder people were joining gangs, because it was a free money tree.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents funding of community/rehabilitation programmes as 'giving money to gangs' — a strawman.

civility.statement: Why is it that Black Power insignia is named and a swastika isn’t? Why aren’t white supremacist gangs named? Why is it just those of us who are brown?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory in tone but engages a real feature of the bill.

civility.statement: This law is an affront to everything decent that we as a society should stand for, and it is exactly the sort of lockjaw, right-wing rubbish that we do not need in this world.
civility.explanation: Dismissive insult ('right-wing rubbish') rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: I acknowledge the kōrero of the previous member James Meager. It is a rightful kōrero and it’s something that many of us have dealt with for many, many years. However, we cannot go along with this type of legislation.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the other side while disagreeing on the policy.

civility.statement: This heavy-handed approach is doing no good in terms of our community. We’re just pandering to the “Let’s be tough on crime brigade”, rather than finding actual solutions.
civility.explanation: Critical label ('tough on crime brigade') but aimed at the approach rather than an individual.

civility.statement: Willie Jackson says there are better ways. Well, frankly, I don’t want to understand gangs, because we know enough. We know enough about the misery that they peddle in our community.
civility.explanation: Dismissive refusal to engage with the opposing argument.

civility.statement: hearing from the contributions from the other side of the House that are vacuous, silly, lightweight, and pathetic, including some of the contributions that have been made here today. All due respect to the member from the ACT Party, but his opening spiel told us nothing about the problem. You’re on the wrong track, buddy
civility.explanation: String of personal disparagements ('vacuous, silly, pathetic', 'buddy') rather than engagement with argument.

civility.statement: What made “Goldie” buckle? We just want to know. It would be interesting to think, you know, was he threatened? Was he worried? Did he get a report from somewhere? What made him change his mind?
civility.explanation: Speculates about the Minister's fear/motive (ruled unparliamentary on a point of order) rather than critiquing the decision on substance.

specificity.statement: It brings together four different Acts to provide a modern legislative framework for Parliament and the agencies that support it. The Acts are the Parliamentary Privilege Act, which was passed in 2014; the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Act 2013; the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988; and the Parliamentary Service Act 2000.
specificity.explanation: Names each of the four Acts and their years precisely.

specificity.statement: the Government will be nominating the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe, former Speaker, to chair the committee, and I think that's very appropriate and look forward to his erstwhile chairmanship of the committee.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete appointment (chair of the committee).

specificity.statement: It gives the PSOs powers of consent search, denial of entry, temporary seizure of specified items, and temporary detention. It also provides immunity for good-faith execution by PSOs of their functions and powers. These provisions are based on the legislation that empowers court security officers
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the exact powers granted and the statutory model they are drawn from.

specificity.statement: too few people in New Zealand take an interest in our constitutional arrangements, and this is one of those rare occasions when Parliament is considering constitutional legislation, and it's important that we get it right.
specificity.explanation: A general reflection with little concrete detail.

specificity.statement: The bill proposes giving the parliamentary security officers statutory powers to carry out a consented search, a denial of entry, a temporary seizure of specified items, and a temporary detention.
specificity.explanation: Lists the specific statutory powers proposed.

specificity.statement: These powers will apply to the parliamentary precinct and in respect of any other parliamentary meetings, including select committee meetings, that take place off the precinct. These powers may also apply to electorate and community offices in certain circumstances
specificity.explanation: Specifies where the new powers apply, including off-precinct and electorate offices.

specificity.statement: While we support the establishment of a select committee—we think that's a very good idea and we should do that—we oppose the increase of power to Parliament security.
specificity.explanation: Clear on what is supported and opposed, though without detailed alternative.

specificity.statement: For Māori particularly, whānau is so much more than just a mother and father. Government definitions of "whānau" don't work for us; whānau stretches wider and is never restricted to only shared toto.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete cultural critique of the bill's 'family member' definitions, though not a drafted alternative.

specificity.statement: Ours is a small, intimate, and sometimes imperfect little democracy, but it's our democracy. I think it's something that we should cherish, something that we should honour, and something that we should respect
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical and general, with no concrete detail.

specificity.statement: The definition of a "dependent" also will be amended to include any child over the age of 18 who's still at secondary school, or anyone over the age of 18 for that family who is, due to a disability, dependent on the MP for their daily care
specificity.explanation: Precisely states the amended eligibility criteria for a 'dependent'.

specificity.statement: The changes set out in the bill give the security officers the powers of search, the powers to deny entry and ability to seize items as specified, and temporarily detain people, if necessary, similar to those used by court officers.
specificity.explanation: Lists the specific powers and the court-officer model they mirror.

specificity.statement: the fact that this entrenches a greater separation of powers, because it does not allow a situation where a future Government could defund the operation of Parliament, the operation of the Opposition, and, therefore, the function of our democracy.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concrete mechanism (removing government defunding power) behind the principle.

specificity.statement: At present, Parliament security officers have no more powers than private security guards hired to man the door of a downtown nightclub.
specificity.explanation: Concrete comparison illustrating the current lack of statutory powers.

specificity.statement: Households with children are directly better off by an average of $78 a fortnight; hard cash in their bank accounts, opposed by every member of the Opposition, who would have said that those households did not deserve that money.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise average figure ($78 a fortnight).

specificity.statement: a little-known fact is that two-thirds of the new spending in our Budget goes to three key areas: health, education, and law and order.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the allocation (two-thirds) across three named areas.

specificity.statement: This Budget delivers $23 billion of reprioritisation over the next four years so that we can make the sorely needed investments in more front-line police officers, in more funding for our health system
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure ($23 billion), timeframe (four years), and target areas.

specificity.statement: meaning that we can forecast the books coming back into balance and a surplus in 2027-28.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific target year for surplus.

specificity.statement: The money that we spend is matched with targets with fair reporting on quarterly, and we take very seriously our duty to be good custodians of public money.
specificity.explanation: Mentions quarterly reporting against targets but without concrete measures here.
