forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether Government policy constitutes ethnocide, he neither agrees nor rebuts the charge but pivots to a list of targets.

forthrightness.statement: I stand by the commitment made in the coalition agreement with ACT to review whether the firearms registry is effectively improving public safety, and I stand by my role as Minister of Police to advocate for police around the Cabinet table. No such paper has been brought to Cabinet; therefore, such a question would be hypothetical.
forthrightness.explanation: Reaffirms the review commitment but avoids the direct question of whether he would block scrapping the registry by declaring it hypothetical.

forthrightness.statement: I think the member is grasping at straws. There have been no papers taken to Cabinet at all for any decisions. The member is trying to fearmonger. She doesn’t, in my view, have a very good relationship with facts, whereas my colleague Minister Nicole McKee deals with facts.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address whether excluding A-category firearms would weaken the registry; deflects to attacking the member.

forthrightness.statement: It’s a very interesting question because, of course, the member wrote to me, I think, yesterday about this issue, and there was an attachment to her letter, which says that in Norway the standard speed limit in urban areas is 50kph. In Sweden—ditto; 50kph is standard. Denmark—ditto; 50kph is standard. So the member is trying to make a point, but the information she’s provided to me, in my office, actually, I think, backs up what is in the proposed rule.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages Genter's premise about the six countries, though it doesn't concede the residential/rural nuance she raises.

forthrightness.statement: I assure the member that I will take safety into account as part of the process of finalising and signing the new rule.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a reassurance responsive to the safety question but no specific commitment on whether councils would be required to raise limits.

charisma.statement: Can I congratulate the Minister and the Government for concluding this agreement.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party congratulation from an Opposition spokesperson; builds bridges and finds common ground.

charisma.statement: I too rise as the Green Party spokesperson for trade, and, firstly, also to congratulate the Minister for Trade, the Hon Todd McClay, on this Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
charisma.explanation: Congratulates a government minister across party lines before raising concerns.

charisma.statement: Well, there’s an old adage: “A problem shared is a problem halved”, and this is so true. There are a number of organisations that can offer an ear to listen—but also just leaning over the gate and talking to your neighbour about how they are going.
charisma.explanation: Warm, empathetic and inclusive messaging aimed at supporting struggling farmers rather than scoring political points.

civility.statement: Can I congratulate the Minister and the Government for concluding this agreement.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of a political opponent's achievement.

civility.statement: I too rise as the Green Party spokesperson for trade, and, firstly, also to congratulate the Minister for Trade, the Hon Todd McClay, on this Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
civility.explanation: Respectful, policy-focused opening acknowledging an opponent's work.

civility.statement: Well, those who like to spend a lot of time on Treasure Island probably shouldn’t be talking about L-plates.
civility.explanation: A dismissive retort in kind; a cheap shot rather than engagement, though provoked by an equally rhetorical question.

civility.statement: Well, I am very pleased that the member is getting her head around the impacts of high debt, because that is the same member who went on Radio New Zealand and said that she thought the New Zealand Government should be borrowing more.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the member's prior position rather than a purely personal insult.

civility.statement: Who is to blame for the coalition’s differing of opinions and the chaos that has ensued: the current Deputy Prime Minister; the man who will replace the Deputy Prime Minister in six months’ time; the finance Minister, who has stalled at the lights; or the Prime Minister, who is clearly still driving with his L-plates on?
civility.explanation: Uses a mocking 'L-plates' characterisation of the Prime Minister's competence — a personal jab dressed as a question.

civility.statement: I’ve got to say, some of these questions are like a hāngī on repeat, reheat.
civility.explanation: A mildly dismissive quip belittling the questioner's line of questioning rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: I think the member is grasping at straws. There have been no papers taken to Cabinet at all for any decisions. The member is trying to fearmonger. She doesn’t, in my view, have a very good relationship with facts, whereas my colleague Minister Nicole McKee deals with facts.
civility.explanation: Personal attack asserting the questioner has a poor 'relationship with facts' rather than engaging her 70% seizure statistic.

civility.statement: It’s a very interesting question because, of course, the member wrote to me, I think, yesterday about this issue, and there was an attachment to her letter, which says that in Norway the standard speed limit in urban areas is 50kph. In Sweden—ditto; 50kph is standard. Denmark—ditto; 50kph is standard. So the member is trying to make a point, but the information she’s provided to me, in my office, actually, I think, backs up what is in the proposed rule.
civility.explanation: Pointed and slightly needling but stays on the substance of the evidence rather than attacking her personally.

rigor.statement: Trade agreements can’t be relied upon to cure all of the ills in the world. It’s unrealistic to expect that trade agreements will have binding environmental and labour obligations that are so high that they will cure all of the labour and environmental problems in the world, but trade agreements ought to do the lifting that they are able to do in advance of those very worthy goals.
rigor.explanation: Measured, non-fallacious reasoning that sets realistic expectations and distinguishes what trade deals can and cannot achieve.

rigor.statement: Considering the announcement that the Minister has made, my first question is: what public consultation has actually taken place? Based on the time line that is available, there are a lot of conversations between the two parties involved, but I’m not seeing a lot of consultation with the general public, particularly, in this case.
rigor.explanation: Grounds a critique of the treaty process in the published timeline and the Standing Orders review; reasoned rather than rhetorical.

rigor.statement: Free trade is a win-win. Kiwi dairy farmers, meat producers, and manufacturers will be able to sell more products at competitive prices to the people of the UAE, who will, in turn, benefit from greater choice and competition.
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent mutual-benefit argument but leans on the 'win-win' framing without engaging costs or trade-offs.

rigor.statement: ACT is strongly pro-trade. We believe that the free exchange of goods between different countries is key to lifting human prosperity.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a broad prosperity claim as self-evident rather than supporting it with evidence.

rigor.statement: the $100 million that we’ve spent over the last three years was 2.3 times more expensive than other, similar courses offered free of charge. There was anywhere between a 50 and 60 percent completion rate; it was not NZQA accredited; there were no qualifications gained; there was no evidence of improved student outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based case (cost, completion, accreditation, outcomes) rather than mere assertion, though the comparators are unspecified.

rigor.statement: Does he consider that excluding A category firearms from the registry would weaken it, given that these rifles and shotguns currently account for 70 percent of all firearms seized by police from offenders?
rigor.explanation: Links a specific statistic to a logical inference about the registry's effectiveness — evidence-based reasoning framed as a question.

rigor.statement: It’s a very interesting question because, of course, the member wrote to me, I think, yesterday about this issue, and there was an attachment to her letter, which says that in Norway the standard speed limit in urban areas is 50kph. In Sweden—ditto; 50kph is standard. Denmark—ditto; 50kph is standard. So the member is trying to make a point, but the information she’s provided to me, in my office, actually, I think, backs up what is in the proposed rule.
rigor.explanation: Turns the questioner's own supplied evidence against her claim — an evidence-based rebuttal, though it addresses only the urban-limit point and not her rural/30kph argument.

rigor.statement: the six countries he has referred to as having the lowest road deaths—Iceland, Norway, Sweden, the UK, Japan, Denmark—allow and actively encourage councils to extensively use safer speeds, like permanent 30kph speed limits in residential areas and 70 or 80kph on undivided, windy, rural highways
rigor.explanation: Draws on comparative international practice to argue the Minister's own examples support lower, not blanket-higher, limits; reasoned though selectively framed.

specificity.statement: this Government is focused on the highest-risk times, locations, and behaviours on our roads. Alcohol and drugs are the highest-risk contributors to deaths on our roads. That’s why we’re ensuring the Police are consistently doing over 3 million breath tests on our roads. That’s why we’re introducing oral roadside drug testing.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures — 3 million breath tests, oral roadside drug testing — though without timeframes.

specificity.statement: How many additional people being fatally or seriously injured does he believe is acceptable in order to save 14 to 20 seconds on an average 20-minute car journey?
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (14–20 seconds on a 20-minute trip).

specificity.statement: we are going to have a balanced approach to this issue, whereby we have slower speed limits around schools during pick-up and drop-off times, but it doesn’t make any sense to make a shift worker going to work at 4 o’clock in the morning have to crawl around their suburb at 30kph.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (variable school-zone limits at drop-off times) with a scenario, though no scope or timeline.

specificity.statement: That’s why we provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to disability support services in this year’s Budget.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure ($1.1 billion) tied to a specific budget.

specificity.statement: How is she supporting disabled people when parents in their 60s and 70s are writing to her to say their disabled adult children were on the waiting list for residential homes but now have been told the list has been scrapped because of the Government’s funding freeze on residential care facilities?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the challenge in a concrete constituent scenario (elderly parents, scrapped waiting list).

specificity.statement: We must look at flexible funding, and the disability community will be engaged and consulted before any changes are made.
specificity.explanation: 'Flexible funding' and 'engaged and consulted' are directional but uncommitted.

specificity.statement: My four priorities for the corrections portfolio are increasing staff safety, ensuring prison capacity, improving staffing levels, and reducing reoffending through effective rehabilitation.
specificity.explanation: Names four clear priority areas, though without figures at this point.

specificity.statement: Since September 2023, Corrections has reopened approximately 1,300 previously closed beds across the network. By the end of March next year, Corrections will reopen another 460. There’ll be an additional 600 beds added to Waikeria, as well as the Budget 2024 investment of over 810 more.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures and dates (1,300 beds since Sep 2023, 460 by March, 600 at Waikeria, 810 more).

specificity.statement: The Corrections Amendment Bill, which passed last night, delivers on our coalition commitments. For the first time, remand, accused, and convicted prisoners will receive access to rehabilitation programmes. The coalition Government has invested $78 million to support this great initiative.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the beneficiaries, and a $78 million figure.

specificity.statement: For the first time in a long time, Corrections are now recruiting above the level of attrition. This means that we are starting to make progress on staff shortages.
specificity.explanation: Concrete metric (recruitment vs attrition) but no numbers.

specificity.statement: when we look on the Government’s “red list”—which is now up to 20 projects nationally—and when we look and compare that to six months ago, the costs have gone up hugely. Of those same 18 comparable projects, none of which have moved off that “red list” but the amount of money that is concerned with those projects has risen by $640 million already.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (20 projects, 18 comparable, $640 million over six months).

specificity.statement: since the 2017 business case, the cost per square meter to build the hospital has tripled, from $10,000 per square meter to $30,000 per square meter.
specificity.explanation: Precise per-square-metre figures and a baseline year.

specificity.statement: We will invest more money in this, but we’ll also deliver plans and budgets that work.
specificity.explanation: Commits directionally to more investment and workable plans but with no figures, scope, or timeline.

specificity.statement: Suggesting that $3 billion for health for the deep South is unaffordable—$3 billion for a hospital complex, when the Government tells us that $10 billion to explore a possible tunnel for Wellington is cheap as chips.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete dollar figures to draw a spending-priority contrast.

specificity.statement: As a cost blowout, $3 billion is an order of magnitude above the $1.2 billion to $1.4 billion where this project started out, and the $1.6 billion when we came in—
specificity.explanation: Traces specific cost figures over the project's history ($1.2–1.4bn start, $1.6bn on entry, $3bn now).

specificity.statement: it was the wrong site, it was incredibly expensive to buy that site, the demolition costs were incredibly high, it was contaminated, it’s flood-prone, it’s on reclaimed land, it’s had piling difficulties, and they didn’t even provision for parking. Within the rescoped work that Mr Rust has done in his report, he’s had to add in $400 million for auxiliary stuff that wasn’t originally budgeted for.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete site issues and a dollar figure for unbudgeted items.

specificity.statement: The growth is in Central Otago. There needs to be capacity added in Central Otago. We need to use this point to fully address that. When you’ve got 10 percent growth a year, we need to be facing that reality as well.
specificity.explanation: Cites a 10 percent annual growth figure and a concrete regional recommendation.

specificity.statement: It’s not too different from KiwiRail’s iReX ferry terminal project, which blew out from $700 million to over $3 billion.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific before/after figures for a comparator project.

specificity.statement: if there is a fixed budget and there’s a time constraint—we want a new facility developed and delivered in a certain time frame—then we need to look at public-private partnerships (PPPs), where you can outsource the delivery risk, you can agree a fixed cost and a fixed time, and if it’s not delivered on time and to budget, that liability sits with the contractor.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (PPP with transferred delivery risk, fixed cost and time).

specificity.statement: The people of Dunedin need a new hospital; their current hospital is unsuitable and it is unsafe—500 instances of surgical equipment being contaminated every year.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (500 contamination instances annually) to support the safety claim.

specificity.statement: The fact is that if this Government wasn’t so reckless with its $2.9 billion tax cuts for landlords, there would be money to meet the needs of New Zealanders... If they weren’t giving $216 million... to a single tobacco party, we would be able to give New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures ($2.9bn landlord tax cuts, $216m tobacco) tied to a spending-priority argument.

specificity.statement: National made many promises about this hospital. They promised that any changes that Labour had made to decrease the scope—so by two operating theatres and a positron emission tomography (PET) scanner, and some shelled beds. They said, “We’re going to undo that.” ... What do we get when National is in Government? We just get cuts. That is all we can expect from this Government: cuts, cuts, cuts.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific scope items National promised to restore (two theatres, PET scanner, shelled beds).

specificity.statement: in my electorate about a quarter of the population are over the age of 60, so healthcare is really important.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete demographic figure to explain why healthcare dominates local concerns.

specificity.statement: All the issues that were mentioned by Nicola Willis have already been resolved. It was 2.7 percent of the total budget to do that remediation and all of that work is now complete. The land was bought actually incredibly cheaply—$11 million—because Cadbury wanted to get out of town, so there was already value for money in that purchase.
specificity.explanation: Rebuts with concrete figures (2.7% remediation cost, $11m land price).

specificity.statement: the former Southern Partnership chair, the Hon Pete Hodgson... his word is “absurd”. What they have done to concoct this narrative is add pathology, the car park, and a refurbishment costed at $400 million.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific cost components ($400m pathology, car park, refurbishment) she says inflate the figure.

specificity.statement: It’s going to be very topical in the House this afternoon—41 percent increase in construction costs since 2019, a huge additional amount, even leaving aside the cock-ups and the poor decision-making in relation to this hospital particularly.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (41% construction cost rise since 2019).

veracity.statement: this Government is focused on the highest-risk times, locations, and behaviours on our roads. Alcohol and drugs are the highest-risk contributors to deaths on our roads. That’s why we’re ensuring the Police are consistently doing over 3 million breath tests on our roads. That’s why we’re introducing oral roadside drug testing.
veracity.explanation: Alcohol and drugs being a leading contributor to road deaths is broadly supported; the 3 million breath test figure is a specific claim taken at face value.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister believe that the chief trauma surgeon Dr Christopher Wakeman is wrong when he says, “If you hit a pedestrian at 30 kilometres an hour, there’s a 90 percent chance they survive the crash. If you hit at 50 kilometres an hour, there’s a 10 percent chance that they’ll survive.”, and, if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: The directional claim (survival falls sharply with impact speed) is well supported; the precise 90%/10% figures are a commonly cited but simplified version.

veracity.statement: the reality is that this Government is not going to just simply slow every New Zealander down to crawl around our cities and towns around this country, which is what the last Government wanted to do.
veracity.explanation: Misrepresents the prior policy as blanket slowing of everyone, which exaggerates targeted speed reductions.

veracity.statement: That’s why we provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to disability support services in this year’s Budget.
veracity.explanation: A specific, verifiable budget figure asserted as fact; framing as 'record' is a claim taken at face value.

veracity.statement: It’s also why we have taken immediate action to stabilise the disability support system after an independent review found that the Ministry of Disabled People, Whaikaha, was ill-prepared to deliver these services when it was established in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Cites an independent review's finding; broadly consistent with the public record though selectively framed.

veracity.statement: There is not a funding freeze on residential facilities. There is no admissions freeze on residential services. The needs assessment and service coordination centres (NASCs) are making decisions based on need and there are still residential spaces available.
veracity.explanation: A direct factual denial contradicting the questioner's claim; correctness cannot be resolved from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Since September 2023, Corrections has reopened approximately 1,300 previously closed beds across the network. By the end of March next year, Corrections will reopen another 460. There’ll be an additional 600 beds added to Waikeria, as well as the Budget 2024 investment of over 810 more.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable figures presented as fact; taken at face value.

veracity.statement: For the first time in a long time, Corrections are now recruiting above the level of attrition. This means that we are starting to make progress on staff shortages.
veracity.explanation: A specific operational claim (recruitment exceeding attrition) presented as fact.

veracity.statement: when we look on the Government’s “red list”—which is now up to 20 projects nationally—and when we look and compare that to six months ago, the costs have gone up hugely. Of those same 18 comparable projects, none of which have moved off that “red list” but the amount of money that is concerned with those projects has risen by $640 million already.
veracity.explanation: Presents specific project-cost figures as fact; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: I would ask members opposite to desist from the false claim that we have reduced funding for this project. In fact, one of our most significant decisions was to immediately increase funding for this project in recognition of the fact that the costs have blown out so significantly that it would be impossible to deliver it without that extra funding.
veracity.explanation: Claims the Government added rather than cut funding ($300m); a specific, contestable factual assertion presented against the opposition's framing.

veracity.statement: since the 2017 business case, the cost per square meter to build the hospital has tripled, from $10,000 per square meter to $30,000 per square meter.
veracity.explanation: A specific cost-escalation claim attributed to expert advice; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: the actual business case for the project was still being developed while the project was being built—I’d love to hear members opposite explain to me how that is good practice; that despite the years that had been spent on the project, there was still no clear plan for the pathology lab, no plan for the refurbishment of the existing facilities, no plan for the car parking.
veracity.explanation: Specific process claims (business case developed during construction; no plans for lab, refurbishment, car parking) presented as fact; contested by Labour but detailed.

veracity.statement: This Government is bleeding our health system to death to fund trickle-down tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic and causally loaded ('bleeding to death', 'trickle-down') framing that overstates and simplifies.

veracity.statement: Suggesting that $3 billion for health for the deep South is unaffordable—$3 billion for a hospital complex, when the Government tells us that $10 billion to explore a possible tunnel for Wellington is cheap as chips.
veracity.explanation: 'Cheap as chips' caricatures the Government's position; the $10bn tunnel-exploration framing is a rhetorical juxtaposition rather than a like-for-like comparison.

veracity.statement: As a cost blowout, $3 billion is an order of magnitude above the $1.2 billion to $1.4 billion where this project started out, and the $1.6 billion when we came in—
veracity.explanation: 'An order of magnitude above' is inaccurate — $3bn is roughly double $1.4bn, not tenfold — exaggerating the escalation.

veracity.statement: It’s not too different from KiwiRail’s iReX ferry terminal project, which blew out from $700 million to over $3 billion.
veracity.explanation: The iReX cost-escalation figures are broadly consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: The people of Dunedin need a new hospital; their current hospital is unsuitable and it is unsafe—500 instances of surgical equipment being contaminated every year.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable statistic presented as fact; plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: The word “$3 billion” is not in the report; it’s nowhere... The Rust review says it probably could not be achieved within the existing appropriation—that doesn’t mean certainly; that might mean it’s a 50 percent probability or a 40 percent probability. It is certainly not the case that the Government has the right to claim that it’s going to cost $3 billion.
veracity.explanation: Claims the $3bn figure does not appear in the report; a specific, checkable assertion undermining the Government's number.

veracity.statement: They said Health New Zealand was $1.4 billion over budget and they had to fire the board... They said it was because there was 14 layers of management; well, we found out that was untrue. We found out that they didn’t have the organisational chart that Dr Reti said there was. We found out that they actually hired more nurses.
veracity.explanation: Several specific factual assertions about disproven Government claims; plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: The fact is that if this Government wasn’t so reckless with its $2.9 billion tax cuts for landlords, there would be money to meet the needs of New Zealanders... If they weren’t giving $216 million... to a single tobacco party, we would be able to give New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
veracity.explanation: The figures are specific but the 'tax cuts for landlords' and 'tobacco party' framings are partisan characterisations.

veracity.statement: There’s never been any dispute until today when I hear from the Hon Mark Patterson that perhaps the tertiary hospital should be in Central Otago. That is a totally new thing to be hearing, because it has always been based in Dunedin, as the city that then has to do that tertiary-level care for the wider Otago and Southland regions.
veracity.explanation: Accurate framing that Dunedin has historically hosted the tertiary/training hospital for the southern region.

veracity.statement: in my electorate about a quarter of the population are over the age of 60, so healthcare is really important.
veracity.explanation: A plausible, checkable demographic claim about the Taieri electorate.

veracity.statement: All the issues that were mentioned by Nicola Willis have already been resolved. It was 2.7 percent of the total budget to do that remediation and all of that work is now complete. The land was bought actually incredibly cheaply—$11 million—because Cadbury wanted to get out of town, so there was already value for money in that purchase.
veracity.explanation: Specific counter-claims that directly contradict Willis's account of site costs; correctness cannot be settled from the text.

veracity.statement: The fact of the matter is that this Government basically hates the South Island.
veracity.explanation: An unfalsifiable, hyperbolic characterisation presented as 'fact'.

veracity.statement: It’s going to be very topical in the House this afternoon—41 percent increase in construction costs since 2019, a huge additional amount, even leaving aside the cock-ups and the poor decision-making in relation to this hospital particularly.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable cost-inflation statistic presented as fact.

veracity.statement: We are putting in additional funding. It is simply not accurate to characterise that as any kind of a cut. Dunedin does not have a hospital now that was promised by the previous Government. It will because we are promising to get on and do it.
veracity.explanation: The 'not a cut, additional funding' claim is contested; accurate that no hospital has yet been delivered.

rigor.statement: this Government is focused on the highest-risk times, locations, and behaviours on our roads. Alcohol and drugs are the highest-risk contributors to deaths on our roads. That’s why we’re ensuring the Police are consistently doing over 3 million breath tests on our roads. That’s why we’re introducing oral roadside drug testing.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable evidence-based framing (target highest-risk factors) but asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: How many additional people being fatally or seriously injured does he believe is acceptable in order to save 14 to 20 seconds on an average 20-minute car journey?
rigor.explanation: Frames a genuine cost-benefit trade-off (deaths vs seconds saved) with a specific quantified time figure; slightly loaded but evidence-anchored.

rigor.statement: Does the Minister believe that the chief trauma surgeon Dr Christopher Wakeman is wrong when he says, “If you hit a pedestrian at 30 kilometres an hour, there’s a 90 percent chance they survive the crash. If you hit at 50 kilometres an hour, there’s a 10 percent chance that they’ll survive.”, and, if not, why not?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in an expert clinical source and specific survival figures; strong evidentiary structure.

rigor.statement: we are going to have a balanced approach to this issue, whereby we have slower speed limits around schools during pick-up and drop-off times, but it doesn’t make any sense to make a shift worker going to work at 4 o’clock in the morning have to crawl around their suburb at 30kph.
rigor.explanation: Uses a relatable anecdote (4am shift worker) to make the point rather than data.

rigor.statement: How is she supporting disabled people when parents in their 60s and 70s are writing to her to say their disabled adult children were on the waiting list for residential homes but now have been told the list has been scrapped because of the Government’s funding freeze on residential care facilities?
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific case to imply a systemic policy effect; persuasive but a single anecdote.

rigor.statement: They have broken their promises not only to the people of Dunedin but the people of Otago, the rural communities of Otago, South Otago, and Southland—throughout a huge and important regional part of this country—for no other reason than some basic cost saving.
rigor.explanation: 'For no other reason than some basic cost saving' asserts motive without engaging the cost-blowout evidence the Government cites.

rigor.statement: I was quite surprised that when I came to the cost recommendations, whilst almost all of it is redacted... it wasn’t that emphatic. There were lots of lots of sentences that used the words “probably” and “possibly” and things like that. I think for the Government to catastrophise on the basis of this report and break its promise to the people of Dunedin and Otago is disgraceful.
rigor.explanation: Engages directly with the report's hedged language ('probably', 'possibly') to argue the crisis is overstated, though limited by redactions.

rigor.statement: when we look on the Government’s “red list”—which is now up to 20 projects nationally—and when we look and compare that to six months ago, the costs have gone up hugely. Of those same 18 comparable projects, none of which have moved off that “red list” but the amount of money that is concerned with those projects has risen by $640 million already.
rigor.explanation: Uses the rising 'red list' costs to argue delay increases cost — a reasoned, evidence-anchored point.

rigor.statement: since the 2017 business case, the cost per square meter to build the hospital has tripled, from $10,000 per square meter to $30,000 per square meter.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete cost data to support the argument that the project is unaffordable as scoped.

rigor.statement: the actual business case for the project was still being developed while the project was being built—I’d love to hear members opposite explain to me how that is good practice; that despite the years that had been spent on the project, there was still no clear plan for the pathology lab, no plan for the refurbishment of the existing facilities, no plan for the car parking.
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific planning gaps to support the claim of haphazard management.

rigor.statement: This Government is bleeding our health system to death to fund trickle-down tax cuts.
rigor.explanation: Emotive slogan with a false-dichotomy causal claim, no evidence.

rigor.statement: Suggesting that $3 billion for health for the deep South is unaffordable—$3 billion for a hospital complex, when the Government tells us that $10 billion to explore a possible tunnel for Wellington is cheap as chips.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts two unlike projects to imply hypocrisy without establishing comparability.

rigor.statement: it was the wrong site, it was incredibly expensive to buy that site, the demolition costs were incredibly high, it was contaminated, it’s flood-prone, it’s on reclaimed land, it’s had piling difficulties, and they didn’t even provision for parking. Within the rescoped work that Mr Rust has done in his report, he’s had to add in $400 million for auxiliary stuff that wasn’t originally budgeted for.
rigor.explanation: Assembles a specific list of site problems and a $400m omitted-cost figure to support the affordability argument.

rigor.statement: The growth is in Central Otago. There needs to be capacity added in Central Otago. We need to use this point to fully address that. When you’ve got 10 percent growth a year, we need to be facing that reality as well.
rigor.explanation: Links a population-growth premise to a capacity conclusion, though the growth figure is asserted.

rigor.statement: It’s not too different from KiwiRail’s iReX ferry terminal project, which blew out from $700 million to over $3 billion.
rigor.explanation: Uses an analogy to a comparable blowout — illustrative but not itself proof of the Dunedin case.

rigor.statement: The previous Labour Government had a health Minister who went mountain biking during COVID. The next one, Hipkins, he decided to try to restructure the entire health system while the pandemic was still going.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem framing to imply negligence rather than argue from the project evidence.

rigor.statement: I’m a civil engineer. I’ve never started a project without having the client confirm the budget. Yet, apparently, the previous Government made a series of instructions to the extent that piling was under way without a business case being approved.
rigor.explanation: Draws on professional experience (appeal to his own authority) plus a specific process claim (piling before business-case approval).

rigor.statement: if there is a fixed budget and there’s a time constraint—we want a new facility developed and delivered in a certain time frame—then we need to look at public-private partnerships (PPPs), where you can outsource the delivery risk, you can agree a fixed cost and a fixed time, and if it’s not delivered on time and to budget, that liability sits with the contractor.
rigor.explanation: Logical premise-to-solution reasoning about risk allocation, though asserting PPP superiority without evidence.

rigor.statement: Imagine if Labour had had any appetite at all to involve the private sector in actually funding, financing, and delivering this project—it’s quite likely that it would have been delivered by now within the original budget committed to.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a favourable counterfactual outcome without evidence.

rigor.statement: The word “$3 billion” is not in the report; it’s nowhere... The Rust review says it probably could not be achieved within the existing appropriation—that doesn’t mean certainly; that might mean it’s a 50 percent probability or a 40 percent probability. It is certainly not the case that the Government has the right to claim that it’s going to cost $3 billion.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes the report's hedged probability language from the Government's asserted certainty — a disciplined evidentiary point.

rigor.statement: The scope reductions that will be entailed by what the Government is embarking on will cause additional cost. That always happens when you build a hospital that is too small: it ends up costing you more down the line.
rigor.explanation: General principle ('always happens') applied to the case; plausible but stated as a universal.

rigor.statement: They said Health New Zealand was $1.4 billion over budget and they had to fire the board... They said it was because there was 14 layers of management; well, we found out that was untrue. We found out that they didn’t have the organisational chart that Dr Reti said there was. We found out that they actually hired more nurses.
rigor.explanation: Builds a pattern argument by citing specific prior claims she says were disproven (14 layers, org chart, back-office bloat).

rigor.statement: The fact is that if this Government wasn’t so reckless with its $2.9 billion tax cuts for landlords, there would be money to meet the needs of New Zealanders... If they weren’t giving $216 million... to a single tobacco party, we would be able to give New Zealanders the healthcare that they deserve.
rigor.explanation: Implies a direct fungibility between those spends and hospital funding — a contested, oversimplified trade-off.

rigor.statement: There’s never been any dispute until today when I hear from the Hon Mark Patterson that perhaps the tertiary hospital should be in Central Otago. That is a totally new thing to be hearing, because it has always been based in Dunedin, as the city that then has to do that tertiary-level care for the wider Otago and Southland regions.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes tertiary from regional hospitals to rebut the Central Otago suggestion.

rigor.statement: At least Labour was building things. You can’t knock things over if you’re not building them in the first place.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical retort defending Labour's record rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: National made many promises about this hospital. They promised that any changes that Labour had made to decrease the scope—so by two operating theatres and a positron emission tomography (PET) scanner, and some shelled beds. They said, “We’re going to undo that.” ... What do we get when National is in Government? We just get cuts. That is all we can expect from this Government: cuts, cuts, cuts.
rigor.explanation: Ends in a sweeping 'cuts, cuts, cuts' generalisation that overreaches the specific example.

rigor.statement: What a shameful day to go out and election campaign to deliberately mislead voters, knowing that they had no intention of ever delivering on the promise of Dunedin Hospital.
rigor.explanation: Asserts intent ('no intention of ever delivering') without evidence for the internal motive claimed.

rigor.statement: All the issues that were mentioned by Nicola Willis have already been resolved. It was 2.7 percent of the total budget to do that remediation and all of that work is now complete. The land was bought actually incredibly cheaply—$11 million—because Cadbury wanted to get out of town, so there was already value for money in that purchase.
rigor.explanation: Engages Willis's specific points with counter-figures rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: The fact of the matter is that this Government basically hates the South Island.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping claim of emotional motive ('hates') with no evidentiary basis.

rigor.statement: the former Southern Partnership chair, the Hon Pete Hodgson... his word is “absurd”. What they have done to concoct this narrative is add pathology, the car park, and a refurbishment costed at $400 million.
rigor.explanation: Cites an expert's view and itemises the disputed additions, though 'concoct' asserts bad faith.

rigor.statement: I wonder if the members opposite might remember who was in Government for the last six years—that did not deliver such a hospital. This entire discussion would not be necessary if the Government of the day, six years ago, had gotten under way and actually built the damn thing.
rigor.explanation: Points to the previous Government's six years of non-delivery as the root cause — a fair factual point, though it sidesteps the current scope decision.

forthrightness.statement: Well, this Government is incredibly focused on road safety, and in terms of the number of actions this Government has under way to improve road safety... We need to ensure we’re focused on the highest-risk times, locations, and behaviours rather than just blanket speed limits, like the last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many additional deaths are acceptable to save seconds; never gives a number, pivots to breath-test talking points.

forthrightness.statement: There is not a funding freeze on residential facilities. There is no admissions freeze on residential services. The needs assessment and service coordination centres (NASCs) are making decisions based on need and there are still residential spaces available.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of the question with a flat denial and an explanation of how decisions are made.

forthrightness.statement: I know that it is incredibly challenging for families who are looking after disabled children. That is why it is absolutely critical that we have taken urgent action to stabilise the disability support service so that disabled people with the highest needs can continue to get fair and consistent access to the services they need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a specific nurse losing respite care, she acknowledges difficulty but pivots to generic 'stabilise the system' messaging without addressing the case.

forthrightness.statement: I’m standing here as the Minister of Disability Issues, and assessments around disability support services are done by the NASCs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about MSD dropping telehealth autism diagnoses, she deflects to portfolio boundaries and the NASCs rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: We must look at flexible funding, and the disability community will be engaged and consulted before any changes are made.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to confirm she will not change autism eligibility criteria, she promises consultation instead of confirming or denying the change.

forthrightness.statement: My four priorities for the corrections portfolio are increasing staff safety, ensuring prison capacity, improving staffing levels, and reducing reoffending through effective rehabilitation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers how the department is delivering on his priorities by enumerating them.

forthrightness.statement: I will not sugar-coat this. This is not the news that southern New Zealand wanted to hear today, but it is important that we are honest with them.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly acknowledges the news is unwelcome rather than spinning it away.

charisma.statement: Well, this Government is incredibly focused on road safety, and in terms of the number of actions this Government has under way to improve road safety... We need to ensure we’re focused on the highest-risk times, locations, and behaviours rather than just blanket speed limits, like the last Government.
charisma.explanation: Rallies against 'the last Government' rather than engaging the questioner's point.

charisma.statement: I know that it is incredibly challenging for families who are looking after disabled children. That is why it is absolutely critical that we have taken urgent action to stabilise the disability support service so that disabled people with the highest needs can continue to get fair and consistent access to the services they need.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic tone but largely restates talking points.

charisma.explanation: Defensive and combative toward the opposing member rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: Who are New Zealanders meant to believe: a Minister who says she’s prioritising disabled people and families, or the hundreds of disabled people and families, some of whom, I understand, are in the gallery today, whose daily realities are very different and are urging her Government to stop their cost-cutting exercise and actually support them to be able to live with dignity?

charisma.statement: Members across this House agree that the people of Dunedin and its surrounding regions deserve and need a modern, fit for purpose set of hospital facilities.

charisma.statement: It has been enlightening to hear from the National Party, with two National Ministers in Dunedin today willing to say anything to get elected, but simply can’t be trusted... We can’t trust this Government one iota. They slither and squirm away from any clear answer.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them rhetoric that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: I will not sugar-coat this. This is not the news that southern New Zealand wanted to hear today, but it is important that we are honest with them.
charisma.explanation: Honest, level-headed framing that seeks to bring people along even with bad news.

charisma.statement: Sometimes really tough decisions come down the pipe. Sometimes you inherit a mess. Sometimes you’re in charge of sorting it out, and this is the place we find ourselves in today.
charisma.explanation: Sober, responsibility-taking tone that appeals beyond the partisan base.

charisma.statement: One of the lessons that they taught me when I was learning to be a doctor was to take responsibility. Well, this Government needs to stop blaming other people for its problems. It needs to take responsibility.
charisma.explanation: Uses a personal anecdote to make a moral appeal, but directed at rallying against the Government.

charisma.statement: At least Labour was building things. You can’t knock things over if you’re not building them in the first place.
charisma.explanation: A partisan applause line rather than a bridge-building appeal.

charisma.statement: National made many promises about this hospital. They said, “We’re going to undo that.” ... What do we get when National is in Government? We just get cuts. That is all we can expect from this Government: cuts, cuts, cuts.
charisma.explanation: Repetitive attack chant that rallies rather than persuades.

civility.statement: the reality is that this Government is not going to just simply slow every New Zealander down to crawl around our cities and towns around this country, which is what the last Government wanted to do.
civility.explanation: Strawmans the opposing position ('crawl around', 'slow every New Zealander down') rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: They can believe and have confidence in a Government that is investing an additional $1.1 billion in disability services, and not a member who completely disrespects their ability to understand that $1.1 billion of extra funding is not a cut.
civility.explanation: Turns to accuse the questioning member of 'completely disrespecting' disabled people rather than addressing the substance.

civility.statement: Who are New Zealanders meant to believe: a Minister who says she’s prioritising disabled people and families, or the hundreds of disabled people and families, some of whom, I understand, are in the gallery today, whose daily realities are very different and are urging her Government to stop their cost-cutting exercise and actually support them to be able to live with dignity?
civility.explanation: A pointed rhetorical framing that implies the Minister is untrustworthy, but grounded in constituents' stated experiences rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: They have broken their promises not only to the people of Dunedin but the people of Otago, the rural communities of Otago, South Otago, and Southland—throughout a huge and important regional part of this country—for no other reason than some basic cost saving.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of breaking promises for cost-saving — pointed but aimed at a decision/policy rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I was quite surprised that when I came to the cost recommendations, whilst almost all of it is redacted... it wasn’t that emphatic. There were lots of lots of sentences that used the words “probably” and “possibly” and things like that. I think for the Government to catastrophise on the basis of this report and break its promise to the people of Dunedin and Otago is disgraceful.
civility.explanation: 'Disgraceful' and 'catastrophise' are charged, but the criticism targets the Government's use of the report.

civility.statement: this Minister is not competent to make the tough decisions and to do it when needed.
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on the Minister's competence rather than on the policy.

civility.statement: Members across this House agree that the people of Dunedin and its surrounding regions deserve and need a modern, fit for purpose set of hospital facilities.
civility.explanation: Respectful, consensus-oriented framing.

civility.statement: I would ask members opposite to desist from the false claim that we have reduced funding for this project. In fact, one of our most significant decisions was to immediately increase funding for this project in recognition of the fact that the costs have blown out so significantly that it would be impossible to deliver it without that extra funding.
civility.explanation: 'False claim' is sharp but a legitimate challenge to a factual characterisation, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: the actual business case for the project was still being developed while the project was being built—I’d love to hear members opposite explain to me how that is good practice; that despite the years that had been spent on the project, there was still no clear plan for the pathology lab, no plan for the refurbishment of the existing facilities, no plan for the car parking.
civility.explanation: Harsh but substantive criticism of project management rather than personal abuse.

civility.statement: It has been enlightening to hear from the National Party, with two National Ministers in Dunedin today willing to say anything to get elected, but simply can’t be trusted... We can’t trust this Government one iota. They slither and squirm away from any clear answer.
civility.explanation: Characterises Ministers as untrustworthy and 'slithering'/'squirming' — personal disparagement rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: This Government is bleeding our health system to death to fund trickle-down tax cuts.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist framing counts against civility.

civility.statement: I will not sugar-coat this. This is not the news that southern New Zealand wanted to hear today, but it is important that we are honest with them.
civility.explanation: Measured, respectful tone toward the affected public and opponents.

civility.statement: Sometimes really tough decisions come down the pipe. Sometimes you inherit a mess. Sometimes you’re in charge of sorting it out, and this is the place we find ourselves in today.
civility.explanation: Reflective, non-abusive framing of the situation, though it does gesture at inheriting a 'mess'.

civility.statement: The previous Labour Government had a health Minister who went mountain biking during COVID. The next one, Hipkins, he decided to try to restructure the entire health system while the pandemic was still going.
civility.explanation: Leads with a personal jab (mountain biking) about a former Minister rather than the project's substance.

civility.statement: I’m a civil engineer. I’ve never started a project without having the client confirm the budget. Yet, apparently, the previous Government made a series of instructions to the extent that piling was under way without a business case being approved.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of process ('quite outrageous') that stays on the project rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: if we admitted Chris Bishop to the gastroenterology department at Dunedin Hospital, we might be able to get a scope and find out where that $3 billion figure came from, because that is utterly made up.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at a named Minister (colonoscopy pun) rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: they are trying to play other communities off against New Zealand. That is so dirty. It’s disgraceful.
civility.explanation: 'So dirty' and 'disgraceful' are strong condemnations of motive, verging on character attack though aimed at the Government's tactic.

civility.statement: One of the lessons that they taught me when I was learning to be a doctor was to take responsibility. Well, this Government needs to stop blaming other people for its problems. It needs to take responsibility.
civility.explanation: Rebukes the Government for blame-shifting; critical but framed around conduct rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: What a shameful day to go out and election campaign to deliberately mislead voters, knowing that they had no intention of ever delivering on the promise of Dunedin Hospital.
civility.explanation: Alleges deliberate, knowing deception — an accusation of bad faith rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: The fact of the matter is that this Government basically hates the South Island.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic imputation of animus rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: I wonder if the members opposite might remember who was in Government for the last six years—that did not deliver such a hospital. This entire discussion would not be necessary if the Government of the day, six years ago, had gotten under way and actually built the damn thing.
civility.explanation: Sharp and rhetorical but aimed at the record rather than personal insult.

strength.statement: That’s why we provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to disability support services in this year’s Budget.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for an allocated funding boost — an enacted budget decision, though delivery of services is disputed by the questioner.

strength.statement: Since September 2023, Corrections has reopened approximately 1,300 previously closed beds across the network. By the end of March next year, Corrections will reopen another 460. There’ll be an additional 600 beds added to Waikeria, as well as the Budget 2024 investment of over 810 more.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered capacity (1,300 beds reopened) alongside forward commitments still to be delivered.

strength.statement: The Corrections Amendment Bill, which passed last night, delivers on our coalition commitments. For the first time, remand, accused, and convicted prisoners will receive access to rehabilitation programmes. The coalition Government has invested $78 million to support this great initiative.
strength.explanation: Points to legislation actually passed and funding committed — a concrete, enacted deliverable rather than an announcement.

strength.statement: For the first time in a long time, Corrections are now recruiting above the level of attrition. This means that we are starting to make progress on staff shortages.
strength.explanation: Describes in-progress delivery on staffing, an outcome rather than a mere promise.

strength.statement: We will invest more money in this, but we’ll also deliver plans and budgets that work.
strength.explanation: A forward promise of delivery with no concrete mechanism yet enacted.

strength.statement: We are putting in additional funding. It is simply not accurate to characterise that as any kind of a cut. Dunedin does not have a hospital now that was promised by the previous Government. It will because we are promising to get on and do it.
strength.explanation: Restates a forward promise to deliver the hospital with no concrete plan or delivery yet — aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

authenticity.statement: It’s also why we have taken immediate action to stabilise the disability support system after an independent review found that the Ministry of Disabled People, Whaikaha, was ill-prepared to deliver these services when it was established in 2022.
authenticity.explanation: Justifies action by reference to a review; a stated rationale that aligns with the Government's cost-control positioning.

authenticity.statement: The Corrections Amendment Bill, which passed last night, delivers on our coalition commitments. For the first time, remand, accused, and convicted prisoners will receive access to rehabilitation programmes. The coalition Government has invested $78 million to support this great initiative.
authenticity.explanation: Claims the passed bill matches prior coalition commitments — words backed by a legislative act.

divination.statement: Since September 2023, Corrections has reopened approximately 1,300 previously closed beds across the network. By the end of March next year, Corrections will reopen another 460. There’ll be an additional 600 beds added to Waikeria, as well as the Budget 2024 investment of over 810 more.
divination.explanation: Predicts 460 more beds by end of March next year — plausible given the recruitment/capacity pipeline described.

divination.statement: Sitting around and reviewing this hospital again will not do anything other than cost more money. That, therefore, leaves us in a situation where we have a lesser hospital that costs more than what we could have if we’d just done it properly in the first place.
divination.explanation: Predicts further review will raise costs and yield a lesser, more expensive hospital — directionally plausible given construction inflation, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: If this Government gets one vote out of Dunedin at the next election I will be surprised because this Government has accelerated a funding crisis for universities as well, including the University of Otago.
divination.explanation: Predicts the Government will win almost no Dunedin votes — rhetorical hyperbole, unlikely to hold literally.

divination.statement: Imagine if Labour had had any appetite at all to involve the private sector in actually funding, financing, and delivering this project—it’s quite likely that it would have been delivered by now within the original budget committed to.
divination.explanation: A counterfactual prediction that PPP delivery would have hit the original budget — speculative and contradicted by the project's documented site problems.

divination.statement: The scope reductions that will be entailed by what the Government is embarking on will cause additional cost. That always happens when you build a hospital that is too small: it ends up costing you more down the line.
divination.explanation: Predicts scope cuts will raise long-run costs — directionally supported by the cited Health NZ advice, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: there is a reality that can’t be voted away: New Zealand probably has too many doctors. Over the next 10 years, we will need fewer hospital beds than we currently do.
divination.explanation: A late-1990s prediction (quoted by Brooking) that NZ would need fewer hospital beds and had too many doctors — contradicted by subsequent bed and workforce shortages.

veracity.statement: The analysis found that if even a minor incursion of foot-and-mouth disease was found here, our access to foreign markets for animal products would stop, and the cost to our economy would be $1.5 billion in export revenue per month
veracity.explanation: Cites an independent economic assessment; the figure is presented as sourced and is broadly consistent with published FMD impact modelling.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research estimated that if we did nothing to return to normal trade, nominal GDP would fall by 11 percent.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named institute (NZIER); presented as a sourced estimate.

veracity.statement: So the Government will continue to invest in a robust biosecurity system with the highest border standards in the world.
veracity.explanation: "Highest border standards in the world" is an unsubstantiated superlative/hyperbole.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister deny that the chance of a pedestrian surviving when hit by a car at 30 kilometres an hour is around 90 percent, whereas the chance of surviving at 50 kilometres an hour drops to only 20 percent
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with established road-safety survivability research on impact speed.

veracity.statement: Up to two-thirds of New Zealanders supported the direction of travel.
veracity.explanation: "Up to two-thirds" is a hedged ceiling figure repeated as if a firm mandate; likely overstates consultation support.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Transport advised that reversing reduced speed limits would likely result in an increase in the average speeds of these roads. Where the average speed increases, the risk of fatal and serious crashes also increases.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays the regulatory impact analysis, including the adverse finding.

veracity.statement: many of those people left because of the climate that was engaged without their permission or knowledge by November 2023, when 133,000 net had come into the country with no warning to the people of New Zealand about hospitals, schools, roads, or any infrastructure required to accommodate them.
veracity.explanation: The net migration figure is in the right range, but the causal claim that this drove emigration is asserted, not evidenced.

veracity.statement: The reality is, we’ve seen a massive drop off of those people dependent upon the State, as a consequence of this Government
veracity.explanation: Runs against the question's premise of 26,000 more beneficiaries; a "massive drop off" is misleading.

veracity.statement: just overnight, on the question of Palestinian recognition, New Zealand voted to support a UN General Assembly resolution affirming our longstanding position that Israel’s presence in the occupied Palestine territories is unlawful.
veracity.explanation: Factual, verifiable reference to a specific UNGA vote.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that Kiwis do not see a future under his Government and are leaving in record numbers, with net 55,800 New Zealanders having left the country for the year ending July 2024?
veracity.explanation: The 55,800 net departure figure for the year to July 2024 is consistent with Stats NZ migration data.

veracity.statement: How does he reconcile the Government’s target to reduce job seeker beneficiaries by 50,000 with an increase of 26,000 more beneficiaries since he took office?
veracity.explanation: Contrasts a stated target with a benefit-increase figure; broadly consistent with the trend at the time.

veracity.statement: only about one in 400 adult New Zealanders are gang members—one in 400—yet they are associated with one in five serious violent crime offences and, actually, one in four kidnappings.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with commonly cited NZ Police figures on gang association with serious violent offending.

veracity.statement: the vast majority of Māori are not in gangs and the focus of this legislation is to reduce the number of victims of crime and Māori are more likely to be victims of crime.
veracity.explanation: Both claims (few Māori in gangs; Māori over-represented as victims) align with available data.

veracity.statement: This showed that economic activity fell 0.2 percent compared to the previous quarter. This follows a string of mostly low and negative GDP results going back to late 2022.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays the Stats NZ June-quarter GDP result and the preceding trend.

veracity.statement: in its August Monetary Policy Statement, the Reserve Bank forecast negative 0.5 percent growth in the June quarter, considerably higher than this result.

civility.explanation: A dig at opposition members for lacking hands-on building experience; a mild personal jab wrapped around a substantive point.

civility.statement: We’ve been very critical of what the Government is doing around social housing. We believe that they’re taking the wrong approach.
civility.explanation: States clear policy disagreement on social housing directly and respectfully, without personal attack.

charisma.statement: Don’t the National Party dare use my community as an excuse to downgrade the facilities for Dunedin or any other community in this country.
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them framing that rallies her own side rather than seeking any common ground.

charisma.statement: I stand here in solidarity as a Nelson MP because every single community in this country, in Aotearoa, deserves a decent public hospital.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to a shared national value (every community deserving a hospital), though delivered within a partisan attack.

charisma.statement: I’m certainly very happy to contemplate any suggestions that they might make for change.
charisma.explanation: Openly invites input from the select committee and sector, a consensus-building, collaborative posture.

charisma.statement: Labour supports this bill because it builds on Labour’s work to make building products cheaper and the market more competitive, which started with the Commerce Commission’s report
charisma.explanation: Endorses a Government bill across party lines while linking it to prior work, a bridge-building stance.

charisma.statement: The Green Party is supporting this bill. I note that the work on this did begin under the last Government, and I think that what is contained in this bill has the potential to be hugely beneficial.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party support and generous acknowledgement of the bill's origins under the previous Government; consensus-building.

charisma.statement: The approach that we are taking when it comes to housing and building and construction is that we intend and genuinely hope to be able to be as constructive as possible... Where there is something that we agree on, we will say so, and where there is something that is in the right direction... we’ll approach the debate in that manner.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly commits to a constructive, cross-party posture and distinguishes genuine disagreement from politicking; strongly consensus-building.

charisma.statement: a lot of this bill hinges on the word “similar”... I hope that the select committee, when they’re looking at this, will reflect on, and ask questions about, what sort of overseas standards organisations are similar to New Zealand and, even, which ones are not similar to New Zealand
charisma.explanation: Frames the concern as a constructive question for the select committee rather than an attack.

charisma.statement: I would say to the Government, when they are looking at the price of buildings and how to build in more efficient ways, that they go back to these pieces of work. They’re good pieces of work and were going to improve New Zealand’s economy.
charisma.explanation: Constructively urges the Government to revive prior cross-cutting work (building accord, industry transformation plan) rather than scoring political points.

charisma.statement: I look forward to the cross-party collaboration and making real progress in this sector, and I commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes cross-party collaboration and invites public submissions; inclusive and consensus-oriented.

rigor.statement: my message to Simon Court is that public-private partnerships do not work. They cost more money. They take more time. They cut corners and they do not deliver for the people in the community.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping categorical claim ('do not work') asserted without evidence; PPP outcomes are mixed in reality, so this is an unsupported generalisation.

rigor.statement: It’s gone to landlords; it’s gone to tobacco companies.
rigor.explanation: Emotive juxtaposition with no causal link established between the tax measures and the health capital shortfall.

rigor.statement: We should be building hospitals that the medical professionals say are the best for patients, because they are the experts, and this Government is failing to listen to them.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable appeal to clinical expertise for the 'clinically preferred option', but leans on an appeal to authority without engaging cost/trade-off arguments.

rigor.statement: There is a massive opportunity cost associated with the huge rise in construction costs—since 2019 alone, an increase of some 40 percent.
rigor.explanation: Uses the cost rise to motivate the opportunity-cost argument; reasoning follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: I note that the Commerce Commission report of 2022 highlighted very particularly the fact that we have an uncompetitive sector taken as a whole.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in an authoritative independent report and acknowledges variation across product types rather than overclaiming.

rigor.statement: we need credible and comparable jurisdictions—credible ones being those nations and States that have good building standards. And some places in the world, frankly, have better building standards, I would say, than those in this country, but others have worse, and we need to choose carefully in that regard.
rigor.explanation: Carefully qualifies the reform: distinguishes credible from comparable jurisdictions and acknowledges variation and risk, rather than overselling the benefit.

rigor.statement: We’re cautious about product substitutions for plasterboard being approved in groups, which this legislation would allow, because they’re used in structurally different ways in other jurisdictions.
rigor.explanation: A specific, technically-grounded concern about group substitution given structural usage differences between jurisdictions.

rigor.statement: building consent authorities are going to be responsible for more under the new regime, which will add to their time and process costs for those consents.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned inference from the bill's shifting of liability/oversight onto councils to a cost consequence.

rigor.statement: We do have to recognise that New Zealand’s supply chain has been dominated by a few major companies and, essentially, that oligopoly—you know, it is an oligopoly—has allowed some companies to make excessive profits on products that, frankly, are not the best.
rigor.explanation: Consistent with market-study findings, but the profit and quality claims are asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It’s less money spent on hospital bills, it’s more productivity, it’s lower power bills for people. If the Government can lead by example through procurement, then, over time, we can step our Building Code up.
rigor.explanation: Coherent chain from higher build quality via procurement to health, productivity and energy savings; plausible but the links are asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: it is not a monopoly, as a previous speaker has spoken about, because of some oligopoly; it is a situation in which councils make it so hard to achieve standards in New Zealand for new products to enter the market that it is not a surprise that our cost of building is so high.
rigor.explanation: Engages a prior speaker's framing and offers an alternative causal explanation (council barriers), but shifts blame wholly to councils without evidence and against the Commerce Commission's competition findings.

rigor.statement: To the members of the House who haven’t swung a hammer in the last, well, ever—especially on the other side—I can tell you that these acceptable solutions and verification methods are how we get things approved in New Zealand
rigor.explanation: Appeals to his own trade credential (authority/experience) to bolster the point rather than to evidence.

rigor.statement: if you use in good faith a product which the Crown has said is a product which should be able to be used, you won’t be liable for that, and I think that’s a very, very important message.
rigor.explanation: Accurately identifies the bill's liability-shield mechanism for risk-averse councils and explains why it matters; clear reasoning grounded in how the scheme works.

rigor.statement: the cost of building in New Zealand is currently close to around about 50 percent more expensive than trying to build a standalone house in Australia. You wonder why our young people are saying, “No, stuff this, we’re off to Aussie.”
rigor.explanation: Attributes youth emigration to building costs via a rhetorical anecdote, with no evidence for the causal link.

rigor.statement: many councils don’t have the funding to be able to put the infrastructure in beforehand... We’d like the assistance of funding to come at the start of the process so we can get some infrastructure put in at the start, and that’ll mean that land will be able to be developed, rather than at the end, because some councils can’t bridge that gap.
rigor.explanation: Clear cause-and-effect argument: funding timing → councils can bridge the gap → land gets developed.

rigor.statement: Removing barriers to high-quality and innovative products entering the New Zealand market could increase consumer choice, increase competition, and provide greater security against supply disruptions.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable, hedged causal claim linking barrier removal to competition and resilience.

rigor.statement: a lot of this bill hinges on the word “similar”... I hope that the select committee, when they’re looking at this, will reflect on, and ask questions about, what sort of overseas standards organisations are similar to New Zealand and, even, which ones are not similar to New Zealand
rigor.explanation: Precise textual analysis identifying that the bill's operation turns on the undefined word 'similar', and connecting it to the Minister's own point about differing standards.

rigor.statement: Some of these changes have been positive, but others have gone way beyond what is necessary for public safety and we are now at risk of losing safe venues for licence holders to use firearms safely due to overly burdensome regulatory requirements.
rigor.explanation: Concedes some 2020 changes were positive before arguing others overshoot, a balanced framing, though the harm claim is unquantified.

rigor.statement: amendments will be made to the annual 12-event participation requirement for pistol endorsement holders. Once these regulations are in place, attendance at any organised shooting event in the host club’s calendar will count towards these 12 annual shoots. Currently, only those undertaken at the pistol shooter’s home club count, which was nonsensical considering pistol shooters regularly travel to compete.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete flaw (home-club-only counting) and gives a logical justification (shooters travel to compete) for the change.

veracity.statement: my message to Simon Court is that public-private partnerships do not work. They cost more money. They take more time. They cut corners and they do not deliver for the people in the community.
veracity.explanation: PPPs have variable records internationally; the blanket claim that they never work and always cut corners is an overstatement not supported by evidence.

veracity.statement: How much did the Government put into Budget 2024? They put in $100 million—literally nothing.
veracity.explanation: The $100m figure may be defensible for a specific capital line, but calling $100 million 'literally nothing' is hyperbole that misleads about scale.

veracity.statement: It’s gone to landlords; it’s gone to tobacco companies.
veracity.explanation: Rhetorical framing implying health capital was diverted to landlords and tobacco firms; conflates separate tax policy decisions with the health budget in a misleading way.

veracity.statement: She has also shortchanged the entire health system by $1.4 billion for operational costs in that health system.
veracity.explanation: The $1.4 billion 'shortchanged' figure is a contested Labour framing of Health NZ's funding gap; presented as settled fact, it lacks the context that would qualify it.

veracity.statement: There is a massive opportunity cost associated with the huge rise in construction costs—since 2019 alone, an increase of some 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: A ~40% rise in construction costs since 2019 is broadly consistent with NZ cost indices over that period.

veracity.explanation: Accurately references the 2022 Commerce Commission market study, which found the building supplies sector lacked competition.

veracity.explanation: Broadly supported by the Commerce Commission's findings of concentration in NZ building supplies, though 'excessive profits' and 'not the best' are contestable characterisations.

veracity.statement: Construction is 20 percent of the jobs in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Overstated: construction is roughly 8-10% of NZ employment, not 20%; the figure appears inflated.

veracity.statement: the cost of timber here is, I think, what, 30 percent more? Something like that—30 percent more than the cost across the Tasman.
veracity.explanation: NZ timber prices being materially higher than Australia's is broadly credible, though the hedged '30 percent' figure is approximate and uncertain.

veracity.statement: it was 36 square metres for $49,000—really, really inexpensive. The people who are wanting to bring these in looked at the cost of doing that in New Zealand, and it was about $90,000-something without all the fit-out.
veracity.explanation: An anecdotal price comparison relayed second-hand ('I was shown'); plausible but unverifiable and not like-for-like given the fit-out caveat.

veracity.statement: the fact that we’ve had a 41 percent increase in construction costs since 2019 is disgraceful.
veracity.explanation: A ~41% construction cost rise since 2019 aligns with the figure cited elsewhere in the debate and with cost indices.

veracity.explanation: The '50% more than Australia' figure is a repeated Government talking point of contested precision; the migration causal gloss is anecdotal.
