veracity.explanation: saveBOARD is a real Hamilton-based manufacturer making board from recycled material; the description is accurate.

veracity.statement: As the Rt Hon Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said a bit earlier this year, it is currently 50 percent more expensive to build a standalone home in New Zealand than in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays a claim Luxon made; the underlying '50% more' figure is a contested but widely-cited estimate of the NZ-Australia build cost gap.

specificity.explanation: Precise detail: the 12-event annual requirement, the exact rule change, and the reason it currently fails.

authenticity.statement: I am bloody proud to be a member of a Labour Party that has a history in this country of building infrastructure, building hospitals, and investing properly in public health
authenticity.explanation: Aligns her stance with a claimed party record of health investment; broadly consistent with Labour's positioning, though the self-praising record is asserted rather than evidenced here.

authenticity.statement: Labour supports this bill because it builds on Labour’s work to make building products cheaper and the market more competitive, which started with the Commerce Commission’s report
authenticity.explanation: Claims continuity with Labour's own record on building competition, consistent with the party's stated position.

authenticity.statement: During the campaign, ACT went about with a building material equivalency register policy. I’m glad to see that such a policy has been adopted into this bill
authenticity.explanation: Ties current support to an explicit prior campaign commitment now reflected in the bill; words and prior position line up.

authenticity.statement: We’ve been very critical of what the Government is doing around social housing. We believe that they’re taking the wrong approach.
authenticity.explanation: Openly reconciles support for this bill with continued opposition elsewhere, showing a consistent stated principle of issue-by-issue judgement.

strength.statement: We are walking and chewing gum, we’re getting it done, we’re trying to reform the system so that we have greater competition, better choice for the consumer, and of course more affordable homes and other buildings in this country.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a bill that is only at first reading; intent and framework are real but nothing is yet enacted or delivered.

strength.statement: During the campaign, ACT went about with a building material equivalency register policy. I’m glad to see that such a policy has been adopted into this bill
strength.explanation: Points to a campaign policy carried into legislation, but the bill is only at first reading so delivery is in progress, not complete.

strength.explanation: A stated commitment on a bill at first reading; intent is clear but delivery is not yet demonstrated.

veracity.statement: What we do know is once they did get oversight, 267 safety improvement notices were issued to the pistol clubs for failing to meet safety standards in the past.

veracity.statement: There are 230,000 licence holders, which is around 4 percent of the population.

veracity.statement: As a firearm owner, I certainly do not support relaxing controls, and most other Kiwis do not support relaxing controls either.

veracity.statement: It might have been the middle of last year, we had two of our whānau going to check out a house in the Whangārei Heads area and ended up being shot by the gentleman that was living in that house.

veracity.explanation: The Arms Act 1983 is indeed around 41 years old in 2024; accurate framing.

rigor.statement: the Ministry of Health, right now, is consulting on their three-year strategy to prevent and minimise gambling harm, which is actually looking at the regulation of overseas online casino gambling in Aotearoa, and yet we're expanding on this form of online gambling. Where is the thinking in terms of the joining-up of these reviews and inputting into ministry strategy right now?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine policy-coherence gap between expanding online gambling and a concurrent harm-minimisation review.

rigor.statement: it's created, actually, in our communities, a pro-gambling constituency who come into select committees and come into spaces to promote the fact that they need to access this gambling funding in order to be sustainable.
rigor.explanation: Offers a structural analysis of how reliance on gambling funding creates its own political constituency.

rigor.statement: class 3 is about non-continuous gambling. It's not like ones when you bid, you lose, you have another go, and it sucks people in—"I can win it if I just keep trying"—and people whittle away money that they maybe cannot afford to lose. In this case, you buy a ticket and you wait
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent distinction between continuous machine gambling and delayed-draw lotteries to support the low-harm argument.

rigor.statement: As the Heart Foundation shared with us, they actually collect all the information they would have if it were done in person. They said they have names and addresses; they can really angle in on people to make sure there are no issues with problem gambling.
rigor.explanation: Uses submitter evidence about data collection to support the claim that harm can be monitored.

rigor.statement: The Government could have said, "While we're doing the policy work, let's do a short exemption of a couple of months or so while we're actually doing that policy work." They could have also brought the bill to the House a little bit sooner.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts Foster's false-dilemma framing by offering concrete alternative pathways to the same end.

rigor.statement: There are currently no laws or regulations explicitly requiring specific harm prevention and minimisation practices of Class 3 lottery operators.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her harm-minimisation argument in the official report text rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: I do support this bill going forward, because I think when you weigh up the benefits against the risks, I think the benefits far outweigh the risks that are there. That is our job as legislators sometimes, to make that line call, but I do still think there is still some potential for harm
rigor.explanation: Explicit benefit-risk weighing that reaches a proportionate conclusion while acknowledging residual risk.

rigor.statement: I don't think it would be unreasonable for class 3 operators under the regulations to have to outline what is a basic harm minimisation approach. I don't think that's onerous. The Heart Foundation already do it... It actually would probably only be a one-page document on how to prevent harm.
rigor.explanation: Supports the feasibility claim with the existing Heart Foundation practice as evidence.

rigor.statement: ultimately, gambling is not a great thing. I'm not a gambler, and so I always think that the dollar is better in your pocket and being put to better use, but this is an occasion where this is a good use.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a personal-preference premise but the 'good use' conclusion leans on assertion more than evidence.

rigor.statement: Labour members at that select committee called for a specific clause to be considered or added to the bill to directly address harm minimisation. I think that would have been a responsible approach.
rigor.explanation: Argues for a specific legislative fix, though the 'responsible' judgement is partly assertion.

rigor.statement: right now, today, as the Israel Defense Forces are burning children in Gaza this week, the idea that we can simply designate a group as a terrorist organisation has its challenges because of the nature of alliances.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an emotive appeal and the 'one man's terrorist' cliché rather than a structured argument.

rigor.statement: I have seen in this country myself—personally, in the case of Ahmed Zaoui—where someone is falsely accused of terrorism and gets on the wrong list and finds themselves in Pāremoremo prison.
rigor.explanation: Uses a single, apt anecdote to illustrate the risk, but generalises from one case.

rigor.statement: This Government has chosen not to implement eight of the 44 recommendations of the royal commission, and I believe that is an affront to the victims, the survivors, and all the communities at risk of hate crimes in our country.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the critique in a specific figure but the leap to 'affront to the victims' is an emotional appeal.

rigor.statement: one of the failings of our way of seeing the world is that we can fail to notice, as our security services did, that the greatest threat was not coming from the Muslim community; it was coming from the white supremacist community.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference from the inquiry's conclusions, though stated broadly.

rigor.statement: Terror doesn't start with bullets and bombs; it starts with hate speech. Especially when left unchecked, it can lead to violence.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical causal claim asserted rather than evidenced; plausible but presented as a slogan.

divination.statement: The Department of Internal Affairs said there is no issue, the submitters were not able to identify any issue in terms of harm, and we haven't seen any issue in terms of harm over the last four years of the operation of class 3 online. What that suggests to me is that there is very little likelihood of harm
divination.explanation: Prediction that harm is very unlikely going forward; reasonable given four years of data but not certain.

divination.statement: another tūpatotanga I want to put here today that I think we need to be prepared for is an influx of applications we're going to have from charities who want to become eligible to raise funds in this manner.
divination.explanation: Predicts a rise in class 3 applications following the change; plausible directionally but unquantified and uncertain.

divination.statement: we were showing him their intentions there to build a floating wharf that will reduce their response time, in many instances, from the currently 45 minutes, while they get it off the boat trailer, to fewer than five minutes.
divination.explanation: Predicts a large response-time reduction; plausible for a floating berth but the specific '45 to under 5 minutes' is optimistic and unverified.

civility.statement: I guess that is what the Opposition is supposed to do, to raise concerns about legislation from the Government. That's what they're doing, and good on them for doing that, but I don't think that those positions hold a lot of water.
civility.explanation: Respectfully legitimises the Opposition's scrutiny role while disagreeing on the merits, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Te Pāti Māori acknowledges the negative impact this industry has had on our people and commits to monitoring the gambling industry in legislation made by this House to further enable it.
civility.explanation: Balances support for the bill with respectful acknowledgement of harm, no personal attacks.

civility.statement: the six days that the community were allowed or enabled to provide submissions were short. For this type of issue, it would have been good to allow for more community voice to come into the select committee process
civility.explanation: Criticises the process, not any person; focused on substance of consultation.

civility.statement: I'm not a big gambling guy—not a huge fan of it in some contexts—so I had a little bit of sympathy for the Salvation Army when they came and spoke to us at the Governance and Administration Committee in opposition to the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill.
civility.explanation: Respectfully engages with an opposing submitter's position and grants it sympathy.

civility.statement: One submitter told the committee that they weren't able to put together a fulsome written submission to present to the committee. We offered them an opportunity for an oral submission, and they said they didn't have time to prepare for that. That was very real, because we literally only had a couple of days for submissions to be presented to the committee.
civility.explanation: Substantive procedural criticism without attacking individuals.

civility.statement: We know the damage that gambling has done to several of our families across Aotearoa, so I hope that the guarantees we've heard today and, of course, the steps that charities themselves are taking to keep our whānau safe from harm will go some way to once again allaying the concerns of our whānau
civility.explanation: Balances support with acknowledgement of community concern, respectful throughout.

civility.statement: It's disappointing to hear that that call from the Labour Party members of that select committee fell on deaf ears and was not supported
civility.explanation: Mild, policy-focused expression of disappointment about a committee outcome, no personal attack.

civility.statement: right now, today, as the Israel Defense Forces are burning children in Gaza this week, the idea that we can simply designate a group as a terrorist organisation has its challenges because of the nature of alliances.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist, emotionally charged framing rather than measured engagement with the designation issue.

civility.statement: This Government has chosen not to implement eight of the 44 recommendations of the royal commission, and I believe that is an affront to the victims, the survivors, and all the communities at risk of hate crimes in our country.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the Government's choices but directed at policy/record rather than personal character; the 'affront' framing edges toward emotive.

charisma.statement: I guess that is what the Opposition is supposed to do, to raise concerns about legislation from the Government. That's what they're doing, and good on them for doing that, but I don't think that those positions hold a lot of water.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opponents' valid function, a mildly bridge-building gesture, though still dismissive of their case.

charisma.statement: it's created, actually, in our communities, a pro-gambling constituency who come into select committees and come into spaces to promote the fact that they need to access this gambling funding in order to be sustainable.
charisma.explanation: Raises a systemic concern that implicitly invites the whole House to reflect, though framed from the Green side.

charisma.statement: I'm not a big gambling guy—not a huge fan of it in some contexts—so I had a little bit of sympathy for the Salvation Army when they came and spoke to us at the Governance and Administration Committee in opposition to the Gambling (Definition of Remote Interactive Gambling) Amendment Bill.
charisma.explanation: Shows willingness to acknowledge the other side's valid concerns before disagreeing.

charisma.statement: The Government could have said, "While we're doing the policy work, let's do a short exemption of a couple of months or so while we're actually doing that policy work." They could have also brought the bill to the House a little bit sooner.
charisma.explanation: Constructive rather than combative — suggests how the Government could have done better while still supporting the bill.

charisma.statement: I don't think it would be unreasonable for class 3 operators under the regulations to have to outline what is a basic harm minimisation approach. I don't think that's onerous. The Heart Foundation already do it... It actually would probably only be a one-page document on how to prevent harm.
charisma.explanation: Frames the ask as modest and already-practised, seeking to bring the Government along.

charisma.statement: This is a really pragmatic change to legislation to allow organisations like the Heart Foundation and The Operating Theatre Trust to increase their revenue and to continue to support the work they do.
charisma.explanation: Positive, consensus-aligned framing but appeals mainly to the shared support already in the room.

charisma.statement: COVID was a disruptive event that took much away, but it also gave us a couple of things, and one of them was innovation. We have seen the efficacy that it has brought to this particular area of fund-raising for that vital charitable sector.
charisma.explanation: Warm, unifying tone celebrating a shared outcome, but appeals to consensus already present.

charisma.statement: Not only should New Zealand be continuing the work that was agreed to in 2001 at the Council of Europe level but we should also be looking for opportunities to improve our arrangements. The EU provides good examples for New Zealand to do this.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, forward-looking framing that invites the House toward an improvement agenda rather than division.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First is committed to policies that protect and enhance our communities, and I suggest that allowing these great organisations to continue to raise funds in this way in an efficient, practical way is good common sense.
authenticity.explanation: States a party value consistent with supporting the bill, but no independent action verifies the broad claim.

authenticity.statement: Te Pāti Māori acknowledges the negative impact this industry has had on our people and commits to monitoring the gambling industry in legislation made by this House to further enable it.
authenticity.explanation: States a monitoring commitment consistent with the party's stance, but it is a forward promise with no action yet visible.

authenticity.statement: I do support this bill going forward, because I think when you weigh up the benefits against the risks, I think the benefits far outweigh the risks that are there. That is our job as legislators sometimes, to make that line call, but I do still think there is still some potential for harm
authenticity.explanation: Position (support with reservations) is consistent with the concerns she raised throughout her speech.

authenticity.statement: ultimately, gambling is not a great thing. I'm not a gambler, and so I always think that the dollar is better in your pocket and being put to better use, but this is an occasion where this is a good use.
authenticity.explanation: States a personal anti-gambling view and reconciles it with her vote, an openly reasoned position rather than contradiction.

authenticity.statement: Labour members at that select committee called for a specific clause to be considered or added to the bill to directly address harm minimisation. I think that would have been a responsible approach.
authenticity.explanation: His stated value aligns with the concrete action Labour members took at committee, showing consistency between words and record.

veracity.statement: as Minister Penk mentioned in his opening speech, it affected 11 percent of New Zealanders just in 2023 alone
veracity.explanation: Factual claim attributed to Minister Penk that cyber-crime affected 11% of New Zealanders in 2023; plausible but 'affected' is undefined and the figure is hard to verify.

veracity.statement: The SecurityBrief New Zealand report reported a total of $6.8 million in losses to cyber-crime between 1 April and 30 June 2024
veracity.explanation: Specific sourced figure; plausible and attributed to a named report, though not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: A significant portion of this amount totalled $5.5 million and stemmed from 11 large incidents, which were a reported loss exceeding $100,000.
veracity.explanation: Detailed sourced breakdown; internally coherent and plausible.

veracity.statement: As best I could see, we weren't actually a signatory of the convention
veracity.explanation: Later speakers (Meager, Brewer) state NZ IS a signatory but not a party; Foster's claim is inaccurate, though softened by the hedge 'as best I could see'.

veracity.statement: This Parliament itself has been subject to a cyber-attack
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the known cyber-attacks on New Zealand's Parliament.

veracity.statement: the report on the Māori economy, which calculated that it grew at nearly twice the rate of the total economy between 2013 and 2018
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named economic report and broadly consistent with published Māori-economy growth figures for that period.

veracity.statement: It wasted $8.5 million of the country's money while they were at it.
veracity.explanation: Cost figure for the Tūhoe raids operation; in the right order of magnitude but hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is not a party to the convention, but it is a signatory to the Budapest Convention.
veracity.explanation: Accurate legal distinction between signatory and party.

veracity.statement: those conventions and those treaties do not have force of law in New Zealand unless incorporated into domestic statute and domestic legislation, and that is what we are doing here today
veracity.explanation: Accurate statement of New Zealand's dualist treaty-incorporation constitutional principle.

veracity.statement: 51 percent of media and telecom businesses and 46 percent of technology firms identified cyber-security as a major risk.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named industry risk report; specific figures that are plausible and sourced.

veracity.statement: more than half of businesses in New Zealand have been targeted by a ransomware attack just in the past year, and one in five of those businesses have said that that attack caused serious disruption to operations
veracity.explanation: Sourced to commissioned research; plausible though survey-based and self-reported.

veracity.statement: One in five of those businesses estimates their organisation is affected by 16 or more ransomware attacks not per year but per quarter—that's 64 per year.
veracity.explanation: A striking figure that reads as an overstatement or misreading of the survey; the arithmetic is emphasised but the underlying claim strains plausibility.

veracity.statement: two-thirds of businesses—and this is quite concerning—admit that they would pay a ransom to retrieve data after a ransomware attack. One in 10 of those would consider paying more than $50,000.
veracity.explanation: Survey-based proportions attributed to the commissioned research; plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: this omnibus bill is 75 pages.
veracity.explanation: A checkable, concrete factual detail about the bill.

veracity.statement: the convention was signed in 2001—23 years ago—and now has 65 member States, predominantly from Europe but also from Asia, North and South America, Australia, and the Pacific. It entered into force in July 2004.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical facts about the Budapest Convention's signing, entry into force, and membership.

veracity.statement: Our Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade wrote to the Council of Europe in 2020 expressing interest, and so today we are beginning that pathway
veracity.explanation: Specific, plausible procedural fact about NZ's accession pathway.

veracity.statement: cyber-crime and fraud at this stage makes up 11 percent of all scam victims in New Zealand and is increasing rapidly
veracity.explanation: The '11 percent of all scam victims' framing is muddled and differs from Trask's earlier '11 percent of New Zealanders'; likely imprecise.

veracity.statement: we repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act before Christmas last year
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the repeal timing.

veracity.statement: the National Policy Statement on Urban Development (NPSUD) 2020, which, of course, actually started life in 2016 but was significantly strengthened in 2020 under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the NPSUD's development timeline.

veracity.statement: Most of New Zealand's wetlands, more than 90 percent of them, have been lost
veracity.explanation: Consistent with well-established estimates of NZ wetland loss (~90%).

veracity.statement: until we moved against the nixing of wetlands, a further 5 percent of the remaining proportion had been lost in the last 10 years
veracity.explanation: Plausible directional claim about recent additional loss, though the precise figure is harder to verify.

veracity.statement: The coal that they run on the West Coast is hard coal for coking purposes; it's not the sort of coal that you'd poke through Huntly in a dry year.
veracity.explanation: Accurate distinction between West Coast coking (bituminous) coal and thermal coal used at Huntly, rebutting the PM's substitution claim.

veracity.statement: In a couple of decades, we had something like a 600 percent increase in nitrogenous fertiliser use in New Zealand, and an increasing intensity of farm practice, particularly in dairying.
veracity.explanation: Large fertiliser-use increase over recent decades is well documented; the exact 600% figure is approximate ('something like').

veracity.statement: The Growing for Good report came out in 2002 from the then Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, Morgan Williams, reporting that we had a growing problem.
veracity.explanation: Accurate reference to a real PCE report and author.

veracity.statement: it was about 100 people who had to get a resource consent because the permitted activity pathway worked and was practical.
veracity.explanation: Presents a specific low figure to counter the 'tens of thousands' claim; plausible but unsourced here.

veracity.statement: the disaster in Havelock North, where people got very sick—people died, in fact. It was a consequence of agricultural contamination of drinking water
veracity.explanation: The 2016 Havelock North campylobacter outbreak caused mass illness and deaths were linked to it; the agricultural-contamination cause is broadly supported by the inquiry.

veracity.statement: the biggest cause of nitrate contamination is dairy cow urine
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the scientific consensus that intensive dairying (cow urine) is a leading source of freshwater nitrate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has cleared more of its lowland rainforest than the United States, than Canada, and than Australia. We have 7 percent of our lowland rainforest left.
veracity.explanation: NZ's extensive lowland forest loss is real, but the specific cross-country ranking and 7% figure are contestable as stated.

veracity.statement: though we've destroyed 90 percent of our wetlands in this country, we're going to make it easy to destroy some of the last 10 percent to mine coal
veracity.explanation: The ~90% wetland-loss figure is sound; the characterisation of the bill's coal-mining wetland provision is a contested interpretation.

veracity.statement: Councils can't even interpret this themselves. They're saying to us that they don't understand it
veracity.explanation: Attributed to select-committee submissions from councils; plausible but a generalisation from unspecified submissions.

specificity.explanation: Cites a percentage and year, but the metric ('affected') is loosely defined.

specificity.explanation: Names a source, exact dollar figure, and a precise date range.

specificity.explanation: Breaks the figure down with a count of incidents and a per-incident threshold.

specificity.statement: From a mana Māori or Te Pāti Māori policy position, we're fundamentally opposed to the bill—we'll just make that clear; fundamentally opposed—and we're opposed on the basis of mana motuhake
specificity.explanation: Clear position with named grounds (mana motuhake, mana ōrite) but no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: the report on the Māori economy, which calculated that it grew at nearly twice the rate of the total economy between 2013 and 2018

specificity.explanation: Names the exact instrument and the precise change being made.

specificity.statement: following recent court decisions that I don't think were expected, that time-critical amendments to section 107 were needed to give councils and consent applicants from several sectors clarity about the law and the certainty they need to plan.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the section, the trigger (court decisions), and the intended effect.

specificity.statement: it was about 100 people who had to get a resource consent because the permitted activity pathway worked and was practical.

specificity.statement: we worked with the Southland Regional Council in league with DairyNZ, Federated Farmers, and Beef + Lamb... and we developed a new variant of that that did work.
specificity.explanation: Names the partners and describes the practical rules (low vs steep slopes, ploughing direction).

specificity.explanation: Names the event and its consequences and cause.

specificity.explanation: Gives a comparative claim and a concrete remaining percentage.

specificity.statement: It's an omnibus apocalypse bill, this one.
specificity.explanation: A vivid label that conveys no concrete content.

divination.statement: the perniciousness and the amount of cyber-crime and the effects of cyber-crime are only going to grow
divination.explanation: Open-ended prediction of rising cyber-crime, consistent with current trends but no timeframe or magnitude.

divination.statement: cyber-crime and fraud at this stage makes up 11 percent of all scam victims in New Zealand and is increasing rapidly
divination.explanation: Predicts continued rapid increase; directionally supported but vague on magnitude.

divination.statement: It's going to take a generation to clean up, but at least under the last Government we were actually on a track to start that cleaning up.
divination.explanation: Predicts a generation-long cleanup timeframe—directionally plausible but imprecise and unfalsifiable in the near term.

divination.statement: We are going to see more degraded waterways, we're going to see more contaminated drinking water, we're going to see a more polluted marine coastal environment... and we're also going to see more destruction of biodiversity.
divination.explanation: A cluster of directional predictions about environmental decline following the bill—plausible in direction but unquantified and unfalsifiable in the near term.

civility.statement: I wish the select committee which is hearing these submissions all the very best in trying to work their way through this.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful remark toward the process and colleagues.

civility.statement: It's good to see that the House is interested in upholding its international treaties, and we look forward to seeing that spread across all of the treaties that pertain to the House and the Treaty partners in it.
civility.explanation: Barbed but not a personal attack; makes its point through irony.

civility.statement: Given the history of Māori being falsely accused of terrorism and other crimes... like we saw in the Tūhoe raids, in a shameful operation that inflicted intergenerational trauma into the Tūhoe people and the Māori people at large.
civility.explanation: Strong language directed at a past state operation rather than at a person present.

civility.statement: We don't have really any recent examples in New Zealand of such a thing, so it's good to be able to talk about a positive coalition in this House.
civility.explanation: A partisan swipe at the governing coalition dressed as a wordplay aside, not policy substance.

civility.statement: I am struggling a little bit with the notion of Māori sovereignty of data. It's not the sovereignty—I get all that and I accept that—but this is about protecting it from overseas people.
civility.explanation: Respectfully engages a coalition partner's position, conceding the valid part before disagreeing.

civility.statement: I think that that's an altogether different conversation that we need to have; a valid one, none the less.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of another party's point.

civility.statement: one of the failings, I would argue, of the RMA in 1991 to actually operate properly is the failure of successive Governments to use national direction properly.
civility.explanation: Criticises 'successive Governments' generally, including his own side, rather than attacking opponents.

civility.statement: It's not just industry—you're letting your prejudices get in the way of a good story there.
civility.explanation: A retort to an interjection that lightly impugns the interjector's motives, though it stays about the argument.

civility.statement: I know the ACT Party, to get elected, went around the country and said, "Tens of thousands of New Zealand farmers were going to have to get a resource consent." No, they didn't; it was about 100 people
civility.explanation: Accuses ACT of campaigning on a false figure; a substantive rebuttal but framed as bad-faith electioneering.

civility.statement: Te Mana o Te Wai is a concept which was originally a National Party term. They've turned against it now because it's a Māori phrase, I think; not because of what's in it.
civility.explanation: Imputes a discreditable (implicitly racial) motive to opponents rather than engaging their stated reasons.

civility.statement: When you hear this Government talking about balance, you know that it's not right. They talk about balance, when, really, what they mean is more pollution.
civility.explanation: Restates opponents' position in its worst form ('what they mean is more pollution')—a strawman.

civility.statement: I do not hate farmers, and I object to the way I was misrepresented by members of the then Opposition at that time.
civility.explanation: Calls out a misrepresentation of himself firmly but without a reciprocal personal attack.

civility.statement: what we need to be able to do is have a mature conversation in this country about the system causes of harm to our environment... without people feeling like we're making a personal affront to farmers. We love farmers and we need farmers.
civility.explanation: Frames the debate around systems, not individuals, and affirms respect for farmers.

civility.statement: farmers are not sociopaths. They do not want to see their animals suffer; they do not want to see their animals die
civility.explanation: Respectful characterisation of opponents' constituency.

civility.statement: It's an omnibus apocalypse bill, this one.
civility.explanation: Sensational hyperbole ('apocalypse') aimed at the legislation.

civility.statement: It turns out that safe drinking water is an unnecessary regulatory burden and it is a barrier to the exploitation of nature.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic restatement of the Government's rationale in its most damning form—a strawman.

civility.statement: What I would love tonight is if the farmers in the room can get their big-boy pants on

forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly answers both parts (yes / no, not concerned) and gives her reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: I think that's something the Auditor-General is looking into right now, and I'll comment once that inquiry is over.

forthrightness.statement: I will not apologise for putting children first and I will not apologise for not accepting the status quo. rigor.statement: When will she admit that she forced Oranga Tamariki into a rushed and confusing contracting process that risks harm to our most vulnerable children because her Government wanted to save 6.5 percent for tax cuts?

veracity.statement: We are well back in the target range of inflation at just 2.2 percent.

veracity.explanation: Loaded partisan framing; much of the inflation was global/post-COVID, so attributing 'six long years' of mismanagement is one-sided and misleading.

veracity.statement: By 2050, more than 10,000 homes of whānau in our biggest cities will become uninsurable.
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported by climate/insurance analyses, though presented as certain when it is a projection.

veracity.statement: why did the Government reject the Dunedin City Council’s plea for $132.5 million to help the city cope with climate impacts earlier this year?
veracity.explanation: References a concrete, checkable funding request; embedded factual claim is plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: On cost of living: we’ve had it announced that inflation is down to a record 2.2 percent, interest rates 4.75 percent.
veracity.explanation: Inflation 2.2% and OCR 4.75% (after the Oct 2024 cut) are accurate; 'record' is loose since inflation has been lower before, mildly overstated.

veracity.statement: Business confidence is the highest in nearly a decade.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with 2024 business-confidence surveys reaching multi-year highs; broadly accurate but survey-dependent.

veracity.statement: I want to thank those in the police force for bringing to justice 40 Comancheros, and that is having positive ripples throughout our country. We’ve had a 22 percent reduction in serious assaults in Auckland.
veracity.explanation: The 22% reduction is a specific statistic asserted without a source or period; plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: We’ve axed wasteful spending projects like light rail, three waters, Let’s Get Wellington Moving, Lake Onslow, contracts and consultants, and back-office staff, which has saved taxpayers billions of dollars.
veracity.explanation: The projects were indeed cancelled, but 'saved taxpayers billions' bundles disputed accounting and is partly rhetorical.

veracity.statement: he’s cancelled local classroom buildings, he’s closing North Shore Women’s Centre, he’s cancelled the counselling services at the Salvation Army, he’s reduced our police numbers, he’s cut funding to Kaipātiki projects, and he’s cut jobs
veracity.explanation: A list of specific claims attributing local service losses to the local MP; plausible but presented one-sidedly and unverified here.

veracity.statement: The Government has cut $564 million from the next three years of Auckland’s long-term plan in the National Land Transport Programme 2024 to 2027
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable claim about NLTP allocations; plausible but the 'cut' framing depends on the baseline chosen.

veracity.statement: In the year ending July 2024, 27 deaths were recorded in the year, down from six fatalities in the previous 12 months
veracity.explanation: Internally contradictory — 27 cannot be 'down from six' — the figures as stated are garbled or misstated.

veracity.statement: For the first time, Māori on the Māori roll now out-populate Māori on the general roll
veracity.explanation: Following the 2023 roll changes more Māori were on the Māori roll than the general roll — consistent with Electoral Commission data.

veracity.statement: If I just pick one university, a top university—University of Auckland—it is no longer in the top 150 universities. It’s quite disappointing to see that we don’t have any universities in the top 150

veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the announced 15-point compulsory course; broadly correct as reported.

veracity.statement: Today’s Stats New Zealand announcement that the Consumers Price Index is back to 2.2 percent from its high of 7 percent in 2022 is indeed great news.
veracity.explanation: CPI 2.2% (Sept 2024 qtr) and a 2022 peak near 7.3% are both accurate.

veracity.statement: Tax cuts have been delivered into our homes, FamilyBoost is helping families, and interest rates are now down by 75 basis points

specificity.statement: We are well back in the target range of inflation at just 2.2 percent.

specificity.statement: We're extending breast screening to women aged 70 to 74. At the outset, that should save about 22 lives a year, and at its full implementation, about 65 lives a year.
specificity.explanation: Names the age band, the mechanism, and quantified life-saving estimates at two stages.

specificity.statement: One of my big key priorities as the Minister for Women is bringing down that very, very stubborn gender pay gap. I'm going to be announcing the work that we're going to be doing on that very, very shortly
specificity.explanation: States a priority but supplies no mechanism, target, or firm date — 'very shortly' commits to nothing concrete.

specificity.statement: We are putting more cops back on the beat, keeping our people safe.
specificity.explanation: General claim of more police with no numbers, timeframe, or named programme.

specificity.statement: On 2 May, I asked the first question of the Minister about the contracts that were coming up for expiry, and she said in the answer, “I expect that these reviews will prioritise the outcomes for children. [And] Some of these decisions are still Budget-sensitive, and we will find out more when the Budget is announced.”
specificity.explanation: Precise dates and verbatim quotes anchoring the timeline of the procurement process.

specificity.statement: By 2050, more than 10,000 homes of whānau in our biggest cities will become uninsurable.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure (10,000+ homes), a date (2050), and a scope (biggest cities).

specificity.statement: why did the Government reject the Dunedin City Council’s plea for $132.5 million to help the city cope with climate impacts earlier this year?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise dollar figure ($132.5m) and a specific request from a named council.

specificity.statement: On cost of living: we’ve had it announced that inflation is down to a record 2.2 percent, interest rates 4.75 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two precise current figures cited.

specificity.statement: I want to thank those in the police force for bringing to justice 40 Comancheros, and that is having positive ripples throughout our country. We’ve had a 22 percent reduction in serious assaults in Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures — 40 gang members, 22% assault reduction in Auckland.

specificity.statement: We’ve axed wasteful spending projects like light rail, three waters, Let’s Get Wellington Moving, Lake Onslow, contracts and consultants, and back-office staff, which has saved taxpayers billions of dollars.
specificity.explanation: Names specific cancelled projects, though 'billions' is an imprecise aggregate.

specificity.statement: he’s cancelled local classroom buildings, he’s closing North Shore Women’s Centre, he’s cancelled the counselling services at the Salvation Army, he’s reduced our police numbers, he’s cut funding to Kaipātiki projects, and he’s cut jobs
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete named local cuts (women's centre, Salvation Army counselling, Kaipātiki projects).

specificity.statement: This is a Government that is choosing to spend $2 million for landlords and $216 million for tobacco companies.
specificity.explanation: Two precise dollar figures tied to named beneficiaries.

specificity.statement: The Government has cut $564 million from the next three years of Auckland’s long-term plan in the National Land Transport Programme 2024 to 2027
specificity.explanation: Names the figure ($564m), the timeframe (2024-2027), and the specific programme.

specificity.statement: Cycleways will lose about $90 million, or 35 percent of their funding. Electrification of ferries will have $89 million deferred, and buses will get $59 million less
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise dollar figures and percentages broken down by transport mode.

specificity.statement: For the first time, Māori on the Māori roll now out-populate Māori on the general roll
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable demographic claim, though without exact numbers.

specificity.statement: If we are 20 percent of the population, that would translate into more seats in this House if all of our people were on the Māori roll—18 to 20 seats. But because we have people still on the general roll—Māori people on the general roll—we get half of what we should be getting, which is seven Māori seats
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the population share (20%) and projected seat counts (7 now vs 14-20).

specificity.statement: E hika mā, get on the Māori roll, ensure that we have more on the Māori roll to ensure we have more Māori seats for more Māori voices.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, actionable ask (enrol on the Māori roll) tied to a clear goal, though no numbers.

specificity.statement: If I just pick one university, a top university—University of Auckland—it is no longer in the top 150 universities. It’s quite disappointing to see that we don’t have any universities in the top 150
specificity.explanation: Names the specific ranking threshold (top 150) and university.

specificity.statement: the University of Auckland has announced that they are going to introduce a compulsory course to teach the Treaty of Waitangi and Māori world view. This is a compulsory course worth 15 points for all undergraduate degrees
specificity.explanation: States the course content, that it is compulsory, its point value (15), and its scope (all undergraduate degrees).

specificity.statement: Today’s Stats New Zealand announcement that the Consumers Price Index is back to 2.2 percent from its high of 7 percent in 2022 is indeed great news.
specificity.explanation: Cites both the current figure and the 2022 peak with the source (Stats NZ).

specificity.statement: Tax cuts have been delivered into our homes, FamilyBoost is helping families, and interest rates are now down by 75 basis points
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policies and a precise rate movement (75 basis points).

specificity.statement: scrapping fair pay agreements—agreements that would have led to higher wages and better conditions for some of our most vulnerable workers: bus drivers, cleaners, early childhood education teachers, supermarket workers, security guards—reinstating 90-day trials
specificity.explanation: Names specific policy reversals (fair pay agreements, 90-day trials) and the concrete worker groups affected.

specificity.statement: the Global Slavery Index says, on even any given day, 8,000 people in New Zealand are living in modern slavery.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named source and a precise figure.

specificity.statement: inflation today, Stats NZ, the number is out: 2.2 percent... I remember, when I came into Parliament about 2½ years ago, we were sitting at over 7 percent, and then it was 5.6 percent last year, and here we are with a National-led Government in charge: 2.2 percent.
specificity.explanation: A precise trajectory of figures across three time points.

specificity.statement: The Mood of the Boardroom survey recently had confidence in the economy at 3.23 out of five. That’s the highest it has been since 2016... You compare that to where the Mood of the Boardroom was last year, at 1.82 over 5.
specificity.explanation: Named survey, exact scores, and a comparison year.

specificity.statement: The Infrastructure Commission estimates that every year we spend $1.3 billion on the time taken to get a resource consent, and that has nearly doubled in the last five years.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, a dollar figure ($1.3bn/year), and a five-year trend.

specificity.statement: It’s unacceptable to spend six years in a consenting process for something that was included in the Regional Coastal Environment Plan 30 years ago.
specificity.explanation: Concrete timeframes (six years, 30 years ago) tied to the Port of Tauranga consent.

specificity.statement: the Bell Road Limited Partnership in Wairakei South is going to add 2,000 to 3,000 new homes. We’ve got the Tauriko West housing and land development. There’s another 1,250 homes... Now, we look at the fast-track and we have got 58 housing and land development projects; opening up 55,000 homes
specificity.explanation: Named developments with precise home counts (2,000-3,000; 1,250; 55,000 total across 58 projects).

specificity.statement: This bill enables people to move on immediately, and it came about because of three women.
specificity.explanation: States the concrete effect of the bill (immediate dissolution) and its origin, though the mechanism is elaborated elsewhere.

specificity.statement: instead of waiting for two years for a divorce to become final, in fact that could happen within six months.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after mechanism — two-year stand-down reduced to six months in family-violence cases.

strength.statement: We're increasing paid parental leave by 6 percent.
strength.explanation: A concrete deliverable, but this is the routine annual indexation adjustment rather than a discretionary policy win; partial follow-through claim.

strength.statement: We're extending breast screening to women aged 70 to 74. At the outset, that should save about 22 lives a year, and at its full implementation, about 65 lives a year.
strength.explanation: A concrete announced extension, but at this date it is a stated policy in progress rather than fully implemented and verified delivery.

strength.statement: One of my big key priorities as the Minister for Women is bringing down that very, very stubborn gender pay gap. I'm going to be announcing the work that we're going to be doing on that very, very shortly
strength.explanation: A promise to announce future work; announcement of intent to announce is aspiration, not demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: We are putting more cops back on the beat, keeping our people safe.
strength.explanation: Points to a policing commitment in progress, but no delivered figures are given to substantiate follow-through.

strength.statement: We’ve axed wasteful spending projects like light rail, three waters, Let’s Get Wellington Moving, Lake Onslow, contracts and consultants, and back-office staff, which has saved taxpayers billions of dollars.
strength.explanation: Cancelling named projects is demonstrable action, but the 'billions saved' claim is an unverified aggregate and labelling them 'wasteful' is contestable.

strength.statement: Tax cuts have been delivered into our homes, FamilyBoost is helping families, and interest rates are now down by 75 basis points
strength.explanation: Points to delivered measures (tax cuts, FamilyBoost) rather than mere promises, though rate cuts are the RBNZ's action not the government's.

strength.statement: This bill enables people to move on immediately, and it came about because of three women.
strength.explanation: She has shepherded the bill to its third reading — a concrete legislative change actually being delivered, not merely promised.

divination.statement: We're extending breast screening to women aged 70 to 74. At the outset, that should save about 22 lives a year, and at its full implementation, about 65 lives a year.
divination.explanation: Predicts 22 then 65 lives saved annually; consistent with health modelling but the magnitude is an estimate and unverified.

divination.statement: By 2050, more than 10,000 homes of whānau in our biggest cities will become uninsurable.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable long-range forecast to 2050; directionally consistent with insurance-retreat modelling but the specific magnitude is uncertain.

divination.statement: if the student doesn’t like this course, of course the grades won’t be what overall we would like to see, and the overall grades of that student will suffer.
divination.explanation: Predicts falling student grades; speculative and not grounded in evidence.

divination.statement: because of this space that is going to be created for this compulsory Treaty of Waitangi and Māori world view course, other components will be pushed on to the rest of the time that is left for that degree and that is going to create more pressure on students. So who is going to suffer? Students. And, in the long run, our country is going to suffer.
divination.explanation: Predicts national-level harm from a single 15-point paper; implausibly large effect from a small cause.

divination.statement: when the Labour Government is re-elected in 2026, you will know us by our actions, because we are the true party of working people. We will be reinstating all of these policies that have been cruelly taken away
divination.explanation: Predicts Labour's 2026 re-election as a given; an optimistic partisan forecast with uncertain evidence.

divination.statement: the Bell Road Limited Partnership in Wairakei South is going to add 2,000 to 3,000 new homes. We’ve got the Tauriko West housing and land development. There’s another 1,250 homes... Now, we look at the fast-track and we have got 58 housing and land development projects; opening up 55,000 homes
divination.explanation: Projects tens of thousands of homes will be delivered via fast-track; an optimistic forecast contingent on the projects actually proceeding.

civility.statement: We are not a Government that is spraying a fire hose of cash across this economy—which caused the Reserve Bank to ratchet up interest rates harder and faster than many of us have seen in our lifetime.
civility.explanation: Pointed dig at the previous government's fiscal approach, but aimed at policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: We know families have been bearing the brunt of the economic mismanagement of the previous Labour Government for six long years
civility.explanation: Harsh characterisation ('economic mismanagement') of opponents, but directed at their record rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: It has been an absolutely shambolic process, so I welcome the Auditor-General’s inquiry into this process.
civility.explanation: 'Shambolic' is a harsh but legitimate criticism of the process rather than a personal attack on the Minister.

civility.statement: We are seeing the devastating impact for our social service providers, but, more importantly, the vulnerable children and families who they serve, who are in absolute disarray because of this Minister’s cruel cuts that are absolutely front-line services to our most vulnerable children and tamariki.
civility.explanation: 'Cruel cuts' and 'absolute disarray' escalate into emotive characterisation of the Minister's motives rather than sticking to the substance.

civility.statement: the planet’s on fire and all we’re hearing from this Government is lukewarm, lame excuses.
civility.explanation: 'Lame excuses' is dismissive rhetoric aimed at the government rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Members opposite surely know that sniffing fossil fuels damages brain cells. Addiction to fossil fuels is dangerous, and I can see droopy heads opposite
civility.explanation: Personal jibe implying opponents are brain-damaged/impaired ('droopy heads') — an insult, not policy critique.

civility.statement: all we’ve heard from the Government is that it will look to develop a national climate change adaptation framework by some time next year. It is pathetic.
civility.explanation: 'Pathetic' is a dismissive value judgement on the government's pace rather than substantive engagement, though it targets the policy.

civility.statement: If the opposite side was keen on seeing stuff built in this country, they’d come on board and support our fast-track legislation.
civility.explanation: Implies bad faith of opponents but stays on the policy terrain of the fast-track bill.

civility.statement: since Scar took over this kingdom and the darkness invaded our lives and communities in Tāmaki-makau-rau
civility.explanation: Casts the government as the villain 'Scar' bringing 'darkness' — theatrical demonisation rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: We have for too long been over-investigated, over-convicted, over-policed, over-stereotyped, over-incarcerated, overlooked, over-regulated, undereducated, undervalued, under-classed, assimilated, and subjugated in a racist and white supremacist system to make tangata whenua more like settlers.
civility.explanation: Sweeping 'racist and white supremacist system' framing is confrontational, though aimed at institutions/systems rather than a named individual.

civility.statement: You’re not Māori.
civility.explanation: A personal interjection targeting another member's identity rather than any argument.

civility.statement: Our Government inherited a complete shemozzle, rivalled only by the woes of Wellington City Council right now—inflation at a high; interest rates, high; and the only solution, it seemed, was for the previous Government to throw some more money at it, run for the hills, and hope that it might go away.
civility.explanation: 'Run for the hills' mocks the previous government's approach; harsh but aimed at their fiscal conduct rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I challenge that member to take that course. Personal challenge: take that course and tell me after you’ve finished it if you don’t think of it and your mind doesn’t turn to it every single day
civility.explanation: A pointed but good-faith challenge that engages the substance of the disagreement rather than attacking the member personally.

civility.statement: I say to those parties: show me that you are the party of working people by your actions. When I look over them, all I see is the biggest attack on workers’ rights since 30 years ago, when the Employment Contracts Act came in.
civility.explanation: Confrontational framing ('attack on workers') but directed at the parties' policy record rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Thank you, Labour!
civility.explanation: A sarcastic jab blaming Labour for rising consent costs; mild, aimed at the party's record.

civility.statement: Here, I’d also like to thank the Hon Chris Bishop for the work that he did to support Ashley as she was putting together her work in this area.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's contribution.

rigor.statement: We are not a Government that is spraying a fire hose of cash across this economy—which caused the Reserve Bank to ratchet up interest rates harder and faster than many of us have seen in our lifetime.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between fiscal spending and rate rises with colourful metaphor but no evidence; a plausible but unsubstantiated causal claim.

rigor.statement: On 2 May, I asked the first question of the Minister about the contracts that were coming up for expiry, and she said in the answer, “I expect that these reviews will prioritise the outcomes for children. [And] Some of these decisions are still Budget-sensitive, and we will find out more when the Budget is announced.”
rigor.explanation: Builds a case with a dated, sourced chronology (2 May, Budget, 17 June, 1 July) quoting specific answers, letting the conclusion follow from evidence.

rigor.statement: We are seeing the devastating impact for our social service providers, but, more importantly, the vulnerable children and families who they serve, who are in absolute disarray because of this Minister’s cruel cuts that are absolutely front-line services to our most vulnerable children and tamariki.
rigor.explanation: Emotive appeal ('devastating', 'cruel') asserting front-line harm without the evidence of impact offered elsewhere in the speech.

rigor.statement: the planet’s on fire and all we’re hearing from this Government is lukewarm, lame excuses.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbole ('planet's on fire') and appeal to emotion with no evidence in this sentence.

rigor.statement: Members opposite surely know that sniffing fossil fuels damages brain cells. Addiction to fossil fuels is dangerous, and I can see droopy heads opposite
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem dressed as a metaphor; no logical connection between the quip and any argument.

rigor.statement: If the opposite side was keen on seeing stuff built in this country, they’d come on board and support our fast-track legislation.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — opposing this particular bill is equated with not wanting anything built.

rigor.statement: In the year ending July 2024, 27 deaths were recorded in the year, down from six fatalities in the previous 12 months
rigor.explanation: The statistic he cites to make his safety argument is self-contradictory, undermining the reasoning.

rigor.statement: If we are 20 percent of the population, that would translate into more seats in this House if all of our people were on the Māori roll—18 to 20 seats. But because we have people still on the general roll—Māori people on the general roll—we get half of what we should be getting, which is seven Māori seats
rigor.explanation: A genuine proportional-representation argument with a stated premise and conclusion, though it simplifies how Māori seat numbers are actually calculated.

rigor.statement: We have for too long been over-investigated, over-convicted, over-policed, over-stereotyped, over-incarcerated, overlooked, over-regulated, undereducated, undervalued, under-classed, assimilated, and subjugated in a racist and white supremacist system to make tangata whenua more like settlers.
rigor.explanation: The disproportionate-incarceration/policing claims have real evidentiary support, but the rhetorical pile-up substitutes emphasis for cited evidence.

rigor.statement: if the student doesn’t like this course, of course the grades won’t be what overall we would like to see, and the overall grades of that student will suffer.
rigor.explanation: Assumes not liking a course necessarily lowers grades and drags down the whole GPA — an unsupported causal leap.

rigor.statement: because of this space that is going to be created for this compulsory Treaty of Waitangi and Māori world view course, other components will be pushed on to the rest of the time that is left for that degree and that is going to create more pressure on students. So who is going to suffer? Students. And, in the long run, our country is going to suffer.
rigor.explanation: The 'crowding-out' point has a kernel of logic, but the escalation to 'the country is going to suffer' is a slippery-slope leap without evidence.

rigor.statement: Our Government inherited a complete shemozzle, rivalled only by the woes of Wellington City Council right now—inflation at a high; interest rates, high; and the only solution, it seemed, was for the previous Government to throw some more money at it, run for the hills, and hope that it might go away.
rigor.explanation: Caricatures the prior government's policy as just 'throwing money' with no evidence — a strawman of their approach.

rigor.statement: It’s ironic that in the recent economic growth statistics and report, Tāirāwhiti was leading the country in economic growth... that is money largely being spent in the construction sector on fixing up Tāirāwhiti after the cyclone.
rigor.explanation: Adds context that undercuts a headline statistic, showing disciplined reasoning rather than spin.

rigor.statement: If we can create more jobs, then we can get more people off the benefit, into work—that brings more to people’s self-worth than we might imagine. It brings them a new community, a sense of achievement, and a future.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable causal chain (jobs → off benefit → wellbeing), but leans on assertion and emotional appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Then we heard during the election campaign a reassuring word from the now Prime Minister: “We are going to not be reducing sick pay.”, he said. And what do we see when we see this Government come in? We see one of the proposals is to reduce sick pay for part-time workers.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes a quoted campaign statement against a specific subsequent proposal — an evidence-based words-vs-actions contrast.

rigor.statement: I say to those parties: show me that you are the party of working people by your actions. When I look over them, all I see is the biggest attack on workers’ rights since 30 years ago, when the Employment Contracts Act came in.
rigor.explanation: The 'biggest attack since the ECA' is a strong comparative claim; she partly substantiates it with a list, but the superlative is asserted.

rigor.statement: The Infrastructure Commission estimates that every year we spend $1.3 billion on the time taken to get a resource consent, and that has nearly doubled in the last five years.
rigor.explanation: Backs the case for fast-track with a cited estimate from a named body and a trend — evidence-based reasoning.

rigor.statement: It’s unacceptable to spend six years in a consenting process for something that was included in the Regional Coastal Environment Plan 30 years ago.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete example to support the fast-track argument, though it relies on one case to indict the whole regime.

charisma.statement: Members opposite surely know that sniffing fossil fuels damages brain cells. Addiction to fossil fuels is dangerous, and I can see droopy heads opposite
charisma.explanation: Mocking, us-vs-them ridicule of opponents that shuts down rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: If the opposite side was keen on seeing stuff built in this country, they’d come on board and support our fast-track legislation.
charisma.explanation: Frames opponents as not wanting things built — a wedge rather than an attempt to win them over.

charisma.statement: since Scar took over this kingdom and the darkness invaded our lives and communities in Tāmaki-makau-rau
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-them narrative that rallies his own side by villainising opponents.

charisma.statement: E hika mā, get on the Māori roll, ensure that we have more on the Māori roll to ensure we have more Māori seats for more Māori voices.
charisma.explanation: Rousing and effective at mobilising his own constituency, but inward-directed rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: I’m calling on the University of Auckland to be inclusive and be forward-looking in their approach. I would like to see that they create the environment where all perspectives are respected, not just a one-sided view enforced on students.
charisma.explanation: Frames her ask in inclusive language ('all perspectives respected'), though it is one-sided in treating the course itself as the imposition.

charisma.statement: I took a compulsory course on Te Tiriti o Waitangi when I was a university student in my 20s, and I have used that information and knowledge every single day that I have been working in New Zealand since that date.
charisma.explanation: Uses personal testimony to persuade, but is essentially arguing against the opposing member rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I challenge that member to take that course. Personal challenge: take that course and tell me after you’ve finished it if you don’t think of it and your mind doesn’t turn to it every single day
charisma.explanation: An invitational challenge that tries to bring the opponent to a shared experience, though framed adversarially.

charisma.statement: Here, I’d also like to thank the Hon Chris Bishop for the work that he did to support Ashley as she was putting together her work in this area.
charisma.explanation: Warmly credits a senior Government minister from the opposing side, building cross-party goodwill on a shared cause.

charisma.statement: Thank you to everyone across the House who’s worked on this bill, especially the members of the Justice Committee. Thank you to all those who have supported it.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying thanks that spans the whole House and seeks common ownership of the achievement.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I’m going to explain that, because this course is—all students will have to study. forthrightness.explanation: In response to the interjection 'How? How will it create suffering?' she does begin to answer, but the answer is a speculative illustration rather than direct evidence of harm.

authenticity.statement: I took a compulsory course on Te Tiriti o Waitangi when I was a university student in my 20s, and I have used that information and knowledge every single day that I have been working in New Zealand since that date.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds her position in her own consistent lived experience — words matched by her stated personal use of the knowledge.

authenticity.statement: when the Labour Government is re-elected in 2026, you will know us by our actions, because we are the true party of working people. We will be reinstating all of these policies that have been cruelly taken away
authenticity.explanation: Commits to reinstating the named policies, tying future action to stated values, though it is a forward promise not yet backed by deeds.

authenticity.statement: I replied that the previous Government had declined a proposal. What I should have said was that the previous Government did not fund the proposal.
