forthrightness.statement: Let me say that we're willing to look into all information, but the country that I belong to is a country called New Zealand, and it will be that way until the New Zealand people decide to change its name—not by some elite purpose, but because we believe in referendum and consensus.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about police data on faith-motivated hate crimes targeting Muslims, he pivots to litigating the use of 'Aotearoa' and never addresses the substance.

forthrightness.statement: To address this, we are moving to a single-supervisor model, with the Department of Internal Affairs taking the lead. This consolidation will simplify compliance, ensure more efficient decision making, and ensure that guidance and support to businesses is provided sooner.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how the supervisory model change will cut red tape by naming the specific structural reform.

forthrightness.statement: It is my recollection that there were two interactions with the individual. That doesn't change the overall picture of events, where I acknowledge that I caused offence. I accept that, and that is why I've apologised. However, as I've repeatedly said, I did not have any alcohol prior to any interactions with the individual. I did have a small wine tasting at the end of the day.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question about the number of interactions (two, not three) and addresses alcohol, but hedges on the substance of what was said.

forthrightness.statement: The important thing is that I had an interaction which caused offence, and for that reason I have apologised unreservedly.
forthrightness.explanation: Woods repeatedly asks what he actually said to the worker; he pivots each time to the apology and never states the words.

forthrightness.statement: To spell it out for the member: someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Of course, avoiding this or any other sanction is simple. Beneficiaries only need comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the framing of money management as 'non-financial' by explaining beneficiaries keep the full benefit, though it sidesteps the hardship-assistance restriction raised.

forthrightness.statement: We inherited from the last Government no regime, no Cabinet decisions—there was some consultation—but the good news is that the Government will have a bill in the House by the end of the year to introduce an offshore regulatory regime, and that will provide the opportunities for many companies to investigate and get access to our amazing offshore wind regime.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines responsibility for BlueFloat's withdrawal but does directly own the regulatory work and commit to a bill timeline.

forthrightness.statement: Parents and caregivers can receive 25 percent of their early childhood education fees after the 20 hours' early childhood education and Ministry of Social Development childcare subsidy have been taken into account, up to a maximum fortnightly payment of $150. Payments are made quarterly as a lump sum, so parents and caregivers can receive up to $975 in a three-month period. This is the maximum payment, and people will receive a range of amounts depending on their particular circumstances. To ensure the support is well targeted, the maximum payment reduces for family incomes over $140,000 a year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers how much parents can receive.

forthrightness.statement: The previous Government contributed to significant building of warm and dry homes, but unfortunately did that in an absurdly unsustainable manner. Now, we know that many of the children that have left emergency housing have gone into houses that were built under the previous National Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Pressed on how many houses his Government built, he concedes many were built under the previous Government but does not give the number asked for.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Government is bringing back three-strikes legislation. Just this week, my excellent colleague Minister McKee announced the Government will recommend modifications to three strikes to strengthen the regime. Next Tuesday, public submissions to the Justice Committee close on the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what other actions the Government is taking with named measures.

forthrightness.statement: At the end of the day, I am really proud of the fact that, under this programme, more young people will be receiving food than were receiving it before, and we are actually spending the same amount of money doing what this Government promised to do and bringing back some discipline to our finances.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about the procurement process for primary schools, she pivots entirely to talking points about pride and finances.

forthrightness.statement: What I would say is that I am proud of the fact that every student that is receiving a meal today will receive a meal on the first day of term 1 next year, plus an extra 10,000 young people who really need that food will be provided with food.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about staff losses and the March advice, restating the continuity/expansion message instead.

forthrightness.statement: The Police-led change programme to triple one calls to a multi-agency response is a three- to five-year programme that myself and Mark Mitchell are taking back to Cabinet at the end of this year, because the last Labour Government cancelled that programme when they came into office, so we've lost six years.
forthrightness.explanation: Clarifies the questioner's conflation of two programmes and gives the timeline, though partly redirecting blame.

forthrightness.statement: There is a programme called the New Zealand Police Change Programme. It's not actually happening next week, but it's happening on 4 November. There are three succinct changes, and one is around the request to transport patients.
forthrightness.explanation: Corrects the premise and gives a concrete date and detail in response to the safety question.

forthrightness.statement: I've made it very clear to my officials that we are in this direction of travel, because it is better to have a mental health response than a police response to mental distress, unless, of course, the individual or people around them are at risk. I've made it very clear that an agreed action plan needs to be in place that safely allows that change. If that plan is not in place between Police and Health, then that stage will not be activated.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the consultation/safety concern by setting out the conditional gating of the change, though not confirming whether workers were consulted.

forthrightness.statement: That member can ask that question, but she might like to reflect on how we lost six years in the change programme to responding to police crisis calls because, for all their talk about mental health, the first thing those members did was come in and cancel the mental health call-out programme—the co-response programme.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he is 'building the plane while flying it', he does not engage and instead redirects to attacking the opposition's record.

charisma.statement: Not at this stage, but I'm always open to a discussion.
charisma.explanation: Mild, cooperative tone that leaves the door open to the opposition on scheduling.

charisma.statement: Let me say that we're willing to look into all information, but the country that I belong to is a country called New Zealand, and it will be that way until the New Zealand people decide to change its name—not by some elite purpose, but because we believe in referendum and consensus.
charisma.explanation: 'Not by some elite purpose' is an us-vs-them framing rather than a bridge-building response.

charisma.statement: Mr Goldsmith is making sure the laws are fit for purpose, and we're not going to go around as some silly elitist Māori extremists supporting gangsters.
charisma.explanation: Pure demonising us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: What would I know? Well, a whole lot more than you, sunshine. I've been around—in fact, your tribe is where it is today because of a young lawyer called Winston Peters, who started the case against the Labour Party and the Crown, and he won. And there you sit, a beneficiary, with no appreciation. Start being Māori—
charisma.explanation: Aggressive and alienating, the opposite of consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I've said it before and I'll say it again: the parties on this side of the House are on the side of the working people.
charisma.explanation: A partisan rally line that appeals to her own side rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: I'm committed to supporting Te Rōpū Whakahaere to reach an enduring solution by consensus, especially given the legacy of raupatu; multiple whakapapa connections and interests in this whenua; and the use of nearly $30 million of taxpayer funding, effectively under land for housing, for this project under the previous Government.
charisma.explanation: Frames the goal as consensus-building and acknowledges the complexity of competing interests.

charisma.statement: I'm happy to say that this appointment was consulted on and is supported across the House. I think that's a really, really important thing. He certainly is someone who the Labour Party is confident has the skills but also the independence and integrity for this role, which is so critical to our democracy.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-House support and lends the opposition's confidence to a government appointment — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I'd like to thank Dame Marie Shroff for her mahi in maintaining public confidence in our elections—in contrast to the growing distrust of elections around the world.
charisma.explanation: Unifying tone that praises institutional stewardship across party lines.

civility.statement: The deceit and underhandedness shown by Verrall throughout her constant political attacks and smear campaign against one of my Ministers has now writ large, having simultaneously misled the leader of the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack imputing 'deceit and underhandedness' to a named MP rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Using a personal explanation not only to reiterate an unsubstantiated accusation but also build on that, to me, seems to be a questionable approach.
civility.explanation: Challenges Peters' procedural use rather than his character; a measured process objection.

civility.statement: What you've got here is someone asking the same stupid question when she's had the answer and she's got no evidence that what she's got to say is being backed up at all. It's typical of her style.
civility.explanation: Calls a colleague's questions 'stupid' and disparages her 'style' — a personal put-down rather than engagement.

civility.statement: To spell it out for the member: someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Of course, avoiding this or any other sanction is simple. Beneficiaries only need comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work.
civility.explanation: 'To spell it out for the member' is mildly condescending but the substance is policy-focused.

civility.statement: Mr Goldsmith is making sure the laws are fit for purpose, and we're not going to go around as some silly elitist Māori extremists supporting gangsters.
civility.explanation: Derides opponents as 'silly elitist Māori extremists supporting gangsters' — a slur rather than engagement.

civility.statement: What would I know? Well, a whole lot more than you, sunshine. I've been around—in fact, your tribe is where it is today because of a young lawyer called Winston Peters, who started the case against the Labour Party and the Crown, and he won. And there you sit, a beneficiary, with no appreciation. Start being Māori—
civility.explanation: Belittling personal attack ('sunshine', 'a beneficiary, with no appreciation', 'Start being Māori') aimed squarely at another member.

civility.statement: The previous administration couldn't run a school tuck shop. We're showing them how it's done now.
civility.explanation: A dismissive jibe at opponents' competence rather than substantive criticism.

civility.statement: But I'll tell you what we won't be doing: we won't be putting in place building blocks for a massive dam in the bottom of the South Island that stymied investment into the renewables sector, otherwise known as Lake Onslow, advanced by that previous Minister.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig at the previous Minister's Lake Onslow project, but aimed at a policy rather than the person.

civility.statement: Under the last Government's watch, we had an emergency housing catastrophe. Tamariki and whānau deserve better than growing up stuck in dank emergency hotels.
civility.explanation: 'Catastrophe' and 'dank emergency hotels' are heated but aimed at the previous Government's policy record.

civility.statement: I am very committed to supporting Te Rōpū Whakahaere to come to an enduring solution for Ihumātao. What I'm not supportive of is the member and others inventing stories out of the Brothers Grimm, or fables curated from the Waatea news room.
civility.explanation: Accuses the questioner of 'inventing stories' — a dismissive characterisation rather than engaging the documents cited.

civility.statement: That member can ask that question, but she might like to reflect on how we lost six years in the change programme to responding to police crisis calls because, for all their talk about mental health, the first thing those members did was come in and cancel the mental health call-out programme—the co-response programme.
civility.explanation: A jab at the opposition's record ('for all their talk'), pointed but about their policy decision.

civility.statement: I'm happy to say that this appointment was consulted on and is supported across the House. I think that's a really, really important thing. He certainly is someone who the Labour Party is confident has the skills but also the independence and integrity for this role, which is so critical to our democracy.
civility.explanation: Gracious, substance-focused endorsement with no partisan edge.

civility.statement: I'd like to thank Dame Marie Shroff for her mahi in maintaining public confidence in our elections—in contrast to the growing distrust of elections around the world.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an outgoing chair's service.

rigor.statement: The deceit and underhandedness shown by Verrall throughout her constant political attacks and smear campaign against one of my Ministers has now writ large, having simultaneously misled the leader of the Labour Party.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion of deceit rests on assertion and characterisation, not laid-out evidence.

rigor.statement: Using a personal explanation not only to reiterate an unsubstantiated accusation but also build on that, to me, seems to be a questionable approach.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point grounded in the accepted purpose of personal explanations (correcting a statement).

rigor.statement: To spell it out for the member: someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Of course, avoiding this or any other sanction is simple. Beneficiaries only need comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work.
rigor.explanation: A logical comparison (full vs reduced benefit) but leaves out the restrictions on where money can be spent that the questioner flagged.

rigor.statement: Does she accept the overwhelming evidence presented by her officials that shows that compulsory money management can prevent people from shopping at cheaper alternatives and prevent people from paying their rent, and, if so, are increased living costs an intended outcome of her non-financial sanction?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in officials' own evidence about concrete harms rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: Mr Goldsmith is making sure the laws are fit for purpose, and we're not going to go around as some silly elitist Māori extremists supporting gangsters.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem caricature standing in for an argument.

rigor.statement: She is making sure the focus is on the basics of reading, writing, and maths—structured literacy and numeracy—giving our young generation the tools they need to succeed in life and taking us back to where we should be, at the top of the educational chart.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a return to 'the top of the educational chart' as an aspiration without evidence linking the policy to that outcome.

rigor.statement: But I'll tell you what we won't be doing: we won't be putting in place building blocks for a massive dam in the bottom of the South Island that stymied investment into the renewables sector, otherwise known as Lake Onslow, advanced by that previous Minister.
rigor.explanation: Asserts Lake Onslow 'stymied investment' without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: Well, because New Zealanders are sick and tired of the prevalence of violent and serious crime in our communities, and the majority want to see a stronger response.
rigor.explanation: Leans on appeal to popularity ('the majority want') rather than evidence of the policy's effect.

rigor.statement: Who is correct: David Seymour, who has bragged about reducing the cost of meals to $3; or the March Cabinet paper, which highlighted that changes to the school lunch programme would risk achievement, attendance, nutrition, and the wellbeing of children?
rigor.explanation: Sets up a documented contradiction between a Minister's cost claim and a Cabinet paper's risk warning — evidence-anchored, though framed as a false-choice question.

rigor.statement: I've made it very clear to my officials that we are in this direction of travel, because it is better to have a mental health response than a police response to mental distress, unless, of course, the individual or people around them are at risk. I've made it very clear that an agreed action plan needs to be in place that safely allows that change. If that plan is not in place between Police and Health, then that stage will not be activated.
rigor.explanation: States a clear conditional (no agreed plan → phase not activated) with a stated rationale.

veracity.statement: The official I mentioned in my general debate is Ayesha Verrall's sister-in-law, Emily Revell, who attended multiple meetings with the Minister, worked on tobacco reform legislation advice, and who did not declare to the Minister that she was a close relative nor did she declare that there was a massive conflict of interest.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claims about relationship and undeclared conflict, directly contested in the House (Verrall said the person is a distant relative and conflicts were declared); accuracy is unresolved from the text.

veracity.statement: We implemented 36 of the 44 recommendations, demonstrating the Government's commitment to ensuring the intent of the royal commission of inquiry is still met with the ongoing work that Government agencies are still doing to keep New Zealanders safe.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about implementation of royal commission recommendations; plausible but not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: How will the Government address the fact that police data shows that 58 percent of all reported faith-motivated hate crimes target Aotearoa's Muslim community?
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific police-data statistic; the figure is falsifiable and plausibly sourced but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: It is my recollection that there were two interactions with the individual. That doesn't change the overall picture of events, where I acknowledge that I caused offence. I accept that, and that is why I've apologised. However, as I've repeatedly said, I did not have any alcohol prior to any interactions with the individual. I did have a small wine tasting at the end of the day.
veracity.explanation: Factual claims about interaction count and no alcohol beforehand that are disputed by the complainant; unresolved from the text.

veracity.statement: Minister Louise Upston is announcing positive feedback that the traffic-light system has shown promising results in the first four months, with 98 percent of beneficiaries meeting their obligations, and now aims to have 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker by 2030—just a snapshot of the many things that we're doing positively.
veracity.explanation: The 98 percent figure is presented as fact but 'promising results' framing may be selective; unverified here.

veracity.statement: So far, $11.5 million has been paid into people's bank accounts. This is only after three weeks of claims being open, and this amount is going up every day.
veracity.explanation: A specific dollar figure attributed to IRD data; checkable and plausible though unverified here.

veracity.statement: The number of households in emergency housing has dropped by 62 percent—our starting point of 3,141 households in December 2023 to the 1,179 households as at 30 September this year.
veracity.explanation: Checkable statistical claim; plausible and consistent with the target framing, though selection of endpoints could flatter.

veracity.statement: If the previous programme had been designed like this, we would have saved over $800 million over the last five years.
veracity.explanation: A counterfactual savings figure presented as fact; the '$800 million' rests on unstated assumptions and is hard to verify.

veracity.statement: The Police-led change programme to triple one calls to a multi-agency response is a three- to five-year programme that myself and Mark Mitchell are taking back to Cabinet at the end of this year, because the last Labour Government cancelled that programme when they came into office, so we've lost six years.
veracity.explanation: The 'lost six years' / cancellation claim is a contestable characterisation of the previous Government's decision.

specificity.statement: We implemented 36 of the 44 recommendations, demonstrating the Government's commitment to ensuring the intent of the royal commission of inquiry is still met with the ongoing work that Government agencies are still doing to keep New Zealanders safe.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete count (36 of 44 recommendations) but not which ones or timeframes.

specificity.statement: The question concerns a subject that is a work in progress at this point of time. The Government has committed to a significant programme to reform firearms law over this parliamentary term and work is substantially already under way.
specificity.explanation: Gives one concrete detail (Arms Act responsibility moved to justice in January) but otherwise general.

specificity.statement: To address this, we are moving to a single-supervisor model, with the Department of Internal Affairs taking the lead. This consolidation will simplify compliance, ensure more efficient decision making, and ensure that guidance and support to businesses is provided sooner.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (single-supervisor model, DIA lead) but no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: This model will include an industry levy that is fair and manageable, particularly for small businesses. Alongside this, we will be developing a national strategy and work programme designed to ensure the system delivers regulatory relief and operational efficiencies for businesses across New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names an industry levy and a national strategy but no rates, thresholds, or timing.

specificity.explanation: Cites a percentage, a timeframe (first four months) and a numeric target with a date (50,000 fewer by 2030).

specificity.statement: Ministers Chris Bishop and Shane Jones are fast-tracking 149 infrastructure projects to boost economic growth, create jobs, and address New Zealand's housing, energy, and transportation needs.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count of 149 projects, though no named projects or timelines.

specificity.statement: She is making sure the focus is on the basics of reading, writing, and maths—structured literacy and numeracy—giving our young generation the tools they need to succeed in life and taking us back to where we should be, at the top of the educational chart.
specificity.explanation: Names structured literacy and numeracy but no measures, targets, or timeframes.

specificity.explanation: Commits to a bill 'by the end of the year', a concrete timeframe.

specificity.statement: Parents and caregivers can receive 25 percent of their early childhood education fees after the 20 hours' early childhood education and Ministry of Social Development childcare subsidy have been taken into account, up to a maximum fortnightly payment of $150. Payments are made quarterly as a lump sum, so parents and caregivers can receive up to $975 in a three-month period. This is the maximum payment, and people will receive a range of amounts depending on their particular circumstances. To ensure the support is well targeted, the maximum payment reduces for family incomes over $140,000 a year.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures: 25 percent, $150 fortnightly cap, $975 quarterly, $140,000 income threshold.

specificity.explanation: Concrete amount ($11.5 million) with the timeframe (three weeks).

specificity.explanation: Cites the nearly $30 million funding figure but the 'enduring solution' itself is undefined.

specificity.explanation: Precise figures with dates: 3,141 in December 2023 down to 1,179 at 30 September, a 62 percent drop.

specificity.explanation: Concrete counts (726 households, nearly 1,500 tamariki, five months) tied to a named pathway.

Just this week, my excellent colleague Minister McKee announced the Government will recommend modifications to three strikes to strengthen the regime. Next Tuesday, public submissions to the Justice Committee close on the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill.
specificity.explanation: Names specific legislation, a modification, and a concrete deadline (submissions close next Tuesday).

specificity.statement: If the previous programme had been designed like this, we would have saved over $800 million over the last five years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure and period but the derivation is opaque.

specificity.statement: What I would say is that I am proud of the fact that every student that is receiving a meal today will receive a meal on the first day of term 1 next year, plus an extra 10,000 young people who really need that food will be provided with food.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (extra 10,000 students) and a date (first day of term 1).

specificity.explanation: Names the programme, its three-to-five-year span, and the Cabinet timing.

specificity.statement: There is a programme called the New Zealand Police Change Programme. It's not actually happening next week, but it's happening on 4 November. There are three succinct changes, and one is around the request to transport patients.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact date (4 November) and one of the three specific changes.

strength.explanation: Legislation in progress with defined next steps, not yet enacted.

authenticity.explanation: Apologises 'unreservedly' while simultaneously disputing several of the complainant's facts, creating tension between the apology and the defence.
