specificity.explanation: Gives named faults, magnitudes, probabilities and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: we had something like over 7,000 buildings across the country which were designated as earthquake-prone buildings, and about 2,000 of those have been resolved.
specificity.explanation: Concrete totals for buildings designated and resolved.

specificity.statement: Without the amendments we discuss today, many of our marae would have been at risk of closure and would be forced to be demolished if they had failed to meet the original deadlines.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the affected group (marae) and the consequence but no figures on how many were actually at risk.

specificity.statement: The Government should fully fund seismic strengthening for marae.
specificity.explanation: A clear policy demand but with no cost, mechanism, eligibility, or timeframe attached.

civility.statement: very ably chaired by one of the previous contributors, James Meager; I’ll just throw him a wee comment because it felt like he needed it from over here
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of a chair from an opposing party; no attack, purely collegial.

civility.statement: this is a Government bill in the name of the Hon Mark Mitchell, our Minister of Police, and an excellent Minister of Police at that.
civility.explanation: Respectful and free of any attack, though it adds praise rather than substance.

civility.statement: there is a large degree of non-compliance currently because of the operation of the rules, implemented, as they were, in good faith a decade ago
civility.explanation: Diagnoses the policy problem while explicitly crediting the earlier rule-makers with good faith rather than blaming them.

civility.statement: It’s admirable for members of the Opposition to spend taxpayers’ money on offering incentives to say that we could give loans to be paid back on completion on a sale of a building, but, actually, that’s taxpayer money, and we need to make sure that we’re putting the money to work in a good way that is actually sustainable.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab at the Opposition ('admirable') but engages the policy substance (fiscal sustainability of loan incentives) rather than attacking anyone personally.

civility.statement: Arena Williams spoke about the previous Government’s funding regime, but my recollection is that I don’t think anybody actually got through the hoops to actually get anything.
civility.explanation: Rebuts a rival party's claim on the merits (whether the fund actually helped anyone) without personal attack, and hedges honestly with 'my recollection'.

charisma.statement: very ably chaired by one of the previous contributors, James Meager; I’ll just throw him a wee comment because it felt like he needed it from over here
charisma.explanation: Good-humoured cross-party praise that builds goodwill across the aisle, though it is a light aside rather than substantive bridge-building.

charisma.statement: this is a Government bill in the name of the Hon Mark Mitchell, our Minister of Police, and an excellent Minister of Police at that.
charisma.explanation: Confident and positive but a partisan compliment to her own side's minister; appeals inward rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: let’s go—let’s work on that together because bipartisanship and a long-term vision on this is really important, but let’s make sure it’s independent.
charisma.explanation: Explicit, genuine invitation to cross-party collaboration on a long-term solution — inclusive and consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: This bill has cross-party support, but we need to go further and get cross-party support on really sustainable solutions that address the fiscal issues faced
charisma.explanation: Frames the way forward as a shared, cross-party endeavour and invites others toward a durable solution.

rigor.statement: why is a framework important, in particular a statutory one? It’s for consistency. Consistency is so important. It’s so important, particularly when you’re dealing with people’s private information.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reasonable rationale (consistency in handling private information) but leans on assertion and repetition rather than developed evidence.

rigor.statement: there is a large degree of non-compliance currently because of the operation of the rules, implemented, as they were, in good faith a decade ago
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal account (rule design causing non-compliance) though the scale of non-compliance is asserted rather than quantified here.

rigor.statement: Of course, we could have simply just said that it was six years from the outset, but I do want to hold my own feet to the fire, and those of the Government and of lawmakers in general, to try and get a result more quickly than that.
rigor.explanation: Coherent justification for the four-plus-two structure over a flat six years, tied to the goal of reducing real-world risk sooner.

rigor.statement: if it is only a constraint on the Public Service which requires it to be six years, then that is not a good enough reason for the legislation to be extended—not by Parliament
rigor.explanation: Draws a principled distinction between a legitimate trigger (a disruptive event) and mere administrative convenience for granting the extra two years; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: If you have a multi-storey apartment building that people are living in, or a commercial building that hundreds of people are working in, clearly that is a greater risk to life and wellbeing than a one-storey, hundred-year-old tennis club that doesn’t have anyone in it most of the time.
rigor.explanation: Sound risk-based reasoning for prioritisation — occupancy and height as proxies for risk to life — with the conclusion clearly following from the premises.

rigor.statement: It’s admirable for members of the Opposition to spend taxpayers’ money on offering incentives to say that we could give loans to be paid back on completion on a sale of a building, but, actually, that’s taxpayer money, and we need to make sure that we’re putting the money to work in a good way that is actually sustainable.
rigor.explanation: Raises a legitimate fiscal-sustainability concern but asserts rather than demonstrates that the loan scheme is not a good use of funds.

rigor.statement: Arena Williams spoke about the previous Government’s funding regime, but my recollection is that I don’t think anybody actually got through the hoops to actually get anything.
rigor.explanation: Fair evidential challenge to the effectiveness of the prior scheme, appropriately qualified as recollection rather than asserted as certain fact.

rigor.statement: marae are some of the only spaces left in the country built off stolen whenua and Māori labour.
rigor.explanation: Emotionally powerful but rests on a sweeping historical assertion offered without supporting evidence in the text (appeal to emotion / broad generalisation).

authenticity.statement: Of course, we could have simply just said that it was six years from the outset, but I do want to hold my own feet to the fire, and those of the Government and of lawmakers in general, to try and get a result more quickly than that.
authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily sets a tighter default (four years) to keep himself accountable rather than taking the easier six-year option — words aligned with a self-imposed constraint.

authenticity.statement: Labour will be tentatively supporting the bill at this stage, and that is a change in position from the first reading.
authenticity.explanation: Openly declares a reversal from opposing at first reading, giving the reason (submissions and worked-through policy issues) — a transparent, defensible shift rather than hidden inconsistency.

forthrightness.statement: Labour will be tentatively supporting the bill at this stage, and that is a change in position from the first reading.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly states the party's position and candidly flags that it has changed rather than obscuring the shift.

strength.statement: Labour had a scheme called the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme, which offered up to $250,000 for the below-market rates payable on sale to protect those homeowners who would have been at a significant financial disadvantage because of the compliance that was being put on them.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a solution that was largely undelivered in practice — the scheme was hard to access and later pulled, so it reflects intent more than delivered results.

divination.statement: in the next 50 years, there was an 80 percent chance of an Alpine Fault event of 8-plus—80 percent—a 25 percent chance of a Hikurangi Fault event of 8-plus; a 1 percent chance—God help us—of a Hikurangi Fault event of 9.1; and a 5 percent chance on the Wellington Fault.
divination.explanation: Probabilistic 50-year seismic forecasts sourced from expert/crisis-management assessment; broadly consistent with published GNS-type hazard estimates, though inherently uncertain.

charisma.statement: I actually want to acknowledge and mihi to you, Minister Penk, for reaching out to us early. Your office did a really great job at reaching out to myself and my colleague Julie Anne Genter, as the Wellington City MPs, to brief us on some of these changes, and I really appreciated having that early notice and being communicated with about what your intentions are.
charisma.explanation: A Green MP going out of her way to warmly acknowledge a National minister across the House — inclusive, bridge-building, genuinely consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: We're happy to support this bill at this stage of its passage, but I just want to reiterate our desire to make sure that that financial burden isn't impossible or insurmountable, and we also want to acknowledge the really important role of human safety.
charisma.explanation: Balances competing concerns (cost vs safety) constructively and signals cross-party support rather than combat.

charisma.statement: it's great that common sense has broken out on the other side of the House and they've finally seen the light and decided to support this bill
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side by scoring a point off opponents even while thanking them; more crowing than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: it has been a very collegial select committee on this one, to be fair.
charisma.explanation: Genuine acknowledgement of cross-party cooperation, softening the earlier jab.

charisma.statement: The tentative—and very tentative—support for this bill really comes with the plea to know what you are doing, to really understand that the difference between four years and six years is huge, to take responsibility for those implications, and to not lose the speed that should be given to this.
charisma.explanation: Earnest and emotionally resonant, but appeals to caution from the Opposition benches rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Just acknowledging the prior contributor—Reuben Davidson—for his heartfelt and genuine contribution on that, and he did make some really valid points in what he's been saying.
charisma.explanation: Government MP crediting an Opposition speaker's valid points — generous, consensus-building acknowledgement across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I'm really proud of Labour for having put its money where its mouth was. In the scheme that it put forward, it was prepared to spend money on the situation, and that, unfortunately, is no longer an option available.
charisma.explanation: Confident partisan pride that appeals mainly to her own side.

charisma.statement: I think getting to the committee stage is going to be a good space for us to debate and thrash some of these concepts and ideas out, and, again, come to a bipartisan agreement on which we can move forward feeling comfortable, together.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks a bipartisan, collaborative path forward — inclusive and consensus-oriented.

charisma.statement: I do wonder, just very quickly, incidentally, kind sir, why you're now sitting in Opposition. There you go: an abandonment of rural New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Scores points against the Opposition to please his own side rather than building any consensus.

civility.statement: I actually want to acknowledge and mihi to you, Minister Penk, for reaching out to us early. Your office did a really great job at reaching out to myself and my colleague Julie Anne Genter, as the Wellington City MPs, to brief us on some of these changes, and I really appreciated having that early notice and being communicated with about what your intentions are.
civility.explanation: Respectful and gracious toward a political opponent, focused on process and cooperation rather than any personal jab.

civility.statement: it's great that common sense has broken out on the other side of the House and they've finally seen the light and decided to support this bill
civility.explanation: A light partisan jab ('finally seen the light') that is condescending toward the Opposition but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: it has been a very collegial select committee on this one, to be fair.
civility.explanation: Fair-minded, respectful recognition of the committee's collaborative work.

civility.statement: Even a stopped clock is right twice a day.
civility.explanation: A witty heckle implying the government is only occasionally right; teasing rather than a serious personal attack.

civility.statement: We've all seen the speed that things can be done with—bad things—when this Government sets their minds to it. They can railroad things through. How come this isn't being given the same priority? It is, instead, being slowed down, pushed out, and given a more distant horizon.
civility.explanation: 'Railroad' and 'bad things' are pointed, but the criticism targets the government's legislative prioritisation rather than any person.

civility.statement: Just acknowledging the prior contributor—Reuben Davidson—for his heartfelt and genuine contribution on that, and he did make some really valid points in what he's been saying.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with an opponent's contribution.

civility.statement: But the idiots on that side of the House are going to open the door
civility.explanation: Direct insult ('idiots') aimed at government members — a personal attack rather than policy criticism.

civility.statement: Saying that one believes in climate change and then doing all the things that make climate change worse has the same effect as denying that climate change exists in the first place. That is what this Government is doing with bill after bill after bill.
civility.explanation: Equates the government's action with climate denial — a harsh characterisation of their position, pointed but aimed at policy rather than a person.

civility.statement: the biggest, most powerful lobbyist in this country is Fonterra. It is the dairy industry, and these guys are doing their bidding. This Government is doing the bidding of the big bully in the room, and that is Fonterra.
civility.explanation: Characterises Fonterra as a 'big bully' and accuses the government of doing its bidding — accusatory and belittling rather than substance-focused.

civility.statement: I'm fascinated by some of the language that I've just heard shared from the Hon Damien O'Connor. “Idiots” I think was the language on this side of the House—an inference to my rural friends.
civility.explanation: Calls out an opponent's insult rather than returning one; a legitimate, relatively measured rebuke.

civility.statement: I do wonder, just very quickly, incidentally, kind sir, why you're now sitting in Opposition. There you go: an abandonment of rural New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic jab ('kind sir') and accusation of abandoning rural NZ — a partisan cheap shot at an opponent.

civility.statement: What percentage are we talking about here? Carbon dioxide is 0.04 percent. Gracious me, Mr O'Connor. Methane is two parts per million, and we're having this hyperbolic runaway conversation, end of days—two parts per million. That, Steve, is a nonsense.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' case as 'nonsense' and mocks the debate ('end of days'), harsh but directed at the argument.

specificity.statement: We're happy to support this bill at this stage of its passage, but I just want to reiterate our desire to make sure that that financial burden isn't impossible or insurmountable, and we also want to acknowledge the really important role of human safety.
specificity.explanation: States a clear direction (limit the financial burden, protect safety) but names no mechanism, figure, or threshold.

specificity.statement: we'd be making sure that the buildings that have the most people going through them and the highest risk are prioritised in those deadlines, above some of the more random, smaller, less consequential buildings that exist out there
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete prioritisation mechanism (occupancy and risk) but without thresholds or timeframes.

specificity.statement: Our solution when we were in Government was the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme—which this Government cancelled—and, under Labour, owner-occupiers of units and apartments living in earthquake-prone buildings could apply for financial support to fix their homes.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy and who was eligible for it.

specificity.statement: in Christchurch, that was the loss of 185 lives, and what we need to remember is that 115 of those lives—115 people—died in one building alone. The collapse of one building killed 115 people.
specificity.explanation: Precise casualty figures tied to a single building.

specificity.statement: The tentative—and very tentative—support for this bill really comes with the plea to know what you are doing, to really understand that the difference between four years and six years is huge, to take responsibility for those implications, and to not lose the speed that should be given to this.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete change at issue (four vs six years) but frames its concern in general terms of 'implications'.

specificity.statement: For us on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, we heard from 23 submitters on this piece of legislation. It was not a huge amount, but it was still really vital and important, and the majority of the submitters spoke in favour of the bill
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (23 submitters) and characterises their stance.

specificity.statement: Clause 17, inserts new section 133AMC, which is an amendment to make it clearer that a further deadline extension by Order in Council would apply both to deadlines originally extended by four years as well as to earthquake-prone building notices issued following commencement of the amendment Act.
specificity.explanation: Highly precise legislative detail — names the clause, the inserted section, and exactly what the amendment does.

specificity.statement: I was part of the earthquake response, and I led a trauma research team in the Pyne Gould building at the time. During continuous aftershocks, I stood in that building, clutching a vial of ketamine and a saw, ready to crawl through the building to assist some of the people who were stuck in that building.
specificity.explanation: Vivid, concrete personal detail — the building, the role, the equipment.

specificity.statement: we had owned a heritage building on The Terrace that was at about 15 percent of code, and when we went through the process to redevelop that building and had the business case for it, it looked like we could afford it. However, when the project started, inevitably there were foundation issues that pushed out the costs, and we didn't achieve the business that we thought we would afterwards. As a result, the New Zealand Medical Association, which had started in the 1880s and was over 130 years old—we had to wind that up.
specificity.explanation: Concrete case study with figures (15% of code, 130+ years old) illustrating the economic risk of heritage strengthening.

specificity.statement: Everyone assumes that Taranaki is this dormant cone that erupted the last time in 1690, or something like that, but, actually, a report came out two years ago that it has a 50 percent chance of erupting within the next 50 years.
specificity.explanation: Cites a probability and timeframe drawn from a report.

specificity.statement: if you look around the streets of Wellington, there are more than 800 buildings within a short walk or drive from here which are actually earthquake-prone and need remediation work done.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough count but only a vague geographic scope ('short walk or drive').

specificity.statement: in the 1990s, this building was strengthened... As a Government, I think it was about $75 million that was spent. I mean, I know it included some refurbishment work as well, but it was around the strengthening of these buildings
specificity.explanation: Provides an approximate cost and the mechanism (base isolators).

specificity.statement: That is why we have brought forward the review of the earthquake-prone building system that was scheduled to take place in 2027. We have brought that forward to make sure that we can do this in a timely manner, but it is one of the reasons why we do need to extend the deadlines out, because, of course, there's no point doing a review after a deadline has already passed.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete action (review moved earlier than 2027) and its rationale.

specificity.statement: This bill will alleviate the stress and sleepless nights as people struggle to get their building back in shape, whether it be their house or whether it be their place of work.
specificity.explanation: Frames the benefit in general emotional terms without measures.

specificity.statement: In the year 31 March 2024, the food and fibre sector accounted for 80.9 percent of New Zealand's merchandise exports.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentage tied to a defined reporting year.

specificity.statement: Over the last 10 years, food and fibre exports have grown by an average of 3.6 percent per year, whereas other elements of export growth have only grown by 1.6 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two precise growth rates over a stated period.

specificity.statement: we have also committed to replacing it with a fair and sustainable pricing system outside of the ETS by 2030 to ensure that we do not send production or jobs overseas.
specificity.explanation: Gives a deadline (2030) but no mechanism for the promised 'fair and sustainable pricing system'.

specificity.statement: The requirements for farmers to report and pay for their emissions would likely require up to 100,000 animal farmers to be registered and begin reporting and paying for those emissions under the emissions trading scheme.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and described mechanism.

specificity.statement: The committee received 581 submissions and 26 oral submissions during this consultation process. Of these total submissions, approximately two-thirds were supportive of this bill, with the remainder one-third being against the bill.
specificity.explanation: Exact submission numbers and a proportional breakdown.

specificity.statement: We tried, in 2000, in a Labour Government. We came in and we talked about a carbon tax. That was rejected by farmers—called a “fart tax”—and so we moved on to create an emissions trading scheme as the next best option. It was accepted.
specificity.explanation: Names the policies and rough timeframe.

specificity.statement: even though the concession for agriculture was 95 percent discount; so, effectively, facing a 5 percent impost on the methane and other emissions from the agricultural system.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for the discount and effective impost.

specificity.statement: Nitrous oxide from fertiliser and manure is about 300 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and methane is about 27 times more potent over a 100-year period.
specificity.explanation: Precise potency multipliers with a stated time horizon.

specificity.statement: The dairy farmer who presented to us from the Waikato, a guy farming 300 cows, who has eliminated synthetic nitrogen fertiliser from his production system and has cut his emissions by 25 percent, has done that unacknowledged.
specificity.explanation: Concrete example with herd size, the practice change, and a quantified emissions cut.

specificity.statement: This legislation takes away the requirement for processes to monitor and report the agricultural emissions under the emissions trading scheme. We're not even going to look and see how things are going.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific reporting requirement being removed.

specificity.statement: if we remain part of this Paris Agreement and these agreements to deal with climate change, we face a future bill of between $3 billion and $23 billion to buy overseas carbon credits to account for our failure to reduce our emissions in the way that we've committed to.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified cost range and its cause, though the range is very broad.

specificity.statement: We heard a lot of submissions, 581 submissions; 26 were heard orally—gracious me. And 65 percent, give or take a bit, were in support of this bill; about 30 percent opposed; and, depending on who you asked on the day, about 5 percent disagreed.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts and percentage breakdown.

rigor.statement: we'd be making sure that the buildings that have the most people going through them and the highest risk are prioritised in those deadlines, above some of the more random, smaller, less consequential buildings that exist out there
rigor.explanation: Risk-based reasoning: prioritise remediation by occupancy and hazard, which follows logically from the safety-vs-cost trade-off.

rigor.statement: We've all seen the speed that things can be done with—bad things—when this Government sets their minds to it. They can railroad things through. How come this isn't being given the same priority? It is, instead, being slowed down, pushed out, and given a more distant horizon.
rigor.explanation: An argument from inconsistency (urgent for some bills, slow for this one) that is rhetorically effective but not evidenced beyond the assertion.

rigor.statement: It became institutionally acceptable to actually defraud about the risk of that product, and I am very mindful that it's really easy to go to sleep about these issues because they seem a long way out.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Grenfell analogy to warn about complacency; a reasonable cautionary parallel but leaning on the single example.

rigor.statement: However, those buildings have stood through quite a few shakes already, and so I think that that doesn't take away all risk, but there is some piece of mind. Most of the buildings in Christchurch that were problematic have gone, and we need to acknowledge that.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference that surviving prior shakes lowers (but doesn't eliminate) risk; qualified appropriately but not backed by data.

rigor.statement: we had owned a heritage building on The Terrace that was at about 15 percent of code, and when we went through the process to redevelop that building and had the business case for it, it looked like we could afford it. However, when the project started, inevitably there were foundation issues that pushed out the costs, and we didn't achieve the business that we thought we would afterwards. As a result, the New Zealand Medical Association, which had started in the 1880s and was over 130 years old—we had to wind that up.
rigor.explanation: Uses a detailed real example to support the claim that redevelopment costs are unpredictable, though it is a single anecdote.

rigor.statement: That is why we have brought forward the review of the earthquake-prone building system that was scheduled to take place in 2027. We have brought that forward to make sure that we can do this in a timely manner, but it is one of the reasons why we do need to extend the deadlines out, because, of course, there's no point doing a review after a deadline has already passed.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument linking bringing the review forward to the logic of extending deadlines so the review can inform them.

rigor.statement: In 1992, a National Government committed to a Kyoto Protocol, an international movement to reduce emissions. A National Government, in 2015, reiterated its commitment to emissions reduction, at Paris. Through that period, the National Government did nothing to implement any progress in the area where 50 percent of our emissions come from: agriculture.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument from the historical record that National committed internationally yet did not act on agriculture; partly evidenced but leans on the absolute 'nothing'.

rigor.statement: opening the door to foreign investment in farmland will destroy opportunities for future generations of New Zealand farmers, and that's what is being considered on that side of the House, supported by Federated Farmers.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a sweeping negative consequence without supporting evidence for the causal claim.

rigor.statement: the absence of a clear alternative to give market signals to farmers to reduce their emissions, to get money to help them make that transition, will mean that our country, our economy, is at huge risk from this piece of legislation.

veracity.statement: What percentage are we talking about here? Carbon dioxide is 0.04 percent. Gracious me, Mr O'Connor. Methane is two parts per million, and we're having this hyperbolic runaway conversation, end of days—two parts per million. That, Steve, is a nonsense.
veracity.explanation: The concentrations (~0.04% CO2, ~2 ppm methane) are roughly correct, but using them to imply the gases are climatically insignificant is misleading — potency, not concentration, drives warming.

civility.statement: race relations deteriorating to the worst point it has been in over 40 years
civility.explanation: Harsh but aimed at government conduct rather than a person; the exaggeration undercuts it.

civility.statement: put tens of thousands of New Zealanders out of work during a very tough part of the economic cycle so that they can, among other things, fund $2.9 billion worth of tax cuts for landlords; and give over $200 million in tax cuts to Philip Morris, the country's largest supplier of cigarettes
civility.explanation: Pointed policy attack; edges toward imputing bad motive but stays on fiscal choices.

civility.statement: All we've seen is the promise of weaker firearms regulations, making it easier for gang members to get access to guns.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy's alleged effect rather than a person, but with an inflammatory framing.

civility.statement: the Prime Minister was spotted sneaking in through the back door of the Dunedin Public Art Gallery to avoid Dunedin people
civility.explanation: A personal characterisation of the PM as sneaky/evasive rather than engaging with policy.

civility.statement: This demolition Government is well known for its shiftiness.
civility.explanation: Name-calling ('demolition', 'shiftiness') with no substantive content.

civility.statement: I have become very concerned about the climate impacts of the amount of hot air coming from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: A partisan jibe, but light/rhetorical rather than a personal attack; still dismissive of opponents.

civility.statement: Recently, the Opposition spokesperson for finance, Barbara Edmonds, appears to have done a complete 180 on FamilyBoost. She's now saying there aren't enough families getting it. Of course, this completely contrasts to her vote on FamilyBoost, which legislated when she voted for zero families in this country to receive it.
civility.explanation: Charges an opponent with a U-turn; substantive but pointed and framed to embarrass.

civility.statement: This is being rushed for political expediency, not what is in the best interests of children and young people.
civility.explanation: Imputes a motive to the government but stays focused on the policy process.

civility.statement: This Government is setting up a structure whereby third-party providers... are going to provide these boot camps. How are we supposed to know what level of training they're going to get? Well, we don't know that—at all.
civility.explanation: Critical of the policy design rather than the person, with some rhetorical exaggeration.

civility.statement: I want to speak particularly to the National Party, who actually have a long and honourable tradition in upholding the principles of Te Tiriti and making really good progress. I think to the work that Jim Bolger and Doug Graham did, and I think to the work that Christopher Finlayson did
civility.explanation: Respectful, names their record positively rather than attacking.

civility.statement: As we see the bill introduced tomorrow, snuck in while many will be distracted by international events, snuck in so that the hīkoi so carefully planned won't be there when it's introduced
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad-faith timing ('snuck in') to opponents rather than engaging the merits.

rigor.statement: a fall in inflation and a fall in interest rates, which is almost exclusively because of the actions of the Reserve Bank and nothing to do with this Government
rigor.explanation: A defensible causal point (monetary policy drives rates), but 'almost exclusively/nothing to do with' overstates and ignores fiscal contribution.

rigor.statement: this Government has borrowed more money in this year's Budget than in any of the Budgets that we delivered, except for one, which was in 2020 when we were at the height of the global pandemic
rigor.explanation: Uses a like-for-like comparison with a stated exception, a reasonably disciplined argument.

rigor.statement: The Government has also announced two new tunnels for Wellington to make traffic and pollution worse. So how many more minutes will those new tunnels—costing somewhere between $3 billion or more—save us? About 10 minutes, we're told.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a cost-benefit contrast, but the 'make traffic and pollution worse' assertion is stated rather than shown.

rigor.statement: it was a Cabinet decision approved in June—and he chairs Cabinet
rigor.explanation: Uses the PM chairing Cabinet to counter his claimed unawareness — a valid inference, though it doesn't prove recollection.

rigor.statement: the advice from her officials is very clear that there is a risk that abuse could occur, that harm could be done to young people
rigor.explanation: Grounds the concern in officials' advice rather than assertion alone.

rigor.statement: This Government is setting up a structure whereby third-party providers... are going to provide these boot camps. How are we supposed to know what level of training they're going to get? Well, we don't know that—at all.
rigor.explanation: Methodically tests the Minister's three distinguishing criteria; the training point is a reasonable inference, though 'could literally be anybody' overstates.

rigor.statement: The boot camps that the John Key National Government started were a failure because a significant majority of those young people went on to reoffend later in life.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'failure' claim with a reoffending outcome rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: My niece is one of them—reading at three years above the age that she is, which is incredible.
rigor.explanation: A single family anecdote offered as evidence for a programme's effectiveness — appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: the Crown, in bringing this bill to this House, has breached the principle of good government in its pursuit of a policy that's not evidence-based, has not been adequately tested, has not been consulted upon, and fails regulatory standards
rigor.explanation: Grounds criticism in a specific institutional finding rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: New Zealand missed out on Taylor Swift... for one reason: the resource consent for Eden Park is only limited to six concerts per year. Missing out on Tay Tay was a lay lay for our economies and the estimated $70 million of economic activities we lost
rigor.explanation: Attributes a complex touring decision to a single cause (the six-concert cap), a mono-causal oversimplification.

strength.statement: Today, over 30,000 households have received their first payment under the FamilyBoost childcare payment scheme
strength.explanation: Claims actual delivery (payments made) on a pre-election commitment, though the scheme's uptake was modest.

strength.statement: Our goal is to double New Zealand's renewable energy by 2050
strength.explanation: A long-horizon aspiration with no delivery yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: From 1 January next year—2025—135 central Government agencies must pay 90 percent of invoices within 10 business days. This increases to 95 percent from the start of 2026.
strength.explanation: A concrete rule change she has made, though delivery/impact is prospective.

divination.statement: Inland Revenue estimating that, from 1 October 2024 to 1 October 2025, 100,000 families will be eligible
divination.explanation: A forward eligibility forecast attributed to IRD; plausible but eligibility rarely equals uptake, so uncertain.

divination.statement: we've listed 22 energy projects with a combined capacity of 3 gigawatts to be fast tracked under legislation. This will help to ensure clean, reliable energy that is affordable to supply New Zealanders, and that will increase generation capacity by nearly 30 percent.
divination.explanation: Predicts a ~30% generation increase contingent on projects being consented and built — uncertain delivery.

divination.statement: we prepare for the biggest hīkoi that this country will ever see—bigger than any other hīkoi in history
divination.explanation: A forecast about turnout; directionally the hīkoi was very large, but 'biggest ever' is a superlative prediction that was uncertain when stated.

authenticity.statement: We had the National Party campaign on delivering this hospital but now they've come and said, "Oh, maybe we'll go back into the old building"—that is leaky.
authenticity.explanation: Charges National with reversing a campaign commitment — a low-authenticity signal about that opponent, contrasting their campaign words with the paused delivery.

forthrightness.statement: The age range is 62 to 100, and it will be around about 19,434 people. That estimated figure was put in the table in the departmental report and was put together by Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials using data from the 2021 Samoan national census.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Rachel Boyack's question about how many people the pre-1962 amendment would affect, with a specific figure and its source.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that's the establishment of the Samoan State.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Boyack's 'why 1962?' question with a concrete rationale (the establishment of the Samoan State), though brief.

specificity.statement: The age range is 62 to 100, and it will be around about 19,434 people. That estimated figure was put in the table in the departmental report and was put together by Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials using data from the 2021 Samoan national census.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise figure (19,434), an age range, and names the data source (departmental report, MFAT, 2021 census).

specificity.statement: The rationale for change was that I was proposing to amend the bill to reduce the application fee for citizenship under this bill to zero dollars—currently, it's set at $177—because we don't believe that it is appropriate to impose an application fee on people who had a right taken away from them.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact current fee ($177), the proposed change (zero), and the clause it applies to.

specificity.statement: Now, can I just note on the record that the Labour Party will be supporting this amendment in the committee today, and so I thank the member for putting forward this amendment.
specificity.explanation: Clear, committed position on a named amendment (AP 139) rather than a vague sentiment.

specificity.statement: We had the situation where Falema‘i Lesa was told, "You're an overstayer.", and she took that all the way to the Privy Council... The Privy Council actually overrode all the New Zealand courts and said, "Actually, we agree.", and then, of course, what happened was that the New Zealand Government—and it was the Muldoon Government, but it was also supported by the other parties who were then in Parliament; so both Labour and Social Credit—said, "No, we're going to overrule that."
specificity.explanation: Names the individual, the court, the government, and the parties involved.

specificity.statement: What my Amendment Paper says is that you pay the fee, but when you're successful—and it can only be those 3,500-odd people who are aged 76 to 100, who were born between 1924 and 1948, who are the only ones who would be able to be successful.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism (pay-then-refund) with the exact eligible cohort, count (~3,500), age range and birth years.

specificity.statement: Of course, to gain New Zealand Superannuation, merely being a citizen is not enough. There's a sliding scale there, depending on how old you are, but for people who were born before 1959, you have to have been in New Zealand for 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete residence threshold and birth-year cutoff.

specificity.statement: One of the key reasons why we as the National Party voted in support of it at the second reading was because we had got a change in the first place during the select committee phase around rather than a repealing piece of legislation, it was an amendment to the number one legislation of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact structural change (repeal vs amendment) and names the 1982 Act as the reason for the vote.

specificity.statement: As I said in my first reading speech, the ACT Party believes in fairness, we believe in equality, we believe in justice. We also believe that when we talk about fairness, when we talk about justice, it cannot be delivered partially.
specificity.explanation: Abstract values (fairness, equality, justice) with no concrete mechanism or measure attached.

specificity.statement: I would argue that, actually, the Government parties have a choice around whether they commit to adequately resourcing those departments to accommodate justice being delivered... This can include things like even temporarily bolstering the workforce and having a task force that it is very specifically in charge of processing these applications.
specificity.explanation: Names actual mechanisms (temporary workforce, dedicated processing task force) though without figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: The reason it's important to include the descendants is, as we know, the case that perhaps someone was born in Samoa in 1924, qualifies for this, maybe moved to Australia, for example, after World War II, and had children there in 1948. Those children may have never lived in New Zealand, they may have never lived in Samoa, but as a result of the bill as it stands, they can apply for New Zealand citizenship.
specificity.explanation: Concrete illustrative scenario with dates and the resulting legal entitlement.

specificity.statement: It is no mistake they were chosen, and we know that the 1924 date actually stems from 1914, 1921, and 1923 legislation—it's not just a date that was plucked as an arbitrary marker. The 1949 date comes from legislation started, obviously, in 1946, under Fraser and Savage.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the cutoff dates to specific years of legislation rather than treating them as arbitrary.

veracity.statement: The age range is 62 to 100, and it will be around about 19,434 people. That estimated figure was put in the table in the departmental report and was put together by Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials using data from the 2021 Samoan national census.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the estimate to official MFAT extrapolation and candidly flags it as 'a guesstimate', reducing overstatement risk.

veracity.statement: And, just to note, it is extremely unusual for a bill that addresses an historical wrong to require those who've been wronged to pay for an act of restoration.
veracity.explanation: Broadly plausible as a characterisation of restitution legislation, but unverified and somewhat rhetorical ('extremely unusual').

veracity.statement: It's the only country that we have a Treaty of Friendship with, so making sure that we do everything that we can to make that relationship as strong as possible is important.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the 1962 Treaty of Friendship with Samoa is New Zealand's only such treaty.

veracity.statement: During the select committee process, Labour and the Greens both voted in favour of legislation that would have allowed for that first group of descendants who were born before 1 January 1962 to be eligible.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about committee voting presented factually; plausible and consistent with the debate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand held Samoa—or Western Samoa, originally, as it was—as a protectorate under the League of Nations after the German occupation was removed, essentially, during the First World War, and, essentially, New Zealand held a role of looking after Samoa for good or bad—and often, sadly, it wasn't done well—right the way through until Samoan independence in 1961.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate (NZ administered Western Samoa under a League of Nations mandate from WWI), but 'protectorate' is loose and independence was formalised on 1 January 1962, not 1961.

veracity.statement: We had the situation where Falema‘i Lesa was told, "You're an overstayer.", and she took that all the way to the Privy Council... The Privy Council actually overrode all the New Zealand courts and said, "Actually, we agree.", and then, of course, what happened was that the New Zealand Government—and it was the Muldoon Government, but it was also supported by the other parties who were then in Parliament; so both Labour and Social Credit—said, "No, we're going to overrule that."
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 1982 Lesa Privy Council decision and the Muldoon Government's legislative override, with the cross-party support fairly noted.

veracity.statement: What my Amendment Paper says is that you pay the fee, but when you're successful—and it can only be those 3,500-odd people who are aged 76 to 100, who were born between 1924 and 1948, who are the only ones who would be able to be successful.
veracity.explanation: Cohort figures align with the select committee's defined scope as described throughout the debate.

veracity.statement: Of course, to gain New Zealand Superannuation, merely being a citizen is not enough. There's a sliding scale there, depending on how old you are, but for people who were born before 1959, you have to have been in New Zealand for 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Correctly notes citizenship alone doesn't confer Super and that a residence requirement applies; the specific '10 years for those born before 1959' reflects the pre-transition NZ Super residence rule, broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: You heard during that time how the National Party at the first reading didn't support the legislation, for a couple of key reasons, but then, through the select committee process, myself and my colleagues Cameron Brewer and Tim Costley were able to work with the other members of the Governance and Administration Committee to refine the bill to a place that we thought as a political party we could support it, hence why you saw us at the second reading change our position on the legislation and vote in support of it.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes National's first-reading opposition and second-reading support, matching the recorded course of the bill.

veracity.statement: We heard from the former Prime Minister of Samoa during the select committee process, and we heard from the Samoan Government.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual claim about who was heard at select committee; plausible and consistent with the debate, though unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: I also want to highlight that when the bill came through for the first reading, the ACT Party was the first Government party to stand up and support this bill because we assessed the bill and we thought that this bill must go to the select committee process and then very soon we were joined by New Zealand First.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about ACT being the first Government party to support; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: In the select committee, we heard from around 25,000 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate figure, consistent with other members' counts (24,500/25,000), i.e. a rounded rather than misleading number.

veracity.statement: It is no mistake they were chosen, and we know that the 1924 date actually stems from 1914, 1921, and 1923 legislation—it's not just a date that was plucked as an arbitrary marker. The 1949 date comes from legislation started, obviously, in 1946, under Fraser and Savage.
veracity.explanation: Cites a chain of historical statutes underpinning the dates; broadly credible, though 'Fraser and Savage' is loose since Savage died in 1940 and the 1948 citizenship reforms were under Fraser.

veracity.statement: The other point I wonder if the member has considered is just around section 32 of the Legislation Act, which says that, when a bill is repealed, it doesn't change or remove the impact or the operational effect of that bill from the time that it was enforced.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the general effect of savings provisions on repeal, applied to s32 of the Legislation Act.

veracity.statement: The Treaty of Friendship requires that the New Zealand Government consult with the Samoan Government on all matters of foreign affairs, citizenship.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate characterisation of the consultation obligations under the NZ–Samoa Treaty of Friendship, though stated somewhat sweepingly.

rigor.statement: The rationale for change was that I was proposing to amend the bill to reduce the application fee for citizenship under this bill to zero dollars—currently, it's set at $177—because we don't believe that it is appropriate to impose an application fee on people who had a right taken away from them.
rigor.explanation: Premise (a right was taken away) leads to conclusion (they shouldn't pay to restore it); a coherent principled argument, though it leans partly on fairness intuition.

rigor.statement: And, just to note, it is extremely unusual for a bill that addresses an historical wrong to require those who've been wronged to pay for an act of restoration.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable general claim used to support the no-fee position, but asserted without supporting examples or evidence of comparators.

rigor.statement: I note that the member from New Zealand First Andy Foster has an amendment on the Table that would achieve the same outcome, but my reluctance on this matter is that people would still have to put up the cost up front—they'd still have to come forward with the cash in order to apply.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete practical distinction (up-front cost vs no fee) as the basis for preferring one amendment over another.

rigor.statement: We had very, very strong advice from Immigration New Zealand, the Department of Internal Affairs, etc., saying, "Please don't do that, because what we know will happen is that people will have a go, and you could end up with thousands and thousands and thousands of people having a go. That will put a significant burden on the administration system."
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in official advice (appeal to authority), which is legitimate here, but the 'thousands and thousands' figure is asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: One of the key reasons why we as the National Party voted in support of it at the second reading was because we had got a change in the first place during the select committee phase around rather than a repealing piece of legislation, it was an amendment to the number one legislation of the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982.
rigor.explanation: Links the vote to a concrete legal concern about the Treaty of Friendship, a coherent reasoned basis.

rigor.statement: I did think it was really important that we were very, very specific, and you'll see it in the report back from the select committee, so that if this were to be brought before the courts in the future, you could see what was quite clearly defined around who was eligible through the legislation and who wasn't.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification for precise drafting—clear definitions to avoid future litigation—linking cause to consequence.

rigor.statement: You may have a cohort who had applied and got it for free. And then three, six, twelve months down the track, you had people then having to pay for their application. It created an in-between phase, a no-man's land, which would have been, I think, detrimental to the impact of what this bill is actually trying to legislate and change.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete inconsistency risk (an interim no-fee window then a fee) as a reasoned objection to the zero-fee amendment.

rigor.statement: Going with this approach of refunding the fee for applications that are approved I think is going to be a practical approach, because this will also put some personal responsibility on people to really consider and see that they do qualify before they apply.
rigor.explanation: Offers a behavioural rationale (self-screening) for the refund model; reasonable but asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: I would argue that, actually, the Government parties have a choice around whether they commit to adequately resourcing those departments to accommodate justice being delivered... This can include things like even temporarily bolstering the workforce and having a task force that it is very specifically in charge of processing these applications.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the administrative-burden objection by proposing concrete remedies (temporary staffing, a dedicated task force), a logical counter rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: If members across the Chamber are going to acknowledge that there was an injustice done in the past, the least we can do is genuinely commit to going all the way, as far as we can and within the scope of the bill, to deliver some sort of adequate response and justice.
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument (if you accept the injustice, act fully on it) with some logical force, though it relies on a moral premise more than evidence.

rigor.statement: The reason it's important to include the descendants is, as we know, the case that perhaps someone was born in Samoa in 1924, qualifies for this, maybe moved to Australia, for example, after World War II, and had children there in 1948. Those children may have never lived in New Zealand, they may have never lived in Samoa, but as a result of the bill as it stands, they can apply for New Zealand citizenship.
rigor.explanation: Works through a precise worked example to illustrate the legal effect of the existing clause, tightly reasoned from premises to conclusion.

rigor.statement: It is no mistake they were chosen, and we know that the 1924 date actually stems from 1914, 1921, and 1923 legislation—it's not just a date that was plucked as an arbitrary marker. The 1949 date comes from legislation started, obviously, in 1946, under Fraser and Savage.
rigor.explanation: Argues the dates are principled, not arbitrary, by tracing their legislative provenance.

rigor.statement: The other point I wonder if the member has considered is just around section 32 of the Legislation Act, which says that, when a bill is repealed, it doesn't change or remove the impact or the operational effect of that bill from the time that it was enforced.
rigor.explanation: Introduces a specific statutory provision to test whether repeal would achieve the intended restoration—evidence-based legal reasoning.

civility.statement: The rationale for change was that I was proposing to amend the bill to reduce the application fee for citizenship under this bill to zero dollars—currently, it's set at $177—because we don't believe that it is appropriate to impose an application fee on people who had a right taken away from them.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused, engages the substance of the fee question without any personal attack.

civility.statement: I want to put on record my thanks to all of the parties who have gotten us this far—and noting this is as far as we've ever got as a Parliament to getting some form of restitution; some form of restoration for our Samoan aiga.
civility.explanation: Respectful and gracious toward all parties involved.

civility.statement: I note that the member from New Zealand First Andy Foster has an amendment on the Table that would achieve the same outcome, but my reluctance on this matter is that people would still have to put up the cost up front—they'd still have to come forward with the cash in order to apply.
civility.explanation: Disagrees with a rival amendment on substance while remaining respectful of its author.

civility.statement: First of all say congratulations to Teanau Tuiono for getting the bill through the process... I also acknowledge Rachel Boyack for chairing us, and all of my colleagues on the Governance and Administration Committee. I think it was a very, very collegial process, and I thought we worked really, really well together to try and nut out these issues.
civility.explanation: Respectful and collegial toward colleagues across parties.

civility.statement: We here in the National Party won't be supporting that Amendment Paper because we made it pretty clear through the select committee process that we needed to get the bill refined to a place that we could support it, and it was that initial original cohort and not the descendants of them, for a variety of different reasons.
civility.explanation: States disagreement on scope grounds without disparaging the member or other parties.

civility.statement: Going with this approach of refunding the fee for applications that are approved I think is going to be a practical approach, because this will also put some personal responsibility on people to really consider and see that they do qualify before they apply.
civility.explanation: Engages the policy mechanism constructively without attacking other parties.

civility.statement: Can I begin by acknowledging my friend and colleague Teanau Tuiono for the amazing work that he has done in shepherding this bill. I want to acknowledge the broader Samoan community here in Aotearoa and throughout the world and their homeland for their amazing contributions to the select committee stage.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious acknowledgement with no attacks.

charisma.statement: I want to put on record my thanks to all of the parties who have gotten us this far—and noting this is as far as we've ever got as a Parliament to getting some form of restitution; some form of restoration for our Samoan aiga.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-party thanks that builds consensus and credits opponents rather than attacking them.

charisma.statement: But, as a backbench MP in an Opposition party, if you don't ask, you don't get. I'm pretty certain the community wanted me to ask; so I'm asking.
charisma.explanation: Candid and relatable framing, but appeals to his own side/community rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: Now, can I just note on the record that the Labour Party will be supporting this amendment in the committee today, and so I thank the member for putting forward this amendment.
charisma.explanation: Constructive and appreciative toward the member in charge across party lines.

charisma.statement: The Labour Party's position is that we support Teanau Tuiono's amendment and we are happy to have continued discussions around the amendment proposed by Andy Foster.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking: signals openness to a rival party's alternative while stating a clear preference.

charisma.statement: First of all say congratulations to Teanau Tuiono for getting the bill through the process... I also acknowledge Rachel Boyack for chairing us, and all of my colleagues on the Governance and Administration Committee. I think it was a very, very collegial process, and I thought we worked really, really well together to try and nut out these issues.
charisma.explanation: Warm, cross-party acknowledgement that emphasises collaboration and common purpose.

charisma.statement: If members across the Chamber are going to acknowledge that there was an injustice done in the past, the least we can do is genuinely commit to going all the way, as far as we can and within the scope of the bill, to deliver some sort of adequate response and justice.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared acknowledgement across the Chamber, but frames it as a challenge to opponents rather than a bridge.

charisma.statement: Can I begin by acknowledging my friend and colleague Teanau Tuiono for the amazing work that he has done in shepherding this bill. I want to acknowledge the broader Samoan community here in Aotearoa and throughout the world and their homeland for their amazing contributions to the select committee stage.
charisma.explanation: Warm and appreciative, but largely rallies his own side and the community rather than reaching across the aisle.

authenticity.statement: But, as a backbench MP in an Opposition party, if you don't ask, you don't get. I'm pretty certain the community wanted me to ask; so I'm asking.
authenticity.explanation: Frames his amendments as consistent with his role and the community's expressed wishes, and he is in fact tabling the amendments he describes—words matching action.

authenticity.statement: During the select committee process, Labour and the Greens both voted in favour of legislation that would have allowed for that first group of descendants who were born before 1 January 1962 to be eligible.
authenticity.explanation: Her stated support for the broadening amendment is backed by Labour's prior select-committee votes she cites—words consistent with the record.

authenticity.statement: You heard during that time how the National Party at the first reading didn't support the legislation, for a couple of key reasons, but then, through the select committee process, myself and my colleagues Cameron Brewer and Tim Costley were able to work with the other members of the Governance and Administration Committee to refine the bill to a place that we thought as a political party we could support it, hence why you saw us at the second reading change our position on the legislation and vote in support of it.
authenticity.explanation: Openly explains and owns National's shift from opposing to supporting, giving a defensible reason (bill refined via select committee)—a transparent position change rather than hidden inconsistency.

authenticity.statement: We here in the National Party won't be supporting that Amendment Paper because we made it pretty clear through the select committee process that we needed to get the bill refined to a place that we could support it, and it was that initial original cohort and not the descendants of them, for a variety of different reasons.
authenticity.explanation: National's opposition to the descendants amendment is consistent with the position it says it held throughout the select committee—stated position matches prior conduct.

authenticity.statement: I also want to highlight that when the bill came through for the first reading, the ACT Party was the first Government party to stand up and support this bill because we assessed the bill and we thought that this bill must go to the select committee process and then very soon we were joined by New Zealand First.
authenticity.explanation: Claims consistent early support by ACT; presented as matching the party's first-reading conduct, though partly self-crediting.

authenticity.statement: As I said in my first reading speech, the ACT Party believes in fairness, we believe in equality, we believe in justice. We also believe that when we talk about fairness, when we talk about justice, it cannot be delivered partially.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value position she links to a consistent ACT stance, but with limited visible action tying words to deeds here.

divination.statement: We had very, very strong advice from Immigration New Zealand, the Department of Internal Affairs, etc., saying, "Please don't do that, because what we know will happen is that people will have a go, and you could end up with thousands and thousands and thousands of people having a go. That will put a significant burden on the administration system."
divination.explanation: Predicts a waiving of fees would trigger a large surge of applications burdening the system; plausible but uncertain in magnitude.

divination.statement: I did think it was really important that we were very, very specific, and you'll see it in the report back from the select committee, so that if this were to be brought before the courts in the future, you could see what was quite clearly defined around who was eligible through the legislation and who wasn't.
divination.explanation: Implicitly predicts vague wording would spawn court cases; directionally plausible but speculative.

divination.statement: The reason I ask some of these questions, although they may seem obvious to some, is that I foresee, like we heard from Mr Rutherford earlier, a time when this ultimately may be challenged, when other descendants might say, "Well, what about those that were born in"—I don't know—"1975?
