strength.statement: Don't forget the $1.9 billion in new funding to deliver 810 extra beds, deliver new front-line staff
strength.explanation: Cites a budgeted Government commitment to deliver beds and staff; funding allocated but delivery is in-progress, not yet demonstrated complete.

strength.statement: You can add to that list that you can blame us for the largest ever financial commitment for victims... To 93,000 more people being able to access legal aid... And for banning the ability to charge interest on legal aid debt
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered policy from Labour's time in government rather than mere aspiration.

forthrightness.statement: That question was put, I think, to the Prime Minister yesterday, and, as the Prime Minister said, the bill will have a full select committee.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Government would move to report the Treaty principles bill back immediately and why not; he confirms it will get a full select committee (implicitly a no) but does not directly address the 'immediate report-back' mechanism or reasons.

forthrightness.statement: As that member will know, we’re about to re-engage with an administration where we got right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement; where he turned in front of the then Prime Minister—because of the work we’d done—and said to his team, “Well, why not?” We missed a chance then; we don’t intend to miss that chance this time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about tariff, AUKUS and climate risks to NZ; he pivots to an FTA anecdote and answers none of the three risks raised.

forthrightness.statement: I have no intention of answering a question made so malignantly as that without any shred of evidence whatsoever.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly declines to answer the question about AUKUS/foreign policy.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that question is littered with assumptions, many of which are completely wrong.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about advice on adding trucks to roads by attacking its premises rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: I’m really proud of the Government school lunch programme because, in effect, what we are doing is actually providing school lunch to an additional 10,000 children that we know are struggling—their families are struggling with food.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she was advised that school lunch and transport changes would worsen child-poverty progress; she pivots to praising the programme and never addresses the advice.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. I reject the member’s assertion that I was unaware an unredacted version had not been released, because she has mischaracterised my personal explanation from yesterday. And I would point out that while the member continues to fixate on old news and trying to find links where there aren’t any, this Government is getting on with actually supporting smokers to quit cigarettes...
forthrightness.explanation: Rejects the premise and pivots to attacking the questioner's motives ('fixate on old news') rather than explaining how the unredacted document was never released.

forthrightness.statement: That is a written question that the member can send to my office, but what I can say is that by September, over 2,000 tamariki had left emergency housing in the nine months to date.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many people have been declined emergency housing since the criteria changed; he declines to give the number, redirecting to a written question and a different statistic.

forthrightness.statement: I believe that many, many Māori communities are very enthusiastic about the number of Māori tamariki who have left emergency housing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Rahui Papa is correct that the Government's bills/policies are racist; he changes the subject entirely to emergency-housing numbers.

forthrightness.statement: the scope of this bill is really answering one simple question: should agriculture enter the emissions trading scheme (ETS) on 1 January of next year or not? It is a view on this side of the House that it should not.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers his own bill's purpose clearly but uses 'scope of the bill' to avoid the substantive certainty question repeatedly put by Luxton.

rigor.statement: The Treaty principles bill being proposed violates this constitutional relationship by overriding decades of judicial decisions.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the objection in a named Standing Order and the legislative/judicial separation, but the 'overriding decades of judicial decisions' claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: that member’s party was part and parcel of that arrangement—begun with a commissioned paper in September of 2021 under the then Labour Government; a report in October 2021—on which we have worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all; so much so that the former defence Minister Andrew Little says that we have got it about right.
rigor.explanation: Cites a documented timeline and an opposing minister's endorsement to rebut the AUKUS criticism; reasoning is grounded, though 'no changes at all' is a strong claim.

rigor.statement: a question that begins “Isn’t it actually the case” is not a question; it’s a statement. And the members are asked here to come to Parliament to ask questions properly, not to make a statement and ask for somebody to confirm it or otherwise.
rigor.explanation: A correct procedural point about the form of parliamentary questions.

rigor.statement: Ministers’ assessments was that Project iReX was inherently flawed, with large cost blowouts for landside infrastructure, and the project needed to be reset.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from cost blowouts to the 'reset' conclusion; premise stated but not quantified here.

rigor.statement: if the member for Rongotai wishes to tell the people of Miramar that they don’t deserve a duplicate Mount Victoria tunnel, that they should sit in traffic, that their buses should go slowly, and that they should have inadequate ability to cycle through the tunnel to get to work, then she is welcome to go and campaign on her commitment to get rid of the second tunnel. Good luck.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/false dichotomy: recasts a question about spending priorities as the member wanting people to 'sit in traffic'.

rigor.statement: Why has she considered that $3 billion for this iReX project, which had a business case and clear strategic value of retaining a rail connection between the North and South Islands, was unaffordable but, yesterday, has committed to at least $3 billion to add less than 2 kilometres of one-car lane in each direction in central Wellington before an investment case has even begun?
rigor.explanation: Draws an evidence-based inconsistency between rejecting one $3b project and committing to another before its business case; the framing is pointed but the comparison is substantive.

rigor.statement: How can he credibly claim this policy is a success when his official advice was that these changes to entry criteria for emergency housing would increase homelessness, and when asked why 20 percent of people that have left emergency housing are now homeless, his response was “I’m not worried.”?
rigor.explanation: Builds the challenge on cited official advice and a figure; the '20 percent are now homeless' inference is contested by the Minister but the argument is evidence-referencing.

rigor.statement: how can just simply removing agriculture from the ETS with no other plan in place and just simply saying, “We will look to price emissions no later than 2030.”, give farmers certainty? How on earth does that give farmers certainty about what’s next?
rigor.explanation: Logical challenge: removing a backstop and deferring to a mechanism-free 2030 date does not deliver the certainty the Minister claims farmers want.

rigor.statement: Why, then, remove the ETS backstop at 2025 and not move that to 2030 if the Minister is so intent on doing some sort of pricing of methane by 2030?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a logical tension between removing the backstop entirely and the stated intent to price by 2030, proposing a coherent alternative.

civility.statement: The Treaty principles bill being proposed violates this constitutional relationship by overriding decades of judicial decisions.
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive, procedural criticism of the bill with no personal attack.

civility.statement: The articles are a complete fabrication and a bastardisation of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic, charged language ('complete fabrication', 'bastardisation') rather than measured critique.

civility.statement: We congratulate President Trump and J D Vance on their election victory, and we look forward to working with them and their incoming administration. But also, we acknowledge the contribution of outgoing President Joe Biden and his administration towards relations between New Zealand and the United States.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious tone acknowledging opponents' contributions.

civility.statement: I have no intention of answering a question made so malignantly as that without any shred of evidence whatsoever.
civility.explanation: Characterises the question as 'malignant' rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: We cannot have these members so sensitive. All I said in Spanish was “Goodbye, my friend.”, but he’s offended by that. Now, for goodness’ sake, we have a very diverse Parliament.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a colleague's objection as over-sensitivity rather than engaging it; mildly belittling.

civility.statement: a question that begins “Isn’t it actually the case” is not a question; it’s a statement. And the members are asked here to come to Parliament to ask questions properly, not to make a statement and ask for somebody to confirm it or otherwise.
civility.explanation: Corrective and slightly condescending ('they should know it after all this time') but focused on procedure, not the person.

civility.statement: Well, that question is littered with assumptions, many of which are completely wrong.
civility.explanation: Dismissive but aimed at the question's assumptions, not the member personally.

civility.statement: if the member for Rongotai wishes to tell the people of Miramar that they don’t deserve a duplicate Mount Victoria tunnel, that they should sit in traffic, that their buses should go slowly, and that they should have inadequate ability to cycle through the tunnel to get to work, then she is welcome to go and campaign on her commitment to get rid of the second tunnel. Good luck.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic ('Good luck') and dismissive rather than engaging the funding comparison raised.

civility.statement: Why has she considered that $3 billion for this iReX project, which had a business case and clear strategic value of retaining a rail connection between the North and South Islands, was unaffordable but, yesterday, has committed to at least $3 billion to add less than 2 kilometres of one-car lane in each direction in central Wellington before an investment case has even begun?
civility.explanation: Adversarial but focused on the policy/spending decision, not the person.

civility.statement: We saw six years of the previous Government; material hardship went up by 4,100 when it was supposedly the priority.
civility.explanation: Critical of the opponent's record on the substance rather than personally.

civility.statement: Yes. I reject the member’s assertion that I was unaware an unredacted version had not been released, because she has mischaracterised my personal explanation from yesterday. And I would point out that while the member continues to fixate on old news and trying to find links where there aren’t any, this Government is getting on with actually supporting smokers to quit cigarettes...
civility.explanation: Characterises the opposition as fixating and dealing in 'headline-catching, misdirected slogans' rather than engaging the OIA substance.

civility.statement: The member may use chicanery and innuendo to try and trap me into an answer, but I’ll repeat that, in this House, we are absolutely dedicated to ensuring that those with genuine need for short-term stays in temporary accommodation... can access that.
civility.explanation: Accuses the questioner of 'chicanery and innuendo' rather than engaging the point about cost reduction.

civility.statement: How can he credibly claim this policy is a success when his official advice was that these changes to entry criteria for emergency housing would increase homelessness, and when asked why 20 percent of people that have left emergency housing are now homeless, his response was “I’m not worried.”?
civility.explanation: Sharp but targets the policy and the Minister's stated position rather than his character.

civility.statement: This Government does not tolerate gangs and the misery that they peddle, and refuses to allow others to come into our country and glorify that misery.
civility.explanation: Charged rhetoric aimed at gangs (not a political opponent); harsh but not a personal attack on a member.

civility.statement: how can just simply removing agriculture from the ETS with no other plan in place and just simply saying, “We will look to price emissions no later than 2030.”, give farmers certainty? How on earth does that give farmers certainty about what’s next?
civility.explanation: Explicitly non-partisan ('I'm not being political'), acknowledges farmers' efficiency, and engages the policy substance.

civility.statement: Why, then, remove the ETS backstop at 2025 and not move that to 2030 if the Minister is so intent on doing some sort of pricing of methane by 2030?
civility.explanation: Measured, substantive questioning focused on evidence and policy design.

veracity.statement: The articles are a complete fabrication and a bastardisation of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: The bill's articles being a 'complete fabrication' is a contestable, exaggerated characterisation of a genuine legislative-drafting dispute.

veracity.statement: that member’s party was part and parcel of that arrangement—begun with a commissioned paper in September of 2021 under the then Labour Government; a report in October 2021—on which we have worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all; so much so that the former defence Minister Andrew Little says that we have got it about right.
veracity.explanation: The 2021 origins under Labour are broadly accurate; the characterisation of Little's view and 'no changes at all' is harder to verify.

veracity.statement: core Crown revenue in the first three months of the year totalled $32.3 billion and core Crown expenses totalled $34.9 billion... the OBEGAL deficit was $700 million larger than forecast, at $4.2 billion for the quarter, and net core Crown debt was also $700 million larger than forecast, at $177.6 billion.
veracity.explanation: Presented as the just-released Treasury financial statements; figures are checkable and framed as official.

veracity.statement: That extra debt amounts to $118 billion, which for the members’ knowledge is the equivalent of $22,000 for every person in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The per-person figure and attribution of all 2017–2023 debt to the previous Government omits context (COVID response), giving a directionally true but partisan-framed claim.

veracity.statement: Treasury modelling shows the investments in Budget 2024 are estimated to lift around 17,000 children out of poverty, on the after-housing-cost measure, by 2026-27.
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites modelling but presents a projected estimate as established, omitting countervailing advice raised by the questioner.

veracity.statement: during the last full four years of the previous National-led Government, from the year 2013 to 2017, the number of children in material hardship fell by 56,200.
veracity.explanation: A checkable statistic used selectively (chosen window) to credit her party; directionally plausible but framing-dependent.

veracity.statement: We saw six years of the previous Government; material hardship went up by 4,100 when it was supposedly the priority.
veracity.explanation: A specific stat aimed at the previous Government; checkable but the chosen measure/period is used to make a partisan contrast.

veracity.statement: I reject the assertions in that question. I did not apologise yesterday; I sought leave to make a clarification and correction of what was said.
veracity.explanation: Verrall immediately tables Hansard of Costello's prior statement containing 'and I apologise for any confusion to the House', directly contradicting the claim that she did not apologise.

veracity.statement: none of the 726 households and 1,452 tamariki living in emergency housing and transitioned through priority one by 30 September 2024 into social housing were homeless when placed. Every single one of those 1,452 children were placed into warm, dry homes.
veracity.explanation: 'None were homeless when placed' is narrowly framed to the moment of placement, sidestepping the questioner's point about people homeless after leaving emergency housing.

veracity.statement: I can also confirm that when we arrived, we were spending around a million dollars a day on emergency housing, and now it’s less than half a million.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim of halved spending, presented as fact without a cited source in the exchange.

veracity.statement: Yesterday, police arrested three associates of the Mongols gang in Christchurch, recovering stolen property from the gang’s headquarters.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable operational claim reported as fact.

veracity.statement: Data shows that women who participate in the BreastScreen Aotearoa programme are 34 percent less likely to die from breast cancer.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to programme data with a specific figure; broadly consistent with screening-benefit evidence.

veracity.statement: New Zealand’s agricultural sector is one of the most carbon-efficient sectors in the world and is the backbone of the New Zealand economy.
veracity.explanation: A commonly-stated but contested efficiency claim; hedged as 'one of the most', which the opposition specifically probes for evidence.

veracity.statement: it currently reflects around 53 percent of New Zealand’s total emissions. New Zealand has one of the highest proportions of methane from livestock emissions of any country in the world
veracity.explanation: The ~50% agricultural share is well-established for NZ; broadly accurate.

charisma.statement: We congratulate President Trump and J D Vance on their election victory, and we look forward to working with them and their incoming administration. But also, we acknowledge the contribution of outgoing President Joe Biden and his administration towards relations between New Zealand and the United States.
charisma.explanation: Diplomatic and inclusive, extending goodwill to both the incoming and outgoing administrations across the political divide.

divination.statement: The result of every US presidential election, as in the last 100 years, has had and will have a significant impact on New Zealand, our region, and indeed, the world.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the new US administration will significantly affect NZ; well-supported by historical pattern, though 'significant impact' is broad.

divination.statement: Treasury modelling shows the investments in Budget 2024 are estimated to lift around 17,000 children out of poverty, on the after-housing-cost measure, by 2026-27.
divination.explanation: A forecast of poverty reduction by 2026-27; modelled but uncertain and contested by other advice referenced in the exchange.

divination.statement: This age extension could potentially save 22 lives per year.
divination.explanation: A forecast of lives saved annually; plausible and modelled but hedged ('could potentially').

specificity.statement: As that member will know, we’re about to re-engage with an administration where we got right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement; where he turned in front of the then Prime Minister—because of the work we’d done—and said to his team, “Well, why not?” We missed a chance then; we don’t intend to miss that chance this time.
specificity.explanation: Evocative anecdote but no concrete detail on the trade, security or climate risks asked about.

specificity.statement: Ministers’ assessments was that Project iReX was inherently flawed, with large cost blowouts for landside infrastructure, and the project needed to be reset.
specificity.explanation: Identifies landside-infrastructure blowouts as the flaw, but without figures in this sentence.

specificity.statement: core Crown revenue in the first three months of the year totalled $32.3 billion and core Crown expenses totalled $34.9 billion... the OBEGAL deficit was $700 million larger than forecast, at $4.2 billion for the quarter, and net core Crown debt was also $700 million larger than forecast, at $177.6 billion.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures, comparison to forecast, and a named reporting period.

specificity.statement: That extra debt amounts to $118 billion, which for the members’ knowledge is the equivalent of $22,000 for every person in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Gives a total figure and a per-capita conversion.

specificity.statement: Treasury modelling shows the investments in Budget 2024 are estimated to lift around 17,000 children out of poverty, on the after-housing-cost measure, by 2026-27.
specificity.explanation: Named figure, measure and target year, attributed to Treasury modelling.

specificity.statement: during the last full four years of the previous National-led Government, from the year 2013 to 2017, the number of children in material hardship fell by 56,200.
specificity.explanation: Specific figure and date range.

specificity.statement: none of the 726 households and 1,452 tamariki living in emergency housing and transitioned through priority one by 30 September 2024 into social housing were homeless when placed. Every single one of those 1,452 children were placed into warm, dry homes.
specificity.explanation: Exact household/child counts, a date, and the priority-one pathway named.

specificity.statement: This Government has a target—target No. 8—to reduce the number of households living in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030. We are up to 62 percent in nine months.
specificity.explanation: Named target, percentage, deadline and progress figure.

specificity.statement: I can also confirm that when we arrived, we were spending around a million dollars a day on emergency housing, and now it’s less than half a million.
specificity.explanation: Concrete before/after daily-spend figures.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, police arrested three associates of the Mongols gang in Christchurch, recovering stolen property from the gang’s headquarters.
specificity.explanation: Specific event: number arrested, gang, location and outcome.

specificity.statement: This Government does not tolerate gangs and the misery that they peddle, and refuses to allow others to come into our country and glorify that misery.
specificity.explanation: Statement of stance with emotive framing but no concrete mechanism or measure in this sentence.

specificity.statement: free breast-screening is being extended for 70- to 74-year-old women, starting in the Nelson-Marlborough district, ahead of a national roll-out late next year.
specificity.explanation: Named age band, starting district and rough roll-out timing.

specificity.statement: Data shows that women who participate in the BreastScreen Aotearoa programme are 34 percent less likely to die from breast cancer.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentage tied to a named programme.

specificity.statement: We’ve also introduced a target for faster cancer treatment, increased access to CT scanning, expanded access to life-extending cancer medicines through our transformative $604 million investment in Pharmac, and started building a new cancer radiotherapy machine at Whangārei Hospital.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete actions with a dollar figure and a named hospital project.

specificity.statement: This work will consolidate the three current regulators: the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, the Financial Markets Authority, and the Department of Internal Affairs into a single regulatory body under the Department of Internal Affairs. This consolidation will cut red tape, streamline processes, and reduce the high compliance costs that the report identifies as obstacles for small businesses.
specificity.explanation: Names the three regulators and the concrete structural change; the benefit claims are less concrete.

specificity.statement: New Zealand’s agricultural sector is one of the most carbon-efficient sectors in the world and is the backbone of the New Zealand economy.
specificity.explanation: General assertion without a metric or comparison basis.

specificity.statement: it currently reflects around 53 percent of New Zealand’s total emissions. New Zealand has one of the highest proportions of methane from livestock emissions of any country in the world
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage figure and a comparative characterisation.

specificity.statement: under this Government, we have signalled our intent that by 2030 we will be putting in place a pricing system in order to price agricultural emissions.
specificity.explanation: A date is given but no mechanism, price or design for the pricing system.

authenticity.statement: I reject the assertions in that question. I did not apologise yesterday; I sought leave to make a clarification and correction of what was said.
authenticity.explanation: Denying an apology that the record shows she made is an inconsistency between her account and her own words in the House.

strength.statement: This Government has a target—target No. 8—to reduce the number of households living in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030. We are up to 62 percent in nine months.
strength.explanation: Reports concrete measured progress (62% in nine months) toward a stated target, though delivery mechanism (criteria changes) is contested.

strength.statement: free breast-screening is being extended for 70- to 74-year-old women, starting in the Nelson-Marlborough district, ahead of a national roll-out late next year.
strength.explanation: An announced extension with a starting location; delivery is beginning but the national roll-out is future, so partial follow-through.

strength.statement: We’ve also introduced a target for faster cancer treatment, increased access to CT scanning, expanded access to life-extending cancer medicines through our transformative $604 million investment in Pharmac, and started building a new cancer radiotherapy machine at Whangārei Hospital.
strength.explanation: Claims a mix of delivered and in-progress actions (funding made, machine 'started building'); some follow-through demonstrated, some still underway.

strength.statement: under this Government, we have signalled our intent that by 2030 we will be putting in place a pricing system in order to price agricultural emissions.
strength.explanation: Signals intent by 2030 but with no mechanism and having removed the existing backstop, so aspiration rather than demonstrated delivery.

specificity.statement: It extends the time frame to implement an emissions measurement scheme by six months, meaning that this would be required by 1 July 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (measurement scheme) and a precise date (1 July 2025).

specificity.statement: The purpose here is to stop the pricing of agriculture in 55 days from today. That is the reality. It is a position that, as I said, is one of consensus support, and I am surprised by those that aren’t supporting it.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe (55 days) but the 'consensus' claim is unquantified.

specificity.statement: there are 50,000 GST-registered farmers, and, in addition to that, there are 56,000 “others”, including small-block holders—so 106,000; we’re in that ballpark.
specificity.explanation: Breaks the figure into named components (50,000 GST-registered + 56,000 others).

specificity.statement: We are working with the sector, not against them.
specificity.explanation: A slogan with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: The Hon Rachel Brooking’s point in regards to agricultural emissions, the 53 percent: the source for that is part of the 2022 New Zealand greenhouse gas inventory, which can be found on the Ministry for the Environment’s website.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact document and where to find it.

specificity.statement: some of our customers—that is, some of the big players; Nestlé in particular—are prepared to pay bonuses for lower carbon ingredients.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific customer (Nestlé) but no figures or terms.

specificity.statement: I record all the emissions that are happening on-farm. I have an insights report by Fonterra that gives me ideas on how to improve my efficiency on-farm and improve the greenhouse gas emissions from my farm. I do not see anything in this bill that will stop that from carrying on.
specificity.explanation: Concrete personal example (Fonterra insights report) but no figures.

specificity.statement: voluntary mechanisms and taking our time to take action is actually not going to cut it. We will not only need to put in legislative mechanisms and pricing mechanisms; we’re also really going to have to have that whole carrot and stick approach.
specificity.explanation: Refers to 'legislative', 'pricing' and 'carrot and stick' mechanisms without concrete detail.

specificity.statement: I note that the Minister has announced previously—I think it was—a $400 million investment in tech and tools there, and that the Government has signalled intention to equip farmers, but what I’ve been hearing is that that’s still quite a way off and does not necessarily mean that the tools and technologies will be available in order for pricing to be put in place by 2030.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure ($400 million) but hedges on timeframe.

rigor.statement: One of the most vital things we need in understanding any environmental problem is solid data on the pollution, on the emissions, on what is the nature of the problem, and if you take away the requirement for processes or farmers to report, you basically remove the ability of us to understand the scale of the problem and, likewise, the ability to understand the scale of success when we do manage to reduce emissions.
rigor.explanation: Coherent premise-to-conclusion reasoning (no data → no ability to measure the problem or progress), though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It seems obvious, it seems axiomatic, that if you remove any of the incentives, any promise of a forthcoming pricing regime, any sort of backstop, those emissions are going to start increasing again.
rigor.explanation: Leans on 'obvious/axiomatic' assertion (appeal to self-evidence) rather than presenting evidence for the causal claim.

rigor.statement: The processor-level reporting obligations that the bill removes are entirely separate from the national accounting of agricultural emissions. The New Zealand accounting standards around national emissions uses data sets from a wide range of sources, including Statistics New Zealand and other aspects—Beef + Lamb New Zealand, DairyNZ, etc. It does not use ETS data, which was last updated in 2012.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes two data systems and reasons from that distinction to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: It would be simply inefficient of any Government to look to put agricultural into the ETS and then to take it out—that is ridiculous. I’m not sure why members of the Opposition would think that that would be a sensible thing to do. Well, I probably do know, but I’m not going to get into that.
rigor.explanation: Relies on ridicule and innuendo rather than engaging the Opposition's actual argument for extending the backstop.

rigor.statement: It doesn’t take agricultural activities at all out of the ETS. It takes or removes what was a backstop obligation for biogenic methane and nitrous oxide... the bill is actually quite misleading.
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in the bill's actual coverage of energy vs biogenic emissions.

rigor.statement: the animal ruminant sector has been falling since about 2010, so the overall contribution of methane by virtue of that is diminishing, notwithstanding that we are talking about a short-lived gas that decays back to carbon dioxide.
rigor.explanation: Draws a reassuring conclusion from a partial trend without accounting for offsetting increases.

rigor.statement: we are well on track to meet obligations that we have made in this House and internationally. We are actually catastrophising about a problem that actually isn’t existing in real time.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping reassurance ('a problem that isn't existing in real time') offered without evidence and against expert advice.

rigor.statement: the large amount of risk for the rural industries in respect of methane disappeared the moment the last Government—with New Zealand First at the time, actually—introduced the split gas target, so that the amount of emission reduction expected from short-lived gases like biogenic methane was a lot lower than the reduction in emissions required from carbon dioxide
rigor.explanation: Grounds the risk claim in the specific policy mechanism that changed the numbers.

rigor.statement: Can I also ask the Minister to confirm that the backstop included 95 percent free allocation of emissions based on 1990 emissions. There was no great financial risk to those sectors that I’ve heard some other members in this House say the rural industry was exposed to, because there was 95 percent free allocation. There was only exposure for risk for the last 5 percent of emissions.
rigor.explanation: Quantified rebuttal of the 'huge cost to farmers' claim, following logically from the allocation percentage.

rigor.statement: there is a fallacy in taking a 30-year offset in respect of a carbon dioxide emission that lasts 1,000 years, whereas there is good sense in enabling farmers to have the benefit of a forestry offset to offset methane emissions if they couldn’t reduce them otherwise.
rigor.explanation: Cites the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment and reasons carefully from gas-lifetime matching between forestry offsets and short-lived methane.

rigor.statement: there’s also another sector that has a short-lived gas, methane, which is in the emissions trading scheme, and that’s the waste sector. Now, the waste sector still has to reduce their methane; it’s still in the emissions trading scheme. If the logic is “because it’s a methane”, “because it’s a short-lived gas”—well, most of the emissions from waste is also a short-lived gas—would we, on that basis, also seek to exclude waste from the emissions trading scheme?
rigor.explanation: Consistency argument by counter-example: applies the Government's own 'short-lived methane' rationale to the waste sector to expose the inconsistency.

rigor.statement: If the kind of logic for exempting agriculture from paying for emissions is because it’s efficient, should we not apply that logic wider to the rest of the economy? That is correctly what the inter-sectoral analysis is revealing here, because it’s actually not very fair.
rigor.explanation: Tests the 'agriculture is efficient' rationale for generality and ties it to the regulatory impact statement's inter-sectoral equity finding.

rigor.statement: why not change it so that the Climate Change Commission has a role in monitoring and reporting on the progress of the Government’s initiatives to price on-farm emissions by 2030?... we can have a blue-green deal across this House. None of the other parties need to vote for it. I hope they’d vote for it, of course, but I’m very interested in the Minister’s views on that particular section.
rigor.explanation: Argues that if the Government is serious about 2030 pricing, independent monitoring logically supports that aim.

rigor.statement: the Minister alluded to the fact that we were already on track, according to the projections of the second emissions reduction plan. Now, I checked back to that document, and it said that that was with the assumption that a methane inhibitor was developed.
rigor.explanation: Checks the source behind the Minister's 'on track' claim and identifies the load-bearing assumption (a methane inhibitor).

rigor.statement: Profitability is quite important. You know, I do like to make a profit—obviously, you’re not too interested in farmers making money.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: attributes an anti-farmer-profit motive to opponents that they did not state.

rigor.statement: what happens if this all falls apart, if we don’t bring to fruition the technologies that they’re heavily investing in and it puts us at risk of not meeting our methane reduction targets? Therefore, why is it not then OK or worth thinking about moving the backstop of bringing agriculture into the emissions trading scheme to further beyond or to 2030?
rigor.explanation: Reasonable contingency argument: if the technology bet fails, an extended backstop preserves the target.

rigor.statement: there are significant risks to meeting the second and third emissions budgets and the 2030 biogenic methane target. The agriculture and transport sectors show the largest risks, and insufficient action to reduce emissions in these sectors will put the second and third emissions budgets at risk.
rigor.explanation: Deploys an authoritative, cited source directly against the 'on track' claim.

rigor.statement: just because something is related to an animal—that one gas is sometimes related to an animal, but sometimes it is not; sometimes it is related to fertiliser. That seems like a very good reason to treat that nitrous oxide that’s coming from the fertiliser differently from the nitrous oxide that is coming from the animals.
rigor.explanation: Exposes the inconsistency in bundling fertiliser-source nitrous oxide with animal-source gases, and in treating waste methane differently from ag methane.

rigor.statement: I wonder what the Minister’s feelings are about the total abandonment of the “polluter pays” principle, because that is where all these conversations are about climate emissions. They are pollution and we have a “polluter pays” principle.
rigor.explanation: Invokes an established policy principle to frame the critique, though 'total abandonment' is somewhat rhetorical.

rigor.statement: voluntary mechanisms and taking our time to take action is actually not going to cut it. We will not only need to put in legislative mechanisms and pricing mechanisms; we’re also really going to have to have that whole carrot and stick approach.
rigor.explanation: States a position with general reasoning but leans on assertion ('not going to cut it') rather than presenting evidence.

rigor.statement: I note that the Minister has announced previously—I think it was—a $400 million investment in tech and tools there, and that the Government has signalled intention to equip farmers, but what I’ve been hearing is that that’s still quite a way off and does not necessarily mean that the tools and technologies will be available in order for pricing to be put in place by 2030.
rigor.explanation: Questions whether announced funding translates to available tools in time, distinguishing announcement from delivery.

rigor.statement: the Minister mentioned a number—that was 100,000—and I did hear colleagues on this side of the Chamber query that number. I don’t see an explanation within the RIS, as far as I can tell, that tells us how that number was arrived at. I would appreciate some clarification from the Minister around that.
rigor.explanation: Probes the evidentiary basis of the 100,000-farmer figure against the regulatory impact statement.

civility.statement: One of the most vital things we need in understanding any environmental problem is solid data on the pollution, on the emissions, on what is the nature of the problem, and if you take away the requirement for processes or farmers to report, you basically remove the ability of us to understand the scale of the problem and, likewise, the ability to understand the scale of success when we do manage to reduce emissions.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the reporting question with no personal attack.

civility.statement: It would be simply inefficient of any Government to look to put agricultural into the ETS and then to take it out—that is ridiculous. I’m not sure why members of the Opposition would think that that would be a sensible thing to do. Well, I probably do know, but I’m not going to get into that.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' position as 'ridiculous' and adds an unspoken insinuation about their motives.

civility.statement: It doesn’t take agricultural activities at all out of the ETS. It takes or removes what was a backstop obligation for biogenic methane and nitrous oxide... the bill is actually quite misleading.
civility.explanation: Calls the bill 'misleading' (a claim about the legislation, not a personal attack), but the framing is pointed.

civility.statement: we are well on track to meet obligations that we have made in this House and internationally. We are actually catastrophising about a problem that actually isn’t existing in real time.
civility.explanation: 'Catastrophising' characterises opponents' concern dismissively but stops short of a personal attack.

civility.statement: why not change it so that the Climate Change Commission has a role in monitoring and reporting on the progress of the Government’s initiatives to price on-farm emissions by 2030?... we can have a blue-green deal across this House. None of the other parties need to vote for it. I hope they’d vote for it, of course, but I’m very interested in the Minister’s views on that particular section.
civility.explanation: Constructive, good-faith engagement with the Government's stated goal.

civility.statement: Profitability is quite important. You know, I do like to make a profit—obviously, you’re not too interested in farmers making money.
civility.explanation: Personal jab imputing to opponents that they don't care about farmers' incomes.

civility.statement: what happens if this all falls apart, if we don’t bring to fruition the technologies that they’re heavily investing in and it puts us at risk of not meeting our methane reduction targets? Therefore, why is it not then OK or worth thinking about moving the backstop of bringing agriculture into the emissions trading scheme to further beyond or to 2030?
civility.explanation: Poses it as a 'genuine question' engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: just because something is related to an animal—that one gas is sometimes related to an animal, but sometimes it is not; sometimes it is related to fertiliser. That seems like a very good reason to treat that nitrous oxide that’s coming from the fertiliser differently from the nitrous oxide that is coming from the animals.
civility.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated logic on its merits without personal attack.

civility.statement: I wonder what the Minister’s feelings are about the total abandonment of the “polluter pays” principle, because that is where all these conversations are about climate emissions. They are pollution and we have a “polluter pays” principle.
civility.explanation: Frames a substantive policy question and directs it at the coalition partners' stated positions.

civility.statement: the Minister mentioned a number—that was 100,000—and I did hear colleagues on this side of the Chamber query that number. I don’t see an explanation within the RIS, as far as I can tell, that tells us how that number was arrived at. I would appreciate some clarification from the Minister around that.
civility.explanation: Politely requests clarification, focused on the substance.

veracity.statement: What about the long-lived nature of nitrous oxide, which is a 300 times more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and is a long-lived gas?
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: nitrous oxide is roughly 270–300x more potent than CO2 and is long-lived (~114-year atmospheric lifetime).

veracity.statement: The processor-level reporting obligations that the bill removes are entirely separate from the national accounting of agricultural emissions. The New Zealand accounting standards around national emissions uses data sets from a wide range of sources, including Statistics New Zealand and other aspects—Beef + Lamb New Zealand, DairyNZ, etc. It does not use ETS data, which was last updated in 2012.
veracity.explanation: Largely accurate: the national GHG inventory draws on Stats NZ and sector bodies rather than ETS processor data.

veracity.statement: diesel going into a ute or petrol going into a farm bike is covered under the ETS and will continue to be so.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: transport fuels are priced at point of sale under the ETS and are unaffected by this bill.

veracity.statement: That plan signalled and indicated that we are broadly on track to meet the 2030 methane reduction targets, today, where we stand—no pricing, no other aspects. We are on track, where we are today, in terms of meeting that target.
veracity.explanation: Contested and missing context: the projection assumes a methane inhibitor is developed, and the Climate Change Commission warns of significant risk to the 2030 methane target.

veracity.statement: there are 50,000 GST-registered farmers, and, in addition to that, there are 56,000 “others”, including small-block holders—so 106,000; we’re in that ballpark.
veracity.explanation: Plausible sourcing but the count of 'others/small-block holders' as ETS entrants is an estimate presented as fact.

veracity.statement: Fertiliser accounts for around 18 percent of ag emissions—nitrous oxide—and the total contribution from fertiliser is around 3.8 percent. Nitrous oxide is around 9 percent of total emissions
veracity.explanation: Figures are roughly in the right range but presented in a muddled way that conflates shares of ag vs total emissions.

veracity.statement: The Hon Rachel Brooking’s point in regards to agricultural emissions, the 53 percent: the source for that is part of the 2022 New Zealand greenhouse gas inventory, which can be found on the Ministry for the Environment’s website.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: agriculture is around half of NZ's gross emissions per the GHG inventory.

veracity.statement: It doesn’t take agricultural activities at all out of the ETS. It takes or removes what was a backstop obligation for biogenic methane and nitrous oxide... the bill is actually quite misleading.
veracity.explanation: Substantially correct: the bill leaves agricultural energy emissions (diesel, coal) in the ETS and only removes the biogenic backstop, as the Minister later confirms.

veracity.statement: some of our customers—that is, some of the big players; Nestlé in particular—are prepared to pay bonuses for lower carbon ingredients.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and directionally accurate: major food companies including Nestlé run low-carbon sourcing incentives, though 'bonuses' is generalised.

veracity.statement: the animal ruminant sector has been falling since about 2010, so the overall contribution of methane by virtue of that is diminishing, notwithstanding that we are talking about a short-lived gas that decays back to carbon dioxide.
veracity.explanation: Selective: sheep numbers have declined but dairy intensification offset much of it, so 'the ruminant sector is falling / methane diminishing' omits context.

veracity.statement: we are well on track to meet obligations that we have made in this House and internationally. We are actually catastrophising about a problem that actually isn’t existing in real time.
veracity.explanation: Contradicts Climate Change Commission advice of significant risk to the second and third budgets and the 2030 methane target.

veracity.statement: the large amount of risk for the rural industries in respect of methane disappeared the moment the last Government—with New Zealand First at the time, actually—introduced the split gas target, so that the amount of emission reduction expected from short-lived gases like biogenic methane was a lot lower than the reduction in emissions required from carbon dioxide
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the split-gas target set a lower reduction requirement for biogenic methane than for long-lived gases, reducing the sector's exposure.

veracity.statement: Can I also ask the Minister to confirm that the backstop included 95 percent free allocation of emissions based on 1990 emissions. There was no great financial risk to those sectors that I’ve heard some other members in this House say the rural industry was exposed to, because there was 95 percent free allocation. There was only exposure for risk for the last 5 percent of emissions.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the design featured 95% free allocation, so priced exposure was limited to ~5% of emissions.

veracity.statement: The ETS, as originally designed—and I did it way back when, in about 2007—was designed to be at the processor level.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Parker was involved in the ETS's establishment in the late 2000s and it was designed at processor level.

veracity.statement: there’s also another sector that has a short-lived gas, methane, which is in the emissions trading scheme, and that’s the waste sector. Now, the waste sector still has to reduce their methane; it’s still in the emissions trading scheme. If the logic is “because it’s a methane”, “because it’s a short-lived gas”—well, most of the emissions from waste is also a short-lived gas—would we, on that basis, also seek to exclude waste from the emissions trading scheme?
veracity.explanation: Accurate: waste-sector methane is covered by the ETS.

veracity.statement: the Minister alluded to the fact that we were already on track, according to the projections of the second emissions reduction plan. Now, I checked back to that document, and it said that that was with the assumption that a methane inhibitor was developed.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the ERP relying on assumed technology uptake to hit the target.

veracity.statement: there are significant risks to meeting the second and third emissions budgets and the 2030 biogenic methane target. The agriculture and transport sectors show the largest risks, and insufficient action to reduce emissions in these sectors will put the second and third emissions budgets at risk.
veracity.explanation: Accurately quotes the Climate Change Commission's published risk assessment.

veracity.statement: I note that the Minister has announced previously—I think it was—a $400 million investment in tech and tools there, and that the Government has signalled intention to equip farmers, but what I’ve been hearing is that that’s still quite a way off and does not necessarily mean that the tools and technologies will be available in order for pricing to be put in place by 2030.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a previously announced investment figure with an explicit hedge ('I think it was').

divination.statement: It seems obvious, it seems axiomatic, that if you remove any of the incentives, any promise of a forthcoming pricing regime, any sort of backstop, those emissions are going to start increasing again.
divination.explanation: Falsifiable prediction that emissions will rise once incentives are removed; directionally plausible but magnitude and timing uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: The processor-level reporting obligations that the bill removes are entirely separate from the national accounting of agricultural emissions. The New Zealand accounting standards around national emissions uses data sets from a wide range of sources, including Statistics New Zealand and other aspects—Beef + Lamb New Zealand, DairyNZ, etc. It does not use ETS data, which was last updated in 2012.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Abel's question about whether removing reporting harms understanding of emissions.

forthrightness.statement: diesel going into a ute or petrol going into a farm bike is covered under the ETS and will continue to be so.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers O'Connor's question about whether the energy/fuel component of agriculture stays in the ETS.

forthrightness.statement: there are 50,000 GST-registered farmers, and, in addition to that, there are 56,000 “others”, including small-block holders—so 106,000; we’re in that ballpark.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Radhakrishnan's challenge about where the 100,000-farmer figure came from.

forthrightness.statement: the points in regards to the future models that the Government may be considering in regards to policy of the pricing mechanisms of which we have committed to by 2030 are not part of the scope of this bill, but we will be taking into account all considerations as part of that process.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer Parker's question on why delaying the backstop was rejected, deflecting to 'scope' and vague future consideration.

forthrightness.statement: Fertiliser accounts for around 18 percent of ag emissions—nitrous oxide—and the total contribution from fertiliser is around 3.8 percent. Nitrous oxide is around 9 percent of total emissions
forthrightness.explanation: Attempts a direct, numerical answer to repeated questions about nitrous oxide.

forthrightness.statement: The Hon Rachel Brooking’s point in regards to agricultural emissions, the 53 percent: the source for that is part of the 2022 New Zealand greenhouse gas inventory, which can be found on the Ministry for the Environment’s website.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Brooking's demand for the evidence that ~50% of emissions come from agriculture, and cites the source.

charisma.statement: The purpose here is to stop the pricing of agriculture in 55 days from today. That is the reality. It is a position that, as I said, is one of consensus support, and I am surprised by those that aren’t supporting it.
charisma.explanation: Asserts consensus while expressing surprise at dissenters, appealing to his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: It would be simply inefficient of any Government to look to put agricultural into the ETS and then to take it out—that is ridiculous. I’m not sure why members of the Opposition would think that that would be a sensible thing to do. Well, I probably do know, but I’m not going to get into that.
charisma.explanation: Alienating rather than bridge-building; shuts down rather than invites the other side.

charisma.statement: We are working with the sector, not against them.
charisma.explanation: Frames his side as with farmers, implicitly casting opponents as against them rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: why not change it so that the Climate Change Commission has a role in monitoring and reporting on the progress of the Government’s initiatives to price on-farm emissions by 2030?... we can have a blue-green deal across this House. None of the other parties need to vote for it. I hope they’d vote for it, of course, but I’m very interested in the Minister’s views on that particular section.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks a cross-party 'blue-green deal', invites the Minister in, and offers to bring his own colleagues along.

charisma.statement: Profitability is quite important. You know, I do like to make a profit—obviously, you’re not too interested in farmers making money.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them dig rather than a persuasive appeal.

charisma.statement: what happens if this all falls apart, if we don’t bring to fruition the technologies that they’re heavily investing in and it puts us at risk of not meeting our methane reduction targets? Therefore, why is it not then OK or worth thinking about moving the backstop of bringing agriculture into the emissions trading scheme to further beyond or to 2030?
charisma.explanation: Frames a compromise (extending rather than removing) but is aimed mainly at pressing the Minister.

authenticity.statement: The ETS, as originally designed—and I did it way back when, in about 2007—was designed to be at the processor level.
authenticity.explanation: His advocacy for processor-level pricing is consistent with his own record as an architect of the original ETS design.

authenticity.statement: I record all the emissions that are happening on-farm. I have an insights report by Fonterra that gives me ideas on how to improve my efficiency on-farm and improve the greenhouse gas emissions from my farm. I do not see anything in this bill that will stop that from carrying on.
authenticity.explanation: As a farmer, cites his own on-farm practice, consistent with his stated position that market-led measurement continues.

forthrightness.statement: The answer will be no. I will not be supporting that amendment. ... The reason is that the Climate Change Commission has actually delivered that advice and, therefore, the function is no longer required as part of that law. Therefore, the clause is coming out.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and unambiguously answers whether he will support the amendment ('no') and supplies a reason. Fully addresses the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: I'll tell the member that I've spent a long time agonising in regards to the question and the points that the member's raised, but it's not in the scope of this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Abel's direct question about whether the Government is agnostic on land use, he declines to answer on scope grounds, avoiding the substance entirely.

forthrightness.statement: no, we won't be accepting that amendment. It's not helpful because agriculture isn't going to stay within the emissions trading scheme (ETS). Why would you leave clauses in there in that regard when that is not the intent, and, actually, that is a consensus intent by not just the Government but by the Opposition, who were also in that position, regarding taking the agricultural elements out of the ETS?
forthrightness.explanation: Directly declines the amendment and gives a reason, addressing Willis's request head-on.

specificity.statement: The answer will be no. I will not be supporting that amendment. ... The reason is that the Climate Change Commission has actually delivered that advice and, therefore, the function is no longer required as part of that law. Therefore, the clause is coming out.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (Commission advice delivered -> function redundant -> clause removed), though no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Are you agnostic about land use change, or is this simply about fiercely defending a specific kind of land use, i.e., pastoral livestock farming?
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete examples (Canterbury Plains dairy conversion, Southland barley/oats, nitrate leachate) but the core ask is a general question about policy stance.

specificity.statement: Was there a cost-benefit analysis done on the other proposals? ... that seems to be not evidence-based policy if we're just evaluating the status quo and not comparing the relativity of the options. The cost-benefit analysis shows that it does have a positive cost-benefit ratio—1.24 or 1.13 without the premium for carbon action
specificity.explanation: Cites clause 32, Schedule 2, three named policy options, and precise cost-benefit ratios (1.24 / 1.13).

specificity.statement: why repeal legislation that was actually set up during a previous National Government, the Key Government, which was just set up to enable participants to actually measure their emissions and report on them? ... If you're not measuring it, how can you manage it?
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes clause 35(1) reporting from clause 35(2) ETS mandate and identifies the regulation's role as an emissions-factor baseline.

specificity.statement: with the repeal of the requirement to report—and also with the repeal of the requirement to do anything at all other than rely on ... the technological mitigation and the methane inhibitors ... is there a concern that, by repealing all these mechanisms, there's a further emissions gap that's been opened in the nationally determined contribution?
specificity.explanation: References the nationally determined contribution, the emissions gap, and CIPA (Climate Implications of Policy Assessment) but no numbers.

specificity.statement: methane—often related to ruminants but also related to landfills—is treated separately and ... the landfills are still in the ETS and they're not being removed despite the fact that methane is also related to ruminants. The logic just doesn't seem to be there.
specificity.explanation: Cites clause 37, the specific 3.8% fertiliser figure, and named definitions being revoked (calf, cow, heifer, milk solids, synthetic fertilisers).

specificity.statement: I'm suggesting that the title should be the "Climate Change Response (Removing Agriculture Despite Agreeing that it Makes up over 50 Percent of our Emissions) Amendment Act 2024".
specificity.explanation: A slogan-style title; gestures at the ~50% agriculture figure but is a rhetorical device rather than a substantive proposal.

specificity.statement: I'm aware that the Minister is placing a lot of faith in the magic bullet approach to agricultural emissions and in unproven technologies, and we are concerned that by shutting the door to ensuring that we can reduce agricultural emissions through the emissions trading scheme, we are not going to be able to meet our commitments.
specificity.explanation: Proposes deleting clause 37 and retaining specific named definitions (calf, cow, heifer, milk solids, synthetic fertilisers, vealer) to preserve a future pricing framework, with precise definitional detail.

specificity.statement: It is correct that 3.8 percent of total agricultural emissions come from nitrous oxide from synthetic fertiliser. ... the uptake in regards to that is progressing already without any incentives by Government in order to achieve that. ... The current status quo in terms of the trajectory of emissions reduction for methane in particular is on track in regards to our 2030 target.
specificity.explanation: Cites 3.8%, the draft emissions reduction plan, and the 2030 target, but no mechanism detail or figures on the technology uptake.

specificity.statement: It's an unnecessary administrative burden; it doesn't change the outcome very much. It's much better to have a processor-level obligation, which is a lot more efficient administratively, with volunteers being rewarded and the bulk of the price signal flowing through from the processor, based on reporting at the processor level.
specificity.explanation: Cites clause 35(1), the Climate Change (Agriculture Sector) Regulations 2010, and Regulation 9's requirement to record tonnes of milk solids at dairy processing.

specificity.statement: that report actually said "Be careful about that breather", because they referenced a Chapman Tripp report which showed that 80 percent—80 percent—of the exports from New Zealand to international markets require climate change reporting obligations.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete sources (Rabobank, Chapman Tripp, Reserve Bank), buyers (Nestle, Tesco), and the 80% figure.

specificity.statement: we actually had the climate commission come in and they talked about their first monitoring report ... they really stressed the significant risks to the second and third budgets. This is primarily ... with agriculture and transport sectors. ... in the absence of pricing mechanisms or any incentives, these provide headwinds to genuine emissions reduction.
specificity.explanation: Includes the 4.2% 2022 figure and the specific second/third budget risks, but the proposed 'Global Climate Train Wreck' title is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: The answer will be no. I will not be supporting that amendment. ... The reason is that the Climate Change Commission has actually delivered that advice and, therefore, the function is no longer required as part of that law. Therefore, the clause is coming out.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion (remove the clause) follows from a stated premise (advice already delivered), though the premise is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Are you agnostic about land use change, or is this simply about fiercely defending a specific kind of land use, i.e., pastoral livestock farming?
rigor.explanation: Builds a coherent argument that emissions pricing should incentivise land-use change, using the parallel of nitrate leachate being regulated despite being a biological process; some steps are asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Was there a cost-benefit analysis done on the other proposals? ... that seems to be not evidence-based policy if we're just evaluating the status quo and not comparing the relativity of the options. The cost-benefit analysis shows that it does have a positive cost-benefit ratio—1.24 or 1.13 without the premium for carbon action
rigor.explanation: Structured, evidence-based argument that only analysing the status quo (not the alternative options) undermines evidence-based policy; references the multi-criteria analysis directly.

rigor.statement: why repeal legislation that was actually set up during a previous National Government, the Key Government, which was just set up to enable participants to actually measure their emissions and report on them? ... If you're not measuring it, how can you manage it?
rigor.explanation: Argues repealing a reporting/measurement framework risks knock-on effects for climate reporting and emissions factors; the 'can't manage what you don't measure' point is a reasonable maxim rather than hard evidence.

rigor.statement: with the repeal of the requirement to report—and also with the repeal of the requirement to do anything at all other than rely on ... the technological mitigation and the methane inhibitors ... is there a concern that, by repealing all these mechanisms, there's a further emissions gap that's been opened in the nationally determined contribution?
rigor.explanation: Reasons that removing both measurement and action mechanisms could widen the existing NDC emissions gap, noting there was already a gap requiring international credits; asks for quantification rather than asserting a figure.

rigor.statement: methane—often related to ruminants but also related to landfills—is treated separately and ... the landfills are still in the ETS and they're not being removed despite the fact that methane is also related to ruminants. The logic just doesn't seem to be there.
rigor.explanation: Identifies an inconsistency in the Minister's rationale: nitrous oxide from fertiliser is bundled out with ruminants, yet landfill methane (same gas as ruminant methane) stays in the ETS. A clear consistency argument.

rigor.statement: he said that 3.8 percent of our emissions are from nitrous oxide relating to synthetic fertilisers. ... 3.8 percent is still a lot, and if we can get rid of 3.8 percent, then we should, because a lot of time and effort goes into reducing that methane by quite small increments, and every increment counts.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the 'polluter pays' principle and the marginal-effort point that a removable 3.8% source should be retained; a reasonable, if partly value-laden, argument.

rigor.statement: I'm aware that the Minister is placing a lot of faith in the magic bullet approach to agricultural emissions and in unproven technologies, and we are concerned that by shutting the door to ensuring that we can reduce agricultural emissions through the emissions trading scheme, we are not going to be able to meet our commitments.
rigor.explanation: Argues that relying on unproven technology while removing the ETS lever risks missing targets; the 'magic bullet' characterisation is rhetorical but the risk logic is sound.

rigor.statement: It's an unnecessary administrative burden; it doesn't change the outcome very much. It's much better to have a processor-level obligation, which is a lot more efficient administratively, with volunteers being rewarded and the bulk of the price signal flowing through from the processor, based on reporting at the processor level.
rigor.explanation: Coherent efficiency argument: per-farmer reporting is costly and low-value versus processor-level obligation that preserves the price signal; conclusion follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: that report actually said "Be careful about that breather", because they referenced a Chapman Tripp report which showed that 80 percent—80 percent—of the exports from New Zealand to international markets require climate change reporting obligations.
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based case (Rabobank 'Maintaining our emissions edge' paper, Chapman Tripp report, Reserve Bank Financial Stability Report) that deferring pricing raises export costs and risk.

rigor.statement: we actually had the climate commission come in and they talked about their first monitoring report ... they really stressed the significant risks to the second and third budgets. This is primarily ... with agriculture and transport sectors. ... in the absence of pricing mechanisms or any incentives, these provide headwinds to genuine emissions reduction.
rigor.explanation: Cites the Commission's evidence to argue against removing agriculture from the ETS, but the argument is wrapped in an Austin Powers steamroller / train-wreck analogy (appeal to analogy).

rigor.statement: When the Luxon Government says it believes in climate change and then does all the things to make climate change worse, it has the same effect as if it did not believe in climate change in the first place
rigor.explanation: The 'delay has the same effect as denial' argument is a reasonable equivalence claim but relies on assertion ('does all the things to make climate change worse') rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: The bill is currently called the Climate Change Response (Emissions Trading Scheme Agricultural Obligations) Amendment Bill, but there will no longer be agricultural obligations. It's utterly incorrect to call it that, because it's explicitly taking out agricultural obligations.
rigor.explanation: Logical point that the title references obligations the bill removes; the inference is sound, though 'utterly incorrect' overstates a titling convention.

civility.statement: Are you agnostic about land use change, or is this simply about fiercely defending a specific kind of land use, i.e., pastoral livestock farming?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory toward Government policy ('fiercely defending') but frames it as a critique of a policy stance rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: why repeal legislation that was actually set up during a previous National Government, the Key Government, which was just set up to enable participants to actually measure their emissions and report on them? ... If you're not measuring it, how can you manage it?
civility.explanation: The jab that 'that was the last National Government that actually cared about climate change' is a swipe at the current party rather than engagement with its argument.

civility.statement: I'm suggesting that the title should be the "Climate Change Response (Removing Agriculture Despite Agreeing that it Makes up over 50 Percent of our Emissions) Amendment Act 2024".
civility.explanation: A rhetorical mock title used to make a point; more theatrical needling than personal attack, but leans on sensationalism rather than engaging the Minister's substance.

civility.statement: I'm aware that the Minister is placing a lot of faith in the magic bullet approach to agricultural emissions and in unproven technologies, and we are concerned that by shutting the door to ensuring that we can reduce agricultural emissions through the emissions trading scheme, we are not going to be able to meet our commitments.
