These are very small steps to start, but we remain hopeful that bigger strides are taken at pace
charisma.explanation: Supportive of the government's bill while pushing for more; cooperative rather than combative.

charisma.statement: Now, we can talk about changing the system, or we can change the system. We can tinker, or we can transform. Anything less than transformation is, as one young person put it to me, “just a pastel coat of paint on the same old kid prisons.”
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically vivid but rallies her own side and frames the bill's supporters as merely 'tinkering'.

authenticity.statement: Today, I stand before you as the representative of not only this Government but of all the Governments that have gone before us, to offer a formal and unreserved apology for the abuse that you suffered while in State care, churches, and other faith-based places.
authenticity.explanation: The apology is paired with concrete action announced the same day (bill introduced, funding), so words are broadly matched by deeds; not fully verifiable on delivery yet.

authenticity.statement: When survivors tried to raise the alarm, representatives of Labour also played a role in ignoring, punishing, and shaming survivors, drowning them out so they could never be heard. That was wrong.
authenticity.explanation: Self-critical acknowledgement of his own party's culpability rather than deflecting — words consistent with owning the record.

authenticity.statement: I am sorry that the last Labour Government did not act more quickly to put in place an independent redress system.
authenticity.explanation: Directly admits the failing of his own recent government, a consistent and candid position rather than self-serving.

authenticity.statement: In 2018, we started the long-overdue process of acknowledging that the abuse happened, and so we could hear from those who have had to live with the repercussions of that.
authenticity.explanation: Claim of initiating the inquiry is consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in State Care was the largest, the longest, and the most complex public inquiry ever held in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Royal Commission is widely and correctly described as the largest and most complex public inquiry in NZ history.

veracity.statement: More than 2,400 of you were incredibly brave and shared your experiences of the abuse that you suffered while in State care, churches, and other faith-based places
veracity.explanation: Roughly accurate; the Commission heard from well over two thousand survivors in person, though the total who registered was higher.

veracity.statement: The royal commission made 138 recommendations for change.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the final report made 138 recommendations.

veracity.statement: I am pleased to announce today the Government has completed or started work on 28 recommendations in the report.
veracity.explanation: Plausible self-reported claim; 'started work' is a low bar and not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: It is important to note that not all care was abusive, and certainly not all caregivers.
veracity.explanation: Accurate qualification consistent with the Commission's own findings that much care was not abusive.

veracity.statement: As the royal commission found, around 250,000 people were abused, and an even higher, untold number neglected.
veracity.explanation: In the ballpark of the Commission's estimate (up to ~256,000), but 'around 250,000' sits at the top of the range rather than the central estimate, slightly overstating.

veracity.statement: In 2018, we started the long-overdue process of acknowledging that the abuse happened, and so we could hear from those who have had to live with the repercussions of that.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Labour-led government established the Royal Commission in 2018.

veracity.statement: It is discrimination that led to the disproportionately high numbers of Māori, Pasifika, poor, disabled, and rainbow people being put into State care in the first place—often on the assumption they couldn’t be well cared for by their own whānau.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the inquiry's documented findings on disproportionate placement of these groups.

veracity.statement: Sir Robert Martin was brain damaged at birth. He was locked away in State facilities to be cared for due to what was deemed mental deficiency. He wasn’t cared for; he was abused.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of Sir Robert Martin's documented life, consistent with his own published biography.

veracity.statement: the system of power and secrets which enabled at least a quarter of a million mōrehu, pēpē, tamariki, and rangatahi to be abused through the decades was brought to this land and established through colonisation and oppression. That is how this State was established. It shouldn’t be a controversial thing to say. These are facts.
veracity.explanation: The abuse figure is supported, but the broad causal framing of the State's origins presented as settled fact is contestable and one-sided.

veracity.statement: Just a few weeks ago, rangatahi were once again protesting on the roof of one of those youth justice facilities. It was reported that they were protesting about access to food and fresh air. And politicians currently in power—not between 1950 and 1999; currently in power—joked about how these kids wouldn’t be getting access to KFC.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a genuine protest and a reported ministerial comment, though characterised in the most unfavourable framing.

veracity.statement: As of June 2023, around 4,500 young people are in State care in this country.
veracity.explanation: In the right order of magnitude for Oranga Tamariki care/custody figures around that period.

veracity.statement: The abuse in State care has filled our prisons and grown gang numbers. That is what the State is responsible for.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported (over-representation of care-experienced people in prison) but overstated as the singular cause.

veracity.statement: This week, tens of thousands—in the largest mobilisation that our country has seen in living memory—are marching to this place
veracity.explanation: The hikoi that week was very large, but 'largest mobilisation in living memory' is a hyperbolic and contestable superlative.

specificity.statement: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in State Care was the largest, the longest, and the most complex public inquiry ever held in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Superlatives with no figures or dates, though it names the specific inquiry.

specificity.statement: The royal commission made 138 recommendations for change.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure tied to a named document.

specificity.statement: I am pleased to announce today the Government has completed or started work on 28 recommendations in the report.
specificity.explanation: Names a count (28) but not which recommendations or timeframes.

specificity.statement: today I am announcing the Government will invest an additional $32 million to increase capacity in the current system while we work on the new redress system.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure ($32m) and its purpose.

specificity.statement: it is our intention to have a new single redress system operating next year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough timeframe ('next year') but no detail on the system's design or scale.

specificity.statement: Today, I am announcing a National Remembrance Day will be held on 12 November next year to mark the one-year anniversary of this apology.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete date and event.

specificity.statement: this afternoon a bill that will introduce a range of measures to improve the safety of children and vulnerable adults in State care will have its first reading here in Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Names the action and timing but describes contents only as 'a range of measures'.

specificity.statement: We have started the process to remove the ability to strip search children in care, provide new search powers for people visiting youth justice facilities, and to strengthen restrictions for people working with young children.
specificity.explanation: Lists three concrete legislative measures.

specificity.statement: As the royal commission found, around 250,000 people were abused, and an even higher, untold number neglected.
specificity.explanation: Gives an approximate figure sourced to the Commission.

specificity.statement: It will add requirements to the Oranga Tamariki Act to develop search plans with the children and young people in secure residential care who may be subject to searches. These plans will enable their preferences and experiences to be considered when searches are undertaken. The ability to undertake strip searches will also, importantly, be removed.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act, the mechanism (search plans), and the concrete change (removing strip searches).

specificity.statement: As the Minister of Education, I am proposing an improved process in the Children's Act for the vetting of people seeking to work with children and young people by making provisions for New Zealand citizens or residents who have worked overseas to be required to disclose overseas convictions.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the precise mechanism (mandatory disclosure of overseas convictions for core children's workers).

specificity.statement: The bill also amends the Crimes Act 1961 so that a disability is included as a specific factor in the definition of a “vulnerable adult”.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statute and the precise definitional change.

specificity.statement: As of June 2023, around 4,500 young people are in State care in this country.
specificity.explanation: Gives an approximate figure with a date.

strength.statement: I am pleased to announce today the Government has completed or started work on 28 recommendations in the report.
strength.explanation: Claims work started or completed on 28 recommendations, but 'started' is largely in-progress and self-reported, not demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: today I am announcing the Government will invest an additional $32 million to increase capacity in the current system while we work on the new redress system.
strength.explanation: A funding announcement, not yet delivered spending or outcomes — announcement alone is not follow-through.

strength.statement: it is our intention to have a new single redress system operating next year.
strength.explanation: Stated intention with no mechanism or delivery yet; redress systems have repeatedly stalled.

strength.statement: Today, I am announcing a National Remembrance Day will be held on 12 November next year to mark the one-year anniversary of this apology.
strength.explanation: A definite commitment to a scheduled event; low-cost to deliver but concrete.

strength.statement: this afternoon a bill that will introduce a range of measures to improve the safety of children and vulnerable adults in State care will have its first reading here in Parliament.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislative action taken the same day (the bill did have its first reading), demonstrating follow-through rather than mere aspiration.

strength.statement: We have started the process to remove the ability to strip search children in care, provide new search powers for people visiting youth justice facilities, and to strengthen restrictions for people working with young children.
strength.explanation: Backed by the bill introduced the same day, so more than announcement; 'started the process' means not yet enacted.

strength.statement: In 2018, we started the long-overdue process of acknowledging that the abuse happened, and so we could hear from those who have had to live with the repercussions of that.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered action (establishing the inquiry) that his government actually saw through.

strength.statement: It will add requirements to the Oranga Tamariki Act to develop search plans with the children and young people in secure residential care who may be subject to searches. These plans will enable their preferences and experiences to be considered when searches are undertaken. The ability to undertake strip searches will also, importantly, be removed.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislative measure being progressed the same day, though still at first reading.

strength.statement: As the Minister of Education, I am proposing an improved process in the Children's Act for the vetting of people seeking to work with children and young people by making provisions for New Zealand citizens or residents who have worked overseas to be required to disclose overseas convictions.
strength.explanation: A concrete proposed measure within the bill, in progress rather than enacted.

strength.statement: Three months ago, this bill was just an idea. To have it before us has been a cross-parliamentary effort carried by mutual good faith and a commitment to today’s apology being accompanied by tangible action.
strength.explanation: Points to rapid delivery of a bill from idea to first reading in three months, though the substantive change is still pending.

divination.statement: it is our intention to have a new single redress system operating next year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a new redress system operating within a year; redress reform has historically been very slow, making the timeframe optimistic and uncertain.

divination.statement: This week, tens of thousands—in the largest mobilisation that our country has seen in living memory—are marching to this place
divination.explanation: Predicts a mass march arriving that week — highly likely given it was already underway, and it did occur.

rigor.statement: It is important to note that not all care was abusive, and certainly not all caregivers.
rigor.explanation: Adds nuance and avoids overgeneralisation, distinguishing the system's failures from all individual carers.

rigor.statement: There will be a big bill, but it's nothing compared to the debt that we owe those survivors. It must not be the reason for any further delay.
rigor.explanation: Pre-empts a cost objection with a reasoned proportionality argument, though it leans on moral framing rather than figures.

rigor.statement: I believe this bill strikes the right balance in strengthening the ability for Oranga Tamariki to identify contraband before it enters a residence, while removing the legislative provision for the harmful and unnecessary practice of strip searches.
rigor.explanation: Articulates a reasoned trade-off between safety and dignity rather than a one-sided claim.

rigor.statement: If this change prevents even one person from working with children who should not, then it will have done its job.
rigor.explanation: A 'if it saves even one' justification — emotionally persuasive but sidesteps proportionality and cost-benefit reasoning.

rigor.statement: It is discrimination that led to the disproportionately high numbers of Māori, Pasifika, poor, disabled, and rainbow people being put into State care in the first place—often on the assumption they couldn’t be well cared for by their own whānau.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim grounded in the Commission's findings on discriminatory over-representation, though asserted rather than evidenced in the speech.

rigor.statement: Government rhetoric and policy should not and cannot reflect these views, or we risk making the same mistakes that we are apologising for today.
rigor.explanation: Draws a logical link between present discriminatory attitudes and repeating past harms, though the connection is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: the system of power and secrets which enabled at least a quarter of a million mōrehu, pēpē, tamariki, and rangatahi to be abused through the decades was brought to this land and established through colonisation and oppression. That is how this State was established. It shouldn’t be a controversial thing to say. These are facts.
rigor.explanation: Labels a sweeping interpretive/causal claim as 'facts' without supplying evidence, foreclosing debate by assertion.

rigor.statement: The systemic abuse of at least a quarter of a million people in the past several decades was not only evil, but it was by definition systematic and, therefore, deeply, profoundly, horrifically ordinary and banal.
rigor.explanation: Deploys a structured argument (Arendt's 'banality of evil') to make a substantive point about systemic vs individual causes, though it leans on the authority of the concept.

rigor.statement: The abuse in State care has filled our prisons and grown gang numbers. That is what the State is responsible for.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping near mono-causal claim; there is real evidence linking care experience to later incarceration, but stated as a direct cause without qualification.

rigor.statement: Now, we can talk about changing the system, or we can change the system. We can tinker, or we can transform. Anything less than transformation is, as one young person put it to me, “just a pastel coat of paint on the same old kid prisons.”
rigor.explanation: Rests on a false dichotomy (tinker vs transform) that dismisses incremental reform without argument.

civility.statement: When survivors tried to raise the alarm, representatives of Labour also played a role in ignoring, punishing, and shaming survivors, drowning them out so they could never be heard. That was wrong.
civility.explanation: Takes responsibility for own side's failings; no personal attack or blame-shifting.

civility.statement: We welcome the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill but recognise wholeheartedly that many of the survivors of abuse in State care will feel that this doesn’t go far enough. These are very small steps to start, but we remain hopeful that bigger strides are taken at pace
civility.explanation: Constructive criticism focused on the policy's adequacy while still supporting it — engages substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: Just a few weeks ago, rangatahi were once again protesting on the roof of one of those youth justice facilities. It was reported that they were protesting about access to food and fresh air. And politicians currently in power—not between 1950 and 1999; currently in power—joked about how these kids wouldn’t be getting access to KFC.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of sitting politicians' conduct; references a real reported incident, but singling out an unnamed 'joke' carries a cheap-shot edge.

civility.statement: It’s a welcome change, but the bar really is that low.
civility.explanation: Backhanded acknowledgement — credits the reform while belittling it; harsh but aimed at the policy, not a person.

veracity.statement: Tā Robert was born in 1925, and, falsifying his age in order to be able to enlist, he sailed as a reinforcement for the 28th Māori Battalion in July 1943.

veracity.explanation: The underlying event is real, but the date '1923' is impossible (before his 1925 birth); the year is wrong, undermining accuracy.

veracity.statement: He was appointed as a knight not only by the Italian Republic but, of course, of New Zealand in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record: knighted in New Zealand in 2022 and honoured by Italy; accurate.

veracity.statement: Born in Hawke’s Bay on 14 February 1925—meaning he was 99 years old at his death.
veracity.explanation: Date and resulting age are internally consistent and match the record.

veracity.statement: This was actually his third attempt to enlist and he was only successful after giving a false date of birth.
veracity.explanation: Matches the well-documented account of Gillies' enlistment.

veracity.statement: in 2022, he was finally honoured with a knighthood. This is something that he had actually turned down multiple times before this.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: he repeatedly declined a knighthood before accepting in 2022.

veracity.statement: I do want to take a moment to reflect on the hīkoi activations across the motu this week, where tens of thousands are marching to Pāremata in a peaceful protest—
veracity.explanation: The November 2024 hīkoi drawing tens of thousands to Parliament is well documented; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: He was first awarded the Order of Merit by the Italian Government in 2019, which is our country’s equivalent of a knighthood.

veracity.statement: to pay respect to the many 3,600 men who enlisted in the 28th Māori Battalion during World War II.

veracity.explanation: The Budget 2024 Defence funding uplift is broadly real, though '$450m operating' and 'massively underfunded' are her characterisation.

veracity.statement: No, I have not been informed of that, but I can say that I’m happy to say that after some excellent work done by the Minister of Finance, the inflation rate is dropping.
veracity.explanation: Inflation was falling in late 2024; the factual claim holds.

veracity.explanation: The Manawanui sinking (Oct 2024) is factual and NZDF staffing shortfalls were widely reported; broadly accurate.

The new offence comes as a part of a wider package of changes... including a change to prevent those convicted of a stalking offence from holding a firearms licence.

specificity.explanation: References the 1975 legislative gap concretely, but the benefits are described in broad terms.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m not responsible for what that previous Government might have done with its resources or what was done under previous Ministers. What I can say is that I’ve been the Minister for a year and I have not had to use this power before, but I am certainly doing it now.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for any prior precedent of using s9(2) after a zero offer; she deflects and only speaks to her own tenure.

forthrightness.statement: No, I have not been informed of that, but I can say that I’m happy to say that after some excellent work done by the Minister of Finance, the inflation rate is dropping.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'No' to whether she was advised on the workers' real-wage effect, but then pivots to inflation.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don’t have the full details of who is on strike, but I can say that it’s hard for people to be on strike if they’ve already made themselves redundant.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether roles are vacancies/redundancies or strike-driven; she concedes she lacks details and answers only partially.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I’m fully aware that we have followed the law. In fact, I’ve had advice on that and, as one would expect, I have read my advice and taken it on board.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'Yes' to whether she followed the Employment Relations Act and gives the basis.

forthrightness.statement: Well, thank you for the question. I’m pleased that the member’s clearly going to support any increase in the Defence budget... The point is that we cannot simply not have these jobs undertaken; they are critical to the safety of the New Zealand Defence Force.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she sought alternatives to using armed forces; she does not address alternatives and instead justifies the decision.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it’s an operational matter, of course, for the Chief of Defence Force. But I’d say, too, that I’m very pleased that at the last Budget—which the member did not support—Defence was able to get close to half a billion dollars for operational costs.

forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Ministers undermine the Tribunal without censure; he sidesteps into whether the Tribunal's role should be reviewed.

forthrightness.statement: We didn’t get what we wanted; the ACT Party didn’t get what they wanted. We came to a sensible compromise. We’re supporting it at first reading, not beyond that.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly addresses how the compromise supposedly resolves concerns, though skirts the 'prejudice to Māori' point raised.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we’re not supporting the bill into law; we’re not supporting the bill out to a national referendum. We’ve been very clear about that from the get-go.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he didn't tell voters his 'won't support' pledge was tradeable; he ignores that and restates the current position.

forthrightness.statement: I had looked at the different reporting mechanisms. The weekly reporting is very volatile and the more detailed analysis that’s provided in the monthly and quarterly report provides us the ability to do what we want to do, which is to support more people into work.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the cancellation came at MSD's or her own request; she gives a rationale but never says whose decision it was.

forthrightness.statement: No. Unfortunately, as the Minister of Finance said, the economic climate that we took over, with a recession that was deeper and longer, has meant that unemployment has continued to rise... For every single person that loses their job, I feel for them.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'No' to whether reporting was stopped to hide rising numbers, and concedes numbers rose.

forthrightness.statement: I’m advised that this quote is not one of the over 500 findings in the royal commission’s final report... it’s not possible for me to either agree or disagree with the statement. However... it is clear that racism was a contributing factor to Māori tamariki and rangatahi being disproportionately taken into care, where many experienced abuse and neglect.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to agree/disagree on a technicality about sourcing, but does concede the core point that racism contributed to disproportionate uplift.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, in the context of the findings of the royal commission of inquiry, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, yes, absolutely.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers both parts of the question directly and unambiguously.

forthrightness.statement: the core reason for looking at section 7AA was to bring clarity to the fact that we need to put the safety and the wellbeing of our young people at the forefront of every decision we’re making when it comes to placements... So I have thought about the safety and wellbeing of children.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for empirical evidence justifying the repeal; she restates her rationale rather than naming evidence.

forthrightness.statement: Whilst I appreciate that question, we have spent years and years going back to when I was dealing with Child, Youth and Family Services over 20 years ago doing reports. I’m sick of reports that say the same thing over and over again from multiple spaces that take resources away from our young people, when we know what the problem is and we just need to get on with it and deliver for our children.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she is removing the reporting requirement on Māori outcomes; she voices frustration with reports rather than answering the specific point.

forthrightness.statement: The Treaty principles bill is very clear that in clause 8 it says it should not be used in interpreting any statute in relation to a Treaty settlement... my advice is to read the bill because you will find such details as that that often show you there’s nothing to worry about.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether the bill affects Treaty settlements, citing the relevant clause.

forthrightness.statement: As I said at Waitangi last year, one of my goals is ki a maimoatia te reo me te ahurea Māori—that is, to cherish the Māori language and culture. The Treaty principles bill protects the rights of hapū and iwi Māori as they stood in 1840. It also ensures that those basic rights of tino rangatiratanga and self-determination extend to all New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Reasonably addresses the question about the bill and te reo/culture.

civility.statement: The Defence Force was massively underfunded and massively under stress when we became the Government. We were able to secure, despite the very difficult fiscal circumstances, well over $450 million extra of operating costs in the Budget just passed.
civility.explanation: Criticism aimed at the prior government's funding rather than the person, but pointed.

civility.statement: I am appalled that the former Minister does not understand what a shocking state we were left with.
civility.explanation: A personalised swipe at the former Minister's understanding rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: I will never leave Defence to be defenceless, like that previous Government did.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical jab contrasting herself with the previous government.

civility.statement: Well, it’s an operational matter, of course, for the Chief of Defence Force. But I’d say, too, that I’m very pleased that at the last Budget—which the member did not support—Defence was able to get close to half a billion dollars for operational costs.
civility.explanation: Partisan dig ('which the member did not support') rather than engaging the premise.

civility.statement: In the opinion of the New Zealand Labour Party, the circumstances we are facing here today are of the Government’s making. They chose to underfund parts of the Defence budget, which resulted in the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) offering nothing of substance to civilian workers.
civility.explanation: Criticism directed at government budget choices, not personal attack.

civility.statement: Using armed forces for civilian functions is a significant decision and should not be taken lightly and it requires adequate scrutiny.
civility.explanation: Measured, principle-focused framing without personal attack.

civility.statement: it cannot be separated from decisions that the executive has taken in terms of how they choose to resource Public Service entities, because, at the end of the day, those operational issues play out reflecting the austerity politics or otherwise that we’re seeing right now.
civility.explanation: Contests the government's characterisation on substance rather than personally.

civility.statement: I couldn’t help but wonder at Opposition members who, until recently, were part of a Government that put half the New Zealand Defence Force as de facto guards of hotel rooms for two years while the other half were lost to attrition, who drove Defence Force capability into the ground while inflation went through the roof and they crashed the economy, and are now trying to play politics out of this difficult circumstance.
civility.explanation: A sustained partisan broadside ('drove capability into the ground', 'crashed the economy') aimed at opponents.

civility.statement: When he told New Zealanders before the election that he thought the Treaty principles bill was divisive and that National would not support it, why didn’t he tell them that commitment was something he was willing to trade away in coalition negotiations?
civility.explanation: Pointed accusation of bad faith, but grounded in a specific prior commitment rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I’m advised that this quote is not one of the over 500 findings in the royal commission’s final report... it’s not possible for me to either agree or disagree with the statement. However... it is clear that racism was a contributing factor to Māori tamariki and rangatahi being disproportionately taken into care, where many experienced abuse and neglect.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused response acknowledging harm.

civility.statement: It hasn’t created any divisiveness. What it has done has revealed the divisiveness of people—
civility.explanation: Turns a divisiveness charge back on opponents rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: I can’t miss the opportunity to say to those principals that they have a duty to adhere to political neutrality, and there is nothing in the Treaty principles bill that will disadvantage any student even one iota. However, students are disadvantaged by missing school.
civility.explanation: Critical of principals' conduct but frames it around a duty argument rather than personal insult.

charisma.statement: I will never leave Defence to be defenceless, like that previous Government did.
charisma.explanation: Us-versus-them framing that rallies rather than persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: I couldn’t help but wonder at Opposition members who, until recently, were part of a Government that put half the New Zealand Defence Force as de facto guards of hotel rooms for two years while the other half were lost to attrition, who drove Defence Force capability into the ground while inflation went through the roof and they crashed the economy, and are now trying to play politics out of this difficult circumstance.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-versus-them; makes no attempt to persuade the other side.

charisma.statement: Our message is very simple: if you are perpetrating a culture of fear in your community—whether that’s breaking into a shop or stalking and intimidating someone—we are coming after you.
charisma.explanation: A tough-on-crime applause line that rallies supporters rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: We didn’t get what we wanted; the ACT Party didn’t get what they wanted. We came to a sensible compromise. We’re supporting it at first reading, not beyond that.
charisma.explanation: Even-handed 'no one got what they wanted' framing, but appeals mainly to defend the coalition.

charisma.statement: It hasn’t created any divisiveness. What it has done has revealed the divisiveness of people—
charisma.explanation: Combative reframing that entrenches division rather than bridging it.

charisma.statement: it will fill in the blanks that this House left in 1975 when it said that there were Treaty principles but failed to define what they were. It will give us a conception of our founding document that is based upon equal rights for all... that, in short, will allow New Zealanders to overcome our real and tangible challenges with a shared and equal understanding of our citizenship and our rights in this country.
charisma.explanation: Invokes shared citizenship and 'equal rights for all' and solving challenges 'together' — an inclusive appeal, though it will not persuade the bill's opponents.

charisma.statement: As I said at Waitangi last year, one of my goals is ki a maimoatia te reo me te ahurea Māori—that is, to cherish the Māori language and culture. The Treaty principles bill protects the rights of hapū and iwi Māori as they stood in 1840. It also ensures that those basic rights of tino rangatiratanga and self-determination extend to all New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Seeks to reassure and include ('extend to all New Zealanders'), reaching beyond his base.

charisma.statement: I was quite humbled by something that was said to me by a staff member of Oranga Tamariki: “Every kid, or every young person, that comes to the attention of Oranga Tamariki, or is in the care of Oranga Tamariki, has a name. We know their names, and we must base it on their needs and every young person deserves the same level of care and protection no matter what their ancestry is.”
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive framing centred on every child's needs regardless of ancestry.

rigor.statement: Well, thank you for the question. I’m pleased that the member’s clearly going to support any increase in the Defence budget... The point is that we cannot simply not have these jobs undertaken; they are critical to the safety of the New Zealand Defence Force.
rigor.explanation: Supports the safety point with concrete evidence (trained firefighters, Port Hills deployment, Linton), though it answers a different question.

rigor.statement: In the opinion of the New Zealand Labour Party, the circumstances we are facing here today are of the Government’s making. They chose to underfund parts of the Defence budget, which resulted in the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) offering nothing of substance to civilian workers.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain (underfunding → zero offer → strike) that is plausible but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: if you’re offered a zero percent increase and you put that and match it with inflation, you’re, effectively, asking civilian staff to perform their same duties with less resources in real time, because of inflationary pressures on things like housing.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point that a 0% nominal offer is a real-terms pay cut once inflation is accounted for; logically sound.

rigor.statement: it cannot be separated from decisions that the executive has taken in terms of how they choose to resource Public Service entities, because, at the end of the day, those operational issues play out reflecting the austerity politics or otherwise that we’re seeing right now.
rigor.explanation: Links the 'operational' framing to executive resourcing choices, but 'austerity politics' is asserted.

rigor.statement: I couldn’t help but wonder at Opposition members who, until recently, were part of a Government that put half the New Zealand Defence Force as de facto guards of hotel rooms for two years while the other half were lost to attrition, who drove Defence Force capability into the ground while inflation went through the roof and they crashed the economy, and are now trying to play politics out of this difficult circumstance.
rigor.explanation: Stacks unquantified accusations and hyperbole ('crashed the economy') without evidence.

rigor.statement: What I’d say to that member is that many commentators have said in a post-Treaty settlement world it’s quite a legitimate question to ask what the role of the Waitangi Tribunal is going forward. That is something that we as a coalition Government will explore in due course.
rigor.explanation: Leans on unnamed 'many commentators' (appeal to authority) rather than an argued case.

rigor.statement: When he told New Zealanders before the election that he thought the Treaty principles bill was divisive and that National would not support it, why didn’t he tell them that commitment was something he was willing to trade away in coalition negotiations?
rigor.explanation: Contrasts a documented pre-election position with subsequent action to argue inconsistency.

rigor.statement: Economic forecasts have generally changed for the worse over successive updates, as it became clear that the current recession started earlier, was deeper, and persisted for longer than was earlier understood... earlier forecasts attributed too much weight to an apparent pick-up in productivity over the COVID period. This pick-up proved to be illusory.
rigor.explanation: Coherent evidence-based explanation of why forecasts were revised down (productivity assumptions), logically connected.

rigor.statement: the core reason for looking at section 7AA was to bring clarity to the fact that we need to put the safety and the wellbeing of our young people at the forefront of every decision we’re making when it comes to placements... So I have thought about the safety and wellbeing of children.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a safety objective without the empirical support the question sought.

rigor.statement: Whilst I appreciate that question, we have spent years and years going back to when I was dealing with Child, Youth and Family Services over 20 years ago doing reports. I’m sick of reports that say the same thing over and over again from multiple spaces that take resources away from our young people, when we know what the problem is and we just need to get on with it and deliver for our children.
rigor.explanation: Relies on personal experience and 'we know what the problem is' in place of evidence.

rigor.statement: it will fill in the blanks that this House left in 1975 when it said that there were Treaty principles but failed to define what they were. It will give us a conception of our founding document that is based upon equal rights for all... that, in short, will allow New Zealanders to overcome our real and tangible challenges with a shared and equal understanding of our citizenship and our rights in this country.
rigor.explanation: The historical premise (undefined 1975 principles) is fair, but the leap to solving health/housing challenges is asserted.

rigor.statement: I can’t miss the opportunity to say to those principals that they have a duty to adhere to political neutrality, and there is nothing in the Treaty principles bill that will disadvantage any student even one iota. However, students are disadvantaged by missing school.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point about lost schooling, though 'nothing will disadvantage any student one iota' is an unqualified assertion.

rigor.statement: I was quite humbled by something that was said to me by a staff member of Oranga Tamariki: “Every kid, or every young person, that comes to the attention of Oranga Tamariki, or is in the care of Oranga Tamariki, has a name. We know their names, and we must base it on their needs and every young person deserves the same level of care and protection no matter what their ancestry is.”
rigor.explanation: Rests on a single anecdote/quotation rather than evidence.

authenticity.statement: Well, we’re not supporting the bill into law; we’re not supporting the bill out to a national referendum. We’ve been very clear about that from the get-go.
authenticity.explanation: Tension with his pre-election stance that the bill was divisive and National would not support it; now backing it at first reading.

divination.statement: Treasury will release a full set of economic and fiscal forecasts in the half-year update on 17 December. I expect those forecasts will show a strengthening economy, lower interest rates, and reducing unemployment over the next few years.
divination.explanation: A forecast of a strengthening economy and falling rates over coming years—plausible and consistent with mainstream expectations, but uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: I say over and over again: whakapapa, working with whānau, hapū, and iwi is important, but the safety and wellbeing must be the first thing we think about in every decision we make about our young people.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why she is repealing section 7AA given the Whanaketia recommendation on ethnicity-specific data, she pivots to a general statement of values about safety and never addresses section 7AA or the data-collection point.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm sure there's a wide variety of views amongst iwi leaders, but there are still plenty who are very keen to make progress on Treaty negotiations.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the bill restores momentum given iwi leaders' condemnation, he sidesteps the momentum question and asserts unnamed 'plenty' of supporters instead.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not sure it will make any difference whatsoever, but I did write a book about that particular fellow 20-odd years ago, and that's on the record.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees Don Brash is a 'true New Zealand patriot', he neither agrees nor disagrees, deflecting to the fact he wrote a biography.

forthrightness.statement: Now, it's true that one year in, I have not yet concluded a settlement with Ngāpuhi, and that is challenging work and many Ministers in the past have worked in that way. Ultimately, it requires engagement on both sides, and that's what we're doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about Nicola Willis's 'dangerous' warning by redirecting to Treaty settlement progress, though he does volunteer a concession about Ngāpuhi.

forthrightness.statement: Well, clearly, the other side have woken up this morning and decided to have every question on this particular area today in the House, and so they're straining to draw different bills into different ministerial responsibilities.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government is proceeding with a divisive select committee process despite warnings, he dismisses the questioning as tactical and never answers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the new offence will capture patterns of behaviour, being three specified acts occurring within a 12-month period that amount to stalking and harassment. It includes damaging reputation, recording, tracking, loitering, as well as the use of technology and modern stalking methods.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers 'what will be covered by the new offence'.

forthrightness.statement: So, yes, the Government's decided that a stalking and harassment conviction will disqualify the offender from holding a firearms licence.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a stalking conviction will disqualify someone from a firearms licence, he answers 'yes' directly and completely.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do, which is why, when designing the pilot programme, we took on lessons from examples in New Zealand and internationally. In fact, in this process, over 75 formal lessons were identified and collated from these reviews of previous programmes, both in New Zealand and internationally.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly accepts the officials' advice ('Yes, I do') and explains how it shaped the design, though she does not name the specific counter-evidence asked for.

forthrightness.statement: I think a 90 percent pass rate from the first part of the pilot programme shows that it's actually done a pretty damn good job.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what evidence would make her pause and reflect, she does not answer, instead citing a pass rate as vindication.

forthrightness.statement: I don't recall saying that or even implying that. I think that young people deserve to be in a safe environment, which they call their home, which is why in response to the abuse in care inquiry and to that report, I have tabled, in the omnibus bill yesterday, ways to keep young people safe within these facilities
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the premise and points to concrete action (the tabled omnibus bill) in response.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that 863 expressions of interest have been received from staff. To the second part of the member's question... As at 8 November, Health New Zealand advises that 224 offers have been made to people whose applications were originally declined by their immediate managers.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers both parts of a precise question with specific numbers (863 EOIs; 224 offers made against manager recommendations).

forthrightness.statement: I'm assured by Health New Zealand that the net front line of clinical staff is safe, that patients are safe, and that outcomes will improve work.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a specific question about doctors filling registration forms and reconsidering 777 emergency calls due to clerical shortages, he offers a general safety assurance and never addresses the specifics.

forthrightness.statement: I do agree with those statements—that reflected the previous Government's position—and what I would say is that voluntary redundancies are an operational matter for Health New Zealand. But I'm assured that senior leaders take wider strategic matters, including the one the member raises, into account when they make their decisions.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why local managers were overridden in 80%+ of accepted redundancies given his 'local solutions' statement, he affirms the statement but deflects the override contradiction to 'operational matters'.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. And we have decentralised the four regions, but that previous Government did not.
forthrightness.explanation: Reaffirms belief in decentralisation but does not engage the specific example of the deputy chief executive limiting Bay of Plenty recruitment approvals to 10 a week.

forthrightness.statement: What I admit is that we're fixing the botched reforms of the previous Government and looking to improve patient outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when he will admit his cuts have tied up clinicians in paperwork and cost more, he refuses the premise and pivots to attacking the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: As at end September 2024, Hamilton and Wellington had the most households in emergency housing. In Kirikiriroa, there were 225 households in emergency housing, and around two-thirds are singles or couples with no tamariki. In Te Upoko o Te Ika / Wellington, there were 216 households in emergency housing; the overwhelming majority were singles with no children.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why the trial is in Wellington and Hamilton with specific supporting data.

forthrightness.statement: The trial's expected to support between 50 and 100 people total across both regions over the two years... Officials will use the Integrated Data Infrastructure from data received from providers and set up an evaluative process alongside the Social Investment Agency to inform future insights and actions.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers both how many participants and how the trial will be monitored.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in particular, my decision to reprioritise $30 million in funding to provide maths workbooks, guidebooks, resources to students across New Zealand, and as of today 400,000 primary and intermediate school students around New Zealand in schools and kura will receive these books.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly stands by her actions and specifies which one, though the answer is framed to the resourcing decision rather than Te Ahu o te Reo Māori itself.

forthrightness.statement: The evaluation said exactly that. There was no link between the course and student achievement. The fact is that's what the report said... And when 12 percent of tamariki Māori are at curriculum for maths, I've got decisions to make, and I made the decision to reprioritise that money
forthrightness.explanation: Directly defends the disputed claim, though she restates rather than engages the fact-check's distinction that 'no link found' reflects the evaluation's scope, not the programme's ineffectiveness.

forthrightness.statement: No, because we in the Ministry of Education and under this Government invest a huge amount in te reo Māori... we also have $43 million in Māori language programme funding for schools, teaching te reo Māori as a subject in any setting, and $3.5 million for Māori medium and kura professional learning and development in te reo language development.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'No' to whether she agrees the move was cultural suppression and supports it with funding detail.

civility.statement: I say over and over again: whakapapa, working with whānau, hapū, and iwi is important, but the safety and wellbeing must be the first thing we think about in every decision we make about our young people.
civility.explanation: Respectful, policy/values-focused, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Sir, I would ask that you take some time to reflect on the questions that we've just had to endure for the last five minutes. It's quite clear there is no scope for repetitive questioning going over the same ground all the time, and, more importantly, we've suffered enough harassment in terms of that side of the House of that Minister.
civility.explanation: Characterises legitimate opposition questioning as 'harassment' and something to be 'endured', dismissing scrutiny rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: How does introducing the Treaty Principles Bill "restore some of that momentum." when the bill has been described by iwi leaders as "reckless", "dishonourable", and "callous"?
civility.explanation: Pointed, quoting others' harsh descriptors, but the challenge engages the substance of the bill's effect on Treaty progress rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Well, clearly, the other side have woken up this morning and decided to have every question on this particular area today in the House, and so they're straining to draw different bills into different ministerial responsibilities.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of opponents' motives but no personal insult.

civility.statement: In light of the above facts, does it not show that maybe, actually, it is possible to advance some matters while disagreeing on others, and that is how mature people conduct business?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical and slightly barbed ('mature people') but broadly issue-oriented.

civility.statement: Does she see that the moral panic around youth delinquency that was used to justify the boot camps of the past, outlined in the abuse in care report, is the same moral panic around youth crime that she is whipping up today to justify her boot camps?
civility.explanation: The 'whipping up... moral panic' framing imputes bad-faith motive to the Minister rather than engaging only the policy.

civility.statement: to say that it's just a moral panic—tell that to the people who have been attacked in their dairies and have been attacked doing their jobs every day and are left injured and traumatised by some of the crimes that these young people have committed.
civility.explanation: Forceful but directed at the substance of the crime problem, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: What I admit is that we're fixing the botched reforms of the previous Government and looking to improve patient outcomes.
civility.explanation: 'Botched reforms' is harsh criticism of policy, which is legitimate, but adds no substance.

civility.statement: What a deeply cynical, extreme, and jaundiced view of the world expressed by that member, the leader of the Greens
civility.explanation: Labels the member's outlook 'cynical, extreme, and jaundiced'—a characterisation of the person's worldview rather than a substantive rebuttal.

civility.statement: I once did read that biography of Don Brash that was written by Paul Goldsmith. I have never had such a good sleep in my entire life!
civility.explanation: A personal jab mocking a colleague's book as boring; a cheap shot rather than substantive.

civility.statement: They told New Zealanders before the election that they thought it was divisive. They told New Zealanders before the election that they would not support it... and yet here we are: now the National Party tomorrow voting in favour of the Treaty principles bill—a bill that takes race relations in New Zealand backwards, despite the fact that the National Party said they would not do that.
civility.explanation: Harsh but engages the substance of a policy reversal rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: That is a betrayal of the people who voted for this Government... Their principles and their values are up for sale on that side of the House, and I think New Zealanders have every right to be upset about that.
civility.explanation: 'Principles and values up for sale' and 'betrayal' impute bad faith to opponents, edging toward character rather than policy.

civility.statement: That was, New Zealanders, a man affectionately known as "Chippy"—sadly, not a chip off the old block of Norman Kirk, David Lange, or indeed Helen Clark—a temporary occupant at the back of the waka.
civility.explanation: Personal belittling of Hipkins as a lesser, 'temporary' leader unfavourably compared to predecessors, rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: if you spend more time talking about pronouns, if you spend more time obsessed with narrow marginal issues adversely related to the economic challenges of the day-to-day lives of Kiwis, you will never hold power
civility.explanation: Dismissive caricature of opponents' priorities rather than engagement with them.

civility.statement: The Treaty of Waitangi is not a creed; it is not a basis for a separate sovereignty. It does not in any way at all uphold, mandate, 78 separate sovereignties from the Foveaux Strait to Te Rerenga Wairua.
civility.explanation: Argumentative but framed around constitutional ideas rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: You want to be a lawyer? Don't try and hop in bed with the Labour Party unless you're already there. And most certainly do not go around inflating the expectations of people who have a lifetime of misery as it is.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on a named lawyer (Sonja Cooper), imputing partisan motive and unprofessionalism rather than addressing substance.

civility.statement: Ngāti Ruanui, a tribe of Taranaki who should be using their money to educate their mokopunas, have tried to pay for the cost... I know no hapū who goes 30 kilometres off the shoreline of our country to either get crayfish, either get shellfish—it's that level of distortion
civility.explanation: Lectures a named iwi on how it should spend its money and dismisses its concerns as 'distortion' and 'falsehood', disrespectful rather than substantive.

civility.statement: It is important that we give due recognition to those who have served our country with distinction over the years... We stand here exercising our freedom of speech in this general debate as a result of the actions, the courage, the comradeship, and the commitment of those who have served this nation previously
civility.explanation: Wholly respectful, no attack, focused on honouring veterans.

civility.statement: In 2040, the Treaty principles bill being debated tomorrow will be remembered as an ugly mistake in an otherwise honourable record of a country that has always been proud of the way we have done right by our citizens. It should be remembered as a political stunt, because it is and it's only that. It's a creature of a coalition agreement because it will help a minor party drum up votes using the politics of fear.
civility.explanation: 'Political stunt' and 'politics of fear' attribute cynical motive, though aimed at the bill's design more than a person.

civility.statement: the ACT Party is there, the tail wagging the big, fat, ugly dog, whilst the puppy dog in the other corner isn't getting a look-in at all, and I am shocked that the party on the other side—the National Party—is being led by the nose.
civility.explanation: Name-calling ('big, fat, ugly dog', 'puppy dog') aimed at the coalition parties rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: What they're trying to do is vicious, it's divisive, it's racist, it's dishonest, it's illegitimate, and it's unconstitutional.
civility.explanation: A stacked series of severe pejoratives ('vicious', 'racist', 'dishonest') aimed at opponents' motives rather than continuing the reasoned argument he had built.

specificity.statement: these are children that come to the attention of Oranga Tamariki, often broken, often not been treated with the dignity and respect they should have been, and Oranga Tamariki has to pick up those pieces and make decisions for these young people.
specificity.explanation: Some concrete framing about children in care but no figures, mechanisms, or how the section 7AA change addresses it.

specificity.statement: How does introducing the Treaty Principles Bill "restore some of that momentum." when the bill has been described by iwi leaders as "reckless", "dishonourable", and "callous"?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bill and cites specific characterisations, though relies on quoted labels rather than mechanism.

specificity.statement: The Government has agreed to introduce legislation this year which will make stalking an illegal and jailable offence for up to five years. It is often a precursor to more serious and violent crime—there are established links between stalking and intimate partner violence—which is increasing in prevalence.
specificity.explanation: Names the offence, the penalty (up to five years), and a timeframe (this year).

specificity.statement: Well, the new offence will capture patterns of behaviour, being three specified acts occurring within a 12-month period that amount to stalking and harassment. It includes damaging reputation, recording, tracking, loitering, as well as the use of technology and modern stalking methods.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism: three specified acts within 12 months, with an enumerated list of covered behaviours.

specificity.statement: So, yes, the Government's decided that a stalking and harassment conviction will disqualify the offender from holding a firearms licence.
specificity.explanation: Clear, concrete policy consequence stated.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do, which is why, when designing the pilot programme, we took on lessons from examples in New Zealand and internationally. In fact, in this process, over 75 formal lessons were identified and collated from these reviews of previous programmes, both in New Zealand and internationally.
