The fact of the matter is that even if you take those two documents, its true intent is not always clear to see, and there's a way around that. Just like a contract that is incomplete... we do go to the courts.
rigor.explanation: Concedes genuine complications (two versions, non-signatories) then reasons by analogy to incomplete contracts and judicial interpretation—a structured, honest argument.

rigor.statement: it was in 1994, in the State-owned Enterprises case, that the Privy Council looked at this for us... They said that "the 'principles' are the underlying mutual obligations and responsibilities which the Treaty places on the parties. They reflect the intent of the Treaty as a whole... With the passage of time, the 'principles' which underlie the Treaty have become much more important than its precise terms."
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in cited case law and a direct judicial quotation, a strong evidential basis for the point about Treaty principles.

divination.statement: I think a 90 percent pass rate from the first part of the pilot programme shows that it's actually done a pretty damn good job.
divination.explanation: Implicitly predicts 'positive results these young people show for their future'; too optimistic given weak evidence for boot-camp effectiveness.

divination.statement: In 2040, the Treaty principles bill being debated tomorrow will be remembered as an ugly mistake in an otherwise honourable record of a country that has always been proud of the way we have done right by our citizens. It should be remembered as a political stunt, because it is and it's only that. It's a creature of a coalition agreement because it will help a minor party drum up votes using the politics of fear.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will be 'remembered as an ugly mistake' by 2040; a long-horizon, partly subjective forecast that is plausible but not clearly falsifiable.

civility.statement: it is giving unprecedented powers to politicians who have deliberately chosen to remove Te Tiriti and who are doing everything they can to resurrect zombie projects previously turned down by every court that exists in Aotearoa. That’s not progress. That is not economic progress; that wreaks of desperation.
civility.explanation: Harsh, loaded framing ('zombie projects', 'wreaks of desperation') that imputes bad faith rather than engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: I call BS on this Minister—Minister Jones—because not once has any of this gone back to his backyard. I’ve just come from there, and there’s no way, with all the anti-mining signs I saw, that they would allow him to do that in his own backyard.
civility.explanation: 'I call BS' is a personal jab at the Minister, though it is tied to a claim about local opposition.

civility.statement: what you don’t realise is you’re fast tracking your way out of Parliament, and let this be a one-term Government, for all we can do.
civility.explanation: A combative political flourish rather than a personal insult, but aimed at rallying against the Government.

civility.statement: One term is actually one term too many for a Government intent on trashing our environment, running roughshod over our communities, and destroying our children’s future.
civility.explanation: Sweeping, emotive accusations ('trashing', 'destroying our children's future') rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: This fast-track bill is simply a dog’s breakfast and it deserves to be consigned to the bin.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the legislation rather than a person, but a colourful put-down that adds no substance.

civility.statement: Now, our world is burning, and if you look around at what is going on, I feel like this Government is just throwing fuel into that fire, literally—literally. Nature is in retreat, it is under attack, and this Government is fast tracking its way to collapse those things.
civility.explanation: Emotive, accusatory framing of the Government's intent rather than engaging the bill's mechanics.

civility.statement: Thank you, sir, I really appreciate that comment, but it’s no laughing matter, actually, when we talk about things like the destruction of our ecosystems and the destruction of things like birds and creatures that have lived here for millions and billions of years, and that you choose just to make a joke about it is unacceptable.
civility.explanation: Rebukes an interjector but does so on substance, criticising the act of joking rather than launching a personal insult.

civility.statement: Oh, Labour is very rare in New Plymouth.
civility.explanation: A heckling cheap shot at Labour's electoral standing rather than engagement with the debate.

civility.statement: Radio New Zealand did a great job: $500,000 of donations from people who are on the fast-track list, and there’s no good explanation for that. I’m concerned that there are close connections between donors, members of the National Party, and the fact that they’re on this list.
civility.explanation: Raises conflict-of-interest concerns but with an insinuation of impropriety ('no good explanation') against named opponents.

civility.statement: I’m deeply concerned that this country’s position as somewhere where people do business honestly, transparently, by the rules, and on an equal footing is at risk.
civility.explanation: Frames the worry about integrity in institutional terms rather than as a direct personal attack.

civility.statement: I have hesitated while I’ve been listening to the member on his feet making inappropriate imputations and assertions and veiled allegations that are inappropriate in a debate of this sort. I would invite you to consider the content of the words that he has been making, in consideration of appropriate Standing Orders, and ask him to desist from this type of insinuation during this debate.
civility.explanation: Raises a procedural objection to insinuations in measured, rule-based language rather than trading insults.

civility.statement: if there was any doubt where the Grinch was going to be hiding this Christmas, I’d be looking in central Christchurch, because what we’ve heard is an Opposition and a Labour Party—
civility.explanation: A 'Grinch' jibe aimed at an opponent (Christchurch-based Webb) rather than the substance of the argument.

civility.statement: They don’t just want to kill this bill; they want to kill 55,000 new homes for hard-working Kiwis that just want to get a chance... Then they’re saying, “We don’t just want to kill them, we want to kill 180 kilometres of new roads.”
civility.explanation: Repeated 'they want to kill' framing misrepresents opponents' position for effect.

civility.statement: just like they killed the Ōtaki to North of Levin Expressway in 2018. Everyone in our region, in Horowhenua, knows exactly the impact that had—the needless deaths that we experienced on that road—because of the six years of delay.
civility.explanation: Emotive attribution of deaths to opponents' decision heightens the charge beyond policy critique.

civility.statement: Scott Simpson, at one level, did a very pleasant job of administering the chair for this bill—and he is a decent chair—but, by goodness, he’s going to be at risk in the Coromandel election next time, isn’t he, because he has, effectively, brought through legislation which is incompatible with the values of most of his voters in the Coromandel.
civility.explanation: Politically pointed but opens by genuinely acknowledging Simpson as a 'decent chair', keeping it above a personal attack.

civility.statement: I do also want to acknowledge a point that was emphasised during the second reading debate—particularly by members opposite, and I think that had a good point—which was, first, that this should not be an exercise in kicking the can down the road.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with the substance of opponents' concerns.

civility.statement: Labour supports this bill, but we’ll work through clause by clause to ask the Minister to clarify some points which came up not only from submitters in the select committee stage but also in the contributions in the second reading, because there are remaining questions there.
civility.explanation: Wholly policy-focused, respectful engagement with the Minister and the process.

rigor.statement: it is giving unprecedented powers to politicians who have deliberately chosen to remove Te Tiriti and who are doing everything they can to resurrect zombie projects previously turned down by every court that exists in Aotearoa. That’s not progress. That is not economic progress; that wreaks of desperation.
rigor.explanation: Leans on emotive characterisation ('desperation') rather than evidence; the 'turned down by every court' claim is asserted, not substantiated.

rigor.statement: When we see nearly 27,000 submitters, 83 percent of whom are opposed and many of whom weren’t heard because they were relegated to a ballot system over 23 days, it sort of tells you how desperate this Government is.
rigor.explanation: Uses real submission data but jumps to an emotive conclusion ('how desperate'); a submission count is not a measure of merit.

rigor.statement: I call BS on this Minister—Minister Jones—because not once has any of this gone back to his backyard. I’ve just come from there, and there’s no way, with all the anti-mining signs I saw, that they would allow him to do that in his own backyard.
rigor.explanation: Relies on personal anecdote ('anti-mining signs I saw') to infer the Minister lacks a mandate at home.

rigor.statement: There were 53,000 submitters, including petitions, individual submitters, and a thousand organisation submitters. Of those, 0.3 percent gave outright support to the bill—0.3 percent—1.1 percent gave support in principle, 5.7 percent had an unclear position, and 92.9 percent outright opposed the bill.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in submission data, though volume of opposition does not by itself establish the bill's merits.

rigor.statement: One term is actually one term too many for a Government intent on trashing our environment, running roughshod over our communities, and destroying our children’s future.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion with unsupported absolute claims.

rigor.statement: It’s a proposal to burn toxic waste in a small, rural community, in Waimate in South Canterbury, and we heard in their submission that this is a project that will increase harmful climate emissions... It is proposed on a site on a flood plain—it could all wash out to sea—and it’s located within two kilometres of a school. On 5 November, the Waimate District Council passed a motion to request that the Government remove the toxic waste plant from the fast-track list.
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific evidence toward the conclusion, though the harm claims rest on one side's submission.

rigor.statement: we used to be a country that got stuff done and now, quite simply, we’re a country where it’s become impossibly hard to actually get anything done at all in a timely and cost-effective manner, and that’s despite a housing crisis, despite a roading crisis, despite an energy crisis, and despite an economic crisis
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical framing ('obstruction economy') asserting multiple 'crises' without evidence in the statement itself.

rigor.statement: We can create jobs, we can create economic growth, we can create export income that helps us pay our bills and provide the services to New Zealanders... or we can have no jobs, no economic growth, and no export income, and continue to import those minerals that we need in our everyday lives and have no control whatsoever on the environmental impacts.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — presents mining under this bill vs. 'no jobs, no growth' as the only two options.

rigor.statement: Therefore, Mr Deputy Chair, why not ensure that Kāinga Ora is building the houses that we in Government actually put in place? Why not come to New Plymouth and make sure that those houses that we had planned and that were budgeted for were actually being built?
rigor.explanation: A pointed rhetorical challenge; identifies a specific counter-example but argues by question rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Now, our world is burning, and if you look around at what is going on, I feel like this Government is just throwing fuel into that fire, literally—literally. Nature is in retreat, it is under attack, and this Government is fast tracking its way to collapse those things.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbole ('throwing fuel into that fire, literally') and appeal to emotion in place of evidence.

rigor.statement: when you look at 90 percent of seabirds being under threat, when you look at 84 percent of reptiles being under threat, when you look at 76 percent of freshwater fish being under threat—when you look at all of these things, and this is an underestimation of what is potentially happening, we need to make sure that nature and that the environment is in this bill.
rigor.explanation: Uses real biodiversity data to support the call for environmental provisions in the bill.

rigor.statement: When we listened to the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, the Hon Simon Upton, a previous National Party Minister... he talked about this bill lacking many of the environmental safeguards that the predecessor legislation contained... He even talked about Muldoon’s National Development Act of 1979 having far more environmental protections in place than this piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: Cites the independent Commissioner (and notes he is a former National Minister) to pre-empt bias claims; relies on his authority but with a concrete comparison to the 1979 Act.

rigor.statement: As I listened to this farmer speak, he was vehemently opposed at the beginning to this wind farm being built next to his farm... through the process we currently have, they worked, they listened, the company understood the challenges, then they made changes to the design and to the placement of that wind farm, to the point where this farmer said that he and his community sat comfortably with that wind farm being built near them, because they had been listened to.
rigor.explanation: A single anecdote used to argue the existing process works, illustrative but not generalisable evidence.

rigor.statement: members opposite are talking a lot about the nature of the bill as it was introduced, but it’s important to remind those who are listening of both sides of this, because, of course, it was a draft. It’s the first reading when it’s introduced... They were honest about the fact that it could have been better, and, of course, that was the part that we played, as a select committee.
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasonable procedural point that the introduced bill was a draft intended to change through select committee.

rigor.statement: this is not a poll. It is not our job to weigh each individual submission; it’s our job to consider them, and, because of that, the bill is now in a better place.
rigor.explanation: Draws a valid distinction between counting submissions and evaluating them, rebutting the 'majority opposed' argument on principle.

rigor.statement: I have a power station in my electorate, up in Tūai, a very remote part of New Zealand, and this power station provides power to almost the entire settlement of Wairoa... One of the projects that could get fast-track consent is the hydro energy station in Tūai. Now, this is just reconsenting... the processes that they have to go through, as it stands, are so complicated that we are risking cutting the power to the entire settlement of Wairoa.
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific case to argue complicated processes—not just controversial projects—drive the delays; the 'risking cutting the power' claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: In Canterbury, one of those projects was the Carter Group project. Philip Carter of Carter Holdings, uncle to Matt Doocey—donor of $60,000. I asked the Prime Minister, in written question No. 66395... The Prime Minister gave me a long answer. I needed one word—“no”—and he didn’t give me that word.
rigor.explanation: Builds a specific circumstantial case, but infers a conflict from association rather than demonstrating improper influence.

rigor.statement: They don’t just want to kill this bill; they want to kill 55,000 new homes for hard-working Kiwis that just want to get a chance... Then they’re saying, “We don’t just want to kill them, we want to kill 180 kilometres of new roads.”
rigor.explanation: Strawman — recasts opposition to the bill's process as wanting to 'kill' the homes and roads themselves.

rigor.statement: just like they killed the Ōtaki to North of Levin Expressway in 2018. Everyone in our region, in Horowhenua, knows exactly the impact that had—the needless deaths that we experienced on that road—because of the six years of delay.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion and local consensus ('everyone knows') plus an unsupported causal link.

rigor.statement: when we were in Government there was a study done, led by the Infrastructure Commission, proving that New Zealand’s cost of consenting mid-size infrastructure was higher than the top end of the range for Europe. Over 5 percent of the project cost was being spent on the consenting process, which was far too high.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a cited study and draws a proportionate conclusion.

rigor.statement: There is one aspect of this legislation that I do support in principle, which is combining the decision making under various other pieces of legislation, including the Conservation Act and the Reserves Act, but only if the tests that apply under those pieces of legislation still apply and are not overridden in the process
rigor.explanation: Draws a precise distinction between combining process and overriding substantive statutory tests.

rigor.statement: the current process doesn’t just change the process; it enables the decision maker to override RMA plans to actually allow activities that are prohibited under the Resource Management Act or under Resource Management Act plans, or are contrary to the legal requirements of the Conservation Act or the Wildlife Act or the heritage protection legislation, to name but some. That is the major difference between this legislation and that.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion contrast between changing process and overriding environmental tests.

rigor.statement: The Rt Hon Simon Upton has in the past been the secretary for the environment for the OECD, probably the highest environmental office ever held by a New Zealander. He is a former National Minister for the Environment, and he said that this legislation is wrong and is worse than the National Development Act under Muldoon
rigor.explanation: Bolsters the argument by establishing the authority's credentials and cross-party standing, though it remains an appeal to authority.

rigor.statement: The Raetihi Hydro Dam—an existing dam—took 18 years to reconsent... the Mill Creek wind farm took 1,437 days to consent, and we’ve just heard from the other side that re-consenting is different to new. This was a new thing. It was a wind farm that took close to four years to actually gain a consent.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete case timelines to rebut the opposition's process-vs-substance point.

rigor.statement: the UK currently actually has a centralised planning process like this for large infrastructure projects. Did they mention that? No, they didn’t. The EU has adopted a fast-track permit-granting process for renewable energy projects. They’re also exploring options to speed up permitting for critical raw materials
rigor.explanation: Brings comparative international evidence to rebut the trade/reputation argument, though analogies gloss over key differences between regimes.

rigor.statement: it is only now, or, rather, at the third reading and then at the Royal assent of this bill, that the legislation will become effective as a matter of law. We’re saying that back to that date at which we announced that that change will be made, that’s when the rule shall apply, with the rule being that an additional four years shall be allowed to remediate buildings in accordance with the earthquake-prone building regime as it currently stands.
rigor.explanation: Clear, orderly explanation of how and when the rule takes effect.

rigor.statement: we’re getting the balance here right between the safety of people who are in buildings which we know are earthquake-prone and the ability of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) and of Government to work through the issues which need to be resolved and need to be resolved quickly underlying some of those decisions. It’s really important that MBIE is well resourced and well equipped
rigor.explanation: Frames the issue as a reasoned trade-off between building safety and administrative capacity.

rigor.statement: First, let me move to clause 5, the unsexy part of the bill which gives stand-alone building consent authorities (BCAs) more direction in terms of paying their levies. I want to ask the Minister to explain the status quo to the committee and how it came to be... and whether this change interacts at all with his proposals generally to change the rules for BCAs, and then whether regional and consolidated BCAs of the future will be liable to pay under this provision.
rigor.explanation: Methodical, clause-level scrutiny probing how the change interacts with wider BCA reform.

rigor.statement: One of the issues that we have, particularly in lesser populated areas, is that there are some very significant historic buildings that are not utilised very often, are uneconomic to repair, and are risky if people were in them infrequently... there is a case, according to some of the people who live in those areas, that they would like, with appropriate notification, to actually be able to, as a community, take the risk. Now, obviously, you wouldn’t want to be doing that for schools and hospitals, but will there be consideration given to that trade-off between frequency of use and economics of repair
rigor.explanation: Frames a nuanced trade-off (use-frequency vs. repair economics) and pre-empts the obvious objection by excluding schools and hospitals.

veracity.statement: it is giving unprecedented powers to politicians who have deliberately chosen to remove Te Tiriti and who are doing everything they can to resurrect zombie projects previously turned down by every court that exists in Aotearoa. That’s not progress. That is not economic progress; that wreaks of desperation.
veracity.explanation: Some listed projects were indeed declined by courts/panels, but 'every court that exists' is hyperbolic and unverified as a blanket claim.

veracity.statement: When we see nearly 27,000 submitters, 83 percent of whom are opposed and many of whom weren’t heard because they were relegated to a ballot system over 23 days, it sort of tells you how desperate this Government is.
veracity.explanation: Submission figures are checkable and broadly consistent with other speakers, though her totals differ from Willis's 53,000 count.

Of those, 0.3 percent gave outright support to the bill—0.3 percent—1.1 percent gave support in principle, 5.7 percent had an unclear position, and 92.9 percent outright opposed the bill.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable figures presented consistently; plausible against the official submission analysis.

veracity.statement: It’s a proposal to burn toxic waste in a small, rural community, in Waimate in South Canterbury, and we heard in their submission that this is a project that will increase harmful climate emissions... It is proposed on a site on a flood plain—it could all wash out to sea—and it’s located within two kilometres of a school. On 5 November, the Waimate District Council passed a motion to request that the Government remove the toxic waste plant from the fast-track list.
veracity.explanation: The dated council motion and location are checkable facts; the emissions/pollution characterisations are drawn from opposing submissions and are contestable.

veracity.statement: In regards to the 149 projects included in Schedule 2 of the bill, they include housing, aquaculture, infrastructure—including 180 kilometres of new road, rail, and public transport routes—quarries, renewable energy, and, yes, mining.
veracity.explanation: Describes the Schedule 2 contents in checkable, factual terms.

veracity.explanation: Figures align closely with NZ conservation status reporting (high proportions of native species threatened/at risk).

veracity.statement: When we listened to the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, the Hon Simon Upton, a previous National Party Minister... he talked about this bill lacking many of the environmental safeguards that the predecessor legislation contained... He even talked about Muldoon’s National Development Act of 1979 having far more environmental protections in place than this piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the Commissioner's publicly reported criticisms of the bill.

veracity.statement: I just wanted to highlight in this legislation the many different laws and Acts that the bill will go through: the Resource Management Act... the Conservation Act, the Reserves Act, the Wildlife Act, the Heritage New Zealand Act, the Freshwater Fisheries Regulations, the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Act, the Crown Minerals Act, the Public Works Act, and the Fisheries Act.
veracity.explanation: Factual, checkable list of the statutes engaged by the regime.

veracity.statement: Radio New Zealand did a great job: $500,000 of donations from people who are on the fast-track list, and there’s no good explanation for that. I’m concerned that there are close connections between donors, members of the National Party, and the fact that they’re on this list.

veracity.statement: In Canterbury, one of those projects was the Carter Group project. Philip Carter of Carter Holdings, uncle to Matt Doocey—donor of $60,000. veracity.statement: just like they killed the Ōtaki to North of Levin Expressway in 2018. Everyone in our region, in Horowhenua, knows exactly the impact that had—the needless deaths that we experienced on that road—because of the six years of delay.
veracity.explanation: The 2018 project change is real, but attributing specific 'needless deaths' directly to the delay is an unproven causal claim.

veracity.statement: Ninety-five percent of the applications that were made through our fast-track process were approved and, indeed, of the 5 percent that weren’t, there were probably some applications that were withdrawn or that proceeded through some other process outside of fast track. We had a process that was principled and worked.
veracity.explanation: The 95% figure is plausible but is contested moments later by Campbell's differing breakdown (65% consented); no source cited.

veracity.statement: the current process doesn’t just change the process; it enables the decision maker to override RMA plans to actually allow activities that are prohibited under the Resource Management Act or under Resource Management Act plans, or are contrary to the legal requirements of the Conservation Act or the Wildlife Act or the heritage protection legislation, to name but some. That is the major difference between this legislation and that.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the bill's override of RMA/Conservation Act prohibitions.

veracity.statement: The Rt Hon Simon Upton has in the past been the secretary for the environment for the OECD, probably the highest environmental office ever held by a New Zealander. He is a former National Minister for the Environment, and he said that this legislation is wrong and is worse than the National Development Act under Muldoon
veracity.explanation: Upton's OECD and former National ministerial roles, and his criticism of the bill, are accurately stated.

veracity.statement: The Raetihi Hydro Dam—an existing dam—took 18 years to reconsent... the Mill Creek wind farm took 1,437 days to consent, and we’ve just heard from the other side that re-consenting is different to new. This was a new thing. It was a wind farm that took close to four years to actually gain a consent.

veracity.statement: I will get to some of those numbers: 65 percent were actually consented through that legislation, 16 percent are still in the process, and 11 percent fell into a black hole of who knows what.
veracity.explanation: Directly contradicts Parker's 95% approval figure for the same regime; one of the two is materially off and neither cites a source.

The EU has adopted a fast-track permit-granting process for renewable energy projects. They’re also exploring options to speed up permitting for critical raw materials
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — the UK's NSIP regime and EU renewable/critical-raw-materials permitting reforms exist, though the comparison to this bill's override powers is loose.

specificity.statement: Absolutely, we should progress—absolutely, and there’s no debate on this side—but “At the cost of what?” is what we’re really, really opposing you on.

On 5 November, the Waimate District Council passed a motion to request that the Government remove the toxic waste plant from the fast-track list.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, location, a dated council motion, and concrete risk factors (flood plain, 2km from a school).

specificity.explanation: References concrete planned/budgeted New Plymouth Kāinga Ora housing, though without figures.

specificity.statement: when you look at 90 percent of seabirds being under threat, when you look at 84 percent of reptiles being under threat, when you look at 76 percent of freshwater fish being under threat—when you look at all of these things, and this is an underestimation of what is potentially happening, we need to make sure that nature and that the environment is in this bill.

specificity.explanation: Names the source, his office, and a specific historical comparator.

specificity.statement: I have a power station in my electorate, up in Tūai, a very remote part of New Zealand, and this power station provides power to almost the entire settlement of Wairoa... One of the projects that could get fast-track consent is the hydro energy station in Tūai. Now, this is just reconsenting... the processes that they have to go through, as it stands, are so complicated that we are risking cutting the power to the entire settlement of Wairoa.
specificity.explanation: Concrete named example (Tūai hydro station, Wairoa) illustrating the reconsenting problem.

specificity.statement: I just wanted to highlight in this legislation the many different laws and Acts that the bill will go through: the Resource Management Act... the Conservation Act, the Reserves Act, the Wildlife Act, the Heritage New Zealand Act, the Freshwater Fisheries Regulations, the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Act, the Crown Minerals Act, the Public Works Act, and the Fisheries Act.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise Acts the one-stop-shop consolidates to substantiate the 'parallel processes' argument.

specificity.statement: Radio New Zealand did a great job: $500,000 of donations from people who are on the fast-track list, and there’s no good explanation for that. I’m concerned that there are close connections between donors, members of the National Party, and the fact that they’re on this list.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific reported donations figure and links it to the fast-track list.

specificity.statement: In Canterbury, one of those projects was the Carter Group project. Philip Carter of Carter Holdings, uncle to Matt Doocey—donor of $60,000. I asked the Prime Minister, in written question No. 66395... The Prime Minister gave me a long answer. I needed one word—“no”—and he didn’t give me that word.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, the donor, the family relationship, a dollar figure, and the exact written question number.

specificity.statement: I’m deeply concerned that this country’s position as somewhere where people do business honestly, transparently, by the rules, and on an equal footing is at risk.
specificity.explanation: A general expression of concern with no concrete measure attached.

specificity.statement: They don’t just want to kill this bill; they want to kill 55,000 new homes for hard-working Kiwis that just want to get a chance... Then they’re saying, “We don’t just want to kill them, we want to kill 180 kilometres of new roads.”
specificity.explanation: Attaches concrete figures (55,000 homes, 180km of roads) to the claim.

specificity.statement: when we were in Government there was a study done, led by the Infrastructure Commission, proving that New Zealand’s cost of consenting mid-size infrastructure was higher than the top end of the range for Europe. Over 5 percent of the project cost was being spent on the consenting process, which was far too high.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Infrastructure Commission) and a concrete figure (>5% of project cost).

specificity.statement: Ninety-five percent of the applications that were made through our fast-track process were approved and, indeed, of the 5 percent that weren’t, there were probably some applications that were withdrawn or that proceeded through some other process outside of fast track. We had a process that was principled and worked.
specificity.explanation: Gives an approval-rate figure, though hedges on the fate of the remainder.

specificity.statement: the current process doesn’t just change the process; it enables the decision maker to override RMA plans to actually allow activities that are prohibited under the Resource Management Act or under Resource Management Act plans, or are contrary to the legal requirements of the Conservation Act or the Wildlife Act or the heritage protection legislation, to name but some. That is the major difference between this legislation and that.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the precise mechanism (overriding substantive tests across named Acts) that distinguishes the two regimes.

specificity.statement: The Raetihi Hydro Dam—an existing dam—took 18 years to reconsent... the Mill Creek wind farm took 1,437 days to consent, and we’ve just heard from the other side that re-consenting is different to new. This was a new thing. It was a wind farm that took close to four years to actually gain a consent.
specificity.explanation: Cites named projects with precise durations (18 years; 1,437 days).

specificity.statement: I will get to some of those numbers: 65 percent were actually consented through that legislation, 16 percent are still in the process, and 11 percent fell into a black hole of who knows what.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage breakdown of the earlier regime's outcomes.

specificity.statement: the UK currently actually has a centralised planning process like this for large infrastructure projects. Did they mention that? No, they didn’t. The EU has adopted a fast-track permit-granting process for renewable energy projects. They’re also exploring options to speed up permitting for critical raw materials
specificity.explanation: Names specific overseas regimes and their purposes.

specificity.statement: In Schedule 2, there are projects that, if approved, will deliver up to 55,000 sections, 3,000 megawatts of renewable energy, and 43 infrastructure projects enabling 180 kilometres for roads, rail, and public transport routes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete quantified projections (55,000 sections, 3,000 MW, 180km).

specificity.statement: It’s about creating a future where all New Zealanders can have access to affordable housing, where our economy is powered by clean energy, and where our communities are connected by modern and efficient infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational vision statement with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: it is only now, or, rather, at the third reading and then at the Royal assent of this bill, that the legislation will become effective as a matter of law. specificity.explanation: Precisely sets out the retrospective effective date and the concrete rule (an additional four years to remediate).

specificity.statement: my assurance is that we will not use that power unless it is needed... if additional time should be needed following the review and any legislation needed to give effect to new settings, and then to allow a reasonable period of time for people to comply with the settings, particularly if they are in any way more onerous... That additional time may be needed for people to get up to those standards.
specificity.explanation: Explains the contingency (review, new settings, compliance time) but no concrete triggers or limits.

specificity.statement: we’re getting the balance here right between the safety of people who are in buildings which we know are earthquake-prone and the ability of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) and of Government to work through the issues which need to be resolved and need to be resolved quickly underlying some of those decisions. It’s really important that MBIE is well resourced and well equipped
specificity.explanation: Identifies the relevant agency and the affected groups, but no concrete resourcing measure.

specificity.statement: First, let me move to clause 5, the unsexy part of the bill which gives stand-alone building consent authorities (BCAs) more direction in terms of paying their levies. I want to ask the Minister to explain the status quo to the committee and how it came to be... and whether this change interacts at all with his proposals generally to change the rules for BCAs, and then whether regional and consolidated BCAs of the future will be liable to pay under this provision.
specificity.explanation: Drills into a precise clause and a detailed, technical set of questions about BCA levy liability.

specificity.statement: One of the issues that we have, particularly in lesser populated areas, is that there are some very significant historic buildings that are not utilised very often, are uneconomic to repair, and are risky if people were in them infrequently... there is a case, according to some of the people who live in those areas, that they would like, with appropriate notification, to actually be able to, as a community, take the risk. Now, obviously, you wouldn’t want to be doing that for schools and hospitals, but will there be consideration given to that trade-off between frequency of use and economics of repair
specificity.explanation: Describes the rarely-used-heritage-building problem concretely, though the proposed solution is left as a question for consideration.

charisma.statement: Absolutely, we should progress—absolutely, and there’s no debate on this side—but “At the cost of what?” is what we’re really, really opposing you on.
charisma.explanation: Concedes shared support for progress, but frames the dispute as us-vs-you rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: One term is actually one term too many for a Government intent on trashing our environment, running roughshod over our communities, and destroying our children’s future.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them rhetoric that alienates rather than persuades the other side.

charisma.statement: As I listened to this farmer speak, he was vehemently opposed at the beginning to this wind farm being built next to his farm... through the process we currently have, they worked, they listened, the company understood the challenges, then they made changes to the design and to the placement of that wind farm, to the point where this farmer said that he and his community sat comfortably with that wind farm being built near them, because they had been listened to.
charisma.explanation: Uses a constructive, consensus-building example (community and company reaching agreement) to make the case for engagement.

charisma.statement: Oh, Labour is very rare in New Plymouth.
charisma.explanation: A partisan quip that scores points against the other side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: members opposite are talking a lot about the nature of the bill as it was introduced, but it’s important to remind those who are listening of both sides of this, because, of course, it was a draft. It’s the first reading when it’s introduced... They were honest about the fact that it could have been better, and, of course, that was the part that we played, as a select committee.
charisma.explanation: Measured and explanatory in tone, though still defending her side's process.

charisma.statement: if there was any doubt where the Grinch was going to be hiding this Christmas, I’d be looking in central Christchurch, because what we’ve heard is an Opposition and a Labour Party—
charisma.explanation: A partisan applause line that mocks the other side instead of persuading it.

charisma.statement: There is one aspect of this legislation that I do support in principle, which is combining the decision making under various other pieces of legislation, including the Conservation Act and the Reserves Act, but only if the tests that apply under those pieces of legislation still apply and are not overridden in the process
charisma.explanation: Concedes a genuine merit in the opponents' bill and states a condition for support, seeking common ground rather than blanket opposition.

charisma.statement: It’s about creating a future where all New Zealanders can have access to affordable housing, where our economy is powered by clean energy, and where our communities are connected by modern and efficient infrastructure.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'all New Zealanders' framing, but a broad rally-the-vision line rather than a bridge to opponents.

charisma.statement: I do also want to acknowledge a point that was emphasised during the second reading debate—particularly by members opposite, and I think that had a good point—which was, first, that this should not be an exercise in kicking the can down the road.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits opponents with a good point and adopts it, a genuine cross-aisle, consensus-building gesture.

charisma.statement: Labour supports this bill, but we’ll work through clause by clause to ask the Minister to clarify some points which came up not only from submitters in the select committee stage but also in the contributions in the second reading, because there are remaining questions there.
charisma.explanation: Signals cross-party support while flagging constructive scrutiny — collaborative rather than combative.

charisma.statement: One of the issues that we have, particularly in lesser populated areas, is that there are some very significant historic buildings that are not utilised very often, are uneconomic to repair, and are risky if people were in them infrequently... there is a case, according to some of the people who live in those areas, that they would like, with appropriate notification, to actually be able to, as a community, take the risk. Now, obviously, you wouldn’t want to be doing that for schools and hospitals, but will there be consideration given to that trade-off between frequency of use and economics of repair
charisma.explanation: Constructive, problem-solving question to the Minister across the aisle rather than a partisan attack.

divination.statement: what you don’t realise is you’re fast tracking your way out of Parliament, and let this be a one-term Government, for all we can do.
divination.explanation: Predicts a one-term government at the 2026 election; partisan and uncertain given no polling basis is offered.

divination.statement: Scott Simpson, at one level, did a very pleasant job of administering the chair for this bill—and he is a decent chair—but, by goodness, he’s going to be at risk in the Coromandel election next time, isn’t he, because he has, effectively, brought through legislation which is incompatible with the values of most of his voters in the Coromandel.
divination.explanation: Predicts Simpson will be electorally 'at risk' in Coromandel next election — partisan and speculative.

divination.statement: In Schedule 2, there are projects that, if approved, will deliver up to 55,000 sections, 3,000 megawatts of renewable energy, and 43 infrastructure projects enabling 180 kilometres for roads, rail, and public transport routes.
divination.explanation: Predicts delivery of these outputs, hedged with 'if approved' and 'up to'; realisation is uncertain and depends on later consenting decisions.

authenticity.statement: There is one aspect of this legislation that I do support in principle, which is combining the decision making under various other pieces of legislation, including the Conservation Act and the Reserves Act, but only if the tests that apply under those pieces of legislation still apply and are not overridden in the process
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his record as author of the earlier fast-track regime; supports the process element he himself introduced while opposing the override.

strength.statement: Ninety-five percent of the applications that were made through our fast-track process were approved and, indeed, of the 5 percent that weren’t, there were probably some applications that were withdrawn or that proceeded through some other process outside of fast track. We had a process that was principled and worked.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a fast-track regime he introduced that was enacted and processed applications at a high approval rate — delivered policy, not just rhetoric.

forthrightness.statement: it is only now, or, rather, at the third reading and then at the Royal assent of this bill, that the legislation will become effective as a matter of law. We’re saying that back to that date at which we announced that that change will be made, that’s when the rule shall apply, with the rule being that an additional four years shall be allowed to remediate buildings in accordance with the earthquake-prone building regime as it currently stands.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly acknowledges the retrospectivity element and explains its scope rather than glossing over it.

forthrightness.statement: my assurance is that we will not use that power unless it is needed... if additional time should be needed following the review and any legislation needed to give effect to new settings, and then to allow a reasonable period of time for people to comply with the settings, particularly if they are in any way more onerous... That additional time may be needed for people to get up to those standards.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the 'Henry VIII' power concern directly and states the condition under which it would be used, though the assurance rests on future good faith.

strength.statement: That's what people told me they wanted, that's what I fought hard for, and today it has been delivered.
strength.explanation: The 110km/h Kāpiti Expressway speed limit was actually implemented, and he credibly links it to his own petition advocacy — a stated commitment followed through to delivery.

strength.statement: if you buy a house today at the median house price, you put down a 20 percent deposit, you will be saving exactly $110 per week on your mortgage thanks to this Government and our efforts to cut inflation
strength.explanation: Claims credit for interest-rate relief largely driven by monetary policy, not delivered by his Government.

strength.statement: I looked at the number of nurses that we have trained—almost 2,600—it’s almost 110 new nurses that we have employed every fortnight for the last year since we came into Government.
strength.explanation: Claims workforce delivery, but the causal contribution and the conflated metric make follow-through unclear.

strength.statement: One of the first things that the new coalition Government did before Christmas last year was to repeal Labour’s very ill-conceived natural and built environment legislation. It was full of red tape; it had slowed down the economy
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete delivered action — the Government did repeal the Natural and Built Environment/Spatial Planning Acts in December 2023.

authenticity.statement: That's what people told me they wanted, that's what I fought hard for, and today it has been delivered.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his campaigning/petitioning for 110; words match a visible action he pursued.

authenticity.statement: There was a period of time that I had arrogated that distinction to my good self, but I’m a member of a Cabinet that is blessed with common sense… That’s why a High Court judge or an Environment Court judge will chair the panels
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges reversing his earlier wish to be the decision-maker in favour of judge-chaired panels — a candid, defensible shift in position.

specificity.statement: More than 2,000 people signed that petition in support; 3,000 people submitted to the New Zealand Transport Agency, and 93 percent of them said, “Make it 110.”
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for signatures, submissions and support percentage.

specificity.statement: if you buy a house today at the median house price, you put down a 20 percent deposit, you will be saving exactly $110 per week on your mortgage thanks to this Government and our efforts to cut inflation
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete dollar figure and scenario, though the assumptions are cherry-picked.

specificity.statement: Now, I’m sure it’s not just those that are 10 percent better; our streets are probably 10 percent safer.
specificity.explanation: A number is cited but it is arbitrary and attached to nothing measurable.

specificity.statement: I looked at the number of nurses that we have trained—almost 2,600—it’s almost 110 new nurses that we have employed every fortnight for the last year since we came into Government.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete numbers and a timeframe, even if the framing is strained.

specificity.statement: the next stage, Ōtaki to north of Levin, all the way to the north of Levin, construction starting next year.
specificity.explanation: Names the route and a rough start timeframe, but no cost or completion detail.

specificity.statement: the very next day, as in this morning, there was a regulatory impact statement released that detailed the impact of the military boot camps that this Government is currently experimenting with
specificity.explanation: Points to a specific document and timing, though not to its contents.

specificity.statement: where he was subject to seclusion—which is solitary confinement for kids—where he was subject to a number one diet, where he was showered by being hosed down with a fire hose.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, detailed account of specific practices (seclusion, number-one diet, fire hose).

specificity.statement: the inflation genie is well back in the box. It was down to 2.2 percent for the year ended September
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact figure and period, wrapped in a metaphor.

specificity.statement: 80 percent of our export income comes from our food and fibre sector, 70,000 businesses are involved in the sector, and 360,000 people work in it—one in six New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise statistics on export share, businesses and employment.

specificity.statement: there were nigh on 390 to 400 projects, but we showed judiciousness on this side of the House… and we said we’d settle upon 149 projects.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers for applications received and projects listed.

specificity.statement: There was a period of time that I had arrogated that distinction to my good self, but I’m a member of a Cabinet that is blessed with common sense… That’s why a High Court judge or an Environment Court judge will chair the panels
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete change: judge-chaired expert panels as final decision-makers.

specificity.statement: Government bills are there for the general New Zealanders—they’re not specific. We have local bills when councils want to change the status of a reserve or something like that, and we have private bills when private entities such as trusts want to change something about their trust deed.
specificity.explanation: Precisely identifies the categories of legislation and their proper uses.

specificity.statement: we heard from people that there are only 16 water conservation orders in New Zealand over 16 pristine water bodies, and it’s a very long and arduous process to get a water conservation order, but these projects can just ignore the water conservation orders
specificity.explanation: Cites the number of orders and the specific mechanism being overridden.

specificity.statement: Clause 3, as in the bill that was introduced, said something about processes to facilitate development and projects, and now that “process” word has been deleted—to make it very clear that this is a substantive bill. The purpose does not refer to the environment, and it does not refer to sustainable management
specificity.explanation: Points to the exact clause and wording change.

specificity.statement: We had the media point out, even just at a cursory glance, that $500,000 in donations have been linked to companies that are on that Schedule 2 fast-track list, and we really welcome the Auditor-General launching their inquiry into how Ministers managed conflicts of interest with the fast-track process.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, the schedule, and the specific oversight body.

specificity.statement: despite the 27,000 submissions that we got on the bill and the 23 days of public hearings that the Environment Committee went through… quite incredibly, this bill has now emerged that is actually worse than when it first started out.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete submission and hearing-day counts.

specificity.statement: The Green Party proposed at select committee that we would actually define what constitutes significant, regional, and national benefits, and we proposed that this would mean public infrastructure, like transport, water, hospitals, education, renewable energy generation, and telecommunications.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, enumerated proposal for narrowing the bill's scope.

specificity.statement: they would rather open up swaths of the Mackenzie Basin for massive solar farms than actually do the policy work to enable the use of the millions of existing square metreage available on industry and domestic roofs that could be used instead.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete location and an alternative mechanism.

specificity.statement: a system that’s been running with the handbrake on, getting nowhere, and, in fact, costing $1.3 billion per annum, according to the Infrastructure Commission, to consent infrastructure projects alone in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Precise annual cost figure with an attributed source.

specificity.statement: New Zealanders are currently forced to get about 40,000-odd consents a year, as at the most recent peak of our construction boom. In the 1990s, and a few years after the Resource Management Act was passed, about 5,000 consents were required every year.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete before/after figures across time.

specificity.statement: a friend of mine building a house at Mangawhai… his 1-metre-high retaining wall, according to a council officer, was actually 1.2 metres, and that was a $4,000 cost and a six-week delay to building a family home.
specificity.explanation: Concrete details: location, measurements, cost and delay.

veracity.statement: More than 2,000 people signed that petition in support; 3,000 people submitted to the New Zealand Transport Agency, and 93 percent of them said, “Make it 110.”
veracity.explanation: Specific, plausible figures but presented by an interested party and not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: You’ll remember the dark days of Labour Governments, when it was a windy road; it was a dangerous road. People died on that road.
veracity.explanation: The old SH1 route did have a poor safety record, but pinning fatalities on “Labour Governments” is misleading causal spin.

veracity.statement: if you buy a house today at the median house price, you put down a 20 percent deposit, you will be saving exactly $110 per week on your mortgage thanks to this Government and our efforts to cut inflation
veracity.explanation: The “exactly $110” figure is contrived to fit his 110 theme, and crediting mortgage-rate falls to the Government understates the Reserve Bank's independent role.

veracity.statement: Now, I’m sure it’s not just those that are 10 percent better; our streets are probably 10 percent safer.
veracity.explanation: Unsupported claim hedged with “probably”; the “10 percent” is a rhetorical flourish tied to his motif, with no evidence.

veracity.statement: I looked at the number of nurses that we have trained—almost 2,600—it’s almost 110 new nurses that we have employed every fortnight for the last year since we came into Government.
veracity.explanation: The framing is arithmetically massaged to hit “110” and blends trained vs employed nurses; the underlying figure is dubious and hard to verify.

veracity.statement: the tax relief that the Opposition opposed. They didn’t want people in our community to have anything. Labour didn’t want you to have it.
veracity.explanation: Misleading caricature of Labour's stance on tax.

veracity.statement: the very next day, as in this morning, there was a regulatory impact statement released that detailed the impact of the military boot camps that this Government is currently experimenting with
veracity.explanation: The release of a regulatory impact statement on the youth boot-camp pilot is a checkable factual claim consistent with the timing.

veracity.statement: State abuse did not end in 1999; it continues to this day.
veracity.explanation: A defensible claim; the Royal Commission and ongoing Oranga Tamariki concerns support that abuse in care did not neatly end in 1999, though “continues” is a strong generalisation.

veracity.statement: David Seymour wants to lock up the parents of truants.
veracity.explanation: A simplified, sharpened characterisation of a truancy-enforcement position; captures the gist but strips nuance.

veracity.statement: Mark Mitchell is building a mega-prison at Waikeria and at Auckland Prison to continue to funnel our people into prisons.
veracity.explanation: The Waikeria expansion is real, but “mega-prison… to funnel our people” is loaded framing that imputes intent.

veracity.statement: where he was subject to seclusion—which is solitary confinement for kids—where he was subject to a number one diet, where he was showered by being hosed down with a fire hose.

veracity.statement: the inflation genie is well back in the box. It was down to 2.2 percent for the year ended September
veracity.explanation: Accurate: annual CPI inflation was 2.2% for the year ended September 2024.

veracity.statement: 80 percent of our export income comes from our food and fibre sector, 70,000 businesses are involved in the sector, and 360,000 people work in it—one in six New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with Ministry for Primary Industries figures for the food and fibre sector.

veracity.statement: They’d tax our land, they’d tax our beds, they’d tax the tables upon which we’re fed.
veracity.explanation: Misleading exaggeration of Labour's tax positions.

veracity.statement: Of course, we all know that this is modelled on Labour Party legislation. We all know it was the Labour Party who originally introduced the fast-track legislation, and included a list of projects
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Labour's COVID-era fast-track consenting regime included a project list and is a genuine antecedent.

veracity.statement: we are not going to get into a situation of developments’ progress and jobs held ransom to or hijacked by a random frog, a multicoloured skink, or other such elements of the natural world when there’s thousands and millions of them around us.
veracity.explanation: Misleading: the native frogs and skinks at issue are threatened/endemic species, not present in “thousands and millions.”

veracity.statement: there were nigh on 390 to 400 projects, but we showed judiciousness on this side of the House… and we said we’d settle upon 149 projects.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reported scale of applications and the ~149 listed projects.

veracity.statement: it enables coalmining in kiwi habitats. That is just mind-blowingly bad… kiwi are regarded as taonga species in New Zealand, and that project has already been declined. It can’t get through the current environmental tests, and yet with this bill it will be able to

veracity.explanation: The count of around 16 water conservation orders is broadly accurate, and the bill does subordinate them.

veracity.statement: Clause 3, as in the bill that was introduced, said something about processes to facilitate development and projects, and now that “process” word has been deleted—to make it very clear that this is a substantive bill. The purpose does not refer to the environment, and it does not refer to sustainable management
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about the amended purpose clause omitting environmental/sustainable-management references.

veracity.statement: We had the media point out, even just at a cursory glance, that $500,000 in donations have been linked to companies that are on that Schedule 2 fast-track list, and we really welcome the Auditor-General launching their inquiry into how Ministers managed conflicts of interest with the fast-track process.
veracity.explanation: References a reported donations figure and a genuine Auditor-General inquiry; the linkage is as reported rather than proven wrongdoing.

veracity.statement: despite the 27,000 submissions that we got on the bill and the 23 days of public hearings that the Environment Committee went through… quite incredibly, this bill has now emerged that is actually worse than when it first started out.

veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific cost figure to a named source; broadly consistent with Infrastructure Commission estimates, though the exact number is contestable.

veracity.explanation: Coal does have chemical/industrial uses; true as far as it goes, but omits context about the bill's actual coal projects.

veracity.statement: final decisions on projects will not sit with a group of Ministers but with the expert panel… in fact, it’s identical to the same system that the Labour Government had when they were in power, so I’m sure that they’ll be supporting that.

civility.statement: You’ll remember the dark days of Labour Governments, when it was a windy road; it was a dangerous road. People died on that road.
