civility.statement: tomorrow, this Government will introduce a Treaty principles bill that will absolutely underpin harm that is completely irreversible.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnation of a policy rather than a person; heated but aimed at the bill.

civility.statement: David Seymour wants to lock up the parents of truants.
civility.explanation: Pointed framing of an opponent's policy, but directed at the policy rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Mark Mitchell is building a mega-prison at Waikeria and at Auckland Prison to continue to funnel our people into prisons.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy/record with charged language rather than the person directly.

civility.statement: They’d tax our land, they’d tax our beds, they’d tax the tables upon which we’re fed.
civility.explanation: Mocking doggerel caricaturing opponents rather than engaging their tax policy.

civility.statement: it’s not hard to come to the conclusion that the Labour Party seems to be fixated not only on more rules but on more tax. They seem quite addicted to tax.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as “addicted to tax” — a jab at the party rather than a substantive policy critique.

civility.statement: This bill will take New Zealand backwards under this Government. It will take Māori-Crown relations back to the dark ages. It is divisive, it is destructive, it is an absolute waste of money.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic “dark ages” condemnation of the bill; heated but targets the policy not a person.

civility.statement: Last week, I watched in disbelief as “Simeon Seymour” tabled the Treaty principles bill.
civility.explanation: A mocking portmanteau nickname conflating two ministers — a cheap shot rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: we move beyond the cobweb of green, red, and brown tapeworm-like obstructiveness that has impeded the development of our economy
civility.explanation: Colourful denigration (“tapeworm-like”) of environmental and consenting processes; rhetorical rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I’ll take jobs for Māoris before surfing for hippies any time of the day.
civility.explanation: Dismissive labelling (“hippies”) and a sneering framing of opponents' concerns.

civility.statement: we are not going to get into a situation of developments’ progress and jobs held ransom to or hijacked by a random frog, a multicoloured skink, or other such elements of the natural world when there’s thousands and millions of them around us.
civility.explanation: Trivialises opponents' conservation concerns with mocking language.

civility.statement: a lot of the Māori hogwash that I have to tolerate… This notion that tikanga Māori applies 30 kilometres off the coast, and you can’t go exploring and creating wealth looking at ironsands… shows how ideology has weaponised our Māori identity.
civility.explanation: Derides opposing cultural arguments as “hogwash” rather than engaging them.

civility.statement: the Minister is just yelling out “red tape” because that is how he holds the constitutional norms in New Zealand: with disdain. It is a disgrace.
civility.explanation: Sharp “disdain… a disgrace” language, but aimed at the Minister's conduct/approach in debate rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: they would rather open up swaths of the Mackenzie Basin for massive solar farms than actually do the policy work to enable the use of the millions of existing square metreage available on industry and domestic roofs that could be used instead.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of laziness in policy-making — a jab, but tied to a substantive point.

civility.statement: I would call on all members of this House to quit the catastrophising, quit the use of these terms like “ecocide” and a “war on nature”, and go back and tell your supporters… that there’s a way through this, and we’re going to participate in a constructive way
civility.explanation: Calls for cooler debate while itself belittling opponents' language.

civility.statement: New Zealanders do share values about our love of the environment, but, by goodness, we also want to live in affordable homes, we want to be able to drive at a decent clip on modern roads, we want to be able to get into ports and airports
civility.explanation: Frames the disagreement around competing goods rather than attacking opponents.

civility.statement: not have a whole bunch of nimbies and people who catastrophise the impact of land development on the environment to such an extent that, essentially, they’ll say that we can’t build anything anywhere, ever.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents “nimbies” and caricatures their position.

civility.statement: We simply can’t, as a nation, continue to divide the pie into ever-decreasing slivers… we actually have to grow the pie. I know that that is a difficult concept for members of the Opposition to grasp
civility.explanation: The “difficult concept… to grasp” aside is a condescending swipe at opponents' intelligence.

civility.statement: One of the first things that the new coalition Government did before Christmas last year was to repeal Labour’s very ill-conceived natural and built environment legislation. It was full of red tape; it had slowed down the economy
civility.explanation: “Ill-conceived… full of red tape” is harsh but aimed at the legislation, not a person.

rigor.statement: the tax relief that the Opposition opposed. They didn’t want people in our community to have anything. Labour didn’t want you to have it.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: opposing a specific tax package is recast as wanting people to have nothing.

rigor.statement: They end up in our youth justice residences—the same ones that those kids were up on the roof for—and then they end up getting involved in gangs because those are the only people who can relate to their experiences of abuse and trauma, and then for their entire life they end up in and out of prison. It is a vicious cycle.
rigor.explanation: A plausible causal narrative from state-care abuse to gangs to imprisonment, but asserted rather than evidenced with data.

rigor.statement: Karen Chhour and her boot camps: we just need to read the report to see how those boot camps inevitably will end.
rigor.explanation: Relies on analogy to a historical report rather than evidence specific to the current pilot.

rigor.statement: They’d tax our land, they’d tax our beds, they’d tax the tables upon which we’re fed.
rigor.explanation: Pure caricature/hyperbole with no evidence; the listed taxes are invented for effect.

rigor.statement: it’s not hard to come to the conclusion that the Labour Party seems to be fixated not only on more rules but on more tax. They seem quite addicted to tax.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion rests on a single anecdote and characterisation, not evidence.

rigor.statement: A business owner came up to me the other week in Masterton. He was actually quite incredulous at the comments he’d heard from the previous administration… In his comment to me, he said, “That’s how we ended up in the recession we did.”
rigor.explanation: Argues from a single unnamed anecdote to a sweeping causal conclusion about the recession — an appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: we move beyond the cobweb of green, red, and brown tapeworm-like obstructiveness that has impeded the development of our economy
rigor.explanation: Emotive imagery substitutes for an evidenced case that the processes are the problem.

rigor.statement: I’ll take jobs for Māoris before surfing for hippies any time of the day.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy pitting jobs against “surfing,” ignoring the substantive environmental objection.

rigor.statement: we are not going to get into a situation of developments’ progress and jobs held ransom to or hijacked by a random frog, a multicoloured skink, or other such elements of the natural world when there’s thousands and millions of them around us.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses biodiversity impacts by assertion, contrary to the ecological evidence.

rigor.statement: a lot of the Māori hogwash that I have to tolerate… This notion that tikanga Māori applies 30 kilometres off the coast, and you can’t go exploring and creating wealth looking at ironsands… shows how ideology has weaponised our Māori identity.
rigor.explanation: Asserts ideology has “weaponised” identity without engaging the actual legal/tikanga argument he dismisses.

rigor.statement: Government bills are there for the general New Zealanders—they’re not specific. We have local bills when councils want to change the status of a reserve or something like that, and we have private bills when private entities such as trusts want to change something about their trust deed.
rigor.explanation: A careful, evidence-based constitutional distinction (public vs local vs private bills) supporting her conclusion that private-benefit projects don't belong in a Government bill.

rigor.statement: it enables coalmining in kiwi habitats. That is just mind-blowingly bad… kiwi are regarded as taonga species in New Zealand, and that project has already been declined. It can’t get through the current environmental tests, and yet with this bill it will be able to
rigor.explanation: Concrete argument: a project already declined under current tests could proceed under the bill, demonstrating it overrides protections rather than merely speeding them.

rigor.statement: we heard from people that there are only 16 water conservation orders in New Zealand over 16 pristine water bodies, and it’s a very long and arduous process to get a water conservation order, but these projects can just ignore the water conservation orders
rigor.explanation: Uses the concrete example to substantiate the general claim that protections are overridden.

rigor.statement: Clause 3, as in the bill that was introduced, said something about processes to facilitate development and projects, and now that “process” word has been deleted—to make it very clear that this is a substantive bill. The purpose does not refer to the environment, and it does not refer to sustainable management
rigor.explanation: Traces a specific textual change to the purpose clause and explains why it matters for how decision-makers must weigh factors.

rigor.statement: We had the media point out, even just at a cursory glance, that $500,000 in donations have been linked to companies that are on that Schedule 2 fast-track list, and we really welcome the Auditor-General launching their inquiry into how Ministers managed conflicts of interest with the fast-track process.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the conflict-of-interest concern in reporting and an independent inquiry rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The Green Party proposed at select committee that we would actually define what constitutes significant, regional, and national benefits, and we proposed that this would mean public infrastructure, like transport, water, hospitals, education, renewable energy generation, and telecommunications.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a defined criterion to the conclusion that the rejected scope reveals the bill's true purpose.

rigor.statement: they would rather open up swaths of the Mackenzie Basin for massive solar farms than actually do the policy work to enable the use of the millions of existing square metreage available on industry and domestic roofs that could be used instead.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts a specific policy path (rooftop solar) with the criticised one, though the “millions of square metres” capacity is asserted.

rigor.statement: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment so accurately described this as there being one set of rules for everyone and then there being special, fast-track rules “for the big end of town”.
rigor.explanation: Supports her point by citing an independent office-holder, though it leans on that authority rather than her own analysis.

rigor.statement: a system that’s been running with the handbrake on, getting nowhere, and, in fact, costing $1.3 billion per annum, according to the Infrastructure Commission, to consent infrastructure projects alone in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Cites a source to substantiate the cost claim rather than merely asserting it.

rigor.statement: New Zealanders are currently forced to get about 40,000-odd consents a year, as at the most recent peak of our construction boom. In the 1990s, and a few years after the Resource Management Act was passed, about 5,000 consents were required every year.
rigor.explanation: Uses a quantified comparison to argue the system has ballooned, though “all paperwork” is an overreach.

rigor.statement: a friend of mine building a house at Mangawhai… his 1-metre-high retaining wall, according to a council officer, was actually 1.2 metres, and that was a $4,000 cost and a six-week delay to building a family home.
rigor.explanation: A single vivid anecdote used to indict the whole consenting system — an appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: coal is not just something to be burned; it is a chemical. It contains carbon. It is used to turn into products like the coal tar in our trading partners like Japan and South Korea, which is then used to make those wonderful waterproof backpacks and rain jackets
rigor.explanation: Makes a valid point that coal has non-fuel industrial uses, but selectively frames it to sidestep that most NZ coal extraction is for combustion.

rigor.statement: not have a whole bunch of nimbies and people who catastrophise the impact of land development on the environment to such an extent that, essentially, they’ll say that we can’t build anything anywhere, ever.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — attributes an absolutist “can’t build anything anywhere, ever” position no one stated.

rigor.statement: we don’t accept that having protection, enhancement, and maintenance of the environment and having a growing, thriving economy are binary options, and that you can’t have one without the other. In fact, you must have both—you must have both.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly rejects a false dichotomy and argues both goals can be pursued, though he asserts the compatibility rather than showing how.

rigor.statement: We simply can’t, as a nation, continue to divide the pie into ever-decreasing slivers… we actually have to grow the pie. I know that that is a difficult concept for members of the Opposition to grasp
rigor.explanation: Relies on the “grow the pie” analogy as argument rather than evidence.

divination.statement: the next stage, Ōtaki to north of Levin, all the way to the north of Levin, construction starting next year.
divination.explanation: Forecast that construction of the next expressway stage will start in 2025 — plausible given it is a funded RoNS, but timelines commonly slip.

divination.statement: Karen Chhour and her boot camps: we just need to read the report to see how those boot camps inevitably will end.
divination.explanation: Predicts the boot camps will end badly by analogy to past institutions; directionally supported by history but stated as inevitability.

divination.statement: tomorrow, this Government will introduce a Treaty principles bill that will absolutely underpin harm that is completely irreversible.
divination.explanation: Forecasts irreversible harm from the bill; the bill's introduction is certain, but “absolutely… completely irreversible” overstates a contested outcome.

divination.statement: This bill will take New Zealand backwards under this Government. It will take Māori-Crown relations back to the dark ages. It is divisive, it is destructive, it is an absolute waste of money.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will set back Māori-Crown relations — a contested, unfalsifiable-in-degree forecast.

charisma.statement: This bill will take New Zealand backwards under this Government. It will take Māori-Crown relations back to the dark ages. It is divisive, it is destructive, it is an absolute waste of money.
charisma.explanation: Rallies those already opposed rather than persuading the undecided.

charisma.statement: I particularly throw the tono out to those that sit on the Māori Affairs Committee with me, to the chair, to members that sit across the other side of the House in Government. I’m calling them to do what is right: to not put New Zealand through a six-month process of destruction that whips up racism.
charisma.explanation: Directly appeals across party lines to Government committee colleagues' conscience, though framed combatively (“process of destruction”).

charisma.statement: I just want to acknowledge all of the people, Māori and non-Māori alike, that crossed that bridge today; that stood for something; that stood for unity, Māori and non-Māori alike.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unity-focused language emphasising Māori and non-Māori together, though addressed to sympathisers.

charisma.statement: Of course, we all know that this is modelled on Labour Party legislation. We all know it was the Labour Party who originally introduced the fast-track legislation, and included a list of projects
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opponents' authorship of the concept, though deployed to needle rather than to build bridges.

charisma.statement: The Green Party proposed at select committee that we would actually define what constitutes significant, regional, and national benefits, and we proposed that this would mean public infrastructure, like transport, water, hospitals, education, renewable energy generation, and telecommunications.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive alternative rather than pure opposition, though it appeals mainly to her own side's framing.

charisma.statement: I would call on all members of this House to quit the catastrophising, quit the use of these terms like “ecocide” and a “war on nature”, and go back and tell your supporters… that there’s a way through this, and we’re going to participate in a constructive way
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites a constructive, shared path forward, but simultaneously dismisses opponents' concerns as “catastrophising,” limiting the bridge-building.

charisma.statement: New Zealanders do share values about our love of the environment, but, by goodness, we also want to live in affordable homes, we want to be able to drive at a decent clip on modern roads, we want to be able to get into ports and airports
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared values and common ground before making the case for development.

charisma.statement: we don’t accept that having protection, enhancement, and maintenance of the environment and having a growing, thriving economy are binary options, and that you can’t have one without the other. In fact, you must have both—you must have both.
charisma.explanation: Frames a both/and position that could appeal beyond his own side.

charisma.statement: final decisions on projects will not sit with a group of Ministers but with the expert panel… in fact, it’s identical to the same system that the Labour Government had when they were in power, so I’m sure that they’ll be supporting that.
charisma.explanation: Reaches for cross-party common ground by aligning the change with Labour's own past approach.

specificity.statement: That we amend this extension motion to replace “14 February 2025” with “17 December 2024”.
specificity.explanation: A precise, concrete amendment naming exact dates and the mechanism of change.

specificity.statement: What that will mean is if the Minister does wish for a further extension, she can come to Parliament and explain why and can justify it, and, in doing so, potentially give an update as to the negotiations and the industrial action where appropriate, because the House deserves to know.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete accountability mechanism (return to Parliament to justify) though without figures.

specificity.statement: The International Labour Organization, which New Zealand participates in, has ratified many, many different conventions on this; and a lot of our domestic legislation, including the Employment Relations Act, recognises the right of freedom of association and sees the right to strike as a corollary to the right of the freedom of association.
specificity.explanation: Names specific bodies and legislation, though the conventions themselves are not enumerated.

specificity.statement: requires the Minister to report to the House every two weeks on the status of the resolution of the industrial action
specificity.explanation: Concrete accountability mechanism with a defined reporting interval.

specificity.statement: if you read the Defence Act 1990, if you look at section 9, you will see how seriously the Parliament who passed this Act took this exceptional power. The reason that they put in the 14 days is, I think, reflective of how serious they thought utilisation of this power is.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific Act, section, and the 14-day review period.

specificity.statement: Of this $571 million increase, $163 million would go to improving remuneration for the New Zealand Defence Force personnel and $408 million to upgrading equipment and infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar breakdown of the funding allocation.

specificity.statement: the Government Workforce Policy Statement that the public services Minister, the Hon Nicola Willis, published earlier this year—I think it was in August—said that remuneration had to be met within baseline.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the responsible Minister, and an approximate date.

specificity.statement: all Government departments made cuts between, I believe, 5 to 7.5 percent, and that included the Ministry of Defence
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage range and names the affected department.

specificity.statement: The Great Strike was in 1913... That was the first time that I can recall—not that I was there, but the first time I can recall in terms of my history lessons—when the New Zealand Defence Force was actually brought in to actually deal with things like transportation, things even like waste, etc., and the movement of people
specificity.explanation: Anchors to a dated historical event but the role described is broad-brush.

specificity.statement: That after the words “camps and bases” the following words are added: “as long as the above authorisations are in place, the Minister will update the House on the progress being made to settle this industrial dispute on a weekly basis or on the next sitting day.”
specificity.explanation: Concrete amendment text specifying a weekly reporting obligation and trigger condition.

specificity.statement: authority for the use of appropriately trained members of the armed forces located at Devonport Naval Base, RNZAF Base Auckland, Papakura Military Camp, RNZAF Base Ōhakea, Linton Military Camp, Trentham Military Camp, Burnham Military Camp, RNZAF Base Woodbourne, and Headquarters, Joint Force New Zealand
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the exact list of bases, maximising precision of the amendment.

specificity.statement: Part 1, section 9(2)—it does indicate in that piece of governing legislation that the “authority shall specify the part or parts of the Armed Forces that may be used and the public service or public services that may be provided.”
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact Part and subsection and quotes it.

specificity.statement: he’s identified that the strike notice ends on 31 January. The extension is sought through to 14 February, which in itself is questionable. Is he aware as to whether or not those involved would be, effectively, within the time period within which that ends and the extension ends—whether a lockout is going to be on the cards
specificity.explanation: Pins down the two competing dates and the concrete concern (a possible lockout).

rigor.statement: What that will mean is if the Minister does wish for a further extension, she can come to Parliament and explain why and can justify it, and, in doing so, potentially give an update as to the negotiations and the industrial action where appropriate, because the House deserves to know.
rigor.explanation: Clear logical link: a shorter deadline forces accountability and disclosure; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: I don’t believe that the Ministry of Defence can act in good faith if this Parliament sends them a message that they actually don’t need to engage with the union or engage with the workers until next year
rigor.explanation: Reasonable incentive argument, but partly speculative about the Ministry's future motives.

rigor.statement: The International Labour Organization, which New Zealand participates in, has ratified many, many different conventions on this; and a lot of our domestic legislation, including the Employment Relations Act, recognises the right of freedom of association and sees the right to strike as a corollary to the right of the freedom of association.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based legal reasoning grounding the right to strike in ILO conventions and domestic statute.

rigor.statement: if you read the Defence Act 1990, if you look at section 9, you will see how seriously the Parliament who passed this Act took this exceptional power. The reason that they put in the 14 days is, I think, reflective of how serious they thought utilisation of this power is.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the statute's text, though the inference about legislative intent is interpretive.

rigor.statement: Of this $571 million increase, $163 million would go to improving remuneration for the New Zealand Defence Force personnel and $408 million to upgrading equipment and infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Uses the disaggregated figures to build a clear evidence-based argument.

rigor.statement: the $163 million increase for remuneration was for uniformed personnel only; I guess that’s the key distinction here. The reason why the defence force is actually having trouble meeting the needs of the civilian workers who are striking is because the funding increase which was tagged to remuneration was for uniformed personnel in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Draws a logically clean causal link between the earmarked funding and the civilian pay impasse.

rigor.statement: Part 1, section 9(2)—it does indicate in that piece of governing legislation that the “authority shall specify the part or parts of the Armed Forces that may be used and the public service or public services that may be provided.”
rigor.explanation: Grounds the amendment in the precise wording of the enabling statute.

rigor.statement: he’s identified that the strike notice ends on 31 January. The extension is sought through to 14 February, which in itself is questionable. Is he aware as to whether or not those involved would be, effectively, within the time period within which that ends and the extension ends—whether a lockout is going to be on the cards
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine gap between the strike-notice end date and the sought extension and reasons about its implication.

rigor.statement: there appears to be, perhaps, a lot of repetition more targeted on the resolution of industrial disputes and funding, not the use of defence force personnel under section 9 of the Act, which is indeed the question.
rigor.explanation: Correctly distinguishes the section 9 question before the House from the broader pay-dispute arguments.

civility.statement: I don’t believe that the Ministry of Defence can act in good faith if this Parliament sends them a message that they actually don’t need to engage with the union or engage with the workers until next year
civility.explanation: Criticises the Ministry's likely conduct, not a personal attack, but imputes bad faith.

civility.statement: She made a good point that you wouldn’t ever expect to be in a civilian aeroplane and not have those emergency firefighting rescue services available, even at a domestic airport, and you certainly shouldn’t expect that either at a defence airport
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with the substance of an opponent's argument.

civility.statement: We do not begrudge the Minister taking responsible decisions in terms of health and safety—that is, of course, important
civility.explanation: Acknowledges the legitimacy of the Minister's health-and-safety concerns; policy-focused.

civility.statement: there appears to be, perhaps, a lot of repetition more targeted on the resolution of industrial disputes and funding, not the use of defence force personnel under section 9 of the Act, which is indeed the question.
civility.explanation: A measured, respectful procedural point focused on relevance rather than personal attack.

authenticity.statement: the fact is that is why they are striking, and the Labour Party will always support their right to do so.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's long-standing and well-known pro-union, pro-strike position; words match the party's record.

divination.statement: the Government hasn’t confirmed this, but chances are Parliament’s going to knock off on Wednesday, 18 December of that week... The 18th December is likely to be the last sitting day
divination.explanation: Near-term, checkable forecast grounded in Business Committee signals; hedged and plausible.

divination.statement: we’re just going to be sitting here again on 14 February with the Ministry of Defence again asking for this motion to be extended.
divination.explanation: Plausible directional prediction that the dispute won't be resolved by February and a further extension will be sought; magnitude/timing uncertain.

charisma.statement: What could possibly be wrong with coming back to Parliament on the last sitting week of the year for, say, an hour, an hour-and-a-half , or two-hour debate to justify why they need to extend it further?
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective challenge, but framed to put the Government on the spot rather than to build cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: She made a good point that you wouldn’t ever expect to be in a civilian aeroplane and not have those emergency firefighting rescue services available, even at a domestic airport, and you certainly shouldn’t expect that either at a defence airport
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits the Minister's valid point, conceding common ground while making her own case.

charisma.statement: We do not begrudge the Minister taking responsible decisions in terms of health and safety—that is, of course, important
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory framing that narrows the disagreement and avoids demonising the Minister.

veracity.statement: The International Labour Organization, which New Zealand participates in, has ratified many, many different conventions on this; and a lot of our domestic legislation, including the Employment Relations Act, recognises the right of freedom of association and sees the right to strike as a corollary to the right of the freedom of association.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ is an ILO member, and the Employment Relations Act does recognise freedom of association and the right to strike.

veracity.statement: Of this $571 million increase, $163 million would go to improving remuneration for the New Zealand Defence Force personnel and $408 million to upgrading equipment and infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Presents specific budget figures consistent with the debate's context; checkable against Budget documents.

veracity.statement: the $163 million increase for remuneration was for uniformed personnel only; I guess that’s the key distinction here. The reason why the defence force is actually having trouble meeting the needs of the civilian workers who are striking is because the funding increase which was tagged to remuneration was for uniformed personnel in the first place.

veracity.explanation: Specific attributed factual claim about a named policy statement; hedged on the date, otherwise checkable.

veracity.statement: all Government departments made cuts between, I believe, 5 to 7.5 percent, and that included the Ministry of Defence
veracity.explanation: Quantified claim about the baseline savings exercise; hedged and broadly consistent with the reported targets.

veracity.statement: The Great Strike was in 1913... That was the first time that I can recall—not that I was there, but the first time I can recall in terms of my history lessons—when the New Zealand Defence Force was actually brought in to actually deal with things like transportation, things even like waste, etc., and the movement of people
veracity.explanation: The 1913 Great Strike and use of special constables/military-linked forces is historically real, though the exact 'Defence Force' characterisation is loose.

veracity.statement: Part 1, section 9(2)—it does indicate in that piece of governing legislation that the “authority shall specify the part or parts of the Armed Forces that may be used and the public service or public services that may be provided.”
veracity.explanation: Direct citation of the statutory text supporting his amendment; checkable and consistent.

veracity.statement: I understand the last time that it was enacted was back in 2001, so it means that this is not an issue or an item that has been placed before the Parliament on a frequent or regular basis.
veracity.explanation: A specific, hedged historical claim about the last use of the power; plausible and checkable.

authenticity.statement: The coalition agreement between ACT and National stipulates that National will support the Treaty principles bill for its first reading and to select committee, and that's what we're doing today.
authenticity.explanation: States National is acting exactly as its coalition agreement requires; the described vote (support to first reading only) matches the stated commitment.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has a very long and consistent history on our position regarding the Treaty principles.
authenticity.explanation: Claim of consistency backed later in the speech by the 2005 deletion bill and long-stated position; largely supported by the record.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First will, as we've committed to, support this bill to the first reading; it is our commitment to this Government and to this democracy.
authenticity.explanation: States the party is honouring its stated commitment; the vote matches the declared position.

authenticity.statement: National's long-held position is that a referendum on the Treaty would be divisive and would not deliver an outcome that takes our country forward.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a consistent, publicly held position; aligns with National voting against the bill at later stages.

authenticity.statement: Too often, those with the highest needs are Māori, and, in many cases, Māori have the answers. I'm proud of the work that we do to support a by Māori, for Māori approach.
authenticity.explanation: Praising a "by Māori, for Māori" approach sits in tension with the same speech's opposition to Māori-specific co-governance and the Māori Health Authority; a defensible but unresolved distinction.

authenticity.statement: Successive National Governments have worked well with Māori on Treaty issues. We have a proud track record of progressive Treaty settlements to address historic wrongdoings.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's stated case-by-case approach and its historical settlement record.

authenticity.statement: National has made a commitment to our coalition partner that we will support this bill to select committee, and we will honour that commitment today by voting as such. However, National is united in our view that this bill should not pass into law, and that is why we will vote against it at second reading.
authenticity.explanation: Openly reconciles the coalition obligation with the pre-election promise; the described votes match both commitments.

authenticity.statement: Our coalition agreement with ACT stipulates we will "introduce a Treaty principles bill based on existing ACT policy and support it to a select committee as soon as practicable." We will honour this commitment and support this bill to select committee. We will also honour our pre-election commitment and vote against the bill at second reading.
authenticity.explanation: Quotes the exact commitment and shows the planned votes honour both the coalition agreement and the pre-election promise.

specificity.statement: The coalition agreement between ACT and National stipulates that National will support the Treaty principles bill for its first reading and to select committee, and that's what we're doing today.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific mechanism (coalition agreement) and the precise limit of support (first reading and select committee).

specificity.statement: That's why we have reasserted the principle that healthcare should be delivered on the basis of need alone. That's why we're pushing back against the previous Government's move against equal voting rights in local government. That's why we're unwinding co-governance arrangements in core public services and a separate Māori Health Authority.
specificity.explanation: Lists several concrete named policies and actions rather than platitudes.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First brought legislation in 2005, the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Deletion Bill, which was voted down.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact bill, year, and outcome.

specificity.statement: We are not a people who should fear debate, ideas, or difference of opinion.
specificity.explanation: General value statement with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: First, we need to do what we need to do to get rid of this Government. This must be a one-term Government. How do we do that? E te iwi Māori, we must all register on the Māori roll.
specificity.explanation: Concrete political strategy (register on the Māori roll, add Māori seats) with a clear stated goal, though the mechanism of effect is asserted not detailed.

specificity.statement: We have reversed a number of Labour's divisive co-governance policies, like three waters and the Māori Health Authority.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policies reversed.

specificity.statement: When we look back and we think of the Maori Prisoners Act 1880, suspending trial rights for Māori at Parihaka; the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, confiscating land after the Tainui wars; the Tohunga Suppression Act 1907, banning traditional practices; and the Native Schools Act 1867, banning the use of te reo
specificity.explanation: Names four Acts with dates and their effects.

specificity.statement: National has made a commitment to our coalition partner that we will support this bill to select committee, and we will honour that commitment today by voting as such. However, National is united in our view that this bill should not pass into law, and that is why we will vote against it at second reading.
specificity.explanation: Specifies exactly how National will vote at each stage.

specificity.statement: What are we grappling with? It's simple: honour the Treaty; no grapple involved.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like assertion that offers no concrete mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: The people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti brought me to this House with hope—hope that we might actually address the real issues that whānau are facing, issues like housing, employment, education, and economic development.
specificity.explanation: Names several issue areas but no policies, figures, or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: we don't need to change the Treaty—we do not need to change the Treaty—we need to change this Government.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical slogan with no policy content.

specificity.statement: Our coalition agreement with ACT stipulates we will "introduce a Treaty principles bill based on existing ACT policy and support it to a select committee as soon as practicable." We will honour this commitment and support this bill to select committee. We will also honour our pre-election commitment and vote against the bill at second reading.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the precise wording of the commitment and states the exact voting behaviour at each stage.

specificity.statement: a thousand defence force personnel have given notice to go on strike, and the dates that they have proposed to go on strike are from 6 November until 31 January.
specificity.explanation: Gives the number of staff and precise strike dates.

specificity.statement: This is a very, very rare power... used on a few occasions in our recent history; once in 1996 and in 2001, as has been recently covered in the media, and again, I understand, in 2018 by Ron Mark.
specificity.explanation: Gives specific years and a named prior minister.

specificity.statement: I would like to move, That the words "14 February 2025" be replaced with the words "31 January 2025"... I cannot see any logical reason why these authorisations need to go on for two weeks longer than the strike notices.
specificity.explanation: Precise, concrete amendment with exact dates and a clear rationale.

specificity.statement: the Government regards it as prudent to provide a notice that will be long enough, at least until such time as the industrial action takes place, and a bit longer... as a matter of practicality to allow a couple of weeks for rosters to be put on so that people know, from one day to the next, when they are going to be required to turn up and do their shifts.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete operational reasons (rostering, standby for accidents, security gates) rather than generalities.

specificity.statement: The defence budget—total Vote Defence—was $4.949 billion for this financial year, which was a $308 million reduction on the budget for the preceding year.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures for the vote and the reduction.

specificity.statement: Why couldn't we apply the same rationale and approve an extension of 14 days, exactly the same amount that the Minister has available to her under the Defence Act, and then come back to Parliament and justify it?
specificity.explanation: Proposes a precise alternative (14-day extension mirroring the Act) with a clear mechanism.

civility.statement: This is a crude way to handle a very delicate subject. With a wave of the wand, as it were, we would unwind more than 30 years of jurisprudence—winner takes all.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the bill's process ("crude") but aimed at the method, not a person; mild rhetorical flourish.

civility.statement: Well, I was interrupted half a dozen times by the barracking and intimidation on the other side.
civility.explanation: Complaint about opponents' conduct; characterises barracking as "intimidation," mildly loaded but a legitimate point of order.

civility.statement: I may not agree with what you say, but I will defend your right to say it.
civility.explanation: Explicitly respects opponents' right to speak; frames disagreement as legitimate rather than personal.

civility.statement: ACT are seen to be pulling the strings and running the country, like the KKK with a swipe card to the Beehive, and Luxon doesn't even care. There's a ghost in his chair.
civility.explanation: Extreme personal attack: likens ACT to the KKK and derides the Prime Minister as an absent "ghost."

civility.statement: Everybody, every single one of the members sitting on that side of the House have enabled this bill to be introduced to the House. You are complicit in the harm and the division that this presents and are complicit in the euthanising of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Accuses the whole government benches of complicity in "harm"; broad-brush condemnation over engagement with substance.

civility.statement: E taku iwi: 35,000 people marched yesterday across that bridge, and they will arrive here, at Parliament. And one message to you, David, is "See you next Tuesday."
civility.explanation: "See you next Tuesday" is a well-known veiled obscenity directed personally at David Seymour; a deliberate insult.

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon, you are presiding over the most racist piece of legislation in a hundred years.
civility.explanation: Directly names and accuses the Prime Minister of the "most racist" legislation; personal and sensational.

civility.statement: It's not realistic to suggest that almost 200 years of debate over what is an incredibly complex and challenging issue would be resolved by the passing of a single piece of legislation. It is too blunt and simplistic and risks stoking grievance and driving division.
civility.explanation: Criticises the bill's approach, not people; measured tone.

civility.statement: today Hikurangi is on the move, supporting the thousands descending upon Parliament to condemn this divisive moumou moni, moumou tāima [waste of money, waste of time] bill.
civility.explanation: Attacks the bill as a waste of money/time; harsh but directed at the legislation, not individuals.

civility.statement: as chair of the Justice Committee and out of respect for our parliamentary process and the institutions of this House, it is my job to ensure submissions are heard respectfully and in line with the Standing Orders, and it is my commitment to do just that. So I just simply and respectfully ask that all members do the same as this bill is considered over the coming months.
civility.explanation: Commits to a respectful, procedurally fair process and calls on all members to do likewise.

civility.statement: these circumstances, I would offer, are entirely of the Government's making. They have chosen to cut parts of the defence budget, which has resulted in this quite astonishing zero percent offer to staff. This is the cause of this strike.
civility.explanation: Assigns blame to Government choices rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: I'm sure that member has as much respect as I do for the civilians in the defence force who are on strike at the moment, and additionally for the members of the defence force who have been, as a result of this motion, asked to perform the work of the civilian defence force.
civility.explanation: Responds to a heckle by attributing good faith to the interjector and respect to both groups of workers.

civility.statement: I also just finally add the obvious point that the notice can be cancelled at any time, so we're very hopeful that the matter will be able to be resolved not only before 14 February but also before 30 or 31 January, and, indeed, as soon as possible.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with the opposition's concern and good wishes to all parties.

civility.statement: It is the choices this Government has made when it promised tax cuts to landlords, tax cuts to tobacco companies, and set commitments about their Budget prior to the election that did not add up.
civility.explanation: Pointed attack on Government fiscal choices; directed at policy but with loaded characterisations.

civility.statement: this Government has demonised public servants. They have just used that demonisation to justify large-scale cuts of the Public Service. Defence is only one of many agencies having 6 percent cuts across the board.
civility.explanation: "Demonised" is a charged characterisation of opponents' conduct, though aimed at Government behaviour rather than a named individual.

civility.statement: Well, I just welcome the member who has so much to say about this to come over here and run a response to a national emergency, and then can lecture me about what to do in that situation. When you've saved 20,000 lives in a health emergency, come and tell me how to run a Government.
civility.explanation: Combative, personalised put-down of an interjector rather than engagement with his point.

civility.statement: thanks to the Associate Minister of Defence for that contribution. I really enjoy and value his plain-spoken presentations in the House.
civility.explanation: Warm, genuine acknowledgement of an opponent across the aisle.

civility.statement: I find the Associate Minister to be a reasonable man and indeed it was a reasonable response, but it did make me wonder: what is the purpose of this extension?
civility.explanation: Credits the opposing minister as reasonable while pressing a substantive question.

rigor.statement: This is a crude way to handle a very delicate subject. With a wave of the wand, as it were, we would unwind more than 30 years of jurisprudence—winner takes all.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point about referendum overturning decades of case law, but leans on the vivid "wave of the wand" image rather than detailed argument.

rigor.statement: Think of the UK House of Lords or the fact that voters in the US Senate elections in Wyoming have a much greater say than voters in California.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete comparative examples to support the claim that democracies contain historical inequalities; sound analogy though only illustrative.

rigor.statement: Our leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, has referred often to the great Māori leaders who forged the path for a better New Zealand: Sir Apirana Ngata, Sir Peter Buck, Sir Māui Pōmare, Sir James Carroll. They all shared the position that there were no principles to the Treaty
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority; attributes a modern legal-drafting stance ("no principles") to historical figures who predate the principles jurisprudence, a strained inference.

rigor.statement: Te Tiriti o Waitangi is superior to any person and any law ever created in this House. It is the constitutional document by which this House and democracy is established here in Aotearoa.
rigor.explanation: Strong constitutional assertion stated as fact without supporting argument; contestable as a matter of NZ constitutional law where parliamentary sovereignty prevails.

rigor.statement: ACT are seen to be pulling the strings and running the country, like the KKK with a swipe card to the Beehive, and Luxon doesn't even care. There's a ghost in his chair.
rigor.explanation: Inflammatory analogy and ad hominem with no evidence.

rigor.statement: It is simply not realistic to suggest 184 years of debate can be settled with the broad stroke of a pen.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable argument that a single law cannot resolve a long-contested issue, though it rests on assertion rather than detailed evidence.

rigor.statement: When we look back and we think of the Maori Prisoners Act 1880, suspending trial rights for Māori at Parihaka; the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, confiscating land after the Tainui wars; the Tohunga Suppression Act 1907, banning traditional practices; and the Native Schools Act 1867, banning the use of te reo
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific historical statutes to support the argument that Parliament has passed harmful anti-Māori laws; evidence-based even if selectively deployed.

rigor.statement: Christopher Luxon, you are presiding over the most racist piece of legislation in a hundred years.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping superlative ("most racist in a hundred years") asserted without comparative evidence; rhetorical hyperbole.

rigor.statement: This bill is a bill that's so obnoxious that 40 King's Counsel have spoken out against it.
rigor.explanation: Leans partly on appeal to authority (number of KCs), though the letter's substance is also quoted.

rigor.statement: even if Parliament can legislate like this, it should not, because it's not for the Government of the day to retrospectively and unilaterally reinterpret constitutional treaties—that would offend the basic principles which underpin New Zealand's representative democracy.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes legal capacity from legitimacy and gives a constitutional-principle reason; a structured argument, though drawing on the KCs' authority.

rigor.statement: It's not realistic to suggest that almost 200 years of debate over what is an incredibly complex and challenging issue would be resolved by the passing of a single piece of legislation. It is too blunt and simplistic and risks stoking grievance and driving division.
rigor.explanation: Argues the bill is too blunt for a complex issue; a coherent point, though largely asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: compromises like this are at the heart of the MMP system that New Zealanders voted to introduce before the 1996 election and reaffirmed their support of at the 2011 referendum.
rigor.explanation: Uses the electoral history to justify why coalition compromises occur; a sound contextual argument.

rigor.statement: these circumstances, I would offer, are entirely of the Government's making. They have chosen to cut parts of the defence budget, which has resulted in this quite astonishing zero percent offer to staff. This is the cause of this strike.
rigor.explanation: Draws a causal chain from budget cuts to the zero percent offer to the strike; plausible but presented as "entirely" causal without accounting for other factors.

rigor.statement: I would like to move, That the words "14 February 2025" be replaced with the words "31 January 2025"... I cannot see any logical reason why these authorisations need to go on for two weeks longer than the strike notices.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the mismatch between authorisation end date and strike end date; a logical, evidence-anchored point.

rigor.statement: The defence budget—total Vote Defence—was $4.949 billion for this financial year, which was a $308 million reduction on the budget for the preceding year.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in specific budget numbers to explain the zero percent offer.

rigor.statement: It is the choices this Government has made when it promised tax cuts to landlords, tax cuts to tobacco companies, and set commitments about their Budget prior to the election that did not add up.
rigor.explanation: Links budget choices to policy priorities, but "tax cuts to tobacco companies" and "did not add up" are contested framings offered without figures here.

rigor.statement: this Government has demonised public servants. They have just used that demonisation to justify large-scale cuts of the Public Service. Defence is only one of many agencies having 6 percent cuts across the board.
rigor.explanation: Asserts motive (demonisation to justify cuts) alongside a concrete figure (6 percent); the motive claim is unevidenced.

rigor.statement: Well, I just welcome the member who has so much to say about this to come over here and run a response to a national emergency, and then can lecture me about what to do in that situation. When you've saved 20,000 lives in a health emergency, come and tell me how to run a Government.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to her own authority/credentials to dismiss the interjection rather than address it.

rigor.statement: How is it good faith for this Parliament to send a message to those workers that they shouldn't expect a resolution until at least 14 February? Now, that's not good faith.
rigor.explanation: Argues the long authorisation undercuts good-faith bargaining; a coherent inference, though the "message" it sends is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Why couldn't we apply the same rationale and approve an extension of 14 days, exactly the same amount that the Minister has available to her under the Defence Act, and then come back to Parliament and justify it?
rigor.explanation: Argues from the statutory 14-day limit that any longer extension should be justified incrementally; logically structured.

divination.statement: That would risk stoking an already keen sense of grievance. It would risk increasing divisions in our country rather than reducing them.
divination.explanation: Prediction that passing the bill/referendum would increase division; directionally plausible but hedged ("risk") and unfalsifiable in magnitude.

divination.statement: 35,000 people marched yesterday across that bridge, and they will arrive here, at Parliament.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the marchers will reach Parliament; short-timeframe and highly likely.

divination.statement: National's long-held position is that a referendum on the Treaty would be divisive and would not deliver an outcome that takes our country forward.
divination.explanation: Prediction that a referendum would be divisive; plausible but unfalsifiable as stated.

divination.statement: Will a later Parliament look back at the conduct of Christopher Luxon presiding over this bill and put it alongside those Parliaments which drove a wedge in our society and caused generations of harm? I think so.
divination.explanation: Prediction of future historical judgement; inherently speculative and value-laden, hard to falsify.

strength.statement: That's why we have reasserted the principle that healthcare should be delivered on the basis of need alone. That's why we're pushing back against the previous Government's move against equal voting rights in local government. That's why we're unwinding co-governance arrangements in core public services and a separate Māori Health Authority.
strength.explanation: Claims a series of concrete actions the Government is taking; several (Māori Health Authority disestablishment) are being delivered, though some are in progress.

strength.statement: New Zealand First will, as we've committed to, support this bill to the first reading; it is our commitment to this Government and to this democracy.
strength.explanation: Follows through on a coalition commitment, though supporting to first reading only is a limited action.

strength.statement: First, we need to do what we need to do to get rid of this Government. This must be a one-term Government. How do we do that? E te iwi Māori, we must all register on the Māori roll.
strength.explanation: A call to action / stated intent rather than delivered outcome.

strength.statement: We have reversed a number of Labour's divisive co-governance policies, like three waters and the Māori Health Authority.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered action; the Māori Health Authority was disestablished and Three Waters repealed, so the delivery claim is largely borne out.

strength.statement: Successive National Governments have worked well with Māori on Treaty issues. We have a proud track record of progressive Treaty settlements to address historic wrongdoings.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered record of Treaty settlements; National governments did progress numerous settlements, so the follow-through claim is broadly supported.

strength.statement: I would like to move, That the words "14 February 2025" be replaced with the words "31 January 2025"... I cannot see any logical reason why these authorisations need to go on for two weeks longer than the strike notices.
strength.explanation: Moves a concrete amendment, though as an opposition MP she cannot guarantee it is adopted.

charisma.statement: The Government will never lose sight of the reality that the things that most Māori want are the same as what most other New Zealanders want: a strong economy that can deliver jobs and incomes and sustain a good standing of living, decent housing, to feel safe in their community, and for their kids to access great education that sets them up to succeed.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground by framing Māori and non-Māori aspirations as shared; inclusive tone amid a divisive debate.

charisma.statement: We are not a people who should fear debate, ideas, or difference of opinion.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to shared democratic values inviting all sides into debate.

charisma.statement: I may not agree with what you say, but I will defend your right to say it.
charisma.explanation: Draws on a shared free-speech ideal to appeal beyond her own side, though in service of a contested bill.

charisma.statement: ACT are seen to be pulling the strings and running the country, like the KKK with a swipe card to the Beehive, and Luxon doesn't even care. There's a ghost in his chair.
charisma.explanation: Purely divisive us-vs-them rhetoric that alienates rather than persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: Everybody, every single one of the members sitting on that side of the House have enabled this bill to be introduced to the House. You are complicit in the harm and the division that this presents and are complicit in the euthanising of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
charisma.explanation: Sharpens division by casting opponents as complicit wrongdoers.

charisma.statement: As I reflect on the 16 years that I've been a member of Parliament, as a country we have faced some significant challenges, and I know that we are better when we face them together, when we are united.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to unity and shared national effort; inclusive framing.

charisma.statement: Too often, those with the highest needs are Māori, and, in many cases, Māori have the answers. I'm proud of the work that we do to support a by Māori, for Māori approach.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory acknowledgement that Māori have solutions, reaching across the debate.

charisma.statement: today Hikurangi is on the move, supporting the thousands descending upon Parliament to condemn this divisive moumou moni, moumou tāima [waste of money, waste of time] bill.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective and rallying, but appeals to those already opposed rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: The people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti brought me to this House with hope—hope that we might actually address the real issues that whānau are facing, issues like housing, employment, education, and economic development.
charisma.explanation: Frames priorities around shared everyday concerns, but within a one-side appeal.

charisma.statement: we don't need to change the Treaty—we do not need to change the Treaty—we need to change this Government.
charisma.explanation: Punchy rally line for opponents of the bill; combative rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: as chair of the Justice Committee and out of respect for our parliamentary process and the institutions of this House, it is my job to ensure submissions are heard respectfully and in line with the Standing Orders, and it is my commitment to do just that. So I just simply and respectfully ask that all members do the same as this bill is considered over the coming months.
charisma.explanation: Appeals across the House to shared respect for process, inviting cooperation.

charisma.statement: I also just finally add the obvious point that the notice can be cancelled at any time, so we're very hopeful that the matter will be able to be resolved not only before 14 February but also before 30 or 31 January, and, indeed, as soon as possible.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory, expresses hope for early resolution and good faith on all sides.

charisma.statement: thanks to the Associate Minister of Defence for that contribution. I really enjoy and value his plain-spoken presentations in the House.
charisma.explanation: Builds goodwill by praising an opposing minister before disagreeing.

veracity.statement: Think of the UK House of Lords or the fact that voters in the US Senate elections in Wyoming have a much greater say than voters in California.
veracity.explanation: Factually accurate: the Lords is unelected and small-state US Senate representation is disproportionate.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First brought legislation in 2005, the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Deletion Bill, which was voted down.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical fact: NZ First's 2005 deletion bill existed and was defeated.

veracity.statement: Our leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, has referred often to the great Māori leaders who forged the path for a better New Zealand: Sir Apirana Ngata, Sir Peter Buck, Sir Māui Pōmare, Sir James Carroll. They all shared the position that there were no principles to the Treaty
veracity.explanation: Contestable: the "principles of the Treaty" as a legal concept postdates these leaders, so claiming they held a position on it is anachronistic and misleading.

veracity.statement: 35,000 people marched yesterday across that bridge, and they will arrive here, at Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Crowd-size figure for the hīkoi; plausible and in line with reported estimates but such counts are uncertain.

veracity.statement: We have reversed a number of Labour's divisive co-governance policies, like three waters and the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that these policies were reversed; "divisive" is an editorial characterisation.

veracity.statement: When we look back and we think of the Maori Prisoners Act 1880, suspending trial rights for Māori at Parihaka; the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, confiscating land after the Tainui wars; the Tohunga Suppression Act 1907, banning traditional practices; and the Native Schools Act 1867, banning the use of te reo
veracity.explanation: The Acts and their broad effects are real; some characterisations are simplified (e.g. Native Schools Act's role in te reo suppression).

veracity.statement: This bill is a bill that's so obnoxious that 40 King's Counsel have spoken out against it.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a real open letter from senior KCs, but the number is stated as 40 here and 42 later in the same speech, an internal inconsistency.

veracity.statement: compromises like this are at the heart of the MMP system that New Zealanders voted to introduce before the 1996 election and reaffirmed their support of at the 2011 referendum.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: MMP was adopted via the 1993 referendum (first used 1996) and retained in the 2011 referendum.

veracity.statement: a thousand defence force personnel have given notice to go on strike, and the dates that they have proposed to go on strike are from 6 November until 31 January.
veracity.explanation: Concrete factual claim about the strike notice; consistent with the rest of the debate.

veracity.statement: This is a very, very rare power... used on a few occasions in our recent history; once in 1996 and in 2001, as has been recently covered in the media, and again, I understand, in 2018 by Ron Mark.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific prior uses of the power, attributed to Parliamentary Library research; hedged ("I understand") appropriately.

veracity.statement: The defence budget—total Vote Defence—was $4.949 billion for this financial year, which was a $308 million reduction on the budget for the preceding year.
veracity.explanation: Specific budget figures presented as fact; broadly consistent with Budget documents she says she consulted, though such year-on-year comparisons can hinge on definitions.

veracity.statement: It is the choices this Government has made when it promised tax cuts to landlords, tax cuts to tobacco companies, and set commitments about their Budget prior to the election that did not add up.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: interest-deductibility changes and tobacco excise decisions are real, but "tax cuts to landlords/tobacco companies" is a contested characterisation and "did not add up" is disputed.

forthrightness.statement: the Government regards it as prudent to provide a notice that will be long enough, at least until such time as the industrial action takes place, and a bit longer... as a matter of practicality to allow a couple of weeks for rosters to be put on so that people know, from one day to the next, when they are going to be required to turn up and do their shifts.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the opposition's question of why the authorisation runs to 14 February, giving practical roster/lead-time reasons.

civility.statement: amendments were put forward by members up to the new amendment from the Government—they were put forward in good faith and it was actually quite a good exchange; the Minister was answering questions even though there was no requirement, and it was good and it was reasonable.
civility.explanation: Gracious, acknowledges the Minister's cooperation and characterises the exchange positively; respectful and constructive.

civility.statement: with legal advice having been provided, it's within the Government's power to waive that privilege. We do not intend to do so.
civility.explanation: Measured, policy-focused reply with no personal attack.

civility.statement: we don't undermine the good-faith bargaining efforts on both sides, and we expect and hope that the matter will be resolved as soon as possible.
civility.explanation: Respectful toward both parties, no attack, focused on outcome.

civility.statement: If it was interchangeable, if military could do anything, if they could be out the front gate of Parliament today, we would have a military State.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic but aimed at the policy principle rather than at a person.

civility.statement: they haven't got money to throw around and they've got a few other things, including a sunken vessel, to spend their money on at the moment.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic jab (the 'sunken vessel' dig at the HMNZS Manawanui loss) that scores a political point rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: This is a Government that likes using the private sector. The first resort should be to go out and use contractors, because this is, essentially, standing at the front gate to make sure people who come in have ID, and yet they're going to use military personnel to do this role.
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the substance of the staffing decision rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: Although I don't 100 percent agree with the member on other elements that the member has raised, in this particular case... I believe that the upgrading of the software package with SH-2G(I) system potentially does require a level of security clearance that a contractor may not have.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance and openly grants a point that cuts against his own side.

civility.statement: I don't think for a second that the Government intended to do this on Thursday last week. I reckon they entered into that in good faith.
civility.explanation: Generous, non-accusatory reading of the Government's conduct.

civility.statement: this is a man with a military background instead sitting there arrogantly and criticising those who are trying to get it right.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on Tim Costley ('arrogantly'), targeting the individual rather than any argument.

civility.statement: Oh, it wasn't the Minister? I do apologise. It was his very loud and irritating friend next to him. That's all that member has done throughout this entire debate.
civility.explanation: Direct personal insult ('very loud and irritating') aimed at a member rather than at a policy point.

civility.statement: How can they realistically expect the House to give them carte blanche until the 14th, with what has proven to be a realistic prospect that we're going to have to come back regardless?
civility.explanation: Challenges the Government's position pointedly but on process substance, not personally.

civility.statement: There is no suggestion on this side of the House that the Minister of Defence is not authorised to take the action that she has taken—that is, clearly, not in dispute—however, what is the requirement of how long those particular extensions would remain in place?
civility.explanation: Explicitly concedes the Minister's authority before narrowing the dispute to the substantive question of duration and oversight.

civility.statement: I would just place on record, I suppose, the disappointment that that's the view that the Government have formed in terms of not effectively landing on a date that is much earlier than 14 February.
civility.explanation: Registers disagreement as measured disappointment about a policy choice, without any personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, do your research. Of course it's meaningful.
civility.explanation: Dismissive interjection ('do your research') that belittles the speaker rather than engaging the point.

civility.statement: Surely, it can't get worse.
civility.explanation: Sniping interjection aimed at disparaging another member's contribution rather than addressing the substance.

charisma.statement: amendments were put forward by members up to the new amendment from the Government—they were put forward in good faith and it was actually quite a good exchange; the Minister was answering questions even though there was no requirement, and it was good and it was reasonable.
charisma.explanation: Generous toward the opposing Minister, crediting good faith and finding common ground on process.

charisma.statement: we don't undermine the good-faith bargaining efforts on both sides, and we expect and hope that the matter will be resolved as soon as possible.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges good faith on both sides of the industrial dispute and expresses hope for resolution — inclusive framing.

charisma.statement: Although I don't 100 percent agree with the member on other elements that the member has raised, in this particular case... I believe that the upgrading of the software package with SH-2G(I) system potentially does require a level of security clearance that a contractor may not have.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges disagreement with a colleague respectfully while conceding the Government's point on clearance — bridges rather than polarises.

charisma.statement: I don't think for a second that the Government intended to do this on Thursday last week. I reckon they entered into that in good faith.
charisma.explanation: Extends good faith to opponents, defusing conflict and attributing benign intent to the Government.

charisma.statement: There is no suggestion on this side of the House that the Minister of Defence is not authorised to take the action that she has taken—that is, clearly, not in dispute—however, what is the requirement of how long those particular extensions would remain in place?
charisma.explanation: Frames disagreement narrowly and reasonably, avoiding an us-vs-them posture.

veracity.statement: it was on 5 November that the New Zealand Defence Force first received a notice from the Public Service Association ( PSA) of strike action that would take place the following day until 31 January.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable factual claim about the timeline of the PSA strike notice; presented plainly and consistent with the surrounding debate.

veracity.statement: there is already a combination of civilian and uniformed personnel undertaking those tasks, not only historically but even into the present day.
veracity.explanation: Plausible factual claim about mixed staffing used to rebut the 'civilian roles' objection; consistent with defence practice but unverified in detail.

veracity.statement: It is that army personnel, military personnel, are never to use their powers of force in a civilian sphere except in cases of utmost emergency. We saw that in the Christchurch earthquakes, where the military personnel were used to secure damaged buildings, and some of us are very well aware of that.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the constitutional principle and the earthquake precedent for emergency military deployment.

veracity.statement: they haven't got money to throw around and they've got a few other things, including a sunken vessel, to spend their money on at the moment.
veracity.explanation: The sunken-vessel reference is factually grounded, but 'no money to throw around' is loose characterisation of the defence budget.

veracity.statement: Section 9 makes it very, very clear that this should be something which only happens in rare circumstances.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of section 9's high reporting bar and its intent to confine such deployments to rare cases.

specificity.statement: it was on 5 November that the New Zealand Defence Force first received a notice from the Public Service Association ( PSA) of strike action that would take place the following day until 31 January.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise date, the named body (PSA), and an end date (31 January).

specificity.statement: We think that the calibration of the dates that we've provided so far is the right one, which is to say it's the full length of the strike notice plus two weeks in order for transitional arrangements to be made as to personnel turning up for duty and so forth.
specificity.explanation: Explains the date as a defined formula — strike notice length plus two weeks — though without exact figures beyond that.

specificity.statement: It is that army personnel, military personnel, are never to use their powers of force in a civilian sphere except in cases of utmost emergency. We saw that in the Christchurch earthquakes, where the military personnel were used to secure damaged buildings, and some of us are very well aware of that.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named provision and a specific historical example, though paraphrasing the section rather than quoting it.

specificity.statement: I would be minded to amend my amendment, following the amendment by the Government, to change what I originally had, That 31 January 2025—which aligned with the end of the strike notice—be amended to 3 December 2025.
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete date change tied to the strike-notice end plus a defined accountability window, though she misspoke the year (2025 for 2024).

specificity.statement: When it's around providing security guard services for Defence House and for Pipitea House, that is not something that I believe meets the threshold of why section 9(2) of the Defence Act 1990 should be triggered. For all intents and purposes, to provide security guard services for these two particular areas can very much be conducted by a contractor.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact section (9(2)), the Act, the specific buildings, and the precise task at issue.

specificity.statement: Now, my original amendment was that "14 February 2025" be replaced by "17 December 2024"... I'll just amend it and bring it forward a week—to the 10th. Why do I propose the 10th? Well, for practical reasons. If we said, "Why don't we just leave it for the 14 days that are available to the Minister?", that would fall within scrutiny week.
specificity.explanation: Names precise dates and ties the choice of 10 December to concrete calendar/procedural constraints (scrutiny week, sitting days).

forthrightness.statement: with legal advice having been provided, it's within the Government's power to waive that privilege. We do not intend to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Webb's question about legal advice — confirms advice exists and states plainly the Government will not waive privilege, though he declines to share the substance.

forthrightness.statement: We think that the calibration of the dates that we've provided so far is the right one, which is to say it's the full length of the strike notice plus two weeks in order for transitional arrangements to be made as to personnel turning up for duty and so forth.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why the Government rejects earlier dates, giving a concrete rationale rather than deflecting.
