rigor.statement: We think that the calibration of the dates that we've provided so far is the right one, which is to say it's the full length of the strike notice plus two weeks in order for transitional arrangements to be made as to personnel turning up for duty and so forth.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification (strike length plus transition buffer) that logically supports the chosen end date.

rigor.statement: there is already a combination of civilian and uniformed personnel undertaking those tasks, not only historically but even into the present day.
rigor.explanation: Supports the argument that using uniformed personnel is not a bright-line breach by pointing to existing practice.

rigor.statement: It is that army personnel, military personnel, are never to use their powers of force in a civilian sphere except in cases of utmost emergency. We saw that in the Christchurch earthquakes, where the military personnel were used to secure damaged buildings, and some of us are very well aware of that.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the statute (section 9) and a concrete precedent (Christchurch earthquakes); premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: If it was interchangeable, if military could do anything, if they could be out the front gate of Parliament today, we would have a military State.
rigor.explanation: Slippery-slope / reductio to an extreme ('military State') that does not follow from a limited, statutorily-authorised deployment.

rigor.statement: This is a Government that likes using the private sector. The first resort should be to go out and use contractors, because this is, essentially, standing at the front gate to make sure people who come in have ID, and yet they're going to use military personnel to do this role.
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasoned case that a low-skill guarding task could be contracted, but leans partly on a 'you usually prefer contractors' tu quoque framing.

rigor.statement: Section 9 makes it very, very clear that this should be something which only happens in rare circumstances.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the objection in the statute's reporting requirements, which she lays out as evidence for the 'rare circumstances' reading.

rigor.statement: I would be minded to amend my amendment, following the amendment by the Government, to change what I originally had, That 31 January 2025—which aligned with the end of the strike notice—be amended to 3 December 2025.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned link between the two-week accountability period and section 9's regular reporting requirement.

rigor.statement: When it's around providing security guard services for Defence House and for Pipitea House, that is not something that I believe meets the threshold of why section 9(2) of the Defence Act 1990 should be triggered. For all intents and purposes, to provide security guard services for these two particular areas can very much be conducted by a contractor.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes this task from clearance-sensitive ones and argues from the specific statutory threshold; conclusion follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: Although I don't 100 percent agree with the member on other elements that the member has raised, in this particular case... I believe that the upgrading of the software package with SH-2G(I) system potentially does require a level of security clearance that a contractor may not have.
rigor.explanation: Draws a principled clearance-based distinction between which roles can and cannot be contracted out.

rigor.statement: Even if the House had voted in favour or in support of the motion on Thursday, we'd be here again, probably tomorrow, debating another extension, because there was another ministerial statement today.
rigor.explanation: Infers the recurring-debate problem from concrete evidence (the new amendment and the day's further statement).

rigor.statement: Now, my original amendment was that "14 February 2025" be replaced by "17 December 2024"... I'll just amend it and bring it forward a week—to the 10th. Why do I propose the 10th? Well, for practical reasons. If we said, "Why don't we just leave it for the 14 days that are available to the Minister?", that would fall within scrutiny week.
rigor.explanation: Steps through practical reasons — sitting weeks, the risk of a gap in authorisation — to justify the specific date; conclusion follows the premises.

rigor.statement: How can they realistically expect the House to give them carte blanche until the 14th, with what has proven to be a realistic prospect that we're going to have to come back regardless?
rigor.explanation: Argues from demonstrated fact (the Government itself had to amend) that a long blanket extension is unwarranted; a rhetorical question but evidence-backed.

authenticity.statement: I know that we've spoken, on this side, of the belief that the Labour Party has always had in the right for people to take industrial action.
authenticity.explanation: Aligns her stance with Labour's long-standing and consistent support for the right to strike — words matching the party's known record.

divination.statement: Even if the House had voted in favour or in support of the motion on Thursday, we'd be here again, probably tomorrow, debating another extension, because there was another ministerial statement today.
divination.explanation: Near-term prediction that further extension debates were inevitable; plausible given the fresh ministerial statement, but hedged and contingent.

civility.statement: I'm concerned, based on what happened—the coordinated level of disruptiveness and the prevention of votes being cast—at whether or not the Standing Orders that we currently have are still of the level of robustness that will provide protection to the essence of our democracy.
civility.explanation: Criticises conduct and process (disruptiveness, prevention of votes) rather than launching a personal attack, though 'essence of our democracy' leans to hyperbole.

civility.statement: I move, That this House note that today in 2010, 29 miners lost their lives while at work in the Pike River Mine, express its condolences to family and friends who will forever be profoundly impacted, and thank rescue and support teams for their service on that day and the days that followed.
civility.explanation: Respectful, unifying commemoration with no partisan content.

civility.statement: it's as recently as the period of the last Government in which New Zealand Defence Force personnel, both uniform and civilian, were offered zero percent pay increases for a much longer period of time than is contemplated in this motion. I think those members would be surprised to understand that members of political parties that now form the Opposition have discovered an intense interest in their pay and conditions in this way.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab implying the Opposition's interest is opportunistic rather than engaging the substance of the question.

civility.statement: the effect of inflation and those cost of living pressures on our defence force is much less than it would have been had the previous Government continued its spendthrift ways to continue to drive up inflation and the cost of living. We are pleased as a Government as a whole to be doing something about that situation.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government's fiscal record; harsh but aimed at policy, with 'spendthrift' edging toward rhetoric.

civility.statement: I consider that I have responded. If the member doesn't like the responses, that is his problem, not mine, and it's not the problem of the Government.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'his problem, not mine' framing rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I'm not a research assistant for either of the members of Parliament opposite who have asked me a question that is not directly relevant to the motion today. If they wish to know the history and the background of industrial relations, they are welcome to research that themselves.
civility.explanation: The 'not a research assistant' retort is a dismissive put-down rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I must express surprise to the Government that, having asked that question last week, the Minister's not in a position to answer it today.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Minister's preparedness but focused on the failure to answer, not on his character.

civility.statement: we acknowledge that this fiscal environment did not just happen organically. It was due to political decisions by successive Governments, including this one that led to the strike action. Can I ask: what level of advocacy has the Minister done to alleviate the so-called strained fiscal environment?
civility.explanation: Presses the Minister on responsibility while keeping to policy and process.

civility.statement: In answer to part of the question, no, we're not at risk of civil war in New Zealand. That's inflammatory language.
civility.explanation: Rejects the framing as inflammatory rather than attacking the questioner personally.

civility.statement: Is it not the case that in classical Māori behaviour in former times and around the rohe of late is to, when they want to speak to someone, ask them to come and speak, but in this case they did not ask political party leaders to speak; more importantly, Te Pāti Māori told them not to come?
civility.explanation: A framed question that turns the point into a criticism of Te Pāti Māori rather than a neutral inquiry.

civility.statement: Could I ask the Minister as to why he would have regard to someone who has his shingles up acting for Treaty of Waitangi claimants and claiming to be independent on this matter?
civility.explanation: Impugns Finlayson's independence and motives ('shingles up') rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: it would be a contrast between people who want to have a respectful and rational debate about our constitutional future and the way the principles of the Treaty have evolved in recent years, versus people who resort to name calling, abuse, and theatrics but not actually engaging with the argument
civility.explanation: Casts opponents as resorting to name-calling and theatrics, characterising the other side rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, it's possible to walk and chew gum at the same time, and while the National Party has a different view to one of the governing parties in the coalition on the Treaty principles bill—that's been well canvassed—what I can say... is that Minister Seymour is intensely focused on productivity and is leading the charge on foreign investment reform
civility.explanation: Defends a colleague on policy grounds without attacking the questioner.

civility.statement: the only person who, I think, has got very excited about it and distracted is members of the Labour Party, including herself.
civility.explanation: A tu-quoque jab at the questioner rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: I would also like to note for the House that the document we launched last week contains a foreword from the Prime Minister and myself and the under-secretary, and I would like to publicly thank Barbara Edmonds from the Labour Party on behalf of the Opposition for putting forward a foreword to the document.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful recognition of an opponent.

civility.statement: I always take the comments of former colleagues with great interest but also with a grain of salt, because things have sometimes moved on from where they were when they were in the House. But that former Minister has a lot to say on many issues, and it's always very entertaining to hear what he has to say.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive of Finlayson but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: we have a long tradition of robust debate within the National Party. We're not sort of all having to believe the same thing at the same moment at the same time... the most important thing is that we conduct ourselves with good grace, listen to the other side, and have a good, honest conversation, and that's what we're about.
civility.explanation: Emphasises respectful, honest conversation over conflict.

civility.statement: it's a snide and unhelpful comment, and this is a Government that is absolutely determined to ensure that we work collaboratively with Māori on all sides of the House, recognising that when he talks about Māori as if they all think alike and have the same view on any given topic, it's completely nuts. There is a wide variety of views
civility.explanation: Labels the question 'snide' and 'completely nuts'; partly engages substance but with dismissive edge.

civility.statement: Does he agree with former Prime Minister John Key that "philosophically it's bad policy. I'll tell you why I think it's bad - if you write down the principles, if you think they're going to stay like that, you're a dreamer."; if so, why did he decide that it was worth making coalition negotiations a little easier to advance such a destructive and defective policy?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded ('destructive and defective policy') but directed at the policy and the decision, not personal character.

civility.statement: Can she explain how Te Tiriti o Waitangi has been embedded and authentically reflected in the refreshed curriculum following the outright removal and erasure of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the curriculum framework Te Mātaiaho and dismissal of Māori advisers on the curriculum refresh working group?
civility.explanation: Charged terms ('erasure', 'dismissal') frame the question as an accusation, though aimed at policy decisions.

civility.statement: Speakers' rulings make it quite clear that Ministers are not to introduce new material into the answers. The question was quite clear... the question was about charter schools. It wasn't about fast track, it wasn't about deep-sea mining or anything else that the Prime Minister introduced. He shouldn't have been allowed to carry on with that.
civility.explanation: A procedural objection focused on the rules, not on the Prime Minister personally.

rigor.statement: I'm concerned, based on what happened—the coordinated level of disruptiveness and the prevention of votes being cast—at whether or not the Standing Orders that we currently have are still of the level of robustness that will provide protection to the essence of our democracy.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned concern linking observed disruption to a question about rule robustness, but the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: it is very important, in my view, that the House and New Zealanders see you take this position and this issue incredibly seriously and provide back to us a level of guidance, whether or not the deterrence, the range of censure options, are such that we now need to reform, sharpen, and bring the Standing Orders into a world where it is apparent that a host of members no longer fear the consequences.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a premise (members no longer fear consequences) to a need for reform, but the premise is asserted.

rigor.statement: I think some of the changes, particularly around the use of social media, have changed the incentives for people's behaviour around the rules of Parliament and that perhaps an early Standing Orders Committee could be convened to address those changes.
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible causal mechanism (social media altering behavioural incentives) linked to a concrete institutional response.

rigor.statement: the effect of inflation and those cost of living pressures on our defence force is much less than it would have been had the previous Government continued its spendthrift ways to continue to drive up inflation and the cost of living. We are pleased as a Government as a whole to be doing something about that situation.
rigor.explanation: Attributes inflation to the opponent's 'spendthrift ways' as a partisan causal assertion rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: we acknowledge that this fiscal environment did not just happen organically. It was due to political decisions by successive Governments, including this one that led to the strike action. Can I ask: what level of advocacy has the Minister done to alleviate the so-called strained fiscal environment?
rigor.explanation: Reasonably argues the fiscal environment is a product of political choices rather than inevitable, but the claim is asserted without specifics.

rigor.statement: it would be a contrast between people who want to have a respectful and rational debate about our constitutional future and the way the principles of the Treaty have evolved in recent years, versus people who resort to name calling, abuse, and theatrics but not actually engaging with the argument
rigor.explanation: Frames the debate as a false dichotomy between his 'rational' side and an 'abusive' side.

rigor.statement: it's a snide and unhelpful comment, and this is a Government that is absolutely determined to ensure that we work collaboratively with Māori on all sides of the House, recognising that when he talks about Māori as if they all think alike and have the same view on any given topic, it's completely nuts. There is a wide variety of views
rigor.explanation: Makes the reasonable point that Māori are not monolithic, but does so via characterising the questioner's premise rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The science of learning is a well-known, well-documented, and well-evidenced way to improve the outcomes of our students. If that member wants to see some evidence of that, she should go and look at the structured literacy Better Start Literacy Approach results for tamariki Māori, because they are outstanding.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to a specific evidence base (Better Start Literacy Approach results) rather than mere assertion, though 'outstanding' is unquantified.

rigor.statement: Gang membership recorded on the National Gang List grew 1 percent to October this year. Last year for the same period, it grew by 10 percent. Under this coalition Government, gang membership growth has slowed tenfold.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the slowdown to the Government from a year-on-year comparison without controlling for other factors.

rigor.statement: How can he stand in this House and speak about the strengthened Māori-Crown relationship when Māori die seven years earlier than non-Māori, Māori are overrepresented in the justice system, and are overrepresented in emergency housing?
rigor.explanation: Marshals concrete disparities to challenge the 'strengthened relationship' claim, a reasonable evidentiary contrast.

rigor.statement: Does he agree with former Prime Minister John Key that "philosophically it's bad policy. I'll tell you why I think it's bad - if you write down the principles, if you think they're going to stay like that, you're a dreamer."; if so, why did he decide that it was worth making coalition negotiations a little easier to advance such a destructive and defective policy?
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority (quoting John Key) rather than developing the argument, and loads the question with 'destructive and defective'.

rigor.statement: Speakers' rulings make it quite clear that Ministers are not to introduce new material into the answers. The question was quite clear... the question was about charter schools. It wasn't about fast track, it wasn't about deep-sea mining or anything else that the Prime Minister introduced. He shouldn't have been allowed to carry on with that.
rigor.explanation: Cites the specific procedural rule (Speakers' rulings on new material) and applies it precisely to what was asked versus answered.

specificity.statement: I'm concerned, based on what happened—the coordinated level of disruptiveness and the prevention of votes being cast—at whether or not the Standing Orders that we currently have are still of the level of robustness that will provide protection to the essence of our democracy.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concern (Standing Orders robustness, blocked votes) but proposes no concrete mechanism at this point.

specificity.statement: it is very important, in my view, that the House and New Zealanders see you take this position and this issue incredibly seriously and provide back to us a level of guidance, whether or not the deterrence, the range of censure options, are such that we now need to reform, sharpen, and bring the Standing Orders into a world where it is apparent that a host of members no longer fear the consequences.
specificity.explanation: Names the levers (deterrence, censure options, Standing Orders reform) but gives no specific proposed change.

specificity.statement: I think some of the changes, particularly around the use of social media, have changed the incentives for people's behaviour around the rules of Parliament and that perhaps an early Standing Orders Committee could be convened to address those changes.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific cause (social media) and a specific vehicle (an early Standing Orders Committee).

specificity.statement: the situation arose where minimum pay was set for members of the army who were doing certain work for the Government. It included a military factor—or "mil factor"... For reservists who did not receive that mil factor, their hourly pay rate fell below that of the minimum wage. Now, technically—technically—that's not a breach of the law... but we did something about it—that was our advocacy among other things.
specificity.explanation: Explains the precise mechanism (mil-factor component, reservists, effect on hourly rate) with concrete detail.

specificity.statement: My understanding is that the strike notice, or the industrial action, generally has a specified date at the end of January to which it can take place. A further two weeks from that seems prudent for the purpose then of resetting normal arrangements, whereby rosters can be made, people can be given notice for duties... The date of mid-February seems to us prudent.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete timing (end of January plus two weeks) and the operational rationale (rostering, notice).

specificity.statement: Our position is very clear. We had a delegation from the National Party representing our position, receiving the hīkoi, and making clear our point of view, which is that we're not supporting the bill beyond first reading, therefore it won't become law.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete position: not supporting the bill beyond first reading so it will not become law.

specificity.statement: When we see 12 percent of Māori getting to high school at the standard they need to be for on mathematics because of the previous Government, that's not great.
specificity.explanation: Offers a figure and named policy areas (maths standard, emergency motels, Waikato-Tainui social housing) but loosely.

specificity.statement: Partnership, protection, and other things that have discussed over many years—over 184 years.
specificity.explanation: Names partnership and protection but leaves the rest as 'other things' without detail.

specificity.statement: This is the first time in our history that all New Zealanders have been offered an equal chance to have a say on what our constitutional future means under the Treaty of Waitangi, and I'd encourage people to get along to the Justice Committee website and have their voice heard.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete process (first reading, referral to Justice Committee, public submissions) though the historic claim is loose.

specificity.statement: from now until 11.59 p.m. on 7 January, the Justice Committee will be accepting submissions, and I think it's very important that people have a view on this bill and the issues surrounding it; actually have their say, and make sure that they do it in a respectful and constructive way
specificity.explanation: Names the exact cut-off (11.59 p.m. on 7 January) and the body receiving submissions.

specificity.statement: We've made six targeted changes to the framework, involving smarter allocation of risk; recognising, and in some cases reimbursing bid costs; stronger collaboration between the Crown and bidders in the tendering phase; and ensuring the upcoming National Infrastructure Agency provides robust and centralised PPP expertise and improvements to the dispute resolution process.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete changes (risk allocation, bid-cost reimbursement, tender collaboration, dispute resolution) though without figures.

specificity.statement: PPPs in New Zealand are not new; there have been eight since 2011, including three bundles of primary and secondary schools that were carried on through the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Gives a number, a start year, and named examples (school bundles).

specificity.statement: On Thursday, I announced alongside the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, that the Government and Auckland Council have delivered contactless payments on Auckland's public transport network, to enable commuters to tag on and off public buses, trains, and ferries travelling across the region.
specificity.explanation: Names the partners, modes (bus, train, ferry) and the region, though light on cost detail.

specificity.statement: The roll-out of contactless payments will expand to Timaru and Christchurch in early 2025 and it will reach other regions by the end of 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names specific locations and timeframes for the roll-out.

specificity.statement: Rolling out contactless debit and credit card payments for public transport users will be a game-changer.
specificity.explanation: 'Game-changer' is a vague booster with no measure of the benefit.

specificity.statement: we are putting student achievement at the heart of every single thing that we do. If we want to honour the Treaty, it means closing the equity gap so that decades of disparity that have pervaded our system and the disproportionate representation of tamariki Māori and rangatahi Māori in the lower quartiles of our education and achievement system is closed.
specificity.explanation: Names the goal (closing the equity gap, lower-quartile representation) but no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: I answered this last week, and I'll repeat myself: Te Mātaiaho has not been developed yet. There are only two learning areas—English and maths—that have been put out... it's only a shell. We are working on that framework and it will be consulted on in the same way that all of the learning areas are being consulted on. But I'll reiterate: it hasn't been written yet, so the member needs to understand that.
specificity.explanation: Specifies that only English and maths are released and the framework is a 'shell' awaiting consultation.

specificity.statement: The science of learning is a well-known, well-documented, and well-evidenced way to improve the outcomes of our students. If that member wants to see some evidence of that, she should go and look at the structured literacy Better Start Literacy Approach results for tamariki Māori, because they are outstanding.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme and cohort as supporting evidence.

specificity.statement: yes, especially my recently announced maths pilot to lift student achievement and close the equity gap. From term 1 and 2 next year, around 2,000 year 7 and 8 students who need the most help will take part in an intensive programme to support them to progress towards the required curriculum levels in mathematics.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete numbers (2,000 students), year levels, terms, and the programme's aim.

specificity.statement: I highlighted a 3 percent reduction in victimisations, an increase of over 30 percent in foot patrols, ram raids dropping by 60 percent, and aggravated robberies down by 11 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures across four distinct metrics.

specificity.statement: Gang membership recorded on the National Gang List grew 1 percent to October this year. Last year for the same period, it grew by 10 percent. Under this coalition Government, gang membership growth has slowed tenfold.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise comparative growth figures and the source list.

specificity.statement: In May, the European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) entered into force many months sooner than predicted, providing $46 million of tariffs saved for Kiwi exporters this year... In September, we concluded the New Zealand - United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, our first FTA in the Middle East... Last month, we concluded a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)—unfinished business for successive Governments over 18 years
specificity.explanation: Names specific agreements, months, a dollar figure, and historical context.

specificity.statement: in September—after just four months of negotiation—we concluded a trade deal with the UAE delivering 98.5 percent tariff elimination on New Zealand exports on entry into force, rising to 99 percent after three years.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages, negotiation duration, and phase-in period.

specificity.statement: Twenty-four agreements and memorandums of understanding between New Zealand and Chinese companies were signed during the visit, worth an additional $340 million in export revenue to New Zealand over the next three years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count of agreements and a dollar value with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: How can he stand in this House and speak about the strengthened Māori-Crown relationship when Māori die seven years earlier than non-Māori, Māori are overrepresented in the justice system, and are overrepresented in emergency housing?
specificity.explanation: Cites specific disparities (life expectancy, justice, emergency housing).

charisma.statement: I think some of the changes, particularly around the use of social media, have changed the incentives for people's behaviour around the rules of Parliament and that perhaps an early Standing Orders Committee could be convened to address those changes.
charisma.explanation: Offers cross-bench support for a shared process, mildly consensus-oriented but within the governing bloc.

charisma.statement: This is the first time in our history that all New Zealanders have been offered an equal chance to have a say on what our constitutional future means under the Treaty of Waitangi, and I'd encourage people to get along to the Justice Committee website and have their voice heard.
charisma.explanation: Invites broad public participation, though framed to advance his own bill rather than build cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: PPPs in New Zealand are not new; there have been eight since 2011, including three bundles of primary and secondary schools that were carried on through the previous Government.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the previous Government's continuation of PPPs, a mildly cross-partisan note.

charisma.statement: I would also like to note for the House that the document we launched last week contains a foreword from the Prime Minister and myself and the under-secretary, and I would like to publicly thank Barbara Edmonds from the Labour Party on behalf of the Opposition for putting forward a foreword to the document.
charisma.explanation: Publicly acknowledges an Opposition MP's constructive contribution, building cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: we have a long tradition of robust debate within the National Party. We're not sort of all having to believe the same thing at the same moment at the same time... the most important thing is that we conduct ourselves with good grace, listen to the other side, and have a good, honest conversation, and that's what we're about.
charisma.explanation: Frames internal disagreement positively and calls for good grace and listening to the other side.

veracity.statement: I move, That this House note that today in 2010, 29 miners lost their lives while at work in the Pike River Mine, express its condolences to family and friends who will forever be profoundly impacted, and thank rescue and support teams for their service on that day and the days that followed.
veracity.explanation: The factual claim that 29 miners died at Pike River in 2010 is accurate.

veracity.statement: it's as recently as the period of the last Government in which New Zealand Defence Force personnel, both uniform and civilian, were offered zero percent pay increases for a much longer period of time than is contemplated in this motion. I think those members would be surprised to understand that members of political parties that now form the Opposition have discovered an intense interest in their pay and conditions in this way.
veracity.explanation: The claim about prior zero-percent offers under the last Government is plausible but presented without figures and framed to score points.

veracity.statement: It's my understanding that in 2001, the Department of Corrections workers, who were at that time undertaking industrial action, were effectively—or, their duties were authorised to be carried out in the manner equivalent to that which we are discussing in today's motion by New Zealand Defence Force personnel. I don't know the detail in terms of a zero increase pay offer having been made
veracity.explanation: The 2001 precedent is presented as best understanding and is broadly plausible, though hedged.

veracity.statement: the effect of inflation and those cost of living pressures on our defence force is much less than it would have been had the previous Government continued its spendthrift ways to continue to drive up inflation and the cost of living. We are pleased as a Government as a whole to be doing something about that situation.
veracity.explanation: A contestable counterfactual claim that the previous Government drove inflation, stated without evidence.

veracity.statement: the situation arose where minimum pay was set for members of the army who were doing certain work for the Government. It included a military factor—or "mil factor"... For reservists who did not receive that mil factor, their hourly pay rate fell below that of the minimum wage. Now, technically—technically—that's not a breach of the law... but we did something about it—that was our advocacy among other things.
veracity.explanation: A detailed, plausible technical account, though unverifiable from the text and self-serving.

veracity.statement: When we see 12 percent of Māori getting to high school at the standard they need to be for on mathematics because of the previous Government, that's not great.
veracity.explanation: Cites a low Māori maths-achievement figure but the '12 percent' statistic is imprecisely framed and attributed wholly to the previous Government.

veracity.statement: Is it not the case that in classical Māori behaviour in former times and around the rohe of late is to, when they want to speak to someone, ask them to come and speak, but in this case they did not ask political party leaders to speak; more importantly, Te Pāti Māori told them not to come?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Te Pāti Māori told leaders not to come, an unverified partisan claim.

veracity.statement: This is the first time in our history that all New Zealanders have been offered an equal chance to have a say on what our constitutional future means under the Treaty of Waitangi, and I'd encourage people to get along to the Justice Committee website and have their voice heard.
veracity.explanation: The sweeping 'first time in our history' framing overstates; public submission processes on Treaty-related matters are not unprecedented.

veracity.statement: PPPs in New Zealand are not new; there have been eight since 2011, including three bundles of primary and secondary schools that were carried on through the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable count of PPPs since 2011 that is broadly consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: On Thursday, I announced alongside the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, that the Government and Auckland Council have delivered contactless payments on Auckland's public transport network, to enable commuters to tag on and off public buses, trains, and ferries travelling across the region.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about a delivered, publicly announced service.

veracity.statement: The science of learning is a well-known, well-documented, and well-evidenced way to improve the outcomes of our students. If that member wants to see some evidence of that, she should go and look at the structured literacy Better Start Literacy Approach results for tamariki Māori, because they are outstanding.
veracity.explanation: The claim that science of learning is well-evidenced is defensible; the results characterisation is unverified here.

veracity.statement: I highlighted a 3 percent reduction in victimisations, an increase of over 30 percent in foot patrols, ram raids dropping by 60 percent, and aggravated robberies down by 11 percent.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable statistics presented favourably; broadly consistent with reported police data but selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Gang membership recorded on the National Gang List grew 1 percent to October this year. Last year for the same period, it grew by 10 percent. Under this coalition Government, gang membership growth has slowed tenfold.
veracity.explanation: The figures may be accurate, but 'slowed tenfold' compares two single-year snapshots and implies causation the data alone doesn't establish.

veracity.statement: In May, the European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) entered into force many months sooner than predicted, providing $46 million of tariffs saved for Kiwi exporters this year... In September, we concluded the New Zealand - United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, our first FTA in the Middle East... Last month, we concluded a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)—unfinished business for successive Governments over 18 years
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claims about concluded trade deals; the '$46 million saved' figure is a stated estimate.

veracity.statement: in September—after just four months of negotiation—we concluded a trade deal with the UAE delivering 98.5 percent tariff elimination on New Zealand exports on entry into force, rising to 99 percent after three years.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable claims about the UAE deal's tariff coverage.

veracity.statement: How can he stand in this House and speak about the strengthened Māori-Crown relationship when Māori die seven years earlier than non-Māori, Māori are overrepresented in the justice system, and are overrepresented in emergency housing?
veracity.explanation: The life-expectancy gap and over-representation claims are broadly supported by New Zealand data, though 'seven years' is a rounded figure.

veracity.statement: Can she explain how Te Tiriti o Waitangi has been embedded and authentically reflected in the refreshed curriculum following the outright removal and erasure of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the curriculum framework Te Mātaiaho and dismissal of Māori advisers on the curriculum refresh working group?
veracity.explanation: Asserts 'outright removal and erasure' as fact, which the Minister disputes as a mischaracterisation of an unwritten framework.

forthrightness.statement: It's my understanding that in 2001, the Department of Corrections workers, who were at that time undertaking industrial action, were effectively—or, their duties were authorised to be carried out in the manner equivalent to that which we are discussing in today's motion by New Zealand Defence Force personnel. I don't know the detail in terms of a zero increase pay offer having been made
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Parker's question about a prior precedent by naming the 2001 Corrections case, but explicitly cannot confirm the zero-percent aspect actually asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Suffice to say that inflationary pressures have affected many workers throughout New Zealand, again both civilian and uniform, within the Defence Act.
forthrightness.explanation: Parker asked specifically about the effect of inflation on the real terms and conditions of the workers since their last increase; the answer offers a generality and no figure.

forthrightness.statement: I consider that I have responded. If the member doesn't like the responses, that is his problem, not mine, and it's not the problem of the Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer Parker's repeated request for the specific information, asserting responsiveness instead of providing it.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not a research assistant for either of the members of Parliament opposite who have asked me a question that is not directly relevant to the motion today. If they wish to know the history and the background of industrial relations, they are welcome to research that themselves.
forthrightness.explanation: Refuses outright to answer Menéndez March's question about his advocacy on the fiscal environment.

forthrightness.statement: My understanding is that the strike notice, or the industrial action, generally has a specified date at the end of January to which it can take place. A further two weeks from that seems prudent for the purpose then of resetting normal arrangements, whereby rosters can be made, people can be given notice for duties... The date of mid-February seems to us prudent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains why mid-February was chosen for the authorisation window, responsive to the question about dates.

forthrightness.statement: Our position is very clear. We had a delegation from the National Party representing our position, receiving the hīkoi, and making clear our point of view, which is that we're not supporting the bill beyond first reading, therefore it won't become law.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Paul's 'why won't he front the crowd' by pointing to a delegation and restating the position, but does not directly address why he personally would not go out.

forthrightness.statement: When we see 12 percent of Māori getting to high school at the standard they need to be for on mathematics because of the previous Government, that's not great.
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots from Paul's question about killing the bill to unrelated achievement and housing statistics.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to part of the question, no, we're not at risk of civil war in New Zealand. That's inflammatory language.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Hipkins's question about Shipley's 'civil war' warning with a clear rejection.

forthrightness.statement: Partnership, protection, and other things that have discussed over many years—over 184 years.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Hipkins's direct question about what he believes the Treaty principles are, naming two but trailing into vagueness.

forthrightness.statement: We are not supporting the bill. As you know, we are not supporting the bill beyond first reading and it will not become law. I've been clear from day one. That is exactly our position and it remains unchanged.
forthrightness.explanation: Reiterates the standing position but sidesteps Hipkins's underlying point that National still supports first reading of a bill Luxon dislikes.

forthrightness.statement: from now until 11.59 p.m. on 7 January, the Justice Committee will be accepting submissions, and I think it's very important that people have a view on this bill and the issues surrounding it; actually have their say, and make sure that they do it in a respectful and constructive way
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how New Zealanders can have their say, giving the precise deadline and channel.

forthrightness.statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, it's possible to walk and chew gum at the same time, and while the National Party has a different view to one of the governing parties in the coalition on the Treaty principles bill—that's been well canvassed—what I can say... is that Minister Seymour is intensely focused on productivity and is leading the charge on foreign investment reform
forthrightness.explanation: Sidesteps Edmonds's quoted criticism that Seymour is the wrong person, pivoting to praise of Seymour's productivity work.

forthrightness.statement: the only person who, I think, has got very excited about it and distracted is members of the Labour Party, including herself.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects Edmonds's question about the Government being distracted by turning the charge back on her rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: I always take the comments of former colleagues with great interest but also with a grain of salt, because things have sometimes moved on from where they were when they were in the House. But that former Minister has a lot to say on many issues, and it's always very entertaining to hear what he has to say.
forthrightness.explanation: Avoids saying whether he agrees with Finlayson, deflecting with 'a grain of salt' and 'entertaining'.

forthrightness.statement: we are putting student achievement at the heart of every single thing that we do. If we want to honour the Treaty, it means closing the equity gap so that decades of disparity that have pervaded our system and the disproportionate representation of tamariki Māori and rangatahi Māori in the lower quartiles of our education and achievement system is closed.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'how' she honours the Treaty by reframing it as closing the equity gap, an on-topic but high-level response.

forthrightness.statement: I answered this last week, and I'll repeat myself: Te Mātaiaho has not been developed yet. There are only two learning areas—English and maths—that have been put out... it's only a shell. We are working on that framework and it will be consulted on in the same way that all of the learning areas are being consulted on. But I'll reiterate: it hasn't been written yet, so the member needs to understand that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of the 'erasure' question by explaining the framework is unwritten, though it also serves to sidestep the erasure charge.

forthrightness.statement: As I said today, all schools should be open for instruction, and the most important thing for our tamariki Māori is that they are in front of a teacher, learning, every single day that they possibly can if we're going to close the equity gap.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about why tamariki must attend a hīkoi instead of relying on her, reframing to school attendance.

forthrightness.statement: If it's required by law then yes we will.
forthrightness.explanation: Only conditionally commits to releasing the consultation report, leaving the core 'will you release it' unanswered unless legally compelled.

strength.statement: the situation arose where minimum pay was set for members of the army who were doing certain work for the Government. It included a military factor—or "mil factor"... For reservists who did not receive that mil factor, their hourly pay rate fell below that of the minimum wage. Now, technically—technically—that's not a breach of the law... but we did something about it—that was our advocacy among other things.
strength.explanation: Claims to have acted on the below-minimum-wage issue ('we did something about it') but delivery is asserted, not evidenced.

strength.statement: We've made six targeted changes to the framework, involving smarter allocation of risk; recognising, and in some cases reimbursing bid costs; stronger collaboration between the Crown and bidders in the tendering phase; and ensuring the upcoming National Infrastructure Agency provides robust and centralised PPP expertise and improvements to the dispute resolution process.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered framework refresh, but it is an announcement of settings rather than demonstrated built outcomes.

strength.statement: On Thursday, I announced alongside the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, that the Government and Auckland Council have delivered contactless payments on Auckland's public transport network, to enable commuters to tag on and off public buses, trains, and ferries travelling across the region.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete capability actually delivered and rolled out, not merely promised.

strength.statement: yes, especially my recently announced maths pilot to lift student achievement and close the equity gap. From term 1 and 2 next year, around 2,000 year 7 and 8 students who need the most help will take part in an intensive programme to support them to progress towards the required curriculum levels in mathematics.
strength.explanation: An announced pilot with a defined scope but delivery is still prospective.

strength.statement: I highlighted a 3 percent reduction in victimisations, an increase of over 30 percent in foot patrols, ram raids dropping by 60 percent, and aggravated robberies down by 11 percent.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for measurable early results as police Minister, though attribution to policy is partly asserted.

strength.statement: In May, the European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) entered into force many months sooner than predicted, providing $46 million of tariffs saved for Kiwi exporters this year... In September, we concluded the New Zealand - United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, our first FTA in the Middle East... Last month, we concluded a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)—unfinished business for successive Governments over 18 years
strength.explanation: Points to concluded, in-force agreements as delivered outcomes he was responsible for.

authenticity.statement: Our position is very clear. We had a delegation from the National Party representing our position, receiving the hīkoi, and making clear our point of view, which is that we're not supporting the bill beyond first reading, therefore it won't become law.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the position he repeats throughout the session; words align with the stated intended action of blocking the bill.

authenticity.statement: We are not supporting the bill. As you know, we are not supporting the bill beyond first reading and it will not become law. I've been clear from day one. That is exactly our position and it remains unchanged.
authenticity.explanation: Emphasises an unchanged position held throughout, consistent with his repeated statements this session.

divination.statement: The roll-out of contactless payments will expand to Timaru and Christchurch in early 2025 and it will reach other regions by the end of 2026.
divination.explanation: A forecast delivery timeline (Timaru/Christchurch early 2025, other regions by end 2026); plausible but dependent on execution.

divination.statement: Twenty-four agreements and memorandums of understanding between New Zealand and Chinese companies were signed during the visit, worth an additional $340 million in export revenue to New Zealand over the next three years.
divination.explanation: The '$340 million over the next three years' is a forward projection of export revenue, plausible but contingent on delivery of the MOUs.

specificity.statement: as long as the above authorisations are in place, the Minister will update the House on the progress being made to settle this industrial dispute on a weekly basis or on the next sitting day.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (weekly ministerial update to the House) with a defined trigger and timeframe.

specificity.statement: I really feel and believe that democracy needs accountability and so, therefore, having the Minister having to report back to this House is something that must be considered. Nowhere within this motion and the amendment to the motion is there anywhere that says that the Minister needs to keep this House informed.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete deficiency and remedy, though the accountability framing is partly abstract.

specificity.statement: Democracy can take time, democracy can be messy, but none the less we've got to ensure that democracy is the pinnacle and the foundation of this House and of any kind of legislation, any kind of motion, any kind of mahi that is done here.
specificity.explanation: Platitude about democracy with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to restoring law and order and strengthening democracy and freedoms.
specificity.explanation: Broad mission-statement slogan with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: To commit the offence, a person's conduct must include all of the following elements: it must be undertaken for, or on behalf of, a foreign power; and be covert, deceptive, corruptive, or coercive; and, thirdly, be meant to compromise protected New Zealand interests.
specificity.explanation: Lays out the precise legal elements of the new offence.

specificity.statement: The offence will also not apply to people who do not know, and have no reasonable way of determining, that they are being used by a foreign State to undertake foreign interference against New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete carve-out, though it glosses the precise statutory test.

specificity.statement: We're delivering on our promise to make New Zealand safer and more secure and a place where everyone can enjoy the guaranteed rights and freedoms afforded to them under our laws.
specificity.explanation: General claim of 'delivering' safety without measurable outcomes.

specificity.statement: In essence, it doubles the current financial jurisdiction of the Disputes Tribunal from $30,000 to $60,000, and this will improve access to justice for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures and the concrete change.

specificity.statement: Around 2,000 claimants per year will experience improved access to justice as a result of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number and timeframe.

specificity.statement: A new filing fee of $468 for claims of more than $30,000 will aid in cost recovery and help maintain current service levels.
specificity.explanation: Exact fee and the claim threshold it applies to.

specificity.statement: you can file a claim for up to $350,000 in the District Court for $260. There's a real mismatch when you can go to the District Court for $260 but the Disputes Tribunal, which doesn't apply the law and doesn't have a judge, is $468 as well.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact fee figures and jurisdictional limits.

specificity.statement: in the District Court and every other court, if you can't afford the filing fee, you can apply for a waiver, but in the Disputes Tribunal you can't. If you're going to put up a barrier of $468, you need to be able to have a hardship waiver as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact fee and the missing waiver mechanism.

specificity.statement: For example, parliamentary question No. 64705 to the Minister asked, "Is the Minister aware that the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command has a missile defense battery with radar in Israel and if so, will this prohibit further launches from New Zealand and if not, why not?"
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific numbered written question and its precise content to support his point about the 'New Zealand interest' test.

specificity.statement: The penalties for such actions are severe: up to 14 years in prison for intentional conduct, and up to 10 years for reckless behaviour.
specificity.explanation: Precise penalty figures for the two conduct standards.

specificity.statement: there is a filing fee of $468 proposed, and that is higher than the fee in the District Court, but then, of course, you've got half-day hearings of $1,200 and judicial settlement conferences of $1,200 in the District Court, so there are those other costs to consider as well when you're going through that process.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact hearing and conference fee figures.

specificity.statement: this work actually commenced under the last Labour Government, and the intention to introduce this legislation—at that stage, not drafted—was announced by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins in 2023.
specificity.explanation: Names the person and year of the original announcement.

specificity.statement: the wording in the legislation is slightly different and uses the words "the person knows, or ought to know", which is a different wording... maybe the select committee can look as to whether those words in new section 78AAA(3)(b) that are being inserted by clause 10 of the bill—as to whether that is the appropriate articulation of recklessness.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact section, clause, and disputed wording.

specificity.statement: This is something that we have seen increase a number of times over the years, noting that, for example, in 2009 the limit was only $7,500 at that stage.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete year and dollar figure.

specificity.statement: Fundamentally, we are seeing that our court systems are systemically underfunded in this environment and something like this is mainly pushing a certain section of the bill around within that greater ecosystem of the court system.
specificity.explanation: General diagnosis of underfunding without figures or specific programmes.

specificity.statement: This is a very important but small amendment, upping the amount that the Disputes Tribunal can look at, adding this extra tier—basically increasing it up to S60,000—and then adding this filing tier. This will make a material difference for people wanting to use this avenue to get disputes resolved.
specificity.explanation: Names the $60,000 figure and the mechanism, though the 'material difference' benefit stays general.

specificity.statement: There is also the knock-on effect that it does empower our small businesses and our communities to be a bit more brave, to be a bit less risk-averse, and to challenge things a bit more.
specificity.explanation: Directional benefit claim with no mechanism or measure of 'braver' behaviour.

civility.statement: I don't think they should really be laughing when it seems like it's a bit of their own inability to get this right that we're having to go through this process.
civility.explanation: Pointed pushback against being heckled, aimed at the drafting process rather than a personal insult, but somewhat combative.

civility.statement: I think the challenge we have here, as the Hon Dr Webb did say earlier—the member for Christchurch Central—is that this should be a last resort, not a first resort. The challenge we have is that we're rushing things through and mistakes are being made.
civility.explanation: Criticises the process, not people; engages the substance of how the motion is being handled.

civility.statement: That's the bit that took all the thought?
civility.explanation: A mocking interjection belittling a colleague's contribution rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: we need to be very careful before we make that an offence which is criminal and imprisonable by 14 years. I think we need to test that degree of intention required very, very carefully indeed.
civility.explanation: Substantive, policy-focused caution with no personal attack.

civility.statement: this Government has got a certain affection for warrantless search powers, it appears, and I'm a bit concerned that they're not going to turn their mind to the very question of whether this is essential.
civility.explanation: A barbed characterisation of the Government's tendencies, but tied to a genuine policy concern rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Some foreign influence, it seems, is OK, while others is not.
civility.explanation: Challenges a perceived double standard about the substance of the bill rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: just to touch base on the previous speaker Teanau Tuiono's notes around AUKUS, they're not knocking on our door. We've not even been invited to join at this point, so I think that rhetoric is kind of somewhat harmful and just adds to that sort of hype
civility.explanation: Corrects a colleague's characterisation and labels it 'harmful', but engages the claim rather than the person.

civility.statement: it would seem odd for this not to get at least the same level of time, scrutiny, and resource, being a bill that the Government is in favour of, as a bill that the Government isn't in favour of is getting—so a full and deep select committee process
civility.explanation: Presses the Government on process fairness through comparison rather than personal attack.

rigor.statement: I think the challenge we have here, as the Hon Dr Webb did say earlier—the member for Christchurch Central—is that this should be a last resort, not a first resort. The challenge we have is that we're rushing things through and mistakes are being made.
rigor.explanation: Uses the concrete drafting inconsistencies he identified as evidence that rushing causes errors; reasonable but leans on a general 'rushing' claim.

rigor.statement: I really feel and believe that democracy needs accountability and so, therefore, having the Minister having to report back to this House is something that must be considered. Nowhere within this motion and the amendment to the motion is there anywhere that says that the Minister needs to keep this House informed.
rigor.explanation: Principle (accountability) tied to a concrete gap in the motion (no reporting requirement); conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: To commit the offence, a person's conduct must include all of the following elements: it must be undertaken for, or on behalf of, a foreign power; and be covert, deceptive, corruptive, or coercive; and, thirdly, be meant to compromise protected New Zealand interests.
rigor.explanation: Structured, element-by-element explanation of how the offence is bounded to avoid over-reach.

rigor.statement: we need to be very careful before we make that an offence which is criminal and imprisonable by 14 years. I think we need to test that degree of intention required very, very carefully indeed.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific concern (criminalising reckless, non-intentional conduct) and reasons about the intent threshold and penalty.

rigor.statement: you can file a claim for up to $350,000 in the District Court for $260. There's a real mismatch when you can go to the District Court for $260 but the Disputes Tribunal, which doesn't apply the law and doesn't have a judge, is $468 as well.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete cost comparison to argue the fee is disproportionate; conclusion follows from the figures cited.

rigor.statement: in the District Court and every other court, if you can't afford the filing fee, you can apply for a waiver, but in the Disputes Tribunal you can't. If you're going to put up a barrier of $468, you need to be able to have a hardship waiver as well.
rigor.explanation: Points to a concrete inconsistency (no hardship waiver) and draws a proportionate remedy from it.

rigor.statement: the Government Communications Security Bureau, or GCSB, between 2013 and 2020—seven years—had a spy agency parked up at that bureau, which points to the fact that we actually have had foreign influence within our sphere.
rigor.explanation: Offers a concrete example to support the 'some interference is tolerated' point, but the inference is loosely drawn.

rigor.statement: there is an assessment process where things might be deemed at risk of being contrary to the New Zealand interest, but the kicker is that none of those assessment analyses has actually ever happened.
rigor.explanation: Backs the argument that 'New Zealand interest' is undefined in practice with a concrete claim that no assessments have occurred.

rigor.statement: just to touch base on the previous speaker Teanau Tuiono's notes around AUKUS, they're not knocking on our door. We've not even been invited to join at this point, so I think that rhetoric is kind of somewhat harmful and just adds to that sort of hype
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the AUKUS claim on the factual ground that no invitation exists.

rigor.statement: there is a filing fee of $468 proposed, and that is higher than the fee in the District Court, but then, of course, you've got half-day hearings of $1,200 and judicial settlement conferences of $1,200 in the District Court, so there are those other costs to consider as well when you're going through that process.
rigor.explanation: Answers Webb's fee-comparison point by adding the District Court's downstream hearing costs — relevant context that qualifies the comparison.

rigor.statement: the wording in the legislation is slightly different and uses the words "the person knows, or ought to know", which is a different wording... maybe the select committee can look as to whether those words in new section 78AAA(3)(b) that are being inserted by clause 10 of the bill—as to whether that is the appropriate articulation of recklessness.
rigor.explanation: Precise textual analysis contrasting the Minister's characterisation with the actual statutory wording and citing the exact clause.

rigor.statement: most foreign interference now is actually through AI-generated bots that are using social media channels to influence people... internet service providers, including social media companies, have no liability for third-party content—none. They've got no duty of care to prevent it
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete gap (no ISP/social-media liability) and links it to the AI-bot threat the bill omits; reasoning is coherent though the 'most' claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: we have recently seen quite large trims to the budgets for both the Security Intelligence Service and the Government Communications Security Bureau; so needing to be assured that we have the resourcing there for those agencies
rigor.explanation: Links a claimed resourcing cut to the practical question of whether agencies can enforce the new law.

rigor.statement: it would seem odd for this not to get at least the same level of time, scrutiny, and resource, being a bill that the Government is in favour of, as a bill that the Government isn't in favour of is getting—so a full and deep select committee process
rigor.explanation: Argues by consistency that a supported bill deserves at least the scrutiny given an unsupported one.

rigor.statement: we simply don't have the data right now of the number of civil claims that are between $30,000 and $100,000 at all, and they are not currently captured in the legal system. We also don't really know what is the maximum intent and the maximum benefit that we will see with this particular bill.
rigor.explanation: Flags a genuine evidence gap and links it to uncertainty about whether the bill will achieve its purpose.

rigor.statement: Fundamentally, we are seeing that our court systems are systemically underfunded in this environment and something like this is mainly pushing a certain section of the bill around within that greater ecosystem of the court system.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable systemic point, but the 'systemically underfunded' claim is asserted rather than evidenced here.

veracity.statement: we've heard that the last time this was used was 23 years ago, so this is a rare occurrence and we need to make sure that the Minister is speaking to this
veracity.explanation: The '23 years ago' claim (last such motion ~2001) is plausibly accurate and used proportionately, though presented second-hand.

veracity.statement: The offence will also not apply to people who do not know, and have no reasonable way of determining, that they are being used by a foreign State to undertake foreign interference against New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: David Parker later notes the bill's actual wording is 'the person knows, or ought to know', a lower threshold than this characterisation suggests, making the description arguably misleading.

veracity.statement: In essence, it doubles the current financial jurisdiction of the Disputes Tribunal from $30,000 to $60,000, and this will improve access to justice for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's core provision.

veracity.statement: you can file a claim for up to $350,000 in the District Court for $260. There's a real mismatch when you can go to the District Court for $260 but the Disputes Tribunal, which doesn't apply the law and doesn't have a judge, is $468 as well.
veracity.explanation: The District Court filing-fee comparison is broadly accurate; 'doesn't apply the law' is a fair gloss on the tribunal's equity-based standard.

veracity.statement: the Government Communications Security Bureau, or GCSB, between 2013 and 2020—seven years—had a spy agency parked up at that bureau, which points to the fact that we actually have had foreign influence within our sphere.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a reported foreign-partner presence at the GCSB; the broad framing is hard to fully verify and stated pointedly.

veracity.statement: they've got AUKUS knocking on our door—knocking on our door—for New Zealand to join.
veracity.explanation: Overstates the situation; Laura McClure rebuts that New Zealand has not been invited to join AUKUS, making 'knocking on our door' misleading.

veracity.statement: there is an assessment process where things might be deemed at risk of being contrary to the New Zealand interest, but the kicker is that none of those assessment analyses has actually ever happened.
veracity.explanation: A specific factual assertion sourced to his written questions, but not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: just to touch base on the previous speaker Teanau Tuiono's notes around AUKUS, they're not knocking on our door. We've not even been invited to join at this point, so I think that rhetoric is kind of somewhat harmful and just adds to that sort of hype
veracity.explanation: Correctly notes New Zealand has not been invited to join AUKUS, rebutting the earlier 'knocking on our door' framing.

veracity.statement: The penalties for such actions are severe: up to 14 years in prison for intentional conduct, and up to 10 years for reckless behaviour.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the bill's stated penalties as described elsewhere in the debate.

veracity.statement: by my count, this is the 27th bill that the Justice Committee will receive this term and consider. It's another absolute masterclass from Minister Paul Goldsmith in getting the simple changes that the country needs in order to get us back on track.
veracity.explanation: The bill-count figure is a specific claim he stakes on his own count; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: this work actually commenced under the last Labour Government, and the intention to introduce this legislation—at that stage, not drafted—was announced by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins in 2023.
veracity.explanation: A checkable historical claim about the bill's origin under the previous government; presented with a specific attribution and date.

veracity.statement: most foreign interference now is actually through AI-generated bots that are using social media channels to influence people... internet service providers, including social media companies, have no liability for third-party content—none. They've got no duty of care to prevent it
veracity.explanation: The liability point is broadly accurate; 'most foreign interference now is... AI-generated bots' is a strong quantitative claim offered without a source.

veracity.statement: we have recently seen quite large trims to the budgets for both the Security Intelligence Service and the Government Communications Security Bureau; so needing to be assured that we have the resourcing there for those agencies
veracity.explanation: Asserts recent budget cuts to the SIS and GCSB as fact to support a resourcing concern; plausible but not substantiated in the text.

veracity.statement: This is something that we have seen increase a number of times over the years, noting that, for example, in 2009 the limit was only $7,500 at that stage.
veracity.explanation: A specific historical figure for the tribunal's earlier jurisdiction limit, offered as verifiable context.

charisma.statement: Democracy can take time, democracy can be messy, but none the less we've got to ensure that democracy is the pinnacle and the foundation of this House and of any kind of legislation, any kind of motion, any kind of mahi that is done here.
charisma.explanation: Reaches for a unifying appeal to shared democratic values, but rhetorical and aimed at his own argument.

charisma.statement: I think it is really important when we come to matters such as foreign interference that we, wherever possible, reach a position which is agreed across all parties and endures.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-party consensus and durable agreement on a sensitive issue.

charisma.statement: by my count, this is the 27th bill that the Justice Committee will receive this term and consider. It's another absolute masterclass from Minister Paul Goldsmith in getting the simple changes that the country needs in order to get us back on track.
charisma.explanation: Partisan praise of his own side's Minister; rallies his own benches rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I also endorse Duncan Webb's comments that, if possible around these issues, it's good if we can reach a cross-party accord at least with a substantial majority of the votes in the House.
charisma.explanation: Seeks cross-party accord and common ground on a security matter.

strength.statement: We're delivering on our promise to make New Zealand safer and more secure and a place where everyone can enjoy the guaranteed rights and freedoms afforded to them under our laws.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery, but this is a first reading of a bill only introduced, not yet enacted — announcement, not delivered result.

strength.statement: The Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill fulfils both the National Party's election manifesto commitment to raise the tribunal's financial jurisdiction, allowing it to resolve disputes of a higher value, and this Government's justice priority to improve timely access to dispute resolution.
strength.explanation: Follows through on a manifesto pledge, but at first reading it is delivery-in-progress, not yet enacted.

divination.statement: Around 2,000 claimants per year will experience improved access to justice as a result of this bill.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable forecast of ~2,000 affected claimants a year; plausible from ministry modelling but uncertain in practice.

divination.statement: There is also the knock-on effect that it does empower our small businesses and our communities to be a bit more brave, to be a bit less risk-averse, and to challenge things a bit more.
divination.explanation: Predicts a behavioural effect (businesses taking more risks) from raising the jurisdiction; plausible but unmeasured and uncertain.

authenticity.statement: The Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill fulfils both the National Party's election manifesto commitment to raise the tribunal's financial jurisdiction, allowing it to resolve disputes of a higher value, and this Government's justice priority to improve timely access to dispute resolution.
authenticity.explanation: Action (introducing the bill) is explicitly consistent with a prior manifesto commitment — words matching a stated promise.

authenticity.statement: As Minister of Customs and the Minister responsible for combating transnational organised crime, we have a daily reminder of the amount of interference and the high need of protection that we have.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds her support in her own portfolio experience, consistent with her stated ministerial roles, though it offers no verifiable detail.

forthrightness.statement: the Greens won't be supporting this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: States the party's position on the bill plainly and unambiguously.

charisma.statement: I note that Dr Duncan Webb made some interesting points about the gaps that remain. I also noted that Paul Goldsmith seemed willing to consider those and I hope that the committee will look at them.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges a cross-party colleague's willingness to engage and invites collaborative committee consideration — consensus-seeking rather than combative.

charisma.statement: The submitters, I think, would be welcome to focus on things like whether, in fact, that is the right amount—whether it should be $60,000, whether it should be $70,000, or whether it should be $100,000... but it does seem that that would be a situation where submissions would be very helpful from real, live New Zealanders who have suffered harm under a system that has not necessarily catered for them as well as it should.
charisma.explanation: Openly invites public submissions and defers to affected New Zealanders — inclusive and bridge-building.

charisma.statement: we are supportive of the legislation and the trajectory and the journey where we are heading in terms of strengthening the protections for young smokers and particularly in the vape space, but also we need a system and we need the many cogs in the public health service to be ready to implement the legislation when it comes into effect.
charisma.explanation: Endorses the shared direction and frames the issue collaboratively rather than as opposition.

civility.statement: I note that Dr Duncan Webb made some interesting points about the gaps that remain. I also noted that Paul Goldsmith seemed willing to consider those and I hope that the committee will look at them.
civility.explanation: Respectful reference to members across the House, focused on ideas and process.

civility.statement: The questions that we will have will be: why the truncated process, why the very restrictive bill—which the regulatory impact statements acknowledge is restrictive and therefore deems many things out of scope—when there was an opportunity to do something much more ambitious?
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's process, but engages the substance and cites the RIS rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: why had the Associate Minister of Health, the Hon Casey Costello, made decisions—and why had Cabinet made decisions—prior to the second regulatory impact statement being made? That seems to be a little bit the wrong way round.
civility.explanation: Names the Minister but frames a legitimate process critique rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that there has been a really unfortunate narrative that has been around this vaping space—that, somehow, when we were talking about vaping, we were talking about the situation where it was safer. Unfortunately, I think that the language got away, and we ended up with it being discussed as if it was safe.
civility.explanation: Reflective and self-critical about messaging failures, no personal attacks or blame-shifting onto opponents.
