divination.explanation: Forecast that the page and contact centre go live by Friday; operational and within DIA's control.

authenticity.statement: I also know that we’ve still got a way to go to make sure that our actions match up with the words in that apology.
authenticity.explanation: Frankly acknowledges a gap between the Dawn Raids apology's words and follow-through actions rather than claiming the work is done.

authenticity.statement: I’m very proud to stand here today to say Labour has supported this bill at every step of the way.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's record, which backed the bill from the first reading; the claim matches the party's actions.

strength.statement: Normally, it takes 10 to 20 years to get superannuation, depending on the age, but that is something that New Zealand First will give very careful thought to.
strength.explanation: Only a vague commitment to 'give very careful thought' — no concrete action or delivery pledged on superannuation eligibility.

civility.statement: If only this House could stop creating harm.
civility.explanation: A pointed lament about the institution's record rather than a personal attack on any member.

charisma.statement: The real test of politicians is our ability to get in behind that idea and put aside the party political agendas and to support with seeing the policy or law through to fruition. This was not a problem for Labour in this instance.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly praises cross-party cooperation and getting behind an opponent's good idea — consensus-building rather than us-vs-them.

charisma.statement: Although we don’t agree with a lot of the New Zealand First policy agenda, the one thing that the Rt Hon Winston has demonstrated over the years is a level of commitment to our Pacific region and a respectful relationship with our Pasifika communities.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges an opponent's valid record while noting disagreement — reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I often find it difficult to comprehend David Seymour’s views on matters, let alone agree with him, but the words he shared, whilst they were insightful and genuine
charisma.explanation: Finds common ground with a figure she usually opposes, modelling cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: The redeeming factor for National here is despite opposing the bill at first reading, National was able to listen to the voices of over 24,000 Samoans who submitted on this bill and then work with other political parties to form a consensus on this bill.
charisma.explanation: Credits an opponent for coming around and building consensus — generous, bridge-building framing.

charisma.statement: As politicians from across political parties, we should be continually seeking out opportunities for actions to match the words of that apology through our policy, through our funding, and our legislative decisions.
charisma.explanation: Frames the task as a shared cross-party obligation, inviting others in.

charisma.statement: What we achieved today is unprecedented: the first time in history that a trustee administered country will be given citizenship in this way. No other mandated country has ever taken this step.
charisma.explanation: Rallying rhetoric of national significance, but appeals to the shared occasion rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: Most importantly, today we’ve demonstrated how Parliament can work together constructively to achieve meaningful change.
charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party cooperation and unity rather than partisan advantage.

charisma.statement: Let them see how we can strengthen relationships with our Pacific neighbours through actions, not just words.
charisma.explanation: Unifying, forward-looking framing that invites collective ownership.

charisma.statement: My ask is that we continue as tangata moana to stand in solidarity with our tēina who are feeling the weight of decisions being made without them—much like why we are here today.
charisma.explanation: Appeals for solidarity and unity across communities, drawing a connecting theme.

charisma.statement: We will only move forward together if we face our past honestly and with integrity.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'move forward together' framing appealing to shared national responsibility.

charisma.statement: Last but not least, I would like to acknowledge my National Party colleagues, Cameron Brewer and all of the members in the select committee and the National Party for supporting this bill. It is wonderful that it is a bill that is unanimously supported, because it is the right thing for all of us to support it unanimously in restoring justice for our Samoan people.
charisma.explanation: Warmly credits political opponents and celebrates unanimous, cross-party support.

charisma.statement: It would be hard to find a stronger and more voiceful advocate for victims in our caucus and in the Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Warm praise of a colleague, but appeals to his own side rather than persuading across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I’m not going to blame the Government members any more than I would blame the prior Labour administration, but there is a bad habit forming here that we are filibustering members’ bills.
charisma.explanation: Non-partisan appeal to shared parliamentary norms that both sides can accept.

authenticity.statement: The real test of politicians is our ability to get in behind that idea and put aside the party political agendas and to support with seeing the policy or law through to fruition. This was not a problem for Labour in this instance.
authenticity.explanation: States a value (backing good ideas regardless of party) that Labour is actually acting on by voting for another party's bill — words match the deed visible in the text.

authenticity.statement: As politicians from across political parties, we should be continually seeking out opportunities for actions to match the words of that apology through our policy, through our funding, and our legislative decisions.
authenticity.explanation: Calls for words (the Dawn Raids apology, made under Labour) to be matched by action — consistent with supporting this bill, though the demand is broader than the visible deed.

authenticity.statement: Labour commits to giving consideration to these next steps, but given the reins of power sit squarely with National, ACT, and New Zealand First, we encourage you to keep the pressure on.
authenticity.explanation: A stated intent with no delivery either way; honest about lacking power but non-committal.

civility.statement: Although we don’t agree with a lot of the New Zealand First policy agenda, the one thing that the Rt Hon Winston has demonstrated over the years is a level of commitment to our Pacific region and a respectful relationship with our Pasifika communities.
civility.explanation: Respectful of a political opponent, credits his genuine commitment despite policy differences.

civility.statement: I often find it difficult to comprehend David Seymour’s views on matters, let alone agree with him, but the words he shared, whilst they were insightful and genuine
civility.explanation: A mild jab softened by a genuine, generous acknowledgement of an opponent's sincerity — criticism stays civil.

civility.statement: Turning to National, I think they underestimated their two coalition partners on this matter and I will also add I feel they did themselves a disservice by voting against this bill at first reading.
civility.explanation: Criticises a political decision (the first-reading vote) rather than attacking anyone personally.

civility.statement: The redeeming factor for National here is despite opposing the bill at first reading, National was able to listen to the voices of over 24,000 Samoans who submitted on this bill and then work with other political parties to form a consensus on this bill.
civility.explanation: Gives credit across party lines rather than scoring points.

civility.statement: Last but not least, I would like to acknowledge my National Party colleagues, Cameron Brewer and all of the members in the select committee and the National Party for supporting this bill. It is wonderful that it is a bill that is unanimously supported, because it is the right thing for all of us to support it unanimously in restoring justice for our Samoan people.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of the other side.

civility.statement: This is disrespectful to the member, to filibuster your own member’s bill.
civility.explanation: A pointed, legitimate criticism of the conduct (filibustering) rather than a personal insult, but sharply worded.

civility.statement: I just wanted to clarify with the member if she considered, potentially, a broader title to encompass those that she believes were under the focus of the bill, which is about people under a protection order, and if there were other alternative titles that she considered to make this more encompassing for the focus of the bill.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill respectfully and constructively.

civility.statement: I’m not going to blame the Government members any more than I would blame the prior Labour administration, but there is a bad habit forming here that we are filibustering members’ bills.
civility.explanation: Criticises a practice even-handedly, explicitly refusing to make it partisan.

civility.statement: The way to deal with issues that are not agreed to by other political parties through the members’ ballot is to vote them down. It’s actually not to delay their consideration so as to stop more bills being drawn from the ballot.
civility.explanation: Focuses on process and principle, not personalities.

veracity.statement: The redeeming factor for National here is despite opposing the bill at first reading, National was able to listen to the voices of over 24,000 Samoans who submitted on this bill and then work with other political parties to form a consensus on this bill.
veracity.explanation: The figure of over 24,000 submissions matches the record for this bill.

veracity.statement: Labour and the Greens heard the call from the community to extend eligibility to descendants born prior to 1 January 1962; this was not supported.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes a debated eligibility extension that was not adopted.

veracity.statement: we are about to pass this bill that rights a historic wrong for those born in Samoa who had their citizenship revoked under the 1982 Act when they were rightly entitled to it.
veracity.explanation: The Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act 1982 did revoke citizenship affirmed by the Lesā Privy Council case — accurate.

veracity.statement: What we achieved today is unprecedented: the first time in history that a trustee administered country will be given citizenship in this way. No other mandated country has ever taken this step.
veracity.explanation: A sweeping 'first in history/never' claim that is broadly defensible but grandiose and hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: The strength of feeling on this issue was demonstrated by more than 24,000 submissions received by the Governance and Administration Committee, one of which represented the views of nearly 6,000 people.
veracity.explanation: Submission figures are consistent with the record for this bill.

veracity.statement: We also clarified the bill’s scope of eligibility to the cohort of approximately 3,500 individuals who were born between 1924 and 1948 and lost their citizenship when this law was changed in 1982.
veracity.explanation: Cohort and dates align with the Lesā-era affected group and the bill's stated scope.

veracity.statement: The bill establishes a straightforward application process through the Department of Internal Affairs, with a modest application fee of $177. Importantly, as agreed during the committee of the whole House stage, this fee will be refunded to successful applicants
veracity.explanation: Describes concrete, checkable features of the enacted process.

veracity.statement: the hundreds of cleaners, kitchen hands, and supermarket workers in our Samoan community in the 1970s and 1980s who organised to raise the funds for the Privy Council taken by Falema‘i Lesā, who tested the law, succeeded, and ultimately has paved the path to where we are today.
veracity.explanation: Accurately recounts the community fundraising behind the Lesā Privy Council case that shaped this history.

veracity.statement: I’d like to acknowledge the approximately 24,581 people, groups, individuals that made submissions.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the ~24,000+ submissions cited by other members.

veracity.statement: Tens of thousands of Samoans have been affected by the Citizenship (Western Samoa) Act, which was passed in this Parliament in 1982, and as we have heard through the thousands of submissions, that Act effectively revoked the citizenship of Samoans who were rightfully entitled to New Zealand citizenship.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 1982 Act's effect of overriding the Lesā ruling and stripping entitlement.

veracity.statement: In 1914, New Zealand established a military occupation on behalf of Great Britain to take possession of Samoa from Germany. In 1920, this colonial role was affirmed by the League of Nations as the administrator of Samoa.
veracity.explanation: Historically accurate: NZ's 1914 occupation and the 1920 League of Nations mandate over Western Samoa.

veracity.statement: New Zealand’s role as colonial administrator continued right up until 1962.
veracity.explanation: Correct — Western Samoa gained independence in 1962.

veracity.statement: Nearly 50 percent of my electorate are Pacific people.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the high Pacific population of Panmure-Ōtāhuhu.

veracity.statement: It’s an important moment for the class of ’23 in our caucus too, because this is the first member’s bill that has come from the National Party through the Justice Committee.
veracity.explanation: A checkable procedural claim about the first National member's bill through that committee.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Law Society, in their submission to the Justice Committee—which, I believe, are on their 28th bill, if I’m correct, Mr Meager—noted that the word “victim” is not defined in either the Corrections Act or in this bill specifically.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports that 'victim' is undefined in the principal Act and the bill, per the submission.

specificity.statement: Labour and the Greens heard the call from the community to extend eligibility to descendants born prior to 1 January 1962; this was not supported.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy ask (descendants born before 1 Jan 1962) and its outcome.

specificity.statement: The strength of feeling on this issue was demonstrated by more than 24,000 submissions received by the Governance and Administration Committee, one of which represented the views of nearly 6,000 people.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete numbers (24,000+ submissions, one representing nearly 6,000 people).

specificity.statement: We also clarified the bill’s scope of eligibility to the cohort of approximately 3,500 individuals who were born between 1924 and 1948 and lost their citizenship when this law was changed in 1982.
specificity.explanation: Precise cohort size and birth-year window define exactly who is covered.

specificity.statement: The bill establishes a straightforward application process through the Department of Internal Affairs, with a modest application fee of $177. Importantly, as agreed during the committee of the whole House stage, this fee will be refunded to successful applicants
specificity.explanation: Names the administering agency, exact fee ($177), and the refund mechanism and when it was agreed.

specificity.statement: All documentation, guidance, and support will be provided in both English and Samoan, ensuring the process is truly accessible to all those who are eligible.
specificity.explanation: A concrete accessibility commitment (bilingual materials) though without detail on delivery timing.

specificity.statement: the hundreds of cleaners, kitchen hands, and supermarket workers in our Samoan community in the 1970s and 1980s who organised to raise the funds for the Privy Council taken by Falema‘i Lesā, who tested the law, succeeded, and ultimately has paved the path to where we are today.
specificity.explanation: Concrete actors, era, and the specific legal case named.

specificity.statement: I’d like to acknowledge the approximately 24,581 people, groups, individuals that made submissions.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise submission count rather than a round gesture.

specificity.statement: In 1914, New Zealand established a military occupation on behalf of Great Britain to take possession of Samoa from Germany. In 1920, this colonial role was affirmed by the League of Nations as the administrator of Samoa.
specificity.explanation: Precise dates, actors, and institutions.

specificity.statement: Nearly 50 percent of my electorate are Pacific people.
specificity.explanation: A concrete proportion, though approximate.

specificity.statement: When this bill passes in a few minutes and she submits her application on Monday, her mother Alofa will again be a citizen of Niu Sila.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, the timing (Monday), and the concrete outcome.

specificity.statement: Tomasi found a job, worked incredibly hard, and over the next six years was able to bring both his parents and siblings to New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A concrete personal illustration with a timeframe, used to humanise the bill's stakes.

specificity.statement: Essentially, what this bill aims to do is to protect victims—victims of crime, those that have a protection order for their benefit from unwanted contact from people that are under the supervision of Corrections that are located within prisons.
specificity.explanation: Clearly delineates who the bill protects and the exact scenario (unwanted contact from prisoners under Corrections' supervision).

specificity.statement: It’s an important moment for the class of ’23 in our caucus too, because this is the first member’s bill that has come from the National Party through the Justice Committee.
specificity.explanation: Concrete institutional detail anchoring the point.

specificity.statement: The New Zealand Law Society, in their submission to the Justice Committee—which, I believe, are on their 28th bill, if I’m correct, Mr Meager—noted that the word “victim” is not defined in either the Corrections Act or in this bill specifically.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific source and the specific drafting gap.

strength.statement: Labour commits to giving consideration to these next steps, but given the reins of power sit squarely with National, ACT, and New Zealand First, we encourage you to keep the pressure on.
strength.explanation: Only commits to 'giving consideration', and from opposition with no levers to deliver — aspiration, not action.

strength.statement: The bill establishes a straightforward application process through the Department of Internal Affairs, with a modest application fee of $177. Importantly, as agreed during the committee of the whole House stage, this fee will be refunded to successful applicants
strength.explanation: Concrete mechanism being delivered through legislation passing today, not merely promised.

strength.statement: All documentation, guidance, and support will be provided in both English and Samoan, ensuring the process is truly accessible to all those who are eligible.
strength.explanation: A commitment tied to a bill actually passing, giving it more backing than pure aspiration.

divination.statement: When this bill passes in a few minutes and she submits her application on Monday, her mother Alofa will again be a citizen of Niu Sila.
divination.explanation: A near-term, falsifiable prediction with high likelihood given the bill's imminent passage and the individual's eligibility.

rigor.statement: The advice from the Corrections officials was that, if they included it, if we were to amend the bill and include a definition for “victims”, essentially, it would need significant resource to operationalise.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her decision in the departmental report and officials' operational advice rather than assertion, quoting paragraph 25.

rigor.statement: The New Zealand Law Society, in their submission to the Justice Committee—which, I believe, are on their 28th bill, if I’m correct, Mr Meager—noted that the word “victim” is not defined in either the Corrections Act or in this bill specifically.
rigor.explanation: Backs a drafting concern with the Law Society's submission rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: I just wanted to clarify with the member if she considered, potentially, a broader title to encompass those that she believes were under the focus of the bill, which is about people under a protection order, and if there were other alternative titles that she considered to make this more encompassing for the focus of the bill.
rigor.explanation: Raises a substantive scope point — that protection-order beneficiaries are not necessarily victims — rather than a rhetorical one.

rigor.statement: The way to deal with issues that are not agreed to by other political parties through the members’ ballot is to vote them down. It’s actually not to delay their consideration so as to stop more bills being drawn from the ballot.
rigor.explanation: A clean logical argument: identifies the legitimate mechanism (voting down) and why delay undermines the ballot's purpose, conclusion following from premises.

forthrightness.statement: The advice from the Corrections officials was that, if they included it, if we were to amend the bill and include a definition for “victims”, essentially, it would need significant resource to operationalise.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Rutherford's question on whether she'd amend the title/add a definition, explaining why she will not.

civility.statement: I thank the Leader of the House for the update. In previous parliaments, when a members’ day was scheduled on the likely last week of the sitting calendar, there have been provisions made for an extended sitting so that the House doesn’t lose its members’ day. Would the Leader of the House consider such an arrangement this year?
civility.explanation: Courteous, procedural request that thanks the minister and engages the substance without any attack.

civility.statement: That’s a case of what I might call “res ipsa loquitur”—the thing speaks for itself.
civility.explanation: Dismissive and evasive but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: How long have you been here? Yeah, it shows—it shows.
civility.explanation: A personal put-down of Shanan Halbert’s experience rather than engagement with the point.

civility.statement: No evidence whatsoever—there’s no New World in Ponsonby—and she got away with it.
civility.explanation: A pointed gotcha rather than a personal insult, but scored to undermine rather than engage.

civility.statement: Who is correct: David Seymour, who thinks Treaty principles should be unilaterally rewritten by the Crown; Winston Peters, who thinks they don’t even exist; or Christopher Luxon, who thinks they are “Partnership, protection, and other things”?
civility.explanation: Sharp but engages the substance of the ministers’ stated positions rather than personal traits.

civility.statement: Obviously, geographical knowledge in that part of Auckland is enjoyed by my leader—something sadly absent from the intellect of the questions offered by the Green Party.
civility.explanation: A personal attack on the 'intellect' of Green Party questions rather than their substance.

civility.statement: Is he confident that his Cabinet colleagues, including the Prime Minister, were fully informed in making the decision to allow commercial fishing in the high protection areas despite official advice based on Fisheries New Zealand data clearly stating that the commercial operators could still catch fish in the over 90 percent of the Gulf outside of the high protection areas with “minimal impact on their businesses”?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the substance of the decision and the evidence, not the minister personally.

civility.statement: Well, they can have confidence because there are a number of things that this Government has undertaken since the report has been tabled... this Government had the courage to acknowledge that the torture of young people that took place at Lake Alice was, in fact, torture—a finding that was found by the UN under the previous Government’s watch and that they did nothing about.
civility.explanation: Contrast with the previous government ('did nothing about') is a partisan swipe within an otherwise substantive answer.

civility.statement: As I said, this is an operational matter for the Ministry of Education. I would also like to point out that in 2023, under that member’s Government, 29 routes were cancelled.
civility.explanation: 'Under that member’s Government' is a partisan counter-jab rather than engagement with the safety concern.

civility.statement: What does it say about her coordination and the Government’s response when the Government is doing things contrary to the royal commission’s recommendations, like repealing section 7AA and legislating for failed boot camps?
civility.explanation: Sharp but targets policy actions and consistency rather than the minister personally.

civility.statement: How does he reconcile telling the House on two separate occasions that gang members were not practising on gun ranges when a police email on 9 September 2024 released under the Official Information Act states, “I’ve included images of those gang members shooting .50 calibre in the South Island, one being overseen by a senior NZ pistol shooter.”?
civility.explanation: Accusatory but grounded in evidence about the minister’s statements rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Electoral boundaries are important, but, at the same time, it is important that there’s a fair degree of distance between those who are directly affected by it and those who make those decisions... we absolutely support these appointments. We think there’s a high degree of competence and, also, the right approach of the public service by these appointees, notwithstanding the political backgrounds that exist there as well.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful endorsement across the aisle with reasoned support.

civility.statement: I stand on behalf of the Green Party to endorse and support the appointment of these representatives of the Government and the Opposition today... May I also comment that I note there’s no wāhine being appointed—just pause on that—but the credentials of those who have been appointed are great.
civility.explanation: Supportive and respectful, raising the absence of women appointees as a measured observation, not an attack.

civility.statement: for those members of the public who might be watching... who despair sometimes at the partisan argument that is such a feature of political life in this Parliament, the process and the collaborative work on this bill... the engagement by parties across the House, I think is a refreshing case study in the way that colleagues in the House here can from time to time come together and work in a very collegial way.
civility.explanation: Wholly constructive, focused on collegial process rather than any attack.

civility.statement: I’m really glad to hear that the issue around joint and several liability will be considered as part of this review, and I thank the Minister for taking that on board. I’ll leave it there.
civility.explanation: Thanks the minister and engages substantively with the liability review — cooperative and respectful.

charisma.statement: I thank the Leader of the House for the update. In previous parliaments, when a members’ day was scheduled on the likely last week of the sitting calendar, there have been provisions made for an extended sitting so that the House doesn’t lose its members’ day. Would the Leader of the House consider such an arrangement this year?
charisma.explanation: Constructive, cooperative tone seeking a cross-house accommodation rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: Well, I always consider the good ideas, so let’s wait and see. We’ve got a few sitting days left in the year and a lot of Government business to get to, but I’m also conscious that members’ business is important, so let’s see how we go.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the value of members’ business and stays cordial, but non-committal.

charisma.statement: It is something that I would like to see the whole of Parliament get behind and so I’m encouraging all political parties to meet with the Infrastructure Commission to be briefed on the plan. I know some political parties have taken up that opportunity already and I really welcome that and encourage them to do that.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites all parties in and seeks cross-party buy-in on the infrastructure plan.

charisma.statement: Well, the difference between some political parties and ones on this side of the House is that we treat every member as an equal. We don’t think we’re superior... The second thing is: by a process of consultation, they came to a conclusion together.
charisma.explanation: Frames an us-vs-them contrast with 'some political parties' rather than persuading across the aisle.

charisma.statement: we got there with legislation—not Labour’s, but designed by New Zealand First... Every change that Labour made between 2020 and 2023 was never coming into effect until 2027, so they can take no credit whatsoever. New Zealand First—with Action on Smoking and Health, I might add—can take all the credit.
charisma.explanation: Purely partisan credit-grabbing that denigrates the opposition rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: Mr Jones is quite different from a lot of people in this Parliament; he’s an action man. Some talk and some act. Mr Jones is an action man. If you don’t know that, go down to Ōpōtiki, go down to Hawke’s Bay... go down to Invercargill. All over this country, they are seeing a revival of action politics from somebody who knows what he’s doing.
charisma.explanation: Rallying praise of a colleague with a 'some talk and some act' jab at opponents.

charisma.statement: I have announced a series of 15 nationwide summits, where the audiences have applauded the fact that, at long last, after three years of absence, a regional development Minister willing to be bold and make allocative decisions has arrived. Over 150 applications for the Regional Infrastructure Fund have been received, and in those regions, work is already taking place on fixing up the neglected flood management systems as a consequence of the Budget allocation of $100 million initially, up possibly to $200 million.
charisma.explanation: Self-congratulatory ('audiences have applauded... at long last') and contrastive rather than unifying.

charisma.statement: we have already allocated a $5.8 million grant at historic site Parihaka... I’m going to extol the virtues of ironsand mining. I’m going to remind the audience that vanadium and other minerals are essential for the climate change journey. Unlike other MPs, we’re prepared to make the hard trade-off decisions. I’m also going to share with the Taranaki audience that soon the oil and gas ban, which destroyed the oil and gas industry, by the last Government will pass through Parliament.
charisma.explanation: 'Unlike other MPs, we’re prepared to make the hard trade-off decisions' is a divisive contrast.

charisma.statement: So much of politics is about hope. Underlying these regional summits and the existence of the pūtea—$1.2 billion—is a demonstration on the part of our Government that we are willing to co-invest. We believe in public-private collaborative efforts... But people have to have confidence that solutions that are discovered in the regions won’t be squashed by Wellington advisers or timid politicians, far too many of whom sit on the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Opens with hope and collaboration but closes with a jab at 'timid politicians' opposite.

charisma.statement: Obviously, geographical knowledge in that part of Auckland is enjoyed by my leader—something sadly absent from the intellect of the questions offered by the Green Party.
charisma.explanation: Belittling the opposing party, the opposite of consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Yes, I do, because the previous Government accepted an increase in gang-related violence, and this Government doesn’t.
charisma.explanation: Confident but framed as a partisan contrast rather than persuasion across the House.

charisma.statement: I think we can agree that legislation is not always the answer to every problem. There is common ground with both parties, and we are working to achieve those positive outcomes without the need for the legislative process.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises common ground and working with both associations.

charisma.statement: Electoral boundaries are important, but, at the same time, it is important that there’s a fair degree of distance between those who are directly affected by it and those who make those decisions... we absolutely support these appointments. We think there’s a high degree of competence and, also, the right approach of the public service by these appointees, notwithstanding the political backgrounds that exist there as well.
charisma.explanation: Bipartisan tone backing government-nominated appointees despite their political backgrounds.

charisma.statement: I stand on behalf of the Green Party to endorse and support the appointment of these representatives of the Government and the Opposition today... May I also comment that I note there’s no wāhine being appointed—just pause on that—but the credentials of those who have been appointed are great.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party endorsement with an inclusive, celebratory framing.

charisma.statement: for those members of the public who might be watching... who despair sometimes at the partisan argument that is such a feature of political life in this Parliament, the process and the collaborative work on this bill... the engagement by parties across the House, I think is a refreshing case study in the way that colleagues in the House here can from time to time come together and work in a very collegial way.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly praises cross-party collaboration and models consensus-building for the public.

charisma.statement: this problem has spanned now three different Governments and the best part of a decade, and the Parliament hasn’t really covered itself in glory in dealing effectively and decisively with the problem at hand... Labour had a scheme in place that provided concessionary loan finance up to $250,000. We are not dying in the ditch to protect that policy. Having taken feedback from the sector and from building owners, Labour colleagues on the committee have taken an open-minded approach.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building, willing to compromise and credit the process across parties.

charisma.statement: It does affect the 808 earthquake-prone buildings that were registered in Wellington on the earthquake-prone buildings register as of 30 April 2024. It is particularly a concern for us, an issue that is live and something that any Government has to work on.
charisma.explanation: Frames the issue as one 'any Government has to work on' and offers Labour’s support.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I always consider the good ideas, so let’s wait and see. We’ve got a few sitting days left in the year and a lot of Government business to get to, but I’m also conscious that members’ business is important, so let’s see how we go.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he would arrange an extended sitting, he neither commits nor refuses — leaves it open with 'we’ll see'.

forthrightness.statement: the infrastructure needs assessment is about looking at our needs over the next five to 30 years and looking at demand drivers, including population growth, renewals, inflation, resilience, and increasing living standards. The needs analysis will set a benchmark so that we can look at what we have against that need and then what we need to do to close that infrastructure deficit over the long term.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the patsy question about the role of the needs assessment.

forthrightness.statement: We’re picking up some ideas that have been used overseas, most notably in parts of Australia where independent agencies take a structured, independent assessment of priority problems and projects... Anyone can submit a proposal through the Infrastructure Commission website into the Infrastructure Priorities Programme—the IPP—and then that will go to the Government, and it will be, ultimately, over to the decision makers to make investment decisions. But we need to be well informed by good data and good evidence around that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains how the priorities programme works, as asked.

forthrightness.statement: That’s a case of what I might call “res ipsa loquitur”—the thing speaks for itself.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which of three coalition figures is correct on Treaty principles, he refuses to answer entirely with a Latin quip.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the difference between some political parties and ones on this side of the House is that we treat every member as an equal. We don’t think we’re superior... The second thing is: by a process of consultation, they came to a conclusion together.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not explain why Potaka was overruled on the fishing decision; deflects into a partisan contrast.

forthrightness.statement: Over the last five years, the Māori smoking rate has halved, while smoking rates are lowest in our young people, signalling a generational shift away from cigarettes. The smoking rate for 18- to 24-year-olds is now down to 4.2 percent, for 15- and 17-year-olds it is down now to less than 1 percent, and daily smoking rates have declined amongst all people.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses smoking trends but reframes the question’s '16,000 rise' claim rather than engaging it directly.

forthrightness.statement: Again, I’m very grateful for that question, because, first of all, it’s based on some experience in rail, where we turned it around between ’17 and ’20, and we saved rail in this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he is considering non-rail-enabled ferries against the coalition agreement, he pivots to past rail record rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that we inherited a seriously failing economy, much worse than many people thought, and a power system that was the most costly in the world.
forthrightness.explanation: Only partially addresses the point of the Regional Infrastructure Fund before shifting to blaming the inherited economy.

forthrightness.statement: We engaged with Ngāi Tahu and the civic leadership of Southland Murihiku... the many thousands of hectares of aquaculture space, as a consequence of the historic aquaculture settlement, was announced. We also visited a host of developments, and I can say that in Bluff we saw pāua being grown.
forthrightness.explanation: Reports concretely on the Southland summit as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, well, obviously, I’m not responsible for the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill. However, I am a champion of the fishing industry. Consultation, from time to time, does take place between Ministers, but, of course, decisions are made by Cabinet, and those discussions are tapu.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice he gave the Conservation Minister, he declines to say, sheltering behind Cabinet confidentiality.

forthrightness.statement: At no time have I shared the name of that company with that Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: A direct, unambiguous denial to the specific question about Leigh Fisheries.

forthrightness.statement: Well, obviously, the price of fish is slightly beyond my grasp. However, as a consequence of quota allocation decisions, not the least of which is a massive expansion of the catchable amount of snapper in New Zealand, I imagine that the value of fish is going to shrink.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the affordability-assurance question ('beyond my grasp') and offers only a general expectation.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, these harmless refinements that were introduced at the point of which the Cabinet discussions process was taking place... are like a beauty spot: they are so small. The vast majority of the Tīkapa Moana reserve areas remain as they were originally introduced.
forthrightness.explanation: Minimises rather than confirming whether Cabinet was fully informed of the official advice.

forthrightness.statement: Tiny, beauty, star, little infinitesimal points will enable four or five additional fishers to provide kaimoana during the months of winter, and it will be thoroughly appreciated by working-class families in “Strugglers’ Gully” that they will have access to affordable kaimoana.
forthrightness.explanation: Sidesteps the fairness question about overriding a decade-long collaborative process with rhetoric about 'infinitesimal' impacts.

forthrightness.statement: There is too much hyperbole in that rendition of official advice. I couldn’t imagine officials would use such imaginative and wild language.
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the question rather than addressing the quoted official advice that the fishing is 'incompatible with the purpose'.

forthrightness.statement: As the lead coordination Minister, it is my responsibility to draw Ministers’ attention to the recommendations that are relevant to their portfolios. It is then the relevant Minister’s or Cabinet’s responsibility to take those decisions.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question of responsibility clearly, but the answer functions to disclaim accountability for outcomes.

forthrightness.statement: That is one of the recommendations that has been considered by the group that I lead, and we will report back in time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether she will meet recommendation 131’s four-month deadline, she neither confirms nor commits.

forthrightness.statement: Well, they can have confidence because there are a number of things that this Government has undertaken since the report has been tabled... this Government had the courage to acknowledge that the torture of young people that took place at Lake Alice was, in fact, torture—a finding that was found by the UN under the previous Government’s watch and that they did nothing about.
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots from the accountability question to a favourable example and a jab at the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, this is an operational matter for the Ministry of Education. I would also like to point out that in 2023, under that member’s Government, 29 routes were cancelled.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines responsibility for the cancelled bus routes as 'operational' and deflects with a tu quoque.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve asked all of the relevant Ministers to write to me with the relevant recommendations that pertain to their portfolios and have asked them to ensure that their work programme reflects those recommendations.
forthrightness.explanation: Describes concrete coordination action taken, though still stops short of addressing the contradictions raised.

forthrightness.statement: Apart from the enforcement action at 2.03 this morning, I’m advised that there has been a high level of compliance with the ban. I’m told that this morning a gang member was arrested in Wairoa for wearing gang insignia to the supermarket and a patched gang member was arrested standing on the street in Papakura. Both patches have been seized.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about further examples of the ban in effect.

forthrightness.statement: When the member asks me a question in the House, I’ll respond with the information I’ve had at the time. It’s very simple.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he lacked information already provided in briefings, he restates a general principle instead of explaining the discrepancy.

forthrightness.statement: Police did provide advice, and I forwarded my recommendations to Cabinet. Cabinet’s made a decision and that’s the end of it.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms advice was given and forwarded but closes down the question of why the advice was not reflected.

forthrightness.statement: We’re banning gang patches because for a gang member to have a gang patch, they have to have shown they have a propensity to commit violent crime. So there is a trail of tears and victims sitting behind each one of those gang patches. They’re designed to intimidate the communities that they operate in, and that’s why we ban them.
forthrightness.explanation: Restates the rationale for the patch ban rather than answering the gun-range and 'blind eye' question put to him.

forthrightness.statement: Poultry farmers should be taking steps to enhance on-farm biosecurity such as investing in secure enclosures to keep birds away from wildlife and from open waterways where wild birds tend to gather. Good on-farm biosecurity and animal husbandry practices like good maintenance, security of feed and water supplies, staff hygiene, and wild bird control have the potential to make a big difference in avoiding infection and limiting spread.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers what poultry farmers can do to prepare.

forthrightness.statement: My plan includes three key components: first, better information sharing across Government and its agencies; second, work with telcos, social media platform providers, and banks to develop industry-led solutions; and, third, engage with ministerial counterparts in Australia and Singapore to look at regional solutions.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what measures he will take.

forthrightness.statement: I think we can agree that legislation is not always the answer to every problem. There is common ground with both parties, and we are working to achieve those positive outcomes without the need for the legislative process.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains an alternative to legislation but does not address the timeline concern squarely.

forthrightness.statement: I will continue to—and do—meet with the residents’ association to identify those key issues... and, on average, the sale of those occupancy rights has been within the nine-month period.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly addresses the residents’ struggle but reframes rather than confronting the hardship raised.

forthrightness.statement: As I have said, there is very good common ground. A lot of the initiatives that we’re hoping will be achieved under this legislation are under way or in action... that is why I’m continuing to meet with those groups and addressing those practical issues to get the job done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the review was pushed to the next parliamentary term, she reiterates 'common ground' without answering the delay.

forthrightness.statement: This bill’s key purpose is to extend the remediation time frames by four years, with a limited power to extend the deadlines by a further two years by Order in Council. The reason is clear: there are many buildings, the length of New Zealand, that would not meet the current deadlines, and they would simply be sitting there empty.
forthrightness.explanation: Clearly states the bill’s purpose and rationale as intended by the debate.

forthrightness.statement: Last Thursday, sadly for the dignity of the House, I was absent. We engaged with Ngāi Tahu and the civic leadership of Southland Murihiku, where the many thousands of hectares of aquaculture space, as a consequence of the historic aquaculture settlement, was announced.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly reports on the Southland summit as asked, including his absence from the House.

specificity.statement: the infrastructure needs assessment is about looking at our needs over the next five to 30 years and looking at demand drivers, including population growth, renewals, inflation, resilience, and increasing living standards. The needs analysis will set a benchmark so that we can look at what we have against that need and then what we need to do to close that infrastructure deficit over the long term.
specificity.explanation: Names a time horizon (5–30 years) and concrete demand drivers, though no figures.

specificity.statement: We’re picking up some ideas that have been used overseas, most notably in parts of Australia where independent agencies take a structured, independent assessment of priority problems and projects... Anyone can submit a proposal through the Infrastructure Commission website into the Infrastructure Priorities Programme—the IPP—and then that will go to the Government, and it will be, ultimately, over to the decision makers to make investment decisions. But we need to be well informed by good data and good evidence around that.
specificity.explanation: Describes a named mechanism (the IPP) and the submission/decision pathway.

specificity.statement: It is something that I would like to see the whole of Parliament get behind and so I’m encouraging all political parties to meet with the Infrastructure Commission to be briefed on the plan. I know some political parties have taken up that opportunity already and I really welcome that and encourage them to do that.
specificity.explanation: A direction (all parties briefed, a debate later next year) with only rough timing.
