veracity.explanation: A widely-repeated claim about NZ farming efficiency that is broadly defensible but often stated more absolutely than evidence supports.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has just fallen seven places in the Climate Change Performance Index released overnight—seven places; not one, not two, but seven places based on the climate inaction—of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific, dated index movement; the drop is checkable, though attributing it wholly to 'this Government' adds spin.

specificity.statement: This year, we had 11 young people begin the 12-month military-style academy pilot, with one young person deciding not to take up the opportunity.
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers (11 participants, 12-month, one opt-out) rather than vague description.

specificity.statement: A young person will be eligible for a young serious offender (YSO) declaration if they are 14 to 17 years old at the time of offending, have committed at least two serious offences, and are likely to go on offending, committing crimes with a sentence of 10 years or more.
specificity.explanation: Precise eligibility mechanism: age band, offence count, and sentence threshold.

specificity.statement: Each one has a mentor who is working with them for 30 hours face to face every week, and there is intensive, tailored support for each young person while they reintegrate into the community.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism and quantity (30 hours weekly), though 'intensive, tailored support' is looser.

specificity.statement: That is why today I’m proud to introduce legislation that builds on the success of the pilot and will be a key to achieving the Government’s target of reducing child and youth offending.
specificity.explanation: Points at a target but gives no measure or timeframe for the reduction.

specificity.statement: This bill is taking us backwards. This bill is seriously dangerous for our young people.
specificity.explanation: A strong characterisation with no mechanism or measure attached in this line.

specificity.statement: An Oranga Tamariki briefing paints a stark picture of the background of these tamariki: 80 percent have a confirmed or suspected mental health - or disability-related diagnosis—80 percent; 20 percent have attempted suicide; 90 percent face significant learning difficulties.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named source and precise figures for the cohort's background.

specificity.statement: I want to shout out to Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services, specifically for their Mahuru programme... Through Mahuru, tamariki remain in their Whare Tapu o Ngāpuhi, where they can reconnect with their culture and heritage and learn about their identity in a supportive and familiar environment.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative programme and provider, though without outcome figures.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First have always consistently championed policies that prioritise public safety, but also with a balance of ensuring that victims are heard and the offenders have the opportunity to rehabilitate.
specificity.explanation: General statement of values without concrete mechanisms.

specificity.statement: This is the reality for our tamariki Māori, who constitute 70 percent of children in State care—70 percent of children in State care.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage, though without the source or year.

specificity.statement: This must not be commended; this must be burnt down. I’m tempted to rip it up.
specificity.explanation: Expressive denunciation with no substantive content.

specificity.statement: They could be required to wear electronic bracelets so that they will be ensured to be identified and made accountable if they were to violate the conditions of their residence.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (electronic monitoring) tied to the residence conditions.

specificity.statement: I’ll tell you what works, Minister: not American-style boot camps. Tikanga Māori works. It’s proven. Talk to Dr Mason Durie. He will tell you to embed our young people in tikanga, te reo, aroha, manaakitanga.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative approach and its elements, though without programmes or figures.

specificity.statement: What did we lose in terms of te reo Māori? Thirty million dollars.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise number but not the programme or timeframe it refers to.

specificity.statement: Ram raids have gone down from 410 in January to September 2023, to 161 between January to September 2024. Note that we used the same months as a comparison. That is a reduction of 61 percent in one year.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts, matched months, and computed percentage change.

specificity.statement: There are 877 fourteen- to 16-year-olds who faced police action in the last year ending June 2023. This was for theft causing injury, and burglary.
specificity.explanation: Exact number, age band, timeframe, and offence types.

specificity.statement: the reoffending rate for young people who have been through these military academies is around 80 percent, whereas for the young people who go through programmes like Kotahi te Whakaaro... the reoffending rate is the opposite. Around 80-plus percent do not go on to reoffend.
specificity.explanation: Contrasts two programmes with concrete reoffending figures.

specificity.statement: I think in Christchurch we’ve seen it more than double from about 46 serious repeat offenders to about 105 young offenders.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete before/after numbers for a named city.

specificity.statement: The sector is our top export earner, contributing to 10.5 percent of GDP, 13 percent of employment, and close to 82 percent of all goods exported.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise percentages quantifying the sector's economic weight.

specificity.statement: Food and fibre export revenue is expected to reach $54.6 billion this year and will hit a record $66.6 billion in 2028.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures and years.

specificity.statement: the Government, in partnership with industry, has committed $400 million over the next four years to accelerate the commercialisation of tools and technology to reduce on-farm emissions.
specificity.explanation: Names an amount, timeframe, and purpose.

specificity.statement: I look forward to working collaboratively with the sector, with iwi Māori, and with New Zealanders on a fair and sustainable pricing system for agricultural emissions for the future.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational tone with 'fair and sustainable' but no mechanism yet defined.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has just fallen seven places in the Climate Change Performance Index released overnight—seven places; not one, not two, but seven places based on the climate inaction—of this Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the index, the magnitude, and the timing of the ranking change.

specificity.statement: This bill does not provide certainty for farmers going forward, and that is why we cannot support it.
specificity.explanation: States the specific objection (lack of certainty) and the resulting position, though 'certainty' stays general.

strength.statement: These young people engaged in three months of the programme without incident and without any safety concerns.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered result from her own pilot, but it is only three of twelve months in and unevaluated, so follow-through is unproven.

strength.statement: Ram raids have gone down from 410 in January to September 2023, to 161 between January to September 2024. Note that we used the same months as a comparison. That is a reduction of 61 percent in one year.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered reduction under this Government's approach with concrete figures, though causation is asserted.

strength.statement: the Government, in partnership with industry, has committed $400 million over the next four years to accelerate the commercialisation of tools and technology to reduce on-farm emissions.
strength.explanation: A concrete funding commitment, but stated as committed spending over four years rather than delivered outcomes.

divination.statement: That is why today I’m proud to introduce legislation that builds on the success of the pilot and will be a key to achieving the Government’s target of reducing child and youth offending.
divination.explanation: Forecasts reduced youth offending from this approach; the weight of cited evidence (high reoffending after boot camps) runs against it, though uncertain.

divination.statement: We also wanted to ensure that inside this bill there is an effective deterrent so that prior to offending, someone may think, “I don’t think I’ll do this because the pain of doing this is not worth it”.
divination.explanation: Predicts would-be offenders will be deterred; weakly supported given evidence on this cohort.

divination.statement: Consequences for crime will bring a drop in youth offending, which has already happened. We’ve seen it.
divination.explanation: Predicts consequences drive down offending; the ram-raid fall she cites is directionally supportive but causation is unestablished.

divination.statement: Food and fibre export revenue is expected to reach $54.6 billion this year and will hit a record $66.6 billion in 2028.
divination.explanation: A dated revenue forecast to 2028; consistent with official projections but subject to commodity and market uncertainty.

civility.statement: How did that work for Labour? These kids were in and out. No help, no support—well done, Labour!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic interjection aimed at scoring against Labour rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: This bill is taking us backwards. This bill is seriously dangerous for our young people.
civility.explanation: Harsh but directed at the policy rather than the person.

civility.statement: You’re giving police greater powers to allow them to designate somebody a serious young offender—children—and arrest those deemed serious young offenders without a warrant and sentence them to your boot camp experiment.
civility.explanation: 'Boot camp experiment' is pointed but the critique targets the policy's substance.

civility.statement: These so-called new boot camps are nothing more than a rehash of past failures—untrained staff, no meaningful oversight, and isolated settings. These were the very conditions that allowed abuse to flourish in the 1970s.
civility.explanation: Strong criticism aimed at the policy design and its history, not at individuals.

civility.statement: Those Ministers who cannot boast toto Māori... hide behind their colleagues’ struggles with disconnection to advance their own bigoted, autocratic agendas.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack imputing bigoted and autocratic motives to named Ministers.

civility.statement: This must not be commended; this must be burnt down. I’m tempted to rip it up.
civility.explanation: Inflammatory theatrics rather than engagement with the bill's substance.

civility.statement: New Zealand First and Winston Peters thought it was 22,000, which shows how stupid New Zealand First are—they don’t know how to count.
civility.explanation: Personal insult ('how stupid') aimed at another party rather than the argument.

civility.statement: There’s what you call the three Ps, just for the Minister... It’s called participation, protection, and partnership... Participation-wise, Māori do not want to participate in your rotten, useless boot camps.
civility.explanation: Condescending framing ('just for the Minister') plus 'rotten, useless' dismissal rather than respectful engagement.

civility.statement: The answer is that it’s the same as with the Treaty principles bill: it ticks a box in their voter base to keep their voters happy, to show that they’re tough... that they can lock up 14-year-olds.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad political motive to the Government rather than engaging its stated rationale.

civility.statement: Deep down, I really believe that Karen Chhour knows that this is a mistake. I think she believes that this is the wrong thing to do for rangatahi and tamariki in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Personalises the debate by speculating about the Minister's private beliefs, though not an insult.

civility.statement: Where’s the balance in manhandling our kids?
civility.explanation: A heckle using the loaded term 'manhandling'; more interjection than engagement, though it gestures at the use-of-force issue.

charisma.statement: How did that work for Labour? These kids were in and out. No help, no support—well done, Labour!
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them jab that rallies her own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I want to shout out to Ngāpuhi Iwi Social Services, specifically for their Mahuru programme... Through Mahuru, tamariki remain in their Whare Tapu o Ngāpuhi, where they can reconnect with their culture and heritage and learn about their identity in a supportive and familiar environment.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive alternative vision, though framed within a strongly oppositional speech.

charisma.statement: I can speak also from personal experience, having been an army reservist: the army isn’t what it used to be. The army is not the place of physical discipline, of overtly aggressive behaviour, and bullying.
charisma.explanation: Engages opponents' stated concern directly and calmly rather than dismissing it.

charisma.statement: Those Ministers who cannot boast toto Māori... hide behind their colleagues’ struggles with disconnection to advance their own bigoted, autocratic agendas.
charisma.explanation: Alienating framing that attacks colleagues' identity rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: a person who is not embedded within their culture burns it to the ground to feel the warmth.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically striking but used to indict opponents rather than build a bridge.

charisma.statement: A lot of us are parents in this House... at some point in time, when our young people... go out and offend—and repetitively offend—then they may need to be put into spaces where they are strongly held into a structure.
charisma.explanation: Measured, inclusive tone ('a lot of us are parents') aimed at common ground.

charisma.statement: New Zealand First and Winston Peters thought it was 22,000, which shows how stupid New Zealand First are—they don’t know how to count.
charisma.explanation: Divisive mockery of opponents, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: But his mum sent him to LSV—the Limited Service Volunteer course... He graduated from LSV. He won many of the awards at LSV... He now runs three businesses, he has a social media following of 40,000 people.
charisma.explanation: A humanising local story that draws the House in, though it appeals mainly to the government side's case.

charisma.statement: Deep down, I really believe that Karen Chhour knows that this is a mistake. I think she believes that this is the wrong thing to do for rangatahi and tamariki in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Attempts a note of shared conscience but frames it as the opponent secretly agreeing, which is not genuinely bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I look forward to working collaboratively with the sector, with iwi Māori, and with New Zealanders on a fair and sustainable pricing system for agricultural emissions for the future.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, collaborative closing that reaches across sectors and to iwi Māori.

charisma.statement: There is something that I absolutely agree on with the previous speaker, the Hon Andrew Bayly, and that is that our farmers here are the most carbon emissions - efficient in the world.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges common ground with the Minister opposite before disagreeing.

charisma.statement: they threw out the baby with the bathwater. There should have been some parts that could have been kept and built on and worked on, rather than putting a new group in place, waiting on more technology, crossing our fingers, and hoping that it will be ready in time.
charisma.explanation: Concedes He Waka Eke Noa's failure while pressing the point, a relatively even-handed tone.

rigor.statement: This pilot hasn’t even finished yet and the Minister is introducing this law today to entrench boot camps. The pilot was a 12-month pilot. We’ve only finished three months of in-residence. It hasn’t even been evaluated.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based objection: legislating before a 12-month pilot has finished or been evaluated is a genuine logical gap.

rigor.statement: It goes against officials’ advice, goes against the Children’s Commissioner’s advice, goes against things that the Chief Judge of the Youth Court is saying works and is needed.
rigor.explanation: Marshals multiple expert sources against the bill; leans partly on appeal to authority but names relevant bodies.

rigor.statement: An Oranga Tamariki briefing paints a stark picture of the background of these tamariki: 80 percent have a confirmed or suspected mental health - or disability-related diagnosis—80 percent; 20 percent have attempted suicide; 90 percent face significant learning difficulties.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited data to argue the cohort needs a therapeutic rather than punitive response; conclusion follows from the evidence.

rigor.statement: These so-called new boot camps are nothing more than a rehash of past failures—untrained staff, no meaningful oversight, and isolated settings. These were the very conditions that allowed abuse to flourish in the 1970s.
rigor.explanation: Draws a historical analogy to past abuse conditions; reasonable but relies on the analogy holding rather than evidence the new model replicates it.

rigor.statement: I can speak to this having been a youth advocate in the courts, having been a defence lawyer in courts across New Zealand, worked in prisons across New Zealand, worked as a mental health advocate across New Zealand. There are some who continue to come back time and time and time again to the courts.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in relevant first-hand professional experience, but rests on appeal to that experience rather than data.

rigor.statement: I can speak also from personal experience, having been an army reservist: the army isn’t what it used to be. The army is not the place of physical discipline, of overtly aggressive behaviour, and bullying.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a concern via personal anecdote about the army; addresses the objection but is an appeal to personal experience.

rigor.statement: It takes time to change behaviour. It doesn’t happen in a few weeks, doesn’t even happen in a couple of months. I know this having had many, many, many clients across New Zealand who have had a desire to change... but they have struggled in rehabilitation programmes to stay focused.
rigor.explanation: Argues the case for a longer intervention from experience; reasonable but anecdotal rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We also wanted to ensure that inside this bill there is an effective deterrent so that prior to offending, someone may think, “I don’t think I’ll do this because the pain of doing this is not worth it”.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a deterrent effect on youth reasoning without evidence, contrary to research opponents cite on repeat youth offenders.

rigor.statement: Those Ministers who cannot boast toto Māori... hide behind their colleagues’ struggles with disconnection to advance their own bigoted, autocratic agendas.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem attack on motive substituting for argument about the policy.

rigor.statement: a person who is not embedded within their culture burns it to the ground to feel the warmth.
rigor.explanation: An evocative aphorism/analogy standing in for an argument about cultural disconnection.

rigor.statement: I have been involved in a United Nations consultative body on the welfare of children for many years, for over 20 years, and accountability is a big factor in the structure that helps to form young people.
rigor.explanation: Supports the accountability point by citing his own long involvement; an appeal to authority/experience rather than evidence on outcomes.

rigor.statement: A lot of us are parents in this House... at some point in time, when our young people... go out and offend—and repetitively offend—then they may need to be put into spaces where they are strongly held into a structure.
rigor.explanation: Reasons by parenting analogy; relatable but leans on the analogy rather than evidence the structure reduces offending.

rigor.statement: I’ll tell you what works, Minister: not American-style boot camps. Tikanga Māori works. It’s proven. Talk to Dr Mason Durie. He will tell you to embed our young people in tikanga, te reo, aroha, manaakitanga.
rigor.explanation: Asserts an approach 'works' and 'is proven' but substantiates it by appeal to an authority (Dr Mason Durie) rather than cited outcomes.

rigor.statement: There’s what you call the three Ps, just for the Minister... It’s called participation, protection, and partnership... Participation-wise, Māori do not want to participate in your rotten, useless boot camps.
rigor.explanation: Structures an argument around Treaty principles but folds in loaded assertions rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Ram raids have gone down from 410 in January to September 2023, to 161 between January to September 2024. Note that we used the same months as a comparison. That is a reduction of 61 percent in one year.
rigor.explanation: Controls for seasonality by matching months, but attributes the fall to police/processes without isolating causes.

rigor.statement: But his mum sent him to LSV—the Limited Service Volunteer course... He graduated from LSV. He won many of the awards at LSV... He now runs three businesses, he has a social media following of 40,000 people.
rigor.explanation: A single success anecdote used to support the policy; also elides that LSV is voluntary, unlike the compulsory MSA.

rigor.statement: Consequences for crime will bring a drop in youth offending, which has already happened. We’ve seen it.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal claim from a correlation without ruling out other drivers.

rigor.statement: the reoffending rate for young people who have been through these military academies is around 80 percent, whereas for the young people who go through programmes like Kotahi te Whakaaro... the reoffending rate is the opposite. Around 80-plus percent do not go on to reoffend.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative outcome data to argue for the evidence-based alternative; conclusion follows if the figures hold.

rigor.statement: the programmes that were put in place—like Kotahi te Whakaaro, like Circuit Breaker, like Fast Track—have been working and contributed to a decrease in youth offending. That is why they have continued to be funded and extended under this Government.
rigor.explanation: Turns the Government's own decision to keep funding these programmes into evidence they work; a coherent argument.

rigor.statement: The answer is that it’s the same as with the Treaty principles bill: it ticks a box in their voter base to keep their voters happy, to show that they’re tough... that they can lock up 14-year-olds.
rigor.explanation: Motive-based explanation (appeal to political cynicism) rather than an evidenced rebuttal.

rigor.statement: She said she saw a multidisciplinary team working on a one-on-one basis, focusing on their trauma, wrapping therapeutic and rehabilitative approaches around the individual.
rigor.explanation: Answers a heckle by citing the Chief Children's Commissioner's first-hand observation of the pilot; relevant sourced evidence.

rigor.statement: I had a mother in my electorate office this week in tears because we are not doing enough to help her child get on the straight and narrow.
rigor.explanation: Emotive constituent anecdote used to justify the bill; appeal to emotion rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The removal of process and reporting obligations... will not affect the ability of the Government to report agricultural emissions. New Zealand’s official estimates of agricultural emissions don’t use this data, and instead use input data from several sources—chiefly Statistics New Zealand, but also DairyNZ, Livestock Improvement Corporation, and Beef + Lamb New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a specific objection by explaining that inventory reporting draws on separate named data sources; a substantive, evidenced response.

rigor.statement: New Zealand has just fallen seven places in the Climate Change Performance Index released overnight—seven places; not one, not two, but seven places based on the climate inaction—of this Government.
rigor.explanation: Uses an external index as evidence, but leaps to sole causation by the Government.

rigor.statement: they threw out the baby with the bathwater. There should have been some parts that could have been kept and built on and worked on, rather than putting a new group in place, waiting on more technology, crossing our fingers, and hoping that it will be ready in time.
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasoned continuity argument that scrapping He Waka Eke Noa entirely discarded usable work, leaving a gap.

rigor.statement: This bill does not provide certainty for farmers going forward, and that is why we cannot support it.
rigor.explanation: Ties the stated conclusion (opposition) to the argued premise that no replacement pricing plan is ready.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First have always consistently championed policies that prioritise public safety, but also with a balance of ensuring that victims are heard and the offenders have the opportunity to rehabilitate.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent party stance on public safety; a defensible positioning statement with no contradicting action shown in the text.

rigor.statement: Saying you believe in climate change and then doing all the things that make climate change worse has exactly the same effect as denying climate change exists in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorically forceful equation of belief-plus-inaction with denial, but asserted rather than demonstrated and glosses the causal nuance.

rigor.statement: how are you to monitor who is doing well in terms of the methods of working out how to reduce emissions and who is doing badly if you don't even keep a track of the reporting and the data?
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that removing measurement/reporting undermines the ability to manage emissions.

rigor.statement: it's been higher in our history, 10 times higher, and here we all are, we're surviving, and things are going along tickety-boo.
rigor.explanation: Appeal-to-nature/false-reassurance that downplays present risk without engaging the actual warming trend.

rigor.statement: The left loves the catastrophisation—end of days, everyone's burning. I heard it yesterday in the House. Arena Williams: we're all boiling, literally boiling, she said.
rigor.explanation: Strawman that caricatures the opposing position.

rigor.statement: It's not all inflation, it's not all competition with the foreign market; it has a lot to do with regulatory burden.
rigor.explanation: Attributes food-price rises to regulation as the cause without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: We've led, as we often do, by having a split gas approach that recognises that methane is a short-lived gas: it dissipates after about a decade. It is part of a natural cycle.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned scientific basis for the split-gas approach, though somewhat selective in framing.

rigor.statement: The Government's own figures from the second emissions reduction plan, the draft consultation document, shows that we're off track to meet the 2050 target. We were on track in the first emissions reduction plan, and now we're off track
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the Government's own published figures.

rigor.statement: I asked the Minister repeatedly, during several stages of the debate, for the cost-benefit analysis for the other options other than the status quo option that was modelled. The Minister didn't even aim to answer that question.
rigor.explanation: Presses for the evidence/cost-benefit basis behind the decision.

rigor.statement: That shift of production overseas, to less-efficient producers, means an increase in global emissions.
rigor.explanation: Coherent emissions-leakage argument, though it rests on the assumed NZ-efficiency premise.

rigor.statement: Try telling the people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti that everything is tickety-boo—tickety-boo when they're watching erosion to the scale where they're not building anymore. Farmers have lost so much land through climate change.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'tickety-boo' claim with a regional example, but largely anecdotal.

rigor.statement: it feels like this Government just does nothing. It just repeals stuff and then doesn't think it through.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping generalisation offered with little supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: The honest response is that I don't want to see agriculture in the emissions trading scheme (ETS) either, but is completely removing them out of it right now, when the Government hasn't got a plan in place to address it, the right response? Well, my honest answer to that would have to be no.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the principle (ag out of ETS) from the timing and the missing plan.

rigor.statement: our reputation and our contribution to the world determines the price that we can get for our products overseas... the free-trade agreements this country has recently signed, in particular the European Union—hugely, hugely beneficial to this country; however, only if we live up to our obligations on climate change.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based linkage between climate obligations, trade access and export prices.

rigor.statement: This is too important for this country to simply have a debate that says, “We love farmers; they hate farmers.”, “They hate farmers; we love farmers.” It's too important for that, because it's not honest and it's also not accurate.
rigor.explanation: Explicitly names the false-dichotomy framing distorting the debate.

charisma.statement: Saying you believe in climate change and then doing all the things that make climate change worse has exactly the same effect as denying climate change exists in the first place.
charisma.explanation: Effectively brands the Government climate deniers — combative framing that shuts down rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: We are the most efficient farmers in the world—second to none; I'm not going to apologise for that.
charisma.explanation: Defiant rallying of the rural base rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: stop the wokery. Start protecting everyday mums and dads—
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing aimed at rallying supporters.

charisma.statement: This isn't your fathers' or your grandfathers' National Party; these are people who have got into bed with people who fundamentally don't believe in the science of climate change
charisma.explanation: Divisive framing that alienates the other side.

charisma.statement: Here on this side of the House, we absolutely know the amazing contribution farmers make to Aotearoa—
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opponents' valid point about farmers and seeks common ground before dissenting.

charisma.statement: unlike that speaker who just spoke, Glen Bennett, on this side of the House, we have real farmers—real farmers
charisma.explanation: In-group/out-group framing rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: They vilified our farmers, they went to war with our farmers, and we are saying no.
charisma.explanation: Rallies the base against the other side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: The honest response is that I don't want to see agriculture in the emissions trading scheme (ETS) either, but is completely removing them out of it right now, when the Government hasn't got a plan in place to address it, the right response? Well, my honest answer to that would have to be no.
charisma.explanation: Concedes shared ground before setting out the disagreement, inviting the other side in.

charisma.statement: if this bill was proposing that the deadline, so to speak, was to be pushed out, say, three years, as an example, I think there's a very good chance that there'd be a lot more support in this House than what there is tonight.
charisma.explanation: Offers a concrete compromise that could win cross-House support.

charisma.statement: This is too important for this country to simply have a debate that says, “We love farmers; they hate farmers.”, “They hate farmers; we love farmers.” It's too important for that, because it's not honest and it's also not accurate.
charisma.explanation: Calls out the false binary and appeals for a higher, shared debate.

charisma.statement: This is a man who has been on fewer farms than Erica Stanford has called Jan Tinetti names... Remember that time he stood on the side of the road with a shovel and pretended he would dig a hole? His shovel wasn't even dirty and his boots weren't even dirty.
charisma.explanation: An in-group applause line that alienates the other side.

charisma.statement: How can the Government form a partnership, not necessarily in the form of a rinky-dink scheme like He Waka Eke Noa, but actually genuinely to partner, to understand what's going on, to support that, to invest, to enable the investment, including the technology?
charisma.explanation: Partnership framing that reaches out, though still partisan in tone.

charisma.statement: we cannot ignore, however, that vaping has been a contributor as a lower-harm product that has allowed people to exit from smoking.
charisma.explanation: Balanced framing acknowledging the trade-off, aimed at bringing both sides along.

veracity.statement: This Government has systematically, over the course of its term, cancelled just about every single climate initiative that there is.
veracity.explanation: Directionally true that many climate policies were reversed, but 'every single' is hyperbole that overstates the record.

veracity.statement: They've brought back the oil and gas industry, they're going to fast track the coal industry, and they're telling the dairy industry, “You're exempt from your emissions pricing.”
veracity.explanation: Oil/gas exploration reversal and agriculture leaving the ETS are real; 'fast track the coal industry' is an overstatement.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has dropped seven places to 41st in the global Climate Change Performance Index, which ranks countries based on their emissions
veracity.explanation: Direct quotation of the CCPI result; accurate and sourced.

rigor.statement: Racing is inherently dangerous for dogs. On any given day at a greyhound race, dogs risk suffering from broken bones, dislocations, ruptured muscles, spinal damage, and wounds.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'inherently dangerous' premise with a concrete enumeration of injury types.

rigor.statement: In the most recent 2023 to 2024 season, Greyhound Racing New Zealand’s animal welfare report said nine dogs were euthanised because of injuries suffered during a race, up from seven the season before; 224 dogs suffered serious injuries; and a further 672 had injuries classified as minor or medium in the past season, according to the report.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited statistics to substantiate the animal-welfare case.

rigor.statement: when 70 percent of the injuries occur on the corner and even now we don’t have the level of infrastructure to get around that—we have no real choice but to race them around on tight tracks—we weren’t making the improvements that would’ve been necessary for greyhound racing to maintain its social licence.
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific statistic and a structural cause (corners/tracks) that logically supports the conclusion.

rigor.statement: if the task itself is so dangerous that it leads to unacceptable levels of injury and unacceptable levels of death, then this was the only conclusion that we could reach.
rigor.explanation: Clean conditional argument tying the danger premise to the closure conclusion.

rigor.statement: The Animal Welfare Act doesn’t create a right to life or restrict owners from killing healthy dogs for solely economic purposes, so what this bill will do is create an offence of imprisonment of up to 12 months or fines of up to $50,000 if someone were to breach the law that we’re going to pass today.
rigor.explanation: Explains the legal gap and how the bill fills it — premise-to-conclusion reasoning.

rigor.statement: I understand that people, like Edward, were working and had introduced a trial of a straight track at Whanganui, but in my view it didn’t go far enough—it didn’t go fast enough—and we hadn’t seen enough change to say that this industry had changed
rigor.explanation: Grounds the 'lost social licence' judgement in a specific unmet reform (straight tracks).

rigor.statement: there are too many animals injured, too many animals that needed to be euthanised, and a number of—a small number, I might add—contributors to the industry that weren’t doing their part. I do want to acknowledge those that have contributed to the industry in a positive way over many years
rigor.explanation: Gives injury/euthanasia grounds for the decision, though stated loosely.

rigor.statement: There is a lesson in here for the horse racing industry: to make sure that we do everything we can to look after the animals and give them a good life.
rigor.explanation: Draws an analogy/lesson to another code, reasonable but not evidenced.

civility.statement: The industry has made genuine efforts, particularly within recent years, to address the animal welfare issues, and this should be acknowledged, especially in regard to dog deaths.
civility.explanation: Credits the affected industry even while closing it; respectful, no personal attack.

civility.statement: could I thank, across the political divide, the other parties in Parliament—all the other parties in Parliament—for their committed support for this action.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgment of opponents.

civility.statement: We met with Edward Rennell from Greyhound Racing New Zealand, and I came away from that meeting convinced that he had a genuine commitment to trying to achieve the best outcomes for dogs.
civility.explanation: Names and credits an industry figure's good faith despite opposing the industry.

civility.statement: I am sure that 90 or 99 percent of people in the industry will be doing that, but this legislation is to protect from that small percentage who may not be.
civility.explanation: Emphasises that the vast majority of the industry acts well; avoids demonising.

civility.statement: I also want to acknowledge those organisations who have advocated so long and hard for the protection of greyhounds—Save Animals from Exploitation, Helping You Help Animals, Veterinarians for Animal Welfare Aotearoa, Dogwatch, and the SPCA
civility.explanation: Respectful, credit-sharing tone.

civility.statement: As has been already acknowledged in this House, the vast majority of dog owners do care for their animals, and I want to stress that.
civility.explanation: Explicitly defends the affected owners rather than attacking them.

civility.statement: [We would like to add our support of this bill. It is amazing to see the huge support from all parties on this bill, despite the pressures brought upon by politics at this time. I am delighted to see the immense support by all parties on this bill.]
civility.explanation: Positive, cooperative framing toward all parties.

civility.statement: I just want to make the point that although we are rushing through this legislation, it is to safeguard the welfare of animals and not because we inherently believe that all greyhound owners are bad people.
civility.explanation: Explicitly avoids demonising owners while justifying urgency.

civility.statement: it’s one of those rare moments people keep asking us for, where the whole Parliament works together and we don’t take political potshots at each other; we acknowledge the work that our opponents have done to lead to this.
civility.explanation: Explicitly renounces personal attacks and honours opponents' work.

civility.statement: if the task itself is so dangerous that it leads to unacceptable levels of injury and unacceptable levels of death, then this was the only conclusion that we could reach.
civility.explanation: Focuses on the task, not on blaming owners ('no matter how much love').

civility.statement: We have seen a reduction in deaths. Unfortunately, we haven’t seen a big enough reduction in the number of injuries that are occurring to dogs.
civility.explanation: Fairly credits the industry's progress before criticising.

civility.statement: I understand that people, like Edward, were working and had introduced a trial of a straight track at Whanganui, but in my view it didn’t go far enough—it didn’t go fast enough—and we hadn’t seen enough change to say that this industry had changed
civility.explanation: Acknowledges industry effort while criticising pace, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge previous racing Ministers Grant Robertson and Kieran McAnulty, who did a lot of that initial work, and now the Minister, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who has taken that step.
civility.explanation: Credits predecessors across the aisle and the current Minister.

civility.statement: there are too many animals injured, too many animals that needed to be euthanised, and a number of—a small number, I might add—contributors to the industry that weren’t doing their part. I do want to acknowledge those that have contributed to the industry in a positive way over many years
civility.explanation: Distinguishes a 'small number' of bad actors from the majority, crediting the latter.

civility.statement: I would wish that we could do more of this and have more support generally for positive bills across the House.
civility.explanation: Constructive, non-adversarial appeal.

charisma.statement: The industry has made genuine efforts, particularly within recent years, to address the animal welfare issues, and this should be acknowledged, especially in regard to dog deaths.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the other side's good faith, softening a hard decision.

charisma.statement: could I thank, across the political divide, the other parties in Parliament—all the other parties in Parliament—for their committed support for this action.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party, unifying, invites shared credit.

charisma.statement: We met with Edward Rennell from Greyhound Racing New Zealand, and I came away from that meeting convinced that he had a genuine commitment to trying to achieve the best outcomes for dogs.
charisma.explanation: Generous, bridge-building acknowledgment of the other side.

charisma.statement: I am sure that 90 or 99 percent of people in the industry will be doing that, but this legislation is to protect from that small percentage who may not be.
charisma.explanation: Reassuring, inclusive framing toward the affected group.

charisma.statement: [We would like to add our support of this bill. It is amazing to see the huge support from all parties on this bill, despite the pressures brought upon by politics at this time. I am delighted to see the immense support by all parties on this bill.]
charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party unity, inclusive tone.

charisma.statement: it’s one of those rare moments people keep asking us for, where the whole Parliament works together and we don’t take political potshots at each other; we acknowledge the work that our opponents have done to lead to this.
charisma.explanation: Strongly unifying, credits opponents, seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge previous racing Ministers Grant Robertson and Kieran McAnulty, who did a lot of that initial work, and now the Minister, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who has taken that step.
charisma.explanation: Generous, credit-sharing, cross-party tone.

charisma.statement: I would wish that we could do more of this and have more support generally for positive bills across the House.
charisma.explanation: Calls for more cross-party cooperation; unifying.

authenticity.statement: In 2006, when previously the Minister for Racing, I launched the first Greyhounds as Pets adoption scheme, and that was 18 years ago.
authenticity.explanation: Current action on greyhound welfare is consistent with a long-standing prior initiative under him — words match a demonstrated record.

authenticity.statement: I said that the Governor-General was in the Chatham Islands and therefore couldn’t sign the document today. Her flight got cancelled, so she can sign the document.
authenticity.explanation: Proactively corrects his own earlier statement on the record — words revised to match reality.

authenticity.statement: I regret that because Cyclone Gabrielle hit when it did, and the direction was that cyclone-related pieces of legislation would take priority and other things would need to take a step back, this could’ve happened before the last election. I personally regret that it hasn’t
authenticity.explanation: Candid, self-critical admission his own government did not deliver sooner; consistent but partly self-justifying via the cyclone reason.

authenticity.statement: I mentioned the petitioner who has taken a number of petitions to ban greyhound racing, but I said “Steve Cross”... I meant to say “Aaron Cross”, who is also an agitator and stands up for fairness, but this time for dogs.
authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily corrects her own earlier misstatement on the record — a candid accuracy correction.

forthrightness.statement: clearly in the veterinary practices, the vet is able to assign qualified people within his organisation—not necessarily veterinarians but oversight is still his or hers, and that’s how the job’s done.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Utikere's question about why the vet-student wording differs, explaining the oversight mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: a year in prison, or $50,000, is a pretty stiff fine and enough to be a serious consideration if someone’s thinking about offending. As to where it fits into the criminological code, well, who knows—it depends who you’re talking to and which side of the House you’re on on this matter, so I don’t want to go there at this time of bipartisan approach.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers that the penalty is a strong deterrent but explicitly declines the core of the question — whether it is consistent with other offences.

civility.statement: Once again, this Government is the Grinch that stole Christmas.
civility.explanation: A sensationalist seasonal jibe casting the Government as a villain; rhetorical, not a personal insult of an individual, but demonising rather than substantive.

civility.statement: This legislation is appalling. The Government is introducing legislation that will make it easier to penalise workers fighting for better pay and conditions. It is dire, Draconian, and outright disgraceful, even by this own Government’s standards.
civility.explanation: Harsh, hyperbolic condemnation of the policy ('dire, Draconian, disgraceful') rather than a personal attack; criticises the bill but with sensational language.

civility.statement: Workers should be getting ready to organise against this Government and make them a one-term Government.
civility.explanation: A campaigning call to action against the Government; combative but aimed at political mobilisation rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I have worked in transport for most of my career, and I have seen examples where bus drivers will turn up for work and they will drive around the route with the door closed and refuse to let passengers on, or they will refuse to take revenue to subsidise the ratepayer-funded public transport.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused explanation of the bill's rationale with no personal attack on opponents.

civility.statement: We are reintroducing a piece of legislation that was revoked in 2018, which is not saying that nobody can strike, which is not saying that nobody can partially strike; it’s to say that there actually has to be a consequence for the impact that this has on a business, on the Public Service, on the customer, on the member of the public that is entitled to that public service.
civility.explanation: Pre-empts and engages the opposing argument on its substance rather than caricaturing it.

civility.statement: We have always believed in the egalitarian principle that a fair day’s work deserves a fair day’s pay, but both of those things need to go together. To get your fair day’s pay, you do have to do a fair day’s work, and to be able to withdraw your labour and still get paid doesn’t balance, in our view.
civility.explanation: States a principled position in measured terms without attacking opponents personally.

civility.statement: We continuously hear from and see from the Government for the elite, by the elite, from the elite; out there to make sure that they’ve demonised every hard-working person, every community, anyone that wants to fight for their rights.
civility.explanation: Sweeping imputation of bad motive ('for the elite, by the elite') and the charge that the Government has 'demonised' workers; caricature rather than engagement with the bill.

civility.statement: This bill is not about protecting workers or the general public; it’s about protecting unfair, bad employers from any consequences.
civility.explanation: Attributes bad faith to the bill's purpose ('protecting unfair, bad employers') rather than engaging its stated rationale.

civility.statement: it did not fall on deaf ears when Te Pāti Māori referred to the work that is being done, that these employees are partially striking from, as being the “bits and pieces”.
civility.explanation: Misattributes and recasts an offhand phrase ('bits and pieces', actually used by the Green speaker) as disrespect for workers—a strawman used to score a point.

civility.statement: That was a shocking speech—absolute shocker—and par for the course from an ill-informed National Party, who, sadly, are being led around by the one and only David Seymour over there, who is taking all their votes at the moment, as you can see. The puppet master is leading them.
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of colleagues as 'ill-informed' and 'puppet'/'puppet master'; attacks people rather than the argument.

civility.statement: he was bravely standing three kilometres from the hīkoi with all his police escorts around him, but the very brave and courageous David Seymour was there and he was looking out at the hīkoi.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic personal mockery of an individual member's courage; a cheap shot unrelated to the bill's substance.

civility.statement: on that hīkoi, 60,000-plus—so many workers were protesting against his dirty, rotten ACT Party and this coalition.
civility.explanation: 'Dirty, rotten ACT Party' is a personal/party insult rather than substantive criticism.

civility.statement: That’s not an incentive to settle a dispute—it’s actually an incentive to go all the way and not protest by a partial withdrawal of labour, but it actually incentivises a full withdrawal of labour. It’s completely impractical. It doesn’t do what it says on the tin.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy's logic and workability rather than the people proposing it.

civility.statement: A very simple principle in life: if you want to get the full pay, do the full day.
civility.explanation: States a principle plainly without attacking opponents, though dismissive of the opposing case.

civility.statement: the amendments in Amendment Paper 238 in my name are matters of public policy as described in Standing Order 257 and, therefore, more than appropriate for consideration as an Amendment Paper. I would point you, sir, to the example of the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Bill considered by the last Parliament, which also included a list of projects in its schedule, with some promoted by private entities.
civility.explanation: Vigorous but procedurally focused disagreement with the ruling, without personal attack.

civility.statement: if we are going to today decide that matters of a private nature which confer private benefits can be lumped into public bills, we are fundamentally changing some of the constitutional precepts which underpin this Parliament.
civility.explanation: Argues the constitutional substance without denigrating the bill's proponents personally.

civility.statement: I wonder if you might draw the member speaking’s attention to Standing Order 112. She’s so far spoken for a minute and hasn’t actually addressed the bill. She has made a number of imputations about the motivations of the Government to which you might draw your attention.
civility.explanation: A procedurally grounded point of order citing specific standing orders; legitimate, though used tactically to interrupt an opponent.

civility.statement: the Government of the day chose to issue a guarantee to the BNZ as a matter of public policy to protect the banking system and the depositors—clearly a matter of benefit to the public and a matter of public policy. I don’t think that’s a precedent that the Minister can rely upon, because it wasn’t conferring a private benefit to the BNZ; it was conferring a benefit to the banking system and to the depositors.
civility.explanation: Substantive, respectful legal rebuttal addressed to the argument, not the person.

charisma.statement: Once again, this Government is the Grinch that stole Christmas.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than building any cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: The Greens will continue to fight this legislation every step of the way.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative rallying of his own side; no attempt to persuade the undecided or find common ground.

charisma.statement: Workers should be getting ready to organise against this Government and make them a one-term Government.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly divisive us-vs-them mobilisation, shutting down consensus.

charisma.statement: This is a proportionate response to something that has a disproportionate impact on the public, and I think that when we go through the select committee process, we will hear just that.
charisma.explanation: Measured and confident, appealing to process, but ultimately a defence of her own side's position.

charisma.statement: The employer, if there is a partial strike going on, is still paying a price—they’ve lost that productivity during that period—and the chance of a spurious walkout is mitigated because there are consequences for people withdrawing their labour, workers withdrawing their labour.
charisma.explanation: Frames the bill as balanced and mutual rather than adversarial, an appeal to fairness beyond his own base.

charisma.statement: We continuously hear from and see from the Government for the elite, by the elite, from the elite; out there to make sure that they’ve demonised every hard-working person, every community, anyone that wants to fight for their rights.
charisma.explanation: Highly divisive elite-vs-workers framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: productivity, fundamentally, is about these workers earning money at a value for the roles that they play.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to reclaim a contested term in workers' favour, but embedded in a partisan rebuttal.

charisma.statement: That was a shocking speech—absolute shocker—and par for the course from an ill-informed National Party, who, sadly, are being led around by the one and only David Seymour over there, who is taking all their votes at the moment, as you can see. The puppet master is leading them.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing attack on opponents with no attempt at persuasion or common ground.

charisma.statement: Who are employers? They’re mums and dads that work hard.
charisma.explanation: Attempts a relatable, humanising frame for employers, but rests on an emotive appeal.

specificity.statement: This legislation is appalling. The Government is introducing legislation that will make it easier to penalise workers fighting for better pay and conditions. It is dire, Draconian, and outright disgraceful, even by this own Government’s standards.
specificity.explanation: Strings of adjectives with only a general characterisation of what the bill does; no figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: If you want to minimise disruptions to public services, you pay people properly—you pay the nurses, you pay the teachers, you pay people properly.
specificity.explanation: 'Pay people properly' names the direction but no amount, mechanism, or how it would be funded.

specificity.statement: I have worked in transport for most of my career, and I have seen examples where bus drivers will turn up for work and they will drive around the route with the door closed and refuse to let passengers on, or they will refuse to take revenue to subsidise the ratepayer-funded public transport.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete, illustrative behaviours (doors closed, refusing revenue) that make the abstract concept tangible.

specificity.statement: We are reintroducing a piece of legislation that was revoked in 2018, which is not saying that nobody can strike, which is not saying that nobody can partially strike; it’s to say that there actually has to be a consequence for the impact that this has on a business, on the Public Service, on the customer, on the member of the public that is entitled to that public service.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the bill to a specific prior legislative state (pre-2018) and its purpose, though without the deduction mechanics.

specificity.statement: Wāhine Māori and Pasifika are, effectively, working for free for the rest of the year when they compare the pay to the average Pākehā man’s salary. Over a lifetime, Māori women will have earned over $400,000 less than Pākehā men.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete comparative figure and framing (lifetime earnings gap vs Pākehā men).

specificity.statement: Approximately 93 percent of Māori have experienced some form of workplace discrimination, as disclosed in findings released just last year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise percentage and attributes it to recent findings.

specificity.statement: This bill is not about protecting workers or the general public; it’s about protecting unfair, bad employers from any consequences.
specificity.explanation: A characterisation of intent with no concrete mechanism or evidence attached.

specificity.statement: A broken workforce means broken services—whether it’s healthcare, education, or public safety.
specificity.explanation: Names the affected sectors but offers no measure or mechanism of the claimed harm.

specificity.statement: if we go to the regulatory impact statement on this bill, it says in paragraph 32 that “Enabling employers to make partial pay deductions in response to partial strikes would be consistent”—would be consistent—“with the approach in Australia (from 2009)”... It goes on to say, “and the United Kingdom (UK)(in case law from the 1980s).”
specificity.explanation: Names the document, paragraph number, jurisdictions, and dates.

specificity.statement: This is a cynical move by the Government. They’re amending our work from 2018, and it weakens workers’ ability to ask for better conditions and pay; that’s just the reality. It’s part of this wider Government’s strategy in terms of rolling back workers’ rights, including getting rid of fair pay agreements, 90-day trials.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete related measures and the 2018 baseline being amended.

specificity.statement: we had the president, Rachel Mackintosh, calling on political parties to vote down this terrible piece of legislation. She said that it will undermine the ability of workers to engage in industrial action and may even lead to workers losing pay for simply doing their job.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, her role, and the substance of her stated concern.

specificity.statement: the simple act of, for example, a nurse who’s part of industrial action wearing a union T-shirt, which includes a demand for better pay, for example, instead of their uniform at their place of work, could actually be penalised, could have their pay deducted by 10 percent or whatever it would be under the formula in the bill.
specificity.explanation: Uses a concrete worked example (T-shirt, 10 percent deduction, formula) to illustrate the bill's operation.

specificity.statement: every single time—every single time—a bill comes before this House that has the potential either to increase incomes or to diminish them, that side of the House always votes to reduce the incomes and the bargaining power of workers in this country. We saw it in the demolition of fair pay agreements earlier in the term. We saw it in the minimum wage increase that wasn’t actually a real increase; it was a real reduction in the minimum wage. We saw it in the restoration of the 90-day, fire-at-will trial legislation, and now this.
specificity.explanation: Cites multiple concrete, named measures to substantiate the pattern claim.

specificity.statement: A very simple principle in life: if you want to get the full pay, do the full day.
specificity.explanation: A pithy slogan capturing the bill's principle but with no mechanism, figure, or detail.

specificity.statement: the amendments in Amendment Paper 238 in my name are matters of public policy as described in Standing Order 257 and, therefore, more than appropriate for consideration as an Amendment Paper. I would point you, sir, to the example of the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Bill considered by the last Parliament, which also included a list of projects in its schedule, with some promoted by private entities.
specificity.explanation: Names the standing order, the amendment paper, and a directly comparable prior bill.

specificity.statement: a wind farm listed in the Fast-track Approvals Bill by Government-owned Meridian Energy would be able to be listed because it is a 51 percent-owned Crown mixed-ownership company; however, a hydroelectric power scheme seeking to be listed in the bill by privately owned Contact Energy... would not be able to be listed because it is a listed public company, despite the reason for the listing being the exact same reason.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific companies, ownership percentages, and project types to make the point concrete.

specificity.statement: We have three instances here—in 2003, 2006, and 2018—when this ruling was made and upheld. In fact, we would put to you that if you were to rule against the presiding officer—and then, in doing so, against the advice of the Clerk—that would actually be unprecedented.
specificity.explanation: Gives three dated precedents and identifies the exact procedural stakes.

specificity.statement: a development in Ōhoka in Canterbury is one of them. They have lost in the courts, and by coming into this schedule, they are, essentially, trying to use this House as a final court of appeal to confer a private benefit.
specificity.explanation: Names the Ōhoka development and its court history to ground the objection.

specificity.statement: where the Speaker was returned to the chair in that case and backed the ruling of the chair of the committee, it was because the private benefit conferred at an amendment stage went to the heart of what a private bill is meant to be, which is promoted by the promoter so that there is sufficient public scrutiny that has been invited by that promoter, and that the private benefit was well understood. Neither of those two things were met in that case.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific features (promotion by promoter, public scrutiny) that define a private bill and maps them onto the case.

specificity.statement: the question of whether the benefits given by this bill is public or private is actually moot. It doesn’t give any benefit. It doesn’t take from one and give to another. It simply allows people to use their property rights with a little bit less bureaucracy and rigmarole than they’d otherwise face under laws made by this House.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism in general terms (reduced bureaucracy on property rights) without engaging the specific schedule items.

specificity.statement: the Government of the day chose to issue a guarantee to the BNZ as a matter of public policy to protect the banking system and the depositors—clearly a matter of benefit to the public and a matter of public policy. I don’t think that’s a precedent that the Minister can rely upon, because it wasn’t conferring a private benefit to the BNZ; it was conferring a benefit to the banking system and to the depositors.
specificity.explanation: Engages the specific cited precedent and the exact basis on which it differs.

specificity.statement: This legislation changes the Conservation Act, the Resource Management Act, the normal protections in the Wildlife Act, and many other pieces of legislation, for the benefit of the people that get that special leg-up.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutes affected to substantiate the claim that the bill alters legal rights, not just process.

specificity.statement: It is not sustainable to continue to argue that the impact of this schedule will be enjoyed by a narrow range of New Zealanders. It is profound. It is not inconsistent with the public welfare, which this bill seeks to produce.
specificity.explanation: Claims wide impact in general terms without naming projects, beneficiaries, or scale.

specificity.statement: These are not broad impacts. This is about a specific set of 149 projects that specifically impacts quite a narrow group of people, and I want to give one example, being the Waimate waste incineration plant. This is an entirely private company. It impacts one school, a very set amount of farmers.
specificity.explanation: Cites the number of projects (149) and a named example (Waimate incineration plant) with its specific, limited footprint.

rigor.statement: If you want to minimise disruptions to public services, you pay people properly—you pay the nurses, you pay the teachers, you pay people properly.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal claim (better pay → fewer strikes → less disruption) but asserted without evidence and reliant on repetition for emphasis.

rigor.statement: Everybody across the House likes to talk a big game about the brain drain, but where do you think these people go? Where do people go when they lose their jobs? They get on a plane and they get out of here to find better work and conditions.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical-question reasoning; plausible link but leans on assertion and anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: I have worked in transport for most of my career, and I have seen examples where bus drivers will turn up for work and they will drive around the route with the door closed and refuse to let passengers on, or they will refuse to take revenue to subsidise the ratepayer-funded public transport.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in first-hand sector experience with concrete examples of partial-strike conduct; persuasive but rests on personal anecdote rather than systematic data.

rigor.statement: We have always believed in the egalitarian principle that a fair day’s work deserves a fair day’s pay, but both of those things need to go together. To get your fair day’s pay, you do have to do a fair day’s work, and to be able to withdraw your labour and still get paid doesn’t balance, in our view.
rigor.explanation: A reciprocity argument that follows logically from its stated premise, though the premise itself is asserted as principle rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The employer, if there is a partial strike going on, is still paying a price—they’ve lost that productivity during that period—and the chance of a spurious walkout is mitigated because there are consequences for people withdrawing their labour, workers withdrawing their labour.
rigor.explanation: Presents a two-sided incentive argument (both parties bear cost), which is internally coherent, though the claim that this incentivises settlement is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: particularly, I know from personal experience, the teachers’ strikes under the last Government, where the teachers were just striking and striking and striking, and the inconvenience to the general public was enormous.
rigor.explanation: Relies on personal anecdote and repetition rather than data on frequency or impact.

rigor.statement: Approximately 93 percent of Māori have experienced some form of workplace discrimination, as disclosed in findings released just last year.
rigor.explanation: Uses a cited statistic to support the argument for strike rights, though the causal link is asserted.

rigor.statement: A broken workforce means broken services—whether it’s healthcare, education, or public safety.
rigor.explanation: A plausible slogan-like causal chain across named sectors, but asserted as a truism without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: if we go to the regulatory impact statement on this bill, it says in paragraph 32 that “Enabling employers to make partial pay deductions in response to partial strikes would be consistent”—would be consistent—“with the approach in Australia (from 2009)”... It goes on to say, “and the United Kingdom (UK)(in case law from the 1980s).”
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a cited official document and specific comparators (Australia 2009, UK case law), with the conclusion following from the source.

rigor.statement: productivity, fundamentally, is about these workers earning money at a value for the roles that they play.
rigor.explanation: Reframes 'productivity' against the opposition's characterisation; a reasonable definitional point but asserted rather than argued from evidence.

rigor.statement: This is a cynical move by the Government. They’re amending our work from 2018, and it weakens workers’ ability to ask for better conditions and pay; that’s just the reality. It’s part of this wider Government’s strategy in terms of rolling back workers’ rights, including getting rid of fair pay agreements, 90-day trials.
rigor.explanation: Situates the bill within a pattern of named policy changes (fair pay agreements, 90-day trials), which strengthens the argument, though 'cynical' imputes motive without proof.

rigor.statement: Who are employers? They’re mums and dads that work hard.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to sympathy that generalises all employers as hardworking 'mums and dads'; rhetorical framing rather than reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: We’ve also heard about people heading across the Ditch for the brain drain. Well, you’ve got to ask yourself: why are they going? It’s because of a recession forced by the administration.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical-question reasoning asserting a single cause for a complex trend, without evidence.

rigor.statement: the simple act of, for example, a nurse who’s part of industrial action wearing a union T-shirt, which includes a demand for better pay, for example, instead of their uniform at their place of work, could actually be penalised, could have their pay deducted by 10 percent or whatever it would be under the formula in the bill.
rigor.explanation: Illustrative example supports the 'unfair' claim; hedged ('or whatever it would be'), and the worst-case reading is asserted rather than tested.

rigor.statement: That’s not an incentive to settle a dispute—it’s actually an incentive to go all the way and not protest by a partial withdrawal of labour, but it actually incentivises a full withdrawal of labour. It’s completely impractical. It doesn’t do what it says on the tin.
rigor.explanation: A genuine counter-incentive argument: penalising partial strikes may push toward full strikes; logically coherent, though the behavioural claim is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: the amendments in Amendment Paper 238 in my name are matters of public policy as described in Standing Order 257 and, therefore, more than appropriate for consideration as an Amendment Paper. I would point you, sir, to the example of the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Bill considered by the last Parliament, which also included a list of projects in its schedule, with some promoted by private entities.
rigor.explanation: Frames the test correctly (public-policy vs private benefit) and supports it with a specific, on-point precedent; argument follows from the cited rule and example.

rigor.statement: a wind farm listed in the Fast-track Approvals Bill by Government-owned Meridian Energy would be able to be listed because it is a 51 percent-owned Crown mixed-ownership company; however, a hydroelectric power scheme seeking to be listed in the bill by privately owned Contact Energy... would not be able to be listed because it is a listed public company, despite the reason for the listing being the exact same reason.
rigor.explanation: A tight reductio: two functionally identical projects treated differently by ownership status, exposing an inconsistency in the opposing interpretation.

rigor.statement: if the position is taken that the Government is unable to propose legislation like this to Parliament, it will set a dangerous precedent that will fundamentally undermine the executive’s power to progress matters of public policy through legislation and will potentially lead to perverse outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A consequentialist argument that edges toward a slippery-slope, though grounded in a genuine institutional concern.

rigor.statement: We have three instances here—in 2003, 2006, and 2018—when this ruling was made and upheld. In fact, we would put to you that if you were to rule against the presiding officer—and then, in doing so, against the advice of the Clerk—that would actually be unprecedented.
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific precedents to argue the ruling is well-established and that overturning it would be the true departure; conclusion follows from the cited instances.

rigor.statement: a development in Ōhoka in Canterbury is one of them. They have lost in the courts, and by coming into this schedule, they are, essentially, trying to use this House as a final court of appeal to confer a private benefit.
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific case to argue the schedule confers private benefits on parties who failed in court, tying the general principle to a concrete instance.

rigor.statement: if we are going to today decide that matters of a private nature which confer private benefits can be lumped into public bills, we are fundamentally changing some of the constitutional precepts which underpin this Parliament.
rigor.explanation: A constitutional-principle argument distinguishing private from public bills, coherent and consistent with the cited scholarship, though the stakes are stated in strong terms.

rigor.statement: New Zealand’s Parliament has the fewest veto points of any Western Parliament. The Speaker is one of them, and you are being asked to use that power today to preserve the constitutional arrangements of New Zealand’s democracy.
rigor.explanation: Situates the Speaker's decision within a structural argument about checks on power; the framing supports the request, if somewhat elevated.

rigor.statement: where the Speaker was returned to the chair in that case and backed the ruling of the chair of the committee, it was because the private benefit conferred at an amendment stage went to the heart of what a private bill is meant to be, which is promoted by the promoter so that there is sufficient public scrutiny that has been invited by that promoter, and that the private benefit was well understood. rigor.explanation: Closely reads the Ngāti Mutunga precedent, distinguishing it precisely and applying its ratio to the current facts; disciplined analogical reasoning.

rigor.statement: I have never seen the ruling of a presiding officer, a Chair of the committee of the whole House, on the admissibility of an Amendment Paper... overruled by the Speaker during the time that I have been here.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to consistent institutional practice to argue against overruling; reasonable but partly an appeal to precedent/experience.

rigor.statement: the question of whether the benefits given by this bill is public or private is actually moot. It doesn’t give any benefit. It doesn’t take from one and give to another. rigor.statement: I was the Minister responsible for the overseas investment legislation, where the exemption that was given to a development up North was ruled out by the Speaker. I accepted that ruling as being proper, and I think the same principle applies here.

rigor.statement: It is not sustainable to continue to argue that the impact of this schedule will be enjoyed by a narrow range of New Zealanders. It is profound. It is not inconsistent with the public welfare, which this bill seeks to produce.

veracity.explanation: NZ's unicameral, no-upper-house system does have unusually few institutional veto points; broadly defensible, though 'fewest of any Western Parliament' is a strong comparative claim.

veracity.statement: I have never seen the ruling of a presiding officer, a Chair of the committee of the whole House, on the admissibility of an Amendment Paper... overruled by the Speaker during the time that I have been here.
veracity.explanation: A first-hand claim over 16 years in the House; plausible and specific, though inherently a claim about his own experience rather than an exhaustive record.

veracity.statement: This legislation changes the Conservation Act, the Resource Management Act, the normal protections in the Wildlife Act, and many other pieces of legislation, for the benefit of the people that get that special leg-up.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track regime did override provisions across the named conservation/planning statutes; accurate in substance, framed critically.

veracity.statement: These are not broad impacts. This is about a specific set of 149 projects that specifically impacts quite a narrow group of people, and I want to give one example, being the Waimate waste incineration plant. This is an entirely private company. It impacts one school, a very set amount of farmers.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track schedule did contain a fixed list of projects and the Waimate proposal was a private venture; the characterisation is specific and broadly accurate.

divination.statement: This is a proportionate response to something that has a disproportionate impact on the public, and I think that when we go through the select committee process, we will hear just that.
