divination.statement: if the position is taken that the Government is unable to propose legislation like this to Parliament, it will set a dangerous precedent that will fundamentally undermine the executive’s power to progress matters of public policy through legislation and will potentially lead to perverse outcomes.

divination.statement: you’ll find yourself recalled very, very frequently if that becomes your practice.
divination.explanation: Predicts frequent future recalls if the Speaker overrules presiding officers; a plausible behavioural forecast about how parties would exploit the change, but uncertain.

strength.statement: The Greens will continue to fight this legislation every step of the way.

authenticity.statement: every single time—every single time—a bill comes before this House that has the potential either to increase incomes or to diminish them, that side of the House always votes to reduce the incomes and the bargaining power of workers in this country. veracity.statement: the economy has reached a turning point. Inflation is back under control... The Reserve Bank has begun reducing interest rates.

specificity.statement: the new Dunedin Hospital, that started life as $1.2 billion and ended up on the thick end of $3 billion. It's a bit like with iReX... two new ferries for $700 million. Except, they forgot about the $3 billion on top of that to actually house the ferries.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific project costs and escalations.

rigor.statement: net core Crown debt under the previous Government went from $57 billion to $175 billion; more than $100 billion added to debt in just five years under the past Government, going from 19.5 percent of GDP to over 40 percent of GDP.
rigor.explanation: Cites concrete data to support the claim of fiscal deterioration; conclusion follows, though it omits the COVID context driving much of the borrowing.

rigor.statement: spending was so lavish—went up by more than 80 percent on things like light rail phantom projects that went nowhere... that operating Crown expenses went from under 30 percent of GDP, 27 percent, to more than 33 percent. And all of that spending, what did it do? It drove inflation to 7.2 percent, creating the worst cost of living crisis in a generation.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause reasoning ('all of that spending... drove inflation') ignores global inflation drivers; a causal leap beyond the evidence.

rigor.statement: As recently as March—just eight months ago, colleagues—she told Radio New Zealand that a future Labour Government would consider taking on more debt... Just two weeks ago at the Labour Party conference... she argued that surplus... is a moot point. This kind of mixed position is very hard to take seriously.
rigor.explanation: Attempts to show inconsistency in an opponent's position using dated references; a reasonable argument but relies on paraphrase the House can't verify.

rigor.statement: This time last year, HYEFU was projecting a 1.5 percent growth this year; now, the actual rate is minus 0.2 percent. Next year's growth, at the Budget in May, was projected to be 1.7 percent, but it's now projected to be 0.5 percent.
rigor.explanation: Uses the Government's own forecast revisions as evidence that conditions worsened; conclusion supported by the cited figures.

rigor.statement: This is the austerity playbook. It is to defund public services to failure, to watch them fail, point that out to the public, and then say, "Hey, we should privatise that." Mark my words: that is the next thing on the agenda.
rigor.explanation: Imputes deliberate intent ('defund to failure') without evidence—an inference about motive presented as established fact.

rigor.statement: the top 311 households in this country hold more wealth combined than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders... those at the top pay an effective tax rate less than half that of the average New Zealander.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the inequality argument in a specific IRD report; reasoning follows, though 'effective rate' includes unrealised gains that complicate the comparison.

rigor.statement: the economy is not a car. The economy is all of us, the stuff that we create, and the rules that we put in place in order to try and get certain outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the Minister's analogy with a reframing, but the counter-claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: in 2018, 2019, when Chlöe Swarbrick was on the Government benches, voting for every Budget, the Government spent 27 percent, 28 percent at max; today, in this statement, the Government is spending 33 percent of GDP. Only Chlöe Swarbrick can point to a Government that's spending five percentage points more of the economy than she was responsible for spending and then say that this is an austerity Government.
rigor.explanation: Uses spending-as-share-of-GDP data to challenge the 'austerity' label; a coherent evidence-based rebuttal, though it sidesteps the year-on-year cuts Swarbrick was describing.

rigor.statement: a political career is a little bit like one of those polaroid photos: slowly, people see your true form. Chlöe Swarbrick is increasingly being found out for having great-sounding rhetoric, but when you look at even the most basic facts... she doesn't stack up.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an ad hominem framing and an analogy in place of evidence for the specific claim.

rigor.statement: the spending was made necessary by the excessive response to COVID... the spending kept on going, even after COVID had ended.
rigor.explanation: A defensible argument that post-COVID spending was not wound back, though 'excessive response' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: look no further than the massive growth in export income coming from the primary sector announced last week. Fisheries up. Horticulture up. Farming up. Forestry increasing.
rigor.explanation: Cites recent export data as evidence the 'recipe' works, but attributing the gains to the Government's regulatory changes is asserted, not demonstrated.

rigor.statement: This is what happens when you put a landlord who flips houses for profit in charge of the country.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem framing that attributes economic outcomes to a leader's personal property dealings without evidence of causation.

rigor.statement: When you're the Minister of Finance, it costs $1 million an hour. That is how much this Government is borrowing to make up the services they cut.
rigor.explanation: Vivid figure deployed for effect with no shown calculation; appeal to emotion over evidence.

rigor.statement: When we see in this Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update that transitional housing has been removed as a risk... Sure, the expenditure on motels has been reduced, but I can tell you, Mr Speaker—and we have many, many cases—they are living in their cars.
rigor.explanation: Links a fiscal line-item change to human impact via constituent cases; a reasonable inference but relying on anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: Revenue forecast, as a result of that constriction in our economy, is down $13 billion over the forecast period, peaking at around a $4 billion reduction per annum over that period... The likely comparative numbers around that are the Defence budget and the Police budget. Together, they do not even add up to $13 billion.
rigor.explanation: Uses a relatable comparison to convey the scale of the shortfall; evidence-based, though attributing all of it to the prior Government is a partisan simplification.

rigor.statement: On page 67, these statements tell us that the Health New Zealand operating deficit is a risk. What does that tell you about the attitude of that Government? It says that people and their health are a risk, a real risk.
rigor.explanation: Trades on an equivocation—'fiscal risk' in the document is budget-terminology, not a claim that people are a risk; a strawman reading.

rigor.statement: if we lift tertiary education, if we ensure that around about 80 percent of New Zealanders have a diploma or a degree, then productivity will lift, but... the funding for tertiary education... doesn't change at all. In fact, it stays at around about $5 billion. There is no investment in tertiary education.
rigor.explanation: Connects a stated productivity goal to the flat funding line in the document to expose a gap; a coherent evidence-based argument, though the 80% target link to productivity is asserted.

rigor.statement: their novel financial measure, OBEGAL... Alas, that standard measure did not show what the Government wanted, so they've created a new measure called OBEGALx, which does give a measure that the Government likes. They have engaged in some more creative accounting.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine measurement change and argues it flatters the books; a reasonable point, though it doesn't detail why the excluded items are illegitimate.

rigor.statement: Having taken net core Crown debt from $57 billion... to $175 billion in just five years, their solution is to borrow more, spend more, and tax more.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the attack in real debt figures but caricatures the opponents' position rather than engaging their actual argument.

rigor.statement: the new Dunedin Hospital, that started life as $1.2 billion and ended up on the thick end of $3 billion. It's a bit like with iReX... two new ferries for $700 million. Except, they forgot about the $3 billion on top of that to actually house the ferries.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete cost-overrun examples to argue projects were under-costed; the examples support the point, though presented one-sidedly.

civility.statement: what she's surrounded by is a group of people who wouldn't know how to run a business and a set of accounts if it rolled them over.
civility.explanation: Personal, disparaging attack on the competence of opponents rather than engagement with their arguments.

civility.statement: As recently as March—just eight months ago, colleagues—she told Radio New Zealand that a future Labour Government would consider taking on more debt... Just two weeks ago at the Labour Party conference... she argued that surplus... is a moot point. This kind of mixed position is very hard to take seriously.
civility.explanation: Pointed critique of an opponent's contradictory positions—harsh but aimed at the substance of her stance rather than pure insult.

civility.statement: we are setting up for a two-track economy—that is, wage and salary earners, beneficiaries, and small businesses all going backwards. Meanwhile, the oligopolies—that is, our banks, our supermarkets, and our gentailers—will continue to compound their power and their profits under decisions made by this Government.
civility.explanation: Attacks Government policy and 'oligopolies' on substance rather than making personal attacks on members.

civility.statement: a political career is a little bit like one of those polaroid photos: slowly, people see your true form. Chlöe Swarbrick is increasingly being found out for having great-sounding rhetoric, but when you look at even the most basic facts... she doesn't stack up.
civility.explanation: Personalised attack on an opponent's character ('true form', 'found out') rather than her specific argument.

civility.statement: Yes, you'll hear all sorts of strange, bizarre rationalisations from the cooker, lentil speakers from that side of the House.
civility.explanation: Name-calling ('cooker, lentil speakers') directed at opponents rather than their arguments.

civility.statement: the Māori Party won't be here at the next election. If the Serious Fraud Office doesn't drive them out, the people who voted them in will turn their backs on them.
civility.explanation: Invokes an SFO matter to disparage a rival party's continued existence—an attack rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: It was a very bleak day that, in a tawdry attempt to capture public attention, members on the other side of the House sought to stigmatise, demonise, and spread a whole host of mythology about applicants... I want to apologise to the people associated with projects on that list, including the Winton company, that they were dragged through muck.
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of a 'tawdry' smear campaign; harsh characterisation of their conduct, though framed around a defence of named applicants.

civility.statement: You get a Prime Minister who makes $769,500 in untaxed capital gains while he cuts school lunches.
civility.explanation: A pointed personal attack on the Prime Minister's finances rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: This is what happens when you put a landlord who flips houses for profit in charge of the country.
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of the Prime Minister ('a landlord who flips houses') rather than engagement with policy.

civility.statement: Be afraid, be very, very afraid, of Budget 2025 and what it is going to bring. It is going to bring more cuts. It certainly isn't going to bring more spending.
civility.explanation: Uses fear-based rhetoric ('be very, very afraid') but is directed at Government policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Nicola Willis has given a clear message to the country today that she has prioritised tax cuts for landlords and tax breaks to tobacco companies over the fact that New Zealand needs more spending.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Minister's priorities pointedly but on the substance of her policy choices.

civility.statement: They are like crickets. They are crickets because they do not take accountability for their actions.
civility.explanation: A mocking characterisation of opponents ('crickets') rather than engagement with their position.

civility.statement: On page 67, these statements tell us that the Health New Zealand operating deficit is a risk. What does that tell you about the attitude of that Government? It says that people and their health are a risk, a real risk.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Government's 'attitude' by reinterpreting a technical term, but stops short of a personal insult.

civility.statement: I thought it was interesting when Barbara Edmonds led off the debate... but actually we spent 90 seconds with a sob story. It was sort of like a year 10 debating speech that somehow made its way into Parliament.
civility.explanation: Belittles an opponent's speech ('sob story', 'year 10 debating speech') rather than engaging its content.

charisma.statement: what she's surrounded by is a group of people who wouldn't know how to run a business and a set of accounts if it rolled them over.
charisma.explanation: Demeaning us-vs-them jab that rallies her own side rather than persuading anyone.

charisma.statement: the economy is not a car. The economy is all of us, the stuff that we create, and the rules that we put in place in order to try and get certain outcomes.
charisma.explanation: An inclusive 'all of us' framing, though delivered as a rebuttal to opponents rather than a bridge to them.

charisma.statement: a political career is a little bit like one of those polaroid photos: slowly, people see your true form. Chlöe Swarbrick is increasingly being found out for having great-sounding rhetoric, but when you look at even the most basic facts... she doesn't stack up.
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing attack line aimed at diminishing an opponent, not building consensus.

charisma.statement: I'm confident we will see a turn-around that will keep these people far away from any levers of power for a generation to come.
charisma.explanation: Triumphalist us-vs-them line aimed at his own side, not at persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: Yes, you'll hear all sorts of strange, bizarre rationalisations from the cooker, lentil speakers from that side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Derisive labelling of opponents; divisive rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This piece of legislation is built on an innovation that the Hon David Parker introduced during COVID, into this House, to fast track the consideration of proposals dedicated to boosting New Zealand's resilience.
charisma.explanation: Credits an opponent's earlier work as the foundation of the bill—an uncharacteristic cross-party acknowledgement.

charisma.statement: there can be no fiscal wellbeing without Māori wellbeing. Deficits will not disappear until Māori are at the table.
charisma.explanation: An inclusive appeal to bring Māori 'to the table', though framed within an otherwise combative speech.

charisma.statement: They are like crickets. They are crickets because they do not take accountability for their actions.
charisma.explanation: A dismissive applause line for his own side, not an attempt to persuade the other.

charisma.statement: I thought it was interesting when Barbara Edmonds led off the debate... but actually we spent 90 seconds with a sob story. It was sort of like a year 10 debating speech that somehow made its way into Parliament.
charisma.explanation: A mocking put-down aimed at his own benches, not at persuading across the aisle.

divination.statement: the economy has reached a turning point. Inflation is back under control... The Reserve Bank has begun reducing interest rates.
divination.explanation: The 'turning point' framing forecasts sustained recovery; plausible given easing inflation and rate cuts, but growth forecasts were being revised down.

divination.statement: we are now able to forecast confidently a sustained period of economic growth.
divination.explanation: Prediction of sustained growth, but the same HYEFU downgraded near-term growth forecasts, so 'confidently' is optimistic relative to the evidence.

divination.statement: This is the austerity playbook. It is to defund public services to failure, to watch them fail, point that out to the public, and then say, "Hey, we should privatise that." Mark my words: that is the next thing on the agenda.
divination.explanation: Predicts a future move to privatisation; falsifiable but speculative, with no cited evidence of a privatisation plan in the documents.

divination.statement: we are setting up for a two-track economy—that is, wage and salary earners, beneficiaries, and small businesses all going backwards. Meanwhile, the oligopolies—that is, our banks, our supermarkets, and our gentailers—will continue to compound their power and their profits under decisions made by this Government.
divination.explanation: Predicts diverging outcomes between ordinary earners and large firms; directionally plausible but the magnitude and mechanism are asserted, not modelled.

divination.statement: We are going to reduce wasteful Government spending. I predict we're going to have to reduce it by around $6 billion and find ways to do stuff better and smarter.
divination.explanation: A quantified forecast of ~$6bn in spending reductions; plausible as an intention but uncertain in delivery.

divination.statement: I'm confident we will see a turn-around that will keep these people far away from any levers of power for a generation to come.
divination.explanation: A partisan prediction that opponents will be out of power 'for a generation'—highly uncertain and not evidence-based.

divination.statement: the Māori Party won't be here at the next election. If the Serious Fraud Office doesn't drive them out, the people who voted them in will turn their backs on them.
divination.explanation: Predicts Te Pāti Māori will be eliminated at the next election; speculative and contradicted by their electoral trajectory.

divination.statement: Be afraid, be very, very afraid, of Budget 2025 and what it is going to bring. It is going to bring more cuts. It certainly isn't going to bring more spending.
divination.explanation: Predicts further cuts in Budget 2025; directionally supported by the document's flagged 'optionality' around future savings, though the magnitude is asserted.

authenticity.statement: there's now a fiscally disciplined team in charge... It is why we have instilled a disciplined fiscal stance with very tight operating allowances.
authenticity.explanation: Claims fiscal discipline while the same update forecasts rising debt-to-GDP and continued deficits; a stated stance whose delivery is genuinely in progress and unproven.

authenticity.statement: The operating balance was in deficit for five years, and now Barbara Edmonds stands up and says, "Nicola Willis is running deficits." Yep, we are running deficits, and we're determined to get back to surplus as quickly as we can.
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges the Government is running deficits rather than denying it, aligning words with the acknowledged fiscal reality while asserting a surplus goal.

strength.statement: We are going to reduce wasteful Government spending. I predict we're going to have to reduce it by around $6 billion and find ways to do stuff better and smarter.
strength.explanation: A concrete stated commitment to cut spending, but delivery is prospective and unproven at this point.

strength.statement: I move, That the Fast-track Approvals Bill be now read a third time.
strength.explanation: Jones is actually carrying a coalition-negotiated bill through its third reading into law—a stated commitment being delivered, not merely announced.

veracity.statement: And the progress that we are making by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years, having inflation at 2.2 percent to have wages growing faster than inflation for the first four quarters of this Government versus 13 under the last one where it went backwards, having the official cash rate and interest rates down, having actually business sentiment and confidence up and consumer confidence up—we're making good progress. A long way to go, but we're on the right track.
veracity.explanation: Inflation ~2.2% and lower OCR/interest rates broadly match late-2024 data; 'tax relief for the first time in 14 years' and the wages-vs-inflation framing are selectively favourable but directionally defensible.

veracity.statement: We have actually had stable rents under this Government versus $180 per week under Labour. Our source of data, from memory, is the tenancy bond data.
veracity.explanation: Calling rents 'stable' while official annual rent inflation was 4.5% is misleading; selects tenancy-bond data over the cited Stats NZ figure.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his claim, "We haven't had a single rent increase; it's been stable rents over the last 12 months."; if so, how does he reconcile that with Statistics New Zealand's annual rent inflation figure of 4.5 percent over that time, over twice the rate of headline inflation?
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites Stats NZ annual rent inflation of 4.5% to challenge the PM's 'stable rents' claim; a verifiable, well-sourced factual point.

veracity.statement: Well, I don't agree with that, but I'll just say to you members: the New Zealand public can see that this is a Government that's getting the work done. They can see that inflation's down, they can see that interest rates are down, they can see that crime is down, and—compared to the ungodly mess that that Government left us—they can see we're making progress.
veracity.explanation: Inflation and interest rates down are accurate; 'crime is down' is contested and depends on measure/timeframe.

veracity.statement: Well, the member makes a very good point. It should be remembered that by the time we came into Government, the cost of the ferries—the ships themselves—was just 21 percent of the total cost of iReX. That is to say, four in every five dollars was going towards costs that weren't even ships, with the blowout having been overseen by members who were in that Cabinet and sat by while New Zealanders' money was recklessly put at risk.
veracity.explanation: The '21% of total cost' figure is plausible and consistent with the reported iReX blowout, though presented in the most damaging light.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge that's an incredibly tough situation. There are many New Zealanders that have had a very difficult year and continue to do so, and that is directly a function of economic mismanagement over the previous six years. When Government spending goes up 84 percent, when inflation goes up to 7.3 percent, and when interest rates go up 12 or 13 times and you end up putting an economy into recession, people start losing their jobs—it's tough.
veracity.explanation: 'Spending up 84 percent' and 'inflation to 7.3 percent' cite real datapoints but attribute the child-poverty situation wholly to Labour, which is contestable.

veracity.statement: What's not fair is that 23,000 children were put into poverty in the last year under the Labour Government. Thanks to our Budget actions, 17,000 children are being moved out of poverty, and that is because we're offering tax relief, that's because we're getting inflation relief, that's because we're getting interest rate relief.
veracity.explanation: The 23,000/17,000 figures are drawn from official poverty projections but are framed one-sidedly; the same Budget report warned of children pushed into poverty.

veracity.statement: But I also want to say that Oji, the company that is behind the mill, is a large multinational corporation with billions of dollars of investment. They have said for some time that the paper mill is unprofitable, and it hasn't been helped by the Labour-Greens energy policy, which ended up creating high electricity wholesale prices, because the Green Party thought it was a great idea to import Indonesian coal rather than to use domestic gas.
veracity.explanation: Oji's unprofitability claims are real, but pinning high wholesale power prices on 'the Green Party' importing Indonesian coal is a simplified, contestable causal claim.

veracity.statement: Well, I would encourage Te Pāti Māori and the Greens and Labour—if they cared about the environment, if they cared about our energy policy, they would back us in ending the oil and gas ban. They would back the legislation around fast-track legislation that is building 30 percent more renewable electricity into this country.
veracity.explanation: '30 percent more renewable electricity' is an aspirational projection tied to fast-track projects, not an established figure.

veracity.statement: It was suggested that a young person had died in the military-style academy pilot. This is simply untrue. A young person has tragically died in the community whilst in whānau placement. The attempt to use the death of a young person for political gain is absolutely shameful and disgusting, and that statement was actually shared on social media by someone who should have known better, and that was Green MP Tamatha Paul.
veracity.explanation: Draws a factual distinction—death occurred in community whānau placement, not in the pilot—that is verifiable and material, though presented forcefully.

veracity.statement: Even Auckland Transport's recent annual report highlighted that only 29 percent of Aucklanders felt the organisation listens and responds to their needs.
veracity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure attributed to a named report; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: I'm pleased to say that we have recently expanded the Ministry of Social Development's phone-based case management service to support 10,000 job seekers. This has increased the total number of people who are being supported by an MSD employment case manager at any time to 70,000.
veracity.explanation: Specific operational figures presented as fact; plausible and checkable against MSD data.

veracity.statement: Yes, I do: victimisations are down, ram raids are down, aggravated robberies are down, serious assaults are down, burglaries are down, crime in the Auckland CBD is down. Foot patrols are up. Police are back on their core role, keeping communities safe. Gang patches are banned.
veracity.explanation: A rapid-fire list of 'down' metrics presented without timeframe; several are directionally supported but selectively framed to credit his tenure.

veracity.statement: he was correct in stating that the funding by this Government goes through to June 2026. That's how appropriations work. But he would also agree with me and say that under this coalition Government, an excellent recruitment policy... for 500 additional police officers is to be delivered in November of this year, unlike the previous Government, who promised 1,800 and only delivered 1,500.
veracity.explanation: The 1,800-promised/1,500-delivered comparison is a contested characterisation of Labour's record used to frame his own target favourably.

veracity.statement: The context is that since 2019, the cost of construction increased by 40 percent. That was due to many different factors, including additional costs imposed by the rules in the form that they were imposed that came into effect late last year.
veracity.explanation: 'Construction cost up 40% since 2019' is broadly in line with reported cost inflation, though attributing it partly to recent insulation rules is a narrower, contestable claim.

veracity.statement: Sadly, the security was undermined as the closure of the Marsden Point refinery was green lighted by the Labour Government. To reverse that imperilment... we have announced that new rules are about to be put in place to ensure that we have at least 10 days of jet fuel at the country's busiest airport.
veracity.explanation: Marsden Point's conversion did occur under Labour, but 'green lighted by the Labour Government' overstates government agency in what was a commercial decision by the operator.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister explain how it was that a commission of $400 million to buy two ferries ended up at $3.2 billion, and 80 percent of that money was not to do with the ferries but with infrastructure that was not required in the first tender that was put out in 2020, when somebody who knew what he was doing was running the outfit?
veracity.explanation: The $400m-to-$3.2b escalation and the roughly four-fifths non-ship cost share align with reported iReX figures, presented in the most damaging framing.

specificity.statement: And the progress that we are making by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years, having inflation at 2.2 percent to have wages growing faster than inflation for the first four quarters of this Government versus 13 under the last one where it went backwards, having the official cash rate and interest rates down, having actually business sentiment and confidence up and consumer confidence up—we're making good progress. A long way to go, but we're on the right track.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (2.2% inflation, four quarters, 14 years) but bundles them into a general progress claim.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, the Government announced it is proceeding with plans to provide Kiwibank with access to more capital. The Treasury and Kiwibank's parent company, Kiwi Group Capital, will talk to New Zealand KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups about a potential investment of up to $500 million in the bank.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism, the parties, and a concrete figure (up to $500m).

specificity.statement: I've been advised that an additional $500 million of capital could support up to $4 billion of business lending or $10 billion of home lending. That is sufficient to add competitive pressure to the market. Treasury calculates that even a 0.25 percent drop in personal and business lending rates across all banks would save customers $1.5 billion to $2 billion a year.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures: $4b/$10b lending, 0.25% rate drop, $1.5–2b annual savings.

specificity.statement: A future Government may consider the possibility of a public share offering at some point, but, at this stage, the potential offering would be limited to KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups... Therefore, the Government is not considering a market float during this term of Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the eligible investor classes and a concrete date (2028) constraining any float.

specificity.statement: What's not fair is that 23,000 children were put into poverty in the last year under the Labour Government. Thanks to our Budget actions, 17,000 children are being moved out of poverty, and that is because we're offering tax relief, that's because we're getting inflation relief, that's because we're getting interest rate relief.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific child numbers and the policy levers, though the causal attribution is broad.

specificity.statement: We're going to do everything we can to meet some very ambitious goals.
specificity.explanation: 'Do everything we can' commits to nothing measurable.

specificity.statement: The new legislation will allow the ability for a judge or a court to decide on the level of intensive response that is needed for a young person based on their needs. It is to be no less than three months, but no more than 12 months.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete bounds (no less than 3, no more than 12 months) and the decision mechanism.

specificity.statement: There's some questions in there that I may not be able to answer because they may not be to my knowledge, but there have been three young people that have had accusations of reoffending.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete figure though notes it may not capture all offending asked about.

specificity.statement: On Friday, I announced, alongside Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown, that our Government is restoring democratic accountability to transport decision-making in Auckland, ensuring voters can hold their elected representatives accountable for the city's transport policies.
specificity.explanation: Names the announcement and partner but the 'democratic accountability' claim is high-level until the mechanisms are spelled out.

specificity.statement: Well, our reforms will return regional transport policy and planning to Auckland Council; establish a new Auckland regional transport committee, which will develop a 30-year integrated transport plan for Auckland, designate Auckland Council as Auckland's road-controlling authority, and empower Auckland Council to have control over its council-controlled transport organisation.
specificity.explanation: Lists four concrete structural changes and a 30-year planning horizon.

specificity.statement: Unsurprisingly, yes, I am. Last week's changes to the around $78 million Marsden Fund ensure our limited funding is focused on the areas of science research with the greatest potential to grow our economy while enhancing quality of life for New Zealanders. The Marsden Fund will continue to support blue-skies research, but will now focus on those core science areas more likely to lead to scientific breakthroughs.
specificity.explanation: Gives the fund size ($78m) and the refocusing criterion, though 'core science areas' is left somewhat open.

specificity.statement: it's wrong to say that the entire focus will be on economic gain; only 50 percent of the applications, or around that, will need to show that they can actually start to grow the economy and they have potential to do so. There is still blue-skies research, but it will be on science.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the economic-relevance requirement rather than speaking only in generalities.

specificity.statement: most of those that he's named are not science. They are, however, very important, and many of those are already funded through the funding that the universities get—if I think about things like, for instance, the Performance-based Research Fund, the centres of research excellence, and tuition subsidies. In addition to that, many Government departments commission research to support policy objectives.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete funds and agencies (PBRF, CoREs, Treasury, Reserve Bank, MBIE, etc.).

specificity.statement: I do not think $360,000 of taxpayer money to look at what are the implications of policing climate justice activism—nah, that's not science... I'm not happy with things like $360,000 going for Big Things, Complex Shadows: Investigating Intersecting Stories Of Place, Identity, And Erasure Through Aotearoa's Large Roadside Sculptures... this is all about, basically, the carrot outside Paeroa. No, I don't think that's science.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact dollar figures and named grants to illustrate her point.

specificity.statement: I'm pleased to say that we have recently expanded the Ministry of Social Development's phone-based case management service to support 10,000 job seekers. This has increased the total number of people who are being supported by an MSD employment case manager at any time to 70,000.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers for the expansion (10,000) and total coverage (70,000).

specificity.statement: people under the age of 25 who come on to a main benefit are currently forecast to spend an average of about 20 future years on welfare over their lifetime. This is a 49 percent increase over the figures in 2017.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise figures: ~20 future years, 49% increase, 2017 baseline.

specificity.statement: The figures provided by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment in relation to the first part of the consultation... indicates that up to $15,000 may be saved in the case of each new build.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete potential saving ($15,000 per build) and its source (MBIE consultation).

specificity.statement: Sadly, the security was undermined as the closure of the Marsden Point refinery was green lighted by the Labour Government. To reverse that imperilment... we have announced that new rules are about to be put in place to ensure that we have at least 10 days of jet fuel at the country's busiest airport.
specificity.explanation: Concrete measure: at least 10 days of jet fuel at the busiest airport under new rules.

specificity.statement: The new rules will be in place by November 2026. This is to ensure that no indiscriminate decisions are made which have unintended consequences... They have to respect that if they want their social licence to be esteemed in New Zealand, they have to step up to the plate and not further undermine our fuel security.
specificity.explanation: Gives a firm implementation date (November 2026) though the enforcement expectations on fuel companies are stated in general terms.

specificity.statement: Well, obviously the oil and gas industry is about to be re-established, but I'm confident that the 21-day cover for diesel or for jet fuel as a stockholding rule will boost our resilience. We are also completing an independent study on the options as to how Marsden Point may further play a role in respect of fuel security... given it was trashed over the last three years.
specificity.explanation: Cites a 21-day stockholding cover and an independent study on Marsden Point, though 'about to be re-established' is vague on timing.

strength.statement: And the progress that we are making by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years, having inflation at 2.2 percent to have wages growing faster than inflation for the first four quarters of this Government versus 13 under the last one where it went backwards, having the official cash rate and interest rates down, having actually business sentiment and confidence up and consumer confidence up—we're making good progress. A long way to go, but we're on the right track.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivered macro outcomes (tax relief, lower rates); some are Reserve Bank driven rather than direct government delivery.

strength.statement: Yesterday, the Government announced it is proceeding with plans to provide Kiwibank with access to more capital. The Treasury and Kiwibank's parent company, Kiwi Group Capital, will talk to New Zealand KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups about a potential investment of up to $500 million in the bank.
strength.explanation: An announcement of intent to raise capital, not yet delivered—Cabinet decision still pending mid-next-year.

strength.statement: What's not fair is that 23,000 children were put into poverty in the last year under the Labour Government. Thanks to our Budget actions, 17,000 children are being moved out of poverty, and that is because we're offering tax relief, that's because we're getting inflation relief, that's because we're getting interest rate relief.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of poverty reduction via Budget measures that are forecast rather than yet realised outcomes.

strength.statement: Yes, in the context in which I said and did them; in particular, my statements that Oranga Tamariki does not have the ability to restrict the movement of these young people, or the choices they make once they leave the residence and return to the community, and also my statement that we have already seen success with the military-style academy, including involvement for the participants in jobs, education, and training.
strength.explanation: Claims early 'success' for a pilot on the basis of participation in jobs/education, which is in-progress rather than a durable delivered outcome.

strength.statement: On Friday, I announced, alongside Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown, that our Government is restoring democratic accountability to transport decision-making in Auckland, ensuring voters can hold their elected representatives accountable for the city's transport policies.
strength.explanation: An announced reform delivered jointly with the mayor, but implementation is prospective.

strength.statement: I'm pleased to say that we have recently expanded the Ministry of Social Development's phone-based case management service to support 10,000 job seekers. This has increased the total number of people who are being supported by an MSD employment case manager at any time to 70,000.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered expansion of a service, not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: Yes, I do: victimisations are down, ram raids are down, aggravated robberies are down, serious assaults are down, burglaries are down, crime in the Auckland CBD is down. Foot patrols are up. Police are back on their core role, keeping communities safe. Gang patches are banned.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a range of crime measures and the enacted gang-patch ban, mixing genuinely legislated change with trend claims.

strength.statement: So after 12 months of hearing from those commentators and others that the police didn't have the capability and the gangs were too strong, I think the police have answered that one in the last two weeks. They've done an outstanding job in policing the new gang legislation, and they've let the country know... that they are controlling the streets, not the gangs.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted gang-patch legislation being actively enforced as evidence of follow-through, not just intent.

strength.statement: The new rules will be in place by November 2026. This is to ensure that no indiscriminate decisions are made which have unintended consequences... They have to respect that if they want their social licence to be esteemed in New Zealand, they have to step up to the plate and not further undermine our fuel security.
strength.explanation: A committed timeline for rules not yet in force; delivery remains prospective.

charisma.statement: And the progress that we are making by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years, having inflation at 2.2 percent to have wages growing faster than inflation for the first four quarters of this Government versus 13 under the last one where it went backwards, having the official cash rate and interest rates down, having actually business sentiment and confidence up and consumer confidence up—we're making good progress. A long way to go, but we're on the right track.
charisma.explanation: Confident and reassuring but framed against 'the last' government, appealing mainly to his own side.

charisma.statement: Well, I don't agree with that, but I'll just say to you members: the New Zealand public can see that this is a Government that's getting the work done. They can see that inflation's down, they can see that interest rates are down, they can see that crime is down, and—compared to the ungodly mess that that Government left us—they can see we're making progress.
charisma.explanation: 'Ungodly mess that that Government left us' is combative us-vs-them framing rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This is a Government that believes we should celebrate people who have been successful and that are working incredibly hard to get ahead. If you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you are a fiscal conservative, unlike the last Labour-led Government.
charisma.explanation: Defines caring about workers as being a 'fiscal conservative, unlike' Labour—an us-vs-them framing that excludes rather than persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: Well, I would encourage Te Pāti Māori and the Greens and Labour—if they cared about the environment, if they cared about our energy policy, they would back us in ending the oil and gas ban. They would back the legislation around fast-track legislation that is building 30 percent more renewable electricity into this country.
charisma.explanation: 'If they cared about the environment' impugns opponents' motives rather than inviting them in—divisive rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: In all seriousness, I came into this role to make the lives of young people better. Children and young people have been hurt and harmed for over 20 to 30 years... What I can say is I will put all safety mechanisms that I can in place to keep these young people safe, but we cannot continue to do what we were doing, which was absolutely nothing.
charisma.explanation: Earnest, values-based appeal, but 'which was absolutely nothing' frames predecessors dismissively.

charisma.statement: On Friday, I announced, alongside Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown, that our Government is restoring democratic accountability to transport decision-making in Auckland, ensuring voters can hold their elected representatives accountable for the city's transport policies.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises working alongside the Auckland mayor—a cross-institutional, collaborative note.

charisma.statement: Yes, I do: victimisations are down, ram raids are down, aggravated robberies are down, serious assaults are down, burglaries are down, crime in the Auckland CBD is down. Foot patrols are up. Police are back on their core role, keeping communities safe. Gang patches are banned.
charisma.explanation: Rallying, side-affirming delivery ('them who control the streets') aimed at his base more than persuasion across the aisle.

charisma.statement: So after 12 months of hearing from those commentators and others that the police didn't have the capability and the gangs were too strong, I think the police have answered that one in the last two weeks. They've done an outstanding job in policing the new gang legislation, and they've let the country know... that they are controlling the streets, not the gangs.
charisma.explanation: Confident, morale-boosting framing directed at supporters and against 'those commentators'.

forthrightness.statement: We have actually had stable rents under this Government versus $180 per week under Labour. Our source of data, from memory, is the tenancy bond data.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile with Stats NZ's 4.5% rent inflation figure; he reasserts 'stable rents' and cites a different data source rather than addressing the discrepancy.

forthrightness.statement: I find it ironic, from that member, getting lectured about rent increases, don't you think? It's $180 per week that it went up under his Government. We have stable rents under this Government. Why is that? Because we've taken the costs off landlords, we've actually got the balance right between tenants and landlords, and we've pulled the brightline test back to two years.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how a 4.5% rise squares with his promise rents would fall, he pivots to attacking Labour's record rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can guarantee that member they will cost less than the $3.2 billion he let that project grow out to. It'll be less than that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee the new ferries cost less than the cancelled $551m Hyundai contract, he only guarantees they beat the wider $3.2b iReX blowout—a much easier bar than the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: We haven't had that conversation in Government, but I can assure you we are focused on improving public safety.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to assure the public he won't liberalise sale of military-style semi-automatics; he neither rules it in nor out, pivoting to a generic public-safety line.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don't agree with that, but I'll just say to you members: the New Zealand public can see that this is a Government that's getting the work done. They can see that inflation's down, they can see that interest rates are down, they can see that crime is down, and—compared to the ungodly mess that that Government left us—they can see we're making progress.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the premise (that Peters thinks he's struggling) but then pivots to campaign lines rather than the leadership-respect question.

forthrightness.statement: A future Government may consider the possibility of a public share offering at some point, but, at this stage, the potential offering would be limited to KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups... Therefore, the Government is not considering a market float during this term of Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether Kiwibank will be floated, she gives a clear answer: not this term, with reasons (systems not upgraded until 2028).

forthrightness.statement: Yes. I stand by the statement which was referring to the Government's decision to decline a request from KiwiRail to contribute additional funding to the iReX project. And, yes, I'm confident that the Government's alternative ferry solution for the Cook Strait will cost less than the iReX project that was started under the previous Government and which blew out to a cost of at least $3 billion.
forthrightness.explanation: The question asked whether the alternative would cost less than the $551m Hyundai ferry contract; she instead compares to the whole $3b iReX project, dodging the specific benchmark.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member may like to pretend you can have ships without berths and you don't need to consider the cost of port-side infrastructure, but we here in the real world understand that the two must come together.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the specific ferry-cost question by invoking commercial sensitivity and a broadened project scope.

forthrightness.statement: I regret and will always remember an incoming Government being faced with a situation where they were set a deadline of a matter of weeks to determine whether we would shovel more cash into a failing project that had had multiple cost blowouts, that had gone completely off the rails, and that the last Government had not acted on.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she regrets refusing KiwiRail funding given the write-offs, she reframes her 'regret' onto the situation she inherited rather than her own decision.

forthrightness.statement: As I have said, it would not have been a good deal for New Zealanders to have shovelled more cash at a failing project which had blown out to more than $3 billion in cost... It was a failed project, and the member's defence of it tells me that she does not take value for taxpayers' money seriously.
forthrightness.explanation: Restates the cost-blowout case but does not confirm the specific write-off/cancellation figures put to her.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge that's an incredibly tough situation. There are many New Zealanders that have had a very difficult year and continue to do so, and that is directly a function of economic mismanagement over the previous six years. When Government spending goes up 84 percent, when inflation goes up to 7.3 percent, and when interest rates go up 12 or 13 times and you end up putting an economy into recession, people start losing their jobs—it's tough.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked his message to hungry tamariki, he briefly acknowledges then pivots to blaming the prior government rather than offering a message or remedy.

forthrightness.statement: Again, I refer the member to my former answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage a follow-up on tamariki asking for food instead of presents, offering no substantive response.

forthrightness.statement: We're going to do everything we can to meet some very ambitious goals.
forthrightness.explanation: Pressed for a yes/no on committing to the 2030 NDC, he offers an effort platitude that avoids the binary asked.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government's very committed to delivering on our net carbon 2050 goals and doing everything we can to deliver on NDC 2030.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked specifically about the 2030 NDC, he affirms the 2050 target firmly but only 'doing everything we can' on the actual NDC in question.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in the context in which I said and did them; in particular, my statements that Oranga Tamariki does not have the ability to restrict the movement of these young people, or the choices they make once they leave the residence and return to the community, and also my statement that we have already seen success with the military-style academy, including involvement for the participants in jobs, education, and training.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly stands by her statements and restates their substance rather than evading.

forthrightness.statement: The new legislation will allow the ability for a judge or a court to decide on the level of intensive response that is needed for a young person based on their needs. It is to be no less than three months, but no more than 12 months.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question about her '12 months in' statement by clarifying the actual legislated range (3–12 months at judicial discretion).

forthrightness.statement: This is a pilot that is ongoing that has worked with Defence and has worked with multiple agencies to make sure that we get the best outcomes for these young people, and those will be future discussions to be had.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out NZDF or Corrections involvement in future academies, she declines to rule it out and defers to 'future discussions'.

forthrightness.statement: There's some questions in there that I may not be able to answer because they may not be to my knowledge, but there have been three young people that have had accusations of reoffending.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the limits of her knowledge but does give a specific number (three) in response to the reoffending question.

forthrightness.statement: In all seriousness, I came into this role to make the lives of young people better. Children and young people have been hurt and harmed for over 20 to 30 years... What I can say is I will put all safety mechanisms that I can in place to keep these young people safe, but we cannot continue to do what we were doing, which was absolutely nothing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she'll promise to shut the academies down if harm occurs, she commits to safety mechanisms but does not give the yes/no shutdown promise sought.

forthrightness.statement: Unsurprisingly, yes, I am. Last week's changes to the around $78 million Marsden Fund ensure our limited funding is focused on the areas of science research with the greatest potential to grow our economy while enhancing quality of life for New Zealanders. The Marsden Fund will continue to support blue-skies research, but will now focus on those core science areas more likely to lead to scientific breakthroughs.
forthrightness.explanation: Owns the decision plainly ('yes, I am') and explains the rationale rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: it's wrong to say that the entire focus will be on economic gain; only 50 percent of the applications, or around that, will need to show that they can actually start to grow the economy and they have potential to do so. There is still blue-skies research, but it will be on science.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of the question with a concrete proportion (50%).

forthrightness.statement: most of those that he's named are not science. They are, however, very important, and many of those are already funded through the funding that the universities get—if I think about things like, for instance, the Performance-based Research Fund, the centres of research excellence, and tuition subsidies. In addition to that, many Government departments commission research to support policy objectives.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the substance of Willis's list rather than deflecting, though sidesteps whether the cut narrows the system.

forthrightness.statement: But I don't think that Māori or anyone else in New Zealand, apart from a few, might be that excited about the fact that they want to look at the history of big things that were put outside towns in the 1980s. I mean, next thing the member will be suggesting that we fund a study into those great big pou that are around those wonderful roads of national significance, but I actually don't think that's science.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the changes align with Te Tiriti obligations to protect mātauranga Māori, she dodges into ridicule of a roadside-sculpture grant.

forthrightness.statement: he was correct in stating that the funding by this Government goes through to June 2026. That's how appropriations work. But he would also agree with me and say that under this coalition Government, an excellent recruitment policy... for 500 additional police officers is to be delivered in November of this year, unlike the previous Government, who promised 1,800 and only delivered 1,500.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly reconciles the deputy commissioner's June 2026 statement with his own November target, though blurs funding dates against delivery dates.

forthrightness.statement: Well, they're both right. Casey Costello's absolutely 100 percent correct, as we are committed to delivering 500 police officers in November of this year. The Police Commissioner is also correct in saying there'll be 500 additional police officers in 2026, because there will be—they would've been delivered in November 2025.
forthrightness.explanation: Attempts a direct 'both right' reconciliation of two conflicting public statements, though the logic elides the tension the question highlighted.

forthrightness.statement: The problem the member has is she's got no credibility around her information sources and figures, so that's a whole lot of rambling mumbo-jumbo. I just want to say that on this side of the House, in this coalition Government, we are deadly serious about public safety and we are focused on making sure that we're a safer country.
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the question about contradictory delivery dates without addressing which account is correct.

forthrightness.statement: Oh no, don't worry. I front up all right—don't worry about that. I get around the country and I constantly get asked, "Where's that Chris Hipkins and Ginny Andersen that walked around with—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he regrets not fronting up to scrutiny week, he deflects into an anecdote taking aim at his questioners.

rigor.statement: Does he stand by his claim, "We haven't had a single rent increase; it's been stable rents over the last 12 months."; if so, how does he reconcile that with Statistics New Zealand's annual rent inflation figure of 4.5 percent over that time, over twice the rate of headline inflation?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes an official statistic against the PM's own quoted words to expose a contradiction—evidence-based rather than an appeal.

rigor.statement: I've been advised that an additional $500 million of capital could support up to $4 billion of business lending or $10 billion of home lending. That is sufficient to add competitive pressure to the market. Treasury calculates that even a 0.25 percent drop in personal and business lending rates across all banks would save customers $1.5 billion to $2 billion a year.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the case in Treasury modelling and quantified lending multipliers; conclusion about competitive pressure follows, though the rate-drop is a hypothetical.

rigor.statement: Well, the member makes a very good point. It should be remembered that by the time we came into Government, the cost of the ferries—the ships themselves—was just 21 percent of the total cost of iReX. That is to say, four in every five dollars was going towards costs that weren't even ships, with the blowout having been overseen by members who were in that Cabinet and sat by while New Zealanders' money was recklessly put at risk.
rigor.explanation: Uses a genuine cost-ratio to argue that ferry-only comparisons are misleading; reasoning largely follows from the figure cited.

rigor.statement: Yes. It may be the case that some members might like to pretend that you can buy ships without caring about supporting infrastructure, but I would say that is as fantastical as promising 100,000 KiwiBuild houses—
rigor.explanation: The infrastructure point is fair, but the KiwiBuild analogy is a rhetorical appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Is it the Minister's understanding that the whole point of ferries is to transport people and goods between points on the land, and therefore focusing on the price of the ferries without thinking about where they would dock is not only totally impractical but grossly fiscally irresponsible?
rigor.explanation: Makes a valid point that ferries need docks, but loads it as a rhetorical patsy question rather than a reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: I acknowledge that's an incredibly tough situation. There are many New Zealanders that have had a very difficult year and continue to do so, and that is directly a function of economic mismanagement over the previous six years. When Government spending goes up 84 percent, when inflation goes up to 7.3 percent, and when interest rates go up 12 or 13 times and you end up putting an economy into recession, people start losing their jobs—it's tough.
rigor.explanation: Chains the outcome to 'economic mismanagement' via selective figures; a partisan causal story more than a demonstrated one.

rigor.statement: But I also want to say that Oji, the company that is behind the mill, is a large multinational corporation with billions of dollars of investment. They have said for some time that the paper mill is unprofitable, and it hasn't been helped by the Labour-Greens energy policy, which ended up creating high electricity wholesale prices, because the Green Party thought it was a great idea to import Indonesian coal rather than to use domestic gas.
rigor.explanation: Attributes the mill's troubles to opponents' energy policy without establishing the causal chain; leans on a partisan narrative.

rigor.statement: Even Auckland Transport's recent annual report highlighted that only 29 percent of Aucklanders felt the organisation listens and responds to their needs.
rigor.explanation: Backs the case for reform with a specific, sourced statistic from AT's own annual report.

rigor.statement: most of those that he's named are not science. They are, however, very important, and many of those are already funded through the funding that the universities get—if I think about things like, for instance, the Performance-based Research Fund, the centres of research excellence, and tuition subsidies. In addition to that, many Government departments commission research to support policy objectives.
rigor.explanation: Supports the claim that social research is still funded by naming specific alternative funding streams; reasoning mostly follows, though 'not science' is asserted rather than argued.

rigor.statement: I do not think $360,000 of taxpayer money to look at what are the implications of policing climate justice activism—nah, that's not science... I'm not happy with things like $360,000 going for Big Things, Complex Shadows: Investigating Intersecting Stories Of Place, Identity, And Erasure Through Aotearoa's Large Roadside Sculptures... this is all about, basically, the carrot outside Paeroa. No, I don't think that's science.
rigor.explanation: Uses cherry-picked grant titles to characterise a whole funding class—vivid examples standing in for a general argument about what counts as science.

rigor.statement: But I don't think that Māori or anyone else in New Zealand, apart from a few, might be that excited about the fact that they want to look at the history of big things that were put outside towns in the 1980s. I mean, next thing the member will be suggesting that we fund a study into those great big pou that are around those wonderful roads of national significance, but I actually don't think that's science.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a mocking slippery-slope ('next thing...') and an appeal to what most people would find exciting rather than addressing the Treaty question.

rigor.statement: people under the age of 25 who come on to a main benefit are currently forecast to spend an average of about 20 future years on welfare over their lifetime. This is a 49 percent increase over the figures in 2017.
rigor.explanation: Uses actuarial lifetime-liability forecasts to justify intervention; a reasoned, data-grounded argument, though the 2017 baseline is a favourable comparator.

rigor.statement: Well, they're both right. Casey Costello's absolutely 100 percent correct, as we are committed to delivering 500 police officers in November of this year. The Police Commissioner is also correct in saying there'll be 500 additional police officers in 2026, because there will be—they would've been delivered in November 2025.
rigor.explanation: Reconciles the November-2025 and 2026 claims by asserting one implies the other rather than resolving the apparent contradiction with evidence.

rigor.statement: The context is that since 2019, the cost of construction increased by 40 percent. That was due to many different factors, including additional costs imposed by the rules in the form that they were imposed that came into effect late last year.
rigor.explanation: Links the reform to a cost figure and identified causes; reasoning is coherent though the causal weight on 'the rules' is asserted.

civility.statement: I find it ironic, from that member, getting lectured about rent increases, don't you think? It's $180 per week that it went up under his Government. We have stable rents under this Government. Why is that? Because we've taken the costs off landlords, we've actually got the balance right between tenants and landlords, and we've pulled the brightline test back to two years.
civility.explanation: 'Getting lectured' is a mild dig but the response stays largely on policy substance (brightline test, landlord costs).

civility.statement: Well, the member may like to pretend you can have ships without berths and you don't need to consider the cost of port-side infrastructure, but we here in the real world understand that the two must come together.
civility.explanation: Strawmans the questioner as pretending ships need no berths; belittling framing rather than engaging her actual point about ferry cost.

civility.statement: Well, the member makes a very good point. It should be remembered that by the time we came into Government, the cost of the ferries—the ships themselves—was just 21 percent of the total cost of iReX. That is to say, four in every five dollars was going towards costs that weren't even ships, with the blowout having been overseen by members who were in that Cabinet and sat by while New Zealanders' money was recklessly put at risk.
civility.explanation: 'Sat by while New Zealanders' money was recklessly put at risk' is an accusatory jab at named opponents, but tied to the substance of cost overruns.

civility.statement: Yes. It may be the case that some members might like to pretend that you can buy ships without caring about supporting infrastructure, but I would say that is as fantastical as promising 100,000 KiwiBuild houses—
civility.explanation: Repeats the strawman and lands a mocking KiwiBuild jibe at the opposition rather than addressing substance.

civility.statement: I regret and will always remember an incoming Government being faced with a situation where they were set a deadline of a matter of weeks to determine whether we would shovel more cash into a failing project that had had multiple cost blowouts, that had gone completely off the rails, and that the last Government had not acted on.
civility.explanation: Charged language ('shovel more cash', 'off the rails') aimed at the previous government's handling, but focused on the project record.

civility.statement: As I have said, it would not have been a good deal for New Zealanders to have shovelled more cash at a failing project which had blown out to more than $3 billion in cost... It was a failed project, and the member's defence of it tells me that she does not take value for taxpayers' money seriously.
civility.explanation: Closes with a personal imputation that Edmonds 'does not take value for taxpayers' money seriously' rather than sticking to the project's merits.

civility.statement: Is it the Minister's understanding that the whole point of ferries is to transport people and goods between points on the land, and therefore focusing on the price of the ferries without thinking about where they would dock is not only totally impractical but grossly fiscally irresponsible?
civility.explanation: Attacks the opposition framing ('grossly fiscally irresponsible') but targets the argument, not a person.

civility.statement: This is a Government that believes we should celebrate people who have been successful and that are working incredibly hard to get ahead. If you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you are a fiscal conservative, unlike the last Labour-led Government.
civility.explanation: Partisan but focused on values and the opposing party's stance rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: But I also want to say that Oji, the company that is behind the mill, is a large multinational corporation with billions of dollars of investment. They have said for some time that the paper mill is unprofitable, and it hasn't been helped by the Labour-Greens energy policy, which ended up creating high electricity wholesale prices, because the Green Party thought it was a great idea to import Indonesian coal rather than to use domestic gas.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at the previous government's policy rather than personal attacks.

civility.statement: It was suggested that a young person had died in the military-style academy pilot. This is simply untrue. A young person has tragically died in the community whilst in whānau placement. The attempt to use the death of a young person for political gain is absolutely shameful and disgusting, and that statement was actually shared on social media by someone who should have known better, and that was Green MP Tamatha Paul.
civility.explanation: 'Absolutely shameful and disgusting' plus naming Tamatha Paul is a pointed personal condemnation, though anchored to a specific alleged misstatement.

civility.statement: I do not think $360,000 of taxpayer money to look at what are the implications of policing climate justice activism—nah, that's not science... I'm not happy with things like $360,000 going for Big Things, Complex Shadows: Investigating Intersecting Stories Of Place, Identity, And Erasure Through Aotearoa's Large Roadside Sculptures... this is all about, basically, the carrot outside Paeroa. No, I don't think that's science.
civility.explanation: Mocks specific funded projects ('the carrot outside Paeroa') rather than a person; dismissive but aimed at policy choices.

civility.statement: But I don't think that Māori or anyone else in New Zealand, apart from a few, might be that excited about the fact that they want to look at the history of big things that were put outside towns in the 1980s. authenticity.statement: Yes. I stand by the statement which was referring to the Government's decision to decline a request from KiwiRail to contribute additional funding to the iReX project. authenticity.statement: That is quite wrong—we are neither of those things. We had the Spatial Planning Act and the Natural and Built Environment Act, which included a fast track, which will remain on the books for some time.

specificity.statement: That is quite wrong—we are neither of those things. We had the Spatial Planning Act and the Natural and Built Environment Act, which included a fast track, which will remain on the books for some time.

specificity.statement: In the last 10 years, we’ve seen politicians and senior leaders take more accountability for the infrastructure projects that they are championing. civility.statement: I agree with Chris Bishop that not all projects with a public benefit are necessarily owned by the Government or local government. I agree with that

civility.statement: the idea of Debbie Ngarewa-Packer running anything in this Government fills me with dread

divination.statement: This is a great bill, and this will get our infrastructure and our economy back on track.

divination.statement: On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things, and the people of New Zealand will say no to them at the 2026 election.

rigor.statement: we have had the delivery of some of the information about those applications for the 149 listed projects and we can see from those that there is no change from what was applied for and what was declined in the past

rigor.statement: We spend, according to the Infrastructure Commission, over $1.3 billion a year on consenting.

rigor.statement: That is why we are 30 percent poorer than Australia, because for 30 years we have grown, on average, at a lower rate than they have.

rigor.statement: I accept that he dislikes the comparison between the COVID-19 fast-track legislation, but it is true in the most obvious sense that the COVID-19 fast-track legislation is the building block for this legislation. rigor.explanation: Concedes the differences Parker raised while defending the continuity claim, distinguishing architecture from machinery.

rigor.statement: how many millions will the Winton Land company make when this bill passes? What is the value of Winton’s land before these projects made their way on to the 149-project list, compared to later in this week when this bill becomes law?
rigor.explanation: Frames the private-benefit case as testable valuation questions, though it presumes the conclusion it demands answers to.

rigor.statement: In the last 10 years, we’ve seen politicians and senior leaders take more accountability for the infrastructure projects that they are championing. rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative example (Victoria) to argue for a better process, though the analogy is asserted rather than evidenced.

veracity.statement: we have had the delivery of some of the information about those applications for the 149 listed projects and we can see from those that there is no change from what was applied for and what was declined in the past

veracity.statement: We spend, according to the Infrastructure Commission, over $1.3 billion a year on consenting.

veracity.statement: Trans-Tasman Resources, who promised to bring $1 billion to Aotearoa’s economy and, in fact, their promises were so bad, they had to do a formal retraction to the Australian Stock Exchange.

veracity.statement: there is absolutely no accountability to the 83 percent who voted against it

veracity.statement: It has been kicked back by the Supreme Court. It has been kicked back by every consideration body in the country.
