veracity.statement: More than 90 percent of the projects that went through that fast track were eventually consented. Less than 10 percent were declined, and they were declined for good reasons.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable statistics on Labour's COVID/NBEA fast-track outcomes; plausible and consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: We consented wind farms, solar farms—the biggest solar farms ever to be built in New Zealand were consented under our fast track. We consented roads; we consented geothermal.
veracity.explanation: Specific claims about projects consented; consistent with the known record of the prior fast-track regime.

veracity.statement: the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, Simon Upton, a former National Party Minister for the Environment... came to the Environment Committee and said that this legislation is worse than the National Development Act—1979, I think it was—passed by Muldoon
veracity.explanation: Reports the Commissioner's submission; plausible characterisation, hedged ('I think it was') on the year.

veracity.statement: This is the man that would double New Zealand’s electricity price by importing liquefied natural gas (LNG).
veracity.explanation: 'Double the price of electricity' is a strong quantitative claim that reads as hyperbolic without cited evidence.

veracity.statement: the Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991 has been a wrecking ball through the New Zealand economy, and you can directly trace the onset of our housing affordability crisis to the RMA 1991.
veracity.explanation: Directionally defensible (planning rules affect housing costs) but the sweeping 'directly trace' overstates a contested causal claim.

veracity.statement: It took 10 years to re-consent an existing geothermal power station that got built in the 1950s.
veracity.explanation: Specific anecdotal claim used as evidence of consenting delay; plausible but uncorroborated here.

veracity.statement: That is why we are 30 percent poorer than Australia, because for 30 years we have grown, on average, at a lower rate than they have.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with long-run NZ–Australia productivity/GDP-per-capita gaps, though '30 percent' is a rounded headline figure.

veracity.statement: We are telling Waka Kotaki and New Zealand Transport Agency officials that they must acquire land from a specific developer who has now benefited to the tune of tens of millions of dollars for the project that they were going to do at a much cheaper rate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 'tens of millions' developer benefit as fact; the magnitude is an unverified estimate.

charisma.statement: We of course—and I’ll talk about this in the next bill, as well—have made bipartisan offers to talk with the Government, and they’ve come to nothing.
charisma.explanation: Notes attempts at cross-party engagement, though framed as blaming the Government for their failure.

charisma.statement: if these companies want to come and give so little disregard to Te Tiriti, to our democratic process, and to our environmental protections, then there is no security for them in that and they have no future here in Aotearoa—and we make absolutely no apology for that
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them warning to companies; makes no attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: Do not insult our intelligence. Do not insult those communities that live there and know their communities better than the Government ever will that this is what this bill is about.
charisma.explanation: Rallies the represented communities but frames the Government as the adversary.

charisma.statement: If this was a bill that sought to find a means to fast-track renewable energy projects or housing projects and took into account Te Tiriti o Waitangi and took into account the environment and the climate, the conversation would be very different.
charisma.explanation: Signals openness to a fast-track approach on different terms — offering common ground rather than blanket opposition.

charisma.statement: I stand in support of the Fast-track Approvals Bill, a bill which says yes to jobs, yes to opportunities, yes to energy security, yes to building the roads that are needed to unlock economic growth and opportunity, yes to houses
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically upbeat but purely one-sided rallying, no reach across the House.

charisma.statement: On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things, and the people of New Zealand will say no to them at the 2026 election.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that caricatures opponents; no consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I agree with Chris Bishop that not all projects with a public benefit are necessarily owned by the Government or local government. I agree with that
charisma.explanation: Explicitly concedes a valid point made by an opponent, building toward common ground before drawing the distinction.

charisma.statement: I actually think there’s broad consensus around the Parliament across that—and that, at least, is progress, because, for quite a long time, that was denied.
charisma.explanation: Seeks and names cross-party common ground (that building is too hard), framing it as shared progress.

charisma.statement: In the last 10 years, we’ve seen politicians and senior leaders take more accountability for the infrastructure projects that they are championing. Politicians in Australia, in the state of Victoria, getting out in front of their infrastructure projects, leading people along with them, winning the argument in people’s hearts, convincing people that these are important projects and they should happen.
charisma.explanation: Points to a positive, persuasion-based model of leadership (winning hearts) as the constructive alternative.

charisma.statement: The Fast-track Approvals Bill is a crucial step in unlocking New Zealand’s potential. Whether it’s housing or renewable energy or aquaculture, this bill aims to streamline the approval process for infrastructure and development projects which are of significant regional and national benefit.
charisma.explanation: Positive framing around shared national benefit, but a standard one-sided commendation.

strength.statement: We absolutely commit to reviewing and potentially revoking every consent rammed through under this fast-track bill
strength.explanation: A firm commitment, but it is a future/opposition promise contingent on winning office, with no delivery to show.

strength.statement: the worst of these projects, as my colleague has said, shall be subject to re-evaluation in a new Government. We reserve the right to revoke and rescind the permits issued for them
strength.explanation: A conditional future commitment from opposition; no ability to deliver now.

strength.statement: We consented wind farms, solar farms—the biggest solar farms ever to be built in New Zealand were consented under our fast track. We consented roads; we consented geothermal.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivery under his own fast-track legislation — projects actually consented, not merely promised.

authenticity.statement: As part of the agreements with our coalition partners, New Zealand First and the ACT Party, this Government has committed to introducing dedicated legislation for gene technology. This bill is a result of that commitment and the commitment we made to the New Zealand public to bring our regulations for gene technology into the 21st century.
authenticity.explanation: Words match action: she frames a coalition commitment and is at that moment delivering the promised bill to the House, a consistent follow-through on a stated position.

authenticity.statement: I think that most of us in this House, like most New Zealanders, would support the use of GMO and gene editing techniques for medical applications. Indeed, Labour as a Government was working towards updating our rules for exactly that purpose.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent position: she supports medical gene tech and notes Labour was itself moving to update rules for that purpose, so her objection is to scope, not the technology — words align with her party's prior stance.

authenticity.statement: Genetic medicine is not contentious and has always been supported by the Greens, from insulin through to vaccines, and so too is contained precision fermentation. The release of live, self-replicating organisms into the environment and agricultural systems is a different story.
authenticity.explanation: Draws a consistent line — long-standing Green support for medical and contained applications versus opposition to environmental release — situating the objection within a stable party record rather than blanket opposition.

strength.statement: As part of the agreements with our coalition partners, New Zealand First and the ACT Party, this Government has committed to introducing dedicated legislation for gene technology. This bill is a result of that commitment and the commitment we made to the New Zealand public to bring our regulations for gene technology into the 21st century.
strength.explanation: A committed policy actually being introduced (first reading), but introduction is not enactment — delivery is only in-progress, so partial strength.

veracity.statement: Our current regulations for genetically modified organisms are some of the most backward looking in the world.
veracity.explanation: NZ's HSNO/GMO regime is genuinely among the more restrictive, but 'most backward looking in the world' is a hyperbolic, evaluative overstatement of a defensible underlying point.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has lagged behind other countries, such as Australia, Canada, and England, which have safely embraced these technologies for the benefit of their people and their economies.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that Australia/Canada and others have more permissive gene-tech regimes; 'safely' and 'for the benefit of their economies' add contestable framing.

veracity.statement: Despite gene technologies having been in use in New Zealand since the 1970s, the restrictive rules and time-consuming processes we have imposed on researchers have made testing and embracing innovation outside the lab all but impossible.
veracity.explanation: Recombinant/gene technology has been used in NZ labs since the 1970s and field release is tightly restricted; 'all but impossible' outside the lab is a mild exaggeration of a largely true point.

veracity.statement: They can opt in. They do not have to opt out. They’d have to opt in in order to use them.
veracity.explanation: Frames the regime as opt-in for adopters; critics (Abel) contend non-GMO producers will bear certification costs, so the 'no obligation on others' implication is contestable.

veracity.statement: I can assure you that the genetic engineering of human embryos will remain banned.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the bill's stated scope and existing NZ prohibitions on human germline modification.

veracity.statement: This change does not mean we can no longer have organics or be GE-free. Genetically engineered products have been in New Zealand for years, in things such as soy milk... The US is the largest organics producer in the world while also being the largest producer of genetically modified food.
veracity.explanation: The US is indeed both a top organic market and the largest GM producer, and imported GE-derived products are sold in NZ; 'largest organics producer in the world' is roughly but not precisely accurate, and the coexistence claim omits the certification-cost issue opponents raise.

veracity.statement: Think of genetically edited apples that take one year to grow, fruit, and produce, rather than the five to seven years of other apples... I’ve seen this in one of our labs in a Crown research institute already being done here, but they can’t take it out the lab.
veracity.explanation: Fast-flowering/early-fruiting gene-edited apple lines do exist in research; the sweeping one-year field claim is plausible but somewhat idealised.

veracity.statement: The CRISPR process was announced in 2012, and it won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. That changed everything, because it means that we’re not splicing together genes from different species but that we’re editing existing genes.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the CRISPR-Cas9 method was published in 2012 and Doudna and Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the editing-vs-splicing distinction is broadly correct.

veracity.statement: The Minister says that we’re bringing our rules into alignment with other countries and, in particular, Australia, but there’s a critical difference... we would allow non-regulation of SDN-2 processes, where other countries such as Australia allow non-regulation of only SDN-1 processes.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record that Australia deregulated only SDN-1 (no-template) edits while NZ's bill extends non-regulation to SDN-2; a technically precise, defensible claim.

veracity.statement: The second gap in this proposed legislation, unlike Australia, is that there has been no public consultation. There has been targeted consultation, but it has been conducted primarily with those who stand to benefit from the legislation.
veracity.explanation: The process did rely on targeted rather than full public consultation; the claim that it was 'primarily with those who stand to benefit' is a fair but somewhat one-sided characterisation.

veracity.statement: One study showed that when it comes to gene editing and genetic modification, 11 percent of Māori and 12 percent of non-Māori were strongly supportive, and 33 percent of Māori and 23 percent of non-Māori leaned supportive.
veracity.explanation: Presented as direct study figures with attribution; accepted as accurately quoted, though the underlying study can't be verified from the text.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research has quantified the possible costs and they estimate that the effect on our exports might be in the order of $10 billion to $20 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes a specific figure to NZIER; the estimate itself is a modelled worst-case range, so the underlying magnitude is uncertain even if the citation is faithful.

veracity.statement: The regulator is required to set up a technical advisory committee, but that committee has no space for an ethicist. And while the regulator is also required to set up a Māori advisory committee, they are not required to consult that committee.
veracity.explanation: Reads as a faithful account of gaps in the bill's advisory provisions; not independently confirmable from the text but specific and falsifiable.

veracity.statement: It is extraordinary that this Government has not done a full economic analysis of the impact of this legislation, and the only one done by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research finds a potential $10 billion to $20 billion cost of our existing value-added component to our primary production sector.
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites the NZIER estimate and the absence of a full government economic analysis; the $10–20bn figure is itself a modelled potential cost, not a realised one.

veracity.statement: In the Australian canola example, the additional certifications costs were estimated to be A$14.00 per tonne... you no longer are maintaining your current GE-free status, you in fact are having to pay the cost of obtaining it.
veracity.explanation: Quotes a specific figure from the regulatory impact statement and correctly infers the burden-shift that certification costs impose on non-GMO producers; the interpretive leap to 'forfeits GE-free status' is arguable but grounded.

veracity.statement: There are only actually 27 countries in the world that have commercial production of GE crops, out of 195 countries. Most of those countries are in the Americas and, of the four main commodity crops produced, 99 percentage of the global acreage is four crops: soy, maize, cotton, canola. They mostly end up as animal feed or as biofuels.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with ISAAA-type data: roughly 26–29 countries grow biotech crops, dominated by soy, maize, cotton and canola, much of it for feed and fuel; figures are approximately accurate.

veracity.statement: There is no single product that has high commercial value that is sold as direct human food in the global market—after 40 years of billions of dollars of investment in the United States and thousands of field trials.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supportable that GE commodity crops are predominantly feed/fuel/processing rather than premium direct human food, but 'no single product' is an absolute that overlooks GE products marketed for human consumption (e.g. Arctic apples, GM sweet corn, papaya).

civility.statement: Our current regulations for genetically modified organisms are some of the most backward looking in the world.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the regulatory regime rather than a person; harsh framing but aimed at policy/rules.

civility.statement: This change does not mean a free-for-all on genetic technologies in New Zealand. This change simply means that gene technologies have a pathway to regulatory assessment that is designed to ensure the public and environmental safety of New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Directly addresses public concerns/'rhetoric' with reassurance rather than attacking opponents; engages the substance of the fear.

civility.statement: I would like to thank all the members and staff from around the House who engaged with myself and my office on these changes. As this bill progresses through the parliamentary process, I encourage all parties not to lose sight of the real aims of this new legislation.
civility.explanation: Respectful, appreciative of colleagues across the House, focused on process.

civility.statement: The Minister says that we’re bringing our rules into alignment with other countries and, in particular, Australia, but there’s a critical difference... we would allow non-regulation of SDN-2 processes, where other countries such as Australia allow non-regulation of only SDN-1 processes.
civility.explanation: Points to a gap between the Minister's claim and the detail, but engages the policy substance rather than attacking her character.

civility.statement: The second gap in this proposed legislation, unlike Australia, is that there has been no public consultation. There has been targeted consultation, but it has been conducted primarily with those who stand to benefit from the legislation.
civility.explanation: Implies the consultation was captured by beneficiaries — a pointed critique of process, edging toward impugning motives but still about the policy process.

civility.statement: I think that most of us in this House, like most New Zealanders, would support the use of GMO and gene editing techniques for medical applications. Indeed, Labour as a Government was working towards updating our rules for exactly that purpose.
civility.explanation: Respectful, acknowledges shared ground and opponents' valid aims.

civility.statement: It doesn’t just liberalise our rules around genetic engineering; it takes us out in advance of other countries, and it does so with no public consultation, no analysis of the impact on trade, no certain role for tangata whenua, no ethics input. There simply are too many gaps in this bill.
civility.explanation: Sustained substantive critique of the legislation's content and process, no personal attack.

civility.statement: This particular legislation is a reckless rush job of potentially monumental proportions, because it has failed to take into account those who are most impacted by this liberalisation of the current regime.
civility.explanation: 'Reckless rush job of monumental proportions' is heated, hyperbolic language, though aimed at the legislation and process rather than a person.

civility.statement: The evidence of genetic engineering is that the hyperbolic claims made by the Luxon Government for what it can do are not borne out by what we’ve seen in 30 years of commercial production of GE crops.
civility.explanation: Names 'the Luxon Government' and calls its claims 'hyperbolic', but the charge is against the Government's arguments, not a personal attack on an individual's character.

The US is the largest organics producer in the world while also being the largest producer of genetically modified food.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real comparative example (US coexistence of organic and GM sectors) to support the coexistence claim; reasonable but glosses over segregation costs.

rigor.statement: The Minister says that we’re bringing our rules into alignment with other countries and, in particular, Australia, but there’s a critical difference... we would allow non-regulation of SDN-2 processes, where other countries such as Australia allow non-regulation of only SDN-1 processes.

charisma.statement: I would like to thank all the members and staff from around the House who engaged with myself and my office on these changes. As this bill progresses through the parliamentary process, I encourage all parties not to lose sight of the real aims of this new legislation.

charisma.statement: I think that most of us in this House, like most New Zealanders, would support the use of GMO and gene editing techniques for medical applications. Indeed, Labour as a Government was working towards updating our rules for exactly that purpose.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly finds common ground across the House and with New Zealanders on medical uses before dissenting on scope — a consensus-acknowledging, bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: Genetic medicine is not contentious and has always been supported by the Greens, from insulin through to vaccines, and so too is contained precision fermentation. The release of live, self-replicating organisms into the environment and agricultural systems is a different story.
charisma.explanation: Concedes shared ground on medical genetic technology before distinguishing the contested case, an attempt to appear reasonable to the wider House.

divination.statement: The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research has quantified the possible costs and they estimate that the effect on our exports might be in the order of $10 billion to $20 billion a year.
divination.explanation: Forecast of $10–20bn annual export impact if the regime damages NZ's status; directionally plausible risk but a wide, uncertain range dependent on market reactions.

civility.statement: This legislation, as we have heard, as we have seen, as we continue to see just runs roughshod over our democracy.
civility.explanation: Harsh, hyperbolic framing ('runs roughshod') aimed at the legislation rather than a person; sensationalist but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Our world is burning, and this Government is just throwing more fuel on that fire.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic, sensationalist metaphor directed at the Government; more rhetoric than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: there’s a private company in this bill and all they’re going to do is dig up and suck up all the sand off the bottom of our beautiful Taranaki ocean, and then the profits go over to Australia, where the company’s from, and they jeopardise the fact that offshore wind is viable.
civility.explanation: Pointed characterisation of a company's project; emotive ('suck up all the sand') but aimed at the project, not a person.

civility.statement: As has been said, there’s renewable energy projects in this bill, but it is just smoke and mirrors—it is just smoke and mirrors—in terms of what they are wanting to achieve.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation ('smoke and mirrors') that imputes bad faith without detailing it.

civility.statement: We don’t want to be fossil fools on this side of the House.
civility.explanation: A 'fossil fools' pun implicitly disparaging the other side; a cheap shot dressed as wordplay.

civility.statement: The previous speaker, Mike Butterick, just talked about the fact that the Resource Management Act (RMA) is broken and needs to be fixed, but I would say that this legislation is more about tinkering than fixing anything.
civility.explanation: Engages the opposing argument directly and critiques the bill's substance rather than the person.

civility.statement: Do you know what is truly despicable? It’s that members opposite talked about respecting Te Tiriti, but guess what! Last week, there was an Amendment Paper put forward to remove Mana Ahuriri from this bill.
civility.explanation: Opens with 'truly despicable' and a gotcha framing charging opponents with hypocrisy rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: This is a very bad way to make laws, and it seems that the Prime Minister does not understand that fundamental need for laws to be scrutinised.
civility.explanation: Shifts from process critique to a personal claim that the PM 'does not understand', impugning competence.

civility.statement: it’s a win for the nimbies in Epsom, and it will allow for discharges into polluted water bodies and override local decision-making.
civility.explanation: 'Nimbies in Epsom' is a mild jab; the rest targets policy effects rather than a person.

civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith ('as an excuse') to the Government; strong but aimed at Government motive rather than a named person.

civility.statement: Go for it, sit comfortably for two years. After two years, you will be gone.

civility.statement: I have not an iota, iota, iota of consideration for the authority of this House, the authority of that side, and the people seated there that are carrying out the activities of the Government.

specificity.statement: This legislation, as we have heard, as we have seen, as we continue to see just runs roughshod over our democracy.

specificity.statement: Now, more than 27,000 people submitted on this piece of legislation. Not all of them had the opportunity to speak to their submissions to the Environment Committee

specificity.statement: We’ve got the Crown Minerals Act 1991. We’ve got the Wildlife Act 1953. We’ve got the Reserves Act 1977. We’ve got the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Act 2012.

specificity.statement: councils must decide renewable energy generation consents within one year of application; consents for renewable energy generation will receive 35-year consents by default. veracity.statement: Today, in fact, this very day, is the final ever Kāpiti News publication, the last newspaper for the Kāpiti Coast. Friday will see the last ever Horowhenua Chronicle.
veracity.explanation: Presented as concrete, checkable facts about local newspaper closures consistent with the period's reporting.

veracity.statement: There is no reason that this bill needs to be amended to allow a handful of fishers to contribute to the 57 percent decline of key fish stocks in the gulf, a 67 percent decline in seaboard birds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
veracity.explanation: The decline figures echo commonly cited Hauraki Gulf state-of-environment data, but are hard to verify precisely as stated.

veracity.statement: what was being proposed was legislation that would see the protected area in the gulf—largely through a new concept of high protection area... go from a very meagre 0.3 percent to just 6 percent. That would be, undoubtedly, the largest attempt, or the most significant protection attempt in the history of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: The protection percentages and 'largest attempt' characterisation align with how the bill was described publicly.

veracity.statement: the Minister, Minister Potaka, added in commercial fishing at the eighth hour before the first reading. That has created a level of uncertainty. This is after decades of people advocating and campaigning to protect Tīkapa Moana
veracity.explanation: Aligns with other speakers' accounts of a late change allowing fishing, though 'betrayal' framing is his characterisation.

civility.statement: I stand on behalf of the Labour Party to support and endorse the recommendation of the Government for this appointment. Mr Horsley brings significant experience to the role.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful cross-party endorsement with no personal attack.

civility.statement: this week—this week—the Minister for broadcasting wrote in and announced a repeal totalling 73 words. If he'd written a word a day, he could have done it in two months, not eight.
civility.explanation: Mocking, sarcastic jab aimed at ridiculing the Minister's diligence rather than engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: the Minister wasn't in the House last night to speak to the introduction of the bill, and we were surprised. He wasn't at select committee this morning to hear from NZ On Air, to hear from RNZ, and to hear from TVNZ, and I thought: "This is how the industry feels." They want engagement... and the Minister is simply missing in action.
civility.explanation: 'Missing in action' is a pointed personal characterisation, though tied to specific absences from the House and committee.

civility.statement: This is a woeful, woeful, embarrassing bill. It shows a complete lack of engagement with the industry, a complete lack of understanding for exactly what is at stake with the losses that we are seeing across our media sector, and a blatant disregard for the threat to our democracy that the inaction from this Government to look after our local media presents.
civility.explanation: Heavy pejorative language ('woeful', 'embarrassing') and sweeping condemnation over substantive critique.

civility.statement: That member was part of a Government, and Labour had six years in which they were actually able to enact changes, and what did they do? They didn't make any changes at all.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opponent's record on policy grounds rather than personally, but framed as a rhetorical gotcha.

civility.statement: I'm just reflecting on the speech we've just heard from Labour's Helen White, and I'm contrasting it with what we heard from Labour's Reuben Davidson... On the one hand, we're hearing, "We need to act."... On the other hand, we're hearing, "Don't do anything."
civility.explanation: Engages opposing arguments by name and substance rather than resorting to personal insult.

civility.statement: Te Pāti Māori supports aspirations for the protection and restoration of Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana. Te Pāti Māori does not support efforts to undermine the protection and restoration of the moana, and while the bill may have started with the right intentions, it has landed in the wrong place. Therefore, Te Pāti Māori oppose this bill.
civility.explanation: Frames opposition around the bill's substance and cited concerns, not personal attack.

civility.statement: New Zealand First have ruined what should have been a happy story for the National Party at the last minute by allowing Shane Jones to lobby the Minister of Conservation after he himself had been lobbied by the fishing industry.
civility.explanation: Accuses a named MP of doing the fishing industry's bidding — a pointed attack on motive rather than policy substance.

civility.statement: This a very dangerous precedent that this Government is getting into. We've seen it with the fast track last week, and then it seems like we're going to see this with this bill when it's in committee stage... If the changes are so important and if they are significant changes that are going to give benefits to individuals, then, at the very least, put it back through a select committee process.
civility.explanation: Sharp but legitimate criticism of process, with a constructive proposed remedy rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: In respect of the reference that is made to people catching fish who need to catch fish to eat, I think we have to be careful that we don't create different standards of access to the recreational fishery. That would be a big step in New Zealand that we've so far avoided and would lead to conflicts within communities that I think are best avoided.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the proposed change respectfully, focused on policy consequences.

civility.statement: We saw great evidence in the select committee about kina barrens and other things that are plaguing the gulf, and I think it's really important that we can extend the protection of the gulf since so little of it is currently protected.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges that not everyone will be happy and engages the issue constructively.

civility.statement: I think it's a really very nuanced issue as we did all vote unanimously. We do feel very strongly that protection is required, but one thing of interest and of note is the variety of submissions that we heard... There is a lot of care for this area, but there are so many different people that are involved.
civility.explanation: Even-handed acknowledgement of the range of views and the unanimous committee support.

civility.statement: Can I just say to all the families and the partners of all of the MPs here in Parliament: merry Christmas. You make the sacrifices that allow each and every one of us to be here, and we want to say thank you to you.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful remarks directed to the whole House and its staff.

charisma.statement: I stand on behalf of the Labour Party to support and endorse the recommendation of the Government for this appointment. Mr Horsley brings significant experience to the role.
charisma.explanation: Bridges party lines to back a government proposal, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: there's two essential functions, as I understand it: an investigation function with appropriate supporting powers to scrutinise in response to issues that have occurred; and an assessment function to assess processes, procedures, and policies, and identify gaps to prevent issues from occurring in the future.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive cross-party support, explaining the role plainly for those 'listening at home'.

charisma.statement: This is a woeful, woeful, embarrassing bill. It shows a complete lack of engagement with the industry, a complete lack of understanding for exactly what is at stake with the losses that we are seeing across our media sector, and a blatant disregard for the threat to our democracy that the inaction from this Government to look after our local media presents.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative attack on the Government; makes no attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: not everything is something that you leave to the market... this is what happens when you're just totally hands off and there are no rules. What you have is big businesses actually ruling the roost and doing exactly what they want, because it's a cowboy world.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective appeal to fairness, but framed as a partisan critique of the Government's ideology.

charisma.statement: this is a really good example of where leadership involves actually making some rules, making it fair for people, thinking about the contribution that people make to this community, and fostering it... We need a Government that's prepared to lead. Please do so.
charisma.explanation: An appeal for the Government to act, but framed from opposition rather than genuinely reaching across.

charisma.statement: Why would we go and place what now seem like arbitrary rules on top of our free-to-air media, local media, New Zealand media? Why would we restrict them when not everyone else in the market is? Surely we believe in one rule for all.
charisma.explanation: Frames the change around a broadly shared principle of fairness, inviting agreement.

charisma.statement: The Department of Conservation advice said that changes would be incompatible with the purpose, will undermine biodiversity outcomes, and create significant equity issues. I urge the Minister of Conservation to reconsider. I urge the National Party to step up to your better instincts.
charisma.explanation: Ends by appealing to National's 'better instincts', inviting them to act rather than only condemning.

charisma.statement: Is this piece of legislation perfect? No... Is this piece of legislation better than nothing? Absolutely yes... we should not in this Parliament let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-building appeal that invites all sides to accept an imperfect but worthwhile step.

charisma.statement: I think it's a really very nuanced issue as we did all vote unanimously. We do feel very strongly that protection is required, but one thing of interest and of note is the variety of submissions that we heard... There is a lot of care for this area, but there are so many different people that are involved.
charisma.explanation: Recognises the many stakeholders and the shared care for the area, adopting an inclusive tone.

charisma.statement: Can I just say to all the families and the partners of all of the MPs here in Parliament: merry Christmas. You make the sacrifices that allow each and every one of us to be here, and we want to say thank you to you.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-party acknowledgement of all MPs' families and Parliament's staff, building goodwill across the House.

rigor.statement: it's extremely unlikely that relaxing advertising rules on Christmas Day, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Anzac Day morning will make the slightest difference to the difficulties overall that New Zealand media organisations are facing.
rigor.explanation: Weighs the modest revenue against the structural drivers (offshore big tech) and presents both a case and counter-case for the $6m estimate.

rigor.statement: this week—this week—the Minister for broadcasting wrote in and announced a repeal totalling 73 words. If he'd written a word a day, he could have done it in two months, not eight.
rigor.explanation: The word-count-per-day quip is rhetorical ridicule, not a substantive argument about the bill's merits.

rigor.statement: let's be under no illusion: the media bargaining bill is a very small solution to a much bigger challenge, which is the upending of the media business models, and it's incumbent on the organisations in those sectors to innovate and create new business models
rigor.explanation: Reasonable framing that the bargaining bill is minor relative to structural disruption, but the 'must innovate' conclusion is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: not everything is something that you leave to the market... this is what happens when you're just totally hands off and there are no rules. What you have is big businesses actually ruling the roost and doing exactly what they want, because it's a cowboy world.
rigor.explanation: Makes an ideological case against a hands-off approach but leans on characterisation ('cowboy world') rather than specific evidence.

rigor.statement: I'm just reflecting on the speech we've just heard from Labour's Helen White, and I'm contrasting it with what we heard from Labour's Reuben Davidson... On the one hand, we're hearing, "We need to act."... On the other hand, we're hearing, "Don't do anything."
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine tension between two opposition speakers, though it somewhat flattens their positions to make the point.

rigor.statement: Why would we go and place what now seem like arbitrary rules on top of our free-to-air media, local media, New Zealand media? Why would we restrict them when not everyone else in the market is? Surely we believe in one rule for all.
rigor.explanation: A coherent level-playing-field argument, though it rests partly on the 'one rule for all' appeal rather than evidence of impact.

rigor.statement: Te Pāti Māori notes concerns from the Hauraki Gulf Forum... and this statement by the forum's co-chair Nicola MacDonald: "Years of collaboration with successive Governments with iwi, communities, and industries have been undermined."
rigor.explanation: Builds the opposition case on cited submissions from the Forum, Te Ohu Kaimoana, and the Hauraki Māori Trust Board rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: There is no reason that this bill needs to be amended to allow a handful of fishers to contribute to the 57 percent decline of key fish stocks in the gulf, a 67 percent decline in seaboard birds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
rigor.explanation: Marshals quantified ecological decline to argue against the amendment, though the causal link to 'a handful of fishers' is rhetorically compressed.

rigor.statement: Commercial fishers will still be able to operate in over 90 percent of the gulf outside the high protection areas. The Government's most recent amendments will allow commercial fishing in 52 square kilometres of the gulf's high protection areas.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete proportions to rebut the idea that fishers are being shut out, strengthening the argument.

rigor.statement: The Department of Conservation advice said that changes would be incompatible with the purpose, will undermine biodiversity outcomes, and create significant equity issues. I urge the Minister of Conservation to reconsider. I urge the National Party to step up to your better instincts.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the appeal in cited official DOC advice rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: Is this piece of legislation perfect? No... Is this piece of legislation better than nothing? Absolutely yes... we should not in this Parliament let the perfect be the enemy of the good.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned cost-benefit framing acknowledging the bill's imperfections while arguing it is a net improvement.

rigor.statement: When I last checked about an hour ago on the legislation website, there were no Amendment Papers explaining what the Minister's intentions are. It's very upsetting that this legislation could be turned on its head at this late stage and that the only opportunity for scrutiny of the benefit to private individuals... seems to be in a committee stage of the whole House.
rigor.explanation: Builds a procedural-scrutiny argument from the absence of published amendments rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: There are land-use pressures coming down from the Firth of Thames—a huge sediment load from some of those rivers. The Piako River is—there's an old post about 100 metres from the mouth of the river which marks where the mouth of the river used to be. That is the amount of accretion of land at the mouth of the river caused by sediment flows.
rigor.explanation: Explains the gulf's decline through named, physical causal mechanisms (population, land-use, sediment) rather than generalities.

rigor.statement: In respect of the reference that is made to people catching fish who need to catch fish to eat, I think we have to be careful that we don't create different standards of access to the recreational fishery. That would be a big step in New Zealand that we've so far avoided and would lead to conflicts within communities that I think are best avoided.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a principled concern (differential access to the fishery) and reasons about its downstream consequences.

rigor.statement: In farming parlance, the gulf's overgrazed and the best remedy is to shut the gate and let it recover—and this is what this bill seeks to do by creating 19 new protection areas.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an agricultural analogy ('overgrazed', 'shut the gate') rather than evidence to justify the approach.

rigor.statement: We saw great evidence in the select committee about kina barrens and other things that are plaguing the gulf, and I think it's really important that we can extend the protection of the gulf since so little of it is currently protected.
rigor.explanation: References specific select-committee evidence (kina barrens) to support extending protection, though stated generally.

divination.statement: it's extremely unlikely that relaxing advertising rules on Christmas Day, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Anzac Day morning will make the slightest difference to the difficulties overall that New Zealand media organisations are facing.
divination.explanation: Predicts the repeal will have negligible effect on the sector's overall difficulties; plausible given the scale of the structural pressures she describes.

divination.statement: until we find a satisfactory solution to our old media / new media dilemma, until that can be engineered, and until the question of trust in news is addressed and we return to more rigour in our journalism—and we are seeing some green shoots of that—the migration of audience from our old media to our new media will continue, and this is putting a strain on our mainstream media.
divination.explanation: Predicts continued audience migration from old to new media absent a solution; directionally well-supported by current trends.

forthrightness.statement: my colleague Minister Goldsmith is working very, very hard and diligently in this portfolio. He does have COVID, which is why he wasn't able to be at the select committee
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the prior criticism of the Minister's absence with a concrete reason (COVID).

forthrightness.statement: Te Pāti Māori supports aspirations for the protection and restoration of Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana. Te Pāti Māori does not support efforts to undermine the protection and restoration of the moana, and while the bill may have started with the right intentions, it has landed in the wrong place. Therefore, Te Pāti Māori oppose this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: States the party's position and reasoning plainly — supports protection in principle but opposes this bill.

forthrightness.statement: I want to put on record that I am in favour of more protection, not less, and I know that there are many members of this House that share the same view that I have.
forthrightness.explanation: Plainly states his own position on the record without hedging.

authenticity.statement: I'm going to support the bill, but the bill is, basically, going to produce $6 million in an industry that is absolutely on its feet.
authenticity.explanation: Supports the bill while candidly acknowledging its inadequacy — a consistent, non-tribal position rather than blanket opposition.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First have ruined what should have been a happy story for the National Party at the last minute by allowing Shane Jones to lobby the Minister of Conservation after he himself had been lobbied by the fishing industry.
authenticity.explanation: As a low-authenticity charge against Jones/NZ First: alleges they overturned a multipartisan agreement to serve industry lobbyists (a claim about that opponent, not the speaker).

authenticity.statement: I want to put on record that I am in favour of more protection, not less, and I know that there are many members of this House that share the same view that I have.
authenticity.explanation: As a government MP openly stating a preference at odds with his own side's late amendment allowing more fishing — a principled, consistent stance.

authenticity.statement: Labour introduced this bill. We got it off the ground. I was there on the day that Chris Hipkins announced it, alongside Rachel Brooking and Willow-Jean Prime and Helen White. We absolutely believe in this.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit for originating the bill and ties it to a consistent Labour position; corroborated by other speakers' accounts of the bill's origin.

strength.statement: Labour introduced this bill. We got it off the ground. I was there on the day that Chris Hipkins announced it, alongside Rachel Brooking and Willow-Jean Prime and Helen White. We absolutely believe in this.
strength.explanation: Claims Labour introduced and progressed the bill — a genuine legislative step, though final passage and outcome remain in the current Government's hands.

charisma.statement: In stark contrast to years gone by, Ministers in this Government have actually got things done.
charisma.explanation: Partisan, us-vs-them framing that praises his own side by contrast with the previous government; rallies rather than builds cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: There are friendships across this floor, so I really do want to wish you all a merry Christmas and a happy New Year with your whānau and loved ones.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building acknowledgement of cross-party goodwill; reaches across the aisle rather than demonising opponents.

charisma.statement: I just want to reflect for a moment on the fact that nobody comes to this Chamber with bad intentions, in my view. Nobody comes to this place wanting to make things worse. We may disagree and have strong views strongly expressed, and sometimes sung, about how to achieve the making of things better, but we all have that objective.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, consensus-seeking; invites the whole House into a shared purpose and finds common ground across parties.

charisma.statement: This is a place where strong views should be strongly held and strongly expressed, but with respect to each other, in my view.
charisma.explanation: Unifying appeal to a shared norm of mutual respect that speaks to all sides.

charisma.statement: I want to wish colleagues from around the House—from my own party, from our coalition partners in New Zealand First and in ACT, and from the other parties in the Opposition—a warm summer welcome to the beautiful Coromandel
charisma.explanation: Deliberately names every party, including the Opposition, in an inclusive gesture of goodwill; bridge-building rather than tribal.

charisma.statement: Chris Bishop made the point about how many bills have been passed and how many questions have been asked and all that sort of thing, and I think we’ve actually collectively as a Parliament achieved a lot.
charisma.explanation: Frames the year's output as a collective parliamentary achievement rather than a partisan win, drawing the whole House in.

specificity.statement: In stark contrast to years gone by, Ministers in this Government have actually got things done.
specificity.explanation: Vague boast with no named policy, figure, or mechanism to substantiate 'got things done'.

specificity.statement: We had 149 projects—that were included in the bill.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise figure tied to a named piece of legislation, though little further detail.

specificity.statement: We’ve had 93 first readings, 60 bills reported back from select committees, and 60 third readings. Ministers have answered 87,000 written parliamentary questions.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise numeric figures for legislative throughput and written questions.

specificity.statement: In the first year in Government, the Nats forgot Kiwis: $12 billion borrowed, jobs down the gurgler, tens of thousands leaving, Seven Luxon houses, tax breaks for landlords— Forty thousand marched, three strikes is back, tobacco, and guns,
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures and policies ($12b, seven houses, forty thousand marchers, three strikes) but in compressed slogan form without sourcing or context.

civility.statement: Simeon Brown has had to sell precisely zero shares in Auckland Airport. In fact, he sold zero shares in the entities he’s responsible for, in stark contrast to the last Minister of Transport.
civility.explanation: A pointed jibe alluding to the previous Transport Minister's (Michael Wood's) share-holding scandal; a personal cheap shot at an opponent rather than engagement with policy substance, albeit delivered as end-of-year humour.

civility.statement: There are friendships across this floor, so I really do want to wish you all a merry Christmas and a happy New Year with your whānau and loved ones.
civility.explanation: Respectful, warm, and focused on shared humanity across party lines.

civility.statement: In the first year in Government, the Nats forgot Kiwis: $12 billion borrowed, jobs down the gurgler, tens of thousands leaving, Seven Luxon houses, tax breaks for landlords— Forty thousand marched, three strikes is back, tobacco, and guns,
civility.explanation: Partisan attack song; largely aimed at policies and record rather than personal insult, but hyperbolic ('forgot Kiwis') and mocking in tone.

civility.statement: I just want to reflect for a moment on the fact that nobody comes to this Chamber with bad intentions, in my view. Nobody comes to this place wanting to make things worse. We may disagree and have strong views strongly expressed, and sometimes sung, about how to achieve the making of things better, but we all have that objective.
civility.explanation: Explicitly attributes good faith to opponents and frames disagreement as being about means, not motives — the antithesis of personal attack.

civility.statement: This is a place where strong views should be strongly held and strongly expressed, but with respect to each other, in my view.
civility.explanation: Directly endorses respectful disagreement over personal attack as the standard for debate.

veracity.statement: We had 149 projects—that were included in the bill.
veracity.explanation: Verifiable factual claim about the Fast-track Approvals Bill, which did list 149 projects; consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: We’ve had 93 first readings, 60 bills reported back from select committees, and 60 third readings. Ministers have answered 87,000 written parliamentary questions.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable parliamentary tally figures presented as fact; plausible and of a kind drawn from official House statistics, though not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: In the first year in Government, the Nats forgot Kiwis: $12 billion borrowed, jobs down the gurgler, tens of thousands leaving, Seven Luxon houses, tax breaks for landlords— Forty thousand marched, three strikes is back, tobacco, and guns,
veracity.explanation: A mix of broadly accurate references (Luxon's property holdings, the reinstatement of three strikes, the large Treaty Principles hīkoi) and rhetorical framing ('the Nats forgot Kiwis', 'jobs down the gurgler') that overstates for effect; partly true but selectively framed.

veracity.statement: Kiwis have seen inflation down to 2.2 percent, down from 7.3 percent; they've seen three interest rate cuts after 12 rises
veracity.explanation: CPI inflation did fall to ~2.2% (Q3 2024) from a 7.3% peak, and the RBNZ made three OCR cuts in late 2024 after the prior hiking cycle — figures are broadly accurate, though the fall is largely global and not solely government-driven.

veracity.statement: their wages are rising faster than inflation for four quarters in a row, after 13 quarters of declining real wages
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with real-wage data returning to positive as inflation fell, though the precise quarter counts are selectively framed.

veracity.statement: there is tax relief for 3.5 million New Zealanders for the first time in 14 years
veracity.explanation: Income tax thresholds were adjusted in July 2024 (thresholds had been static since 2010/2011), affecting a large number — broadly accurate, though '14 years' and the headcount are generous framings.

veracity.statement: Gang patches are banned, ram raids are down 60 percent, and the foot patrols are up 30 percent.
veracity.explanation: The gang-patch ban was enacted (in force Nov 2024); the 60% and 30% figures are selectively chosen point-in-time comparisons that overstate a settled trend.

veracity.statement: Phones are banned from classrooms, we've got structured literacy and maths in place to teach our kids the basics brilliantly, and school attendance is up six points.
veracity.explanation: The phone ban was implemented in Term 1 2024; the 'up six points' attendance claim is a favourable reading of volatile term-by-term data.

veracity.statement: In health, we've invested a record $16.7 billion more. We've rolled out 26 new cancer treatments as part of 54 new medicines helping 175,000 Kiwis, and we've hired 2,900 more nurses.
veracity.explanation: The Pharmac funding boost (~$604m, 54 medicines) is real; the '$16.7 billion' is a multi-year cumulative figure and nurse-hiring counts are net-vs-gross ambiguous — accurate in outline, generously framed.

veracity.statement: we've had total victimisations down, after violent crime was up 33 percent and retail crime doubled
veracity.explanation: The '33 percent' and 'doubled' figures describe the prior period and are cherry-picked comparisons; the claimed reduction is early and contested.

veracity.statement: They have committed to pulling in $200 billion through a capital gains tax—or about half the size of the New Zealand economy.
veracity.explanation: Misrepresents Te Pāti Māori tax policy; the '$200 billion' framing is a cumulative-over-decades construction presented as if a single grab, which is misleading.

veracity.statement: when they spend a year in Opposition ostensibly working on policy, the three things that they come up with are: (1) not joining a security agreement; (2) building a hospital that they've already failed to deliver and build; and (3) working up some new taxes that they've actually been talking about for over a decade
veracity.explanation: A caricatured summary that strips context; reductive but loosely tied to real Labour positions.

veracity.statement: And Simon Watts, who is delivering net-zero six years earlier while still growing our economy.
veracity.explanation: 'Delivering net-zero six years earlier' overstates policy that at best sets a pathway; framed as accomplished fact when it is aspiration.

veracity.statement: the $2.9 billion tax cut they gave to landlords whilst cutting the support for first-home buyers
veracity.explanation: Refers to restored interest deductibility; the '$2.9 billion' figure is a contested cost estimate and 'tax cut to landlords' is a loaded framing of a policy reversal.

veracity.statement: repealing smoke-free legislation while giving over $200 million in tax breaks to tobacco companies
veracity.explanation: The smokefree repeal happened, but '$200 million tax breaks to tobacco companies' is a contested characterisation of excise/policy decisions, not a direct corporate handout.

veracity.statement: the 13,000 people in that industry who have lost their jobs in the last year because of the decisions of this Government
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses did occur, but attributing all 13,000 solely to government decisions ignores interest-rate and cycle effects — partly true, over-attributed.

veracity.statement: while they won't build any more State houses, they'll spend seven million bucks on a couple of new ministerial offices for their staff
veracity.explanation: The office-fitout spend was reported; the state-house 'won't build any more' claim is an overstatement of a funding reduction — mostly grounded but sharpened.

veracity.statement: There are 22,000 more New Zealanders on a jobseeker benefit under this Government.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker numbers did rise materially over 2024; the figure is in the right range, though driven substantially by the wider economic slowdown.

veracity.statement: a Prime Minister that thinks that those on low incomes are "bottom feeders"
veracity.explanation: Misattributes context; the 'bottom feeders' phrase was not a blanket description of low-income people, so this is a misleading characterisation.

veracity.statement: They've changed the goal posts on child poverty reduction targets after it became clear they weren't going to meet them.
veracity.explanation: The government did revise child-poverty targets, consistent with the claim; 'after it became clear' imputes motive that is arguable.

veracity.statement: They've cut the pay equity task force because they don't think women should earn the same amount of pay as men for the same amount of work.
veracity.explanation: The stated motive ('don't think women should earn the same') is asserted, not evidenced — a misleading imputation even if a body was disestablished.

veracity.statement: There is not a reputable economist in this country who would argue against a capital gains tax—so do it.
veracity.explanation: Overstated: economists are divided on CGT design; the sweeping 'not one' claim is not supportable.

veracity.statement: Prime Minister, you yourself have acknowledged that your Government's decisions have inflamed race relations in this country—so stop it.
veracity.explanation: Luxon did make comments acknowledging tension around race relations, so the attribution is broadly fair though paraphrased.

veracity.statement: during the election you said that the policies of one of your new coalition parties targeting the rainbow community were "on another planet", but those same policies now underpin your coalition agreements
veracity.explanation: Luxon did use dismissive language about some ACT positions during the campaign; whether those exact policies now 'underpin' the agreements is a debatable stretch.

veracity.statement: If the estimated 100,000 people that this Government has managed to mobilise against their attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi tell us anything, it is that your power, Mr Prime Minister, will be fleeting.
veracity.explanation: The '100,000' hīkoi figure sits at the high end of contested crowd estimates (police put it far lower).

veracity.statement: Our minimum wage is one of the highest in the developed world—I think it's the fifth highest—compared with the median wage
veracity.explanation: NZ's minimum-to-median wage ratio is indeed among the highest in the OECD; the specific 'fifth highest' rank is plausible but hedged and unverified.

veracity.statement: I look at the work that Brooke van Velden is doing, the youngest Cabinet Minister in 40 years and taking to it like a duck to water, going out and listening to people about health and safety for three months so she is formulating policy informed by the experiences of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: The 'youngest Cabinet Minister in 40 years' is a plausible but unverified superlative; the consultation description is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: This party is a party of frauds. They've broken the Electoral Act, they've broken the Charities Act, they've made tens of millions on the backs of their people
veracity.explanation: Presents allegations then under investigation as established fact ('have broken'), which is misleading.

veracity.statement: why doesn't your party chairman practise law? Let's start. He declared war upon us, and do you know why he doesn't practise law? Because he got convicted of forging and uttering
veracity.explanation: An unverifiable-in-context personal claim presented as certain fact.

veracity.statement: we've been overseas about 112 days this year, but I've spent more time in Parliament than all those put together
veracity.explanation: 'More time in Parliament than all of Te Pāti Māori put together' is a rhetorical boast that is not readily substantiated.

veracity.statement: I can remember David Caygill as the finance Minister. He reported in 1990 a $89 million surplus, and it ended up a $3.2 billion deficit.
veracity.explanation: Points to a real episode of forecast-to-outturn deterioration around 1990, though the exact figures are recalled and rounded.

veracity.statement: we see over here where they don't even turn up at Parliament, don't even turn up at select committees, don't even do their jobs properly and they're getting away with it
veracity.explanation: Sweeping attendance claim asserted without evidence and likely exaggerated.

veracity.statement: one party set it out last year that we're in a far, far worse situation. It's horrifying to be proven right—horrifying to be proven right.
veracity.explanation: 'Proven right' about the economy being worse than known is arguable and selectively framed.

veracity.statement: who stood shoulder to shoulder to unite on a hīkoi from both ends of Aotearoa that saw 100,000 of our people converge on the lawns of this very Parliament
veracity.explanation: The 100,000 figure is the organisers' high-end estimate for the Te Tiriti hīkoi; official estimates were substantially lower, so it is contested.

veracity.statement: he has delivered less than half of the 670 chargers that he promised
veracity.explanation: EV-charger rollout did lag the stated target, consistent with the claim, though the precise ratio is debatable.

veracity.statement: Last year, she was on it as the Grinch who stole Christmas when she cancelled the $551 million interisland ferries.
veracity.explanation: The iRex ferry project was cancelled; the '$551 million' figure references a contract sum but the wider project cost was far larger, so the framing is partial.

specificity.statement: Kiwis have seen inflation down to 2.2 percent, down from 7.3 percent; they've seen three interest rate cuts after 12 rises
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and counts (2.2% vs 7.3%, three cuts vs 12 rises).

specificity.statement: their wages are rising faster than inflation for four quarters in a row, after 13 quarters of declining real wages
specificity.explanation: Quantified with quarter counts, but no wage figures.

specificity.statement: there is tax relief for 3.5 million New Zealanders for the first time in 14 years
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (3.5 million) and timeframe (14 years).

specificity.statement: Gang patches are banned, ram raids are down 60 percent, and the foot patrols are up 30 percent.
specificity.explanation: Named policy plus two percentage figures.

specificity.statement: Phones are banned from classrooms, we've got structured literacy and maths in place to teach our kids the basics brilliantly, and school attendance is up six points.
specificity.explanation: Named policies plus an attendance figure, though 'brilliantly' is filler.

specificity.statement: In health, we've invested a record $16.7 billion more. We've rolled out 26 new cancer treatments as part of 54 new medicines helping 175,000 Kiwis, and we've hired 2,900 more nurses.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures: dollar amount, treatment counts, beneficiary and staffing numbers.

specificity.statement: we've had total victimisations down, after violent crime was up 33 percent and retail crime doubled
specificity.explanation: Percentages given, but 'total victimisations down' lacks a magnitude.

specificity.statement: that's a lot of progress represented by 160 actions in our quarterly action plans alone
specificity.explanation: Cites a count (160 actions) but 'actions' is an undifferentiated measure of activity rather than outcomes.

specificity.statement: the $2.9 billion tax cut they gave to landlords whilst cutting the support for first-home buyers
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and the beneficiary/loser groups.

specificity.statement: repealing smoke-free legislation while giving over $200 million in tax breaks to tobacco companies
specificity.explanation: Names a figure and the two paired actions.

specificity.statement: the 13,000 people in that industry who have lost their jobs in the last year because of the decisions of this Government
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, sector and timeframe.

specificity.statement: while they won't build any more State houses, they'll spend seven million bucks on a couple of new ministerial offices for their staff
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure, though 'a couple of' is vague.

specificity.statement: There are 22,000 more New Zealanders on a jobseeker benefit under this Government.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure attributed to a defined period.

specificity.statement: Politics does not have to be this cynical game. Politics can and should be about regular people working together to solve the big issues.
specificity.explanation: An idealistic sentiment with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: Our minimum wage is one of the highest in the developed world—I think it's the fifth highest—compared with the median wage
specificity.explanation: Gives a ranking and the correct comparator (relative to median wage), though self-hedged.

specificity.statement: I was so proud of launching seven charter schools—among other things I have done myself—up and down New Zealand, from all different cultural backgrounds, with so many different pedagogical approaches
specificity.explanation: Gives a number and some texture, but no locations, funding, or roll figures.

specificity.statement: I look at the work that Brooke van Velden is doing, the youngest Cabinet Minister in 40 years and taking to it like a duck to water, going out and listening to people about health and safety for three months so she is formulating policy informed by the experiences of everyday New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names a process (three-month consultation on health and safety) but no policy detail.

specificity.statement: we've been overseas about 112 days this year, but I've spent more time in Parliament than all those put together
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (112 days) though the comparison is loose.

specificity.statement: I can remember David Caygill as the finance Minister. He reported in 1990 a $89 million surplus, and it ended up a $3.2 billion deficit.
specificity.explanation: Names person, year, and two dollar figures.

specificity.statement: who stood shoulder to shoulder to unite on a hīkoi from both ends of Aotearoa that saw 100,000 of our people converge on the lawns of this very Parliament
specificity.explanation: Names a crowd figure and location.

specificity.statement: he has delivered less than half of the 670 chargers that he promised
specificity.explanation: Names the target figure (670) and quantifies the shortfall.

specificity.statement: Last year, she was on it as the Grinch who stole Christmas when she cancelled the $551 million interisland ferries.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure and the specific decision.

strength.statement: there is tax relief for 3.5 million New Zealanders for the first time in 14 years
strength.explanation: A campaigned-on tax change that was actually enacted this term; delivery is real, magnitude modest.

strength.statement: Gang patches are banned, ram raids are down 60 percent, and the foot patrols are up 30 percent.
strength.explanation: The gang-patch ban was a specific commitment legislated and delivered this term.

strength.statement: Phones are banned from classrooms, we've got structured literacy and maths in place to teach our kids the basics brilliantly, and school attendance is up six points.
strength.explanation: Phone ban and structured-literacy rollout are concrete delivered actions this term.

strength.statement: In health, we've invested a record $16.7 billion more. We've rolled out 26 new cancer treatments as part of 54 new medicines helping 175,000 Kiwis, and we've hired 2,900 more nurses.
strength.explanation: The medicines funding was announced and rolled out this term — concrete delivery, though staffing claims are harder to verify.

strength.statement: that's a lot of progress represented by 160 actions in our quarterly action plans alone
strength.explanation: Counting completed action-plan items evidences follow-through, but activity counts are not the same as delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: And Simon Watts, who is delivering net-zero six years earlier while still growing our economy.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a long-horizon target not yet delivered — announcement rather than delivery.

strength.statement: I was so proud of launching seven charter schools—among other things I have done myself—up and down New Zealand, from all different cultural backgrounds, with so many different pedagogical approaches
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of a concrete, countable policy (seven charter schools launched) that he was responsible for — genuine follow-through, though early.

civility.statement: They have committed to pulling in $200 billion through a capital gains tax—or about half the size of the New Zealand economy.
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature of an opponent's policy ('Grinch stealing every Christmas'), though aimed at policy not person.

civility.statement: when they spend a year in Opposition ostensibly working on policy, the three things that they come up with are: (1) not joining a security agreement; (2) building a hospital that they've already failed to deliver and build; and (3) working up some new taxes that they've actually been talking about for over a decade
civility.explanation: Dismissive of Labour's output but engages with actual policy positions rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: it's just great—it's just great—to see the Greens live those values by being a parody of themselves each and every single day
civility.explanation: A mocking jab at a whole party ('a parody of themselves') with no policy substance.

civility.statement: the $2.9 billion tax cut they gave to landlords whilst cutting the support for first-home buyers
civility.explanation: Pointed but criticises a policy choice rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: repealing smoke-free legislation while giving over $200 million in tax breaks to tobacco companies
civility.explanation: Sharp juxtaposition but policy-focused.

civility.statement: while they won't build any more State houses, they'll spend seven million bucks on a couple of new ministerial offices for their staff
civility.explanation: Contrast framing to imply bad priorities; policy-based but rhetorically loaded.

civility.statement: a Prime Minister that thinks that those on low incomes are "bottom feeders"
civility.explanation: Imputes a demeaning belief to the PM personally — closer to character attack than policy critique.

civility.statement: They've changed the goal posts on child poverty reduction targets after it became clear they weren't going to meet them.
civility.explanation: Accuses of moving goalposts but centres on a policy record.

civility.statement: They've cut the pay equity task force because they don't think women should earn the same amount of pay as men for the same amount of work.
civility.explanation: Ascribes a discriminatory intent to opponents rather than engaging the policy rationale.

civility.statement: We have two men propping up this dead old guy and trying to pretend that he's still alive.
civility.explanation: Comedic 'Weekend at Bernie's' analogy but personalises coalition leaders as propping up a 'dead' figure — a personal jab.

civility.statement: There is not a reputable economist in this country who would argue against a capital gains tax—so do it.
civility.explanation: Direct challenge to the PM on policy, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Prime Minister, you yourself have acknowledged that your Government's decisions have inflamed race relations in this country—so stop it.
civility.explanation: Confrontational but addresses the PM's own stated position and policy consequences.

civility.statement: during the election you said that the policies of one of your new coalition parties targeting the rainbow community were "on another planet", but those same policies now underpin your coalition agreements
civility.explanation: Charges inconsistency but does so by quoting the PM's own words and coalition record.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge members across the House, particularly our friends in Labour and Te Pāti Māori, for the aroha that you wrapped around us that day and in those following weeks. We will never forget that.
civility.explanation: Gracious tribute honouring colleagues from other parties after the death of Efeso Collins.

civility.statement: Just this past month, we lost the Hon Nikki Kaye. She was respected across this House because she stood so strongly for things—she even crossed the floor to do that.
civility.explanation: Respectful cross-party tribute focused on character and principle.

civility.statement: I've been here so long I can remember when Chlöe Swarbrick was actually fun. I can even remember when she talked about the environment, unlike that speech which made no reference to it whatsoever.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at an opponent's character/appeal, though the environment point is a fair critique of the speech.

civility.statement: What I can see is an Opposition that is still going through the stages of grief. Man, they pick some tiny issues—tiny minds, tiny people, and tiny issues
civility.explanation: 'Tiny minds, tiny people' is a direct belittling personal attack on opponents.

civility.statement: This party is a party of frauds. They've broken the Electoral Act, they've broken the Charities Act, they've made tens of millions on the backs of their people
civility.explanation: Blanket 'party of frauds' accusation — a serious personal/collective slur, not policy critique.

civility.statement: why doesn't your party chairman practise law? Let's start. He declared war upon us, and do you know why he doesn't practise law? Because he got convicted of forging and uttering
civility.explanation: Airs a damaging personal allegation about a named individual to discredit opponents — a cheap shot under parliamentary privilege.

civility.statement: we've been overseas about 112 days this year, but I've spent more time in Parliament than all those put together
civility.explanation: Used to imply opponents are absentee — a needling attack on their diligence.

civility.statement: I have no difficulty in withdrawing and apologising. I didn't mean any offence at all. I just happened to admire someone who used to do projects because she understood who in Parliament might help her get the job done. But if that causes offence, well, I'm apologising, I'm very, very sorry.
civility.explanation: Gracious, full withdrawal and apology in response to Willie Jackson's point of order — respectful de-escalation.

civility.statement: we see over here where they don't even turn up at Parliament, don't even turn up at select committees, don't even do their jobs properly and they're getting away with it
civility.explanation: 'Lazy, idle' style attack on opponents' work ethic; disparaging rather than substantive.

civility.statement: Oh no, no. Listen, sunshine, I'll be around long after you've gone because nobody wants the "Midnight Cowboy" any more.
civility.explanation: Condescending 'sunshine' and a mocking nickname aimed personally at Rawiri Waititi.

civility.statement: E kai i ō rongoa, e koro. [Take your medicine, old man.]
civility.explanation: A dismissive personal jab directed at Winston Peters ('old man').

civility.statement: Maybe if the Government cared less about three strikes and more about the three articles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, this year could have gone differently.
civility.explanation: A pointed contrast that criticises priorities via a rhetorical device rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: he has delivered less than half of the 670 chargers that he promised
civility.explanation: Mocking in tone but grounded in a delivery-against-target critique of Simeon Brown.

civility.statement: Last year, she was on it as the Grinch who stole Christmas when she cancelled the $551 million interisland ferries.
