civility.explanation: Uses a festive caricature ('Grinch') of Nicola Willis but anchored to a real policy decision.

rigor.statement: They've cut the pay equity task force because they don't think women should earn the same amount of pay as men for the same amount of work.
rigor.explanation: Attributes an extreme motive to a policy decision without evidence — closer to strawman than reasoned inference.

rigor.statement: There is not a reputable economist in this country who would argue against a capital gains tax—so do it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority stated as an absolute ('not a reputable economist') to close off debate, without citing the reasoning.

rigor.statement: Our minimum wage is one of the highest in the developed world—I think it's the fifth highest—compared with the median wage
rigor.explanation: Uses a relevant statistical framing to support a cost-on-business argument, but relies on a self-recalled figure.

rigor.statement: Does it mean that we are a combination of two collectives where for ever and a day we'll be recognised based on who our ancestry was and given rights based on our ancestry? Or are we indeed a liberal, democratic society filled with thinking and valuing individuals who are able to make the most of their time on Earth without discrimination
rigor.explanation: Frames the Treaty debate as a binary between 'two collectives' and 'individuals' — a false dichotomy that excludes middle positions.

rigor.statement: This party is a party of frauds. They've broken the Electoral Act, they've broken the Charities Act, they've made tens of millions on the backs of their people
rigor.explanation: Asserts guilt without adjudicated evidence; conclusion outruns the premises.

rigor.statement: I can remember David Caygill as the finance Minister. He reported in 1990 a $89 million surplus, and it ended up a $3.2 billion deficit.
rigor.explanation: Uses a historical analogy to argue forecasts can be badly wrong — relevant but anecdotal support for the broader claim.

rigor.statement: We may be the minority in Parliament, but our movement is the majority across Aotearoa.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping 'majority across Aotearoa' claim asserted without evidence; rhetorical rather than substantiated.

divination.statement: If the estimated 100,000 people that this Government has managed to mobilise against their attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi tell us anything, it is that your power, Mr Prime Minister, will be fleeting.
divination.explanation: A prediction that the PM's power will be short-lived; directional and politically motivated, no defined timeframe, genuinely uncertain.

divination.statement: Oh no, no. Listen, sunshine, I'll be around long after you've gone because nobody wants the "Midnight Cowboy" any more.
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that Waititi will be gone from Parliament while Peters remains — highly uncertain and self-serving.

divination.statement: You watch the next election, and that goes for Te Pāti Māori sitting on the left-hand side of them as well.
divination.explanation: Predicts the Greens and Te Pāti Māori will fare badly at the next election — no timeframe detail beyond 'next election' and highly uncertain.

charisma.statement: If the estimated 100,000 people that this Government has managed to mobilise against their attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi tell us anything, it is that your power, Mr Prime Minister, will be fleeting.
charisma.explanation: Rallies her own movement but frames the PM as adversary rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Politics does not have to be this cynical game. Politics can and should be about regular people working together to solve the big issues.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, aspirational appeal to collaboration over cynicism.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge members across the House, particularly our friends in Labour and Te Pāti Māori, for the aroha that you wrapped around us that day and in those following weeks. We will never forget that.
charisma.explanation: Warm, cross-party acknowledgement that builds goodwill across the House.

charisma.statement: Just this past month, we lost the Hon Nikki Kaye. She was respected across this House because she stood so strongly for things—she even crossed the floor to do that.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across party lines to honour a National MP for principled conduct.

charisma.statement: What I can see is an Opposition that is still going through the stages of grief. Man, they pick some tiny issues—tiny minds, tiny people, and tiny issues
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side by demeaning the other; divisive rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: Does it mean that we are a combination of two collectives where for ever and a day we'll be recognised based on who our ancestry was and given rights based on our ancestry? Or are we indeed a liberal, democratic society filled with thinking and valuing individuals who are able to make the most of their time on Earth without discrimination
charisma.explanation: Confident and values-driven, but poses an either/or that appeals to his own base rather than bridging.

charisma.statement: We may be the minority in Parliament, but our movement is the majority across Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Rousing to supporters but frames the country in majority/minority terms that speak mainly to his own base.

charisma.statement: Maybe if the Government cared less about three strikes and more about the three articles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, this year could have gone differently.
charisma.explanation: Clever framing that appeals to his own side more than it persuades opponents.

charisma.statement: our tangata moana, tangata Tiriti, who rose up and marched alongside, who educated one another, who understood that this wasn't a single issue but a shared responsibility to rise up for the Aotearoa our mokopuna deserve
charisma.explanation: Inclusive language embracing non-Māori allies ('tangata Tiriti') and framing a shared cause, though within an oppositional movement.

authenticity.statement: one party set it out last year that we're in a far, far worse situation. It's horrifying to be proven right—horrifying to be proven right.
authenticity.explanation: Claims his 2023 warnings about the economy are consistent with events; a plausible self-consistency claim but self-assessed and unverified.

authenticity.statement: Te Pāti Māori have consistently remained mokopuna-focused
authenticity.explanation: A self-consistency claim about his party's steadfast focus; plausible but self-assessed with no external test in the text.

veracity.statement: Lyn Fleming was an exceptional police officer with 38 years of front-line service. Her policing career started in 1986 as a traffic officer in Auckland before joining the Police in 1992, when the organisations merged. She spent 32 years on the front line of Nelson, spending the last seven years as Nelson Bay's area response manager.
veracity.explanation: A detailed, internally consistent biographical account (dates, roles, tenure) consistent with the public record of the officer's career; no misleading framing.

veracity.statement: The respect that the community holds for Lyn was evident when 2,000 people came together for a candlelit vigil in the rain to honour Lyn's legacy and show their support for the local police
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable claim about vigil attendance; consistent with contemporaneous reporting of the Nelson vigil.

veracity.statement: Those qualities drew more than 1,200 people to remember Senior Sergeant Fleming at her funeral in Nelson.
veracity.explanation: Specific, falsifiable attendance figure consistent with reports of the funeral; the '1,200' aligns with the scale others described ('hundreds').

veracity.statement: a woman who gave 38 years and seven months of service to her community
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the 38-year figure cited by other speakers; a precise, checkable factual claim.

veracity.statement: a defining moment in her career, as mentioned earlier, came in 2004 when she, along with Matua Tā Pita Sharples, Matua Whatarangi, and a whole host of hōia came together to establish the Māori Party—Te Pāti Māori.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 2004 founding of the Māori Party by Turia and Sharples; matches the historical record.

veracity.statement: In 2008, Te Pāti Māori entered into an agreement, a cooperation agreement with our National Party, and while maintaining its toka tū moana—an independent stance—the parties worked together to create policies that would benefit Māori and indeed all New Zealanders, especially through Whānau Ora.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Māori Party signed a confidence-and-supply/cooperation arrangement with National after the 2008 election, with Whānau Ora a flagship outcome.

veracity.statement: I think about when she crossed the floor... the kaupapa, which at the time was the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical reference to Turia crossing the floor over the Foreshore and Seabed legislation in 2004.

veracity.statement: she was the only Te Pāti Māori MP from 2004. She spoke on every single Government bill, she never missed a vote, and she attended select committees.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate about her lone-MP status and diligence, but the absolute claims ('every single', 'never missed a vote') are strong assertions that risk mild overstatement.

veracity.statement: I'm proud to say, as Sir Micheal Cullen noted at the time, that ACT was the only party that stood consistently with that position in favour of the rule of law at that time.
veracity.explanation: Substantially accurate that ACT opposed the 2004 legislation on rule-of-law grounds, though the 'only party' claim is a self-flattering characterisation attributed to Cullen.

veracity.statement: it was because of Dame Tariana's advocacy in the background that while we were in Government, our two parties, for nine years, were able to bring about and sustain partnership schools or kura hourua.
veracity.explanation: Partnership schools were established (2014) and operated for several years; the 'nine years' framing is loose given they were closed under Labour before their 2024 reintroduction.

veracity.statement: But as we see new kura hourua opening up and down New Zealand this week, that is one of the ways that I remember her
veracity.explanation: Accurate present-tense claim: charter schools were being reopened around early 2025 under Seymour's policy.

veracity.statement: She understood that the health of our lungs was related to, and could be not removed from, the health of the air around us in the mahi that she did on Smokefree.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes Smokefree advocacy to Turia, who championed the Smokefree 2025 goal as Associate Health Minister.

specificity.statement: Lyn Fleming was an exceptional police officer with 38 years of front-line service. Her policing career started in 1986 as a traffic officer in Auckland before joining the Police in 1992, when the organisations merged. She spent 32 years on the front line of Nelson, spending the last seven years as Nelson Bay's area response manager.
specificity.explanation: Concrete years (1986, 1992), durations (38 years, 32 years, seven years) and named roles — highly specific rather than a vague tribute.

specificity.statement: The respect that the community holds for Lyn was evident when 2,000 people came together for a candlelit vigil in the rain to honour Lyn's legacy and show their support for the local police
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure (2,000) and setting, though rounded and without further detail.

specificity.statement: Those qualities drew more than 1,200 people to remember Senior Sergeant Fleming at her funeral in Nelson.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure and location, anchoring the tribute in concrete detail.

specificity.statement: a woman who gave 38 years and seven months of service to her community
specificity.explanation: Unusually precise (to the month) length-of-service claim rather than a round approximation.

specificity.statement: a defining moment in her career, as mentioned earlier, came in 2004 when she, along with Matua Tā Pita Sharples, Matua Whatarangi, and a whole host of hōia came together to establish the Māori Party—Te Pāti Māori.
specificity.explanation: Names the year, the party, and the key co-founders.

specificity.statement: In 2008, Te Pāti Māori entered into an agreement, a cooperation agreement with our National Party, and while maintaining its toka tū moana—an independent stance—the parties worked together to create policies that would benefit Māori and indeed all New Zealanders, especially through Whānau Ora.
specificity.explanation: Dates the arrangement (2008), names the parties and the concrete resulting policy.

specificity.statement: she was the only Te Pāti Māori MP from 2004. She spoke on every single Government bill, she never missed a vote, and she attended select committees.
specificity.explanation: Concrete claims about attendance, voting record and legislative participation.

specificity.statement: it was because of Dame Tariana's advocacy in the background that while we were in Government, our two parties, for nine years, were able to bring about and sustain partnership schools or kura hourua.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy and a duration, but the timeframe is imprecise.

civility.statement: I'd like to extend my condolences to the entire Police family. I have seen how much this has impacted you all and how you have rallied around to support each other during this very difficult time.
civility.explanation: Respectful, supportive language focused on acknowledging others' grief; no attack or provocation.

civility.statement: I want to endorse all of the words just spoken by the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of a rival leader, prioritising shared mourning over partisanship.

civility.statement: But we growl and we come in here and we get grumpy... One of the things that I want to do is remind ourselves, as the year starts, of the legacy of Whaea Tariana... I promise this year I'll try, Chris Bishop, not to show my teeth so much.
civility.explanation: Openly reflecting on her own combativeness and committing to more respectful conduct; models civility rather than attacking.

civility.statement: Everybody should return home safe after mahi.
civility.explanation: A universal, inclusive value statement about worker safety, offered respectfully with no partisan edge.

charisma.statement: I want to endorse all of the words just spoken by the Prime Minister.
charisma.explanation: As Leader of the Opposition, explicitly endorsing his political opponent's words — a cross-party, consensus-building gesture.

charisma.statement: Whaea Tariana had the rare ability to bridge different hues of the political rainbow and bring people together for the greater good.
charisma.explanation: A National minister warmly praising a Māori Party leader's cross-party bridge-building — inclusive, consensus-affirming framing.

charisma.statement: But we growl and we come in here and we get grumpy... One of the things that I want to do is remind ourselves, as the year starts, of the legacy of Whaea Tariana... I promise this year I'll try, Chris Bishop, not to show my teeth so much.
charisma.explanation: Self-deprecating and reaching across the aisle by name to a Government minister, inviting a shared, less combative tone — bridge-building rather than partisan.

divination.statement: Unfortunately, in September this year, on Police Remembrance Day, another name will be added to the column.
divination.explanation: A near-certain prediction: with a serving officer killed on duty, her name being added at the September 2025 Police Remembrance Day is virtually assured; falsifiable and well-founded.

authenticity.statement: I'm proud to say, as Sir Micheal Cullen noted at the time, that ACT was the only party that stood consistently with that position in favour of the rule of law at that time.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent principled ACT position on the Foreshore and Seabed / rule-of-law question, broadly borne out by ACT's opposition at the time — words match the party's record.

strength.statement: it was because of Dame Tariana's advocacy in the background that while we were in Government, our two parties, for nine years, were able to bring about and sustain partnership schools or kura hourua.
strength.explanation: Seymour, the policy's champion, claims credit for delivering and sustaining charter schools — they were established and ran under National-ACT, though later abolished by Labour, so follow-through is real but was reversed.

strength.statement: But as we see new kura hourua opening up and down New Zealand this week, that is one of the ways that I remember her
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete, in-progress delivery (new schools opening) that he is responsible for, though it is early-stage rollout rather than completed at scale.

specificity.statement: Over the past month, I've announced a high income threshold for unjustified dismissal personal grievances, the removal of remedies for personal grievances in cases where the employee contributed to the grievance, the reintroduction of wage deductions for partial strikes, I've asked my officials to develop an hours-based accrual system for annual leave, and today I announced the new minimum wage rate for 2025 in order to give businesses certainty leading into the new year.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates named, concrete policy changes across the portfolio.

specificity.statement: Together, these changes will help rebalance the employment relations landscape, make it easier to hire workers, and reduce compliance costs so that both workers and employers can focus on what they do best.
specificity.explanation: Directional claim of benefit with no figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: In the last three months, we've completed 42 actions designed to lift New Zealand's economic performance, restore law and order, and improve the public services that all of us rely upon.
specificity.explanation: Cites a count (42 actions) but the actions themselves are summarised in broad categories.

specificity.statement: Our Government's working incredibly hard to raise incomes, to provide economic growth, and to lower the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Vague statement of effort with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: We have adjusted tax for low and middle income working New Zealanders. We have increased the Working for Families credits. We have also provided FamilyBoost for people dealing with expensive childcare. We have provided inflation, interest rate, rent stability, and also tax relief for low and middle income working New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Lists named measures but no figures on their distributional impact.

specificity.statement: I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries.
specificity.explanation: Gives a date (2029) and number/type (two rail-compatible ferries).

specificity.statement: 20 hospitals will receive additional funding for security, and further funding will be available if there is a major incident or event that requires a greater security presence.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (20 hospitals) and a contingency funding mechanism.

specificity.statement: I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it's not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.
specificity.explanation: Attaches concrete targets (30% renewables, 55,000 houses, 180km roads).

specificity.statement: There is no justification to take 19 months to build a three- to four-bedroom home that's 50 percent more expensive than the same home in Australia.
specificity.explanation: Gives a duration and a percentage cost comparison.

specificity.statement: Earlier today, I released the Budget Policy Statement. At the same time, Treasury released its half-year update, which contains the latest set of forecasts. They tell a positive story about growth returning to the New Zealand economy, and they also highlight some challenges for the Government's books.
specificity.explanation: Names the documents but keeps the substance high-level.

specificity.statement: The Budget Policy Statement sets four priorities for Budget 2025: (1) lifting economic growth through measures to address New Zealand's long-term productivity challenges; (2) implementing a social investment approach to drive better results from the Government's investment in social services; (3) keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of high-priority Government policy commitments and cost pressures that cannot be met from reprioritisation; and (4) developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investment.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four defined Budget priorities with some mechanism detail.

specificity.statement: Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures linking a GDP delta to a dollar revenue figure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: now more than ever is a time for disciplined Government spending and a focus on driving economic growth.
specificity.explanation: A general statement of stance with no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: Isn't it the case that there will be $58.7 billion more debt, peaking at $235 billion, than what was forecast in her Budget only six months ago?
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures and a peak and comparison point.

specificity.statement: This side of the House did have interest deductibility, but it was for the build of new houses. It was to incentivise the building of new houses.
specificity.explanation: Clarifies the precise scope (new builds) of the deductibility policy.

specificity.statement: This afternoon, the Fast-track Approvals Bill will receive its third reading, fulfilling one of the actions in the Quarter Four Action Plan. The new system will be up and running in early February 2025, with listed projects able to apply directly to the Environmental Protection Authority for their substantive application process to begin.
specificity.explanation: Gives the legislative stage, a start date, and the application mechanism.

specificity.statement: These 149 projects, the initial tranche, will help rebuild our struggling economy and kick-start growth around the country.
specificity.explanation: Cites the count (149 projects) but not the scale or timing of the promised growth.

specificity.statement: we don't go from $401 million—which is what I charged them with in May 2020—to now, according to Treasury, $4 billion. That's inexcusable.
specificity.explanation: Names dollar figures and a date.

specificity.statement: Over the summer, Health New Zealand will increase security in 20 mostly provincial hospitals across the country and have further surge capacity available if additional security is needed... this initiative will provide 44 additional full-time security personnel across our eight high-priority EDs, a flexible funding package to surge security support when needed and further provisioning for 12 security trainers.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures: 20 hospitals, 44 personnel, 8 EDs, 12 trainers.

specificity.statement: After years of deterioration, ED wait times remained relatively the same as they were the year before, whilst seeing roughly 18,000 more people presenting to our EDs.
specificity.explanation: Gives an approximate presentation increase (18,000) and a wait-time comparison.

specificity.statement: we announced reforms to get councils back to basics to reduce pressure on rates, deliver core services, and modernise outdated rules... These measures include removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act, benchmarking council performance to hold them accountable.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (removing well-beings, benchmarking) though outcomes stay general.

specificity.statement: The evidence shows that when the four “well-beings” were in legislation, rates increased approximately 2 percent more per year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified claim (about 2% more per year).

specificity.statement: the first benchmarking report on local councils will be released in the middle of 2025, ahead of the 2025 local elections. This report will give hard-working ratepayers and residents across the country clear information about their council's financial performance prior to going to the polls in October 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names a release window (mid-2025) and ties it to the October 2025 elections.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister wish to confirm that the minimum wage in New Zealand, at around 70 percent of the median wage, is among the very highest in the developed world, and does he believe it important that publicly owned companies have directors that are remunerated at a rate that is comparable and perhaps almost competitive with the rates paid to directors of privately owned companies so they can be productive and efficient for the public?
specificity.explanation: Cites the ~70% ratio and frames a concrete governance argument.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that we have a fair tax system when the IRD told us all last year that the wealthiest 311 households in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander, and his Government has chosen to re-entrench those settings?
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact figure (311 households) and the effective-rate comparison.

strength.statement: Over the past month, I've announced a high income threshold for unjustified dismissal personal grievances, the removal of remedies for personal grievances in cases where the employee contributed to the grievance, the reintroduction of wage deductions for partial strikes, I've asked my officials to develop an hours-based accrual system for annual leave, and today I announced the new minimum wage rate for 2025 in order to give businesses certainty leading into the new year.
strength.explanation: Mostly announcements/in-progress (officials 'developing' the accrual system); only the minimum wage is actually set, so partial delivery.

strength.statement: In the last three months, we've completed 42 actions designed to lift New Zealand's economic performance, restore law and order, and improve the public services that all of us rely upon.
strength.explanation: Claims completed follow-through on an action plan, though 'actions' vary in substance.

strength.statement: I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries.
strength.explanation: 'Delivered' overstates: only an option has been chosen after the earlier iReX deal was cancelled; no build contract yet.

strength.statement: 20 hospitals will receive additional funding for security, and further funding will be available if there is a major incident or event that requires a greater security presence.
strength.explanation: Concrete commitment building on a delivered prior-year programme.

strength.statement: This afternoon, the Fast-track Approvals Bill will receive its third reading, fulfilling one of the actions in the Quarter Four Action Plan. The new system will be up and running in early February 2025, with listed projects able to apply directly to the Environmental Protection Authority for their substantive application process to begin.
strength.explanation: Legislation actually reaching third reading is concrete delivery, not mere announcement.

strength.statement: Over the summer, Health New Zealand will increase security in 20 mostly provincial hospitals across the country and have further surge capacity available if additional security is needed... this initiative will provide 44 additional full-time security personnel across our eight high-priority EDs, a flexible funding package to surge security support when needed and further provisioning for 12 security trainers.
strength.explanation: Concrete funded programme extending a prior-year initiative, with named numbers.

strength.statement: we announced reforms to get councils back to basics to reduce pressure on rates, deliver core services, and modernise outdated rules... These measures include removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act, benchmarking council performance to hold them accountable.
strength.explanation: Announced reforms with defined mechanisms, at the announcement stage.

strength.statement: the first benchmarking report on local councils will be released in the middle of 2025, ahead of the 2025 local elections. This report will give hard-working ratepayers and residents across the country clear information about their council's financial performance prior to going to the polls in October 2025.
strength.explanation: A dated future commitment, not yet delivered.

divination.statement: Together, these changes will help rebalance the employment relations landscape, make it easier to hire workers, and reduce compliance costs so that both workers and employers can focus on what they do best.
divination.explanation: Predicts labour-market effects of the reforms; plausible but unproven, no timeframe.

divination.statement: the 1.5 percent increase to the minimum wage rate that I've announced today will make sure young people continue to have the opportunity to get their first job, enjoy their newfound sense of responsibility, and build those necessary life skills that will take them far in their career ahead.
divination.explanation: Predicts a sub-inflation minimum-wage rise preserves youth employment; contestable and directional.

divination.statement: under Budget '24, with all the cost of living measures that this Government delivered for low and middle income New Zealanders, 17,000 children are going to be taken out of poverty—compared to the last year of the Labour Government, where 23,000 more children were put in poverty.
divination.explanation: Forecasts 17,000 children lifted from poverty; a modelled future outcome, uncertain.

divination.statement: I can tell you that would not be the case. That would be a wrecking ball through our economy, because we have been in recession for three years
divination.explanation: Predicts a capital gains tax would wreck the economy; sweeping and unsupported.

divination.statement: I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries.
divination.explanation: Predicts the service will be operating in 2029; a firm forecast on a troubled procurement.

divination.statement: I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it's not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.
divination.explanation: Projects large outputs from the fast-track regime; aspirational figures, uncertain.

divination.statement: Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period.
divination.explanation: Forecasts revenue effect by end of the forecast period; conditional and uncertain.

divination.statement: This afternoon, the Fast-track Approvals Bill will receive its third reading, fulfilling one of the actions in the Quarter Four Action Plan. The new system will be up and running in early February 2025, with listed projects able to apply directly to the Environmental Protection Authority for their substantive application process to begin.
divination.explanation: Predicts the system running by early February 2025; near-term and largely within his control.

divination.statement: These 149 projects, the initial tranche, will help rebuild our struggling economy and kick-start growth around the country.
divination.explanation: Forecasts economic revival from the project list; directional and uncertain.

divination.statement: the first benchmarking report on local councils will be released in the middle of 2025, ahead of the 2025 local elections. This report will give hard-working ratepayers and residents across the country clear information about their council's financial performance prior to going to the polls in October 2025.
divination.explanation: Near-term, within-control commitment to a report by mid-2025; likely deliverable.

forthrightness.statement: Dealing with vexatious personal grievances can be extremely stressful for employers, who can find themselves facing large and unanticipated costs. An employer's own wellbeing and reputation can be harmed throughout the grievance process, yet for employers there is no recourse.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the patsy 'how will your changes affect employers?' with substantive reasons.

forthrightness.statement: the Deputy Prime Minister did an excellent job of completing his two actions of the 43 in the quarter four action plan, which were to help the racing industry get ahead, and also to make sure we deal with the greyhound industry, which he did very, very effectively and very, very well.
forthrightness.explanation: Hipkins asked how to reconcile Luxon praising the plan with Peters calling such plans 'crap'; Luxon deflects with humour and never addresses the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: for the first time in 14 years this Government has delivered tax relief, inflation relief, and interest rate relief. Importantly, every quarter of this Government, wages have grown faster than prices, unlike the 13 quarters in a row under the previous administration.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was about director fees rising 39-104% versus a below-inflation minimum wage; he pivots to general tax-relief talking points.

forthrightness.statement: With respect to professional directors that we're asking to run some of our largest entities, they are not paid market rates, they won't still be, but it's actually acknowledging that we want to attract good people to make sure we have high-quality governance. I'm sure the member would understand that, given the variety of messes that he left behind in the last Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a rationale for director pay but does not engage the minimum-wage contrast in the question.

forthrightness.statement: under Budget '24, with all the cost of living measures that this Government delivered for low and middle income New Zealanders, 17,000 children are going to be taken out of poverty—compared to the last year of the Labour Government, where 23,000 more children were put in poverty.
forthrightness.explanation: Waititi cited CPAG's claim of 20,000 more children into poverty; Luxon answers with his own counter-figures rather than the claim asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge that across New Zealand, it's a pretty tough time. That's what happens when you don't run an economy well. If you care about low and middle income New Zealanders, you run the books well. You don't spend more, tax more, borrow more, and deliver less.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he'd say to a 7-year-old who wrote to Santa for a burger, he pivots to economic talking points and never addresses the child.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government's working incredibly hard to raise incomes, to provide economic growth, and to lower the cost of living.
forthrightness.explanation: Swarbrick asked whether it is the job of his Government to decrease wealth inequality; he neither confirms nor denies, offering a slogan.

forthrightness.statement: We have adjusted tax for low and middle income working New Zealanders. We have increased the Working for Families credits. We have also provided FamilyBoost for people dealing with expensive childcare. We have provided inflation, interest rate, rent stability, and also tax relief for low and middle income working New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Names policies in response to 'name one policy that will decrease inequality', though whether they reduce inequality is left unargued.

forthrightness.statement: It's well established by Treasury that, you've heard them say, we have a progressive tax system.
forthrightness.explanation: Swarbrick cited the IRD finding that the 311 wealthiest households pay under half the average effective rate; he sidesteps with a general claim about income-tax progressivity.

forthrightness.statement: I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it's not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.
forthrightness.explanation: Lan Pham asked whether environmental protections would remain under fast-track; he rejects the premise and pivots to build targets.

forthrightness.statement: A hypothetical question—I'm not answering it.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly declines to answer whether he'd reconsider projects if the Auditor-General finds the process mishandled.

forthrightness.statement: The Budget Policy Statement sets four priorities for Budget 2025: (1) lifting economic growth through measures to address New Zealand's long-term productivity challenges; (2) implementing a social investment approach to drive better results from the Government's investment in social services; (3) keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of high-priority Government policy commitments and cost pressures that cannot be met from reprioritisation; and (4) developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investment.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers the patsy 'what does the BPS say about Budget 2025?'

forthrightness.statement: It is also the case that in the past five years, the last Labour Government added more than $100 billion to New Zealand's debt.
forthrightness.explanation: Edmonds asked whether debt at 46.5% of GDP was last this high in 1994; Willis answers with a counter-attack rather than the comparison.

forthrightness.statement: I won't take responsibility for the mistakes of the last Government, but I will take responsibility for fixing it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she'll take responsibility for the downward growth revision since her own Budget, she reframes to blame predecessors.

forthrightness.statement: I reject the characterisations of the member's question.
forthrightness.explanation: Wholly declines to engage the question about shifting the OBEGAL and child-poverty definitions.

forthrightness.statement: Nothing has been ruled in or out. We are looking at all the options—the costs and benefits, and the pluses and minuses—and we'll make decisions based on the best interests of our country. We are not going to make silly pledges before the work is done, and we can guarantee the member that we are not going to be asleep at the wheel like his colleagues were for the last three years.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee the new ferries will be rail-enabled, he explicitly refuses to commit either way.

forthrightness.statement: In response to the first arm of that question, yes, it is well known that where technical or detailed operational matters are concerned, it is an operational matter for Health New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects Verrall's question about lost after-hours services in Porirua by categorising it as 'operational' rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: I reject the assertions in that question and would point to the fact that we are trying to turn around the reset from the botched two years of health reforms that member was a part of.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address the substance of the cuts question; reframes to blame the questioner.

rigor.statement: Dealing with vexatious personal grievances can be extremely stressful for employers, who can find themselves facing large and unanticipated costs. An employer's own wellbeing and reputation can be harmed throughout the grievance process, yet for employers there is no recourse.
rigor.explanation: Leans on anecdote ('I've met a lot of employers up and down the country') rather than data.

rigor.statement: I acknowledge that across New Zealand, it's a pretty tough time. That's what happens when you don't run an economy well. If you care about low and middle income New Zealanders, you run the books well. You don't spend more, tax more, borrow more, and deliver less.
rigor.explanation: Asserted causal chain (poor economic management → hardship) with no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: I can tell you that would not be the case. That would be a wrecking ball through our economy, because we have been in recession for three years
rigor.explanation: Dismisses cited Treasury analysis with an unevidenced 'wrecking ball' assertion.

rigor.statement: There is no justification to take 19 months to build a three- to four-bedroom home that's 50 percent more expensive than the same home in Australia.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete comparison to support the argument, though the causal link to consenting alone is assumed.

rigor.statement: Why has his Government agreed to increase the fees paid to directors of Government companies by between 39 percent and 104 percent while increasing the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation?
rigor.explanation: Poses a clear evidence-based contrast between two specific decisions.

rigor.statement: So who is correct, then: the Prime Minister, who says that his whole Government is relentlessly focused on his quarterly action plan, or his Deputy Prime Minister, who says—and I quote—“I don't have this sort of dashboard crap that I see other people perform on and a 50-point plan, or a 100-point plan, or a quarter-year plan”, and if Winston Peters thinks that his plans are crap, why should Kiwis think otherwise?
rigor.explanation: Uses the Deputy PM's own quoted words to expose a genuine internal contradiction.

rigor.statement: Who's correct: Nicola Willis, who claims she has “delivered” new interisland ferries, despite not knowing who will build them, how much they'll cost, or who's going to pay for them; or Winston Peters, who said, “There are far more viable propositions that are yet to be considered.”?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two ministers' statements and lists concrete unknowns undercutting the 'delivered' claim.

rigor.statement: Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period.
rigor.explanation: A quantified, plausible fiscal argument, though the estimate is stated without workings.

rigor.statement: Does she plan on shifting any other goalposts to help reach her targets, like she has done with the definition of “OBEGAL” and with child poverty targets?
rigor.explanation: Names two specific alleged redefinitions but folds them into a loaded rhetorical question.

rigor.statement: We take responsibility for our spending that saved lives, that ensured families and employees stayed connected to their workers. We take responsibility for that, because 20,000 people did not die because of those decisions.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to a life-saving figure to justify spending without citing the underlying analysis.

rigor.statement: this Government is borrowing for the groceries, is borrowing for tax cuts, and has made deliberate choices to make it hard on every single body except for their mates.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorically punchy but the 'borrowing for groceries/tax cuts' claim is asserted, not demonstrated.

rigor.statement: This side of the House did have interest deductibility, but it was for the build of new houses. It was to incentivise the building of new houses.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent distinction between incentivising new builds and a general landlord tax break.

rigor.statement: Why is he evading questions on the operational realities of how New Zealanders are cared for in our health system and the consequences that stem from his direction to cut $1.4 billion in health spending?
rigor.explanation: Links the alleged spending cut to service consequences, though the causal figure is asserted.

rigor.statement: The evidence shows that when the four “well-beings” were in legislation, rates increased approximately 2 percent more per year.
rigor.explanation: Invokes 'the evidence' and a number, but treats correlation as causation.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that we have a fair tax system when the IRD told us all last year that the wealthiest 311 households in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander, and his Government has chosen to re-entrench those settings?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the fairness question in a specific empirical finding.

rigor.statement: Will his Government's benefit sanctions help to put more kai on the table or less kai on the table this Christmas for the thousands of hungry tamariki in Aotearoa?
rigor.explanation: Poses a loaded either/or ('more or less kai') that forecloses nuance.

veracity.statement: the 1.5 percent increase to the minimum wage rate that I've announced today will make sure young people continue to have the opportunity to get their first job, enjoy their newfound sense of responsibility, and build those necessary life skills that will take them far in their career ahead.
veracity.explanation: Frames a real-terms cut as protecting youth jobs; the causal claim is unverified.

veracity.statement: In the last three months, we've completed 42 actions designed to lift New Zealand's economic performance, restore law and order, and improve the public services that all of us rely upon.
veracity.explanation: Self-reported count against the Government's own action plan; broadly accurate but self-defined.

veracity.statement: for the first time in 14 years this Government has delivered tax relief, inflation relief, and interest rate relief. Importantly, every quarter of this Government, wages have grown faster than prices, unlike the 13 quarters in a row under the previous administration.
veracity.explanation: Selective framing; the 'every quarter wages beat prices' claim is contestable and cherry-picks the comparison window.

veracity.statement: under Budget '24, with all the cost of living measures that this Government delivered for low and middle income New Zealanders, 17,000 children are going to be taken out of poverty—compared to the last year of the Labour Government, where 23,000 more children were put in poverty.
veracity.explanation: A contested projection presented as settled; comparison statistics are selectively framed.

veracity.statement: It's well established by Treasury that, you've heard them say, we have a progressive tax system.
veracity.explanation: True of the income-tax schedule but ignores the capital-income point that made the system regressive at the top in the IRD study.

veracity.statement: I can tell you that would not be the case. That would be a wrecking ball through our economy, because we have been in recession for three years
veracity.explanation: 'in recession for three years' is an exaggeration of the actual recessionary period.

veracity.statement: There is no justification to take 19 months to build a three- to four-bedroom home that's 50 percent more expensive than the same home in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures on build time and trans-Tasman cost gap that are broadly in the right range but rounded/asserted.

veracity.statement: Why has his Government agreed to increase the fees paid to directors of Government companies by between 39 percent and 104 percent while increasing the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation?
veracity.explanation: Cites concrete percentage figures for director fee rises and characterises the minimum-wage rise as below inflation.

veracity.statement: Earlier today, I released the Budget Policy Statement. At the same time, Treasury released its half-year update, which contains the latest set of forecasts. They tell a positive story about growth returning to the New Zealand economy, and they also highlight some challenges for the Government's books.
veracity.explanation: Accurately references the documents while framing the mixed forecasts as a 'positive story', a selective emphasis.

veracity.statement: I recently received a letter from 15 economists telling me to increase current and future Government spending. I noticed that several people who signed this letter telling me to spend more were advisers to the previous Minister of Finance, and two are currently on the Labour Party policy council. I wasn't surprised... This actually did surprise me, because it came from Barbara Edmonds.
veracity.explanation: The affiliations may be accurate but the framing implies bias to dismiss the advice.

veracity.statement: It is also the case that in the past five years, the last Labour Government added more than $100 billion to New Zealand's debt.
veracity.explanation: Debt did rise sharply over the period, though it spans the COVID response; broadly accurate figure.

veracity.statement: Isn't it the case that there will be $58.7 billion more debt, peaking at $235 billion, than what was forecast in her Budget only six months ago?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific HYEFU figures against the prior Budget; drawn directly from the fiscal documents.

veracity.statement: We take responsibility for our spending that saved lives, that ensured families and employees stayed connected to their workers. We take responsibility for that, because 20,000 people did not die because of those decisions.
veracity.explanation: The '20,000 people did not die' figure is a modelled counterfactual stated as fact.

veracity.statement: We are having more New Zealanders—almost every five minutes—leave this country because they don't see any hope.
veracity.explanation: 'Almost every five minutes' and 'no hope' are hyperbolic and impute a single cause to migration.

veracity.statement: we don't go from $401 million—which is what I charged them with in May 2020—to now, according to Treasury, $4 billion. That's inexcusable.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific cost figures for the ferry project's escalation, broadly consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: After years of deterioration, ED wait times remained relatively the same as they were the year before, whilst seeing roughly 18,000 more people presenting to our EDs.
veracity.explanation: Presents flat wait times against rising presentations as an achievement; the framing is favourable but the figures are cited.

veracity.statement: Why is he evading questions on the operational realities of how New Zealanders are cared for in our health system and the consequences that stem from his direction to cut $1.4 billion in health spending?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $1.4 billion cut directed by the Minister; a contested characterisation of Health NZ's savings.

veracity.statement: The evidence shows that when the four “well-beings” were in legislation, rates increased approximately 2 percent more per year.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure but attributes rate rises causally to the well-beings, a contested inference.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister wish to confirm that the minimum wage in New Zealand, at around 70 percent of the median wage, is among the very highest in the developed world, and does he believe it important that publicly owned companies have directors that are remunerated at a rate that is comparable and perhaps almost competitive with the rates paid to directors of privately owned companies so they can be productive and efficient for the public?
veracity.explanation: NZ's minimum wage as a share of the median is genuinely among the highest in the OECD.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe that we have a fair tax system when the IRD told us all last year that the wealthiest 311 households in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander, and his Government has chosen to re-entrench those settings?
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the 2023 IRD high-wealth study's headline finding on effective tax rates.

civility.statement: With respect to professional directors that we're asking to run some of our largest entities, they are not paid market rates, they won't still be, but it's actually acknowledging that we want to attract good people to make sure we have high-quality governance. I'm sure the member would understand that, given the variety of messes that he left behind in the last Government.
civility.explanation: Substantive point on governance undercut by a personal jab about the 'messes' Hipkins left behind.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that across New Zealand, it's a pretty tough time. That's what happens when you don't run an economy well. If you care about low and middle income New Zealanders, you run the books well. You don't spend more, tax more, borrow more, and deliver less.
civility.explanation: Turns a question about a hungry child into a jab at the opposition's economic record.

civility.statement: Why has his Government agreed to increase the fees paid to directors of Government companies by between 39 percent and 104 percent while increasing the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation?
civility.explanation: Pointed but focused on Government decisions and policy, not personal attack.

civility.statement: So who is correct, then: the Prime Minister, who says that his whole Government is relentlessly focused on his quarterly action plan, or his Deputy Prime Minister, who says—and I quote—“I don't have this sort of dashboard crap that I see other people perform on and a 50-point plan, or a 100-point plan, or a quarter-year plan”, and if Winston Peters thinks that his plans are crap, why should Kiwis think otherwise?
civility.explanation: Repeats a crude word ('crap') but it is a direct quotation used to make a substantive point.

civility.statement: Who's correct: Nicola Willis, who claims she has “delivered” new interisland ferries, despite not knowing who will build them, how much they'll cost, or who's going to pay for them; or Winston Peters, who said, “There are far more viable propositions that are yet to be considered.”?
civility.explanation: Sharp but engages the substance of the ferry decision using both ministers' own positions.

civility.statement: I recently received a letter from 15 economists telling me to increase current and future Government spending. I noticed that several people who signed this letter telling me to spend more were advisers to the previous Minister of Finance, and two are currently on the Labour Party policy council. I wasn't surprised... This actually did surprise me, because it came from Barbara Edmonds.
civility.explanation: Discredits the letter by imputing partisan motive and singles out Edmonds for a personal jab.

civility.statement: Does she plan on shifting any other goalposts to help reach her targets, like she has done with the definition of “OBEGAL” and with child poverty targets?
civility.explanation: Accusatory 'shifting goalposts' framing, though it references identifiable definitional changes.

civility.statement: not just their mates in the tobacco companies, not just their mates who are landlords, not just their mates who are getting far higher remuneration than minimum-wage earners.
civility.explanation: Repeated 'their mates' framing imputes corrupt favouritism to opponents.

civility.statement: this Government is borrowing for the groceries, is borrowing for tax cuts, and has made deliberate choices to make it hard on every single body except for their mates.
civility.explanation: Sharp policy critique undercut by the 'their mates' insinuation of cronyism.

civility.statement: We are having more New Zealanders—almost every five minutes—leave this country because they don't see any hope.
civility.explanation: Emotive but aimed at policy outcomes rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: If we want a brighter future for New Zealand, we have to stop giving in to a nimby, low-growth, status quo minority.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents 'nimby' and a 'status quo minority' rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: Nothing has been ruled in or out. We are looking at all the options—the costs and benefits, and the pluses and minuses—and we'll make decisions based on the best interests of our country. We are not going to make silly pledges before the work is done, and we can guarantee the member that we are not going to be asleep at the wheel like his colleagues were for the last three years.
civility.explanation: Legitimate 'don't pre-empt the work' point paired with an 'asleep at the wheel' jab at opponents.

civility.statement: we don't go from $401 million—which is what I charged them with in May 2020—to now, according to Treasury, $4 billion. That's inexcusable.
civility.explanation: 'Inexcusable' is harsh but directed at the cost blowout, a legitimate target.

civility.statement: I reject the assertions in that question and would point to the fact that we are trying to turn around the reset from the botched two years of health reforms that member was a part of.
civility.explanation: Rejects the question and pivots to a jab at Verrall's role in 'botched' reforms rather than the $1.4bn cut asked about.

civility.statement: Why is he evading questions on the operational realities of how New Zealanders are cared for in our health system and the consequences that stem from his direction to cut $1.4 billion in health spending?
civility.explanation: Accuses the Minister of evasion but ties it to a specific policy figure rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister wish to confirm that the minimum wage in New Zealand, at around 70 percent of the median wage, is among the very highest in the developed world, and does he believe it important that publicly owned companies have directors that are remunerated at a rate that is comparable and perhaps almost competitive with the rates paid to directors of privately owned companies so they can be productive and efficient for the public?
civility.explanation: A friendly 'patsy' framed to make the Opposition's position look absurd, more debating tactic than personal attack.

civility.statement: Will his Government's benefit sanctions help to put more kai on the table or less kai on the table this Christmas for the thousands of hungry tamariki in Aotearoa?
civility.explanation: Emotive framing tied to a real policy (benefit sanctions), not a personal attack.

charisma.statement: I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it's not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.
charisma.explanation: Invites the Greens to 'get on board' but frames it as them being late/obstructive rather than genuine bridge-building.

charisma.statement: not just their mates in the tobacco companies, not just their mates who are landlords, not just their mates who are getting far higher remuneration than minimum-wage earners.
charisma.explanation: Purely us-vs-them; rallies her side by casting the Government as serving cronies.

charisma.statement: If we want a brighter future for New Zealand, we have to stop giving in to a nimby, low-growth, status quo minority.
charisma.explanation: Rallies supporters by casting critics as an obstructive minority; divisive rather than unifying.

authenticity.statement: I won't take responsibility for the mistakes of the last Government, but I will take responsibility for fixing it.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with her stated 'inherited a mess' position, but avoids owning her own forecast's revision.

authenticity.statement: now more than ever is a time for disciplined Government spending and a focus on driving economic growth.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with her repeated fiscal-discipline positioning throughout the session.

authenticity.statement: We take responsibility for our spending that saved lives, that ensured families and employees stayed connected to their workers. We take responsibility for that, because 20,000 people did not die because of those decisions.
authenticity.explanation: Openly owns and defends her party's spending record rather than distancing from it.

authenticity.statement: This side of the House did have interest deductibility, but it was for the build of new houses. It was to incentivise the building of new houses.
authenticity.explanation: Defends the consistency and intent of her own party's prior policy against the implied hypocrisy charge.

veracity.statement: It was an agreement that was delivered in just four months after talks began—New Zealand’s fastest ever trade negotiation.
veracity.explanation: The NZ–UAE CEPA was concluded unusually fast; the four-month/fastest-ever framing is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: What it means is that duties on 98.5 percent of exports to the UAE are gone
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the tariff-elimination coverage reported for the UAE deal.

veracity.statement: Wages are now growing faster than inflation, and cost pressures, like the Auckland regional fuel tax, have now been removed from the system.
veracity.explanation: Wage growth outpacing inflation was accurate by early 2025, and the Auckland fuel tax was removed; largely correct.

veracity.statement: Interest rates are falling—falling—and the Reserve Bank is forecasting that more relief is on the way very, very shortly.
veracity.explanation: The RBNZ had been cutting rates from late 2024; the factual claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: We delivered tax relief last year, and that means that Kiwis are keeping more of their money for the first time in 14 long years.
veracity.explanation: Tax cuts were delivered in 2024, but 'first time in 14 years' is a rhetorical overstatement of threshold history.

veracity.statement: applications for 149 projects from Kaikohe to Stewart Island open next week... I’m proud to say that there are 49 of those projects that are in the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Fast-track project figures are broadly consistent with the scheme as launched.

veracity.statement: every single member of the Opposition parties voted against those fast-track projects, right? They voted against creating opportunities for Kiwis. Labour: they voted against jobs and housing. The Greens: they voted against wind and solar farms.
veracity.explanation: Technically true they voted against the bill, but the 'voted against jobs/housing' gloss is misleading.

veracity.statement: We’ve got record new investment in health, with $17 billion extra going in, and 26 new cancer treatments.
veracity.explanation: The 26 cancer treatments claim is accurate; the '$17 billion extra' is a multi-year figure that flatters the scale.

veracity.statement: Over the next three years, we’re investing $33 billion into our transport network, which includes 17 roads of national significance
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the government's stated transport investment programme.

veracity.statement: we’ve already kicked off the Hawke’s Bay expressway, which I know Katie Nimon and Catherine Wedd are greatly appreciative of.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and specific, though 'kicked off' covers early-stage work.

veracity.statement: in the last year, 700,000 first specialist appointments happened. There were 200,000 elective surgeries that took place, and today there are 50,000 Kiwis getting in to see their GP.
veracity.explanation: Broad activity figures that are plausible but presented without baseline for comparison.

veracity.statement: not having 35 percent of their week tied up in filling out paperwork.
veracity.explanation: A precise-sounding figure for farmer compliance time that is not well substantiated.

veracity.statement: It’s only at 86 percent of pre-COVID levels
veracity.explanation: Tourism recovery around mid-80s percent of pre-COVID levels is consistent with the data.

veracity.statement: when you have six years in power, with the last three with an absolute majority, and you do absolutely nothing, you then get buyer’s regret on the other side
veracity.explanation: 'Absolutely nothing' is a misleading overstatement of the previous government's record; Labour also lacked a majority for the full three years.

veracity.statement: they have driven New Zealand into the worst economic recession since 1991 might have been a good place to start. An acknowledgment that the deepest cuts to Government spending since 1991 made that situation so much worse
veracity.explanation: The 2024 downturn was severe but 'worst since 1991' and 'deepest cuts since 1991' are contestable superlatives.

veracity.statement: $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords because they promised that rents were going to go down—what’s happened? Rents have continued to go up under this Government
veracity.explanation: Interest-deductibility restoration cost and continued rent rises are broadly accurate, though causation is asserted.

veracity.statement: like $200 billion in tax cuts for tobacco companies while our health system descends further into crisis
veracity.explanation: '$200 billion' is wildly wrong by orders of magnitude — the smokefree repeal figure was in the low hundreds of millions.

veracity.statement: look at the HSBC’s estimates that said that New Zealand’s economy had the largest contraction in GDP last year in the world.
veracity.explanation: Reflects commentary on NZ's sharp contraction, but 'largest in the world' is a strong claim dependent on a specific comparison.

veracity.statement: Just last year, the Commonwealth Fund studied 10 health systems around the world, including New Zealand, Australia, the UK, and the US. They found that privatised health systems came in last for administrative efficiency. New Zealand was third.
veracity.explanation: Broadly reflects the Commonwealth Fund Mirror, Mirror findings, though 'privatised systems came last' compresses the ranking.

veracity.statement: why is it that the privatised American health system costs more per person than just about any other health system in the world and yet delivers worse health outcomes?
veracity.explanation: The US spends the most per capita on health with comparatively poor outcomes — well supported.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has five times the fatality rate at work of the United Kingdom, twice the rate of Australia, and yet this Government seems to think that health and safety is the problem.
veracity.explanation: NZ's workplace fatality rate is markedly higher than the UK's and Australia's; the ratios are in the right ballpark.

veracity.statement: In New Zealand, 5,000 to 6,000 hospitalisations happen every year because of injury and illness caused by work.
veracity.explanation: Plausible order of magnitude for work-related hospitalisations, presented without a cited source.

veracity.statement: They cut $500 million of investment from science in last year’s Budget; 500 science and research jobs have been cut. Take GNS... they cut 59 science jobs... The National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research... 90 jobs down the drain
veracity.explanation: Science-sector job losses at Crown Research Institutes occurred; the headline '$500m cut' framing is contestable.

veracity.statement: before the Government goes gutting health and safety regulations and rules that are designed to ensure that Kiwis can be healthy at work and make it home at the end of the day, they should understand why those rules were put in place in the first place, because, actually, most of them were put in place under the last National Government
veracity.explanation: The current H&S regime largely followed the post-Pike River reforms under the previous National government.

veracity.statement: today in this country, 311 households hold more wealth combined than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Reflects Green Party wealth-concentration analysis; a striking figure whose exact basis is contestable.

veracity.statement: The wealthiest 311 households, who hold more wealth than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders, pay an effective tax rate of less than half that of the average New Zealander.
veracity.explanation: Aligns with IRD's high-wealth study showing effective rates roughly half those of middle earners.

veracity.statement: the United States of America, where the Government spends over 16 percent of GDP on an almost fully privatised healthcare system, compared to around 10 percent for most OECD countries. Meanwhile, Americans gets comparatively lower lifespans and much poorer health outcomes
veracity.explanation: US health spending as a share of GDP and worse outcomes are accurate; 'almost fully privatised' overstates given large public programmes.

veracity.statement: Two-hundred years ago, there was no concept of the idea of the cost of living in Aotearoa. There was no idea of private ownership here. There was no notion of profit.
veracity.explanation: An idealised historical generalisation; pre-colonial Māori society had property and exchange concepts, so this overstates.

specificity.statement: It was an agreement that was delivered in just four months after talks began—New Zealand’s fastest ever trade negotiation.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete timeframe and a specific superlative claim.

specificity.statement: What it means is that duties on 98.5 percent of exports to the UAE are gone
specificity.explanation: Precise figure tied to a named agreement.

specificity.statement: applications for 149 projects from Kaikohe to Stewart Island open next week... I’m proud to say that there are 49 of those projects that are in the South Island.
specificity.explanation: Concrete project counts and a near-term timeframe.

specificity.statement: We’ve got record new investment in health, with $17 billion extra going in, and 26 new cancer treatments.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figure and count of treatments.

specificity.statement: Over the next three years, we’re investing $33 billion into our transport network, which includes 17 roads of national significance
specificity.explanation: Precise amount, timeframe and named programme.

specificity.statement: this year, we won’t debate and discuss it and have endless hui and discussion, but we’re going to fix it and replace it with a system that’s fairer, faster, and cheaper.
specificity.explanation: Names RMA replacement but only via vague adjectives (fairer/faster/cheaper), no mechanism.

specificity.statement: we want 20,000 fewer victims of violent crime, and we want youth offending cut by 15 percent
specificity.explanation: Quantified targets with clear metrics.

specificity.statement: in the last year, 700,000 first specialist appointments happened. There were 200,000 elective surgeries that took place, and today there are 50,000 Kiwis getting in to see their GP.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures for health system throughput.

specificity.statement: It’s only at 86 percent of pre-COVID levels
specificity.explanation: Precise recovery percentage.

specificity.statement: This House has no confidence in this coalition Government because under its incompetent, arrogant, shambolic, and divisive leadership, New Zealand is going backwards, Kiwis are losing their jobs, record numbers are leaving the country, and their priorities are wrong and out of touch.
specificity.explanation: Some concrete claims (job losses, emigration) mixed with broad characterisation.

specificity.statement: they have driven New Zealand into the worst economic recession since 1991 might have been a good place to start. An acknowledgment that the deepest cuts to Government spending since 1991 made that situation so much worse
specificity.explanation: Anchors claims to a historical benchmark year.

specificity.statement: look at the HSBC’s estimates that said that New Zealand’s economy had the largest contraction in GDP last year in the world.
specificity.explanation: Attributes to a named source (HSBC) but the comparison basis is unstated.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has five times the fatality rate at work of the United Kingdom, twice the rate of Australia, and yet this Government seems to think that health and safety is the problem.
specificity.explanation: Concrete comparative multiples against named countries.

specificity.statement: In New Zealand, 5,000 to 6,000 hospitalisations happen every year because of injury and illness caused by work.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete annual range.

specificity.statement: They cut $500 million of investment from science in last year’s Budget; 500 science and research jobs have been cut. Take GNS... they cut 59 science jobs... The National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research... 90 jobs down the drain
specificity.explanation: Names institutions (GNS, NIWA) and specific job counts.

specificity.statement: the Regulatory Standards Bill is a bill that has no place in this House, and I can guarantee you this: in the first hundred days of the next Labour Government, it will be repealed
specificity.explanation: Names the bill and a concrete timeframe (first 100 days) for repeal.

specificity.statement: today in this country, 311 households hold more wealth combined than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts on both sides of the comparison.

specificity.statement: The wealthiest 311 households, who hold more wealth than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders, pay an effective tax rate of less than half that of the average New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Quantified comparison of effective tax rates.

specificity.statement: the United States of America, where the Government spends over 16 percent of GDP on an almost fully privatised healthcare system, compared to around 10 percent for most OECD countries. Meanwhile, Americans gets comparatively lower lifespans and much poorer health outcomes
specificity.explanation: Concrete GDP percentages and outcome comparison.

specificity.statement: Government is supposed to make the best possible decisions on behalf of the welfare of everybody in the country. It is supposed to be about ensuring that everybody gets access to what they need not only to survive but to thrive.
specificity.explanation: High-level principle with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: At the end of last year, the Green Party released He Ara Anamata, our alternative emissions reduction plan... a green jobs guarantee: planting native trees instead of pine, efficient public transport, sustainable food production, restoring our wetlands, designing our cities better, distributed and resilient renewable energy, real just transition plans led by local communities
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete plan and a list of measures, though without figures or timeframes.

strength.statement: It was an agreement that was delivered in just four months after talks began—New Zealand’s fastest ever trade negotiation.
strength.explanation: A concluded, signed trade agreement — actual delivery, not just an announcement.

strength.statement: Wages are now growing faster than inflation, and cost pressures, like the Auckland regional fuel tax, have now been removed from the system.
strength.explanation: Removal of the Auckland regional fuel tax is a delivered, verifiable action.

strength.statement: We delivered tax relief last year, and that means that Kiwis are keeping more of their money for the first time in 14 long years.
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment on tax relief that was actually enacted.

strength.statement: We’ve got record new investment in health, with $17 billion extra going in, and 26 new cancer treatments.
strength.explanation: Funded cancer treatments were delivered; the headline funding figure is partly forward-looking.

strength.statement: Over the next three years, we’re investing $33 billion into our transport network, which includes 17 roads of national significance
strength.explanation: A funded programme largely still in progress rather than delivered.

strength.statement: we’ve already kicked off the Hawke’s Bay expressway, which I know Katie Nimon and Catherine Wedd are greatly appreciative of.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete project start; delivery of commencement rather than completion.

strength.statement: this year, we won’t debate and discuss it and have endless hui and discussion, but we’re going to fix it and replace it with a system that’s fairer, faster, and cheaper.
strength.explanation: Stated intent to replace the RMA, in progress but not yet delivered.

strength.statement: we want 20,000 fewer victims of violent crime, and we want youth offending cut by 15 percent
strength.explanation: Targets set with progress claimed but outcomes still in train.

strength.statement: one year ago, I promised that this would be a Government of action, one that takes on the big challenges facing our country and actually delivers... A year on, I have to say I am incredibly proud of the progress that we have made
strength.explanation: Claims follow-through on a 'government of action' promise, with delivery genuinely mixed.

divination.statement: Interest rates are falling—falling—and the Reserve Bank is forecasting that more relief is on the way very, very shortly.
divination.explanation: Predicts further OCR relief; consistent with RBNZ's easing cycle and subsequently borne out by the Feb 2025 cut.

authenticity.statement: We delivered tax relief last year, and that means that Kiwis are keeping more of their money for the first time in 14 long years.
authenticity.explanation: Words match deeds: campaigned on tax relief and delivered it.

authenticity.statement: one year ago, I promised that this would be a Government of action, one that takes on the big challenges facing our country and actually delivers... A year on, I have to say I am incredibly proud of the progress that we have made
authenticity.explanation: Self-assessment that words matched deeds; a plausible but self-serving consistency claim not independently verified here.
