authenticity.statement: the Regulatory Standards Bill is a bill that has no place in this House, and I can guarantee you this: in the first hundred days of the next Labour Government, it will be repealed
authenticity.explanation: A firm commitment consistent with Labour's stated opposition to the bill, but no action possible from opposition yet.

civility.statement: every single member of the Opposition parties voted against those fast-track projects, right? They voted against creating opportunities for Kiwis. Labour: they voted against jobs and housing. The Greens: they voted against wind and solar farms.
civility.explanation: Recasts votes against a bill as votes 'against jobs and housing' — misrepresentation rather than engaging the actual objections.

civility.statement: the members opposite remind me of a cat pawing at the ranch slider, yowling away, trying to get in, and then you open the door, and they don’t move. They refuse to come in.
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature of opponents rather than engagement with their positions.

civility.statement: we are a coalition on this side; they’re a “no-alition” on that side—that’s what they’re about. They’re all about no; we’re all about yes, on this side.
civility.explanation: A rhetorical jibe, but aimed at political stance rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: the country’s productivity would actually be improved if the members opposite did just stay at home. I’d encourage them to do that.
civility.explanation: Personal put-down implying opponents are worthless, not policy criticism.

civility.statement: While we have been back at work for weeks pushing through changes to make Kiwis so much better off, Chris Hipkins is barely out of his jandals.
civility.explanation: Personal jab about Hipkins being idle rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Farmers and rural communities are the backbones of our economy and they were treated like villains—absolute villains—under that last Labour Government.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic characterisation of the previous government's treatment of farmers.

civility.statement: when you have six years in power, with the last three with an absolute majority, and you do absolutely nothing, you then get buyer’s regret on the other side
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of opponents rather than engagement with their actual record.

civility.statement: This House has no confidence in this coalition Government because under its incompetent, arrogant, shambolic, and divisive leadership, New Zealand is going backwards, Kiwis are losing their jobs, record numbers are leaving the country, and their priorities are wrong and out of touch.
civility.explanation: String of character adjectives ('incompetent, arrogant, shambolic') aimed at leadership rather than specific policy.

civility.statement: you could see them pulling out their phones after only a few minutes and frantically dusting off their CVs.
civility.explanation: Mocking depiction of the government benches rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: like $200 billion in tax cuts for tobacco companies while our health system descends further into crisis
civility.explanation: Legitimate policy attack line, though framed emotively.

civility.statement: Forget the rock star economy; Nicola Willis is aiming for rock-bottom!
civility.explanation: Personalised zinger against the minister rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: We see businesses every week going to the wall as company liquidations continue to go through the roof. Companies that survived COVID can’t survive National.
civility.explanation: Punchy attack line, aimed at the party's record rather than a person.

civility.statement: He’s like a walking Dale Carnegie seminar.
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation of Luxon as all talk; a personal jab.

civility.statement: the people who choose to teach, the people who choose to be nurses, the people who choose to become police, and the people who enter the Defence Force are mediocre according to this Government. Those with disabilities: mediocre, according to this Government.
civility.explanation: Extends Seymour's 'mediocre' remark into a caricature the government never stated; Seymour objected it was a misrepresentation.

civility.statement: He does know quite a lot about tourism, though. In fact, he visited Te Puke so many times that he forgot he was actually in Hawaii.
civility.explanation: Personal jibe about Luxon's holiday rather than a policy point.

civility.statement: the same guy who is doing his best to currently tell everybody in this country that Māori are apparently coming to take more and more rights is the same guy who is trying to sell off New Zealanders’ rights to access public healthcare.
civility.explanation: Pointed personal framing of Seymour's motives rather than engaging his stated arguments.

civility.statement: Privatisation means that if you can’t afford it, you don’t get it. It literally means that people who cannot afford their medicine die.
civility.explanation: Charged framing of opponents' agenda, though directed at policy consequences.

civility.statement: To completely misrepresent what someone has said in a way that reflects badly on, for example, the police of this country, I think, brings this House into disrepute, and he should withdraw the comment.
civility.explanation: A measured procedural objection to being misrepresented, focused on conduct rather than insult.

civility.statement: There are some of us that think that the standards of this House have seriously declined. Now, when you’re giving a ruling, it is not right for a member of Parliament to stand there impatiently waiting for you to stop. That shows no respect for you or this institution.
civility.explanation: Appeals to respect for the Speaker and institutional standards, though delivered as a rebuke of Hipkins.

civility.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. Happy New Year. It’s nice to see you, and I hope that you have had a sunny summer down in Christchurch.
civility.explanation: Warm, courteous opening addressed respectfully to the Speaker.

rigor.statement: every single member of the Opposition parties voted against those fast-track projects, right? They voted against creating opportunities for Kiwis. Labour: they voted against jobs and housing. The Greens: they voted against wind and solar farms.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: infers opposition to outcomes from opposition to a specific legislative mechanism.

rigor.statement: Farmers and rural communities are the backbones of our economy and they were treated like villains—absolute villains—under that last Labour Government.
rigor.explanation: Emotive assertion ('absolute villains') offered without evidence.

rigor.statement: $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords because they promised that rents were going to go down—what’s happened? Rents have continued to go up under this Government
rigor.explanation: Points to a stated prediction vs outcome, but treats a single trend as proof the policy failed.

rigor.statement: We see businesses every week going to the wall as company liquidations continue to go through the roof. Companies that survived COVID can’t survive National.
rigor.explanation: Slogan-style causal claim; 'through the roof' and 'can't survive National' are hyperbole without evidence.

rigor.statement: Just last year, the Commonwealth Fund studied 10 health systems around the world, including New Zealand, Australia, the UK, and the US. They found that privatised health systems came in last for administrative efficiency. New Zealand was third.
rigor.explanation: Cites a named study to support the argument, a reasonable evidentiary appeal.

rigor.statement: why is it that the privatised American health system costs more per person than just about any other health system in the world and yet delivers worse health outcomes?
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based comparison, though used to argue against a privatisation the government hasn't fully proposed.

rigor.statement: the people who choose to teach, the people who choose to be nurses, the people who choose to become police, and the people who enter the Defence Force are mediocre according to this Government. Those with disabilities: mediocre, according to this Government.
rigor.explanation: Strawman that puts words in the government's mouth and generalises from a single speech.

rigor.statement: New Zealand has five times the fatality rate at work of the United Kingdom, twice the rate of Australia, and yet this Government seems to think that health and safety is the problem.
rigor.explanation: Marshals comparative data to rebut the deregulation argument.

rigor.statement: before the Government goes gutting health and safety regulations and rules that are designed to ensure that Kiwis can be healthy at work and make it home at the end of the day, they should understand why those rules were put in place in the first place, because, actually, most of them were put in place under the last National Government
rigor.explanation: Historical point that many H&S rules were introduced under National supports the argument against deregulation.

rigor.statement: the United States of America, where the Government spends over 16 percent of GDP on an almost fully privatised healthcare system, compared to around 10 percent for most OECD countries. Meanwhile, Americans gets comparatively lower lifespans and much poorer health outcomes
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based comparison, slightly weakened by mischaracterising the US system as fully private.

rigor.explanation: Sweeping ideological assertion presented as axiom without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: the same guy who is doing his best to currently tell everybody in this country that Māori are apparently coming to take more and more rights is the same guy who is trying to sell off New Zealanders’ rights to access public healthcare.

veracity.statement: When this Government was elected, inflation was running at 5.6 percent per annum, and it peaked at 7.3 percent per annum a year prior to that. Today, it is down almost at the mid-point of the target band—2 percent inflation.
veracity.explanation: The figures broadly match official StatsNZ CPI data: ~5.6% annual inflation to Sep 2023, a 7.3% peak in mid-2022, and ~2.2% by late 2024. Accurate.

veracity.statement: While prices may still be high, they have stopped rising because this Government has killed inflation.
veracity.explanation: Misleading: 2% inflation means prices are still rising, just more slowly. 'Prices have stopped rising' is false, and 'killed inflation' is hyperbole.

veracity.statement: For example, we have a Reserve Bank Governor who put in place capital requirements that have pushed up the price of borrowing to every firm, every farm, and every family in this country.
veracity.explanation: Bank capital requirements do raise funding costs somewhat, but 'pushed up the price of borrowing to every firm, farm and family' overstates the size and directness of the effect.

veracity.statement: The Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA) changes that his Government brought in at the end of 2021, effectively, tanked the housing market that November... because people went along to their bank and they found that to get a minor increase to their credit limit, they had to tell the bank how much they spent each month on pet food.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported: the Dec 2021 CCCFA changes did tighten lending and drew complaints about intrusive expense scrutiny; the 'pet food' example and 'tanked the market' framing are dramatised.

veracity.statement: In the last five years, we’ve increased spending by $10 billion and still most New Zealanders would say we have First World people with a system that is letting down those doctors, nurses, orderlies, and allied health professionals while still failing to satisfy the desires and the needs of every single patient.
veracity.explanation: Health spending has risen substantially over five years, though the exact '$10 billion' framing and the sweeping 'every single patient' claim are imprecise.

veracity.statement: We’re a Government with $200 billion of debt, scheduled to pay nearly $10 billion of interest on the debt. That’s real money. That is, doing quick mental arithmetic, $2,000 per New Zealander in interest payments next year.
veracity.explanation: In the right ballpark: gross Crown debt and finance costs are of this order, and ~$2,000 per capita is roughly consistent, though which debt/interest measure is used affects precision.

veracity.statement: In 2023, the dire state the economy was in was grossly understated and not understood by most. It was part of the New Zealand First speeches leading all the way up to the election and pointing out that we were heading for a recession and that we would have a serious battle on our hands to turn our economy around.
veracity.explanation: NZ did enter a period of economic weakness/technical recession, so the recession warning is defensible, though 'grossly understated' is a subjective characterisation.

veracity.statement: I’ll make one very certain judgment for you right here: there’s nobody in the labouring workforce out there that supports Labour any more.
veracity.explanation: Categorical claim that is demonstrably false; Labour retains substantial worker and union support. Hyperbole presented as fact.

veracity.statement: Now, he could have gone on to talk about the $3.1 billion light rail... The $54 million spent on the cycleway across the Harbour Bridge. How many metres were built?... the Cook Strait ferries blowing out to what? $4.2 billion. They were charged in May of 2020 with $401 million to find two ferries.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: the cancelled harbour cycleway (~$51m spent, nothing built) and the ferry cost blowout are broadly real, but the '$3.1 billion light rail' and '$4.2 billion' figures are projected/contested totals presented as wasted spend.

veracity.statement: Oh, and here’s the one: the $4 million playing whale music to save kauri trees.
veracity.explanation: A mocking mischaracterisation: a kauri dieback research project involving sound/vibration existed, but 'playing whale music to save kauri trees' distorts what it was, and the figure is presented for ridicule.

veracity.statement: here you are, your family’s saved up, you want to buy your first house, you want to build your first house, and your greatest obstruction—about 30 percent of the cost—is planning permission... If that was true, why haven’t they got that in Canada, the United States, and Australia?
veracity.explanation: The '30 percent of the cost is planning permission' figure is overstated for most builds; regulatory/consenting costs are real but rarely that share. Comparison countries also have significant planning regimes.

veracity.statement: the greatest privatisation we ever saw in this country was 1984 and 1990 with the BNZ being flogged off... Then you had... Electricorp. He paid $6 million for it, and he got $1 million for redundancies.

veracity.statement: This country is called New Zealand, and the mass majority of New Zealanders want it that way. And the mass majority of New Zealanders want equality, where everybody’s treated the same.
veracity.explanation: Asserts majority opinion on the country's name/'Aotearoa' without polling support; contestable claim stated as fact.

veracity.statement: which saw 14,000 bureaucrats taken on that we didn’t need.

rigor.statement: Perhaps what she forgot to say is that 200 years ago, life expectancy in New Zealand was 40. That tells you about the sense of rationality that we’re getting from the Green Party.

rigor.statement: These capital requirements were put in place in order for us to get through a major shock, and when the shock of COVID-19 came along, guess what! Actually, we were fine with the old capital requirements. We never needed to have them phased in at all, and we should drop them today.
rigor.explanation: Plausible argument but leans on a single case (COVID) to conclude the buffers were never needed, ignoring that the higher requirements were largely not yet phased in during COVID.

rigor.statement: The Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA) changes that his Government brought in at the end of 2021, effectively, tanked the housing market that November... because people went along to their bank and they found that to get a minor increase to their credit limit, they had to tell the bank how much they spent each month on pet food.
rigor.explanation: Gives a real example to support the point, but relies on an anecdote and hyperbole ('tanked') for the causal claim.

rigor.statement: Perhaps we could have a grown-up discussion about it. How do they do it in France? rigor.explanation: Uses comparative examples (France, East Asia) to argue a mixed system is normal; reasonable but the comparisons are asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: here you are, your family’s saved up, you want to buy your first house, you want to build your first house, and your greatest obstruction—about 30 percent of the cost—is planning permission... If that was true, why haven’t they got that in Canada, the United States, and Australia?
rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative appeal (other countries) but the premise that they lack such protections is inaccurate, weakening the inference.

veracity.statement: In the latest figures that we had for the 12 months to October 2024, we had 24,000 fewer victims of crimes than they did in the 12 months to June 2024.
veracity.explanation: A specific statistical claim from the NZ Crime and Victims Survey; plausible and drawn from official data, though he compares overlapping non-standard periods (12 months to October vs 12 months to June), which can flatter the trend.

veracity.statement: We've seen, actually, already a lift in business confidence levels, notwithstanding all the challenges, and that's because they see help is on its way.
veracity.explanation: Business confidence surveys did rise over this period, so the factual core is broadly supported; the causal attribution ('because they see help is on its way') is unverifiable.

veracity.statement: Isn't it great to be able to have gone around over the summer and not seen gang patches everywhere where we went? Thanks to the work of the police and the legislation that's passed.
veracity.explanation: Anecdotal observation credited to the new gang-patch ban; the law's effect on visible patches is plausible but the personal-impression evidence is weak.

veracity.statement: They took $30 million from Te Ahu o te Reo Māori to pay for these amazing resources for our schools.
veracity.explanation: Specific funding-reallocation claim; the framing of one programme's funds directly 'paying for' another is a contestable characterisation of budget decisions.

veracity.statement: Last year, this Government made a decision about indexing benefits that put 7,000 children, estimated at up to 13,000 children—more children—into poverty.
veracity.explanation: Cites modelled estimates on the benefit-indexing change that align with published projections, presented with a range rather than overstated.

veracity.statement: Research released last year shows that teenagers who don't get enough to eat end up two to four years behind their peers in subjects like maths and reading.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific effect size to unnamed research; directionally consistent with food-insecurity literature but the precise '2–4 years' figure is unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: We hear this Government going on about numeracy and literacy and their investment and focus on that, yet they are reducing Ka Ora, Ka Ako, the school lunches programme, from a lunch to a snack.
veracity.explanation: The school-lunch changes did reduce provision; 'from a lunch to a snack' is a pointed but broadly fair characterisation of the cost-cutting.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's snapshot of the Māori economy... shows that the Māori asset base has grown exponentially from $68 billion in 2018 to $118 billion in 2023, with more Māori in high-skilled jobs than low-skilled jobs for the first time ever.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific MBIE snapshot with figures broadly matching published Māori-economy estimates; attributed to a named source.

veracity.statement: The evidence shows in the officials' advice that 80 to 85 percent of the young people who will be classed as young serious offenders will be Māori.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific proportion to officials' advice on the boot-camp cohort; plausible given over-representation data but the exact figure rests on the cited advice.

veracity.statement: Right now, this Government is planning to remove or replace more than 28 legislative provisions for Te Tiriti o Waitangi from legislation. That is a New Zealand First - National coalition agreement.
veracity.explanation: References a specific coalition-agreement commitment to review Treaty clauses across legislation; the '28 provisions' figure reflects the review's scope.

veracity.statement: When it comes to the gang legislation—the Hon Paul Goldsmith referred to it—it's been outstanding. It's working, without a doubt. It's tipped the balance back to our police. Our front-line police have reseized the initiative when it comes to organised crime and gangs.
veracity.explanation: 'Working, without a doubt' overstates certainty about outcomes for legislation only recently in force.

veracity.statement: In the 17 pages of this statement to Parliament by our Prime Minister, there is not one mention of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in this speech, which is ironic given that the bill... is the most submitted-on bill in the history of this country.
veracity.explanation: The absence of any Te Tiriti reference and the record submission count for the Treaty Principles Bill are both checkable factual claims that are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: The way that this Government has treated its indigenous people has made us the laughing stock of this planet. We were once known for punching well above our weight and now we're just known for punching down on the first people that were on this whenua.
veracity.explanation: 'Laughing stock of this planet' is an unfalsifiable exaggeration of NZ's international standing.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has signed up to 1,900 treaties; we are a party to 1,900 treaties, and the one that founded our own Parliament is the one that our Government does not give a toss about.
veracity.explanation: The treaty count is a specific checkable figure; the 'does not give a toss' characterisation is opinion layered onto it.

veracity.statement: We know the Government's fast-track bill overrides almost every existing protection that we have, and it even gives life to zombie projects already declined by the courts.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track regime does allow reconsideration of previously declined projects; 'overrides almost every existing protection' is a contestable overstatement of its scope.

veracity.statement: Flying across to the United Arab Emirates with me to put on paper the ink that signed the free-trade agreement with the UAE—one of the highest quality on entry into force we've negotiated and negotiated very, very quickly.
veracity.explanation: The UAE FTA signing is real; 'one of the highest quality on entry into force' is a self-serving qualitative claim.

veracity.statement: When we came into Government and during the course of last year, confidence in the rural sector was at an all-time low. Year upon year over the last six years of the previous Government, rural confidence was shattered.
veracity.explanation: Rural confidence surveys did hit very low points, but 'all-time low' and a uniform six-year decline are overstatements of a more variable record.

veracity.statement: Senior Sergeant Fleming had given 38 years of service to the community as a police officer. She was known as the matriarch of the Nelson police station, where she was a trusted mentor, quiet leader, and kind friend to many.
veracity.explanation: Straightforward biographical facts about the officer's service, presented accurately.

veracity.statement: If you look at GDP growth, it has plummeted from what was 2.4 percent under Labour and is now on its steepest decline since 1991—if you take aside the blip of COVID-19.
veracity.explanation: GDP did contract sharply over this period, but selectively comparing a peak Labour figure and excluding COVID frames the trend to maximum effect.

veracity.statement: Back in the 1990s, the then National Government sold off more than 11,500 State houses around Aotearoa New Zealand, and in New Plymouth, in Marfell, where I live, that ravaged the community.
veracity.explanation: The 1990s state-house sell-off is a real historical event with figures in this range; the local 'ravaged the community' impact is his characterisation.

veracity.statement: One of the big overseas companies has already exited New Zealand because they realise that offshore wind is no longer a possibility because of fast track, because of the fact that they just want to do dirty mining offshore, at sea. Seabed mining cannot coexist with offshore wind.
veracity.explanation: An offshore-wind developer did scale back NZ involvement, but attributing it solely to fast-track/seabed-mining and the blanket 'cannot coexist' claim compress a more complex picture.

specificity.statement: In the latest figures that we had for the 12 months to October 2024, we had 24,000 fewer victims of crimes than they did in the 12 months to June 2024.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure (24,000) and defined timeframes.

specificity.statement: That's why we've already brought back three-strikes legislation. We've passed the gang laws which give the police extra powers to deal with gangs who are a tiny fraction of the population but are responsible for a very significant amount of the violent crime in our community.
specificity.explanation: Names specific enacted laws and their purpose, though no figures on the 'significant amount' of crime.

specificity.statement: They get paid more in Australia because Australia does more things. They dig stuff out of the ground, and they make some money.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at 'doing more things' and mining without any mechanism, figures, or policy detail.

specificity.statement: They took $30 million from Te Ahu o te Reo Māori to pay for these amazing resources for our schools.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact figure ($30m), the source programme, and the destination.

specificity.statement: Last year, this Government made a decision about indexing benefits that put 7,000 children, estimated at up to 13,000 children—more children—into poverty.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and gives concrete figures with an estimated range.

specificity.statement: Research released last year shows that teenagers who don't get enough to eat end up two to four years behind their peers in subjects like maths and reading.
specificity.explanation: Concrete effect size and named subjects, but the study itself is unidentified.

specificity.statement: The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's snapshot of the Māori economy... shows that the Māori asset base has grown exponentially from $68 billion in 2018 to $118 billion in 2023, with more Māori in high-skilled jobs than low-skilled jobs for the first time ever.
specificity.explanation: Named source, two dated dollar figures, and a concrete labour-market milestone.

specificity.statement: The evidence shows in the officials' advice that 80 to 85 percent of the young people who will be classed as young serious offenders will be Māori.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage range tied to a defined policy population.

specificity.statement: Right now, this Government is planning to remove or replace more than 28 legislative provisions for Te Tiriti o Waitangi from legislation. That is a New Zealand First - National coalition agreement.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count of provisions and the specific agreement it stems from.

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister talks a big game—he talks a big game about economic growth—but words mean nothing when so many Kiwis are struggling just to make ends meet.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical contrast with no figures or mechanism attached.

specificity.statement: When it comes to the gang legislation—the Hon Paul Goldsmith referred to it—it's been outstanding. It's working, without a doubt. It's tipped the balance back to our police. Our front-line police have reseized the initiative when it comes to organised crime and gangs.
specificity.explanation: General claims of success with no metrics on crime or enforcement.

specificity.statement: In the 17 pages of this statement to Parliament by our Prime Minister, there is not one mention of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in this speech, which is ironic given that the bill... is the most submitted-on bill in the history of this country.
specificity.explanation: Cites the document length, the specific omission, and the record-submission claim.

specificity.statement: New Zealand has signed up to 1,900 treaties; we are a party to 1,900 treaties, and the one that founded our own Parliament is the one that our Government does not give a toss about.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number but the substantive claim about the Government's attitude is vague.

specificity.statement: The Treaty principles bill, yeah, it's going to die, but there are other bills that this Government has signed up to and agreed to legislate within their coalition agreement... that will remove Te Tiriti as a lawmaking principle within this country.
specificity.explanation: Clear on the bill's fate but vague about which 'other bills' and how they remove the principle.

specificity.statement: We know the Government's fast-track bill overrides almost every existing protection that we have, and it even gives life to zombie projects already declined by the courts.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill and a concrete effect (reviving declined projects) but quantifies nothing.

specificity.statement: They are a very big part of the Government's plan not only to provide greater income to all New Zealanders through the doubling of the value of exports over a decade.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target (double exports) and a timeframe (a decade), but no mechanism for how.

specificity.statement: We're setting up a new agency which will not be bureaucratic, it won't be large, and it won't be expensive. It will be charged with working with New Zealanders to attract investment overseas that is good for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deliverable (a new investment agency) but describes it only by negatives — no size, budget, or mandate detail.

specificity.statement: When we came into Government and during the course of last year, confidence in the rural sector was at an all-time low. Year upon year over the last six years of the previous Government, rural confidence was shattered.
specificity.explanation: References confidence trends over a defined period but cites no survey figures.

specificity.statement: We should, as a House, be united in our desire to lighten the load and the burden on those farmers so they can farm more, to have fewer regulations, better ones, and regulations that focus on an outcome that actually achieves something.
specificity.explanation: 'Fewer, better, outcome-focused regulations' states a direction without naming which rules or how.

specificity.statement: If you look at GDP growth, it has plummeted from what was 2.4 percent under Labour and is now on its steepest decline since 1991—if you take aside the blip of COVID-19.
specificity.explanation: Cites a percentage and a historical benchmark (since 1991).

specificity.statement: Back in the 1990s, the then National Government sold off more than 11,500 State houses around Aotearoa New Zealand, and in New Plymouth, in Marfell, where I live, that ravaged the community.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and named locality tied to a specific policy.

strength.statement: That's why we've already brought back three-strikes legislation. We've passed the gang laws which give the police extra powers to deal with gangs who are a tiny fraction of the population but are responsible for a very significant amount of the violent crime in our community.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of concrete legislation (three-strikes, gang laws) that the coalition did in fact pass — action backing the rhetoric, not just an announcement.

strength.statement: When it comes to the gang legislation—the Hon Paul Goldsmith referred to it—it's been outstanding. It's working, without a doubt. It's tipped the balance back to our police. Our front-line police have reseized the initiative when it comes to organised crime and gangs.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for enacted gang legislation and asserts it is working; the law passed, but the 'it's working, without a doubt' delivery-of-results claim is early and self-assessed.

strength.statement: Flying across to the United Arab Emirates with me to put on paper the ink that signed the free-trade agreement with the UAE—one of the highest quality on entry into force we've negotiated and negotiated very, very quickly.
strength.explanation: Points to a concluded, signed FTA — a concrete delivered outcome he was responsible for, not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: We're setting up a new agency which will not be bureaucratic, it won't be large, and it won't be expensive. It will be charged with working with New Zealanders to attract investment overseas that is good for New Zealanders.
strength.explanation: A stated intention to set up an agency; announcement stage with no delivery yet demonstrated.

rigor.statement: We've seen, actually, already a lift in business confidence levels, notwithstanding all the challenges, and that's because they see help is on its way.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a cause for the confidence lift without evidence beyond assertion.

rigor.statement: They get paid more in Australia because Australia does more things. They dig stuff out of the ground, and they make some money.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping single-cause explanation of the trans-Tasman wage gap; mining is one factor but the reasoning is a simplification presented as sufficient.

rigor.statement: We had a revolving door of police Ministers and justice Ministers in the last legislation, and they kept on coming and going. They were soft, they came up with excuses for crime, and it was always everybody else's fault and not the criminals' fault for crime.
rigor.explanation: Attributes a crime increase to the previous government's attitude via assertion, with no evidence linking their decisions to outcomes.

rigor.statement: Isn't it great to be able to have gone around over the summer and not seen gang patches everywhere where we went? Thanks to the work of the police and the legislation that's passed.
rigor.explanation: Draws a causal conclusion from personal summer observation — anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: Research released last year shows that teenagers who don't get enough to eat end up two to four years behind their peers in subjects like maths and reading.
rigor.explanation: Cites research to support the point, though the source is not named and the magnitude is asserted.

rigor.statement: We hear this Government going on about numeracy and literacy and their investment and focus on that, yet they are reducing Ka Ora, Ka Ako, the school lunches programme, from a lunch to a snack.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes the stated literacy/numeracy goal against the lunch cut to argue inconsistency — a coherent point, though the causal link to learning outcomes is compressed.

rigor.statement: I listened to the contribution from David Seymour, who says, 'I still doubt that it will not pass.' It suggests that he's calling the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister... liars, because he said... he still doubts that it will not pass.
rigor.explanation: Builds the 'liars' conclusion on a strained reading of a single hedged quote.

rigor.statement: The fields that he wants to farm on, the mines that he wants to ram raid, the streams that he wants to pipe underground, the mega-prisons that he wants to build and fill my people up with, they all rest on stolen land.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical listing with charged verbs; asserts conclusions ('stolen land') without argument.

rigor.statement: It is truly extraordinary how hollow the claims are of this Government around evidence-based decision-making. They persist in saying that they're committed to it, while directly reducing the processes and funding that allow them to be informed.
rigor.explanation: Argues an inconsistency between stated commitment to evidence and funding cuts to science/data — a coherent point, though the funding claims are asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: The PM was equally confused and backwards when he said that they were replacing the Resource Management Act with a system that will 'continue protecting our natural environment'. Unfortunately, just because one says it's so doesn't make it so.
rigor.explanation: Raises a fair point that assertion isn't proof, but supports it with characterisation more than evidence.

rigor.statement: They've 'roared out of the blocks'—his words—with a big bulldozing 'No' to environmental protections. They say no to honouring Te Tiriti obligations and to climate action; no to protecting marine areas... no to protecting and restoring our polluted waterways, no to even basic levels of funding for our environmental agencies.
rigor.explanation: Turns the PM's own phrase into an anaphoric list of 'no's; rhetorically effective but each claim is asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: Our dairy industry will be able to produce more dairy for exactly the same number of cows as they had last year, but they will produce more, and that makes the country richer.
rigor.explanation: Links favourable pasture conditions to higher output — a reasonable inference, but stated as a certainty.

rigor.statement: If you look at GDP growth, it has plummeted from what was 2.4 percent under Labour and is now on its steepest decline since 1991—if you take aside the blip of COVID-19.
rigor.explanation: Uses real figures but curates the comparison ('take aside the blip of COVID') to strengthen the conclusion.

rigor.statement: One of the big overseas companies has already exited New Zealand because they realise that offshore wind is no longer a possibility because of fast track, because of the fact that they just want to do dirty mining offshore, at sea. Seabed mining cannot coexist with offshore wind.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a single cause for the company's exit and an absolute incompatibility without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: It's not about our economy; it's about unleashing meanness, about unleashing division, about unleashing environmental degradation, and about unleashing economic hardship.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical anaphora of accusations with no evidence attached to any of them.

civility.statement: We had a revolving door of police Ministers and justice Ministers in the last legislation, and they kept on coming and going. They were soft, they came up with excuses for crime, and it was always everybody else's fault and not the criminals' fault for crime.
civility.explanation: Characterises predecessors as 'soft' making 'excuses' — a broad-brush attack on their motives rather than engagement with specific policy.

civility.statement: My plea to the many different hapū of Ngāpuhi is: let's listen to some of the ones who say yes; let's see if we can make a deal. Let's see if we can make some progress so that we can get Northland cooking with gas over the next little while.
civility.explanation: Respectful, constructive framing aimed at reaching a deal.

civility.statement: I listened to the contribution from David Seymour, who says, 'I still doubt that it will not pass.' It suggests that he's calling the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister... liars, because he said... he still doubts that it will not pass.
civility.explanation: Uses a coalition partner's ambiguous remark to imply the PM and DPM are 'liars'; an inference about honesty rather than direct engagement with policy.

civility.statement: The Prime Minister talks a big game—he talks a big game about economic growth—but words mean nothing when so many Kiwis are struggling just to make ends meet.
civility.explanation: Criticises the PM's rhetoric-vs-reality gap; pointed but aimed at the record rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: She gave 38 years of public service to our country, and when you think about the amount of people's lives that she has touched, that is extraordinary and that deserves all of our respect and acknowledgment.
civility.explanation: A respectful tribute to a fallen officer with no partisan edge.

civility.statement: The fields that he wants to farm on, the mines that he wants to ram raid, the streams that he wants to pipe underground, the mega-prisons that he wants to build and fill my people up with, they all rest on stolen land.
civility.explanation: Loaded framing ('ram raid', 'fill my people up with') attributes malign intent rather than engaging the policies on their merits.

civility.statement: The way that this Government has treated its indigenous people has made us the laughing stock of this planet. We were once known for punching well above our weight and now we're just known for punching down on the first people that were on this whenua.
civility.explanation: Sweeping condemnation ('laughing stock of this planet') using hyperbole rather than specific criticism.

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon, you are not God and you cannot change the facts, history, or the founding of this country, and the Government should stop acting like they are more important than the people that were first here.
civility.explanation: Directly addresses and belittles the Prime Minister ('you are not God'), a personal rather than policy-focused rebuke.

civility.statement: That will be your legacy, Prime Minister—that will be your legacy: mobilising and agitating the entire population to get rid of him.
civility.explanation: A taunt framed as a prediction, addressed personally to the PM.

civility.statement: It is truly extraordinary how hollow the claims are of this Government around evidence-based decision-making. They persist in saying that they're committed to it, while directly reducing the processes and funding that allow them to be informed.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's credibility but directed at its policy conduct rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: The PM was equally confused and backwards when he said that they were replacing the Resource Management Act with a system that will 'continue protecting our natural environment'. Unfortunately, just because one says it's so doesn't make it so.
civility.explanation: 'Confused and backwards' characterises the PM's grasp rather than debating the RMA replacement on substance.

civility.statement: They've 'roared out of the blocks'—his words—with a big bulldozing 'No' to environmental protections. They say no to honouring Te Tiriti obligations and to climate action; no to protecting marine areas... no to protecting and restoring our polluted waterways, no to even basic levels of funding for our environmental agencies.
civility.explanation: Sharp critique of the Government's policy direction, aimed at actions rather than persons.

civility.statement: Senior Sergeant Fleming had given 38 years of service to the community as a police officer. She was known as the matriarch of the Nelson police station, where she was a trusted mentor, quiet leader, and kind friend to many.
civility.explanation: A respectful, non-partisan tribute to a fallen officer.

civility.statement: Every person who goes to work should come home safely to their family, and this includes our police and other first responders who work to keep our community safe.
civility.explanation: A unifying, respectful sentiment with no partisan or personal edge.

civility.statement: It's not about our economy; it's about unleashing meanness, about unleashing division, about unleashing environmental degradation, and about unleashing economic hardship.
civility.explanation: Ascribes 'meanness' and intent to divide to the Government — a motive attack rather than substantive critique.

charisma.statement: My plea to the many different hapū of Ngāpuhi is: let's listen to some of the ones who say yes; let's see if we can make a deal. Let's see if we can make some progress so that we can get Northland cooking with gas over the next little while.
charisma.explanation: An invitation to negotiate and find agreement on the Ngāpuhi settlement, though it privileges the 'ones who say yes' rather than fully bringing sceptics along.

charisma.statement: Christopher Luxon, you are not God and you cannot change the facts, history, or the founding of this country, and the Government should stop acting like they are more important than the people that were first here.
charisma.explanation: Confrontational and us-vs-them; rallies opponents of the Government rather than persuading the undecided.

charisma.statement: We should, as a House, be united in our desire to lighten the load and the burden on those farmers so they can farm more, to have fewer regulations, better ones, and regulations that focus on an outcome that actually achieves something.
charisma.explanation: Appeals for cross-House unity on regulation, though framed around the Government's own agenda rather than genuine common ground.

charisma.statement: Every person who goes to work should come home safely to their family, and this includes our police and other first responders who work to keep our community safe.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal to a shared value that everyone in the House can endorse.

divination.statement: That will be your legacy, Prime Minister—that will be your legacy: mobilising and agitating the entire population to get rid of him.
divination.explanation: Predicts the PM's actions will mobilise the population to remove him; a directional forecast, but 'entire population' overstates and the outcome is far from certain.

divination.statement: The Treaty principles bill, yeah, it's going to die, but there are other bills that this Government has signed up to and agreed to legislate within their coalition agreement... that will remove Te Tiriti as a lawmaking principle within this country.
divination.explanation: Predicts the Treaty Principles Bill will not pass — well-supported given the PM's public commitment that it would not proceed past second reading.

divination.statement: They are a very big part of the Government's plan not only to provide greater income to all New Zealanders through the doubling of the value of exports over a decade.
divination.explanation: Refers to the target of doubling export value in ten years; an ambitious forecast/goal that current growth rates make uncertain.

divination.statement: Our dairy industry will be able to produce more dairy for exactly the same number of cows as they had last year, but they will produce more, and that makes the country richer.
divination.explanation: Predicts higher dairy output from the same herd this season; plausible given good grass growth but weather-dependent and uncertain.

charisma.statement: I move, That this House send its condolences and best wishes to the people and Government of Vanuatu following yesterday's devastating earthquake.
charisma.explanation: A cross-party humanitarian motion seeking the whole House's agreement; unifying rather than partisan.

charisma.statement: Right. Well, in that case, sir, I would endorse the Deputy Prime Minister's statements. I'm sure that the House would be interested to know when it is that New Zealand aircraft are likely to be able to actually land and take assistance to the people in Vanuatu. I wish the members of the New Zealand Defence Force and supporting agencies who will likely be working through the Christmas period—I thank them for their service on behalf of New Zealand and the assistance that they are giving to the people of Vanuatu.
charisma.explanation: Openly endorses a Government minister's statement across party lines and thanks the NZDF; consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Yes, I do. And absolutely, what a year. Inflation is down, interest rates are down, tax relief has been delivered, fast track delivered, confidence is rising, growth is coming back, crime is falling, police are on the beat, gangs are on the run, phones are gone from class, and kids are getting back to school. We don't need a year of delivery. Every year this team delivers. And that's what we're doing—we're getting New Zealand back on track and cleaning up Labour's mess.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side and ends with the divisive 'cleaning up Labour's mess' framing rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: Well, Nicola Willis is going to go down as the best finance Minister this country has ever seen, because by God what a mess she has picked up. She is cleaning house and she's getting the job done. And she has delivered a value-for-money, reliable, sensible ferry solution of rail-compatible ferries.
charisma.explanation: Effusive praise for a colleague that appeals only to his own side; does not engage the critique.

charisma.statement: That member, on the other hand, within the space of two radio interviews this morning, managed to want more borrowing, less borrowing, more tax, less tax. She needs to make up her mind.
charisma.explanation: Scores a point with her own side; makes no attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: No. This Government's Christmas present to Kiwis is inflation under control for the first time in three years. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is official cash rate reductions, meaning cheaper mortgages. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is tax relief for the first time in 14 years, including FamilyBoost payments for kids in early childhood education. And here's the best present of all: next year we will deliver a growing economy with more opportunities and more choices for New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: A polished festive frame that plays to supporters rather than reaching the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: OMV, an international gas and oil explorer, announced at 6:30 a.m. this morning they are no longer withdrawing from New Zealand; as a consequence of the advocacy and the confidence instilled by this Government, they are staying to salvage the oil and gas industry in New Zealand. And on your behalf, New Zealand, I claim a little credit for that.
charisma.explanation: Confident and effective for supporters but framed combatively toward critics.

charisma.statement: Occasionally, there have been one or three protesters as I've sought to engage with garden-variety Kiwis, but the days of those mung bean-meddlers are over.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than builds consensus.

civility.statement: I move, That this House send its condolences and best wishes to the people and Government of Vanuatu following yesterday's devastating earthquake.
civility.explanation: Wholly respectful and constructive, focused on shared compassion.

civility.statement: Right. Well, in that case, sir, I would endorse the Deputy Prime Minister's statements. I'm sure that the House would be interested to know when it is that New Zealand aircraft are likely to be able to actually land and take assistance to the people in Vanuatu. I wish the members of the New Zealand Defence Force and supporting agencies who will likely be working through the Christmas period—I thank them for their service on behalf of New Zealand and the assistance that they are giving to the people of Vanuatu.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful, focused on the substance of the relief effort.

civility.statement: My goodness! The member has no economic credibility. I mean, this was a Prime Minister that increased spending by 84 percent, drove up domestic inflation, drove up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and that raises unemployment. And he has the audacity to stand up and ask us questions on economics.
civility.explanation: 'No economic credibility' and 'the audacity' are personal attacks on the questioner rather than engagement with the point.

civility.statement: Oh, I mean, that is a bit rich, isn't it? Isn't that a bit rich? How are the conversations with David Parker and Kieran McAnulty working out, son?
civility.explanation: The condescending 'son' and personal needling are cheap shots rather than substance.

civility.statement: The fact that Te Pāti Māori hasn't had a conversation about why nine out of 10 young Māori students heading into high school are not where they need to be in mathematics is shameful.
civility.explanation: 'Shameful' targets the opposing party's priorities rather than engaging their argument on Te Aka Whai Ora.

civility.statement: Why are he and Nicola Willis the only people surprised to learn that when you slash jobs, the bill for unemployment benefits goes up, the tax take goes down, and the economy stalls; or is this one of the economic lessons from the last 35 years that he thinks he needs to relearn?
civility.explanation: Largely policy-focused but the 'needs to relearn' jab edges toward personal derision.

civility.statement: Does his definition of "delivery" include an announcement about an announcement with no budget, no build specifications, no builder, no concrete time frame, no actual ships, and, if not, what exactly has Nicola Willis actually delivered when it comes to the Interislander?
civility.explanation: Pointed and mocking ('announcement about an announcement') but aimed at the policy record, not the person.

civility.statement: Does his definition of "dumb stuff" that he said he was going to cut include spending nearly $14 million on the administration of the flailing FamilyBoost scheme that's only paid out $16 million so far, and is helping fewer than half the families he promised?
civility.explanation: 'Flailing' and quoting his own 'dumb stuff' line is sharp but attacks the scheme, not the man.

civility.statement: Is the reason Andrew Bayly faced no sanction for calling someone working late "a loser", he defended Penny Simmonds' claims that disability support workers were ripping off the system, and his Government passed law changes stripping away workers' rights because those actions actually reflect what his Government thinks, which is that Kiwis who work hard for a living are losers and—to use his own words—"bottom feeders"?
civility.explanation: Imputes a contemptuous motive ('thinks Kiwis are losers') to the whole Government, an inflammatory generalisation.

civility.statement: So why does he think he's the most unpopular Prime Minister in New Zealand's history, and what does he think Nicola Willis is more likely to replace next year: the interisland ferries, or him, as Prime Minister?
civility.explanation: A personal, leadership-instability jibe rather than a substantive policy question.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that "We've set ambitious goals for ourselves.", and, if so, can he please outline for the House what exactly is ambitious about his Government's goals to decrease emissions and persistent child poverty by just 1 percent?
civility.explanation: Challenges the substance of the targets; mildly loaded but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that his Government has cut services for vulnerable children and whānau, increased benefit sanctions by 133 percent, and cut 9,000 jobs from the public sector, with 1,500 more to go at Health New Zealand, while setting aside $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords, in just this year alone?
civility.explanation: Hard-hitting but directed at Government actions and figures rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: So why did his Government decide to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, because the authority was unable to unwind 182 years of oppression and unequal treatment in only nine months?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing but aimed at the policy decision, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: How can her target to reduce jobseeker beneficiary numbers by 50,000 be on track when the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts there will still be 204,000 people on jobseeker benefit in 2029, and her target for 2030 is 140,000 jobseeker beneficiaries?
civility.explanation: A tough but wholly policy- and data-focused question.

civility.statement: As I shared with the House yesterday, net core Crown debt went from $57 billion to $175 billion during the six years of the Labour Government, and now their position is that somehow that's our fault.
civility.explanation: Attributes blame pointedly but engages the debt argument on substance.

civility.statement: That member, on the other hand, within the space of two radio interviews this morning, managed to want more borrowing, less borrowing, more tax, less tax. She needs to make up her mind.
civility.explanation: A dismissive 'make up her mind' jab characterising the opponent as incoherent rather than engaging her policy.

civility.statement: How can New Zealanders take her financial management seriously when she cancelled the ferries, costing the taxpayer hundreds of millions of dollars, undertook creative accounting to make her books look better, and has delivered the highest debt in decades?
civility.explanation: 'Creative accounting' and 'take her seriously' edge toward impugning competence/integrity while stringing together assertions.

civility.statement: Occasionally, there have been one or three protesters as I've sought to engage with garden-variety Kiwis, but the days of those mung bean-meddlers are over.
civility.explanation: Derides opponents as 'mung bean-meddlers', a dismissive personal-category insult.

civility.statement: Obviously, aquaculture is now going to enjoy an amazing growth period because for the next 20 years there will be no need for any more resource consents; they have been guaranteed. No more meddling from the Department of Conservation, no more interfering from unwise decision makers and regional councils. Certainty, confidence, and growth is about to hit regional New Zealand in the aquaculture sector, despite the best efforts of narrow-minded critics.
civility.explanation: 'Meddling', 'unwise decision makers', 'narrow-minded critics' disparage those who disagree.

civility.statement: It doesn't take a lot of parliamentary time, it doesn't take a lot of select committee time, but it is an important check on the ability of the executive to increase the costs on society, the most important of which, probably most years, is adjusting the excise and excise duties, the equivalent duties, on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products. That should be done every year so that they keep pace with inflation and don't decline in real terms.
civility.explanation: Measured, substantive, and non-partisan explanation of the bill's purpose.

civility.statement: We do think that the Government has used secondary legislation to update some things but also to advance a political agenda due to its inclusion of reduced excise for heated tobacco products in this bill, and we think that's actually not the way to go. … I also want to note the social security changes, particularly the changes that mean that benefits will now be changed to an index with the Consumers Price Index (CPI). That, actually, is also problematic because … those things will lead to lower increases to income support rather than if we adjusted those to wages, or whichever was higher.
civility.explanation: Disagrees on policy substance without personal attack, acknowledging much of the bill is technical and necessary.

civility.statement: Did the Government cut taxes for landlords or simply restore the very consistent and sensible tax policy that was the case for the first four years of the Labour-Green Government?
civility.explanation: Partisan framing but engages the tax-policy substance without personal insult.

civility.statement: Going from the first supplementary question that you were asked, how can the Minister be responsible for the greatest debt ever when 80 percent of the Crown debt incurred here, at this point in time, was incurred under Labour?
civility.explanation: Focused on the debt figures rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Is she seriously saying that cutting Stand Tū Māia's contract in April next year—an organisation that provides specialised trauma treatment and intensive wraparound family support for thousands of highly vulnerable children and their families, with a waiting list of over 450 children—is the right thing to do?
civility.explanation: 'Is she seriously saying' is pointed, but the question engages a specific programme cut on its merits.

civility.statement: Is maintaining the rail freight connection between the North and South Islands by ensuring we have at least one rail-enabled ferry important for the economic prosperity of the regions, particularly in the South Island?
civility.explanation: A calm, substantive, non-adversarial policy question.

specificity.statement: I move, That this House send its condolences and best wishes to the people and Government of Vanuatu following yesterday's devastating earthquake.
specificity.explanation: Names the country and the event but is a general expression of condolence.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do. And absolutely, what a year. Inflation is down, interest rates are down, tax relief has been delivered, fast track delivered, confidence is rising, growth is coming back, crime is falling, police are on the beat, gangs are on the run, phones are gone from class, and kids are getting back to school. We don't need a year of delivery. Every year this team delivers. And that's what we're doing—we're getting New Zealand back on track and cleaning up Labour's mess.
specificity.explanation: A rapid-fire list of slogans with no figures, timeframes, or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: We've got 100,000 people eligible, we've got 60,000 that have actually claimed, and we've got about 42,000 that are actually settled. When you talk to people, they say it's a simple process: get on myIR.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for eligibility, claims, and settlements.

specificity.statement: I can tell you that average rents since we've come into power are stable and not up $180 per week, as they were under the Labour Government.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete $180/week comparison figure.

specificity.statement: Wages grew slower than inflation for 13 quarters in a row under a Labour Government. They've had four quarters of wages growing faster than inflation under this Government.
specificity.explanation: Precise quarter counts for both periods.

specificity.statement: Does his definition of "delivery" include an announcement about an announcement with no budget, no build specifications, no builder, no concrete time frame, no actual ships, and, if not, what exactly has Nicola Willis actually delivered when it comes to the Interislander?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates precisely what is missing (budget, specs, builder, timeframe, ships).

specificity.statement: Does his definition of "dumb stuff" that he said he was going to cut include spending nearly $14 million on the administration of the flailing FamilyBoost scheme that's only paid out $16 million so far, and is helping fewer than half the families he promised?
specificity.explanation: Names dollar amounts and a coverage benchmark ('fewer than half').

specificity.statement: Which of the following best reflects his Government's priorities: $3 billion in tax cuts for landlords while cutting first-home buyer grants, $200 million in tax cuts for tobacco companies while the number of daily smokers increases for the first time in recent history, real-terms cuts to the minimum wage while directors' fees increase by up to 100 percent, or saying that he wouldn't borrow for tax cuts, only to increase Government borrowing by a record amount?
specificity.explanation: Stacks several precise figures and named policies into the question.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that "We've set ambitious goals for ourselves.", and, if so, can he please outline for the House what exactly is ambitious about his Government's goals to decrease emissions and persistent child poverty by just 1 percent?
specificity.explanation: Pins the challenge to a concrete '1 percent' figure for both emissions and child-poverty goals.

specificity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that his Government has cut services for vulnerable children and whānau, increased benefit sanctions by 133 percent, and cut 9,000 jobs from the public sector, with 1,500 more to go at Health New Zealand, while setting aside $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords, in just this year alone?
specificity.explanation: Dense with precise figures — 133 percent, 9,000 jobs, 1,500, $2.9 billion.

specificity.statement: What does the Prime Minister say about the economist Bernard Hickey's statement that "Treasury reports public service spending cuts to pay for lower taxes for landlords are shrivelling the economy, lifting spending on benefits, pumping up public debt & will put 20,000 more out of work"?
specificity.explanation: Attributes a concrete '20,000 more out of work' claim to a named source.

specificity.statement: Yes, absolutely. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030 and achieving this target is a priority for our Government. Jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022 and are expected to peak in January 2025. The forecast has always been for the numbers to get worse before they get better.
specificity.explanation: Gives the target (50,000 by 2030) and a concrete forecast peak (January 2025).

specificity.statement: I would like to go through that list of all the things we've done in the last 12 months, but you have said to keep my answers brief. So what I would say is: our plan is working. In the last five months, we have seen over 30,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit exit into work despite very challenging economic conditions, and that's what I'm proud of.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete number and timeframe (over 30,000 in five months).

specificity.statement: When jobseeker numbers started increasing during the global financial crisis in May 2008, there were around 85,000 people on the equivalent of jobseeker benefit; our starting point was 190,000.
specificity.explanation: Specific dates and headcounts (May 2008, 85,000, 190,000).

specificity.statement: How can her target to reduce jobseeker beneficiary numbers by 50,000 be on track when the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts there will still be 204,000 people on jobseeker benefit in 2029, and her target for 2030 is 140,000 jobseeker beneficiaries?
specificity.explanation: Marshals precise figures — 50,000, 204,000 in 2029, 140,000 target for 2030.

specificity.statement: The simplest way to look through them is to take ACC revenue and expenses out of the OBEGAL. That is what we've done by creating a new measure called OBEGALx, which is simply OBEGAL excluding ACC. People who are attached to OBEGAL … if they are attached to OBEGAL, that measure will continue to be reported as a fiscal indicator.
specificity.explanation: Explains the exact mechanism of the new OBEGALx indicator and what it excludes.

specificity.statement: As I shared with the House yesterday, net core Crown debt went from $57 billion to $175 billion during the six years of the Labour Government, and now their position is that somehow that's our fault.
specificity.explanation: Precise start and end debt figures over a defined period.

specificity.statement: No. This Government's Christmas present to Kiwis is inflation under control for the first time in three years. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is official cash rate reductions, meaning cheaper mortgages. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is tax relief for the first time in 14 years, including FamilyBoost payments for kids in early childhood education. And here's the best present of all: next year we will deliver a growing economy with more opportunities and more choices for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete items (inflation, OCR cuts, tax relief, FamilyBoost) but the 'growing economy' promise lacks figures.

specificity.statement: How can New Zealanders take her financial management seriously when she cancelled the ferries, costing the taxpayer hundreds of millions of dollars, undertook creative accounting to make her books look better, and has delivered the highest debt in decades?
specificity.explanation: References concrete grievances but keeps costs vague ('hundreds of millions').

specificity.statement: Obviously, aquaculture is now going to enjoy an amazing growth period because for the next 20 years there will be no need for any more resource consents; they have been guaranteed. No more meddling from the Department of Conservation, no more interfering from unwise decision makers and regional councils. Certainty, confidence, and growth is about to hit regional New Zealand in the aquaculture sector, despite the best efforts of narrow-minded critics.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete '20 years, no new resource consents' policy mechanism.

specificity.statement: This includes the installation of 1,337 piles; use of over 10,000 cubic metres of concrete; more than 5 kilometres of road has been repaved; and 50,000 square metres of asphalt installed, which is around the size of seven rugby fields, I am told. These critical works have addressed 36 slips to increase resilience on this critical route and get Northlanders where they want to go quickly and safely.
specificity.explanation: Highly precise engineering detail — pile count, concrete volume, road length, asphalt area, slip count.

specificity.statement: For one last time this year: there has not been a cut to the overall amount Oranga Tamariki is spending on contracted providers. There are contracts that will expire and not be renewed, some that Oranga Tamariki has decided to reduce, and others that will be increased. Oranga Tamariki spent more than $500 million with providers last year, and I'm advised we're on track to do so again this year.
specificity.explanation: Gives the overall spend figure and categorises the types of contract change.

specificity.statement: I'm pleased to announce the first three recipients of the Government's Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund: Youthline, the Sir John Kirwan Foundation, and MATES in Construction. … The first three organisations being announced today will share more than $2 million from the mental health innovation fund, with this being matched with an additional $2 million in philanthropic funding, meaning the total investment in new mental health services announced today doubles to $4 million.
specificity.explanation: Names the three recipients and the exact matched-funding figures ($2m + $2m = $4m).

specificity.statement: The Commerce Commission has today released a draft proposal to significantly lower card fees. The commission estimates that Kiwi businesses and consumers will save $260 million every year.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the expected saving ($260 million a year) and identifies the source (Commerce Commission).

specificity.statement: It doesn't take a lot of parliamentary time, it doesn't take a lot of select committee time, but it is an important check on the ability of the executive to increase the costs on society, the most important of which, probably most years, is adjusting the excise and excise duties, the equivalent duties, on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products. That should be done every year so that they keep pace with inflation and don't decline in real terms.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific instruments (excise on alcohol and tobacco) and why annual confirmation matters.

specificity.statement: We do think that the Government has used secondary legislation to update some things but also to advance a political agenda due to its inclusion of reduced excise for heated tobacco products in this bill, and we think that's actually not the way to go. … I also want to note the social security changes, particularly the changes that mean that benefits will now be changed to an index with the Consumers Price Index (CPI). That, actually, is also problematic because … those things will lead to lower increases to income support rather than if we adjusted those to wages, or whichever was higher.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provisions objected to and the indexation mechanism at issue.

specificity.statement: The report makes 15 recommendations to modernise and simplify regulations across ECE so that service providers can get on with what they do best … The ministry has recommended removing, changing, or merging approximately three-quarters of the 98 licensing criteria for centre-based services … I've accepted all 15 of the review's recommendations for regulatory changes … I'll be taking a paper to Cabinet in the new year with the intention of implementing these recommendations.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures — 15 recommendations, three-quarters of 98 licensing criteria — and a named next step.

specificity.statement: Is she seriously saying that cutting Stand Tū Māia's contract in April next year—an organisation that provides specialised trauma treatment and intensive wraparound family support for thousands of highly vulnerable children and their families, with a waiting list of over 450 children—is the right thing to do?
specificity.explanation: Names the provider, the service, the timing (April), and a concrete waiting-list figure (over 450 children).

specificity.statement: Is maintaining the rail freight connection between the North and South Islands by ensuring we have at least one rail-enabled ferry important for the economic prosperity of the regions, particularly in the South Island?
specificity.explanation: Frames a concrete policy condition ('at least one rail-enabled ferry') tied to regional freight.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do. And absolutely, what a year. Inflation is down, interest rates are down, tax relief has been delivered, fast track delivered, confidence is rising, growth is coming back, crime is falling, police are on the beat, gangs are on the run, phones are gone from class, and kids are getting back to school. We don't need a year of delivery. Every year this team delivers. And that's what we're doing—we're getting New Zealand back on track and cleaning up Labour's mess.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes, I do stand by' the question before listing claims.

forthrightness.statement: We've got 100,000 people eligible, we've got 60,000 that have actually claimed, and we've got about 42,000 that are actually settled. When you talk to people, they say it's a simple process: get on myIR.
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots away from Hipkins' actual question about high administration cost relative to payout.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd just reject the characterisation of that question, because we've had a very good uptake, having inherited very low immunisation rates from the last Labour Government. I'm proud of the work that we've done in partnering with iwi to drive immunisation rates with Māori under-two-year-olds. That's great work. Actually, we have a whooping cough epidemic in this country, and the task for parents—and we're making it as easy as possible—is to go get your kids vaccinated, and get yourself vaccinated, as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly to admit the immunisation cuts were a mistake given the epidemic; concedes the epidemic exists but never answers the mistake question, deflecting to blame and uptake.

forthrightness.statement: If you take the full year, which is including the period of a Labour-Greens Government, rents are up as you've talked about. But you've taken an annual number, rather than the number from when we came to office. That's what we measure ourselves against.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly acknowledges the figure rather than denying it, while defending his chosen framing.

forthrightness.statement: Oh, I mean, that is a bit rich, isn't it? Isn't that a bit rich? How are the conversations with David Parker and Kieran McAnulty working out, son?
forthrightness.explanation: Completely ignores the question about being the most unpopular PM, deflecting with a jibe about Labour leadership.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd just say, on the point about emissions, I'm very proud that our emissions reduction plan 2, delivered by an excellent climate change Minister, who is actually managing to deliver net zero six years earlier and keep our economy growing—well done. I'm very, very proud of that. We're on track to deliver net carbon zero 2050, as we've committed to doing.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage Swarbrick's specific point that the emissions target is only a 1 percent reduction, pivoting to praise.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, absolutely. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030 and achieving this target is a priority for our Government. Jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022 and are expected to peak in January 2025. The forecast has always been for the numbers to get worse before they get better.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly restates and stands by the target and confronts the forecast tension rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: I would like to go through that list of all the things we've done in the last 12 months, but you have said to keep my answers brief. So what I would say is: our plan is working. In the last five months, we have seen over 30,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit exit into work despite very challenging economic conditions, and that's what I'm proud of.
forthrightness.explanation: Sidesteps the question about whether economic conditions and mass job losses put the target at risk, redirecting to a positive metric.

forthrightness.statement: The simplest way to look through them is to take ACC revenue and expenses out of the OBEGAL. That is what we've done by creating a new measure called OBEGALx, which is simply OBEGAL excluding ACC. People who are attached to OBEGAL … if they are attached to OBEGAL, that measure will continue to be reported as a fiscal indicator.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what change was made and how, including that the old measure will still be reported.

forthrightness.statement: For one last time this year: there has not been a cut to the overall amount Oranga Tamariki is spending on contracted providers. There are contracts that will expire and not be renewed, some that Oranga Tamariki has decided to reduce, and others that will be increased.
