Oranga Tamariki spent more than $500 million with providers last year, and I'm advised we're on track to do so again this year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the 'do you stand by the cuts' question, distinguishing overall spend from individual contract changes.

forthrightness.statement: I campaigned saying that more money does not fix a problem. What fixes a problem is actually making sure that we're delivering the outcomes that are needed for our most vulnerable children.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she broke a promise that front-line services would not be impacted, she restates philosophy rather than confronting the specific promise.

veracity.statement: Yes, I do. And absolutely, what a year. Inflation is down, interest rates are down, tax relief has been delivered, fast track delivered, confidence is rising, growth is coming back, crime is falling, police are on the beat, gangs are on the run, phones are gone from class, and kids are getting back to school. We don't need a year of delivery. Every year this team delivers. And that's what we're doing—we're getting New Zealand back on track and cleaning up Labour's mess.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: inflation and rate falls are broadly accurate, but 'crime is falling', 'gangs are on the run' are contestable rhetorical claims presented as settled fact.

veracity.statement: My goodness! The member has no economic credibility. I mean, this was a Prime Minister that increased spending by 84 percent, drove up domestic inflation, drove up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and that raises unemployment. And he has the audacity to stand up and ask us questions on economics.
veracity.explanation: The '84 percent' spending figure is a contested/selectively-framed number, and the causal chain to recession is oversimplified.

veracity.statement: Well, Nicola Willis is going to go down as the best finance Minister this country has ever seen, because by God what a mess she has picked up. She is cleaning house and she's getting the job done. And she has delivered a value-for-money, reliable, sensible ferry solution of rail-compatible ferries.
veracity.explanation: Claims a ferry solution has been 'delivered' when by his own later words new ferries only arrive in 2029; overstated.

veracity.statement: We've got 100,000 people eligible, we've got 60,000 that have actually claimed, and we've got about 42,000 that are actually settled. When you talk to people, they say it's a simple process: get on myIR.
veracity.explanation: Offers plausible specific figures, though the anecdotal 'when you talk to people' portion is unverifiable.

veracity.statement: Well, I'd just reject the characterisation of that question, because we've had a very good uptake, having inherited very low immunisation rates from the last Labour Government. I'm proud of the work that we've done in partnering with iwi to drive immunisation rates with Māori under-two-year-olds. That's great work. Actually, we have a whooping cough epidemic in this country, and the task for parents—and we're making it as easy as possible—is to go get your kids vaccinated, and get yourself vaccinated, as well.
veracity.explanation: Acknowledges the whooping cough epidemic (accurate) but frames immunisation record selectively.

veracity.statement: I can tell you that average rents since we've come into power are stable and not up $180 per week, as they were under the Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Uses a start-date chosen to flatter; he later concedes that on the full-year measure rents are up, so the 'stable' framing is misleading.

veracity.statement: If you take the full year, which is including the period of a Labour-Greens Government, rents are up as you've talked about. But you've taken an annual number, rather than the number from when we came to office. That's what we measure ourselves against.
veracity.explanation: Honestly concedes rents are up on the annual measure and explains the alternative baseline he prefers.

veracity.statement: Wages grew slower than inflation for 13 quarters in a row under a Labour Government. They've had four quarters of wages growing faster than inflation under this Government.
veracity.explanation: The direction of real-wage trends is broadly supportable, though quarter counts are the kind of figure that can be framed selectively.

veracity.statement: Well, I'd just say, on the point about emissions, I'm very proud that our emissions reduction plan 2, delivered by an excellent climate change Minister, who is actually managing to deliver net zero six years earlier and keep our economy growing—well done. I'm very, very proud of that. We're on track to deliver net carbon zero 2050, as we've committed to doing.
veracity.explanation: 'Delivering net zero six years earlier' is an optimistic characterisation of a modelled plan rather than an achieved result.

veracity.statement: But what we're not going to do is what the last Labour-Greens Government did, which is have low unemployment at 3.2 percent and yet 70,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures (3.2% unemployment, 70,000) whose juxtaposition is presented pointedly but is broadly in the ballpark.

veracity.statement: The fact that Te Pāti Māori hasn't had a conversation about why nine out of 10 young Māori students heading into high school are not where they need to be in mathematics is shameful.
veracity.explanation: The 'nine out of 10' maths figure is a strong claim asserted without a cited source.

veracity.statement: Does his definition of "dumb stuff" that he said he was going to cut include spending nearly $14 million on the administration of the flailing FamilyBoost scheme that's only paid out $16 million so far, and is helping fewer than half the families he promised?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific admin-cost, payout, and coverage figures; broadly aligned with the numbers the PM concedes, though framed to maximise contrast.

veracity.statement: Which of the following best reflects his Government's priorities: $3 billion in tax cuts for landlords while cutting first-home buyer grants, $200 million in tax cuts for tobacco companies while the number of daily smokers increases for the first time in recent history, real-terms cuts to the minimum wage while directors' fees increase by up to 100 percent, or saying that he wouldn't borrow for tax cuts, only to increase Government borrowing by a record amount?
veracity.explanation: Figures are pointed and framed adversarially (e.g. 'tax cuts for landlords' for interest deductibility), mixing defensible and contestable characterisations.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that his Government has cut services for vulnerable children and whānau, increased benefit sanctions by 133 percent, and cut 9,000 jobs from the public sector, with 1,500 more to go at Health New Zealand, while setting aside $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords, in just this year alone?
veracity.explanation: Cites concrete numbers; the '$2.9 billion tax cuts for landlords' label is a contested characterisation of interest deductibility.

veracity.statement: Yes, absolutely. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030 and achieving this target is a priority for our Government. Jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022 and are expected to peak in January 2025. The forecast has always been for the numbers to get worse before they get better.
veracity.explanation: The 'always forecast to get worse before better' framing is a defensible but self-serving characterisation.

veracity.statement: I would like to go through that list of all the things we've done in the last 12 months, but you have said to keep my answers brief. So what I would say is: our plan is working. In the last five months, we have seen over 30,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit exit into work despite very challenging economic conditions, and that's what I'm proud of.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific 30,000-exits figure; 'our plan is working' is an interpretive gloss over gross flows that omit inflows.

veracity.statement: When jobseeker numbers started increasing during the global financial crisis in May 2008, there were around 85,000 people on the equivalent of jobseeker benefit; our starting point was 190,000.
veracity.explanation: Historical comparison figures presented as fact; broadly plausible but the 'equivalent of jobseeker' comparison across benefit regimes is imprecise.

veracity.statement: As I shared with the House yesterday, net core Crown debt went from $57 billion to $175 billion during the six years of the Labour Government, and now their position is that somehow that's our fault.
veracity.explanation: The debt-growth figures are broadly consistent with the record, though the framing omits the COVID context of much of that increase.

veracity.statement: No. This Government's Christmas present to Kiwis is inflation under control for the first time in three years. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is official cash rate reductions, meaning cheaper mortgages. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is tax relief for the first time in 14 years, including FamilyBoost payments for kids in early childhood education. And here's the best present of all: next year we will deliver a growing economy with more opportunities and more choices for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Inflation and OCR claims are broadly accurate; 'cheaper mortgages' and the growth promise are forward-leaning framings.

veracity.statement: How can New Zealanders take her financial management seriously when she cancelled the ferries, costing the taxpayer hundreds of millions of dollars, undertook creative accounting to make her books look better, and has delivered the highest debt in decades?
veracity.explanation: Mixes a defensible ferry-cost point with contested characterisations ('creative accounting', 'highest debt in decades').

veracity.statement: OMV, an international gas and oil explorer, announced at 6:30 a.m. this morning they are no longer withdrawing from New Zealand; as a consequence of the advocacy and the confidence instilled by this Government, they are staying to salvage the oil and gas industry in New Zealand. And on your behalf, New Zealand, I claim a little credit for that.
veracity.explanation: The OMV announcement may be real, but the causal attribution to Government advocacy is asserted without evidence.

veracity.statement: This includes the installation of 1,337 piles; use of over 10,000 cubic metres of concrete; more than 5 kilometres of road has been repaved; and 50,000 square metres of asphalt installed, which is around the size of seven rugby fields, I am told. These critical works have addressed 36 slips to increase resilience on this critical route and get Northlanders where they want to go quickly and safely.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable delivery figures presented plainly; the rugby-field analogy is illustrative rather than misleading.

veracity.statement: For one last time this year: there has not been a cut to the overall amount Oranga Tamariki is spending on contracted providers. There are contracts that will expire and not be renewed, some that Oranga Tamariki has decided to reduce, and others that will be increased. Oranga Tamariki spent more than $500 million with providers last year, and I'm advised we're on track to do so again this year.
veracity.explanation: Cites a $500m figure and 'on track'; the 'no cut overall' claim may sit in tension with individual provider cuts raised later.

veracity.statement: The Commerce Commission has today released a draft proposal to significantly lower card fees. The commission estimates that Kiwi businesses and consumers will save $260 million every year.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes the estimate to the commission, though it is a projected saving from a draft proposal, not a realised one.

veracity.statement: Going from the first supplementary question that you were asked, how can the Minister be responsible for the greatest debt ever when 80 percent of the Crown debt incurred here, at this point in time, was incurred under Labour?
veracity.explanation: The '80 percent under Labour' figure is a specific but selectively framed apportionment of accumulated Crown debt.

strength.statement: Yes, I do. And absolutely, what a year. Inflation is down, interest rates are down, tax relief has been delivered, fast track delivered, confidence is rising, growth is coming back, crime is falling, police are on the beat, gangs are on the run, phones are gone from class, and kids are getting back to school. We don't need a year of delivery. Every year this team delivers. And that's what we're doing—we're getting New Zealand back on track and cleaning up Labour's mess.
strength.explanation: Claims broad delivery ('this team delivers') but attributes are asserted rather than demonstrated with implemented specifics.

strength.statement: Well, Nicola Willis is going to go down as the best finance Minister this country has ever seen, because by God what a mess she has picked up. She is cleaning house and she's getting the job done. And she has delivered a value-for-money, reliable, sensible ferry solution of rail-compatible ferries.
strength.explanation: An announced/procured intention is presented as delivery, but nothing is yet built or operating.

strength.statement: OMV, an international gas and oil explorer, announced at 6:30 a.m. this morning they are no longer withdrawing from New Zealand; as a consequence of the advocacy and the confidence instilled by this Government, they are staying to salvage the oil and gas industry in New Zealand. And on your behalf, New Zealand, I claim a little credit for that.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete corporate decision as a result, but the link to delivered policy action is claimed rather than demonstrated.

strength.statement: This includes the installation of 1,337 piles; use of over 10,000 cubic metres of concrete; more than 5 kilometres of road has been repaved; and 50,000 square metres of asphalt installed, which is around the size of seven rugby fields, I am told. These critical works have addressed 36 slips to increase resilience on this critical route and get Northlanders where they want to go quickly and safely.
strength.explanation: Describes a tangible completed reopening of a route with quantified works, not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: I'm pleased to announce the first three recipients of the Government's Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund: Youthline, the Sir John Kirwan Foundation, and MATES in Construction. … The first three organisations being announced today will share more than $2 million from the mental health innovation fund, with this being matched with an additional $2 million in philanthropic funding, meaning the total investment in new mental health services announced today doubles to $4 million.
strength.explanation: A concrete funding allocation with named recipients, though it is an announcement of new services rather than demonstrated outcomes.

strength.statement: The Commerce Commission has today released a draft proposal to significantly lower card fees. The commission estimates that Kiwi businesses and consumers will save $260 million every year.
strength.explanation: This is a draft proposal at consultation stage; delivery ('sleighed' surcharges) is claimed ahead of implementation.

strength.statement: The report makes 15 recommendations to modernise and simplify regulations across ECE so that service providers can get on with what they do best … The ministry has recommended removing, changing, or merging approximately three-quarters of the 98 licensing criteria for centre-based services … I've accepted all 15 of the review's recommendations for regulatory changes … I'll be taking a paper to Cabinet in the new year with the intention of implementing these recommendations.
strength.explanation: Accepts all recommendations but implementation is still a future Cabinet paper; this is commitment, not yet delivery.

rigor.statement: My goodness! The member has no economic credibility. I mean, this was a Prime Minister that increased spending by 84 percent, drove up domestic inflation, drove up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and that raises unemployment. And he has the audacity to stand up and ask us questions on economics.
rigor.explanation: Leans on ad hominem and a sweeping causal claim rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Wages grew slower than inflation for 13 quarters in a row under a Labour Government. They've had four quarters of wages growing faster than inflation under this Government.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative data to support the claim, though attribution of wage movements solely to government is a stretch.

rigor.statement: But what we're not going to do is what the last Labour-Greens Government did, which is have low unemployment at 3.2 percent and yet 70,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit.
rigor.explanation: Uses a genuine statistical tension as an argument, though it dodges Swarbrick's underlying question about job availability.

rigor.statement: The fact that Te Pāti Māori hasn't had a conversation about why nine out of 10 young Māori students heading into high school are not where they need to be in mathematics is shameful.
rigor.explanation: Deflects the question with an emotive charge rather than addressing the disestablishment reasoning.

rigor.statement: Why are he and Nicola Willis the only people surprised to learn that when you slash jobs, the bill for unemployment benefits goes up, the tax take goes down, and the economy stalls; or is this one of the economic lessons from the last 35 years that he thinks he needs to relearn?
rigor.explanation: Sets out a coherent fiscal-multiplier argument, though wrapped in a rhetorical 'only people surprised' framing.

rigor.statement: Does his definition of "delivery" include an announcement about an announcement with no budget, no build specifications, no builder, no concrete time frame, no actual ships, and, if not, what exactly has Nicola Willis actually delivered when it comes to the Interislander?
rigor.explanation: Builds the 'no delivery' case from a concrete checklist of absent elements.

rigor.statement: Which of the following best reflects his Government's priorities: $3 billion in tax cuts for landlords while cutting first-home buyer grants, $200 million in tax cuts for tobacco companies while the number of daily smokers increases for the first time in recent history, real-terms cuts to the minimum wage while directors' fees increase by up to 100 percent, or saying that he wouldn't borrow for tax cuts, only to increase Government borrowing by a record amount?
rigor.explanation: A structured juxtaposition, but the multi-part 'which reflects his priorities' framing is rhetorical rather than analytic.

rigor.statement: Is the reason Andrew Bayly faced no sanction for calling someone working late "a loser", he defended Penny Simmonds' claims that disability support workers were ripping off the system, and his Government passed law changes stripping away workers' rights because those actions actually reflect what his Government thinks, which is that Kiwis who work hard for a living are losers and—to use his own words—"bottom feeders"?
rigor.explanation: Leaps from selected incidents to a sweeping inference about what the Government 'thinks' — a strawman-adjacent generalisation.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that "We've set ambitious goals for ourselves.", and, if so, can he please outline for the House what exactly is ambitious about his Government's goals to decrease emissions and persistent child poverty by just 1 percent?
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the 'ambitious' rhetoric against the stated numeric target to expose a gap.

rigor.statement: So why did his Government decide to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, because the authority was unable to unwind 182 years of oppression and unequal treatment in only nine months?
rigor.explanation: A loaded rhetorical question that presumes its own conclusion rather than making an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: What does the Prime Minister say about the economist Bernard Hickey's statement that "Treasury reports public service spending cuts to pay for lower taxes for landlords are shrivelling the economy, lifting spending on benefits, pumping up public debt & will put 20,000 more out of work"?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a named economist citing Treasury, rather than bare assertion.

rigor.statement: How can her target to reduce jobseeker beneficiary numbers by 50,000 be on track when the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts there will still be 204,000 people on jobseeker benefit in 2029, and her target for 2030 is 140,000 jobseeker beneficiaries?
rigor.explanation: Directly juxtaposes the official forecast against the target to test the 'on track' claim.

rigor.statement: The simplest way to look through them is to take ACC revenue and expenses out of the OBEGAL. That is what we've done by creating a new measure called OBEGALx, which is simply OBEGAL excluding ACC. People who are attached to OBEGAL … if they are attached to OBEGAL, that measure will continue to be reported as a fiscal indicator.
rigor.explanation: Gives a clear rationale (ACC is a self-sustaining long-term scheme) linking premise to the reporting change.

rigor.statement: It doesn't take a lot of parliamentary time, it doesn't take a lot of select committee time, but it is an important check on the ability of the executive to increase the costs on society, the most important of which, probably most years, is adjusting the excise and excise duties, the equivalent duties, on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products. That should be done every year so that they keep pace with inflation and don't decline in real terms.
rigor.explanation: Clear constitutional reasoning: taxes require parliamentary confirmation, with a concrete example and the inflation rationale.

rigor.statement: We do think that the Government has used secondary legislation to update some things but also to advance a political agenda due to its inclusion of reduced excise for heated tobacco products in this bill, and we think that's actually not the way to go. … I also want to note the social security changes, particularly the changes that mean that benefits will now be changed to an index with the Consumers Price Index (CPI). That, actually, is also problematic because … those things will lead to lower increases to income support rather than if we adjusted those to wages, or whichever was higher.
rigor.explanation: Gives concrete, reasoned objections (heated-tobacco excise, CPI vs wage indexation of benefits) rather than blanket opposition.

rigor.statement: Did the Government cut taxes for landlords or simply restore the very consistent and sensible tax policy that was the case for the first four years of the Labour-Green Government?
rigor.explanation: A leading, false-dichotomy question that presupposes its favoured answer ('simply restore … sensible tax policy').

rigor.statement: Going from the first supplementary question that you were asked, how can the Minister be responsible for the greatest debt ever when 80 percent of the Crown debt incurred here, at this point in time, was incurred under Labour?
rigor.explanation: Poses a genuine attribution challenge but as a friendly leading question that presumes its own answer.

authenticity.statement: If you take the full year, which is including the period of a Labour-Greens Government, rents are up as you've talked about. But you've taken an annual number, rather than the number from when we came to office. That's what we measure ourselves against.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent choice of baseline, though selecting the flattering measure sits in tension with the fuller picture.

authenticity.statement: OMV, an international gas and oil explorer, announced at 6:30 a.m. this morning they are no longer withdrawing from New Zealand; as a consequence of the advocacy and the confidence instilled by this Government, they are staying to salvage the oil and gas industry in New Zealand. And on your behalf, New Zealand, I claim a little credit for that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his pro-extraction stance; the self-credit ('I claim a little credit') is a candid claim of ownership.

authenticity.statement: I campaigned saying that more money does not fix a problem. What fixes a problem is actually making sure that we're delivering the outcomes that are needed for our most vulnerable children.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly ties her current position back to what she campaigned on — words consistent with a stated prior position.

divination.statement: Well, I'd just say, on the point about emissions, I'm very proud that our emissions reduction plan 2, delivered by an excellent climate change Minister, who is actually managing to deliver net zero six years earlier and keep our economy growing—well done. I'm very, very proud of that. We're on track to deliver net carbon zero 2050, as we've committed to doing.
divination.explanation: Predicts net-zero delivery by 2050 (and 'six years earlier'); a long-horizon forecast that is plausible but far from assured on current trajectory.

divination.statement: Yes, absolutely. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030 and achieving this target is a priority for our Government. Jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022 and are expected to peak in January 2025. The forecast has always been for the numbers to get worse before they get better.
divination.explanation: Predicts jobseeker numbers will peak in January 2025 — a near-term, checkable forecast that is plausible but uncertain given the deteriorating outlook.

divination.statement: No. This Government's Christmas present to Kiwis is inflation under control for the first time in three years. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is official cash rate reductions, meaning cheaper mortgages. Our Christmas present to Kiwis is tax relief for the first time in 14 years, including FamilyBoost payments for kids in early childhood education. And here's the best present of all: next year we will deliver a growing economy with more opportunities and more choices for New Zealanders.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'next year we will deliver a growing economy' — an optimistic forecast against a deteriorating HYEFU outlook.

divination.statement: Obviously, aquaculture is now going to enjoy an amazing growth period because for the next 20 years there will be no need for any more resource consents; they have been guaranteed. No more meddling from the Department of Conservation, no more interfering from unwise decision makers and regional councils. Certainty, confidence, and growth is about to hit regional New Zealand in the aquaculture sector, despite the best efforts of narrow-minded critics.
divination.explanation: Predicts an 'amazing growth period' for aquaculture over 20 years; directionally plausible but the magnitude is asserted optimistically.

specificity.statement: It’s my hope that we can get some really good wins for everybody who wants to do better for themselves and for their families this year and into the future.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspirational platitude with no mechanism, measure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: it’s really good that in 2025, entering the year, we are seeing the official cash rate in the actual band that we want to see, between 1 and 3 percent
specificity.explanation: Cites a numeric band, but the referent is muddled.

specificity.statement: we're still going to really work hard to get that down so that there’s more money in people’s pockets and the value of every dollar isn’t being sucked away by inflation
specificity.explanation: General intent to lower costs, no policy mechanism or target.

specificity.statement: We have campaigned in ACT on reducing wasteful spending so more Kiwis do have more money in their own back pocket
specificity.explanation: Names a theme (wasteful spending) but no figures or named cuts.

specificity.statement: We found savings of $421 million last year alone, and that work will continue into this year
specificity.explanation: Names a precise dollar figure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: we managed to find savings even within Fire and Emergency, so that people who pay for Fire and Emergency through a levy don’t have to pay as much as what Fire and Emergency was originally asking
specificity.explanation: Direction (lower levy) with no figure or date.

specificity.statement: We managed to get that child into a school so that that mother could return back to work and get back into the workforce.
specificity.explanation: Concrete case but individual, without named school or measures.

specificity.statement: Alcohol and drugs, as I think most members will know, are the number one contributing factor in fatal road crashes in New Zealand. In 2022, they were contributors to 200 fatal crashes on our roads.
specificity.explanation: Gives year and crash count.

specificity.statement: only 26 percent of drivers think they are likely to be caught while driving under the influence of drugs.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage figure.

specificity.statement: From 2019 to 2023, crashes involving drug-drivers claimed the lives of 108 people each year on average. That is 30 percent of road deaths annually
specificity.explanation: Date range, annual average, and percentage.

specificity.statement: The provisions require two positive screening tests at the roadside before a person is prohibited from driving for 12 hours.
specificity.explanation: Precise procedural detail: two tests, 12-hour stand-down.

specificity.statement: even the Attorney-General, the Hon Judith Collins, in her report on this bill, indicated that anything above 15 minutes, basically, called into question this issue of what is an unreasonable period of time to detain someone.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete threshold (15 minutes) and its statutory source.

specificity.statement: When we turn our mind to other jurisdictions, like Australia, where, in some situations, a first screening test could be up to 10 minutes, in other circumstances, a second oral fluid test could be up to 40 minutes
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete time figures for each test stage.

specificity.statement: People killed per year by sharks, four people; by a wolf, 10 people; 1,000 people killed by crocodiles; 475,000 killed by humans intentionally; 725,000 killed by mosquitoes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete per-category annual figures.

veracity.statement: it’s really good that in 2025, entering the year, we are seeing the official cash rate in the actual band that we want to see, between 1 and 3 percent
veracity.explanation: Conflates the OCR with the 1–3% inflation target band; the OCR in Jan 2025 was around 4.25%, so the claim as stated is inaccurate/misleading.

veracity.statement: We found savings of $421 million last year alone, and that work will continue into this year
veracity.explanation: Specific self-reported DIA savings figure; plausible but unverifiable from the text and how the saving is defined is unclear.

veracity.statement: we managed to find savings even within Fire and Emergency, so that people who pay for Fire and Emergency through a levy don’t have to pay as much as what Fire and Emergency was originally asking
veracity.explanation: Self-reported, unquantified, unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Alcohol and drugs, as I think most members will know, are the number one contributing factor in fatal road crashes in New Zealand. In 2022, they were contributors to 200 fatal crashes on our roads.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with NZ crash data, though 'number one factor' relies on combining drugs and alcohol (a framing Genter later challenges).

veracity.statement: only 26 percent of drivers think they are likely to be caught while driving under the influence of drugs.
veracity.explanation: Specific survey-style statistic presented as fact; plausible and consistent with the deterrence argument, unverified here.

veracity.statement: From 2019 to 2023, crashes involving drug-drivers claimed the lives of 108 people each year on average. That is 30 percent of road deaths annually
veracity.explanation: Specific averaged figure and proportion presented as fact; plausible and consistent with official framing.

veracity.statement: The last legislation, introduced by the previous Government, did not work as there was no commercially available testing device that met the criteria, so we committed to solving this problem, and, indeed, that is what this bill does.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises why the earlier regime never operated (no compliant device available).

veracity.statement: the land transport amendment Act 1991, from memory, got a section 7 report under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and Parliament went ahead and did it anyway because they thought it was the right thing to do.
veracity.explanation: Hedged with 'from memory'; broadly accurate historical account of the breath-testing precedent.

veracity.statement: even the Attorney-General, the Hon Judith Collins, in her report on this bill, indicated that anything above 15 minutes, basically, called into question this issue of what is an unreasonable period of time to detain someone.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific position to the AG's report; plausible and specific, unverified here.

veracity.statement: When we turn our mind to other jurisdictions, like Australia, where, in some situations, a first screening test could be up to 10 minutes, in other circumstances, a second oral fluid test could be up to 40 minutes
veracity.explanation: Specific comparative claim about Australian testing durations; plausible but not verified in the text.

veracity.statement: People killed per year by sharks, four people; by a wolf, 10 people; 1,000 people killed by crocodiles; 475,000 killed by humans intentionally; 725,000 killed by mosquitoes.
veracity.explanation: Figures match the widely circulated 'deadliest animals' infographic; broadly accurate order-of-magnitude data.

veracity.statement: The numbers that are being used, the statistics that have been cited by the Government to say that drugs and alcohol are the single largest contributing factor—well, that’s only because they’ve combined drugs and alcohol. If we split out drugs and alcohol, speed trumps both of them.
veracity.explanation: The disaggregation point and speed being a leading separate factor are consistent with NZ crash data.

veracity.statement: a number of studies have shown that doctors after work, or even medical students, people who’ve been working 24- or 36-hour shifts with no sleep, were more likely to be in a seriously damaging car crash or a fatal car crash than people who were severely impaired by alcohol.
veracity.explanation: Fatigue-impairment research broadly supports the comparison, though 'more likely than severely alcohol-impaired' is at the strong end and study-dependent.

veracity.statement: unlike with alcohol, for most of these substances, the presence of the substance in the blood or in saliva cannot be sufficiently correlated to impairment.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with expert evidence that oral-fluid drug concentration is a poor proxy for impairment, unlike blood alcohol.

veracity.statement: I’ll quote the Law Society, which recommended that the bill not proceed, and quoted the Independent Expert Panel on Drug Driving in its submission
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays the submitters' recommendation; plausible and specific.

strength.statement: we're still going to really work hard to get that down so that there’s more money in people’s pockets and the value of every dollar isn’t being sucked away by inflation
strength.explanation: Stated intent with no concrete action or delivery attached.

strength.statement: We found savings of $421 million last year alone, and that work will continue into this year
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivered result (savings achieved) rather than a mere aspiration.

strength.statement: we managed to find savings even within Fire and Emergency, so that people who pay for Fire and Emergency through a levy don’t have to pay as much as what Fire and Emergency was originally asking
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of a levy reduction, but no amount or confirmation of enactment given.

strength.statement: We managed to get that child into a school so that that mother could return back to work and get back into the workforce.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete constituent outcome actually delivered through electorate office work.

authenticity.statement: We have campaigned in ACT on reducing wasteful spending so more Kiwis do have more money in their own back pocket
authenticity.explanation: States a campaign position consistent with the party's stated in-government focus; plausible but general, no specific action cross-referenced in the text.

authenticity.statement: We supported this bill at first reading, we supported it through select committee, and we’ll continue to support it at second reading, with a couple of caveats there.
authenticity.explanation: States a position held consistently across all stages of the bill, backed by the party's own earlier introduction of a regime.

authenticity.statement: Road safety was a huge priority for me, always has been, and was when I was the Minister and developed the evidence-based road safety strategy and action plan, which was trying to address the biggest factors.
authenticity.explanation: Claim of a consistent priority backed by her documented record as Associate Minister responsible for road safety.

authenticity.statement: Last term, we none the less opposed that bill finally after submissions at select committee, and this bill amends that legislation.
authenticity.explanation: Notes a principled, consistent prior opposition, framing her current critical stance as continuous with her record.

civility.statement: I want to start by acknowledging the work of my predecessor, the Hon Simeon Brown... I also want to acknowledge the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—very ably chaired by Andy Foster—and sound contributions from across the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of predecessor, chair and cross-party contributors.

civility.statement: The last legislation, introduced by the previous Government, did not work as there was no commercially available testing device that met the criteria, so we committed to solving this problem, and, indeed, that is what this bill does.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government but on the substantive, factual failure rather than personally.

civility.statement: Can I acknowledge the chair, Andy Foster, for chairing us through this process... I also, along with the Minister, want to acknowledge Dr Helen Poulsen
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the chair, advisers and an expert witness across party lines.

civility.statement: I have to say that I’m very disappointed to hear from the Minister that one of the issues that was in the select committee—a possible maximum time by which a driver would be detained on the roadside—which the committee was really encouraging the Government to turn its mind to, is something that the Government is not prepared to pursue.
civility.explanation: Expresses disappointment but stays focused on the policy decision, not the person.

civility.statement: I’ll start by congratulating the new Minister on his role as Minister of Transport—very exciting.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful congratulation of a political opponent.

civility.statement: The numbers that are being used, the statistics that have been cited by the Government to say that drugs and alcohol are the single largest contributing factor—well, that’s only because they’ve combined drugs and alcohol. If we split out drugs and alcohol, speed trumps both of them.
civility.explanation: Substantive critique of the argument's statistical basis, not of any person.

charisma.statement: I want to start by acknowledging the work of my predecessor, the Hon Simeon Brown... I also want to acknowledge the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—very ably chaired by Andy Foster—and sound contributions from across the House.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, credits contributions from across the House, builds goodwill.

charisma.statement: Can I acknowledge the chair, Andy Foster, for chairing us through this process... I also, along with the Minister, want to acknowledge Dr Helen Poulsen
charisma.explanation: Collegial, credits others including the Minister; builds cooperative tone.

charisma.statement: we could have a different outcome to make it more workable, more fair, and get some consensus across the House on what is a pretty important issue.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-House consensus and a workable compromise.

charisma.statement: I’ll start by congratulating the new Minister on his role as Minister of Transport—very exciting.
charisma.explanation: Generous, bridge-building opening across party lines.

charisma.statement: it is important that there is some deterrent factor that people don’t believe they can use an impairing substance and then drive. It is really, really important that we do something about that.
charisma.explanation: Despite opposing the bill, concedes the legitimacy of the Government's underlying deterrence goal, finding common ground.

rigor.statement: Alcohol and drugs, as I think most members will know, are the number one contributing factor in fatal road crashes in New Zealand. In 2022, they were contributors to 200 fatal crashes on our roads.
rigor.explanation: Cites statistics to support the case for the bill; the combined-category framing is a mild gap.

rigor.statement: From 2019 to 2023, crashes involving drug-drivers claimed the lives of 108 people each year on average. That is 30 percent of road deaths annually
rigor.explanation: Evidence marshalled directly to justify the policy conclusion.

rigor.statement: The last legislation, introduced by the previous Government, did not work as there was no commercially available testing device that met the criteria, so we committed to solving this problem, and, indeed, that is what this bill does.
rigor.explanation: Diagnoses prior failure and links it to the current fix, though 'that is what this bill does' is asserted.

rigor.statement: the land transport amendment Act 1991, from memory, got a section 7 report under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and Parliament went ahead and did it anyway because they thought it was the right thing to do.
rigor.explanation: Uses a genuine historical precedent to reason by analogy about rights concerns.

rigor.statement: legislating a time frame potentially incentivises drivers to prolong the process in order to avoid undergoing a test. That would send the wrong message and incentive, clearly, and it would completely undermine the effectiveness of the regime.
rigor.explanation: Coherent incentive-based argument for why a statutory time limit is counterproductive; conclusion follows from the premise, though 'completely undermine' is somewhat strong.

rigor.statement: even the Attorney-General, the Hon Judith Collins, in her report on this bill, indicated that anything above 15 minutes, basically, called into question this issue of what is an unreasonable period of time to detain someone.
rigor.explanation: Grounds his argument in the Attorney-General's report and an existing 15-minute statutory identity provision; conclusion follows from cited authority.

rigor.statement: When we turn our mind to other jurisdictions, like Australia, where, in some situations, a first screening test could be up to 10 minutes, in other circumstances, a second oral fluid test could be up to 40 minutes
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative evidence to argue a reasonable maximum detention time is definable.

rigor.statement: I don’t think it’s appropriate to have a situation where the decisions as to what is going to be in the bill or in the legislation, or what is not, is going to be driven by an ability to, basically, procure devices or otherwise
rigor.explanation: Principled argument that policy content should drive procurement, not vice versa; logically ordered.

rigor.statement: People killed per year by sharks, four people; by a wolf, 10 people; 1,000 people killed by crocodiles; 475,000 killed by humans intentionally; 725,000 killed by mosquitoes.
rigor.explanation: Vivid comparison to make a point about risk perception, but somewhat of a tangential rhetorical device rather than direct evidence for the bill.

rigor.statement: The numbers that are being used, the statistics that have been cited by the Government to say that drugs and alcohol are the single largest contributing factor—well, that’s only because they’ve combined drugs and alcohol. If we split out drugs and alcohol, speed trumps both of them.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a category-combination framing in the Government's headline statistic and offers a specific counter-claim (speed) that can be checked.

rigor.statement: a number of studies have shown that doctors after work, or even medical students, people who’ve been working 24- or 36-hour shifts with no sleep, were more likely to be in a seriously damaging car crash or a fatal car crash than people who were severely impaired by alcohol.

specificity.statement: blue shoots—the country has reached the Government target, reducing by 81 percent the number of households living in emergency housing.

rigor.statement: The last Government was obsessed with imposing illogical and untargeted speed limit reductions on State highways and local roads. We are reversing that.

strength.statement: On Monday, I joined immigration Minister Erica Stanford and tourism Minister Louise Upston to announce the relaxation of visitor visa requirements to allow tourists to work remotely while visiting New Zealand. strength.explanation: A specific policy change actually announced and taking effect, though delivery of the economic benefit is unproven.

strength.statement: this year we are saying yes to economic growth. We have said yes to a trade deal with the UAE to boost exports and lift incomes. We've said yes to Invest New Zealand so we can attract more foreign direct investment in New Zealand into infrastructure and energy and manufacturing. We said yes to digital nomads—we actually did something about it—and said yes to more tourism and more hospitality.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a list of announced actions; several are announcements rather than delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: What I can rule in is that we're going to be Government that actually doubles the amount of renewable energy in this country and we'll make sure that we can also keep the lights on and keep electricity abundant and affordable for New Zealanders. strength.statement: We've announced 38 roads for which the speed limits will revert back to what they were pre-2020. strength.statement: the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill passed its second reading last night, which brings New Zealand into line with other jurisdictions, in which we will be able to test people by the roadside for whether or not they have recently used drugs.
strength.explanation: Legislation progressed to second reading — real progress, though not yet enacted.

strength.statement: This year, 65,000 young New Zealanders starting school will benefit from an internationally comparable, knowledge-rich, and structured curriculum in English and maths, that has been very well received by the sector.
strength.explanation: A curriculum change actually rolling out this school year, not merely promised.

strength.statement: Eighteen thousand teachers have already been trained or are in training. Phonics checks are available after 20 and 40 weeks at school to catch our young learners who are falling behind. Schools across the country are getting up to $5,000 for additional structured literacy resources each year for four years. And, finally, 970 schools applied for and received staffing allocations for reading intervention teachers for young learners who are falling behind in their reading.

strength.statement: Nearly half a million maths workbooks, textbooks, and teacher guides are being shipped to primary and intermediate schools around New Zealand where they will benefit over 430,000 students as they engage with their new maths curriculum this year.
strength.explanation: Materials actually being distributed — delivery underway rather than an aspiration.

strength.statement: blue shoots—the country has reached the Government target, reducing by 81 percent the number of households living in emergency housing.

strength.statement: Invest New Zealand will be a new agency modelled on the Irish and Singaporean best practice. civility.statement: This rubbish—this lie—about us being a special privileged people must stop, and it's the Prime Minister's job to get this ACT Party in line.
civility.explanation: 'Rubbish'/'lie' is heated, but attacks an argument/policy narrative rather than a person's character.

civility.explanation: Characterises the Government as captured by tobacco/lobbyists/landlords — an uncharitable framing rather than engagement with its arguments.

civility.statement: We think that Seymour's either wilfully blind or wilfully deaf because he consistently says "I don't know what they're talking about. Can someone explain it to me?"

civility.statement: I apologise to my good friend the Minister; I know he's a sensitive soul.

civility.statement: The allegation of a relationship that is completely fallacious should be rescinded.

civility.statement: A name is a taonga, and to have that taonga erased, assimilated, and suppressed is an act of deliberate colonial violence.
civility.explanation: Forceful language about historical Crown conduct, directed at actions rather than any present member.

civility.explanation: Frank criticism of past Crown conduct, not of any current member.

civility.statement: our tūpuna never ceded sovereignty over our maunga—no raupatu, no Act of Government, no colonial decree could ever sever our connection with our maunga.
civility.explanation: Emphatic assertion of principle, not a personal attack on any member.

veracity.statement: He is the most principled of the Māori MPs—of that there is no doubt—because he didn't want to deliver this Government's terrible Health budget: underfunding, under-resourcing this country.
veracity.explanation: 'Underfunding, under-resourcing' is a contested characterisation of the health budget, and the imputed motive for Reti is speculative.

veracity.statement: If we were privileged, we wouldn't die seven years earlier than everyone else. If we were privileged, we wouldn't be 50 percent of the prison population. If we were privileged, we wouldn't be three times more unemployed than Pākehā people.
veracity.explanation: Life-expectancy gap (~7 yrs), Māori share of the prison population (~50%) and higher unemployment ratio are broadly consistent with official data, though the multiples are approximate.

veracity.statement: It's yes to the tobacco companies, right? It's yes to the lobbyists. Who else is it a yes to? ... to landlords—but, most of all, what we've heard lately is that it's yes to privatisation.
veracity.explanation: Some threads are grounded (smokefree repeal, privatisation discussion) but the sweeping 'yes to' list overstates and misleads.

veracity.statement: In 1865, the Crown unfairly punished Māori by confiscating 1.2 million acres of Taranaki land, including the mountain.
veracity.explanation: The 1865 Taranaki confiscation of roughly 1.2 million acres is well documented in the historical record and Tribunal findings.

veracity.statement: In 1770, Captain Cook sighted Taranaki Maunga while sailing down the western coast of the North Island. Cook decided to name the mountain Mt Egmont after the Earl of Egmont, who had a been a key supporter of Cook's voyages.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of Cook's 1770 sighting and naming after the Earl of Egmont.

veracity.statement: The Parliamentary Council Office, through quality assurance processes, identified seven incorrect cross references within Te Pire Whakatupua mō Te Kāhui Tupua/Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Bill—for example, where a reference to section 86(3) was intended to be section 87(3).
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable procedural claim consistent with routine PCO quality-assurance corrections.

veracity.statement: Through the eight individual settlements for the iwi of Taranaki, the Crown promised that it would return to negotiate collective redress over the maunga. Today, the Crown fulfils this agreement.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the settlement history in which collective maunga redress was deferred from the individual iwi settlements.

veracity.statement: These tensions came to a head in 1850, when the Crown used military force to seize Waitara, sparking war, and in 1865, the Crown compounded this injustice by confiscating 1.2 million acres of Māori land, including Taranaki Maunga itself.
veracity.explanation: The 1865 confiscation figure is accurate, but the Crown's military move on Waitara that sparked the Taranaki war was 1860, not 1850 (Goldsmith gave 1860).

veracity.statement: The Crown sought to name and claim our wāhi tapu, our takiwā, as a strategy of cultural genocide.
veracity.explanation: 'Strategy of cultural genocide' is a strong interpretive characterisation that overstates a documented but contested historical intent.

veracity.statement: Rights have been trampled by the Crown; violence, injustice has been given out; the Crown has told lies and damaged te mana, the respect, that it claims but, perhaps, didn't deserve.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the documented historical record of Crown breaches in Taranaki set out in the bill.

veracity.statement: In 2014, Te Urewera was delisted as a national park to become the first ecosystem in the world to be recognised as having legal personhood.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Te Urewera Act 2014 granted Te Urewera legal personhood and removed its national park status.

veracity.statement: the Whanganui awa became the first river to be recognised as an indivisible and living being—the first river in the world to be granted legal personhood status
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River) settlement recognised the river as a legal person, widely reported as a world first.

He also wanted me to mention that he has put money into upgrading 23 marae in the Taranaki region
veracity.explanation: PGF investment in the Taranaki Crossing and regional marae is broadly documented, though the specific '23 marae' figure is relayed on Jones's word.

veracity.statement: probably our most famous mountaineer, Sir Edmund Hillary, climbed it for the first time at the age of 24. ... In fact, he went and climbed it a hundred more times
veracity.explanation: Hillary did climb Taranaki, but 'a hundred more times' is an unverified, likely hyperbolic figure.

veracity.statement: The bill doesn't return ownership.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the bill vests the maunga in a legal-personhood entity rather than returning fee-simple ownership to iwi.

veracity.statement: There was also recognition in the Taranaki tribunal reports—which I take every opportunity in this House to mention—of the kaupapa tuatahi of the Waitangi Tribunal, which noted that what happened to Taranaki Māori in the 1860s as being akin to holocaust
