civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive — tests a stated value against attendance record rather than insulting the person.

civility.statement: Why do wealthy people applying for her investor visa not need to meet English language requirements but hard-working migrants on other visas do?
civility.explanation: Frames a fairness contrast; sharp but engages a real policy asymmetry rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: We had a golden goose that was absolutely destroyed by the previous Government and that was replaced with a lame duck … In the last almost three years, 31 applicants were approved in principle, with a total of $70 million invested, compared to $2.2 billion in the two years prior to 2020.
civility.explanation: Colourful ('golden goose … lame duck') but aimed at the policy settings, not a person.

specificity.statement: the concern for the public and mana whenua on the danger that that vehicle could have had and the breach of the tikanga around those pou … there is a tikanga around protecting these pou as well that I think that the Speaker needs to consider in his investigation address as well.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete concern (safety and the pou/tikanga) but without further detail or remedy.

specificity.statement: I'd take my line-up over his every day of the week, because inflation is beat, interest rates are falling, and exports are rising fast thanks to our farmers and growers competing so well on the world stage.
specificity.explanation: Cites directional economic indicators but no figures, mechanisms, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: That means promoting more tourism, more investment, more infrastructure, more farming, more fishing and mining, and we're doubling down on all of that so we get this economy moving.
specificity.explanation: A list of sectors with 'more' of each, but no policies, amounts, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his comment that David Seymour has not breached the Cabinet Manual … given recent revelations that David Seymour intervened in a police murder investigation, referred a sexual abuse survivor to an ACT Party lawyer rather than to the police, and, just yesterday—potentially illegally—attempted to drive a Land Rover up the front steps of Parliament?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates three concrete alleged incidents and cites the Cabinet Manual standard by wording.

specificity.statement: Well, does he agree with Christopher Luxon, who said of Ministers involving themselves in police matters, "This would not be tolerated under a National government I lead. New Zealanders expect Ministers to hold themselves to the highest standards."; if so, what happened to those standards?
specificity.explanation: Quotes a specific prior statement to frame the challenge.

specificity.statement: Before the last Labour Government made some very restrictive changes to the active investor visa, this was a country that benefited by $2.2 billion from investment … Under the changes of the "no" Government of Labour … there was $70 million raised over 13 projects in a two-year period.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures, project counts, and a time window.

specificity.statement: No, we have a justice system that we want to make sure the public have great confidence in. That's what we keep perfecting.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration ('perfecting' the justice system) with no mechanism.

specificity.statement: Last month, Statistics New Zealand reported annual Consumers Price Index (CPI) inflation of 2.2 percent for the December quarter. That was the same rate as the September quarter and well within the Reserve Bank's target range of 1 percent to 3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the figure, the quarter, and the target range.

specificity.statement: annual CPI inflation in the December quarter was 2.2 percent. In the same period, according to the quarterly employment survey, wages rose 4.2 percent. … it is true that with inflation now under control, on average, wages are now rising faster than prices.
specificity.explanation: Two named statistics with their sources and the period.

specificity.statement: Infometrics has estimated that by the end of this year, households will have another $45 million to spend every week due to lower mortgage interest costs.
specificity.explanation: Attributed forecast with a dollar figure, cadence, and timeframe.

specificity.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that 13,000 jobs in the building and construction sector have been lost during the time he has been Prime Minister, particularly given industry statements that his Government's decision to slash house building, pause or cancel major infrastructure projects, and cut Government investment are to blame?
specificity.explanation: A specific job-loss figure tied to named government decisions and industry attribution.

specificity.statement: We're going to build infrastructure, not just talk about it—like Auckland light rail and harbour crossings and a bunch of other kumbaya and mush from the muppets on the other side.
specificity.explanation: Names Auckland light rail and harbour crossings but the delivery claim is unquantified.

specificity.statement: The Infrastructure Commission's latest pipeline actually had, I think, $148 billion worth of work. We have $33 billion in the transport Government policy statement over the next three years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for the pipeline and the transport GPS with a three-year horizon.

specificity.statement: If New Zealand is back on track, why are company liquidations in the building and construction sector up 41 percent, up 55 percent in hospitality, and a whopping 79 percent in transport, all under his watch; or will he now admit that under his leadership, the country's being derailed?
specificity.explanation: Three sector-specific liquidation percentages anchoring the challenge.

specificity.statement: Does he think the fact that 70,000 New Zealanders have left the country since he became Prime Minister—equivalent to the population of Napier—is one of the reasons over half the country think that things are heading in the wrong direction?
specificity.explanation: A net-migration figure with a vivid comparator and a polling reference.

specificity.statement: What's Nicola Willis more likely to replace this year: the interisland ferries or him as Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: A quip with no substantive content.

specificity.statement: We have inflation down. We have interest rates down. We have confidence up. We had exports in December up 17 percent—that's brilliant news.
specificity.explanation: Mostly directional but includes a concrete 'exports up 17 percent in December' figure.

specificity.statement: as of last Friday, the coalition Government's fast-track approvals scheme is officially open for business. … People are now able to apply into the approvals scheme if their proposed projects have significant regional or national benefits.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme, its open date, and the applicant criteria.

specificity.statement: Last week, we announced that retired Environment Court Judge Jane Borthwick has been appointed as the fast-track panel convener, Helen Atkins and Jennifer Caldwell as associate conveners.
specificity.explanation: Names specific appointees and their roles.

specificity.statement: Yes, I often agree with myself. … in Budget 2024, we allocated $140 million to fund 1,500 new places to June 2027. Kāinga Ora will also be delivering an additional 2,650 housing places to June 2026.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, place counts, and dated targets.

specificity.statement: Since we came to Government, the social housing wait-list has declined by around 5,000 households. … Despite record debt by Kāinga Ora and billions of dollars given to the organisation, the social housing wait-list quadrupled.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for the change in the wait-list under both governments.

specificity.statement: around 1,900 children in emergency housing motels have been moved into social and affordable housing. It's a totemic achievement, and the Government is very proud of the fact that there are thousands of children now living in social houses who were previously living in cold, dark, dank motels.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (1,900 children) though 'thousands' is looser.

specificity.statement: From 1 April, this Government will introduce two new investment categories … The Growth category focuses on high-risk investments like Kiwi start-ups, with a minimum of $5 million for three years, while the Balanced category targets lower-risk investments, requiring $10 million over five years.
specificity.explanation: Names both categories, dollar thresholds, holding periods, and the start date.

specificity.statement: In 2019, 217 applications were approved and $1.1 billion was invested into New Zealand. I've been advised that there are already over 50 investors who are ready to apply on 1 April. This represents a minimum of $250 million.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures: approvals, dollars invested, prospective applicants, and a minimum sum.

specificity.statement: the question has to be put by the public to that member why on earth they approved 212,000 resident visas under RV21 with almost no health requirements at all, even though they were warned by their officials that it would have a huge impact on our health system. But here the previous Minister is worried about 219 multimillionaires.
specificity.explanation: Cites the RV21 visa count and the investor-visa headcount.

specificity.statement: Multimillion-dollar investors coming into New Zealand are not required to speak English, for two reasons: firstly, it's insulting that we ask them to sit a high school test to show that they can speak English when they're worth millions of dollars … and secondly … actually we have people in our businesses who speak Mandarin; we don't need them to speak English.
specificity.explanation: Explains the concrete rule (no English test for investors) and contrasts it with lower-skilled visa protections.

specificity.statement: I think what's important is that we actually are expanding access for 10,000 more kids, and the money saved is actually going into delivering better resources in education and healthcare.
specificity.explanation: Cites '10,000 more kids' but is vague on where savings go ('better resources').

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the people delivering the Healthy School Lunches Programme, the School Lunch Collective, are highly qualified and skilled in delivering food, unlike Chlöe Swarbrick … "Received our first lunches from the new lunch programme today and the students and staff were very impressed! Lunches arrived on time and they were nice and hot …"?
specificity.explanation: Names the provider and quotes concrete positive feedback about the delivery.

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that yesterday, the school lunch programme achieved 100 percent on-time delivery in every region, with two exceptions, where, in one case, 95 percent delivery was achieved, and, in the other case, 92 percent on-time delivery was achieved?
specificity.explanation: Precise on-time-delivery percentages by region.

specificity.statement: In January, Germany confirmed an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in cattle for the first time in 40 years. The risk to New Zealand is low, but we take it very seriously because of how devastating this disease would be for our primary sector and for the New Zealand economy.
specificity.explanation: Names the disease, country, timing, and the 40-year framing.

specificity.statement: Tracing has not detected any HPAI-infected chickens beyond the farm where the disease originated. Given we have now had enough time to move through two incubation periods, our focus has shifted on to decontamination of the affected property.
specificity.explanation: Concrete status update: containment to one farm, two incubation periods elapsed, shift to decontamination.

specificity.statement: New Zealand's robust biosecurity system, and the relative freedom from pests and disease that it protects, is a massive part in our farmers' competitive advantage. It underpins a $53 billion export industry.
specificity.explanation: Includes a concrete export-value figure ($53 billion) but the causal 'underpins' claim is broad.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, "Despite tension, despite frustration, we still show up and actually engage in a process, in a conversation, on this day."; if so, why does he keep avoiding significant events like the Treaty principles bill first reading, the arrival of the hīkoi to Parliament, and Waitangi?
specificity.explanation: Names three specific events and quotes the PM's own words to frame a consistency challenge.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that his Government's decision to cut funding for school lunches by up to 75 percent per child has reduced the quality of those lunches?
specificity.explanation: Puts a concrete figure (up to 75 percent per child) on the funding cut.

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his Government's choice to stop contracts with local providers and procure school lunches from a large corporation has cost approximately 2,000 local jobs in communities, as well as a reduction in the quality of this food?
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete job figure (~2,000) and the mechanism (local providers → single large supplier).

specificity.statement: Did she share with Cabinet the Australian Productivity Commission report that found their investor visa was costing Australia more in health than it was bringing in?
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific report and its finding to frame a pointed policy question.

specificity.statement: We had a golden goose that was absolutely destroyed by the previous Government and that was replaced with a lame duck … In the last almost three years, 31 applicants were approved in principle, with a total of $70 million invested, compared to $2.2 billion in the two years prior to 2020.
specificity.explanation: Concrete approval count and dollar contrast between the two visa regimes.

veracity.statement: I'd take my line-up over his every day of the week, because inflation is beat, interest rates are falling, and exports are rising fast thanks to our farmers and growers competing so well on the world stage.
veracity.explanation: Inflation at 2.2% and falling rates are broadly accurate for the period; 'inflation is beat' overstates a still-live cost-of-living situation.

veracity.statement: actually, we're funded by the taxpayer, just like everybody in this House. We are not funded by particular people, and I think it is quite wrong for him to get away with implying otherwise.
veracity.explanation: Conflates MPs' parliamentary funding with party political donations; parties do receive private donations, so the rebuttal is partly misleading.

veracity.statement: Before the last Labour Government made some very restrictive changes to the active investor visa, this was a country that benefited by $2.2 billion from investment … Under the changes of the "no" Government of Labour … there was $70 million raised over 13 projects in a two-year period.
veracity.explanation: The $2.2 billion vs ~$70 million contrast is repeated by Stanford with figures and broadly matches the visa's history, though framing is selective.

veracity.statement: Last month, Statistics New Zealand reported annual Consumers Price Index (CPI) inflation of 2.2 percent for the December quarter. That was the same rate as the September quarter and well within the Reserve Bank's target range of 1 percent to 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Accurately cites the official StatsNZ CPI figure and the RBNZ target band.

veracity.statement: annual CPI inflation in the December quarter was 2.2 percent. In the same period, according to the quarterly employment survey, wages rose 4.2 percent. … it is true that with inflation now under control, on average, wages are now rising faster than prices.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific CPI and wage figures with sources; the 'on average … faster than prices' claim is hedged appropriately ('many people are still doing it tough').

veracity.statement: What responsibility does he take for the fact that 13,000 jobs in the building and construction sector have been lost during the time he has been Prime Minister, particularly given industry statements that his Government's decision to slash house building, pause or cancel major infrastructure projects, and cut Government investment are to blame?
veracity.explanation: The 13,000 construction-sector job-loss figure is broadly consistent with the sector's downturn, though causal attribution is contested.

veracity.statement: The Infrastructure Commission's latest pipeline actually had, I think, $148 billion worth of work. We have $33 billion in the transport Government policy statement over the next three years.
veracity.explanation: Figures are in the right ballpark for the pipeline and GPS, hedged with 'I think', but conflates a pipeline value with delivered spend.

veracity.statement: If New Zealand is back on track, why are company liquidations in the building and construction sector up 41 percent, up 55 percent in hospitality, and a whopping 79 percent in transport, all under his watch; or will he now admit that under his leadership, the country's being derailed?
veracity.explanation: Cites concrete liquidation increases consistent with reported insolvency trends, though the 'derailed' framing is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: Does he think the fact that 70,000 New Zealanders have left the country since he became Prime Minister—equivalent to the population of Napier—is one of the reasons over half the country think that things are heading in the wrong direction?
veracity.explanation: Net departure figures of this order are broadly reported, though 'left the country' blurs gross vs net migration.

veracity.statement: We have inflation down. We have interest rates down. We have confidence up. We had exports in December up 17 percent—that's brilliant news.
veracity.explanation: Directional claims align with the period and the export figure is plausible, though presented selectively.

veracity.statement: Since we came to Government, the social housing wait-list has declined by around 5,000 households. … Despite record debt by Kāinga Ora and billions of dollars given to the organisation, the social housing wait-list quadrupled.
veracity.explanation: The wait-list decline figure is repeated and defensible, but 'quadrupled' and the register's acknowledged imperfections (which Bishop later concedes) add missing context.

veracity.statement: The member's question is completely factually inaccurate. We have funded more social houses than the last Government did. … the Kāinga Ora and social housing build programme stopped as per the settings left by the last Government's Budget in May 2023. There were no social housing places funded beyond June 2025.
veracity.explanation: The 'fiscal cliff'/no funding beyond June 2025 framing is a contested but arguable characterisation of prior Budget settings.

veracity.statement: around 1,900 children in emergency housing motels have been moved into social and affordable housing. It's a totemic achievement, and the Government is very proud of the fact that there are thousands of children now living in social houses who were previously living in cold, dark, dank motels.
veracity.explanation: The 1,900 figure is plausible, but attributing all improvement to policy and omitting emergency-housing gateway tightening leaves out context.

veracity.statement: In 2019, 217 applications were approved and $1.1 billion was invested into New Zealand. I've been advised that there are already over 50 investors who are ready to apply on 1 April. This represents a minimum of $250 million.
veracity.explanation: The historical figures are plausible; the '50 investors / $250 million' is an advised projection presented as near-fact.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that yesterday, the school lunch programme achieved 100 percent on-time delivery in every region, with two exceptions, where, in one case, 95 percent delivery was achieved, and, in the other case, 92 percent on-time delivery was achieved?
veracity.explanation: A specific operational claim presented favourably; unverifiable from the text and selective (delivery timeliness, not food quality).

veracity.statement: In January, Germany confirmed an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in cattle for the first time in 40 years. The risk to New Zealand is low, but we take it very seriously because of how devastating this disease would be for our primary sector and for the New Zealand economy.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the January 2025 German FMD outbreak and characterises the risk proportionately ('risk is low').

veracity.statement: New Zealand's robust biosecurity system, and the relative freedom from pests and disease that it protects, is a massive part in our farmers' competitive advantage. It underpins a $53 billion export industry.
veracity.explanation: The primary-export figure is in the right order of magnitude; the framing of biosecurity as underpinning all of it is somewhat sweeping.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that his Government's decision to cut funding for school lunches by up to 75 percent per child has reduced the quality of those lunches?
veracity.explanation: The per-child funding-reduction framing is contested and depends on how the saving is calculated; presented as settled.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his Government's choice to stop contracts with local providers and procure school lunches from a large corporation has cost approximately 2,000 local jobs in communities, as well as a reduction in the quality of this food?
veracity.explanation: The 2,000-jobs and quality claims are asserted as fact but are estimates/contested.

veracity.statement: We had a golden goose that was absolutely destroyed by the previous Government and that was replaced with a lame duck … In the last almost three years, 31 applicants were approved in principle, with a total of $70 million invested, compared to $2.2 billion in the two years prior to 2020.
veracity.explanation: The dollar figures are consistent with the department's account, but the 'golden goose/lame duck' framing selectively omits the prior visa's design problems.

charisma.statement: I'd take my line-up over his every day of the week, because inflation is beat, interest rates are falling, and exports are rising fast thanks to our farmers and growers competing so well on the world stage.
charisma.explanation: Confident boosterism that rallies his own side ('I'd take my line-up over his') without reaching across the aisle.

strength.statement: That means promoting more tourism, more investment, more infrastructure, more farming, more fishing and mining, and we're doubling down on all of that so we get this economy moving.
strength.explanation: States broad intent to 'double down' without concrete delivery or mechanism.

strength.statement: as of last Friday, the coalition Government's fast-track approvals scheme is officially open for business. … People are now able to apply into the approvals scheme if their proposed projects have significant regional or national benefits.
strength.explanation: Announces an actually-implemented scheme (open for applications), a concrete delivery rather than mere aspiration.

strength.statement: Last week, we announced that retired Environment Court Judge Jane Borthwick has been appointed as the fast-track panel convener, Helen Atkins and Jennifer Caldwell as associate conveners.
strength.explanation: Concrete appointments made, evidence of the scheme being operationalised.

strength.statement: Yes, I often agree with myself. … in Budget 2024, we allocated $140 million to fund 1,500 new places to June 2027. Kāinga Ora will also be delivering an additional 2,650 housing places to June 2026.
strength.explanation: Funded and dated build programme, but places are future-dated (to 2026/2027), so delivery is in progress rather than complete.

strength.statement: Since we came to Government, the social housing wait-list has declined by around 5,000 households. … Despite record debt by Kāinga Ora and billions of dollars given to the organisation, the social housing wait-list quadrupled.
strength.explanation: Claims a measurable reduction in the wait-list as a delivered result, though partly driven by register operation, not just builds.

strength.statement: around 1,900 children in emergency housing motels have been moved into social and affordable housing. It's a totemic achievement, and the Government is very proud of the fact that there are thousands of children now living in social houses who were previously living in cold, dark, dank motels.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered outcome (children moved out of motels), a follow-through claim rather than aspiration.

strength.statement: Tracing has not detected any HPAI-infected chickens beyond the farm where the disease originated. Given we have now had enough time to move through two incubation periods, our focus has shifted on to decontamination of the affected property.
strength.explanation: Describes a response actually carried through (containment and decontamination) rather than a promise.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I said yesterday, I made my position clear: he wrote the letter before he was actually a Government Minister and before the Government was formed.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers a question about whether Seymour breached the Cabinet Manual by pivoting to the timing of the letter rather than addressing the standard asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Because the Minister was not a Minister at the time in which he sent the letter. He was an MP outside the Government and not a Minister—it's very simple.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he hasn't asked Seymour about donations/conflict of interest, he repeats the timing point instead of answering whether he asked.

forthrightness.statement: It would be the easiest thing in the world for me to just stand up and say that there's been no such donation to me, but I'm not going to do that. I would urge all members of the House to think very carefully about the implications of every member declaring every possible donation, or not, at every point of questioning.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly declines to answer whether he received a donation from Polkinghorne, pivoting to a warning about precedent.

forthrightness.statement: I'm just reminded of the words of the Canadian songstress Alanis Morissette, who said, "Isn't it ironic?", because let me give you four names: Michael Wood, Meka Whaitiri, Stuart Nash, and how about Kiri Allan?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he hasn't demanded a resignation letter from Seymour, he deflects to naming former Labour ministers rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: No, we have a justice system that we want to make sure the public have great confidence in. That's what we keep perfecting.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether an election should be used to grant/extend name suppression, he gives a generic justice-confidence line without answering.

forthrightness.statement: That member is like the arsonist that lit the fire and now criticises the fire brigade for putting it out, right? … He put the economy into recession and the consequence was unemployment. If he cared about working people, he would have managed the economy well, but he didn't.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what responsibility he takes for 13,000 lost construction jobs, he redirects blame to Labour rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Ha, ha! Oh my goodness! What I'd just say to that member is we know that it's a tough time for New Zealanders. … thank you, Labour! Thank you, Labour, for running the economy into the ditch!
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about rising liquidations across sectors, he acknowledges hardship but answers with blame rather than the figures.

forthrightness.statement: Firstly, he's not the chief executive; he's left. Secondly, he is right. The register is imperfect … There are people in housing need who aren't on the register … I'm not pretending that it's a perfect measure of housing need, but it's what we have.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes the challenging point (the register understates need) rather than dodging it.

forthrightness.statement: Well, once again, the member has his facts wrong; it seems to be a trend. We've already started work on the visa, and I look to announce that visa later this year.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the parent visa is delayed, she partly answers (work started, announcement later this year) but doesn't give a firm start date.

forthrightness.statement: I think what's important is that we actually are expanding access for 10,000 more kids, and the money saved is actually going into delivering better resources in education and healthcare.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the funding cut reduced lunch quality, he pivots to expanded access and savings without addressing quality.

forthrightness.statement: Well I'm more worried about which children are missing out on those lunches that you've nicked them from.
forthrightness.explanation: Wholly evades the question about lunches ending up in landfill.

forthrightness.statement: I had a series of engagements on the 5th, including with Ngāi Tahu leadership, to discuss how we work together to advance the interests of Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he didn't attend the Government pōwhiri at Waitangi and travel to Ōnuku like colleagues, he cites other engagements but doesn't directly explain the choice.

divination.statement: Infometrics has estimated that by the end of this year, households will have another $45 million to spend every week due to lower mortgage interest costs.
divination.explanation: A cited prediction about year-end household spending capacity; plausible given falling rates but dependent on rate paths and behaviour.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I often agree with myself. … in Budget 2024, we allocated $140 million to fund 1,500 new places to June 2027. Kāinga Ora will also be delivering an additional 2,650 housing places to June 2026.
authenticity.explanation: Affirms consistency with his own 2022 statement ('I often agree with myself') and backs it with funded commitments.

authenticity.statement: Firstly, he's not the chief executive; he's left. Secondly, he is right. The register is imperfect … There are people in housing need who aren't on the register … I'm not pretending that it's a perfect measure of housing need, but it's what we have.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges limits of his own headline metric, consistent rather than spin.

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced that $200 million in funding will be used to accelerate the delivery of 400 affordable rentals by Māori housing providers in areas of high need.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure ($200m), a concrete output (400 rentals), and a mechanism (Māori housing providers).

specificity.statement: Since coming into administration in November 2023, including this recent announcement, this Government has enabled the delivery of around a thousand homes for whānau to be built across the country through the Māori housing programme.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and a programme, though 'around a thousand' and 'enabled...to be built' hedge on actual completion.

specificity.statement: These 1,000 homes are intended to be delivered by Māori housing providers by end of June 2027. In terms of where: the developments are focused but not exclusive to high-needs priority rohe against the backdrop of severe housing deprivation and acute shortage of quality affordable rental homes. Priority regions include Te Tai Tokerau, Te Tairāwhiti, and the mighty Waikato.
specificity.explanation: Provides a timeframe and named priority regions, though the 'focused but not exclusive' caveat softens the 'where'.

specificity.statement: We know from the 2021 housing economic survey that around half of Māori households spend more than 30 percent of their disposable income on housing costs and more than a third spend more than 50 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the data source and gives concrete percentages.

specificity.statement: We know, for example, that in one region alone, very close to this House, there are over 600 vacancies—600 vacancies.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (600 vacancies) but leaves the region unnamed ('very close to this House').

specificity.statement: In 2017, if you turned up in an emergency department (ED), 90 percent of people were being seen within six hours. When the last Government left office, when we started recording again, it had dropped below 70 percent.
specificity.explanation: Concrete before/after percentages against a named target and timeframe.

specificity.statement: When it came to elective surgeries, those critically important planned surgeries... when we left office in 2017, 97.3 percent of New Zealanders were getting elective surgeries within four months. When they left office, it had dropped to 62 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages (97.3% vs 62%) with a defined threshold (four months).

specificity.statement: So what have we done? We’ve invested another $16.68 billion additional into health services. We’ve hired thousands more nurses.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure ($16.68b) and a workforce claim, though 'thousands more nurses' is looser.

specificity.statement: Because we have a workforce that is stressed, we cannot turn our back on what our nurses and what our unions are telling us. They are telling us very clearly they need to be resourced better. We need a dollar into the health system that genuinely funds a public health sector.
specificity.explanation: Direction (better resourcing/funding) without amounts, mechanisms, or targets.

specificity.statement: One obviously very dear to my heart is Pharmac and the massive fiscal cliff that was left in Pharmac, which would have seen medicines—many of them cancer medicines—not continue to be funded. Again, this Government had to come in and clean up that mess.
specificity.explanation: Names Pharmac and the funding-cliff issue but gives no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: There had not been a change in the capitation model for over 20 years. They were already stretched; their business models were already breaking.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe (over 20 years) tied to a named mechanism (capitation model).

specificity.statement: We have, throughout this Parliament, put an additional $16.8 billion into the health system, into the front line, where it’s most important.
specificity.explanation: Cites the headline figure but attributes it broadly 'into the front line' without breakdown.

specificity.statement: It has taken that forensic work by Dr Verrall... to be able to show that while the Government is saying it’s funding health, actually, in all the regions, the funding has been dropped by 6 to 14 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete range (6–14%) and scope (all regions), though without the underlying source detail.

specificity.statement: There are 650 mental health vacancies; 130 of those are psychiatrists. The Wairarapa doesn’t have a single resident psychiatrist, and yet it has New Zealand’s highest suicide rate.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (650 vacancies, 130 psychiatrists) plus a named region and a concrete claim.

specificity.statement: The people in Dunedin: 35,000 people had to march to get the Dunedin Hospital. It still doesn’t have pathology.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure (35,000 marchers) and a specific deficiency (no pathology in the building).

specificity.statement: it was that Government that spent $1.9 billion that no one could point to where it went to in mental health, and the Auditor-General said it made no material improvement; so did the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission.

charisma.explanation: Dismissive and alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: this country has never seen such a shambolic and incompetent and divisive Government.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing.

charisma.statement: Well, thankfully the fanciful and far-fetched fiction flowing forth from the former Minister Jan Tinetti is finished.
charisma.explanation: Scores a point with his own side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: All of these things that we hear from the other side are very important, and indeed they are, and we agree with that, but, actually, you cannot fund them without a strong economy
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the other side's priorities as valid before pivoting — a partial bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: There's a lot of negativity on that side of the House—a lot of "no". It's time to be positive. It's time to say, "yes".
charisma.explanation: Upbeat tone but framed as a partisan contrast against "that side" rather than reaching across.

divination.statement: When you do not put the health and safety of young people at the centre, there will be catastrophic consequences. That's not saying that that's a "maybe"; that is a "will be".
divination.explanation: Predicts catastrophic outcomes from ECE deregulation with stated certainty; directionally arguable but the absolute "will be" overstates confidence, timeframe unspecified.

divination.statement: We're committed to extending the Waikato Expressway. The plan is to go all the way through to Tauranga; four lanes … we're hoping to be turning dirt on that next year.
divination.explanation: "Turning dirt next year" is a forecast of a large project's start; NZ RoNS timelines frequently slip.

divination.statement: Recent forecasts actually show that the New Zealand apple industry is about to hit $1 billion for the very first time, and against the odds, following the cyclone.
divination.explanation: A near-term forecast of the apple sector reaching $1b in exports; plausible and directionally supported but not yet realised.

divination.statement: $3 million for the Tukituki water storage scheme. This has the potential to provide over 22,000 hectares of irrigation and environmental flows … forecasting up to $300 million of GDP impact, and create over 3,000 jobs.
divination.explanation: The $300m GDP and 3,000-job projections are optimistic "potential" forecasts contingent on the scheme proceeding.

strength.statement: We're committed to extending the Waikato Expressway. The plan is to go all the way through to Tauranga; four lanes … we're hoping to be turning dirt on that next year.
strength.explanation: A stated commitment still at the planning stage — announcement, not yet delivery.

strength.statement: The Telephone Road intersection a great example of that. Simeon Brown, the transport Minister at the time, agreed that we needed to reopen that intersection and it's going to happen.
strength.explanation: A decision to reopen is confirmed but delivery ("going to happen") is still pending.

strength.statement: We have new agreements with the United Arab Emirates, with the Gulf Cooperation Council as well … Ninety-nine percent of goods are going in tariff-free, once that's up and running
strength.explanation: Concluded trade agreements are a tangible deliverable, though ratification/implementation was still pending.

strength.statement: $3 million for the Tukituki water storage scheme. This has the potential to provide over 22,000 hectares of irrigation and environmental flows … forecasting up to $300 million of GDP impact, and create over 3,000 jobs.
strength.explanation: Funding support is announced, but the scheme's benefits are prospective, not delivered.

strength.statement: the four-laning of the Hawke's Bay Expressway. This is the first road of national significance to start, and it has actually started. We've got shovels in the ground. We've got diggers on site. We've got hard hats.
strength.explanation: Points to construction actually underway rather than merely announced — demonstrable follow-through, if verifiable.

strength.statement: he announced over $60 million into healthcare in Hawke's Bay: a new radiology department, a new cancer treatment machine.
strength.explanation: An announcement of funding — commitment stated but delivery not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Labour had talked about that cancer treatment machine for a very long time but never actually delivered. Well, we are delivering
strength.explanation: Claims delivery in progress contrasted with prior non-delivery; the machine was announced/funded but not yet installed, so it is delivery-in-train rather than completed.

strength.statement: just simple policies that have been introduced, like banning cell phones in schools … teachers and principals, who say, "We're actually seeing the students engaging. They're actually learning, and they're actually talking to each other."
strength.explanation: A specific policy actually implemented, with follow-through claimed.

strength.statement: we are putting those speed limits back up to 100 … State Highway 5 between Napier and Taupō, but also State Highway 51 between Clive and Napier obviously going back up to 100
strength.explanation: A concrete, named policy action being implemented.

strength.statement: in Hawke's Bay, we have one of the largest populations of gangs in the country. I've been talking to police in the region and they're just so happy that they've now got this tool kit where they can crack down on the gangs. They have the ability to be able to stop gangs from consorting. They can actually do something when they're wearing gang patches.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted gang legislation (patch ban, consorting powers) now in force — a delivered policy.

strength.statement: We delivered tax relief, putting more money in the back pockets of hard-working families—the first time in 14 years Kiwis felt a difference in their household budgets.
strength.explanation: Tax relief was actually enacted (July 2024 threshold changes), so a stated commitment was delivered.

strength.statement: In just the first 15 days of this year, nearly 22,000 FamilyBoost claims were paid, providing immediate financial relief for parents.
strength.explanation: Points to an implemented policy actually paying out, but modest and partial delivery against the original promise.

strength.statement: We are going to add another 3,000 megawatts of new renewable energy capacity, boosting New Zealand’s electricity generation by almost 30 percent, removing regulations and making it easier to build.
strength.explanation: Stated future intent ('going to add'); announcement not yet delivered.

strength.statement: As part of that policy, the first two new bills were passed in August, providing councils with the certainty and clarity of a pathway to develop their water service delivery plans.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislation actually enacted, with follow-through described.

strength.statement: Let me start with fast track, which is traceable back to the coalition agreement agreed to between my leader and the leader of the National Party: 149 projects.
strength.explanation: Fast-track legislation was actually passed and projects listed; real delivery claimed.

strength.statement: The party I belong to will never ever agree to buying Congo carbon credits.
strength.explanation: A stance/commitment to block a policy, not a delivered outcome.

strength.statement: In the event that they cannot deliver, I look forward, along with my colleagues, to ramming changes through to finally tame the beast that represents the unaccountable forces inside our electricity sector.
strength.explanation: Conditional future threat of reform, not a delivered action.

strength.statement: I’m proud that we’ve started to make some inroads on that by getting inflation under control.
strength.explanation: Claims partial progress ('started to make some inroads'), appropriately hedged rather than overclaiming delivery.

strength.statement: Over the last couple of weeks, we’ve seen the launch of the first of the charter schools.
strength.explanation: A concrete policy actually implemented, with the government responsible.

strength.statement: We’ve brought back interest deductibility for residential rental properties, which will ease the pressure on rents.
strength.explanation: Interest deductibility was actually restored; a delivered policy.

strength.statement: The restoration of 90-day trials, the repeal of the so-called fair pay agreements, consultation and work being under way on the Holidays Act, and a nationwide roadshow for improvements to health and safety law, which is being led by our wonderful Minister Brooke van Velden.
strength.explanation: Mixes delivered actions (90-day trials restored, fair pay agreements repealed) with in-progress work; genuine follow-through on several.

strength.statement: With ACT in Government, we have introduced legislation to improve recognition of products from overseas so that buildings can be built efficiently, effectively, and at a more affordable price.
strength.explanation: Legislation introduced, but introduction is not yet delivery/implementation.

strength.statement: The introduction of pet bonds allows for tenants to have their animal companion with them without being a burden on their landlord.
strength.explanation: A concrete tenancy reform actually legislated, described accurately.

veracity.statement: We delivered tax relief, putting more money in the back pockets of hard-working families—the first time in 14 years Kiwis felt a difference in their household budgets.
veracity.explanation: Tax cuts were delivered (true), but 'first time in 14 years Kiwis felt a difference' is a rhetorical claim that overstates and is not really verifiable.

veracity.statement: In just the first 15 days of this year, nearly 22,000 FamilyBoost claims were paid, providing immediate financial relief for parents.
veracity.explanation: Claims-paid figure is plausible, though FamilyBoost uptake overall fell well short of projections.

veracity.statement: We have seen inflation come down, an encouraging step in terms of us getting economic stability back.
veracity.explanation: Inflation did fall back within the RBNZ target band over 2024; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: As part of that policy, the first two new bills were passed in August, providing councils with the certainty and clarity of a pathway to develop their water service delivery plans.
veracity.explanation: Local Water Done Well legislation was passed in 2024; accurate.

veracity.statement: We’ve lost over 10,000 jobs in the public sector, which that side of the House seems to want to celebrate.
veracity.explanation: Public sector job reductions in the thousands are broadly supported; the '10,000' figure is in the plausible range though rounded up.

veracity.statement: There have been 13,000 jobs lost in building and construction.
veracity.explanation: Construction employment fell substantially over 2024; figure is plausible and roughly consistent with reported data.

veracity.statement: We’re losing record numbers of New Zealanders going overseas because that side of the House have not taken care of what is fundamentally important to New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Net departures of NZ citizens did hit record highs in 2024 (true); the causal attribution to the government is contestable.

veracity.statement: They are struggling with their rents, despite a promise from that Government that if they gave landlords a tax cut of over $2 billion, then that would help with the cost of rent for New Zealanders. Well, it hasn’t helped, and rent continues to go up.
veracity.explanation: Rents did continue rising through 2024 and interest deductibility is a multi-billion-dollar cost; broadly accurate though the '$2 billion' figure and framing are debatable.

veracity.statement: He did not show up to Waitangi for Waitangi Day. Why did he not show up? Because he did not want to face the criticism that was going to come his way.
veracity.explanation: The factual claim that Luxon did not attend Waitangi is accurate; the imputed motive is speculation.

veracity.statement: Let me start with fast track, which is traceable back to the coalition agreement agreed to between my leader and the leader of the National Party: 149 projects.
veracity.explanation: The fast-track regime listing 149 projects is accurate.

veracity.statement: I may make a few remarks about a dolphin that doesn’t exist, otherwise known as the Māui dolphin. It was a contrivance, a fiction, put together by some underemployed academic down in the South Island.
veracity.explanation: The Māui dolphin is a real, critically endangered subspecies; the claim that it 'doesn't exist' is demonstrably false.

veracity.statement: In relation to water storage, it was extraordinary to see the Labour Party member gushing enthusiastically about Waimea. They voted against the Waimea dam, and it took New Zealand First to rescue the scheme.
veracity.explanation: Claims about Labour's Waimea vote and NZ First's role are specific and checkable, plausibly accurate but presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: I had a little bit of a scour through the Prime Minister’s statement... and I failed to find any mention of Te Tiriti in any part of his statement.
veracity.explanation: A directly checkable claim about the content of the PM's statement; plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: He knows like I do that the degradation that we have seen just in the last couple of generations has actually meant that it’s hard to find mullet and flounder—flounder that I grew up enjoying in the Hokianga.
veracity.explanation: Anecdotal but consistent with documented declines in inshore fisheries; personal-observation claim, hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: Growth is forecast to reach 2.1 percent of GDP this year, according to Treasury, and businesses will be excited about that.
veracity.explanation: Cites a Treasury forecast figure; accurate as an attributed forecast (though forecasts carry uncertainty).

veracity.statement: Compared to this time last year, look at where we are now. We’ve got falling interest rates, lower inflation.
veracity.explanation: Interest rates were falling and inflation lower than a year earlier; broadly accurate for early 2025.

veracity.statement: With inflation now under control and interest rates coming down, and wages rising faster than inflation, we expect the unemployment rate to start to decrease. It has been increasing.
veracity.explanation: Wages rising faster than inflation and unemployment increasing were broadly true late 2024; the forward claim is a projection.

veracity.statement: This has got the potential for over 6,000 houses, to house over 15,000 people. Twenty years, the developers have been wanting to go on this, and here we are stuck with some of the most expensive housing in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The housing-capacity and delay figures are plausible; 'most expensive housing in NZ' is a defensible characterisation of Tauranga's affordability.

veracity.statement: I’m proud that we’ve started to make some inroads on that by getting inflation under control.
veracity.explanation: Inflation had fallen back into the target band; 'under control' is broadly accurate though inflation is not solely a government lever.

veracity.statement: Over the last couple of weeks, we’ve seen the launch of the first of the charter schools.
veracity.explanation: The first charter schools were being launched in early 2025; accurate.

specificity.statement: We delivered tax relief, putting more money in the back pockets of hard-working families—the first time in 14 years Kiwis felt a difference in their household budgets.
specificity.explanation: References a 14-year timeframe but gives no dollar figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: In just the first 15 days of this year, nearly 22,000 FamilyBoost claims were paid, providing immediate financial relief for parents.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure (22,000 claims) and precise timeframe (first 15 days).

specificity.statement: We are going to add another 3,000 megawatts of new renewable energy capacity, boosting New Zealand’s electricity generation by almost 30 percent, removing regulations and making it easier to build.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures (3,000 MW, ~30% boost) and the mechanism (deregulation, fast track).

specificity.statement: Our plan shows that we can grow the economy and deliver our climate commitments—effective policies that can lay the foundation to meet net zero targets as early as 2044.
specificity.explanation: Gives a date (2044) but no concrete mechanism for how it is reached.

specificity.statement: As part of that policy, the first two new bills were passed in August, providing councils with the certainty and clarity of a pathway to develop their water service delivery plans.
specificity.explanation: Names the bills and timing (August) but not the substantive content.

specificity.statement: We’re not just talking about growth; we’re going to deliver it.
specificity.explanation: Slogan with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We’ve lost over 10,000 jobs in the public sector, which that side of the House seems to want to celebrate.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number for the claim.

specificity.statement: There have been 13,000 jobs lost in building and construction.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure tied to a named sector.

specificity.statement: They are struggling with their rents, despite a promise from that Government that if they gave landlords a tax cut of over $2 billion, then that would help with the cost of rent for New Zealanders. Well, it hasn’t helped, and rent continues to go up.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a dollar magnitude and a concrete claim (rents up).

specificity.statement: Kiwis want to be able to feed their whānau—a pretty simple ask. They want to be able to pay for the roof over their heads, they want to have a job... and they want to live in communities that support and care for each other.
specificity.explanation: General values (jobs, housing, community) with no policy or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Let me start with fast track, which is traceable back to the coalition agreement agreed to between my leader and the leader of the National Party: 149 projects.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count (149 projects) and provenance (coalition agreement).

specificity.statement: Coal will be available and used in New Zealand well towards 2050, and if it comes to pass that from time to time we can create wood pellets without a Crown subsidy and we can move on from coal, let the market make that choice.
specificity.explanation: Gives a horizon (2050) but no volumes or mechanism.

specificity.statement: He knows like I do that the degradation that we have seen just in the last couple of generations has actually meant that it’s hard to find mullet and flounder—flounder that I grew up enjoying in the Hokianga.
specificity.explanation: Names a place and species but no measures or data.

specificity.statement: How about a culture of yes to protecting our taiao? How about a culture of yes to Te Tiriti bringing us together? How about a culture of yes to ending poverty and making sure our tamariki in schools, for example, get quality, healthy, and on-time lunches?
specificity.explanation: Mostly aspirational, with the school-lunches example providing a single concrete anchor.

specificity.statement: Growth is forecast to reach 2.1 percent of GDP this year, according to Treasury, and businesses will be excited about that.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure with a named source.

specificity.statement: This has got the potential for over 6,000 houses, to house over 15,000 people. Twenty years, the developers have been wanting to go on this, and here we are stuck with some of the most expensive housing in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (6,000 houses, 15,000 people, 20 years) about the Te Tumu development.

specificity.statement: Over the last couple of weeks, we’ve seen the launch of the first of the charter schools.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and rough timing but no numbers or detail.

specificity.statement: We really do want this to be a country of hope, a country where people do want to bring up their children and, actually, a place where Kiwis can live and thrive as they want.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: We’ve brought back interest deductibility for residential rental properties, which will ease the pressure on rents.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete policy but not the size or timing of any rent effect.

specificity.statement: The restoration of 90-day trials, the repeal of the so-called fair pay agreements, consultation and work being under way on the Holidays Act, and a nationwide roadshow for improvements to health and safety law, which is being led by our wonderful Minister Brooke van Velden.
specificity.explanation: Lists named, concrete policy actions.

specificity.statement: With ACT in Government, we have introduced legislation to improve recognition of products from overseas so that buildings can be built efficiently, effectively, and at a more affordable price.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area but no product details, thresholds, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: The introduction of pet bonds allows for tenants to have their animal companion with them without being a burden on their landlord.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (pet bonds) but not amounts or timing.

divination.statement: We are going to add another 3,000 megawatts of new renewable energy capacity, boosting New Zealand’s electricity generation by almost 30 percent, removing regulations and making it easier to build.
divination.explanation: A capacity target rather than an assured outcome; plausible but delivery uncertain, no clear timeframe.

divination.statement: Our plan shows that we can grow the economy and deliver our climate commitments—effective policies that can lay the foundation to meet net zero targets as early as 2044.
divination.explanation: A ~20-year prediction of meeting net zero by 2044; optimistic and dependent on unspecified future policy.

divination.statement: Coal will be available and used in New Zealand well towards 2050, and if it comes to pass that from time to time we can create wood pellets without a Crown subsidy and we can move on from coal, let the market make that choice.
divination.explanation: Prediction that coal use continues toward 2050; plausible given current industrial reliance but uncertain against decarbonisation pressure.

divination.statement: I want to say to Māoridom as well that the bill which you are jumping up and down over will never pass.
divination.explanation: Prediction the Treaty Principles Bill will not pass; well supported since National and NZ First had already signalled they would not back it past select committee.

divination.statement: Growth is forecast to reach 2.1 percent of GDP this year, according to Treasury, and businesses will be excited about that.
divination.explanation: A near-term growth forecast; plausible and consensus-based but uncertain.

divination.statement: With inflation now under control and interest rates coming down, and wages rising faster than inflation, we expect the unemployment rate to start to decrease. It has been increasing.
divination.explanation: Predicts unemployment will start falling; optimistic given it was still rising, with lagged labour-market effects making timing uncertain.

divination.statement: We’ve brought back interest deductibility for residential rental properties, which will ease the pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Predicts it 'will ease the pressure on rents'; contestable, as rents continued rising and the link is disputed.

divination.statement: When the crash inevitably comes—because it will come—the result lies on the workers, the tradies, and the families who carry the pain for the profligacy.
divination.explanation: Predicts an inevitable future 'crash' with no timeframe; too generic to be strongly grounded, framed as a certainty.

charisma.statement: We’re not just talking about growth; we’re going to deliver it.
charisma.explanation: Rallying line aimed at the government's own side, not persuasion across the aisle.

charisma.statement: What we’ve seen is divisiveness caused mostly as part of their absolute attack on Māori, whether it be the Treaty principles bill or the undermining of te reo Māori, even the undermining of Māori names for Public Service agencies.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that indicts the other side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: Kiwis want to be able to feed their whānau—a pretty simple ask. They want to be able to pay for the roof over their heads, they want to have a job... and they want to live in communities that support and care for each other.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared, universal aspirations, mildly unifying, though framed to contrast with the government.

charisma.statement: Well, there’ll be no more clutter, no more ideological bum fluff from my opposition—no, straight down the guts.
charisma.explanation: Combative crowd-pleaser that demeans the other side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: I firstly must acknowledge the aroha from across the House that I was very privileged to receive in noting my return back to Parliament after some time away on medical treatment. It is a really human and beautiful thing to be able to share collectively when we are watching another member of this House going through tough times.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, cross-party acknowledgement that draws the whole House together.

charisma.statement: We have not once seen polluted rivers end poverty. We have not once seen destroyed oceans end homelessness. We have not once seen ruined soils uplift everyone’s lives.
charisma.explanation: Powerful for supporters but framed against the government rather than persuading it.

charisma.statement: How about a culture of yes to protecting our taiao? How about a culture of yes to Te Tiriti bringing us together? How about a culture of yes to ending poverty and making sure our tamariki in schools, for example, get quality, healthy, and on-time lunches?
charisma.explanation: Language of 'bringing us together' and yes-framing is inclusive in tone, though delivered as a partisan counter-vision.

charisma.statement: We really do want this to be a country of hope, a country where people do want to bring up their children and, actually, a place where Kiwis can live and thrive as they want.
charisma.explanation: Warm, aspirational tone but aimed at articulating the party's own vision rather than reaching across the aisle.

civility.statement: We’ve lost over 10,000 jobs in the public sector, which that side of the House seems to want to celebrate.
civility.explanation: The 'seems to want to celebrate' imputes motive, a mild strawman on top of legitimate criticism.

civility.statement: What we’ve seen is divisiveness caused mostly as part of their absolute attack on Māori, whether it be the Treaty principles bill or the undermining of te reo Māori, even the undermining of Māori names for Public Service agencies.
civility.explanation: 'Absolute attack on Māori' is a sweeping, characterisation-heavy accusation rather than measured critique.

civility.statement: He did not show up to Waitangi for Waitangi Day. Why did he not show up? Because he did not want to face the criticism that was going to come his way.
civility.explanation: Factual point paired with an attack on the PM's courage/motives rather than substance.

civility.statement: The most recent example being with David Seymour and his ill-advised letter to support Mr Polkinghorne and his contradictory position compared to Prime Minister Luxon.
civility.explanation: Criticism of a named minister's conduct; pointed ('ill-advised') but tied to a specific action rather than pure insult.

civility.statement: Well, there’ll be no more clutter, no more ideological bum fluff from my opposition—no, straight down the guts.
civility.explanation: Dismissive, mocking language ('bum fluff') aimed at opponents rather than their arguments.

civility.statement: We won’t have these grandees, self-appointed, trying to block development, squash initiative, ruin entrepreneurialism, and, quite frankly, imperil regional fiscal solvency.
civility.explanation: Belittles opponents ('grandees') rather than engaging their case.

civility.statement: I may make a few remarks about a dolphin that doesn’t exist, otherwise known as the Māui dolphin. It was a contrivance, a fiction, put together by some underemployed academic down in the South Island.
civility.explanation: Personal denigration of scientists rather than argument.

civility.statement: In the event that they cannot deliver, I look forward, along with my colleagues, to ramming changes through to finally tame the beast that represents the unaccountable forces inside our electricity sector.
civility.explanation: Aggressive 'ramming through' framing, combative toward the sector.

civility.statement: I want to say to Māoridom as well that the bill which you are jumping up and down over will never pass.
civility.explanation: 'Jumping up and down' is dismissive of Māori concerns while making a substantive point.

civility.statement: Stop believing in the shrill, green rhetoric that, somehow, Māori can solve the problems of China, Russia, and India with some mātauranga Māori and stop them from generating coal-fired power stations.
civility.explanation: 'Shrill' and mocking framing rather than engagement.

civility.statement: I firstly must acknowledge the aroha from across the House that I was very privileged to receive in noting my return back to Parliament after some time away on medical treatment. It is a really human and beautiful thing to be able to share collectively when we are watching another member of this House going through tough times.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful, explicitly praises goodwill from opponents.

civility.statement: My uncle from the North, Minister Jones, has just finished minimising the power of community by trying to say that it’s only a few voices trying to protect our environment... How dare he? I heard you; I heard those people.
civility.explanation: A direct rebuke of Jones but engages his actual claim (that opposition is 'only a few voices') rather than attacking him personally.

civility.statement: That Government, that Minister over—I’m not going to call him out on it. I won’t; I’d feel a bit mean doing that. The previous Government had the opportunity to deal with that. They had the opportunity and they squandered it.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous government's record and even declines to name-and-shame, though 'squandered it' is a pointed characterisation.

civility.statement: You can’t turn around the mismanagement—the economic mismanagement—of the last few years in a matter of days or months; it is going to take time.
civility.explanation: Blames the previous government ('mismanagement') but as a policy/record critique rather than personal attack.

rigor.statement: We’re losing record numbers of New Zealanders going overseas because that side of the House have not taken care of what is fundamentally important to New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation between emigration and government policy without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: What we’ve seen is divisiveness caused mostly as part of their absolute attack on Māori, whether it be the Treaty principles bill or the undermining of te reo Māori, even the undermining of Māori names for Public Service agencies.
rigor.explanation: Cites specific examples (Treaty principles bill, te reo, agency names) but frames them as a single intentional 'attack' without argument.

rigor.statement: We won’t have these grandees, self-appointed, trying to block development, squash initiative, ruin entrepreneurialism, and, quite frankly, imperil regional fiscal solvency.
rigor.explanation: Caricatures opponents as wanting to 'ruin' the economy — a strawman with no evidence.

rigor.statement: I may make a few remarks about a dolphin that doesn’t exist, otherwise known as the Māui dolphin. It was a contrivance, a fiction, put together by some underemployed academic down in the South Island.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem ('underemployed academic') substituted for any evidence.

rigor.statement: Stop believing in the shrill, green rhetoric that, somehow, Māori can solve the problems of China, Russia, and India with some mātauranga Māori and stop them from generating coal-fired power stations.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — no one claims mātauranga Māori will stop foreign coal plants; the position is caricatured to dismiss it.

rigor.statement: We have not once seen polluted rivers end poverty. We have not once seen destroyed oceans end homelessness. We have not once seen ruined soils uplift everyone’s lives.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorically effective and directionally reasonable, but relies on emotive parallelism rather than evidence linking extraction to poverty outcomes.

rigor.statement: You can’t turn around the mismanagement—the economic mismanagement—of the last few years in a matter of days or months; it is going to take time.
rigor.explanation: Asserts prior 'mismanagement' as premise without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: The basic law of supply and demand says that when supply is low and prices are driven up, you’ll get more supply. Interest deductibility encourages investment and development so that more houses can be built for the rental stock.
rigor.explanation: Applies a standard economic mechanism with a coherent chain, but leans on textbook theory without evidence that this policy actually increased rental supply.

authenticity.statement: The party I belong to will never ever agree to buying Congo carbon credits.
authenticity.explanation: A firm stated position consistent with NZ First's known opposition to offshore carbon purchasing; no visible contradiction but unverified in-text.

civility.statement: This House has no confidence in this coalition Government because under its incompetent, arrogant, shambolic, and divisive leadership, New Zealand is going backwards, Kiwis are losing their jobs, record numbers are leaving the country, and their priorities are wrong and out of touch.
civility.explanation: String of character-based insults ('incompetent, arrogant, shambolic') rather than engagement with specific policy substance.

civility.statement: We know Kiwis are doing it tough. When they’re walking through our offices, they’re doing it tough, but instead, all we see from this Government is continual name-calling, a lowest common denominator approach.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government's conduct critically but as a general 'name-calling' charge rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: It’s been 16 months. Where were you for the first 15 months?
civility.explanation: A pointed interjection questioning the member's diligence; a jab rather than an outright personal insult.

civility.statement: unlike the negative Nellies on the other side, I’m delighted to speak in favour of the Prime Minister’s statement
civility.explanation: 'Negative Nellies' is a mild dismissive label aimed at opponents rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: It’s really interesting, because some of the things that that member spoke about was absolutely at the heart of why growth is important. She spoke with passion about the people she represents, because what she wants to see is an improvement in the quality of their lives, of whānau, of hapū, of iwi—their ability to live in warm homes, to have stable jobs, and to put great kai on the table.
civility.explanation: Respectful, credits the opposing member's sincerity and the substance of her concerns.

civility.statement: I reflected on how if there was a university degree in saying no, the other side of the House would have PhDs in saying no... no to banning gang patches in public... no to making sure that repeat offenders are not given more than three chances to smash up shops; no to adjusting tax brackets... and no to removing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
civility.explanation: The 'Doctors of No' mockery is a rhetorical dig, though it is tethered to actual votes rather than pure insult.

civility.statement: and the “Minister of No” at the time—who criticised it for a long time—and who is now the leader of the Opposition, the Hon Chris Hipkins, then actually said, “Well, actually, we’re opening a road. I’ll go and open it, even though I opposed it all the way through.”... He used to call it a “holiday highway”. Actually, it’s now open.
civility.explanation: Charges an opponent with hypocrisy via the 'Minister of No' label; tied to a specific record but delivered as a jab.

civility.statement: I’d like to welcome the former member for Northland—who I wish had actually done her job last time and stood up for that road. It would have been great if she had, but never mind.
civility.explanation: Personal dig implying a named member (Willow-Jean Prime) failed to do her job, rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: This Government has had no growth. There is more growth on my face than this Government has had, and that’s a fact!
civility.explanation: A jokey hyperbolic line rather than a personal attack, but sensationalises rather than engages substance.

civility.statement: how about focusing on David Seymour’s behaviour when he interfered with a police prosecution and tried to get the police to stop investigating someone who was ultimately charged with murder.
civility.explanation: Serious personal accusation against a named member, contested on a point of order for misrepresenting the facts.

civility.statement: David Seymour seems to be running the country—running the country into the ground with his divisive and racist Treaty principles bill, with his surreptitious Regulatory Standards Bill, with the legislation that puts the Treaty second and puts himself first. This Government is a disgrace.
civility.explanation: Labels a member's bill 'racist' and calls the Government 'a disgrace' — characterisation and personal framing rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Anyone who thinks you can make a lunch and deliver it 90 kilometres for $3 really shouldn’t be purporting to be the economic geniuses that this Government are.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'economic geniuses' jab, but anchored to a concrete cost-versus-distance argument.

civility.statement: In an earlier contribution from the other side of the House, during this debate, the Green leader said no one is entitled to make a profit. Now, that’s an outrageous statement, and that is a statement which shows absolute poverty of consciousness—it’s conditioned thinking; it’s negative, constrictive thinking.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opponent's mindset ('poverty of consciousness', 'negative thinking') and likely paraphrases the Green leader unfavourably rather than engaging the actual argument.

charisma.statement: This House has no confidence in this coalition Government because under its incompetent, arrogant, shambolic, and divisive leadership, New Zealand is going backwards, Kiwis are losing their jobs, record numbers are leaving the country, and their priorities are wrong and out of touch.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing; rallies her own side, makes no attempt to persuade the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: These organisations, among others, are confident to grow. They can see that the economic tide is turning and they know that the future of our country, for the services everybody wants, lies in economic growth—not in handing out money. It takes hard decisions, fortitude... You don’t get growth by giving away money; you get it by providing opportunities for everybody.
charisma.explanation: Aspirational and confident but appeals to its own side's framing rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: It’s really interesting, because some of the things that that member spoke about was absolutely at the heart of why growth is important. She spoke with passion about the people she represents, because what she wants to see is an improvement in the quality of their lives, of whānau, of hapū, of iwi—their ability to live in warm homes, to have stable jobs, and to put great kai on the table.
charisma.explanation: Genuinely acknowledges an opponent's (Cushla Tangaere-Manuel's) passion and shared goals, seeking common ground before disagreeing on means.

charisma.statement: I reflected on how if there was a university degree in saying no, the other side of the House would have PhDs in saying no... no to banning gang patches in public... no to making sure that repeat offenders are not given more than three chances to smash up shops; no to adjusting tax brackets... and no to removing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
charisma.explanation: Effective partisan applause line that caricatures opponents rather than persuading them.

charisma.statement: One of the things they asked for: “Please, bring in that FamilyBoost”... “Please adjust the tax brackets like you’re saying you will. Please get rid of the Auckland fuel tax.” And I said, “I promise you: what I know is that we will be doing this.” I’m so happy, and relieved for them, that those are just a few of the changes that we’ve managed to make
charisma.explanation: Personal, relatable door-knock storytelling, though aimed at reinforcing her own side's narrative.

charisma.statement: David Seymour seems to be running the country—running the country into the ground with his divisive and racist Treaty principles bill, with his surreptitious Regulatory Standards Bill, with the legislation that puts the Treaty second and puts himself first. This Government is a disgrace.
charisma.explanation: Highly divisive; targets and demonises rather than building any cross-bench bridge.

charisma.statement: In spite of this Government’s attempts to dim the light, it shines bright in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti... they have the power to change this Government in just over a year and they’re just waiting.
charisma.explanation: Rousing for her own constituents but framed as opposition rather than cross-bench persuasion.

charisma.statement: the roots don’t cause the growth; it is the creation of a fertile soil in which you plant the seed to germinate, to grow, and to multiply itself again and again and again, so that what was originally one small seed becomes countless millions.
charisma.explanation: Vivid, positive imagery reframing the debate's 'roots' motif, but pitched to reinforce her side's 'abundance' framing.
