veracity.statement: How about we talk about that Minister of Finance and that one out of three National Party voters don’t believe can make this economy grow? How about we talk about that Minister of Finance where 50 percent of New Zealanders do not trust her to make this economy grow?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific poll-style figures on trust in the Finance Minister; plausible and consistent with reported polling of the period, but unsourced and hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: When the Prime Minister says that New Zealand has been in a recession for the last three years, well, let’s fact-check that. I did. I asked the Treasury chief economist, “Has New Zealand been in a recession for the past three years?” Well, actually, just for nine months in 2024.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate that NZ was not in continuous three-year recession; the technical recession fell in 2024, though 'just nine months' simplifies a more complex growth record.

veracity.statement: Again, it was the Labour Government that funded those 2,000 homes and continued the build, which is why we have 2,000 more homes.
veracity.explanation: Housing completions often reflect prior-government funding pipelines, so the claim is plausible; exact attribution of all 2,000 is contestable.

veracity.statement: Those unemployment numbers would actually be higher had 125,000 New Zealanders not left New Zealand for overseas. They’re going to Australia.
veracity.explanation: Net migration losses of this magnitude are broadly consistent with 2024 departure figures, though '125,000 to Australia' conflates gross departures with net loss.

veracity.statement: When this Government came in, within their 100-day plan, they removed the remit for maximum sustainable employment for the Reserve Bank... Yet in Australia, there is lower unemployment, their inflation levels are better, and 125,000 Kiwis, a large portion of them, are going to Australia because they know there are jobs. Yet the Reserve Bank of Australia, guess what they have which this Government removed in the first 100 days!
veracity.explanation: The core factual claim — removal of the Reserve Bank's maximum-sustainable-employment remit early in the term — is accurate.

veracity.statement: which is why one in two Pacific children is going hungry, which is why one in 10 Pacific people does not have a job. All these figures are evidence. There is data about it
veracity.explanation: 'One in two Pacific children going hungry' likely overstates food-insecurity survey data; Pacific unemployment near 10% is closer to reported figures.

veracity.statement: This project has not only created jobs but it also positions the Waitaki electorate as a leader in renewable energy creation.
veracity.explanation: The hydro scheme exists and generates renewable power, but the 'leader' framing and job claims are unquantified.

veracity.statement: So far, we’ve done fast track, 149 projects on the list; inflation’s down; interest rates are down; we have stopped wasteful spending because taxpayers expect better outcomes for their money; we’ve done the Resource Management Act (RMA) reform first tranche... and we’ve dealt with ram raids, reducing those down significantly.
veracity.explanation: Inflation and interest rates did fall over 2024; '149 projects' and 'ram raids down significantly' are broadly supportable, though some claims are selectively framed.

veracity.statement: In my answer to oral question No. 5 today in the House, I was so excited about the 33,000 people that exited the jobseeker benefit into jobs that I said it was 29 percent more than the same period in 2023. It was actually 22 percent.
veracity.explanation: Proactively replaces an inaccurate figure (29%) with the correct one (22%).

veracity.statement: With that figure that I gave before—33,000 job seekers in the six months to December who exited into a job in this challenging labour market—is an extraordinary result. It didn’t come by accident; it came by very deliberate, targeted, integrated work to get an outcome—22 percent increase on the same period a year ago.
veracity.explanation: Uses the corrected figure and a defined period, consistent with the personal explanation given earlier.

veracity.statement: That’s why, despite knowing unemployment was due to go up—the same forecasts the previous Minister of Finance had; we had the same forecast projection in terms of the unemployment rate getting to 5.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Forecasts of unemployment rising toward ~5.1% were consistent with Treasury projections of the period; framing that Labour held 'the same' forecasts is defensible.

veracity.statement: It is absolutely appalling that we are sitting at 84 percent of the international visitor numbers that we had in 2019... since 2019, 30,000 jobs were lost in tourism and hospitality—30,000.
veracity.explanation: International arrivals recovering to roughly 80–85% of 2019 levels and sizeable tourism job losses since 2019 are consistent with reported data.

veracity.statement: and, do you know what? One percent—only 1 percent of our job seekers—aren’t complying with their obligations and under a sanction, which is a remarkable result
veracity.explanation: The 1% under-sanction figure is plausible but the 'remarkable result' framing may understate broader non-compliance not yet sanctioned.

veracity.statement: In the last election campaign, the number one issue in Northland was roads, well above cost of living. The irony being that, in 2017, we recognised that and we announced that we were going to put a four-lane highway all the way up to Whangārei, but guess what! Guess what happened when the other lot got in! They cancelled it.
veracity.explanation: The prior Government did pause/rescope Northland highway plans, so the core claim is broadly accurate, though 'cancelled' simplifies a more mixed record.

veracity.statement: The fact of the matter is that we handed over an economy that was growing—an economy that had 2.4 percent growth per annum. How much growth has this Government had? None. They have gone backwards for every single quarter.
veracity.explanation: The handover-growth figure is cherry-picked and 'backwards for every single quarter' overstates the sequence of GDP prints, which were mixed rather than uniformly negative.

veracity.statement: We have got 30,000 people more unemployed than when you took your job. That is enough people to fill Sky Stadium.
veracity.explanation: An increase of roughly 30,000 unemployed over the period is in the ballpark of reported figures; the stadium comparison is illustrative, not misleading.

veracity.statement: how about focusing on David Seymour’s behaviour when he interfered with a police prosecution and tried to get the police to stop investigating someone who was ultimately charged with murder.
veracity.explanation: The claim conflates cases and was challenged as inaccurate — Webb himself then reframed it, indicating the original assertion was misleading.

veracity.statement: Businesses like Kai Aio in Ruatōria, who will continue to deliver 500 school lunches between Tokomaru Bay and Wharekāhika, a 90-kilometre one-way trip, and inland 37 kilometres to Mata School, at a loss, subsidising it with other areas of this business.
veracity.explanation: Concrete local example; the geography is verifiable and the 'at a loss' claim is plausible for a rural provider, though unaudited.

veracity.statement: cutting initiatives like progressive procurement.”, an initiative that has been directly credited with opening and then keeping open roads in Tairāwhiti during and after Cyclone Gabrielle, mainly on State Highway 35
veracity.explanation: Progressive procurement did support local roading contractors post-Gabrielle; 'directly credited' is defensible but somewhat asserted.

veracity.statement: a region with, incidentally, the highest proportion of reo Māori speakers, a region where, in Tairāwhiti, Māori collectives hold 73 percent of the food and fibre sector asset base... In Kahungunu, 61 percent and in Wairarapa, a whopping 87 percent
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures consistent with regional Māori economy reporting; not independently sourced in the text but concrete and checkable.

veracity.statement: In Waitangi, the Treaty grounds have received $10.2 million. Now, not only is it the location of the first signing of the Treaty of Waitangi but also it’s our number one tourism destination: 160,000 people visited the Treaty grounds over the last year.
veracity.explanation: Funding and visitor figures are specific and plausible; the 'number one tourism destination' claim is a looser superlative.

veracity.statement: The wild-caught spat has a very limited ability to survive when it’s been transferred on to the mussel farms. Only about 5 percent of the wild-caught spat actually survive, so there is a project under way—alongside the University of Auckland, the Coromandel Marine Farmers’ Association... to develop an innovative nursery culture system
veracity.explanation: The low survival rate for wild mussel spat is broadly consistent with industry knowledge; presented as a factual basis for the project.

veracity.statement: Just very briefly, I’d like to also talk about sustainability being a bottom line for our fishing industry, which is an absolute success story in New Zealand. It generates about $1.6 billion in exports each year—we should be pleased about that. It employs 9,000 people directly.
veracity.explanation: Seafood export value near $1.6–2 billion and direct employment around 9,000 are consistent with sector figures of the period.

specificity.statement: How about we talk about that Minister of Finance and that one out of three National Party voters don’t believe can make this economy grow? How about we talk about that Minister of Finance where 50 percent of New Zealanders do not trust her to make this economy grow?
specificity.explanation: Attaches concrete proportions (one in three, 50 percent) rather than vague claims, though the underlying poll is unnamed.

specificity.statement: which is why one in two Pacific children is going hungry, which is why one in 10 Pacific people does not have a job. All these figures are evidence. There is data about it
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete ratios but does not cite the specific dataset or period behind them.

specificity.statement: Not only have we delivered legislation that will play a crucial role in progress, like the fast-track consenting Act and the Resource Management Act reforms, we are also ensuring that we have a Budget that will allow economic recovery to occur.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete Acts, though the 'economic recovery' claim remains general.

specificity.statement: It is under his stewardship that we have seen a focused drive not only towards economic growth but also towards enhancement of the services that a modern-day society demands, from healthcare—and, yes, this will include delivering Dunedin Hospital, which services not only Dunedin but a much wider area including the Waitaki electorate—to education, infrastructure, and digital connectivity.
specificity.explanation: Names Dunedin Hospital but lists other areas (education, infrastructure, connectivity) only as broad headings.

specificity.statement: This project has not only created jobs but it also positions the Waitaki electorate as a leader in renewable energy creation.
specificity.explanation: Refers to the Waitaki Hydro Scheme but supplies no figures on jobs created or capacity.

specificity.statement: So far, we’ve done fast track, 149 projects on the list; inflation’s down; interest rates are down; we have stopped wasteful spending because taxpayers expect better outcomes for their money; we’ve done the Resource Management Act (RMA) reform first tranche... and we’ve dealt with ram raids, reducing those down significantly.
specificity.explanation: Cites a project count and named reforms, though several items ('wasteful spending', 'significantly') lack figures.

specificity.statement: How good was it yesterday to see the news with the announcement of the reopening of the Juken sawmill, where an investor has stepped in, bought the mill, and is looking to put back 500 jobs into the Tairāwhiti community.
specificity.explanation: Names the mill, the location, and a concrete job figure (500).

specificity.statement: What about in Kawerau, where next month a large processor will celebrate a $20 million investment into switching a massive manufacturing and processing entity from natural gas to geothermal steam.
specificity.explanation: Gives location, timeframe (next month), dollar figure ($20 million), and the concrete nature of the switch.

specificity.statement: With that figure that I gave before—33,000 job seekers in the six months to December who exited into a job in this challenging labour market—is an extraordinary result. It didn’t come by accident; it came by very deliberate, targeted, integrated work to get an outcome—22 percent increase on the same period a year ago.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (33,000), timeframe (six months to December), and corrected comparison (22%).

specificity.statement: Often, the Opposition will kind of criticise me and my or our Government’s ambition to reduce the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by 2030. So, yes, the numbers have gone up and that is, unfortunately, the reality of a low-growth environment.
specificity.explanation: States a numeric target (50,000) with a deadline (2030).

specificity.statement: That’s why, despite knowing unemployment was due to go up—the same forecasts the previous Minister of Finance had; we had the same forecast projection in terms of the unemployment rate getting to 5.1 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific projected rate (5.1 percent).

specificity.statement: It is absolutely appalling that we are sitting at 84 percent of the international visitor numbers that we had in 2019... since 2019, 30,000 jobs were lost in tourism and hospitality—30,000.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete recovery percentage and a jobs-lost figure with a baseline year.

specificity.statement: and, do you know what? One percent—only 1 percent of our job seekers—aren’t complying with their obligations and under a sanction, which is a remarkable result
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise compliance figure (1 percent).

specificity.statement: I reflected on how if there was a university degree in saying no, the other side of the House would have PhDs in saying no... no to banning gang patches in public... no to making sure that repeat offenders are not given more than three chances to smash up shops; no to adjusting tax brackets... and no to removing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete policies the Opposition opposed (gang patches, tax brackets, fuel tax), giving the attack some substance.

specificity.statement: We’re saying yes—yes to FamilyBoost, which we have said; yes to a new school for 600 students in Flat Bush; and, in particular, the crème de la crème of yesses on this side of the House is yes to Mill Road—yes, that’s going to happen.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete deliverables (600-student Flat Bush school, Mill Road), though without dates or costs.

specificity.statement: In the last election campaign, the number one issue in Northland was roads, well above cost of living. The irony being that, in 2017, we recognised that and we announced that we were going to put a four-lane highway all the way up to Whangārei, but guess what! Guess what happened when the other lot got in! They cancelled it.
specificity.explanation: Gives a year and project (2017, four-lane to Whangārei) but not the segments or funding detail.

specificity.statement: The fact of the matter is that we handed over an economy that was growing—an economy that had 2.4 percent growth per annum. How much growth has this Government had? None. They have gone backwards for every single quarter.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete growth rate (2.4 percent per annum) as a comparison anchor.

specificity.statement: We have got 30,000 people more unemployed than when you took your job. That is enough people to fill Sky Stadium.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure with a relatable scale reference.

specificity.statement: Businesses like Kai Aio in Ruatōria, who will continue to deliver 500 school lunches between Tokomaru Bay and Wharekāhika, a 90-kilometre one-way trip, and inland 37 kilometres to Mata School, at a loss, subsidising it with other areas of this business.
specificity.explanation: Names the business, lunch count (500), and precise distances (90 km, 37 km) to illustrate the delivery burden.

specificity.statement: I was able to visit another home, land which just recently landed for a whānau with six children, one of many homes initiated and actually delivered by Labour. We understand that, when you have a roof over your head, the world is your oyster.
specificity.explanation: Gives a location and family detail but no figures on how many homes overall.

specificity.statement: a region with, incidentally, the highest proportion of reo Māori speakers, a region where, in Tairāwhiti, Māori collectives hold 73 percent of the food and fibre sector asset base... In Kahungunu, 61 percent and in Wairarapa, a whopping 87 percent
specificity.explanation: Supplies precise regional percentages of Māori asset ownership in the primary sector.

specificity.statement: We have been able, through our coalition negotiations, to develop the Regional Infrastructure Fund—also known as the RIF... We are able to, through Matua Jones, spread out that $1.2 billion across the regions.
specificity.explanation: Names the fund, its predecessor (PGF), and the concrete quantum ($1.2 billion).

specificity.statement: Flood resilience has been a really important part of the RIF, and $200 million has been set aside for various projects... 42 projects have been identified, $101 million there, and they’ll be co-partnered alongside their relevant local authorities... Stopbanks, pumping stations, groynes, and culverts—that is the really sensible, practical, and pragmatic solution
specificity.explanation: Provides dollar allocations ($200m, $101m), project count (42), and concrete infrastructure types (stopbanks, pumping stations, groynes, culverts).

specificity.statement: In Waitangi, the Treaty grounds have received $10.2 million. Now, not only is it the location of the first signing of the Treaty of Waitangi but also it’s our number one tourism destination: 160,000 people visited the Treaty grounds over the last year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise funding figure ($10.2m) and visitor number (160,000).

specificity.statement: I have some time left and I really want to talk about the blue economy... Our blue economy is an economy that can grow, and we can increase the sector to $3 billion by 2035.
specificity.explanation: States a target value ($3 billion) and date (2035).

specificity.statement: The wild-caught spat has a very limited ability to survive when it’s been transferred on to the mussel farms. Only about 5 percent of the wild-caught spat actually survive, so there is a project under way—alongside the University of Auckland, the Coromandel Marine Farmers’ Association... to develop an innovative nursery culture system
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete survival rate (~5%) and names the collaborating institutions and the project's aim.

specificity.statement: Just very briefly, I’d like to also talk about sustainability being a bottom line for our fishing industry, which is an absolute success story in New Zealand. It generates about $1.6 billion in exports each year—we should be pleased about that. It employs 9,000 people directly.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete export value and direct-employment figures.

rigor.statement: When the Prime Minister says that New Zealand has been in a recession for the last three years, well, let’s fact-check that. I did. I asked the Treasury chief economist, “Has New Zealand been in a recession for the past three years?” Well, actually, just for nine months in 2024.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a claim by appealing to a named authoritative source (Treasury chief economist) rather than assertion; conclusion follows from the cited evidence.

rigor.statement: Those unemployment numbers would actually be higher had 125,000 New Zealanders not left New Zealand for overseas. They’re going to Australia.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal point that emigration flatters the jobless rate, but presented without the labour-force mechanics that would firm it up.

rigor.statement: When this Government came in, within their 100-day plan, they removed the remit for maximum sustainable employment for the Reserve Bank... Yet in Australia, there is lower unemployment, their inflation levels are better, and 125,000 Kiwis, a large portion of them, are going to Australia because they know there are jobs. Yet the Reserve Bank of Australia, guess what they have which this Government removed in the first 100 days!
rigor.explanation: Factually correct that the employment mandate was removed and that the RBA retains one, but the implied causation between mandate and unemployment gap is asserted, not demonstrated.

rigor.statement: We know Kiwis are doing it tough. When they’re walking through our offices, they’re doing it tough, but instead, all we see from this Government is continual name-calling, a lowest common denominator approach.
rigor.explanation: Leans on anecdote (people in her office) and characterisation rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: These organisations, among others, are confident to grow. They can see that the economic tide is turning and they know that the future of our country, for the services everybody wants, lies in economic growth—not in handing out money. It takes hard decisions, fortitude... You don’t get growth by giving away money; you get it by providing opportunities for everybody.
rigor.explanation: Frames growth vs 'handing out money' as a clean dichotomy; asserts rather than evidences the mechanism.

rigor.statement: This Government has had no growth. There is more growth on my face than this Government has had, and that’s a fact!
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical hyperbole dressed as 'a fact'; no evidence supplied at this point.

rigor.statement: What’s their answer to this so-called crisis they find themselves in? Asset sales. They’re going to sell our prized assets, but they’re cagey. They’re not going to tell us what they’re going to sell... Sell our rail again? How did that work out last time? We had to buy it back and fix it up.
rigor.explanation: The rail buy-back point is a real historical example, but the overall argument attributes an unannounced plan and reasons from it.

rigor.statement: Anyone who thinks you can make a lunch and deliver it 90 kilometres for $3 really shouldn’t be purporting to be the economic geniuses that this Government are.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real cost/logistics illustration to challenge the $3 lunch figure, though it generalises from one route.

rigor.statement: In an earlier contribution from the other side of the House, during this debate, the Green leader said no one is entitled to make a profit. Now, that’s an outrageous statement, and that is a statement which shows absolute poverty of consciousness—it’s conditioned thinking; it’s negative, constrictive thinking.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a possibly strawmanned quote and dismisses it via characterisation rather than counter-evidence.

rigor.statement: the roots don’t cause the growth; it is the creation of a fertile soil in which you plant the seed to germinate, to grow, and to multiply itself again and again and again, so that what was originally one small seed becomes countless millions.
rigor.explanation: An extended agricultural analogy standing in for economic argument; rhetorically neat but reasons by metaphor rather than evidence.

authenticity.statement: Again, it was the Labour Government that funded those 2,000 homes and continued the build, which is why we have 2,000 more homes.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated housing-build record while in government; claims credit for a program her party actually initiated.

authenticity.statement: In my answer to oral question No. 5 today in the House, I was so excited about the 33,000 people that exited the jobseeker benefit into jobs that I said it was 29 percent more than the same period in 2023. It was actually 22 percent.
authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily corrects her own overstated figure on the record, aligning words with the accurate number.

authenticity.statement: One of the things they asked for: “Please, bring in that FamilyBoost”... “Please adjust the tax brackets like you’re saying you will. Please get rid of the Auckland fuel tax.” And I said, “I promise you: what I know is that we will be doing this.” I’m so happy, and relieved for them, that those are just a few of the changes that we’ve managed to make
authenticity.explanation: Points to campaign promises (FamilyBoost, tax brackets, fuel tax) that were subsequently enacted, matching prior words to delivered action.

authenticity.statement: I was able to visit another home, land which just recently landed for a whānau with six children, one of many homes initiated and actually delivered by Labour. We understand that, when you have a roof over your head, the world is your oyster.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's housing record; claims delivery of homes her party actually funded, backed by a concrete local instance.

strength.statement: Not only have we delivered legislation that will play a crucial role in progress, like the fast-track consenting Act and the Resource Management Act reforms, we are also ensuring that we have a Budget that will allow economic recovery to occur.
strength.explanation: Names specific legislation (fast-track consenting Act, RMA reforms) that was in fact passed, demonstrating delivery rather than mere announcement.

strength.statement: It is under his stewardship that we have seen a focused drive not only towards economic growth but also towards enhancement of the services that a modern-day society demands, from healthcare—and, yes, this will include delivering Dunedin Hospital, which services not only Dunedin but a much wider area including the Waitaki electorate—to education, infrastructure, and digital connectivity.
strength.explanation: 'Will include delivering Dunedin Hospital' is a forward commitment on a much-delayed project, not evidence of delivery.

strength.statement: So far, we’ve done fast track, 149 projects on the list; inflation’s down; interest rates are down; we have stopped wasteful spending because taxpayers expect better outcomes for their money; we’ve done the Resource Management Act (RMA) reform first tranche... and we’ve dealt with ram raids, reducing those down significantly.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted measures (fast-track list, RMA first tranche) as delivered, not merely promised.

strength.statement: With that figure that I gave before—33,000 job seekers in the six months to December who exited into a job in this challenging labour market—is an extraordinary result. It didn’t come by accident; it came by very deliberate, targeted, integrated work to get an outcome—22 percent increase on the same period a year ago.
strength.explanation: Claims a measurable delivered outcome attributed to MSD case-management work, though 'exits into jobs' can partly reflect labour-market churn.

strength.statement: One of the things they asked for: “Please, bring in that FamilyBoost”... “Please adjust the tax brackets like you’re saying you will. Please get rid of the Auckland fuel tax.” And I said, “I promise you: what I know is that we will be doing this.” I’m so happy, and relieved for them, that those are just a few of the changes that we’ve managed to make
strength.explanation: The named commitments (FamilyBoost, tax-bracket changes, fuel-tax removal) were in fact delivered.

strength.statement: cutting initiatives like progressive procurement.”, an initiative that has been directly credited with opening and then keeping open roads in Tairāwhiti during and after Cyclone Gabrielle, mainly on State Highway 35
strength.explanation: Attributes concrete regional benefit to a Labour initiative, though the delivery credit is framed rather than evidenced here.

strength.statement: We have been able, through our coalition negotiations, to develop the Regional Infrastructure Fund—also known as the RIF... We are able to, through Matua Jones, spread out that $1.2 billion across the regions.
strength.explanation: Points to an established, funded programme delivered through the coalition agreement rather than an aspiration.

strength.statement: Flood resilience has been a really important part of the RIF, and $200 million has been set aside for various projects... 42 projects have been identified, $101 million there, and they’ll be co-partnered alongside their relevant local authorities... Stopbanks, pumping stations, groynes, and culverts—that is the really sensible, practical, and pragmatic solution
strength.explanation: Names allocated funding and identified projects; delivery is partly in-progress (projects 'identified', co-investment pending).

divination.statement: How good was it yesterday to see the news with the announcement of the reopening of the Juken sawmill, where an investor has stepped in, bought the mill, and is looking to put back 500 jobs into the Tairāwhiti community.
divination.explanation: Prediction that ~500 jobs will return depends on the buyer's plans materialising; plausible but contingent on an announced, not yet realised, restart.

divination.statement: What about in Kawerau, where next month a large processor will celebrate a $20 million investment into switching a massive manufacturing and processing entity from natural gas to geothermal steam.
divination.explanation: Near-term forecast of a specific, already-committed investment event; likely to occur as described.

divination.statement: Often, the Opposition will kind of criticise me and my or our Government’s ambition to reduce the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by 2030. So, yes, the numbers have gone up and that is, unfortunately, the reality of a low-growth environment.
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast that the 50,000-by-2030 target is achievable, currently running against a rising-unemployment trend.

divination.statement: We’re saying yes—yes to FamilyBoost, which we have said; yes to a new school for 600 students in Flat Bush; and, in particular, the crème de la crème of yesses on this side of the House is yes to Mill Road—yes, that’s going to happen.
divination.explanation: 'Mill Road—that's going to happen' predicts completion of a road repeatedly scaled back before; assertion outruns current certainty.

divination.statement: What’s their answer to this so-called crisis they find themselves in? Asset sales. They’re going to sell our prized assets, but they’re cagey. They’re not going to tell us what they’re going to sell... Sell our rail again? How did that work out last time? We had to buy it back and fix it up.
divination.explanation: Predicts the Government will pursue asset sales; speculative and not clearly supported by a stated policy at the time.

divination.statement: In spite of this Government’s attempts to dim the light, it shines bright in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti... they have the power to change this Government in just over a year and they’re just waiting.
divination.explanation: Implied prediction that voters will change the Government at the next election, over a year out; speculative and outcome-uncertain.

divination.statement: I have some time left and I really want to talk about the blue economy... Our blue economy is an economy that can grow, and we can increase the sector to $3 billion by 2035.
divination.explanation: Ten-year growth target for the marine sector; directionally plausible but a long-horizon aspiration with uncertain realisation.

forthrightness.statement: In my answer to oral question No. 5 today in the House, I was so excited about the 33,000 people that exited the jobseeker benefit into jobs that I said it was 29 percent more than the same period in 2023. It was actually 22 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely corrects the specific error without hedging.

forthrightness.statement: Often, the Opposition will kind of criticise me and my or our Government’s ambition to reduce the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by 2030. So, yes, the numbers have gone up and that is, unfortunately, the reality of a low-growth environment.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly concedes the numbers have risen rather than dodging the unflattering trend.

rigor.statement: It is well-established practice in this House that making comments about the Speaker and questioning the Speaker's judgment outside the House is a question of privilege—I know this for a fact because I was referred to the Privileges Committee for doing exactly that
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in a concrete precedent (his own referral) applied consistently to Seymour; conclusion follows from the cited practice.

rigor.statement: Issues of ministerial conduct are absolutely questions for the Prime Minister, not for the Speaker... Actually, regardless of what decisions you have taken, the Prime Minister is responsible for determining whether a Minister's conduct is acceptable or not. He can't deflect the question by saying it's not his responsibility; it is.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument with an apt analogy (a Minister charged by police is still the PM's responsibility); conclusion follows from the premise about who sets ministerial standards.

rigor.statement: Now, he either is unable to read the captions at the bottom of the screen or he was deliberately misleading the House about what that says, and I'd put it to you that that actually is a breach of privilege
rigor.explanation: Explicit false dichotomy (can't read vs deliberately lying) that excludes honest disagreement over the broadcast.

rigor.statement: I should stress that forecasts aren't reality, and as the shifting GDP figures show, even reality can be hard to pin down and measure. But forecasts do contain valuable information for people and businesses making economic and financial decisions, including the Government.
rigor.explanation: Disciplined, well-calibrated reasoning that distinguishes forecasts from outcomes and acknowledges measurement uncertainty rather than overclaiming.

rigor.statement: It was to be 5.4 percent in 2025; HYEFU has it at 5.4 percent for 2025. It was to be 4.8 percent for 2026; HYEFU has it at 4.8 percent for 2026. It was to be 4.6 percent for 2027, and HYEFU has it at 4.5 percent. So if the member is suggesting that somehow it is the actions of this Government that have led to unemployment, she needs to explain why her previous Government was forecasting exactly the same levels of unemployment that are occurring today.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based rebuttal comparing pre-election forecasts to HYEFU figures; the conclusion (unemployment tracking pre-existing forecasts) follows from the numbers cited.

rigor.statement: My job is to create the conditions in which growth can occur. Do you know who's going to deliver it?... it's the New Zealanders who get up in the morning, the farmers who milk their cows and get more for their milk, it's the businesses who choose to hire more people, it's the entrepreneurs who decide to start a new business. This is a Government that is on their side.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable framing of government's enabling role, but leans on appeal to shared values rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, the Speaker has dealt to the issue, but we don't need to take 12 to 16 contraventions of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
rigor.explanation: Whataboutism (tu quoque) — the Wood comparison does not bear on whether Seymour's conduct met standards.

rigor.statement: I'm proud of the standing that New Zealand has in the world around transparency and no corruption... it's a little bit ironic, as I said yesterday, that we're being lectured by someone who took 16 goes of contravention of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
rigor.explanation: Whataboutism that does not address the substance of the transparency-ranking question.

rigor.statement: this will overturn the worst energy decision made in the history of New Zealand, where an entire oil and gas sector was snuffed out by juvenile, childish green thinking, which is now being proven to have been shallow and irrelevant
rigor.explanation: Sweeping hyperbole ('worst decision in history') and name-calling substituting for evidence.

rigor.statement: The people who didn't fund it, my friend, were you, who, in Budget 2023, pretended that there would be no ongoing operational funding required for Kāinga Ora. It was a fiscal cliff left by Grant Robertson to try and make the books look better in the lead-up to the 2023 election.
rigor.explanation: Makes a causal argument about the funding shortfall with a factual anchor, though motive is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: I don't know many New Zealanders who think it is an economic use of land and houses for Kāinga Ora to own around 200 houses, most of them in Auckland, worth $2 million or more.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable value-for-money point, but partly rests on an appeal to popular common sense rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The real issue here is no one can surely be condemned for expecting immigrants to come to this country to be grateful to the country they've come to. What's wrong with us when that is a complaint from that side of the House? It's virtue-signalling nonsense and he's misleading Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal to tradition ('when in Rome') and reframing rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: This is the most constrained one now because some members here can't take it when somebody hits back at them. It's an essential part of this Parliament that we have a vigorous debate.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an anecdotal comparison to other parliaments and assertion rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: You cannot manage what you don't measure, and they got rid of the health targets, and I just say shame on them. People are waiting too long to get an elective surgery, waiting longer at emergency departments, immunisation rates declining.
rigor.explanation: A coherent management argument (removing targets undermined accountability) but leans on an aphorism and 'shame on them' rhetoric.

specificity.statement: It is well-established practice in this House that making comments about the Speaker and questioning the Speaker's judgment outside the House is a question of privilege—I know this for a fact because I was referred to the Privileges Committee for doing exactly that
specificity.explanation: Names a specific parliamentary practice and a concrete precedent rather than a vague complaint.

specificity.statement: Westpac expects growth in the economy to be positive in the December quarter of last year, and it is forecasting growth to pick up across 2025, and reach 3 percent in 2026. It also expects inflation to stay within the 1 to 3 percent target band and expects the current account deficit to narrow.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, quarters, a 3% figure, and the target band.

specificity.statement: A heavy traffic index continues to trend upwards, being 4.1 percent higher than a year ago on a three-month rolling average.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentage, comparison period, and methodology (three-month rolling average).

specificity.statement: the market and most economists are expecting a 50-basis point reduction in the OCR. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates, lower mortgage rates, which in turn will support a growing economy.
specificity.explanation: Names magnitude (50bp), the resulting rate (3.75%), and the transmission channel.

specificity.statement: It was to be 5.4 percent in 2025; HYEFU has it at 5.4 percent for 2025. It was to be 4.8 percent for 2026; HYEFU has it at 4.8 percent for 2026. It was to be 4.6 percent for 2027, and HYEFU has it at 4.5 percent. So if the member is suggesting that somehow it is the actions of this Government that have led to unemployment, she needs to explain why her previous Government was forecasting exactly the same levels of unemployment that are occurring today.
specificity.explanation: Multiple exact figures matched year-by-year against a named source.

specificity.statement: Wages are rising faster than inflation, goods exports in December were up 17 percent, average mortgage rates have fallen now for two months in a row, and economists... are now predicting we'll have more interest rate relief very, very shortly.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and timeframes rather than slogans.

specificity.statement: Absolutely, and that's why this year's Budget package takes 17,000 children out of poverty compared to the last year of the Labour-Greens Government, which put 23,000 more children in poverty.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (17,000; 23,000) tied to specific periods.

specificity.statement: Because that Minister—Minister Potaka—has done an exceptionally good job getting almost 2,000 children out of motel accommodation in emergency motels. He has also delivered $200 million recently to Māori social housing.
specificity.explanation: Names the minister, a ~2,000 count, and a $200 million figure.

specificity.statement: Yes, and we're on track to do that. But what we will not be doing is driving up house prices 50 percent, adding $180 of rent per week, having a fourfold increase in the social house wait-list, and putting 3,000 to 4,000 families into motel accommodation in emergency motels.
specificity.explanation: Several concrete figures on prices, rent, wait-list, and motel families.

specificity.statement: the $3 billion target that has been set for this sector—clear and measurable—will [be] achieved by 2035, but it will only be achieved as we operationalise fast track
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar target and a date.

specificity.statement: considering the Salvation Army's State of the Nation report found that, in the past year, most of the indicators monitored showed worsening or unchanged outcomes for children and youth
specificity.explanation: Attributes a specific finding to a named source, though without individual figures.

specificity.statement: considering she is repealing the protections for tamariki Māori in section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, despite the Salvation Army finding that tamariki Māori still make up more than two-thirds of children in care?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutory clause and a concrete proportion.

specificity.statement: since 27 November 2023, when this Government took office and we got sworn in as Ministers, over 2,000 net new social houses have been built in Auckland. So we're well on the way to meeting the 1,000 per year commitment
specificity.explanation: Concrete count, date, and reference to the annual commitment.

specificity.statement: I don't know many New Zealanders who think it is an economic use of land and houses for Kāinga Ora to own around 200 houses, most of them in Auckland, worth $2 million or more.
specificity.explanation: Names a count (~200), location, and value threshold ($2m+).

specificity.statement: Brougham Street carries 45,000 vehicles per day, a critical route servicing the commercial, industrial, and residential areas of Christchurch.
specificity.explanation: Exact daily vehicle count and the road's function.

specificity.statement: It also includes an overbridge between Collins... and Simeon Street to ensure local residents and school children can safely cross over the highway. I'm advised it's about a thousand people... that cross over that very busy section of State Highway 76
specificity.explanation: Names the specific overbridge location, the highway, and a ~1,000-people figure.

specificity.statement: The number of children in a benefit-dependent household in September 2017 was around 172,000. This increased by around 50,200, or 29 percent, to 222,500 by December 2023. Since then, it has increased to 232,800 as at December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts, percentages, and dated reference points.

specificity.statement: we've had 33,000 people exit the jobseeker benefit into jobs in the last six months—29 percent more than the same time a year ago when the economic conditions were better.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count, timeframe, and year-on-year comparison.

specificity.statement: which is why our Government is focused on reducing the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by the year 2030.
specificity.explanation: A quantified target with a date.

specificity.statement: Why has Kāinga Ora cancelled at least 103 public housing projects—comprised of 965 much-needed houses, including 398 houses in the last five months—if the Government is using every lever?
specificity.explanation: Exact numbers of projects, houses, and a recent time window.

specificity.statement: How does the Minister reconcile his statement ruling out a mass sell-off of State houses when he is increasing annual State house sales by 2,000 percent, compared with 2017 to 2023?
specificity.explanation: Cites a percentage and comparison period, though the base is not stated.

specificity.statement: How can we trust that she is going for growth, when we have record unemployment, 13,000 less construction roles in the economy, record net migration, record company liquidations, more hungry children and homelessness, all because of her choices
specificity.explanation: Lists several concrete indicators including a 13,000 figure.

specificity.statement: Right now, for the first time ever, we are delivering, to 310 classrooms across the country, nationally consistent maths resources including student workbooks, teacher guides, and tactile materials in te reo Māori... will benefit 27,000 ākonga across the country, learning in immersion settings.
specificity.explanation: Names classroom count (310), student count (27,000), and the resource types.

specificity.statement: Students will be checked at 20, 40, and 55 weeks of schooling to see how they're progressing with identifying sounds, letters, and words, if they can segment and write words, and whether or not they can read sentences
specificity.explanation: Precise checkpoints (20/40/55 weeks) and the specific reading skills assessed.

specificity.statement: note that it does report on the number of households in emergency housing being the lowest in eight years, and reducing over 80 percent... These reductions have happened, notwithstanding the increase in the number of people being reported as in severe housing deprivation, which rose by 10 percent between 2018 and 2023.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures and time periods.

specificity.statement: Between 2017 and 2023, Kāinga Ora tenant debt increased from $1 million to $21 million, with some whānau struggling to repay their debt.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures and a defined period.

specificity.statement: we continue to be committed to facilitating the use of taxpayer funds to build houses through community housing providers—1,500 by June 2027, Kāinga Ora is probably 2,650 by June 2026
specificity.explanation: Named build targets with dates for two delivery channels.

specificity.statement: when the last Government came into office in 2017, there were 918 people waiting longer than four months to get their first specialist assessments. When we came to office, it was 59,000
specificity.explanation: Exact counts and clearly defined metric (four-month FSA waits).

specificity.statement: Why are one in four children reported going without food sometimes or often—and for Pasifika, it's one in two—and how does she reconcile this with fewer Ministry of Social Development (MSD) hardship grants being granted and less money for food banks?
specificity.explanation: Concrete ratios (one in four; one in two for Pasifika) tied to a policy contrast.

civility.statement: It is well-established practice in this House that making comments about the Speaker and questioning the Speaker's judgment outside the House is a question of privilege—I know this for a fact because I was referred to the Privileges Committee for doing exactly that
civility.explanation: Procedural argument focused on conduct and precedent rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: He has not apologised to the House, he has not apologised to the public; he has only apologised to you, and I think it is very appropriate that the New Zealand public actually sees an apology from a Minister who has clearly broken both the rules of the House and, potentially, the law of the land.
civility.explanation: Harsh and accusatory (implying lawbreaking) but directed at conduct and process rather than personal character.

civility.statement: Issues of ministerial conduct are absolutely questions for the Prime Minister, not for the Speaker... Actually, regardless of what decisions you have taken, the Prime Minister is responsible for determining whether a Minister's conduct is acceptable or not. He can't deflect the question by saying it's not his responsibility; it is.
civility.explanation: Pointed but substantive procedural argument about accountability, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Now, he either is unable to read the captions at the bottom of the screen or he was deliberately misleading the House about what that says, and I'd put it to you that that actually is a breach of privilege
civility.explanation: Personal jab implying the opponent is either illiterate or a liar.

civility.statement: Does this Government have any plans to go through the telephone book and find homebuyers with Chinese-sounding names?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic cross-House jab referencing a past Labour episode rather than engaging any substance.

civility.statement: The only one who wants to say the sky is falling is you, Barb.
civility.explanation: Personal jab using a diminutive nickname (which Edmonds raised a point of order over), not engaging substance.

civility.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, the Speaker has dealt to the issue, but we don't need to take 12 to 16 contraventions of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
civility.explanation: Tu quoque deflection targeting a past opponent rather than answering.

civility.statement: I'm proud of the standing that New Zealand has in the world around transparency and no corruption... it's a little bit ironic, as I said yesterday, that we're being lectured by someone who took 16 goes of contravention of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
civility.explanation: Tu quoque directed at Hipkins' handling of former ministers.

civility.statement: this will overturn the worst energy decision made in the history of New Zealand, where an entire oil and gas sector was snuffed out by juvenile, childish green thinking, which is now being proven to have been shallow and irrelevant
civility.explanation: Dismissive, hyperbolic language ('juvenile, childish') aimed at opponents' views.

civility.statement: Also it's my pleasure to tell the House that most of the people there reminded me they never left the Labour Party; the Labour Party left them.
civility.explanation: A partisan needle at Labour, unsupported anecdote rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: The people who didn't fund it, my friend, were you, who, in Budget 2023, pretended that there would be no ongoing operational funding required for Kāinga Ora. It was a fiscal cliff left by Grant Robertson to try and make the books look better in the lead-up to the 2023 election.
civility.explanation: Accusatory ('pretended') but anchored to a substantive fiscal argument.

civility.statement: Was she going for growth when she put the country in the deepest recession for the last 30 years with the exception of COVID, and the accelerating number of company liquidations and closures?
civility.explanation: A sharp attack on the government's economic record, but on policy outcomes rather than personal character.

civility.statement: The real issue here is no one can surely be condemned for expecting immigrants to come to this country to be grateful to the country they've come to. What's wrong with us when that is a complaint from that side of the House? It's virtue-signalling nonsense and he's misleading Parliament.
civility.explanation: Dismissive framing ('virtue-signalling nonsense') and an accusation of misleading the House rather than engaging the point.

civility.statement: My question to the Minister is: given the inability for some members to understand the facts that are being told by you in the answers, could he configure the future answers in cartoon form to make it more understandable?
civility.explanation: A mocking jab implying opposition members cannot understand the answers.

civility.statement: This is the most constrained one now because some members here can't take it when somebody hits back at them. It's an essential part of this Parliament that we have a vigorous debate.
civility.explanation: Argues for robust exchange; a mild swipe at colleagues' sensitivity rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: You cannot manage what you don't measure, and they got rid of the health targets, and I just say shame on them. People are waiting too long to get an elective surgery, waiting longer at emergency departments, immunisation rates declining.
civility.explanation: 'Shame on them' is pointed but aimed at a policy decision (removing targets), not personal character.

civility.statement: Well, I have been called many things in my career in politics and I'm sure that's probably not the worst.
civility.explanation: Responds to an insulting quote with grace instead of a counter-attack.

civility.statement: Why should New Zealanders take him seriously when he has broken his promise to build more houses than the previous Labour Government; when Chris Bishop broke his promise to build enough houses to eliminate the housing waiting list; and when this pledge, signed by Nicola Willis, promised a net increase of 1,000 State homes in Auckland but demonstrates that her word is worth nothing?
civility.explanation: Frames the case as broken promises (substantive) but tips into a personal denigration ('her word is worth nothing').

veracity.statement: He has not apologised to the House, he has not apologised to the public; he has only apologised to you, and I think it is very appropriate that the New Zealand public actually sees an apology from a Minister who has clearly broken both the rules of the House and, potentially, the law of the land.
veracity.explanation: The apology-only-to-Speaker point is factual, but 'potentially, the law of the land' is an unsubstantiated escalation hedged by 'potentially'.

veracity.statement: I haven't insisted I be allowed to; I've actually accepted your ruling and given you an apology. I have not attacked a security guard; I've simply described the facts.
veracity.explanation: A disputed framing of his own behaviour; the claim of not criticising the guard clashes with the reported footage.

veracity.statement: Westpac expects growth in the economy to be positive in the December quarter of last year, and it is forecasting growth to pick up across 2025, and reach 3 percent in 2026. It also expects inflation to stay within the 1 to 3 percent target band and expects the current account deficit to narrow.
veracity.explanation: An accurate relay of a named external forecast (Westpac's 'Turning the corner' report) with figures that can be checked against it.

veracity.statement: A heavy traffic index continues to trend upwards, being 4.1 percent higher than a year ago on a three-month rolling average.
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable figure attributed to the ANZ Truckometer report.

veracity.statement: the market and most economists are expecting a 50-basis point reduction in the OCR. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates, lower mortgage rates, which in turn will support a growing economy.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of market and economist expectations at the time.

veracity.statement: It was to be 5.4 percent in 2025; HYEFU has it at 5.4 percent for 2025. It was to be 4.8 percent for 2026; HYEFU has it at 4.8 percent for 2026. It was to be 4.6 percent for 2027, and HYEFU has it at 4.5 percent. So if the member is suggesting that somehow it is the actions of this Government that have led to unemployment, she needs to explain why her previous Government was forecasting exactly the same levels of unemployment that are occurring today.
veracity.explanation: Specific forecast figures presented accurately, though selectively framed to shift causation.

veracity.statement: Wages are rising faster than inflation, goods exports in December were up 17 percent, average mortgage rates have fallen now for two months in a row, and economists... are now predicting we'll have more interest rate relief very, very shortly.
veracity.explanation: A run of broadly supportable economic claims (17% goods export rise, falling mortgage rates), though selectively upbeat.

veracity.statement: Absolutely, and that's why this year's Budget package takes 17,000 children out of poverty compared to the last year of the Labour-Greens Government, which put 23,000 more children in poverty.
veracity.explanation: Uses modelled/projected figures presented as settled fact and contrasts them with a contestable characterisation of the previous government's record.

veracity.statement: Because that Minister—Minister Potaka—has done an exceptionally good job getting almost 2,000 children out of motel accommodation in emergency motels. He has also delivered $200 million recently to Māori social housing.
veracity.explanation: Delivery figures broadly consistent with the emergency-housing reduction cited elsewhere in the session, though favourably framed.

veracity.statement: Yes, and we're on track to do that. But what we will not be doing is driving up house prices 50 percent, adding $180 of rent per week, having a fourfold increase in the social house wait-list, and putting 3,000 to 4,000 families into motel accommodation in emergency motels.
veracity.explanation: A mix of accurate and inflated characterisations of the previous government's housing record.

veracity.statement: the power companies today are now underwriting the importation of Indonesian coal
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — NZ coal imports rose in recent years — though the causal link to the exploration ban is contested.

veracity.statement: considering the Salvation Army's State of the Nation report found that, in the past year, most of the indicators monitored showed worsening or unchanged outcomes for children and youth
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of a named, citable report's findings.

veracity.statement: considering she is repealing the protections for tamariki Māori in section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, despite the Salvation Army finding that tamariki Māori still make up more than two-thirds of children in care?
veracity.explanation: Both the section 7AA repeal and the two-thirds-in-care figure are accurate and checkable.

veracity.statement: since 27 November 2023, when this Government took office and we got sworn in as Ministers, over 2,000 net new social houses have been built in Auckland. So we're well on the way to meeting the 1,000 per year commitment
veracity.explanation: The 2,000 figure is defensible but conflates 'social housing' broadly with the specific 'net additional public homes in Auckland' the question asked about.

veracity.statement: The people who didn't fund it, my friend, were you, who, in Budget 2023, pretended that there would be no ongoing operational funding required for Kāinga Ora. It was a fiscal cliff left by Grant Robertson to try and make the books look better in the lead-up to the 2023 election.
veracity.explanation: A partisan framing of the Budget 2023 funding arrangements with some factual basis but a contestable characterisation of intent.

veracity.statement: Brougham Street carries 45,000 vehicles per day, a critical route servicing the commercial, industrial, and residential areas of Christchurch.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable traffic-volume figure for a specific corridor.

veracity.statement: The number of children in a benefit-dependent household in September 2017 was around 172,000. This increased by around 50,200, or 29 percent, to 222,500 by December 2023. Since then, it has increased to 232,800 as at December 2024.
veracity.explanation: Precise, checkable figures presented without cherry-picking to hide the recent increase.

veracity.statement: we've had 33,000 people exit the jobseeker benefit into jobs in the last six months—29 percent more than the same time a year ago when the economic conditions were better.
veracity.explanation: A specific delivery statistic, plausible though the 'into jobs' framing may include other exit types.

veracity.statement: Why has Kāinga Ora cancelled at least 103 public housing projects—comprised of 965 much-needed houses, including 398 houses in the last five months—if the Government is using every lever?
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable project and house-count figures underpinning the question.

veracity.statement: How does the Minister reconcile his statement ruling out a mass sell-off of State houses when he is increasing annual State house sales by 2,000 percent, compared with 2017 to 2023?
veracity.explanation: The '2,000 percent' framing is dramatic and dependent on a very low 2017–2023 baseline, which risks being misleading despite a real increase.

veracity.statement: Was she going for growth when she put the country in the deepest recession for the last 30 years with the exception of COVID, and the accelerating number of company liquidations and closures?
veracity.explanation: 'Deepest recession in 30 years' is a contestable superlative and attributing it wholly to the current minister overstates the causal claim.

veracity.statement: How can we trust that she is going for growth, when we have record unemployment, 13,000 less construction roles in the economy, record net migration, record company liquidations, more hungry children and homelessness, all because of her choices
veracity.explanation: Mixes some supportable figures (construction roles) with overstated 'record' claims (unemployment was not at a record) and a sweeping sole-causation attribution.

veracity.statement: Right now, for the first time ever, we are delivering, to 310 classrooms across the country, nationally consistent maths resources including student workbooks, teacher guides, and tactile materials in te reo Māori... will benefit 27,000 ākonga across the country, learning in immersion settings.
veracity.explanation: Specific delivery claims that are checkable, framed as currently happening.

veracity.statement: note that it does report on the number of households in emergency housing being the lowest in eight years, and reducing over 80 percent... These reductions have happened, notwithstanding the increase in the number of people being reported as in severe housing deprivation, which rose by 10 percent between 2018 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: The emergency-housing figures are accurate but the 'reduction' is challenged as partly driven by policy restricting access, which the framing does not concede.

veracity.statement: Between 2017 and 2023, Kāinga Ora tenant debt increased from $1 million to $21 million, with some whānau struggling to repay their debt.
veracity.explanation: Specific debt figures consistent with the ~$22m peak he cites later; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: when the last Government came into office in 2017, there were 918 people waiting longer than four months to get their first specialist assessments. When we came to office, it was 59,000
veracity.explanation: Specific figures used to contrast 2017 and 2023 waitlists; broadly checkable though favourably chosen.

veracity.statement: Why are one in four children reported going without food sometimes or often—and for Pasifika, it's one in two—and how does she reconcile this with fewer Ministry of Social Development (MSD) hardship grants being granted and less money for food banks?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific food-insecurity proportions consistent with the report under discussion.

veracity.statement: Yeah, look, he's built 2,000 houses already.
veracity.explanation: A round claim challenged in the House (McAnulty's point of order) that conflates broad social-housing builds with the specific Auckland net-additional metric asked about.

authenticity.statement: I haven't insisted I be allowed to; I've actually accepted your ruling and given you an apology. I have not attacked a security guard; I've simply described the facts.
authenticity.explanation: Self-defence asserting his words match his conduct (accepting the ruling), but the characterisation is contested by Hipkins' account of the TV footage.

authenticity.statement: Well, it's a three-year term in Government. We are 15 months in... Three-year commitments are not broken within 15 months; you've got to wait till the end. We will honour that commitment.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a prior commitment as still binding; consistency cannot yet be verified either way.

authenticity.statement: How does the Minister reconcile his statement ruling out a mass sell-off of State houses when he is increasing annual State house sales by 2,000 percent, compared with 2017 to 2023?
authenticity.explanation: Frames the sales increase as inconsistent with Bishop's prior 'no mass sell-off' assurance — a hypocrisy charge directed at the minister.

authenticity.statement: I am very concerned by the number of people with severe housing deprivation throughout the country, and this is some of the legacy that we've inherited over the last 15 months.
authenticity.explanation: States genuine concern but attributes the outcome to the previous government, a defensible but unverified shift of responsibility.

authenticity.statement: Why should New Zealanders take him seriously when he has broken his promise to build more houses than the previous Labour Government; when Chris Bishop broke his promise to build enough houses to eliminate the housing waiting list; and when this pledge, signed by Nicola Willis, promised a net increase of 1,000 State homes in Auckland but demonstrates that her word is worth nothing?
authenticity.explanation: Levels a hypocrisy/broken-promise charge at ministers — a low-consistency signal directed at the opponents, not the speaker.

charisma.statement: Does this Government have any plans to go through the telephone book and find homebuyers with Chinese-sounding names?
charisma.explanation: Partisan needle aimed at scoring against opponents, not persuasive or bridge-building.

charisma.statement: My job is to create the conditions in which growth can occur. Do you know who's going to deliver it?... it's the New Zealanders who get up in the morning, the farmers who milk their cows and get more for their milk, it's the businesses who choose to hire more people, it's the entrepreneurs who decide to start a new business. This is a Government that is on their side.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective and evocative, but appeals to its own base rather than reaching across to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: Also it's my pleasure to tell the House that most of the people there reminded me they never left the Labour Party; the Labour Party left them.
charisma.explanation: An in-group applause line, not a bridge-building appeal.

charisma.statement: Well, I have been called many things in my career in politics and I'm sure that's probably not the worst.
charisma.explanation: Disarming, good-humoured deflection that defuses a hostile characterisation rather than escalating.

divination.statement: the market and most economists are expecting a 50-basis point reduction in the OCR. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates, lower mortgage rates, which in turn will support a growing economy.
divination.explanation: Short-horizon prediction (next week's MPS) consistent with market consensus and prevailing conditions; well-founded though contingent on the committee.

divination.statement: the $3 billion target that has been set for this sector—clear and measurable—will [be] achieved by 2035, but it will only be achieved as we operationalise fast track
divination.explanation: A long-horizon (2035) prediction of a specific export/value target; plausible but optimistic and contingent on policy delivery.

forthrightness.statement: It was to be 5.4 percent in 2025; HYEFU has it at 5.4 percent for 2025. It was to be 4.8 percent for 2026; HYEFU has it at 4.8 percent for 2026. It was to be 4.6 percent for 2027, and HYEFU has it at 4.5 percent. So if the member is suggesting that somehow it is the actions of this Government that have led to unemployment, she needs to explain why her previous Government was forecasting exactly the same levels of unemployment that are occurring today.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages the question about unemployment with data rather than deflecting, though pivots to blame.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, the Speaker has dealt to the issue, but we don't need to take 12 to 16 contraventions of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Seymour's conduct was acceptable, he pivots to attacking a former Labour minister without addressing the question.

forthrightness.statement: As I've said before, this is an issue for the Speaker, and the Speaker has comprehensively dealt with the issue.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether Seymour's conduct met his expectations as PM, he deflects to the Speaker despite ministerial conduct being his own responsibility.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, with respect to parliamentary security, that is a decision for the Speaker. I have confidence in all of my Ministers.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeats a non-answer to a specific question about whether Seymour's conduct met ministerial standards.

forthrightness.statement: Well, in answer to the last part of that question: I have huge confidence in the Deputy Prime Minister, who really believes in the Mexico - New Zealand relationship and visited the country and cares deeply about those relationships.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether specific anti-immigrant remarks met his expectations, he answers only the last clause and recasts it as being about the NZ-Mexico relationship.

forthrightness.statement: I think you've actually heard from, in all of those cases, members expressing in the heat of the moment in this place that they may not have got their language perfect, and they've admitted as much.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages the question about ministerial remarks but minimises rather than saying whether the conduct met his standards.

forthrightness.statement: I'm proud of the standing that New Zealand has in the world around transparency and no corruption... it's a little bit ironic, as I said yesterday, that we're being lectured by someone who took 16 goes of contravention of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage the specific claims about the Corruption Perceptions Index decline; pivots to attacking the questioner's record.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and we're on track to do that. But what we will not be doing is driving up house prices 50 percent, adding $180 of rent per week, having a fourfold increase in the social house wait-list, and putting 3,000 to 4,000 families into motel accommodation in emergency motels.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'yes... on track' to the 1,000-homes question before pivoting to attack the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: Yeah, I reject the premise and the conflation of all those issues in that question.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage the substance of a multi-part question by rejecting its premise wholesale.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it's a three-year term in Government. We are 15 months in... Three-year commitments are not broken within 15 months; you've got to wait till the end. We will honour that commitment.
forthrightness.explanation: Reaffirms the commitment but sidesteps the specific yes/no on whether 1,000 net new homes will exist in 2026.

forthrightness.statement: The number of children in a benefit-dependent household in September 2017 was around 172,000. This increased by around 50,200, or 29 percent, to 222,500 by December 2023. Since then, it has increased to 232,800 as at December 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question comparing current benefit-dependent child numbers to 2023, including the unflattering rise on her own watch.

forthrightness.statement: I want to start by addressing the question around less food grants because, on investigation, there have been fewer requests for food hardship grants. So I would say to any New Zealander who is struggling right now, please seek assistance from MSD. There is assistance available
forthrightness.explanation: Offers a partial explanation (fewer requests) but pivots to encouragement rather than reconciling this with the reported rise in food insecurity.

forthrightness.statement: note that it does report on the number of households in emergency housing being the lowest in eight years, and reducing over 80 percent... These reductions have happened, notwithstanding the increase in the number of people being reported as in severe housing deprivation, which rose by 10 percent between 2018 and 2023.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers with data and openly notes the rise in severe housing deprivation alongside the favourable numbers.

forthrightness.statement: I am very concerned by the number of people with severe housing deprivation throughout the country, and this is some of the legacy that we've inherited over the last 15 months.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the problem raised (a rough-sleeping pregnant woman) but deflects responsibility to an inherited legacy rather than his policies.

strength.statement: Because that Minister—Minister Potaka—has done an exceptionally good job getting almost 2,000 children out of motel accommodation in emergency motels. He has also delivered $200 million recently to Māori social housing.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivery (children out of motels, funding delivered) attributed to a responsible minister, not merely an announcement.

strength.statement: Yes, and we're on track to do that. But what we will not be doing is driving up house prices 50 percent, adding $180 of rent per week, having a fourfold increase in the social house wait-list, and putting 3,000 to 4,000 families into motel accommodation in emergency motels.
strength.explanation: Reaffirms an in-progress commitment (on track for 1,000 homes) without yet demonstrating the target delivered.

strength.statement: the $3 billion target that has been set for this sector—clear and measurable—will [be] achieved by 2035, but it will only be achieved as we operationalise fast track
strength.explanation: A target announced, not delivered; follow-through remains speculative.

strength.statement: since 27 November 2023, when this Government took office and we got sworn in as Ministers, over 2,000 net new social houses have been built in Auckland. So we're well on the way to meeting the 1,000 per year commitment
strength.explanation: Points to concrete delivery against a stated commitment, though the metric definition is disputed.

strength.statement: It also includes an overbridge between Collins... and Simeon Street to ensure local residents and school children can safely cross over the highway. I'm advised it's about a thousand people... that cross over that very busy section of State Highway 76
strength.explanation: Describes an announced project component rather than completed delivery.

strength.statement: we've had 33,000 people exit the jobseeker benefit into jobs in the last six months—29 percent more than the same time a year ago when the economic conditions were better.
strength.explanation: Points to a measurable outcome under her portfolio, though modest against the overall rise in benefit numbers she also reported.

strength.statement: which is why our Government is focused on reducing the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by the year 2030.
strength.explanation: A stated aspiration with a distant target and no delivery yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Right now, for the first time ever, we are delivering, to 310 classrooms across the country, nationally consistent maths resources including student workbooks, teacher guides, and tactile materials in te reo Māori... will benefit 27,000 ākonga across the country, learning in immersion settings.
strength.explanation: Describes delivery in progress ('right now... we are delivering') rather than a mere announcement, with concrete outputs.

strength.statement: we continue to be committed to facilitating the use of taxpayer funds to build houses through community housing providers—1,500 by June 2027, Kāinga Ora is probably 2,650 by June 2026
strength.explanation: Forward commitments with dates; delivery not yet demonstrated ('probably').

strength.statement: Yeah, look, he's built 2,000 houses already.
strength.explanation: Asserts concrete delivery attributed to the housing minister, though the figure and its definition are contested.

civility.statement: The Greens are the official de-growth party. They're not in favour of economic growth, but most rational political parties are, apart from the Māori Party—they're also not in favour of growth.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents and implies only 'rational' parties favour growth; dismissive rather than engaging their actual position.

civility.statement: Let's leave Te Pāti Māori and the Green Party out of this, and let's just pretend that this conversation is happening amongst rational, normal people.
civility.explanation: Implies two parties are neither rational nor normal — a personal/collective slight rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: We've got "Mr No" and "Mr Slow", and then we've got "Miss No-show" over there—the finance spokesperson for the Labour Party—who is just not part of the economic debate.
civility.explanation: Mocking nicknames aimed at individuals rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: This Government is arrogant, it is incompetent, it is disingenuous, it is heartless, and it is cruel.
civility.explanation: A string of pejorative characterisations rather than engagement with policy substance.
