civility.statement: That was pathetic. Did you see the level of energy? The most energy that Chris Bishop could bring up... was when Mark Mitchell crossed his arms—that was it. That was the best they could come up with.
civility.explanation: Personal mockery of Bishop's delivery rather than his argument.

civility.statement: Well, I guess if you're bereft of your own ideas, you just start talking about everybody else's, because I didn't hear one idea on how to actually improve the quality of life for everyday Kiwis in that last 10 minutes of whatever that was.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the previous speaker's contribution as ideas-free; more jab than engagement.

civility.statement: It's just a mystery to people like their finance spokesperson how we landed up in the worst recession in 30 years.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic swipe at an opponent's competence rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: The ideology, of the last century, at least, has been growth for growth's sake, and that is the ideology of the cancer cell.
civility.explanation: Attacks an ideology rather than a person, but the 'cancer cell' comparison is deliberately provocative.

civility.statement: Then they say we're the irrational ones—projection, much? I mean, the least rational thing you can do is keep doing the same thing and expect to get a different result.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab implying opponents are irrational, though aimed at their approach rather than personal character.

civility.statement: The future ex-Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour has set up a few white-elephant bureaucracies. He's degraded the school lunches programme so that, where there were once healthy, nutritious lunches for kids, they're feeding them inedible slop. Earlier this week he ram-raided Parliament.
civility.explanation: Personal attacks on Seymour with loaded language ('slop', 'ram-raided') rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: We've already seen what one year of her economic stewardship has delivered to this country: unemployment at record levels, poverty at record levels, the economy breaking at the seams, and more and more New Zealanders leaving this country in record numbers.
civility.explanation: Aggressive but aimed at the record and policy rather than personal character.

civility.statement: We're growing our economy, especially needed after the last effort of the last Government and their "drunk uncle" ways of spending taxpayer money with no accountability.
civility.explanation: The 'drunk uncle' metaphor mocks opponents' fiscal conduct rather than engaging specifics.

civility.statement: The public and parents, they are sick of education being a political football. They want us to all get along. They want to have choice where they send their children... My challenge to the Opposition is to go and visit these schools, see what they're about, get on board... we can all have a bright future.
civility.explanation: Frames the disagreement respectfully and challenges opponents to engage rather than attacking them.

charisma.statement: The Greens are the official de-growth party. They're not in favour of economic growth, but most rational political parties are, apart from the Māori Party—they're also not in favour of growth.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that excludes two parties rather than persuading or building consensus.

charisma.statement: Let's leave Te Pāti Māori and the Green Party out of this, and let's just pretend that this conversation is happening amongst rational, normal people.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly excludes opponents from the conversation; alienating, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: We've got "Mr No" and "Mr Slow", and then we've got "Miss No-show" over there—the finance spokesperson for the Labour Party—who is just not part of the economic debate.
charisma.explanation: Applause-line ridicule of opponents; rallies his own side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: This Government is arrogant, it is incompetent, it is disingenuous, it is heartless, and it is cruel.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative opener that rallies opponents of the Government, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: That was pathetic. Did you see the level of energy? The most energy that Chris Bishop could bring up... was when Mark Mitchell crossed his arms—that was it. That was the best they could come up with.
charisma.explanation: Derisive, in-group ridicule; alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: Well, I guess if you're bereft of your own ideas, you just start talking about everybody else's, because I didn't hear one idea on how to actually improve the quality of life for everyday Kiwis in that last 10 minutes of whatever that was.
charisma.explanation: Opens by belittling the opponent rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: If we want to pay for more doctors, if we want more teachers and more nurses and more social workers, if we want to have better welfare, if we want to have better public services, we have to pay for it, and that means we need growth.
charisma.explanation: Frames growth as serving broadly shared goals, a mildly inclusive appeal, but stays within his side's framing.

charisma.statement: That's what every community, every hapū, every family in this country wants. They want the ability to be able to look after themselves. They want the ability to be able to create employment and care for their own.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying framing that appeals to shared aspirations across communities.

charisma.statement: The ideology, of the last century, at least, has been growth for growth's sake, and that is the ideology of the cancer cell.
charisma.explanation: Vivid but polarising framing that speaks to her own side rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: If you designed a transport system where more people can walk, cycle, take public transport for the short trips, then the roads we have would work perfectly to move freight and to move the things that need to be moved by road.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to reframe as non-culture-war and universal, but delivered within a combative exchange.

charisma.statement: Then they say we're the irrational ones—projection, much? I mean, the least rational thing you can do is keep doing the same thing and expect to get a different result.
charisma.explanation: Scores a rhetorical point against opponents rather than inviting them in.

charisma.statement: The public and parents, they are sick of education being a political football. They want us to all get along. They want to have choice where they send their children... My challenge to the Opposition is to go and visit these schools, see what they're about, get on board... we can all have a bright future.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites opponents in and seeks common ground on education, a consensus-building appeal.

rigor.statement: The Greens are the official de-growth party. They're not in favour of economic growth, but most rational political parties are, apart from the Māori Party—they're also not in favour of growth.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: attributes a self-identified 'de-growth' stance the Greens do not claim, with no evidence.

rigor.statement: What are the countries that look after the environment the best? Wealthy countries that grow. The poorest economies in the world desecrate the environment. They ravage the environment.
rigor.explanation: Gestures at the environmental Kuznets idea but overstates it as a sweeping generalization without evidence.

rigor.statement: Wealth taxes are stupid and capital gains taxes are stupid.
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion with name-calling of the ideas and no supporting argument.

rigor.statement: This Government is arrogant, it is incompetent, it is disingenuous, it is heartless, and it is cruel.
rigor.explanation: Assertion by adjective; the supporting evidence comes later, but this line itself is unsupported invective.

rigor.statement: Homelessness is growing. That is proven in the Salvation Army State of the Nation 2025 report released today.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a specific external source rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The example today is a Rotorua mother who's pregnant and who is sleeping in a doorway; the man from Christchurch who was sent out of hospital, denied emergency housing—readmitted to hospital from complications from sleeping in his car; the mother with a four-month-old in Tauranga who was denied the opportunity to apply for emergency housing and is living in a tent.
rigor.explanation: Illustrative anecdotes marshalled for emotional force; supports the point but is not systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: The failed policy of privatisation—the very policy that has led to unaffordable energy bills, because John Key sold 49 percent of the power companies. Apparently, the solution to that is to sell the rest!
rigor.explanation: Draws a causal line from the 2013 float to today's power prices; a contestable single-cause argument, though it identifies a real policy.

rigor.statement: If we want to pay for more doctors, if we want more teachers and more nurses and more social workers, if we want to have better welfare, if we want to have better public services, we have to pay for it, and that means we need growth.
rigor.explanation: A coherent means-ends argument linking growth to fiscal capacity, though stated as a general principle without figures.

rigor.statement: Real wealth is not measured in GDP; it is measured in the time that we are able to spend with our children.
rigor.explanation: A value proposition rather than an evidenced argument, though a coherent premise for what follows.

rigor.statement: The ideology, of the last century, at least, has been growth for growth's sake, and that is the ideology of the cancer cell.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an inflammatory analogy rather than evidence to characterise growth policy.

rigor.statement: A proposal for a road tunnel that is going to cost billions of dollars. Just in the news yesterday, it's been reconfirmed that the Government's own documents show it doesn't save travel time; it makes traffic worse.
rigor.explanation: Cites the Government's own documents as evidence against the project, a specific evidentiary appeal.

rigor.statement: If you designed a transport system where more people can walk, cycle, take public transport for the short trips, then the roads we have would work perfectly to move freight and to move the things that need to be moved by road.
rigor.explanation: A logically structured argument with an appeal to how comparable cities function; some empirical backing.

rigor.statement: The future ex-Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour has set up a few white-elephant bureaucracies. He's degraded the school lunches programme so that, where there were once healthy, nutritious lunches for kids, they're feeding them inedible slop. Earlier this week he ram-raided Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Emotive, exaggerated characterisations offered without evidence.

rigor.statement: We're growing our economy, especially needed after the last effort of the last Government and their "drunk uncle" ways of spending taxpayer money with no accountability.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a colourful analogy in place of evidence for the spending claim.

rigor.statement: Catherine wrote me a letter to tell me, "I can't even open a bank account for my child. I can't do that anymore." The reason why is because the AML/CFT regime is so strict that unless she can prove that her child lives in that house and has some sort of letter that has the child's name and address on it, she can't prove the existence of the child and can't open a bank account for her child.
rigor.explanation: Argues the case for reform via a single constituent anecdote rather than systematic evidence.

veracity.statement: The Greens are the official de-growth party. They're not in favour of economic growth, but most rational political parties are, apart from the Māori Party—they're also not in favour of growth.
veracity.explanation: The Greens do not describe themselves as a 'de-growth party'; a misleading caricature of their platform.

veracity.statement: We wake up in 2025 and we find ourselves 35 to 40 percent poorer than Australia.
veracity.explanation: The NZ-Australia GDP-per-capita gap is large and roughly in this range on some measures, though rounded and measure-dependent.

veracity.statement: What are the countries that look after the environment the best? Wealthy countries that grow. The poorest economies in the world desecrate the environment. They ravage the environment.
veracity.explanation: Partly true (wealth funds some environmental protection) but misleading as an absolute claim; wealthy nations also have large footprints.

veracity.statement: They have failed the economy: 2.4 percent growth in GDP when they took office, and now we're in recession.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate — growth on entering office turned to recession — though the precise figure is approximate.

veracity.statement: We've been in recession for nine months—entirely in your time.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the recession timing at the time; the exact duration and attribution are contestable but defensible.

veracity.statement: They have built zero houses. The only houses that have been built are the houses that the previous Government paid for.
veracity.explanation: 'Zero' is hyperbolic and misleading; construction pipelines were funded under both governments, so an absolute claim overstates the case.

veracity.statement: They stand there after firing thousands upon thousands of people, after pulling funding out of hospital builds and school builds and social house builds—to the tune of 14,000 people have lost their jobs in construction.
veracity.explanation: Construction employment did fall materially in the period, but the precise 14,000 figure and its sole attribution to Government decisions are debatable.

veracity.statement: Homelessness is growing. That is proven in the Salvation Army State of the Nation 2025 report released today.
veracity.explanation: Cites a same-day named report as the basis; consistent with reported trends, though 'proven' overstates a single report.

veracity.statement: The failed policy of privatisation—the very policy that has led to unaffordable energy bills, because John Key sold 49 percent of the power companies. Apparently, the solution to that is to sell the rest!
veracity.explanation: The 49% sell-down is accurate; the claim that it caused unaffordable bills is an oversimplification of multiple price drivers.

veracity.statement: There are over 20,000 people on the social housing waiting list, and their solution is to fund 750 a year, but the thing that I find most egregious and most disingenuous is the claim that they have met their emergency housing target five years early. It's just not true.
veracity.explanation: Waitlist figure and funding numbers are broadly accurate; the disputed 'five years early' claim is a genuine contested characterisation rather than clearly false.

veracity.statement: It's just a mystery to people like their finance spokesperson how we landed up in the worst recession in 30 years.
veracity.explanation: 'Worst recession in 30 years' is a superlative that overstates the downturn's severity relative to prior recessions.

veracity.statement: I'm proud that we've done stuff like going from almost 5,000 households in emergency accommodation, to 591 in a year. We set a target of six years; we did it five years early.
veracity.explanation: The headline numbers are real but their meaning is disputed (people diverted rather than housed), so the framing is partly misleading.

veracity.statement: I was speaking with Horowhenua District Council staff about this; more than $35,000 in traffic management for an Anzac Day parade.
veracity.explanation: A plausible sourced anecdote, though a single unverified figure used to illustrate a broader claim.

veracity.statement: Under NZTE, in just three years, Invest New Zealand has backed 324 Māori businesses, generating $753 million in investments.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about programme outputs; plausible but not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: In my electorate of Rongotai, we have a predator-free peninsula. We have record numbers of native birds coming back to the city.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Wellington's well-documented predator-free efforts and rising native bird counts.

veracity.statement: A proposal for a road tunnel that is going to cost billions of dollars. Just in the news yesterday, it's been reconfirmed that the Government's own documents show it doesn't save travel time; it makes traffic worse.
veracity.explanation: A concrete claim about official documents; plausible but a contestable characterisation of modelling.

veracity.statement: His newly minted Minister of Health confirmed that the hospital rebuild would proceed but it would proceed with less beds than the current Dunedin Hospital.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim consistent with the reported Dunedin Hospital scaling-back debate at the time.

veracity.statement: The future ex-Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour has set up a few white-elephant bureaucracies. He's degraded the school lunches programme so that, where there were once healthy, nutritious lunches for kids, they're feeding them inedible slop. Earlier this week he ram-raided Parliament.

charisma.statement: I’d like to commend the Hon Ginny Andersen, the Minister from the Labour Party who brought it to this House before the election with the support of many in the House, and I’d like to commend the Minister of Justice from the National Party who carried on the work and has ensured that this bill has gotten right through the process.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits ministers from both Labour and National, modelling cross-party cooperation.

charisma.statement: people sometimes don’t believe that parliamentarians agree on things, but there are times when we actually do get together and agree on things because it is the right thing to do.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared purpose across the House and counters cynicism about Parliament — unifying.

charisma.statement: We should feel pleased about the degree of agreement across the House on it, but we shouldn’t pat ourselves on the back too much. There is much more to be done in this space, and I hope that people right across the House are committed to getting more work done in this area.
charisma.explanation: Balances celebration with a call to continued cross-House effort; inclusive and forward-looking.

charisma.statement: There have been many speeches given this afternoon on the importance of this legislation, and I commend members from across the House for their delivery on this.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and praises members across party lines.

charisma.statement: Many of the initial changes for anti - money-laundering (AML) came through under the previous John Key National Government, and I remember working on those and identifying where the weaknesses were in the New Zealand system in order to make some of the changes that closed loops and made it harder for organised criminal groups to exploit New Zealand as a way of cleaning dirty money.
charisma.explanation: Credits a political opponent's past government for the original reforms — a bridge-building acknowledgement.

charisma.statement: what’s the point of taking a gang patch off someone if you’re enabling them to peddle meth and clean that money in a dirty business?
charisma.explanation: A partisan zinger aimed at her own side more than at persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: We make laws to protect people, to protect our communities, and to protect our businesses, and I believe that red tape is important, but as was just said by the previous speaker, Dr Vanessa Weenink, at times we need to consider that.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle by explicitly agreeing with a National member's point about red tape.

civility.statement: I’m glad that the Parliament can agree on this one, and I look forward to much more agreement as we move through our justice programme later on today.
civility.explanation: Respectful, focused on shared agreement across the House.

civility.statement: It’s one thing to talk tough about crime and it’s one thing to rattle off a list of things that are happening in the Justice Committee, but whether they are efficacious or not, whether they’re grounded in decent policy formation or not, or whether they’re just a signal to people to emphasise the fact that the Government thinks they’re tough on crime is a whole other conversation.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's approach but engages the substance (efficacy, policy formation) rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: It must be painful sitting on that side of the House and not being able to imagine a world where you can do more than one thing at once and where you can address both the drivers of crime and address those that have committed a crime.
civility.explanation: Mocks the intelligence/capacity of the opposition rather than engaging their argument.

civility.statement: It must be difficult for those who have left these benches because they weren’t effective at doing anything, to see effectiveness on this side of the House.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on opponents' competence and effectiveness.

civility.statement: I will put on record my concern that it’s taken until now for this bill to actually work its way through.
civility.explanation: Mild criticism of the legislative timeline; process-focused, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I want to thank all members of this House who are voting for this today, and the Justice Committee for doing the work that they did.
civility.explanation: Gracious and respectful toward colleagues.

civility.statement: I’d like to commend the Hon Ginny Andersen, the Minister from the Labour Party who brought it to this House before the election with the support of many in the House, and I’d like to commend the Minister of Justice from the National Party who carried on the work and has ensured that this bill has gotten right through the process.
civility.explanation: Generous and respectful toward political opponents.

civility.statement: We should feel pleased about the degree of agreement across the House on it, but we shouldn’t pat ourselves on the back too much. There is much more to be done in this space, and I hope that people right across the House are committed to getting more work done in this area.
civility.explanation: Humble and constructive, no attacks.

civility.statement: There have been many speeches given this afternoon on the importance of this legislation, and I commend members from across the House for their delivery on this.
civility.explanation: Respectful and collegial.

civility.statement: what’s the point of taking a gang patch off someone if you’re enabling them to peddle meth and clean that money in a dirty business?
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's priorities via policy contrast rather than personal attack, but the 'dirty business' jab sharpens it.

civility.statement: There were some really surprising remarks, actually, from the Acting Prime Minister, Winston Peters, saying he thought we didn’t actually deserve the first place in the first place, which I found quite astounding.
civility.explanation: Characterises an opponent's remarks as astounding — a jab at Peters, but mild and tied to a real statement rather than an insult.

civility.statement: We make laws to protect people, to protect our communities, and to protect our businesses, and I believe that red tape is important, but as was just said by the previous speaker, Dr Vanessa Weenink, at times we need to consider that.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's contribution.

veracity.statement: whether we see the increase in unemployment, whether we see the continuing bite of the cost of living—all of those things impact crime.
veracity.explanation: Claims of rising unemployment and cost-of-living pressure are directionally accurate for the period, though stated loosely.

veracity.statement: Some of that work has included the biggest ever investment in family violence and sexual violence prevention and support services.
veracity.explanation: Superlative claim about record investment is broadly supported for the previous Labour government but 'biggest ever' is hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: Approximately one-quarter of submitters raised various concerns about the bill’s impact on children, and the select committee made amendments in that regard. Submitters expressed concern that provisions could harm victims, and there were safeguards put in place to address that.
veracity.explanation: Description of the committee process is plausible and checkable against the committee report.

veracity.statement: in doing this process of making it harder for money-laundering and for crime, we’ve made it harder for businesses, we’ve made it harder for everyday New Zealanders just to get a loan, just to get a mortgage—
veracity.explanation: AML customer due-diligence genuinely does add friction to loans/mortgages; broadly accurate though generalised.

veracity.statement: Now, all the research shows that there is actually no such thing as parental alienation syndrome. It’s been dreamed up.
veracity.explanation: It is true that 'parental alienation syndrome' lacks recognition as a formal diagnosis, but 'all the research shows...no such thing' overstates a genuinely contested area.

veracity.statement: Many of the initial changes for anti - money-laundering (AML) came through under the previous John Key National Government, and I remember working on those and identifying where the weaknesses were in the New Zealand system in order to make some of the changes that closed loops and made it harder for organised criminal groups to exploit New Zealand as a way of cleaning dirty money.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the foundational AML/CFT Act 2009 and subsequent reforms did originate under a National-led government.

veracity.statement: In the past year—roughly a year, year and a half—we have seen an exponential increase in the prevalence of methamphetamine in our waste-water testing. We have the highest levels of meth coming into New Zealand that we have ever seen.
veracity.explanation: Wastewater testing did show record methamphetamine consumption in this period, so directionally accurate, though 'exponential' is loose.

veracity.statement: The last big update of this particular Act was in 2017, and since then two major assessments have been completed, one of them by the Financial Action Task Force in 2019-21 as part of some of our agreements and obligations under the mutual evaluation of New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Accurate legislative and evaluation history (2017 update, FATF mutual evaluation, 2022 statutory review).

veracity.statement: This bill amends the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, and that’s the principal Act, to strengthen New Zealand’s regime against financial crimes. This amendment bill responds to two pieces of work that we’ve already heard about from other members—the Financial Action Task Force that was held between 2019 and 2021, and, secondly, it’s a statutory review of the original Act; that is, the 2009 Act.
veracity.explanation: Correctly identifies the principal Act (2009) and the two review processes the bill responds to.

veracity.statement: This week, New Zealand lost its coveted first place, not in a sporting event but actually in the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index, and we dropped from first to fourth.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes New Zealand's slide down the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index, though the exact ranking specifics can vary by year.

veracity.statement: The 26 proposals that are in this were looked at from the 2020 review, which was including internal and external connections and recommendations that were made. There were people like Crown Law Office, Department of Corrections, Department of Internal Affairs, Inland Revenue Department, Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, just to name a few.
veracity.explanation: Description of the review process and consulted agencies is plausible and checkable.

authenticity.statement: Some of that work has included the biggest ever investment in family violence and sexual violence prevention and support services.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated priorities on family violence; claim aligns with the party's record.

authenticity.statement: In 2022, I was approached by two women in Nelson—one Adele Keefe, who’s part of an organisation called Mana Wāhine, and another woman who I won’t name. I have permission to share her story, but I’m going to keep her name secret.
authenticity.explanation: Recounts her own direct constituency casework that led to the bill, consistent with the advocacy role she claims.

authenticity.statement: Everything that this Government is doing—everything that we’re doing—to support children through the education system and help them to learn, everything that we’re doing to boost and grow our economy, is so that we can make people’s incomes better, we can reduce the stress of the cost of living, and so that we can actually help families to thrive.
authenticity.explanation: Stated alignment between government actions and its family-wellbeing goal, with no visible action-vs-words tension but also no delivery shown.

divination.statement: This bill makes 26 amendments that will improve the effectiveness, the efficiency, and consistency of the anti-money laundering regulatory regime for the benefit of Kiwi businesses; support the better functioning of the responsible agencies; and improve New Zealand’s compliance with international standards.
divination.explanation: Predicts the amendments 'will improve' effectiveness and compliance ahead of the 2029 FATF assessment — plausible but unproven until enacted and evaluated.

civility.statement: Perhaps a word of advice to this Government, as we've seen a whole number of bills that impact on Māori and indeed this nation as they have been pushed through the submission process: perhaps we should take more to the marae, where our people can be heard; where the issues that they raise can be actually heard and felt, as it was for myself and the committee members on Pārāwera Marae that day.
civility.explanation: Frames a criticism of the Government's submission process as constructive advice, engaging the substance (how consultation is done) rather than attacking anyone personally.

civility.statement: Let's take them to the marae. Zoom committee meetings just aren't good enough, and I think our people, and New Zealanders right across, deserve so much more.
civility.explanation: Pointed but focused on process quality, not personal attack.

civility.statement: we are, as a Crown, recognising the blood on our hands—perhaps, as the previous speaker, Steve Abel, would say; I am going to quibble and say I don't want to hear someone say there's blood on my children's hands. I don't think that's going to help, so I repudiate that, but I do think the Crown has got a debt to pay and this is a very small part of paying it.
civility.explanation: Disagrees directly with a colleague's framing but does so respectfully, engaging the idea ('blood on my children's hands') rather than the person, and concedes the Crown's debt.

civility.statement: I recently asked our whānau who were only here last week on the return of Maunga Taranaki, and them expressing their feelings in the constant contradiction of one day turning up to Parliament to an important day like this, and then another day slamming that side of the Government in oral submissions for the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill.
civility.explanation: Raises a real perceived inconsistency in Government conduct; pointed and accusatory ('slamming') but aimed at conduct, not personal insult.

specificity.statement: Perhaps a word of advice to this Government, as we've seen a whole number of bills that impact on Māori and indeed this nation as they have been pushed through the submission process: perhaps we should take more to the marae, where our people can be heard; where the issues that they raise can be actually heard and felt, as it was for myself and the committee members on Pārāwera Marae that day.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (hold hearings on marae) but no detail on which bills, how, or when.

specificity.statement: Let's take them to the marae. Zoom committee meetings just aren't good enough, and I think our people, and New Zealanders right across, deserve so much more.
specificity.explanation: A concrete proposal (marae over Zoom) but no process detail or timeframe.

specificity.statement: One of the key ways we can do that, in encouraging our young people to continue to carry on those stories in that rich tapestry of our heritage and our history, is we must continue to support local stories and local communities for local people.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at 'support local stories and communities' but names no mechanism, funding, or measure.

specificity.statement: During 2017 and 2020, my leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, encouraged me to find some pūtea to address the outstanding matters of rehabilitating Ruapekapeka, Rangiriri Pā, and other places of such significance.
specificity.explanation: Names the years, the funder role, and specific sites (Ruapekapeka, Rangiriri Pā) but no dollar figures.

specificity.statement: The 28th of October is held as a national day of significance for the Land Wars of Aotearoa. Te Pāti Māori states that this day should be held as a national public holiday, just as we commemorate Anzac.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific date and a concrete, measurable proposal (make it a public holiday) with a clear comparator (Anzac).

specificity.statement: This brings me to stress to this coalition statement of "Rebalancing of the current history's education curriculum to be less focused on te ao Māori." We must keep the New Zealand history curriculum in schools.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific policy statement and takes a clear position (keep the curriculum) but offers no detail on how.

specificity.statement: The vesting and ownership arrangements in this bill are not redress provided in settlement of any historical claims under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, but the Ō-Rākau deed and this bill instead reflect the desire of all parties to acknowledge the history associated with, and the national significance of, the Battle of Ō-Rākau.
specificity.explanation: Precisely describes the legal character of the bill—not Treaty settlement redress but a distinct acknowledgement deed.

specificity.statement: This bill enables the record of title for the Ō-Rākau site to be held in the names of the ancestors who fought at the Battle of Ō-Rākau or had other connections with the land. It enables Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato to jointly have, and exercise, the rights and obligations of the registered owner of the site.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail on the legal mechanism—title held in ancestors' names, joint ownership by the three named iwi.

charisma.statement: Perhaps a word of advice to this Government, as we've seen a whole number of bills that impact on Māori and indeed this nation as they have been pushed through the submission process: perhaps we should take more to the marae, where our people can be heard; where the issues that they raise can be actually heard and felt, as it was for myself and the committee members on Pārāwera Marae that day.
charisma.explanation: Offers cross-cutting advice but mildly partisan, directed at 'this Government' rather than fully bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I think of the many from where I come from in the Far North to the many across the Waikato and right across the country, Bay of Plenty, so many other places where we know that if actions weren't taken—by, in particular, Māori ancestors but I will also say Pākehā farmers—to protect this land, it wouldn't have happened.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately inclusive, crediting both Māori ancestors and Pākehā farmers, seeking a shared national ownership of the story.

charisma.statement: One of the key ways we can do that, in encouraging our young people to continue to carry on those stories in that rich tapestry of our heritage and our history, is we must continue to support local stories and local communities for local people.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive framing about carrying stories forward, but appeals in general terms.

charisma.statement: It occurs to me that we of British descent—we New Zealanders—must own our part in the Battle of Ō-Rākau and in the Waikato Wars. We cannot be responsible personally for the actions of our ancestors, but we must account for the consequences of those actions, and we must, for the good of our descendants, seek to dull the blood on our hands.
charisma.explanation: Seeks collective national ownership and reconciliation, but the 'blood on our hands' framing risks alienating (the next speaker explicitly pushed back on it).

charisma.statement: If the objective of the invasion was land, then, surely, the recompense must be the return of land.
charisma.explanation: Persuasive framing for land return, though it appeals mainly to those already sympathetic.

charisma.statement: we are, as a Crown, recognising the blood on our hands—perhaps, as the previous speaker, Steve Abel, would say; I am going to quibble and say I don't want to hear someone say there's blood on my children's hands. I don't think that's going to help, so I repudiate that, but I do think the Crown has got a debt to pay and this is a very small part of paying it.
charisma.explanation: Finds common ground (Crown debt) while pushing back, but the pushback frames one side of the earlier speaker.

charisma.statement: I suppose I'll just finish by saying that this is something that the ACT Party supports because it continues New Zealand on a path where we recognise our history and come together as a people for the betterment of the future, but recognising and acknowledging the past and the mamae, the pain, that is still with us to this day.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly unifying—'come together as a people'—while acknowledging pain, inviting all sides in.

charisma.statement: any fair-minded New Zealander, once they are told the broad and factual story, has no hesitation in embracing the entirety of our history.
charisma.explanation: Invites a shared national embrace of history, though the 'fair-minded' framing subtly implies dissenters are not.

charisma.statement: This bill, which is about to pass, ought to be seen as an opportunity for not only the broader Waikato community but for all Kiwis to acknowledge and to learn about the history as we march towards 2040, because there are no saints, purely; there are no sinners, solely, in our history.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive ('all Kiwis') and nuanced 'no saints, no sinners' framing that invites people across divides to engage.

charisma.statement: Not often does this House come together—all six parties. I often say that the last time we were all on the same waka in this House was a tribute we had for Kiingi Tuheitia. Today, I'm heartened that the House unites again to pass this bill in honour of our late King, and all those who fought at Ō-Rākau.
charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party unity and frames the moment as bringing all six parties together—consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This brings me to stress to this coalition statement of "Rebalancing of the current history's education curriculum to be less focused on te ao Māori." We must keep the New Zealand history curriculum in schools.
charisma.explanation: A clear stance that rallies her own side against the coalition position rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: This is a major step in the Crown acknowledging the past so that we and iwi and the Crown can focus on the future. It was my privilege to help shepherd this bill through the House as part of the select committee process.
charisma.explanation: Forward-looking, inclusive framing (we, iwi, Crown together) though fairly conventional.

charisma.statement: Every member in this House should remember that, in 161 years, they're going to judge what we're doing today. My message to everyone in this room: be on the right side of history.
charisma.explanation: Addresses every member across the House with a unifying appeal to shared judgement by future generations.

charisma.statement: I look around this House today and in this spirit I ask all of us that we continue that mahi to do what's right to create better outcomes for Māori and for all of Aotearoa.
charisma.explanation: Directly invites the whole House to keep working together for shared outcomes—inclusive and consensus-oriented.

charisma.statement: I learnt more from this demonstration than I learnt from the movie, because the stories are real. They come from a different place. They come from our whānau and they come from lived history.
charisma.explanation: A warm, personal reflection valuing first-hand testimony; mildly persuasive but not aimed at bridging divides.

veracity.statement: Governor Grey himself visited the district in 1849 and he said that he had never seen a more thriving or contented population in any part of the world—he had never seen a more thriving and contented population in any part of the world.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the documented historical record of Grey's account of the prosperous Waikato Māori economy of the 1840s; framing is accurate though quoted from memory.

veracity.statement: It is that very same Governor Grey who led the deliberate war of conquest of the Waikato to steal that abundance from tangata whenua Māori.
veracity.explanation: Grey did initiate the 1863 Waikato invasion; historians broadly agree land/economic acquisition was a core motive. 'Deliberate war of conquest' is a defensible characterisation, mildly rhetorical.

veracity.statement: The worst atrocities in the New Zealand Wars were committed in Waikato and Bay of Plenty in the 1860s.
veracity.explanation: Defensible given events like Rangiaowhia; 'the worst' is a comparative judgement that is hard to establish definitively, so partly opinion.

veracity.statement: It is 161 years since the Battle of Ō-Rākau, and finally, here today, we are returning a portion of that land.
veracity.explanation: 1864 to 2025 is 161 years; accurate.

veracity.statement: Let's recall that 10 days after, after the Rangiaowhia horrors, the surveyors were in Kihikihi, dividing up the land and giving it out to the soldiers who'd fought in the battle—10 days.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical pattern of rapid confiscation and military settlement of Waikato land; the precise '10 days' is a specific claim not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: History did not begin just when the Treaty of Waitangi was signed; the history goes well before the Treaty of Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: Trivially accurate—Māori history long predates 1840.

veracity.statement: These were the Land Wars that were inflicted on our people of Waikato and Māori throughout the country—300 people to defend Ō-Rākau against 1,500 soldiers. This lasted over three days and 12,000 square kilometres of land.
veracity.explanation: The ~300 defenders, ~1,500 troops, and three-day siege match the historical record; the '12,000 square kilometres' figure (a reference to the wider confiscation) is loosely attached and less precise.

veracity.statement: The 28th of October is held as a national day of significance for the Land Wars of Aotearoa. Te Pāti Māori states that this day should be held as a national public holiday, just as we commemorate Anzac.
veracity.explanation: 28 October (Te Pūtake o te Riri) is indeed the recognised national commemoration day for the Land Wars.

veracity.statement: Growing up in Aotearoa New Zealand, I did not learn that at school, and so I wanted to briefly acknowledge the day, acknowledge the significance of it.
veracity.explanation: A personal historical claim consistent with the widely documented absence of NZ Wars history in the school curriculum of earlier decades.

veracity.statement: The vesting and ownership arrangements in this bill are not redress provided in settlement of any historical claims under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, but the Ō-Rākau deed and this bill instead reflect the desire of all parties to acknowledge the history associated with, and the national significance of, the Battle of Ō-Rākau.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the bill's legal status as separate from Treaty settlement redress.

veracity.statement: I'm also pleased the land is going back to this entity, because we should note that, in the 1880s, the Crown explored acquiring the battle site to gift to Te Kooti to keep him from returning to the East Coast.
veracity.explanation: A specific historical claim about an 1880s Crown proposal regarding Te Kooti; plausible and detailed but not independently verifiable from the text alone.

rigor.statement: It is that very same Governor Grey who led the deliberate war of conquest of the Waikato to steal that abundance from tangata whenua Māori.
rigor.explanation: Connects Grey's earlier praise of the district to his later invasion to establish motive; reasoning is grounded but the 'steal that abundance' causal claim is asserted rather than fully evidenced.

rigor.statement: It occurs to me that we of British descent—we New Zealanders—must own our part in the Battle of Ō-Rākau and in the Waikato Wars. We cannot be responsible personally for the actions of our ancestors, but we must account for the consequences of those actions, and we must, for the good of our descendants, seek to dull the blood on our hands.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clear distinction between personal guilt and collective responsibility for consequences—a coherent moral argument.

rigor.statement: If the objective of the invasion was land, then, surely, the recompense must be the return of land.
rigor.explanation: Clean if-then reasoning where the conclusion follows from the stated premise about the invasion's motive.

rigor.statement: we are, as a Crown, recognising the blood on our hands—perhaps, as the previous speaker, Steve Abel, would say; I am going to quibble and say I don't want to hear someone say there's blood on my children's hands. I don't think that's going to help, so I repudiate that, but I do think the Crown has got a debt to pay and this is a very small part of paying it.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes inherited personal guilt from institutional Crown responsibility—a reasoned distinction, though asserted rather than argued at length.

rigor.statement: any fair-minded New Zealander, once they are told the broad and factual story, has no hesitation in embracing the entirety of our history.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a no-true-Scotsman style appeal ('any fair-minded' person agrees) rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: This bill, which is about to pass, ought to be seen as an opportunity for not only the broader Waikato community but for all Kiwis to acknowledge and to learn about the history as we march towards 2040, because there are no saints, purely; there are no sinners, solely, in our history.
rigor.explanation: The 'no saints, no sinners' point acknowledges historical complexity and resists a simple good/evil dichotomy.

rigor.statement: History did not begin just when the Treaty of Waitangi was signed; the history goes well before the Treaty of Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: Uses the point to argue against confining discussion to Tribunal-era history; a sound if brief argument.

strength.statement: During 2017 and 2020, my leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, encouraged me to find some pūtea to address the outstanding matters of rehabilitating Ruapekapeka, Rangiriri Pā, and other places of such significance.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete past action—securing funding for heritage/battle site rehabilitation—consistent with NZ First's Provincial Growth Fund record; delivery on named sites is broadly supported.

strength.statement: This is a major step in the Crown acknowledging the past so that we and iwi and the Crown can focus on the future. It was my privilege to help shepherd this bill through the House as part of the select committee process.
strength.explanation: Claims a real role in shepherding the bill through committee; modest, in-progress delivery of a bill about to pass.

authenticity.statement: During 2017 and 2020, my leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, encouraged me to find some pūtea to address the outstanding matters of rehabilitating Ruapekapeka, Rangiriri Pā, and other places of such significance.
authenticity.explanation: Aligns his current support for the bill with a documented prior record of funding similar sites.

veracity.statement: This bill will, essentially, as we've heard, give effect to a deed of agreement between the Crown and Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato-Tainui iwi, and this deed of agreement will, essentially, place a piece of land that's almost about 10 hectares in size under a title with the names of people long gone
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's effect and the parties to the deed; the ~10 hectare Ō-Rākau site vesting matches the legislation.

veracity.statement: the story that my colleague before me spoke about saw 300 iwi defenders protecting this piece of land and all that dwelt on it, against all odds, against about 1,500 British troops
veracity.explanation: Roughly matches the historical record of the 1864 Battle of Ō-Rākau (~300 Māori defenders against a much larger colonial force of well over a thousand); figures are approximate but defensible.

veracity.statement: For instance, I was looking at the pūtea—you know, $1.7 million for the transfer of the Ō-Rākau site at no cost to iwi, $75,000 to fund the establishment of managing entity for the Ō-Rākau site, $306,000 to fund historical research. It's chump change, really.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific funding figures presented as fact; consistent with the deed's financial terms.

veracity.statement: It's wonderful to talk about the 300 against 1,500, but right now we've got Māori who are feeling under threat and we've got 400,000 people who've been making submissions to a select committee.
veracity.explanation: The Treaty Principles Bill submissions were around 300,000; '400,000' appears to overstate the recorded figure.

veracity.statement: Just two weeks ago in this House, we acknowledged the legal personhood of Taranaki Maunga—it was an amazing day.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Taranaki Maunga collective redress legislation granting legal personhood passed in late January 2025, roughly two weeks prior.

veracity.statement: the imprisonment rate for burglary, which has a maximum penalty of 10 years, reduced from 50 percent in 2016-17 to 39 percent in 2022-23. The imprisonment rate for robbery, which has a 14-year maximum penalty, dropped from 74 percent to 58 percent in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Presents specific, checkable imprisonment-rate statistics that are consistent with Ministry of Justice data; treated as accurate absent contrary evidence.

veracity.statement: The bill builds on the Government's ongoing effort to restore law and order, and we started off with passing legislation to tackle gangs and to reinstate the three-strikes regime.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of legislation the coalition has passed.

veracity.statement: This Government is increasing police numbers—500 more by the end of 2025.
veracity.explanation: Reflects a real coalition commitment; framed as fact but is a forward target that was still in progress.

veracity.statement: The impact of all these laws, according to the legal experts of the country, is that the number of Māori incarcerated within the justice system will increase—increase!
veracity.explanation: Consistent with regulatory-impact analyses warning of disproportionate effects on Māori.

veracity.statement: The departments within the justice system have already researched these phenomena. They already know: the impact of the law on Māori is not the same as the impact of the law on other people.

civility.statement: Does he expect this loose-change announcement to distract the New Zealand public from the fact that his Government continues to put commercial interests over protecting te taiao for future generations?
civility.explanation: 'Loose-change announcement' and imputing an intent to 'distract' is combative framing rather than engaging the policy on its merits.

civility.statement: Can the Minister confirm that parliamentary activities, including the member for Auckland Central commuting to work by aeroplane every week, contributes to climate change?
civility.explanation: A pointed personal jab singling out a named member's commuting to score a rhetorical point rather than engaging the emissions debate substantively.

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. How proper is it for a member to ask a question and, when the question is being answered, shout out and hold up the paper to the Minister, “You gave us the numbers.”? So he’s asking a question about numbers he already had in his hand. How professional, in a political sense and a parliamentary sense, is that?
civility.explanation: Criticises a member's conduct pointedly but frames it around parliamentary propriety rather than a personal insult.

specificity.statement: Tourism is an absolutely critical industry for this great country of ours. It drives almost $38 billion, employs almost 200,000 people up and down the country.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete dollar and employment figures rather than a vague claim about the sector's importance.

specificity.statement: There’s $33 billion in the national transport plan; there’s $148 billion in the Infrastructure Commission pipeline. There’s work coming and it’s starting to happen. We’re getting roads built: Brougham St’s starting, Hawke’s Bay’s started.
specificity.explanation: Names dollar figures and specific projects (Brougham St, Hawke's Bay) rather than generic promises of infrastructure.

specificity.statement: Construction on Takitimu North Link stage one—a four-lane expressway between Tauranga and Te Puna—is now past the halfway point. So we know there’s $33 billion set aside in our National Land Transport Programme.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project, its scope (four-lane, Tauranga–Te Puna), progress (past halfway), and a funding figure.

specificity.statement: In terms of manufacturing, the index lifted sharply in January to its highest level since September 2022. And while, of course, individual manufacturers will have their own sets of circumstances, manufacturing on the whole is now expanding after 22 months of contraction.
specificity.explanation: Cites the named index, the timeframe, and the 22-month contraction figure.

specificity.statement: The market and most economists are expecting a reduction in the OCR of 50 basis points. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates which, in turn, support a growing economy, jobs, and incomes for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names the magnitude (50bp), resulting rate (3.75%), and mechanism.

specificity.statement: Taxpayers deserve to know that when a dollar of theirs that’s been taken out of their household budget is being spent by Ministers, it is going to its absolute best value and impact.
specificity.explanation: A general value-for-money principle without figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: I’ve announced a plan to reintroduce pay deductions for partial strikes. This will be discussed at select committee this week. This Government has committed to this change because we need to restore balance to the rights and consequences of collective bargaining. If workers are partially striking by refusing to do their normal work, why should they get paid a normal wage?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy (pay deductions for partial strikes) and its immediate legislative stage (select committee this week).

specificity.statement: When teachers refused to teach certain year groups on particular days, it was parents who paid the price by having to take unplanned leave from work in order to take care of their kids who were rostered home, not to mention the cost of lost learning for the students. When hospital-based nuclear medicine technologists limited the number of scans completed each day, it was patients waiting for their results who suffered.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific real-world examples (teacher rosters, nuclear-medicine scan limits) rather than abstractions.

specificity.statement: There’ll be a cap on total sentencing discounts of 40 percent, and there will no longer be repeated discounts for remorse. You can’t be remorseful repeatedly. The bill also makes a number of other changes, including the addition of a range of new aggravating factors, such as for adults who offend in crimes alongside young people, such as in ram raids.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete mechanism (40% discount cap, removal of repeat remorse discounts, new aggravating factors) rather than a general 'tough on crime' claim.

specificity.statement: That’s why the Government set an ambitious target of seeing a reduction of 20,000 fewer victims of assault, robbery, and sexual assault by 2029. The data has long lead times, but early results from our work have been encouraging. There have been 24,000 fewer victims over the year ending October 2024 compared to the year ending June 2024.
specificity.explanation: Provides a numeric target, categories, deadline, and a cited figure.

specificity.statement: I especially stand by my actions to provide funding of $30.6 million over four years to continue the fast-track youth offending programme and extend the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds, which will contribute to Government Target 3, a 15 percent reduction in the total number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending behaviour.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact funding ($30.6m over four years), the age extension, and the linked target (15% reduction).

specificity.statement: My measure of its success is around making sure that our communities are safe, and we are also putting in place opportunities for young people to be the best version of themselves. What they do with that is ultimately up to them.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspirational language ('best version of themselves') with no measurable indicators.

specificity.statement: These young people right now, currently, under the current legislation, are ending up in youth justice facilities. They are repeat, serious youth offenders who to qualify to be part of the MSA programme must have committed two crimes with a sentence of 10 years or more. They will end up in a youth justice facility anyway.
specificity.explanation: States the concrete qualifying criteria for the programme.

specificity.statement: I recently had the pleasure of opening a new motorway interchange, building on 20 years of long-term planning and infrastructure development... And with the $18 million that was allocated several years ago, it was a pleasure—with Tapuika, the tangata whenua—to open the infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names the $18m allocation, the 20-year planning horizon, and the local partners.

specificity.statement: Just this week, new stats show a 12 percent increase in international visitor arrivals compared to December 2023. That’s an 85 percent recovery of international visitor arrivals compared to 2019. Visitor numbers from Australia are currently at about 90 percent, compared to 2019, so we know there’s more room to grow.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete percentages for growth, overall recovery, and the Australian market specifically.

specificity.statement: The benefits of growing these visitor numbers will reach beyond our cities and into our regions: 93 percent of New Zealanders see benefits from increased tourism.
specificity.explanation: Offers a specific figure but attaches it to a broad claim about regional benefit.

specificity.statement: Well, I’ll tell the member what action we’ve taken... So I’ll tell you what I did: I brought together a stakeholders group, with everyone working together: residents and ratepayers groups, business associations, social service providers, Government agencies, and the police. We’re making big progress and we’ve made massive steps in terms of making sure that our CBD is now a safer place.
specificity.explanation: Names the composition of the stakeholder group but not measurable actions or outcomes tied to the meth figures asked about.

specificity.statement: Why is he comfortable with his Government only investing a mere 0.88 percent of the value of tourism on conservation land at the same time as it is enabling more mining in Aotearoa?
specificity.explanation: Derives a precise ratio (0.88%) from the $30m spend against the ~$3.4bn conservation-land tourism value.

specificity.statement: Is he aware that the coal set to be mined by just one of his fast-track projects would increase emissions by 66.5 million tonnes, meanwhile his latest international commitment to reduce emissions is just 42 million tonnes?
specificity.explanation: Cites precise figures (66.5Mt project emissions vs 42Mt reduction commitment) to sharpen the contrast.

specificity.statement: Inanahi—yesterday—I announced a $30 million investment from the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy to fund more than a dozen projects to boost biodiversity—kanorautanga—and manuhiri infrastructure in tourism. Tourism is a key critical economic driver, and nature, alongside culture, are our biggest drawcards for international tourists. Around 50 percent of tourists—manuhiri—cite it as their primary reason for coming here.
specificity.explanation: Names the $30m source (IVL), the number of projects, and a specific tourist-motivation statistic.

specificity.statement: We are investing $19 million into protecting biodiversity by reducing the spread of pests, predators, and weeds. This includes stopping the spread of wallabies in renowned and spectacular places like the Te Arawa Lakes district; managing deer and goat populations... targeted predator control to protect native species, especially the critically endangered tuturuatu, or southern dotterel birds, in Rakiura National Park; and stopping and removing wilding pines.
specificity.explanation: Breaks the $19m into named activities, locations, and target species rather than a general biodiversity claim.

specificity.statement: The bill vests title to this 9.7 hectare site, 5 kilometres east of Kihikihi, in those tūpuna of Ō-Rākau, the ancestors of Ō-Rākau... the site, once this bill is passed, will transfer 21 working days after the Royal assent by our Governor-General, Cindy Kiro, which will provide for it to be vested before the 161st anniversary of this battle.
specificity.explanation: States the exact site area, location, transfer mechanism, timeframe (21 working days post-assent), and the anniversary deadline.

specificity.statement: I look forward to engaging with nearly 30 percent of the entire whenua of Aotearoa to generate more revenue, and to do that in an appropriate manner with reference to iwi and hapū relationships, speeding up concessions and ensuring expedited, appropriate statutory planning.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at the scale (30% of the land) and direction (speeding concessions) but without concrete measures or timelines.

specificity.statement: Does announcing $500,000 of additional spending for tourism marketing make up for the $20 million that was cut from the “marketing New Zealand as a tourist destination” fund at Budget 2024?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact amounts and the specific fund and budget year.

specificity.statement: It’s important that the House note that the value of the fishing industry is well over $1.6 billion. A part of that broader marine industry is aquaculture that has been turbocharged as a consequence of extending marine farming permits.
specificity.explanation: Cites a sector value and names the permit-extension mechanism, though 'turbocharged' is imprecise.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge that, under his last year in Government, there were 43,000 New Zealand citizens that left New Zealand. That number has crept up—up to 47,000 in the last year—and that is why this Government’s working incredibly hard on improving the economy so that there are opportunities for people here.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about infrastructure delays driving engineers to Australia, he pivots to aggregate citizen-departure numbers and blames the previous government rather than addressing the engineering question.

forthrightness.statement: Isn’t it ironic that the member that caused the grief in the New Zealand economy is now criticising us for trying to fix it?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Engineering NZ chief executive's specific statement was wrong, he does not engage with it and deflects to a rhetorical jab.

forthrightness.statement: We’re embracing “Everything must go!”, like high inflation, like high interest rates, like wasteful spending, like cycle bridges, like Let’s Get Wellington Moving. We’re saying everything must go, including gang members going up, violent crime going up, retail crime going up. And who was the police Minister for five years?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about health-system leadership departures, he ignores the question entirely to deliver a scripted list and a jab.

forthrightness.statement: I’d just say we took the public approach to the Labour Party at the last election, where they said, “Everyone must go.”, and, actually, the member is the only member who hasn’t got anywhere else to go.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a pointed question about David Seymour's conduct and promotion, he does not address it at all and delivers a joke at Hipkins' expense.

forthrightness.statement: That is rich coming from that member, because that Government presided over an absolute shameful record on emergency housing. When we came to Government, there was 3,200 households living in motels—
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about where emergency-housing residents have gone and rising homelessness by attacking the previous record instead of explaining.

forthrightness.statement: I’m actually incredibly proud of that investment, and I’d hope that the member would get behind it. Surely the member is saying yes to $30 million going in for this particular task.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how a $30m announcement offsets $47.2m in DOC cuts, he restates pride in the investment without addressing the net shortfall.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I mean, I think the Minister’s done a very good job, actually, identifying 37 critical minerals, of which 21 of them we think are actually in this country. Importantly, coal and metallurgical coal and gold are actually really important for our mining industry.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why coal (a fossil fuel, not a mineral) was added to the critical minerals list, he praises the Minister and asserts coal's importance without addressing the classification point.

forthrightness.statement: This is an outrageous conversation we’re actually having here, because this country needs to grow. We need to have economic growth. Are the Greens not for economic growth? I mean, what’s the position? You have to grow an economy. You need to have energy to do it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to Rod Carr's 'crimes against humanity' remark, he does not engage with it and pivots to growth talking points.

forthrightness.statement: Did the member just say the $125 billion that was cut from conservation spending? Because that would be a ludicrous figure to use in this House.
forthrightness.explanation: Seizes on a likely misspeak ('billion' vs 'million') rather than answering the substance about conservation cuts.

forthrightness.statement: On the other side of the House, they’ve got to make up their mind. Should we be investing more in attracting tourists, as these questions seem to suggest, or does she not think tourism is a good idea, as other of her members have suggested? I don’t know which way is up or down with you guys.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether $500k offsets a $20m cut, she pivots to attacking Labour's supposed inconsistency rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Taxpayers deserve to know that when a dollar of theirs that’s been taken out of their household budget is being spent by Ministers, it is going to its absolute best value and impact.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially addresses the cycle-trail cut question with a value-for-money principle but does not engage the specific $24m reduction.

forthrightness.statement: Well, look, our primary target is to reduce the number of victims of crime, and that is what this Government is focused on. As that member is well aware, sadly, Māori are more likely to be victims of crime than the general public. That is why we are absolutely focused on reducing the number of victims of crime.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will commit to setting the three justice-sector CEOs targets to reduce Māori overrepresentation, he redirects to the victims target and never answers the commitment question.

forthrightness.statement: My measure of its success is around making sure that our communities are safe, and we are also putting in place opportunities for young people to be the best version of themselves. What they do with that is ultimately up to them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for her specific measures of success for the 12-month MSA pilot, she offers general aims (community safety, opportunity) rather than defined metrics.

forthrightness.statement: These young people right now, currently, under the current legislation, are ending up in youth justice facilities. They are repeat, serious youth offenders who to qualify to be part of the MSA programme must have committed two crimes with a sentence of 10 years or more. They will end up in a youth justice facility anyway.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly engages the 'what works' challenge by reframing the cohort, though she does not directly rebut the evidence the Commissioner cites.

forthrightness.statement: As I’ve said, there are a couple of areas—Tekapō is one—where I know the mayor is concerned about it. But the reality is the majority of New Zealand recognise that we want more visitors; 93 percent of New Zealanders realise how it’s good for New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about Tekapō's infrastructure deficits and inequitable ratepayer burden, she acknowledges the concern but pivots to overall public support rather than addressing the cost burden.

forthrightness.statement: No, I’m not concerned at all about the gangs controlling the streets in Auckland, because the police are doing an outstanding job in policing the gangs in Auckland, and that’s certainly the feedback that I get.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'are you concerned' with a clear no and a reason, though he sidesteps the 129% meth-consumption figure embedded in the question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don’t know whether that’s dealers dumping methamphetamine or not. We know that we have got a problem in this country with methamphetamine. We know that it’s a wrecking ball through people’s lives in every part of society.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether record wastewater meth levels make New Zealanders feel safer, he casts doubt on the data ('dealers dumping') and speaks generally rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’ll tell the member what action we’ve taken... So I’ll tell you what I did: I brought together a stakeholders group, with everyone working together: residents and ratepayers groups, business associations, social service providers, Government agencies, and the police. We’re making big progress and we’ve made massive steps in terms of making sure that our CBD is now a safer place.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what action addresses the Salvation Army's 32.4kg/week meth and $34m weekly harm findings, he describes an Auckland CBD stakeholder group rather than the drug-consumption data.

forthrightness.statement: I look forward to engaging with nearly 30 percent of the entire whenua of Aotearoa to generate more revenue, and to do that in an appropriate manner with reference to iwi and hapū relationships, speeding up concessions and ensuring expedited, appropriate statutory planning.
forthrightness.explanation: Broadly endorses the premise of the friendly question about growing conservation-estate revenue, but keeps the 'appropriate manner' caveat rather than fully committing to the 'accelerated pace' framing.

rigor.statement: Isn’t it ironic that the member that caused the grief in the New Zealand economy is now criticising us for trying to fix it?
rigor.explanation: Answers a factual challenge with an ad hominem about who ‘caused the grief’ instead of evidence.

rigor.statement: This is an outrageous conversation we’re actually having here, because this country needs to grow. We need to have economic growth. Are the Greens not for economic growth? I mean, what’s the position? You have to grow an economy. You need to have energy to do it.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a false dichotomy (growth vs the Greens' position) rather than reasoning about the emissions point raised.

rigor.statement: Having an oil and gas ban that that member signed up for, which has led us to import in huge amounts of Indonesian coal— to keep our lights on when we don’t have rain and wind in this economy isn’t good.
rigor.explanation: Draws a direct causal line from the ban to coal imports while omitting the multiple other drivers of the electricity situation.

rigor.statement: I’ve announced a plan to reintroduce pay deductions for partial strikes. This will be discussed at select committee this week. This Government has committed to this change because we need to restore balance to the rights and consequences of collective bargaining. If workers are partially striking by refusing to do their normal work, why should they get paid a normal wage?
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent reciprocity argument (no normal work, no normal pay), though it leans on a rhetorical question rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: When teachers refused to teach certain year groups on particular days, it was parents who paid the price by having to take unplanned leave from work in order to take care of their kids who were rostered home, not to mention the cost of lost learning for the students. When hospital-based nuclear medicine technologists limited the number of scans completed each day, it was patients waiting for their results who suffered.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete illustrative cases to support the claim that partial strikes harm third parties; persuasive but anecdote-based rather than data-driven.

rigor.statement: These young people right now, currently, under the current legislation, are ending up in youth justice facilities. They are repeat, serious youth offenders who to qualify to be part of the MSA programme must have committed two crimes with a sentence of 10 years or more. They will end up in a youth justice facility anyway.
rigor.explanation: Responds to the Children's Commissioner point with a specific eligibility-threshold argument (two 10-year-plus offences) rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: No, I’m not concerned at all about the gangs controlling the streets in Auckland, because the police are doing an outstanding job in policing the gangs in Auckland, and that’s certainly the feedback that I get.
rigor.explanation: Rests the reassurance on anecdotal 'feedback that I get' rather than data, especially given the cited surge.

rigor.statement: How can he be proud of that $30 million funding announcement for conservation tourism when, in the past year alone, the Department of Conservation (DOC) has been forced to make $47.2 million in cuts, so that, overall, this announcement doesn’t even cover the hole that this Government created?
rigor.explanation: Directly contrasts the announced $30m against $47.2m in cuts to argue the announcement is net-negative — a coherent evidence-based comparison.

rigor.statement: Why is he comfortable with his Government only investing a mere 0.88 percent of the value of tourism on conservation land at the same time as it is enabling more mining in Aotearoa?
rigor.explanation: Uses a quantified proportion to press the point, though it bundles in a contested 'enabling more mining' premise.

rigor.statement: Is he aware that the coal set to be mined by just one of his fast-track projects would increase emissions by 66.5 million tonnes, meanwhile his latest international commitment to reduce emissions is just 42 million tonnes?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two quantified figures to argue an inconsistency, though comparing a single project's lifetime emissions to an NDC is not strictly like-for-like.

rigor.statement: Why has he added coal to the critical minerals list when coal is not a mineral but a fossil fuel?
rigor.explanation: Raises a specific classification objection (coal as a fossil fuel rather than a mineral) as a factual challenge to the policy.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree with the member that spending more money is a goal in itself, or does he alternatively believe that the Government’s objective is to get greater value out of spending less money, just as every firm, farm, and family has had to for the last few years?
rigor.explanation: Frames a false dichotomy (spending as a goal in itself vs value-for-money) and leans on a folksy 'firm, farm and family' analogy rather than argument.

rigor.statement: Does announcing $500,000 of additional spending for tourism marketing make up for the $20 million that was cut from the “marketing New Zealand as a tourist destination” fund at Budget 2024?
rigor.explanation: Poses a quantified net comparison ($500k new vs $20m cut) to test whether the announcement is genuinely additive.

strength.statement: There’s $33 billion in the national transport plan; there’s $148 billion in the Infrastructure Commission pipeline. There’s work coming and it’s starting to happen. We’re getting roads built: Brougham St’s starting, Hawke’s Bay’s started.
strength.explanation: Points to funding pipelines and some starting projects, but most is planned/announced rather than delivered, so follow-through is partial.

strength.statement: Construction on Takitimu North Link stage one—a four-lane expressway between Tauranga and Te Puna—is now past the halfway point. So we know there’s $33 billion set aside in our National Land Transport Programme.
