strength.explanation: Points to a concrete project genuinely under construction, though delivery is in progress rather than complete.

strength.statement: I’ve announced a plan to reintroduce pay deductions for partial strikes. This will be discussed at select committee this week. This Government has committed to this change because we need to restore balance to the rights and consequences of collective bargaining. If workers are partially striking by refusing to do their normal work, why should they get paid a normal wage?
strength.explanation: A committed change progressing through select committee, but announced/in-progress rather than enacted.

strength.statement: There’ll be a cap on total sentencing discounts of 40 percent, and there will no longer be repeated discounts for remorse. You can’t be remorseful repeatedly. The bill also makes a number of other changes, including the addition of a range of new aggravating factors, such as for adults who offend in crimes alongside young people, such as in ram raids.
strength.explanation: A committed reform progressing to second reading, but not yet enacted at the time of speaking.

strength.statement: I especially stand by my actions to provide funding of $30.6 million over four years to continue the fast-track youth offending programme and extend the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds, which will contribute to Government Target 3, a 15 percent reduction in the total number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending behaviour.
strength.explanation: A concrete funded commitment with follow-through on an existing programme, though outcomes are still to be delivered.

strength.statement: I recently had the pleasure of opening a new motorway interchange, building on 20 years of long-term planning and infrastructure development... And with the $18 million that was allocated several years ago, it was a pleasure—with Tapuika, the tangata whenua—to open the infrastructure.
strength.explanation: Describes an actually-opened piece of infrastructure with named funding, indicating delivered follow-through.

strength.statement: The gang legislation has been in force for nearly three months and has changed the way gangs are policed in New Zealand. Police now control our streets, not the gangs... I was pleased to note in recent reporting late last year, or last year, that for the first time since 2018, we have seen an annual drop in violent crime.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted gang legislation in force and some early results, credible delivery though causal claims are early.

strength.statement: Inanahi—yesterday—I announced a $30 million investment from the International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy to fund more than a dozen projects to boost biodiversity—kanorautanga—and manuhiri infrastructure in tourism. Tourism is a key critical economic driver, and nature, alongside culture, are our biggest drawcards for international tourists. Around 50 percent of tourists—manuhiri—cite it as their primary reason for coming here.
strength.explanation: An announced funded package; concrete but delivery is prospective.

strength.statement: The bill vests title to this 9.7 hectare site, 5 kilometres east of Kihikihi, in those tūpuna of Ō-Rākau, the ancestors of Ō-Rākau... the site, once this bill is passed, will transfer 21 working days after the Royal assent by our Governor-General, Cindy Kiro, which will provide for it to be vested before the 161st anniversary of this battle.
strength.explanation: Carrying settlement legislation to third reading with a concrete transfer timeline shows follow-through on the commitment.

charisma.statement: We’re embracing “Everything must go!”, like high inflation, like high interest rates, like wasteful spending, like cycle bridges, like Let’s Get Wellington Moving. We’re saying everything must go, including gang members going up, violent crime going up, retail crime going up. And who was the police Minister for five years?
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-them rally line for his own side; entertaining but not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This is an outrageous conversation we’re actually having here, because this country needs to grow. We need to have economic growth. Are the Greens not for economic growth? I mean, what’s the position? You have to grow an economy. You need to have energy to do it.
charisma.explanation: Combative 'are the Greens not for growth' framing rallies his side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: On the other side of the House, they’ve got to make up their mind. Should we be investing more in attracting tourists, as these questions seem to suggest, or does she not think tourism is a good idea, as other of her members have suggested? I don’t know which way is up or down with you guys.
charisma.explanation: Scores a debating point against the other side rather than persuading or seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: It comes to me as very bleak news—and I will look into it this afternoon—that the Marlborough District Council is meddling and trying to impose their view of the law on marine farming. Marine farming represents the interests of mothers and fathers and households, and we’re not going to tolerate bureaucrats and that particular council repeating the perfidy of what they did with seabed and foreshore.
charisma.explanation: Populist framing ('mothers and fathers') that rallies rather than builds cross-party consensus.

divination.statement: The market and most economists are expecting a reduction in the OCR of 50 basis points. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates which, in turn, support a growing economy, jobs, and incomes for New Zealanders.
divination.explanation: A near-term forecast of a 50bp OCR cut consistent with market/economist consensus at the time; timeframe is the next day, so well-grounded.

divination.statement: That’s why the Government set an ambitious target of seeing a reduction of 20,000 fewer victims of assault, robbery, and sexual assault by 2029. The data has long lead times, but early results from our work have been encouraging. There have been 24,000 fewer victims over the year ending October 2024 compared to the year ending June 2024.
divination.explanation: A 2029 victim-reduction target; plausible as a goal but its achievement is uncertain and dependent on many factors.

charisma.statement: As kāwana, we won't always agree with rangatira throughout the motu. We could all do better. But the key is to keep engaging respectfully, in the same waka, in a timely manner, to uphold the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, humble ('we could all do better'), invites continued respectful engagement rather than combat.

charisma.statement: I am absolutely encouraging of all members, and in fact all New Zealanders, to have a very basic and fundamental understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, a bilingual and bicultural document, which is the founding document of this great nation.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal directed at all members and all New Zealanders, unifying rather than partisan.

charisma.statement: Well, the reality is that those two Ministers were making statements about different matters. It's an awful conflict when you have to choose between two geniuses!
charisma.explanation: Witty deflection that plays to his own side but resolves nothing.

charisma.statement: So here we go again with a judgment that was artificial all along, and rather than make these proud boasts, I think our country should be doing better to be a more corruption-free land.
charisma.explanation: Ends on a unifying note that NZ should aspire to do better, softening the defensive stance.

charisma.statement: I'm not sure where that member has got those numbers from and I can neither confirm nor deny those numbers, because I am not going to constantly drag these young people down when they have come to this programme voluntarily to make their lives better. Parliament is not here to destroy young people's lives; Parliament is here to support them and get behind them to succeed.
charisma.explanation: Frames refusal around a positive, protective appeal, though it appeals mainly to her own side.

civility.statement: As kāwana, we won't always agree with rangatira throughout the motu. We could all do better. But the key is to keep engaging respectfully, in the same waka, in a timely manner, to uphold the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Respectful tone, concedes fallibility, no personal attack.

civility.statement: If the Minister's party is truly opposed to the Treaty principles bill, why are his colleagues questioning and badgering submitters who oppose the bill during the select committee process?
civility.explanation: Pointed accusation of 'badgering' submitters; targets conduct/hypocrisy rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: And I note that despite a bit of criticism from members opposite in the past, they very quietly rolled over a few education and school public-private partnerships during their time in Government because they were working so successfully.
civility.explanation: Pointed jab at opponents but engages the policy record rather than personal character.

civility.statement: The reality is that the judgment being made on that standard is set against the actions of a sworn Minister of the Crown. In this case, they weren't; they were made by a backbench member of Parliament, and the standards and criteria are massively different. I suggest you ask Willie Jackson about that because he'd be very knowledgable about it.
civility.explanation: Ends with a personal jab redirecting at another member instead of answering.

civility.statement: We tried to be as open and transparent as possible when it came to this pilot programme, but then it became very apparent that the Opposition used that opportunity to drag these young people through the mud with venom, trying to make them be unsuccessful.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Opposition of acting 'with venom' and trying to make young people fail — a personal-motive attack rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: I actually think that, as Prime Minister, the Prime Minister has responsibility for all of his Cabinet Ministers, including his Deputy Prime Minister and including his incoming Deputy Prime Minister. My question was to the Prime Minister on whether or not he thought it was an acceptable standard.
civility.explanation: Presses on ministerial accountability and standards without personal insult, focusing on the responsibility question.

civility.statement: How can New Zealanders expect environmental protection to improve when she has not brought one piece of legislation to this House to protect the environment, has made significant cuts to staff and funding of her agencies, and has disregarded the very evidence which could enable her to make better decisions in actually protecting the environment?
civility.explanation: Sharp but substantive critique itemising legislative record, cuts, and evidence use rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: What does she say to Sonya Cameron, the food security manager at the Salvation Army, who said that "The government's turning down people for food, they're sending them to foodbanks. Now they're not funding foodbanks. Foodbanks around the country are either overstretched like ourselves or they're starting to close down."?
civility.explanation: Confronts the Minister with a named front-line source's testimony; pointed but grounded in substance, not personal attack.

specificity.statement: In the past week alone, we've seen many examples of this Government upholding the responsibilities under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—for example, Minister Goldsmith attending Kororipo Pā to encourage the return of Kororipo Pā to Ngāti Rēhia as a catalyst for the Ngāpuhi settlement; Minister Stanford announcing structured literacy and numeracy materials in te reo Māori out at Panguru; Minister Mitchell and Minister Watts attending Mātihetihe Marae, out at Mitimiti, to activate further funding for a climate change pilot project; Minister Jones announcing various Regional Infrastructure Fund support for marae up in Northland
specificity.explanation: Names specific Ministers, locations, and concrete actions rather than generalities.

specificity.statement: I am absolutely encouraging of all members, and in fact all New Zealanders, to have a very basic and fundamental understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, a bilingual and bicultural document, which is the founding document of this great nation.
specificity.explanation: A general encouragement; no mechanism or concrete measure.

specificity.statement: I can guarantee that my quest, and my parliamentary experiences now and into the future, is to ensure equality of opportunity and equal citizenship and to ensure that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is recognised as the founding document of this nation.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational values statement with no concrete policy, measure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: On Monday, the Prime Minister and I announced we'll be hosting an international investment summit in March, with about a hundred of the world's highest-profile investors in super funds, construction companies, engineers, and business leaders coming.
specificity.explanation: Names timeframe (March), scale (~100 investors) and sectors.

specificity.statement: Non-financial sanctions allow job seekers who fail to meet obligations for the first time to continue receiving their full benefit payments while still being required to complete activities such as the new Report Job Search, where job seekers must perform a minimum of three job-search activities every week for four weeks and report this to the Ministry of Social Development, and upskilling, where job seekers must attend and participate in employment-related training for at least five hours a week over a four-week period.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanics: three activities/week, four weeks, five hours/week of training.

specificity.statement: Between July and December, more than 33,000 people moved off the jobseeker benefit into work, a 22 percent increase compared to the same period in 2023. It's also positive to see that 98.6 percent of clients are complying with their obligations, while only 0.4 percent are in orange and 1 percent in red.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures, percentages, and comparison periods.

specificity.statement: In December 2023, 123,000 people were unemployed in New Zealand, and in December 2024, this figure sat at 156,000, in line with Treasury forecasts.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts for two dated periods.

specificity.statement: When I referred to the 33,000 people that have cancelled their jobseeker benefit because they found work, disproportionately, in a positive way, Pasifika job seekers exited at a rate of 30 percent higher than the same time a year ago.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete comparative figure, though the underlying claim is selectively framed.

specificity.statement: You see, our farmers are world best, with food and fibre exports set to reach $56.9 billion this year, with sheep and beef farmers alone contributing the equivalent of $3,300 for every Kiwi household.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise export figure and a per-household contribution.

specificity.statement: We've invested $400 million over four years in emissions-reduction technology that will increase production, not decrease it. We've passed legislation to remove agriculture from the emissions trading scheme so that we can work constructively with the rural community.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, timeframe, and specific legislative change.

specificity.statement: there are real signs of green shoots ahead. Already we've seen a lift in sheep meat prices over recent months with December lamb prices exceeding the five-year average, record high cattle prices, and rising demand for key red meat markets that could see an additional $1 billion in export revenue for our farms this year.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete price signals and a dollar figure, though the projection is a rough estimate.

specificity.statement: yes, there have been quite substantial staff reductions at the Ministry for the Environment, but in the last year the Ministry for the Environment has managed to lead a cross-agency team and establish the fast-track regime—the one-stop shop. We have already done one RMA amendment bill and there is a second amendment bill before the Parliament right now, before the select committee.
specificity.explanation: Names the fast-track regime and the count of RMA amendment bills.

specificity.statement: In December last year, I launched an ambitious review of competition settings. The reason for doing this is that New Zealand lags behind many other countries when it comes to competition. This has led to low productivity, limited choice, and higher prices for Kiwis. The first component includes a fundamental review of the Commerce Act to see whether merger settings are appropriate. The second element is that I've commissioned an independent group led by Dame Paula Rebstock to look at the governance structures of the Commerce Commission.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete review components, the statute, and the person leading the independent group.

specificity.statement: Our Government has invested more in health than ever before: a record investment of $16.68 billion.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise dollar figure, though without context on real-terms change.

specificity.statement: The initial consultation on the much-anticipated rewrites of the Arms Act 1983 is off to a strong start, with 577 submissions received as of today, and the accompanying discussion document has been downloaded 1,758 times, showing that many New Zealanders are taking the opportunity to have their say—an opportunity which they were not afforded in 2019.
specificity.explanation: Precise submission and download counts and a dated comparison.

veracity.statement: In the past week alone, we've seen many examples of this Government upholding the responsibilities under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—for example, Minister Goldsmith attending Kororipo Pā to encourage the return of Kororipo Pā to Ngāti Rēhia as a catalyst for the Ngāpuhi settlement; Minister Stanford announcing structured literacy and numeracy materials in te reo Māori out at Panguru; Minister Mitchell and Minister Watts attending Mātihetihe Marae, out at Mitimiti, to activate further funding for a climate change pilot project; Minister Jones announcing various Regional Infrastructure Fund support for marae up in Northland
veracity.explanation: Cites checkable events; presented as fact and largely plausible, though 'upholding Te Tiriti' framing is interpretive.

veracity.statement: Our 30-year failure to embrace opportunities has produced anaemic levels of growth and lower productivity growth than we need to drive higher living standards.
veracity.explanation: NZ's weak productivity growth is real, but the blanket characterisation is rhetorical and imprecise.

veracity.statement: The reality is that that is not a matter that's currently on the present agenda. The last time that happened, of course, was in 2002, when the Labour Party did precisely that in their free-trade deal with Singapore.
veracity.explanation: Reference to the 2002 Singapore free-trade deal and its investment provisions is broadly accurate, though 'precisely that' overstates equivalence.

veracity.statement: Smack in the middle of the wine-box inquiry and the BNZ inquiry and every other fraud I saw, we were still rating number one and we've only slipped to number four.
veracity.explanation: NZ has historically ranked near the top and has slipped; the framing selectively marshals detail to dismiss the ranking.

veracity.statement: Minister, is it not a fact that the Treasury forecast was, as Labour left office, that this unemployment rate right now would be 5.3 percent, when in fact it's down to 5.1 percent?
veracity.explanation: A specific, falsifiable comparison of forecast (5.3%) vs actual (5.1%); plausible but presented to favour the Government and unverified here.

veracity.statement: Between July and December, more than 33,000 people moved off the jobseeker benefit into work, a 22 percent increase compared to the same period in 2023. It's also positive to see that 98.6 percent of clients are complying with their obligations, while only 0.4 percent are in orange and 1 percent in red.
veracity.explanation: Specific official-sounding statistics presented as fact; plausible but the 'into work' framing may overstate, as leaving jobseeker benefit is not always a move into employment.

veracity.statement: In December 2023, 123,000 people were unemployed in New Zealand, and in December 2024, this figure sat at 156,000, in line with Treasury forecasts.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable unemployment figures consistent with the rising trend she acknowledges.

veracity.statement: Eligibility requirements for food and other special needs grants haven't changed, and I have no plans to change them. As I said in the House yesterday, we have seen a reduction in applications, so I would encourage people who need help to get in touch with the Ministry of Social Development, as there is assistance available.
veracity.explanation: Claim that formal eligibility rules are unchanged is plausible; leaves open whether practical access tightened, as the report alleged.

veracity.statement: while we've worked hard to reduce inflation from 7.3 percent to 2.2 percent, and that's helping to bring costs down and put more money in people's pockets
veracity.explanation: The 7.3%→2.2% inflation figures are broadly accurate, but 'we've worked hard to reduce' overstates a Government's direct control over inflation.

veracity.statement: You see, our farmers are world best, with food and fibre exports set to reach $56.9 billion this year, with sheep and beef farmers alone contributing the equivalent of $3,300 for every Kiwi household.
veracity.explanation: The $56.9b forecast aligns with MPI projections; 'world best' is boosterish but the figures are broadly credible.

veracity.statement: We've also concluded two high-quality trade deals with the United Arab Emirates and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries last year, which will eliminate 99 percent of all tariffs over time, including sheep and beef meat exports.
veracity.explanation: The UAE and GCC trade agreements and the ~99% tariff elimination are accurately described.

veracity.statement: The third point I'd make is this—and it's the point I made in the debate last night—which is that wealthy countries look after the environment better. That is a simple fact. So if we can grow our economy and grow our national prosperity, we can do all sorts of amazing things for our biodiversity and for our endangered species. Countries that are poor trash the environment; wealthy countries look after it.
veracity.explanation: There is some correlation between wealth and certain environmental metrics, but the absolute claim is an overgeneralisation.

veracity.statement: I actually would say it's too early to say whether the pilot has been a success or not. We are still in the middle of the pilot. That is why we are evaluating its progress and we'll be releasing the first evaluation shortly. What I would say is evidence tells us that what we were doing was not working. Evidence tells us that youth crime was at an all-time high, and something needed to happen.
veracity.explanation: The claim that 'youth crime was at an all-time high' is contestable and not clearly supported by the record.

veracity.statement: The competition settings in the Commerce Act haven't been significantly reviewed for more than 20 years. Over that time, market conditions have changed, with many sectors becoming more concentrated.
veracity.explanation: The Commerce Act's core competition settings have indeed gone long without major review; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Our Government has invested more in health than ever before: a record investment of $16.68 billion.
veracity.explanation: The nominal figure may be accurate, but 'more than ever before' as record spending is a common claim that ignores inflation and demand growth, so potentially misleading.

veracity.statement: The initial consultation on the much-anticipated rewrites of the Arms Act 1983 is off to a strong start, with 577 submissions received as of today, and the accompanying discussion document has been downloaded 1,758 times, showing that many New Zealanders are taking the opportunity to have their say—an opportunity which they were not afforded in 2019.
veracity.explanation: The counts are specific factual claims; the '2019' comparison is a contestable characterisation of the earlier post-Christchurch process.

forthrightness.statement: I can guarantee that my quest, and my parliamentary experiences now and into the future, is to ensure equality of opportunity and equal citizenship and to ensure that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is recognised as the founding document of this nation.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Ferris's question about supporting a Te Tiriti commissioner, he restates general commitments rather than answering yes/no.

forthrightness.statement: I think the answer to that question lies with the person three over to your right in the Speaker's Chair.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether driving a car up Parliament's steps meets expected standards; deflects to the Speaker rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: All the comments the Prime Minister wishes to make on this matter have been made.
forthrightness.explanation: Refuses to engage the repeated question about acceptable standards; a non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that the judgment being made on that standard is set against the actions of a sworn Minister of the Crown. In this case, they weren't; they were made by a backbench member of Parliament, and the standards and criteria are massively different. I suggest you ask Willie Jackson about that because he'd be very knowledgable about it.
forthrightness.explanation: Offers a partial rationale (backbencher vs Minister) but pivots to deflect at Willie Jackson rather than defending the standard.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that that is not a matter that's currently on the present agenda. The last time that happened, of course, was in 2002, when the Labour Party did precisely that in their free-trade deal with Singapore.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers (not on the agenda) but avoids a direct yes/no, adding a counter-attack.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the reality is that those two Ministers were making statements about different matters. It's an awful conflict when you have to choose between two geniuses!
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile two Ministers' conflicting positions on English requirements; dodges with a joke and does not pick a side.

forthrightness.statement: As that member will be aware, in a recession, unfortunately, there are jobs that are lost across a range of industries, and I'm very confident in the Minister for Media and Communications' plan in that sector.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she had discussed a media-sector plan with Minister Goldsmith; does not say whether she did, offering general reassurance instead.

forthrightness.statement: When I referred to the 33,000 people that have cancelled their jobseeker benefit because they found work, disproportionately, in a positive way, Pasifika job seekers exited at a rate of 30 percent higher than the same time a year ago.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she scrapped targeted Māori/Pacific employment plans; pivots to a favourable Pasifika statistic without addressing the scrapping.

forthrightness.statement: Eligibility requirements for food and other special needs grants haven't changed, and I have no plans to change them. As I said in the House yesterday, we have seen a reduction in applications, so I would encourage people who need help to get in touch with the Ministry of Social Development, as there is assistance available.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the eligibility point directly but sidesteps the Salvation Army claim that access was effectively reducing.

forthrightness.statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister, yes. If the member wants to think about a simple illustration of that, I invite the member to reflect on the attempted establishment of a McDonalds in Wānaka, which has gone to extraordinary hearings, public submissions, and has been turned down. Meanwhile, there are developments up and down this country tied up in acres and acres of red and green tape who are just trying to do something quite simple—use their land to build stuff.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly reaffirms the Minister's contested statement when asked if she stands by it.

forthrightness.statement: yes, there have been quite substantial staff reductions at the Ministry for the Environment, but in the last year the Ministry for the Environment has managed to lead a cross-agency team and establish the fast-track regime—the one-stop shop. We have already done one RMA amendment bill and there is a second amendment bill before the Parliament right now, before the select committee.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the staff cuts directly and responds to the criticism with specific counter-examples.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not sure where that member has got those numbers from and I can neither confirm nor deny those numbers, because I am not going to constantly drag these young people down when they have come to this programme voluntarily to make their lives better. Parliament is not here to destroy young people's lives; Parliament is here to support them and get behind them to succeed.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to confirm the reoffending figures asked about, citing privacy rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: under the last National Government 89 percent of Kiwis were waiting six hours in emergency departments. When this coalition Government took office, that was down to 67 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify GP-related cuts; answers with unrelated ED/FSA/elective statistics instead.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, I don't have that answer. If he'd like to put that in writing, it will be answered.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked what his expectation would be about ring-fencing the Masterton settlement; provides no expectation, deferring to a written question.

forthrightness.statement: I plan on listening to New Zealanders and making sure that their views are heard, because what we have discovered in the past is that they never got that opportunity.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether she intends to rewrite the review's findings; does not answer yes or no, restating a general commitment to listen.

strength.statement: On Monday, the Prime Minister and I announced we'll be hosting an international investment summit in March, with about a hundred of the world's highest-profile investors in super funds, construction companies, engineers, and business leaders coming.
strength.explanation: An announcement of a planned event; delivery/outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Non-financial sanctions allow job seekers who fail to meet obligations for the first time to continue receiving their full benefit payments while still being required to complete activities such as the new Report Job Search, where job seekers must perform a minimum of three job-search activities every week for four weeks and report this to the Ministry of Social Development, and upskilling, where job seekers must attend and participate in employment-related training for at least five hours a week over a four-week period.
strength.explanation: A concrete, announced-and-implemented policy change, though downstream results not yet shown.

strength.statement: We've invested $400 million over four years in emissions-reduction technology that will increase production, not decrease it. We've passed legislation to remove agriculture from the emissions trading scheme so that we can work constructively with the rural community.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered action (passed legislation, committed funding) rather than mere aspiration.

strength.statement: We've also concluded two high-quality trade deals with the United Arab Emirates and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries last year, which will eliminate 99 percent of all tariffs over time, including sheep and beef meat exports.
strength.explanation: Concluded trade deals are delivered outcomes attributable to the Government.

strength.statement: In December last year, I launched an ambitious review of competition settings. The reason for doing this is that New Zealand lags behind many other countries when it comes to competition. This has led to low productivity, limited choice, and higher prices for Kiwis. The first component includes a fundamental review of the Commerce Act to see whether merger settings are appropriate. The second element is that I've commissioned an independent group led by Dame Paula Rebstock to look at the governance structures of the Commerce Commission.
strength.explanation: A launched review and commissioned group are concrete steps, though outcomes are pending.

strength.statement: This Government campaigned on ensuring New Zealanders could have their say on the future of the Arms Act, and we are delivering on that commitment.
strength.explanation: Consultation is under way as promised, though the substantive rewrite is not yet delivered.

rigor.statement: Our 30-year failure to embrace opportunities has produced anaemic levels of growth and lower productivity growth than we need to drive higher living standards.
rigor.explanation: Directionally supported by NZ's known productivity lag, but sweeping '30-year failure' framing asserts causation without evidence.

rigor.statement: And I note that despite a bit of criticism from members opposite in the past, they very quietly rolled over a few education and school public-private partnerships during their time in Government because they were working so successfully.
rigor.explanation: Uses opponents' own past behaviour as evidence for the argument; broadly accurate reasoning though 'so successfully' is asserted.

rigor.statement: Smack in the middle of the wine-box inquiry and the BNZ inquiry and every other fraud I saw, we were still rating number one and we've only slipped to number four.
rigor.explanation: Argues the corruption index is unreliable by anecdote from past inquiries; a plausible skeptical point but not systematically evidenced.

rigor.statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister, yes. If the member wants to think about a simple illustration of that, I invite the member to reflect on the attempted establishment of a McDonalds in Wānaka, which has gone to extraordinary hearings, public submissions, and has been turned down. Meanwhile, there are developments up and down this country tied up in acres and acres of red and green tape who are just trying to do something quite simple—use their land to build stuff.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a single anecdote (Wānaka McDonald's) to generalise about the whole planning system; illustrative rather than evidential.

rigor.statement: The third point I'd make is this—and it's the point I made in the debate last night—which is that wealthy countries look after the environment better. That is a simple fact. So if we can grow our economy and grow our national prosperity, we can do all sorts of amazing things for our biodiversity and for our endangered species. Countries that are poor trash the environment; wealthy countries look after it.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping 'simple fact' dichotomy (poor trash / wealthy protect) ignores counterexamples; asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: I actually would say it's too early to say whether the pilot has been a success or not. We are still in the middle of the pilot. That is why we are evaluating its progress and we'll be releasing the first evaluation shortly. What I would say is evidence tells us that what we were doing was not working. Evidence tells us that youth crime was at an all-time high, and something needed to happen.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to 'evidence' and a claimed all-time high but presents no figures; reasoning that action was needed is reasonable but under-supported.

rigor.statement: The competition settings in the Commerce Act haven't been significantly reviewed for more than 20 years. Over that time, market conditions have changed, with many sectors becoming more concentrated.
rigor.explanation: Links long-unrevised settings to concentration as a reasoned case, though without cited data here.

rigor.statement: under the last National Government 89 percent of Kiwis were waiting six hours in emergency departments. When this coalition Government took office, that was down to 67 percent.
rigor.explanation: Switches the metric to ED wait times rather than answering the GP-funding question; comparison is deployed selectively.

rigor.statement: I actually think that, as Prime Minister, the Prime Minister has responsibility for all of his Cabinet Ministers, including his Deputy Prime Minister and including his incoming Deputy Prime Minister. My question was to the Prime Minister on whether or not he thought it was an acceptable standard.
rigor.explanation: Makes a coherent argument that the PM bears responsibility for his Ministers' conduct.

rigor.statement: How can New Zealanders expect environmental protection to improve when she has not brought one piece of legislation to this House to protect the environment, has made significant cuts to staff and funding of her agencies, and has disregarded the very evidence which could enable her to make better decisions in actually protecting the environment?
rigor.explanation: Builds the challenge on specific claimed facts (no protective legislation, staff cuts, disregarded evidence).

divination.statement: there are real signs of green shoots ahead. Already we've seen a lift in sheep meat prices over recent months with December lamb prices exceeding the five-year average, record high cattle prices, and rising demand for key red meat markets that could see an additional $1 billion in export revenue for our farms this year.
divination.explanation: Predicts up to an additional $1b in export revenue this year; directionally plausible given rising prices but magnitude uncertain.

authenticity.statement: This Government campaigned on ensuring New Zealanders could have their say on the future of the Arms Act, and we are delivering on that commitment.
authenticity.explanation: Ties current consultation to a stated campaign commitment, with the action broadly matching the prior position.

civility.statement: This is a bill that's really hard to hear the Government talk about, because they are extremely pompous in the way they're talking about it and they're extremely out of touch.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government as 'pompous' and 'out of touch' — a personal/character swipe rather than engagement with the policy substance.

civility.statement: a melodramatic appeal to them by somebody who barely understands what it is to be one is actually really offensive
civility.explanation: Personal attack impugning an opponent's understanding and sincerity rather than addressing the argument.

civility.statement: And what do we do? We make sure that we look good by taking away their discretion to do their job well. That's what we are doing today in this court. We are making ourselves look good and doing very little to address the problem.
civility.explanation: Imputes a self-serving 'look good' motive to the Government rather than engaging its stated rationale.

civility.statement: Do you know what I call that? I call it arrogance. I call it arrogance and I call it pontificating, and I call it actually something less than the duty we have in here
civility.explanation: Labels the Government's conduct 'arrogance' and 'pontificating' — character-based rather than substantive criticism.

civility.statement: real people will become victims again if we allow laws like this to rule us because it happens to make us a little bit more popular when we're down in the polls
civility.explanation: Imputes a cynical poll-driven motive to the Government.

civility.statement: which has been a debate that has focused on politicians talking about being tough on crime and not on being tough on the causes of crime
civility.explanation: Critiques the framing of the debate rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: It is certainly not looking after the victims when the Minister of Justice's own advice says that this is not something that will help victims, that victims will actually be negatively affected by these reforms.
civility.explanation: Pointed but attacks the policy on its merits and its own advice, not a person.

civility.statement: I do want some action—I do, Grant McCallum. These sorts of debates call for some soberness and some dignity
civility.explanation: Calls for dignity and sobriety in the debate; a restrained response to heckling.

civility.statement: We all know that there is political hay to be made out of looking tough in sentencing reform.
civility.explanation: Imputes a political-gain motive to opponents rather than engaging their stated aims.

civility.statement: We're not heckling. Do you want heckling? Do you want some heckling? You sure?
civility.explanation: Taunting interjection that disrupts rather than engages the speaker's argument.

civility.statement: Don't be serious! Don't laugh!
civility.explanation: Mocking heckle aimed at the speaker rather than the substance.

civility.statement: I truly believe people on the other side of the House are good people, decent people, but I can't believe, sometimes, the world view that is shared with us.
civility.explanation: Separates the people from their views, respectful in tone.

civility.statement: "What do we say"—and she was speaking against the bill—"to an 11-year-old girl that was very violently sexually abused and the perpetrator was given home detention?" … He was given 75 percent discount because of this reason and this reason and this reason. It is shameful.
civility.explanation: Harsh and emotive but directed at a sentencing outcome/policy rather than a member personally.

civility.statement: Well, maybe I'm missing something. I mean, I did pretty well at School C English, so I don't quite understand what the member's saying. It's "20 or more", which is the same as "at least 20". So, yeah, I think that deals with that, right?
civility.explanation: The 'School C English' quip mildly belittles the questioner rather than addressing the point respectfully.

civility.statement: the member is, essentially, arguing for something that brings it closer to running into problems with the foreign-buyers ban, because if you have a lower threshold in the regions … the closer you get to kind of one, by definition the closer you get to allowing overseas investment into existing homes.
civility.explanation: Attacks the argument's implications, not the member, though it misstates his position.

civility.statement: Now, while the Minister of Housing's cracking himself up at his own jokes, I'll ask a few more questions.
civility.explanation: A mild jab at the Minister's levity before returning to substance; needling but not a serious attack.

civility.statement: At no point have we advocated for the threshold to be one, and at no point have we advocated for the rules to be loosened. What we have advocated for is a recognition that the minimum threshold that's outlined in this bill would be hard to meet for many areas of the country.
civility.explanation: Firmly but respectfully clarifies rather than escalating.

civility.statement: It would be helpful if the Minister was prepared to perhaps make that available, rather than have us rely on the Official Information Act for it … I invite the Minister to maybe think about proactively releasing that information.
civility.explanation: Courteous, substance-focused request for transparency with no personal edge.

charisma.statement: This is a bill that's really hard to hear the Government talk about, because they are extremely pompous in the way they're talking about it and they're extremely out of touch.
charisma.explanation: Opens combatively against the other side; alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Do you know what I call that? I call it arrogance. I call it arrogance and I call it pontificating, and I call it actually something less than the duty we have in here
charisma.explanation: Rallies against opponents rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: it is sadly the result of a very well-meaning but misguided sentencing system that wanted to believe that these guys were ready for release. They weren't.
charisma.explanation: Concedes good intent ('well-meaning') to the system he criticises, softening the attack.

charisma.statement: and I agree that signalling to judges is sometimes required, but it is also really important to give judges the role that they do in our justice system, which is to assess the appropriate sentencing and the appropriate conditions in each case.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly concedes a point to the other side ('signalling … is sometimes required') before making her own — bridging rather than combative.

charisma.statement: I do want some action—I do, Grant McCallum. These sorts of debates call for some soberness and some dignity
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared standards of conduct, though addressed pointedly at a heckler.

charisma.statement: I truly believe people on the other side of the House are good people, decent people, but I can't believe, sometimes, the world view that is shared with us.
charisma.explanation: Extends good faith to opponents as 'good, decent people' while disagreeing with their views — a bridging gesture.

charisma.statement: no one pretends that this is the sole answer to New Zealand's housing woes—I think everyone would acknowledge that—but it's one of those things you can chip away at to make a difference. Build-to-rent has got a role to play
charisma.explanation: Measured, non-overclaiming framing that invites shared acknowledgement across the House.

charisma.statement: I've gone away, I've taken some advice on it, I appreciate that members are raising these issues in good faith, I'm happy to make it available, but, in answer to Mr Utikere's question, I'm not proposing to advance any amendments.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opponents' good faith while declining their ask.

charisma.statement: So, look, I've not got a closed mind to it. In three or four years' time, if we wake up and it turns out there's a proliferation of foreign money that wants to enter into the regions and buy 10- or 12-bedroom units, OK, let's have a look at it, but the advice is that that's not necessary.
charisma.explanation: Signals openness to revisit and frames disagreement congenially rather than shutting it down.

charisma.statement: The fact of the matter is we support this bill and actually don't intend to take too much time up in this committee stage, but the point that was raised by Tangi Utikere, my friend and colleague, is one that we do wish to explore
charisma.explanation: States cross-party support for the bill up front and frames the exchange as constructive rather than obstructive.

charisma.statement: It would be helpful if the Minister was prepared to perhaps make that available, rather than have us rely on the Official Information Act for it … I invite the Minister to maybe think about proactively releasing that information.
charisma.explanation: Constructive framing that invites cooperation from the Minister.

rigor.statement: It is complex because our victims actually tend to also be our perpetrators, because there are mental health issues, because there are issues of youth, because we had a long time in this country where we let people go into State care, we kicked them out of the system at 16, and they have alcohol issues and we've had methamphetamine.
rigor.explanation: Builds a causal picture of offending drivers; reasoning is coherent but relies on assertion rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: And what do we do? We make sure that we look good by taking away their discretion to do their job well. That's what we are doing today in this court. We are making ourselves look good and doing very little to address the problem.
rigor.explanation: Asserts motive and ineffectiveness without evidence; leans on characterisation.

rigor.statement: children's brains are plastic. They are changing. Men don't actually have a fully set brain until their mid-20s. They are still developing their brain.
rigor.explanation: Uses a developmental-science premise to justify considering youth in sentencing; the conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: She went on to explain to me that earlier that week she'd come in from her back garden there on Campbell Road to be confronted with two masked gentlemen … in her kitchen. They threatened her, they made her lie on the ground … they took her car … by the time the police caught these two guys, they were in East Auckland repeating their home invasion on another two victims. When the police did finally apprehend them, they discovered both of them were wearing monitoring bracelets.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single vivid anecdote to justify a systemic conclusion (appeal to anecdote).

rigor.statement: it is sadly the result of a very well-meaning but misguided sentencing system that wanted to believe that these guys were ready for release. They weren't.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from one case to a system-wide verdict; charitable framing but the inference is thin.

rigor.statement: which has been a debate that has focused on politicians talking about being tough on crime and not on being tough on the causes of crime
rigor.explanation: Frames the debate around a tough-on-causes distinction; a reasonable framing but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: and I agree that signalling to judges is sometimes required, but it is also really important to give judges the role that they do in our justice system, which is to assess the appropriate sentencing and the appropriate conditions in each case.
rigor.explanation: Grants the opposing premise and argues from judicial function; reasoned and balanced.

rigor.statement: That is why Parliament doesn't set compulsory sentences for every type of crime and every type of offending. There is a reason why this House is not the court that decides every sentence for every person in every case
rigor.explanation: Coherent separation-of-powers argument; the conclusion (leave discretion to judges) follows from the premise about case-by-case assessment.

rigor.statement: None of the victims of violent crime that I have spoken with in my electorate, after really horrific events like jewellery store owners being bashed, like store owners who have been the target of ram raids, have spoken first about the need for sentencing reform.
rigor.explanation: Uses her own constituency conversations as evidence — an anecdotal basis.

rigor.statement: It is certainly not looking after the victims when the Minister of Justice's own advice says that this is not something that will help victims, that victims will actually be negatively affected by these reforms.
rigor.explanation: Turns the Government's own advice against the policy — an evidence-based line of argument.

rigor.statement: all of the research, all of best practice in our lawmaking in this country and in other jurisdictions that have tried reforms like this, show that this kind of reform doesn't have a positive outcome for victims, because it disincentivises people to come forward and to admit their offending
rigor.explanation: Supplies a plausible causal mechanism (reduced incentive to admit offending), but the sweeping 'all of the research' is asserted, not shown.

rigor.statement: Absolutely we want to punish people further. There's a reason why we want to punish people further, because my neighbours in Takanini were telling me over and over and over again that there seem to be no more consequences for violent crime, for all types of crime.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the policy by constituent anecdote and the sweeping 'no more consequences' claim — appeal to anecdote plus hyperbole.

rigor.statement: "What do we say"—and she was speaking against the bill—"to an 11-year-old girl that was very violently sexually abused and the perpetrator was given home detention?" … He was given 75 percent discount because of this reason and this reason and this reason. It is shameful.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a single emotionally charged case to justify the whole reform — appeal to emotion and anecdote.

rigor.statement: that is, I'm advised, the threshold used in the Act and the definition of build-to-rent land in the Income Tax Act 2007 … A higher limit restricts access to capital for large housing developments, which discourages investment, but a lower limit exempts small overseas property developers from the on-sale requirements, which, people would argue, is inconsistent with the foreign-buyers ban.
rigor.explanation: Lays out the trade-off on both sides of the threshold with a clear rationale for the chosen number.

rigor.statement: Well, maybe I'm missing something. I mean, I did pretty well at School C English, so I don't quite understand what the member's saying. It's "20 or more", which is the same as "at least 20". So, yeah, I think that deals with that, right?
rigor.explanation: Asserts the two phrasings are equivalent without addressing the member's careful boundary-case argument.

rigor.statement: the member is, essentially, arguing for something that brings it closer to running into problems with the foreign-buyers ban, because if you have a lower threshold in the regions … the closer you get to kind of one, by definition the closer you get to allowing overseas investment into existing homes.
rigor.explanation: Logical in form but characterises McAnulty as heading 'closer to one' — a position he expressly denied holding (a mild strawman).

rigor.statement: in new clause 11A(1)(a) it says, "with 1 or more buildings that, taken together, consist of 20 or more dwellings", but then in subclause (1)(b) it says, "at least 20…dwellings". With subclause (1)(a), 20 is included as part of "20 or more", but in subclause (1)(b), 20 is not, because "at least 20" would imply 21. If we're taking the two of them together, with subclauses (1)(a) and (1)(b) using the conjunction "and", it means that both must be met
rigor.explanation: Careful, disciplined close reading of the conjunctive test that isolates a genuine boundary-case ambiguity.

rigor.statement: Is this Government really telling Parliament that it wants build-to-rents to become a significant part of our housing portfolio in this country, but only in Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, and Christchurch?
rigor.explanation: Exposes a logical gap — if the on-sale rationale holds, it should apply beyond the big cities — though framed rhetorically.

rigor.statement: At no point have we advocated for the threshold to be one, and at no point have we advocated for the rules to be loosened. What we have advocated for is a recognition that the minimum threshold that's outlined in this bill would be hard to meet for many areas of the country.
rigor.explanation: Corrects the Minister's characterisation and restates his actual position precisely — repairs a strawman.

rigor.statement: keep the threshold as it is for the cities and look at the requirement that if, say, 100 percent of the development—let's say it's above eight. So you've got eight to 20—nine, 10, 11, 12, etc.; all of those options. If all of them were build-to-rent … I guarantee that there would be more build-to-rent developments built because they would benefit from this.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned proposal following from the on-sale logic, though the 'I guarantee' outcome is asserted.

specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme (Clendon Pride's Mangōpare), its location, and what it does.

divination.explanation: Predicts the law will produce fresh victims; directionally plausible on a rehabilitation-vs-deterrence argument but unquantified and uncertain.

strength.explanation: Stated commitment to more rehabilitation investment with no delivery or mechanism yet shown — aspiration/announcement.

strength.explanation: A conditional future commitment to repeal from Opposition — intent stated, delivery necessarily unproven.

veracity.explanation: Unemployment did rise between the Oct 2023 election and early 2025, so the direction is accurate; the specific 'families with an unemployed parent' framing is plausible but not precisely verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Families still see their grocery bills going up each week under this Government. And let's not forget power prices going up every month under this Government.
veracity.explanation: Groceries and power prices were rising, so directionally true, but 'each week' and 'every month' are hyperbolic overstatements of continuous increase.

veracity.statement: hocking off half the power companies actually contributed to the current power crisis that we're seeing at the moment, because those power companies decided to gouge more profits out of consumers rather than actually invest in new power generation.
veracity.explanation: The 2013 partial float and gentailer profits are real, but attributing the current supply crunch primarily to privatisation is contested and simplifies multiple causes.

veracity.explanation: Cites a specific, checkable Federated Farmers survey result; the figures are precise and plausible for early 2025, though presented selectively to flatter the Government.

veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with MBIE modelling that wind and solar are among the cheapest new generation, though 'offshore wind' specifically is more costly than onshore.

veracity.statement: Whilst the average age of the Pākehā or European population in New Zealand is around 42, the average age of Māori is between 27 and 28.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with census data — median age for Māori is roughly 27 and for European New Zealanders around 41-42; accurate to within normal rounding.

veracity.statement: Māori freehold land, which comprises around 5 percent of the total land of New Zealand—1.5 million hectares of this country.
veracity.explanation: Māori freehold land is commonly cited at roughly 1.4–1.5 million hectares, about 5% of NZ's land area; the figures are accurate.

veracity.statement: over the last 10 years there's been a growth of nearly 50 percent of the total Māori population in this country.
veracity.explanation: Overstated — the Māori population grew substantially over the decade but not by nearly 50 percent; the true increase is closer to 20–30 percent depending on measure.

veracity.explanation: Presented explicitly as 'one estimate' and broadly consistent with reported science-sector job losses over 2024, though the round 500 figure is an approximation.

veracity.explanation: The National Science Challenges wound up and Marsden's blue-sky/humanities funding was cut under this Government — substantially accurate, though 'cut research funds' broadly is more debatable.

veracity.explanation: Attributed to specific ANZ domestic-spending analysis for mid-Dec to mid-Jan; plausible and sourced, though not independently verifiable here.

veracity.explanation: The RBNZ cut the OCR by 50 basis points on 19 February 2025; an accurate factual report.

veracity.statement: Today, we saw a 50 basis point cut in the official cash rate by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Now, the Reserve Bank is independent; the Government did not make them do that, but the Government did create the conditions for an official cash rate cut.
veracity.explanation: Accurate on the cut and on RBNZ independence; the fiscal-conditions attribution is a defensible but contestable interpretation.
