civility.statement: Families still see their grocery bills going up each week under this Government. And let's not forget power prices going up every month under this Government.
civility.explanation: Harsh but legitimate criticism of cost-of-living outcomes, focused on policy impact rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: We now have a future Deputy Prime Minister... who thinks it's OK for members of Parliament to interfere in murder investigations, who thinks it's OK to drive a Land Rover up the front steps of Parliament, who thinks it's OK to refer a victim of sexual abuse at the hands of that member's party president to a lawyer supplied by the party rather than to Victim Support or the Police.
civility.explanation: String of character-based accusations against an opponent, 'thinks it's OK to...' framing imputes bad motive rather than engaging policy substance.

civility.statement: stringing together a bunch of slogans will not make up for the fact that they simply don't have a plan. They don't have any idea how they're actually going to turn around the fortunes of the country.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the Government's approach, but 'don't have any idea' verges on dismissive characterisation rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: the reason that it is tough for New Zealanders is six years of economic vandalism and mismanagement and creating rules and costs on New Zealanders to control every single part of their lives, because that's a Labour Party and a Government that thinks they know best.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist characterisation of opponents' record rather than engagement with specific policies.

civility.statement: the war against farmers from Wellington is over, and we're working hard to make sure we get Wellington out of farming.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic 'war against farmers' framing, though aimed at policy/regulation rather than a person.

civility.statement: First, I really want to congratulate the Minister Simon Watts for his elevation to energy Minister, because it is a positive sign that the Minister, in his new role, has made it clear that we need a market that works in the interests of New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent, entirely policy-focused.

civility.statement: It thinks if it says the words, then it will just happen. What are their big ideas about getting growth growing in our economy? Import some rich people from overseas—and that's it.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation ('cargo-cult', 'that's it') rather than engagement with the actual policy program.

civility.statement: They've cut research funds for science, got rid of the National Science Challenges, got rid of the blue-sky element of the Marsden funding, and, while they're at it, they knifed the humanities in the back.
civility.explanation: Largely policy-focused list, but 'knifed the humanities in the back' is a sensationalist flourish.

civility.statement: Never let it be forgotten in this House or across the nation that that member who's just resumed her seat, Deborah Russell, was part of the failed last administration that led our country into the financial abyss that we find ourselves in today.
civility.explanation: Personalises the attack onto the named member and uses hyperbole ('financial abyss') rather than engaging her science arguments.

civility.statement: I want to make one thing very clear: takatāpui are our whānau. In the recent events we have witnessed following Pride week, we saw our takatāpui communities being devastatingly targeted for simply being themselves.
civility.explanation: Advocacy focused on protecting a community; 'devastatingly targeted' is emotive but not a personal attack on a named member.

civility.statement: That side just loves me, don't they, Mr Speaker? Any little thing—from my stickers, to my shoes, to whatever it is. They love it! They just keep picking, and, honestly, it doesn't do them any favours.
civility.explanation: A pointed but light retort to a point of order; mildly combative ('doesn't do them any favours') without being a personal insult.

rigor.statement: hocking off half the power companies actually contributed to the current power crisis that we're seeing at the moment, because those power companies decided to gouge more profits out of consumers rather than actually invest in new power generation.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal chain (partial privatisation → profit-seeking → underinvestment → price crisis) but relies on the loaded 'gouge' framing and asserts the mechanism without evidence.

rigor.statement: Emergency accommodation is not a solution, it is a stopgap measure while we build more houses, but they're not doing that any more either. They cancelled the new State house build programme when they became the Government, and all New Zealanders will pay the price for that.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable framing of emergency accommodation as a stopgap, but 'cancelled the new State house build programme' overstates a scaling-back/reprioritisation and the closing line is an unsupported assertion.

rigor.statement: the reason that it is tough for New Zealanders is six years of economic vandalism and mismanagement and creating rules and costs on New Zealanders to control every single part of their lives, because that's a Labour Party and a Government that thinks they know best.
rigor.explanation: Attributes all current hardship to the previous Government via loaded labels ('economic vandalism') and a strawman ('control every single part of their lives') with no evidence.

rigor.statement: We know the least-cost solutions to meet new demand are offshore wind and solar, according to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in a named expert source (MBIE) rather than assertion; conclusion follows from the cited evidence, though 'least-cost' depends on assumptions.

rigor.statement: I heard a submission the other day in the Treaty principles submission hearings about how it takes 26 steps to get an easement for Māori land but it only takes about five steps to get an easement on general land.
rigor.explanation: Uses a single submission as an anecdote to illustrate regulatory burden; the 26-vs-5 contrast is vivid but rests on one unverified account (appeal to anecdote).

rigor.statement: It thinks if it says the words, then it will just happen. What are their big ideas about getting growth growing in our economy? Import some rich people from overseas—and that's it.
rigor.explanation: Reduces the Government's growth agenda to a single caricatured policy ('import some rich people') — a strawman that ignores its stated measures.

rigor.statement: any other activities beyond this will no longer be funded from 30 June 2025... science activities to stop—that's 60 to 70 scientists whose jobs are going at Callaghan Innovation.
rigor.explanation: Builds the conclusion (scientists losing jobs) from a documented source — the letter of expectations — rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: Today, we saw a 50 basis point cut in the official cash rate by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Now, the Reserve Bank is independent; the Government did not make them do that, but the Government did create the conditions for an official cash rate cut.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes RBNZ independence from Government 'conditions', avoiding the fallacy of directly claiming credit — a disciplined caveat, though the causal 'created the conditions' claim is still asserted.

rigor.statement: at the heart of it, we had a Government for too long that created too much money and ended up producing too few goods. They spent billions and billions and billions that they couldn't afford... If there's more money hanging around than there is stuff to buy, then the prices go up.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a coherent monetary/supply story for inflation with a stated mechanism, but oversimplifies (ignores global supply shocks) and leans on 'billions and billions' rhetoric.

rigor.statement: It was colonisation that started criminalising and oppressing our people for being simply who they are. We must speak up... Fighting for our rights as indigenous peoples means we must fight for all rights of oppressed communities.
rigor.explanation: Historically grounded point about colonial-era criminalisation, but stated as broad assertion without specific evidence.

rigor.statement: We are the world-class innovators; remember it was we in New Zealand that split the atom.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to national pride using a historical claim that doesn't actually support 'we in New Zealand' as the site of the achievement.

rigor.statement: the very effervescent Winston Churchill said, "Trying to tax your way out of prosperity is like standing in a bucket and trying to lift it up by the handles." And he's quite right.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority plus an analogy ('and he's quite right') rather than evidence for the claim that taxation harms prosperity.

rigor.statement: for every Jimmy, that's about $15,500 a year we pay in the jobseeker benefit for Jimmy... for every thousand Jimmies, that's $15 million. And for every 10,000, that's $156 million that, if we aren't paying jobseeker benefits because we've had growth... we can spend on everything.
rigor.explanation: Extended hypothetical ('Jimmy') to illustrate savings, with loose and inconsistent arithmetic (1,000 × $15,500 = $15.5m, and 10,000 = $155m, not $156m) and assuming growth automatically converts beneficiaries to workers.

divination.statement: Emergency accommodation is not a solution, it is a stopgap measure while we build more houses, but they're not doing that any more either. They cancelled the new State house build programme when they became the Government, and all New Zealanders will pay the price for that.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'all New Zealanders will pay the price' — directionally plausible if state housing supply slows, but vague on magnitude and open-ended in timeframe.

charisma.statement: We now have a future Deputy Prime Minister... who thinks it's OK for members of Parliament to interfere in murder investigations, who thinks it's OK to drive a Land Rover up the front steps of Parliament, who thinks it's OK to refer a victim of sexual abuse at the hands of that member's party president to a lawyer supplied by the party rather than to Victim Support or the Police.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them attack; makes no attempt to persuade the unconvinced or build common ground.

charisma.statement: stringing together a bunch of slogans will not make up for the fact that they simply don't have a plan. They don't have any idea how they're actually going to turn around the fortunes of the country.
charisma.explanation: Rallying attack aimed at his own side; no bridge-building or acknowledgement of opponents' points.

charisma.statement: the war against farmers from Wellington is over, and we're working hard to make sure we get Wellington out of farming.
charisma.explanation: Rallies the rural base with an us-vs-them 'war' frame; energising to one side but divisive and not consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: First, I really want to congratulate the Minister Simon Watts for his elevation to energy Minister, because it is a positive sign that the Minister, in his new role, has made it clear that we need a market that works in the interests of New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Congratulates a Government minister across the aisle and frames shared purpose; genuinely bridge-building.

charisma.statement: It's in this House, with my Labour colleagues, my Te Pāti Māori colleagues, and I know even across the House with National, with New Zealand First, and possibly even ACT, people understand that we've got a broken electricity system and we need action.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly names every party as sharing common ground on the problem; strongly inclusive and consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: My bill, the Electricity Industry (Separation of Generation and Retail Businesses) Amendment Bill, is prepared and is in the ballot and can be acted on now by the Government if the Government wishes, and everyone seems to agree this is necessary.
charisma.explanation: Frames the bill as something all can support and invites the Government to act; inclusive tone.

charisma.statement: We need a delivery of the national energy strategy—and it would be good if it was bipartisan. It was supposed to be delivered last December. It would be good if it can be delivered in 2025. I'll reach across the House to ask the Government to work on that together.
charisma.explanation: Repeated explicit offers to work bipartisanly and 'reach across the House'; consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Never let it be forgotten in this House or across the nation that that member who's just resumed her seat, Deborah Russell, was part of the failed last administration that led our country into the financial abyss that we find ourselves in today.
charisma.explanation: Combative partisan framing aimed at his own side; no attempt at persuasion across the House.

charisma.statement: it allows New Zealanders freedom—freedom to choose how their own life story turns out without excessive hectoring, lecturing, and waste from a Government.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective appeal to freedom, but framed to rally his own side rather than to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: I want to make one thing very clear: takatāpui are our whānau. In the recent events we have witnessed following Pride week, we saw our takatāpui communities being devastatingly targeted for simply being themselves.
charisma.explanation: Warm and inclusive toward the takatāpui community, but framed around 'targeting' by opponents rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: It was colonisation that started criminalising and oppressing our people for being simply who they are. We must speak up... Fighting for our rights as indigenous peoples means we must fight for all rights of oppressed communities.
charisma.explanation: Seeks solidarity across oppressed groups, which is unifying within her frame, but the message rallies her side rather than reaching political opponents.

strength.statement: Over the last 12 months, we've undone more than 20 rules and regulations holding rural New Zealand back that were just the cost.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivery (20+ rules removed) rather than mere intent; follow-through is plausible but the vague 'more than 20' and unnamed rules limit verification.

strength.statement: As per our coalition agreement, last year legislation was placed "to restore the right to local referendum on the establishment of ongoing use of Māori wards."—promise delivered, along with our coalition partners.
strength.explanation: Points to actual legislation enacted to match a coalition commitment, not just an announcement; delivery is verifiable.

strength.statement: in the coalition agreement, we secured to refocus the curriculum on academic achievement and not ideology, including the removal and replacement of gender, sexuality, and relationship-based education guidelines. This is another promise that we are delivering on.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a coalition commitment, but 'delivering on' signals work in progress rather than completed implementation of the curriculum change.

strength.statement: this Government has put its money where its mouth is. It is funding the Waikare Gorge realignment, which is a massive project... that realignment means everything to the economic future and sustainability of regions like Tairāwhiti and Wairoa.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete funded project (Waikare Gorge realignment) rather than aspiration, though it is a recent funding announcement whose delivery is still ahead.

authenticity.statement: As per our coalition agreement, last year legislation was placed "to restore the right to local referendum on the establishment of ongoing use of Māori wards."—promise delivered, along with our coalition partners.
authenticity.explanation: Words match deeds — the coalition-agreement commitment is backed by the passed legislation she cites.

authenticity.statement: back in July 2023, Mr Peters—once again, a very busy leader—committed, in Whangārei, that we would have the second COVID inquiry. He also committed that we would have wider terms of reference, which is what the people wanted. This was secured in the coalition agreement with our partners beside me here.
authenticity.explanation: Ties a specific pre-election commitment (July 2023, Whangārei) to a delivered coalition outcome (Phase 2 inquiry with wider terms); a consistent words-to-deeds link.

forthrightness.statement: That side just loves me, don't they, Mr Speaker? Any little thing—from my stickers, to my shoes, to whatever it is. They love it! They just keep picking, and, honestly, it doesn't do them any favours.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to Seymour's objection that she was reading, she deflects with banter before returning to her theme rather than directly addressing the point.

veracity.statement: In June of last year, Mr Walker was referred to Nelson Hospital by his GP for suspected testicular cancer. The referral was urgent and he was supposed to be seen within a two-week time frame, but in fact it took nine weeks for Mr Walker to be seen—nine weeks.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced factual claim drawn from clinical records; plausible and detailed, though not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: who had to go on to a jobseeker benefit even though he has a job. The man has a job and he had to go on to a jobseeker benefit and take $10,000 out of his KiwiSaver because of financial hardship.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claim about the constituent's circumstances; plausible but unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: it has been initially capitalised with $1.31 billion from the divestment of Auckland Council - owned shares in Auckland International Airport Ltd.
veracity.explanation: Matches the widely reported ~$1.3bn Auckland Airport share sale proceeds.

veracity.statement: Our city drives over 38 percent of our national economy.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with commonly cited estimates that Auckland accounts for roughly 38% of NZ GDP.

veracity.statement: The $400 million in additional revenue that this fund will provide is dwarfed by the $1.2 billion that Auckland lost in revenue when the Government removed the regional fuel tax.
veracity.explanation: The regional fuel tax figure is in the reported range, but the '$400 million' framing sits oddly against the fund's ~$40m/year distribution, making the comparison potentially misleading.

veracity.statement: In the year to September 2024, Auckland saw an increase of 5,200 in the number of young people who are not engaged in education or training.
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claim; plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: As a result of National’s economic mismanagement and lack of action from the Minister for Auckland, Simeon Brown, Aucklanders continue to face a transport deficit of $564 million and a higher unemployment rate than the rest of Aotearoa New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The transport-deficit figure and higher-than-average unemployment are plausible, but causally attributing them to the government is contestable.

veracity.statement: This bill doesn’t even actually establish the Auckland Future Fund. What it does is put legislation and statutory protection around the kind of what we would call “raid protections” against the future potential use of that fund.
veracity.explanation: Accurate clarification of what the bill does versus common misconceptions; corrects the record.

veracity.statement: In the OECD, the average amount of spending that occurs at a local government level is approximately—and, again, these will be really old figures—30 percent, but here in Aotearoa, from what I recall of about nine years ago, it was far lower than half of that at around 12 percent.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with NZ's low share of local-government spending; she openly flags the figures are old/from memory, reducing overstatement.

veracity.statement: All of those inquiries and reports and all of that evidence has told us that local government does not have the resources necessary to do its damn job.
veracity.explanation: The general finding of under-resourced local government is well supported, though summarised sweepingly.

veracity.explanation: Auckland Airport's long-run share appreciation is broadly in this range; figures are approximate but reasonable.

veracity.explanation: The adequacy of iwi consultation is contested — Cheung later asserts a Māori Advisory Group was consulted — so the 'no proper consultation' claim is partly disputed.

veracity.statement: How can we talk about benefiting future generations, when Māori, who have the largest-growing populations in Tāmaki Makaurau—250,000 living in our city—are not explicitly included in decision making?
veracity.explanation: The order-of-magnitude Māori population figure for Auckland is plausible.

veracity.statement: I think it was something like $1.3 billion that they raised through the sale of the Auckland Airport shares.

veracity.statement: It’s not the councillors who will be making decisions on the investment that they will actually make with the fund but the experts in the Auckland Future Fund (AFF). They will make decisions on the investments that they will invest in to grow the pot
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the fund's independent, expert-governed structure as set out in the bill.

veracity.explanation: Auckland ~1.7 million and being the most populous region is accurate, but 'growing at 1 percent per day' is grossly wrong (that would be implausibly fast) — a misleading exaggeration.

specificity.explanation: Names dates, the referral, the two-week standard, and the actual nine-week wait — concrete and precise.

I can tell you that in terms of the set-up of that Auckland Future Fund, basically they have consulted with the Māori Advisory Group as well, and they are actually working on developing and achieving a Māori outcome plan

rigor.explanation: False dichotomy/strawman: implies opposing him equals opposing tackling bureaucracy.

rigor.statement: this Government inherited a botched merger of the healthcare system. Health outcomes went backwards under the last Government and we are doing everything we can to turn it around.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation without evidence.

rigor.statement: Well, what we're not going to do is run the economy into the ground like the Labour-Greens Government did in the last administration.
rigor.explanation: Assertion without evidence.

rigor.statement: ED wait times, which declined from 89.2 percent of people being seen within six hours when National left office to 67.5 percent when Labour left office.
rigor.explanation: Uses a defined metric to support the decline claim.

rigor.statement: There are 128,000 vintage vehicles in New Zealand and about 40,000 private motorhomes. They have to spend time and money getting a WoF or a CoF every six months. That is despite the fact that they travel less compared to modern cars. Evidence shows faults in these vehicles are half as likely to contribute to serious crashes.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy change in mileage and crash-contribution evidence.

rigor.statement: the National Government in 2014 started the funding for the Transmission Gully motorway. It finished in 2022, but I noticed that didn't stop Jacinda Ardern and Grant Robertson riding out in the Crown limos to spend up roughly $400,000 opening Transmission Gully, even though they campaigned against it in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete examples to argue projects span governments, though delivered with a partisan barb.

rigor.statement: the Government is not responsible for mill closures. Ultimately, those are economic decisions made by the owners of particular businesses.
rigor.explanation: Coherent point distinguishing macro policy from individual business decisions.

rigor.explanation: A reasoned incentive argument, though the causal claim is speculative and unevidenced.

rigor.statement: in the 1880s and 1890s, a white colonist popularised that name. Before that, no Māori ever thought that was the name for this country, because it comes from French Polynesia.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping historical assertion presented without evidence.

rigor.statement: Why is someone who applied to come to this country as an immigrant in 2006, when it was called New Zealand, allowed, in this House, to change the country's name without the mandate, the approval, or referendum of the New Zealand people?
rigor.explanation: Uses a member's origin to dismiss their point rather than addressing it (ad hominem).

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister telling Chlöe Swarbrick that we will not be following the Marxist model of wealth redistribution that she advocates?
rigor.explanation: Strawman framing of the opponent's position.

rigor.statement: Can his Government finally admit that after firing the Health New Zealand board, overseeing a health leadership exodus, and appointing one man who has delivered nothing but cuts, running the health system is not as simple as running an aeroplane?
rigor.explanation: Lists real events but wraps them in a loaded rhetorical question.

strength.statement: since this Government was elected, we have now had 175 basis points of interest rate reductions for New Zealanders.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for rate cuts that are the independent RBNZ's decisions, not a government delivery.

strength.statement: we have stable rents, we have a reduction in people on the social housing wait-list, and, most importantly, we have 2,000 kids out of emergency housing in good, safe, dry homes.
strength.explanation: Points to a measurable delivered outcome on emergency housing.

strength.statement: Already, the Government, in slightly more than 12 months, has taken over 20 actions to slash red tape and get Wellington out of farming. forthrightness.statement: Well, none, because, as the member knows, funding is allocated two or three years out from when the funding starts, and the Government took office on 27 November 2023, so it's a little bit difficult to allocate funding and have a house built the day or the month afterwards. civility.explanation: Critiques the bill's scope while explicitly protecting the member from personal criticism.

civility.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party to also support this bill, and I would like to thank the Hon Dr Deborah Russell for bringing this bill to the House and for highlighting the importance and also the potential risks that having your personal and private address being published in the Companies Register may bring.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused acknowledgement of the bill's sponsor.

civility.statement: Yes, it is potentially just a band-aid at this point.

civility.statement: New Zealand First will not support the bill as it is our view that there is a more comprehensive approach required. We will stand and stick with that.

civility.statement: I think it's just a simple and smart idea; and thought up by women, obviously, so we're really good with that. That makes complete, good women's sense to me and to our party.
civility.explanation: Light-hearted and supportive; no attack on anyone.

civility.statement: Remind us how many times you've used urgency.

civility.statement: There seems to be agreement across the House this evening that we safeguard company directors and those that cohabit from the risks associated with public disclosure of their residential addresses.

charisma.statement: We invite him to actually do a comprehensive view. civility.statement: can I just take the opportunity to congratulate the member Camilla Belich for taking this diligently through the hard-working Education and Workforce Committee and the various oral submissions and written submissions that we had the opportunity to engage in, and for the thoughtful debate we had through the select committee stage.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's work; opens debate on constructive terms.

civility.statement: I wondered if this title, Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill, would more appropriately be named something like the “Crimes (We Think All Employers Are Thieves) Amendment Bill”

civility.statement: we in the National Party want to just thank New Zealand First for bringing this Amendment Paper to the Table and indicate that we’ll be supporting the amendment.
civility.explanation: Cordial cross-party acknowledgement and support for another party's amendment.

civility.statement: I would like to just reject Carl Bates’ allegation that this is about calling employers thieves, or that there was any suggestion that all employers are involved in this type of behaviour. civility.explanation: Rebuts the characterisation on substance and affirms most employers are good, without personal attack.

civility.statement: It is very ironic to hear members of the National Party stand up and take calls wanting people who have committed crimes against their employees not to face justice as a result of that; that is the effective nature of that submission and something that I reject.

civility.statement: I would also like to thank our former colleague Sarah Pallett, who was the person who first authored this bill. When Sarah wasn’t re-elected to Parliament, I took over the bill.

charisma.statement: can I just take the opportunity to congratulate the member Camilla Belich for taking this diligently through the hard-working Education and Workforce Committee and the various oral submissions and written submissions that we had the opportunity to engage in, and for the thoughtful debate we had through the select committee stage.
charisma.explanation: Generous, bridge-building tone toward the member across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I wondered if this title, Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill, would more appropriately be named something like the “Crimes (We Think All Employers Are Thieves) Amendment Bill”
charisma.explanation: Partisan, mocking framing that plays to his own side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: An example of what I’m saying would be the removal of accredited employer status for employers who are caught doing wrong in terms of this type of intent.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, solution-oriented suggestion rather than pure opposition.

charisma.statement: we in the National Party want to just thank New Zealand First for bringing this Amendment Paper to the Table and indicate that we’ll be supporting the amendment.
charisma.explanation: Signals cooperation across the House, building consensus around the amendment.

charisma.statement: I would like to just reject Carl Bates’ allegation that this is about calling employers thieves, or that there was any suggestion that all employers are involved in this type of behaviour. Of course, we know that the vast majority are very good employers, just like most New Zealanders, but there is a place for the criminal law in New Zealand when crimes are committed.
charisma.explanation: Seeks to reassure the other side that good employers are not the target.

charisma.statement: It is very ironic to hear members of the National Party stand up and take calls wanting people who have committed crimes against their employees not to face justice as a result of that; that is the effective nature of that submission and something that I reject.
charisma.explanation: Partisan 'ironic to hear National' jab that rallies her side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I encourage all members across the House, even if you’re not voting for the substantive bill—I would like to request that you consider this Amendment Paper, because I do think it is beneficial and makes the bill, hopefully, a better piece of legislation.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive appeal inviting even opponents of the bill to back a specific improvement.

charisma.statement: Maybe if that member had sat through the process themselves, they would have actually been able to see what was being said and then would appreciate the new title that I’m suggesting.
charisma.explanation: Dismissive of an opponent rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: That might be 1 June because the financial year—the people on the other side who’ve never run a business and don’t understand what the rural sector’s like, this is actually quite an important time.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: if we could get a breakdown of the data, if it does exist, of small business versus large business, just to see where the burden sits in this space
charisma.explanation: Frames a concrete, reasonable ask that could inform members on both sides.

charisma.statement: did you consider using the word “pilfer” or “pilferage” by an employer? That is really a much better description of the kinds of things that we are dealing with. Or “peculation” or “rapacity”—these are words that potentially could have been better used.
charisma.explanation: Light, non-hostile in tone but adds little that persuades.

charisma.statement: The reason New Zealand First is speaking on this legislation is because we recognise that just as we have hard-working Kiwi businesses, we have hard-working employees who on occasion can be victimised because of that power imbalance.
charisma.explanation: Balanced framing that honours both employers and workers, seeking common ground across the debate.

charisma.statement: thank you to the member Casey Costello for that very thoughtful contribution to this debate, which I think does really sum up the purpose of this legislation.
charisma.explanation: Reinforces cross-party goodwill and shared purpose.

divination.statement: Now, ultimately, for how often the Opposition members talk about their concerns around us filling up our prisons with too many prisoners, this could ultimately result, potentially, in people filling up or clogging up our justice system.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the bill will clog the justice system; heavily hedged and speculative, no evidence of volume, and prosecution thresholds make it unlikely.

rigor.statement: Now, ultimately, for how often the Opposition members talk about their concerns around us filling up our prisons with too many prisoners, this could ultimately result, potentially, in people filling up or clogging up our justice system.
rigor.explanation: Attempts a consistency gotcha about prison numbers, but the causal chain to a clogged justice system is asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: I wondered if this title, Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill, would more appropriately be named something like the “Crimes (We Think All Employers Are Thieves) Amendment Bill”
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts a targeted theft offence as branding all employers thieves.

rigor.statement: Frankly, when I’m door knocking, like I was on Sunday, in Whanganui, meeting members of my own constituency, the everyday worker’s focus was on how their wages can increase.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an anecdote from door-knocking rather than evidence to support a policy point.

rigor.statement: I wonder if the member would consider as an alternative, as an amendment to that, the “Crimes (Theft (Even if it is an Accident) by Employer) Amendment Bill
rigor.explanation: Argument built on a misreading of the offence's intent requirement.

rigor.statement: would the member consider aligning, if it was to pass, the commencement to be 1 April 2026 so that, first of all, it is aligned, as I’ve said, with the life cycle of the business year—that naturally sits at the start of the financial year, being 1 April—then, secondly, allowing sufficient time for not only the communication out of this House to get through to employers, through appropriate different channels, but also for HR practitioners to get the appropriate up-skilling and up-training?
rigor.explanation: Coherent, reasoned case linking the date to the business cycle and readiness, though the burden it assumes is disputed.

rigor.statement: An example of what I’m saying would be the removal of accredited employer status for employers who are caught doing wrong in terms of this type of intent.
rigor.explanation: Offers a targeted, defensible alternative aimed at the migrant-exploitation cases actually raised.

rigor.statement: The first part of his question, on why it’s in the Crimes Act as opposed to a personal grievance, is really the entire purpose of this bill. It’s to recognise the fact that there isn’t a criminal sanction available for employees who suffer theft as a result of the actions of their employer.
rigor.explanation: Clear reasoning: the gap in criminal sanction is the stated rationale for the drafting choice.

rigor.statement: There are existing provisions in the Immigration Act which criminalise theft by an employer for recent migrants, and often—and inequitably, in my view—employees who do steal from their employers are referred to police and treated in the criminal law.
rigor.explanation: Uses the existing legal asymmetry as evidence that the bill corrects an imbalance.

rigor.statement: I would like to just reject Carl Bates’ allegation that this is about calling employers thieves, or that there was any suggestion that all employers are involved in this type of behaviour. Of course, we know that the vast majority are very good employers, just like most New Zealanders, but there is a place for the criminal law in New Zealand when crimes are committed.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes a targeted criminal offence from a blanket accusation coherently.

rigor.statement: It is very ironic to hear members of the National Party stand up and take calls wanting people who have committed crimes against their employees not to face justice as a result of that; that is the effective nature of that submission and something that I reject.
rigor.explanation: Borders on strawman by equating title/commencement objections with wanting crimes to go unpunished.

rigor.statement: This bill covers intentional theft—not mistakes, not mishaps, not people being forgetful: intentional theft—and that links to his suggestion that the commencement should be delayed.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the rebuttal in the offence's intent element, which follows from the drafting.

rigor.statement: In respect to his question in relation to data, the document I pointed out to him earlier that was provided by the Ministry of Justice to the Education and Workforce Committee states that in 2020, there were 77 cases of wage arrears in the Employment Relations Authority; 2021, 61 cases; 2022, 107 cases; 2023, 130 cases; and 2024, 30 cases. Now, not all of these cases will necessarily reach the higher threshold of theft, but some of them may.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based response with a careful qualification about what the numbers do and don't show.

rigor.statement: In terms of the drafting of the Education and Workforce Committee being deficient, he is a member of that select committee. He has the numbers by majority on that select committee, so if there’s any issue with the drafting, then he is, if not just as responsible as myself, more so. Additionally, the select committee changes were agreed unanimously with, in fact, his vote.
rigor.explanation: Turns the deficient-drafting charge back with a factual point about committee majority and his own vote.

rigor.statement: That might be 1 June because the financial year—the people on the other side who’ve never run a business and don’t understand what the rural sector’s like, this is actually quite an important time.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem substituting for argument about the commencement date.

rigor.statement: I would suggest 1 June 2026 might suit the dairy sector, because it gives them time to really understand that, actually, this is a potential criminal act that they could deal with.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned link to the dairy financial year, though the underlying need for delay is contested.

rigor.statement: One of the other things that does worry me about the bill is the list of the punishments that you’ve got here in terms of imprisonment of not exceeding a year. Is that really appropriate in this situation? That seems to me to be very heavy-handed, along with a fine of up to $5,000.
rigor.explanation: Raises a legitimate proportionality question but leans on assertion ('heavy-handed') rather than comparison.

rigor.statement: if we could get a breakdown of the data, if it does exist, of small business versus large business, just to see where the burden sits in this space
rigor.explanation: Constructive, evidence-seeking request to disaggregate the data by business size.

rigor.statement: did you consider using the word “pilfer” or “pilferage” by an employer? That is really a much better description of the kinds of things that we are dealing with. Or “peculation” or “rapacity”—these are words that potentially could have been better used.
rigor.explanation: Tangential wordsmithing on the title rather than a substantive argument; Belich notes 'theft' is defined in the Crimes Act.

rigor.statement: I just think that this is one of those examples, potentially, where we’ve got a bill that’s looking for a problem to solve, and it’s not necessarily that we’ve got a huge background problem here that we’re trying to amend.
rigor.explanation: Asserts no real problem exists; contradicted by the Ministry of Justice wage-arrears data cited in the debate.

rigor.statement: Our concern that New Zealand First had in this—and it’s been touched on in the discussion so far—was that we needed to ensure that there were not only intentional actions, not only the mens rea to deprive, but that there was no reasonable excuse. That will capture, I think, a lot of the concerns that have been raised in the committee today: that if there’s a payroll glitch, if there is a delayed time sheet, if there is a dispute over a time sheet, if there is a cash-flow issue—all of those factors that would generate a reasonable excuse would ensure that this component of legislation is really focused on those who we are targeting
rigor.explanation: Precise legal reasoning tying the intent and 'reasonable excuse' elements to the specific edge cases raised.

rigor.statement: The reason New Zealand First is speaking on this legislation is because we recognise that just as we have hard-working Kiwi businesses, we have hard-working employees who on occasion can be victimised because of that power imbalance.
rigor.explanation: Grounds support in a coherent power-imbalance rationale rather than slogans.

rigor.statement: The solution we have in place through this bill is a bit of a band-aid but, for the time being, a band-aid will do. ... The solution proposed by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs will be a better solution, but that solution is not available yet.
rigor.explanation: Honest cost-benefit framing of an interim measure versus a fuller reform not yet available.

rigor.statement: He said it was coming “soon”, but “soon” is a very slippery word: “soon” can mean five minutes, “soon” can mean three months, “soon” can mean five years—what does “soon” mean in this case?
rigor.explanation: Fair point about an unfalsifiable timeframe, though rhetorical rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Think we could have a delay on murder as well?
rigor.explanation: A flippant reductio that ridicules rather than reasons.

veracity.statement: there was no data able to substantiate the size of the problem that the member is trying to solve.
veracity.explanation: Contestable claim; Belich points to Ministry of Justice wage-arrears data supplied to the committee, so 'no data' is misleading.

veracity.statement: I wonder if the member would consider as an alternative, as an amendment to that, the “Crimes (Theft (Even if it is an Accident) by Employer) Amendment Bill
veracity.explanation: Mischaracterises the bill as catching accidental non-payment; Belich confirms it covers only intentional theft.

veracity.statement: There are existing provisions in the Immigration Act which criminalise theft by an employer for recent migrants, and often—and inequitably, in my view—employees who do steal from their employers are referred to police and treated in the criminal law.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Immigration Act does criminalise migrant exploitation, and employee theft is dealt with criminally; supports her balance argument.

veracity.statement: In respect to his question in relation to data, the document I pointed out to him earlier that was provided by the Ministry of Justice to the Education and Workforce Committee states that in 2020, there were 77 cases of wage arrears in the Employment Relations Authority; 2021, 61 cases; 2022, 107 cases; 2023, 130 cases; and 2024, 30 cases. Now, not all of these cases will necessarily reach the higher threshold of theft, but some of them may.
veracity.explanation: Cites a sourced Ministry of Justice figure and appropriately caveats that not all cases meet the theft threshold.

veracity.statement: there are special penalties already for the exploitation of employees and temporary workers that are made under the employment legislation, and that comes with a penalty of up to seven years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $100,000.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states existing Immigration Act exploitation penalties.

veracity.statement: In terms of the drafting of the Education and Workforce Committee being deficient, he is a member of that select committee. He has the numbers by majority on that select committee, so if there’s any issue with the drafting, then he is, if not just as responsible as myself, more so. Additionally, the select committee changes were agreed unanimously with, in fact, his vote.
veracity.explanation: Assertion about unanimous agreement and his vote is a checkable procedural claim presented as fact.

veracity.statement: We heard Ibrahim Omer—the first person who brought this bill to the House, in the 53rd Parliament—speak of two examples of wage theft that he had suffered himself.
veracity.explanation: Verifiable factual claim about the bill's origin and Omer's testimony.

veracity.statement: I just think that this is one of those examples, potentially, where we’ve got a bill that’s looking for a problem to solve, and it’s not necessarily that we’ve got a huge background problem here that we’re trying to amend.
veracity.explanation: Claim that there is no big background problem is misleading given the case-count data and select-committee testimony.

veracity.statement: what it does is it creates the capacity for directors of companies—and, by the time it came out of the select committee, it’s directors of companies who are also shareholders in those companies—to have their home addresses removed from the Companies Register and replaced with an alternate address.
veracity.explanation: Accurate factual description of the bill's effect.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Super Fund supported it, and so did the Restaurant Association and Retail New Zealand. Russell McVeagh supported it; so did Business New Zealand and the Institute of Directors and one of our big insurance companies, IAG, who also put in a submission on it.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claims about which organisations submitted in support.

specificity.statement: Frankly, when I’m door knocking, like I was on Sunday, in Whanganui, meeting members of my own constituency, the everyday worker’s focus was on how their wages can increase.
specificity.explanation: Names the place (Whanganui) and time (Sunday) but the underlying claim about workers' focus is impressionistic.

specificity.explanation: Proposes a precise commencement date (1 April 2026) with a concrete rationale tied to the financial year and communication lead time.

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative mechanism (removing accredited employer status) rather than a vague objection.

Now, not all of these cases will necessarily reach the higher threshold of theft, but some of them may.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise annual case counts and their source.

Is that really appropriate in this situation? That seems to me to be very heavy-handed, along with a fine of up to $5,000.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact penalties (up to a year's imprisonment, $5,000 and later $30,000 fines) at issue.

specificity.statement: the background on this space is that I have done a lot of work in the labour exploitation area and recognise the vulnerability of these communities and, therefore, have had to rely a lot on the immigration legislation that looks at the protections for temporary workers and unlawful workers in this country.
specificity.explanation: References her area of work and the relevant immigration protections, though without specific cases.

specificity.statement: Our concern that New Zealand First had in this—and it’s been touched on in the discussion so far—was that we needed to ensure that there were not only intentional actions, not only the mens rea to deprive, but that there was no reasonable excuse. That will capture, I think, a lot of the concerns that have been raised in the committee today: that if there’s a payroll glitch, if there is a delayed time sheet, if there is a dispute over a time sheet, if there is a cash-flow issue—all of those factors that would generate a reasonable excuse would ensure that this component of legislation is really focused on those who we are targeting
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete scenarios (payroll glitch, delayed or disputed time sheet, cash-flow issue) the amendment addresses.

specificity.explanation: Clearly and precisely states the mechanism and the select-committee narrowing to director-shareholders.

specificity.explanation: Names specific supporting submitters rather than asserting vague 'broad support'.

forthrightness.statement: The first part of his question, on why it’s in the Crimes Act as opposed to a personal grievance, is really the entire purpose of this bill. It’s to recognise the fact that there isn’t a criminal sanction available for employees who suffer theft as a result of the actions of their employer.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Bates's question about why the offence sits in the Crimes Act.

forthrightness.statement: This bill covers intentional theft—not mistakes, not mishaps, not people being forgetful: intentional theft—and that links to his suggestion that the commencement should be delayed.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the banking-mishap scenario by stating the intent requirement plainly.

forthrightness.statement: In respect to his question in relation to data, the document I pointed out to him earlier that was provided by the Ministry of Justice to the Education and Workforce Committee states that in 2020, there were 77 cases of wage arrears in the Employment Relations Authority; 2021, 61 cases; 2022, 107 cases; 2023, 130 cases; and 2024, 30 cases. Now, not all of these cases will necessarily reach the higher threshold of theft, but some of them may.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the repeated demand for year-by-year data with the actual figures.

authenticity.statement: the background on this space is that I have done a lot of work in the labour exploitation area and recognise the vulnerability of these communities and, therefore, have had to rely a lot on the immigration legislation that looks at the protections for temporary workers and unlawful workers in this country.
authenticity.explanation: Positions her support consistent with a stated record of work on labour exploitation, matching words to prior focus.

authenticity.statement: The solution we have in place through this bill is a bit of a band-aid but, for the time being, a band-aid will do. ... The solution proposed by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs will be a better solution, but that solution is not available yet.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly concedes her own bill is an interim fix and credits the Minister's forthcoming approach as better, matching rhetoric to a realistic assessment.

specificity.statement: The Labour Party supports this bill, the Overseas Investment (Build-to-rent and Similar Rental Developments) Amendment Bill, but we wouldn’t support the bill if went any further.
specificity.explanation: Clear stated position with a defined limit (supports this, not further loosening), though the boundary is qualitative.

specificity.statement: This Government has done that by reversing the interest deductibility rules to back to where they were, and already we have seen the number of consents for new builds fall, and we have seen the level of lending to investors increase.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (interest deductibility reversal) and directional effects but no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: All they needed to do was to look at a two-tier system: that the 20-unit minimum applied in the cities, and a proportional threshold outside of that; so as long as it’s above six units and 100 percent.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism with named thresholds (20 units in cities, above six units at 100 percent in regions).

specificity.statement: Housing is a human right.
specificity.explanation: A value slogan with no mechanism, figure, or commitment.

specificity.statement: Just in my own electorate of Rongotai alone, I talked to a builder who said they had $70 million worth of new builds, redevelopment of public land, that would have supplied more homes into Rongotai, cancelled now by the existing Government.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure ($70 million), location (Rongotai) and source, though number of homes is not given.

specificity.statement: The real problem we have in New Zealand is that we have just harsh and unworkable, sometimes unmovable, and designed-to-say-no legislation and problems in this country that this Government is working incredibly hard on addressing, through things like reforming the Resource Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the RMA reform as the mechanism but no detail on how it changes outcomes.

specificity.statement: so that everybody in this big boat we call New Zealand or Aotearoa—we all are paddling in the same direction, we all feel like we have a place here, and New Zealanders can look at their country with pride when we have the places to house New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Uplifting but vague — no concrete content.

specificity.statement: When I was the Mayor of Wellington, I saw KO projects, and most of them were sitting at around $900,000 to a million dollars—for the building; probably excluding the land. That is for a one- or two-bedroom house.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures ($900k–$1m) and dwelling type.

specificity.statement: I had a quick look last week at the number of houses which are $2 million - plus which were listed on TradeMe... In Auckland, out of 15,196 listings, approximately 12 percent were $2 million or above... In Queenstown Lakes, it was 45 percent of the 469 listings.
specificity.explanation: Precise listing counts and percentages by region to support the $2m-threshold argument.

specificity.statement: just before I started this job, I built 16 homes in a tiny little place in the very Far North... We built four-bedroom, three-bedroom, and two-bedroom homes on a piece of dirt in Te Kao.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail — 16 homes, dwelling types, location (Te Kao), road and water infrastructure added.

specificity.statement: We’ve lifted the brightline test to 10 years. We’ve brought back deductibility, treating interest as a genuine expense. We’ve brought back no-cause terminations on 90-day contracts... We’ve put more competition into building products.
specificity.explanation: Names specific, checkable policy changes (brightline 10 years, deductibility, 90-day terminations).

specificity.statement: you will see on that buildtorentnz.co.nz website all of what’s under construction, with 1,800 completed units, 736 under construction, and nearly 3,000 in the pipeline as of the end of December.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts (1,800 completed, 736 under construction, ~3,000 pipeline) with a dated source.

specificity.statement: we are the party for mum and dad landlords, we are the party for homeowners, and now this is just another step to confirm that we are the party for renters.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-style branding with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: It is under way because, when we were in Government, we put in place the regime that allowed it to happen. We created the asset class. We made it clear that build-to-rent was part of solving our housing crisis.
specificity.explanation: Concrete on the achievement (creating the asset class) though light on figures here.

specificity.statement: Under this asset class, those people renting those apartments have the right for leases up to 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail — leases up to 10 years.

specificity.statement: we will not solve a housing crisis until we resurrect that piece of housing that sits between the market and public housing, which we had in New Zealand for decades—decades and decades, since the 1930s.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a category (between-market-and-public housing) with historical framing but no numbers.

specificity.statement: Of course, it was great news, only yesterday, to have the official cash rate drop by 50 basis points.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact figure (50 basis points) and timing.

specificity.statement: I have a rental property on the same street as one owned by a friend, and they are similar properties. My property was rented in two days, although I did reduce the rent by $70, but my friend reduced his rent by $150 and he still hasn’t rented it.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($70, $150, two days) though as an illustrative single case.

specificity.statement: all it does is create a streamlined process through the Overseas Investment Act, right. All the other requirements of that office still apply, so there are still protections in there for New Zealand in terms of the sale of land.
specificity.explanation: Explains the actual mechanism of the bill clearly, though without clause detail.

specificity.statement: It means, also, for the local businesses, as the developments take shape, more cafes, more coffee, more sandwiches, more hardware stores, more service providers.
specificity.explanation: An evocative list of downstream benefits but no figures, mechanisms or measurable targets.

specificity.statement: we’re saying yes to solutions, yes to actions, yes to more income, yes to a stronger economy for all Kiwis in the country.
specificity.explanation: Pure slogan with no content.

specificity.statement: As part of the Finance and Expenditure Committee process, we received 27 submissions on this, including from a local iwi, which I acknowledged in the second reading of the House.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count of submissions and reference to an iwi submission.

specificity.statement: It does streamline the test in order to make things slightly quicker for those who have the volume of build-to-rent units. It has not removed some of those protections from the Overseas Investment Act, which is why this side of the House is supporting it.
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism (streamlined test, retained protections, 20-unit volume) with reasonable precision.

specificity.statement: I think all that has been said in this House is relevant. I don’t have much more to contribute other than to say I agree with the statements made from many sides of this part of the House.
specificity.explanation: Adds no concrete content of his own.

authenticity.statement: The Labour Party supports this bill, the Overseas Investment (Build-to-rent and Similar Rental Developments) Amendment Bill, but we wouldn’t support the bill if went any further.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's record of creating the build-to-rent asset class; a principled, bounded position later echoed by his colleagues.

authenticity.statement: The Green Party is not going to support this bill.
authenticity.explanation: Position consistent with the party's stated preference for public housing and renter protection over easing foreign investment; matched by the final vote.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has always been very wary of foreign investment in New Zealand. What we want to do is to make sure that where there is foreign investment in New Zealand, it is to the benefit of New Zealand.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-standing, well-known stance on foreign investment and their objection to the lower $2m threshold.

authenticity.statement: just before I started this job, I built 16 homes in a tiny little place in the very Far North... We built four-bedroom, three-bedroom, and two-bedroom homes on a piece of dirt in Te Kao.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds her community-development argument in her own demonstrated action of building homes.

authenticity.statement: It is under way because, when we were in Government, we put in place the regime that allowed it to happen. We created the asset class. We made it clear that build-to-rent was part of solving our housing crisis.

civility.explanation: Attacks 'looking after the rich mates' framing; heated but aimed at policy priorities.
