civility.explanation: Charged historical framing directed at a class ('they') rather than a personal attack on a member.

civility.statement: before we talk about the fact that we have seen a Prime Minister who consistently uses the term “ruthlessly in pursuit of growth”, I would like to remind the House that the adverb “ruthlessly” has never been used in any positive light. That is only ever used to describe cruel and cold-blooded intent.
civility.explanation: Uses the PM's own word choice to characterise him as cold-blooded — pointed but tied to his actual phrasing.

civility.statement: What we are hearing, for those that are upset about this reconfirmation of the 2024-25 tax year, is their anti-ness of hard-working Kiwis getting some tax relief.
civility.explanation: Recasts the Opposition's position as being 'anti' hard-working Kiwis — a strawman rather than engaging their fiscal argument.

civility.statement: We did have that under the previous Labour Government and also under the previous National Government, who dealt with other disasters.
civility.explanation: Even-handedly credits both Labour and National governments for the emergency tax measures.

civility.statement: the thing with tax cuts is timing is really important. It was a very difficult time, and we’re seeing the consequences of that through our health system. We are seeing consequences of that through other programmes, like the school lunch programme, which has had a reduction in funding.
civility.explanation: Frames the disagreement as a matter of principle and timing, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: we do recognise the hard work that has actually come about through not just this Government but also the previous Labour Government, and possibly even previous Governments to that, in working towards building better taxation systems. Not everything in a bill is always something that is bad.
civility.explanation: Gracious, substance-focused recognition of opponents' contributions.

civility.statement: that side of the House thinks Government knows best. That’s why we’re now having reforms with tertiary, hospital, tax—just a mess everywhere we go, because they think Wellington knows best. Well, we like to give money back to the Kiwis that earn it.
civility.explanation: Caricatures the other side ('Government knows best') and calls their legacy 'a mess'; partisan but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Note, Te Pāti Māori were not present to cast a vote, so there aren’t many surprises there.
civility.explanation: A dismissive dig at another party's attendance rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: I know that many people in the National Party that I meet with and talk with do believe in that. They believe that we as a society are judged by how we treat our most vulnerable, and being a member of the New Zealand society, being a New Zealand taxpayer, is around our contribution.
civility.explanation: Respectful, assumes good faith in political opponents.

specificity.statement: the Labour Party will be voting against this bill. The reason is not the particular tax measures, but the bill does contain the annual rates for 2024-25, and unfortunately, we do not see in those rates any response to the fiscal needs of this country.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact objection (the 2024-25 annual rates) but the 'fiscal needs' claim is left general.

specificity.statement: One of the jobs for the revenue system in this country is to ensure that it supplies enough Government revenue—gathered from all citizens, all residents—to ensure that Government can do the things that Government ought to do, like paying for a health system, like paying for an education system, like paying for decent school lunches, and like paying for the increased defence spending we’re likely to need in this increasingly uncertain world.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete spending areas (health, education, school lunches, defence) but no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: we will be voting in favour of all the amendments to the bill at committee stage, but we will not be supporting Part 1 of the bill, and alas, we cannot support the bill overall because of the annual rates in it.
specificity.explanation: Precise about voting intentions at each stage and the exact reason (Part 1 annual rates).

specificity.statement: the top two quintiles—that is, 40 percent of households—gain $1.6 billion or 55 percent of the total of the value of those tax cuts. Those top two quintiles, that top 40 percent, it must be noted, also benefit from $750 million a year from the landlord tax cut reduction. When that is included, that top 40 percent in our country ends up getting 64 percent of the value of the Government’s tax cuts.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, percentages and source for the distribution of the tax cuts.

specificity.statement: the lowest quintile, the bottom 20 percent of New Zealanders, are getting just 5.4 percent of the total over here. Even more than that—and the Government knows this—we are seeing 130,000 households get nothing at all. Meanwhile, 8,000 households are worse off.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages and household counts.

specificity.statement: these tax cuts were paid for by the reintroduction of prescription fees, by increases in bus fares, by increases in vehicle registration fees, by increased and raised immigration levies, by higher tertiary education fees, by more toll roads, by increased court fees... and by cuts—cuts, cuts, cuts: cuts to Dunedin Hospital plans, cuts to the per child cost of the school lunch programme.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates many concrete offsetting measures by name.

specificity.statement: This was spelled out by research done by the Inland Revenue Department in 2023, which told us that the top 311 households in Aotearoa hold more wealth than 2.5 million New Zealanders. That report also spelled out that... those at the top pay an effective tax rate that is less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, year and precise figures (311 households, 2.5 million, half the effective rate).

specificity.statement: Here I would only just quote from the OECD Economic Surveys: New Zealand 2024, where they say, “There is a need to reduce distortions to household choice of asset allocation. Shares, land and owner-occupied residential property are tax favoured... capital gains taxation reform should be done as part of a review of tax settings for saving.”
specificity.explanation: Names the exact source and quotes its precise recommendation.

specificity.statement: we should be very proud of our tax system. We do actually have a very robust tax system. It actually does have a lot of transparency. We don’t have a lot of deductions. It works very well.
specificity.explanation: Broadly asserts virtues (robust, transparent, few deductions) with one concrete feature but little detail.

specificity.statement: This Government finally made the proactive decision to change the thresholds in the tax rates. That is something that New Zealanders have waited for since 2010 to see changes in the thresholds—2010.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the claim to a specific year (2010) but not to the threshold figures.

specificity.statement: the changes here allow an Order in Council, and I think that is the big thing. Instead of having to have a piece of legislation that goes through the House, an Order in Council can make the necessary, quick changes to actually help people that are in times of need, in times where different emergency events have occurred. It is good that there is consensus across the House on that amendment.
specificity.explanation: Explains the concrete mechanism (Order in Council instead of fresh legislation) and its purpose.

specificity.statement: This Government has given $3 billion tax cuts to landlords while over a million people who are earning less than $30,000 a year will only get $2 a week from their tax cuts.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures, income threshold and beneficiary counts.

specificity.statement: They have taken away public transport subsidies, free prescriptions. They’ve also taken away first-home grants. They’ve increased rates. They’ve cut the minimum wage, cut the benefit, cut 10,000 jobs.
specificity.explanation: A concrete list of measures, including a job-cut figure, though items are unqualified.

specificity.statement: if we had a tax policy... removing GST, removing income tax for whānau on low incomes, we would increase take-home pay for 98 percent of whānau, income tax on those earning more than $200k, the company tax rate from 28 percent to 33 percent. We’ll introduce a wealth tax, foreign companies tax, land banking tax, vacant house tax.
specificity.explanation: Lists named tax instruments and concrete rates/thresholds ($200k, 28%→33%).

specificity.statement: The tax system is broken and it continues to allow the rich to pay only 9 percent while the rest of Aotearoa pays 20.2 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise effective-rate figures (9% vs 20.2%).

specificity.statement: If you are a couple and you are on superannuation and that’s all you are on, you are getting—through the Government’s own budget calculator—$8.62 for the couple, for the two of you, per fortnight. That is $2.16 per week. That is 31c per day. A two litre bottle of milk has gone up by 29c, just most recently. A one kilo block of cheese has gone up by 10c.
specificity.explanation: Highly concrete: exact per-fortnight/week/day amounts and specific grocery price changes.

specificity.statement: We’re seeing shocking stats for child poverty. We’re seeing one in eight of our tamariki living in material hardship, one in five for tamariki Māori, one in four for Pasifika children.
specificity.explanation: Precise ratios broken down by group (1 in 8, 1 in 5 Māori, 1 in 4 Pasifika).

specificity.statement: We’re seeing hack and slash to the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme, and within that we’re seeing the way that this Government chooses to evaluate programmes... Out of the six evaluations that they will be using, three are about cost saving.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and gives a concrete evaluation breakdown (three of six criteria about cost saving).

specificity.statement: Poverty is a political choice, taxation is a political choice, and we have the tools to make those kind of genuine changes based on data, based on what economists around Aotearoa and internationally are telling us.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical framing; gestures at 'tools' and 'data' without naming them here.

specificity.statement: overall, 83 percent of Kiwis or 94 percent of households benefited from the Government’s tax package—personal tax package—that we are confirming today through this taxation bill.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise proportions of individuals and households benefiting.

specificity.statement: The thresholds have risen from $14,000 to $15,600 for the 17.5 percent tax rate. They have risen from $48,000 to $53,500 for those paying the 30 percent tax rate. They’ve risen from $70,000 to $78,100 for the 33 percent tax rate.
specificity.explanation: Exact old and new threshold figures for each rate band.

specificity.statement: you can actually claim FamilyBoost for up to four years. If any family members haven’t claimed... anyone that wants to claim FamilyBoost can actually claim it for up to four years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, actionable detail about the FamilyBoost claim window (up to four years).

specificity.statement: we’re able to get many new Kāinga Ora houses on the schedule to be built—we got many built. In fact, just earlier, or just like last year, we had 48 new beautiful homes open in central New Plymouth. To see, then, the hard work that was done and investment made be cut... has been devastating.
specificity.explanation: Names the location and a concrete figure (48 homes) with timeframe.

specificity.statement: The best way to achieve economic development is actually to make sure hard-working people get to keep more of their hard-working dollars. Wellington does not know best, but people do.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level; no mechanism, figures or policy detail.

rigor.statement: One of the jobs for the revenue system in this country is to ensure that it supplies enough Government revenue—gathered from all citizens, all residents—to ensure that Government can do the things that Government ought to do, like paying for a health system, like paying for an education system, like paying for decent school lunches, and like paying for the increased defence spending we’re likely to need in this increasingly uncertain world.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument linking revenue adequacy to specific public services; reasoned though the conclusion (rates are insufficient) is asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: the top two quintiles—that is, 40 percent of households—gain $1.6 billion or 55 percent of the total of the value of those tax cuts. Those top two quintiles, that top 40 percent, it must be noted, also benefit from $750 million a year from the landlord tax cut reduction. When that is included, that top 40 percent in our country ends up getting 64 percent of the value of the Government’s tax cuts.
rigor.explanation: Argument built on cited official distributional data rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: these tax cuts were paid for by the reintroduction of prescription fees, by increases in bus fares, by increases in vehicle registration fees, by increased and raised immigration levies, by higher tertiary education fees, by more toll roads, by increased court fees... and by cuts—cuts, cuts, cuts: cuts to Dunedin Hospital plans, cuts to the per child cost of the school lunch programme.
rigor.explanation: Strong itemisation but asserts a direct funding link rather than demonstrating it.

rigor.statement: This was spelled out by research done by the Inland Revenue Department in 2023, which told us that the top 311 households in Aotearoa hold more wealth than 2.5 million New Zealanders. That report also spelled out that... those at the top pay an effective tax rate that is less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the inequality argument in a named official study with specific findings.

rigor.statement: Here I would only just quote from the OECD Economic Surveys: New Zealand 2024, where they say, “There is a need to reduce distortions to household choice of asset allocation. Shares, land and owner-occupied residential property are tax favoured... capital gains taxation reform should be done as part of a review of tax settings for saving.”
rigor.explanation: Supports the CGT argument with a direct, relevant quotation from an authoritative external body.

rigor.statement: We know that societies with greater wealth inequality are less cohesive. They are less functional, and they are less healthy than their more equal counterparts.
rigor.explanation: Draws on a real strand of inequality research, but stated as settled fact without citing the specific evidence here.

rigor.statement: after 50-odd years of this playbook, New Zealanders are not safer, New Zealanders are not healthier, and New Zealanders are not happier. In fact, the opposite is true.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical triad asserted without evidence for such a broad claim.

rigor.statement: putting in place a capital gains is a tax on investment, and, in fact, what we need to do is actually have people investing in our businesses to improve productivity—adopting new technology, training their staff, etc., etc. Actually, lower taxes do improve productivity.
rigor.explanation: Chains contestable premises to a flat conclusion ('lower taxes do improve productivity') without evidence; the CGT-as-investment-tax framing is asserted.

rigor.statement: We actually have the Opposition saying to us, “Actually, we don’t support that. We don’t support seeing extra money in New Zealanders’ pockets.” I find that very difficult to understand in a cost of living crisis.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: misrepresents the Opposition's stated reasoning to make it easier to attack.

rigor.statement: It will allow mega landlords to borrow more money to buy more houses until 99 percent of the people in Aotearoa are paying their rent to the 1 percent of homeowners.
rigor.explanation: Slippery-slope hyperbole with no evidence for the 99%/1% end state.

rigor.statement: We have heard a lot of talk about Māori privilege because the super-wealthy need us to blame each other before we blame them. First they stole the land, then they stole our labour.
rigor.explanation: Frames a 'divide and distract' narrative as fact; rhetorically forceful but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: If you are a couple and you are on superannuation and that’s all you are on, you are getting—through the Government’s own budget calculator—$8.62 for the couple, for the two of you, per fortnight. That is $2.16 per week. That is 31c per day. A two litre bottle of milk has gone up by 29c, just most recently. A one kilo block of cheese has gone up by 10c.
rigor.explanation: Concrete comparison of the tax benefit against real price rises; sourced to the Government's calculator, though the milk/cheese anecdote is illustrative.

rigor.statement: before we talk about the fact that we have seen a Prime Minister who consistently uses the term “ruthlessly in pursuit of growth”, I would like to remind the House that the adverb “ruthlessly” has never been used in any positive light. That is only ever used to describe cruel and cold-blooded intent.
rigor.explanation: A semantic/definitional argument used to impute intent; the claim that 'ruthlessly' is 'only ever' negative is an overreach.

rigor.statement: This is a tax cut not for the rich. I reiterate: this is a tax cut for low to middle income workers, and frankly, any dollars earned after $78,100 are not getting a tax cut... It’s effectively capped: the tax-cut benefit stops at every dollar earned after $78,100.
rigor.explanation: Uses a correct mechanical fact (the cap) to support a broader distributional claim it doesn't fully establish.

rigor.statement: the thing with tax cuts is timing is really important. It was a very difficult time, and we’re seeing the consequences of that through our health system. We are seeing consequences of that through other programmes, like the school lunch programme, which has had a reduction in funding.
rigor.explanation: Argues the tax cuts came at the cost of services; reasonable but the causal link is asserted with limited evidence.

rigor.statement: that side of the House thinks Government knows best. That’s why we’re now having reforms with tertiary, hospital, tax—just a mess everywhere we go, because they think Wellington knows best. Well, we like to give money back to the Kiwis that earn it.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a strawman ('Wellington knows best') and a sweeping 'mess everywhere' claim without evidence.

rigor.statement: I just want to read some commentary from Deloitte which was published at the time: “The bill itself is less controversial than some of its predecessors as it largely contains taxpayer friendly measures aimed at reducing compliance costs and increasing productivity.”
rigor.explanation: Supports his characterisation of the bill with an external professional-services assessment.

rigor.statement: The best way to achieve economic development is actually to make sure hard-working people get to keep more of their hard-working dollars. Wellington does not know best, but people do.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a contested economic proposition as self-evident and leans on the 'Wellington knows best' slogan.

charisma.statement: This is a particularly good set of measures—started under the previous Government, quite correctly continued by the current Government, as a way of ensuring that there could be a generic response to emergencies.
charisma.explanation: Credits a political opponent's government for correctly continuing a policy — bridge-building across the aisle.

charisma.statement: when the next black swan event occurs, whoever the Minister of Revenue is, whoever the Minister of Finance is, won’t have to try to design measures from scratch and won’t even have to look back at the measures that have been used previously. They can reach for them from the shelf. That’s an excellent piece of work from across the House.
charisma.explanation: 'Work from across the House' framing praises cross-party collaboration.

charisma.statement: I just wanted to appreciate the contribution made by the Hon Dr Deborah Russell just then, walking us through the changes that were made at the Finance and Expenditure Committee. It is, of course, in those moments that we see that cordial working across the aisle to try and improve pieces of legislation, even if indeed we are opposed to those laws.
charisma.explanation: Praises an opposing party's member and celebrates cross-aisle cooperation.

charisma.statement: It is good to actually have some tax experts like the Hon Dr Deborah Russell on our committee. She’s obviously very interested in some of the issues and a lot of the technicalities, so she does add a lot of value, so it’s good to have her.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party generosity that builds goodwill in the chamber.

charisma.statement: Poverty is a political choice, taxation is a political choice, and we have the tools to make those kind of genuine changes based on data, based on what economists around Aotearoa and internationally are telling us.
charisma.explanation: Aspirational 'hope' appeal, but rallies its own side rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: we do recognise the hard work that has actually come about through not just this Government but also the previous Labour Government, and possibly even previous Governments to that, in working towards building better taxation systems. Not everything in a bill is always something that is bad.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges good-faith cross-government work and concedes merit in the bill — consensus-minded.

charisma.statement: it’s not a binary decision from the first reading to the third reading. It’s actually about looking at the issues and debating them, which this place is all about. I feel really comfortable with the fact that maybe at one stage a party has voted yes and now they’re voting no.
charisma.explanation: Reframes flip-flopping accusations constructively, appealing to shared parliamentary process.

charisma.statement: I know that many people in the National Party that I meet with and talk with do believe in that. They believe that we as a society are judged by how we treat our most vulnerable, and being a member of the New Zealand society, being a New Zealand taxpayer, is around our contribution.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly finds common ground with individual National members, reaching across the aisle.

divination.statement: when the next black swan event occurs, whoever the Minister of Revenue is, whoever the Minister of Finance is, won’t have to try to design measures from scratch and won’t even have to look back at the measures that have been used previously. They can reach for them from the shelf. That’s an excellent piece of work from across the House.
divination.explanation: Predicts future emergency responses will be quicker off-the-shelf; plausible given the legislated generic measures, timeframe open-ended.

divination.statement: It will allow mega landlords to borrow more money to buy more houses until 99 percent of the people in Aotearoa are paying their rent to the 1 percent of homeowners.
divination.explanation: Predicts near-total concentration of home ownership; implausible in magnitude and unbounded in timeframe.

divination.statement: if we had a tax policy... removing GST, removing income tax for whānau on low incomes, we would increase take-home pay for 98 percent of whānau, income tax on those earning more than $200k, the company tax rate from 28 percent to 33 percent. We’ll introduce a wealth tax, foreign companies tax, land banking tax, vacant house tax.
divination.explanation: Claims 98% would be 'better off overnight'; directionally arguable for low earners but the magnitude is unsubstantiated.

authenticity.statement: we will be voting in favour of all the amendments to the bill at committee stage, but we will not be supporting Part 1 of the bill, and alas, we cannot support the bill overall because of the annual rates in it.
authenticity.explanation: Voting record aligns with the stated position — supporting agreed technical amendments while opposing the rates she criticised.

authenticity.statement: it’s not a binary decision from the first reading to the third reading. It’s actually about looking at the issues and debating them, which this place is all about. I feel really comfortable with the fact that maybe at one stage a party has voted yes and now they’re voting no.
authenticity.explanation: Openly defends changing a vote between readings as legitimate deliberation rather than hiding an inconsistency.

veracity.statement: the top two quintiles—that is, 40 percent of households—gain $1.6 billion or 55 percent of the total of the value of those tax cuts. Those top two quintiles, that top 40 percent, it must be noted, also benefit from $750 million a year from the landlord tax cut reduction. When that is included, that top 40 percent in our country ends up getting 64 percent of the value of the Government’s tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Distributional figures attributed to the regulatory impact statement; consistent with published RIS quintile analysis.

veracity.explanation: Specific figures sourced to the RIS; broadly consistent with published distributional analysis.

veracity.explanation: The listed fee increases and cuts are largely real, but framing them all as directly 'paying for' the tax cuts is a contestable causal attribution.

veracity.statement: they have knowingly increased climate changing emissions, they have knowingly increased child material hardship, and they have knowingly increased inequality.
veracity.explanation: Directional trends are debatable but the 'knowingly' framing overstates provable intent.

veracity.statement: This was spelled out by research done by the Inland Revenue Department in 2023, which told us that the top 311 households in Aotearoa hold more wealth than 2.5 million New Zealanders. That report also spelled out that... those at the top pay an effective tax rate that is less than half of that of the average New Zealander.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the 2023 IRD high-wealth individuals research findings on concentration and effective tax rates.

veracity.statement: Here I would only just quote from the OECD Economic Surveys: New Zealand 2024, where they say, “There is a need to reduce distortions to household choice of asset allocation. Shares, land and owner-occupied residential property are tax favoured... capital gains taxation reform should be done as part of a review of tax settings for saving.”
veracity.explanation: Quotation is consistent with OECD's 2024 survey recommendations on NZ tax settings.

veracity.statement: after 50-odd years of this playbook, New Zealanders are not safer, New Zealanders are not healthier, and New Zealanders are not happier. In fact, the opposite is true.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping claim of across-the-board decline over 50 years; on many long-run measures (life expectancy, safety) it is contestable or false.

veracity.statement: we should be very proud of our tax system. We do actually have a very robust tax system. It actually does have a lot of transparency. We don’t have a lot of deductions. It works very well.
veracity.explanation: NZ's low-deduction broad-base system is a fair characterisation, though 'works very well' is a value-laden generalisation.

veracity.statement: putting in place a capital gains is a tax on investment, and, in fact, what we need to do is actually have people investing in our businesses to improve productivity—adopting new technology, training their staff, etc., etc. Actually, lower taxes do improve productivity.
veracity.explanation: The claim that lower taxes improve productivity is presented as settled fact but the evidence is mixed and disputed.

veracity.statement: This Government finally made the proactive decision to change the thresholds in the tax rates. That is something that New Zealanders have waited for since 2010 to see changes in the thresholds—2010.
veracity.explanation: Income tax thresholds had indeed been unchanged since 2010; broadly accurate, though minor prior adjustments existed.

veracity.explanation: The interest-deductibility restoration is in the multi-billion range and low earners gained little, but the '$3 billion' and '$2 a week' figures are rounded/framed for effect.

veracity.explanation: Material-hardship ratios by ethnicity are consistent with published NZ child poverty statistics.

veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about evaluation criteria, presented factually though unverified here.

veracity.explanation: References a same-day statement by the PM on NDC commitment; plausible but the characterisation is one-sided and unverified here.

veracity.statement: overall, 83 percent of Kiwis or 94 percent of households benefited from the Government’s tax package—personal tax package—that we are confirming today through this taxation bill.
veracity.explanation: The 83%/94% benefit figures match the Government's stated tax-package modelling; accurate to its own framing.

veracity.explanation: Accurate that emergency tax relief has been deployed under successive governments (e.g. Kaikōura, COVID).

veracity.explanation: Presents a direct quoted assessment; consistent with the bill's largely technical, taxpayer-friendly content.

veracity.statement: we’re able to get many new Kāinga Ora houses on the schedule to be built—we got many built.
