It does pick up on some of the thrust of where Mr Twyford was taking things when he was housing spokesperson. I am keen to get bipartisan buy-in to these things.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits the Opposition and Twyford's earlier work, offers a briefing, and seeks bipartisan buy-in — genuinely bridge-building.

specificity.statement: And thanks to that funding, Kiwis will see more nurses working in primary care, more international doctors working in their community, more opportunities to enrol with their local doctors, and more choice with the roll-out of a 24/7 digital service.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms (nurses, international doctors, 24/7 digital service) but without figures or dates in this statement itself.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, for example, the latest trade figures were released. These show that in the December quarter of last year, New Zealand exported $26.7 billion worth of goods and services. That's an increase of 9.6 percent over the same period a year earlier. Dairy was particularly strong, making up almost a quarter of our total exports in the quarter.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures, quarter, growth rate, and sectoral breakdown.

specificity.statement: ANZ's Commodity Price Index, which follows movements in prices for New Zealand exports like dairy, meat, horticulture, and forestry, has risen 15 percent in the past year when measured in world prices, and has risen 25 percent in New Zealand dollar terms.
specificity.explanation: Named index with both world-price and NZD-terms figures.

specificity.statement: Well, I'd like to share with you facts from a letter I received from New Zealand Apples and Pears, who tell me that New Zealand's apple and pear industry has achieved $1 billion in orchard-gate returns for the very first time. I would like to congratulate the apple and pear industry, which also has revealed that this is worth $2.5 billion in revenue impact to the New Zealand economy—up 27 percent from 2023—with employment in the sector also increasing to more than 13,700 jobs, and this growth trend looks set to continue.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures (orchard-gate returns, revenue impact, growth %, jobs) with a cited source.

specificity.statement: Yes, and especially our action to support Kiwis with the cost of living. We know it's a tough time for New Zealanders, which is why it's so important to get on top of wasteful spending, inflation, and interest rates. We've made real progress: repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering tax relief, and supporting young families with FamilyBoost.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete delivered actions (fuel tax repeal, tax relief, FamilyBoost) though without amounts.

specificity.statement: Well, I think it's an important thing for kids who come to school with no lunch. We're not willing to let them go hungry, we don't want them not to learn, and we don't want them ending up on, or being consigned to, welfare or other things. We want them to have potential and a future.
specificity.explanation: General aspirational language about potential and avoiding welfare, no mechanisms or measures.

specificity.statement: We weighed that against other advice and considerations, given the fact that New Zealanders currently have citizen's arrest powers for things that happen at night. But then, if the same thing happens during the day, when somebody walks out of a shop with around $900 worth of food or clothing or electronics, nothing can be done about that, and we don't think that's the correct situation.
specificity.explanation: Concrete example (daytime theft of ~$900 of goods) and the specific legal gap being addressed.

specificity.statement: The proposals, in particular, came from the ministry advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal in response to a significant increase in retail crime over the past few years. New Zealanders are fed up with the level of retail crime that they are experiencing in our communities.
specificity.explanation: Names the advisory group and its chair and the select-committee path, but not the consultation detail asked for.

specificity.statement: On 23 February, I announced changes to the Overseas Investment Act. Cabinet has approved a package of legislative reforms that will ensure faster decision-making, greater investor certainty, and stronger national interest protections. Specifically, I announced reforms that will change the presumption of the Act to better acknowledge the benefits that international investment provides to New Zealand's economy. It will reduce the time frames for the regulator's assessment of most applications to 15 days unless escalated to a comprehensive assessment in more sensitive cases.
specificity.explanation: Dated announcement plus concrete mechanism (15-day assessment window, changed presumption, escalation for sensitive cases).

specificity.statement: Because we follow economic evidence. The evidence in particular is clear around productivity. Our growth has stalled. It was at 1.4 percent per year from 1993-2013, but only 0.2 percent over the decade to date.
specificity.explanation: Precise comparative growth rates across defined periods.

specificity.statement: This Government believes in smarter regulation, not more regulation. We are retaining screening for farmland, residential property, and fishing quota, and we're strengthening our ability to intervene if an investment is genuinely against New Zealand's national interests.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific asset classes still screened and the ministerial-directive mechanism.

specificity.statement: We have investigated the cause, which was the overheating of plastic by using the wrong temperature in an oven in one of the 27 regional kitchens and then failing to do correct quality control before they were sent out. The people concerned have been spoken to about this and we are taking steps to ensure that it won't happen again.
specificity.explanation: Concrete account of the failure (wrong oven temperature, one of 27 kitchens, quality-control lapse) and remedial steps.

specificity.statement: And in terms of fixing it, yesterday on 3 March, we achieved 99 percent on-time delivery up and down New Zealand. That's how you start off with a problem—you put on your thinking cap, you solve it, and make the world a better place.
specificity.explanation: Dated, quantified delivery metric.

specificity.statement: Yes, especially our action to build the infrastructure that Kiwis need to get the country moving and our economy growing. That's why it was so positive last week to see the infrastructure pipeline continuing to grow, hitting almost $204 billion last quarter. We know that high inflation and interest rates have hit the construction sector hard in the last few years, and that's why we're so positive to see that $15 billion more than expected is going to be spent on infrastructure this year, with more than half that going to transport. New Zealand won't get rich doing phantom projects like Auckland light rail or Let's Get Wellington Moving.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($204b pipeline, $15b above expectation, >half to transport) though sourced to a pipeline estimate.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister and I announced a boost for primary healthcare to help Kiwis access timely and quality primary care for all New Zealanders. This includes 100 clinical placements for overseas-trained doctors to work in primary care, incentives to recruit up to 400 graduate nurses per year for the next three years, a new 24/7 digital healthcare service for online medical appointments, and a $285 million performance-based uplift for general practice over the next three years.
specificity.explanation: Detailed figures and timeframes (100 placements, up to 400 nurses/yr for 3 yrs, $285m over 3 yrs, 24/7 service).

specificity.statement: Well, we all know that we need more doctors. That's why we are funding a new two-year primary care training programme for up to 100 extra overseas-trained doctors. It makes no sense that overseas-trained doctors living in New Zealand who are willing to work in primary care can't, because there aren't the training opportunities available to them.
specificity.explanation: Names the two-year programme and the 100-placement figure with a clear mechanism.

specificity.statement: On Sunday, I announced that the New Zealand Police will be opening a training base in Auckland, increasing the training capacity of police and supporting the attraction and training of quality new officers from our largest market. This Government is committed to restoring law and order, and adding a training facility in Auckland is another example of what can be achieved with a Government that is backing police.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, dated announcement of an Auckland training base, though without numbers or open date.

specificity.statement: We shared with Hyundai the fact that a two-ferry project in May 2020 involving $400.1 million of Government funding, when I was Minister, was on track to reach over $4 billion under his Government—that is, the Opposition now. The core objective of infrastructure to safely berth ships blew out to involve the highest possible specifications for the renewal of almost every piece of infrastructure, all at the taxpayer's expense.
specificity.explanation: Specific figures and dates ($400.1m in May 2020 rising to over $4b) framing the cost blowout.

specificity.statement: Last Friday, I announced pillar two of the Government's Going for Housing Growth policy, five improvements to infrastructure funding and financing to support urban growth: replacing development contributions with development levies, regulatory oversight of those levies, increasing the flexibility of targeted rates, improving the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act, and broadening existing tools to support value capture.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five concrete, named policy mechanisms with a date of announcement.

specificity.statement: It is true that some councils have not been able to effectively recover growth costs, leaving ratepayers to pick up the cheque and cross-subsidise that growth—for example, at Drury, and there are other examples that members will be aware of around the country.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific case (Drury) and the mechanism (development contributions requiring planned/costed developments).

specificity.statement: What we're committed to doing is going incredibly hard on economic growth and we're going to make sure that it's in our national interest to continue to do so. We'll continue to put Kiwis first and make sure that we're acting in our own national interest. But we are determined to drive for growth, and we are going to do everything we can to deliver on net zero 2050.
specificity.explanation: General commitments to growth and 'do everything we can' with no concrete Paris-specific detail.

divination.statement: And thanks to that funding, Kiwis will see more nurses working in primary care, more international doctors working in their community, more opportunities to enrol with their local doctors, and more choice with the roll-out of a 24/7 digital service.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased workforce/access following the funding; plausible and directionally supported but magnitude and timeframe are uncertain.

divination.statement: Well, I'd like to share with you facts from a letter I received from New Zealand Apples and Pears, who tell me that New Zealand's apple and pear industry has achieved $1 billion in orchard-gate returns for the very first time. I would like to congratulate the apple and pear industry, which also has revealed that this is worth $2.5 billion in revenue impact to the New Zealand economy—up 27 percent from 2023—with employment in the sector also increasing to more than 13,700 jobs, and this growth trend looks set to continue.
divination.explanation: "This growth trend looks set to continue" is a mild forecast — plausible but unquantified and uncertain.

divination.statement: A flood of urban land coming to market plus responsive infrastructure will unlock an abundance of development opportunities, drive down the price of land, and make housing more affordable.
divination.explanation: Predicts more land supply plus responsive infrastructure will lower land prices and improve affordability; directionally supported by economics but magnitude and timeframe uncertain and dependent on execution.

forthrightness.statement: Well, David Seymour is the accountable Minister. I've got every confidence he's all over the detail and he's going to make sure all the food and the meals get up to scratch.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he expressed confidence in Seymour given his own Education Minister had not; deflects to Seymour's accountability rather than explaining his own reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I have clear delegations and clear responsibilities. David Seymour is the accountable Minister for school lunches; he is aware of the issues and he will fix them. Erica Stanford is the accountable Minister for teacher-only days, and she will manage that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Stanford was correct that Seymour overstepped and what he had done about it; answers neither, pivoting to delegation lines.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I said before, I have every confidence that David Seymour is working his way through the issues around the school lunches. He's aware of the detail, he's on top of it, and I have every confidence that he will sort it out.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Stanford is left cleaning up Seymour's messes and why he won't act; repeats a confidence talking point without engaging the question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'll just say to that member, it's a bit rich because we saved school lunches, because that Prime Minister didn't fund school lunches. So we are spending more on school lunches and we are giving them to more kids.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when hungry students can expect the promised quality; pivots to attacking the previous government's funding rather than answering on delivery.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, some of the food is not up to scratch, but the Minister is working his way through the issues and I have every confidence he will resolve it. And I just say to parents that may be listening to this, feel free to prepare a Marmite sandwich and an apple for lunch.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes some food is "not up to scratch" (a partial answer) but does not say what it will take for him to step in, and deflects to parents.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'm proud of it because that member was part of a Government that didn't fund it, and this is a Government that has come in, has funded the programme, and has extended it to more children.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Ka Ora Ka Ako supports tamariki to learn and how he can be proud of the rollout; sidesteps the rollout problems by attacking prior funding.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think it's an important thing for kids who come to school with no lunch. We're not willing to let them go hungry, we don't want them not to learn, and we don't want them ending up on, or being consigned to, welfare or other things. We want them to have potential and a future.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a principal that the programme is one of the most direct ways to tackle intergenerational poverty; broadly endorses the value but does not engage the specific claim.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I do agree with the Minister that there is actually some parental responsibility. We would like not to have a State-funded lunch programme, but we do have one to make sure that we are supporting the kids who don't or can't have lunches, and make sure they can learn.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Peters by stating an actual position (prefers no State programme but supports the current one) — reasonably direct.

forthrightness.statement: Yes—and I agree that many New Zealanders have become exasperated at the high level of crime occurring in our communities and that vigilante justice is not the solution. That's why this Government is focused on restoring law and order, so people are confident that our justice system delivers real consequences for crime.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Mitchell's quoted warning about vigilante action; directly agrees and explains why.

forthrightness.statement: There was a range of advice. The Police, quite frankly, were not broadly in favour of the changes; they had concerns around potential impacts. We weighed that up against our concerns about the current situation, where that, during the day—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice Police gave on public-safety risks; candidly admits Police were not broadly in favour and had concerns — a direct, non-defensive answer.

forthrightness.statement: The proposals, in particular, came from the ministry advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal in response to a significant increase in retail crime over the past few years. New Zealanders are fed up with the level of retail crime that they are experiencing in our communities.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically what consultation occurred with the Police Association; describes the advisory group's origins and says the Association can submit later, rather than answering what consultation happened.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think people would recognise that retail crime costs our community billions of dollars, and all New Zealanders have to pay more for the things that they buy because some New Zealanders steal it and don't pay for it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify $3.6m spend against 72 fewer police and doubled meth use; justifies the spend on cost-of-crime grounds but ignores the police-numbers and meth premises of the question.

forthrightness.statement: There'll be a wide variety of views, and I would note that there is one fellow called Stuart Nash, who said, "I am a fan.", and there's no doubt about that. Of course, I can understand why he's out of step with the current Labour Government, which seems to be wanting to defend the current situation whereby people walk out of stores during the middle of the day and nobody can do anything about it apart from escort them to their car.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he thinks aligning the day/night rule is sensible; answers yes and gives supporting points.

forthrightness.statement: This Government believes in smarter regulation, not more regulation. We are retaining screening for farmland, residential property, and fishing quota, and we're strengthening our ability to intervene if an investment is genuinely against New Zealand's national interests.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what protections remain; directly lists retained screening categories and the intervention power.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement, and the reason is that the programme has been set up to ensure that the nutritional standards under the previous iteration of the school lunch programme will be met under this iteration.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by 'same quality or better' and why; directly affirms and gives the nutritional-standards reason.

forthrightness.statement: We have investigated the cause, which was the overheating of plastic by using the wrong temperature in an oven in one of the 27 regional kitchens and then failing to do correct quality control before they were sent out. The people concerned have been spoken to about this and we are taking steps to ensure that it won't happen again.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains the cause of the melted-plastic incident rather than deflecting, while framing it as an isolated failure.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it's very simple. We had a meeting scheduled, contingent on our respective caucuses finishing on time. But the ACT caucus is a very tight, busy, and productive group of people, and we can't always be ready for that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he won't show up to a meeting with the Education Minister; gives a scheduling excuse laced with self-praise rather than squarely addressing the no-show.

forthrightness.statement: We haven't cut the school lunch programme; we've increased it. We've funded it, which is what the last Government didn't do.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether cutting the programme will make learning harder; directly disputes the premise that it was cut, a clear (if contested) response.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we all know that we need more doctors. That's why we are funding a new two-year primary care training programme for up to 100 extra overseas-trained doctors. It makes no sense that overseas-trained doctors living in New Zealand who are willing to work in primary care can't, because there aren't the training opportunities available to them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the government is increasing overseas-trained doctors in primary care; directly explains the training-bottleneck rationale.

forthrightness.statement: Police now have record numbers of applicants, and having an extra training location will support their efforts to get applicants through the pipeline and into training faster.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the facility complements recruitment; gives a direct, on-point answer about pipeline throughput.

forthrightness.statement: However, that so-called $300 million break fee has been misrepresented by the questioner in the sense that there were a whole lot of infrastructural costs that made up that $300 million, not just the iReX project.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he discussed the break fee and what Hyundai said; declines the substance (says it lies with KiwiRail/Hyundai) but does dispute the questioner's characterisation.

forthrightness.statement: In this Government, we're famous for consulting with each other, and she wished me the very best and hoped that I could fix up the Labour Party's mess.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he consulted Willis and her response; gives a jokey answer implying consultation but no substance on what was discussed.

forthrightness.statement: I agree that we are working incredibly hard to deliver on Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 1 for 2030, and I also note that we have signed up for NDC2 in 2035.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he stands by his climate Minister's statement that the Paris target is 'not a liability... no legal obligation'; does not address that characterisation and pivots to NDC effort.

forthrightness.statement: What we're committed to doing is going incredibly hard on economic growth and we're going to make sure that it's in our national interest to continue to do so. We'll continue to put Kiwis first and make sure that we're acting in our own national interest. But we are determined to drive for growth, and we are going to do everything we can to deliver on net zero 2050.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Government is committed to meeting the Paris Agreement; pivots to growth and net zero 2050 without answering on the Paris/NDC commitment.

forthrightness.statement: We are committed to delivering on net zero 2050, as we have consistently said from the beginning.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether he is committed to meeting the NDC under the Paris Agreement; substitutes a net-zero-2050 commitment for the Paris/NDC commitment asked about.

forthrightness.statement: I've got nothing further to my previous answer.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked again to be specific about commitment to the Paris NDC; declines entirely to answer.

civility.statement: Well, I'll just say to that member, it's a bit rich because we saved school lunches, because that Prime Minister didn't fund school lunches. So we are spending more on school lunches and we are giving them to more kids.
civility.explanation: "It's a bit rich" is a pointed but not personal jab, aimed at the opponent's record.

civility.statement: Yes, some of the food is not up to scratch, but the Minister is working his way through the issues and I have every confidence he will resolve it. And I just say to parents that may be listening to this, feel free to prepare a Marmite sandwich and an apple for lunch.
civility.explanation: The "Marmite sandwich and an apple" aside is dismissive of families raising concerns about the programme.

civility.statement: Has the Government ever considered that there are comparisons of a former time when much poorer Māori families in largely Māori schools nevertheless provided the food for their children every day, with the older students doing the labour—the males—and the girls doing the cooking, and never relying upon the State at that point in time, when we were being better educated at the same time?
civility.explanation: Framed as a policy argument about self-reliance, but the gendered division of labour and dismissal of State support drew objection as demeaning.

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. Mr Speaker, I think that's one of the most chauvinistic displays that we've seen in the House in recent times. I think that is going to prompt a bit of a reaction.
civility.explanation: Sharp characterisation ("chauvinistic") of Peters' remarks — a strong value judgement of the display rather than a substantive engagement, though not a personal insult.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I take objection from a number of people who get up and give their views when questions are being asked of, clearly, events that they know nothing about—poverty: how it smells, how it feels, what it tastes like—and they show it every day in this House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents as knowing nothing about poverty — an accusatory, character-directed retort rather than substantive.

civility.statement: What I can tell that member is that the only person that is responsible for losing a life in a situation like that would be the person that took the life—that swung the axe, that used the weapon to kill or hurt or maim somebody. If that member doesn't understand that and wants to create excuses for that kind of activity, then I don't think they understand how law and order should work in this country.
civility.explanation: Accuses the questioner of wanting to "create excuses" for killers — an inflammatory characterisation rather than engaging the policy risk raised.

civility.statement: Well, look, I think one of the biggest changes in the last year or two in justice policy has been a shift away from a culture of excuses for crime that we inherited under the previous administration, where crimes were the fault of all sorts of reasons other than the actions of an individual. This Government is about restoring responsibility for criminal actions to the people who undertake those actions.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous administration's policy stance; pointed but aimed at approach rather than persons.

civility.statement: There'll be a wide variety of views, and I would note that there is one fellow called Stuart Nash, who said, "I am a fan.", and there's no doubt about that. Of course, I can understand why he's out of step with the current Labour Government, which seems to be wanting to defend the current situation whereby people walk out of stores during the middle of the day and nobody can do anything about it apart from escort them to their car.
civility.explanation: Uses a Labour figure's endorsement to needle the current Labour position; a mild partisan jab, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I beg your pardon? She said it's ChatGPT. I tell you what, if that member used ChatGPT, she'd make a lot more sense. And ChatGPT doesn't hallucinate as much as that member.
civility.explanation: Direct personal mockery of another member's coherence and honesty ("hallucinate as much as that member") — a personal attack, not substance.

civility.statement: I think I addressed this question, and it speaks to the issue of what people are happy to have and not. In this particular instance, I seem to recall it was actually butter chicken. Now, a lot of people I know, if someone gave them butter chicken for free 13 times, they wouldn't be complaining. They'd actually be thrilled. Namaste.
civility.explanation: Trivialises a complaint about repetitive meals and the "Namaste" sign-off reads as mocking; dismissive rather than substantive.

civility.statement: She forgot it was a picture that had been sent to her of the school lunches that she was responsible for. And I've got something else. I've got news for the member. I heard a rumour that cannot be substantiated that that picture was sent to Jan Tinetti by Young ACT.
civility.explanation: Repeats an admittedly unsubstantiated rumour to embarrass the member — a cheap shot rather than argument.

civility.statement: Yes, especially our action to build the infrastructure that Kiwis need to get the country moving and our economy growing. That's why it was so positive last week to see the infrastructure pipeline continuing to grow, hitting almost $204 billion last quarter. We know that high inflation and interest rates have hit the construction sector hard in the last few years, and that's why we're so positive to see that $15 billion more than expected is going to be spent on infrastructure this year, with more than half that going to transport. New Zealand won't get rich doing phantom projects like Auckland light rail or Let's Get Wellington Moving.
civility.explanation: 'Phantom projects' derides opponents' policies (light rail, LGWM) but targets the projects rather than persons.

civility.statement: In this Government, we're famous for consulting with each other, and she wished me the very best and hoped that I could fix up the Labour Party's mess.
civility.explanation: 'Fix up the Labour Party's mess' is a partisan jab folded into the answer.

civility.statement: Well, the responsibility of a good Government is to be as careful about spending the taxpayer's money as they are about spending their own—not borrow and hope, frivolously throwing it away, and running the country into tens of billions of dollars of debt, which is the reason why they're over there and we're over here.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opposition as frivolous 'borrow and hope' spenders — a pointed partisan swipe rather than engagement.

civility.statement: I do want to acknowledge the support of the Opposition on this—genuinely—who said that it seems like a step in the right direction. I'm in the middle of arranging a briefing for the Opposition in relation to these reforms. It does pick up on some of the thrust of where Mr Twyford was taking things when he was housing spokesperson. I am keen to get bipartisan buy-in to these things.
civility.explanation: Respectful and generous toward opponents, acknowledging the merit in their prior contributions.

rigor.statement: Yesterday, for example, the latest trade figures were released. These show that in the December quarter of last year, New Zealand exported $26.7 billion worth of goods and services. That's an increase of 9.6 percent over the same period a year earlier. Dairy was particularly strong, making up almost a quarter of our total exports in the quarter.
rigor.explanation: Claim grounded in cited data rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: Has the Government ever considered that there are comparisons of a former time when much poorer Māori families in largely Māori schools nevertheless provided the food for their children every day, with the older students doing the labour—the males—and the girls doing the cooking, and never relying upon the State at that point in time, when we were being better educated at the same time?
rigor.explanation: Appeal to a romanticised past (appeal to tradition/nostalgia) and unsupported claim that education was better then; no evidence and gendered assumptions.

rigor.statement: We weighed that against other advice and considerations, given the fact that New Zealanders currently have citizen's arrest powers for things that happen at night. But then, if the same thing happens during the day, when somebody walks out of a shop with around $900 worth of food or clothing or electronics, nothing can be done about that, and we don't think that's the correct situation.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument citing the existing night/day inconsistency in citizen's-arrest law as the rationale; logically structured though it downplays the safety concerns just acknowledged.

rigor.statement: Well, I think people would recognise that retail crime costs our community billions of dollars, and all New Zealanders have to pay more for the things that they buy because some New Zealanders steal it and don't pay for it.
rigor.explanation: Cost-of-crime rationale is a reasonable point but the 'billions' figure is asserted without a source and the cheaper premises are unaddressed.

rigor.statement: What I can tell that member is that the only person that is responsible for losing a life in a situation like that would be the person that took the life—that swung the axe, that used the weapon to kill or hurt or maim somebody. If that member doesn't understand that and wants to create excuses for that kind of activity, then I don't think they understand how law and order should work in this country.
rigor.explanation: Deflects a question about second-order consequences of a law change by narrowing responsibility solely to the perpetrator; sidesteps the causal argument being made.

rigor.statement: Well, look, I think one of the biggest changes in the last year or two in justice policy has been a shift away from a culture of excuses for crime that we inherited under the previous administration, where crimes were the fault of all sorts of reasons other than the actions of an individual. This Government is about restoring responsibility for criminal actions to the people who undertake those actions.
rigor.explanation: Characterises the previous approach as a 'culture of excuses' — a strawman framing of criminological context as denying individual responsibility.

rigor.statement: Because we follow economic evidence. The evidence in particular is clear around productivity. Our growth has stalled. It was at 1.4 percent per year from 1993-2013, but only 0.2 percent over the decade to date.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the reform rationale in cited productivity-growth figures and a premise-to-conclusion argument about capital investment.

rigor.statement: New Zealand is currently one of the hardest countries to invest in. Other OECD countries such as Australia, Canada, or the United Kingdom protect their natural interests effectively; meanwhile, they receive billions more foreign direct investment than we do. The reality is that other countries are competing for global capital while we've been scaring it away.
rigor.explanation: Comparative reasoning with named countries, but the FDI difference is partly driven by economy size, which the argument elides.

rigor.statement: I think I addressed this question, and it speaks to the issue of what people are happy to have and not. In this particular instance, I seem to recall it was actually butter chicken. Now, a lot of people I know, if someone gave them butter chicken for free 13 times, they wouldn't be complaining. They'd actually be thrilled. Namaste.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the '13 days same food' criticism with an anecdote about people he knows being 'thrilled' — appeal to anecdote rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: However, that so-called $300 million break fee has been misrepresented by the questioner in the sense that there were a whole lot of infrastructural costs that made up that $300 million, not just the iReX project.
rigor.explanation: Makes a substantive distinction that the figure bundles broader infrastructure costs rather than a single break fee, though without itemisation.

rigor.statement: Well, the responsibility of a good Government is to be as careful about spending the taxpayer's money as they are about spending their own—not borrow and hope, frivolously throwing it away, and running the country into tens of billions of dollars of debt, which is the reason why they're over there and we're over here.
rigor.explanation: Asserts fiscal recklessness and links it to the election outcome without evidence — largely rhetorical.

rigor.statement: It is true that some councils have not been able to effectively recover growth costs, leaving ratepayers to pick up the cheque and cross-subsidise that growth—for example, at Drury, and there are other examples that members will be aware of around the country.
rigor.explanation: Supports the case for reform with a concrete named example (Drury) illustrating cost-recovery failure and cross-subsidy.

rigor.statement: We are a country with a land mass the size of the United Kingdom. With only 5 million people, we have created a housing market that has seen the fastest house price growth in the Western World in the last two decades.
rigor.explanation: Uses the land-vs-population contrast to argue artificial scarcity drives prices — a coherent evidence-linked argument.

strength.statement: Yes, and especially our action to support Kiwis with the cost of living. We know it's a tough time for New Zealanders, which is why it's so important to get on top of wasteful spending, inflation, and interest rates. We've made real progress: repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering tax relief, and supporting young families with FamilyBoost.
strength.explanation: Cites specific policies actually enacted (fuel-tax repeal, tax cuts, FamilyBoost) — demonstrated follow-through, though impact on cost of living is contested.

strength.statement: On 23 February, I announced changes to the Overseas Investment Act. Cabinet has approved a package of legislative reforms that will ensure faster decision-making, greater investor certainty, and stronger national interest protections. Specifically, I announced reforms that will change the presumption of the Act to better acknowledge the benefits that international investment provides to New Zealand's economy. It will reduce the time frames for the regulator's assessment of most applications to 15 days unless escalated to a comprehensive assessment in more sensitive cases.
strength.explanation: Cabinet-approved package announced with concrete detail; delivery is at the legislative-intent stage rather than enacted, so partial follow-through.

strength.statement: And in terms of fixing it, yesterday on 3 March, we achieved 99 percent on-time delivery up and down New Zealand. That's how you start off with a problem—you put on your thinking cap, you solve it, and make the world a better place.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete operational improvement he is responsible for, but on a programme still generating widely reported problems, so delivery is partial.

strength.statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister and I announced a boost for primary healthcare to help Kiwis access timely and quality primary care for all New Zealanders. This includes 100 clinical placements for overseas-trained doctors to work in primary care, incentives to recruit up to 400 graduate nurses per year for the next three years, a new 24/7 digital healthcare service for online medical appointments, and a $285 million performance-based uplift for general practice over the next three years.
strength.explanation: Concrete funded commitments announced; scored as intent/announcement pending delivery of the workforce and service targets.

strength.statement: On Sunday, I announced that the New Zealand Police will be opening a training base in Auckland, increasing the training capacity of police and supporting the attraction and training of quality new officers from our largest market. This Government is committed to restoring law and order, and adding a training facility in Auckland is another example of what can be achieved with a Government that is backing police.
strength.explanation: Announcement of a specific facility to support the 500-police target; delivery still pending.

strength.statement: Last Friday, I announced pillar two of the Government's Going for Housing Growth policy, five improvements to infrastructure funding and financing to support urban growth: replacing development contributions with development levies, regulatory oversight of those levies, increasing the flexibility of targeted rates, improving the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act, and broadening existing tools to support value capture.
strength.explanation: A detailed announced reform package; delivery is at announcement stage pending legislation.

authenticity.statement: Yes, and especially our action to support Kiwis with the cost of living. We know it's a tough time for New Zealanders, which is why it's so important to get on top of wasteful spending, inflation, and interest rates. We've made real progress: repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering tax relief, and supporting young families with FamilyBoost.
authenticity.explanation: Claims align with the government's actual legislative actions on these named items.

authenticity.statement: Well, I do agree with the Minister that there is actually some parental responsibility. We would like not to have a State-funded lunch programme, but we do have one to make sure that we are supporting the kids who don't or can't have lunches, and make sure they can learn.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly states an ideological preference against State-funded lunches while defending running one; a coherent if tension-laden position.

authenticity.statement: There was a range of advice. The Police, quite frankly, were not broadly in favour of the changes; they had concerns around potential impacts. We weighed that up against our concerns about the current situation, where that, during the day—
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges advice against his own policy rather than concealing it, showing consistency between the process described and the decision defended.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement, and the reason is that the programme has been set up to ensure that the nutritional standards under the previous iteration of the school lunch programme will be met under this iteration.
authenticity.explanation: Defends consistency between his prior claim and the programme design; the claim's soundness is contested given documented failures, but he holds the position.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I can commend that, and it is the reason that we recognise that we also need to complement investment and training resources and trainers and capacity to meet the added demands for front-line police.
authenticity.explanation: Endorses his own party's prior police-recruitment record and ties current policy to it; a consistent through-line, though the self-referential framing is unverified here.

authenticity.statement: We shared with Hyundai the fact that a two-ferry project in May 2020 involving $400.1 million of Government funding, when I was Minister, was on track to reach over $4 billion under his Government—that is, the Opposition now. The core objective of infrastructure to safely berth ships blew out to involve the highest possible specifications for the renewal of almost every piece of infrastructure, all at the taxpayer's expense.
authenticity.explanation: Consistently references his own earlier ministerial role and figures; the record he cites aligns with his stated position, though selectively framed.

civility.statement: So having lobbied endlessly to include the Hope Bypass in the fast track, Labour then voted against it. We now have her colleague, who’s also from the South Island, not far from Hope actually, criticising the Hope Bypass project and calling it a National Party—well, I just say good luck telling that to the people of Nelson and the wider Tasman region who are in support of that project
civility.explanation: Pointed critique of Labour's inconsistency on the record, but wrapped in a sarcastic 'good luck telling that to the people' jab rather than pure substance.

civility.statement: In relation to revenue, the member does make a good point around funding pressure on the National Land Transport Fund. That is true.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the opposing member's contribution.

civility.statement: We’ve been immature in our approach as a country to these issues. We’re changing that, as a Government, and building on some of the work that started under the previous Government.
civility.explanation: Constructive, blame-sharing tone.

civility.statement: What they did was they increased the weight of trucks across the network, and, at the same time, they chose a programme which was called “sweat the assets”, which was to squeeze as much out of the roading network as they could with as little maintenance. That has continued to affect and downgrade the network
civility.explanation: Criticism aimed at past policy choices rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: at the heart of it for this Minister of Transport in front of us is the $6 billion funding shortfall that he has to achieve the programme of work that he has promised. Particularly of concern to us on the side of the House is that it is a “roads, roads, and roads” focus for a city that desperately needs solutions to addressing our congestion problem.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of policy priorities ('roads, roads, and roads') that stays on substance rather than the person.

civility.statement: If the member wants to campaign on slapping a tax on Aucklanders again, well, he’s welcome to do that; I suspect that he actually won’t.
civility.explanation: A partisan jab ('slapping a tax') predicting the opponent's cowardice rather than engaging his question.

civility.statement: The Minister hasn’t answered my question. ... The figure that I have—and the Minister didn’t mention the shortfall to investment in Auckland—is $564 million. ... Can the Minister please articulate whereabouts is that in anywhere else but roads
civility.explanation: Direct challenge to the Minister's non-answer, focused on the substance.

civility.statement: very little, if anything, to be honest, has been done in the last six or seven years on the level crossings. We’ve now put in $200 million as an initial kind of down payment. The council has chipped in the equivalent. ... That will allow us to get on with the ones around Takanini and Glen Innes, which I’m advised have the best benefit-cost ratios.
civility.explanation: Blames the previous six or seven years for inaction, but as a policy/system critique rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: no, I was not aware of the rating of the bridge. ... When have I talked to local MPs and councils about it? I haven’t. It has not been raised with me and now it has. I note that I haven’t had any correspondence from the member in relation to the matter either.
civility.explanation: Answers honestly but adds a jab that the member himself never wrote to him.

civility.statement: there has been an under-appreciation of asset maintenance. It’s not just on our roads, by the way. We have done a poor job around our schools, our hospitals, many parts of our public infrastructure. ... there are lots of different reasons for that and they span lots of different Governments as well.
civility.explanation: Constructive, non-partisan concession.

civility.statement: I could spend the next four minutes of this contribution going through the disastrous iReX procurement process from the previous Government in a series of cascading and unfolding series of dumb decisions made by the Cabinet of which he was a member.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'dumb decisions' framing aimed at the opponent's Cabinet record; more cheap shot than substantive.

civility.statement: basically, Labour’s plan was a fantasy dreamt up in the dregs of the election campaign in order to give Michael Wood and Chris Hipkins a photo op ... And then it turned out there was no plan, there was no funding, there was no solution, and there was no options analysis.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'fantasy... photo op' framing targeting named opponents rather than engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: We have put a record spend into Vote Health, a significant increase over the three next Budgets of $16.68 billion. That’s an additional $3.44 billion into hospital and specialist services, an additional $2.12 billion into primary and community care, and an additional $1.77 billion to clean up the Pharmac mess that we inherited.
civility.explanation: Mostly substantive but the 'Pharmac mess that we inherited' is a jab at the previous Government.

veracity.statement: So having lobbied endlessly to include the Hope Bypass in the fast track, Labour then voted against it. We now have her colleague, who’s also from the South Island, not far from Hope actually, criticising the Hope Bypass project and calling it a National Party—well, I just say good luck telling that to the people of Nelson and the wider Tasman region who are in support of that project
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that Boyack lobbied to include the Hope Bypass in fast-track while Labour voted against the bill; plausible and specific but presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: it’s become more pronounced since 2008, when the Clark Government, the fifth Labour Government, merged the New Zealand Transport Agency, Transfund, and the Land Transport Safety Authority into one agency: the New Zealand Transport Agency.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 2008 merger creating NZTA; the causal link to funding pressure is more arguable than the historical fact.

veracity.statement: Tolls are not the answer to everything. ... They are a tool, but they are not a whole funding solution. There are not that many roads in New Zealand with the vehicle volumes and the numbers that would recover huge amounts of money
veracity.explanation: Accurate that few NZ roads have volumes to recover major costs via tolls.

veracity.statement: What we’ve landed on is using the existing tool, which is the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act, which was passed under the last Government in 2020
veracity.explanation: The IFF Act was indeed passed in 2020 under the previous Labour Government.

veracity.statement: it has created an enormous value uplift in the areas around the stations, and we have captured none of that value as a Government—none of it. ... It’s not what Sydney’s just recently done. ... It’s not what London did when they built the Elizabeth Line.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that these jurisdictions use value-capture and NZ largely did not for CRL.

veracity.statement: What they did was they increased the weight of trucks across the network, and, at the same time, they chose a programme which was called “sweat the assets”, which was to squeeze as much out of the roading network as they could with as little maintenance. That has continued to affect and downgrade the network
veracity.explanation: The 'sweat the assets' characterisation and truck-weight increase are broadly grounded, though contestable as the sole cause of decline.

veracity.statement: in the National Land Transport Plan, road maintenance funding was approximately $2.8 billion over three years, from 2021 to 2024. It is $4 billion over the three years that we’re in, from 2024 to 2027 ... 95 percent of pothole repairs within 24 hours for high-classification roads and 85 percent within 24 hours for lower-classification roads. All targets have been met to date.
veracity.explanation: Specific verifiable figures presented confidently; the 'all targets met' claim is the checkable part.

veracity.statement: Most submitters supported the reversal of the speed limit reductions under the previous Government, so that is the position, as it stands
veracity.explanation: Contested factual claim about submitter support that Genter immediately challenges by asking how many councils opposed the rule.

veracity.statement: as the member knows from her time as associate transport Minister, I don’t make funding decisions around those things; they’re made by the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) board. We set the activity classes, we set the overall funding envelope, but the individual project decisions are made by the NZTA board.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes that individual project funding is an NZTA board decision within Ministerial activity classes.

veracity.statement: But the Minister does clearly set a direction through the Government policy statement on transport funding, and it is within the Minister’s ability to amend the Government policy statement so that it would be possible to fund these projects.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the Minister sets direction via the Government Policy Statement on transport.

veracity.statement: he was able to tell me at that time that $13 million had been committed towards that project. Now, the only issue there is that it is in fact only $6.5 million that’s so far been committed to the project. It’s an $80 million project. This bridge is not a nice-to-have; this bridge is the vital lifeline that connects New Brighton to the city
veracity.explanation: Alleges a gap between the committed figure claimed and actually allocated; contested by Bishop, so accuracy is disputed.

veracity.statement: How much money has been allocated? I’m advised $13 million in this year’s National Land Transport Fund, so the project is funded. I hear what he’s saying that that’s not enough to fund the whole project
veracity.explanation: States $13m allocated, directly contradicting Davidson's $6.5m figure; one of the two is inaccurate.

veracity.statement: We did get rid of the Clean Car Discount, because it, essentially, resulted in tradies and farmers paying more to subsidise middle-class and wealthy people in Remuera and Wellington, like myself. ... it was a regressive wealth transfer—from lower-income people ... to people who could afford to buy it.
veracity.explanation: The 'regressive wealth transfer' claim is contestable; the scheme's incidence was mixed rather than clearly poor-to-rich.

veracity.statement: basically, Labour’s plan was a fantasy dreamt up in the dregs of the election campaign in order to give Michael Wood and Chris Hipkins a photo op ... And then it turned out there was no plan, there was no funding, there was no solution, and there was no options analysis.
veracity.explanation: The claim that Labour's second-crossing announcement lacked detailed funding/options is partly grounded but overstated as pure 'fantasy'.

veracity.statement: We have put a record spend into Vote Health, a significant increase over the three next Budgets of $16.68 billion. That’s an additional $3.44 billion into hospital and specialist services, an additional $2.12 billion into primary and community care, and an additional $1.77 billion to clean up the Pharmac mess that we inherited.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific budget figures presented as fact; the 'record spend' and 'Pharmac mess inherited' framing is partisan and checkable.

rigor.statement: So having lobbied endlessly to include the Hope Bypass in the fast track, Labour then voted against it. We now have her colleague, who’s also from the South Island, not far from Hope actually, criticising the Hope Bypass project and calling it a National Party—well, I just say good luck telling that to the people of Nelson and the wider Tasman region who are in support of that project
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete record of behaviour to allege inconsistency, but leans on the rhetorical appeal to Nelson public opinion rather than data.

rigor.statement: a four-lane road from north of Auckland through to Whangārei—the single best thing we could do to unlock growth in a deprived or somewhat deprived area of New Zealand
rigor.explanation: Sweeping 'single best thing' superlative asserted without any comparative evidence.

rigor.statement: it has created an enormous value uplift in the areas around the stations, and we have captured none of that value as a Government—none of it. ... It’s not what Sydney’s just recently done. ... It’s not what London did when they built the Elizabeth Line.
rigor.explanation: Argument for value capture backed by international comparators (Sydney, Singapore, London's Elizabeth Line).

rigor.statement: What they did was they increased the weight of trucks across the network, and, at the same time, they chose a programme which was called “sweat the assets”, which was to squeeze as much out of the roading network as they could with as little maintenance. That has continued to affect and downgrade the network
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal mechanism (heavier trucks + minimal maintenance → degraded network) but asserts it without cited figures.

rigor.statement: the rule is apparently going to force speed limits back up for a couple of hundred metres at a section on Adelaide Road next to two aged-care facilities, a hospital, two early childhood education facilities—South Wellington Intermediate School and Berhampore Primary School? Will the Minister allow there to be an exemption where communities have demonstrated strong support, and there’s no evidence of time savings for motorists, but there is very good evidence of increased risk of serious injury or death
rigor.explanation: Argues from concrete local land-use evidence (schools, hospital, aged care) and cost-benefit (no time saving vs injury risk).

rigor.statement: You can give people discounts to ride public transport; that doesn’t really move the dial. ... The actual thing that drives public transport uptake is reliability and efficiency.
rigor.explanation: A defensible reasoning that service reliability drives patronage more than fare concessions, though asserted without cited data.

rigor.statement: But the Minister does clearly set a direction through the Government policy statement on transport funding, and it is within the Minister’s ability to amend the Government policy statement so that it would be possible to fund these projects.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'not my decision' deflection by correctly identifying the GPS as the lever the Minister does control.

rigor.statement: there are more road-user charges and fuel excise duties generated in Southland than is spent in Southland. rigor.explanation: Chains evidence (RUC/excise raised vs spent) to a coherent conclusion about under-maintenance and economic cost.

rigor.statement: it would be a radical change to divvy up transport funding regionally on the basis of GDP ... or even done on distance or kilometres travelled. ... That would be a drastic change, and it’s not one the Government is contemplating at this point.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the practical difficulty of reallocating funding by GDP or distance, though briefly.

rigor.statement: I could spend the next four minutes of this contribution going through the disastrous iReX procurement process from the previous Government in a series of cascading and unfolding series of dumb decisions made by the Cabinet of which he was a member.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a 'cascading series of dumb decisions' without laying out the actual reasoning.

rigor.statement: when you make something free, people overuse it. It’s free to drive ... rigor.explanation: Applies a sound economic argument (unpriced goods are over-consumed; price signals allocate peak demand) to justify congestion pricing.

rigor.explanation: Distributional argument (fee-payers subsidising EV buyers) is coherent but the 'regressive' framing is asserted without the actual incidence data.

strength.statement: very little, if anything, to be honest, has been done in the last six or seven years on the level crossings. We’ve now put in $200 million as an initial kind of down payment. The council has chipped in the equivalent. ... That will allow us to get on with the ones around Takanini and Glen Innes, which I’m advised have the best benefit-cost ratios.
strength.explanation: Concrete funding committed, though delivery is a 'start' with the work still ahead.

strength.statement: I think we’ve got a solution. The Minister for Rail, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, is leading that work. ... It’s going to result in the Crown spending far less than the failed iReX project.
strength.explanation: Claims a solution exists but delivery is prospective and details withheld as commercial-in-confidence.

strength.statement: What we’re doing on the Auckland Harbour ... is we’re actually doing the work. There’s a barge in the harbour right now doing the geotechnical work, and we’re undertaking market soundings ... there’s no funding for delivery in this National Land Transport Plan.
strength.explanation: Real preparatory work underway but the crossing itself is unfunded and undelivered.

strength.statement: We have put a record spend into Vote Health, a significant increase over the three next Budgets of $16.68 billion. That’s an additional $3.44 billion into hospital and specialist services, an additional $2.12 billion into primary and community care, and an additional $1.77 billion to clean up the Pharmac mess that we inherited.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for committed funding, though the spend spans future Budgets rather than being delivered outcomes.

forthrightness.statement: The short answer in relation to tolling is, yes, there needs to be an alternative.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers O'Connor's question of whether a free alternative to a toll road must exist: yes.

forthrightness.statement: We’ve made a commitment as a Government not to increase fuel excise taxes or road-user charges in this term. That was a campaign commitment, and that remains the position as of today.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers O'Connor's RUC/excise question by stating the no-increase position, though sidesteps what happens after this term.

forthrightness.statement: there’s a whole cadre of South Island National and coalition MPs, including the Hon Mark Patterson from New Zealand First, Penny Simmonds, and other members.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the South Island advocacy question with reassurance and names, but no substantive funding commitment.

forthrightness.statement: for the setting of the speed rule, there’s a judicial review under way, so it’s difficult to comment publicly beyond matters which are already on the public record.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to fully answer Genter's questions about safety advice, but gives a legitimate reason (active litigation).

forthrightness.statement: Well, I thank the member for her spirited advocacy on behalf of her constituency. As the Government, we’re always interested and open to receiving our feedback, particularly that expressed passionately.
forthrightness.explanation: Genter asked directly whether he would grant an exemption; he offers only a compliment and vague openness, never answering yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: I haven’t actually had any conversations with the mayor about it, but I’ve only been the transport Minister for 2½ months or so. ... we haven’t actually talked about the Auckland regional fuel tax.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits he hasn't discussed the fuel tax with the mayor, directly answering Halbert's question about mayoral feedback.

forthrightness.statement: as the member knows from her time as associate transport Minister, I don’t make funding decisions around those things; they’re made by the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) board. We set the activity classes, we set the overall funding envelope, but the individual project decisions are made by the NZTA board.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Genter's project-funding question by drawing a real line of responsibility, but uses it to deflect rather than address the GPS direction she raises.

forthrightness.statement: no, I was not aware of the rating of the bridge. ... When have I talked to local MPs and councils about it? I haven’t. It has not been raised with me and now it has. I note that I haven’t had any correspondence from the member in relation to the matter either.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers each of Davidson's questions, including candidly admitting his own lack of awareness and contact.

forthrightness.statement: How much money has been allocated? I’m advised $13 million in this year’s National Land Transport Fund, so the project is funded. I hear what he’s saying that that’s not enough to fund the whole project
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the funding-amount question with a figure and acknowledges it doesn't cover the whole project.

forthrightness.statement: it would be a radical change to divvy up transport funding regionally on the basis of GDP ... or even done on distance or kilometres travelled. ... That would be a drastic change, and it’s not one the Government is contemplating at this point.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Foster's structural question: the Government is not contemplating GDP-based regional funding.

forthrightness.statement: I could, but I would be breaching commercial-in-confidence negotiations. So I won’t.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines O'Connor's question on cancelled-contract compensation, citing a legitimate confidentiality reason but giving no estimate.

forthrightness.statement: EVs are the way of the future in New Zealand ... Over time, it’s cheaper to own a little Nissan Leaf or a Hyundai IONIQ ... because petrol prices are going to rise, and electricity is a great comparative advantage for New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the 41% 2035 emissions target will be met, he pivots to a general 'long-term game' EV case rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: What we’re doing on the Auckland Harbour ... is we’re actually doing the work. There’s a barge in the harbour right now doing the geotechnical work, and we’re undertaking market soundings ... there’s no funding for delivery in this National Land Transport Plan.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Halbert's investment question, including the honest admission that no delivery money is budgeted.

authenticity.statement: We’ve made a commitment as a Government not to increase fuel excise taxes or road-user charges in this term. That was a campaign commitment, and that remains the position as of today.
authenticity.explanation: Position stated as consistent with the party's campaign commitment.

authenticity.statement: I haven’t actually had any conversations with the mayor about it, but I’ve only been the transport Minister for 2½ months or so. ... we haven’t actually talked about the Auckland regional fuel tax.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the party's two-election repeal position on the regional fuel tax.

authenticity.statement: We did get rid of the Clean Car Discount, because it, essentially, resulted in tradies and farmers paying more to subsidise middle-class and wealthy people in Remuera and Wellington, like myself. ... it was a regressive wealth transfer—from lower-income people ... to people who could afford to buy it.
authenticity.explanation: Notably names himself as the kind of well-off buyer who benefited, disclosing his own stake in the policy he critiques.

divination.statement: I think we’ve got a solution. The Minister for Rail, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, is leading that work. ... It’s going to result in the Crown spending far less than the failed iReX project.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the new ferry solution will cost the Crown far less than iReX; plausible but unproven and undetailed.

divination.statement: EVs are the way of the future in New Zealand ... Over time, it’s cheaper to own a little Nissan Leaf or a Hyundai IONIQ ... because petrol prices are going to rise, and electricity is a great comparative advantage for New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts EV dominance and rising petrol prices over the long term; directionally supported by cost trends but timeframe uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: In the urgent debate yesterday, I misspoke when speaking about former Minister Michael Wood. I said that the Minister was told 17 times by the Cabinet Office to sell his Auckland Transport shares; I should have said “16 times” for his Auckland Airport shares.
forthrightness.explanation: Volunteers a correction to the record without prompting, directly identifying the specific error.

forthrightness.statement: The Government’s four priorities for Budget 2025 are: lifting economic growth through measures to address long-term productivity challenges, implementing a social investment approach, keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of policy commitments and cost pressures, and developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investments.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about Budget priorities with an enumerated list.

forthrightness.statement: What I believe is that we need to help kids who are coming to school with no lunches, and that’s why we saved the school lunch programme that was unfunded. We’ve got some challenges, but we’re working our way through them.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Davidson's question about collective care but pivots to a talking point rather than affirming the principle asked about.

forthrightness.statement: What I’d say is in the last 24 hours the vilification from Labour and the Greens, who are telling working parents across New Zealand who happen to give their kids a Marmite sandwich and apple each and every day that they are bad parents, is not acceptable.
forthrightness.explanation: Dodges Davidson's question about vilifying families by counter-attacking Labour and the Greens.

forthrightness.statement: We are actually funding the school lunch programme. We are feeding more kids than the previous Government did. We are doing so, more efficiently, having saved $130 million, which has been put back into health and education for our kids.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not answer Davidson's specific question about jobs lost, pivoting to funding claims.

forthrightness.statement: What I’m proud about is that, actually, rents under this Government are stable, not up $180 per week. What I’m comfortable about is that house prices didn’t increase 40 to 50 percent, and what I’m comfortable about is that, actually, social housing wait-lists are going down and kids in emergency housing are out of motels.
forthrightness.explanation: Hipkins asked how many lunch programmes the landlord tax cuts could fund; Luxon avoids the comparison entirely and pivots to housing.

forthrightness.statement: As I have previously said, I was made aware of the issue on Thursday, and Andrew Bayly resigned very late on Friday.
forthrightness.explanation: Hipkins asked specifically when Luxon first discussed the allegations with Bayly; he answers a different question about when he was informed.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m not going to comment on individual employment matters; it’s a privacy issue, and, actually, it’s up to Ministerial Services to take it forward from there.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer whether an investigation is ongoing, citing privacy rather than confirming or denying.

forthrightness.statement: I also announced more locally trained doctors in general practice, including increasing the total extra medical school placements to 100 each year over the course of this Government. We’re also boosting our nursing workforce by training more nurse practitioners and supporting advanced education for nurses in general practice.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about healthcare access announcements.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m very happy to talk about the PSA union, led by a failed Labour Party candidate who couldn’t even win her seat, and ultimately the union’s doing what the union does: when the National Party’s in Government, they attack the Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Verrall asked whether named health professionals are 'bureaucrats'; he deflects onto the union leader's credentials.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I acknowledge that there is a need for greater investment in our health system, and I’m proud of the investment this Government has made. We have increased health funding by $16.68 billion over three Budgets.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages Verrall's question after repeated pressing, acknowledging need for investment but not the specific harms cited.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there are hundreds of jobs advertised at Health New Zealand, currently online and available for people to put their names forward. There is no such thing as a hiring freeze.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the freeze question but does not take up the invitation to meet the team, which was the specific ask.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, and in answer to the second part of the question, that depends on the procurement approach and commercial negotiations yet to occur.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the first part directly but leaves the cost question open, citing pending negotiations rather than giving a figure.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I’ve just said, I find it’s always wise to agree with the Minister for Rail.
forthrightness.explanation: Edmonds asked her to confirm the $2 billion Treasury saving figure; she deflects with a quip and never confirms.

forthrightness.statement: Those assessments—literacy and numeracy assessments—are not failing the students. The students are failing the assessments, and it is upon this Government to make sure that every single one of those students gets the assistance that they need to get a base level of literacy and numeracy so that they can live the life that they want.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the premise of Maipi-Clarke's question and states her position, though sidesteps the equity concern about low-income schools.

forthrightness.statement: In Southland, there are five RTs Māori; in Northland, there are only three. Yet rangatahi Māori predominantly are in Northland, in far greater numbers than in Southland. That is the reason why we need to take a look at this resource and work out exactly how we can optimise it.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains the rationale for the consultation rather than evading.

forthrightness.statement: We already, amongst other things, secured funding of $68.5 million through Budget 2024 to upgrade the outdated case management technology system so social workers can have the tools they need, which means they can spend more time with the children and family that they work with. We’ve also recruited 33 allied support workers.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the pressure-on-social-workers question with specific actions taken.

forthrightness.statement: I’m sure the PSA is entitled to their opinion, but, at the end of the day, this Government is committed to making sure that every dollar we spend goes towards our young people, and we are prioritising our front-line staff to make sure that they do have the tools that they need.
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the PSA's specific claim about 400 lost workers as 'opinion' rather than engaging the figure.

forthrightness.statement: This has been an issue for a very long time. This is a four-year report; I’m responsible for this year that has come by. I’m not happy with that report, and I am making sure that we do better in the future.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the report is poor but frames responsibility narrowly to the current year.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. I mean, I think the member is pointing to the fact that there is a widespread variety of views on this matter, but the point I would make is that, in the hospitality context, we have laws in place after 9 p.m. where a citizen’s arrest can be conducted, but before 9 p.m. it can’t be, and so, fundamentally, it’s about trying to rectify that situation.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms he considered Hospitality NZ's view and explains the specific anomaly the policy targets.

forthrightness.statement: Why? Well, because we believe it’s a good policy. The ministerial advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal has a variety of people in it, and they all have their different views. We fully expect that they will come up with proposals which are bold and which may well be pushing the boat out, but we need to experiment and come up with different approaches, otherwise we’re going to have the same outcome.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers why he proceeded but glosses over the point that submissions largely opposed the change.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I did think it was a cheap shot by the New Zealand Herald to refer to Destiny being in support of this proposal. Nobody asked Destiny. Nobody is particularly concerned in the views of the Destiny Church on this matter, and we certainly don’t make our decisions as to whether to progress law and order policies based on the opinions of the good bishop.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the premise that Destiny Church was consulted or influential.

civility.statement: In the urgent debate yesterday, I misspoke when speaking about former Minister Michael Wood. I said that the Minister was told 17 times by the Cabinet Office to sell his Auckland Transport shares; I should have said “16 times” for his Auckland Airport shares.
civility.explanation: Correcting one's own record respectfully; no attack involved.

civility.statement: There is a myth propagated by the New Zealand Public Service Association and others that health funding is being reduced. Nothing could be further from the truth. Billions of dollars of additional funding are going into health to help ensure Kiwis have more access to the care they need where they need it.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents' claim a 'myth' but engages the substance of funding levels.

civility.statement: That is called reprioritisation, for the benefit of members who did not experience this concept when they were last in office.
civility.explanation: A condescending jab at the Opposition's competence rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: What I’d say is in the last 24 hours the vilification from Labour and the Greens, who are telling working parents across New Zealand who happen to give their kids a Marmite sandwich and apple each and every day that they are bad parents, is not acceptable.
civility.explanation: Attributes an inflammatory position to opponents ('bad parents') rather than engaging their actual argument.

civility.statement: Does he agree that providing school lunches is an important collective response and one that is far more helpful than vilifying parents and families doing it tough?
civility.explanation: Presses a policy point but embeds the loaded framing that the Government is 'vilifying parents'.

civility.statement: Well, I’m very happy to talk about the PSA union, led by a failed Labour Party candidate who couldn’t even win her seat, and ultimately the union’s doing what the union does: when the National Party’s in Government, they attack the Government.
