civility.explanation: Personal attack on Fleur Fitzsimons ('failed Labour Party candidate') instead of engaging the report's contents.

civility.statement: Because the point of comparison is Project iReX, the biggest dog of an infrastructure project New Zealand has seen in many years, that blew out, members, from $750 million to $4 billion and climbing, with only 21 percent of the costs actually being for the core project of replacing the ferries.
civility.explanation: 'Biggest dog of an infrastructure project' is colourful hyperbole but aimed at a project, not a person.

civility.statement: Those assessments—literacy and numeracy assessments—are not failing the students. The students are failing the assessments, and it is upon this Government to make sure that every single one of those students gets the assistance that they need to get a base level of literacy and numeracy so that they can live the life that they want.
civility.explanation: 'The students are failing the assessments' is a pointed reframing that engages the policy but risks sounding dismissive of the affected students.

civility.statement: I’m sure the PSA is entitled to their opinion, but, at the end of the day, this Government is committed to making sure that every dollar we spend goes towards our young people, and we are prioritising our front-line staff to make sure that they do have the tools that they need.
civility.explanation: Restrained; disagrees without personal attack but does not substantively rebut.

civility.statement: Well, I did think it was a cheap shot by the New Zealand Herald to refer to Destiny being in support of this proposal. Nobody asked Destiny. Nobody is particularly concerned in the views of the Destiny Church on this matter, and we certainly don’t make our decisions as to whether to progress law and order policies based on the opinions of the good bishop.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of Destiny Church and 'the good bishop' but engages the consultation question.

civility.statement: What you’re saying is no criticism at all can happen. What happened to “Sticks and stones can break my bones, but names will never hurt me.”? Over there, they’re so sensitive to every little issue.
civility.explanation: Mocks the Opposition as oversensitive rather than engaging the point of order's substance.

civility.statement: In line with MP Kahurangi Carter’s recent select committee request, if she offers the issue a hug, will it go away?
civility.explanation: A mocking personal jibe at another MP rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Last week, the Government’s slogan was “Everyone must go.” Andrew Bayly finally got the memo and went. But this week, they’ve changed their slogan, and it seems to be “Let them eat Marmite”, because this is a Government that have absolutely trashed the school lunches programme.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical mockery ('Let them eat Marmite') aimed at the Government's record, with a jab at Bayly.

civility.statement: This was a Government that decided to increase the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation. For those working families that are now being attacked, their incomes have gone backwards because of decisions that this Government took.
civility.explanation: Critical of Government decisions on their merits, with some heightened framing ('attacked').

civility.statement: It would be like Christopher Luxon saying, when at Air New Zealand, “We’re a bit short of pilots, let’s just let the public fly the planes.” I don’t think it’s going to work and I think New Zealanders can see that it’s going to make them less safe.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic analogy targeting the policy and Luxon's background, more mocking than substantive.

civility.statement: They still haven’t taken real action on supermarkets, they’re not fixing the health system as it descends further into crisis, more Kiwis are losing their jobs, and house building has collapsed.
civility.explanation: Sweeping criticism of Government priorities; harsh but issue-focused, though 'descends into crisis' is hyperbolic.

civility.statement: Why, if he’s so committed to patient outcomes, won’t he respond seriously to a report that documents delays in rehab for stroke patients, malnourished cancer patients, and untreated babies left with cleft palates because of his Government’s cuts?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory but grounded in specific report findings rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: What message is the Government sending to young Māori when they stress the importance of literacy, on the one hand, while considering defunding expert teachers who support literacy and te reo Māori, on the other?
civility.explanation: Challenges the policy's coherence without personal attack.

authenticity.statement: In the urgent debate yesterday, I misspoke when speaking about former Minister Michael Wood. I said that the Minister was told 17 times by the Cabinet Office to sell his Auckland Transport shares; I should have said “16 times” for his Auckland Airport shares.
authenticity.explanation: Owning and correcting a mistake shows a commitment to accuracy in one's words.

authenticity.statement: This has been an issue for a very long time. This is a four-year report; I’m responsible for this year that has come by. I’m not happy with that report, and I am making sure that we do better in the future.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges dissatisfaction with the report and accepts responsibility for her period, consistent with a reform stance.

specificity.statement: The Government’s four priorities for Budget 2025 are: lifting economic growth through measures to address long-term productivity challenges, implementing a social investment approach, keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of policy commitments and cost pressures, and developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investments.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete priority areas but no figures or timeframes for most.

specificity.statement: That is the commitment of $1.37 billion a year from 2025 onwards to meet demographic, volume, and price pressures for front-line health services. In total, that comes to an additional $5.48 billion for Health New Zealand over the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures ($1.37b/year, $5.48b) with timeframe and named purpose.

specificity.statement: We are actually funding the school lunch programme. We are feeding more kids than the previous Government did. We are doing so, more efficiently, having saved $130 million, which has been put back into health and education for our kids.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete $130m saving and a claim of feeding more kids, but no per-child or coverage figures.

specificity.statement: What I’m proud about is that, actually, rents under this Government are stable, not up $180 per week. What I’m comfortable about is that house prices didn’t increase 40 to 50 percent, and what I’m comfortable about is that, actually, social housing wait-lists are going down and kids in emergency housing are out of motels.
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete comparators but as talking points rather than sourced figures.

specificity.statement: Two years ago, inflation was running at 7.2 percent; today, it’s 2.2 percent. Two years ago today, the official cash rate was 4.75 percent, and today it is 3.75 percent. Two years ago, food inflation was 10.3 percent, and today it’s just 2.3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures with timeframes for inflation, OCR and food inflation.

specificity.statement: I also announced more locally trained doctors in general practice, including increasing the total extra medical school placements to 100 each year over the course of this Government. We’re also boosting our nursing workforce by training more nurse practitioners and supporting advanced education for nurses in general practice.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (100 placements/year) and specific workforce measures.

specificity.statement: Under our Government, medical school placements have already increased by 75 places each year. Increasing this to 100 places will provide more opportunities for talented Kiwis to train as doctors.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (75 places now, 100 planned) with clear mechanism.

specificity.statement: Our front-line workforce—Health New Zealand—is the largest and strongest it has ever been, with over 2,000 more nurses employed at Health New Zealand since 2023, earning, on average, a salary of $125,000, comparable now with nurses in New South Wales.
specificity.explanation: Cites 2,000+ nurses, $125,000 average salary and a cross-jurisdiction comparison.

specificity.statement: Well, I acknowledge that there is a need for greater investment in our health system, and I’m proud of the investment this Government has made. We have increased health funding by $16.68 billion over three Budgets.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise cumulative figure ($16.68b over three Budgets).

specificity.statement: Because the point of comparison is Project iReX, the biggest dog of an infrastructure project New Zealand has seen in many years, that blew out, members, from $750 million to $4 billion and climbing, with only 21 percent of the costs actually being for the core project of replacing the ferries.
specificity.explanation: Concrete cost blowout figures ($750m to $4b) and a 21 percent core-cost breakdown.

specificity.statement: In 2023, only 433 new classrooms were built; in 2024, 581 were built—a 30 percent increase on the year before because we are driving efficiency, delivering results, and building more classrooms.
specificity.explanation: Precise year-on-year classroom counts (433 vs 581) with percentage.

specificity.statement: The average cost per classroom when we arrived in Government was $1.2 million. This is now down to $870,000—nearly a 30 percent reduction.
specificity.explanation: Exact before/after costs ($1.2m to $870,000) and a percentage reduction.

specificity.statement: In Southland, there are five RTs Māori; in Northland, there are only three. Yet rangatahi Māori predominantly are in Northland, in far greater numbers than in Southland. That is the reason why we need to take a look at this resource and work out exactly how we can optimise it.
specificity.explanation: Names specific numbers and regions to illustrate the inequity.

specificity.statement: We already, amongst other things, secured funding of $68.5 million through Budget 2024 to upgrade the outdated case management technology system so social workers can have the tools they need, which means they can spend more time with the children and family that they work with. We’ve also recruited 33 allied support workers.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($68.5m, 33 support workers) tied to named initiatives.

specificity.statement: Last year, Oranga Tamariki recruited 463 field social workers—410 of these were permanent roles. With attrition, this means that the number of field social workers has increased by more than 200 in the last year.
specificity.explanation: Precise recruitment and net-increase figures (463 recruited, 410 permanent, +200 net).

specificity.statement: As of yesterday, police have laid 385 charges under the Gangs Act 2024, and 3,546 other charges overall against individuals on the National Gang List.
specificity.explanation: Exact charge counts (385 and 3,546) with a dated reference point.

specificity.statement: As at 19 February, police have seized 76 patches and 67 firearms from gang members since the new legislation came into force.
specificity.explanation: Dated, precise seizure figures (76 patches, 67 firearms).

specificity.statement: Last year, reported violent crime dropped for the first time since 2018. With these improved firearms prohibition orders now in force, I am confident this downward trend in violent crime will continue, making our communities safer.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dated statistical turning point but the future claim is directional.

specificity.statement: I have expanded the qualifying criteria, allowing firearms prohibition orders to be issued to gang members and criminals convicted of drug, firearms, and other violent offences. This means senior gang members can no longer avoid firearms prohibition orders by having their prospects commit offences on their behalf.
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete legislative change and its mechanism (broadened qualifying offences).

specificity.statement: They still haven’t taken real action on supermarkets, they’re not fixing the health system as it descends further into crisis, more Kiwis are losing their jobs, and house building has collapsed.
specificity.explanation: Lists several concrete areas (supermarkets, health, jobs, house building) but without figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: Why, if he’s so committed to patient outcomes, won’t he respond seriously to a report that documents delays in rehab for stroke patients, malnourished cancer patients, and untreated babies left with cleft palates because of his Government’s cuts?
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete documented harms (stroke rehab delays, malnourished cancer patients, cleft-palate cases) from the report.

specificity.statement: How does she expect social workers to collect data when their workloads prevent them from visiting all tamariki assigned to them, and what does she say to the 63 percent of tamariki that aren’t receiving the minimum standard of care under the national care standards regulations?
specificity.explanation: Grounds the question in a concrete report figure (63 percent not meeting minimum care standards).

veracity.statement: That is the commitment of $1.37 billion a year from 2025 onwards to meet demographic, volume, and price pressures for front-line health services. In total, that comes to an additional $5.48 billion for Health New Zealand over the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Specific fiscal figures consistent with announced Budget commitments; plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: There is a myth propagated by the New Zealand Public Service Association and others that health funding is being reduced. Nothing could be further from the truth. Billions of dollars of additional funding are going into health to help ensure Kiwis have more access to the care they need where they need it.
veracity.explanation: Health funding is rising in nominal terms, but framing sidesteps the PSA's real-terms/per-capita argument, so partly missing context.

veracity.statement: We are actually funding the school lunch programme. We are feeding more kids than the previous Government did. We are doing so, more efficiently, having saved $130 million, which has been put back into health and education for our kids.
veracity.explanation: Savings figure is defensible, but 'feeding more kids... more efficiently' sits against widely reported quality failures, so context is contested.

veracity.statement: What I’m proud about is that, actually, rents under this Government are stable, not up $180 per week. What I’m comfortable about is that house prices didn’t increase 40 to 50 percent, and what I’m comfortable about is that, actually, social housing wait-lists are going down and kids in emergency housing are out of motels.
veracity.explanation: Directional claims on rents, house prices and social housing wait-lists are partly supported but the specific comparatives ($180/week, 40-50%) are rhetorical framings against the prior term.

veracity.statement: Two years ago, inflation was running at 7.2 percent; today, it’s 2.2 percent. Two years ago today, the official cash rate was 4.75 percent, and today it is 3.75 percent. Two years ago, food inflation was 10.3 percent, and today it’s just 2.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: The cited economic figures track official statistics closely; broadly accurate though selectively favourable.

veracity.statement: Under our Government, medical school placements have already increased by 75 places each year. Increasing this to 100 places will provide more opportunities for talented Kiwis to train as doctors.
veracity.explanation: Placement figures are concrete and checkable against announced policy.

veracity.statement: Our front-line workforce—Health New Zealand—is the largest and strongest it has ever been, with over 2,000 more nurses employed at Health New Zealand since 2023, earning, on average, a salary of $125,000, comparable now with nurses in New South Wales.
veracity.explanation: The headcount and salary figures are specific, but 'largest and strongest ever' is a superlative that omits context on vacancies and hiring constraints raised in the same session.

veracity.statement: Well, I acknowledge that there is a need for greater investment in our health system, and I’m proud of the investment this Government has made. We have increased health funding by $16.68 billion over three Budgets.
veracity.explanation: Cumulative funding figure is concrete and checkable against Budget documents.

veracity.statement: Well, there are hundreds of jobs advertised at Health New Zealand, currently online and available for people to put their names forward. There is no such thing as a hiring freeze.
veracity.explanation: Advertised vacancies can coexist with restrictions on filling roles; a flat 'no such thing as a hiring freeze' likely understates reported approval constraints.

veracity.statement: Because the point of comparison is Project iReX, the biggest dog of an infrastructure project New Zealand has seen in many years, that blew out, members, from $750 million to $4 billion and climbing, with only 21 percent of the costs actually being for the core project of replacing the ferries.
veracity.explanation: The escalation figures broadly match public reporting, though 'and climbing' and the framing are rhetorically loaded.

veracity.statement: In 2023, only 433 new classrooms were built; in 2024, 581 were built—a 30 percent increase on the year before because we are driving efficiency, delivering results, and building more classrooms.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable build figures presented consistently.

veracity.statement: Last year, Oranga Tamariki recruited 463 field social workers—410 of these were permanent roles. With attrition, this means that the number of field social workers has increased by more than 200 in the last year.
veracity.explanation: Counters the PSA's '400 lost' claim with net-increase figures; both can be partly true depending on baseline, so context matters.

veracity.statement: As of yesterday, police have laid 385 charges under the Gangs Act 2024, and 3,546 other charges overall against individuals on the National Gang List.
veracity.explanation: Precise, dated enforcement figures that are checkable against police data.

veracity.statement: Last year, reported violent crime dropped for the first time since 2018. With these improved firearms prohibition orders now in force, I am confident this downward trend in violent crime will continue, making our communities safer.
veracity.explanation: The claim that reported violent crime dropped for the first time since 2018 is a specific, checkable statistic.

veracity.statement: This was a Government that decided to increase the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation. For those working families that are now being attacked, their incomes have gone backwards because of decisions that this Government took.
veracity.explanation: A below-inflation minimum wage rise does reduce real incomes; the factual core is defensible though 'attacked' is rhetorical.

charisma.statement: That is called reprioritisation, for the benefit of members who did not experience this concept when they were last in office.
charisma.explanation: A partisan put-down that plays to its own side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: This morning, our excellent Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, announced more support for nurses so they can play a greater role in primary care. That comes off the back of action yesterday to train more doctors here at home, including in primary care.
charisma.explanation: Ends by suggesting the Opposition should want to support this, a mild reach across framed as a challenge.

charisma.statement: I would like to extend the opportunity for the other members of this House to reach across the divide and approach this in a bipartisan manner, because I think all New Zealanders and all members of this Parliament should be focused on improving the situation that people experience in our community and to restore law and order in this country.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites cross-party cooperation and common ground on a contested issue.

charisma.statement: In line with MP Kahurangi Carter’s recent select committee request, if she offers the issue a hug, will it go away?
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing put-down that appeals to one side and belittles an opponent.

charisma.statement: Last week, the Government’s slogan was “Everyone must go.” Andrew Bayly finally got the memo and went. But this week, they’ve changed their slogan, and it seems to be “Let them eat Marmite”, because this is a Government that have absolutely trashed the school lunches programme.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for his own side but purely combative, not consensus-building.

strength.statement: What I believe is that we need to help kids who are coming to school with no lunches, and that’s why we saved the school lunch programme that was unfunded. We’ve got some challenges, but we’re working our way through them.
strength.explanation: Claims to have saved the programme, but concedes ongoing delivery 'challenges'.

strength.statement: This morning, our excellent Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, announced more support for nurses so they can play a greater role in primary care. That comes off the back of action yesterday to train more doctors here at home, including in primary care.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete announcements on nurses and doctor training, but these are announcements/commitments rather than demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: In 2023, only 433 new classrooms were built; in 2024, 581 were built—a 30 percent increase on the year before because we are driving efficiency, delivering results, and building more classrooms.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered results with concrete build numbers, indicating follow-through on the property programme.

strength.statement: The average cost per classroom when we arrived in Government was $1.2 million. This is now down to $870,000—nearly a 30 percent reduction.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete delivered cost reduction attributable to the standardised-design policy.

strength.statement: We already, amongst other things, secured funding of $68.5 million through Budget 2024 to upgrade the outdated case management technology system so social workers can have the tools they need, which means they can spend more time with the children and family that they work with. We’ve also recruited 33 allied support workers.
strength.explanation: Points to funded and partly-delivered measures, though impact on workloads is still emerging.

strength.statement: As at 19 February, police have seized 76 patches and 67 firearms from gang members since the new legislation came into force.
strength.explanation: Concrete enforcement outcomes demonstrating the legislation being applied.

strength.statement: I have expanded the qualifying criteria, allowing firearms prohibition orders to be issued to gang members and criminals convicted of drug, firearms, and other violent offences. This means senior gang members can no longer avoid firearms prohibition orders by having their prospects commit offences on their behalf.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted legislation now in force, a delivered commitment.

rigor.statement: What I’d say is in the last 24 hours the vilification from Labour and the Greens, who are telling working parents across New Zealand who happen to give their kids a Marmite sandwich and apple each and every day that they are bad parents, is not acceptable.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts opponents' criticism of the programme as an attack on parents who pack lunches.

rigor.statement: Is it the view of his Government that good words and good wishes must be backed up by a fiscally sustainable plan to actually pay for the Government’s programmes, and does he believe it’s credible to have all those good words and good wishes but no plan to afford them?
rigor.explanation: Frames a coherent fiscal-sustainability argument, though as a leading patsy question with rhetorical loading.

rigor.statement: Well, I’m very happy to talk about the PSA union, led by a failed Labour Party candidate who couldn’t even win her seat, and ultimately the union’s doing what the union does: when the National Party’s in Government, they attack the Government.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem: dismisses the report by attacking its author's political background.

rigor.statement: Those assessments—literacy and numeracy assessments—are not failing the students. The students are failing the assessments, and it is upon this Government to make sure that every single one of those students gets the assistance that they need to get a base level of literacy and numeracy so that they can live the life that they want.
rigor.explanation: Makes a coherent argument about not lowering standards, but rests on assertion rather than evidence about the assessments' effect.

rigor.statement: In Southland, there are five RTs Māori; in Northland, there are only three. Yet rangatahi Māori predominantly are in Northland, in far greater numbers than in Southland. That is the reason why we need to take a look at this resource and work out exactly how we can optimise it.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete distributional mismatch (5 vs 3 RTs against population) to justify the review; evidence-based reasoning.

rigor.statement: Yes. I mean, I think the member is pointing to the fact that there is a widespread variety of views on this matter, but the point I would make is that, in the hospitality context, we have laws in place after 9 p.m. where a citizen’s arrest can be conducted, but before 9 p.m. it can’t be, and so, fundamentally, it’s about trying to rectify that situation.
rigor.explanation: Points to a concrete legal inconsistency (before/after 9 p.m.) as the rationale, a reasoned basis.

rigor.statement: Why? Well, because we believe it’s a good policy. The ministerial advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal has a variety of people in it, and they all have their different views. We fully expect that they will come up with proposals which are bold and which may well be pushing the boat out, but we need to experiment and come up with different approaches, otherwise we’re going to have the same outcome.
rigor.explanation: 'We need to experiment' is a reasonable governing rationale but leans on assertion over evidence that this measure will help.

rigor.statement: What you’re saying is no criticism at all can happen. What happened to “Sticks and stones can break my bones, but names will never hurt me.”? Over there, they’re so sensitive to every little issue.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a rhymed truism to dismiss a procedural complaint rather than addressing it.

rigor.statement: This was a Government that decided to increase the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation. For those working families that are now being attacked, their incomes have gone backwards because of decisions that this Government took.
rigor.explanation: Links a specific policy decision to a real-terms income effect, a coherent causal claim.

rigor.statement: It would be like Christopher Luxon saying, when at Air New Zealand, “We’re a bit short of pilots, let’s just let the public fly the planes.” I don’t think it’s going to work and I think New Zealanders can see that it’s going to make them less safe.
rigor.explanation: Uses a vivid analogy (public flying planes) rather than evidence to argue citizen's-arrest powers are unsafe.

rigor.statement: What message is the Government sending to young Māori when they stress the importance of literacy, on the one hand, while considering defunding expert teachers who support literacy and te reo Māori, on the other?
rigor.explanation: Frames an apparent inconsistency between stated literacy goals and defunding RT Māori roles, a reasoned tension though it assumes 'defunding'.

rigor.statement: How does she expect social workers to collect data when their workloads prevent them from visiting all tamariki assigned to them, and what does she say to the 63 percent of tamariki that aren’t receiving the minimum standard of care under the national care standards regulations?
rigor.explanation: Connects workload constraints to a specific data-collection and care-standard failure, a coherent line.

divination.statement: Last year, reported violent crime dropped for the first time since 2018. With these improved firearms prohibition orders now in force, I am confident this downward trend in violent crime will continue, making our communities safer.
divination.explanation: Predicts the violent-crime decline will continue; plausible if the trend holds but attribution to the new orders is uncertain.

specificity.statement: This is a Government that has put student achievement back at the heart of the education system.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-like framing statement with no mechanism, figure, or measure.

specificity.statement: over the last 13-14 months, we have put in place a significant reform package to raise student achievement and to close the equity gap in this country.
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe but describes the work only as a 'significant reform package' without detail at this point.

specificity.statement: I’m pleased that, as of term 1 this year, we now have a curriculum that is consistent across the country. No matter where your child goes to school, they are getting access to a world-leading, knowledge-rich curriculum now.
specificity.explanation: Names a timeframe (term 1 this year) and the new English/maths curriculum, but 'world-leading, knowledge-rich' is qualitative.

specificity.statement: The feedback has been phenomenal.
specificity.explanation: Vague positive assertion with no source, measure, or detail.

specificity.statement: mandated this year, every child who goes to school and learns to read will learn through structured literacy, underpinned by the science of learning, integrated into the curriculum
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (structured literacy), a timeframe (this year), and that it is mandated.

specificity.statement: we have trained—or are in training—18,000 primary school teachers, with another six to come in the next tranche.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete figure (18,000 teachers) and a next tranche.

specificity.statement: They have reported that almost two-thirds of teachers—or 64 percent—report that structured literacy approaches have already changed their teaching practices a lot.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (64 percent) attributed to a named source (ERO).

specificity.statement: Three-quarters of teachers say structured literacy approaches have improved literacy for most students.
specificity.explanation: Gives a proportion (three-quarters) but rests on teacher perception rather than measured outcomes.

specificity.statement: On top of that, this year, we have delivered over half a million maths books, course books, textbooks, and guides for teachers over four different providers that they get to choose from.
specificity.explanation: Concrete quantity (over half a million) and number of providers (four), with a timeframe.

specificity.statement: One thing I always remember in Opposition were those who are teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa saying, “We are always an afterthought.” ... I always knew, in my mind, that we would ensure that everything we did was mirrored in te reo Māori as well. I’m very proud that we have delivered te reo decodables that are consistent across the country, for the first time in this country’s history.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deliverable (te reo decodables, consistent nationally) but without figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Not only that but we’ve also devised our phonics check, which is available in mainstream but now also in te reo Māori as well. That is a world first: four checks over a tamariki’s first two years at school to make sure that they are on track with their reading.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete tool (phonics check) with structure (four checks over the first two years).

specificity.statement: Mark my word, it is world leading. I have been to conferences around the world, and other countries are coming to us because what we are doing is world leading.
specificity.explanation: No named countries, benchmarks, or measures behind the sweeping claim.

strength.statement: This is a Government that has put student achievement back at the heart of the education system.
strength.explanation: Broad claim of action with no concrete delivery attached to this sentence itself.

strength.statement: over the last 13-14 months, we have put in place a significant reform package to raise student achievement and to close the equity gap in this country.
strength.explanation: Claims action underway; delivery is asserted generally, with specifics provided later in the speech.

strength.statement: I’m pleased that, as of term 1 this year, we now have a curriculum that is consistent across the country. No matter where your child goes to school, they are getting access to a world-leading, knowledge-rich curriculum now.
strength.explanation: Describes an implemented change (new curriculum rolled out term 1 2025) rather than a mere announcement.

strength.statement: mandated this year, every child who goes to school and learns to read will learn through structured literacy, underpinned by the science of learning, integrated into the curriculum
strength.explanation: A commitment that has been enacted/mandated for 2025, showing follow-through rather than aspiration.

strength.statement: we have trained—or are in training—18,000 primary school teachers, with another six to come in the next tranche.
strength.explanation: In-progress delivery of a professional development programme, with numbers to back the follow-through.

strength.statement: On top of that, this year, we have delivered over half a million maths books, course books, textbooks, and guides for teachers over four different providers that they get to choose from.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered, tangible output rather than a promise.

strength.statement: One thing I always remember in Opposition were those who are teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa saying, “We are always an afterthought.” ... I always knew, in my mind, that we would ensure that everything we did was mirrored in te reo Māori as well. I’m very proud that we have delivered te reo decodables that are consistent across the country, for the first time in this country’s history.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of te reo decodables nationwide; presented as an implemented output backing the commitment.

strength.statement: Not only that but we’ve also devised our phonics check, which is available in mainstream but now also in te reo Māori as well. That is a world first: four checks over a tamariki’s first two years at school to make sure that they are on track with their reading.
strength.explanation: A delivered assessment tool, including a te reo Māori version.

veracity.statement: I remember coming into my ministership and reading, in the briefing to the incoming Minister, that we were “not delivering excellent or equitable outcomes in education”.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about what the Briefing to the Incoming Minister stated; plausible and consistent with the public BIM, though presented to frame the prior state negatively.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased that, as of term 1 this year, we now have a curriculum that is consistent across the country. No matter where your child goes to school, they are getting access to a world-leading, knowledge-rich curriculum now.
veracity.explanation: The new English and maths curriculum was implemented; the self-praising 'world-leading' descriptor is an unverifiable superlative that inflates the claim.

veracity.statement: we have trained—or are in training—18,000 primary school teachers, with another six to come in the next tranche.
veracity.explanation: A specific numeric claim about teachers trained; plausible but not independently verifiable from the text, and blends completed with in-progress training.

veracity.statement: They have reported that almost two-thirds of teachers—or 64 percent—report that structured literacy approaches have already changed their teaching practices a lot.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to ERO's early findings released the same day; accurate as a report but relies on teacher self-report and very early implementation data.

veracity.statement: Three-quarters of teachers say structured literacy approaches have improved literacy for most students.
veracity.explanation: Reports a survey figure of teacher opinion; measures perception of improvement, not verified literacy gains, so it slightly overstates evidence of impact.

veracity.statement: Not only that but we’ve also devised our phonics check, which is available in mainstream but now also in te reo Māori as well. That is a world first: four checks over a tamariki’s first two years at school to make sure that they are on track with their reading.
veracity.explanation: The 'world first' claim is a superlative that is difficult to substantiate and likely overstated.

veracity.statement: Mark my word, it is world leading. I have been to conferences around the world, and other countries are coming to us because what we are doing is world leading.
veracity.explanation: 'World leading' is repeated hyperbole supported only by vague anecdote, with no comparative evidence.

authenticity.statement: One thing I always remember in Opposition were those who are teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa saying, “We are always an afterthought.” ... I always knew, in my mind, that we would ensure that everything we did was mirrored in te reo Māori as well. I’m very proud that we have delivered te reo decodables that are consistent across the country, for the first time in this country’s history.
authenticity.explanation: Ties a stated prior value (not treating Māori medium as an afterthought) to a concrete delivery (te reo decodables), so words appear consistent with action.

authenticity.statement: in everything that we do, we hold ourselves to account, and I have been incredibly careful to make sure that the Education Review Office (ERO) are watching everything that we do.
authenticity.explanation: Stated commitment to accountability backed by a visible action (commissioning ERO to monitor implementation), though self-reported.

rigor.statement: Mark my word, it is world leading. I have been to conferences around the world, and other countries are coming to us because what we are doing is world leading.
rigor.explanation: Relies on repetition and anecdote (conferences, unnamed countries 'coming to us') rather than evidence to support the 'world leading' conclusion.

charisma.statement: I owe a huge debt of gratitude to our principals, our teachers, our teacher-aides, our support workers, because they are on the ground implementing this world-leading change.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, inclusive acknowledgement of the workforce delivering the reforms, though it appeals within the education sector rather than across party lines.

veracity.statement: Health New Zealand has said that its workforce has “grown dramatically, by the thousands.” That is a very good outcome because there are more doctors and midwives and nurses available to make sure that Health New Zealand can deliver for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Reports a broadly accurate direction (HNZ headcount did grow under Labour's build-up), but 'by the thousands' quotes the entity's own gloss without net figures, and the gains partly precede this Government.

veracity.statement: There’s been increased access to PET and CT scans—1,000 more per year to be publicly funded—a crucial cancer diagnostic tool.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with announced scan-funding expansions; plausible and checkable, though presented as delivered outcome.

veracity.statement: As has been highlighted in this House, wait-lists grew substantially under the previous Government, which removed the health targets and left many thousands of New Zealanders waiting far too long to get the care that they need.
veracity.explanation: Wait-lists did grow and the prior Government did scrap the previous target regime; broadly accurate though causation is contested and partly pandemic-driven.

veracity.statement: Over three Budgets, we are delivering an additional $16.68 billion investment in health, ensuring our hospitals, doctors, and nurses have the resources they need to provide access to timely, quality healthcare.
veracity.explanation: The headline figure matches the Government's stated multi-Budget health uplift, though 'additional' aggregates across years in a favourable framing.

veracity.statement: $300 million attributed to the wrong financial year. Health New Zealand had tried to present the costs of redundancies for jobs that hadn’t even been cut to make it look like they were turning their books around. The Auditor-General was having none of it and made Health New Zealand revise its accounts. If that isn’t cooking the books, I don’t know what is.
veracity.explanation: The accounts were revised after audit scrutiny (factual core), but 'cooking the books' overstates a restatement/timing dispute as deliberate fraud.

veracity.statement: Let’s remember those demonstrably and unbelievably false accounts were being prepared with 70 staff under non-disclosure agreements—a highly unusual arrangement in our Public Service.
veracity.explanation: The NDA claim is checkable, but 'demonstrably and unbelievably false accounts' is charged characterisation layered onto a restatement.

veracity.statement: There was a false claim that there were 16 layers of management at Health New Zealand, but there demonstrably wasn’t. No one in the Beehive was able to back up that claim.
veracity.explanation: The '16 layers' figure was indeed widely disputed and unsubstantiated; her rebuttal is directionally supported.

veracity.statement: In that sentiment, Mr Chair, why did the Minister of Health just express so much concern about the restructuring of the health system when in private—while he’s planning to hock off our hospitals to foreign investors—he’s happy to sing the praises of a centralised health system?
veracity.explanation: The claim that the Minister is 'planning to hock off our hospitals to foreign investors' is an unsubstantiated characterisation.

veracity.statement: It says here—the key finding—“The decline in financial performance … was primarily due to Health NZ losing control of the critical levers that drive financial outcomes.” Moving to a single national system eliminated district governance and management controls such as boards, finance and risk committees, and chief financial officers.
veracity.explanation: Accurately quotes a review's finding; the centralisation-cost link is evidenced though the framing serves his narrative.

veracity.statement: Under the previous Government, vaccination rates for two-year-olds dropped from 92.4 percent to 77.1 percent, and I think all members across the House would agree that we need to be increasing immunisation rates rapidly to ensure that our children are protected from a range of diseases.
veracity.explanation: The cited fall in two-year-old immunisation coverage over that period is consistent with official figures.

veracity.statement: That’s why the previous Minister of Health announced two-year funding, $50 million, towards the Immunising our Tamariki initiative. I understand there’s been many thousands of vaccinations done through that initiative.
veracity.explanation: The $50m two-year funding is accurate; 'many thousands of vaccinations' is a vaguer, self-attributed outcome.

veracity.statement: Māori life expectancy continues to lag behind Pākehā, and, despite repeated promises, there has been little progress. How does Health New Zealand plan to close this gap, beyond the tokenistic strategies?
veracity.explanation: The persistent Māori–Pākehā life-expectancy gap is well documented and accurate.

veracity.statement: This year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding. That was an uplift of $200 million, from Budget 2024. We have been very clear, as has the Commissioner of Health New Zealand, that that is protected.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the ring-fenced mental health funding and Budget 2024 uplift; checkable and broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: She might want to reflect, when her Government came into power in 2017, the first thing they did in mental health was cut the mental health co-response pilot teams. So, because of that, we’ve lost six years where we could have been building out that new service.
veracity.explanation: There was disruption to co-response pilots, but 'the first thing they did' and a clean six-year causal loss are contestable simplifications.

veracity.statement: Under the last six years of the Labour Government, they would have published a mental health and addiction workforce plan, which they didn’t. The Auditor-General was highly critical. That’s why, in the last year, this Government published New Zealand’s first stand-alone mental health and addiction workforce plan.
veracity.explanation: The A-G did criticise workforce planning and this Government published a standalone plan; the 'first' framing is broadly defensible.

veracity.statement: The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission released their report recently, the five-year report. The target was to see 325,000 people a year. It’s only delivering to 207,000, so it only hit two-thirds of its target.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific Commission report and figures; presented accurately as a shortfall against target.

veracity.statement: Health New Zealand’s financial situation was significantly worse than expected, doubling from a $500 million deficit to a billion-dollar deficit in 2022-2023, and then it was a $722 million reported deficit in 2023-2024.
veracity.explanation: The deficit figures are broadly consistent with reported HNZ accounts, though 'doubling from $500m to a billion' compresses a moving picture.

veracity.statement: As the report highlights, whilst they changed the letterhead for Health New Zealand, when they put the letterhead on, the previous Government left the system running on an Excel spreadsheet. The financial system was running on an Excel spreadsheet.
veracity.explanation: Loss of local financial controls is evidenced, but 'the financial system was running on an Excel spreadsheet' is a hyperbolic characterisation.

veracity.statement: We’ve increased, over the term of this Government, the number of doctors being trained in our universities by 150 last year, 25 this year, and 25 more next year. That means we’ll be training 100 more doctors through our universities each and every year.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with announced medical-school place increases, but the arithmetic between the annual additions and '100 more each year' is muddled.

specificity.statement: Health New Zealand has said that its workforce has “grown dramatically, by the thousands.” That is a very good outcome because there are more doctors and midwives and nurses available to make sure that Health New Zealand can deliver for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: 'By the thousands' is a vague magnitude with no net number, roles breakdown, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: There’s been increased access to PET and CT scans—1,000 more per year to be publicly funded—a crucial cancer diagnostic tool.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (1,000 more per year) and the specific diagnostic service.

specificity.statement: There’s been mobile breast screening rolled out in Counties Manukau, expected to reach 6,000 more women per year, an extension in the number of people who can receive breast screening, with 70- to 74-year-olds now included in that cohort.
specificity.explanation: Location, target population (6,000 women/yr), and the specific age-cohort extension are all named.

specificity.statement: We’re all dedicated to improving patient outcomes in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A generic platitude with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Over three Budgets, we are delivering an additional $16.68 billion investment in health, ensuring our hospitals, doctors, and nurses have the resources they need to provide access to timely, quality healthcare.
specificity.explanation: Precise cumulative figure and timeframe (three Budgets).

specificity.statement: Let’s remember those demonstrably and unbelievably false accounts were being prepared with 70 staff under non-disclosure agreements—a highly unusual arrangement in our Public Service.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure (70 staff) and the NDA arrangement.

specificity.statement: The whole debacle should have been stopped when it became hard to find actual savings. But no: Health New Zealand pressed on, cutting Milo and toast for new mums at Wellington Hospital. For months beyond that, they pressed on with chaotic cuts to support staff, and data and digital. Hundreds, if not thousands, of staff have left. Just part of the year under review, $33 million in redundancies were paid out.
specificity.explanation: Concrete examples (Milo and toast, $33 million redundancies) though staff losses hedged 'hundreds, if not thousands'.

specificity.statement: The Director-General of Health, the director of public health, the board of Health New Zealand, the chief executive, the chief financial officer, half the executive leadership team, and we even see reports of tier 3 and 4 leaders in mental health. The result is a culture described as “broken”.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates specific departures to substantiate the destabilisation claim.

specificity.statement: My questions for the Minister are: will he commit to monthly publication of papers and financial statements, as was occurring before the election? Secondly, will he commit to a public part to board meetings? Thirdly, can he commit, in his role as Minister directing Health New Zealand and in the practices in his own office, to make sure that the select committee has all of the annual review documents a week before its hearing next time?
specificity.explanation: Three precise, actionable asks with a clear benchmark (monthly, public, one week before).

specificity.statement: Under the previous Government, vaccination rates for two-year-olds dropped from 92.4 percent to 77.1 percent, and I think all members across the House would agree that we need to be increasing immunisation rates rapidly to ensure that our children are protected from a range of diseases.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after percentages and defined cohort (two-year-olds).

specificity.statement: That’s why the previous Minister of Health announced two-year funding, $50 million, towards the Immunising our Tamariki initiative. I understand there’s been many thousands of vaccinations done through that initiative.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure and initiative, but delivery claim ('many thousands') lacks a number.

specificity.statement: So that has been the expectation I’ve made very clear to Health New Zealand: I’m not going to accept excuses which are using that terminology. I want all funded parties that Health New Zealand fund to deliver vaccine services, to be doing everything they can to be making sure they are reaching the health target when it comes to vaccinating our children.
specificity.explanation: A clear expectation set on providers, but no mechanism, funding, or timeframe attached.

specificity.statement: How many, as directed by the Government, community health plans have been submitted, accepted, and progressed by this Government in the past year? For the money that was allocated for the Iwi Māori Partnership Boards, can the Minister confirm just exactly how much of that has been spent? A percentage would be helpful.
specificity.explanation: Precisely scoped, quantified questions (counts of plans; percentage of funding spent).

specificity.statement: This year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding. That was an uplift of $200 million, from Budget 2024. We have been very clear, as has the Commissioner of Health New Zealand, that that is protected.
specificity.explanation: Concrete total ($2.6b), the uplift ($200m), and its Budget source are all stated.

specificity.statement: That’s why this Government announced New Zealand’s first mental health targets—to hold us to account, as a Government... 80 percent of Kiwis to access primary mental health and addiction services within one week, 80 percent of Kiwis to access specialist mental health and addiction services within three weeks, and 95 percent of Kiwis to be either admitted, discharged, or transferred through emergency departments for mental health and addiction issues within six hours.
specificity.explanation: Three precise targets with percentages and time thresholds.

specificity.statement: The associate psychology role will have students in campuses at the start of next year. They will be entering the workforce at the start of 2027. Their role there is to support—not replace—clinical psychologists, to work under supervision, to work within scope of low-intensity patients, and work within a multi-disciplinary team.
specificity.explanation: Timeline (campus next year, workforce 2027) and a defined scope of practice for the new role.

specificity.statement: Look, I’m excited to announce to the committee, there will actually be increased resources into the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, because that’s an issue we, quite frankly, need to do a lot better in New Zealand responding to.
specificity.explanation: 'Increased resources' with no amount, timeframe, or mechanism.

specificity.statement: The Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission released their report recently, the five-year report. The target was to see 325,000 people a year. It’s only delivering to 207,000, so it only hit two-thirds of its target.
specificity.explanation: Names the report and precise figures (325,000 target vs 207,000 delivered).

specificity.statement: Health New Zealand’s financial situation was significantly worse than expected, doubling from a $500 million deficit to a billion-dollar deficit in 2022-2023, and then it was a $722 million reported deficit in 2023-2024.
specificity.explanation: Precise deficit figures across two named financial years.

specificity.statement: Core financial reporting across Health New Zealand is now on a single Oracle Enterprise Resource Planning system—that actually helps, rather than an Excel spreadsheet. So that’s been put in place.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete system (single Oracle ERP) now implemented.

specificity.statement: We all know that primary care, in fact, is the gatekeeper to our health system. None of us can deny how important our general practices are in our local communities, as they are the first port of call for many. What efforts, for the Minister, have been made to improve access to primary care?
specificity.explanation: General framing of primary care's role; the ask itself is open-ended rather than precise.

specificity.statement: Even today, the Associate Minister of Health David Seymour and myself just announced changes to the Medicines Act, which will allow nurse practitioners to be able to prescribe more medicines, which... will play a critical role as part of the health workforce working in general practice to support patients.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete legislative change (Medicines Act) and its effect (nurse-practitioner prescribing).

specificity.statement: We’ve increased, over the term of this Government, the number of doctors being trained in our universities by 150 last year, 25 this year, and 25 more next year. That means we’ll be training 100 more doctors through our universities each and every year.
specificity.explanation: Year-by-year place figures given, though the reconciliation to '100 more each year' is presented loosely.

specificity.statement: In regards to the questions around health quality and safety... Health New Zealand, on 27 March, released its review of the health quality system, with recommendations and the work programme it has under way in regard to that. In terms of the risk register, the roll-out of the national risk reporting system will be happening over the next 18 months.
specificity.explanation: Names a release date and an 18-month rollout window.

specificity.statement: You’ve said previously, Minister, that Iwi Māori Partnership Boards are not for commissioning, and yet there is a requirement for Health NZ to work with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards on the commissioning of investment into kaupapa Māori services.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the challenge in specific legislation and the commissioning-of-investment requirement.

specificity.statement: Why are Māori and Pacific users not monitored to the same extent as other population groups and why did the under-25-year-old cohort not reach any targets in any regions within the last 12 months in terms of that three-week segue into specialist care?
specificity.explanation: Very precise: named cohorts, the three-week specialist target, regional scope, and 12-month window.

divination.statement: There’s been mobile breast screening rolled out in Counties Manukau, expected to reach 6,000 more women per year, an extension in the number of people who can receive breast screening, with 70- to 74-year-olds now included in that cohort.
divination.explanation: Forecast of reaching 6,000 more women per year; plausible but a projection contingent on uptake and rollout.

divination.statement: The associate psychology role will have students in campuses at the start of next year. They will be entering the workforce at the start of 2027. Their role there is to support—not replace—clinical psychologists, to work under supervision, to work within scope of low-intensity patients, and work within a multi-disciplinary team.
divination.explanation: Forecasts students entering the workforce by 2027; plausible but contingent on training pipeline delivery.

charisma.statement: We’re all dedicated to improving patient outcomes in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'we all', acknowledging shared cross-party purpose after thanking committee members.

charisma.statement: Can I just thank the Health Committee, led by the member Sam Uffindell, and all members of the Health Committee, for their work on the annual reviews. I’m just going to make a few opening remarks, and then I look forward to engaging with members from across the House in regards to the annual review of the health portfolio.
charisma.explanation: Cross-bench courtesy and an invitation to engage with members from across the House.

charisma.statement: My questions for the Minister are: will he commit to monthly publication of papers and financial statements, as was occurring before the election? Secondly, will he commit to a public part to board meetings? Thirdly, can he commit, in his role as Minister directing Health New Zealand and in the practices in his own office, to make sure that the select committee has all of the annual review documents a week before its hearing next time?
charisma.explanation: Constructive, transparency-oriented requests rather than pure combat, though addressed to opponents.

charisma.statement: Under the previous Government, vaccination rates for two-year-olds dropped from 92.4 percent to 77.1 percent, and I think all members across the House would agree that we need to be increasing immunisation rates rapidly to ensure that our children are protected from a range of diseases.
charisma.explanation: Frames the goal as shared ('all members across the House would agree') to build consensus on immunisation.

charisma.statement: That’s why the previous Minister of Health announced two-year funding, $50 million, towards the Immunising our Tamariki initiative. I understand there’s been many thousands of vaccinations done through that initiative.
charisma.explanation: Credits 'the previous Minister' for the funding — an acknowledgement of an opponent's contribution.

charisma.statement: Look, I acknowledge the Minister of Health’s response with respect to the immunisation rates and—agreed—we must get them lifted.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly finds common ground with the Minister across the aisle on lifting immunisation rates.

charisma.statement: In fairness to the last Government, they made a significant investment to roll out health improvement practitioners and health coaches within GPs. But, once again, the legacy of the last Government—it’s all good to announce things, but it’s actually about the implementation.
charisma.explanation: 'In fairness to the last Government' concedes a genuine opponent achievement before pivoting to critique.

charisma.statement: We all know that primary care, in fact, is the gatekeeper to our health system. None of us can deny how important our general practices are in our local communities, as they are the first port of call for many. What efforts, for the Minister, have been made to improve access to primary care?
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'we all know / none of us can deny' framing that seeks shared ground before the question.

rigor.statement: Around the health targets, the removal of the national health targets significantly reduced transparency in the health system, and without clear benchmarks, tracking becomes more challenging.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable logical link (no benchmarks -> harder tracking), but asserts the transparency loss rather than evidencing its magnitude.

rigor.statement: Ultimately, if you’re not measuring it, you’re not managing it. The last Government failed to measure, failed to manage, and we are fixing the problems left behind and the thousands of New Zealanders who are waiting too long.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an aphorism and sweeping 'failed to measure/manage' assertion rather than specific evidence at this point in the speech.

rigor.statement: $300 million attributed to the wrong financial year. Health New Zealand had tried to present the costs of redundancies for jobs that hadn’t even been cut to make it look like they were turning their books around. The Auditor-General was having none of it and made Health New Zealand revise its accounts. If that isn’t cooking the books, I don’t know what is.
rigor.explanation: Cites a concrete figure and the A-G's intervention, but the conclusion of deliberate deception outruns the evidence given.

rigor.statement: There was a false claim that there were 16 layers of management at Health New Zealand, but there demonstrably wasn’t. No one in the Beehive was able to back up that claim.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a specific claim by noting no one could substantiate it, though 'demonstrably' is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: The Director-General of Health, the director of public health, the board of Health New Zealand, the chief executive, the chief financial officer, half the executive leadership team, and we even see reports of tier 3 and 4 leaders in mental health. The result is a culture described as “broken”.
rigor.explanation: Builds the 'chaos at the top' case from a concrete list, though 'broken culture' rests on an attributed description.

rigor.statement: In that sentiment, Mr Chair, why did the Minister of Health just express so much concern about the restructuring of the health system when in private—while he’s planning to hock off our hospitals to foreign investors—he’s happy to sing the praises of a centralised health system?
rigor.explanation: Alleged private hypocrisy is asserted with no evidence; approaches a strawman of the Minister's position.

rigor.statement: Worried about the bureaucracy, worried about the personalities rather than about the patients and about delivery. Nothing in there about wait-lists, nothing in there about elective treatment, nothing in there about actually making sure we get the system delivering more for patients. That is why—and nothing about the targets.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts by recharacterising her speech ('nothing about wait-lists') rather than engaging her governance questions.

rigor.statement: It says here—the key finding—“The decline in financial performance … was primarily due to Health NZ losing control of the critical levers that drive financial outcomes.” Moving to a single national system eliminated district governance and management controls such as boards, finance and risk committees, and chief financial officers.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a named external report (Deloitte) and a specific causal mechanism (loss of district financial controls).

rigor.statement: They created that problem. They centralised the health system. They put a new logo on the top and said “job done” and walked away. That’s what they left behind for this Government to have to fix up.
rigor.explanation: Reduces a major structural reform to 'a new logo' — a strawman that ignores the reform's substance.

rigor.statement: The Government claims to be investing in Māori health, yet the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora has centralised decision making back under Crown control. How can Māori trust this Government when their health sovereignty has been stripped away?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine tension (disestablishment vs stated investment) but rests the conclusion on the loaded 'health sovereignty stripped away'.

rigor.statement: Oh, look, what a list. I suppose that’s what you get when you do your research on talkback radio.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks the source of the questions instead of their substance.

rigor.statement: She might want to reflect, when her Government came into power in 2017, the first thing they did in mental health was cut the mental health co-response pilot teams. So, because of that, we’ve lost six years where we could have been building out that new service.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a single-cause 'lost six years' counterfactual without evidence for the causal chain.

rigor.statement: The member also talked about the associate psychology role. She made a comment that someone might get hurt. What about the Kiwis today who are getting hurt because they can’t get the timely access to mental health and addiction support?
rigor.explanation: A 'what about' deflection that answers a safety concern with a counter-harm rather than addressing the raised risk.

rigor.statement: Under the last six years of the Labour Government, they would have published a mental health and addiction workforce plan, which they didn’t. The Auditor-General was highly critical. That’s why, in the last year, this Government published New Zealand’s first stand-alone mental health and addiction workforce plan.
rigor.explanation: Backs the point with an external critique (Auditor-General) and a specific counter-action.

rigor.statement: The public consultation said there were no clear roles and responsibilities, it wasn’t targeted, and they couldn’t actually measure whether it was making a difference. So those three things will be embedded in our Suicide Prevention Action Plan.
rigor.explanation: Ties the redesign to specified consultation findings and maps each to a corrective change.

rigor.statement: As the report highlights, whilst they changed the letterhead for Health New Zealand, when they put the letterhead on, the previous Government left the system running on an Excel spreadsheet. The financial system was running on an Excel spreadsheet.
rigor.explanation: The 'Excel spreadsheet' line is a rhetorical caricature rather than a documented account of the finance systems.

rigor.statement: I know they’re all feeling rather embarrassed about what they left behind, because—through a pandemic, instead of focusing on patients, outcomes, wait-lists, all of those important things which people actually care about, they were worried about changing a letterhead. That was their priority.
rigor.explanation: Strawman that reduces the opponents' pandemic-era health reform to 'changing a letterhead'.

rigor.statement: The reality is, a focus on wait times and a focus on outcomes will benefit Māori and will benefit non-Māori. That is why we are focused so much on those health targets as a Government, and on delivering against them.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that generic targets close ethnic gaps without addressing the equity mechanism the question raised.

rigor.statement: You’ve said previously, Minister, that Iwi Māori Partnership Boards are not for commissioning, and yet there is a requirement for Health NZ to work with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards on the commissioning of investment into kaupapa Māori services.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete tension between the Minister's stated position and the Pae Ora legislative wording she quotes.

civility.statement: Around the health targets, the removal of the national health targets significantly reduced transparency in the health system, and without clear benchmarks, tracking becomes more challenging.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused criticism of a decision, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Can I just thank the Health Committee, led by the member Sam Uffindell, and all members of the Health Committee, for their work on the annual reviews. I’m just going to make a few opening remarks, and then I look forward to engaging with members from across the House in regards to the annual review of the health portfolio.
civility.explanation: Respectful, collegial framing of the debate.

civility.statement: As has been highlighted in this House, wait-lists grew substantially under the previous Government, which removed the health targets and left many thousands of New Zealanders waiting far too long to get the care that they need.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous Government's policy record, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Ultimately, if you’re not measuring it, you’re not managing it. The last Government failed to measure, failed to manage, and we are fixing the problems left behind and the thousands of New Zealanders who are waiting too long.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-directed criticism of the predecessor's management.

civility.statement: $300 million attributed to the wrong financial year. Health New Zealand had tried to present the costs of redundancies for jobs that hadn’t even been cut to make it look like they were turning their books around. The Auditor-General was having none of it and made Health New Zealand revise its accounts. If that isn’t cooking the books, I don’t know what is.
civility.explanation: 'Cooking the books' is sensationalist framing imputing bad faith, though aimed at the organisation not a person.

civility.statement: The whole debacle should have been stopped when it became hard to find actual savings. But no: Health New Zealand pressed on, cutting Milo and toast for new mums at Wellington Hospital. For months beyond that, they pressed on with chaotic cuts to support staff, and data and digital. Hundreds, if not thousands, of staff have left. Just part of the year under review, $33 million in redundancies were paid out.
civility.explanation: 'Debacle' and 'chaotic' are sharp but the critique targets management decisions, not persons.

civility.statement: In that sentiment, Mr Chair, why did the Minister of Health just express so much concern about the restructuring of the health system when in private—while he’s planning to hock off our hospitals to foreign investors—he’s happy to sing the praises of a centralised health system?
civility.explanation: The 'hock off our hospitals to foreign investors' insinuation imputes a hidden privatisation motive without support.

civility.statement: Worried about the bureaucracy, worried about the personalities rather than about the patients and about delivery. Nothing in there about wait-lists, nothing in there about elective treatment, nothing in there about actually making sure we get the system delivering more for patients. That is why—and nothing about the targets.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opponent as caring about personalities over patients; dismissive but framed around priorities.

civility.statement: They created that problem. They centralised the health system. They put a new logo on the top and said “job done” and walked away. That’s what they left behind for this Government to have to fix up.
civility.explanation: 'Put a new logo on the top and walked away' mockingly caricatures the opponents' reform.

civility.statement: Look, I acknowledge the Minister of Health’s response with respect to the immunisation rates and—agreed—we must get them lifted.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's point before pressing his own questions.

civility.statement: How many, as directed by the Government, community health plans have been submitted, accepted, and progressed by this Government in the past year? For the money that was allocated for the Iwi Māori Partnership Boards, can the Minister confirm just exactly how much of that has been spent? A percentage would be helpful.
civility.explanation: Straightforward, substantive questions with no personal edge.

civility.statement: The Government claims to be investing in Māori health, yet the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora has centralised decision making back under Crown control. How can Māori trust this Government when their health sovereignty has been stripped away?
civility.explanation: Pointed and rhetorical, but attacks the policy/record rather than a person.

civility.statement: Māori life expectancy continues to lag behind Pākehā, and, despite repeated promises, there has been little progress. How does Health New Zealand plan to close this gap, beyond the tokenistic strategies?
civility.explanation: 'Tokenistic strategies' is a jab at the approach, but embedded in a substantive equity question.

civility.statement: Oh, look, what a list. I suppose that’s what you get when you do your research on talkback radio.
civility.explanation: A dismissive personal jab implying the member's questions come from 'talkback radio' rather than serious research.

civility.statement: She might want to reflect, when her Government came into power in 2017, the first thing they did in mental health was cut the mental health co-response pilot teams. So, because of that, we’ve lost six years where we could have been building out that new service.
civility.explanation: Sharp but directed at a past policy decision rather than the member personally.

civility.statement: In fairness to the last Government, they made a significant investment to roll out health improvement practitioners and health coaches within GPs. But, once again, the legacy of the last Government—it’s all good to announce things, but it’s actually about the implementation.
civility.explanation: Balanced acknowledgement plus a policy-level (announce vs implement) criticism, no personal attack.

civility.statement: As the report highlights, whilst they changed the letterhead for Health New Zealand, when they put the letterhead on, the previous Government left the system running on an Excel spreadsheet. The financial system was running on an Excel spreadsheet.
civility.explanation: Mockery ('changed the letterhead', 'running on an Excel spreadsheet') ridiculing the predecessor's competence.

civility.statement: I know they’re all feeling rather embarrassed about what they left behind, because—through a pandemic, instead of focusing on patients, outcomes, wait-lists, all of those important things which people actually care about, they were worried about changing a letterhead. That was their priority.
civility.explanation: Imputes embarrassment and trivial priorities to opponents; a caricature rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: You’ve said previously, Minister, that Iwi Māori Partnership Boards are not for commissioning, and yet there is a requirement for Health NZ to work with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards on the commissioning of investment into kaupapa Māori services.
civility.explanation: Substantive, respectful challenge grounded in the statute, no personal attack.

civility.statement: Why are Māori and Pacific users not monitored to the same extent as other population groups and why did the under-25-year-old cohort not reach any targets in any regions within the last 12 months in terms of that three-week segue into specialist care?
civility.explanation: Detailed, substantive scrutiny questions with no personal attack.

strength.statement: Over three Budgets, we are delivering an additional $16.68 billion investment in health, ensuring our hospitals, doctors, and nurses have the resources they need to provide access to timely, quality healthcare.
strength.explanation: A concrete, budgeted commitment partly delivered via successive Budgets, with delivery of outcomes still in progress.

strength.statement: That is why we’ve brought back the health targets—so we can focus the system back on the patient and make sure that we are delivering more for them.
strength.explanation: A specific policy (reinstating health targets) that has actually been enacted by this Government.

strength.statement: So that has been the expectation I’ve made very clear to Health New Zealand: I’m not going to accept excuses which are using that terminology. I want all funded parties that Health New Zealand fund to deliver vaccine services, to be doing everything they can to be making sure they are reaching the health target when it comes to vaccinating our children.
strength.explanation: States intent and instruction to the system, but this is direction-setting rather than demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: This year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding. That was an uplift of $200 million, from Budget 2024. We have been very clear, as has the Commissioner of Health New Zealand, that that is protected.
strength.explanation: A budgeted, protected commitment; delivery of the funding is credible though outcomes remain in progress.

strength.statement: That’s why this Government announced New Zealand’s first mental health targets—to hold us to account, as a Government... 80 percent of Kiwis to access primary mental health and addiction services within one week, 80 percent of Kiwis to access specialist mental health and addiction services within three weeks, and 95 percent of Kiwis to be either admitted, discharged, or transferred through emergency departments for mental health and addiction issues within six hours.
