strength.explanation: The targets have been announced/established (a delivered policy act), though the access outcomes they set are not yet met.

strength.statement: Under the last six years of the Labour Government, they would have published a mental health and addiction workforce plan, which they didn’t. The Auditor-General was highly critical. That’s why, in the last year, this Government published New Zealand’s first stand-alone mental health and addiction workforce plan.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete deliverable actually produced (first stand-alone workforce plan) under his watch.

strength.statement: Core financial reporting across Health New Zealand is now on a single Oracle Enterprise Resource Planning system—that actually helps, rather than an Excel spreadsheet. So that’s been put in place.
strength.explanation: Points to a specific systems change described as already delivered ('put in place').

strength.statement: Even today, the Associate Minister of Health David Seymour and myself just announced changes to the Medicines Act, which will allow nurse practitioners to be able to prescribe more medicines, which... will play a critical role as part of the health workforce working in general practice to support patients.
strength.explanation: A specific action just announced; between announcement and delivery, so partial follow-through.

strength.statement: We’ve increased, over the term of this Government, the number of doctors being trained in our universities by 150 last year, 25 this year, and 25 more next year. That means we’ll be training 100 more doctors through our universities each and every year.
strength.explanation: Training-place increases are partly enacted (150 last year) with more scheduled — in-progress delivery.

authenticity.statement: That is why we’ve brought back the health targets—so we can focus the system back on the patient and make sure that we are delivering more for them.
authenticity.explanation: Reinstating targets is consistent with the Government's stated commitment and with National's prior use of health targets.

authenticity.statement: The Government claims to be investing in Māori health, yet the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora has centralised decision making back under Crown control. How can Māori trust this Government when their health sovereignty has been stripped away?
authenticity.explanation: Frames a words-vs-deeds gap: claims to invest in Māori health while abolishing the Māori Health Authority — but this targets the Government's consistency, not her own.

forthrightness.statement: Worried about the bureaucracy, worried about the personalities rather than about the patients and about delivery. Nothing in there about wait-lists, nothing in there about elective treatment, nothing in there about actually making sure we get the system delivering more for patients. That is why—and nothing about the targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to Verrall's three specific commit-or-not questions (monthly publication, public board meetings, documents a week early), he answers none and pivots to attacking her focus.

forthrightness.statement: The first question around vaccine hesitancy is a question I am happy to come back to the member in regards to, if you put it in writing, as well as the question around how much has been spent on Iwi Māori Partnership Boards (IMPBs). If you can put those in writing, I can provide an answer to the member on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Henare's specific asks (source of the 7% hesitancy rise; % of IMPB funding spent) are deferred to written questions rather than answered.

forthrightness.statement: The member also talked about the associate psychology role. She made a comment that someone might get hurt. What about the Kiwis today who are getting hurt because they can’t get the timely access to mental health and addiction support?
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots away from Leary's specific safety question about the associate role to a broader access argument.

forthrightness.statement: The public consultation said there were no clear roles and responsibilities, it wasn’t targeted, and they couldn’t actually measure whether it was making a difference. So those three things will be embedded in our Suicide Prevention Action Plan.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains why the plan was delayed (consultation findings) but doesn't give the delivery date Leary specifically pressed for.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I’m excited to announce to the committee, there will actually be increased resources into the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, because that’s an issue we, quite frankly, need to do a lot better in New Zealand responding to.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts Leary's premise (resource-constraint delay) by asserting resources will increase, though without figures.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is, a focus on wait times and a focus on outcomes will benefit Māori and will benefit non-Māori. That is why we are focused so much on those health targets as a Government, and on delivering against them.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Kemp's pointed Māori-equity and 'health sovereignty' questions with a universalist targets answer that sidesteps the Māori-specific concern.

forthrightness.statement: In regards to the questions around health quality and safety... Health New Zealand, on 27 March, released its review of the health quality system, with recommendations and the work programme it has under way in regard to that. In terms of the risk register, the roll-out of the national risk reporting system will be happening over the next 18 months.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Verrall's risk-register question with a concrete date (27 March review) and timeline (18 months), though not confirming outright whether a register currently exists.

veracity.statement: Since the 2014 Veterans' Support Act, a veteran has to have had qualified overseas experience or operational experience or have been in danger.
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of the narrower NZ definition under the Veterans' Support Act 2014 (qualifying operational/overseas service).

veracity.statement: there are a large number of our forces—approximately 40,000 people, but the extra 100,000 to take it to 140,000 people—who are not entitled to any of those things.
veracity.explanation: Order-of-magnitude plausible for ex-service personnel outside the current definition, but the exact numbers are unverified and loosely stated.

veracity.statement: Wool is naturally flame resistant, reducing the risk of fire hazards. Unlike synthetic materials that can melt and release toxic fumes when exposed to flames, wool chars and self-extinguishes—adding an extra layer of safety to our homes and our workplaces.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: wool has high natural flame resistance and self-extinguishes due to its high ignition point and moisture content.

veracity.statement: One of the greatest challenges has been the aggressive marketing from synthetic materials, which have infiltrated the market and overshadowed our natural wool.
veracity.explanation: Partly true that synthetics displaced wool, but the marketing-conspiracy framing overstates a single cause.

veracity.statement: There have been over 7 million people who have died in the conflict—that is a population greater than the entirety of Aotearoa's population—with about 30 percent of them being children.
veracity.explanation: The commonly cited DRC conflict death toll is around 5–6 million since 1996; 'over 7 million' is at the high end and the 30% children figure is not well established.

veracity.statement: those particular ceasefire talks broke down when the Rwanda regime-backed March 23 Movement (M23) pulled out of those discussions at the last minute.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reporting that the March 2025 Doha talks collapsed after M23's withdrawal; the 'Rwanda-backed' characterisation aligns with UN findings.

veracity.statement: Sir Ernest Rutherford—who was of course from Nelson, not from the USA—splitting the atom; Kate Sheppard, the first country to give women the vote.
veracity.explanation: Rutherford was indeed from the Nelson region (Brightwater), and NZ was the first self-governing country to grant women the vote (1893); slightly garbled phrasing but factually sound.

veracity.statement: We've got an organisation which is on track to produce more whitebait than the entire national catch out of a single old, closed meat works near Bluff.
veracity.explanation: Plausible reference to a Bluff whitebait aquaculture venture, but 'more than the entire national catch' is an ambitious claim stated without evidence.

charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the mover's valid goal and frames NZ First as balancing both sides; conciliatory, bridge-building tone.

charisma.statement: If this bill doesn’t go through tonight, then I would hope that members would collectively come together and think of a solution. Because it is absolutely wrong.
charisma.explanation: Appeals across the House to work together on a solution even if the bill fails; consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: I certainly hear that support from this side of the House, and I thank the support of the other parties to do what we have to do with this bill, and that is to kick it back—back into the dim, dark past where it belongs. On that note, I do not commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side and coalition partners but is purely combative toward the Opposition, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: You can choose not to take a side in the debate. You can choose to be for New Zealand... You can choose to determine what’s right in an employment relationship in the context of what is right for a place we call home.
charisma.explanation: Reaches for an inclusive 'for New Zealand' framing, but implicitly casts the other side as taking a narrow side, limiting its bridge-building.

charisma.statement: Easter is a Christian holiday. I am Catholic—I’m not a very good Catholic, but I’m still Catholic. I attend Mass at Easter and at Christmas.
charisma.explanation: Self-deprecating, relatable personal disclosure that disarms the religious objection by speaking from within the tradition.

charisma.statement: I respect those that hold views that would lead them to not want to consume alcohol on those days—absolutely respect that. But what about those people that don’t hold those views? Why should they be prevented?
charisma.explanation: Explicitly respects opposing religious views before making the freedom-of-choice case; inclusive, consensus-seeking framing.

civility.statement: What has happened in this country, with regard to wages, has been a disaster for our people. In a cost of living crisis, we need to face that fact—all of our parties—and we need to put it right.
civility.explanation: Focuses on the collective policy problem, no personal attack, calls for shared responsibility.

civility.statement: There is this myth that somehow the National Party are the people who understand economics. This shows the problem with the myth—it shows the problem—because it’s false economy if you underpay workers, if they never get a share of the wealth of the country, and it all goes offshore and it all goes to the 1 percent, then we end up with a mess of a country. We end up with crime. We end up with mental health issues. We end up with violence.
civility.explanation: Attacks the National Party's economic credibility as a 'myth' but frames it as a policy/ideas critique rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: We need to start being smart in this House and stop this absolute garbage, that fills the head, of an ideology that just cannot see past the word “union”, because that’s what’s going on.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' position as 'absolute garbage' and ideological blindness rather than engaging their substance.

civility.statement: So to hear that it’s about driving up wages makes me think that this is a solution looking for a problem, as is often the case with members’ bills from the opposite side.
civility.explanation: Generalised dig at Opposition members' bills, but stops short of a personal attack and stays on the merits of the bill's purpose.

civility.statement: someone can do exactly the same job as their workmates, under the same conditions, and they might be excluded from union protections just because of who signs their contract. That’s not right—that’s not right at all.
civility.explanation: Argues the substance of the inequity without attacking any person.

civility.statement: We agree with the member—Helen White—that’s proposing the bill. We do want to see real wages rising in this country, but we also quite profoundly believe in flexibility in the labour market. So I guess we try to balance those two aspects out.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with an opponent's aim before disagreeing on means.

civility.statement: There might be a suspicion that, as some of my colleagues over here have alluded to, this is more about appeasing a union base and trying to gain them more influence—which is fair enough; they are the Labour Party after all.
civility.explanation: Imputes an ulterior union motive, but does so mildly and with a good-humoured acknowledgement rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: These actions are not isolated; they are coordinated ideological attacks on the working class, on tangata whenua, on migrants, on women—on those with the least power and the most to lose.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents' policies as deliberate 'attacks' on vulnerable groups, imputing hostile motive rather than debating effects.

civility.statement: yes, I was part of that select committee that the member the Hon Mark Patterson mentioned... We did hear, during that time, some terrible, terrible stories around what was happening in that triangular relationship.
civility.explanation: Graciously affirms a NZ First member's recollection while making her case.

civility.statement: We, unfortunately, have some companies—and I’m not saying all companies—who are going through and making the promises through collective agreement bargaining and then, unfortunately, using labour hire companies to then withdraw on their promises that they made throughout that collective bargaining time.
civility.explanation: Criticises a corporate practice while explicitly avoiding overgeneralisation to all employers.

civility.statement: If this bill doesn’t go through tonight, then I would hope that members would collectively come together and think of a solution. Because it is absolutely wrong.
civility.explanation: Constructive call for collective problem-solving rather than blame.

civility.statement: I find it really ironic that I’m standing here now after having the mover of the bill stand up and talk about the damage that was done to people’s wages in the late 1980s. Well, guess who was in power in the late 80s? Oh, that’s right: it was the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: A pointed partisan jab, but aimed at the party's record rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: this is, by stealth, trying to quietly bring back more and more compulsion around the union movement. So I just have to wonder: who actually wrote this member’s bill? Ooh, might it be the Council of Trade Unions?
civility.explanation: Implies the bill is a covert union front rather than engaging its stated content.

civility.statement: I certainly hear that support from this side of the House, and I thank the support of the other parties to do what we have to do with this bill, and that is to kick it back—back into the dim, dark past where it belongs. On that note, I do not commend this bill to the House.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'dim, dark past' rhetoric relishes defeating the bill rather than engaging the workers' issue it raises.

civility.statement: The seasonal workers in Nelson at Sealord are actually part of a collective agreement, for the record. So Katie Nimon could come and learn a little bit about that.
civility.explanation: Legitimate factual correction, but the 'could come and learn a little bit' framing is a personal dig at a named member.

civility.statement: I’m getting a bit sick of the Opposition talking about their interest in the average New Zealander, when they voted against things that literally put money on the table of those employees in this House last year. Tax cuts, tax cuts and tax relief.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Opposition of insincerity toward workers; a partisan attack on their motives rather than the bill's substance.

civility.statement: I respect those that hold views that would lead them to not want to consume alcohol on those days—absolutely respect that. But what about those people that don’t hold those views? Why should they be prevented?
civility.explanation: Acknowledges and respects opponents' sincerely held beliefs while disagreeing on the policy.

rigor.statement: if they don’t actually have a contract of their own, a collective agreement, but they’re doing the same work as the port workers when they’re brought in, they are entitled to ask to be on those terms and conditions that the primary employer is actually offering its own workers.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned equal-pay-for-equal-work argument tied to the bill's actual mechanism, though leans on a single illustrative case.

rigor.statement: There is this myth that somehow the National Party are the people who understand economics. This shows the problem with the myth—it shows the problem—because it’s false economy if you underpay workers, if they never get a share of the wealth of the country, and it all goes offshore and it all goes to the 1 percent, then we end up with a mess of a country. We end up with crime. We end up with mental health issues. We end up with violence.
rigor.explanation: Chains underpayment to crime, mental health, and violence without evidence for the causal links; a slippery-slope of harms plus an appeal to emotion.

rigor.statement: When I was once involved as a lawyer out at the steel mill, they had something called an equalisation clause. It worked in a very similar way. It said, “If you come on site and you’re a contractor, you should be paid the same amount as the people who are there.” Guess what! Actually, the world didn’t cave in. We still made steel.
rigor.explanation: Offers a real-world precedent to rebut fears of harm, but it is a single anecdote generalised to the whole economy.

rigor.statement: So to hear that it’s about driving up wages makes me think that this is a solution looking for a problem, as is often the case with members’ bills from the opposite side.
rigor.explanation: Points to a genuine mismatch between stated aim and drafting, but the 'always the case' generalisation is an unevidenced appeal.

rigor.statement: Come to Hawke’s Bay for a summer harvest and see why they have to use labour hire contractors for the seasonal work. Go to a wonderful concert, whether it’s at Eden Park in Auckland or whether it’s a Mission concert in Taradale—these are seasonal event-based contracts that need this kind of employment relationship.
rigor.explanation: Illustrates the case for labour-hire flexibility with real examples, but leans on invitation/anecdote rather than evidence that the bill would harm them.

rigor.statement: I would love to know the research behind the assumption that every person working for a labour hire company is earning significantly less. Because that is not the case.
rigor.explanation: Fairly demands evidence for the premise, but then asserts the counter-claim ('that is not the case') without offering its own evidence.

rigor.statement: someone can do exactly the same job as their workmates, under the same conditions, and they might be excluded from union protections just because of who signs their contract. That’s not right—that’s not right at all.
rigor.explanation: Clear statement of the equal-work-unequal-protection problem the bill targets; the conclusion follows from the premise, though asserted as principle.

rigor.statement: What this bill does is, basically, it just extends the powers of unions to third parties in triangular work relationships.
rigor.explanation: Reduces the bill to a single 'union power' framing that omits its equal-pay mechanism; a simplification bordering on strawman.

rigor.statement: a lot of people become employees of labour hire companies only because they want flexibility. We know that people’s circumstances vary. Some people might have responsibilities like young children or maybe an elderly person they’re looking after.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that some workers choose flexibility, supported by relatable scenarios rather than data; an appeal to plausible anecdote.

rigor.statement: But what it will do is it will create more cost for employees because if there is a claim, there are then two parties to deal with that claim rather than one party to deal with that claim. When there are two parties involved, we know it is going to take longer, it is going to be expensive, and there is going to be this big legal risk that the employee will have to go through as well.
rigor.explanation: A coherent procedural-cost argument, but 'we know' substitutes assertion for evidence on the size of the effect.

rigor.statement: I think in a lot of times these temporary workers are actually paid—there’s a premium. To get someone in at short notice, you actually have to pay a premium. So those workers are very valuable to those businesses that need some surge capacity.
rigor.explanation: Conflates the premium paid to the labour-hire company with the worker's take-home pay, weakening the logical link.

rigor.statement: He’s hauling the same timber, pouring the same concrete, and taking the same risks as the workers directly employed by Big Build Ltd. But while those Big Build workers are covered by a union collective agreement... Hēmi gets none of that. Why? Because, he’s technically employed by someone else.
rigor.explanation: Uses a clear illustrative case to make the equal-work-unequal-treatment argument; effective but rests on a constructed example rather than evidence of prevalence.

rigor.statement: These actions are not isolated; they are coordinated ideological attacks on the working class, on tangata whenua, on migrants, on women—on those with the least power and the most to lose.
rigor.explanation: Asserts coordination and intent ('coordinated ideological attacks') as a conclusion without evidence of coordination; strong emotive framing.

rigor.statement: I find it really ironic that I’m standing here now after having the mover of the bill stand up and talk about the damage that was done to people’s wages in the late 1980s. Well, guess who was in power in the late 80s? Oh, that’s right: it was the Labour Party.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque point about which party governed in the 1980s that does not actually address the bill's merits; guilt-by-history rather than argument.

rigor.statement: this is, by stealth, trying to quietly bring back more and more compulsion around the union movement. So I just have to wonder: who actually wrote this member’s bill? Ooh, might it be the Council of Trade Unions?
rigor.explanation: Insinuates hidden authorship and a stealth agenda without evidence; speculation dressed as inference.

rigor.statement: Yes, employers do pay a premium for labour hire workers. But that doesn’t get passed to the worker. There’s a ticket-clipping exercise for the labour hire company... the employer is actually paying more for that worker because there is a percentage being passed on to the labour hire company.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the 'premium reaches the worker' claim by distinguishing what the employer pays from what the worker receives; a logically clean counter.

rigor.statement: The seasonal workers in Nelson at Sealord are actually part of a collective agreement, for the record. So Katie Nimon could come and learn a little bit about that.
rigor.explanation: Offers a concrete counter-example to the claim that seasonal work is inherently outside collective agreements; the 'learn a little bit' aside is a jab rather than argument.

rigor.statement: I have spoken to workers, actual workers in my electorate, who have worked for the same labour hire company at the same large sawmill in Nelson for years—years. This is not about seasonal work.
rigor.explanation: Uses first-hand constituent evidence to counter the 'seasonal flexibility' framing, but relies on personal anecdote rather than systematic data.

rigor.statement: I’ve never, ever, ever talked to a labour hire worker—and I’ve talked to many of them—who doesn’t want a permanent job, who hasn’t asked the employer to be employed permanently.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping universal ('never, ever') drawn from personal anecdote to rebut the 'workers choose flexibility' argument; persuasive but overstated as absolute.

rigor.statement: The member’s been very clear: this only applies when a collective agreement is in place, and the majority of collective agreements are at large employers. It doesn’t add any other, extra party to this. All it’s doing is implying the same wages and conditions.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the small-business/red-tape objection by pointing to the bill's actual trigger condition (existing collective agreement, mostly at large employers).

rigor.statement: The difference is we don’t think we know exactly what that amount of money is for every employee in the country. We don’t believe we should be getting in the middle of the employment relationship and telling the employee, “Hey, this is what you should negotiate with your boss.”
rigor.explanation: States a coherent limited-government principle, but frames the choice as government dictating pay versus not, understating the bill's narrower equal-pay mechanism.

rigor.statement: You can choose not to take a side in the debate. You can choose to be for New Zealand... You can choose to determine what’s right in an employment relationship in the context of what is right for a place we call home.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy between being 'for New Zealand' and supporting the bill, rather than engaging the equal-pay argument.

rigor.statement: I’m getting a bit sick of the Opposition talking about their interest in the average New Zealander, when they voted against things that literally put money on the table of those employees in this House last year. Tax cuts, tax cuts and tax relief.
rigor.explanation: Points to Labour's vote against the tax package but treats it as proof of indifference to workers, ignoring that they opposed the package's design, not worker welfare.

rigor.statement: It seems that this rule is in place because it always has been, and that’s not really a good reason to have a rule.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies and rejects an appeal to tradition as the sole justification for the restriction; sound reasoning.

rigor.statement: At no point in my religion—and, in fact, most; the vast majority of Christian religions—does it prohibit you from drinking alcohol on Good Friday or Easter Sunday... I’m not going to eat meat on Good Friday. Would this Parliament support a ban on serving meat in this country on Good Friday? Of course it wouldn’t. But exactly the same logic applies here.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a parallel-reasoning argument (meat ban analogy) to expose the inconsistency of the alcohol restriction; the analogy is apt and the logic largely holds.

divination.statement: It is our firm belief that this will have a far more perverse impact on small businesses.
divination.explanation: Predicts a net harmful impact on small businesses; plausible directionally but asserted without modelling, and the bill's own scope (collective-agreement workplaces) limits reach.

divination.statement: So at the end of the day—and we have made this very clear—this is not a bill we support. This is a solution looking for a problem, and all we see this doing is discouraging businesses from hiring workers through third-party organisations.
divination.explanation: Predicts businesses will be discouraged from using labour-hire firms; a plausible behavioural response but speculative and unquantified.

divination.statement: But what it will do is it will create more cost for employees because if there is a claim, there are then two parties to deal with that claim rather than one party to deal with that claim. When there are two parties involved, we know it is going to take longer, it is going to be expensive, and there is going to be this big legal risk that the employee will have to go through as well.
divination.explanation: Predicts longer, more expensive claims for employees; plausible mechanism but speculative and unquantified.

divination.statement: To avoid that there might be some businesses who would go out and try to hire staff directly instead of going through labour hire companies... it is going to provide a lot of disadvantage to labour hire companies because they won’t be able to survive.
divination.explanation: Predicts labour-hire firms 'won't be able to survive'; a strong claim that overstates a plausible but far smaller behavioural shift, since the bill only bites where a collective agreement exists.

divination.statement: all we see this doing is discouraging businesses from hiring workers through third-party organisations.
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced use of third-party labour hire if the bill passes; plausible behavioural response but speculative and bounded by the bill's collective-agreement trigger.

authenticity.statement: As we often get the chance to say, at the moment, National’s values are of limited government and personal responsibility.
authenticity.explanation: States a consistent, long-held party value that aligns with National's stated positions on regulation; a principled position statement rather than a contradiction.

authenticity.statement: We have previously supported the primary Act that came to pass in 2019. I was actually on the Education and Workforce Committee when that bill came through and it was clear that we did have to tidy up these triangular employment relationships.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds NZ First's position in its own prior voting record and his personal committee involvement, showing consistency between past and present stance.

authenticity.statement: yes, I was part of that select committee that the member the Hon Mark Patterson mentioned... We did hear, during that time, some terrible, terrible stories around what was happening in that triangular relationship.
authenticity.explanation: Corroborates an opponent's account from her own first-hand involvement, showing consistency and candour across the aisle.

authenticity.statement: The difference is we don’t think we know exactly what that amount of money is for every employee in the country. We don’t believe we should be getting in the middle of the employment relationship and telling the employee, “Hey, this is what you should negotiate with your boss.”
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's stated non-interventionist stance on employment relationships expressed elsewhere in the debate.

authenticity.statement: The Labour Party didn’t support it because we don’t support any changes to what is, essentially, for most workers, guaranteed days off. We also don’t support any changes around labour laws in that.
authenticity.explanation: Openly explains why his party opposed a superficially similar earlier bill, distinguishing it on principle rather than dodging the apparent inconsistency.

forthrightness.statement: The Labour Party didn’t support it because we don’t support any changes to what is, essentially, for most workers, guaranteed days off. We also don’t support any changes around labour laws in that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the expected 'why did you vote down Luxton's bill' challenge and gives a clear reason (guaranteed days off, labour law).

rigor.statement: I would suggest members on the other side actually look at the Act itself because this bill, in my view, is inconsistent with the Act—the inherent inequality in power in the employment relationship between employer and employee. It is inherent.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her opposition in a specific principle of the Employment Relations Act (inherent power imbalance), a reasoned premise, though the entailment to the bill being 'inconsistent' is asserted more than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: It's similar to the power balance you have between a parent and a child; between a landlord and a tenant. These power imbalances are inherent.
rigor.explanation: Uses analogy (parent/child, landlord/tenant) to illustrate the power-imbalance claim; an appeal to analogy that is illustrative but not itself evidence.

rigor.statement: until you actually get to the point of signing, the conversations are what's called "without prejudice", and that's what the member wants to take away: the "without prejudice" conversation. So they don't actually mean that you're getting to a final outcome until such point as you've signed on the dotted line. So you never take away that opportunity for the person to take a grievance or, on the other side, for the employer to actually go through with a dismissal.
rigor.explanation: Explains the mechanism of 'without prejudice' conversations and reasons that removing it forecloses both grievance and dismissal options; a coherent evidence-based argument, though it relies on her characterisation of the bill's effect.

rigor.statement: It is illegal, and you want to make it legal. That's the point—That's kind of the point. It is illegal. It happens all the time, and the member wants to stop it from being illegal and make it legal to have a secret little conversation and get someone to sign away their rights to any kind of process. It's kind of crazy.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the bill would 'make legal' coercive secret meetings, arguably a strawman of a mutual-agreement mechanism that other speakers dispute; the conclusion outruns the premise.

rigor.statement: Personal grievances and the processes around them have become a minor industry for the legal profession.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an anecdote from one board chair to support a broad claim about the system.

rigor.statement: It's not surprising to hear employment lawyers speaking passionately against this because by making this process a very quiet, mutually agreeable way that we can get things done... So of course, all of the unionists and the employment lawyers from the Opposition will speak very passionately about the requirement for employment lawyers to be involved in this.
rigor.explanation: Poisoning-the-well / ad hominem: pre-emptively attributes opponents' arguments to self-interest rather than engaging their substance.

rigor.statement: This is one thing that actually is truly holding back growth in our businesses. This is something where there is the inability to expand the talent pool, because they're stuck with people that don't necessarily fit.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping causal claim that grievance processes are 'truly holding back growth' with no evidence beyond assertion and one anecdote.

rigor.statement: the grievance industry that that person was complaining to you about is not about the fact that there are personal grievances. It's about the fact that there is no regulation on who can take a personal grievance. There are lots of people who are unlicensed, untrained, not lawyers, who take personal grievances on behalf of other people... I am fully in support and in agreement that there should be some regulation around the people who take those claims.
rigor.explanation: Reframes the opponent's 'grievance industry' complaint by drawing a precise distinction (the problem is unregulated advocates, not grievances themselves) and follows it to a concrete remedy; logically tight.

rigor.statement: There is a provision that, in that, you need to seek legal advice. The problem with that is the word "seek". It does not mean "obtain legal advice", it just means "seek". We have other laws in New Zealand, like relationship property settlements, which require legal advice before they're entered into, and I think that would be a much more prudent protective measure to have in a bill like this.
rigor.explanation: Close textual reading distinguishing 'seek' from 'obtain', supported by a concrete precedent (relationship property law requiring advice) to argue for a stronger safeguard; evidence-based and the conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: The whole fundamental basis of that process in New Zealand employment law is the fact that that is not predetermined. If it's a performance issue, they have to give the employee an opportunity to improve. If it's a conduct issue, they have to go into the hearing without preconceived ideas.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies the legal principle (no predetermined outcome) and reasons that the bill undermines it; sound premises supporting the conclusion.

rigor.statement: This will be a negative—negative—thing for New Zealand. It will destroy people's confidence, it will destroy families, it will get rid of livelihoods.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion with escalating unsupported consequences rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: What we need in this country is more productivity. We need the ability to earn the taxes to pay for the things that the Government should provide: First World healthcare, First World education, and restoring law and order, including funding the police.
rigor.explanation: Chains productivity → taxes → services, but the link from the specific employment bill to national productivity is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: we come with a view that is open to the consideration of the underlying reality that not all employment relationships are the same. Not all businesses are the same, and nor are they of the same size.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable premise that employment relationships and firms are heterogeneous, motivating openness to review; sound but general.

rigor.statement: Firstly, where are the boundaries for an off-the-record conversation? When does an off-the-record conversation start... The second issue... is what a reasonable time frame is for both parties to go away and consider what the offer is... Thirdly, we will be looking at safety rails. What are the safeguards... that go around this bill, should it become legislation.
rigor.explanation: Identifies genuine gaps in the bill and structures them as testable issues, showing disciplined engagement with the proposal's weaknesses.

rigor.statement: In New Zealand, judges must retire at 70 under the Senior Courts Act 2016 but may serve further on limited-term contracts up to the age of 75... Most relevant to the proposal in this bill is the retirement age of the Ombudsman, which is set at 72. That informed the drafting of the bill.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the chosen threshold by reasoning from analogous public roles rather than asserting it arbitrarily.

rigor.statement: In England and Wales, 76 is the upper limit for jury service, with those over 70 being able to seek excusal. In Scotland, people over the age of 71 may be excused upon request. In Australia, five states and territories allow those aged 70 or over to permit permanent excusal.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative evidence to argue 72 sits in a reasonable middle range rather than being arbitrary.

rigor.statement: Around 47 percent of excusals are currently granted purely based on the age of the applicant. Even a modest reduction in that number would represent a meaningful improvement in court operations.
rigor.explanation: Links the statistic to the administrative burden (more summonses issued), a coherent efficiency argument.

rigor.statement: I'd be interested in the Greens' view on whether voters should retire at 65, because that's a civic duty. I'd be interested in the view as to whether or not the Greens think that criminals retire at 65... whether they should retire at 65 because it's a civic duty.
rigor.explanation: A reductio that conflates voting and jury excusal with 'criminals retiring', a strained analogy that misrepresents the Greens' position rather than engaging it.

rigor.statement: people expect at the age of 65 that they no longer need to show up. That is actually not what the law says. The law says you have the right to request excusal. And that has resulted in far too many people thinking that they no longer have a requirement to deliver their civic duty of turning up.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the legal text from the popular misunderstanding to justify lifting the expectation age; logically coherent.

rigor.statement: if we really want to have a representative jury, we probably should look at the $31 a half-day that they're paid, because if you're going to take a day off work, $31 a half-day doesn't cut it. Or you could look at the fact that childcare is capped at $80 a day. If you want mums and dads to come along and serve on juries... we want to have a look at that as well and ensure that actual costs of childcare are covered.
rigor.explanation: Argues that pay and childcare barriers skew jury composition, a reasoned point about representativeness backed by the cited figures.

rigor.statement: people who serve on juries are skewed towards people with spare time, people to whom it's interesting and they haven't got a job to hold down, or a child needs attention and can't be put in care. So we do actually already have a skew towards older people who've got time on their hands.
rigor.explanation: Reasons that existing barriers already bias juries toward those with time, using it to question whether raising the age improves representativeness; coherent, drawn partly from his court experience.

rigor.statement: But which generation is under-represented in juries? Is it the greyer generation that is under-represented in juries? I don't think so.
rigor.explanation: Challenges the bill's representativeness rationale by noting older people are not the under-represented group; a pointed logical objection, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It doesn't seem to me to have strong evidence as to whether it should be 65, 72, 103; whether there should be automatic right of refusal, if you like, at any particular age. But given our retirement age is 65... then why not pick an age that we already have generally accepted by the general population?
rigor.explanation: Points to the absence of strong evidence for the specific threshold and offers an alternative anchoring principle (existing retirement age); a fair evidentiary critique.

rigor.statement: when people are on a jury, everything is based on facts. The evidence needs to be taken into consideration. There is no place for emotion in there. It all needs to be based on facts. So that experience of dealing with things, we know that sometimes it comes with age.
rigor.explanation: Correctly notes juries decide on evidence, but the inference that age-earned experience makes older jurors more fact-based leans on an appeal to age rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Just reading the existing legislation at the moment, I found it really confusing. At the moment, in section 15(2) of the principal Act, the Juries Act, there is the term "must excuse"... But then the existing legislation goes on to another section, section 15A(2), where it says that a written application will permanently excuse a person. So it seems that if you're already over the age of 65, you're excluded, but you can also write and be excluded, and I don't quite get the concept there.
rigor.explanation: Identifies an apparent tension between two sections and flags it for officials to clarify; disciplined close reading, honestly acknowledging his own uncertainty.

rigor.statement: the average life expectancy of New Zealanders has increased by broadly one year for every decade over the last 40 years; or in other terms, a month for every year that we've lived for the last 40-odd years. So bringing this into that scope recognises that people are living longer in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Uses the demographic data to support the case that a 65 threshold is outdated; evidence connects to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: at the moment, by having an arbitrary 65 age limit at which you could automatically be excluded, it actually does rob older people of the right to participate in our judicial system. I think it's a pretty important principle.
rigor.explanation: Frames the current threshold as an arbitrary limit denying participation; a reasonable principled argument, though 'rob' overstates a right that remains one of excusal-on-request.

rigor.statement: in the 2023 census, there were actually 466,000 New Zealanders aged between 65 and 74, and that's a 35 percent increase on 2013 stats. So there's a whole lot more people who will be able to partake in jury service.
rigor.explanation: Uses demographic evidence to support the bill's expanded juror-pool rationale.

rigor.statement: I'm grateful that, so far, we've had support across the House—except for the Greens that, for some reason, feel that people don't want to contribute to society after the age of 65.
rigor.explanation: Mischaracterises the Greens' stated reasoning (their objection was about evidence and priorities, not a belief that over-65s don't want to contribute); a strawman.

rigor.statement: that's where maturity on a jury actually really does become quite important... The last thing anyone wants on the jury... is someone who really does not want to be on that jury, who had hoped... they thought that they would get challenged and they didn't. They've probably got places they need to be. And they are the people that most people don't want to have on that jury because they are more likely to influence the jury. They're more likely to make decisions that go against justice.
rigor.explanation: Draws on his court experience to argue that willing, mature jurors serve justice better than reluctant ones, supporting the bill's rationale; experiential rather than data-based reasoning.

civility.statement: I would suggest members on the other side actually look at the Act itself because this bill, in my view, is inconsistent with the Act—the inherent inequality in power in the employment relationship between employer and employee. It is inherent.
civility.explanation: The dig 'actually look at the Act itself' is a mild condescension, but she engages the substance of the legislation rather than attacking the member personally.

civility.statement: It is illegal, and you want to make it legal. That's the point—That's kind of the point. It is illegal. It happens all the time, and the member wants to stop it from being illegal and make it legal to have a secret little conversation and get someone to sign away their rights to any kind of process. It's kind of crazy.
civility.explanation: 'It's kind of crazy' and 'secret little conversation' are dismissive characterisations of the member's bill; directed at the proposal rather than the person, but sensationalised.

civility.statement: It takes away good process—in a time of high unemployment where we do sometimes see people being put on the scrap heap, for whatever reason—and it's easy to discard people without thinking about it.
civility.explanation: Emotive 'scrap heap' framing, but aimed at the policy's consequences rather than any individual.

civility.statement: It's not surprising to hear employment lawyers speaking passionately against this because by making this process a very quiet, mutually agreeable way that we can get things done... So of course, all of the unionists and the employment lawyers from the Opposition will speak very passionately about the requirement for employment lawyers to be involved in this.
civility.explanation: Impugns the motives of unionists and lawyers opposite rather than their arguments, though not a direct personal insult.

civility.statement: This will be a negative—negative—thing for New Zealand. It will destroy people's confidence, it will destroy families, it will get rid of livelihoods.
civility.explanation: Emotive, sensationalised catastrophising ('destroy families') aimed at the policy; hyperbole counts against civility.

civility.statement: Unlike my colleagues on the other side of the House, we are willing to take something to select committee that has a foundation for consideration... The difference on this side of the House, though, is that when we listen to reasonable feedback, we don't consider that we already know the answer.
civility.explanation: Contrasts 'our' open-mindedness against the Opposition having 'already made their minds up'; a swipe at opponents' character/approach rather than their arguments, but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: maybe we need some back-to-basics literacy in the House for some of my colleagues about what "mutual agreement" means. I'm sure that we could take some of our colleagues that aren't necessarily electorate MPs into some schools and show them what we're doing to ensure an hour of reading, writing, and arithmetic, as part of ensuring that they understand the concept of mutual agreement.
civility.explanation: Mocks opposing (notably list) MPs as needing primary-school literacy lessons; a condescending personal jab rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Firstly, where are the boundaries for an off-the-record conversation? When does an off-the-record conversation start... The second issue... is what a reasonable time frame is for both parties to go away and consider what the offer is... Thirdly, we will be looking at safety rails. What are the safeguards... that go around this bill, should it become legislation.
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused critique of his own side's bill, putting concerns on record rather than scoring points.

civility.statement: the member spoke for approximately seven minutes and didn't even address the one question that I asked in relation to the bill. So, hopefully, during the select committee process, that member will be more focused on the question at heart, which is what the exact age should be.
civility.explanation: A pointed but legitimate critique that the opposing speaker failed to engage his specific question, focused on the debate's substance rather than the person.

civility.statement: I'd be interested in the Greens' view on whether voters should retire at 65, because that's a civic duty. I'd be interested in the view as to whether or not the Greens think that criminals retire at 65... whether they should retire at 65 because it's a civic duty.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mischaracterisation of opponents' stance played for effect; borders on strawman.

civility.statement: may I just congratulate Carl Bates, who is in charge of this bill, for speaking for 10 minutes on a bill that does nothing more than raise the age of excusal from 65 to 72... But of all the ways in which we could make New Zealand better, this member has chosen to raise the age at which someone can tap out of jury service. That's it. Well, you know, you have another bill in the ballot. I hope you can do something a little more ambitious next time.
civility.explanation: Backhanded, sarcastic congratulation belittling the bill's ambition; aimed at the proposal but with a condescending edge toward the member.

civility.statement: It's not the worst bill in the universe, but is it really the best use of our time for governance? Should we be sending it to select committee without a really clear case for the time and energy to be engaged in this? At this stage, we say we will not be supporting it.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the bill's priority ('best use of our time') but framed around governance value rather than attacking the mover.

civility.statement: I'm grateful that, so far, we've had support across the House—except for the Greens that, for some reason, feel that people don't want to contribute to society after the age of 65.
civility.explanation: Puts words in opponents' mouths ('for some reason, feel that people don't want to contribute') rather than engaging their actual argument.

authenticity.statement: I've negotiated exit packages, so I have sat around the table and negotiated for people to be able to leave their employment with dignity
authenticity.explanation: Cites her own record as a union organiser negotiating exits to back her stated position on worker protections; words align with claimed personal experience.

authenticity.statement: everybody who's an employer in this place knows that the going rate for a personal grievance is about 10 to 15 grand. And most of the time they're sitting there thinking, "How much can I—are we weighing up?" I would rather just pay them the money; I would pay them to get rid of them.
authenticity.explanation: Draws on her own experience as an employer performance-managing staff, consistent with her pro-bill stance.

authenticity.statement: So the National Party believes in freedom of choice and personal responsibility. So this is one of the ways in which we are showing and sticking by our values. This is definitely in line with our party values and I'm very happy to commend this bill to the House.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly ties her support to consistently-stated National Party values (freedom of choice, personal responsibility); a values-consistency claim that is defensible if unverified from the text.

authenticity.statement: The proposal did not originate from an academic paper; it came from the front lines of our justice system. In October 2024, I visited the Auckland High Court with the Minister of Justice, the Hon Paul Goldsmith. During that visit, Ministry of Justice staff raised the issue directly.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds the bill in a specific personal experience he can be held to, consistent with his framing of it as practically motivated.

authenticity.statement: I've served on juries a couple of times—it's quite a tough experience—and I've also been excused once or twice. I felt the role of being a mayor, leading the long-term plan, probably was a reasonable excuse and they agreed.
authenticity.explanation: Discloses her own jury service and past excusals, giving personal grounding consistent with her sceptical-but-fair stance.

authenticity.statement: in my life experience so far, every time I get the call to jury service, I've been Marlborough district councillor or for certain reasons haven't been able to serve. I had the unusual experience on becoming an MP of being asked to be on a jury... trying to explain through writing some letters that I was no longer eligible because... we can't sit as jurors.
authenticity.explanation: Personal, self-deprecating anecdote about repeatedly being unable to serve, consistent and candid though tangential to the policy merits.

authenticity.statement: I'm someone that is probably very unlikely to end up on a jury where I could be called, being an ex-police officer and an ex-MP. It would be the equivalent of me turning up with an RSA badge on my jacket. Any lawyer with challenges would very quickly isolate me out from the herd. So I say that to make sure there is no vested interest, no conflict of interest in speaking about this.
authenticity.explanation: Openly discloses his background and why he'd be challenged off a jury, pre-empting any conflict-of-interest concern; candid and self-aware.

specificity.statement: I've negotiated exit packages, so I have sat around the table and negotiated for people to be able to leave their employment with dignity
specificity.explanation: References concrete activity (negotiating exit packages) but without particular cases, figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: until you actually get to the point of signing, the conversations are what's called "without prejudice", and that's what the member wants to take away: the "without prejudice" conversation. So they don't actually mean that you're getting to a final outcome until such point as you've signed on the dotted line. So you never take away that opportunity for the person to take a grievance or, on the other side, for the employer to actually go through with a dismissal.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete legal mechanism ('without prejudice') and how it operates up to signing.

specificity.statement: everybody who's an employer in this place knows that the going rate for a personal grievance is about 10 to 15 grand. And most of the time they're sitting there thinking, "How much can I—are we weighing up?" I would rather just pay them the money; I would pay them to get rid of them.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a concrete figure range for the cost of a personal grievance.

specificity.statement: the grievance industry that that person was complaining to you about is not about the fact that there are personal grievances. It's about the fact that there is no regulation on who can take a personal grievance. There are lots of people who are unlicensed, untrained, not lawyers, who take personal grievances on behalf of other people... I am fully in support and in agreement that there should be some regulation around the people who take those claims.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific issue (unlicensed, untrained advocates) and a specific direction (regulation of who can bring claims).

specificity.statement: There is a provision that, in that, you need to seek legal advice. The problem with that is the word "seek". It does not mean "obtain legal advice", it just means "seek". We have other laws in New Zealand, like relationship property settlements, which require legal advice before they're entered into, and I think that would be a much more prudent protective measure to have in a bill like this.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints an exact word in the bill and names a specific comparable statute and the precise fix proposed.

specificity.statement: The whole fundamental basis of that process in New Zealand employment law is the fact that that is not predetermined. If it's a performance issue, they have to give the employee an opportunity to improve. If it's a conduct issue, they have to go into the hearing without preconceived ideas.
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes performance vs conduct processes and their distinct legal requirements.

specificity.statement: We live in a country that we're proud of. We don't have no-fault dismissals—unlike other countries, like in America, where for whatever reason you can be sacked. We proudly do not have laws like this in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete contrast (no-fault/at-will dismissal) and a comparator country.

specificity.statement: What we need in this country is more productivity. We need the ability to earn the taxes to pay for the things that the Government should provide: First World healthcare, First World education, and restoring law and order, including funding the police.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete public goods (healthcare, education, police funding) but leaves the mechanism linking this bill to productivity and taxes unstated.

specificity.statement: Firstly, where are the boundaries for an off-the-record conversation? When does an off-the-record conversation start... The second issue... is what a reasonable time frame is for both parties to go away and consider what the offer is... Thirdly, we will be looking at safety rails. What are the safeguards... that go around this bill, should it become legislation.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates three concrete, well-defined questions (start of off-the-record talks, min/max consideration time, safeguards) for select committee scrutiny.

specificity.statement: which proposes a simple but meaningful change to increase the age at which New Zealanders may request automatic excusal from jury duty from 65 to 72.
specificity.explanation: States the exact change with precise before/after figures (65 to 72) and the mechanism (automatic excusal on request).

specificity.statement: In New Zealand, judges must retire at 70 under the Senior Courts Act 2016 but may serve further on limited-term contracts up to the age of 75... Most relevant to the proposal in this bill is the retirement age of the Ombudsman, which is set at 72. That informed the drafting of the bill.
specificity.explanation: Cites named statutes, specific ages, and the precise benchmark that informed the drafting.

specificity.statement: In England and Wales, 76 is the upper limit for jury service, with those over 70 being able to seek excusal. In Scotland, people over the age of 71 may be excused upon request. In Australia, five states and territories allow those aged 70 or over to permit permanent excusal.
specificity.explanation: Precise jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction ages placing NZ's proposal on an international spectrum.

specificity.statement: Around 47 percent of excusals are currently granted purely based on the age of the applicant. Even a modest reduction in that number would represent a meaningful improvement in court operations.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the argument in a concrete figure (47%) and its operational consequence.

specificity.statement: The proposal did not originate from an academic paper; it came from the front lines of our justice system. In October 2024, I visited the Auckland High Court with the Minister of Justice, the Hon Paul Goldsmith. During that visit, Ministry of Justice staff raised the issue directly.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete origin story with date, place and actors (Oct 2024, Auckland High Court, Ministry staff).

specificity.statement: if we really want to have a representative jury, we probably should look at the $31 a half-day that they're paid, because if you're going to take a day off work, $31 a half-day doesn't cut it. Or you could look at the fact that childcare is capped at $80 a day. If you want mums and dads to come along and serve on juries... we want to have a look at that as well and ensure that actual costs of childcare are covered.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact figures ($31 per half-day juror fee, $80/day childcare cap) and concrete alternative reforms.

specificity.statement: I've served on juries a couple of times—it's quite a tough experience—and I've also been excused once or twice. I felt the role of being a mayor, leading the long-term plan, probably was a reasonable excuse and they agreed.
specificity.explanation: Concrete personal detail (mayoral duties as an excusal ground) though not tied to figures.

specificity.statement: It doesn't seem to me to have strong evidence as to whether it should be 65, 72, 103; whether there should be automatic right of refusal, if you like, at any particular age. But given our retirement age is 65... then why not pick an age that we already have generally accepted by the general population?
specificity.explanation: Engages concrete age options and the retirement-age benchmark, though her own preferred figure is left open.

specificity.statement: As we have heard that 40 percent—47 percent, actually, of excusals are granted because of a juror's age; juror being over 65... And that creates a lot of work for the registrar because when they deal with so many excusals, they have to then approach more people.
specificity.explanation: Uses the concrete figure and explains the specific administrative consequence for registrars.

specificity.statement: Just reading the existing legislation at the moment, I found it really confusing. At the moment, in section 15(2) of the principal Act, the Juries Act, there is the term "must excuse"... But then the existing legislation goes on to another section, section 15A(2), where it says that a written application will permanently excuse a person. So it seems that if you're already over the age of 65, you're excluded, but you can also write and be excluded, and I don't quite get the concept there.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provisions (s15(2), s15A(2)) and quotes the operative language to raise a precise drafting question.

specificity.statement: the average life expectancy of New Zealanders has increased by broadly one year for every decade over the last 40 years; or in other terms, a month for every year that we've lived for the last 40-odd years. So bringing this into that scope recognises that people are living longer in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the demographic claim (one year per decade / a month per year) rather than asserting 'people live longer' vaguely.

specificity.statement: in the 2023 census, there were actually 466,000 New Zealanders aged between 65 and 74, and that's a 35 percent increase on 2013 stats. So there's a whole lot more people who will be able to partake in jury service.
specificity.explanation: Cites an exact population figure, age band, source (2023 census) and rate of change.

specificity.statement: We support this bill because we believe in participation, we believe in inclusion, and we also believe in a justice system that evolves alongside of the society it serves.
specificity.explanation: The justification rests on broad value-words with no mechanism or figure of its own.

specificity.statement: the principal Act with which this bill is seeking to amend is the Juries Act 1981... we're lifting the age with respect to jury duty from when they can be automatically exempt from the age of 65 to the age of 72.
specificity.explanation: Names the principal Act and states the exact age change the bill effects.

specificity.statement: that's where maturity on a jury actually really does become quite important... The last thing anyone wants on the jury... is someone who really does not want to be on that jury, who had hoped... they thought that they would get challenged and they didn't. They've probably got places they need to be. And they are the people that most people don't want to have on that jury because they are more likely to influence the jury. They're more likely to make decisions that go against justice.
specificity.explanation: Concrete observations about juror dynamics, though the claim about outcomes ('decisions that go against justice') is impressionistic.

veracity.statement: until you actually get to the point of signing, the conversations are what's called "without prejudice", and that's what the member wants to take away: the "without prejudice" conversation. So they don't actually mean that you're getting to a final outcome until such point as you've signed on the dotted line. So you never take away that opportunity for the person to take a grievance or, on the other side, for the employer to actually go through with a dismissal.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that without-prejudice negotiations are non-binding until signed; her claim about what the bill 'takes away' is contested by later speakers, so the framing is partly her interpretation.

veracity.statement: It takes away good process—in a time of high unemployment where we do sometimes see people being put on the scrap heap, for whatever reason—and it's easy to discard people without thinking about it.
veracity.explanation: 'High unemployment' is directionally defensible for early 2025 (NZ unemployment was elevated near 5%) but 'high' is a loaded characterisation; 'scrap heap' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: Personal grievances and the processes around them have become a minor industry for the legal profession.
veracity.explanation: A characterisation with a grain of truth about the volume of PG work, but 'minor industry' is an unquantified generalisation presented as fact.

veracity.statement: everybody who's an employer in this place knows that the going rate for a personal grievance is about 10 to 15 grand. And most of the time they're sitting there thinking, "How much can I—are we weighing up?" I would rather just pay them the money; I would pay them to get rid of them.
veracity.explanation: The '$10–15k going rate' is a plausible lower-to-mid ballpark for PG settlements but PG awards vary widely and can be much higher; stated as settled fact.

veracity.statement: This is one thing that actually is truly holding back growth in our businesses. This is something where there is the inability to expand the talent pool, because they're stuck with people that don't necessarily fit.
veracity.explanation: An unsubstantiated and overstated causal claim about the economy-wide effect of employment law on growth.

veracity.statement: There is a provision that, in that, you need to seek legal advice. The problem with that is the word "seek". It does not mean "obtain legal advice", it just means "seek". We have other laws in New Zealand, like relationship property settlements, which require legal advice before they're entered into, and I think that would be a much more prudent protective measure to have in a bill like this.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that NZ relationship property settlements require independent legal advice before signing; the 'seek vs obtain' distinction reflects the drafting.

veracity.statement: The whole fundamental basis of that process in New Zealand employment law is the fact that that is not predetermined. If it's a performance issue, they have to give the employee an opportunity to improve. If it's a conduct issue, they have to go into the hearing without preconceived ideas.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes NZ employment law's requirements: genuine opportunity to improve for performance, and an open mind / no predetermination in disciplinary processes.

veracity.statement: We live in a country that we're proud of. We don't have no-fault dismissals—unlike other countries, like in America, where for whatever reason you can be sacked. We proudly do not have laws like this in this country.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: NZ requires a justified reason and fair process for dismissal, whereas US at-will employment generally permits dismissal without cause; slight simplification of US state variation.

veracity.statement: I just say to the National Party, to the New Zealand First Party, please listen to reason at select committee. Do not vote for this bill. Do not change the fundamental basis of our employment law and allow people—your children, people you know—to be invited into a room and for no reason be told—no "performance reason"... there's not a requirement that there is any performance-related reason to be sacked.
veracity.explanation: Claim that the bill requires no performance-related reason reflects that the exit-by-agreement mechanism is no-fault; a fair reading, though the mutual-agreement framing is contested by the bill's supporters.

veracity.statement: In New Zealand, judges must retire at 70 under the Senior Courts Act 2016 but may serve further on limited-term contracts up to the age of 75... Most relevant to the proposal in this bill is the retirement age of the Ombudsman, which is set at 72. That informed the drafting of the bill.
veracity.explanation: Accurate on the substance: judges have a statutory retirement age of 70 with limited post-retirement service, and the Ombudsman's retirement threshold anchors the choice of 72.

veracity.statement: In England and Wales, 76 is the upper limit for jury service, with those over 70 being able to seek excusal. In Scotland, people over the age of 71 may be excused upon request. In Australia, five states and territories allow those aged 70 or over to permit permanent excusal.
veracity.explanation: The international comparators (England & Wales upper limit 76, over-70 excusal; Scottish and Australian thresholds) are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Around 47 percent of excusals are currently granted purely based on the age of the applicant. Even a modest reduction in that number would represent a meaningful improvement in court operations.
veracity.explanation: A specific statistic attributed to court operations; plausible and consistent with the Ministry rationale he cites, but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: people expect at the age of 65 that they no longer need to show up. That is actually not what the law says. The law says you have the right to request excusal. And that has resulted in far too many people thinking that they no longer have a requirement to deliver their civic duty of turning up.
veracity.explanation: Correctly clarifies that the current law grants a right to request excusal on request, not an automatic exemption from turning up; an accurate legal point.

veracity.statement: if we really want to have a representative jury, we probably should look at the $31 a half-day that they're paid, because if you're going to take a day off work, $31 a half-day doesn't cut it. Or you could look at the fact that childcare is capped at $80 a day. If you want mums and dads to come along and serve on juries... we want to have a look at that as well and ensure that actual costs of childcare are covered.
veracity.explanation: The juror remuneration and childcare cap figures are plausible and consistent with NZ juror fee schedules.

veracity.statement: people who serve on juries are skewed towards people with spare time, people to whom it's interesting and they haven't got a job to hold down, or a child needs attention and can't be put in care. So we do actually already have a skew towards older people who've got time on their hands.
veracity.explanation: A plausible generalisation about self-selection in jury pools, though offered without cited data.

veracity.statement: As we have heard that 40 percent—47 percent, actually, of excusals are granted because of a juror's age; juror being over 65... And that creates a lot of work for the registrar because when they deal with so many excusals, they have to then approach more people.
veracity.explanation: Repeats the 47% age-based excusal figure, self-correcting from 40%; consistent with the mover's cited statistic though not independently verified.

veracity.statement: the average life expectancy of New Zealanders has increased by broadly one year for every decade over the last 40 years; or in other terms, a month for every year that we've lived for the last 40-odd years. So bringing this into that scope recognises that people are living longer in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The '~one year per decade' rise in NZ life expectancy over recent decades is broadly accurate as a long-run trend.

veracity.statement: in the 2023 census, there were actually 466,000 New Zealanders aged between 65 and 74, and that's a 35 percent increase on 2013 stats. So there's a whole lot more people who will be able to partake in jury service.
veracity.explanation: A specific census-based figure (466,000 aged 65–74; ~35% rise on 2013) that is plausible and in line with known NZ ageing trends, presented as sourced data.

veracity.statement: the principal Act with which this bill is seeking to amend is the Juries Act 1981... we're lifting the age with respect to jury duty from when they can be automatically exempt from the age of 65 to the age of 72.
veracity.explanation: Accurately identifies the Juries Act 1981 and the 65-to-72 change.

charisma.statement: I think that as New Zealanders we believe that we should have a fair society. So when I take that lens and I look at this bill, I am struck by the inherent unfairness and way that this bill will try and change the way that employment happens in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Opens by invoking a shared value (fairness) she expects both sides to hold, an attempt to find common ground before her critique.

charisma.statement: the grievance industry that that person was complaining to you about is not about the fact that there are personal grievances. It's about the fact that there is no regulation on who can take a personal grievance. There are lots of people who are unlicensed, untrained, not lawyers, who take personal grievances on behalf of other people... I am fully in support and in agreement that there should be some regulation around the people who take those claims.
charisma.explanation: Concedes ground to the opposing concern ('I am fully in support... that there should be some regulation') before redirecting, an attempt to engage rather than dismiss.

charisma.statement: I just say to the National Party, to the New Zealand First Party, please listen to reason at select committee. Do not vote for this bill. Do not change the fundamental basis of our employment law and allow people—your children, people you know—to be invited into a room and for no reason be told—no "performance reason"... there's not a requirement that there is any performance-related reason to be sacked.
charisma.explanation: Directly appeals to government MPs to reconsider ('please listen to reason', 'your children, people you know'), attempting persuasion, but framed as an urgent warning rather than genuine bridge-building.

charisma.statement: Unlike my colleagues on the other side of the House, we are willing to take something to select committee that has a foundation for consideration... The difference on this side of the House, though, is that when we listen to reasonable feedback, we don't consider that we already know the answer.
charisma.explanation: Us-versus-them framing that flatters his own side while casting the other as closed-minded; rallies rather than unifies.

charisma.statement: we come with a view that is open to the consideration of the underlying reality that not all employment relationships are the same. Not all businesses are the same, and nor are they of the same size.
charisma.explanation: A measured, reasonable tone inviting nuance rather than absolutism.

charisma.statement: maybe we need some back-to-basics literacy in the House for some of my colleagues about what "mutual agreement" means. I'm sure that we could take some of our colleagues that aren't necessarily electorate MPs into some schools and show them what we're doing to ensure an hour of reading, writing, and arithmetic, as part of ensuring that they understand the concept of mutual agreement.
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing put-down of opponents that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: may I just congratulate Carl Bates, who is in charge of this bill, for speaking for 10 minutes on a bill that does nothing more than raise the age of excusal from 65 to 72... But of all the ways in which we could make New Zealand better, this member has chosen to raise the age at which someone can tap out of jury service. That's it. Well, you know, you have another bill in the ballot. I hope you can do something a little more ambitious next time.
charisma.explanation: A witty put-down that plays to his own side rather than persuading across the aisle, softened by the concession to support the bill.

charisma.statement: We support this bill because we believe in participation, we believe in inclusion, and we also believe in a justice system that evolves alongside of the society it serves.
charisma.explanation: Frames support around inclusive values (participation, inclusion, an evolving justice system) in a constructive, consensus-oriented register.

divination.statement: This will be a negative—negative—thing for New Zealand. It will destroy people's confidence, it will destroy families, it will get rid of livelihoods.
