divination.explanation: A prediction that the bill will 'destroy families' and livelihoods; sweeping and hyperbolic, with magnitude far outrunning any evidence offered, though direction (some job losses) is plausible.

forthrightness.statement: the member spoke for approximately seven minutes and didn't even address the one question that I asked in relation to the bill. So, hopefully, during the select committee process, that member will be more focused on the question at heart, which is what the exact age should be.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly identifies the unanswered question and keeps the House's attention on it.

forthrightness.statement: It's not the worst bill in the universe, but is it really the best use of our time for governance? Should we be sending it to select committee without a really clear case for the time and energy to be engaged in this? At this stage, we say we will not be supporting it.
forthrightness.explanation: States the Green position plainly (will not support) and the reason (poor use of governance time), directly declaring her stance.

forthrightness.statement: Just reading the existing legislation at the moment, I found it really confusing. At the moment, in section 15(2) of the principal Act, the Juries Act, there is the term "must excuse"... But then the existing legislation goes on to another section, section 15A(2), where it says that a written application will permanently excuse a person. So it seems that if you're already over the age of 65, you're excluded, but you can also write and be excluded, and I don't quite get the concept there.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly admits he doesn't fully understand the interaction rather than papering over it.

specificity.statement: the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill would finally define the principles in line with the Treaty itself, giving all Kiwis equal rights
specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill and its purpose, but the phrase 'in line with the Treaty itself' and 'equal rights' remain high-level until the principles are read out.

specificity.statement: 40 percent of Māori living in the highest areas of deprivation compared to just 10 percent of Europeans
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete comparative percentages between named groups.

specificity.statement: 90 percent of the submissions opposed—and that's from 307,000 submissions; record-breaking submissions to the Justice Committee—this bill. Also, a record-breaking 80 percent of the oral submissions also opposed this bill, and that is also from 529 oral submissions.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for total submissions, opposition proportion, and oral submission counts.

specificity.statement: National has consistently said that we'll not support it into law, fundamentally because we regard the bill—which seeks to impose a particular interpretation of the Treaty of Waitangi by simple majority and referendum—as a crude way to handle a very sensitive topic.
specificity.explanation: States the position and its rationale clearly but describes the objection ('crude way') in general terms.

specificity.statement: it still generated 300,000 submissions. Of those, more than 16,000 New Zealanders wanted to come and talk to the Justice Committee, and more than 500 actually did. In the meantime, some 40,000 people marched to Parliament to oppose it
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for submissions, would-be oral submitters, actual oral submitters, and marchers.

specificity.statement: That's why we've reasserted the principle that healthcare should be delivered on the basis of need alone.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy principle but no figures, mechanism detail, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: One nation, one flag, one people—that is who we are.
specificity.explanation: A slogan asserting national unity with no concrete content, mechanism, or measurable claim.

specificity.statement: Why would we even entertain the 8 percent divisive rhetoric that this bill tries to achieve, and waste $6 million worth of taxpayers' money when that could have been given and spent on proper food for our tamariki?
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete dollar figure and a percentage, tied to a specific alternative use, though the figures are asserted.

specificity.statement: This bill hasn't been stopped; this bill has been absolutely annihilated.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical flourish about the bill's defeat with no concrete detail beyond the outcome.

specificity.statement: Despite what the New Zealand First member has just told us, they are the ones who want to remove 28 general Treaty clauses across legislation.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise number of clauses and a concrete policy action attributed to the Government.

specificity.statement: We collected 13,000 signatures, we collected 640 postcards, we went into schools, we went to touch tournaments, we went to community hui, and we also went into the clubs and collected submissions.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts of signatures and postcards and a list of named organising venues.

authenticity.statement: the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill would finally define the principles in line with the Treaty itself, giving all Kiwis equal rights
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Seymour's/ACT's long-held one-law-for-all position and their authorship of the bill; words match the party's record.

authenticity.statement: I said before the election, and I will say it again today: I reject both of those approaches, because when Māori thrive in New Zealand, all of us benefit
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent position held before the election and repeated now; plausible and self-consistent within the text, though not independently verifiable here.

authenticity.statement: National has consistently said that we'll not support it into law, fundamentally because we regard the bill—which seeks to impose a particular interpretation of the Treaty of Waitangi by simple majority and referendum—as a crude way to handle a very sensitive topic.
authenticity.explanation: Accurately reflects National's consistent public stance of opposing the bill's passage while allowing its introduction; words match the party's stated position throughout.

authenticity.statement: We battled in the select committee at every single meeting and said, “OK, New Zealand First and National Party, let's get rid of the bill, then, if you don't support it so much.”, and those opportunities were turned down.
authenticity.explanation: Points to consistent action in committee matching the party's stated opposition; a self-account of follow-through, plausible but not independently verified here.

charisma.statement: Let me read those proposed principles, because if anyone wants to vote against this bill in this House today, then let them explain specifically why they oppose the words in the bill.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident and frames a challenge, but it is a combative gauntlet to opponents rather than an attempt to build consensus.

charisma.statement: Finally, some critics say that the debate is divisive. Well, I say it has revealed the division. I say it's revealed a sizeable minority of New Zealanders who oppose equal rights, liberal democracy, and treating each person with the same basic dignity.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that casts a large group of citizens as enemies of democracy; alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: This is a grubby little bill, born of a grubby little deal.
charisma.explanation: A memorable attack line that rallies his own side but does nothing to persuade opponents or build common ground.

charisma.statement: Not one National MP should walk out of this debating chamber today with their head held high, because when it comes to this debate, they led nothing, they stopped nothing, and they stood for nothing
charisma.explanation: Combative and shaming toward MPs who joined the opposition to the bill — divisive rather than an attempt to bring them along.

charisma.statement: when Māori thrive in New Zealand, all of us benefit, all of us will thrive, and non-Māori have nothing to fear from Māori getting ahead here in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, reassuring framing that seeks to defuse fear and unite Māori and non-Māori around a shared benefit.

charisma.statement: Around two-thirds of the settlements have been completed, with many under previous National Governments. It has been a bipartisan effort across many decades
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the cross-party, bipartisan nature of settlements — an inclusive framing that credits opponents' contributions.

charisma.statement: we're proud of those efforts, and this Government will never lose sight of the reality that the things that most Māori want are the same as what most other New Zealanders want.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises shared aspirations across Māori and non-Māori, seeking common ground rather than division.

charisma.statement: One nation, one flag, one people—that is who we are.
charisma.explanation: Aims at a unifying sentiment, but the 'one people' framing appeals mainly to its own side and is contested by those emphasising Treaty partnership.

charisma.statement: We are not divided, but united, with 90 percent of our country's submissions saying no.
charisma.explanation: Frames the outcome as national unity and inclusion, appealing beyond her own base, though within a combative overall speech.

charisma.statement: This bill hasn't been stopped; this bill has been absolutely annihilated.
charisma.explanation: A triumphant applause line that energises supporters but is combative rather than consensus-building.

rigor.statement: Let me read those proposed principles, because if anyone wants to vote against this bill in this House today, then let them explain specifically why they oppose the words in the bill.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable rhetorical move to engage the text of the bill, but presumes the principles are self-evidently unobjectionable, dodging why critics oppose their framing rather than the literal words.

rigor.statement: The end of life choice and abortion law reform both had 90 percent of submissions against them at select committee, but proved overwhelmingly popular with the public
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete precedent to support the argument that submission counts are not a referendum; a relevant evidential analogy, though it leans on it to dismiss the volume of opposition.

rigor.statement: There were two objections that cancelled each other out. One said that the bill isn't needed because Māori don't actually have special rights in New Zealand; other objections said that the bill is an abomination because it denies Māori equal rights. Which one is it? It can't be both.
rigor.explanation: Presents an apparent contradiction, but it is a false dichotomy — different submitters holding different views is not a single incoherent position, so the 'cancelling out' logic does not follow.

rigor.statement: He named his party after a race. Of course you have a problem with race in this country under our current policies.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts 'it's not about race' by pointing to the party's name — a gotcha that conflates 'Māori' as a people with the concept of race, sidestepping Waititi's actual point.

rigor.statement: Having a life expectancy seven years lower than for other New Zealanders is not special privilege. Being twice as likely to die from cancer as others is not special privilege.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete disparity statistics to rebut the 'special privilege' framing; evidence-based and the conclusion follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: Māori are three times more likely to be arrested and convicted of a cannabis-related crime than non-Māori are—but let us be clear—for doing the same thing.
rigor.explanation: Uses a disparity statistic to argue inequity rather than privilege; the 'same thing' qualifier addresses the key confound, though the exact multiplier is asserted rather than sourced.

rigor.statement: Coalitions require compromises. National opposed the bill and would have preferred it not to have gone forward, ACT wanted to have the bill passed into law, but none of us got what we wanted. That is life under MMP.
rigor.explanation: A coherent, evidence-grounded explanation of how coalition trade-offs produced the outcome; the conclusion follows from how MMP coalition-formation works.

rigor.statement: It is plain wrong to take the responsibility of determining the role of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the highest court in the land, to the judiciary, which would have been the outcome of this bill.
rigor.explanation: Argues the bill would perversely shift constitutional questions into the courts; a plausible institutional argument, though asserted rather than demonstrated and slightly garbled in expression.

rigor.statement: Even if we agreed, which we don't, and even if it were to pass—and it won't—a subsequent Parliament could change the definitions, and so the cycle would continue.
rigor.explanation: Sound point about parliamentary sovereignty: ordinary legislation is not entrenched, so a later Parliament could amend it — the conclusion follows from how NZ law works.

rigor.statement: Sir Apirana Ngata, Sir Peter Buck, Sir Māui Pōmare, and Sir James Carroll all shared the position that there were no principles to the Treaty, and this remains New Zealand First's position.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to revered authorities to settle a contemporary legal question those figures never actually addressed in these terms.

veracity.statement: The end of life choice and abortion law reform both had 90 percent of submissions against them at select committee, but proved overwhelmingly popular with the public
veracity.explanation: Directionally correct that both attracted heavily opposed submissions yet passed/were popular; the precise '90 percent' figure is an approximation and 'overwhelmingly popular' overstates margins, but the core claim is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: The Treaty doesn't mention anything by race.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that Te Tiriti does not frame rights in terms of 'race'; it speaks of hapū, iwi and 'all the people of New Zealand', though the point is contestable in interpretation.

veracity.statement: Having a life expectancy seven years lower than for other New Zealanders is not special privilege. Being twice as likely to die from cancer as others is not special privilege.
veracity.explanation: The Māori life-expectancy gap (~7 years) is well documented; the 'twice as likely to die from cancer' figure is broadly supported by mortality data, though it varies by cancer type.

veracity.statement: 40 percent of Māori living in the highest areas of deprivation compared to just 10 percent of Europeans
veracity.explanation: Consistent with NZ deprivation-index data showing Māori heavily over-represented in the most deprived deciles versus Europeans; figures are approximate but in the right range.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon called Te Tiriti o Waitangi “a little experiment”. Winston Peters claims that Māori are not indigenous to Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Both are characterisations of opponents' remarks; Peters has disputed Māori indigeneity in some phrasings and Luxon's 'experiment' quote is contested in context, so the paraphrases carry some risk of stripping context.

veracity.statement: 90 percent of the submissions opposed—and that's from 307,000 submissions; record-breaking submissions to the Justice Committee—this bill. Also, a record-breaking 80 percent of the oral submissions also opposed this bill, and that is also from 529 oral submissions.
veracity.explanation: Broadly matches the reported record submission volumes and lopsided opposition, though exact totals were cited slightly differently by other speakers (e.g. 300,000/270,000).

veracity.statement: Māori are three times more likely to be arrested and convicted of a cannabis-related crime than non-Māori are—but let us be clear—for doing the same thing.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with NZ research showing Māori are markedly more likely to be arrested/convicted for cannabis offences at similar use rates; 'three times' is in the range cited by drug-law reform analyses.

veracity.statement: it still generated 300,000 submissions. Of those, more than 16,000 New Zealanders wanted to come and talk to the Justice Committee, and more than 500 actually did. In the meantime, some 40,000 people marched to Parliament to oppose it
veracity.explanation: Submission and oral-submission figures align with other accounts; the '40,000 marched' figure is lower than the hīkoi estimates others cited (~100,000), suggesting a conservative or contested count.

veracity.statement: It's why we've unwound co-governance arrangements in core public services, and a separate Māori health authority.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Government legislated to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora and unwound co-governance in some public services.

veracity.statement: Around two-thirds of the settlements have been completed, with many under previous National Governments. It has been a bipartisan effort across many decades
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record that a large majority of historical Treaty settlements are done and that the process spanned successive Labour and National governments.

veracity.statement: Sir Apirana Ngata, Sir Peter Buck, Sir Māui Pōmare, and Sir James Carroll all shared the position that there were no principles to the Treaty, and this remains New Zealand First's position.
veracity.explanation: These leaders predate the modern 'principles of the Treaty' concept (a post-1975 legal construction), so attributing to them a stance that 'there were no principles' is anachronistic and reads their historical views selectively.

veracity.statement: Why would we even entertain the 8 percent divisive rhetoric that this bill tries to achieve, and waste $6 million worth of taxpayers' money when that could have been given and spent on proper food for our tamariki?
veracity.explanation: The referendum/process cost has been estimated in the millions, so a '$6 million' figure is plausible but not clearly sourced; the '8 percent' derives from the submission split rather than a measure of the bill's content.

veracity.statement: We are not divided, but united, with 90 percent of our country's submissions saying no.
veracity.explanation: The ~90% opposed submissions figure is accurate, but equating submitters (a self-selected group) with 'our country' being united overstates what the submissions demonstrate.

veracity.statement: Despite what the New Zealand First member has just told us, they are the ones who want to remove 28 general Treaty clauses across legislation.
veracity.explanation: The coalition did commit to reviewing and amending numerous Treaty clauses in legislation; the specific '28 general Treaty clauses' aligns with figures cited about the Treaty-clause review, though the exact count is contested.

civility.statement: He named his party after a race. Of course you have a problem with race in this country under our current policies.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at Rawiri Waititi over his party's name rather than engaging the substance of the interjection that the Treaty makes no reference to race.

civility.statement: Finally, some critics say that the debate is divisive. Well, I say it has revealed the division. I say it's revealed a sizeable minority of New Zealanders who oppose equal rights, liberal democracy, and treating each person with the same basic dignity.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents of the bill as people who oppose equal rights and basic dignity — a strawman attributing bad motives rather than engaging their actual arguments.

civility.statement: This is a grubby little bill, born of a grubby little deal.
civility.explanation: Dismissive, sensationalist language aimed at the bill and the coalition deal; harsh and belittling, though directed at the legislation/process rather than a person.

civility.statement: Not one National MP should walk out of this debating chamber today with their head held high, because when it comes to this debate, they led nothing, they stopped nothing, and they stood for nothing
civility.explanation: A sweeping character attack on National MPs collectively rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: This was an incredible opportunity for the Prime Minister, who is not even here receiving the harm—
civility.explanation: A pointed shot at the Prime Minister's absence; a legitimate criticism of engagement but bordering on a personal jab (partly withdrawn).

civility.statement: We'll hear all sorts of hyperbole today—as we already have from the Leader of the Opposition—about how terrible it is for National to allow this bill to even be introduced. That is just froth and spray.
civility.explanation: Dismisses Hipkins' speech as 'froth and spray' — a swipe at the rhetoric, but aimed at the argument's style rather than the person.

civility.statement: Coalitions require compromises. National opposed the bill and would have preferred it not to have gone forward, ACT wanted to have the bill passed into law, but none of us got what we wanted. That is life under MMP.
civility.explanation: Calm, matter-of-fact framing that lowers the temperature rather than attacking opponents.

civility.statement: So to every tangata Tiriti who made their voices heard and said that that little man does not represent your views, kia ora to you.
civility.explanation: 'That little man' is a belittling personal reference to David Seymour rather than a critique of his argument.

strength.statement: That's why we've reasserted the principle that healthcare should be delivered on the basis of need alone.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered action on a policy the Government has in fact advanced (disestablishing the Māori Health Authority), though 'reasserted the principle' is partly rhetorical rather than a fully evidenced outcome.

strength.statement: It's why we've unwound co-governance arrangements in core public services, and a separate Māori health authority.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete delivered actions — the coalition did disestablish the Māori Health Authority and roll back several co-governance arrangements — so this reflects follow-through, not just aspiration.

strength.statement: We collected 13,000 signatures, we collected 640 postcards, we went into schools, we went to touch tournaments, we went to community hui, and we also went into the clubs and collected submissions.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete organising activity actually undertaken to mobilise opposition, reflecting follow-through on a stated goal.

divination.statement: It is plain wrong to take the responsibility of determining the role of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the highest court in the land, to the judiciary, which would have been the outcome of this bill.
divination.explanation: Predicts the legislation would have driven the issue back into the courts; plausible but uncertain, as the bill's referendum mechanism was intended to do the opposite.

divination.statement: Even if we agreed, which we don't, and even if it were to pass—and it won't—a subsequent Parliament could change the definitions, and so the cycle would continue.
divination.explanation: Predicts an ongoing cycle of redefinition; well-grounded in the non-entrenched nature of the bill, though contingent on future political will.

forthrightness.statement: We battled in the select committee at every single meeting and said, “OK, New Zealand First and National Party, let's get rid of the bill, then, if you don't support it so much.”, and those opportunities were turned down.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly recounts the committee tactic and its rejection, giving a concrete account rather than dodging, in a not-strictly-question context.

veracity.statement: This miracle thread contributed $549 million to our economy in the last financial year, and now it's being prioritised by 130 Government agencies and departments, who are working on our buildings, recognising the immense benefits of our exporters.
veracity.explanation: The wool export figure is plausibly accurate, but 'miracle thread' and '130 agencies prioritising' is boosterish and hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: Two new ferries for the next 30 years—both will move 1,500 people and 2.4 kilometres of lanes for cars, trucks, and rail wagons each movement. That's more than the current fleet. … the Ferry Holdings board has invited six commercial shipyards to compete on price and quality.
veracity.explanation: Capacity claims are specific but unverifiable from the text; 'more than the current fleet' is asserted.

veracity.statement: We are now well on track to be getting our extra 500 people. The intake is the largest it's ever been, and so we're flat out doing it—and do you know something? I think we had sometimes 7,000 applicants to be in the police at the very beginning.
veracity.explanation: 'Largest intake ever' and '7,000 applicants' are hedged with 'I think'; the 500 target is 'on track', not delivered.

veracity.statement: The operating balance has been in deficit for many years. We are now on a path back to surplus. Debt has risen very sharply since 2019. We are now on track to see that debt curve bend then start to decline—that is the crucial role fiscal policy is playing.
veracity.explanation: Deficit and rising-debt-since-2019 claims are broadly accurate; 'on a path back to surplus' is a projection.

veracity.statement: With the official cash rate at 3.5 percent, the Reserve Bank has plenty of room to reduce interest rates, if it needs to.
veracity.explanation: The stated OCR level is consistent with the rate at that date.

veracity.statement: I'd like to make a correction to an answer for oral question No. 3 in the House on Wednesday, 2 April 2025. I inadvertently said that the Ministry of Education report I referred to was 2014. I meant to say 2012.
veracity.explanation: Voluntarily fixes a factual error, improving accuracy of the record.

veracity.statement: The fisheries settlement, otherwise colloquially known as the "Sealord settlement", was settled in 1992. The full and final settlement enabled Māori to receive quota and participate under a general set of rules governing the conduct of commercial fishing.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the 1992 Sealord settlement and how Māori received quota under general rules.

veracity.statement: many taonga species such as tipa—scallops—and koura—crayfish—have become functionally extinct in many areas, leading to the closure of their commercial fisheries and rendering the fisheries settlement assets granted to hapū and iwi in 1992 absolutely worthless
veracity.explanation: Scallop collapse and area closures are real in places, but 'functionally extinct' and 'absolutely worthless' overstate the position.

veracity.statement: Over 300,000 tonnes of fish is commercially harvested from Aotearoa's oceans every year, and exported at rock-bottom prices … the bulk harvesting of kahawai, the people's fish, and exporting them for less than $2 a kilo
veracity.explanation: The tonnage is in the right order of magnitude and low kahawai export prices are plausible, but figures are asserted without source.

veracity.statement: satisfaction with repairs and maintenance has increased from 74 percent in March last year to 83 percent at December 2024, and satisfaction, with MyKāingaOra, which is a metric that Kāinga Ora measures, has gone from 71 percent in March 2024 to 79 percent in December 2024.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific agency-measured figures presented as official data.

veracity.statement: the median rent for new tenancies is sitting at $600 per week; when this Government took office, the figure was $600 … from October 2017 to December 2023, median rents for new tenancies across New Zealand rose by $200 per week.
veracity.explanation: MBIE bond data is cited, but the 'two random dates' comparison is framed to flatter.

veracity.statement: households living in emergency housing motels have reduced by 85 percent under this Government, from over 3,000 in December 2023, to 459 at the end of March.
veracity.explanation: Figures are specific and presented as official; the drop is real though policy tightening drives part of it.

veracity.statement: 85 percent of deaths and serious injuries within 400 metres of a school gate happen outside school drop-off and pick-up times
veracity.explanation: A specific statistic presented as fact; plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: that is why we have provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to Disability Support Services in last year's Budget.
veracity.explanation: A specific budget figure presented as fact; broadly consistent with the DSS funding increase.

veracity.statement: Well, it might interest the member that, actually, that was a decision that was also agreed by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: An assertion about prior-Government agreement that is plausible but unverified and used defensively.

veracity.statement: That member constantly asks this question and talks about cuts. There were no cuts. The money was reprioritised—like we've been talking about—to where the money gets the best outcomes for our children.
veracity.explanation: 'No cuts' vs 'reprioritised' is a contested framing; whether front-line providers lost funding is disputed.

specificity.statement: This miracle thread contributed $549 million to our economy in the last financial year, and now it's being prioritised by 130 Government agencies and departments, who are working on our buildings, recognising the immense benefits of our exporters.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete dollar figure ($549m) and a count of agencies (130).

specificity.statement: It's long been our position that the duopolistic … stranglehold on our grocery sector requires a third entrant. That is why we are replacing the Resource Management Act, the Overseas Investment Act, clamping down on anti-competitive behaviour, and fixing food labelling and import standards to lift competitive products.
specificity.explanation: Names specific mechanisms (RMA/OIA repeal, labelling) but no secured third entrant or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Two new ferries for the next 30 years—both will move 1,500 people and 2.4 kilometres of lanes for cars, trucks, and rail wagons each movement. That's more than the current fleet. … the Ferry Holdings board has invited six commercial shipyards to compete on price and quality.
specificity.explanation: Concrete capacity figures (1,500 people, 2.4km of lanes) and a procurement detail (six shipyards).

specificity.statement: There have been challenges over the last 18 months, and successes too, like Minister Jones' Regional Infrastructure Fund supporting investments in Rātana, Waitangi, and Parihaka; like Treaty settlements led by Minister Goldsmith; the Ō-Rākau bill that transferred the ownership of Ō-Rākau back to Ngā Ahi e Toru … and various fast-track projects—24 of which are either led by, or co-invested with, Māori organisations.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete initiatives, places, and a figure (24 fast-track projects).

specificity.statement: The operating balance has been in deficit for many years. We are now on a path back to surplus. Debt has risen very sharply since 2019. We are now on track to see that debt curve bend then start to decline—that is the crucial role fiscal policy is playing.
specificity.explanation: Directional fiscal claims with a reference year (2019) but no dollar figures or dates.

specificity.statement: at the start of term 2, every kaiako teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa will have received their detailed pāngarau lesson plans, student workbooks, activities, and classroom-ready resources for their tamariki—the first roll-out of high-quality, curriculum-aligned math resources in te reo Māori, delivered by this Government.
specificity.explanation: Names timeframe (start of term 2), audience, and concrete deliverables (lesson plans, workbooks).

specificity.statement: in Northland, for example, we have many kura kaupapa and only two RTs of Māori. The way that we deliver the service is not equitable; it is not optimised. We are going to make sure we take that funding and put it back into Māori education so it is more equitable and it is more optimised
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete example (Northland, two RTs) but the reallocation plan lacks figures or dates.

specificity.statement: the RSE guidelines are not a curriculum. They are causing confusion. They are meaning that some students are learning some things and some are not. What we do need is a year-by-year, knowledge-rich curriculum document that is required to be taught by schools
specificity.explanation: Describes the intended replacement (year-by-year, knowledge-rich) but without content detail or dates.

specificity.statement: the proposed changes that are currently going through the process of consultation will not diminish the mātaitai food-gathering rights of tangata whenua, a feature of the 1992 settlement. Similarly, nothing that is proposed is going to undermine the interests of garden-variety Kiwis, because sustainability will be uppermost in the officials' minds
specificity.explanation: References the 1992 settlement and mātaitai rights, but assurances remain general to consultation.

specificity.statement: The fisheries settlement, otherwise colloquially known as the "Sealord settlement", was settled in 1992. The full and final settlement enabled Māori to receive quota and participate under a general set of rules governing the conduct of commercial fishing.
specificity.explanation: Names the settlement, year, and mechanism (quota under general rules).

specificity.statement: many taonga species such as tipa—scallops—and koura—crayfish—have become functionally extinct in many areas, leading to the closure of their commercial fisheries and rendering the fisheries settlement assets granted to hapū and iwi in 1992 absolutely worthless
specificity.explanation: Names species and links them to the 1992 settlement assets.

specificity.statement: Over 300,000 tonnes of fish is commercially harvested from Aotearoa's oceans every year, and exported at rock-bottom prices … the bulk harvesting of kahawai, the people's fish, and exporting them for less than $2 a kilo
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete tonnage and a per-kilo price figure.

specificity.statement: While the chance of survival is greatest at lower speeds, I'm advised that crash outcomes are influenced by a range of factors. It's not quite as simple as the member is indicating. … the Government has taken steps to improve safety outside schools by requiring variable speed limits to be implemented outside schools by 1 July 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete requirement and date (variable limits by 1 July 2026).

specificity.statement: satisfaction with repairs and maintenance has increased from 74 percent in March last year to 83 percent at December 2024, and satisfaction, with MyKāingaOra, which is a metric that Kāinga Ora measures, has gone from 71 percent in March 2024 to 79 percent in December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after percentages with dates for two named metrics.

specificity.statement: the median rent for new tenancies is sitting at $600 per week; when this Government took office, the figure was $600 … from October 2017 to December 2023, median rents for new tenancies across New Zealand rose by $200 per week.
specificity.explanation: Concrete rent figures, dates, and a regional comparison.

specificity.statement: households living in emergency housing motels have reduced by 85 percent under this Government, from over 3,000 in December 2023, to 459 at the end of March.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage and before/after counts with dates.

specificity.explanation: Precise figure and geographic bound (400 metres, outside peak times).

specificity.statement: that is why we have provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to Disability Support Services in last year's Budget.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure ($1.1b) and the source (last year's Budget).

specificity.explanation: Names concrete milestones and near-term timing (business case approved, go to market next week).

specificity.statement: As we work to double our exports over the next 10 years in places like mining and coal, and see our tourism bounce back, projects like the second Ashburton Bridge are vital to ensuring that New Zealand continues to punch above its weight.
specificity.explanation: Gives a target and timeframe but no mechanism for how doubling is achieved.

specificity.statement: I announced that I have asked Oranga Tamariki to undertake a full scoping review of all existing appropriation measures to ensure that they are focused on the things that matter most to our most vulnerable children and young people.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (scoping review of appropriation measures) but no timeframe or detail on scope.

specificity.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently has a performance measure that the percentage of all service contract funding contracted with iwi and Māori organisations will be greater than 23 percent. These organisations should not just be seen as some sort of quota or tick-box exercise.

forthrightness.statement: It's long been our position that the duopolistic … stranglehold on our grocery sector requires a third entrant. forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether he stands by the comment (yes) and gives the reasoning behind it.

forthrightness.statement: Two new ferries for the next 30 years—both will move 1,500 people and 2.4 kilometres of lanes for cars, trucks, and rail wagons each movement. That's more than the current fleet. … the Ferry Holdings board has invited six commercial shipyards to compete on price and quality.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the rail-ferries question with substantive detail rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: We are now well on track to be getting our extra 500 people. The intake is the largest it's ever been, and so we're flat out doing it—and do you know something? I think we had sometimes 7,000 applicants to be in the police at the very beginning.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was whether the Government will not defund police; he pivots to recruitment numbers rather than addressing funding directly.

forthrightness.statement: Crown-Māori relations are not static—they are tested, they have their ups and downs, and they evolve. … We cannot break Crown-Māori relations. The Crown and iwi and Māori are inextricably tied through the Treaty and obligations and responsibilities that go with kāwanatanga, rangatiratanga, and, most importantly, kotahitanga.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether relations have improved, he reframes to 'not static' rather than giving a clear yes/no.

forthrightness.statement: I am very proud of maintaining a very respectful and dignified posture in this House and out in the electorate that I serve.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he is most proud of among three specific choices, he answers about his 'posture' rather than the substance asked.

forthrightness.statement: There are a number of steps that this Government is absolutely focused on—for example, getting the economy back on track, and that includes Māori and all New Zealanders delivering better public services, including folks who live in Hamilton that are Māori, Pasifika, Asian, or New Zealanders trying to get to the hospital
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how undermining te reo and the Māori Health Authority achieves unity, he pivots entirely to economy and public services.

forthrightness.statement: at the start of term 2, every kaiako teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa will have received their detailed pāngarau lesson plans, student workbooks, activities, and classroom-ready resources for their tamariki—the first roll-out of high-quality, curriculum-aligned math resources in te reo Māori, delivered by this Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'if so, how' part with a concrete example rather than generalities.

forthrightness.statement: when the Ministry of Education are looking to contract writers for the curriculum, they look for experts in curriculum design and in English. forthrightness.statement: in Northland, for example, we have many kura kaupapa and only two RTs of Māori. The way that we deliver the service is not equitable; it is not optimised. We are going to make sure we take that funding and put it back into Māori education so it is more equitable and it is more optimised

forthrightness.statement: I always agree with the Deputy Prime Minister.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees the guidelines are 'woke'/'indoctrinate', she gives a blanket agreement rather than addressing the specific characterisation against her evidence.

forthrightness.statement: the RSE guidelines are not a curriculum. They are causing confusion. They are meaning that some students are learning some things and some are not. What we do need is a year-by-year, knowledge-rich curriculum document that is required to be taught by schools
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether ERO actually recommended removal, she reframes to the guidelines-vs-curriculum distinction rather than directly conceding ERO did not recommend removal.

forthrightness.statement: the proposed changes that are currently going through the process of consultation will not diminish the mātaitai food-gathering rights of tangata whenua, a feature of the 1992 settlement. forthrightness.statement: I cannot respond to a question that's riddled with factual inaccuracies.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to answer the extinction/worthless-assets question outright.

forthrightness.statement: I'm sure that I speak on behalf of a host of the members of the House who love fishing and realise that we need to enhance the value of this valuable stock. But we are not running a Soviet empire here, where politicians dictate what the market should pay.

forthrightness.statement: While the chance of survival is greatest at lower speeds, I'm advised that crash outcomes are influenced by a range of factors. It's not quite as simple as the member is indicating. … the Government has taken steps to improve safety outside schools by requiring variable speed limits to be implemented outside schools by 1 July 2026.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the premise and answers the policy part, though hedges on the direct speed-survival point.

forthrightness.statement: No Minister can guarantee anything, particularly with regard to operational matters for the Chief Executive of Kāinga Ora, but I have stressed to Kāinga Ora that I expect front-line service delivery to not be affected by the change proposal they are undertaking.
forthrightness.explanation: Honestly declines to give the guarantee asked for and explains why, while stating his expectation.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it might interest the member that, actually, that was a decision that was also agreed by the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about the visa exclusion by pointing at the previous Government rather than defending or explaining the current position.

forthrightness.statement: that member would well know that the House is not a place to discuss individual immigration cases, but, as I said, for any family with a child with a disability, it's incredibly challenging, and I accept that.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage the specific case by invoking a procedural convention, offering sympathy rather than an answer.

forthrightness.statement: I announced that I have asked Oranga Tamariki to undertake a full scoping review of all existing appropriation measures to ensure that they are focused on the things that matter most to our most vulnerable children and young people.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly describes the announcement she was asked about.

forthrightness.statement: That member constantly asks this question and talks about cuts. There were no cuts. The money was reprioritised—like we've been talking about—to where the money gets the best outcomes for our children.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers by denying the premise rather than detailing what happened to the specific front-line funding raised.

strength.statement: It's long been our position that the duopolistic … stranglehold on our grocery sector requires a third entrant. That is why we are replacing the Resource Management Act, the Overseas Investment Act, clamping down on anti-competitive behaviour, and fixing food labelling and import standards to lift competitive products.

strength.statement: We are now well on track to be getting our extra 500 people. The intake is the largest it's ever been, and so we're flat out doing it—and do you know something? I think we had sometimes 7,000 applicants to be in the police at the very beginning.

strength.statement: There have been challenges over the last 18 months, and successes too, like Minister Jones' Regional Infrastructure Fund supporting investments in Rātana, Waitangi, and Parihaka; like Treaty settlements led by Minister Goldsmith; the Ō-Rākau bill that transferred the ownership of Ō-Rākau back to Ngā Ahi e Toru … and various fast-track projects—24 of which are either led by, or co-invested with, Māori organisations.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered items (Ō-Rākau bill, settlements) though many are attributed to other ministers.

strength.statement: at the start of term 2, every kaiako teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa will have received their detailed pāngarau lesson plans, student workbooks, activities, and classroom-ready resources for their tamariki—the first roll-out of high-quality, curriculum-aligned math resources in te reo Māori, delivered by this Government.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivery ('will have received', 'first roll-out'), though timing is imminent-future.

strength.statement: satisfaction with repairs and maintenance has increased from 74 percent in March last year to 83 percent at December 2024, and satisfaction, with MyKāingaOra, which is a metric that Kāinga Ora measures, has gone from 71 percent in March 2024 to 79 percent in December 2024.

strength.statement: households living in emergency housing motels have reduced by 85 percent under this Government, from over 3,000 in December 2023, to 459 at the end of March.

strength.statement: we have established lending facilities of up to $150 million for the Community Housing Funding Agency to unlock lower-cost finance for CHPs by pooling their financing requirements.

strength.statement: that is why we have provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to Disability Support Services in last year's Budget.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered budget allocation backing the stated priority.

strength.statement: the second Ashburton Bridge is ready to move ahead at pace. The business case has been approved, geotechnical investigations will begin soon, and next week, we go to market for technical and design support.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered milestone (business case approval) with imminent next steps, though the bridge itself is not built.

rigor.statement: With the official cash rate at 3.5 percent, the Reserve Bank has plenty of room to reduce interest rates, if it needs to.

rigor.explanation: Argues from a distribution-mismatch example, though the causal claim about better outcomes is asserted.

rigor.statement: the RSE guidelines are not a curriculum. They are causing confusion. They are meaning that some students are learning some things and some are not. What we do need is a year-by-year, knowledge-rich curriculum document that is required to be taught by schools

rigor.statement: I'm sure that I speak on behalf of a host of the members of the House who love fishing and realise that we need to enhance the value of this valuable stock. But we are not running a Soviet empire here, where politicians dictate what the market should pay.

rigor.statement: While the chance of survival is greatest at lower speeds, I'm advised that crash outcomes are influenced by a range of factors. rigor.explanation: Acknowledges the survival-vs-speed evidence while qualifying it with multi-factor causation; reasonable if slightly deflective.
