civility.statement: whilst that process was still ongoing, the chairman of the Justice Committee moved the motion to report the bill back to the House 40 days before it was due—whilst we were still working through the submissions... That is shabby—that is shabby process.
civility.explanation: 'Shabby process' criticises the procedure and the chair's decision rather than the person; pointed but substance-focused.

civility.statement: This is a bill that the Prime Minister had the gall to stand up and say that it's not going to pass, and to then bring it to this House is disrespectful to this Chamber, because this Chamber's time is valuable and there should be put before this House laws which are seriously being considered.
civility.explanation: 'Had the gall' is a jab, but the core criticism — legislating a bill known to fail wastes the House's time — engages a real procedural point.

civility.statement: you can't legislate to make the world flat... you cannot legislate the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi out of existence—they might be constitutional truisms... but they're not the Treaty principles. You can't make up the underlying fabric of the Treaty.
civility.explanation: Sharp ('a lie') but directed at the bill's premise, not personal character.

civility.statement: his stooges would front up to the select committee and say, "This is about living in a liberal democracy.", and their concept of a liberal democracy was shallow and impoverished because all it meant was one person, one vote.
civility.explanation: 'Stooges' is a personal disparagement of submitters/opponents, though the following critique engages their argument.

civility.statement: to put a bill into the House that we know is never going to be passed so that we can see some of the hateful rhetoric coming out, is simply divisive, wasteful, and wrong.
civility.explanation: Attributes bad motive ('so that we can see hateful rhetoric') to the Government, though the wastefulness point is substantive.

civility.statement: It's hard to take the Government seriously when they claim that they are focused on healthcare of New Zealanders, when in the context of delivering this bill, the entire health system in this country remains underfunded.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's priorities and consistency rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: we have a situation like we have in Wairarapa where they have literally stolen money that was going to be used for our hospital because they can't make their bills add up.
civility.explanation: 'Literally stolen' is an inflammatory accusation of theft against the Government for a budget reallocation.

charisma.statement: I'd like to acknowledge the work of the clerks and the Select Committee Services team on this bill... at all points they were up front, they were clear in their work, and they provided consistent advice, sometimes in the face of quite significant severe personal reflections from members of the committee.
charisma.explanation: Gracious and consensus-toned toward officials, though it implicitly frames the other side as the problem.

charisma.statement: The purpose of the select committee process is not a poll. It is not a petition. It is not a referendum. It is not a platform for advocacy. It is a process to allow legislators in this House the opportunity to scrutinise legislation, to offer improvements, and to make amendments.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective lecture that appeals to procedural principle but also chides 'members across the hall'.

charisma.statement: There is only one side which has been consistent in our desire to ensure that people have had their say and their voices are heard throughout the entire process—and Tamatha Paul is correct that they did try at every opportunity to stop people from having their say.
charisma.explanation: Sharp us-vs-them framing ('only one side') that alienates rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: For those individuals who were treated disrespectfully by members of Parliament when they gave their submission, I want to apologise to them.
charisma.explanation: Gracious gesture toward the public that reaches beyond his own side.

charisma.statement: This race-baiting political stunt has been a right-wing obscenity masquerading as equality. You should be ashamed on that side of the House—they should all be ashamed for allowing this hate into Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side by demonising opponents; alienating, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I want to thank the former chair the Hon James Meager, who sits beside me, and my colleagues across the committee for the work and for the passion that they put into this kaupapa. It was often very testing and quite emotionally taxing, but I felt privileged throughout the process to see, firsthand, New Zealand's dialogue and history unfolding.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, gracious tone that frames the difficult process positively.

charisma.statement: the National Party strongly asserts that a referendum on the Treaty would be a simplistic approach to a very extremely complex and challenging issue, and so today, we are voting to ensure it will go no further. I say this respectfully to our coalition partners, but this is our strong view.
charisma.explanation: Disagrees with coalition partners while explicitly signalling respect — bridge-building tone.

charisma.statement: friends whom I have sat down with in my home as we've shared Lebanese kai that I've cooked and we have discussed these challenging and complex issues... We've disagreed and we've agreed and we've disagreed again, but all from a place of honesty because we are in this together.
charisma.explanation: Personal, inclusive appeal to shared humanity across both sides of the debate — genuine consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: Let's underpin our conversations, not with our desire for political points, but rather with honest intentions for our collective future.
charisma.explanation: Explicit call to rise above partisanship toward a shared future.

charisma.statement: Hearing speeches of vindication from that side of the House is very hard to swallow, because it has been this National-led Government that has allowed this ugly monster to rear its head in the light of day.
charisma.explanation: Rallies opposition sentiment rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: it's just not realistic to suggest that nearly 200 years of debate, discussion, protest... should be settled just with the stroke of one legislative pen. It's too blunt, it's too simplistic, and it risks, in reality, actually stoking grievance and driving division.
charisma.explanation: Measured, non-inflammatory tone acknowledging the debate's continuity, though addressed to his own governing side.

charisma.statement: Make the time to talk about how we honour the Treaty in a more fulsome way and about how we live together and address some of the gross inequalities which continue in our society.
charisma.explanation: Invites a genuine constitutional conversation and common ground, a more consensus-oriented note than the surrounding attacks.

charisma.statement: We want a thriving, united New Zealand where every Kiwi enjoys equal opportunity and equal citizenship and takes pride in our shared future. Kiwis do best when we are working together in a spirit of unity and mutual respect.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unity-themed framing aimed at a shared national future.

veracity.statement: Most of the decisions in the committee, if not all of them, bar a few, were made unanimously on things like the length of submissions, the number of hours of submissions we would hear, how to treat form and template submissions, and how we would set criteria for what submissions would be heard.
veracity.explanation: Specific procedural claim pointing to Appendix B for verification; plausible and checkable, phrased with hedges ('if not all').

veracity.statement: I want to reassure the public that every submission that has been made to the committee has been read by someone. It has been read by an official in the ministry and the themes from those submissions have been integrated into the departmental report... reading over 300,000 submissions and synthesising them into that document.
veracity.explanation: The 300,000 figure is accurate, but 'read by someone/every submission' is contested by Webb, who says 105,000 were not on the record and only accessible by name — partly true, missing context.

veracity.statement: There has been some misinformation out there that members have not had access to those submissions. Again, if you go through the record, you can see that we agreed to the process of accessing submissions from the clerks' team. All members agreed to that, and it is very disappointing to see suggestions that suggest otherwise out there.
veracity.explanation: Technically points to an agreed process, but Webb's account (24 boxes, submitter-name-only retrieval) suggests access was practically constrained — the 'full access' framing omits material context.

veracity.statement: We were the ones that called for oral submissions to be held; the Opposition called for only written submissions and to prevent every single oral submission from being held.
veracity.explanation: A procedural claim about how the Opposition voted; plausibly grounded in the committee record but presented one-sidedly and disputed in tone by Webb.

veracity.statement: at no time has there been any suggestion of foreign interference or scurrilous behaviour in that process. It is simply a matter of... the website not being able to handle the volume that came through on the very last day.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the website crash to last-day submission volume and explicitly rules out interference; a plausible, non-sensational account.

veracity.statement: Once and for all, for the benefit of David Seymour and his supporters, Treaty rights are not special privileges, or even extra rights... They are rights that were in place before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed. The Treaty simply reaffirms those rights.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with Treaty jurisprudence that Māori rights predate 1840; a defensible characterisation.

veracity.statement: Of the over 300,000 submissions, 90 percent spoke against this lie. Over 100,000 people around the country—100,000 were marching to call the stunt out for what it was.
veracity.explanation: The ~300,000 total and ~90% opposition align with the departmental report; '100,000 marching around the country' overstates crowd estimates for the hīkoi (commonly put near 40,000+ at Parliament) — partly accurate, likely inflated.

veracity.statement: Let's ask the Aboriginal people of Australia what they think of referendums when they were, sadly, defeated in their vote to recognise their indigenous rights last year.
veracity.explanation: The 2023 Australian Voice referendum was indeed defeated — an accurate factual reference.

veracity.statement: his acknowledgment that Māori did not concede tino rangatiratanga, or sovereignty, is the first time that any leader of a mainstream party has admitted that in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: A 'first ever' claim about mainstream party leaders that is difficult to verify and arguably overstated given prior statements by other leaders; plausible but uncertain.

veracity.statement: But, wait a minute, he didn't even have to stand up... this wasn't even a bottom line in negotiations. So much for the great negotiator Christopher Luxon!
veracity.explanation: Reflects the publicly reported position that the bill was an ACT concession rather than a National bottom line; broadly consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: Three-hundred thousand of you presented your opposition to this bill, and behind you was a nation united.
veracity.explanation: ~300,000 submissions is accurate, but characterising all of them as 'opposition' and 'a nation united' overstates (roughly 90% opposed, not all).

veracity.statement: the reversal of a number of divisive co-governance policies from the previous Government... for instance, three waters and the Māori Health Authority... we are restoring the rights of communities to determine whether to introduce Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: These reversals did occur; the 'divisive' and 'worse outcomes' characterisations are contestable framing on an accurate factual base.

veracity.statement: successive National Governments have always worked well with Māori on Treaty issues, and we've always ensured that there are equal citizenship rights and equal opportunity for all New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping 'always' claim that is partly supported (settlement record) but glosses contested episodes.

veracity.statement: there are 105,000 submissions that aren't on the parliamentary record today... There was a room down in the corner with 24 boxes of handwritten and typed submissions—hard-copy submissions—that you had to go in and rifle through... you had to name the submitter, and I'm sorry, but I don't know 307,000 people.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claims (105,000 not on record, 24 boxes, name-to-retrieve) that directly rebut Meager's access assurances; detailed and plausible though contested.

veracity.statement: whilst that process was still ongoing, the chairman of the Justice Committee moved the motion to report the bill back to the House 40 days before it was due—whilst we were still working through the submissions... That is shabby—that is shabby process.
veracity.explanation: A specific timing claim ('40 days before it was due') presented as fact; checkable against the committee record, offered against Meager's 'no further work to do' account.

veracity.statement: The Māori economy has seen remarkable growth, with its asset base rising from $69 billion in 2018 to $119 billion in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with published Te Ōhanga Māori estimates showing the Māori asset base roughly doubling over that period; figures are accurate to a reasonable margin.

veracity.statement: Through partnership with Māori health organisations, over 69,000 vaccinations have been delivered to New Zealanders. We've seen more than 20 Māori-led or Māori-partnered projects placed on the fast-track list. We've also committed over $200 million to Māori housing providers and have helped nearly 2,000 children, many of them Māori, move out of emergency housing.
veracity.explanation: Plausible government delivery figures presented in the party's favour; broadly consistent with announced programmes but not independently checkable from the text.

veracity.statement: National also has a proud record when it comes to Treaty settlements, having made more progress than any other Governments in resolving historical grievances.
veracity.explanation: National did advance many settlements (2008–2017), but the 'more than any other' claim is contestable and lacks the metric to confirm it.

veracity.statement: we saw it from this Government during the campaign. They promised all these medicines. First Budget came and they realised, "Oops, it's actually quite an important thing to deliver on those promises." U-turn—U-turn.
veracity.explanation: Refers to the well-documented controversy over the coalition's cancer/medicines funding pledge and its rocky first Budget; directionally accurate though rhetorically compressed.

veracity.statement: It's hard to take the Government seriously when they claim that they are focused on healthcare of New Zealanders, when in the context of delivering this bill, the entire health system in this country remains underfunded.
veracity.explanation: 'Entire health system remains underfunded' is a contestable evaluative claim rather than a precise figure; a common characterisation but not demonstrable as stated.

veracity.statement: we have a situation like we have in Wairarapa where they have literally stolen money that was going to be used for our hospital because they can't make their bills add up.
veracity.explanation: 'Literally stolen' is hyperbole for a funding reallocation dispute; misleading as a literal factual claim.

veracity.statement: Let's not forget they got rid of free prescriptions, and here they stand up and they talk about improving access to medicines.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the coalition reinstated the $5 prescription co-payment for most people, ending Labour's universal free prescriptions — a real, checkable action.

specificity.statement: Most of the decisions in the committee, if not all of them, bar a few, were made unanimously on things like the length of submissions, the number of hours of submissions we would hear, how to treat form and template submissions, and how we would set criteria for what submissions would be heard.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete categories of decisions and cites the appendix as the record.

specificity.statement: I want to reassure the public that every submission that has been made to the committee has been read by someone. It has been read by an official in the ministry and the themes from those submissions have been integrated into the departmental report... reading over 300,000 submissions and synthesising them into that document.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (ministry officials, departmental report) and figure supplied.

specificity.statement: on bills of significance, we should consider setting those deadlines to be in the middle of the day so that people have a chance to deal with any of those issues.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete process change (midday deadlines for significant bills).

specificity.statement: Of the over 300,000 submissions, 90 percent spoke against this lie. Over 100,000 people around the country—100,000 were marching to call the stunt out for what it was.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures for submissions and marchers.

specificity.statement: I said in the first reading of this koretake bill that we do not need to change the Treaty; we need to change this Government.
specificity.explanation: A memorable line but light on concrete mechanism beyond changing the Government.

specificity.statement: there are 105,000 submissions that aren't on the parliamentary record today... There was a room down in the corner with 24 boxes of handwritten and typed submissions—hard-copy submissions—that you had to go in and rifle through... you had to name the submitter, and I'm sorry, but I don't know 307,000 people.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers and a physical description of the access process.

specificity.statement: We want a thriving, united New Zealand where every Kiwi enjoys equal opportunity and equal citizenship and takes pride in our shared future. Kiwis do best when we are working together in a spirit of unity and mutual respect.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism, figures, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: The Māori economy has seen remarkable growth, with its asset base rising from $69 billion in 2018 to $119 billion in 2023.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures and years.

specificity.statement: Through partnership with Māori health organisations, over 69,000 vaccinations have been delivered to New Zealanders. We've seen more than 20 Māori-led or Māori-partnered projects placed on the fast-track list. We've also committed over $200 million to Māori housing providers and have helped nearly 2,000 children, many of them Māori, move out of emergency housing.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures across vaccinations, fast-track projects, housing funding, and emergency-housing exits.

specificity.statement: So, with caution, we support this bill and we will make sure we interrogate this throughout the entirety of the process... hold the caveat that if we don't agree, we will continue to challenge and even potentially withdraw. But for now, we support it.
specificity.explanation: Explains the conditional nature of support but not the specific criteria that would trigger withdrawal.

specificity.statement: This bill will increase access to medicines for New Zealanders by introducing a streamlined verification pathway for medicines. Faster access to medicines leads to better patient outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism ('streamlined verification pathway') but no figures, timeframe, or which medicines.

specificity.statement: I rise to support the Medicines Amendment Bill. This is about faster and more efficient access to medicines, and it will support better outcomes for families across Aotearoa New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Generic endorsement with no mechanism, figures, or timeframe.

rigor.statement: The purpose of the select committee process is not a poll. It is not a petition. It is not a referendum. It is not a platform for advocacy. It is a process to allow legislators in this House the opportunity to scrutinise legislation, to offer improvements, and to make amendments.
rigor.explanation: Clear, structured constitutional argument with a coherent claim about the committee's function; asserts rather than evidences the normative claim.

rigor.statement: Do not rely on third-party organisations or third-party activists or political parties who go out there and want to collect your data and harvest your data and who purport to provide your submission on your behalf.
rigor.explanation: Asserts data-harvesting motive without evidence; leans on suspicion rather than argument.

rigor.statement: on bills of significance, we should consider setting those deadlines to be in the middle of the day so that people have a chance to deal with any of those issues.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete cause (11.59pm deadline, no staff to help) and proposes a proportionate fix — clean means-ends reasoning.

rigor.statement: Once and for all, for the benefit of David Seymour and his supporters, Treaty rights are not special privileges, or even extra rights... They are rights that were in place before the Treaty of Waitangi was signed. The Treaty simply reaffirms those rights.
rigor.explanation: Coherent legal-historical argument that indigenous rights predate and are reaffirmed (not created) by the Treaty; asserts rather than cites, but logically structured.

rigor.statement: We get it now: property rights only count if you're Pākehā. But if you're Māori—if you're Māori—forget about them.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical strawman of the ACT position; imputes a racial double standard rather than engaging their stated argument.

rigor.statement: Very similar, I might add, are people who believe that the world is still flat and not round, and that sums up him and his nutjob supporters.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem / false analogy with no argumentative content.

rigor.statement: Let's ask the Aboriginal people of Australia what they think of referendums when they were, sadly, defeated in their vote to recognise their indigenous rights last year.
rigor.explanation: Uses real precedents (Australian Voice referendum, NZ homosexual law reform, te reo petition) to argue majorities can err on minority rights; an argument by analogy but a substantive one.

rigor.statement: if I was to withdraw and apologise, it would be an insult to 270,000 select committee submitters who all think that Mr Seymour is a liar also.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to numbers/popularity to justify a personal insult; the '270,000 all think' claim is an unsupported generalisation.

rigor.statement: the National Party strongly asserts that a referendum on the Treaty would be a simplistic approach to a very extremely complex and challenging issue, and so today, we are voting to ensure it will go no further. I say this respectfully to our coalition partners, but this is our strong view.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned position that a single referendum is too blunt for a complex issue, though the complexity claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: it's just not realistic to suggest that nearly 200 years of debate, discussion, protest... should be settled just with the stroke of one legislative pen. It's too blunt, it's too simplistic, and it risks, in reality, actually stoking grievance and driving division.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that a single statute cannot resolve a long, complex constitutional question, with a plausible causal claim about stoking division.

rigor.statement: This is a bill that the Prime Minister had the gall to stand up and say that it's not going to pass, and to then bring it to this House is disrespectful to this Chamber, because this Chamber's time is valuable and there should be put before this House laws which are seriously being considered.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a coherent principle (Parliament's time should be spent on genuinely live legislation).

rigor.statement: you can't legislate to make the world flat... you cannot legislate the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi out of existence—they might be constitutional truisms... but they're not the Treaty principles. You can't make up the underlying fabric of the Treaty.
rigor.explanation: Analogical but substantive argument that a statute cannot redefine principles developed through jurisprudence; cites Chris Finlayson in support.

rigor.statement: We asked the question: "What is the special advantage that Māori have under the Resource Management Act?" No one could put their finger on it. If it's a special advantage for mana whenua to be asked about a project that might impact their customary rights, well, that's a world I want to live in.
rigor.explanation: Tests the opponents' 'special rights' claim empirically at committee, reports no concrete example was given, and reframes consultation as respecting property/customary rights — evidence-seeking reasoning.

rigor.statement: his stooges would front up to the select committee and say, "This is about living in a liberal democracy.", and their concept of a liberal democracy was shallow and impoverished because all it meant was one person, one vote.
rigor.explanation: Substantive critique that reducing liberal democracy to majority voting ignores minority-rights protections, backed by the Cabinet Manual reference.

rigor.statement: is it possible to use the assessment processes of other countries and apply it here to streamline the approval of medication? Fair enough. But are the assessment criteria in other countries suitable for here? Are they as good as our processes here?... We mustn't forget the role that the likes of Medsafe played during the pandemic.
rigor.explanation: Poses focused, testable questions about whether overseas approval criteria are equivalent to NZ's, and grounds concern in Medsafe's pandemic record — disciplined, non-fallacious critique.

forthrightness.statement: the National Party strongly asserts that a referendum on the Treaty would be a simplistic approach to a very extremely complex and challenging issue, and so today, we are voting to ensure it will go no further. I say this respectfully to our coalition partners, but this is our strong view.
forthrightness.explanation: States clearly and directly how and why she is voting, without evasion.

forthrightness.statement: So, with caution, we support this bill and we will make sure we interrogate this throughout the entirety of the process... hold the caveat that if we don't agree, we will continue to challenge and even potentially withdraw. But for now, we support it.
forthrightness.explanation: Clearly states Labour's position — conditional support to select committee with a stated caveat — without evading.

forthrightness.statement: is it possible to use the assessment processes of other countries and apply it here to streamline the approval of medication? Fair enough. But are the assessment criteria in other countries suitable for here? Are they as good as our processes here?... We mustn't forget the role that the likes of Medsafe played during the pandemic.
forthrightness.explanation: States plainly what Labour is and isn't committing to and why.

forthrightness.statement: we're voting it to select committee, but that's all we're committing to, because if the Government doesn't front up and show us the substance that we need and the assurance that we need... we've made that are directly linked to this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Unambiguous about the limits of Labour's support and the conditions attached.

authenticity.statement: I said in the first reading of this koretake bill that we do not need to change the Treaty; we need to change this Government.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly restates a position she took at first reading, signalling consistency of view across the bill's stages.

authenticity.statement: successive National Governments have always worked well with Māori on Treaty issues, and we've always ensured that there are equal citizenship rights and equal opportunity for all New Zealanders.
authenticity.explanation: A claim of consistent principle; plausible in parts (Treaty settlements progress) but 'always worked well' smooths over a contested historical record — defensible but unverified from the text.

authenticity.statement: National also has a proud record when it comes to Treaty settlements, having made more progress than any other Governments in resolving historical grievances.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's long-stated Treaty-settlements stance; 'more progress than any other Governments' is a superlative that is arguable given Labour-era settlements.

strength.statement: the reversal of a number of divisive co-governance policies from the previous Government... for instance, three waters and the Māori Health Authority... we are restoring the rights of communities to determine whether to introduce Māori wards.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete actions the Government has actually delivered (Three Waters repeal, Māori Health Authority disestablishment, Māori wards law change) — enacted, not merely promised.

strength.statement: Through partnership with Māori health organisations, over 69,000 vaccinations have been delivered to New Zealanders. We've seen more than 20 Māori-led or Māori-partnered projects placed on the fast-track list. We've also committed over $200 million to Māori housing providers and have helped nearly 2,000 children, many of them Māori, move out of emergency housing.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered outcomes with numbers; credible as action taken, though 'committed $200m' is a commitment rather than proven delivery and figures aren't independently verified here.

divination.statement: This bill will increase access to medicines for New Zealanders by introducing a streamlined verification pathway for medicines. Faster access to medicines leads to better patient outcomes.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will increase access and improve outcomes; plausible in direction but unquantified and dependent on funding, which critics note is unaddressed.

divination.statement: I rise to support the Medicines Amendment Bill. This is about faster and more efficient access to medicines, and it will support better outcomes for families across Aotearoa New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts better outcomes for families; plausible in direction but unsupported and unquantified.

veracity.statement: I am informed that it reduced the official cash rate by a further 25 basis points, taking the rate down to 3.5 percent. This means that the OCR has now fallen 200 basis points—that is, two whole percentage points—in the past nine months.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the OCR did fall from 5.5% to 3.5% over roughly nine months.

veracity.statement: For someone with a $500,000 mortgage over 25 years, a two-percentage-point drop in their interest rate would reduce their required repayments by around $300 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Broadly in the right order of magnitude, though sensitive to assumptions.

veracity.statement: the way that tariffs work is that any tariffs that are being levied on New Zealand businesses by the Americans are passed through to American consumers.
veracity.explanation: Economically defensible as a general tendency, though incidence is more complex than stated.

veracity.statement: our iwi businesses are doing exceptionally well and are able to do commercial deals and sell their products and services all around the world ... They accompany me on trade delegations—that’s where we’ve been to Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, Korea, the UAE, the Gulf Cooperation Council trade deal, and recently India.
veracity.explanation: The trade delegation destinations are consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: I’m proud of the investment that the Government provides for people that need assistance with food. We have not historically always supported food banks. Over the COVID period we have, with time-limited funding, but, actually, we have money available through the Ministry of Social Development for people who need hardship grants and food support.
veracity.explanation: MSD hardship grants exist; the framing sidesteps the specific food-bank cuts alleged.

veracity.statement: That member was part of a Government where crime went through the roof—violent crime, retail crime, gang membership, ram raids. Now we see crime coming down. We see ram raids down 60 percent. We see police out on the beat up 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Ram-raid declines are broadly supported; the sweeping 'through the roof' framing is selective.

veracity.statement: How can he support his finance Minister refusing to adjust the year’s Budget to account for the US tariffs when they are projected to have the same impact as the 2008 global financial crisis?
veracity.explanation: Equating the tariff shock with the 2008 GFC overstates the likely magnitude.

veracity.statement: Is the Minister able to put the member right in respect to the claim about it being a public resource, when that all changed with the first privatisation of that resource by the Lange Labour Government in 1986?
veracity.explanation: The Quota Management System was introduced in 1986; the characterisation as 'privatisation' is arguable but broadly grounded.

veracity.statement: last week, I was proud to announce as transport Minister that the Melling Road of Regional Significance will begin construction this year. I signed a delivery contract with AECOM and Fletcher Construction to get on with delivering this very important project—40,000 vehicles drive through this bottleneck on State Highway 2 right now.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the public record of the Melling project.

veracity.statement: It’s a billion dollars from the transport agency, $295 million from the Greater Wellington Regional Council, and $180 million from the Hutt City Council.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable funding split consistent with the project's public figures.

veracity.statement: This morning it was reported that not only do 66 percent of New Zealanders feel more safe with police out on the beat, 66 percent of Wellingtonians feel more safe and 48 percent of Green voters feel more safe.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a reported survey; figures are specific but rest on a single cited report.

veracity.statement: the previous Government had underfunded cost pressures by about 4 or 5 percent. The Minister of Finance immediately made a one-off $120 million payment ... There has been $226 million delivered on the extra 500 police officers ... $424.9 million to support front-line policing, $242.2 million to boost police pay, and $62.7 million for front-line police vehicles and marine capability.
veracity.explanation: Specific and checkable, though framed to counter the defunding claim.

veracity.statement: We’ve got the best, world-class police force in the world.
veracity.explanation: Superlative claim not objectively established.

veracity.statement: Ram raids: 293 percent increase under a Labour-Greens Government; 58 percent decrease under a coalition Government.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported by reported ram-raid trends, though partisan framing selects the metric.

veracity.statement: our Government’s already delivering the knowledge-rich curriculum, the 836,000 high-quality maths resources being delivered to students, thousands of students now benefiting from targeted maths acceleration tutoring, and almost 1,000 primary schools benefiting from trained structured literacy teachers to accelerate achievement for year 0 to 2 students.

charisma.explanation: Purely combative, appeals only to her own side.

charisma.statement: his announcement of his resignation from Parliament this week I think is a loss for Parliament, because while I vigorously disagree with some of the policies he’s promoted, at least he had the integrity to fight for what he believed, and I think that Chris Hipkins should take note.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges an opponent's integrity, a bridging gesture, undercut by the closing dig.

charisma.statement: if you seriously think the alternative is Labour, Greens, and Te Pāti Māori managing the economy, that’s not right.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing aimed at rallying his side, not persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: there are thousands and thousands of kind acts of humanity that are shown by our police officers every day in the service of the communities they serve. And let us never forget: yes, they are police officers, but they are mums and dads, they are grandparents, they are sons and daughters.
charisma.explanation: Warm, humanising appeal, but rallies support around a defensive framing.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge that for some people, the presence of police makes them feel safe, especially as communities grapple with soaring crime rates, but I won’t shy away from my view that a more visible police presence does not make me feel safer.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges others' feelings of safety, but ultimately restates a divisive personal stance.

charisma.statement: This is what democracy is: it is people who are not afraid to criticise the systems that we have in place. If you disagree that that is what is happening, then you are part of the problem, and you need to be accountable for the decisions—
charisma.explanation: 'You are part of the problem' frames disagreement as complicity, alienating rather than persuading.

authenticity.statement: Actually, on this side of the House, we can do both. And that’s why we’re working incredibly hard to get our economy well managed and growing again. That’s why you’ve heard me talk about “growth, growth, growth” all year. ... We are backing up our values with actions.
authenticity.explanation: Claims words are matched by action on defence, but offers no specific delivery to verify.

authenticity.statement: the National Party position’s been very clear on the Treaty principles bill, but we had a compromise in an MMP environment ... The ACT Party didn’t get exactly what it wanted, the National Party didn’t get exactly what it wanted, but we found a middle ground and a compromise.
authenticity.explanation: Explains, but does not reconcile, breaking his pre-election position that he wouldn't support the bill.

authenticity.statement: I just think the reference to flip-flops from “Mr Jandals” is probably inappropriate, but our position has been well articulated. I have spoken to it ad nauseam over a number of months, and I’m focused on the things that matter most to New Zealanders, which is actually working out how we navigate choppier waters in a global trading environment.
authenticity.explanation: Defends consistency while the record shows a reversal on supporting the bill.

authenticity.statement: the Rt Hon Winston Peters, the Hon Nicola Willis, and the Hon Mark Patterson have today announced that Government agencies will be directed to use woollen fibre products in construction and refurbishment of Government buildings where practical and appropriate, thus fulfilling a fabulous commitment between the New Zealand First and National coalition.
authenticity.explanation: Presents the move as fulfilling a stated coalition commitment, matching words to action.

authenticity.statement: I acknowledge that for some people, the presence of police makes them feel safe, especially as communities grapple with soaring crime rates, but I won’t shy away from my view that a more visible police presence does not make me feel safer.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent, openly stated personal position she has stood by amid criticism.

strength.statement: last week, I was proud to announce as transport Minister that the Melling Road of Regional Significance will begin construction this year. I signed a delivery contract with AECOM and Fletcher Construction to get on with delivering this very important project—40,000 vehicles drive through this bottleneck on State Highway 2 right now.
strength.explanation: Signed contract and imminent construction indicate concrete delivery, not just announcement.

strength.statement: the previous Government had underfunded cost pressures by about 4 or 5 percent. The Minister of Finance immediately made a one-off $120 million payment ... There has been $226 million delivered on the extra 500 police officers ... $424.9 million to support front-line policing, $242.2 million to boost police pay, and $62.7 million for front-line police vehicles and marine capability.
strength.explanation: Points to money 'delivered', indicating follow-through on police funding.

strength.statement: our Government’s already delivering the knowledge-rich curriculum, the 836,000 high-quality maths resources being delivered to students, thousands of students now benefiting from targeted maths acceleration tutoring, and almost 1,000 primary schools benefiting from trained structured literacy teachers to accelerate achievement for year 0 to 2 students.
strength.explanation: Describes measures presented as already delivered, though outcomes remain to be seen.

strength.statement: if we want to talk about patient safety, how about those people who are stuck on wait-lists, unable to get access to timely mental health addiction support? ... That’s why this Government published New Zealand’s first stand-alone mental health and addiction workforce plan and we’re going to double the amount of clinical psychologists who’ve been trained
strength.explanation: Commitment stated with a plan published, but delivery (2027 workforce) is still ahead.

strength.statement: Two years ago, the Labour Government agreed on a plan to rebuild Nelson Hospital. Last year, National cancelled that plan; they promised a new plan would be finalised by Christmas. Well, it’s April, and the joke’s on us.
strength.explanation: Describes a plan cancelled and a missed deadline — low delivery for those responsible.

strength.statement: Every region deserves a decent hospital. I will stand up for Nelson and every regional hospital in this country.
strength.explanation: Personal commitment to advocate, but from opposition with no delivery attached.

divination.statement: The projections for the sheep and beef sector are looking extremely positive indeed. With much growth predicted to occur in the industry, this Government will continue on its trajectory of backing the industry
divination.explanation: Optimistic sector forecast with no figures or timeframe to assess.

divination.statement: Those students will be on campus at the start of next year and entering the workforce in 2027.
divination.explanation: A dated prediction of workforce entry; plausible but contingent on the training pipeline.

charisma.statement: on behalf of the Labour Opposition, we will be supporting this piece of legislation. It comes at a very important time in international trade, when I think we, more than ever, rely on the rules and the arrangements of trade to give us some security in an otherwise very, very uncertain world.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party support for a Government bill, framed around shared national interest rather than partisan point-scoring.

charisma.statement: Can I say, though, that the incoming Government did pick that up and ran with it, and I want to acknowledge the efforts of Minister McClay, who got stuck into it and, indeed, as it was said, negotiated very quickly a trade agreement.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit a rival minister, actively building cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: I think, as always, it is across the borders and the boundaries of this House and the parties of this House that we see the value in progressing trade agreements.
charisma.explanation: Explicit appeal to cross-party common ground and continuity of national interest.

charisma.statement: With all of these reasons, we love trade, we want trade to benefit everyone, but we do not see that reflected in this agreement.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to soften the opposition by affirming support for trade in principle, but ultimately rallies its own position.

charisma.statement: We know, as opposed to the de-growth Greens, that free trade benefits us. It is huge. We have seen, with the multiple free-trade agreements that this country has entered into, that results have come back to this country.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side by caricaturing opponents rather than persuading them.

charisma.statement: I can't believe what I'm hearing from the Greens over there not supporting this bill. What planet are they on? What world do they live in?
charisma.explanation: Combative, alienating framing that ridicules the other side instead of persuading.

charisma.statement: Todd McClay has done a phenomenal job pulling in not only this trade deal, the New Zealand-Gulf Cooperation Council free-trade agreement, and then following on the good work of the Hon Damien O'Connor in tidying up and finishing the UK and EU trade deal.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges cross-party contributions to trade continuity, though embedded in praise for his own bloc.

charisma.statement: Largely this has been bipartisan. I hope the Greens do reconsider, because we just have not got the ability to turn down these sorts of opportunities from sitting in an ivory tower.
charisma.explanation: Nominally invites reconsideration but frames dissenters as detached and unrealistic, undercutting the outreach.

charisma.statement: the Green Party are just out in the cold on this particular bill, and with trade in general. With that, I'd like to commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Reinforces an us-vs-them line rather than making any persuasive or unifying case.

charisma.statement: As the Hon Damien O'Connor spoke about earlier, the discussions that started on this bill and this agreement happened towards the end of 2023, so we do acknowledge that the Government has picked it up and we've come to this point now.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the Government's role in continuing work started under Labour — cooperative, continuity-focused tone.

charisma.statement: It also speaks to the "Indigenous Peoples Economic and Trade Cooperation" chapter in this particular bill, which seems a little bit ironic given a couple of bills ago, but it's also important to see that this has support from both sides of the House in relation to that chapter.
charisma.explanation: Notes bipartisan support for the indigenous-trade chapter while gently needling the Government.

charisma.statement: The negotiations of these agreements have actually built on the work of successive Governments. The apparent speed with which this agreement was negotiated, I think, is largely because there's now a pretty broad understanding of what a good, comprehensive trade agreement looks like.
charisma.explanation: Frames the achievement as a shared, cumulative effort across successive governments — bridging rather than claiming.

charisma.statement: it's important that a signal is sent to potential trade partners that this isn't a matter where the policy of the Government will change with a change in Government; rather, we will stay the course.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises national unity and continuity across governments — an explicitly consensus-building message.

charisma.statement: I know that there is a practice of taking Opposition members with whoever is in Government on some trade delegations, and I think that's a really good thing, for two reasons: one, for continuity across bargaining teams, but also for a very powerful signal that New Zealand is unified in being an open-trading nation.
charisma.explanation: Advocates cross-party inclusion in delegations for the sake of national unity — bridge-building and inclusive.

charisma.statement: we back our people to be competitive and not to need protection—that they are as good as any other businesses, farmers, game programmers and developers, aerospace engineers, all the things that we're great at—that we're as good or better than anyone in the world and we don't need false protections to prop up our industries.
charisma.explanation: Confident, morale-building appeal to national capability, though it rallies rather than reaches across.

authenticity.statement: on behalf of the Labour Opposition, we will be supporting this piece of legislation. It comes at a very important time in international trade, when I think we, more than ever, rely on the rules and the arrangements of trade to give us some security in an otherwise very, very uncertain world.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's long-standing pro-free-trade position and O'Connor's own record as former Trade Minister.

authenticity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand to oppose both this bill and the NZ-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the Greens' established and repeatedly-stated scepticism of FTAs; position matches the party's record.

veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: the NZ-China FTA was negotiated in that period and signed under the Labour Government (2008), and GCC negotiations were underway.

veracity.statement: the GCC decided to halt that, in 2009, and not proceed with any further trade agreements.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Gulf Cooperation Council suspended its FTA negotiations, including with New Zealand, around 2009.

veracity.statement: in May 2023, when the UAE's Minister of State for International Cooperation came to New Zealand, she sought an assurance from us that we would start and engage on the basis of negotiating a free-trade agreement. Indeed, we confirmed that, in September 2023, we would start negotiations, and then I took a trade delegation to the UAE later on in September.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable chronology consistent with the public record of when NZ-UAE negotiations were launched.

veracity.statement: We set standards in the UK and EU trade agreements that held the rights and opportunities for small to medium enterprises, that protected the rights of workers, protected the rights for women, and advocated for them.
veracity.explanation: The UK and EU agreements do contain labour, gender and SME provisions; broadly accurate though self-favourable framing.

veracity.statement: the tariff that will potentially be removed as a part of this agreement is, at a maximum, worth $42.6 million per annum.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure attributed to official analysis; plausible and consistent with MFAT estimates, though not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: It is also worth noting that the majority of Aotearoa's exports into the UAE currently enter under the unilateral UAE duty-exemption programme.
veracity.explanation: Accurate reflection that many NZ exports already enter the UAE duty-free unilaterally, tempering the deal's marginal benefit.

veracity.statement: proportionally speaking, we have not seen the equal growth in the number of exports in proportion to our GDP through all of these agreements. In fact, the FTAs and CEPAs that we have signed up to have not yielded the kind of return that we are hoping to see.
veracity.explanation: Contested empirical claim; the relationship between FTAs and export-to-GDP growth is genuinely debated and not established here.

veracity.statement: I would also like to draw the House's attention to the ongoing contribution of UAE to the Sudanese civil war, where thousands of people have been killed and also 12 million people have been displaced on the basis of UAE direct involvement in supporting the Rapid Support Forces.
veracity.explanation: UN and multiple reports document UAE support for the Rapid Support Forces and displacement around 11–12 million in Sudan; broadly supported, though 'direct involvement' is asserted more strongly than proven.

veracity.statement: there is currently an application to the International Court of Justice from Sudan against the UAE, and that is also a serious concern we need to mention when we are looking at this agreement
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Sudan filed an application against the UAE at the ICJ in early 2025.

veracity.statement: We have been given the opportunity through outstanding work by our trade officials and our politicians to have this opportunity to get better access into the world's 20th-biggest economy—with the 11th-highest GDP per capita, I might say.
veracity.explanation: The UAE's rankings are overstated/imprecise — its nominal GDP rank is lower than 20th and its per-capita rank varies by measure; directionally right that it is a wealthy sizeable economy.

veracity.statement: So we are a small island nation. We do make our living by trading food and fibre to the world—80 percent of our exports are food and fibre.
veracity.explanation: Food and fibre/primary products do make up roughly 80% of New Zealand's goods exports; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: There are a number of things which for New Zealand's sake mean we have low productivity in our country. Some of them have been traversed quite in depth by the IMF, by the Productivity Commission before it was closed, and the Reserve Bank earlier this year set out what those reasons were. Some of those reasons are education, innovation, technology, and one which this bill seeks to address, and that is around our interconnectedness with the rest of the world.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the diagnosed drivers of NZ's low productivity and that the Productivity Commission was disestablished.

veracity.statement: there was a recognition by both New Zealand and the UAE around the goal of eliminating all forms of forced or compulsory labour, including child labour, and also the importance of supporting women's economic empowerment by adopting, maintaining, and implementing laws, regulations, policies, and best practice, as well as the UN Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against Women.

veracity.explanation: The 98.5% tariff-elimination figure matches the official characterisation of the NZ-UAE CEPA.

veracity.statement: every year, 65,000 young New Zealanders start school
veracity.explanation: In the right order of magnitude — annual new-entrant numbers are roughly 60,000, so slightly high but broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: I'm proud of the progress we've made on attendance, with regular attendance in term 3 2024 up 5.3 percentage points compared to the same term in 2023.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific attendance improvement consistent with the Government's published term 3 attendance data.

veracity.statement: there's a strong, positive correlation between attendance and literacy and numeracy scores over years 4 to 10, as well as attainment across NCEA levels 1, 2, and 3.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with well-established evidence linking school attendance to achievement outcomes.

specificity.explanation: Names the exact instrument being removed (the NELPs) and the specific legislative change.

specificity.explanation: Describes the problem and the principle but names no specific institution or instance.

rigor.statement: I know that there is a practice of taking Opposition members with whoever is in Government on some trade delegations, and I think that's a really good thing, for two reasons: one, for continuity across bargaining teams, but also for a very powerful signal that New Zealand is unified in being an open-trading nation.

rigor.statement: In recent years, some universities seem to have taken a risk-averse approach to discussions about the difficult issues, seeking to protect students and staff from controversial views, but universities should be a place of genuine debate, where diverse opinions can be discussed and challenged.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification for the free-expression duty, but the premise ('some universities seem to have') is impressionistic and unevidenced.

charisma.statement: In a time when so much feels fractured, the presence of a figure who spoke for the possibility of unity, forgiveness, and meaning is not something to take lightly.

civility.statement: No, I don't agree with that sentiment, and, of course, with the passage of time, people and parties sometimes change their views on matters.

forthrightness.statement: Well, what we're doing here is we're making sure that we actually have a process that's more robust, workable, and sustainable. forthrightness.statement: No.

forthrightness.statement: That's exactly why we're here. The Cabinet Manual says that any emails should be kept for the purposes of the Official Information Act. forthrightness.statement: I have not done that, but I have made sure that there is two-factor authentication on my Gmail, which is one of the things that we're required to do.

forthrightness.statement: The Social Security Amendment Bill needs to be enacted by 26 May, and the Government intends to make progress on some other bills that are important to it, including the Racing Industry Amendment Bill. Both of those are second readings, not passing through all stages.

civility.statement: How dare anybody pour shade on the work that has happened since 2020 that had 13—13—pay equity claims be successful in this country, when prior to that we had very few successful pay equity claims.
civility.explanation: Indignant 'how dare' framing; references the substance (13 claims) but delivered as moral outrage rather than argument.

civility.statement: But what this smacks of is that we have a Government that cannot make their Budget balance, and so this is a way that they are actually having to go desperately, to grasp desperately, to make their Budget balance. So what are they doing? They are throwing women under the bus.

civility.statement: We did the same job as our male counterparts, but we were never paid the same equal, fair-pay rate as our male teammates. Every year, we would go to the performance review, fight and prove that we could reach our key performance indicators just as much as our male counterparts. Did we ever get that pay rise? No.

civility.statement: We have Labour crying foul this afternoon, when it took them three years even to get their legislation into this House. During urgency, they introduced a Supplementary Order Paper that fundamentally changed that legislation for the worse.
civility.explanation: 'Crying foul' is a mild jab but the point engages process rather than attacking members personally.

civility.statement: Well, me being angry is not me being emotional.
