civility.explanation: A substantive historical argument for National's record, delivered without personal attack.

civility.statement: This bill is good evidence that we have a two-faced Government.
civility.explanation: 'Two-faced' is a character label applied to the government rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: As our colleague the Minister Louise Upston said, this is not about a collective bargaining tool or where wages are low; it's about a clear framework to assess where pay discrimination is as a result of gender.
civility.explanation: Restates the policy framing calmly without attacking opponents.

authenticity.statement: I was asked whether the budgetary cost of settling pay equity claims was considered when the Government made this decision. What I should have said was that while Cabinet received advice on a range of considerations, our primary motivation was ensuring the regime would be more robust, workable, and sustainable.
authenticity.explanation: A formal correction of the record; reframes the motivation away from budgetary cost, a defensible clarification but one that sits in tension with opposition claims (and later ACT statements) that the change saves money.

authenticity.statement: I have worked nearly my entire working life in male-dominated roles, and I think we can say proudly in New Zealand that we have progressed effectively to ensure that women's work is valued.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value grounded in her own biography, with no visible contradiction but no verifiable link to the bill's effect.

authenticity.statement: We did the same job as our male counterparts, but we were never paid the same equal, fair-pay rate as our male teammates. Every year, we would go to the performance review, fight and prove that we could reach our key performance indicators just as much as our male counterparts. Did we ever get that pay rise? No.
authenticity.explanation: First-hand account consistent with her stance; no visible contradiction, though unverifiable.

authenticity.statement: It was a National-led Government that first introduced the bill to legislate a pay equity system, and we still support pay equity.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts continued support for pay equity while backing a bill that discontinues current claims and removes back-pay — a defensible but tension-laden 'we still support it' framing.

rigor.statement: Health New Zealand admin and clerical staff, as an example, have been compared to mechanical engineers, Health New Zealand librarians have been compared to transport engineers, and Oranga Tamariki's social workers have been compared to air traffic controllers.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete examples to argue comparators have been ill-matched; persuasive but the examples are selected to make the comparisons look self-evidently absurd without engaging the equal-value methodology that justified them.

rigor.statement: How dare anybody pour shade on the work that has happened since 2020 that had 13—13—pay equity claims be successful in this country, when prior to that we had very few successful pay equity claims.
rigor.explanation: Largely an appeal to emotion/indignation rather than a structured argument against the bill's mechanics.

rigor.statement: But what this smacks of is that we have a Government that cannot make their Budget balance, and so this is a way that they are actually having to go desperately, to grasp desperately, to make their Budget balance. So what are they doing? They are throwing women under the bus.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the government's hidden budgetary motive without direct evidence; emotive inference.

rigor.statement: On 22 July 2020, the National Party stood up, and Nicola Willis said she was proud to stand in the House that night and say that National would support the final reading of the Equal Pay Amendment Bill—"I'm proud [of what the National Party] … contributed to crafting this legislation and bringing it to the House."
rigor.explanation: Uses the documented record as evidence of a position reversal; a sound evidentiary point (though the hypocrisy is Willis's, about the opponent).

rigor.statement: That's what this Government has prioritised: tax cuts for landlords, the people who already own the most wealth; tax cuts for tobacco companies.
rigor.explanation: Attributes motive by association rather than establishing the causal link to the pay equity decision.

rigor.statement: Those are the workforces in which we have shortages. We don't have enough teachers, and we don't have enough midwives, because we do not pay them enough.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause explanation for workforce shortages; pay is a genuine factor but the 'because' overstates a monocausal link.

rigor.statement: The first is the blatant—blatant—inaccuracy that this is removing review rights. It's not. It's just putting review rights in a 10-year interval.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason (why revisit within three years) but rests on the assertion that discrimination would be resolved, without evidence.

rigor.statement: when members across the House can muddy the water with a whole lot of issues about pay gaps and underpaid workforces, this is blurring the line about the point of this piece of legislation, which is to raise and resolve the claims.
rigor.explanation: Makes a valid conceptual distinction (pay equity vs general low pay) but asserts rather than demonstrates that opponents' points are irrelevant.

rigor.statement: I have worked nearly my entire working life in male-dominated roles, and I think we can say proudly in New Zealand that we have progressed effectively to ensure that women's work is valued.
rigor.explanation: Leans on personal experience (appeal to anecdote) to support a broad claim of national progress.

rigor.statement: This bill will stop 33 current claims immediately, under urgency, because this Government can afford to give $3 billion to landlords and $13 billion to the military but we cannot afford to pay our wāhine fairly.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical juxtaposition of spending choices rather than a demonstrated fiscal linkage.

rigor.statement: We did the same job as our male counterparts, but we were never paid the same equal, fair-pay rate as our male teammates. Every year, we would go to the performance review, fight and prove that we could reach our key performance indicators just as much as our male counterparts. Did we ever get that pay rise? No.
rigor.explanation: Personal anecdote used as the basis of a broader claim (appeal to anecdote).

rigor.statement: Equal pay is receiving equal pay for equal work. Pay equity is about ensuring that people doing different work in different organisations of similar value are paid at a similar level.
rigor.explanation: A correct definitional clarification, though used to imply opponents don't understand the topic.

rigor.statement: I don't think anyone should be mistaken: this is a war on women.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping characterisation with no supporting reasoning in the statement itself.

rigor.statement: They were more than happy to give $2.9 billion to landlords, more than happy to give the tobacco industry a tax break, more than happy to pay out tax cuts that they were told were unaffordable and that would disproportionately go to those who were on higher incomes.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes spending choices to imply a trade-off rather than establishing one.

rigor.statement: the new law and this bill raises the bar for evidence required to prove historic undervaluation for women's work. Many roles traditionally held by women, like caregiving, nursing, support, and education roles, have complex histories where direct evidence is difficult to find. This bill makes it even harder to find.
rigor.explanation: Makes a structured argument linking the higher evidential threshold to a concrete difficulty for specific female-dominated roles.

rigor.statement: David Seymour today has applauded Brooke van Velden for finding billions of dollars just weeks out from the Budget, when it's most needed. Those are the words used out there on the tiles today, while the Prime Minister has said it's got nothing to do with the Budget.
rigor.explanation: Points to an internal contradiction between two coalition figures' framings as evidence of the budgetary motive.

charisma.statement: I want to remind the House that in 2017 the then National Government settled with Kristine Bartlett. I applaud her determination and her courage in taking that case, and the $2 billion settlement that resulted.
charisma.explanation: Cross-partisan acknowledgement praising a claimant championed by the other side — a bridging gesture within an adversarial debate.

charisma.statement: I accept what members of the House have said about a range of New Zealanders whose pay is too low. That is why we want a growing economy that lifts wages. But that is a very different issue to sex-based discrimination. So let's keep the debate about the issue of the day, which is pay equity.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to concede common ground, though ultimately reframes to advance her own side's position.

charisma.statement: Well, me being angry is not me being emotional. Me being angry for the women who have fought for these pay equity agreements, who have fought for fair pay—me being angry for the Māori and Pacific women who continue to be the people that are paid least in this country is me being angry for the right reasons, actually, and it's not me being emotional.
charisma.explanation: Reframes 'emotional' as justified anger to rally her own side; effective for supporters but not consensus-building.

civility.statement: take a little bit of a story, twist it round, make it into a drama, and talk a load of nonsense
civility.explanation: Characterises the opposition's case as deliberate theatrics and nonsense — a strawman/dismissal rather than engagement with their argument.

civility.statement: it might take a lemon to know a lemon. There you go.
civility.explanation: A personal jab returned at Tracey McLellan rather than a substantive reply.

civility.statement: The rhetoric has already started. You’ve heard it—that women will be paid less as a result of this. What a load of nonsense that we’re throwing out pay equity. We are not doing that. I repeat, this is simply not true.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' arguments as 'nonsense' but frames it around the policy claim rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: You’ve been sold a lemon as well, then, if you believe that.
civility.explanation: Mocking jab implying the member is gullible, aimed at the person's belief rather than the substance.

civility.statement: it reeks of this classic libertarian kind of concept of the unit of analysis being the individual, and that is completely at odds with what the pay equity legislation was designed to do, because it was about rectifying historical undervaluation of what tends to be woman’s work
civility.explanation: Pointed characterisation of the Minister's ideology but engages the conceptual substance rather than the person.

civility.statement: I think the answer is the reason they want to make it harder is because they don’t want to pay out pay equity claims, and they want to have that money—that was set aside for low-paid women who deserve to be paid what they’re worth—available to use for other matters which are not low-paid work of female employees.
civility.explanation: Imputes a self-interested motive to the Government, though framed as inference about policy rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I don’t have the specific 33 claims in front of me at this stage, but I’m sure you can google a few and find them.
civility.explanation: The 'you can google them' retort is dismissive of a reasonable request.

civility.statement: It reeks of ill winds, really, that the Minister has changed this purely—and I want to be convinced here otherwise—as a cost-saving measure, particularly when I see the comments that have been made today in the media... saying this was all about saving billions of dollars.
civility.explanation: 'Reeks of ill winds' is a pointed insinuation of bad motive, though tied to on-the-record cost claims and open to rebuttal ('convince me otherwise').

civility.statement: in that party, there is a value given to a freedom to contract, and yet here we seem to have a whole lot of agreements that have been settled by people... the proposal put forward by the Minister... is to jettison all that work, to basically break those contracts and agreements by overriding them in this piece of legislation.
civility.explanation: Critical but focused on the policy and the party's stated principles rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: where is the Attorney-General’s report? Because the departmental disclosure statement... indicates that there has been an assessment of the bill and whether it’s consistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act... it is shameful that the advice exists and yet it has not been tabled.
civility.explanation: 'Shameful' is harsh but aimed at the process/omission rather than at a person.

civility.statement: sanctity of contract is something that the ACT Party talks about all of the time, and yet here they are legislating away contracts that have been struck between the parties. The process here is appalling and I want to know why the Minister thinks it’s appropriate to retrospectively change contractual agreements.
civility.explanation: 'Appalling' is strong but directed at the process and retrospectivity, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: It’s gone from being a purpose that is to facilitate claims to one that is “The purpose of this Part is to provide a process that facilitates the resolution of pay equity claims”... is that language purposeful?... in the recently passed Fast-track Approvals Act, the purpose of that Act... “is to facilitate the delivery of … projects”... this piece of legislation is doing the exact opposite of that fast-track in terms of the purpose clause.
civility.explanation: A precise, respectful drafting question that engages the legislation on its substance.

civility.statement: at paragraph (d)(ii)... “regarded as not requiring monetary compensation.”... This seems like a higher threshold than is necessary... could that subclause (2)(d)(ii) be regarded as not requiring very much monetary compensation or regarded as low value in terms of monetary compensation, or something to that effect
civility.explanation: Constructive, technically focused suggestion offered without personal edge.

civility.statement: I’ve seen a lot of reporting on the 33 claims that will be discontinued by this legislation but I haven’t seen a list of the 33 claims and which workers are involved in those. Does the Minister have such a list of the 33 parties who are the claims and who it affects? If so, can she share it with the committee?
civility.explanation: A calm, direct, non-hostile question inviting the Minister to share information.

rigor.statement: take a little bit of a story, twist it round, make it into a drama, and talk a load of nonsense
rigor.explanation: Dismisses opponents' position without evidence; relies on caricature rather than reasoning.

rigor.statement: The rhetoric has already started. You’ve heard it—that women will be paid less as a result of this. What a load of nonsense that we’re throwing out pay equity. We are not doing that. I repeat, this is simply not true.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the claim is untrue by repetition rather than by addressing the specific threshold changes opponents cite.

rigor.statement: it reeks of this classic libertarian kind of concept of the unit of analysis being the individual, and that is completely at odds with what the pay equity legislation was designed to do, because it was about rectifying historical undervaluation of what tends to be woman’s work
rigor.explanation: Substantive critique linking the Minister's individual-discrimination framing to a mismatch with the systemic purpose of pay equity law; reasoned though somewhat rhetorical.

rigor.statement: how does she reconcile that with this specific clause which requires 70 percent of the workforce, which is a higher number than previously required, in order to take a pay equity claim? Does she not think... that a workforce of 60 percent or a workforce, indeed, of 50 percent or 50 to 60 percent would not be predominantly female?
rigor.explanation: Directly tests the Government's 'not making it harder' claim against the specific 70% clause; logical and grounded in the bill text.

rigor.statement: I think the answer is the reason they want to make it harder is because they don’t want to pay out pay equity claims, and they want to have that money—that was set aside for low-paid women who deserve to be paid what they’re worth—available to use for other matters which are not low-paid work of female employees.
rigor.explanation: A plausible inference about fiscal motive, but presented as the assumed answer without direct evidence.

rigor.statement: what does she say to a young mother that I met last week at the Maranga Ake protests who is a care and support worker who was seven months pregnant and is on the minimum wage?
rigor.explanation: Relies on an individual anecdote and appeal to emotion to press the point rather than aggregate evidence.

rigor.statement: It is also the case that having a 70 percent threshold is not out of alignment with what we’ve seen internationally. If you look at Manitoba, Canada, they also have a 70 percent threshold for sex-based discrimination.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a single cherry-picked international example as justification without broader comparison.

rigor.statement: you have to draw a line in the sand somewhere, and I believe that having the higher threshold of 70 percent makes us have greater confidence that the analysis that we’re seeing is based on genuine sex-based undervaluation. It makes sense that the higher the threshold is, the more likely it is based on genuine sex-based discrimination.
rigor.explanation: Offers a directional intuition ('higher threshold = more confidence') asserted as self-evident rather than supported by evidence, and doesn't address why 65%/9-year workforces should be excluded.

rigor.statement: When we had that 60 percent threshold, we were successful in getting pay equity claims through, which tells me... that things were working in this space, and are working.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the observed track record of successful claims under 60% to the conclusion that the system worked — reasonable evidential inference.

rigor.statement: when you look at the successful claims of support staff in schools, of science technicians in schools, all of those claims that came through, we saw a change in those workforces. We saw that predominantly female workforce change for the better because of those successful pay equity claims.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'keep 60%' argument with specific real outcomes rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: It reeks of ill winds, really, that the Minister has changed this purely—and I want to be convinced here otherwise—as a cost-saving measure, particularly when I see the comments that have been made today in the media... saying this was all about saving billions of dollars.
rigor.explanation: Infers a cost-saving motive from public 'billions of dollars' comments — plausible and evidenced by the reporting, but an inference about intent.

rigor.statement: It says 10 consecutive years, which means that a company could reasonably change the system in year 10 to reset the 10 consecutive years for them to start again from year one the next year, and there’s nothing that employees can do about it.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a concrete gaming scenario from the wording of the clause to expose a loophole risk — logical, though the risk is hypothetical.

rigor.statement: the current section in the legislation which is section 13F of the equal payment Act actually does have a definitions framework of how they work... we shouldn’t be using a blunt tool of 10 years. That’s very restrictive whereas there are various mechanisms in the existing legislation that already allow for that.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the Minister's 'no clear guidelines' claim by citing an existing statutory framework (s13F) and arguing the 10-year rule is a blunt substitute.

rigor.statement: I had a mother who worked as a teacher in the 1960s. She was paid a quarter what the male standing next to her was being paid for the same job because she was paid as a single person and the male was assumed to have a family of four, and the rate was set to actually be for the family of four.
rigor.explanation: Uses a personal anecdote/appeal to illustrate historical undervaluation; vivid and historically representative but a single-case appeal.

rigor.statement: in that party, there is a value given to a freedom to contract, and yet here we seem to have a whole lot of agreements that have been settled by people... the proposal put forward by the Minister... is to jettison all that work, to basically break those contracts and agreements by overriding them in this piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: Argues an internal inconsistency between ACT's stated freedom-of-contract value and the bill overriding negotiated review clauses — coherent, though it partly rests on characterising the override.

rigor.statement: where is the Attorney-General’s report? Because the departmental disclosure statement... indicates that there has been an assessment of the bill and whether it’s consistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act... it is shameful that the advice exists and yet it has not been tabled.
rigor.explanation: Builds a documented process complaint: the disclosure statement references the advice, therefore it exists and should be tabled.

rigor.statement: we know many of our lowest-paid workers are Māori, and in terms of doing right by Māori and ensuring that they are paid appropriately—our wahine Māori are directly affected by this bill and the Treaty analysis was absolutely necessary.
rigor.explanation: Links the absence of Treaty analysis to a concrete equity consequence via the over-representation of Māori among low-paid workers.

rigor.statement: sanctity of contract is something that the ACT Party talks about all of the time, and yet here they are legislating away contracts that have been struck between the parties. The process here is appalling and I want to know why the Minister thinks it’s appropriate to retrospectively change contractual agreements.
rigor.explanation: Presses an inconsistency between ACT's stated contract principles and the retrospective override, ending in a direct question — reasoned, if rhetorically framed.

rigor.statement: Providing equal pay to women cuts family poverty “in half,”... “falling from 8.0 percent to 3.8 percent.” So that’s over half in terms of family poverty... now, this is US numbers, and it might be different in New Zealand
rigor.explanation: Cites a named research source with figures and explicitly caveats that they are US numbers that may not transfer — disciplined use of evidence.

rigor.statement: It’s gone from being a purpose that is to facilitate claims to one that is “The purpose of this Part is to provide a process that facilitates the resolution of pay equity claims”... is that language purposeful?... in the recently passed Fast-track Approvals Act, the purpose of that Act... “is to facilitate the delivery of … projects”... this piece of legislation is doing the exact opposite of that fast-track in terms of the purpose clause.
rigor.explanation: Close textual analysis contrasting the shift from outcome-focused to process-focused wording, cross-referenced against the Fast-track Act's purpose clause.

rigor.statement: at paragraph (d)(ii)... “regarded as not requiring monetary compensation.”... This seems like a higher threshold than is necessary... could that subclause (2)(d)(ii) be regarded as not requiring very much monetary compensation or regarded as low value in terms of monetary compensation, or something to that effect
rigor.explanation: Identifies that 'not requiring monetary compensation' is an absolute test and reasons, with the cleaner example, that a relative wording would better fit the policy intent.

specificity.statement: This bill is about clearing up what is happening in this system. It is about making the system clearer and better—end of story.
specificity.explanation: Vague characterisation — 'clearer and better' names no mechanism, figure, or concrete change.

specificity.statement: we have 33 current pay equity claims, so by virtue of the fact that we haven’t been through a select committee process and we don’t have a regulatory impact statement, can the Minister take us through all of those 33 existing cases?
specificity.explanation: Concrete request tied to a specific figure and the absence of RIS/select committee process.

specificity.statement: how does she reconcile that with this specific clause which requires 70 percent of the workforce, which is a higher number than previously required, in order to take a pay equity claim? Does she not think... that a workforce of 60 percent or a workforce, indeed, of 50 percent or 50 to 60 percent would not be predominantly female?
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact threshold change and concrete workforce percentages.

specificity.statement: what does she say to a young mother that I met last week at the Maranga Ake protests who is a care and support worker who was seven months pregnant and is on the minimum wage?
specificity.explanation: Concrete, detailed example (care worker, seven months pregnant, minimum wage, named protest).

specificity.statement: It is also the case that having a 70 percent threshold is not out of alignment with what we’ve seen internationally. If you look at Manitoba, Canada, they also have a 70 percent threshold for sex-based discrimination.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete jurisdiction and figure to support the threshold choice.

specificity.statement: The National Party’s original intention when they introduced the law had a threshold of, I believe, 66 percent, which was lowered by the Labour Government down to 60 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific figures and attributes each threshold to a specific government.

specificity.statement: New Zealand’s pay equity system is actually quite unique in terms of international comparisons. The UK and Ireland don’t allow multi-employer claims. They also don’t allow any claims to be made outside of a person’s or the claimant’s workforce... Australia does allow multi-employer claims, but they are usually progressed through a different system... which is the awards system.
specificity.explanation: Names specific jurisdictions and the concrete features (multi-employer claims, awards system) that distinguish them.

specificity.statement: Settlements that have been made are still valid. It is only the review clause that is no longer enforceable... In many of these settlements, the short review period made it difficult to determine whether any remuneration differences were actually due to pay equity issues having re-emerged in such short time frames or, simply, too short-term labour market dynamics.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific mechanism affected (review clauses) and the rationale (short review cycles conflated with labour-market change).

specificity.statement: when you look at the successful claims of support staff in schools, of science technicians in schools, all of those claims that came through, we saw a change in those workforces. We saw that predominantly female workforce change for the better because of those successful pay equity claims.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete claimant groups (school support staff, science technicians) as evidence.

specificity.statement: It says 10 consecutive years, which means that a company could reasonably change the system in year 10 to reset the 10 consecutive years for them to start again from year one the next year, and there’s nothing that employees can do about it.
specificity.explanation: Pins the concern to the exact '10 consecutive years' mechanism and a step-by-step manipulation pathway.

specificity.statement: the current section in the legislation which is section 13F of the equal payment Act actually does have a definitions framework of how they work... we shouldn’t be using a blunt tool of 10 years. That’s very restrictive whereas there are various mechanisms in the existing legislation that already allow for that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the specific section and contrasts it concretely with the new blunt 10-year test.

specificity.statement: I had a mother who worked as a teacher in the 1960s. She was paid a quarter what the male standing next to her was being paid for the same job because she was paid as a single person and the male was assumed to have a family of four, and the rate was set to actually be for the family of four.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail (1960s teacher, quarter pay, family-of-four rate assumption).

specificity.statement: where is the Attorney-General’s report? Because the departmental disclosure statement... indicates that there has been an assessment of the bill and whether it’s consistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act... it is shameful that the advice exists and yet it has not been tabled.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints a specific missing document (the BORA/Attorney-General advice) and grounds the claim in the disclosure statement.

specificity.statement: Providing equal pay to women cuts family poverty “in half,”... “falling from 8.0 percent to 3.8 percent.” So that’s over half in terms of family poverty... now, this is US numbers, and it might be different in New Zealand
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures (8.0% to 3.8%) and the source (Institute for Women's Policy Research).

specificity.statement: this particular report is just full of great big grey redacted paragraphs. So I want to know what advice... what sources of advice the Minister asked for and consulted in terms of looking at the financial implications of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the process complaint in a specific document (MBIE's March 2025 'Reviewing policy settings' paper) and its redactions.

specificity.statement: It’s gone from being a purpose that is to facilitate claims to one that is “The purpose of this Part is to provide a process that facilitates the resolution of pay equity claims”... is that language purposeful?... in the recently passed Fast-track Approvals Act, the purpose of that Act... “is to facilitate the delivery of … projects”... this piece of legislation is doing the exact opposite of that fast-track in terms of the purpose clause.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact old and new purpose wording and a specific comparator statute.

specificity.statement: at paragraph (d)(ii)... “regarded as not requiring monetary compensation.”... This seems like a higher threshold than is necessary... could that subclause (2)(d)(ii) be regarded as not requiring very much monetary compensation or regarded as low value in terms of monetary compensation, or something to that effect
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause (11 / s13F, subclause (2)(d)(ii)) and proposes concrete alternative wording.

specificity.statement: I’ve seen a lot of reporting on the 33 claims that will be discontinued by this legislation but I haven’t seen a list of the 33 claims and which workers are involved in those. Does the Minister have such a list of the 33 parties who are the claims and who it affects? If so, can she share it with the committee?
specificity.explanation: Narrows the request to a single concrete deliverable — the list of the 33 affected claims.

veracity.statement: The National Party began this journey in 2017 to introduce the legislation, and we are not turning our back on our commitment to pay equity.
veracity.explanation: National-led government did begin pay equity legislative work around 2017; broadly accurate though the framing selectively omits that the current bill narrows the regime.

veracity.statement: we have 33 current pay equity claims, so by virtue of the fact that we haven’t been through a select committee process and we don’t have a regulatory impact statement, can the Minister take us through all of those 33 existing cases?
veracity.explanation: The figure of 33 current pay equity claims matches the number widely reported around this bill.

veracity.statement: One thing I do want to make clear right from the start is that we are not taking away a pay equity regime. We still maintain as a Government that we wish to not see discrimination based on sex. That is why the pay equity system will still remain in place.
veracity.explanation: Literally true that a regime remains, but glosses over that the changes materially narrow access — missing context.

veracity.statement: It is also the case that having a 70 percent threshold is not out of alignment with what we’ve seen internationally. If you look at Manitoba, Canada, they also have a 70 percent threshold for sex-based discrimination.
veracity.explanation: Manitoba's pay equity framework does use a female-predominance threshold, but citing one jurisdiction as 'international alignment' overstates the support.

veracity.statement: The National Party’s original intention when they introduced the law had a threshold of, I believe, 66 percent, which was lowered by the Labour Government down to 60 percent.
veracity.explanation: A factual historical claim about prior thresholds; hedged with 'I believe' and broadly consistent with the legislative history.

veracity.statement: this is Budget-sensitive information, which I cannot disclose. What I can say, though, is that pay equity claims have been concentrated in the public sector, and costs to the Crown have become significant. My policy changes will have a significant reduction in costs to the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that pay equity claims have concentrated in the public sector; the 'significant reduction' is an unquantified assertion.

veracity.statement: New Zealand’s pay equity system is actually quite unique in terms of international comparisons. The UK and Ireland don’t allow multi-employer claims. They also don’t allow any claims to be made outside of a person’s or the claimant’s workforce... Australia does allow multi-employer claims, but they are usually progressed through a different system... which is the awards system.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate characterisation of the UK/Ireland/Australia systems relative to NZ's.

veracity.statement: When we had that 60 percent threshold, we were successful in getting pay equity claims through, which tells me... that things were working in this space, and are working.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that multiple pay equity claims were successfully settled under the 60% threshold.

veracity.statement: when you look at the successful claims of support staff in schools, of science technicians in schools, all of those claims that came through, we saw a change in those workforces. We saw that predominantly female workforce change for the better because of those successful pay equity claims.
veracity.explanation: School support staff and related education-sector pay equity settlements did occur and improved pay for those workforces.

veracity.statement: I had a mother who worked as a teacher in the 1960s. She was paid a quarter what the male standing next to her was being paid for the same job because she was paid as a single person and the male was assumed to have a family of four, and the rate was set to actually be for the family of four.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with documented history of the 'family wage' and gendered pay differentials in mid-20th-century NZ teaching.

veracity.statement: we know many of our lowest-paid workers are Māori, and in terms of doing right by Māori and ensuring that they are paid appropriately—our wahine Māori are directly affected by this bill and the Treaty analysis was absolutely necessary.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with data showing Māori, and wāhine Māori in particular, are over-represented in low-paid and female-dominated work.

specificity.statement: the team at the Ministry of Social Development who have dealt with claims already—actually, with the announcement on Friday, as of 2 p.m. yesterday, they have had almost 350 top-up applications. That is delivering for survivors.
specificity.explanation: Precise count and timestamp for the top-up applications.

specificity.statement: I also want to make clear, as she asked me to pass on, that we still are yet to make decisions about those who were abused in faith-based environments.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific outstanding cohort but gives no timeframe or plan.

specificity.statement: MSD supported 71,000 people off benefit and into work, it answered close to 4 million phone calls, it funded community support services accessed by over 135,000 people, and it processed 242,600 student loan and student allowance applications.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures for outputs delivered.

specificity.statement: This on top of all the work that's well under way to reduce the number on jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by the year 2030.
specificity.explanation: Names a numeric target (50,000) and a date (2030).

specificity.statement: this $774 million package includes increasing the average redress payments for new claims from $19,180 to $30,000, so that's a significant increase in the average redress payment for new claims
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures for old and new average payments.

specificity.statement: It is also increasing the system capacity to process claims, from 1,350 to 2,150 per year, from 2027, to reduce wait times for current claimants
specificity.explanation: Precise capacity figures and a start year (2027).

specificity.statement: In 2023-24, the Ministry of Social Development's total revenue was $1.81 billion, which was 3.9 percent more than the previous year as expenditure increased 4.6 percent to $1.73 billion.
specificity.explanation: Precise revenue, expenditure and percentage-change figures.

specificity.statement: It's not easy doing what is right. It is not cheap, doing what is right.
specificity.explanation: Aphoristic generality about 'doing what is right' with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: we need a separate system, and we need the Government to do what they said they were going to do and create a new system.
specificity.explanation: Names the demanded deliverable (a separate/new redress system) but no mechanism or design detail.

civility.statement: Funnelling more money into systems that have harmed them in the past is, without question, the wrong call.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at the policy decision, not at any person; no insult.

civility.statement: instead, the Government have delivered nothing of what they promised—far from what survivors wanted.
civility.explanation: Overstated attack on the Government's record, but directed at the policy delivery rather than persons.

civility.statement: the previous Government received the royal commission redress interim report in December 2021. They had two years to implement a redress entity if they thought that it was important, but they didn't.
civility.explanation: Pointed attack on the previous Government's record, but grounded in dates and actions rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: So it is all very rich for the member to stand up and say that the current system is not appropriate when the previous Government did exactly the same thing after receiving the royal commission design report
civility.explanation: 'All very rich' is a sarcastic tu quoque jab, though it is tied to the opponent's record rather than a personal slur.

civility.statement: At the time, I said to the survivors who were listening in that I acknowledge them, their families, and their supporters. I said that waiting had not been easy.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of survivors and their difficult wait; wholly non-combative.

civility.statement: Seven hundred and seventy-four million dollars is woefully insignificant. It fails to meet the scale of harm done to these survivors, these children, and is well below the international standards for compensation.
civility.explanation: Strong criticism of the amount as tokenistic, but directed at the policy, not persons.

civility.statement: I call on the Government to return to the table and listen to survivors, and I call on my fellow members of the House to stand with me today in ensuring that the Government's response is not the final word on this matter.
civility.explanation: Invitational and respectful call to action rather than an attack.

civility.statement: The previous Government received that redress report and recommendations in December 2021. Then fast forward two years into 2024; the report was finally tabled in this House.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government's delay via the timeline, not via personal attack.

civility.statement: I think it is really important that we do not use this as a political football to kick around this House, using those very voices that we need to be listening to
civility.explanation: Calls for restraint and respect for survivors, but implicitly accuses opponents of exploiting survivors, which is mildly accusatory.

civility.statement: this is a violent regime of disrespect against survivors.
civility.explanation: Inflammatory 'violent regime' characterisation aimed at the Government rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: the Minister should be ashamed—deeply ashamed—just as every other complicit member of Parliament in the coalition Government should be, too.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on the Minister and coalition members ('complicit', 'ashamed').

civility.statement: This Government has offered band-aids for bullet wounds
civility.explanation: A vivid metaphor criticising the policy; more colourful hyperbole than personal insult.

civility.statement: It's only 18 months in, and this is where it's at, at this incredibly insensitive level.
civility.explanation: Charged criticism ('insensitive') of the Government's conduct, bordering on characterising motive but tied to the decision.

civility.statement: I reject the characterisation of this debate and the objection of the Opposition to what has been announced as somehow 'looking for a perfect solution'.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of opponents' argument rather than attacking them personally.

civility.statement: This is an enormous piece of work. It won't be just our Government but Governments of the future, and I think we should focus on the survivors, not on politics.
civility.explanation: Non-combative, calls for focus on survivors over point-scoring.

civility.statement: The member again provides misleading information. The sanctions are only if people don't fulfil their work obligations. They're not sanctioned if they can't find a job.
civility.explanation: Opens by accusing the member of 'misleading information', a mild character-adjacent jab, though aimed at the argument.

civility.statement: what I am seeing is a welfare regime that sanctions people when there is not even enough jobs for every single person who is receiving income support.
civility.explanation: Critiques the policy regime, not the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Why would you go back to your oppressor, with your hands out asking for some crumbs?
civility.explanation: Charged metaphor aimed at the policy of routing redress through the same agencies, not a personal insult.

rigor.statement: Funnelling more money into systems that have harmed them in the past is, without question, the wrong call.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a conclusion 'without question' with reference to past harm, but no evidence marshalled for why topping up cannot work.

rigor.statement: here are some things that we can do now in moving the system towards that end goal. It may well be that in the future, we move to an independent system, but here is what we can do now, we can do quickly, we can get in place so that we can prioritise that certainty and surety for survivors
rigor.explanation: Lays out a reasoned incrementalist argument (act now, evolve later) with a stated trade-off, though the claim that a new system 'may not get us the outcomes' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: the previous Government received the royal commission redress interim report in December 2021. They had two years to implement a redress entity if they thought that it was important, but they didn't.
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific dates and actions to rebut the charge of inaction, a fairly evidence-based argument.

rigor.statement: So it is all very rich for the member to stand up and say that the current system is not appropriate when the previous Government did exactly the same thing after receiving the royal commission design report
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque line of argument—the previous Government's conduct doesn't itself establish the current policy is right, but it is anchored to a real record.

rigor.statement: Of the 138 recommendations made, 105 directly relate to the Government. Of these, only twelve—12—were fully accepted
rigor.explanation: Uses numeric evidence to support the 'not progress' conclusion.

rigor.statement: Seven hundred and seventy-four million dollars is woefully insignificant. It fails to meet the scale of harm done to these survivors, these children, and is well below the international standards for compensation.
rigor.explanation: Backs the claim with an authority (redress design group co-chair) but leans on 'woefully insignificant' rhetoric rather than figures.

rigor.statement: I would rather that all of that $774 million be invested into the survivors than building up a new system that may take years when these survivors have waited long enough to have their claims addressed.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned prioritisation (money to survivors vs to system-building), though it frames the choice as somewhat binary.

rigor.statement: we cannot risk harming those who are seeking support and guidance by making this all about what is missed out and not about what is being delivered... instead of sitting in a paralysis of the perfect solution, is not let that perfect be the enemy of the good.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the 'perfect enemy of the good' aphorism rather than evidence for why the incremental option is adequate.

rigor.statement: $744 million split across 200,000 survivors of abuse in State and faith-based care equates to only $30,000 each.
rigor.explanation: The calculation muddles total fund, claimant numbers and average payment to produce a misleading per-person figure.

rigor.statement: this is a violent regime of disrespect against survivors.
rigor.explanation: Pure emotive/hyperbolic assertion with no supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: This Government has offered band-aids for bullet wounds
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical analogy standing in for an evidenced argument about adequacy.

rigor.statement: I reject the characterisation of this debate and the objection of the Opposition to what has been announced as somehow 'looking for a perfect solution'.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the Government's 'perfect vs good' framing, arguing survivors seek a merely half-decent, non-retraumatising system—a reasoned counter.

rigor.statement: if you're a young person in Auckland, you probably haven't got a lot to put on that CV. And you could write as many CVs as you like and you're not going to move in the stack.
rigor.explanation: Makes a plausible structural point that CV-building can't overcome insufficient job demand, but rests on illustrative reasoning rather than data.

rigor.statement: the Government was faced with a difficult choice. Does the Government spend more time and money on setting up a new scheme, or does it provide more to survivors now through the current redress process?
rigor.explanation: Frames the decision as a binary (new scheme vs money to survivors now), a false dichotomy that the Opposition disputes, since a new system could also deliver payments.

rigor.statement: what I am seeing is a welfare regime that sanctions people when there is not even enough jobs for every single person who is receiving income support.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument that sanctions premised on job-seeking are unfair if jobs are scarcer than jobseekers; the logic follows, though he asserts rather than quantifies the shortfall.

rigor.statement: I want to ask about whether her directive asking to apply sanctions more often has directly contributed to the recent statistics that came out that show that food insecurity is increasing in Aotearoa.
rigor.explanation: Proposes a causal link (sanctions → food insecurity) and cites recent statistics, but leaves the causal claim to be tested rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: In the annual review debate on housing, we heard that everyone who has a genuine need has been granted emergency housing. Can I ask the Minister, therefore: does everyone declined for emergency housing not have a genuine need?
rigor.explanation: Sharp reductio exposing the logical implication of the Government's 'genuine need' claim, a valid probing of the premise.

rigor.statement: Why would you go back to your oppressor, with your hands out asking for some crumbs?
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical question built on an emotive 'oppressor/crumbs' framing rather than reasoned analysis of the redress design.

charisma.statement: Funnelling more money into systems that have harmed them in the past is, without question, the wrong call.
charisma.explanation: Combative framing that rallies opposition rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: We offered to take politics off the table and to work with the Government to make sure we lived up to the words in our formal apologies last year, but the Government chose not to take up this offer.
charisma.explanation: Frames a cross-party offer to collaborate, an attempt at bridge-building, though it also casts the Government as the refuser.

charisma.statement: here are some things that we can do now in moving the system towards that end goal. It may well be that in the future, we move to an independent system, but here is what we can do now, we can do quickly, we can get in place so that we can prioritise that certainty and surety for survivors
charisma.explanation: Measured and confident, acknowledges the future independent-system goal, but largely defends the Government's own position.

charisma.statement: At the time, I said to the survivors who were listening in that I acknowledge them, their families, and their supporters. I said that waiting had not been easy.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic, inclusive tone that seeks to bring the affected audience along.

charisma.statement: I call on the Government to return to the table and listen to survivors, and I call on my fellow members of the House to stand with me today in ensuring that the Government's response is not the final word on this matter.
charisma.explanation: Appeals across the House to unite behind survivors—an attempt to build cross-bench consensus.

charisma.statement: I would rather that all of that $774 million be invested into the survivors than building up a new system that may take years when these survivors have waited long enough to have their claims addressed.
charisma.explanation: Frames the choice as survivor-centred but largely defends the Government line.

charisma.statement: compensation is not just about money. Redress is not just about money. It's also about knowing that our voices are being heard
charisma.explanation: Empathetic framing that acknowledges survivors' non-financial needs.

charisma.statement: I think it is really important that we do not use this as a political football to kick around this House, using those very voices that we need to be listening to
charisma.explanation: Appeals for a less partisan tone, yet can read as deflecting legitimate scrutiny.

charisma.statement: this is a violent regime of disrespect against survivors.
charisma.explanation: Highly divisive, us-vs-them framing.

charisma.statement: the Minister should be ashamed—deeply ashamed—just as every other complicit member of Parliament in the coalition Government should be, too.
charisma.explanation: Alienating and combative; shuts down cross-party dialogue.

charisma.statement: It's only 18 months in, and this is where it's at, at this incredibly insensitive level.
charisma.explanation: Rallies the Opposition side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: This is an enormous piece of work. It won't be just our Government but Governments of the future, and I think we should focus on the survivors, not on politics.
charisma.explanation: Appeals for a survivor-focused, less partisan approach, but also functions to blunt opposition scrutiny.

charisma.statement: Why would you go back to your oppressor, with your hands out asking for some crumbs?
charisma.explanation: Emotive appeal to his own side rather than a bridge to opponents.

charisma.statement: It's not easy doing what is right. It is not cheap, doing what is right.
charisma.explanation: Moralising rhetorical flourish that appeals to the Opposition benches.

charisma.statement: we need a separate system, and we need the Government to do what they said they were going to do and create a new system.
charisma.explanation: A demand that rallies his side around the promise-vs-delivery gap rather than persuading the Government.

strength.statement: it is our intention to have a new single redress system operating next year.
strength.explanation: Commitment (Nov 2024) to stand up a new single redress system in 2025; the actual May 2025 delivery topped up the existing agencies rather than the independent new system, so follow-through fell short of the words.

strength.statement: But what we do know—rather than heckling in this House—is that we have invested $774 million into a process, into redress, into something that is tangible that we can say there are some actions under way.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete allocation with early implementation, though the flagship independent system was not delivered.

strength.statement: the team at the Ministry of Social Development who have dealt with claims already—actually, with the announcement on Friday, as of 2 p.m. yesterday, they have had almost 350 top-up applications. That is delivering for survivors.
strength.explanation: Points to early concrete uptake as evidence of delivery, though it is the topped-up existing scheme, not the promised new system.

strength.statement: This on top of all the work that's well under way to reduce the number on jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by the year 2030.
strength.explanation: A stated target described as 'under way'; delivery is in progress and unproven, and jobseeker numbers were rising per the debate.

authenticity.statement: it is our intention to have a new single redress system operating next year.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between the promised 'new single redress system' and the Government's subsequent decision to invest in the existing system survivors distrust.

forthrightness.statement: I also want to make clear, as she asked me to pass on, that we still are yet to make decisions about those who were abused in faith-based environments.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes an unresolved gap (faith-based redress) that the Opposition had criticised, rather than glossing over it.

forthrightness.statement: The member again provides misleading information. The sanctions are only if people don't fulfil their work obligations. They're not sanctioned if they can't find a job.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the sanctions critique by clarifying the trigger, but sidesteps March's actual question of whether a job exists for every beneficiary.

forthrightness.statement: no, Police has not changed its response to violent crime in the home. They’ll still respond where there is violence in the home. Yes, they are triaging their calls better. They are making sure they are going, again, to jobs that require a police intervention.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to a member's concern about police response to family harm, he answers directly with a clear 'no' and explains the triaging change rather than deflecting.

veracity.statement: no, Police has not changed its response to violent crime in the home. They’ll still respond where there is violence in the home. Yes, they are triaging their calls better. They are making sure they are going, again, to jobs that require a police intervention.
veracity.explanation: Factual assertion that police response to in-home violence is unchanged; plausible but a self-reported claim not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: The measure for violent crime is survey based, so it’s not affected by police attendance. That does not have an impact at all—
veracity.explanation: Accurate methodological point — the main violent-crime measure (NZ Crime and Victims Survey) is survey-based and independent of police attendance rates.

veracity.statement: The only difference is that we have got the prosecution uplift programme that the Police are rolling out. It’s proving to be very effective. It’s building in major efficiencies between Police and the courts system, and we’ve reinvested in that and that is starting to deliver some outstanding results for us.
veracity.explanation: Self-assessment ('very effective', 'outstanding results') presented as fact without supporting data; boosterish and unverifiable.

veracity.statement: The latest survey out from the data is that retail crime has continued to increase during the term of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Cites survey data on rising retail crime; directionally supported by some measures but retail-crime trends are mixed and the specific survey is not identified.

veracity.statement: Police have raised some reasonably serious concerns regarding public safety in the implementation of this law change. ... Police are not convinced that the benefits of these changes outweigh the potential risks. So that’s the Police themselves.
veracity.explanation: Attributes concerns to Police advice on the citizen's-arrest provision; consistent with reported official concerns, though the wording paraphrases.

veracity.statement: Police have also said that there’s a fair chance that when they turn up, they might arrest the retail owner for kidnapping.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a striking scenario to Police; the kidnapping-risk point reflects real concerns raised about citizen's-arrest powers but is stated in a dramatic, unqualified way.

civility.statement: some groups find change hard. They’ve got very used to the police doing things that the police have taken on that they perhaps shouldn’t be doing.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive of critics ('some groups find change hard') but frames it around workload/policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Firstly, I want to thank the Minister for not wasting any more resources or time on a second review of the gun registry.
civility.explanation: Opens by thanking the Minister across party lines and engages on the substance of policy, showing respect.

civility.statement: Police have raised some reasonably serious concerns regarding public safety in the implementation of this law change. ... Police are not convinced that the benefits of these changes outweigh the potential risks. So that’s the Police themselves.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused challenge that grounds criticism in official Police advice rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Police have also said that there’s a fair chance that when they turn up, they might arrest the retail owner for kidnapping.
civility.explanation: A pointed, somewhat sensational framing but attributed to Police advice rather than being a personal attack.

specificity.statement: some groups find change hard. They’ve got very used to the police doing things that the police have taken on that they perhaps shouldn’t be doing.
specificity.explanation: Vague references to 'some groups' and 'things that the police have taken on' with no concrete detail on which functions or groups.

specificity.statement: The only difference is that we have got the prosecution uplift programme that the Police are rolling out. It’s proving to be very effective. It’s building in major efficiencies between Police and the courts system, and we’ve reinvested in that and that is starting to deliver some outstanding results for us.
specificity.explanation: Names the prosecution uplift programme but offers no figures, timeframes, or concrete metrics for the 'outstanding results'.

specificity.statement: The latest survey out from the data is that retail crime has continued to increase during the term of this Government.
specificity.explanation: References 'the latest survey' and a direction of change but gives no figures, source, or magnitude.

rigor.statement: The measure for violent crime is survey based, so it’s not affected by police attendance. That does not have an impact at all—
rigor.explanation: Uses a valid methodological distinction to rebut the implied link between reduced attendance and the crime measure; reasoning is sound though briefly stated.

rigor.statement: those of us who have the privilege of being gun owners have also a responsibility to ensure public safety, and keeping tabs on where guns are, who has them, is a really important part of that, and where they are stored.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned case linking gun-owner responsibility to the public-safety value of tracking firearm location and storage.

rigor.statement: Police have raised some reasonably serious concerns regarding public safety in the implementation of this law change. ... Police are not convinced that the benefits of these changes outweigh the potential risks. So that’s the Police themselves.
rigor.explanation: Backs the critique with a specific evidentiary source (Police advice weighing benefits against risks) and asks the Minister to engage with it.

strength.statement: The only difference is that we have got the prosecution uplift programme that the Police are rolling out. It’s proving to be very effective. It’s building in major efficiencies between Police and the courts system, and we’ve reinvested in that and that is starting to deliver some outstanding results for us.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a named programme that is 'rolling out' and 'starting to deliver' — in-progress delivery rather than a completed, verified outcome.

charisma.statement: Firstly, I want to thank the Minister for not wasting any more resources or time on a second review of the gun registry.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement of a government decision he agrees with, building goodwill rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: those of us who have the privilege of being gun owners have also a responsibility to ensure public safety, and keeping tabs on where guns are, who has them, is a really important part of that, and where they are stored.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'those of us' framing that ties a shared privilege to shared responsibility, appealing beyond one camp.

authenticity.statement: those of us who have the privilege of being gun owners have also a responsibility to ensure public safety, and keeping tabs on where guns are, who has them, is a really important part of that, and where they are stored.
authenticity.explanation: As a self-identified gun owner he supports the registry, framing his position as consistent with his own responsibilities rather than special-interest advantage.

divination.statement: is there a risk that the registry could be moved to another agency other than the Police? Because if this were to happen, it would—certainly as we’ve heard—put the police at greater risk when they’re investigating where guns are or dealing with criminal activity.
divination.explanation: Conditional prediction that moving the registry from Police would increase risk to officers; plausible directionally but hypothetical and unquantified.

forthrightness.statement: I don't have the specific numbers right in front of me of how many reports have come in. If you would like an answer to that I welcome you to just write and ask for those numbers and I shall get them to you.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for specific report numbers, she does not provide them but genuinely offers to supply them on request rather than pivoting to talking points; a partial, good-faith non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: It's also true that I said I was interested in looking into changes to pay equity. Now, I think it's really important to note that that does not mean that that started at that point. This was simply setting out the areas of interest I had... my real work on this area started at the end point of 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses Tinetti's question about when the work started, giving a timeframe (end of 2024) and distinguishing interest from active work, though the distinction is somewhat convenient.

forthrightness.statement: I can't speak to any particular costs. As the member will be aware, we are in a period of Budget sensitivity, and it would not be appropriate for me to give those costs.
forthrightness.explanation: Xu-Nan asked a specific question about the estimated cost of the 33 claims; she declines to answer, citing Budget sensitivity, without providing the figure.

forthrightness.statement: it's not possible to note how many people may or may not be able to take a pay equity claim, because I don't have a crystal ball into the future... There are too many hypotheticals, including whether or not people even wish to continue to progress, to suggest that anyone would or would not miss out.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked how many women would lose out; she declines to give any number, reframing the question as unanswerable rather than engaging its core.

forthrightness.statement: The only one that really comes to mind is that the costs to date to the Crown from the settlements had been $1.78 billion.
forthrightness.explanation: Having earlier declined cost questions, she does supply a specific past-cost figure when pressed.

forthrightness.statement: my officials have provided—180,000 people potentially under those claims. However, that is an estimate.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Tinetti's persistent question about numbers of people represented with an actual figure.

forthrightness.statement: I believe that around 175,000 people had their pay corrected in 15 settlements and one extension in March 2024. The Public Service Commission believes that is still an accurate figure.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Tinetti's repeated question about the number who received pay corrections up to the Budget.

forthrightness.statement: we have gone out for consultation on engineered stone. My understanding of where we are in that process now is that we have received the submissions and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment is working its way through to analyse those submissions. So I haven't yet received any information on my desk as to what the feedback is.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly reports the status (consultation done, submissions under analysis) but honestly cannot yet answer whether engineered stone will be banned.

forthrightness.statement: The Fast Track programme is the responsibility of Oranga Tamariki; that is where the funding sits for that. There certainly has not been a reduction in any funding for our front-line police officers and the engagement that they have with our youth.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Paul's question about where the Fast Track funding went and addresses the funding-reduction concern head-on.

forthrightness.statement: I don't accept for one minute that we have a racist police force; in fact, quite the opposite... In terms of Understanding Police Delivery, that was a piece of work that was commissioned under the last Government; that is not my report. It's not something I asked for... So that's their report.
forthrightness.explanation: States his view on racism plainly, but sidesteps Paul's specific questions about what actions Police took in response to the report's findings by distancing himself from the report.

forthrightness.statement: the police use their discretion in every situation that they deal with... they're pretty sensitive in the way they do that. Kids shouldn't be in gang insignia. They shouldn't be walking around in gang insignia. They become a target themselves... the police will not do it off the profiling of people's skin colour or ethnicity.
forthrightness.explanation: Maipi-Clarke asked what safeguards prevent innocent children being falsely profiled; he asserts police discretion and shifts partial responsibility to the child ('kids shouldn't be in gang insignia') rather than naming a mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: firstly, I've been very clear that yes, I support the firearms register. It is going to be a really useful tool for us to be able to track and have a clear picture of where firearms are, who has got them, who is in possession of them... The register must stay.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Andersen's registry question with an unambiguous 'yes' and states plainly the register must stay.

specificity.statement: we are bringing back Oranga Tamariki to their core purpose and making sure there is a real focus on safety and wellbeing and making sure that young people that do come into care are safe in care and we're not just removing them from one bad situation and putting them into another.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (refocus on safety/core purpose) but names no mechanism, measure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: the first actions I took were to repeal the fair pay agreements and also extend the 90-day trials to all businesses.
specificity.explanation: Names specific named policies (fair pay agreements repeal, 90-day trials extended to all businesses).

specificity.statement: in order to find sex-based discrimination, we believe that a sufficient time period must pass in order to find an evidential basis for sex-based discrimination to return. A period of time of three years is actually a very short amount of time.
specificity.explanation: References concrete review periods (three years vs a longer period) and the mechanism, but no data or thresholds.

specificity.statement: The only one that really comes to mind is that the costs to date to the Crown from the settlements had been $1.78 billion.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise dollar figure for settlements to date.

specificity.statement: my officials have provided—180,000 people potentially under those claims. However, that is an estimate.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete headcount figure for the claims.

specificity.statement: I believe that around 175,000 people had their pay corrected in 15 settlements and one extension in March 2024. The Public Service Commission believes that is still an accurate figure.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 175,000 people, 15 settlements, one extension, dated March 2024, with a source cited.

specificity.statement: the Minister said in the last week that pay equity had been under way since—or had been on her agenda since—the end of 2023. charisma.statement: This Parliament, no matter what side of the political spectrum you come from, must act now to protect our most vulnerable.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly cross-party and inclusive, inviting all sides to a shared cause rather than attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: What we want to do and what we must do is we must make sure that we get the right settings in place, that we don’t just act out of fear and concern and just rush in a piece of legislation that may not work.
charisma.explanation: Reasonable, consensus-oriented tone inviting careful shared deliberation.

charisma.statement: Of course we have seen Labour’s coalition partner, the de-growth Greens, come out with their alternative budget, which focuses on taxing people more and letting debt skyrocket. I think we call it green waste.
charisma.explanation: A partisan applause line that rallies his own side by belittling opponents; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: It is time we stood up as a Parliament. It is time that we said we will come together on this and not play short-term politics.
charisma.explanation: A unifying call for Parliament to come together, though framed within an adversarial speech blaming the other side.

charisma.statement: The only “c” word that’s done more damage to us here in Aotearoa is “colonisation”.
charisma.explanation: A memorable reframing line that appeals strongly to his own base but does not reach across the aisle.

charisma.statement: Self-determination is not divisive. It means Māori designing solutions for Māori, based on our own tikanga, values, and aspirations. It means a future where both Te Tiriti partners thrive in their own right and in mutual respect.
charisma.explanation: Reframes a contested term inclusively, invoking mutual respect and both partners thriving, though within a combative overall speech.

charisma.statement: I can absolutely reassure the House that this was a search for the right person for this job as a result of an absolute understanding of the importance of the role... we have arrived at a decision that has put the right person in this role for the next seven years, Grant Taylor.
charisma.explanation: A cross-party endorsement affirming a collaborative, non-political appointment process; builds consensus around a shared institution.

rigor.statement: What we want to do and what we must do is we must make sure that we get the right settings in place, that we don’t just act out of fear and concern and just rush in a piece of legislation that may not work.
rigor.explanation: Measured reasoning that cautions against reactive legislating and prioritises getting settings right; sensible though not evidence-heavy.

rigor.statement: Just last week in this House, we saw this Government urgently rush through law that means that low-paid women are bearing the burden of this Government’s tax cuts for the wealthy.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a burden-shifting link without laying out the fiscal evidence connecting the two measures.

rigor.statement: It is insulting to hear this Prime Minister declare that New Zealand has been living beyond its means when so many families who are doing their best are struggling to make ends meet.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an emotional appeal (struggling families) to counter a macroeconomic claim rather than engaging the economic argument.

rigor.statement: The reason they put this through in urgency was it silenced voices. It silences the opposition that was going to be seen against this bill.
rigor.explanation: Attributes a single motive (silencing dissent) to the use of urgency without evidence ruling out other reasons.

rigor.statement: It costs money to rectify inequality, but when you do rectify inequality, there are social and fiscal economic benefits for all, and they will ripple right through the community.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned cost-benefit argument, but the claimed downstream benefits are asserted rather than evidenced in the statement itself.

rigor.statement: The job-evaluation process is not about that. It examines the skill, the responsibility, the effort, the experience, and the conditions of work, and it is an extremely robust process that was happening.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the comparator criticism by explaining the actual evaluation criteria, an evidence-based clarification of how assessment works.

rigor.statement: this Government favours the ultra-wealthy big business over the voice of community.
rigor.explanation: Broad motive attribution stated as a given rather than argued from evidence.

rigor.statement: They have managed to find hundreds of millions of dollars for tobacco companies, but at the same time, they give with one hand to tobacco companies and take with the other from the pockets of working women.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes two unrelated fiscal decisions to imply a trade-off without establishing they are actually linked.

rigor.statement: We have seen, since that last Act was passed, 10 settlements that have valued the historically underpaid work of working women. That shows that this process is working.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete count of settlements as evidence that the process functioned, a reasonable evidentiary inference.

authenticity.statement: Let’s reflect on Budget 2024. This Government promised tax relief and delivered it. We promised no new taxes and we delivered it. divination.statement: It costs money to rectify inequality, but when you do rectify inequality, there are social and fiscal economic benefits for all, and they will ripple right through the community.

divination.statement: The legislation will be introduced to the House in the next few months.
