divination.statement: Recently, I announced the next big step for open banking in New Zealand. Cabinet has now signed off on the regulations for open banking, and we're now on a clear path to delivering more choice and better service for Kiwi consumers. The major banks will have until December to get ready for open banking, and that means that there will be certainty that open banking will be live by this Christmas.
divination.explanation: 'Open banking will be live by this Christmas' is a specific, falsifiable near-term prediction backed by a regulatory timetable.

strength.statement: Our work programme is defined by pace, clarity, and outcomes and is delivering exactly what we said we would. We're investing nearly $100 million to ensure that extra help with maths is available across all stages of primary and intermediate schooling so that children get the extra help they need, an approach we're already delivering in reading. We're embedding financial education into the curriculum so students are taught how to budget, save, invest, and understand things like insurance and loans.
strength.explanation: Claims active delivery (maths funding, financial education) with a named investment, though delivery is in progress rather than fully completed.

strength.statement: Twenty-thousand teachers have received high-quality professional development in structured literacy, 15,000 have received structured training in maths, and over 836,000 maths resources have been delivered to students and teachers in primary and intermediate to support the new world-leading maths curriculum. We've delivered on our promise to remove the cost of teacher registration and practising certificates, and that is just the start.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete completed delivery, including a fulfilled promise (removing teacher registration cost).

strength.statement: Yes. Prioritising disabled people, their families, and carers is a priority for this Government, and that's why we provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to Disability Support Services in Budget 2024. The state of affairs left by the last Government needed immediate action to stabilise the disability support system. Just announced today in Budget 2025, the Government has provided $190 million of social investment for vulnerable New Zealanders, including support for Autism New Zealand's early screening and intervention programme.
strength.explanation: Points to concrete delivered funding ($1.1b in 2024, $190m in 2025) backing the stated priority.

strength.statement: During the first month of the traffic light system, obligation failures decreased by 9 percent. Between January and March this year, over 23,000 people cancelled their benefit because they found work. This is an 11 percent increase on the same period from 2024.
strength.explanation: Cites concrete results to argue the welfare reforms are delivering, though causal attribution is asserted.

strength.statement: The Government continues to progress its plan to restore law and order with vigour. We've given Police the additional powers they need to disrupt the activities of gangs. We stopped taxpayers funding the proliferation of cultural reports. We've made sweeping reform to the Sentencing Act to put more serious offenders in prison for longer by restoring three strikes and restricting sentencing discounts by adding additional aggravating factors so that offenders are more appropriately held to account. Our target to reduce the number of victims shows this is working, with more than 28,000 fewer victims recorded in the latest stats.
strength.explanation: Lists concrete enacted measures (gang powers, cultural-report funding cut, Sentencing Act reform, three strikes) rather than mere aspirations.

strength.statement: Recently, I announced the next big step for open banking in New Zealand. Cabinet has now signed off on the regulations for open banking, and we're now on a clear path to delivering more choice and better service for Kiwi consumers. The major banks will have until December to get ready for open banking, and that means that there will be certainty that open banking will be live by this Christmas.
strength.explanation: Reports a concrete step delivered (Cabinet sign-off on regulations) with a set deadline, though full delivery is pending.

strength.statement: Last month, I announced new regulations that will create infringement offences for dog owners who cause their animals harm by leaving them chained up for days on end. Regulations will prohibit chaining vulnerable dogs, like pregnant or young animals, except for very temporary situations, and will give enforcement agencies real teeth to intervene swiftly where there is clearly observable harm associated with the long-term chaining.
strength.explanation: Announced regulations with a concrete mechanism (infringement offences), though this is an announcement rather than fully implemented law.

veracity.statement: New Zealand faces a significant infrastructure deficit. This has spanned generations and different Governments. To acknowledge that fact, to admit that fact, is not a politically partisan point; it is, in fact, simply reality.
veracity.explanation: NZ's infrastructure deficit is widely documented (e.g. Infrastructure Commission reports); accurate and non-misleading.

veracity.statement: take, for example, the previous National Government that brought in “sweat the assets” on the roading infrastructure and then increased the tonnage of the trucks. That actually led to the rapid decline in the roading network that we’re facing across this country
veracity.explanation: Heavier vehicle mass limits did increase road wear, but attributing the network's decline chiefly to this is a contested single-cause claim.

veracity.statement: The National Party and ACT—and New Zealand First too—criticised and slammed the Labour Government for its water initiatives, called “three waters”, and said it would throw that out and would put other alternative initiatives in place. We’re yet to see them.
veracity.explanation: The coalition did repeal Three Waters; replacement policy was at an early stage in 2025, so 'yet to see' is broadly defensible though somewhat understated.

veracity.statement: the vast majority of the transport projects listed in Schedule 2 do not do that. They certainly don’t make improvements in a cost-effective way, and we know that from initial cost-benefit analysis.
veracity.explanation: Several RoNS have had weak benefit-cost ratios, but 'vast majority don't stack up' overstates what the cited analysis shows.

veracity.statement: it is going to come at a cost of hundreds and probably hundreds of millions of dollars because of one person holding out in terms of the Public Works Act.
veracity.explanation: Mt Messenger costs did escalate, but pinning 'hundreds of millions' on one holdout landowner is an exaggerated attribution.

veracity.statement: There’s about 66 million acres of land in this country and, before the signing of the Treaty, Māori owned them all.
veracity.explanation: NZ's land area is roughly 66 million acres and Māori held customary title to all of it before 1840 — broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Māori have suffered loss of land from the Crown through the Public Works Act since 1864, and the scale of that land was probably somewhere in the range of 20 million acres, leading into the 1900s—20 million acres.
veracity.explanation: Massive Māori land loss is real, but the ~20 million acres attributed specifically to the Public Works Act is a hedged ('probably') and likely overstated figure conflating multiple mechanisms.

veracity.statement: do you know what the Public Works Act allowed the Government to do? To put paper roads through that land and carve it up, because the Government was able to then go and take land that was 5 acres either side of that road, even if the road wasn’t built.
veracity.explanation: Historical public works legislation did permit taking of land adjoining roads; the specific '5 acres either side' reflects historical provisions and is broadly credible.

veracity.statement: If you look at the estimates from the Infrastructure Commission, or independent consultant estimates, the need for infrastructure around this country is running into the hundreds of billions of dollars, so I support this bill.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Infrastructure Commission estimates of a multi-hundred-billion-dollar infrastructure need.

veracity.statement: it does identify that depending on the final decisions that are taken, any roads of national significance that are due for construction over that three-year period will need to acquire around 500 properties.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the figure to the bill's RIS, an identifiable and checkable source.

veracity.statement: Gambling is like an addictive substance. It is something that people get into a habit of and find it very hard to stop. It has similar effects on the brain as addictive substances. It is like a stimulant; the thrill of losing and the thrill of winning have a similar chemical effect.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with neuroscience: gambling activates reward pathways similarly to addictive substances.

veracity.statement: From memory, as much as 40 percent of the income of tennis in New Zealand comes from gambling, which is notable.
veracity.explanation: Self-hedged ('from memory') and unverified; a precise 40% figure stated with acknowledged uncertainty.

veracity.statement: betting out of New Zealand on matters such as the NBA finals, which are taking place right now, causes a significant spike in the betting.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with known patterns that major sporting events drive betting surges.

veracity.statement: what actually happened is that the offshore operators, effectively, have captured the market, and TAB was not able to continue to fund the racing industry, which relies very heavily on the TAB revenue to operate.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate account of offshore operators eroding TAB's revenue base and the racing industry's dependence on it.

veracity.statement: when you’re gambling online, through an account, the ability to track gambling behaviour is greatly enhanced, so the TAB and anyone else in that space is able to see problem-gambling behaviour, see repeated gambling, and see the time at which people are gambling
veracity.explanation: Accurate: account-based online betting does generate trackable behavioural data enabling problem-gambling detection.

civility.statement: New Zealand faces a significant infrastructure deficit. This has spanned generations and different Governments. To acknowledge that fact, to admit that fact, is not a politically partisan point; it is, in fact, simply reality.
civility.explanation: Explicitly frames the problem as bipartisan and shared, avoiding blame — respectful, policy-focused.

civility.explanation: Respectfully acknowledges historic land grievance and preserves protections, engaging substance not personalities.

civility.statement: The Labour Party will support this piece of legislation, but we do expect the select committee to scrutinise this very carefully, because there are some serious questions that need to be answered.
civility.explanation: Constructive, offers support while flagging legitimate concerns for scrutiny — no personal attack.

civility.statement: take, for example, the previous National Government that brought in “sweat the assets” on the roading infrastructure and then increased the tonnage of the trucks. That actually led to the rapid decline in the roading network that we’re facing across this country
civility.explanation: Criticises a past policy decision rather than a person, though framed as a partisan jab.

civility.statement: people who think that they’ve got better protection for their property rights, through the RMA reform, are being misled by this Government once again.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of misleading people 'once again' — imputes bad faith rather than engaging the argument.

civility.statement: The National Party and ACT—and New Zealand First too—criticised and slammed the Labour Government for its water initiatives, called “three waters”, and said it would throw that out and would put other alternative initiatives in place. We’re yet to see them.

civility.statement: It’s actually a bit deranged what’s happening. It’s a bit deranged the way they’re so convinced that a four-lane highway is the answer to any problem in the absence of any actual economic analysis.

civility.statement: Go learn something about transport economics.
civility.explanation: Condescending instruction to opponents, dismissive rather than engaging their reasoning.

civility.statement: This is just a Government that is very autocratic and seems to hate the environment and has no concept of the challenges that are actually facing us.
civility.explanation: Sweeping character judgement ('autocratic', 'hate the environment') — an attack on motive, not policy.

civility.statement: I was really sorry that Government MPs did not vote for my colleague Hūhana Lyndon’s member’s bill that would have righted a historical wrong and made sure that Māori land was no longer taken in the same way under the Public Works Act.

civility.statement: So what this bill does is it streamlines the objections process that is experienced when the step of land acquisition comes, and it also introduces some incentives. So what we want to see is that the process is faster but, at the same time, the process is fairer as well.
civility.explanation: Measured, substance-focused, no attacks.

civility.statement: Catch up, junior—you’ll learn about this. You obviously weren’t paying any attention this morning.
civility.explanation: Direct personal put-down ('junior', 'weren't paying attention') aimed at a member — not substance.

civility.statement: don’t throw your things around from that side of the House, because you know absolutely nothing about it.

civility.statement: Māori want roads, too.

civility.statement: I want to reassure people that you’ll get a fair hearing at the select committee, so I’d like to encourage people to submit on this bill.

civility.statement: Yes, I understand what the Government is doing. I understand that they’re moving things through faster. I understand that. But it can’t come at the expense of democracy. civility.explanation: Acknowledges the Government's intent before raising concerns — measured and fair.

civility.statement: will that data be transparently afforded to the New Zealand public? Is it data that could be reviewed and analysed by this House? Is it data that can continue to inform this House’s deliberation on the regulations moving forward?
civility.explanation: Raises a transparency concern constructively as questions to inform future deliberation, not as an attack.

charisma.statement: New Zealand faces a significant infrastructure deficit. This has spanned generations and different Governments. To acknowledge that fact, to admit that fact, is not a politically partisan point; it is, in fact, simply reality.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-building: acknowledges the deficit spans all governments, inviting cross-party agreement rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: The Labour Party will support this piece of legislation, but we do expect the select committee to scrutinise this very carefully, because there are some serious questions that need to be answered.
charisma.explanation: Bipartisan tone, backing a government bill while reserving critique, seeks a workable outcome.

charisma.statement: I want to reassure people that you’ll get a fair hearing at the select committee, so I’d like to encourage people to submit on this bill.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes submitters including those who have gone through land acquisition, seeking to bring people into the process.

charisma.statement: Yes, I understand what the Government is doing. I understand that they’re moving things through faster. I understand that. But it can’t come at the expense of democracy. It can’t come at the expense of those who have skin in the game, whose land it might be, or who might have connections to that space
charisma.explanation: Concedes opponents' aims while advocating for affected people, a bridging tone.

specificity.explanation: Concrete timeframes (60 working days vs 6–12 months) and a named mechanism.

specificity.statement: the bill introduces an incentive payment of 15 percent of the land’s value for those who negotiate and sell early in the process. To ensure the scheme remains affordable, payments will be capped at $150,000, with a minimum payment of $5,000
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages, caps and floors ($150,000 cap, $5,000 minimum) with a named mechanism.

specificity.statement: Protected Māori land, as defined under the Public Works Act, cannot be acquired through the new critical infrastructure process. Owners of this type of land retain their full right to object through the Environment Court.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete carve-out and the retained mechanism (Environment Court objection) for a defined land category.

specificity.statement: we all know that we need to deliver a lot more infrastructure and we need to deliver in a timely manner, in an effective and efficient manner

specificity.statement: So what this bill does is it streamlines the objections process that is experienced when the step of land acquisition comes, and it also introduces some incentives. So what we want to see is that the process is faster but, at the same time, the process is fairer as well.

specificity.statement: That is about making New Zealand fly faster, fly higher, go faster, and that is really important.

specificity.explanation: Gives a date and an acreage figure, though qualified as an estimate.

specificity.statement: it does identify that depending on the final decisions that are taken, any roads of national significance that are due for construction over that three-year period will need to acquire around 500 properties.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (~500 properties) and timeframe drawn from the regulatory impact statement.

specificity.statement: This amendment bill will streamline the land acquisition process under the Public Works Act for critical infrastructure projects, such as the Crosstown Corridor, which involves constructing a railway from Avondale, via Wesley, Mount Roskill, and Onehunga, to KiwiRail Southdown freight hub.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete project and its full route (Avondale–Wesley–Mount Roskill–Onehunga–Southdown).

specificity.statement: People in Mt Roskill will be very happy to have this project fast tracked as it will improve the transport network and benefit people in Mt Roskill. It will be a great day for Mt Roskill.

specificity.statement: New Zealanders wanted a Government to get stuff done, and New Zealanders understand that that takes actually doing things.

specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (30% income vs 20% profits) and a clear policy view on law vs regulation.

specificity.statement: This bill is to safeguard the long-term financial sustainability of New Zealand’s racing industry by extending TAB New Zealand’s existing monopoly on sports and race wagering to include online betting.
specificity.explanation: States the bill's precise mechanism (extending TAB's monopoly to online betting) and purpose.

specificity.statement: One of the obvious things that could be done—as a point of note before I finish—is the prohibition on the advertising by gambling outlets... it would be an easy step to prohibit the advertising of gambling in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (ban gambling advertising) but with no detail on scope or mechanism.

rigor.explanation: Plausible causal argument (heavier trucks → more maintenance) but asserted without data on magnitude.

divination.statement: I'm confident that this bill will promote more harmonious industrial relations across New Zealand.
