specificity.explanation: Cites a specific campus (Wellington) and ongoing consultations, though without naming the site or figures.

specificity.statement: What this bill does is it disestablishes Te Pūkenga and it re-establishes polytechnics. This is to make sure that our vocational education training is aligned with local industry and workforce needs.
specificity.explanation: Accurately describes the bill's core mechanism (disestablish Te Pūkenga, re-establish polytechs) and its stated rationale.

specificity.statement: About the financial viability, what this bill does is it sets up a polytech federation committee to support a designated federation of polytechnics to operate as viable entities. For the entities that will not be designated to the federation committee, they will have to prove that they are able to stand alone financially and academically.
specificity.explanation: Describes concrete mechanisms—the federation committee, designation, and a stand-alone financial/academic test—rather than generalities.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is very in favour of doing this, because we feel that, in the regions, they will be able to more effectively address the needs and do it more efficiently and effectively.
specificity.explanation: States support and a general rationale ('more efficiently and effectively') but no mechanism, figures, or concrete detail.

specificity.statement: When we think of the number of construction projects around the country that have been cancelled by Government, with 13,000 construction workers now leaving New Zealand for other jobs.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a concrete figure (13,000 workers) rather than a vague claim of decline.

specificity.statement: There is no provision in this bill about something that was working incredibly well, that was developed for being an interface between industry and training... The whole problem has been lifted and shifted—she should’ve lifted and shifted it into this bill, and what she’s done is just delayed it, kicked the can down the road.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete gap—workforce development councils not carried into the bill—and what she says should have happened.

specificity.statement: The job losses are happening, Mr Bates, in the following programmes: engineering, beauty therapy, construction, applied science, social services, music, entertainment and events technology, photography, early childhood education, and some business programmes as well.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the exact programmes affected by the UCOL cuts—concrete and precise.

specificity.statement: At Eastern Institute of Technology, this year, the New Zealand Certificate in Ngā Toi is not running... At Tai Poutini Polytechnic, they’re not running the New Zealand Diploma in Arts and Design.
specificity.explanation: Names specific institutions and specific named qualifications no longer running—highly concrete.

specificity.statement: Te Pūkenga has been a failed experiment—a $300 million failed experiment. That’s what it’s cost the New Zealand taxpayer.
specificity.explanation: Attaches a concrete dollar figure ($300 million) but without breaking down what the figure comprises.

specificity.statement: We’re working hard to do what’s best for Northland, and that’s what these adjustments will mean—not being told what’s best for Northland by those that live in other parts of the country.
specificity.explanation: Vague on what 'these adjustments' concretely deliver for Northland—no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: What we really pay judges the big bucks for is that kind of discretion so that they can make a humane and safe decision, not just about the person who has come in front of them but the web of people beyond that, in a society.
specificity.explanation: Grounds the point in a concrete scenario (two sisters, victims in the wings) though without statutory detail.

specificity.statement: The two suggestions that the Labour Party selected to put on the Table in an amendment today are that if the victim of the perpetrator says that they would like the name of the perpetrator to be released, but that identification could result in a hardship or danger to the family of the victim... or... hardship or danger to the family of the offender, then... the judge would retain an ability to look at those as exceptional circumstances.
specificity.explanation: Precisely states the two exceptional-circumstance limbs of the proposed amendment and their trigger conditions.

specificity.statement: Can I just check that this is to do with bringing it up to consistency with what we are seeing in section 128B of the Crimes Act, which has a maximum penalty of 20 years, as well.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact clauses and figures (s132, 14→20 years, s128B) in a precise, technical question.

specificity.statement: My question for the Minister of Justice is in regard to whether there was consideration of section 134(1) of the Crimes Act... an issue that came up in the case of Christian v R, which involved a teenage girl and a significantly older man, where the similar issue played out.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (s134(1)), the affected age group (12–15), the case (Christian v R), and the submission source.

specificity.statement: Sexual violation has a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment, whereas sexual connection with a child has a maximum penalty of 14 years. We didn’t think that that distinction was appropriate, so one of the things that the bill does is increase the maximum penalty to 20 years of imprisonment to align with sexual violation.
specificity.explanation: Gives exact penalties and the concrete rationale for the change.

specificity.statement: The Amendment Paper 289 is clarifying that where it cannot be established whether the child was under or over the age of 12, then, under replacement section 132(6)(a)(ii), the sexual conduct with a child under 12 is treated as if they are under 12.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact replacement provision and states the operative rule precisely.

specificity.statement: In 2023, for example, 76 individuals were convicted and achieved permanent name suppression. Year in, year out, we’re having New Zealanders convicted of sexual offences going off and nobody being able to know who they were.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a concrete year and count to quantify the problem.

specificity.statement: The proposal requires agreement from a layperson who does not necessarily have access to all of the relevant information, including the submissions from counsel and also psychological reports... This change potentially risks undermining the integrity of the justice system, which is based on having impartial parties making decisions.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete unintended consequences—information asymmetry, appeal rights, guilty-plea incentives, no minimum age.

specificity.statement: One of the real centrepieces of our criminal justice system is that the Crown, or the Government, metes out punishment. It stands between victim and offender so that we don’t have personal vengeance. What we have here is, perhaps, a small but critical erosion of that where a victim becomes a judge in this regard.
specificity.explanation: Frames the objection precisely as an absolute veto regardless of gravity and raises a specific BORA/disproportionate-punishment question.

specificity.statement: How much time is considered reasonable? Is it three months? Six months? A year? Three years? What is considered reasonable effort? We know that phone numbers change regularly, particularly mobile phone numbers, email addresses, forgetting passwords, and also the transient nature of renters.
specificity.explanation: Presses for concrete timeframes and grounds the concern in specific practical obstacles to contacting complainants.

veracity.statement: And what do we hear today? She’s renaming it. She’s renaming it to the New Zealand skills institute, taking away the Māori name—of course they did.
veracity.explanation: The factual core—renaming Te Pūkenga to the New Zealand skills institute, dropping the Māori name—is accurate to the bill.

veracity.statement: Under this piece of legislation, she’s given herself more powers—herself more powers—when it comes to the federation of polytechnics, but she’s given less to the sector. And particularly, she’s diluted the representation of Māori within those polytechnics.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the bill's 'as far as is reasonably practicable' Māori-representation wording noted later; directionally supported but a characterisation.

veracity.statement: We know that some campuses, like the one here in Wellington, have already been sold off. We know that there’s already been consultations for more to be sold off.
veracity.explanation: Te Pūkenga did dispose of some property; plausible and directionally supported, though the 'asset sales' framing of the reform is contested.

veracity.statement: What this bill does is it disestablishes Te Pūkenga and it re-establishes polytechnics. This is to make sure that our vocational education training is aligned with local industry and workforce needs.
veracity.explanation: An accurate description of what the bill does.

veracity.statement: When we think of the number of construction projects around the country that have been cancelled by Government, with 13,000 construction workers now leaving New Zealand for other jobs.
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses and emigration were real in this period, but the precise '13,000 leaving NZ' figure and its attribution to cancellations is uncertain.

veracity.statement: The uptake in apprenticeships has dramatically declined in New Zealand, and that is part of the lack of certainty about what is happening in the sector.
veracity.explanation: Apprenticeship uptake did fall from its subsidy-boosted peak; 'dramatically' and the causal link to reform uncertainty are somewhat overstated/unproven.

veracity.statement: I wonder if he’s picked up the phone and talked to his local polytechnic about the 74 job losses at Universal College of Learning (UCOL) being proposed at the moment. I bet he hasn’t.
veracity.explanation: The 74 proposed UCOL job losses is a specific, checkable claim consistent with reported polytechnic restructuring at the time.

veracity.statement: The job losses are happening, Mr Bates, in the following programmes: engineering, beauty therapy, construction, applied science, social services, music, entertainment and events technology, photography, early childhood education, and some business programmes as well.
veracity.explanation: A detailed, checkable list of affected programmes; plausible and consistent with the reported restructure.

veracity.statement: At Eastern Institute of Technology, this year, the New Zealand Certificate in Ngā Toi is not running... At Tai Poutini Polytechnic, they’re not running the New Zealand Diploma in Arts and Design.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable claims of programme cancellations; largely plausible though some are prefaced 'I’ve heard'.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga has been a failed experiment—a $300 million failed experiment. That’s what it’s cost the New Zealand taxpayer.
veracity.explanation: Te Pūkenga ran large deficits, but the '$300 million' cost-to-taxpayer figure conflates deficits/set-up costs and is a contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: Sexual violation has a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment, whereas sexual connection with a child has a maximum penalty of 14 years. We didn’t think that that distinction was appropriate, so one of the things that the bill does is increase the maximum penalty to 20 years of imprisonment to align with sexual violation.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the existing maximum penalties and the bill's alignment to 20 years.

veracity.statement: In 2023, for example, 76 individuals were convicted and achieved permanent name suppression. Year in, year out, we’re having New Zealanders convicted of sexual offences going off and nobody being able to know who they were.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure (76 in 2023) presented as official data; plausible though not independently verified here.

charisma.statement: We have no philosophical objection to the idea that there could be thriving, independent vocational institutions; however, this legislation does not establish that.
charisma.explanation: Concedes shared common ground with the Government's stated aim before objecting, an inclusive framing—though the argument still lands on its own side.

charisma.statement: We’ve heard a lot which essentially is crying wolf from the Opposition. They created this mess, and we said we would fix it.
charisma.explanation: Combative us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: In New Zealand, we have overvalued training and education through universities and have not given, essentially, the mana to the vocational programmes that they should have.
charisma.explanation: Measured, non-combative framing that affirms the value of vocational education rather than attacking opponents.

charisma.statement: We’re working hard to do what’s best for Northland, and that’s what these adjustments will mean—not being told what’s best for Northland by those that live in other parts of the country.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to regional identity and local control, effective for his base but framed as an us (Northland) vs them (elsewhere) contrast.

strength.statement: Through the Education and Workforce Committee, I commit that we will work as judiciously as possible to get this through the select committee and back to this House, because we need strong vocational education around New Zealand.
strength.explanation: A stated commitment about the select committee process; genuine follow-through is not yet demonstrable, so intent-with-unclear-delivery.

authenticity.statement: The feedback I’ve had from actual businesses with apprentices in Nelson is that it was working. They said to me—they pleaded with me, Minister—“Don’t change it.”
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with her stated prior involvement in the polytechnic sector; her position aligns with her declared background and record.

forthrightness.statement: Sexual violation has a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment, whereas sexual connection with a child has a maximum penalty of 14 years. We didn’t think that that distinction was appropriate, so one of the things that the bill does is increase the maximum penalty to 20 years of imprisonment to align with sexual violation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers Xu-Nan's question confirming the penalty increase is for consistency with sexual violation.

forthrightness.statement: The Amendment Paper 289 is clarifying that where it cannot be established whether the child was under or over the age of 12, then, under replacement section 132(6)(a)(ii), the sexual conduct with a child under 12 is treated as if they are under 12.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question about the rationale for the 'cannot be established' clause, though the 'how would you not know' example is brief.

forthrightness.statement: There’s a very simple—and, I think, adequate—answer to that, which is to say, “Nobody’s forced to do anything.” If a victim does not want to make that decision and doesn’t want to engage in the process, then it reverts to the judge making the decision.
forthrightness.explanation: Squarely engages the raised concern rather than deflecting, offering the reversion mechanism as the answer.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can assure the committee and the member that I have considered those risks, and I acknowledge that they are risks and no system can be designed that is perfect, and the current arrangements, of course, bring an enormous number of risks as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms he considered Andersen's enumerated risks but answers at a general level rather than addressing each specific risk she listed.

forthrightness.statement: My advice is that “reasonable efforts” is established in case law. There is not a precise date—you know, you’ve got 15 days or 20 days. Each case can be dealt with on a case by case basis by the courts.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Carter's question honestly but can only say there is no fixed timeframe, so the specific 'how long is reasonable' is left to case law rather than pinned down.

civility.statement: Deliberately disrupting the business of the House is serious, interrupting a vote of Parliament is serious, and I would say to the Māori Party that when you interrupt a vote of the House, you're not just interrupting the votes of those who are voting in favour; you're interrupting the votes of those who are voting against something as well.
civility.explanation: Criticises the conduct (disrupting a vote) on its substance without personal attack, and even-handedly notes it harms all members.

civility.statement: It is never OK to intimidate another member of the House. But the sanction being proposed by the Privileges Committee is totally out of line with existing parliamentary practice, and is disproportionate to the allegations that have been posed.
civility.explanation: Concedes intimidation is wrong while attacking the proposed sanction, not any person; focused on process.

civility.statement: I am not defending the Māori Party, and I'm not saying that their actions should be without sanction—they should be. The motion that we have put forward would see them sanctioned in line with the previous practice of this House, and that would be appropriate.
civility.explanation: Distances from partisan defence and concedes wrongdoing deserves sanction; measured and substance-focused.

civility.statement: I was absolutely shocked to learn that a member of the Privileges Committee asked about the committee's supposed power to imprison a member of the House. That happens in tinpot dictatorships and banana republics.
civility.explanation: Legitimate concern but delivered with sensational 'tinpot dictatorships and banana republics' hyperbole.

civility.statement: Looking around the world—and I say this to all members on all sides of the House—democracy is quite literally hanging by a thread. Days like today hold a razor blade up to that thread.
civility.explanation: Addressed inclusively to all members, but heavy on catastrophic rhetoric.

civility.statement: This particular debate potentially infringes upon the rights of individual members. I think it's not unreasonable, when the Government is moving such an adjournment, to ask them why they are doing so.
civility.explanation: Polite procedural point seeking an explanation, no personal attack.

civility.statement: We had just very recently the cancelling of 33 pay equity claims, just another example of the lack of care, the lack of compassion for workers in our country.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy and imputes 'lack of care/compassion' to the Government generally rather than a person; pointed but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: As we were going through this process, I was waiting for the free speech brigade to get up and to talk about the right of workers... Did we hear from them? No, we did not. We did not hear from the free speech brigade, because often when you hear from that lot all they're really interested in is the free speech of their rich mates and the privileged.
civility.explanation: Derides opponents as the 'free speech brigade' interested only in 'their rich mates', a dismissive characterisation rather than engagement.

civility.statement: What we have here is the tail wagging the dog. We have the ACT Party pushing their agenda through the House.
civility.explanation: Critique of coalition dynamics using a mild idiom; targets a party's influence, not a person.

civility.statement: The argument the Opposition want people to believe is that employees will move from giving up a little bit of their pay for taking a small action, to giving up all of their pay for full strikes. That doesn't add up. All this bill does is say, 'If you take a partial strike, you will have part of your pay deducted.' It's a pretty simple equation.
civility.explanation: Disputes the argument's logic rather than attacking members personally.

civility.statement: New Zealand First believes very, very firmly that a fair day's work deserves a fair day's pay, but if you're not doing a fair day's work—as you're not doing under a partial strike—you don't deserve a full day's pay.
civility.explanation: States the principle without denigrating workers or opponents.

civility.statement: A speaker opposite mentioned the fact that—I couldn't believe this statement—'partial strikes don't affect productivity.' Well, I'm just thinking of a situation whereby if you were a dairy farmer, what happens if they don't milk the last row of cows?... That is absolutely one of the most ridiculous statements I have ever heard.
civility.explanation: 'Most ridiculous statement I have ever heard' derides the argument sharply, though aimed at the statement not the person.

civility.statement: In the time of this Government, we've seen the end of the idea of fair pay agreements... We have had minimum wage increases that are well below what was delivered under Labour. We have had minimum wages for disabled people abandoned... We've got pay equity absolutely gutted, a whole lot of women missing out. And we have had a zero offer to our teacher-aides.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused critique, heated but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: This Government said that it was going to address the cost of living crisis, and what's it doing? It's making our poorest employees pay. It's petty. It's short-sighted.
civility.explanation: 'Petty' and 'short-sighted' are dismissive of the Government's approach, though aimed at policy not a named individual.

civility.statement: A fair day's pay for a fair day's work: I think that's what most Kiwis want in their labour market. Actually, that's what we have in New Zealand's employment relations framework—ever since the 2000s. Our framework is all about engaging in good faith, having fair processes, and having respect for employers' and employees' rights.
civility.explanation: Frames the case respectfully around a shared value and the existing framework.

civility.statement: There is no evidence, right throughout the regulatory impact statement, that this bill will have one iota of difference on productivity or on working... It is simply designed to be able to intimidate workers so that they work longer hours for less money in a cost of living crisis.
civility.explanation: Attributes a bad-faith motive to the Government, sharpening beyond policy critique.

civility.statement: The ACT Party turned up in this House, wearing their lapel badges with 'ACT' on them. In fact, their leader was reprimanded time and time again for continuing to act against a Speaker's ruling, where party political badges were not allowed to be worn within this House. So, in my view, what is good for the goose is good for the gander.
civility.explanation: Points to opponents' inconsistency on badges without personal insult.

civility.statement: The previous Government's mega-merger of polytechnics and industry training organisations was an expensive failure. Its push to centralise and standardise polytechnics and work-based learning was wrong, and it cost this country dearly.
civility.explanation: Attacks the previous Government's policy rather than individuals, though in blunt terms.

rigor.statement: Deliberately disrupting the business of the House is serious, interrupting a vote of Parliament is serious, and I would say to the Māori Party that when you interrupt a vote of the House, you're not just interrupting the votes of those who are voting in favour; you're interrupting the votes of those who are voting against something as well.
rigor.explanation: Logical point that interrupting a vote deprives every member of a recorded vote; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: We've had members undertaking fist fights in the lobbies, and they were not suspended at all. We've had members driving tractors and Land Rovers up the front steps of Parliament, and they were not sanctioned. We have had a recent case where a member left their chair, walked to the other side of the House, and stood over a member and thumped the table, and they were not sanctioned by the House.
rigor.explanation: Marshals concrete comparative precedents to support the disproportionality claim; evidence-based argument by analogy to prior cases.

rigor.statement: The Clerk made the advice clear that suspension of members is a rare occurrence and that a long period of suspension would represent a substantial change in the House's practice... The Clerk further advised that the committee ought to recommend a long suspension only with the broad support of members, not simply a bare majority. That has not happened in this case.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the non-partisan Clerk's formal advice and applies its criteria to the facts; conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: Why do we choose a 24-hour suspension? It's quite simple, Mr Speaker: because it's already in the Standing Orders. Had you, as Speaker, named those members at the time... they would have been suspended for 24 hours, as one of the members was. If they did it again, they'd be suspended for seven days, and if they did it again, they'd be suspended for 28 days. Those are the existing rules of the House.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the alternative sanction by direct reference to codified Standing Orders rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: I was absolutely shocked to learn that a member of the Privileges Committee asked about the committee's supposed power to imprison a member of the House. That happens in tinpot dictatorships and banana republics.
rigor.explanation: Raises a real point but leans on emotive analogy rather than reasoned argument about the imprisonment query.

rigor.statement: Looking around the world—and I say this to all members on all sides of the House—democracy is quite literally hanging by a thread. Days like today hold a razor blade up to that thread.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion via dramatic metaphor rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: It is wrong and against the traditions of our democracy for a Government to use its majority in Parliament to suspend and remove from the service of the people of New Zealand its political opponents.
rigor.explanation: A principled argument grounded in democratic convention, though asserted more than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The effect of the motion that Chris Bishop has just moved potentially removes the ability of the Māori Party to vote on the Budget, because the Budget will not be voted on until after 5 June... If the motion had passed today for 21 days, it's possible that by the time the vote for the Budget came up, they would be back in the House and they got a vote.
rigor.explanation: Works through the timing logic to show a counter-intuitive consequence of the adjournment; reasoning is traceable.

rigor.statement: The Government has come to the view that, given the centrality of the Budget process to Parliament, it would be appropriate for Te Pāti Māori members who may or may not be suspended... to participate in the Budget. There is no more important role for Parliament than scrutinising and debating the Budget. It is a confidence motion... So we are moving to adjourn the debate so that this week can focus, rightfully, on the Budget.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the constitutional role of the Budget as a confidence motion to the conclusion members should participate.

rigor.statement: As we were going through this process, I was waiting for the free speech brigade to get up and to talk about the right of workers... Did we hear from them? No, we did not. We did not hear from the free speech brigade, because often when you hear from that lot all they're really interested in is the free speech of their rich mates and the privileged.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque / motive-attribution rather than an argument on the merits of the bill.

rigor.statement: What we have here is the tail wagging the dog. We have the ACT Party pushing their agenda through the House.
rigor.explanation: Asserts ACT is driving the agenda via metaphor without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: The argument the Opposition want people to believe is that employees will move from giving up a little bit of their pay for taking a small action, to giving up all of their pay for full strikes. That doesn't add up. All this bill does is say, 'If you take a partial strike, you will have part of your pay deducted.' It's a pretty simple equation.
rigor.explanation: Offers a logical rebuttal (proportionate deduction, not escalation) but somewhat simplifies the Opposition's position.

rigor.statement: During the Education and Workforce Committee hearings, we had one member of a particular union acknowledge... that even wearing a branded T-shirt would certainly, and I quote, 'have detrimental effect on businesses—on a business's productivity and brand.'
rigor.explanation: Uses evidence from the hearing, though it generalises from one submitter's concession.

rigor.statement: Just over the weekend, I was talking to a rather large employer in a critical piece of infrastructure, whose vital operation for the movement of freight has been impacted by partial strikes in the past, where the unions will get a key group of workers within the broader network to take out a partial strike, which impacts absolutely everyone and shuts down the whole operation.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single unnamed anecdote to justify the policy; appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: New Zealand First believes very, very firmly that a fair day's work deserves a fair day's pay, but if you're not doing a fair day's work—as you're not doing under a partial strike—you don't deserve a full day's pay.
rigor.explanation: A coherent proportionality principle, but rests on the contestable premise that a partial strike always means not doing a fair day's work.

rigor.statement: This bill allows employers to reduce by 10 percent employees' wages when they have completed all of their tasks in their job, when they have completed all of the duties in their job description and in their employment contract, and they are able to take that 10 percent off their wages without a right for employees being able to challenge that.
rigor.explanation: Builds the unfairness argument on a specific reading of the bill's mechanics; largely follows, though the 'completed all duties' framing is contested by Government members.

rigor.statement: I note that we don't appear to have the regulatory impact statement (RIS) on the table at the moment, but, from memory, in that RIS, it did say that there was no robust, evidential basis for this bill.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the official RIS as evidence against the bill, appropriately flagging the memory caveat.

rigor.statement: This bill is potentially, and I think clearly, against our international obligations. We do have free-trade agreements with the EU and with the UK that prohibit making workers' rights and making labour rights worse under those agreements... it is likely that this is against our International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions, as well.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the objection in specific agreements and ILO conventions rather than assertion, though the breach conclusion is asserted.

rigor.statement: I rise with pride to support the Employment Relations (Pay Deductions for Partial Strikes) Amendment Bill. It is a very simple principle in life: you get paid for the work you do. The work you do is a full day's work, not a partial day's work, and that is how it should be.
rigor.explanation: Restates a general principle rather than engaging the Opposition's specific point about completed duties.

rigor.statement: A speaker opposite mentioned the fact that—I couldn't believe this statement—'partial strikes don't affect productivity.' Well, I'm just thinking of a situation whereby if you were a dairy farmer, what happens if they don't milk the last row of cows?... That is absolutely one of the most ridiculous statements I have ever heard.
rigor.explanation: Uses a vivid dairy-farm analogy but arguably strawmans the Opposition, who distinguished completing duties from affecting the business.

rigor.statement: I worked for the bus drivers up in Auckland and they had a really low wage... because we had a contracting model which meant that the councils were always going to the lowest possible bidder... So they issued that strike notice and they said that they would take their toilet breaks... And you know what that bus company did? It decided to lock them out for that.
rigor.explanation: Uses a detailed first-hand case to illustrate the mechanism, though it remains a single anecdote generalised to the bill's effect.

rigor.statement: I used to work for $6 an hour in a supermarket, and I'll tell you what, most supermarkets, like most businesses out there, don't get involved in politics because they know that their customers don't always agree with them. So when their employees are going around with their T-shirts, with their own political activisms... it does offend a lot of customers, and, therefore, customers may choose to shop elsewhere. That affects productivity.
rigor.explanation: Builds from personal anecdote and assumed customer reactions to a productivity conclusion; several unevidenced links in the chain.

rigor.statement: There is no evidence, right throughout the regulatory impact statement, that this bill will have one iota of difference on productivity or on working... It is simply designed to be able to intimidate workers so that they work longer hours for less money in a cost of living crisis.
rigor.explanation: Anchors part of the argument in the RIS, but imputes intent ('designed to intimidate') without evidence of motive.

rigor.statement: The ACT Party turned up in this House, wearing their lapel badges with 'ACT' on them. In fact, their leader was reprimanded time and time again for continuing to act against a Speaker's ruling, where party political badges were not allowed to be worn within this House. So, in my view, what is good for the goose is good for the gander.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque consistency argument that highlights a genuine parallel but doesn't directly rebut the bill's merits.

rigor.statement: The regulatory impact statement fails to meet quality assurance standards, it has absolutely no qualitative data, and it relies completely on anecdotal and historical examples... That's not even the Labour Party saying that in a differing view; that is the view of the independent review panel that is assessing the regulatory impact statement.
rigor.explanation: Cites an independent, non-partisan source rather than her own assertion to support the no-evidence claim.

rigor.statement: This bill aligns with other jurisdictions—what they're doing in Australia and the UK. Of course, in the Public Service, healthcare and education are really disrupted when we have partial strikes, and this can lead to delayed treatment, and of course disruptions in the classroom.
rigor.explanation: Leans partly on an appeal to what other jurisdictions do, plus asserted disruption effects.

rigor.statement: The previous Government's mega-merger of polytechnics and industry training organisations was an expensive failure. Its push to centralise and standardise polytechnics and work-based learning was wrong, and it cost this country dearly.
rigor.explanation: Asserts failure and cost without presenting supporting figures in the statement.

charisma.statement: It is never OK to intimidate another member of the House. But the sanction being proposed by the Privileges Committee is totally out of line with existing parliamentary practice, and is disproportionate to the allegations that have been posed.
charisma.explanation: Balanced framing that concedes the opponents' point (intimidation is unacceptable) before dissenting, but still argues one side.

charisma.statement: It is wrong and against the traditions of our democracy for a Government to use its majority in Parliament to suspend and remove from the service of the people of New Zealand its political opponents.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared democratic values, but framed to indict the Government rather than build consensus.

charisma.statement: As we were going through this process, I was waiting for the free speech brigade to get up and to talk about the right of workers... Did we hear from them? No, we did not. We did not hear from the free speech brigade, because often when you hear from that lot all they're really interested in is the free speech of their rich mates and the privileged.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side by caricaturing opponents; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: There is another way to calculate this within this bill, which is to look at the proportion of work that someone has completed. Now, I don't agree with this bill but I think that's a more sensible option... I'd like the House to consider this: to remove that arbitrary amount.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive amendment and invites the House to consider it even while opposing the bill.

charisma.statement: This is about bringing balance back to employment relations. That's what we're all about on this side of the House: common sense and practicality.
charisma.explanation: Confident branding that appeals to its own side rather than reaching across the House.

veracity.statement: We've had members undertaking fist fights in the lobbies, and they were not suspended at all. We've had members driving tractors and Land Rovers up the front steps of Parliament, and they were not sanctioned. We have had a recent case where a member left their chair, walked to the other side of the House, and stood over a member and thumped the table, and they were not sanctioned by the House.
veracity.explanation: These are broadly accurate references to real incidents in NZ parliamentary history used to establish a precedent baseline.

veracity.statement: And yet we seem to have gone from a situation where members were not sanctioned to one where a 21-day sanction—the harshest by a factor of seven—is being applied to these members.
veracity.explanation: The 21-day suspension was indeed the harshest ever recommended; the 'factor of seven' comparison to prior suspensions is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: The Clerk made the advice clear that suspension of members is a rare occurrence and that a long period of suspension would represent a substantial change in the House's practice... The Clerk further advised that the committee ought to recommend a long suspension only with the broad support of members, not simply a bare majority. That has not happened in this case.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the Clerk's advisory role and content; presented as fact, plausible though we cannot verify verbatim.

veracity.statement: We had just very recently the cancelling of 33 pay equity claims, just another example of the lack of care, the lack of compassion for workers in our country.
veracity.explanation: The cancellation of 33 pay equity claims is a real, verifiable government action; the '33' figure is accurate.

veracity.statement: During the Education and Workforce Committee hearings, we had one member of a particular union acknowledge... that even wearing a branded T-shirt would certainly, and I quote, 'have detrimental effect on businesses—on a business's productivity and brand.'
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific submitter quote from select committee; plausibly accurate but a single anecdote presented as broadly probative.

veracity.statement: We actually have had wages rising faster than inflation for the last four quarters, so we're starting to win here.
veracity.explanation: A checkable macro claim about real wage growth over four quarters; broadly plausible for the period but stated without source.

veracity.statement: We've also had, of course, importantly within this, things like interest rates trending down, which, as the Prime Minister outlined in question time, is $300 a month for someone on the average mortgage.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific $300/month figure to falling rates via the PM; directionally credible but unverified and cited secondhand.

veracity.statement: The last Labour Government removed the ability for partial strikes to have an associated wage deduction from these types of actions, and the reason that they did was quite simple... partial strikes were taking place... for very minor actions within employment. For example... people wearing a badge, people wearing a T-shirt, people wearing a particular colour or a slogan.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the 2018 Labour change and its stated rationale.

veracity.statement: This bill allows employers to reduce by 10 percent employees' wages when they have completed all of their tasks in their job, when they have completed all of the duties in their job description and in their employment contract, and they are able to take that 10 percent off their wages without a right for employees being able to challenge that.
veracity.explanation: Describes the bill's effect accurately in the 10 percent respect, though the 'completed all tasks' characterisation is disputed.

veracity.statement: I've just got the statistics, now, from my colleague on how many people were supportive of this bill. Apparently, there were four people who were supportive—four submissions in support—606 opposed.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific submission counts (4 for, 606 opposed); presented candidly as secondhand, so plausibly accurate but not independently confirmed.

veracity.statement: I note that we don't appear to have the regulatory impact statement (RIS) on the table at the moment, but, from memory, in that RIS, it did say that there was no robust, evidential basis for this bill.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with later cited RIS criticism, but hedged ('from memory') and the document was not to hand.

veracity.statement: This bill is potentially, and I think clearly, against our international obligations. We do have free-trade agreements with the EU and with the UK that prohibit making workers' rights and making labour rights worse under those agreements... it is likely that this is against our International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions, as well.
veracity.explanation: The EU/UK FTAs contain labour non-regression clauses, so the premise is real; whether this bill breaches them is a contestable legal claim, hedged as 'likely'.

veracity.statement: In the time of this Government, we've seen the end of the idea of fair pay agreements... We have had minimum wage increases that are well below what was delivered under Labour. We have had minimum wages for disabled people abandoned... We've got pay equity absolutely gutted, a whole lot of women missing out. And we have had a zero offer to our teacher-aides.
veracity.explanation: Lists real policy changes (FPA repeal, pay equity changes) accurately, though 'gutted' and some framings are argumentative characterisations.

veracity.statement: I worked for the bus drivers up in Auckland and they had a really low wage... because we had a contracting model which meant that the councils were always going to the lowest possible bidder... So they issued that strike notice and they said that they would take their toilet breaks... And you know what that bus company did? It decided to lock them out for that.
veracity.explanation: Recounts a real Auckland bus-driver dispute; broadly credible as first-hand account, though unverified in specifics.

veracity.statement: A fair day's pay for a fair day's work: I think that's what most Kiwis want in their labour market. Actually, that's what we have in New Zealand's employment relations framework—ever since the 2000s. Our framework is all about engaging in good faith, having fair processes, and having respect for employers' and employees' rights.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the Employment Relations Act 2000 established a good-faith framework; the 'most Kiwis want' claim is an untested assertion.

veracity.statement: There is no evidence, right throughout the regulatory impact statement, that this bill will have one iota of difference on productivity or on working... It is simply designed to be able to intimidate workers so that they work longer hours for less money in a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: The RIS-lacks-evidence claim is later supported by the independent panel quote; the 'designed to intimidate' motive is an inference, not established fact.

veracity.statement: The ACT Party turned up in this House, wearing their lapel badges with 'ACT' on them. In fact, their leader was reprimanded time and time again for continuing to act against a Speaker's ruling, where party political badges were not allowed to be worn within this House. So, in my view, what is good for the goose is good for the gander.
veracity.explanation: References a real episode of ACT MPs wearing party badges against a Speaker's ruling; broadly accurate though the 'time and time again' is emphatic.

veracity.statement: The regulatory impact statement fails to meet quality assurance standards, it has absolutely no qualitative data, and it relies completely on anecdotal and historical examples... That's not even the Labour Party saying that in a differing view; that is the view of the independent review panel that is assessing the regulatory impact statement.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the criticism to the independent RIS review panel and quotes it; a checkable claim presented with its source.

veracity.statement: In 2018, when Labour amended the Employment Relations Act to remove pay deductions for partial strikes, we did so to restore balance in the workplace. We recognised that industrial action is a fundamental right and we understood that partial strikes are a legitimate and proportionate way for workers to express dissatisfaction without resorting to a full withdrawal of labour.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes Labour's 2018 amendment and its stated rationale.

veracity.statement: This bill aligns with other jurisdictions—what they're doing in Australia and the UK. Of course, in the Public Service, healthcare and education are really disrupted when we have partial strikes, and this can lead to delayed treatment, and of course disruptions in the classroom.
veracity.explanation: The Australia/UK comparison is broadly defensible; the disruption claims are plausible generalisations stated without data.

veracity.statement: The previous Government's mega-merger of polytechnics and industry training organisations was an expensive failure. Its push to centralise and standardise polytechnics and work-based learning was wrong, and it cost this country dearly.
veracity.explanation: Te Pūkenga did run large deficits, giving some basis to 'expensive', but 'failure' and 'cost this country dearly' are contestable value-laden characterisations.

veracity.statement: This is about delivering to the 250,000 students, apprentices, trainees annually across construction, engineering, energy, creative, IT, primary industries, healthcare, and the service sector who want training options that are easy to access, responsive, and that will lead to future employment or career pathways.
veracity.explanation: The ~250,000 vocational learner figure is broadly in line with known enrolment scales; presented without a cited source.

specificity.statement: We've had members undertaking fist fights in the lobbies, and they were not suspended at all. We've had members driving tractors and Land Rovers up the front steps of Parliament, and they were not sanctioned. We have had a recent case where a member left their chair, walked to the other side of the House, and stood over a member and thumped the table, and they were not sanctioned by the House.
specificity.explanation: Names specific categories of past conduct (fist fights, tractors, standing over a member) as comparators.

specificity.statement: And yet we seem to have gone from a situation where members were not sanctioned to one where a 21-day sanction—the harshest by a factor of seven—is being applied to these members.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (21 days) and a quantified comparison (harshest by a factor of seven).

specificity.statement: The Clerk made the advice clear that suspension of members is a rare occurrence and that a long period of suspension would represent a substantial change in the House's practice... The Clerk further advised that the committee ought to recommend a long suspension only with the broad support of members, not simply a bare majority. That has not happened in this case.
specificity.explanation: References specific advice (broad support vs bare majority, rationale requirement) rather than vague appeals.

specificity.statement: Why do we choose a 24-hour suspension? It's quite simple, Mr Speaker: because it's already in the Standing Orders. Had you, as Speaker, named those members at the time... they would have been suspended for 24 hours, as one of the members was. If they did it again, they'd be suspended for seven days, and if they did it again, they'd be suspended for 28 days. Those are the existing rules of the House.
specificity.explanation: Lays out the exact escalating penalties (24 hours, 7 days, 28 days) that his amendment relies on.

specificity.statement: Looking around the world—and I say this to all members on all sides of the House—democracy is quite literally hanging by a thread. Days like today hold a razor blade up to that thread.
specificity.explanation: Vague sweeping imagery ('hanging by a thread', 'razor blade') with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: The effect of the motion that Chris Bishop has just moved potentially removes the ability of the Māori Party to vote on the Budget, because the Budget will not be voted on until after 5 June... If the motion had passed today for 21 days, it's possible that by the time the vote for the Budget came up, they would be back in the House and they got a vote.
specificity.explanation: Ties the argument to concrete dates and the 21-day figure.

specificity.statement: The Government has come to the view that, given the centrality of the Budget process to Parliament, it would be appropriate for Te Pāti Māori members who may or may not be suspended... to participate in the Budget. There is no more important role for Parliament than scrutinising and debating the Budget. It is a confidence motion... So we are moving to adjourn the debate so that this week can focus, rightfully, on the Budget.
specificity.explanation: Gives the concrete reason and the adjournment date (Thursday, 5 June 2025).

specificity.statement: This is the partial strikes bill... they are those other actions that people have been able to take. So you could be wearing a badge expressing a particular view on your workplace or you could have a T-shirt... This bill will penalise you and take away your right to be able to do that. That will put on scope that the only thing that people will be able to do is actually move towards full strikes.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete examples (badges, T-shirts) of what the bill affects and the claimed effect of pushing toward full strikes.

specificity.statement: During the Education and Workforce Committee hearings, we had one member of a particular union acknowledge... that even wearing a branded T-shirt would certainly, and I quote, 'have detrimental effect on businesses—on a business's productivity and brand.'
specificity.explanation: Names the committee, the source (a union member), and quotes the wording.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First has always been about balance in employment relations deliberations and bills... we do believe that there needs to be a rebalancing of the partial strikes legislation. It is a powerful mechanism that can impact on productivity in a workplace, and without some guardrails, it could be used—and is used—with impunity.
specificity.explanation: States a position and rationale (guardrails on a productivity-impacting mechanism) but with limited concrete detail here.

specificity.statement: Just over the weekend, I was talking to a rather large employer in a critical piece of infrastructure, whose vital operation for the movement of freight has been impacted by partial strikes in the past, where the unions will get a key group of workers within the broader network to take out a partial strike, which impacts absolutely everyone and shuts down the whole operation.
specificity.explanation: Some detail (freight, key group of workers) but the employer and case are unnamed and unquantified.

specificity.statement: We actually have had wages rising faster than inflation for the last four quarters, so we're starting to win here.
specificity.explanation: Quantified over a defined timeframe (last four quarters).

specificity.statement: We've also had, of course, importantly within this, things like interest rates trending down, which, as the Prime Minister outlined in question time, is $300 a month for someone on the average mortgage.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete dollar figure tied to the average mortgage.

specificity.statement: The last Labour Government removed the ability for partial strikes to have an associated wage deduction from these types of actions, and the reason that they did was quite simple... partial strikes were taking place... for very minor actions within employment. For example... people wearing a badge, people wearing a T-shirt, people wearing a particular colour or a slogan.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete examples of the minor actions at issue.

specificity.statement: This bill allows employers to reduce by 10 percent employees' wages when they have completed all of their tasks in their job, when they have completed all of the duties in their job description and in their employment contract, and they are able to take that 10 percent off their wages without a right for employees being able to challenge that.
specificity.explanation: Precise on the 10 percent figure and the no-challenge mechanism.

specificity.statement: I've just got the statistics, now, from my colleague on how many people were supportive of this bill. Apparently, there were four people who were supportive—four submissions in support—606 opposed.
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers on submissions for and against.

specificity.statement: There is another way to calculate this within this bill, which is to look at the proportion of work that someone has completed. Now, I don't agree with this bill but I think that's a more sensible option... I'd like the House to consider this: to remove that arbitrary amount.
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete alternative mechanism (proportion of work completed) versus the flat 10 percent.

specificity.statement: I rise with pride to support the Employment Relations (Pay Deductions for Partial Strikes) Amendment Bill. It is a very simple principle in life: you get paid for the work you do. The work you do is a full day's work, not a partial day's work, and that is how it should be.
specificity.explanation: Relies on a slogan-level principle with no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: In the time of this Government, we've seen the end of the idea of fair pay agreements... We have had minimum wage increases that are well below what was delivered under Labour. We have had minimum wages for disabled people abandoned... We've got pay equity absolutely gutted, a whole lot of women missing out. And we have had a zero offer to our teacher-aides.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete named changes across several policy areas.

specificity.statement: I worked for the bus drivers up in Auckland and they had a really low wage... because we had a contracting model which meant that the councils were always going to the lowest possible bidder... So they issued that strike notice and they said that they would take their toilet breaks... And you know what that bus company did? It decided to lock them out for that.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail: Auckland bus drivers, contracting/lowest-bidder model, toilet-break action, lockout response.

specificity.statement: I used to work for $6 an hour in a supermarket, and I'll tell you what, most supermarkets, like most businesses out there, don't get involved in politics because they know that their customers don't always agree with them. So when their employees are going around with their T-shirts, with their own political activisms... it does offend a lot of customers, and, therefore, customers may choose to shop elsewhere. That affects productivity.
specificity.explanation: Personal detail ($6/hour supermarket) but the productivity claim is asserted rather than quantified.

specificity.statement: The regulatory impact statement fails to meet quality assurance standards, it has absolutely no qualitative data, and it relies completely on anecdotal and historical examples... That's not even the Labour Party saying that in a differing view; that is the view of the independent review panel that is assessing the regulatory impact statement.
specificity.explanation: Specific findings (no qualitative data, fails QA standards) attributed to a named panel.

specificity.statement: This is about bringing balance back to employment relations. That's what we're all about on this side of the House: common sense and practicality.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level framing ('common sense and practicality') with no mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: This bill reestablishes a network of regional polytechnics... From 1 January 2026, programmes, functions, assets, and staff from Te Pūkenga's on-campus business units will transfer to polytechnics under a transition plan... Te Pūkenga will be referred to as the New Zealand Institute of Skills and Technology and will remain as a transitional entity for a one-year period before being disestablished by 31 December 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete dates (1 Jan 2026, 31 Dec 2026), mechanisms (transition plan), and the entity's interim status.

specificity.statement: To ensure the vocational education and training system is responsive to current new and emerging industry needs, industry skills boards will be established by 1 January next year, replacing the workforce development councils. These boards will be industry-led and tasked with ensuring industry training consistency and quality.
specificity.explanation: Concrete new bodies (industry skills boards), a date (1 January next year), and the councils they replace.

specificity.statement: This is about delivering to the 250,000 students, apprentices, trainees annually across construction, engineering, energy, creative, IT, primary industries, healthcare, and the service sector who want training options that are easy to access, responsive, and that will lead to future employment or career pathways.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (250,000) and enumerates the sectors covered.

forthrightness.statement: Why do we choose a 24-hour suspension? It's quite simple, Mr Speaker: because it's already in the Standing Orders. Had you, as Speaker, named those members at the time... they would have been suspended for 24 hours, as one of the members was. If they did it again, they'd be suspended for seven days, and if they did it again, they'd be suspended for 28 days. Those are the existing rules of the House.
forthrightness.explanation: Poses and then directly and fully answers his own rhetorical question with the mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: This particular debate potentially infringes upon the rights of individual members. I think it's not unreasonable, when the Government is moving such an adjournment, to ask them why they are doing so.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly poses a clear question to the Government about the purpose of the adjournment.

forthrightness.statement: The Government has come to the view that, given the centrality of the Budget process to Parliament, it would be appropriate for Te Pāti Māori members who may or may not be suspended... to participate in the Budget. There is no more important role for Parliament than scrutinising and debating the Budget. It is a confidence motion... So we are moving to adjourn the debate so that this week can focus, rightfully, on the Budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Hipkins' question of why the Government is adjourning, giving the Budget-participation rationale.

authenticity.statement: I am not defending the Māori Party, and I'm not saying that their actions should be without sanction—they should be. The motion that we have put forward would see them sanctioned in line with the previous practice of this House, and that would be appropriate.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his stated position that a proportionate sanction is warranted; puts forward an actual amendment matching the claim.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has always been about balance in employment relations deliberations and bills... we do believe that there needs to be a rebalancing of the partial strikes legislation. It is a powerful mechanism that can impact on productivity in a workplace, and without some guardrails, it could be used—and is used—with impunity.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the stance as consistent with NZ First's long-standing 'balance' brand; plausible but unverified from the text.

authenticity.statement: This Government said that it was going to address the cost of living crisis, and what's it doing? It's making our poorest employees pay. It's petty. It's short-sighted.
authenticity.explanation: Charges the Government with saying it will fix the cost of living while doing the opposite; a words-vs-actions inconsistency alleged against opponents.

authenticity.statement: In 2018, when Labour amended the Employment Relations Act to remove pay deductions for partial strikes, we did so to restore balance in the workplace. We recognised that industrial action is a fundamental right and we understood that partial strikes are a legitimate and proportionate way for workers to express dissatisfaction without resorting to a full withdrawal of labour.
authenticity.explanation: Her opposition today is consistent with Labour's own 2018 legislative action she is defending; words match her party's prior record.

authenticity.statement: This redesign has been a key priority of our Government, with this legislation underpinning a specific commitment in our 100-day plan to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
authenticity.explanation: Ties the bill to an explicit prior commitment (100-day plan to disestablish Te Pūkenga); words match a stated campaign pledge.

divination.statement: This is the partial strikes bill... they are those other actions that people have been able to take. So you could be wearing a badge expressing a particular view on your workplace or you could have a T-shirt... This bill will penalise you and take away your right to be able to do that. That will put on scope that the only thing that people will be able to do is actually move towards full strikes.
divination.explanation: Predicts the bill will push workers toward full strikes; plausible but contested and unquantified.

divination.statement: This, in my view—and in the view of many submitters at select committee—will lead to worse relationships between employers and employees because of these arbitrary amounts that can be taken away from employees' pay packets even if they are still doing the majority of their job.
divination.explanation: Predicts worse employer-employee relationships; plausible and echoed by submitters, but uncertain and unfalsifiable in the near term.

divination.statement: There will be more polarisation, more loss of productivity, because they cannot even take any action.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased polarisation and productivity loss from removing partial-strike options; directionally plausible but uncertain.

divination.statement: What will happen in New Zealand as a result of this is that we will see more strikes. We will see workers who are enabled to do partial strikes, like work to rule or wear a T-shirt, take full strike action, and that is where productivity does get hit.
divination.explanation: Predicts more full strikes and greater productivity loss as a consequence of the bill; plausible mechanism but uncertain and contested.

strength.statement: This redesign has been a key priority of our Government, with this legislation underpinning a specific commitment in our 100-day plan to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
strength.explanation: Advancing a promised policy, but this is only the first reading—commitment stated with delivery still in progress, not yet enacted.

veracity.statement: I have seen a lot of reports recently. Some suggest the Government should impose new taxes, ramp up spending, and increase debt. I completely disagree with those suggestions. An economic recovery is now under way, but we cannot take it for granted. More taxes, more spending, and more debt would kill the recovery and take New Zealand backwards.
veracity.explanation: "An economic recovery is now under way" is a contestable factual claim; plausible but selective.

veracity.statement: In 2023, this Government inherited a structural deficit caused by a sharp and unsustainable increase in spending.
veracity.explanation: The existence of a deficit is real, but attributing it wholly to a "structural" spending increase is a contested political characterisation.

veracity.statement: the current interest bill on our debt is around $9 billion. For context, members, that is enough to pay for the entire operations of the New Zealand Police, the New Zealand Defence Force, the justice department, the Customs Service, and the prison service combined.
veracity.explanation: The ~$9b finance-cost figure is broadly consistent with the fiscal accounts; the agency-cost comparison is a reasonable illustration.

veracity.statement: Treasury’s analysis shows that it’s unwise to have Government debt over 50 percent of GDP. I agree with that ceiling; so did Grant Robertson. Others think debt should go higher, then it shouldn’t, then it should again—it’s hard to keep up.
veracity.explanation: Treasury sustainability commentary exists; the characterisation of opponents flip-flopping is a partisan gloss.

veracity.statement: the last Government never made it transparent that it was allowing to go through to forecasts, the costs of Cabinet decisions that were made to fully fund all private sector claims—that money was never revealed to New Zealand
veracity.explanation: A contested claim about the prior government's fiscal transparency; not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: this is a Government that’s not getting rid of equal pay. We’re not getting rid of collective bargaining. We’re not getting rid of pay equity. We’re not cutting women’s pay. We’re not reversing settled pay equity claims.
veracity.explanation: Technically the regime remains, but the framing omits that 33 active (unsettled) claims were extinguished—true-but-misleading via the "settled" qualifier.

veracity.statement: our Government’s putting more money into healthcare than any other Government in the history of New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Likely true in nominal terms but misleading without adjusting for inflation and rising demand.

veracity.statement: I think there’s been 1,700 more nurses added to our system and 200 more doctors added to our system since we came to power... They are paid on average, I think, $126,000, including allowances, and that is comparable to what they receive in New South Wales, which is, of course, 30 to 35 percent wealthier than New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures hedged with "I think"; broadly plausible but the NSW pay comparison and wealth gap are selective.

veracity.statement: No. I think Māori, when they see inflation down from 7.2 to 2.5 percent, when they see interest rates coming down an extra $300 a fortnight on a $500,000 mortgage over 25 years, and they see a growing economy, and they see iwi doing deals with international infrastructure firms, they understand this is a Government that’s working hard for Māori and non-Māori, women and men, and all New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Inflation falling from ~7.2% to ~2.5% is broadly accurate; the mortgage figure is illustrative and roughly plausible.

veracity.statement: Well, we have official languages in this country—te reo, New Zealand Sign Language, and of course English—and we support all languages.
veracity.explanation: Te reo Māori and NZSL are statutory official languages; English is not formally an official language of NZ, so the list is slightly inaccurate.

veracity.statement: we are on track to meet our emissions carbon net zero 2050. In fact, under emissions reduction plans 1 and 2—and what we see as the outlook for emissions reduction plan 3—while there’s more work to do, there’s even a possibility we could do it six years earlier.
veracity.explanation: "on track" is contested by the sector-viability concerns Swarbrick raised; presents the rosy case.

veracity.statement: It shows that there is $206.9 billion worth of projects in the pipeline—an increase of nearly $3 billion since the last quarter. It also shows the value of projects in the pipeline, where the confirmed funding source has increased by $3.7 billion, up to $111.6 billion. The commission tells me that this year there will be at least $16.6 billion spent across all infrastructure sectors, representing 4 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named Infrastructure Commission quarterly update; verifiable and presented straight.

veracity.statement: When we came into Government, just 30 councils contributed to the pipeline... And now 64—so that’s over double—are now contributing to the pipeline and, as I say, there are 14, I think, that need to lift their game and contribute.
veracity.explanation: Specific before/after council counts; plausible and checkable, presented straightforwardly.

veracity.statement: Budget 2025 allocates $604 million for rail, a sector generating $3.3 billion each year for the economy. This comprises $461 million for the national network and $143 million for Auckland and Wellington metropolitan networks.
veracity.explanation: Budget figures stated as facts; broadly verifiable, though the $3.3b economic value is a rounder estimate.

veracity.statement: More than 22 million commuter journeys use the train in Auckland and Wellington, and that figure will rise once the City Rail Link opens—widely supported across the House—and when new trains arrive in Wellington.
veracity.explanation: Patronage figure plausible; presented as fact.

veracity.statement: last Friday, we officially opened the Hillside Workshops in Dunedin, re-energising mechanical engineering and freeing up land for private industrial development. On the same day, the Hon Shane Jones announced an $8.2 million contribution to Southern Link Logistics.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, verifiable events presented straightforwardly.

veracity.statement: We know that around 450,000 emergency department attendances each year are considered lower urgency, and many of these patients could be suitable for treatment through urgent care services as an alternative to EDs, helping to reduce pressure on our emergency departments.
veracity.explanation: The 450,000 figure is stated as a known fact; plausible order of magnitude, presented without a cited source.

rigor.statement: I have seen a lot of reports recently. Some suggest the Government should impose new taxes, ramp up spending, and increase debt. I completely disagree with those suggestions.
