divination.statement: An 18-year-old New Zealander, as of this year's Budget, is now going to be $66,000 worse off in their retirement.
divination.explanation: A ~47-year projection highly sensitive to return and contribution assumptions.

veracity.statement: Funding of $35 million a year is expected to result in $280 million of extra tax revenue. That's an eight-to-one return on investment.

veracity.statement: I can assure members that adequate funding remains in contingency to meet potential costs of future public sector pay equity settlements under our new regime.

veracity.statement: New funding in Budget 2025, of $646 million operating and $101 million capital, is the largest boost to learning support in a generation.
veracity.explanation: The dollar figures are verifiable; the 'largest in a generation' superlative is an unverified claim.

veracity.statement: Government infrastructure investment over the forecast period now totals around $61.8 billion.

veracity.statement: The Government cannot find one single family—not one single family—that's got the $250 a fortnight that they were promised repeatedly by the Government during the election campaign.

veracity.statement: for 61,000 New Zealand families, their Working for Families is being cut. They're going to be $43 a fortnight, on average, worse off because of this Government.

veracity.statement: An 18-year-old New Zealander, as of this year's Budget, is now going to be $66,000 worse off in their retirement.

authenticity.statement: I can assure members that adequate funding remains in contingency to meet potential costs of future public sector pay equity settlements under our new regime.

authenticity.statement: KiwiSaver, proudly set up by Labour, halved by the last National Government, is being halved again by this National Government.

civility.statement: they are supposedly saving $200 million by denying money to our tiniest New Zealanders. Coincidentally, they could find $200 million for new offshore gasfields.
civility.explanation: Pointed but directed at the Government's policy choices rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: in a climate and inequality crisis, the Government is taking money away from whānau with a new baby at home and setting it on fire by ploughing it into new fossil fuel exploration.
civility.explanation: Emotive but targets Government spending priorities, not individuals.

civility.statement: The Government is not a household. The Minister of Finance talks about maxed-out credit cards, but that is not how it actually works when you are managing a country’s economy.
civility.explanation: Challenges the Minister's framing on substance without personal insult.

civility.statement: Her fixation on reducing debt beyond levels recommended by Treasury—which necessitates these pages and pages of investment cuts—put us all on an incredibly, incredibly dangerous path. The Minister of Finance’s self-imposed fiscal rules and expenditure, gunning for historic lows, will, according to Treasury itself, change—and I quote—“the fundamental role of Government in New Zealand”.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at the Minister's policy choices and framed via evidence, not personal abuse.

civility.statement: This is the “trickle-down Budget”. This is the “no ambition Budget”... This is the “let them eat cake Budget”. This is the “BS Budget”, because the Government is taking New Zealanders for chumps.
civility.explanation: A string of sensationalising labels; harsh and mocking though aimed at the Budget rather than a person.

civility.statement: You see, the Greens are intellectually bankrupt, and if they were over here in Government instead of there in Opposition, the Government would be fiscally bankrupt, as well. But their bankruptcy does not end there. They’re also morally bankrupt
civility.explanation: Escalating 'bankrupt' epithets are denigrating rather than substantive.

civility.statement: Te Pāti Māori probably don’t know what a Budget is or that it was on today, so we needn’t worry about them. They show up to Parliament for TikTok, not for the good of all New Zealanders
civility.explanation: Dismissive personal attack impugning an opposing party's competence and motives.

civility.statement: Then there is the Labour Party. Their whole electoral strategy is kind of the opposite of the Kama Sutra—they don’t have a position on anything.
civility.explanation: A witty jibe, but a mocking characterisation rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Nearly half a billion dollars for locking up more crooks sounds expensive, but if you think crims are expensive in jail, imagine them out on the streets, robbing, raping, and murdering. Locking them up is the best money we’ll ever spend.
civility.explanation: Aimed at policy and offenders generally, but uses lurid, sensational language.

civility.statement: We’re ending the mad experiments of Kāhui Ako—or communities of learning—which were actually “communities of teachers taking time off”. That will save $375.5 million
civility.explanation: The 'teachers taking time off' jibe disparages participants rather than engaging the programme's rationale.

civility.statement: if Labour sold T-shirts, they’d probably say, “I voted Labour and all I got was $100 billion worth of debt.” That’s all we got, and for those who blame COVID, the splurge went on far longer than that.
civility.explanation: A mocking gibe at Labour's record, though directed at policy rather than a person.

charisma.statement: has there ever been a Leader of the Opposition with less substance than Chris Hipkins? What you get is a lot of carping, what you get is a lot of points of order, and you get a lot of wishy-washy
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-vs-them mockery aimed at rallying his own side, not building consensus.

charisma.statement: these people can’t run a bath—they cannot run a bath—let alone run an economy.
charisma.explanation: Demeaning applause line that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: in a climate and inequality crisis, the Government is taking money away from whānau with a new baby at home and setting it on fire by ploughing it into new fossil fuel exploration.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for her base but framed as an attack on the Government's motives.

charisma.statement: In the 1930s and 1940s, after some of the worst atrocities that we have seen in the world, our country decided to create public healthcare, public education, and public housing, and we paid for it with higher taxes on those who had profited handsomely during a time of hardship for many. We have done it before, and we can do it again.
charisma.explanation: An aspirational 'we can do it again' appeal to shared national history and collective capacity.

charisma.statement: We are New Zealanders because we share this country, and our futures are inextricably intertwined. In order for us to move forward, to really, truly, properly move forward, we cannot leave anyone behind.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying language appealing to shared identity and common purpose.

charisma.statement: You see, the Greens are intellectually bankrupt, and if they were over here in Government instead of there in Opposition, the Government would be fiscally bankrupt, as well. But their bankruptcy does not end there. They’re also morally bankrupt
charisma.explanation: Combative, base-rallying attack that shuts down cross-party engagement.

rigor.statement: the constant flip-flopping from the man that I call “Mr Bojandals”
rigor.explanation: Name-calling substitutes an ad hominem label for evidence.

rigor.statement: the last time they were in Government, they added $120 billion extra in debt, and we have nothing to show for it except economic pain and economic suffering.
rigor.explanation: Attributes all outcomes to spending while omitting the pandemic context; conclusion overstated relative to premise.

rigor.statement: these people can’t run a bath—they cannot run a bath—let alone run an economy.
rigor.explanation: Pure ad hominem with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: they are supposedly saving $200 million by denying money to our tiniest New Zealanders. Coincidentally, they could find $200 million for new offshore gasfields.
rigor.explanation: Insinuates a direct trade-off between two unrelated line items, an implied false-cause framing.

rigor.statement: in a climate and inequality crisis, the Government is taking money away from whānau with a new baby at home and setting it on fire by ploughing it into new fossil fuel exploration.
rigor.explanation: Vivid 'setting it on fire' framing asserts wastefulness as fact without establishing the causal claim.

rigor.statement: Our country now is wealthier than it has ever been, but, for some strange reason, half a million New Zealanders are using food banks every week.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes aggregate wealth with hardship to make a distributional point; reasonable but the link is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: In the 1930s and 1940s, after some of the worst atrocities that we have seen in the world, our country decided to create public healthcare, public education, and public housing, and we paid for it with higher taxes on those who had profited handsomely during a time of hardship for many. We have done it before, and we can do it again.
rigor.explanation: Uses a historical precedent to support the argument, though the analogy glosses over very different economic conditions.

rigor.statement: The Government is not a household. The Minister of Finance talks about maxed-out credit cards, but that is not how it actually works when you are managing a country’s economy.
rigor.explanation: Draws a legitimate macroeconomic distinction between household and sovereign budgeting, though stated as assertion without elaboration here.

rigor.statement: Even the Minister of Finance herself admitted the other day—and I quote—“not all spending is a cost. Some spending is investment that provides a social and financial return over the longer-term.”
rigor.explanation: Uses the opponent's own quoted words to support the investment argument, a disciplined evidential move.

rigor.statement: Her fixation on reducing debt beyond levels recommended by Treasury—which necessitates these pages and pages of investment cuts—put us all on an incredibly, incredibly dangerous path. The Minister of Finance’s self-imposed fiscal rules and expenditure, gunning for historic lows, will, according to Treasury itself, change—and I quote—“the fundamental role of Government in New Zealand”.
rigor.explanation: Backs the argument with a named-source quotation, though 'incredibly dangerous' editorialises beyond the evidence.

rigor.statement: This is the “trickle-down Budget”. This is the “no ambition Budget”... This is the “let them eat cake Budget”. This is the “BS Budget”, because the Government is taking New Zealanders for chumps.
rigor.explanation: Sloganeering that asserts characterisations without evidence.

rigor.statement: When a Government spends, it takes from the firms, the farms, and the families that make up our great country. Every dollar that the Government spends cannot be spent by a family paying their groceries or their energy bill or renovating their house
rigor.explanation: A coherent opportunity-cost argument, though it presents a one-sided view that omits public goods and multiplier effects.

rigor.statement: The last time the Greens were in Government, they increased annual Government spending by $52 billion a year. Now, here’s the thing: they can’t have it both ways. Either $52 billion of extra spending was enough to fix all our problems, or $22 billion will not be enough to fix all our problems.
rigor.explanation: A dilemma that relies on a false dichotomy and attributes whole-of-government spending to the Greens' support role.

rigor.statement: You see, the Greens are intellectually bankrupt, and if they were over here in Government instead of there in Opposition, the Government would be fiscally bankrupt, as well. But their bankruptcy does not end there. They’re also morally bankrupt
rigor.explanation: Repeated ad hominem labelling in place of argument.

rigor.statement: Te Pāti Māori probably don’t know what a Budget is or that it was on today, so we needn’t worry about them. They show up to Parliament for TikTok, not for the good of all New Zealanders
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem with no supporting basis.

rigor.statement: inflation is currently at 2.5 percent. The population grew by 0.9 percent, or about 47,000, in the last year, and that means that our population plus inflation is almost 3.5 percent. If the Government’s Budget had grown by 3.5 percent, it would have grown by $5 billion... it increases by only $1.3 billion, and that is the saving.
rigor.explanation: A transparent quantitative argument showing spending growth below population-plus-inflation; premises lead to the conclusion, though the benchmark is a chosen one.

rigor.statement: Nearly half a billion dollars for locking up more crooks sounds expensive, but if you think crims are expensive in jail, imagine them out on the streets, robbing, raping, and murdering. Locking them up is the best money we’ll ever spend.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an emotive worst-case appeal and assumes all additional prisoners would otherwise commit violent crime; conclusion outruns the evidence.

veracity.statement: the last time they were in Government, they added $120 billion extra in debt, and we have nothing to show for it except economic pain and economic suffering.
veracity.explanation: The debt figure is roughly in the ballpark of the COVID-era increase, but 'nothing to show for it' ignores wage subsidies and pandemic support — misleading framing.

veracity.statement: Labour’s regime was unworkable, it was broken, it was unaffordable. We’ve made the sensible changes, and, yes, we’ve saved $12 billion in doing so.
veracity.explanation: The ~$12b saving matches the Government's own pay-equity figure (later stated as $12.8b over four years), though 'unworkable/broken' is contested characterisation.

veracity.statement: within three years, we’ve had four different positions on capital gains tax from the Labour Party.
veracity.explanation: Labour has shifted on CGT/wealth tax, so directionally supportable, but the precise count of 'four positions' is a rhetorical tally that isn't clearly verifiable.

veracity.statement: Treasury’s latest forecasts show that, under this Budget, inflation remains in the band, interest rates will remain low, economic growth is going to average 2.7 percent over the period.
veracity.explanation: Accurately attributes figures to Treasury forecasts, though selectively presents the favourable ones.

veracity.statement: we grew 0.7 percent in the last quarter
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported quarterly GDP growth of about 0.7%.

veracity.statement: their wages after inflation have gone up—listen to this—$1,100 in the short time that we’ve been in Government. Under the last three years of a Labour Government, it went up a measly $80 average after inflation wages
veracity.explanation: A selective real-wage comparison across differently-defined periods; figures are cherry-picked in a way that overstates the contrast.

veracity.statement: changes to Working for Families payments, which means that 142,000 families across this country will receive, on average, an increase of about $14 per fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Matches announced Budget figures for the WFF change.

veracity.statement: if you’re receiving New Zealand super, your payments are going to continue to rise under this Government. In fact, they have already risen $130 for a couple per fortnight since we came to power 18 months ago.
veracity.explanation: Superannuation is indexed and has risen; the specific $130 figure is plausible though unverified here.

veracity.statement: We’ve had years of economic mismanagement and vandalism from the Labour Government and that left a massive financial toll on families up and down this country.
veracity.explanation: Cost-of-living pressures were real but 'vandalism' is hyperbole and ignores the pandemic context.

veracity.statement: they are supposedly saving $200 million by denying money to our tiniest New Zealanders. Coincidentally, they could find $200 million for new offshore gasfields.
veracity.explanation: The Best Start cut and gas-exploration spend figures are broadly cited, but the 'coincidental' equivalence is a rhetorical juxtaposition rather than a genuine budget link.

veracity.statement: Our country now is wealthier than it has ever been, but, for some strange reason, half a million New Zealanders are using food banks every week.
veracity.explanation: Food-bank demand is high and widely reported near this figure, though 'half a million every week' is at the upper end of estimates.

veracity.statement: We rank rock-bottom in OECD countries for children’s wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: NZ ranks poorly on some OECD/UNICEF child-wellbeing measures, but 'rock-bottom' overstates a mixed picture across indicators.

veracity.statement: In the 1930s and 1940s, after some of the worst atrocities that we have seen in the world, our country decided to create public healthcare, public education, and public housing, and we paid for it with higher taxes on those who had profited handsomely during a time of hardship for many. We have done it before, and we can do it again.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate account of NZ's first-Labour-Government welfare-state building funded partly by higher taxes.

veracity.statement: Even the Minister of Finance herself admitted the other day—and I quote—“not all spending is a cost. Some spending is investment that provides a social and financial return over the longer-term.”
veracity.explanation: Presents a direct quotation attributed to the Minister; treated as accurate per convention.

veracity.statement: Her fixation on reducing debt beyond levels recommended by Treasury—which necessitates these pages and pages of investment cuts—put us all on an incredibly, incredibly dangerous path. The Minister of Finance’s self-imposed fiscal rules and expenditure, gunning for historic lows, will, according to Treasury itself, change—and I quote—“the fundamental role of Government in New Zealand”.
veracity.explanation: Cites a Treasury characterisation to support the claim; the debt-below-Treasury framing is contestable but she attributes the specific quote.

veracity.statement: The last time the Greens were in Government, they increased annual Government spending by $52 billion a year. Now, here’s the thing: they can’t have it both ways. Either $52 billion of extra spending was enough to fix all our problems, or $22 billion will not be enough to fix all our problems.
veracity.explanation: The $52b figure conflates total government spending growth with Greens' influence, a misleading attribution.

veracity.statement: inflation is currently at 2.5 percent. The population grew by 0.9 percent, or about 47,000, in the last year, and that means that our population plus inflation is almost 3.5 percent. If the Government’s Budget had grown by 3.5 percent, it would have grown by $5 billion... it increases by only $1.3 billion, and that is the saving.
veracity.explanation: The inflation and population figures are close to actual data; the derivation is internally consistent.

veracity.statement: if a business invests in new plant and equipment, they can write off 20 percent of the value and pay no tax right now.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the announced 20% asset write-off policy.

veracity.statement: The Treasury forecasts that by the time those young Kiwis learning their ABCs I mentioned enter the workforce, wages will be 1.5 percent higher than they would otherwise be, thanks to this policy alone.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the 1.5% figure to Treasury; the attribution is likely accurate though the estimate is model-dependent.

veracity.statement: Today, it’s been revealed the savings of the pay equity changes are $12.8 billion over four years.
veracity.explanation: Cites the Government's own reported savings figure; accurate as a stated number though the framing is contested.

veracity.statement: We’re ending the mad experiments of Kāhui Ako—or communities of learning—which were actually “communities of teachers taking time off”. That will save $375.5 million
veracity.explanation: The savings figure is specific, but the 'time off' characterisation misrepresents the programme's design.

veracity.explanation: The debt rose sharply under Labour, but '$100 billion... all we got' dismisses COVID support and services, an misleading framing.

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete dollar saving, but no mechanism or breakdown of how it is achieved.

specificity.statement: We will generate 240,000 new jobs in the period of this Budget.

specificity.statement: we grew 0.7 percent in the last quarter
specificity.explanation: Precise figure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: changes to Working for Families payments, which means that 142,000 families across this country will receive, on average, an increase of about $14 per fortnight.

specificity.statement: It will require lawmakers to publicly declare what problem their law seeks to solve, it will require them to show the effects on people’s liberties and their property rights, and it will require them to weigh the costs and benefits of a law and publicly state who pays the costs and reaps the benefits.
specificity.explanation: Describes concrete requirements the Regulatory Standards Bill would impose on lawmaking.

strength.statement: Labour’s regime was unworkable, it was broken, it was unaffordable. We’ve made the sensible changes, and, yes, we’ve saved $12 billion in doing so.

divination.statement: here’s my prediction—I’ll tell you what’s going to happen: he is going to come out, flip-flop, and actually desperately try and rule it all out—the Greens’ plan—and then you know what he’s going to do? He’s going to launch a broken tax plan of his own very, very shortly.
divination.explanation: A partisan prediction about Hipkins ruling out the Greens' plan and launching his own; plausible directionally but speculative and framed pejoratively, timeframe 'very shortly'.

divination.statement: when Chris Hipkins actually launches Labour’s plans to smash Kiwis with a capital gains tax, which I guarantee will happen by the end of the year, that will be the biggest flip-flop of them all.
divination.explanation: A dated prediction (a CGT by end of 2025) with a stated timeframe; plausible given Labour's tax review but not certain.

divination.statement: Treasury’s latest forecasts show that, under this Budget, inflation remains in the band, interest rates will remain low, economic growth is going to average 2.7 percent over the period.
divination.explanation: Forecast of ~2.7% average growth with low inflation/rates; a plausible official projection but subject to real uncertainty.

divination.statement: We will generate 240,000 new jobs in the period of this Budget.

authenticity.explanation: Links campaign commitments (maths hour, phone ban) to implementation, consistent words-and-deeds.

specificity.statement: we've had an increase in New Zealand Customs Service staff; Māori wardens are getting more money; that great thing that we championed, the rail; and also Matua Jones around energy.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete Budget items (Customs staff, Māori wardens funding, rail, energy) attributed to NZ First, though without figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: if we can actually take that 20 percent and then still depreciate, what a game-changer that is for businesses.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the 20 percent deduction mechanism plus retained depreciation, but 'game-changer' remains a slogan without magnitudes.

specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill and its purpose (granny flats) and process (select committee), though without policy detail.

strength.statement: this Budget is the real oil, with $200 million dedicated to accelerate, de-risk, enable your nation—our country, fellow MPs—to take a cornerstone in recovering a foundation industry destroyed by the last regime.

strength.statement: that’s why we are repealing the excesses of the Resource Management Act, that’s why we will be fixing up the Wildlife Act, and that’s why my leader, Winston Peters, in negotiating with the National Party, brought forward the fast-track legislation.
strength.explanation: Fast-track legislation was actually enacted (delivered); RMA repeal and Wildlife Act changes are in progress—mixed follow-through.

strength.statement: We’re putting a new board in place, and that board will have the acid on them to ensure that that executive leadership team delivers; if not, consequences will most certainly flow.
strength.explanation: States intent to reform governance; follow-through and results unstated.

veracity.statement: this Budget is the real oil, with $200 million dedicated to accelerate, de-risk, enable your nation—our country, fellow MPs—to take a cornerstone in recovering a foundation industry destroyed by the last regime.
veracity.explanation: "a foundation industry destroyed by the last regime" is hyperbole about the 2018 exploration ban; the gas industry continued operating.

veracity.statement: It is a problem that has been inherited after the worst decision made in the history of our nation, delivered by Jacinda, supported by Megan, and, sadly, acquiesced by the good Matua.
veracity.explanation: "the worst decision made in the history of our nation" is unfalsifiable hyperbole applied to the oil/gas exploration ban.

veracity.statement: we, whether we like it or not, because of the wretched decision of destroying the gas industry four or five years ago, are the only Western nation that I know of that is transitioning to coal
veracity.explanation: Hedged ("that I know of") but misleading; NZ's increased coal use at Huntly is a partial fallback, not a national "transition to coal."

veracity.statement: We were given in the Paris accord, as a food-producing nation, the option of not including food-related emissions. That’s what the law says at the UN
veracity.explanation: Overstates the Paris Agreement, which references not threatening food production but does not grant an "option" to exclude food-related emissions from accounting.

veracity.statement: next Thursday, the Green Party travellers are going to have a protest outside the ANZ Bank. They have decided that banks should no longer fund coal, minerals, and gas.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about a planned protest and its aims; plausible but characterised in his own framing.

veracity.statement: The census told us that the Māori population was just under a million, but they also told us that they only managed to count around 85 percent of us, with this meaning that the 15 percent of Māori who are out there somewhere would naturally take us above 1 million
veracity.explanation: Census undercount of Māori is real, but the precise 85% figure and resulting "above 1 million" inference are approximate.

veracity.statement: Māori imported the first plough in 1820, quickly adapted to new breeds of animals and crops, and steadily moved to import technologies such as the flax and flour mills, whilst simultaneously continuing to export those raw materials, and all of this was before the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the historical record of early Māori agricultural adoption and trade, though the precise "first plough in 1820" claim is specific and hard to verify exactly.

veracity.statement: By 1950, Pākehā returned servicemen had received around a million acres—just short of a million acres—of farmland. They’d been given it free of charge for their service in World War I and World War II... they had received almost a million acres of farmable land and had been advanced more than £28 million in grants and low or no-interest loans.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with documented rehabilitation/land-settlement schemes favouring Pākehā servicemen; the exact acreage and £28m figures are specific and directionally supported by historians.

veracity.statement: by the turn of the 1900s, we would be deemed a dying race, with a population less than 40,000
veracity.explanation: The Māori population fell to roughly 40,000 by the 1890s–1900 and the "dying race" trope is well documented; the figure is close to accurate.

veracity.statement: when it comes to the distribution of Budget funds, Māori are lucky to receive 1 percent
veracity.explanation: A precise-sounding but unsourced and contestable figure; Māori-targeted and general spending that reaches Māori is difficult to reduce to "1 percent."

veracity.statement: They need billions invested into helping them secure a home for their whānau, not a billion-dollar gutting of Kāinga Ora whilst homelessness increases to 53 percent.
veracity.explanation: "homelessness increases to 53 percent" is stated without context or clear referent, making the specific figure misleading.

veracity.statement: we reproduce at a higher rate than anyone else, and so we are, in fact, a numerical inevitability
veracity.explanation: Māori do have a comparatively higher birth rate; the "numerical inevitability" conclusion is rhetorical extrapolation.

veracity.statement: The last Budget returned us to the 1940s, and this Budget, no doubt, will return us to the 1800s.
veracity.explanation: Rhetorical hyperbole equating Budgets with returns to past eras; not a literally accurate claim.

veracity.statement: This bill raises the family income threshold from $42,700, where it has been since 2018, non-adjusted. This bill adjusts it to $44,900 and increases the abatement rate of reduction from 27c for each dollar above the threshold to 27.5c.
veracity.explanation: The Working for Families threshold had indeed been unadjusted since 2018; the factual anchor is accurate.

veracity.statement: Let me stress: the change to Best Start only applies for births on or after 1 April 2026. So no family will see an actual reduction in their current payments, and you’ve all got time to make babies yet.
veracity.explanation: Technically true about current payments, but omits that future families with new babies will lose universal first-year Best Start—context that opponents highlight.

veracity.statement: sitting in the regulatory impact statement we find they considered only two options.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim grounded in the regulatory impact statement; plausible and specifically sourced.

veracity.statement: we asked Treasury, here is what Treasury said about those changes: it turns out that 61,000 families will be $43 a fortnight worse.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific figure to Treasury; sourced and checkable, though the framing selects the losing cohort.

veracity.statement: that Government, we estimate they have taken $66,000 away from a person who’s starting work tomorrow.
veracity.explanation: A modelled long-run estimate presented as a headline figure; directional but assumption-dependent.

veracity.statement: thousands of families having a brand-new baby have their income cut by $3,800 a year by this bill. That’s what the Budget does. It takes money away from families with new babies.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the removal of universal first-year Best Start, though it omits that this applies only to births from 1 April 2026, not current recipients.

civility.statement: The Green Party is likely to say “We can match it with wind.”, but we don’t want your mung bean, pronoun version of wind.
civility.explanation: Mocking, belittling language ("mung bean, pronoun version") rather than engagement with the substance of renewable policy.

civility.statement: It is a problem that has been inherited after the worst decision made in the history of our nation, delivered by Jacinda, supported by Megan, and, sadly, acquiesced by the good Matua.
civility.explanation: Personalises blame by naming individuals, but remains directed at a policy decision.

civility.statement: my advice to Mr Hipkins is you’re going to kiss a lot of frogs before you find the prince. I doubt that they will be able to find anyone worthy of a partner, because his speech today was an obituary. It was an epitaph.
civility.explanation: Mockery of an opponent's speech and coalition prospects; ridicule rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: don’t lecture us about school lunches. Wake up early and make your kids a lunch yourself. When they’re not at school, who’s feeding them? And if they’re not being fed, you don’t deserve the munificence of the State.
civility.explanation: Dismissive lecturing of struggling families rather than respectful engagement.

civility.statement: If you’re 17, 18, 19, or 20 and you’re not willing to stand up and join the ranks of your fellow New Zealanders, prepare to own your own life. Prepare to find a solution to your own problems. We are no longer going to pay you to stay on the couch or be on meth.
civility.explanation: Stereotypes young beneficiaries as idle drug users—a demeaning characterisation rather than policy argument.

civility.statement: no more hakas of victimhood. Don’t tell this House that the reason the haka exists here is because of victim ideology of colonisation.
civility.explanation: Frames a cultural practice as "victimhood," dismissive of Māori opponents' expression.

civility.statement: There’s nothing wrong with aspiring to become wealthy. The Green Party stood against that.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents an opponent's position rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: the banks of New Zealand need to know that you don’t have the moral authority to de-bank farming. You don’t have the moral authority to destroy regional New Zealand, and the Green Party and their fellow travellers—under no circumstances whatsoever should we permit or should we encourage that destructiveness, because of their conceit and the false superiority that they bring to these debates.
civility.explanation: Attributes "conceit" and "false superiority" to opponents—character attack rather than argument.

civility.statement: They need billions invested into helping them secure a home for their whānau, not a billion-dollar gutting of Kāinga Ora whilst homelessness increases to 53 percent.
civility.explanation: "gutting" is charged language, but the criticism is aimed at a policy (Kāinga Ora funding), not a person.

civility.statement: The last Budget returned us to the 1940s, and this Budget, no doubt, will return us to the 1800s.
civility.explanation: Sharp but figurative political criticism of a policy record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: And anyone who opposes this bill may ask themselves why they oppose growth, why they oppose workers, and why they oppose savings. We’re about to find out if people like that exist in this House.
civility.explanation: Provocative but aimed at policy positions rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: the person who has balanced this Budget on the backs of working women, on the backs of families, and on the backs of low-paid workers who rely on that Government contribution to KiwiSaver to save for their old age. Those people are all worse off because of this Budget.
civility.explanation: Strong emotive framing but directed at the Budget's distributional effects rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: A friend of mine messaged me during the speeches earlier saying, “Wow, this Budget is catastrophically bad and cartoonishly evil.”
civility.explanation: Amplifies a charged, sensational characterisation of the Budget.

civility.statement: the members of the Government, clapping like seals in their little chorus of applause for their party leaders and finance Minister, are completely out of touch with what ordinary New Zealanders are having to deal with
civility.explanation: "clapping like seals" is a demeaning personal jibe at opposing members.

civility.statement: stop pretending like you care about the future of this country when all you care about is lining the pockets of your mates and your donors.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motives ("lining the pockets of your mates and your donors")—a personal/character attack.

civility.statement: The member opposite talks about a land tax. How’s that going to help anything? That’s going to discourage you from doing any other investment because you’re too busy paying their death taxes and their land taxes and their capital gains taxes and every other tax there is.
civility.explanation: Dismissive but directed at policy rather than the member personally.

charisma.statement: The Green Party is likely to say “We can match it with wind.”, but we don’t want your mung bean, pronoun version of wind.
charisma.explanation: Alienating us-vs-them ridicule of opponents; shuts down rather than builds consensus.

charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing jab at opponents, not persuasion of the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: don’t lecture us about school lunches. Wake up early and make your kids a lunch yourself. When they’re not at school, who’s feeding them? And if they’re not being fed, you don’t deserve the munificence of the State.
charisma.explanation: Rallies own side by contempt for opponents' constituents; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: no more hakas of victimhood. Don’t tell this House that the reason the haka exists here is because of victim ideology of colonisation.
charisma.explanation: Divisive framing that alienates rather than seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: I hope we all have the courage to challenge ourselves to think of the needs of others before the needs of ourselves, to think of the needs of those who are yet to be born instead of the needs of those who have so much already

charisma.explanation: A daring taunt to opponents rather than an attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: New Zealand is built on small family businesses, and these businesses being able to invest and look for new, productive ideas, improving their business, helps all of New Zealand. This is an absolutely great scheme and I commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Positive, broadly inclusive framing ("helps all of New Zealand"), though still an appeal chiefly to his own side's values.

rigor.statement: The Green Party is likely to say “We can match it with wind.”, but we don’t want your mung bean, pronoun version of wind.
rigor.explanation: Strawman caricature of the wind-energy argument with no engagement of evidence.

rigor.statement: It is a problem that has been inherited after the worst decision made in the history of our nation, delivered by Jacinda, supported by Megan, and, sadly, acquiesced by the good Matua.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping superlative assertion with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: don’t lecture us about school lunches. Wake up early and make your kids a lunch yourself. When they’re not at school, who’s feeding them? And if they’re not being fed, you don’t deserve the munificence of the State.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to a moralising anecdote rather than evidence on child food insecurity.

rigor.statement: If you’re 17, 18, 19, or 20 and you’re not willing to stand up and join the ranks of your fellow New Zealanders, prepare to own your own life. Prepare to find a solution to your own problems. We are no longer going to pay you to stay on the couch or be on meth.
rigor.explanation: Emotive caricature ("on the couch or be on meth") substitutes for evidence on youth welfare.

rigor.statement: There’s nothing wrong with aspiring to become wealthy. The Green Party stood against that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman—attributes to the Greens an opposition to wealth aspiration itself.

rigor.statement: 20 percent of the population who are Māori should expect to see an investment of 20 percent of that $180 billion made in their name. That’s $36 billion, e te whānau—$36 billion.
rigor.explanation: A clearly laid-out proportionality argument, but the naive population-share-equals-spending-share premise is contestable.

rigor.statement: The census told us that the Māori population was just under a million, but they also told us that they only managed to count around 85 percent of us, with this meaning that the 15 percent of Māori who are out there somewhere would naturally take us above 1 million
rigor.explanation: Reasoned extrapolation from a stated undercount, though it assumes the uncounted are all additional Māori.

rigor.statement: it soon became clear, however—and I encourage members to read the regulatory impact statement on this one—that dollar for dollar, Investment Boost has more impact on business investment than a reduction in the company tax rate, as it only applies to new investments and not those made in the past.
rigor.explanation: Cites the regulatory impact statement and gives a coherent reason (new vs past investment) for the comparative judgement.

rigor.statement: And anyone who opposes this bill may ask themselves why they oppose growth, why they oppose workers, and why they oppose savings. We’re about to find out if people like that exist in this House.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy—equates opposing this specific bill with opposing growth, workers, and savings in general.

rigor.statement: the person who has balanced this Budget on the backs of working women, on the backs of families, and on the backs of low-paid workers who rely on that Government contribution to KiwiSaver to save for their old age. Those people are all worse off because of this Budget.
rigor.explanation: Emotive "on the backs of" framing precedes the evidence; the specific claims come later in the speech.

rigor.statement: why did they not look at increasing the low-value asset threshold for writing off a low-value asset? Why did they not look at targeting this measure towards small business?... Why did they not consider an accelerated depreciation rate?
rigor.explanation: Substantive critique naming specific alternative policy options that the analysis allegedly failed to consider.

rigor.statement: A friend of mine messaged me during the speeches earlier saying, “Wow, this Budget is catastrophically bad and cartoonishly evil.”
rigor.explanation: Appeal to an anecdote/emotion ("cartoonishly evil") rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: If the Government was truly serious about tackling low productivity in New Zealand, they would take the mainstream economic advice from institutions like the IMF who have recommended tax reforms, including a comprehensive capital gains tax or a land value tax.
rigor.explanation: Cites institutional (IMF) advice and names concrete policy alternatives—reasoned, though leaning on appeal to authority.

rigor.statement: By using this product, the farmers that use it were getting a 20 percent improvement in pasture production... It leads to a 70 percent reduction in lameness... they were more productive, better working conditions, enjoying their jobs more. The whole business improved.
rigor.explanation: A concrete worked example, but generalises to the whole economy from a single product anecdote.

rigor.statement: The member opposite talks about a land tax. How’s that going to help anything? That’s going to discourage you from doing any other investment because you’re too busy paying their death taxes and their land taxes and their capital gains taxes and every other tax there is.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical escalation piling up assorted taxes ("every other tax there is") rather than engaging the specific land-tax proposal.

rigor.statement: New Zealand is built on small family businesses, and these businesses being able to invest and look for new, productive ideas, improving their business, helps all of New Zealand. This is an absolutely great scheme and I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable link between small-business investment and wider benefit, but rests on assertion rather than evidence.

divination.statement: if it comes to pass that fossil fuels are required in the short to medium or even in the long term, that is the price that we have to pay to ensure that we do not believe falsely in how quickly alternative technologies can develop
divination.explanation: Predicts continued fossil-fuel reliance because renewable/alternative tech will develop more slowly than hoped; plausible but hedged and open-ended in timeframe.

divination.statement: We’re currently 20 percent of the population, steadily moving towards being 30 percent... Young Māori will comprise 30 percent of the future workforce of this country.
divination.explanation: Demographic projection consistent with current younger Māori age structure and higher birth rate; directionally supported but the 30% magnitude and timeframe are uncertain.

divination.statement: Over 20 years, Investment Boost is expected to lift New Zealand’s capital stock by 1.6 percent, GDP by 1 percent, and wages by 1.5 percent.
divination.explanation: A 20-year forecast drawn from officials' modelling; plausible in direction but long-horizon and inherently uncertain (she notes they are orders of magnitude).

specificity.statement: By stopping wasteful spending, inflation is down, interest rates are falling, our economy is expected to grow, on average, 2.7 percent—that means 240,000 new jobs being created in the next four years—and, most importantly, wages are growing faster than inflation.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures: 2.7% average growth, 240,000 jobs, and specific claims about inflation, rates and wages.

specificity.statement: I just disagree completely. This is a Government that makes sure we get maximum value for money out of every dollar that we spend, and we expect each and every year to be looking at the total pool of expenditure, not just the layer cake of new spending but the total spend that happens on a portfolio.
specificity.explanation: Talks about looking at the 'total pool of expenditure' but gives no mechanism, figure, or actual budgeting detail.

specificity.statement: Well, I just say to the member that the feedback that we have had around Government contributions is that people understand we are increasing contribution rates for employers and employees; that's a good pathway for New Zealand to be on. Whether I look at an 18-year-old on minimum wage, whether I look at a 30-year-old on the average wage, typically, it looks like they'll have 25 percent bigger retirement balances.
specificity.explanation: Offers a '25 percent bigger retirement balances' figure but no basis or timeframe, and dodges the specific 80%-offset assumption raised.

specificity.statement: We have house prices stable, we have rents stable, we have taken 7,000 people off the social housing register, and, most importantly, we've taken 2,100 kids out of motel emergency accommodation and they're in great homes with social housing providers and with Kāinga Ora.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures: 7,000 off the register and 2,100 children out of motels, plus claims on prices and rents.

specificity.statement: Does he accept that if the increased KiwiSaver employer-contribution costs must be met out of agency baselines, driving wage growth lower than otherwise, and the cost will be represented in the next Budget, then for all intents and purposes, this is a predictable cost, which the Government has failed to budget for?
specificity.explanation: Names the precise mechanism (employer contributions absorbed by baselines) and the fiscal consequence rather than a vague critique.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister disagree with Treasury when it says, in their Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, that “We have assumed that employers will offset the majority (80 percent) of their higher contributions via lower-than-otherwise wage increases.”?
specificity.explanation: Precisely cites the source and the 80% figure.

specificity.statement: Investment Boost allows New Zealand businesses to immediately deduct 20 percent of the cost of qualifying assets on top of depreciation. That means a much lower tax bill in the year they purchase, create, or construct the asset. The remaining book value of the asset is depreciated at normal rates.
specificity.explanation: Precisely describes the mechanism: 20% immediate deduction on qualifying assets on top of depreciation, with residual value depreciated normally.

specificity.statement: But let me quote from the regulatory impact statement that accompanied this policy... “Our view is the majority of the increase in national income from this policy would flow to workers. And this increase would come from a combination of higher wages and higher employment...”
specificity.explanation: Attributes the claim to a named official document and quotes its wording directly.

specificity.statement: I'm advised that wage growth is forecast by Treasury to be slightly lower across the forecast period because of pay equity and macroeconomic changes, and slightly higher because of Investment Boost. Overall, wage growth is expected to be slightly lower but starts from a higher base, meaning that actual wages in dollar terms... are expected to be higher right across the forecast period compared to the half-year update.
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes wage-growth rate from dollar levels and attributes the drivers (pay equity, macro, Investment Boost).

specificity.statement: Also, WorkSafe's road cone tip line is open and ready for business. You can find this at worksafe.govt.nz/road-cones.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, actionable detail: a named channel and exact URL for the road cone tip line.

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced, alongside the Hon Todd McClay and the Hon Simon Watts, the largest package of changes to national direction rules under the Resource Management Act (RMA)... There are three documents open for consultation now: infrastructure and development, primary sector, and fresh water.
specificity.explanation: Names the three consultation documents and the scope of the national direction package.

specificity.statement: One notable one is to make it easier to consent a quarry or a mine... we are also making changes to the rules around highly productive lands, removing land use class 3 land from protection, letting farmers do more with their own land; we're removing the restrictions on non-intensive grazing of beef, cattle, and deer in wetlands.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates precise rule changes: quarry/mine consenting, removing land use class 3 from protection, and lifting non-intensive grazing restrictions in wetlands.

specificity.statement: They knew that debt was up by 120 billion bucks in six years. They knew that Government spending had risen by around 80 percent in that time.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete dollar and percentage figures over a defined six-year window.

specificity.statement: The operating allowance on this Budget is the lowest it's been for a decade: $1.3 billion.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure ($1.3b) with a comparative claim (lowest in a decade).

specificity.statement: New Zealand's natural gas reserves have been in decline as a consequence of a foolish and dangerous decision. Our Government has set aside a contingency of $200 million to overcome sovereign risk perceptions... specificity.explanation: Gives the $200m contingency and a possible 10–15% Crown commercial stake, though the stake is flagged as tentative.

specificity.statement: Natural gas will continue to produce a critical level of firming, to enable Kiwis to enjoy affordable energy, security of energy, for at least the next 20 years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough horizon ('next 20 years') but no volumes or investment detail.

specificity.statement: This Government has put a record amount of funding into health: $16.68 billion over three years. We're empowering our clinicians by returning decision making as close to the front line as possible, unlike that last Government that took a wrecking ball to the health system in the middle of the pandemic.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($16.68b over three years) and the structural change of returning decision-making to the front line.

specificity.statement: I think that member should get her facts straight. Nothing was declined. What she is referring to is a quality report that went to a quality committee. There was a number of initiatives in that report. Some have been completed, some are under way... including opening up 20 new beds in a ward to ease flow in that ED.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (quality report to a quality committee) and a concrete measure (20 new beds).

specificity.statement: When we left office, the health target for six hours' wait in ED was at 90 percent. In 2023, that went down to 70 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures (90% down to 70%) tied to a defined ED wait-time target.

specificity.statement: If the Minister's claim of record investment is correct, why were clinicians' requests for merely $3 million in one of our largest emergency departments to ensure it was properly staffed turned down by the Government?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the challenge in a precise figure ($3 million) and a specific ED to contrast against the 'record investment' claim.

specificity.statement: We're delivering the expansion of the Early Intervention Service from early childhood to the end of year 1, with an additional 560 fulltime-equivalent specialists... This investment will do two things: it will provide additional support to the 7,000 students already receiving the service and will reduce wait times for the over 3,000 children currently on the wait-list.
specificity.explanation: Highly precise: 560 FTE specialists, service extended to end of year 1, 7,000 current recipients and 3,000+ on the wait-list.

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 delivers a learning support coordinator for every school with a year 0 to 8 student...
