veracity.statement: In a country where over 156,000 children wake up in cold, damp homes; where families are skipping meals to pay the rent; where care-experienced rangatahi are still being harmed by the very systems meant to protect them—this Budget could have prioritised children.
veracity.explanation: The 156,000 figure and cold/damp housing claims are broadly consistent with NZ child-poverty and housing-quality statistics, though the exact figure is not sourced in the text; directionally accurate.

veracity.statement: the Minister has cut funding to independent advocacy services by 37 percent from $6.37 million to $4 million.
veracity.explanation: A checkable budget-line claim stated with exact figures; plausible and internally consistent, though unverified here.

veracity.statement: New Zealand ranks last in the OECD for youth mental wellbeing, 35th out of 41 for child physical health, and our educational inequality gap is widening.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to the recent UNICEF report; the rankings match widely reported UNICEF Report Card findings, so directionally accurate.

veracity.statement: in 18 months—18 short months—we've managed to pull some levers, been able to get the OCR back down to about 3.25 percent.
veracity.explanation: The OCR was indeed around 3.25% in mid-2025; accurate on the number, though attributing the fall to 'pulling levers' overstates government control of the independent Reserve Bank.

veracity.statement: The inflation itself: we went from the highs of over 7 percent—7.3 percent at its highest in recent times—and we're now back down to 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Both figures match official CPI data (peak 7.3%, back to ~2.5% by early 2025).

veracity.statement: unemployment is actually relatively high—it's at about 5.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Matches the reported unemployment rate of ~5.1% for the period; a candid concession of a negative figure.

veracity.statement: our Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, came along and he announced that there will be the extra $59.2 million that's required to complete the build there.
veracity.explanation: A specific announced funding figure, plausible and checkable, presented with acknowledgement the build ran over budget.

veracity.statement: an extra 66,000 SuperGold cardholders are now going to be eligible for the rates rebate scheme... moving the actual threshold of an annual income per household of SuperGold cardholders from $31,500 or thereabouts, up to $45,000... and the rebate itself per annum has had a small increase up to the $805.
veracity.explanation: Detailed policy figures presented with a hedge ('or thereabouts'); checkable and plausible.

veracity.statement: At the moment, we are reliant—when we have no wind blowing, no sun shining, in the middle of the winter when we've got the highest energy requirements of electricity—on burning coal. Natural gas is 40 percent—40 percent—cleaner than coal.
veracity.explanation: Gas does emit substantially less CO2 than coal per unit of energy; '40% cleaner' is in the right ballpark for combustion emissions but simplifies (ignores methane leakage).

veracity.statement: David Seymour's pet ministry, the Ministry for Regulation. Every year, a percent increase whilst Oranga Tamariki is cutting funds... David Seymour's ministry is getting 5 percent more, year on year, for the next four Budget rounds. That's so he can push his vanity bill, the Regulatory Standards Bill.
veracity.explanation: The 5%-per-year funding-increase claim is specific and checkable; plausible but asserted without a cited source.

veracity.statement: the only way that the Government could come anywhere close to having a respectable Budget was by taking $12 billion away from working women.
veracity.explanation: The pay-equity change did produce multi-billion-dollar forecast savings (~$12.8bn cited elsewhere), so the figure is broadly grounded, though 'taking away from working women' is a contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: Te Ao Mārama—one of our most effective programmes to make sure that the experience of the court process is good for victims and is effective in stopping reoffending—is being cut. It was to be rolled out around the country. It's in eight courtrooms at the moment, in the District Court.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claims about a named justice programme, supported by a cited Chief District Court Judge endorsement.

veracity.statement: we had six years of suffering under the lacklustre Labour lot that sent New Zealand into a terrible spin. Inflation at record highs: 7.3 percent—an outrageously high level of inflation—and an extra $100 billion of debt.
veracity.explanation: The 7.3% inflation peak is accurate and debt did rise sharply; but 'record highs' overstates (1980s inflation was far higher) and the $100bn figure is presented without context.

veracity.statement: We know the stats. We know that if you go on a benefit at 18 years old, you are likely to spend, on average, 20 years on that benefit.
veracity.explanation: Echoes an official actuarial-style projection sometimes cited by MSD, but the '20 years on average' figure is contested and oversimplified.

veracity.statement: that $614 million has come from reprioritisation of programmes like Kāhui Ako, which is going to impact—as we know from the leaked documentation—over 4,000 roles, 600 full-time teacher equivalents (FTTEs), over $300 million in funding from an apparently underperforming programme.
veracity.explanation: Checkable claims sourced to leaked documentation; plausible and specific but reliant on an uncited leak.

veracity.statement: over $100 million is being invested into charter schools. Not a single State school has converted in the last financial year. It's five times more per student to fund a charter school than it is to a public school.
veracity.explanation: The 'no conversions' and funding-gap claims are checkable; 'five times more per student' is a contested figure sensitive to how costs are counted, likely overstated.

veracity.statement: this is a "BS Budget". It is a "BS Budget" because it takes $12.8 billion out of the back pockets of women workers: our mums, our sisters, our aunties, our nieces.
veracity.explanation: The $12.8bn pay-equity saving figure is broadly consistent with reported forecasts, though 'out of the back pockets of women workers' is a contestable framing of forgone future claims.

veracity.statement: When unemployment is at its highest, at 5.2 percent, and almost double that for Māori and Pacific, more people are choosing to study, and this Budget does not adequately address training a skilled workforce for the future.
veracity.explanation: 5.2% unemployment and roughly double rates for Māori/Pacific are consistent with official statistics for the period.

veracity.statement: The 4 percent funding increase that equalled $64 million per year for universities has been cut by this Government... Instead, this Government has chosen to only invest in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM) subjects.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable budget claims; the 'only invest in STEM' characterisation may overstate the actual policy scope.

veracity.statement: the reality of Budget 2025 is that students will be paying more to study because of this Government's decision to allow institutions to increase student fees up to 6 percent.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable policy figure that supports the 'students pay more' conclusion.

veracity.statement: Check the unemployment rates out there, Mr MacLeod, and you will see your Māori unemployment rates have gone up considerably. That is because there is no plan. Targeted programmes have been abandoned.
veracity.explanation: Māori unemployment did rise over the period; directionally accurate, though 'considerably' and the sole-cause attribution are asserted.

specificity.statement: In a country where over 156,000 children wake up in cold, damp homes; where families are skipping meals to pay the rent; where care-experienced rangatahi are still being harmed by the very systems meant to protect them—this Budget could have prioritised children.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (156,000) but frames it within a general rhetorical contrast rather than a precise measure.

specificity.statement: the Minister has cut funding to independent advocacy services by 37 percent from $6.37 million to $4 million.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage and before/after dollar figures for a named appropriation.

specificity.statement: New Zealand ranks last in the OECD for youth mental wellbeing, 35th out of 41 for child physical health, and our educational inequality gap is widening.
specificity.explanation: Names precise rankings (last; 35th of 41) sourced to a named report.

specificity.statement: The Green Party has a clear, costed plan to end child poverty, including a family top-up of $220 for the first child and $135 for each additional child, changing the abatement rates for the family tax credit under Working for Families, and doubling the Best Start payment.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete dollar amounts and specific policy mechanisms (abatement rates, Best Start doubling).

specificity.statement: we would commit to real prevention by ensuring that at least 50 percent of Oranga Tamariki's investments go to early intervention, whānau-led, culturally grounded support, and we would legislate to make child impact assessments mandatory in every major decision the Government makes.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete threshold (50%) and a named legislative mechanism, though without dollar figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: our Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, came along and he announced that there will be the extra $59.2 million that's required to complete the build there.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figure tied to a named project (New Plymouth Hospital).

specificity.statement: the Minister of Defence has actually announced that we are aiming for a 2 percent of GDP goal with regards to our defence spend by the year 2032-33.
specificity.explanation: Names a target (2% of GDP) and a target year (2032-33).

specificity.statement: an extra 66,000 SuperGold cardholders are now going to be eligible for the rates rebate scheme... moving the actual threshold of an annual income per household of SuperGold cardholders from $31,500 or thereabouts, up to $45,000... and the rebate itself per annum has had a small increase up to the $805.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures: numbers eligible, income thresholds, and rebate amount.

specificity.statement: Having more teacher-aides in the classroom is of great assistance, and that's to the tune of over 2 million extra hours of teacher-aides—is what the Minister of Education has announced—by the year 2028.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the commitment (2 million extra hours) with a target year (2028).

specificity.statement: I'm very pleased that this Government has actually tagged $200 million to help regain the confidence by playing a stake in that and potentially having a stake of up to 10 to 15 percent in exploration wells.
specificity.explanation: Cites the $200 million figure and a 10-15% stake range for the exploration policy.

specificity.statement: Te Ao Mārama—one of our most effective programmes to make sure that the experience of the court process is good for victims and is effective in stopping reoffending—is being cut. It was to be rolled out around the country. It's in eight courtrooms at the moment, in the District Court.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, its current footprint (eight courtrooms, District Court), and the change (roll-out halted).

specificity.statement: I'm concerned that the biosecurity budget has been slashed overall, and I'm extremely concerned about the issue of Caulerpa up in Northland and the issue it's going to cause and is causing in our underwater seabeds.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete issue (Caulerpa in Northland) but keeps the budget claim general ('slashed overall') without figures.

specificity.statement: you can see clearly now with this new policy that they will have, on average, about $180,000 more by the time they reach retirement age.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete projected figure ($180,000) though the assumptions behind it are unstated.

specificity.statement: the 12-month prescription... to now be able to only do that over a 12-month period, instead of three months. It saves cost in terms of doctors' fees, it saves prescription fees, and it actually frees up capacity at those medical centres.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete change (12-month vs three-month prescriptions) and its stated mechanisms of benefit.

specificity.statement: that $614 million has come from reprioritisation of programmes like Kāhui Ako, which is going to impact—as we know from the leaked documentation—over 4,000 roles, 600 full-time teacher equivalents (FTTEs), over $300 million in funding from an apparently underperforming programme.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures: $614m, 4,000+ roles, 600 FTTEs, $300m+ from a named programme.

specificity.statement: We have this Government investing almost $33 million—$33 million—in their failed boot camp experiment... The Minister will not be honest with the public; the Prime Minister will not be honest with the public and tell the public what the reoffending statistics are.
specificity.explanation: Cites the $33m figure and the specific demand (release reoffending statistics).

specificity.statement: over $100 million is being invested into charter schools. Not a single State school has converted in the last financial year. It's five times more per student to fund a charter school than it is to a public school.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: $100m+, zero conversions, a 5x per-student cost ratio.

specificity.statement: The 4 percent funding increase that equalled $64 million per year for universities has been cut by this Government... Instead, this Government has chosen to only invest in science, technology, engineering, and maths (STEM) subjects.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 4% / $64m per year figure and the STEM-only reallocation.

specificity.statement: the reality of Budget 2025 is that students will be paying more to study because of this Government's decision to allow institutions to increase student fees up to 6 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete mechanism and cap (fee increases up to 6%).

specificity.statement: The Minister's new industry skills boards only receive 46 percent of the funding that workforce development councils had, and they are expected to deliver the same work for the same pay.
specificity.explanation: Precise funding ratio (46%) tied to a named structural change.

specificity.statement: the regulations will be able to be made for two purposes. The first regulation-making power will allow specified benefits to be added or removed from the list, that will be subject to mandatory reviews... this power has been carefully created to ensure that primary legislation includes a list of payments that cannot be added to the list via regulation.
specificity.explanation: Precisely enumerates the two regulation-making powers and the safeguard preserving parliamentary sovereignty.

specificity.statement: my amendment... is to help the Minister maybe delete the whole clause, delete new clause 105. This new clause 105 means a benefit can be reviewed after 52 weeks... beneficiaries have to prepare for a review at very, very short notice.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause (105), the mechanism (review after 52 weeks), and the concrete legislative remedy proposed (deletion).

specificity.statement: I want to know if the Minister has a distributional analysis of where that is coming from... We know that there's around $238 million in savings when it comes to benefit or related expenses... if a beneficiary's relationship status is part of what is being assessed, we could see solo parents, particularly, being disproportionately affected.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question in the exact clause (105(2)(c)), a concrete savings figure ($238m), and a specific at-risk group (solo parents).

divination.statement: It is likely the Government will not meet any of their 2028 child poverty reduction targets.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable forecast about 2028 targets; directionally supported by current trend data cited, but magnitude and timeframe leave real uncertainty.

divination.statement: the Minister of Defence has actually announced that we are aiming for a 2 percent of GDP goal with regards to our defence spend by the year 2032-33.
divination.explanation: Implied forecast of reaching 2% of GDP by 2032-33; the speaker himself calls it 'ambitious', signalling real uncertainty.

divination.statement: you can see clearly now with this new policy that they will have, on average, about $180,000 more by the time they reach retirement age.
divination.explanation: A long-horizon forecast resting on online-calculator assumptions about returns and contributions; plausible but highly sensitive to inputs.

strength.statement: The Green Party has a clear, costed plan to end child poverty, including a family top-up of $220 for the first child and $135 for each additional child, changing the abatement rates for the family tax credit under Working for Families, and doubling the Best Start payment.
strength.explanation: A costed opposition plan, but it is an aspiration/proposal with no delivery power, so demonstrated follow-through is nil.

strength.statement: in 18 months—18 short months—we've managed to pull some levers, been able to get the OCR back down to about 3.25 percent.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a monetary outcome largely set by the independent Reserve Bank; partial at best.

strength.statement: my amendment... is to help the Minister maybe delete the whole clause, delete new clause 105. This new clause 105 means a benefit can be reviewed after 52 weeks... beneficiaries have to prepare for a review at very, very short notice.
strength.explanation: Advances a concrete amendment as an opposition MP, but with little prospect of passage, so it is a proposal rather than delivered action.

civility.statement: Balancing the books on the backs of our most vulnerable children is not fiscal responsibility. None of this is inevitable. It is the result of cruel political choices.
civility.explanation: Charged framing ('cruel political choices') aimed at policy choices rather than a person; heated but stays on the Budget's substance.

civility.statement: There we have a member of the National Party extolling the virtues of a $200 million subsidy to the gas industry... They make the choice not only to open up offshore gas and oil exploration but to pay people to do it, to actually hand over cash.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism but aimed squarely at the policy choice and its dollar figure, not at a person.

civility.statement: David Seymour's pet ministry, the Ministry for Regulation. Every year, a percent increase whilst Oranga Tamariki is cutting funds... David Seymour's ministry is getting 5 percent more, year on year, for the next four Budget rounds. That's so he can push his vanity bill, the Regulatory Standards Bill.
civility.explanation: Labels the ministry 'pet' and the bill a 'vanity bill', personalising the criticism to Seymour, though it also cites a concrete funding contrast.

civility.statement: the only way that the Government could come anywhere close to having a respectable Budget was by taking $12 billion away from working women.
civility.explanation: Pointed but directed at the Budget's fiscal choices rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: money for gas exploration but not for early childhood Best Start payments; money for tax breaks for big businesses but no money for our lowest-paid women workers. That's the choices this Government makes; it's shameful.
civility.explanation: 'Shameful' is heated, but the criticism is framed around policy trade-offs rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I recall the Prime Minister... saying, "We're going to have a laser-sharp focus"... "on the cost of living." Well, I say, from the last two Budgets, the Prime Minister has had a laser-sharp focus on increasing the cost of living.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic turn of the PM's own phrase against him; rhetorical jab but tied to cost-of-living record rather than personal character.

civility.statement: Dan Bidois talked about how wonderful it was that his son was in daycare. That is the value that they put on early childhood education (ECE), by calling it "daycare".
civility.explanation: Seizes on a single word choice to impute contempt for ECE across the government benches; a cheap-shot mischaracterisation.

civility.statement: women who this Government has, basically, said, "You don't matter. Your workers have no value."
civility.explanation: Puts fabricated words in the government's mouth—a strawman/misrepresentation of its position.

civility.statement: we had six years of suffering under the lacklustre Labour lot that sent New Zealand into a terrible spin. Inflation at record highs: 7.3 percent—an outrageously high level of inflation—and an extra $100 billion of debt.
civility.explanation: 'Lacklustre Labour lot' and 'terrible spin' are disparaging labels, though attached to an economic-record argument.

civility.statement: Labour failed to deliver better health outcomes for New Zealanders, they failed to deliver better educational performance for New Zealanders, they failed to keep New Zealanders safer in their communities, and they failed the economy.
civility.explanation: Harsh, sweeping criticism but directed at policy record across portfolios rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: we must have more ambition for our young New Zealanders than letting them suffer in a life of benefit dependency like the Labour Government would have them do. They would have them languish, reliant on the State year after year.
civility.explanation: Attributes to Labour a deliberate wish to make youth 'languish' on benefits—a strawman of their position.

civility.statement: Now, we on this side back pay equity, and that's why we've realigned it to focus specifically on the pay equity piece... under Labour... they'd just given carte blanche to the unions to bring any sort of grievance as a faux mechanism to try and lift pay rates across the board.
civility.explanation: Characterises union claims as a 'faux mechanism', a contestable framing of opponents' motives, but engages the policy mechanism.

civility.statement: We have this Government investing almost $33 million—$33 million—in their failed boot camp experiment... The Minister will not be honest with the public; the Prime Minister will not be honest with the public and tell the public what the reoffending statistics are.
civility.explanation: Directly accuses the Minister and PM of dishonesty ('will not be honest')—a personal integrity attack rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: this is a "BS Budget". It is a "BS Budget" because it takes $12.8 billion out of the back pockets of women workers: our mums, our sisters, our aunties, our nieces.
civility.explanation: The 'BS Budget' epithet is a crude label, though the $12.8bn/women-workers substance follows.

civility.statement: This is a continual punch down from this Government on the groups that don't agree with them, and this Budget is just one more example.
civility.explanation: 'Punch down' is combative characterisation of motive, though aimed at the government's pattern rather than an individual.

civility.statement: it's the stigmatising, in terms of our people at the coalface, that is really, really making us angry on this side, and the punitive nature of this whole bill.
civility.explanation: Emotive language ('stigmatising', 'punitive') but aimed at the bill's effects, not at a person.

civility.statement: Check the unemployment rates out there, Mr MacLeod, and you will see your Māori unemployment rates have gone up considerably. That is because there is no plan. Targeted programmes have been abandoned.
civility.explanation: Pointed direct address to MacLeod but focused on unemployment data and policy, not personal insult.

rigor.statement: if I took the analogy of just our home budget, and we all have one ourselves, we all look on an annual basis and think: well, what kind of income are we actually going to be generating in that 12-month period?
rigor.explanation: Leans on a household-budget analogy to explain government finances; relatable but the analogy elides key differences, so a moderate appeal-to-analogy gap.

rigor.statement: At the moment, we are reliant—when we have no wind blowing, no sun shining, in the middle of the winter when we've got the highest energy requirements of electricity—on burning coal. Natural gas is 40 percent—40 percent—cleaner than coal.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the gas argument in the energy trilemma and a specific emissions comparison; a reasoned case, though the single cleanliness figure is asserted without source.

rigor.statement: There we have a member of the National Party extolling the virtues of a $200 million subsidy to the gas industry... They make the choice not only to open up offshore gas and oil exploration but to pay people to do it, to actually hand over cash.
rigor.explanation: Frames the subsidy as directly funded by KiwiSaver and Best Start cuts ('maybe that's where that cut comes from'), an inferred fungibility link he hedges as speculative.

rigor.statement: Rebekah Hope helps to support my sister in her day-to-day care needs... She said she was furious... "All we want is what we actually deserve to be paid. Maybe they should come and do our job for a day and see what we actually do." I challenge members across the House to take Rebekah up on her invitation.
rigor.explanation: Persuades chiefly through a single sympathetic anecdote and an appeal to emotion rather than data on care-worker pay.

rigor.statement: Labour failed to deliver better health outcomes for New Zealanders, they failed to deliver better educational performance for New Zealanders, they failed to keep New Zealanders safer in their communities, and they failed the economy.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical anaphora of 'failed' assertions with no supporting evidence for any of the four claims.

rigor.statement: We know the stats. We know that if you go on a benefit at 18 years old, you are likely to spend, on average, 20 years on that benefit.
rigor.explanation: Cites a statistic to justify the policy, but asserts it as settled ('we know the stats') without sourcing the modelling.

rigor.statement: Well, unfortunately, the problem is you run out of other people's money to spend, eventually—that's the problem with socialism.
rigor.explanation: A slogan (the classic 'other people's money' line) and a broad-brush label ('socialism') substituting for argument.

rigor.statement: the 12-month prescription... to now be able to only do that over a 12-month period, instead of three months. It saves cost in terms of doctors' fees, it saves prescription fees, and it actually frees up capacity at those medical centres.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned causal chain from longer prescriptions to freed clinic capacity, though supported by constituent anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: When unemployment is at its highest, at 5.2 percent, and almost double that for Māori and Pacific, more people are choosing to study, and this Budget does not adequately address training a skilled workforce for the future.
rigor.explanation: Links rising unemployment and study demand to a workforce-training gap in a coherent argument, though the 'does not adequately address' conclusion is asserted.

rigor.statement: The Minister's new industry skills boards only receive 46 percent of the funding that workforce development councils had, and they are expected to deliver the same work for the same pay.
rigor.explanation: Uses the funding-versus-expectations mismatch to argue the change is unworkable; a reasoned point resting on the cited 46% figure.

rigor.statement: why the Minister for Social Development and Employment decided not to actually elaborate on the nature of those designations. Why are they so open-ended in this situation? If we'd been to a select committee, it would be very likely that we would have more detail.
rigor.explanation: A precise procedural critique—the regulation-making power lacks an attached principle and bypassed select-committee scrutiny—engaging the text of the clause directly.

rigor.statement: I want to know if the Minister has a distributional analysis of where that is coming from... We know that there's around $238 million in savings when it comes to benefit or related expenses... if a beneficiary's relationship status is part of what is being assessed, we could see solo parents, particularly, being disproportionately affected.
rigor.explanation: Builds a clear causal argument: open-ended 'circumstances' wording plus relationship-status checks plus savings targets could disproportionately hit solo parents—each step grounded in the clause and front-line experience.

charisma.statement: Of course, it's in the negative mind-set from the Green Party and my mind-set is absolutely to the positive.
charisma.explanation: Sets up an us-versus-them 'negative Greens vs positive us' framing rather than seeking common ground, though mildly worded.

charisma.statement: Rebekah Hope helps to support my sister in her day-to-day care needs... She said she was furious... "All we want is what we actually deserve to be paid. Maybe they should come and do our job for a day and see what we actually do." I challenge members across the House to take Rebekah up on her invitation.
charisma.explanation: A humanising personal story with a direct invitation to opponents, but the appeal is to her own side's values rather than genuine bridge-building.

authenticity.statement: I recall the Prime Minister... saying, "We're going to have a laser-sharp focus"... "on the cost of living." Well, I say, from the last two Budgets, the Prime Minister has had a laser-sharp focus on increasing the cost of living.
authenticity.explanation: Attacks the PM's consistency (promised focus on cost of living vs. outcome), a low-authenticity signal about him, not the speaker.

authenticity.statement: Now, we on this side back pay equity, and that's why we've realigned it to focus specifically on the pay equity piece... under Labour... they'd just given carte blanche to the unions to bring any sort of grievance as a faux mechanism to try and lift pay rates across the board.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to 'back pay equity' while defending changes widely seen as curtailing pay-equity claims—a tension between the stated value and the action.

forthrightness.statement: I want to bring the committee back to the fact that this is just about regulation-making powers. I've specified the two purposes... I know members have talked about a whole range of other things that are completely irrelevant to this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Helen White's and Menéndez March's specific questions (relationship-status checks, distributional analysis, benefit-name changes), she deflects to 'this is just about regulation-making powers' and dismisses the questions as irrelevant rather than answering them.

specificity.statement: This Government is investing an extra $7 billion in healthcare so that Kiwis can get better access to elective surgeries, GP appointments, and other critical services that they rely on.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure ($7 billion) and specific service areas, though no timeframe or breakdown.

specificity.statement: We’ve increased prescription repeats to 12 months, which means that people don’t need to go to the doctor with the frequency that they need to, reducing costs for households.
specificity.explanation: Concrete named policy change (12-month repeats) with a stated mechanism, though household cost saving unquantified.

specificity.statement: the social housing wait-list is down from 27,000 to 19,000 people, and we have moved from over 5,000 households in motels and emergency accommodation down to 400, and that means 2,100 kids out of motels and into proper homes.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for waitlist, emergency housing households, and children.

specificity.statement: house prices are stable, rents for the first time are actually stable rather than having increased $180 per week.
specificity.explanation: Includes a concrete $180/week figure but attaches it loosely to a general 'stable' claim.

specificity.statement: We don’t just talk about it with bumper stickers; we get things done on this side of the House.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level self-praise with no mechanism, figure, or concrete action.

specificity.statement: we’ve had 63 people who have been ejected from State house tenancies—it was two under the previous Government in their last year—and we have about 1,400 people on first notices.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts for evictions, prior-year comparison, and first notices.

specificity.statement: given that homelessness is rising, rough sleeping is increasing, new State house builds have ground to a halt, consents to build new houses are down, and his Government’s cutting support to first-home buyers?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates several concrete indicators, though without figures.

specificity.statement: taking people off the social housing register has coincided with a 58 percent rise in homelessness in Auckland and a 40 percent rise in homelessness in Wellington?
specificity.explanation: Precise figures tied to named cities.

specificity.statement: Because we have ensured that there is a workable, sustainable pay equity regime in law that will allow claims with merit to be raised and, where appropriate, settled.
specificity.explanation: General assurances ('workable, sustainable', 'where appropriate') with no concrete detail on which claims proceed.

specificity.statement: I would say, quite simply: we value you and we value the work of all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A platitude with no policy content.

specificity.statement: I’m delighted that we have nearly halved the cost of delivering a classroom from $1.2 million down to $626,000.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after unit costs for classroom delivery.

specificity.statement: the Selwyn growth plan is delivering a new primary school in Prebbleton, purchase of land for a new primary school in Lincoln, and an additional 52 classrooms across five existing schools.
specificity.explanation: Named locations and exact classroom counts.

specificity.statement: adopting a “no additional warming” approach for agricultural gases would mean either requiring every other sector of the economy to carry a far higher burden to reduce emissions, or reducing our climate ambition and, therefore, breaching international trade and climate agreements
specificity.explanation: Names the specific policy approach and concrete consequences, though without figures.

civility.statement: the amazing work of our finance Minister, Nicola Willis, who, let's be honest, was dealing with an absolute mess after that side of the House sent us into astronomical debt, a whole lot of wasteful spending, and record inflation.
civility.explanation: Attacks the opposition's record on policy grounds but with sensational language ('absolute mess').

civility.statement: The fact that the Labour Party, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori have hostility to private property explains a lot.
civility.explanation: Strawmans opponents as having 'hostility to private property' rather than engaging their actual positions.

civility.statement: Well, you might say that Labour has begun to swipe right on productivity, but I don't think you're going to find a match. Labour has tried putting numbers out in Opposition; I remember 100,000 houses being one of these.
civility.explanation: A mocking dig at Labour (KiwiBuild jab) that is pointed but references a real policy record rather than a pure personal insult.

civility.statement: It's a balanced Budget, but if you can sleep at night with filling an $88 billion hole by taking from future generations and fuelling the tall poppy dark shadow... It shows Te Pāti Kākāriki are green, they're just green with envy all the way through.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Greens as motivated by 'envy' — a motive-attack framing rather than engaging their alternative budget's substance.

civility.statement: They have room in their Budget—both of them—for tax cuts. They have room to give money to overseas tech giants like Google and Facebook. They have room in their Budget to give money to tobacco companies, and they have money to give landlords a tax cut, but they don't have money to keep kids off the street.
civility.explanation: Sharp juxtaposition attacking priorities; harsh but aimed at policy choices rather than personal character.

civility.statement: What this Government did was compromise a movement towards that kind of freedom to pay for tax cuts for landlords. That's what it did this year.
civility.explanation: A pointed critique of Government priorities on policy grounds.

civility.statement: Because violence will grow. Violence will grow under this Budget and that blood will be on the hands of this Government.
civility.explanation: 'Blood on the hands' is inflammatory hyperbole assigning culpability rather than engaging policy detail.

civility.statement: We have just heard from the Opposition, who, frankly, are trying to pull the wool over the eyes of New Zealanders. They underestimate the intelligence of constituents throughout the country, and I wonder if it's because they don't have constituents, because they no longer have a bunch of electorate MPs to get out around this country.
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of deceit and jibes at their lack of electorate seats rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: Literally, the member was talking about how one of their forebears earned 70 percent of what a male in the same role would have earned. That is something we call equal pay, and that is something that the National Government sorted out in 1972. Pay equity is about ensuring that men and women in comparable industries earn the same
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the opponent's point, albeit with a 'pulling the wool' framing.

civility.statement: This is a Government that is making a historic focus on education, unlike that last Government that had a Prime Minister who before that was an education Minister and, frankly, allowed our education system to slide.
civility.explanation: Criticises the former PM's record on policy grounds but with a dismissive 'allowed to slide' characterisation.

civility.statement: here we have this Government blundering on, making all their decisions not based on evidence and knowledge but based on this false economy where short-term profit and trickle-down economics is some kind of Holy Grail.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government as 'blundering' and driven by greed rather than engaging specific policy detail.

civility.statement: Where's your alternative Budget?
civility.explanation: A challenging interjection but a legitimate substantive challenge rather than a personal insult.

veracity.statement: But what this Budget did was take away the money put aside for these hospice workers, for these Plunket nurses, for these midwives, for these care and support workers... this Government has used money that was set aside to pay them fairly to finance the Budget that they presented two weeks ago.

veracity.statement: The Government was so surprised that a Minister had to come down to the House during the committee of the whole House to find out if it really was true that multinational oil and gas companies would qualify under Investment Boost. And he was told, yes; the answer is yes.

veracity.statement: The growth that is projected by Treasury from Investment Boost is 1 percent over 20 years... wage growth out of that policy: 1.5 percent over 20 years.
veracity.explanation: Roughly reflects Treasury's long-run GDP-level estimate for Investment Boost, though presented as a 'growth rate' which can mislead about magnitude.

veracity.statement: In fact, what we are seeing is, actually, that unemployment is projected to grow under policies put forward by this Government. There'll be fewer jobs; we won't see wage growth.
veracity.explanation: Unemployment was forecast to rise near-term, but wholly attributing it to these policies overstates the causal claim.

veracity.statement: There is a reason why this is the least popular Budget in 30 years, and it's because it is a Government that is not putting New Zealanders at the centre of its decision making.
veracity.explanation: The 'least popular in 30 years' claim is a strong quantitative assertion not clearly substantiated; polling framing is selective.

veracity.statement: Then they scotched 33 existing pay equity claims, took away 33 sets of claims that people had been working on already—claims for 180,000 women.

veracity.explanation: The ~$12.8bn saving is accurate; the 'impossible to get a claim through' is a contested prediction stated as near-fact.

veracity.explanation: Air traffic control in fact requires extensive training and high-complexity work, so the contrast is overstated.

veracity.statement: the amazing work of our finance Minister, Nicola Willis, who, let's be honest, was dealing with an absolute mess after that side of the House sent us into astronomical debt, a whole lot of wasteful spending, and record inflation.
veracity.explanation: Debt and inflation did rise sharply under the previous government, but 'record inflation' and 'astronomical' are hyperbolic characterisations.

veracity.statement: Businesses can deduct 20 percent of new assets' value from their year's taxable income, on top of normal depreciation.

veracity.statement: Tariana Turia... she never missed a vote and she spoke on every single bill before this House, and she was just one member all by herself.
veracity.explanation: Characterization of Turia's diligence is broadly plausible, though 'never missed a vote / every single bill' is a strong absolute that is hard to fully verify.

rigor.statement: In just one example, we have former Prime Minister Mr Muldoon committing some pretty full-on offences, also not turning up to the Privileges Committee, and even then, only getting a three-day suspension.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based comparison to a specific precedent to support the disproportionality argument; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: It is our position that the Privileges Committee is being exploited to do the political bidding of Government MPs, which is an approach we should all treat with disdain.
rigor.explanation: Asserts partisan motive; some support later (consensus broken), but the claim leans on characterization here.

rigor.statement: that bill was designed to provoke. The bill attacked the generosity of Māori despite nearly 200 years of injustice against us. It threatened generations of fundamental relationships... It was political violence trying to uproot the heart of our country.
rigor.explanation: Emotive escalation; 'political violence' is metaphorical overstatement rather than evidenced argument (appeal to emotion).

rigor.statement: you can see that there is no sincerity in what they’re saying, because their speech had to be written for them.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur — a written speech does not entail insincerity.

rigor.statement: haka have been done countless times in this Parliament, but after first consulting the Speaker so that the House and its timing is not disrupted... there was no attempt whatsoever. They told the media they were going to do it, and they didn’t tell the Speaker
rigor.explanation: Grounds the procedural objection in a specific factual distinction (prior consultation vs none).

rigor.statement: I’m glad the ACT Party were intimidated. I think that’s the whole point of doing a haka. The All Blacks don’t do the haka so that the Springboks feel good afterwards.
rigor.explanation: Argues by analogy (All Blacks/haka) — rhetorically effective but an appeal to analogy rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The longest suspension previously was for three days, for Rob Muldoon, for comments that he made about the Speaker. We are talking about three days versus the 21 days for each of the two Te Pāti Māori co-leaders and seven for Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who has already been punished.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based, quantified comparison directly supporting the disproportionality conclusion.

rigor.statement: in fact it was—and here I am reading explicitly from the Privileges Committee report back then—“for the Member, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who knowingly provided false or misleading information on a pecuniary interest”.
rigor.explanation: Uses a documented precedent to support the point that non-consensus rulings have happened and that Peters is not a neutral authority on conduct.

rigor.statement: decides to hand down a punishment that is seven times harsher than the worst punishment that the Privileges Committee has ever handed out before, without any explanatory rationale.
rigor.explanation: Quantifies the disproportion and ties it to the committee's own stated reliance on precedent.

rigor.statement: Suspending the Māori seats of Hauraki-Waikato, Waiariki, and Te Tai Hauāuru is equivalent to suspending 18 general seats. I just want to repeat that again: 18 general seats. That is 210,000 voices being silenced.
rigor.explanation: The equivalence relies on a questionable multiplier rather than sound reasoning.

rigor.statement: MPs are not legally required to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi. There are no provisions in the Constitution Act 1986 for Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: Grounds her reform argument in a correct constitutional fact.

rigor.statement: when it comes to these two-fingered guns, I sat there and had that pointed at me while I was told, “kino”. Now, as a licensed firearm owner, if I were to do that to anybody either in this House or out on the street, I would lose my licence. Why? Because I’d be deemed as no longer being fit and proper.
rigor.explanation: Draws an analogy to firearms-licensing 'fit and proper' standards; a personal-experience argument that is apt but analogical.

rigor.statement: It’s demonstrably clear to me that it is the Government that is punishing the members today, not the Parliament, because if it was the Parliament, we would have the support of every party in this House, like we have had many other times when members have been referred to the Privileges Committee.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument from the convention of cross-party consensus to the conclusion that this is a Government rather than a House decision.

rigor.statement: The Privileges Committee of the future will have a new precedent, without a doubt—a new range of penalties against members who err in the future. You can guarantee that. You can also guarantee that Governments of the day, in the future, will feel very free to use those penalties to punish their opponents.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned from how precedent operates rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: I’ll answer that interjection. You’re here; you’re in this House. You have the opportunity to change it—absolutely change it. You can’t change it by not turning up for a vote in the House. That ain’t going to change anything.
rigor.explanation: Logical point that change comes through participating in votes and Standing Orders processes, not boycotting them.

specificity.statement: the ruling of 21 days’ suspension for the co-leaders with the ruling of seven days on top of seven days already served by Ms Maipi-Clarke is severe and unprecedented and completely out of proportion to the breach of Standing Orders
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete durations (21 days, seven-plus-seven) rather than a vague complaint.

specificity.statement: these dangerously precedent-setting, convention-destroying, consensus-ignoring, Tiriti-trampling, racism-whistling, democracy-mocking, narrowly supported recommendations from the Privileges Committee bring this House into more disrepute than any haka ever has.
specificity.explanation: A string of adjectives conveying direction but little concrete detail.

specificity.statement: I invite the Government parties to support my tabled amendment, which would instead remove suspension for all three MPs as a punishment and leave the penalty to censure.
specificity.explanation: Concrete procedural proposal: replace suspension with censure for all three named MPs.

specificity.statement: you know I love you guys... but a little bit of compromise could help the situation... a little step back—you know, a sorry—wouldn’t go amiss. Like, why not say sorry for Rawiri Waititi abusing the Privileges Committee? Why not say sorry for leaking stuff to social media? Why not say sorry for not turning up to the committee?
specificity.explanation: Names precise things to apologise for (abusing the committee, leaking, non-attendance).

specificity.statement: I implore the Privileges Committee and this House to take on board the recommendation from Labour... that is that Hana Maipi has already served her sentence and to give Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer a day off
specificity.explanation: Concrete alternative sanction: no further penalty for Maipi-Clarke, one day each for the co-leaders.

specificity.statement: I said to the Speaker that I recognise that I disrupted the vote that he had to conduct that day. I took accountability. I apologised directly to the Speaker, accepted the consequences made that day, which was a 24-hour suspension, docked pay, and being named. But I will not apologise for my actions.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete consequences already served (24-hour suspension, docked pay, named).

specificity.statement: Suspending the Māori seats of Hauraki-Waikato, Waiariki, and Te Tai Hauāuru is equivalent to suspending 18 general seats. I just want to repeat that again: 18 general seats. That is 210,000 voices being silenced.
specificity.explanation: Names the three electorates and gives concrete figures.

specificity.statement: The solution is clear: a legal duty for MPs to respect and protect Te Tiriti o Waitangi and a provision of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the Constitution Act 1986. This is my member’s bill, which I introduced last week
specificity.explanation: Concrete legislative proposal (a Treaty duty and a Constitution Act provision) tied to a named, introduced bill.

civility.statement: It is our position that the Privileges Committee is being exploited to do the political bidding of Government MPs, which is an approach we should all treat with disdain.
civility.explanation: Harsh imputation of motive to the committee/Government, but aimed at process rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: these dangerously precedent-setting, convention-destroying, consensus-ignoring, Tiriti-trampling, racism-whistling, democracy-mocking, narrowly supported recommendations from the Privileges Committee bring this House into more disrepute than any haka ever has.
civility.explanation: Targets the recommendations/process rather than a person, but stacks heavy pejorative hyperbole.

civility.statement: that bill was designed to provoke. The bill attacked the generosity of Māori despite nearly 200 years of injustice against us. It threatened generations of fundamental relationships... It was political violence trying to uproot the heart of our country.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist framing of the bill's intent.

civility.statement: you can see that there is no sincerity in what they’re saying, because their speech had to be written for them.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on the opponents' sincerity rather than their argument.

civility.statement: The one in the cowboy hat who hates colonialism—the one that’s shouting down there, with the scribbles on his face; the guy that’s got half the South Island hanging around his neck—can’t keep quiet for five seconds.
civility.explanation: Mocks a member's tā moko and appearance ('scribbles on his face') — a direct personal attack.

civility.statement: The Māori Party are a bunch of extremists, and middle New Zealand and the Māori world has had enough of them.
civility.explanation: Blanket labelling ('extremists') with no engagement of substance.

civility.statement: It’s all there—hundreds of millions of dollars fleeced off the Māori people.
civility.explanation: Accusation of fraud against members without evidence.

civility.statement: I still spent more time in Parliament than all those Māori MPs all together.
civility.explanation: A dig at opponents' attendance framed as self-praise.

civility.statement: Well, if I’ve misdescribed his tā moko, I apologise—I can quite easily do that—but the rest of it, I hope, is understood to be true.
civility.explanation: A partial retraction that simultaneously restates the disputed remarks.

civility.statement: I’m glad the ACT Party were intimidated. I think that’s the whole point of doing a haka. The All Blacks don’t do the haka so that the Springboks feel good afterwards.
civility.explanation: Openly endorses intimidation, though it engages the substance of the dispute rather than insulting a person.

civility.statement: these people on the other side—they’re not all Ku Klux Klan members, as I’ve heard mentioned in different speeches. Some of them are quite good. Some of them make an effort, and I don’t think that we help the situation by saying that everyone’s a racist and everything is racist.
civility.explanation: De-escalatory and respectful toward opponents despite disagreement.

civility.statement: in fact it was—and here I am reading explicitly from the Privileges Committee report back then—“for the Member, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who knowingly provided false or misleading information on a pecuniary interest”.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal to Peters, but sourced to the official record rather than mere insult.

civility.statement: I say to members of the Government: get an absolute grip.
civility.explanation: A dismissive jab directed at Government members rather than engaging their argument.

civility.statement: What I would like to see from Te Pāti Māori is where we look to unify as a country. Where we look to come together to find solutions. But we don’t hear that from Te Pāti Māori. All we hear is aggression. All we hear is bullying. All we hear is yelling.
civility.explanation: Sweeping characterization of opponents as only aggressive/bullying, undercutting the stated wish to unify.

civility.statement: Why don’t you put your brain into gear, get some words in your mouth, and start debating.
civility.explanation: Condescending personal jab rather than engagement with an argument.

civility.statement: It’s demonstrably clear to me that it is the Government that is punishing the members today, not the Parliament, because if it was the Parliament, we would have the support of every party in this House, like we have had many other times when members have been referred to the Privileges Committee.
civility.explanation: Measured, institution-focused critique without personal attack.

civility.statement: There are no winners in this debate—none—especially not this House.
civility.explanation: De-escalatory and respectful of the institution as a whole.

charisma.statement: I invite the Government parties to support my tabled amendment, which would instead remove suspension for all three MPs as a punishment and leave the penalty to censure.
charisma.explanation: Invites Government parties to a compromise, but framed within a partisan opposition case.

charisma.statement: The Māori Party are a bunch of extremists, and middle New Zealand and the Māori world has had enough of them.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: For 53 years, since 1972, under the guise of the “Values Party”, they have never ever been in Cabinet, and they never will be.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative dismissal of an opposing party.

charisma.statement: you know I love you guys... but a little bit of compromise could help the situation... a little step back—you know, a sorry—wouldn’t go amiss. Like, why not say sorry for Rawiri Waititi abusing the Privileges Committee? Why not say sorry for leaking stuff to social media? Why not say sorry for not turning up to the committee?
charisma.explanation: Urges his own allies toward compromise and concrete concession, seeking a path that could unlock cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: these people on the other side—they’re not all Ku Klux Klan members, as I’ve heard mentioned in different speeches. Some of them are quite good. Some of them make an effort, and I don’t think that we help the situation by saying that everyone’s a racist and everything is racist.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges good faith on the other side and warns against blanket accusations — bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I implore the Privileges Committee and this House to take on board the recommendation from Labour... that is that Hana Maipi has already served her sentence and to give Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer a day off
charisma.explanation: Offers a middle-ground proposal aimed at resolving the standoff.

charisma.statement: What I would like to see from Te Pāti Māori is where we look to unify as a country. Where we look to come together to find solutions. But we don’t hear that from Te Pāti Māori. All we hear is aggression. All we hear is bullying. All we hear is yelling.
charisma.explanation: Gestures at unity but frames the other side as wholly unreasonable, which alienates rather than bridges.

charisma.statement: There are no winners in this debate—none—especially not this House.
charisma.explanation: Above-the-fray framing that seeks to reset the tone across the chamber.

charisma.statement: I also implore Te Pāti Māori to actually think about what the Hon Willie Jackson has suggested. It’s not for me to tell colleagues to apologise but, as he said, it might go a long way, and one would need to think clearly about what the long-term strategy is.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party bridge-building: he presses both National to reconsider and Te Pāti Māori to weigh a conciliatory step.

divination.statement: I can see what the end is—I can see what the end is for that party, and it’s not long.
divination.explanation: Prediction of Te Pāti Māori's imminent demise; timeframe vague and polling volatility makes it optimistic against their recent support.

divination.statement: The Privileges Committee of the future will have a new precedent, without a doubt—a new range of penalties against members who err in the future. You can guarantee that. You can also guarantee that Governments of the day, in the future, will feel very free to use those penalties to punish their opponents.
divination.explanation: Institutional prediction that future governments will exploit the new precedent; plausible and directionally reasoned, but not certain.

forthrightness.statement: Well, if I’ve misdescribed his tā moko, I apologise—I can quite easily do that—but the rest of it, I hope, is understood to be true.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the demand to apologise, but narrows it to the tā moko and reasserts the rest of the attack.

forthrightness.statement: I said to the Speaker that I recognise that I disrupted the vote that he had to conduct that day. I took accountability. I apologised directly to the Speaker, accepted the consequences made that day, which was a 24-hour suspension, docked pay, and being named. But I will not apologise for my actions.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, specific account of what she did and accepted.

forthrightness.statement: I’ll answer that interjection. You’re here; you’re in this House. You have the opportunity to change it—absolutely change it. You can’t change it by not turning up for a vote in the House. That ain’t going to change anything.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Ferris's interjected question 'How long do we have to wait?' with a clear response about using the House's mechanisms.

authenticity.statement: I said to the Speaker that I recognise that I disrupted the vote that he had to conduct that day. I took accountability. I apologised directly to the Speaker, accepted the consequences made that day, which was a 24-hour suspension, docked pay, and being named. But I will not apologise for my actions.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent stance: she owns disrupting the vote and accepted the earlier penalty, while distinguishing that from the principle she will not recant.

authenticity.statement: I tore a bill that divided our country. I am now presenting a bill that honours our relationship as a country.
authenticity.explanation: Frames her actions (destroying the Treaty principles bill, introducing her own) as consistent with a stated commitment to Te Tiriti.

strength.statement: The solution is clear: a legal duty for MPs to respect and protect Te Tiriti o Waitangi and a provision of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the Constitution Act 1986. This is my member’s bill, which I introduced last week
strength.explanation: Backed by an actual action — she introduced the member's bill — though as an opposition member's bill its enactment is uncertain.

veracity.statement: We have a Prime Minister, a National-led Government, who traded with Te Tiriti for the principles bill, even though it wasn’t a bottom line.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: National did agree to support the Treaty Principles Bill to first reading under its ACT coalition deal despite it not being a National bottom line, but 'traded with Te Tiriti' is a loaded characterisation.

veracity.statement: Judith Collins, the chair, has called Māori health equity “segregation” and attacked Māori wards as “undemocratic”
veracity.explanation: Paraphrases positions associated with Collins on co-governance and Māori wards; broadly in the ballpark but presented as direct quotation without sourcing.

veracity.statement: We asked to be heard together, as a party: that too was refused. We asked for legal counsel to be properly included: blocked.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claims about process that cannot be verified from the text alone.

veracity.statement: in the 1860s, colonial MPs argued that Māori could not participate in Parliament because they lacked the civil capacity to engage with proper legislative conduct.
veracity.explanation: Broadly reflects 19th-century colonial attitudes (Māori seats were created in 1867), but the specific claim is a generalisation hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: But the fact of the matter is that Te Pāti Māori has made it very clear that this is just the beginning, that they don’t think that they’ve done anything wrong, and that they would do it again.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation: Te Pāti Māori members in this same debate stated they were unapologetic and would act the same way again.

veracity.statement: They chose to hand out a punishment seven times bigger than what has been given before.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record cited across the debate (21 days vs a previous maximum of 3), making the '7 times' figure accurate.

veracity.statement: it is the former Deputy Prime Minister who continuously asks out-of-order questions in the House and challenges the Speakers on an almost weekly basis.
veracity.explanation: Directionally plausible but 'almost weekly basis' is an unverified quantification likely exaggerated.

veracity.statement: Today, we’re debating a privilege from the 1600s, designed to protect MPs for speaking up for the people that they represented to the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: parliamentary privilege has its roots in 17th-century England (e.g. the 1689 Bill of Rights), designed to protect members' speech.

veracity.statement: Twenty-one days is seven times longer than the longest suspension ever recorded.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical record cited (previous longest suspension of three days), making the comparison accurate.

veracity.statement: In over 160 years, only two MPs have ever been suspended: one for a single day, the other for three.
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable historical claim consistent with the record; presented as fact and broadly borne out.

veracity.statement: Standing Order 109 recognises te reo Māori, but not the broader practice of tikanga at all.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable procedural claim that appears accurate about the scope of the Standing Order.

veracity.statement: And not one Privileges Committee member has explained to us where 21 days came from—not once.
veracity.explanation: Aligns with other speakers' claims that the 21-day figure went unexplained; plausible but an absolute ('not once') that is hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: The Regulatory Standards Bill—a Trojan horse designed to chain every future law to corporate profit and to annihilate Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic characterisation of the bill's purpose and effect, presented as fact.

veracity.statement: And the Waitangi Tribunal—the very room where truth about injustice is spoken aloud—heard and legitimised a plan to strip Treaty clauses from 28 pieces of law.
veracity.explanation: There was public reporting about reviewing/removing Treaty references from legislation; the specific '28 pieces' figure is precise but the framing is contested.

veracity.statement: Today, we are ordered from the Chamber for 21 days because we dared to meet the Treaty principles bill with a haka.
veracity.explanation: The haka did occur during the Treaty Principles Bill vote, but the Government's stated basis is the breach of rules during a vote, not the haka itself, so the causal framing is partial.

veracity.statement: We had to suspend the sitting of this House in order to bring it to order.
veracity.explanation: Accurate factual account: the sitting was suspended during the disorder in question.

veracity.statement: a small bill today—a very small bill—that was about to put money in the hands of pensioners was voted down by the two parties that say we’re doing nothing to help people. It was voted down today.
veracity.explanation: References a real vote but the loaded framing ('put money in the hands of pensioners') and characterisation of opponents' position is contestable.

veracity.statement: That is why the legacy of the Māori Party exists today: because they came into this House to change the rules. They worked with the National Party to bring about better outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Historically accurate: the earlier Māori Party held a confidence-and-supply arrangement with National (2008–2017).

veracity.statement: This was not a spur-of-the-moment issue. This was an orchestrated attempt, and that could have easily been facilitated within the rules of this House.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Te Pāti Māori's own statement that their actions were 'purposeful, very measured, and very deliberate', though 'orchestrated' adds a negative gloss.

civility.statement: We have a Prime Minister, a National-led Government, who traded with Te Tiriti for the principles bill, even though it wasn’t a bottom line.
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing of the Government's dealmaking, but aimed at a political action/policy rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Judith Collins, the chair, has called Māori health equity “segregation” and attacked Māori wards as “undemocratic”
civility.explanation: Used to impugn the impartiality of the committee chair; criticises her stated views rather than launching a purely personal attack.

civility.statement: Yet you’re the ones—this Government’s the ones that’s doing the gun laws and doing the bootcamps and reinvesting in military might and trying to mine to be able to sit there and give more blinking military weight. The hypocrisy of this place!
civility.explanation: Sweeping accusation of hypocrisy with sensational phrasing ('military might', 'hypocrisy of this place').

civility.statement: The chair of this committee said the haka lacked “civility”—the same term used in Atlas, the same term used in 19th century debates when Māori were called “savages”, unfit for parliamentary order.
civility.explanation: Implies the chair's language echoes racist historical rhetoric; pointed but tied to a specific word choice rather than a bare insult.

civility.statement: what we’re confronting here is a Government who has a very anti-Māori, anti-Tiriti, anti-women, anti-rainbow agenda
civility.explanation: Attributes a hostile 'anti-' agenda across four fronts; characterisation of motive rather than engagement with policy.

civility.statement: There are ways that we can make changes in this place, but using stand-over tactics and bullying behaviour is not the way to do so.
civility.explanation: Criticises the tactics ('stand-over', 'bullying') rather than the people, but the labelling is a firm characterisation of opponents' conduct.

civility.statement: We want to teach our next generation that you can sit around a table, you can have a debate, and you can disagree, and walk away, agreeing to disagree, without slinging insults at each other and without using bullying tactics to try and get our own way.

civility.statement: So we can talk about one side of the House bullying another side of the House, but two wrongs don’t make a right. We need to address the actual issue that is happening here.
civility.explanation: De-escalatory, steers away from cross-House recriminations.

civility.statement: But the fact of the matter is that Te Pāti Māori has made it very clear that this is just the beginning, that they don’t think that they’ve done anything wrong, and that they would do it again.
civility.explanation: Critical but a fair restatement of the other party's stated position rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I am astounded by the last three ACT Party speakers, who seemed far more offended about alleged finger guns than actual gun violence, children living in poverty, or workers being exploited.

civility.explanation: Mocking 'crocodile tears' plus a personal dig at the ACT leader's conduct.

civility.statement: I found it staggering that when the ACT Party member justified the decision, she didn’t explain why; she just said it was justified. But that’s seven times as much as we’ve had before.
civility.explanation: Criticises the adequacy of an opponent's justification; sharp but engages the substance of the reasoning gap.

civility.statement: I want to speak to every National MP in the House, who I know believe that this House belongs to the people and it must reflect the voices, values, and cultures of those that we serve.
civility.explanation: Respectful, attributes good faith to the other side of the House.

civility.statement: Some members have said there is no remorse—that was a speech of remorse. That was a speech of honesty and moral clarity.

civility.statement: It is an absolute insult to te iwi Māori to hear people’s interpretation of what they believe haka is.
civility.explanation: Expresses strong offence at others' views on haka; heated but directed at their interpretations rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: The Regulatory Standards Bill—a Trojan horse designed to chain every future law to corporate profit and to annihilate Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Aimed at a piece of legislation rather than a person, but framed in extreme terms.

civility.statement: Make no mistake: this Government’s agenda is a war on many. It is a war on Māori. It is a war on wāhine, who refuse to be silent. It is a war to takatāpui, who will not shrink. It is a war on many families living in poverty
civility.explanation: Casts the Government as waging war on multiple groups; combative and sensational.

civility.statement: I acknowledge members across the House for their words, for their passion, and for their commitment to their issues.
civility.explanation: Respectful recognition of other members despite disagreement.

civility.statement: we have the ability to debate, to disagree, to contest each other’s ideas, to heckle, and to be upset, but we do it within the rules of this House so that we can protect the ability to speak.
civility.explanation: Constructive, accepts robust disagreement while advocating mutual restraint.

civility.statement: a small bill today—a very small bill—that was about to put money in the hands of pensioners was voted down by the two parties that say we’re doing nothing to help people. It was voted down today.
civility.explanation: A gotcha aimed at opponents' consistency; sharp but points at their voting record rather than their character.

civility.statement: That is why the legacy of the Māori Party exists today: because they came into this House to change the rules. They worked with the National Party to bring about better outcomes.
civility.explanation: Uses the party's history to criticise its current stance; pointed but grounded in fact.

civility.statement: This was not a spur-of-the-moment issue. This was an orchestrated attempt, and that could have easily been facilitated within the rules of this House.
civility.explanation: Characterises the conduct as premeditated; critical but engages the conduct rather than the person.

specificity.statement: We asked to be heard together, as a party: that too was refused. We asked for legal counsel to be properly included: blocked.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete procedural requests (heard together, legal counsel) and their outcomes.

specificity.statement: We came in and we told our people we are not the moderate, we are not the incremental party; we are the transformational party, because our people are hurting so much and so are our communities.
specificity.explanation: States an identity/direction but no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: They chose to hand out a punishment seven times bigger than what has been given before.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete magnitude of comparison, though the raw figures are not restated here.

specificity.statement: Today, we’re debating a privilege from the 1600s, designed to protect MPs for speaking up for the people that they represented to the Crown.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the argument in a concrete historical origin and purpose.

specificity.statement: Twenty-one days is seven times longer than the longest suspension ever recorded.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and multiple.

specificity.statement: In over 160 years, only two MPs have ever been suspended: one for a single day, the other for three.
specificity.explanation: Names the timeframe and exact prior durations.

specificity.statement: Suspension is not symbolic only; it removes elected representatives and silences those people who brought them here.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete consequence (loss of representation) but no figures.

specificity.statement: Standing Order 109 recognises te reo Māori, but not the broader practice of tikanga at all.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact Standing Order and precisely what it does and does not cover.

specificity.statement: And the Waitangi Tribunal—the very room where truth about injustice is spoken aloud—heard and legitimised a plan to strip Treaty clauses from 28 pieces of law.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete number of statutes affected.

rigor.statement: Yet you’re the ones—this Government’s the ones that’s doing the gun laws and doing the bootcamps and reinvesting in military might and trying to mine to be able to sit there and give more blinking military weight. The hypocrisy of this place!
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes unrelated policies to imply hypocrisy without establishing the logical link.

rigor.statement: The chair of this committee said the haka lacked “civility”—the same term used in Atlas, the same term used in 19th century debates when Māori were called “savages”, unfit for parliamentary order.
rigor.explanation: Guilt-by-association: infers intent from shared use of the word 'civility' across contexts, an appeal to analogy without demonstrated connection.

rigor.statement: There are ways that we can make changes in this place, but using stand-over tactics and bullying behaviour is not the way to do so.

rigor.statement: So we can talk about one side of the House bullying another side of the House, but two wrongs don’t make a right. We need to address the actual issue that is happening here.
rigor.explanation: Rejects tu quoque reasoning and tries to refocus on the substantive question of conduct.

rigor.statement: I am astounded by the last three ACT Party speakers, who seemed far more offended about alleged finger guns than actual gun violence, children living in poverty, or workers being exploited.
rigor.explanation: False-priority framing implying concern for one issue precludes concern for others.

rigor.statement: The ACT Party members may want to tell their leader to stop driving up Parliament steps before they start their crocodile tears about the lowering standards of the House.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: dismisses the standards argument by pointing to unrelated conduct rather than engaging it.

rigor.statement: All rules are made up by humans, and humans can change the rules.
rigor.explanation: A true but rhetorically simplistic premise; correct that rules are human-made and changeable, though it glosses the process for doing so.

rigor.statement: I found it staggering that when the ACT Party member justified the decision, she didn’t explain why; she just said it was justified. But that’s seven times as much as we’ve had before.

rigor.statement: This decision of the Privileges Committee is wrong because it doesn’t do that; and it didn’t even claim to do that. There was no trying to capture the views of not only the minority parties but the major Opposition party too.

rigor.statement: Suspension is not symbolic only; it removes elected representatives and silences those people who brought them here.
rigor.explanation: Sound reasoning linking the penalty to its downstream effect on representation.

rigor.statement: The Regulatory Standards Bill—a Trojan horse designed to chain every future law to corporate profit and to annihilate Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: Loaded 'Trojan horse' metaphor and sweeping claim ('annihilate') asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: If we do nothing, Aotearoa will sprint towards the worst fractures of other nations—division, fear, and resentment—faster than we can say “Kia ora.”

rigor.statement: Make no mistake: this Government’s agenda is a war on many. It is a war on Māori. It is a war on wāhine, who refuse to be silent. It is a war to takatāpui, who will not shrink. It is a war on many families living in poverty
rigor.explanation: Repeated 'war on X' assertion is emotive escalation without supporting evidence.
