civility.statement: This Government has narrowed that test and is giving, basically, a green light to all overseas investment unless it’s farmland, residential land, or fishing quota—basically saying, “Here’s the red carpet; come in.”—never mind whether it creates jobs, never mind if it degrades our environment.

civility.statement: The truth is that David Seymour is not someone who truly believes in liberty. He is a feudalist. He is here to protect the landed gentry, the powerful corporates.

civility.statement: don’t pretend that BlackRock or Stonepeak or any of these huge hedge funds coming over and owning bits of New Zealand is going to benefit New Zealand workers, when, at the same time, they dismantle our employment laws.
civility.explanation: Names funds and policy but engages the substance rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: Well, we know that the bill was part of the coalition agreement, so it’s been around for at least two years, so I don’t know how you haven’t had enough time in two years to consult with any iwi Māori groups out there.
civility.explanation: Critical but focused on process failings rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: This is a bill that exemplifies the cracks in the coalition. This is a bill that exposes that, on one hand, you have the ACT Party that want to sell everything off and, on the other hand, you have a deeply conflicted New Zealand First, who are agreeing to something that they know is not right.
civility.explanation: 'want to sell everything off' strawmans ACT and imputes bad faith to NZ First rather than engaging their stated positions.

civility.statement: Labour is and has always supported high-quality, strategic investment that delivers benefit to New Zealanders... I myself, as a former Associate Minister of Finance, have been a deciding Minister, along with my colleague Damien O’Connor; we were deciding Ministers in the last Government around this.
civility.explanation: Candid, record-based and respectful of the complexity of the decisions.

charisma.statement: There is no magic worker just out there who is going to turn up day after day in a business without a decent wage, and more importantly, without the support of the health system, without the support of the welfare system, without the support of the education system.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective framing of a shared compact, but appeals mainly to her own side.

charisma.statement: To me, it showed an Opposition that hasn’t done the work. They haven’t done the mahi. They haven’t put in the work to understand what is in the Budget, and they don’t get the rewards... don’t do the mahi; don’t get the treats.
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-them applause line aimed at his own side.

charisma.statement: I think we need some greater bipartisanship from across the House on things like superannuation, raising the age, putting in means testing, and other things like that... I would encourage those members from across the House to come to a bipartisan consensus with our side. We’re up for it, we’re ready, we’re focused.
charisma.explanation: Explicit call for cross-party consensus on super, infrastructure and education; invites opponents in.

charisma.statement: This is the message of a country that is open for business and does not fear the world but stands proudly amongst our friends who want to do business with us, trade value for value, and get stronger together.
charisma.explanation: Aspirational, inclusive-of-'friends' framing, but rallies his own pro-market side rather than persuading skeptics.

charisma.statement: I want to first of all congratulate New Zealand First on being able to prevent the foreign buyers ban being reversed under this legislation. It’s good to see that you have held strong that that is a sensitive asset in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges a coalition opponent's contribution and finds common ground across the aisle.

charisma.statement: This Government has narrowed that test and is giving, basically, a green light to all overseas investment unless it’s farmland, residential land, or fishing quota—basically saying, “Here’s the red carpet; come in.”—never mind whether it creates jobs, never mind if it degrades our environment.
charisma.explanation: Persuasive framing aimed at those already worried about foreign ownership.

charisma.statement: The truth is that David Seymour is not someone who truly believes in liberty. He is a feudalist. He is here to protect the landed gentry, the powerful corporates.
charisma.explanation: Alienating, demonising framing that shuts down consensus.

charisma.statement: don’t pretend that BlackRock or Stonepeak or any of these huge hedge funds coming over and owning bits of New Zealand is going to benefit New Zealand workers, when, at the same time, they dismantle our employment laws.
charisma.explanation: Combative framing rallying opponents of foreign ownership; little attempt to persuade the other side.

charisma.statement: That doesn’t mean that we are “Fortress New Zealand”. We are not North Korea. We do rely, and have always relied, on foreign investment to grow our economy and to build our productive capacity.
charisma.explanation: Balances his party's caution with acknowledgement of the case for investment, seeking a reasonable middle ground.

charisma.statement: We can’t survive by selling things to ourselves; we need to open ourselves up to more investment to get things done. Federated Farmers agrees and says that, as a small nation, capital and investment from overseas can help New Zealand to fix infrastructure and drive industry development.
charisma.explanation: Confident framing that appeals mainly to the pro-investment side.

charisma.statement: This is a bill that exemplifies the cracks in the coalition. This is a bill that exposes that, on one hand, you have the ACT Party that want to sell everything off and, on the other hand, you have a deeply conflicted New Zealand First, who are agreeing to something that they know is not right.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to split the coalition rather than build consensus.

charisma.statement: on this side of the House, do we think that processes around making decisions around the Overseas Investment Act could be faster? Certainly... Do we need a bill that removes the benefit to New Zealand test in order to do that? The answer is no.
charisma.explanation: Concedes the opponents' valid point about speed before disagreeing, an attempt at reasoned common ground.

strength.statement: I’m really pleased to announce to the House that more than 1,000 families are no longer in dark, dingy motels. That’s over 2,000 children that are no longer in hotels—
strength.explanation: Claims delivered reduction in emergency housing; plausible against reported declines, though 'no longer in motels' does not confirm stable housing outcomes.

strength.statement: We have seen a dramatic improvement, simply through issuing letters of expectation, that have ensured that consents are processed much faster, with 88 percent of consents recently processed within half of the statutory time frame. That means 88 percent in less than 35 days. The average consent to invest, to send money to New Zealand, is now processed in 28 days.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered administrative improvement he is responsible for, with specific processing metrics.

strength.statement: for a large number of the investments that people would like to make in land that is not farmland—in businesses, for example—we will be consenting—and this is the third point of the bill—within 15 days.
strength.explanation: A forward commitment in a bill at first reading; intent stated but delivery unproven.

divination.statement: I was really pleased to see an item on the news the other day saying that they’re on track to have no emergency motels by the end of this year.
divination.explanation: Prediction of zero emergency motels by end-2025; directionally supported by the downward trend but ambitious and uncertain.

divination.statement: This Government has certainly got a path back to surplus in the 2028-29 period.
divination.explanation: Forecast surplus by 2028-29 restates Treasury projections but such long-range fiscal targets are frequently pushed out.

divination.statement: Treasury’s own forecasts say that debt-to-GDP is going to balloon to over 100 percent of GDP by the time I’ve far left this world.
divination.explanation: Long-horizon projection consistent with current modelling but conditional on policy staying unchanged.

authenticity.statement: I do want to acknowledge that people are still struggling with the cost of living, and we have a construction sector that’s still understanding how that pipeline looks. We’ve got some real big challenges, and I do just want to say that we’ve got a lot of work to do on this side.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly concedes weaknesses and a 'two-stroke economy' rather than only claiming success.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First has drawn a line around farmland, around fishing quota, and, essentially, the stock of family homes. Putting those on the international market and inflating them beyond the means of the average Kiwi is completely anathema to us... It is core to our values. We do not want to be tenants in our own land.
authenticity.explanation: Positions the carve-outs as consistent with NZ First's long-stated protective stance ('it's on the tin; it's in the name').

authenticity.statement: That doesn’t mean that we are “Fortress New Zealand”. We are not North Korea. We do rely, and have always relied, on foreign investment to grow our economy and to build our productive capacity.
authenticity.explanation: Reconciles supporting the bill with NZ First's protective brand consistently.

authenticity.statement: Labour is and has always supported high-quality, strategic investment that delivers benefit to New Zealanders... I myself, as a former Associate Minister of Finance, have been a deciding Minister, along with my colleague Damien O’Connor; we were deciding Ministers in the last Government around this.
authenticity.explanation: Grounds Labour's position in her own record as a deciding Minister under the Act, consistent with the stated principle.

civility.statement: Well, here we are with another attack on workers’ rights by this Government. What a terrible piece of legislation.
civility.explanation: Sensationalist framing ("attack", "terrible") of a policy dispute rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: This is a vehicle for the far-right, libertarian agenda of the ACT Party to be driven into to Parliament and put at the heart of our most important piece of employment legislation.
civility.explanation: Attacks the motive/ideology behind the bill ("far-right agenda") rather than the policy detail.

civility.statement: With one hand they say they’re doing this, but with the real hand, with the actual actions, they continue to erode workers’ rights.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Government of saying one thing and doing another, but stays on their policy conduct rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I’d just like to, in the first instance, acknowledge and thank our community law centres for the services that they provide in our communities and, often, for those who are our most vulnerable.
civility.explanation: Respectful, appreciative, focused on service to constituents.

civility.statement: I understand that it was reported back from the committee by majority, but I also understand that there was a constructive and collegial atmosphere during the select committee hearings, which was good... there are indeed some elements of the bill that other parties in the House support, which is good to see.
civility.explanation: Respectful toward the committee and other parties.

civility.statement: we will move to make the demolition of those disgusting flats up on The Terrace a permitted activity. You might well ask whether it’s a bit ridiculous that Parliament has to legislate to permit the destruction of heritage-listed, earthquake-prone, asbestos-ridden eyesores in Wellington.
civility.explanation: Colourful, disparaging language ("disgusting", "eyesores") but aimed at a building/process, not a person.

civility.statement: Back to the RMA, after a minor diversion into the tawdry embarrassment that is Wellington local body politics and the centre-right in Wellington.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation ("tawdry embarrassment") of local politics, though light and self-deprecating in tone.

civility.statement: I put it to the Minister that if we could see those Amendment Papers before we’re in the committee stage of the bill, that would be a useful thing to do... maybe even talk to Opposition members before the committee stage—so that we can ask good, meaningful questions on those amendments.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused engagement with the Minister.

civility.statement: what I’m absolutely sick and tired of with this Government, is this constant conflation with any form of environmental protection being “anti-farming”. That is absolutely not the case, and, actually, it’s the farmers down there who feel abandoned by this Government.
civility.explanation: Emotive ("sick and tired") criticism of the Government's framing, but engages an argument rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: when more people vote for ACT, you have more ACT MPs in Parliament, more ACT Ministers sitting around the Cabinet table, sometimes the lights come on and good policy gets made.
civility.explanation: Cheeky dig ("the lights come on") but light-touch and not a personal attack.

specificity.statement: Well, here we are with another attack on workers’ rights by this Government. What a terrible piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level opening with no mechanism, figure, or named provision.

specificity.statement: This bill takes that away. It says if you have the word contractor written in a document, then you’re a contractor.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism of the bill — replacing the real-nature test with the written label.

specificity.statement: The first thing that they’re doing is actually making it so anyone earning over $180,000 in New Zealand can be fired at will.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete income threshold and effect of the personal-grievance change.

specificity.statement: This Government has increased unemployment. It has made it harder for New Zealanders to get a job.
specificity.explanation: States a direction but supplies no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Ultimately, this is about increasing opportunities. It’s about going for growth. Economic growth will lead to greater opportunities for workers.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level ("going for growth") with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: record numbers of New Zealanders are leaving our shores... a record number of 47,000 New Zealanders leaving for Australia in the past year
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure, destination, and timeframe.

specificity.statement: It’s a vital rule that enables unions to engage with new employees in those first 30 days to give them the benefit of the collective agreement. By removing that, it means that employers can sign up an individual agreement and undercut the rights and the freedoms of workers.
specificity.explanation: Explains the concrete 30-day rule and the mechanism by which its removal affects workers.

specificity.statement: These changes in the bill will enhance our labour market flexibility, they’ll reduce compliance costs and remove some of that red tape that we all love to hate, and they will bring the balance between employer and employee interests back to a sensible and practical place.
specificity.explanation: Lists intended benefits in general terms with no figures, mechanisms, or targets.

specificity.statement: The changes will provide confidence, and confidence is what enables and promotes positive employment outcomes and opportunities. Outcomes do mean opportunities, and opportunities mean jobs.
specificity.explanation: Abstract slogans with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: Currently, the fund can only directly purchase community legal services, and this expands it to also fund functions that facilitate or support those services. Why this matters? Three points: better use of existing resources, it reduces pressure on Crown funding, and it strengthens community legal services.
specificity.explanation: Clearly states the current limitation, the change, and three concrete rationales.

specificity.statement: If you look back to 2012, for example, the interest received on the fund was actually just under $5 million, which wasn’t anywhere close to the $10.97 million that was needed to fund Community Law at the time. So the Ministry of Justice had to contribute to the budget as well.
specificity.explanation: Precise year and dollar figures for both interest received and funding needed.

specificity.statement: My view is that Community Law do provide a rather special service that ought to be protected by legislation, and so I agree with the framing of the language of the bill as it is. I would just urge the select committee to be very mindful of protecting the scope of the bill as it’s drafted now.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific drafting concern (scope of who provides support functions) though the recommended safeguard is general.

specificity.statement: the special fund is, at present, a fund where the banks still retain 40 percent of the interest from the fund.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete percentage and the party retaining it.

specificity.statement: It requires the council to notify a new plan change by 10 October, and, crucially, it means that the council has to provide as much development capacity as was in PC 78 as it was originally notified.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deadline and a precise substantive requirement (matching original development capacity).

specificity.statement: we will move to make the demolition of those disgusting flats up on The Terrace a permitted activity. You might well ask whether it’s a bit ridiculous that Parliament has to legislate to permit the destruction of heritage-listed, earthquake-prone, asbestos-ridden eyesores in Wellington.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific structure and the concrete intended change (permitted activity), with reasons (earthquake-prone, asbestos).

specificity.statement: section 70... enables regional councils to permit—so something doesn’t need a resource consent—even if it’s going to have an adverse effect to the water body. That just makes no sense.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific provision and its concrete effect on consent requirements.

specificity.statement: in 2021, the Climate Change Commission actually recommended that there be no new gas connections from 2025, and the International Energy Agency has noted that all fossil gas generation should be phased out by 2040. So there is just simply no justifiable need, in this climate crisis, to be giving 35-year consents to fossil fuel infrastructure that will likely not be in use in 25 years.
specificity.explanation: Names bodies, years, and the 35-year consent figure.

specificity.statement: for the first time in the Resource Management Act’s history, they actually permit councils to allow significant adverse pollution in waterways and water bodies where they are already significantly adversely impacted.
specificity.explanation: Points to a specific provision and its concrete effect on already-degraded waterways.

specificity.statement: now we’ve got the New River Estuary in Invercargill, we’ve got the Jacobs River Estuary in Riverton/Aparima, and even Waituna Lagoon near Bluff, all now suffering from those decades of inaction.
specificity.explanation: Names specific estuaries and locations to illustrate the degradation claim.

specificity.statement: Over 90 percent of the land in Southland is covered by catchment groups doing good work on fresh water.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage and region.

specificity.statement: We only need to look at Italy to see Roman aqueducts which have stood for 2,000 years. We are currently designing bridges in New Zealand like up at RiverLink and the Melling Interchange with a 2,000-year design life, yet the Resource Management Act would limit consenting some of these things to just a few decades.
specificity.explanation: Names specific projects (RiverLink, Melling) and design-life figures.

specificity.statement: the Resource Management Act that we’ve got now has, essentially, slowed down the economy, stopped necessary and vital development, and failed to protect the environment.
specificity.explanation: General indictment with no figures or specific cases.

specificity.statement: That’s why New Zealand’s able to grow food for 40 million people, not just the 5 million people who live here.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures contrasting export food output with domestic population.

charisma.statement: Well, here we are with another attack on workers’ rights by this Government. What a terrible piece of legislation.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them framing, rallies own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: With one hand they say they’re doing this, but with the real hand, with the actual actions, they continue to erode workers’ rights.
charisma.explanation: Adversarial framing aimed at own side; no attempt to bring opponents along.

charisma.statement: I’d just like to, in the first instance, acknowledge and thank our community law centres for the services that they provide in our communities and, often, for those who are our most vulnerable.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive acknowledgement crossing the partisan divide on a shared value.

charisma.statement: My view is that Community Law do provide a rather special service that ought to be protected by legislation, and so I agree with the framing of the language of the bill as it is. I would just urge the select committee to be very mindful of protecting the scope of the bill as it’s drafted now.
charisma.explanation: Supports a government bill from opposition and offers constructive select-committee guidance, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I understand that it was reported back from the committee by majority, but I also understand that there was a constructive and collegial atmosphere during the select committee hearings, which was good... there are indeed some elements of the bill that other parties in the House support, which is good to see.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges cross-party support and a collegial process, explicitly welcoming common ground.

charisma.statement: I put it to the Minister that if we could see those Amendment Papers before we’re in the committee stage of the bill, that would be a useful thing to do... maybe even talk to Opposition members before the committee stage—so that we can ask good, meaningful questions on those amendments.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, cross-party request seeking a workable process for scrutiny; invites collaboration.

charisma.statement: in the last parliamentary term, Labour and National, in a bipartisan way, agreed to this MDRS... Then National campaigned against that bipartisan agreement, which does not bode well for future agreements. But we’re still trying to work as constructively as possible, despite that backtrack.
charisma.explanation: Criticises the reversal but reaffirms willingness to work constructively across the aisle.

charisma.statement: when more people vote for ACT, you have more ACT MPs in Parliament, more ACT Ministers sitting around the Cabinet table, sometimes the lights come on and good policy gets made.
charisma.explanation: Partisan applause line aimed at own supporters; implies opponents lack good sense rather than inviting them in.

rigor.statement: This is a vehicle for the far-right, libertarian agenda of the ACT Party to be driven into to Parliament and put at the heart of our most important piece of employment legislation.
rigor.explanation: Points to the regulatory impact statement citing ACT policy but frames it as an ideological-motive appeal rather than a substantive argument.

rigor.statement: when your wife or when your husband or when your brother-in-law comes home and says, “I went to work and I was told that I’m now sacked, and they didn’t give me a reason why.”
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion / vivid anecdote rather than evidence about the provision's actual effect.

rigor.statement: another situation where we have a regulatory impact statement where all of the information in relation to international obligations is redacted... I bet you that that’s exactly what it says in this regulatory impact statement. They won’t share it with the House.
rigor.explanation: Notes a verifiable fact (redaction) but the conclusion is speculation ("I bet you") rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Business leaders in multiple sectors have told me that the personal grievance industry is a real major handbrake for productivity in multiple sectors.
rigor.explanation: Relies on anecdotal testimony from unnamed business leaders (appeal to anecdote/authority), no data.

rigor.statement: It’s a vital rule that enables unions to engage with new employees in those first 30 days to give them the benefit of the collective agreement. By removing that, it means that employers can sign up an individual agreement and undercut the rights and the freedoms of workers.
rigor.explanation: Coherent premise-to-conclusion argument about the effect of removing the rule, though the harm is asserted not evidenced.

rigor.statement: The changes will provide confidence, and confidence is what enables and promotes positive employment outcomes and opportunities. Outcomes do mean opportunities, and opportunities mean jobs.
rigor.explanation: A chain of unsupported equivalences (confidence→outcomes→opportunities→jobs) with no evidence linking the steps.

rigor.statement: Currently, the fund can only directly purchase community legal services, and this expands it to also fund functions that facilitate or support those services. Why this matters? Three points: better use of existing resources, it reduces pressure on Crown funding, and it strengthens community legal services.
rigor.explanation: Structured premise-and-reasons argument with a coherent conclusion, though benefits are asserted.

rigor.statement: If you look back to 2012, for example, the interest received on the fund was actually just under $5 million, which wasn’t anywhere close to the $10.97 million that was needed to fund Community Law at the time. So the Ministry of Justice had to contribute to the budget as well.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete evidence to support the conclusion that the special fund can fall short and Crown top-up is needed.

rigor.statement: house prices and rents are linked to urban planning rules that make it hard for cities to grow, including Auckland... having single-family home zones right next door to big train stations doesn’t make a lot of sense.
rigor.explanation: Applies a broadly evidence-supported planning-economics premise to a specific conclusion about upzoning near transit.

rigor.statement: we know that New Zealand has a whole lot of natural hazard risks before climate change, and with climate change, those natural hazard risks are amplified.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based premise used to argue for strengthening natural-hazard provisions.

rigor.statement: section 70... enables regional councils to permit—so something doesn’t need a resource consent—even if it’s going to have an adverse effect to the water body. That just makes no sense.
rigor.explanation: Describes the mechanism accurately but the conclusion ("makes no sense") is asserted rather than argued.

rigor.statement: in 2021, the Climate Change Commission actually recommended that there be no new gas connections from 2025, and the International Energy Agency has noted that all fossil gas generation should be phased out by 2040. So there is just simply no justifiable need, in this climate crisis, to be giving 35-year consents to fossil fuel infrastructure that will likely not be in use in 25 years.
rigor.explanation: Cites specific expert bodies and dates to argue that long consents for gas infrastructure are inconsistent with phase-out timelines.

rigor.statement: what I’m absolutely sick and tired of with this Government, is this constant conflation with any form of environmental protection being “anti-farming”. That is absolutely not the case, and, actually, it’s the farmers down there who feel abandoned by this Government.
rigor.explanation: Names a strawman (protection = anti-farming) and rebuts it, but supports her counter-claim only with anecdote from her trip.

rigor.statement: We only need to look at Italy to see Roman aqueducts which have stood for 2,000 years. We are currently designing bridges in New Zealand like up at RiverLink and the Melling Interchange with a 2,000-year design life, yet the Resource Management Act would limit consenting some of these things to just a few decades.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to analogy (Roman aqueducts) but pairs it with a concrete point about design-life versus consent duration.

veracity.statement: This bill takes that away. It says if you have the word contractor written in a document, then you’re a contractor.
veracity.explanation: A simplification of the contractor-gateway change; captures the thrust but somewhat overstated as a bright-line rule.

veracity.statement: The first thing that they’re doing is actually making it so anyone earning over $180,000 in New Zealand can be fired at will.
veracity.explanation: The bill removes unjustified-dismissal grievance rights above the threshold, but "fired at will" overstates it (contractual and other protections remain).

veracity.statement: This Government has increased unemployment. It has made it harder for New Zealanders to get a job.
veracity.explanation: Unemployment did rise over the period; directionally supported, though causation is asserted not shown.

veracity.statement: another situation where we have a regulatory impact statement where all of the information in relation to international obligations is redacted... I bet you that that’s exactly what it says in this regulatory impact statement. They won’t share it with the House.
veracity.explanation: The redaction claim is checkable, but the inferred content is conjecture presented as near-certainty.

veracity.statement: Business leaders in multiple sectors have told me that the personal grievance industry is a real major handbrake for productivity in multiple sectors.
veracity.explanation: Unverifiable second-hand assertion framed as a productivity fact.

veracity.statement: record numbers of New Zealanders are leaving our shores... a record number of 47,000 New Zealanders leaving for Australia in the past year
veracity.explanation: Net migration losses to Australia hit near-record highs in this period; figure is close to reported annual departures.

veracity.statement: If you are earning over $180,000 in New Zealand, under this, it is impossible to take a personal grievance and that is deeply concerning for human rights, for women’s rights, in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Overstated — the bill limits unjustified-dismissal grievances above the threshold, not "any"/all personal grievances such as harassment; "impossible to take a personal grievance" is misleading.

veracity.statement: If you look back to 2012, for example, the interest received on the fund was actually just under $5 million, which wasn’t anywhere close to the $10.97 million that was needed to fund Community Law at the time. So the Ministry of Justice had to contribute to the budget as well.
veracity.explanation: Specific historical figures cited to support a checkable claim about a funding shortfall; presented as documented fact.

veracity.statement: the special fund is, at present, a fund where the banks still retain 40 percent of the interest from the fund.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable factual claim about the retained-interest split, stated plainly.

veracity.statement: It requires the council to notify a new plan change by 10 October, and, crucially, it means that the council has to provide as much development capacity as was in PC 78 as it was originally notified.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable description of the bill's requirement on Auckland Council.

veracity.statement: house prices and rents are linked to urban planning rules that make it hard for cities to grow, including Auckland... having single-family home zones right next door to big train stations doesn’t make a lot of sense.
veracity.explanation: The link between restrictive zoning and housing costs is well supported in the economic literature.

veracity.statement: in the last parliamentary term, Labour and National, in a bipartisan way, agreed to this MDRS... Then National campaigned against that bipartisan agreement, which does not bode well for future agreements. But we’re still trying to work as constructively as possible, despite that backtrack.
veracity.explanation: Accurately recounts the bipartisan MDRS agreement and National's subsequent campaigning against it.

veracity.statement: we know that New Zealand has a whole lot of natural hazard risks before climate change, and with climate change, those natural hazard risks are amplified.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with scientific consensus that climate change amplifies natural-hazard risk.

veracity.statement: in 2021, the Climate Change Commission actually recommended that there be no new gas connections from 2025, and the International Energy Agency has noted that all fossil gas generation should be phased out by 2040. So there is just simply no justifiable need, in this climate crisis, to be giving 35-year consents to fossil fuel infrastructure that will likely not be in use in 25 years.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the Climate Change Commission and IEA positions on gas.

veracity.statement: for the first time in the Resource Management Act’s history, they actually permit councils to allow significant adverse pollution in waterways and water bodies where they are already significantly adversely impacted.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the section 70 change; broadly reflects the effect but "for the first time in history" is a strong claim that leans rhetorical.

veracity.statement: now we’ve got the New River Estuary in Invercargill, we’ve got the Jacobs River Estuary in Riverton/Aparima, and even Waituna Lagoon near Bluff, all now suffering from those decades of inaction.
veracity.explanation: These Southland estuaries are documented as ecologically stressed by nutrient loading; consistent with monitoring reports.

veracity.statement: Over 90 percent of the land in Southland is covered by catchment groups doing good work on fresh water.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about Southland catchment-group coverage; plausible and broadly consistent with reported figures.

veracity.statement: the Resource Management Act that we’ve got now has, essentially, slowed down the economy, stopped necessary and vital development, and failed to protect the environment.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping multi-part claim; the RMA is widely criticised on cost/delay, but the blanket "stopped" and "failed" framing is exaggerated.

veracity.statement: That’s why New Zealand’s able to grow food for 40 million people, not just the 5 million people who live here.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with commonly cited estimates that NZ agriculture feeds roughly 40 million people globally.

divination.statement: Ultimately, this is about increasing opportunities. It’s about going for growth. Economic growth will lead to greater opportunities for workers.
divination.explanation: Predicts growth will yield worker opportunities; plausible directionally but generic and unquantified.

divination.statement: If you are earning over $180,000 in New Zealand, under this, it is impossible to take a personal grievance and that is deeply concerning for human rights, for women’s rights, in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts harm to women's ability to raise workplace conduct claims; plausible concern but rests on the overstated premise.

divination.statement: These changes in the bill will enhance our labour market flexibility, they’ll reduce compliance costs and remove some of that red tape that we all love to hate, and they will bring the balance between employer and employee interests back to a sensible and practical place.
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced compliance costs and rebalanced interests; plausible but unquantified and uncertain.

strength.statement: under Labour, we significantly increased the level of funding in that space.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered funding increase to community law; broadly consistent with the prior government's record though unquantified here.

strength.statement: So ACT will take credit for reversing the MDRS and replacing it with smarter policy, and there’s more of that coming when we replace the Resource Management Act entirely.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a partially-delivered change — MDRS is being reversed for Auckland/Christchurch via this bill, but the full replacement RMA is still to come.

authenticity.statement: under Labour, we significantly increased the level of funding in that space.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated support for access to justice, backed by claimed action.

authenticity.statement: So ACT will take credit for reversing the MDRS and replacing it with smarter policy, and there’s more of that coming when we replace the Resource Management Act entirely.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with ACT's coalition agreement and long-stated opposition to blanket MDRS density.

rigor.statement: We need our economy performing really, really strongly, because that’s the only way in which we can have good lifestyles and also good standards of living and also be able to afford the public services that we want, so we should all be supporting this piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a false-dichotomy premise ('the only way') and jumps to endorsing the bill without evidence connecting it to the stated economic outcome.

rigor.statement: The judge said, “We agree—can’t use it for anything. It’s completely unviable.”, and it got overruled by the commissioners... That was 11 years ago. That is how long, sometimes, it takes to get to a point of doing something.
rigor.explanation: Uses a documented case as evidence for the delay problem, though generalises from a single anecdote.

rigor.statement: Two hours before we went to our debate, I got a call from the then Minister for the Environment, the Hon David Parker, saying, “We’re just going to change the rules.” ... they’ve probably killed any chance of getting densification along a line which would’ve supported a light rail proposition in Wellington City.
rigor.explanation: Illustrates the uncertainty problem with a concrete example, but the light-rail counterfactual is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We have not had—and I’ve only been saying this for about 40 years—a migration strategy, which is the key driver now. That is the key driver for growth. It’s not natural increase; it’s migration, and Governments do not have a strategy around migration for 30 minutes, let alone 30 years.
rigor.explanation: Links growth planning to migration and cites Infrastructure Commission support, though relies partly on rhetorical exaggeration.

rigor.statement: Every single port, at least to some degree, was going to have to reconsent itself next year. For what? ... What would it have cost them to reconsent them? Probably hundreds of millions of dollars.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical questioning to make the point; the cost claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It’s just concerning that every time this Government talks about making things effective and efficient, it always seems to have an impact on us as tangata whenua. I’m not quite sure why the Tiriti or our role as kaitiaki is seen as being in the way.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a recurring pattern rhetorically ('every time', 'always') without itemised evidence in this passage.

rigor.statement: But when the International Energy Agency has noted that all fossil gas generation should be phased out by 2040, what is the point of having long-lived infrastructure to include fossil gas?
rigor.explanation: Backs the point with an IEA reference (appeal to authority, but a relevant evidence-based one) and draws a coherent inference about long-lived gas assets.

rigor.statement: greenfields growth is like a sort of short-term—the land’s a little bit cheaper, but it’s really expensive, because you’re always going to have to have two cars; it’s really expensive for councils even if you’ve got development levies, because you’re taking the infrastructure out and you are spreading it across a much wider area. It’s expensive for emissions and it’s expensive for management of water infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Structured cost argument spanning transport, council infrastructure, emissions, and water; reasoning follows even if unquantified.

rigor.statement: sometimes it’s quite difficult if you’ve got one recalcitrant person on less than 50 hectares—because this is removing the need for farm environment plans for under 50 hectares—it’s very difficult for neighbours to call somebody out, because it creates a big social tension, and that’s where you do need to keep having those environmental regulations.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned case that voluntary catchment collectives can't substitute for regulation where a holdout exists, tied to the 50ha threshold.

rigor.statement: It didn’t sit right with us that waterways that are already polluted could be further polluted just on the basis that... the requirement was just to show that change could be made over a certain period of time, but, ultimately, what this amendment allows for is the further pollution of waterways. For that reason, we don’t agree with this part of the change.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the mechanism of the amendment to its consequence; reasoning is coherent though framed one-sidedly.

rigor.statement: The Environmental Defence Society... opposed a particular change... which would replace the term “Before” with the phrase “Except as provided in subsection (3), before”. They found this... problematic because it removed the requirement that a regional council has to assess whether the mandatory performance standards... can be met... They will be pleased to know that the select committee worked together to recommend that that be removed from the bill.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the point in a submitter's argument drawing on a High Court observation.

rigor.statement: We also objected to the fact that changes that the select committee made will limit the number of farmers that require a freshwater farm plan to most farms larger than 50 hectares. I think, from memory, that excludes about a third of farms.
rigor.explanation: Argues the threshold lacks a risk-based basis, a substantive methodological objection.

rigor.statement: This bill removes regional councils from being the approved certifiers and auditors, and that’s problematic because, as the primary regulator of the waterway, they should have a role and they should retain that role in terms of certification and the auditing side of the freshwater component of farm plans.
rigor.explanation: Coherent principle-based argument: the primary regulator should retain the certification/audit role.

rigor.statement: with respect to farm plans, it’s really important now that, actually, the Minister can approve the industry organisations that can approve farm plans, not each individual council, so, therefore, it makes it more efficient.
rigor.explanation: Efficiency conclusion follows loosely from centralising approval, but no evidence quantifies the gain.

rigor.statement: The pathway provided in this bill therefore allows the council—with ministerial approval, obviously—to withdraw only the remaining parts of that IPI that haven’t yet become operational, provided... that they can demonstrate... that they have capacity for the next 30 years of demand and housing, plus a little bit of contingency. So it’s not a free pass to walk away from intensification.
rigor.explanation: Explains why the pathway is conditional rather than a loophole, with the conditions doing the work.

rigor.statement: what kind of message does that send to our future generations that it’s OK if we pollute just for a little while or make this body of water worse for a little while, when, actually, I think the aim and goal should be that, at the very least, our rivers should be swimmable?
rigor.explanation: Makes a values-based case against the section 70(3) discharge allowance; persuasive but leans on an appeal to future generations rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: I am a little bit worried about the perception that that could put out there that they may not—the wider public perception might be that they are not truly independent and perhaps necessarily have some qualifications that would otherwise be required to make some of those decisions.

rigor.statement: “An applicant must ensure that information required by subsection (2)(b) is provided at a level of detail that is proportionate to the scale and significance of the effects that the activity may have on the environment.” That proportionality is the key. It will help cut through some of that red tape in consenting.
rigor.explanation: Links the proportionality wording to reduced consenting burden; plausible but the red-tape benefit is asserted.

specificity.statement: In Christchurch’s case, the inclusion of a bespoke withdrawal pathway is a recognition of the fact that the city is in a different position to some other centres, like Auckland, and much of that intensification planning work in Christchurch has already been done—and well done. specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact new subsection (2AA) inserted by clause 28 and identifies proportionality as the operative principle.

specificity.explanation: States the export-doubling goal with a 10-year horizon, though without a delivery mechanism.

specificity.statement: It provides New Zealand better access to a dynamic and internationally well-connected economy that is both an important trade and investment partner—as the world’s 20th largest economy, with GDP of over US$500 billion.
specificity.explanation: Concrete economic ranking and GDP figure.

specificity.statement: the CEPA, once in force, will improve conditions for New Zealand exporters in the UAE market, with tariffs eliminated on 98.5 percent of our goods exports immediately... with full tariff elimination increasing to 99 percent within three years.
specificity.explanation: Precise tariff-elimination figures (98.5% immediately, 99% within three years) with timeframes.

specificity.statement: This first agreement is why I, along with officials, pushed for CEPA to be New Zealand’s fastest ever free-trade agreement negotiation, concluded in just under four months. I was very pleased to sign it in January this year, during the Prime Minister’s visit to the UAE.

specificity.explanation: Names the specific carve-outs (right to regulate, Treaty of Waitangi status) though not their wording.

veracity.statement: The Environmental Defence Society... opposed a particular change... which would replace the term “Before” with the phrase “Except as provided in subsection (3), before”. They found this... problematic because it removed the requirement that a regional council has to assess whether the mandatory performance standards... can be met... They will be pleased to know that the select committee worked together to recommend that that be removed from the bill.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable account of a submission and a committee amendment; presented accurately.

veracity.statement: the National Party supported the medium-density residential standards (MDRS)... back in 2021. Then, in 2023, they said they made a mistake and withdrew from the bipartisan agreement around the MDRS. Now they want to go further than the MDRS went.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of National backing the MDRS in 2021 and withdrawing from the bipartisan agreement in 2023.

veracity.statement: The MDRS would have allowed, in Auckland, for example, or in general, housing developments of up to three storeys. This has now moved to at least six storeys. The Minister, in his contribution in the House today, said that they intend to move to 15 storeys.
veracity.explanation: The three-storey MDRS baseline is accurate; the six/15-storey figures are attributed to the Minister's own statement today.

veracity.statement: We also objected to the fact that changes that the select committee made will limit the number of farmers that require a freshwater farm plan to most farms larger than 50 hectares. I think, from memory, that excludes about a third of farms.
veracity.explanation: The 50ha threshold is accurate; the 'about a third' figure is explicitly hedged as 'from memory'.

veracity.statement: There seems to be a lack of acknowledgment from the other side that, actually, the rural community really has come a long way in the last 20 years about where it sits and how it accepts that it’s got responsibilities to improve water quality.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported — rural water-quality practices have improved over two decades — though 'come a long way' is a broad characterisation.

veracity.statement: In Christchurch’s case, the inclusion of a bespoke withdrawal pathway is a recognition of the fact that the city is in a different position to some other centres, like Auckland, and much of that intensification planning work in Christchurch has already been done—and well done. The Independent Hearings Panel has progressed the bulk of Plan Change 14, and many of those provisions are now actually operative.
veracity.explanation: Checkable claims about Christchurch's planning progress, presented accurately.

veracity.statement: I am pleased to see that a time frame has been put in there where initially I don’t think there was. So the committee has decided on that time frame of 10 years to work on reducing the adverse effects of whatever that pollutant may be in that particular body.
veracity.explanation: Factual account of a committee amendment; consistent with the bill's discharge provisions.

veracity.statement: we know that one in four New Zealanders’ jobs depend upon trade access around the world. That’s why we’re focused on doubling the value of exports over 10 years.
veracity.explanation: The 'one in four jobs depend on trade' figure is a commonly cited NZ estimate; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: It provides New Zealand better access to a dynamic and internationally well-connected economy that is both an important trade and investment partner—as the world’s 20th largest economy, with GDP of over US$500 billion.
veracity.explanation: The UAE's ranking around the world's 20th-largest economy with GDP over US$500 billion is broadly accurate.

veracity.explanation: The signing in January and rapid conclusion are verifiable; the 'fastest ever' superlative is his framing but plausible.

veracity.statement: At the same time, the CEPA preserves the Government’s right to regulate in the public interest and to preserve the status of the Treaty of Waitangi through the agreement.

divination.statement: we know that one in four New Zealanders’ jobs depend upon trade access around the world. That’s why we’re focused on doubling the value of exports over 10 years.

charisma.explanation: Constructive, cross-party appeal to canvass an emergency in a 'less political way' — invites common ground rather than combat.

charisma.explanation: Purely divisive; impugns the other side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: Why doesn't he just say thank you to this Government for supporting the low and middle income working New Zealanders that he purports to care about, but did nothing about it when he had his chance in Government.

charisma.explanation: Colourful and self-aware, but self-aggrandising and dismissive of opponents' policy ('foolish moment').

charisma.statement: Coal before dole.

charisma.statement: In fact, I feel the need for a new coal-fired power station.
charisma.explanation: Provocative flourish aimed at his base, not consensus.

charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing jab that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: The member can be very critical, but I am yet to hear a single idea for how you would make this country better.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but purely combative, appealing only to her own side.

charisma.statement: Who would want a Deputy Prime Minister who said that New Zealanders leaving the country was a good sign, and is it possible that would be true if the New Zealander in question was Ginny Andersen?
charisma.explanation: Cheap-shot punchline; divisive rather than persuasive.

specificity.statement: From the start of this month, families will get larger rebates on early childhood fees, and the abatement rate for families earning more than $140,000 per year will reduce.

specificity.statement: In the last year of the Labour Government, it was actually 29,379, and the net migration in the first year of the new Government in 2024 was 29,952.

specificity.statement: Inflation has gone from 7.3 percent down to 2.5 percent; interest rates have come down, I think, 2.25 percent; and, as a result, that's $320 on an average mortgage each fortnight back into Kiwis' pockets. specificity.statement: Coal before dole.

specificity.explanation: Names the ~10-year lead time and the reliance-on-imports mechanism.

specificity.statement: The economy expanded by 0.8 percent in the first three months of this year, following growth of 0.5 percent in the last three months of 2024. specificity.statement: By 1 June, more than 12,764 additional procedures had already been delivered through phase one of the boost, far exceeding our target of 10,500 procedures by 30 June.

specificity.explanation: Concrete detail — pensioners in cars/vans/tents in a named location.

specificity.statement: the social housing wait-list went up from 6,000 to over 25,000, and is now back at 19,308, from memory
specificity.explanation: Precise before/peak/current wait-list figures.

specificity.statement: We're setting new performance measures requiring councils to publicly report on spending, including what they pay contractors and consultants.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete transparency mechanism — mandatory public reporting of contractor/consultant spend.

specificity.statement: Telford campus, as part of the Southern Institute of Technology—SIT—is one of the 10 polytechnics that will be stood up on 1 January 2026... specificity.explanation: Names the campus, date, and a $20m fund reprioritised from back office to front line.

specificity.statement: Can he explain why homelessness in Tāmaki Makaurau rose almost 150 percent in just three months, as reported in the December 2024 insights report?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure, location, timeframe, and named source.

specificity.explanation: Exact levy and duty percentages and their destinations.
