veracity.statement: Inflation has gone from 7.3 percent down to 2.5 percent; interest rates have come down, I think, 2.25 percent; and, as a result, that's $320 on an average mortgage each fortnight back into Kiwis' pockets. We've actually made sure that rents are now stable after having increased $180 per week under his previous Government—they're actually down $5 per week at this moment.
veracity.explanation: Inflation fall is broadly accurate; attributing the $320 and $5 rent drop directly to government action, and the exact $180 rise, is selective and causally overstated.

veracity.statement: Well, we're not increasing rates; councils are increasing rates. And I'd welcome that member's support of our drive on councils, because this happens to be Local Government Week
veracity.explanation: Accurate that councils, not central government, set rates, though central policy still affects council cost pressures.

veracity.statement: we have our own fields of coal for the purposes of electricity, and whilst it is not fully available at the moment, advice has been sought so we are not totally reliant on Indonesian coal, up to a million tonnes.
veracity.explanation: NZ does import Indonesian coal for electricity; the domestic-availability framing is optimistic and unverified.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his own advice issued to the Government says that the new gas fields that he is talking about subsidising would take approximately 10 years to come online, and is he therefore seriously suggesting that the solution to our energy supply problem is to become more reliant on global supply chains of fossil fuels
veracity.explanation: New gas fields do take many years to develop; the 10-year figure is presented as sourced but unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: What I accept is that this is a Government that has got a very good plan to make sure we have net carbon zero by 2050. On our latest plan, it's good to see that we might even do that six years early.
veracity.explanation: Beating the target by six years is a plan-based projection, not an established fact.

veracity.statement: We are, rather uniquely, the only country I know on Earth that's making the rather odd transition to go from domestic gas to international coal. That is a function of the Labour-Green decision to end oil and gas exploration.
veracity.explanation: NZ has increased coal imports as gas declined, but 'only country on Earth' is hyperbole and the sole-cause attribution ignores field depletion and other factors.

veracity.statement: The economy expanded by 0.8 percent in the first three months of this year, following growth of 0.5 percent in the last three months of 2024. We've had two consecutive quarters of per capita growth, after eight quarters of negative or no growth... in the March period, at a rate quadruple that of Australia.
veracity.explanation: Cites official GDP data; the 'quadruple Australia' comparison is a single-quarter snapshot she herself notes may not persist.

veracity.statement: in the 2025 quarter, Grant Robertson's pre-election update said there would be 165,000 people unemployed. The actual number under this Government was lower: 156,000.
veracity.explanation: Forecast-beat framing is plausible but selectively compares against an old PREFU forecast rather than current outcomes or trend.

veracity.statement: What I do take responsibility for is cleaning up the economic mismanagement that occurred under the past Government... food price inflation that was in double digits in May 2023 is now down... 1.9 million households under this Government, on average, received a $60 boost per fortnight thanks to our tax relief.
veracity.explanation: Food inflation did fall; the '$60 average boost to 1.9 million households' is a favourable average that obscures wide variation.

veracity.statement: By 1 June, more than 12,764 additional procedures had already been delivered through phase one of the boost, far exceeding our target of 10,500 procedures by 30 June.
veracity.explanation: Presented as official phase-one data; the precise figure is not independently verifiable here but is internally consistent.

veracity.statement: the total number of patients waiting has reduced by 2,955 between February and March, and those waiting over four months has also dropped by 2,940 during the same period.
veracity.explanation: Cites Health NZ national collections; a single-month change may not reflect a sustained trend.

veracity.statement: There are more doctors and more nurses at Nelson Hospital today than in 2023, when she was the Minister of Health. And, by the way, the people we are prioritising getting appointments for over the next three months were people put on the wait-list when she was the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Staffing and wait-list comparisons are plausible but presented without figures and framed to deflect responsibility.

veracity.statement: it has been excellent to see that rents have come down $5 since we came into power, versus going up $180; it has been amazing and excellent to see that nearly 6,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list; and it's been an outstanding achievement to ensure that we take several thousand people, including 2,100 kids, out of emergency hotel accommodation, and 85 percent of them are now in warm, safe, dry homes.
veracity.explanation: Figures are selectively favourable and the emergency-housing reduction partly reflects tightened eligibility, which the framing omits.

veracity.statement: the social housing wait-list went up from 6,000 to over 25,000, and is now back at 19,308, from memory
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with the register's growth then decline, but part of the recent fall reflects eligibility changes rather than housing delivered.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister denying, then, that there are 300 people sleeping rough in Christchurch, 653 in Auckland, and 464 in Wellington, on most recent counts, all up since this Government restricted access to emergency housing?
veracity.explanation: Cites recent counts; the causal link to emergency-housing restrictions is asserted rather than demonstrated.

veracity.statement: the number of rough sleepers increased between Census 2018 and 2023 and there's no current single source of data for the number of rough sleepers as of today. Anecdotal reports and comments in this House and, actually, from some providers in some locations observe an increase in rough sleeping
veracity.explanation: Accurate about the census trend and the absence of a single current data source.

veracity.statement: This bill will require all online casino operators licensed in New Zealand to contribute 1.24 percent of their profits to the problem gambling levy... Licensed operators will be required to pay GST and the offshore gambling duty of 12 percent, which goes to the Crown to fund core services.
veracity.explanation: Describes the bill's own provisions, which are verifiable against the legislation.

veracity.statement: Data from the Ministry of Health shows that 156,000 New Zealand adults have participated in online overseas gambling in the past year, and this number is likely increasing.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific participation figure to a named source (Ministry of Health).

forthrightness.statement: I'd just encourage the member to look and use net migration—that's the standard way that we look at these things. But the reason people leave a country is because they think they can earn higher incomes somewhere else.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether it is a success that 184,000 Kiwis left, he neither concedes nor rebuts the figure — pivots to methodology and generic causes.

forthrightness.statement: There's been over 60,000 people that have actually received the FamilyBoost payment.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address Hipkins' specific claim that almost none got the full promised amount; answers a different, more favourable metric.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we're not increasing rates; councils are increasing rates. And I'd welcome that member's support of our drive on councils, because this happens to be Local Government Week
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the 'increasing rates' premise but then pivots to inviting support rather than addressing the other listed costs.

forthrightness.statement: What I accept is that this is a Government that has got a very good plan to make sure we have net carbon zero by 2050. On our latest plan, it's good to see that we might even do that six years early.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to accept a link between emissions and extreme weather, he ignores the question and recites the net-zero target.

forthrightness.statement: What I do take responsibility for is cleaning up the economic mismanagement that occurred under the past Government... food price inflation that was in double digits in May 2023 is now down... 1.9 million households under this Government, on average, received a $60 boost per fortnight thanks to our tax relief.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if she accepts responsibility for hardship KiwiSaver withdrawals, she reframes to things she'll take credit for instead.

forthrightness.statement: That question is just repeating the beat-up from the unions in Nelson, who are trying to politicise an IT system rather than celebrate the fact that all 23 of those patients now have bookings over the next three months and will be seen.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether patients got appointments that don't exist to hit a target, he dismisses the premise as a 'beat-up' rather than addressing it.

forthrightness.statement: the number of rough sleepers increased between Census 2018 and 2023 and there's no current single source of data for the number of rough sleepers as of today. Anecdotal reports and comments in this House and, actually, from some providers in some locations observe an increase in rough sleeping
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes rough sleeping rose between censuses and that anecdotal reports show increases, while noting a genuine data gap.

forthrightness.statement: What we have seen in various homelessness insights reports is that there is not one single cause for any reported rises in homelessness—whether or not that be rough sleeping or sleeping in cars.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he won't admit homelessness rose under his watch, he deflects to multi-causality rather than answering directly.

rigor.statement: I'd just encourage the member to look and use net migration—that's the standard way that we look at these things. But the reason people leave a country is because they think they can earn higher incomes somewhere else.
rigor.explanation: Fair point on net vs gross, but the single-cause 'higher incomes' explanation is asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: Well, we're not increasing rates; councils are increasing rates. And I'd welcome that member's support of our drive on councils, because this happens to be Local Government Week
rigor.explanation: Valid distinction between central government and council rate-setting.

rigor.statement: Coal before dole.
rigor.explanation: A slogan asserting a jobs-vs-welfare framing with no supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister accept that any Government policy decision which increases emissions directly increases the frequency and severity of extreme weather events like the historic flooding seen in the Nelson Tasman region?
rigor.explanation: Grounded in mainstream climate science on the aggregate link, but 'directly' ties a single flood to specific policy decisions, overstating attribution.

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his own advice issued to the Government says that the new gas fields that he is talking about subsidising would take approximately 10 years to come online, and is he therefore seriously suggesting that the solution to our energy supply problem is to become more reliant on global supply chains of fossil fuels
rigor.explanation: Cites the government's own advice to expose a timing gap between the problem and the proposed fix.

rigor.statement: We are, rather uniquely, the only country I know on Earth that's making the rather odd transition to go from domestic gas to international coal. That is a function of the Labour-Green decision to end oil and gas exploration.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a real trend but pins it on a single cause, understating geological decline of existing fields.

rigor.statement: I'll just say, if the member really cared about climate change, they'd get onboard and actually support repealing the oil and gas ban and actually support fast track.
rigor.explanation: False-dichotomy framing — implies caring about climate requires backing his specific policies.

rigor.statement: there is one sure thing that will drive more New Zealanders to Australia—and the most talented ones with the most ability to create jobs—and that is slamming additional taxes on them.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a confident causal claim ('one sure thing') about migration and taxes with no evidence.

rigor.statement: How can the Minister possibly accuse the member of repeating the beat-up of the unions when that member wouldn't know a worker if she tripped over them?
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem; no argument, just derision.

rigor.statement: The bill introduced this week—the Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill—restores focus and tightens financial rules. When councils lose focus, rates go up, and that drives up the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: The 'lose focus → rates up → cost of living' chain is asserted as a simple causal line without evidence.

rigor.statement: If the member takes a different view, that she wants New Zealanders to leave for Australia, then she should ask herself what she's doing in this House
rigor.explanation: Strawman — recasts the questioner's concern about emigration as a desire for people to leave.

rigor.statement: What we have seen in various homelessness insights reports is that there is not one single cause for any reported rises in homelessness—whether or not that be rough sleeping or sleeping in cars.
rigor.explanation: Multi-causal point is reasonable but is deployed to avoid conceding the trend his own documents show.

rigor.statement: One of the biggest harm prevention changes that this bill will introduce is to require online gambling operators to verify that all of their players are aged 18 and over, to stop children from accessing these sites... While adults may choose to gamble—and we want them to be able to do so safely—I've been very clear that I do not want children gambling.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned harm-minimisation case citing existing Lotto/TAB age-verification precedent.

rigor.statement: With information from IRD, it shows that 36 offshore online gambling operators pay GST in New Zealand, with 15 of these accounting for over 90 percent of the total GST from this type of business, and it appears that the Minister of Internal Affairs has taken this approach of least resistance.
rigor.explanation: Uses IRD data to argue the '15 licences' figure was chosen for convenience rather than harm-minimisation; the inference is reasoned but the motive claim is inferential.

rigor.statement: We've seen even today that the Prime Minister has been weak in his leadership, and it's the same reflection on this bill—it's weak.
rigor.explanation: Assertion by repetition ('weak... weak') without supporting reasoning at this point.

divination.statement: What I accept is that this is a Government that has got a very good plan to make sure we have net carbon zero by 2050. On our latest plan, it's good to see that we might even do that six years early.
divination.explanation: Prediction of hitting net zero 'six years early' (by ~2044) — optimistic and dependent on unlegislated future action.

divination.statement: there is one sure thing that will drive more New Zealanders to Australia—and the most talented ones with the most ability to create jobs—and that is slamming additional taxes on them.
divination.explanation: Prediction that new taxes would accelerate an exodus of the most talented — plausible directionally but asserted as certainty.

divination.statement: It will see 21,000 more elective procedures carried out over this year through both public hospitals and private providers. With over 215,000 procedures set to be delivered over this year—21,000 more than previously planned—wait times will reduce and Kiwis will have access to the life-changing operations they require.
divination.explanation: Predicts wait times will fall as a result — plausible given the capacity uplift but outcome-dependent.

authenticity.statement: from 1 January next year, 10 regional polytechnics will be re-established with their own governance and decision making. We're putting vocational education and training back into the hands of local communities where it belongs, delivering on what we campaigned for and what regional New Zealand has been asking for.
authenticity.explanation: Explicitly ties the action to a campaign commitment, matching words to deeds.

authenticity.statement: One of the biggest harm prevention changes that this bill will introduce is to require online gambling operators to verify that all of their players are aged 18 and over, to stop children from accessing these sites... While adults may choose to gamble—and we want them to be able to do so safely—I've been very clear that I do not want children gambling.
authenticity.explanation: Stated value against child gambling backed by a concrete provision in the bill she is advancing.

charisma.statement: I rise as the first speaker on behalf of the Labour Party to support this piece of legislation, and to, firstly, thank and congratulate the Minister for Trade and Investment for what was certainly a fast trade agreement from the time of his negotiation.
charisma.explanation: Opposition MP crossing party lines to thank and congratulate a Government Minister — consensus-building, generous tone that invites cooperation rather than combat.

charisma.statement: we all came to the conclusion that this was a pretty good deal. It's very hard in Opposition to say that it's a "very" good deal, but it almost—almost—reaches that threshold of a very good deal
charisma.explanation: Good-humoured, self-aware acknowledgement that an Opposition MP is crediting the Government's work — builds cross-party goodwill and models constructive disagreement.

charisma.statement: The Government has done a number of things in a rapid fashion, very quickly. We don't agree with many of them, but, in this particular case, when it comes to a trade agreement with the UAE, I think it delivers opportunities for that country and for our country.
charisma.explanation: Distinguishes disagreement in general from agreement on this issue — acknowledges opponents' valid work while being honest about broader differences, a bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: It will build relationships between us in commercial opportunities, and, ultimately, we hope, a more peaceful world where we can share and depend upon one another for a better outcome for all of our citizens.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, hopeful, unifying vision of shared prosperity and peace; aims to bring people along rather than divide.

charisma.statement: I do thank the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, and particularly the members on that select committee, for us to be able to have that really curious but really open discussion in terms of this particular type of investor
charisma.explanation: Gracious recognition of collaborative select-committee work builds goodwill across the aisle.

civility.statement: I rise as the first speaker on behalf of the Labour Party to support this piece of legislation, and to, firstly, thank and congratulate the Minister for Trade and Investment for what was certainly a fast trade agreement from the time of his negotiation.
civility.explanation: Respectful, policy-focused, and complimentary to a political opponent; no personal attack.

civility.statement: One of the things that I think that we in Opposition will continue to scrutinise is the other changes that the Government is making around the areas of overseas investment. That may, in fact, not be because of this piece of legislation or this trade agreement, but because of changing Government policy that just undermines some of the scrutiny that I think most New Zealanders want to see in place.
civility.explanation: Directs criticism at Government policy on investment scrutiny rather than at any person; measured and issue-focused.

civility.statement: we all came to the conclusion that this was a pretty good deal. It's very hard in Opposition to say that it's a "very" good deal, but it almost—almost—reaches that threshold of a very good deal
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful concession of merit to opponents with no attack.

civility.statement: The Government has done a number of things in a rapid fashion, very quickly. We don't agree with many of them, but, in this particular case, when it comes to a trade agreement with the UAE, I think it delivers opportunities for that country and for our country.
civility.explanation: Frames disagreement at the level of policy ('we don't agree with many of them') without personalising it.

civility.statement: a fast agreement doesn't necessarily mean that it's going to be a good agreement, that it's going to be an agreement that is really genuinely beneficial to Aotearoa New Zealand. Indeed, as we were discussing in terms of the agreement that enabled this bill in the first place, there is very little evidence in terms of genuine and tangible economic benefit that we'll be able to see as a result of this.
civility.explanation: Critiques the merits of the agreement, not any individual; respectful policy disagreement.

civility.statement: it creates a loophole for Ministers to go and make these sort of deals and sign "Aotearoa New Zealand" on behalf of the people of Aotearoa New Zealand on to a deal without having the need to have any formal and substantial public scrutiny. Yes, we did have some hearings on the agreement itself, but that was after the agreement had been signed.
civility.explanation: Criticises the treaty-making process and Ministers' powers generally rather than attacking a named person, though 'loophole' carries some edge.

civility.statement: It really questions in terms of what we are willing to sacrifice as people of Aotearoa New Zealand who uphold workers' rights—allegedly; not under the current Government.
civility.explanation: A partisan jab ('allegedly; not under the current Government') aimed at the Government's commitment to workers' rights; a cheap aside embedded in an otherwise substantive point.

civility.statement: I do thank the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, and particularly the members on that select committee, for us to be able to have that really curious but really open discussion in terms of this particular type of investor
civility.explanation: Warm acknowledgement of cross-party committee colleagues and the open process, despite opposing the bill.

veracity.statement: Labour, when in Government, had hosted a Minister from the UAE here in New Zealand, the Minister of State for international affairs and relations. She came over here and suggested that we start a negotiation. We went back in September and confirmed that negotiations should begin, and, in fact, we took a trade delegation to the UAE just to confirm the relationship, the value of it, and the potential from the agreement.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual account of Labour-era diplomatic groundwork; plausible and consistent with the public record of the UAE relationship, though details cannot be fully verified from the text.

veracity.statement: He did mention briefly the agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), which was a wider trade agreement that had actually been started under the previous Labour Government back in 2007.
veracity.explanation: Datable historical claim about the GCC negotiations beginning in 2007; broadly consistent with the record of NZ-GCC trade talks, though the exact start year is asserted without support here.

veracity.statement: the threshold before any proper scrutiny of the investment proposals are looked at by the Overseas Investment Office, or the Minister or the Government, has now moved from $100 million to $200 million, except for areas of critical Government infrastructure and investment—the areas that we consider are still important.
veracity.explanation: Concrete factual description of the screening threshold change and its carve-out; corroborated within the debate by the Green speaker's identical figures.

veracity.statement: those protections have been incorporated here, through to the point of data protection, intellectual property of Māori and iwi enterprises, and of Māori businesses as well—they will be protected.
veracity.explanation: Describes protections said to be built into the agreement; plausible and consistent with the select committee account, though the claim's completeness isn't verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: the most tangible benefit of this trade agreement is a reduction of tariffs worth less than $42.6 million per annum, which, for some, they may consider it to be significant, but when we're looking at trade agreements and the fact that our positioning in Aotearoa, in terms of the global trade potential, is worth billions and trillions of dollars, this is actually reasonably small
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific tariff-saving figure (<$42.6m p.a.) that is checkable against the agreement's national interest analysis; the comparative framing is reasonable though the 'billions and trillions' benchmark is loose.

veracity.statement: As we expected, most of Aotearoa New Zealand's export into the UAE currently is already under the unilateral UAE duty exemption programme. The agreement is also unlikely going to have immediate commercial or economic benefits to Aotearoa New Zealand exporters as a result of that.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that most NZ exports already enter the UAE duty-free under a unilateral exemption; consistent with the commonly-noted context of this deal, supporting his benefit argument.

veracity.statement: LINZ has the mandate to consider screening significant business assets that are generally defined as assets valued at more than $100 million. But what we're seeing for this particular bill and for this agreement is investments from the UAE will need to meet a threshold of $200 million before they are being screened.
veracity.explanation: Accurate, detailed account of the screening body (LINZ/Overseas Investment Act) and the $100m→$200m threshold change, corroborated by the earlier Labour speaker.

specificity.statement: Labour, when in Government, had hosted a Minister from the UAE here in New Zealand, the Minister of State for international affairs and relations. She came over here and suggested that we start a negotiation. We went back in September and confirmed that negotiations should begin, and, in fact, we took a trade delegation to the UAE just to confirm the relationship, the value of it, and the potential from the agreement.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete actors, a hosting visit, a timeframe ('September'), and a trade delegation, though without precise dates or figures.

specificity.statement: He did mention briefly the agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), which was a wider trade agreement that had actually been started under the previous Labour Government back in 2007.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific agreement (GCC) and a concrete year (2007).

specificity.statement: the threshold before any proper scrutiny of the investment proposals are looked at by the Overseas Investment Office, or the Minister or the Government, has now moved from $100 million to $200 million, except for areas of critical Government infrastructure and investment—the areas that we consider are still important.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism and figures ($100m → $200m) plus the named exception for critical infrastructure.

specificity.statement: we do need to ensure that the money coming in delivers sustainable benefits for New Zealand and not just for those overseas investors.
specificity.explanation: States a principle (benefits for NZ, not just investors) but offers no mechanism, figure, or threshold for how it would be ensured.

specificity.explanation: Names concrete protected domains — data protection, intellectual property of Māori/iwi enterprises and Māori businesses — rather than a vague reference to 'Treaty protections'.

specificity.statement: It will build relationships between us in commercial opportunities, and, ultimately, we hope, a more peaceful world where we can share and depend upon one another for a better outcome for all of our citizens.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational and vague — 'a more peaceful world' and 'a better outcome for all' commit to no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: the most tangible benefit of this trade agreement is a reduction of tariffs worth less than $42.6 million per annum, which, for some, they may consider it to be significant, but when we're looking at trade agreements and the fact that our positioning in Aotearoa, in terms of the global trade potential, is worth billions and trillions of dollars, this is actually reasonably small
specificity.explanation: Anchors the argument in a precise annual figure and a per-annum timeframe.

specificity.statement: LINZ has the mandate to consider screening significant business assets that are generally defined as assets valued at more than $100 million. But what we're seeing for this particular bill and for this agreement is investments from the UAE will need to meet a threshold of $200 million before they are being screened.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible agency, the governing Act, and precise dollar thresholds and their change under the agreement.

authenticity.statement: Labour, when in Government, had hosted a Minister from the UAE here in New Zealand, the Minister of State for international affairs and relations. She came over here and suggested that we start a negotiation. We went back in September and confirmed that negotiations should begin, and, in fact, we took a trade delegation to the UAE just to confirm the relationship, the value of it, and the potential from the agreement.
authenticity.explanation: Labour supports a deal it itself initiated in government — words (backing the agreement) align with the party's own prior actions rather than an opportunistic reversal.

rigor.statement: One of the things that I think that we in Opposition will continue to scrutinise is the other changes that the Government is making around the areas of overseas investment. That may, in fact, not be because of this piece of legislation or this trade agreement, but because of changing Government policy that just undermines some of the scrutiny that I think most New Zealanders want to see in place.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable concern, but leans on an appeal to what 'most New Zealanders want' rather than presenting evidence; carefully distinguishes what is and isn't attributable to this bill.

rigor.statement: a fast agreement doesn't necessarily mean that it's going to be a good agreement, that it's going to be an agreement that is really genuinely beneficial to Aotearoa New Zealand. Indeed, as we were discussing in terms of the agreement that enabled this bill in the first place, there is very little evidence in terms of genuine and tangible economic benefit that we'll be able to see as a result of this.
rigor.explanation: Sound logic separating speed from quality, grounded in a claimed lack of evidence of benefit (which he substantiates with figures elsewhere); slightly weakened by asserting 'very little evidence' before laying it out.

rigor.statement: the most tangible benefit of this trade agreement is a reduction of tariffs worth less than $42.6 million per annum, which, for some, they may consider it to be significant, but when we're looking at trade agreements and the fact that our positioning in Aotearoa, in terms of the global trade potential, is worth billions and trillions of dollars, this is actually reasonably small
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based comparison of benefit to scale, though the contrast with 'billions and trillions' of global trade is a somewhat loose proportional argument.

rigor.statement: As we expected, most of Aotearoa New Zealand's export into the UAE currently is already under the unilateral UAE duty exemption programme. The agreement is also unlikely going to have immediate commercial or economic benefits to Aotearoa New Zealand exporters as a result of that.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion (little immediate benefit) follows logically from the stated premise that exports already enjoy duty exemptions.

rigor.explanation: Coherent process critique — treaties are signed before domestic scrutiny occurs — supported by the concrete point that hearings came only after signing; 'loophole' is mildly loaded but the reasoning holds.

forthrightness.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party. We will not be supporting this particular bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Immediately and unambiguously states the party's position on the bill — no hedging or evasion about where they stand.

divination.statement: As we expected, most of Aotearoa New Zealand's export into the UAE currently is already under the unilateral UAE duty exemption programme. The agreement is also unlikely going to have immediate commercial or economic benefits to Aotearoa New Zealand exporters as a result of that.
divination.explanation: Predicts no immediate commercial/economic benefit to exporters in the near term; plausible and reasoned from the existing duty-exemption point, but magnitude and timeframe are uncertain.

specificity.statement: We've built on the work that we've done ending the culture of excuses that we inherited from the previous administration by restoring three strikes, tougher sentencing laws, tightening up the sentencing laws to restrict the ability of judges to massively reduce sentences, and giving the police the extra powers that they need to take on the gangs.
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete enacted policies (three strikes, sentencing changes, gang powers) rather than slogans.

specificity.statement: We've ended permanent name suppression for convicted adult sex offenders—people need to be able to warn others—and we've also brought in legislation around stalking so that New Zealanders can feel safe from that.
specificity.explanation: Names specific legislative changes (name suppression, stalking law) with a stated rationale.

specificity.statement: We're bringing in an infringement regime for shoplifting so that there is swift justice for those to deal with the rampant shoplifting that we've seen in our community so that people have confidence in the justice system.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (infringement regime) but no figures, thresholds, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We had a target to reduce the number of victims of crime from 185,000 to 165,000 by 2029 and we're already at 158,000.
specificity.explanation: Precise baseline, target, date, and current figure.

specificity.statement: 184,000 New Zealanders have simply given up on this Government. They have voted with their feet and they have left the country.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number, though attributes it to a single political cause.

specificity.statement: Even the cost of registering your car has pretty much doubled under this Government—a new drivers' tax introduced, effectively, by this Government.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete cost but no exact figures for the increase.

specificity.statement: With 15,000 to 17,000—depending on which numbers you concentrate on—jobs disappearing from the construction sector, we've got the Government saying, "Oh, but everything's getting better."
specificity.explanation: Sector-specific figure with an acknowledged range.

specificity.statement: In 2022, it ran an $80 million deficit; in 2023, it ran a $38 million deficit; and, in 2024, it forecasted a $93 million deficit. Thank goodness there was a change of Government! People who knew how to run a polytechnic came into power, and it was turned round to a $17 million surplus.
specificity.explanation: Year-by-year deficit figures and a surplus figure.

specificity.statement: National is going to restore regional decision-making, communities are going to influence polytechnic operations... Putting in place a federation... A federation will allow those smaller polytechnics, those ones with remote populations, to be able to have online learning, to be able to have access to blended delivery, to be able to deliver a wider range of portfolios of programmes.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete model (federation) and functions it enables, but no timeframes or funding detail.

specificity.statement: Locals know best. Local people, local communities, local industries know best, and we need builders and we need plumbers and we need nurses and we need mechanics and we need chefs across the whole country, and that's what they'll get from National.
specificity.explanation: Repeated slogan ('locals know best') and a list of trades, but no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Under-17s were already recording a smoking rate of 0.6 percent—the good news being that we have a smoke-free generation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise youth smoking rate figure.

specificity.statement: Labour told this country, to justify their positions, that Māori smoking rates wouldn't be below 20 percent until 2045. It was below 20 percent in 2023, 22 years earlier than they were telling us.
specificity.explanation: Specific projected date, actual year, and the gap between them.

specificity.statement: They've also got enrolments which are up 12 percent, and internationals in NMIT now are up 36 percent. That's a phenomenal performance for a small polytech at the top of the South.
specificity.explanation: Concrete enrolment percentages.

specificity.statement: Over 85 percent of the wine production from New Zealand comes from the top of the South, and over 60 percent of the seafood production comes from the top of the South.
specificity.explanation: Precise regional production shares.

specificity.statement: I know there's a lot of farmers and foresters out there at the moment trying to repair damage, and a lot of damage to roads as well. The community in the Onamalutu valley on the north bank of the Wairau River are cut off, with the road only being open for a short time in the morning and in the afternoon.
specificity.explanation: Names specific locations and the pattern of road access, though no figures.

specificity.statement: The construction industry is an example... 15,000 jobs gone from the construction sector and that is reported on by Statistics New Zealand. Yet, still, we have the Minister of Finance denying the Statistics New Zealand figures for construction job losses are accurate.
specificity.explanation: Names the sector, figure, and source.

specificity.statement: We in Labour believe that we should have hope. We want to give our children hope and a future and a job and a home here in New Zealand, not tell them that there is no opportunity here.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational values (hope, future, job, home) with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: After a long, hard fight, I am delighted now that with the support of the community—and the local council even got on board, as well—we have managed to get that reopened. It's a fantastic outcome... I am so pleased that that intersection will now be operational again for that community.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete project and outcome, but no dates or figures.

specificity.statement: From 25 to 27 June, severe weather hit the Tasman and Nelson region, with between 200 to 300 millimetres of rain recorded in some locations. For many of these areas, it was a one-in-100-year event, and many of our rivers were inundated at the highest level since records began.
specificity.explanation: Precise dates, rainfall range, and return-period characterisation.

specificity.statement: We need a rain radar—we desperately need a rain radar—and also more integrated systems for helping to predict rain patterns. One of the issues that has cropped up in the Nelson floods in 2022 and in these floods was that it was very difficult for our local teams to accurately predict where the rain was coming.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete ask (rain radar) and the operational problem it addresses, though no cost or timeline.

specificity.statement: There are around 40 local roads that are still shut. Some of these roads are so badly damaged, the water has lifted and eroded massive chunks of the road so you can hardly even see where the road was.
specificity.explanation: Gives a road-closure count and concrete damage description.

specificity.statement: Is Te Whatu Ora really going to prioritise those that die the earliest in our communities, which is Māori—seven to eight years generally in community. But... he shared that, actually, it's 14 years—the age gap between Māori and non-Māori in Ōpōtiki/Whakatane.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific life-expectancy gap figures, including a local figure.

specificity.statement: We're going to fight as tangata whenua. We will fight alongside our health sector colleagues for better pay, for better work conditions, and for our focus on fairness and equity for all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Names broad goals (pay, conditions, equity) but no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: The FamilyBoost, which started last year in July... 25 percent of the cost of early childhood education could be refunded up to $75 per week. But at the beginning of this month, our Government has updated this programme... families can now be refunded 40 percent of their early childhood education costs up to $150 per week.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentages, dollar caps, and dates for the policy and its update.

specificity.statement: In New Lynn alone, 9,000 couples with children are going to benefit from this. There are 3,000 single parent homes in New Lynn who will also benefit from this updated FamilyBoost policy.
specificity.explanation: Concrete local beneficiary counts.

specificity.statement: The Rates Rebate Scheme of this Government, which started on 1 July, has updated the rebate scheme which supports up to 66,000 SuperGold card holders.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme, start date, and beneficiary count.

specificity.statement: We have 70 major river systems in New Zealand. The members may or may not be aware that there is 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers or streams... The 180,000 kilometres I've just referenced is equal to 4½ times the circumference of the planet.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for river systems and mapped length with a comparative scale.

specificity.statement: The actual extraction amount of bottled water doesn't even make 1 percent. It doesn't even make 0.01 percent. It's down to 0.00163 of a percent that is actually in the bottled water.
specificity.explanation: Drills to a precise fraction of total water use.

specificity.statement: There's up to, roughly—I just googled it earlier—about 52 different companies at the moment throughout New Zealand that actually have licences. It is a high-value export market for pure water, and, obviously, the regional jobs and the people that are employed in those companies is where the benefit is.
specificity.explanation: Gives a company count and names the economic benefit, though hedged ('googled it earlier').

strength.statement: We've built on the work that we've done ending the culture of excuses that we inherited from the previous administration by restoring three strikes, tougher sentencing laws, tightening up the sentencing laws to restrict the ability of judges to massively reduce sentences, and giving the police the extra powers that they need to take on the gangs.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of concrete legislation the coalition has largely enacted; follow-through is real for these measures.

strength.statement: We've ended permanent name suppression for convicted adult sex offenders—people need to be able to warn others—and we've also brought in legislation around stalking so that New Zealanders can feel safe from that.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislative action, though some items are 'bringing in' rather than fully enacted.

strength.statement: We're bringing in an infringement regime for shoplifting so that there is swift justice for those to deal with the rampant shoplifting that we've seen in our community so that people have confidence in the justice system.
strength.explanation: Announced/in-progress measure rather than delivered — 'bringing in' signals intent not completion.

strength.statement: We had a target to reduce the number of victims of crime from 185,000 to 165,000 by 2029 and we're already at 158,000.
strength.explanation: Claims measurable progress against a stated target, ahead of schedule.

strength.statement: In 2022, it ran an $80 million deficit; in 2023, it ran a $38 million deficit; and, in 2024, it forecasted a $93 million deficit. Thank goodness there was a change of Government! People who knew how to run a polytechnic came into power, and it was turned round to a $17 million surplus.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered financial turnaround in the sector she administers.

strength.statement: National is going to restore regional decision-making, communities are going to influence polytechnic operations... Putting in place a federation... A federation will allow those smaller polytechnics, those ones with remote populations, to be able to have online learning, to be able to have access to blended delivery, to be able to deliver a wider range of portfolios of programmes.
strength.explanation: Stated policy direction in progress; delivery of the federation model not yet complete.

strength.statement: This success is attributed to practical policy positions that New Zealand First has advocated for since 2017. It was our position to deliver a smoke-free New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivering declines, partly borne out by the trend but the party role is contested.

strength.statement: After a long, hard fight, I am delighted now that with the support of the community—and the local council even got on board, as well—we have managed to get that reopened. It's a fantastic outcome... I am so pleased that that intersection will now be operational again for that community.
strength.explanation: Claims a specific, delivered local outcome (reopening Telephone Road intersection) that he worked to achieve.

strength.statement: The FamilyBoost, which started last year in July... 25 percent of the cost of early childhood education could be refunded up to $75 per week. But at the beginning of this month, our Government has updated this programme... families can now be refunded 40 percent of their early childhood education costs up to $150 per week.
strength.explanation: Describes a delivered and enhanced policy, not merely announced.

civility.statement: Then we had our friend Tamatha Paul from the Greens, who thought it was a good idea to bring up shoplifting in the context of the Greens and said that if people don't have enough money to buy food, they're going to go and look towards shoplifting things, as if there's almost a green light from the Green Party that you should go out and shoplift if you haven't got enough food.
civility.explanation: Recasts an opponent's point into 'a green light to shoplift', a mocking misrepresentation rather than engagement.

civility.statement: The last new law and order policy announced by a Labour MP was announced by Kiri Allan a long time ago. We haven't heard a single thing in terms of new policy on law and order from that side of the House.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the Opposition's productivity but aimed at their policy output, not personal character.

civility.statement: They'll certainly repeal our tough gang legislation because they prefer to give money to the gangs to do meth programmes, remember? Maybe they'll be returning to the policy of funding gangs and gang associates to deliver meth programmes.
civility.explanation: Caricatures Labour policy as 'funding gangs', a loaded misrepresentation of drug-treatment funding.

civility.statement: They are saying they're going to abandon regions that have been affected by severe weather events caused by climate change, first of all by denying that climate change is happening.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Government's policy on affected regions but via an exaggerated characterisation.

civility.statement: I doubted if he knew how to run his own bar, and it came to be true—it came to be true.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at Hipkins's competence rather than engagement with the policy.

civility.statement: Labour told this country, to justify their positions, that Māori smoking rates wouldn't be below 20 percent until 2045. It was below 20 percent in 2023, 22 years earlier than they were telling us.
civility.explanation: Pointed attack on Labour's use of data, bordering on accusing them of bad faith.

civility.statement: We were fed statistics by the Labour Government. As the saying goes, they used statistics like a drunk uses a lamppost, for support rather than illumination.
civility.explanation: Mocking analogy implying Labour used data dishonestly; a cheap shot rather than substantive rebuttal.

civility.statement: I know there's a lot of farmers and foresters out there at the moment trying to repair damage, and a lot of damage to roads as well. The community in the Onamalutu valley on the north bank of the Wairau River are cut off, with the road only being open for a short time in the morning and in the afternoon.
civility.explanation: Respectful, constituent-focused acknowledgement of those affected by flooding.

civility.statement: Then we have Mark Mitchell out in Rotorua, who has told the media, has told people, that people are on the streets of Rotorua because that is a "lifestyle choice"... you have someone who owns seven properties, telling homeless people that they're coming together for a sense of community.
civility.explanation: Contrasts Mitchell's property ownership against homeless comments to imply callous hypocrisy — a character-focused attack.

civility.statement: The pain that people are experiencing right now is directly the fault of this National Government, even though they refuse to take responsibility for it. They have cut jobs, they have cancelled infrastructure projects, and they have driven up costs like rates, insurance, and public transport.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-focused criticism of Government decisions rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: The former member, the Hon Ginny Andersen, talked about Charles Dickens novels; well, I think she just needs to go back to Sesame Street to learn that one and one equals two.
civility.explanation: Belittling personal mockery ('go back to Sesame Street') aimed at the member, not her argument.

civility.statement: I think that's why we see the nastiness—that's why we see the bitterness coming out of that side of the House. It's driven by frustration, because they can see now where they got it wrong. They can't admit it, but they can see it.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as 'nasty' and 'bitter' and imputes hidden motives, a character-based framing.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the other MPs and other leaders who've also been supporting and a couple of the Ministers in particular who've been very communicative: Mark Mitchell and Mark Patterson; my thanks to you both.
civility.explanation: Gracious, cross-party acknowledgement of Government Ministers by an Opposition MP.

civility.statement: The amendments that are coming through the House right now are despicable, because they are turning the back on the Waitangi Tribunal's Wai 2575—the recommendations that paved the way for the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act.
civility.explanation: 'Despicable' is strong, but it targets the legislation and its basis rather than a person.

civility.statement: 56- to 60-odd billion bucks is made by rural people... I am amazed when I come into this building that the advocacy on the left when it comes to the representation of rural New Zealand is missing in action; routinely not mentioning what we do so marvellously well.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the Opposition's priorities framed as neglect, pointed but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, I know why: because there's no one on that side of the House, sadly, that understands this. If they did, they would, because I cannot genuinely reconcile... that $56 billion, Helen White, is so seldomly spoken of. Where are your farmers, I ask you? You do not know because you do not have any.
civility.explanation: Directed jab at Helen White and Labour's rural credentials, combative but issue-adjacent.

civility.statement: So I would argue... that we don't have a shortage of water. Eight out of 10 parts end up in the blissed ocean, so, really, I think the justification for this bill is somewhat ideological... it does look like it runs rough shot over resource management, and assets and consents that have already been given.
civility.explanation: Criticises the bill as ideological/protectionist but engages its substance and even apologises to the member.

civility.statement: We use a very strong term here, especially in resource management, when we use the word "prohibit"... where "prohibit" is used, you can't actually be able to apply even for a consent, and that then becomes a concern... By using the word "prohibit", it actually limits that possibility.
civility.explanation: Engages the bill's wording substantively and respectfully, acknowledging its good intentions.

rigor.statement: Then we had our friend Tamatha Paul from the Greens, who thought it was a good idea to bring up shoplifting in the context of the Greens and said that if people don't have enough money to buy food, they're going to go and look towards shoplifting things, as if there's almost a green light from the Green Party that you should go out and shoplift if you haven't got enough food.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — infers party endorsement of theft from a remark about causes, no logical entailment.

rigor.statement: They'll certainly repeal our tough gang legislation because they prefer to give money to the gangs to do meth programmes, remember? Maybe they'll be returning to the policy of funding gangs and gang associates to deliver meth programmes.
rigor.explanation: Speculative attribution of motive with no evidence; distorts a treatment programme into pro-gang policy.

rigor.statement: A Government that's doubling down on the most expensive source of electricity, which is fossil fuels. When they could be focused on lowering people's power bills, they seem committed to pushing the price of power further and further up.
rigor.explanation: Asserts intent ('committed to pushing the price up') without evidence of deliberate policy to raise prices.

rigor.statement: Government Budgets only record the cost of what Governments are doing; they don't record the cost of what Government is not doing. It's the young people sitting in front of me who are ultimately going to pay that cost.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument about deferred/opportunity costs, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: I doubted if he knew how to run his own bar, and it came to be true—it came to be true.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — competence at running a bar used to dismiss his policy judgement.

rigor.statement: We were fed statistics by the Labour Government. As the saying goes, they used statistics like a drunk uses a lamppost, for support rather than illumination.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a rhetorical analogy rather than showing which statistics were misused and how.

rigor.statement: He tells us the drop is steepest for Māori, with the rates having halved in six years. This progress is exceptional. It took Pākehā more than four decades to achieve the fall achieved by Māori since 2018.
rigor.explanation: Cites an expert authority and a comparative figure, though the argument leans on the authority rather than presenting the underlying data.

rigor.statement: The cost of living is driving New Zealanders offshore in record numbers... those numbers mask the actual unemployment number. If those people had remained in New Zealand, we would have seen an unemployment rate even higher than the one we currently see.
rigor.explanation: A plausible economic argument that emigration suppresses measured unemployment, but asserted without quantification.

rigor.statement: The pain that people are experiencing right now is directly the fault of this National Government, even though they refuse to take responsibility for it. They have cut jobs, they have cancelled infrastructure projects, and they have driven up costs like rates, insurance, and public transport.
rigor.explanation: Attributes all current hardship 'directly' to one cause, a sweeping causal claim without weighing other factors.

rigor.statement: The former member, the Hon Ginny Andersen, talked about Charles Dickens novels; well, I think she just needs to go back to Sesame Street to learn that one and one equals two.
rigor.explanation: Substitutes ridicule for engagement with her economic point.

rigor.statement: We saw inflation go through the roof; we saw interest rates rise to try and counter that—that led to a recession across the country. We then saw homeowners... could get cheap interest rates initially, and then the inflation took hold. They went up multiple percentage points, they lost equity, they were losing homes.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a chain (inflation→rate rises→recession→mortgage stress) that is coherent but assigns it wholly to the prior Government.

rigor.statement: I think that's why we see the nastiness—that's why we see the bitterness coming out of that side of the House. It's driven by frustration, because they can see now where they got it wrong. They can't admit it, but they can see it.
rigor.explanation: Mind-reading — asserts opponents privately know they were wrong, with no evidence.

rigor.statement: We need a rain radar—we desperately need a rain radar—and also more integrated systems for helping to predict rain patterns. One of the issues that has cropped up in the Nelson floods in 2022 and in these floods was that it was very difficult for our local teams to accurately predict where the rain was coming.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the request in a recurring, observed problem across two flood events.

rigor.statement: The amendments that are coming through the House right now are despicable, because they are turning the back on the Waitangi Tribunal's Wai 2575—the recommendations that paved the way for the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the objection in a specific Tribunal report (Wai 2575), though 'despicable' is an emotional appeal.

rigor.statement: We've seen with Local Water Done Well, if they don't have to engage as council with hapū and iwi, they won't, because they didn't. They didn't for Local Water Done Well. So if you take it out of the legislation for Pae Ora, is Te Whatu Ora going to consider equity?
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete precedent (Local Water Done Well) to argue that removing a statutory requirement predicts non-engagement — evidence-based analogy.

rigor.statement: Well, I know why: because there's no one on that side of the House, sadly, that understands this. If they did, they would, because I cannot genuinely reconcile... that $56 billion, Helen White, is so seldomly spoken of. Where are your farmers, I ask you? You do not know because you do not have any.
rigor.explanation: Asserts opponents 'don't understand' rural NZ as the explanation, an unsupported generalisation.

rigor.statement: So I would argue... that we don't have a shortage of water. Eight out of 10 parts end up in the blissed ocean, so, really, I think the justification for this bill is somewhat ideological... it does look like it runs rough shot over resource management, and assets and consents that have already been given.
rigor.explanation: Uses volume statistics to argue no scarcity, but 'ideological' framing and equating total flow with sustainable allocation is a logical gap.

rigor.statement: New Zealand First, in, I believe, around 2017, considered introducing a royalty on bottled water exports, but we found that that was unworkable due to the numerous administration complexities and the limited benefits from that, but it still remains a concern.
rigor.explanation: Gives reasons (administrative complexity, limited benefit) for the party's earlier conclusion.

rigor.statement: The actual extraction amount of bottled water doesn't even make 1 percent. It doesn't even make 0.01 percent. It's down to 0.00163 of a percent that is actually in the bottled water.
rigor.explanation: Uses proportion data to argue the bill's practical effect would be negligible.

rigor.statement: We use a very strong term here, especially in resource management, when we use the word "prohibit"... where "prohibit" is used, you can't actually be able to apply even for a consent, and that then becomes a concern... By using the word "prohibit", it actually limits that possibility.
rigor.explanation: A focused, logical objection to the bill's drafting — that outright prohibition removes even the consent pathway.

veracity.statement: The last new law and order policy announced by a Labour MP was announced by Kiri Allan a long time ago. We haven't heard a single thing in terms of new policy on law and order from that side of the House.
veracity.explanation: A rhetorical 'not a single thing' claim that is likely overstated and hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: We had a target to reduce the number of victims of crime from 185,000 to 165,000 by 2029 and we're already at 158,000.
veracity.explanation: Cites the Government's own victimisation target and a current figure; directionally consistent with reported survey data, though single-source.

veracity.statement: 184,000 New Zealanders have simply given up on this Government. They have voted with their feet and they have left the country.
veracity.explanation: A migration-departures figure that is roughly in the real range, but framing all departures as 'giving up on this Government' overstates causation.

veracity.statement: A Government that's doubling down on the most expensive source of electricity, which is fossil fuels. When they could be focused on lowering people's power bills, they seem committed to pushing the price of power further and further up.
veracity.explanation: The claim that fossil fuels are 'the most expensive source of electricity' is contestable and stated without qualification.

veracity.statement: Even the cost of registering your car has pretty much doubled under this Government—a new drivers' tax introduced, effectively, by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Vehicle registration/ACC levy costs did rise substantially; 'doubled' and 'new drivers' tax' are somewhat rhetorical framings.

veracity.statement: With 15,000 to 17,000—depending on which numbers you concentrate on—jobs disappearing from the construction sector, we've got the Government saying, "Oh, but everything's getting better."
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses of this order are reported by official statistics; the range is presented honestly.

veracity.statement: They are saying they're going to abandon regions that have been affected by severe weather events caused by climate change, first of all by denying that climate change is happening.
veracity.explanation: Claiming the Government denies climate change 'is happening' misstates its stated position and is misleading.

People who knew how to run a polytechnic came into power, and it was turned round to a $17 million surplus.
veracity.explanation: Te Pūkenga deficits and a subsequent surplus are broadly on the record, though the causal 'people who knew how' framing is partisan.

veracity.statement: Under-17s were already recording a smoking rate of 0.6 percent—the good news being that we have a smoke-free generation.
veracity.explanation: Youth smoking rates are indeed very low; the exact 0.6 percent and 'smoke-free generation' claim are somewhat selectively framed.

veracity.explanation: Contrasts a projection with an outcome, but conflating a modelling projection with a claim 'told to justify positions' is a contestable framing.

veracity.statement: He tells us the drop is steepest for Māori, with the rates having halved in six years. This progress is exceptional. It took Pākehā more than four decades to achieve the fall achieved by Māori since 2018.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to expert Beaglehole; the halving of Māori smoking rates is broadly consistent with reported trends.

veracity.statement: They've also got enrolments which are up 12 percent, and internationals in NMIT now are up 36 percent. That's a phenomenal performance for a small polytech at the top of the South.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures presented without source; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: Over 85 percent of the wine production from New Zealand comes from the top of the South, and over 60 percent of the seafood production comes from the top of the South.
veracity.explanation: Marlborough dominates NZ wine; the 85% and 60% figures are broadly in the right range but stated without citation.

veracity.statement: The construction industry is an example... 15,000 jobs gone from the construction sector and that is reported on by Statistics New Zealand. Yet, still, we have the Minister of Finance denying the Statistics New Zealand figures for construction job losses are accurate.
veracity.explanation: Construction job losses of this scale are reported by Stats NZ; the figure is credibly sourced.

veracity.statement: Then we have Mark Mitchell out in Rotorua, who has told the media, has told people, that people are on the streets of Rotorua because that is a "lifestyle choice"... you have someone who owns seven properties, telling homeless people that they're coming together for a sense of community.
veracity.explanation: Selectively characterises Mitchell's remarks; the 'lifestyle choice' quote is paraphrased in the least charitable framing.

veracity.statement: The cost of living is driving New Zealanders offshore in record numbers... those numbers mask the actual unemployment number. If those people had remained in New Zealand, we would have seen an unemployment rate even higher than the one we currently see.
veracity.explanation: Directionally defensible but the magnitude of the masking effect is unverified.

We then saw homeowners... could get cheap interest rates initially, and then the inflation took hold. They went up multiple percentage points, they lost equity, they were losing homes.
veracity.explanation: The macro sequence is broadly accurate, though single-cause attribution to Labour omits global drivers.

veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable meteorological detail consistent with the reported event.

veracity.explanation: Specific on-the-ground figure, plausible and consistent with the event.

veracity.explanation: A ~7-year national Māori/non-Māori life expectancy gap is well established; the 14-year local figure is attributed to a speaker but plausible for a deprived district.

But at the beginning of this month, our Government has updated this programme... families can now be refunded 40 percent of their early childhood education costs up to $150 per week.
veracity.explanation: The FamilyBoost parameters and July uplift are on the record and accurately stated.

veracity.explanation: Specific figures asserted without source; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: The Rates Rebate Scheme of this Government, which started on 1 July, has updated the rebate scheme which supports up to 66,000 SuperGold card holders.
veracity.explanation: Specific figure stated without citation; broadly plausible.

veracity.explanation: The food-and-fibre export contribution is in the tens of billions, broadly consistent; 'the left never mentions it' is rhetorical hyperbole.

forthrightness.statement: This proposed change will align the law from the period between 2015 to 2019 with the current legislative arrangements. This proposed law change is all about ensuring courts have the discretion to come to fair and equitable outcomes.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Justice, I invite that member to actually go to the Beehive website and look at the press release. It talks about having to use reasonable force, which is defined in section 39 of the Crimes Act. It's not about any force; it's about reasonable force.

veracity.statement: It decided to hold the OCR at 3.25 percent, but continued to foreshadow further reduction, saying, "If medium-term inflation pressures continue to ease as projected, the Committee expects to lower the Official Cash Rate further."
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports the Reserve Bank's decision and quotes its statement.

veracity.statement: From late 2021 onwards, the OCR was progressively raised to 5.5 percent to combat inflation spurred on by the previous Government's spending. veracity.statement: I do not accept that that is the primary concern for New Zealand farmers in terms of drinking water—you know, it is a very small amount. strength.statement: That's why we've brought back health targets to focus our health system on delivery for patients, we've increased the number of doctors and nurses caring for patients every day, we're delivering more surgeries like hips, knees, and cataracts through our Elective Boost, and we've delivered a record funding increase for GPs.

strength.statement: This is the third bill that the Government has produced as part of its Local Water Done Well policy programme, which the National Party have campaigned on and is an election promise that we’re delivering.
